## Volume front matter

### Series title page

## COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, AND ECONOMICAL LIBRARY

of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions completed during the last three centuries, together with particular analytical indexes accompanying each volume or each author of some importance; furnished with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, and adorned with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, as well as by works possessing some authority and influence with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be surveyed at a glance; the other, of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers have commented upon the individual books of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they have done so.

A most accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others, if one considers the clarity of its type, the quality of its paper, the integrity of its text, the perfection of its correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the whole work, the modesty of its price, and above all this collection itself—unique, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time brings together in our library six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, collected from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## FIRST SERIES

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Published under the direction of J.-P. Migne, editor of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon

After the recension of the monks of the Order of Saint Benedict from the Congregation of Saint Maur, and especially that of Joannes Martianay of the same order, corrected anew against Roman, Ambrosian, Veronese, and many other manuscripts, as well as against all French and foreign editions; enlarged by very numerous monuments previously entirely unpublished, and by other writings of the holy Doctor previously published only separately; illustrated with innumerable notes, observations, and corrections; through the study and labor of Vallarsi and Maffei, presbyters of Verona, with the assistance of other learned men in that same city.

The latest Parisian edition, revised from the second edition by the later editorial labors of the Veronese editors themselves, and enriched from more recently discovered materials, so that the present edition, by its greater extent alone—apart from all other corrections—materially surpasses all preceding editions, even the Benedictine ones, by a third part or one-third.

Edited and finally revised by J. P. Migne, editor of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# [The Complete Works of Jerome]

[Col. 0009]

# Preface

We include in this ninth volume of his works the Hebrew Canon, or the version of the Old Testament prepared by Jerome from the Hebrew—a portion of his labors and vigils far nobler than any other, and more useful than all the rest. But before I say what this undertaking is, and what our purpose was in preparing this part, or what we have accomplished, I must forestall the judgments of the reader and diligently prevent and avert the reproach that might so easily be brought against our diligence. For I do not doubt that there will be many who, though otherwise neither bad men nor wholly ignorant of divine matters, will at first glance judge this labor either less useful or at least unworthy of inclusion in a collection of Jerome’s writings. They will observe superficially that here they are reading the same things contained in the Latin Vulgate version, and will suppose that this differs scarcely at all from that edition.

They will consequently think that we have appended this work to the Jerome collection merely as something superfluous, or to increase the bulk of the collection: although it is the one approved version among all the Latin interpretations of Sacred Scripture, the best and most faithful of the others, and also, more than any other, the genuine offspring of Jerome’s own genius—of that interpreter who has been recognized as by far the most learned of all ages and of all memory. It is also so widespread and accessible, having been reprinted, embellished, and published so many times, in so many places and forms, and in such variety, ever since the invention of the printing art, and much more especially after the decree of the Council of Trent, that it has truly filled the libraries of the world and is readily available even to those who have adopted an entirely different way of life from the handling of books.

We ourselves, as we readily acknowledge, when nearly five years ago we were considering this new edition of Jerome’s works, hesitated long and earnestly over whether it was in the interest either of ourselves or of our readers to retain this version—although the Benedictine editors had long ago not merely joined it to, but placed it at the head of, the entire collection. Among the many considerations occupying our minds, we were especially concerned that we should not seem to be doing work already done, or fall into the fault of those of our own age who strive toward immortality by wagonloads of paper.

Our plan had almost been to collect into one place only the variant readings supplied by the ancient manuscripts, to explain them with a few customary annotations, and to append and publish them together with the two Psalters and certain other books not contained in the Vulgate. But when, in the prospectus of the edition, we consulted the public and the most learned men throughout Italy by sending letters on this very question, the unanimous opinion of all was that the entire work should be reprinted in its complete sequence. To those who might think otherwise, this is a decisive answer: we rely upon the judgment of the public, and prefer to give greater weight to the votes of learned men than to concede to the laziness—if there should be any such people—of those who might object to this similarity to the Vulgate.

There were, moreover, other most serious reasons that almost against my will led me to undertake this labor; and I do not doubt that they can persuade any sensible reader.

Indeed, we are not the first to have added this material in order to increase the size of the book. It was attached long ago by the Benedictine editors to the edition of Jerome’s works; indeed, they auspiciously began the entire collection with it, since it is the noblest portion of all his labors. Therefore, since we are the first, so to speak, to embrace the entire sphere of Jerome’s writings and have collected monuments—by no means few—that had long been missing, if this complete and finished edition now appearing in public should lack that portion which was the chief part of the earlier edition, we would be said not to have enlarged the work in the customary manner but to have diminished its former dignity.

A person cultivated in literary elegance may rightly regret how much would thereby be lost. For when that edition first appeared, it was especially welcome to the learned world—if we except Richard Simon—not merely because it had been prepared with greater diligence than the other volumes of that edition, and perfected through the combined efforts of Martianay and Pouget, who contributed greatly to it by their labor and learning, but chiefly because of the intrinsic value of the ancient monuments themselves and the almost native dignity of the work. These won it such favor among scholars.

I shall cite as a witness a man whose testimony will be all the more certain and striking because he himself was hostile to the studies of monks and holy Fathers, though otherwise learned, and, having been provoked by Martianay, did everything possible to disparage his labor whenever an opportunity arose. I mean the author of the *Hieronymian Questions*. Although his pen was exercised by hatred, the force of truth compelled him, amid his very quarrels, to make the following admission in praise of his adversary:

> “I cannot refrain from praising Martianay’s plan of publishing Jerome’s Versions as they are found in the most ancient books, without the alterations subsequently made in them, and in the order in which they are found in those same books, without omitting the ancient divisions that appear in them. For we seem to see the Versions as they came from Jerome’s hand, or at least as little altered as possible.”

(Joannes Clericus, *Questions*, 9.2.)

This is a sufficiently good argument when joined to the testimony of a critic. But the principal reason that moved me was different: I learned by my own experience that it is scarcely possible for a scholar to perceive the greatest advantages of this book unless we set out the entire context of its interpretation.

Let us bring forward some examples to make certain of these points clearer. One may run one’s eyes over the immense forest of variant readings in each book, and the enormous abundance of corrections and glosses, either with no benefit at all or at least not with the benefit appropriate to reading, if one presents them piecemeal. If each is noted at its proper place in the context, they stimulate the mind and provoke the reader’s judgment. But if one wishes to refer them only to a particular verse, one must often employ ragged trails of words and stir boredom rather than intellectual interest in a person eager for learning.

Nor can the almost innumerable scholia, especially in the Octateuch, be conveniently presented even by this method. If one praises only what they concern—a word, for example—one joins together, through the very note itself, which is tedious and unwelcome, more words than the context itself contains. When these are set opposite one another, they readily strike the eyes and mind at a single glance.

Exactly the same must be said of the obeli and asterisks. Although they occur everywhere else, they appear especially in those books that have been corrected and revised against the Greek exemplar, and they occur in such numbers that anyone who undertook to remember each one, much less to explain its reasons, would be abusing both his leisure and our patience. How often, moreover, would the same matters have to be repeated in the notes? What limit would there be to the reader’s or the lecturer’s weariness? What method would there be for commending the manuscripts?

As for the ancient division of the verses, which is now held in such high esteem and is so important for preserving the memory of antiquity, I think it can scarcely be represented in words; indeed, I doubt whether anyone could reproduce it usefully at all. Moreover, the very appearance and order of the Hebrew Canon—which they praise so highly—would necessarily be completely disrupted.

In addition, there are certain substantial books of Scripture translated into Latin by Jerome but not received into the Vulgate edition, and these properly claim their own place here. Such is the Psalter from the Hebrew archetype. Since an interpretation from the Greek had long prevailed in the churches, it could not be substituted for it without causing disturbance among the people, who had become accustomed through long usage to those psalms. Yet, being by far the most faithful and prepared with extraordinary learning, it remains almost solely for the private study of readers.

There are also other versions of the sacred books according to the Septuagint interpreters: another version of Job and of Esther, and likewise a double revision of the Psalms—that which is called the Roman Psalter and that called the Gallican Psalter—which are not found in the recension of the Vulgate, either at all or at least in that form. It is of the highest value to know them.

Whoever carefully weighs these considerations and their force, I no longer doubt, will approve our undertaking as fair and reasonable, and will allow us to enjoy the satisfaction of having bestowed our labor properly upon the revision of the entire text.

But perhaps some will attempt to object for another reason and, scarcely having removed that accusation, strive immediately to bring a more serious charge of envy against us. It is well known that Jerome’s version is contained, at least for the most part, in the Vulgate edition, while we are laboring to correct it and restore it to its original integrity.

“Do you not,” someone may perhaps object, “by this recension of yours exclude that edition which the memory of the most remote antiquity, and still more the authority of the ecumenical Council of Trent, together with several subsequent decrees of the popes, have commended to Christians as the one edition of Sacred Scripture?”

But such a thought has never entered my mind; and if it should ever enter anyone’s mind, I would not regard him as thinking wisely. On the contrary, as long as life remains in me, we shall defend the highest praise of that edition. We shall profess that it contains everything weighty and pre-eminent for forming and transmitting the doctrine of faith and morals, and we shall preserve intact the authority it has acquired in these matters.

Nevertheless, if errors introduced into it through either the negligence or misguided diligence of ancient scribes occur in passages that are in no way necessary for establishing the laws of faith and morals, a person who cares about the dignity of sacred matters may correct them with the appropriate degree of probability and reverence. I think he should not be angry with such a person at all; rather, that person will have deserved well of Sacred Scripture through his own ability and diligence.

Men who were supremely Catholic and likewise supreme defenders of the Vulgate did this long ago. Among them—leaving Henry Buchentop aside for the moment—the most learned Franciscus Lucas Brugensis always deserved praise. He either corrected more than four thousand passages that still required correction after the revision of Clement VIII, or indicated with sound arguments that they ought to be corrected. Cardinal Bellarmine, in letters addressed to him, candidly acknowledged that still more passages remained to be improved, if he had the inclination to do so.

Judge our efforts to be of the same mind and intention. And if the passages we propose for correction are truly so numerous and significant, count them among those that have earned so much gratitude from you through the work of others.

Nevertheless, our undertaking is altogether a different enterprise. In preparing it, we did not think that we were charged to examine every third word merely to see whether it differed from the Vulgate edition. For this very reason, the title that preceded us, *Divine Library*, has been retained throughout the work, although we approve little of the rest of it and do not at all believe that it was written by the holy Interpreter.

We know that this title long ago prevailed among ancient writers, both those cited by Martianay and those who escaped his notice. But we also know that other titles are preferred by others, and that, especially in manuscript codices, scribes played with titles according to their individual judgment and ingenuity.

Alcuin, the most celebrated ninth-century corrector of the Latin Bibles—a figure about whom we shall have more to say below—rejected all other titles and entitled the work *Pandect*. He insists that this is its proper name. He emphasizes his view in the following epigram, which was also published among his works and is found at the end of the sacred text that he himself revised and corrected in the Vallicellian manuscript in Rome:

> Remember, reader, to call this sacred body  
> by its proper name, *Pandect*, with your lips.  
> What many now call a library  
> bears a name that is not proper, as the Pelasgian language sounds, etc.

But this is occasioned only by the title; it is not our purpose to pursue how many names the Scriptures have had among the Latins, or how varied those names have been. By retaining the title that has prevailed almost above all others, we wished both to remove ourselves from a slippery dispute and to indicate how far we are from the affected novelty of itching minds.

Our single purpose is to transcribe Jerome’s interpretation from ancient books that, as far as possible, stand closest to the age of the Interpreter himself—before the hands of glossators had invaded them, or before usage of readings from an older version had altered their wording.

Indeed, with the exception of the Octateuch—which the excessive zeal of correctors has corrupted, though to a lesser degree in some books than in others—we derive all the remaining books of the Hebrew Canon from manuscripts and sources so ancient and so pure that it is scarcely possible to doubt the trustworthiness of their readings or the genuineness of Jerome’s work.

Therefore, whenever we say that a verse or sentence must be introduced; whenever we point out that a passage lies in error and offer the true reading; whenever we connect passages differently from the common text; and whenever we observe that even ancient documents diverge in different directions, we act on the authority of our exemplars. Whatever this labor may be, it is undertaken for no other purpose than to assert or vindicate the dignity of Jerome’s version.

To keep this purpose clearly before you, and to make you understand how costly this labor has been for us, we must recall a matter upon which almost the entire history of Jerome’s version depends, and from which judgment of the genuineness we are about to defend may be formed.

Barely four centuries had passed since the version of the holy Doctor had appeared publicly and had everywhere acquired authority among almost all people, when it already seemed to be growing worthless, covered with errors that human diligence could not prevent amid such a multitude of copyists and such variety of users.

The Emperor Charlemagne, distressed by this, was a man born for the building up and adornment of the Church. He exerted himself with the greatest possible zeal and authority to restore the text to its original integrity and to ensure that the most accurate version should be established in all the churches, especially those of Gaul.

“We wish,” he says in the *Capitularies*, “and have so instructed and commanded our envoys, that the canonical books be kept authentic in the churches, just as we have often commanded in another capitulary.”

The task of restoring Scripture was entrusted to Alcuin, or Albinus, who at that time lived in the emperor’s high esteem and personal circle, being the most learned of all whom that age produced.

There are some who report that, unsatisfied with vernacular interpretations, he devoted himself to learning the original languages, Hebrew and Greek, and used them in successfully completing this labor. But the three arguments for his skill in handling the Hebrew text that his recent admirer Hody adduces from the commentaries—where he claims that Albin corrected the version he used from the Hebrew and sometimes explicitly rejected it—are entirely worthless. They are not Albin’s, but Jerome’s own words, which Albin copied verbatim.

They are the following:

In his commentary on Genesis 25:8:

> “How is it compatible with Abraham, so holy a man, that it is said, ‘And, failing, he died’? I answer that in the Hebrew the word ‘failing’ is not present; it was added by the Septuagint interpreters.”

And in Ecclesiastes 9:

> “It should be noted that throughout the entire book, wherever ‘sons of men’ is said, the Hebrew has ‘son of man,’ that is, ‘sons of Adam.’ Nearly all Scripture is full of this idiom, calling the whole human race the sons of Adam.”

Finally, in chapter 12:

> “To become silent, or—as it is better rendered in the Hebrew—to become deaf, refers to the ears.”

All these, I say, are Jerome’s words, pure and unaltered, in his commentaries on those passages of Scripture. I am all the more surprised that this could have escaped such a learned man, since no one is now unaware that almost everything Albin took was drawn from Jerome’s sources.

Therefore, not because I wish, if I may put it so, to begrudge the teacher of Charlemagne some slight breath of Oriental learning, but so that it may be known what resources he used in preparing his edition, I conclude that he did not undertake this task, nor did he intend to consult the original texts and conform himself to the Hebrew and Greek archetypes.

All his diligence was directed to gathering Jerome’s-version manuscripts from every quarter and carefully comparing them with one another, so that he might choose the reading that seemed to him preferable on the authority of those copies that appeared to be of better correction and standing—whether he also weighed it according to sounder critical principles or against Jerome’s own testimony.

The entire work, namely the Old and New Testaments polished and corrected by this new “pumice,” he completed when already an old man, at about eighty-two years of age, in the monastery over which he presided, Saint Martin’s at Tours in Gaul, and presented it to that same emperor, Charlemagne.

The dedicatory letter itself is now counted as the twentieth among the Alcuinian letters. It was sent from the same monastery of Saint Martin, where, addressing the king about the method of his work, he says:

> “I have taken care to send to Your Illustrious Authority the sacred books, joined together into the sanctity of one most distinguished body and carefully corrected.”

There is also another letter to Gisela prefixed to the sixth book of his commentaries on John, where he says that he had undertaken the command of the Lord King concerning the correction of the Old and New Testaments.

Charlemagne himself says something similar:

> “For a long time, with God assisting us in all things, we have corrected with exactness all the books of the Old and New Testament, which had been corrupted by the incompetence of scribes.”

Finally, Sigebert of Gembloux records in his *Chronicle*, under the year 790, that Alcuin corrected the Divine History at the king’s command; and in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 83, he says that Alcuin corrected the Divine Library at the emperor’s command.

We have also cited these testimonies here so that it may be more certain that the edition was not revised against the Hebrew and Greek texts, since those who commended it to posterity make no mention of them even in a single word.

Several codices of this recension still survive. During our residence in Rome, we ourselves handled and sometimes consulted two of them, both of enormous size. One is preserved in the library of Saint Paul Outside the Walls and is often praised by Victorius; the other is in the Vallicellian Library. Baronius regarded the latter as a treasure of immense value, since learned men who labored to reform the Vulgate edition after the decree of the Council of Trent used it, not without a great saving of labor.

There are also certain epigrams at the end of the volume. It will be sufficient to transcribe these few verses, somewhat inelegant by the standards of that age, which name either the author or the instigator of the work:

> For as many little letters of varied form  
> as are depicted in the sacred body of this codex,  
> so many years, by Christ’s gift,  
> may King Charles live, who ordered it to be written.

[Col. 0017]

> Whoever reads these verses, remember to pray for me.  
> I am called Alcuin: may you prosper without end.

It is not now possible to pursue how far and how widely this edition prevailed in the churches, with nearly the whole world obeying the emperor’s authority. Yet it is scarcely possible to say how far the industry of scholars carried it once permission had been granted to correct the sacred text.

The margins of sacred codices were then burdened with scholia and furnished with notes of variant readings or corrections from the Hebrew—not from the archetype itself, but either from a Hebrew text supplied, at someone’s whim, with alternative vowel-points, or from a Latin rendering devised by some modern Judaizer.

I believe that this was more or less the practice of the Hebrew scholiast so called, whom they make a contemporary of Rabanus Maurus. He amassed all those glosses that we too have retained in the margins of the book. Although he often seems more eager to argue than to interpret truly, and sometimes is himself deceived by a false reading or slips through ignorance of a better and deeper meaning, he nevertheless won the approval of the people of his age so completely that scribes had no codices more saleable than those to which they had added his notes.

Why, Jerome himself could have appeared to Martianay to be such a son of the earth, if one considers the great dispute between him and Simon! I shall say nothing for now of others of later times who, when they thought they had acquired some learning in the Hebrew language, applied their efforts to altering the Latin exemplars by their own ingenuity. They supposed that they had deserved better of Sacred Scripture the more widely they departed from the received reading.

A notable passage on this subject occurs in Hugh of Saint Victor, who flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century, in Book 9 of his *On the Sacred Scriptures*:

> “In the eighth place Jerome came forward, no longer translating from Hebrew into Greek, as the earlier translators had done, but transferring the Hebrew into the Latin language. Since his translation was judged to agree more closely with the Hebrew Truth, the Church of Christ throughout the whole world established that this alone should be read and held authoritative above all the other translations, which faulty interpretation had corrupted, whether the first, made from Hebrew into Greek, or the second, made from Greek into Latin.
>
> “But as an evil practice gained strength—one that sometimes seeks what is customary rather than what is true—it happened that, as different people followed different translations, everything eventually became so confused that almost no one now knows what should be attributed to whom.
>
> “From this arose the so-called correctories or castigations. Although they were otherwise composed through the efforts of learned men, they could not follow the same tracks; instead, they introduced new alterations into the sacred text. For some substituted the notes placed in the margins of books for the true readings, while others inserted them alongside the text, and each added, deleted, or altered according to his own judgment.”

Lindanus relates that he saw an extremely ancient exemplar of this kind in the Carthusian monastery at Zeelhem, near Diest. It identified passages in the Bible that ought to be corrected against codices diligently revised by Charlemagne—indeed, in many places, but in no way to be regretted.

Cardinal Bessarion praises another such exemplar in his commentary on the words “I want him to remain so,” against George of Trebizond. More than three hundred years earlier, Nicolaus, a deacon of Saint Damasus and, as he himself says, suffragan of the Vatican Library, had prepared it in Rome. Bessarion quotes its words:

> “As I examined the libraries, I could not attain what I sought—namely, to find accurate exemplars. Even those said to have been corrected by the most learned men differed so greatly, with each person relying on his own judgment, that I found as many exemplars as there were codices.”

It could truly then be said of Jerome’s version what is said of human health: those are more seriously ill who, after seeming to have been relieved of their disease, have fallen back into it completely.

I think the reader now understands from these points what we intended, the purpose with which we undertook this task, and how costly the labor has been. Since Jerome’s version had been corrupted by every kind of fault from the eighth century onward, anyone wishing to represent its native genuineness had to surpass so vast an accumulation of time. His first concern had to be to obtain copies that predated that century, or at least to distinguish by clear indications those that had escaped the hands of critics and of later ages.

In the revision and polishing of all other literary monuments, the age of the exemplar from which they are sought, or against whose authority they are tested, carries very great weight if it stands at a shorter distance from the author’s time. Nevertheless, it can happen—and sometimes does happen—that a copy from a more recent period is greatly preferred to an older one on account of its own quality and correction, because it was copied either from a more faithful exemplar or by a more diligent and learned scribe.

The case is different with the manuscripts of this Latin version: I scarcely think that this—that a later copy should be preferable—ever happens with them, since they were copied not for private study but for public use, and continually bear the corruption of the times in which they were written.

It was not therefore enough, for restoring the version to its original integrity, to consult manuscript books encountered by chance, or the elegant ones—which are certainly numerous—in libraries. It was necessary to seek out, with the greatest possible diligence, the oldest and almost obsolete copies, and to entrust the whole authority to those that the hands of glossators had spared.

After acquiring such books through long labor and investigation from the libraries of Italy, as many as our undertaking required, the one supplied by our Veronese library surpasses all the others both in age and in reputation. It is worth describing briefly as a test, so that you may judge the others by it.

This codex contains the Books of Kings, the most important and noblest part of Scripture, with marks of Jerome’s untouched Version so certain and genuine that I do not hesitate to prefer it to all the others that have so far become known from the libraries of Europe.

It is bound in very thin parchment, in the format called *in-folio*, though almost square in shape. It is entirely written in larger letters, of the kind we see in the most ancient monuments of all.

At times a later hand has colored the letters, which were yellow and escaping the eye, with black ink, following the old strokes, and has renewed writing that had almost become obsolete and faded through such great age. At other times it has made the letters clearer, especially where a small transverse line above forms the letter T, which in the earlier script differs little from I.

Take the following as an example to establish the truth of the matter.

Although the text is continuous throughout, so that no gap appears, and is divided neither into chapters nor into verses, nevertheless, wherever a more important sentence or period comes to an end, it is generally interrupted by a short interval. This gave a later copyist an opportunity to draw there, as he pleased, the mark of punctuation. The orthography likewise bears the ancient character and form of Latin usage, especially in compound words, in which the preposition is preserved intact, as in *subputare*, *adloqui*, and similar forms. The correction, moreover, proves a sufficiently diligent antiquarian, writing in those times that still upheld the glory of the Latin language—except that he often uses the accusative case for the ablative, and the latter in turn for the former. Yet learned men have noted from the testimony of the ancient grammarians that this very feature is an indication of venerable antiquity; and elsewhere we have ourselves made the same point, when we cited the passage from an ancient pagan inscription in our own domestic museum: “WITHOUT. INJURY. TO. EITHER. MIND.” [*SINE ALTERITRUM ANIMI LESIONEM*; the reading is materially uncertain.]

In a word, we attribute such antiquity to this book that among the Hieronymian manuscripts we would wish no other to be its equal; indeed, we would often prefer it even to the much-praised manuscript containing the *Life of Saint Paul the Hermit*, which, from the consular era noted by its copyist, is established as scarcely more than a hundred years later than Jerome. Thus we place this manuscript, which we regard as older than that one, at an even shorter interval from the age of the holy Doctor.

That it presents Jerome’s authentic translation we establish by almost innumerable arguments. We set out in the notes for consideration some of the more significant ones that emerge from the text itself; here let us indicate the evidence drawn from the entire structure of the codex.

First, it assigns the whole history of the Kings to only two books, one entitled Samuel and the other *Malachim*—that is, in accordance with the Hebrew exemplar favored by Jerome, who states in his preface that he had followed this arrangement—not, as in the Vulgate, to four books, the division previously derived from the partition of the Septuagint [*τῶν LXX*, “of the Seventy”]. Then, when the antiquarian wished to call attention to the earlier division before Jerome, he thereby also made clear testimony that the version he was copying was Hieronymian. At the beginning of what we call the second book, after coloring the opening words *Factum est* (“It came to pass”) in red, he wrote opposite them: “In ancient copies this is where the second book begins.”

He would not have called the copies “ancient” except in relation to the new version; nor could any others at that time have been called ancient except those that had long been in circulation and were derived from the Greek, or those that were new in comparison—namely, the version that the holy Father had recently produced from the Hebrew. He taught the same thing, perhaps even more clearly, at the place where the fourth book begins in the Vulgate, by this marginal annotation in the codex: “Here ends the third book according to the Septuagint.” Thus what he had earlier called ancient copies he now identifies by name as those that derived from the translation of the Seventy, and he consequently implies that the book before him had been arranged according to the standard of the Hebrew text, since it follows the division of the Hebrew text rather than that of the Greek. In fact, the codex contains no other title than this one at the end of the second book in the Vulgate: “The book of Samuel ends. The book of Malachim begins.”

Furthermore, the almost complete conformity with the Hebrew text in nearly all the places where it diverges from the Vulgate—whether the manuscript entirely omits additions that had crept in from the older translation, or offers a much better reading and sense, as we have said, explaining these in the notes as occasion requires—is a still clearer indication of the authenticity of Jerome’s version. The more evident this is, the more explicitly the holy Translator declares in his Prologue that he is entirely conscious of having altered nothing of the Hebrew truth [*γνησιότης*, “authenticity,” of Jerome’s version].

There are also other features that commend the excellence of this book: certain notes, written by the same original hand and in the same form of script, though in much smaller letters, are placed here and there in the margin. They are by no means contemptible or useless for the passages they explain, although we have thought it better to omit them, as straying from our purpose. Take, as a specimen of the first that occurs, the note attached to the word *Ramatha*: “This is the city that in the Gospel is called Arimathea, and Joseph was also a decurion there.”

The chapters, or series of headings, although they do not appear to have been prepared by Jerome, are nevertheless extremely ancient and predate the age of Cassiodorus. This one Veronese manuscript, after the editions of the revered Cardinal Tommasi and of the Benedictines, reproduces and restores them in their entirety, and at times supplements them with substantial titles.

Since, then, we used so old and so excellent a manuscript in restoring the Hieronymian translation of this book, even if nothing else had been accomplished, there would nevertheless be ample reason for those devoted to the name and learning of Jerome to acknowledge that they owe us much. Yet in all the remaining books as well we have enjoyed no unfavorable fortune. For although we did not obtain manuscripts of such antiquity or value, we did acquire ancient codices of good quality, and we collated each part of Scripture against the authority of at least one manuscript, and often of two or three. We could have used more, if it had served our purpose to take into account any manuscripts of more recent date—and if our intention had been to admit into consultation not only those that seemed, on sound evidence, to precede the age of Charlemagne and the revision of which we have mentioned by Alcuin, but also those that certainly had not accepted that revision.

[Col. 0021]

This, however, is the real task and labor. Such is the value of the codices of that age, and such mature and acute judgment is required to distinguish the later interventions, that anyone who attributes so much expertise to himself may perhaps appear to be acting more arrogantly and ambitiously than truthfully. Yet this matter was of the utmost importance, since the Benedictine editors themselves admit, in the second Prolegomenon, as they call it, no. 5, that not even a single exemplar of Jerome’s version could be found in other regions outside Gaul. Their entire edition was transcribed from manuscripts that one nation or people had collected for itself. Yet no one even moderately learned in the history of this Latin version can fail to know that the causes of variant readings in the sacred books must be sought in the differing uses and customs of various regions and peoples. Conversely, almost all the manuscripts that served the communities of, so to speak, a single Church are of one tongue and employ the same expressions. It therefore does not seem sufficiently sound to infer the original integrity of a work from copies produced according to the same character. Moreover, the very thing lacking for completing that edition in every respect was what we have attempted to provide by bringing together testimony from all sides.

For although we received all our codices from Italy—and even this was no small advantage for the proposed recension after the merely Gallican resources—we must add that from almost the entire world whatever there was of the most excellent manuscripts had been granted to the Vatican Library, which for us stands in place of all others. Furthermore, we called upon not only those books that present the sacred text in continuous sequence, but also those consisting of Jerome’s commentaries. Above all, we ordered that the commentaries on all the prophets, in which he continuously first presents and explains his translation from the Hebrew, should be brought forward where necessary as witnesses and should support our emendations.

I shall say next what is the heart of the matter: how scrupulously—perhaps even, as others may think, superstitiously—we treated this work with restraint. Even if the immense force of all the variant readings had been indiscriminately approved by us and entered into the official record, no one could rightly complain that the text had ever been rashly altered.

We often kept before our eyes that judgment of Augustine, worthy of being inscribed on cedar, in Book II, chapter 14, of *On Christian Doctrine*: “The diligence of those who desire to know the divine Scriptures must first devote itself to correcting manuscripts.” Yet, on the other hand, there kept returning to our minds the maxim of the Hebrew teachers, devised with remarkable appropriateness to restrain the boldness of ingenuity: “Nothing is to be corrected on conjecture.”

Proceeding according to this principle, we carefully examined whatever the handwritten pages supplied that differed from the reading commonly received—whether in the wording and writing alone, or in the sense itself and the scope of the meaning [*ἐκτάσις*, “extension” or “range”]. If something differed only in sound or wording, without loss of a sound meaning, and no adequate reason existed for adopting it in preference to the received form, it was enough either to place it alongside the text or, if the matter seemed important enough, to indicate it in the appended notes, with a brief explanation.

I truly pity that ill-judged diligence by which nothing, I think, could be more disagreeable to an educated reader: the practice of inserting at every third word mere faults of ancient pronunciation or spelling, which occur in all old books. This was done in a recent edition of an ancient Psalter, provoking universal laughter, when its margins were burdened with almost no other notes than notices that *B* had been substituted for *V*, and *E* for *I*, and conversely, in words such as *brebi* and *bobes* for *brevi* and *boves*, and *intellege*—which is itself also correct—for *intellige*, together with similar letters that had been substituted by the antiquarian.

By contrast, we valued those cases in which we found in manuscripts words, or even commas, that differed specifically in sense, especially where the sense in the Vulgate had been diminished or interpolated. First, if the readings rested upon the testimony of several manuscripts, we investigated them with greater caution. Then we carefully compared the manuscripts with one another and each reading with our Translator; next we tested it against the touchstone of the Hebrew truth. We also scrutinized the Hebrew archetype itself, to see whether it contained a scribal error and whether it could itself be restored according to the traces of the ancient translation—and conversely. More plausibly, we asked whether the Latin scribes’ error in transposing letters might readily become evident from the evidence; by this method of reasoning we seemed more than once to have struck the mark. Finally, we consulted the Greek translators, the Septuagint, to determine whether the proposed reading was that old reading from the edition in circulation before Jerome, which some diligent scholar had rashly brought back into the text, or which the holy Translator himself had retained because it yielded a not unsuitable sense.

We also directed our attention to the remaining translators—Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and others—especially Symmachus, whose talent and learning delighted the holy Father in a remarkable manner. We omitted no word whose difficulty we suspected; we left nothing unattempted and nothing unexamined.

After testing everything against this touchstone, and when judgment still favored the manuscripts, we thought it far better to explain in the notes the reasons for the reading and to confirm with new arguments the interpretation to which we would readily concede, than to lay hands upon the text—even when doing so would not merely have been permissible for the sake of a better meaning, but would also have been safe.

If, nevertheless, we dare to emend the text somewhere, the sincere correction of the passage and its genuine meaning plainly seemed to us to stand forth by themselves; and the reading has been so fortified that no force or critical judgment can later overthrow it. In all other cases, unless the matter itself demanded it, and unless the authority of the original books had made the case secure, or men of great name had opened the way and encouraged us, we religiously refrained. It was enough to point out to others, with a preface of honor, the very blemishes that are marks of venerable antiquity and ought to be washed away.

We have regarded this as the best of all methods for revising a sacred codex. If it achieves nothing else, we at least hope to gain this praise: that we have preserved fidelity to the greatest monument of the Christian religion and have attempted to serve the glory of Jerome and the interests of those devoted to him.

I may now seem to be doing work already done if I wish to bring forward and explain anew whatever concerns the nature and history, so to speak, of this translation. The Benedictine editors have long since satisfied the desire of those who wish to know these matters, and have done so not without learning, in the Prolegomena that we append to this very preface. Other highly learned men have done the same: Natalis Alexander, Du Pin, Frassenius, Simon, Calmet, and a great many other sons of criticism; and above all Humphrey Hody, who holds the foremost place in this field of learning, in his book *On the Original Texts of the Bible*.

Although there are certain points in each of these works, especially in the writings of the earlier authors, that meet with little or no approval from us, it did not seem worthwhile to set out here the arguments by which they should be refuted. Unless I were to undertake to retrace at length, in a manner worthy of the subject, the entire discussion that has commonly been handed down, I could not easily explain each point in its proper place. Those studies are also readily available to everyone. If you compare them with one another and measure them against the portion of the history that we ourselves have touched upon from the period of the Alcuinian recension, you will scarcely continue to desire our labors here.

For they generally err through excessive enthusiasm for the holy Translator. Thus some say that Jerome undertook his version from the Hebrew on behalf of the entire Church; others report that Pope Damasus himself commended it to the universal Church. Platina, in his *Life of that Pontiff*, writes:

“Damasus was the first to give authority to Jerome’s writings, whereas previously only the writings of the Seventy Translators had been held in esteem. For Jerome’s Bible also began to be read, as did his psalms, faithfully translated from the Hebrew, whereas previously they had been read chiefly among the Gauls in a disorderly manner.”

John Francis of Brescia, to say nothing for the moment of others, supports this story in a letter to Pagninus:

“By Damasus’s patronage and care, the Greek texts once corrected by Jerome and the Hebrew monuments of sacred literature translated into Latin . . . . . . time and again require Damasus’s care revived and Jerome’s labor repeatedly renewed.”

They should have said that Damasus favored Jerome’s Hebrew studies, since they were both residing at Rome, as is clear from their reciprocal letters [*ἀμοιβαῖαις*, “mutual”]. For while Damasus was alive, the holy Father had not yet applied himself to translating the Scriptures from the Hebrew. But, as we have said, it is not our purpose to pursue these matters.

Indeed, for this very reason—so that I should not seem to detain you longer or to compile writings that others have long worked out with great credit—I thought it better to omit what I had undertaken and prepared to say about Hebrew poetry, in order to clarify and defend the holy Father’s view against the slanders of his opponents. I had nearly brought that discussion to its conclusion. Experience has confirmed the saying of the Roman orator: “What is excessive offends more forcefully than what appears insufficient.” Moreover, our very learned friend recently took up this subject for cultivation in a work of his own, and has far outstripped our efforts in this field. His book, which will soon be published, will, as I anticipate from its reputation and have learned from the specimen he shared with me, satisfy the desire of learned men.

It would not, however, have been right to pass over in silence anything noticed in the chronological notes of the individual books that conflicts with the opinions of others who have followed the same lines of inquiry. This bears directly upon the proper establishment and interconnection of the sequence of Hieronymian events. If you allow it to be disturbed anywhere by some transposition, the whole structure can easily be shaken.

We readily admit what all agree upon with one voice and what is established, among other evidence, especially by this testimony of Jerome in the *Galeate Prologue*: “Read, then, first my Samuel and Malachim.” The books of Kings, he says, were the first of all to appear in publication. It seems preferable to assign them to approximately the year 390 rather than to 392 or the following year, as is commonly thought.

The reason will become clear from the sequence that we shall immediately set out. We all agree that the Psalter and all the prophets followed them. Jerome testifies in the chapter on Sophronius that in the year 392, when he composed his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, these books had already been translated from Latin into Greek by Sophronius:

“He translated into Greek, in elegant language, the Psalter also and the prophets, which we translated from Hebrew into Latin.”

Martianaeus and others are therefore mistaken in postponing the translation of the Psalter until after the year 393, supposing that the holy Translator still kept it shut away in his cabinet. He writes in Letter 49 to Pammachius, a letter belonging to that year:

“If you read the sixteen books of the Prophets”—without mentioning the Psalms—“which I translated into Latin from the Hebrew language, and I learn that you take pleasure in this work, you will challenge us not to keep the remaining books shut away in our cabinet as well.”

By this silence Jerome may have indicated that he was keeping within his domestic walls the book that he had already dedicated to Sophronius and furnished with a preface addressed to him. I think there is no clearer indication of publication than this. Moreover, Sophronius already knew that Jerome had explained the work in Greek, together with all the prophets, with considerable elegance, and had published it among speakers of that language—an undertaking of such length that it must have begun the preceding year.

Indeed, he places this book before the prophets. From the order of the recension it is therefore more plausible to infer the order of publication as well. The translation of Job followed immediately. In the letter just mentioned the holy Father says that he had recently prepared it and sent a copy to Marcella. It is consequently clear that Martianaeus and others are mistaken when they suppose that Job preceded the prophets.

They commonly add the three books of Solomon. I, however, think that these should be assigned to a later date, on the basis of the words of the Prologue to Chromatius and Heliodorus. Nevertheless, I would not dare oppose the opinion received by everyone.

These, finally, are all the books that we know had already been released for publication at the time when Jerome testified of himself in the *Catalogue*: “I translated the Old Testament according to the Hebrew.” The sons of criticism take this statement [*σχηματικῶς*, “figuratively” or “schematically”] to mean that he had not literally translated the whole of Scripture, but only the portions that we have just listed, by that time.

I believe that the holy Doctor spoke literally and that the entire Old Testament had already been rendered by him into Latin, except perhaps for some small portion that he had no reason to mention there individually. Certainly, at the time when he refers to the translation of Job, he says that he was already keeping “the remaining books shut away in his cabinet.” Although these may subsequently have appeared in different years, their origin must nevertheless be traced back to the point from which he says they had begun; and it is therefore clear that they had already been prepared from the year in which the *Catalogue* was composed.

Of these books, Ezra and Nehemiah appeared first, around the year 394. This is clear from the Prologue, where he says that he is reserving for a larger work the discussion of many passages praised in the Gospels as belonging to the Old Testament but not found in the Septuagint. By the “larger work” he certainly means Letter 57 in our recension, or the booklet *On the Best Kind of Translation*, which we assign to the year 395.

The books of Chronicles followed these. In their Prologue that same booklet, *On the Best Kind of Translation*, is said to have been recently published; thus Chronicles appears to have seen the light in that same year, 395. Those who therefore assert that these books appeared last of all—Du Pin and Martianaeus—are as far as possible from the truth. They could have been instructed by this very testimony, and also by Letter 71 to Lucinius, written almost three years later, in which the holy Translator himself declares that he had published all the books of the Old Testament before the Octateuch:

“I gave the canon of the Hebrew Truth to your boys and secretaries to copy, except for the Octateuch, which I now have in hand.”

He was therefore laboring from the year 398 on the revision of those eight books, which occupy the first place in the order of the sacred text. I am readily persuaded, however, that Genesis was published earlier, since the remaining books of Moses were still being pressed toward their fourth or fifth year.

Joshua did not appear until after the death of the holy Paula. Her death occurred during the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the sixth time and Aristaenetus—that is, in the year 404—as is known from her epitaph.

Finally, the book of Esther must have appeared last of all, if the holy Father includes it among the Octateuch, joining the books of Judges and Ruth into one according to Hebrew custom. On this point, at the end of the matter, we have thought there was nothing to add to the sound calculations of others.

[DIVINE LIBRARY I.]

[Col. 0027]

TO THE MOST HOLY FATHER INNOCENT XII, SUPREME PONTIFF

Jerome, having assumed Christ’s garment in the city of Rome and being joined to the chair of Peter by unbroken communion, once the oracle and delight of Pope Damasus, hastens joyfully to the feet of Your Holiness, most blessed Father, in eager obedience to his vow.

Although your greatness frightens him, your humanity nevertheless invites him. “Let the ambition of the Roman height stand aside,” he says; “I am speaking with the successor of the Fisherman and the disciple of the cross” (Letter 57). For the greatest Doctor of the Church, now a companion of the angels in heaven, knows that if you follow the apostles in honor, you also follow them in merit.

That great man, therefore, prostrate at the feet of Your Beatitude, eagerly desires to offer his Divine Library, which is the head and summit of all his studies, now restored by our labor and indeed by our own hands. Thus, since we are inclined toward the Apostolic See by one and the same act of reverence, we may together celebrate, with joined offices and undivided devotion to honor, the auspicious beginnings of your pontificate (Letter 58).

Nor will we, most holy Father, have any reason to fear even the least of your addresses, since that immortal intellect, together with its most ample gift of sacred interpretations, will grant us a hearing; and we reverently dedicate it to your name. What could be more acceptable or pleasing to the most devout Father of Christians than Jerome’s Divine Library, restored for all the Church’s uses—a treasury, so to speak, of heavenly commands, from which new and old things may be brought forth, so that the good shepherd and faithful steward may nourish himself and the flock entrusted to him?

Why should the sacred volumes of the Scriptures not now have been pleasing to Innocent, which were the chaste delight of the holy Pontiff Damasus, whose distinguished words to Jerome are these:

“I think there is no more worthy subject of our conversation than that we should speak together about the Scriptures—that is, that I should ask and you should answer.” I think there is nothing more delightful in this life than such a way of living; by such nourishment of the soul all honey is surpassed. “How sweet are your words to my palate,” says the prophet, “more than honey to my mouth” (Letter 124).

Many noble actions of yours, most holy Father, when you formerly served as an envoy among princes, kings, and emperors, demonstrated that you were devoted to the divine laws and deeply formed by the teachings of the holy Fathers. Now, however, having become a participant in supreme power and the vicar of Christ, you provide so many and such great proofs of piety that all Christian peoples rejoice that in you they possess a learned scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven, whose will is to meditate day and night upon the law of the Lord.

For whence comes that saying of yours, now celebrated throughout the world: “The house of the Roman Pontiff is the house of the poor”? And again, to the poor who were blind: “I do not take away your freedom; I wish to be your guide and your eye.”

Whence, I ask, do such words come to Your Holiness, words that sound so sweetly in the ears of the virgin Church, unless from the inner sanctuary and oracle of the divine Scriptures, from which you learned to speak in this way: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor” (Job 29)?

What that illustrious prince among the Eastern peoples had once been known to practice through a devout affection for humanity, Your Holiness, now conspicuous throughout the whole world, has proposed to imitate, comforting the members of Christ through the distribution of many gifts and bringing wandering people into the Papal household.

Nor were you content, venerable Pope, to have supported the Church of God by only one act of humanity and mercy. You also wished to warn all the wealthy, striking them with a brazen admonition, not to place their hope in uncertain riches, coveting what belongs to others, failing to distribute what is their own, and using their possessions to their own destruction. For you say: “Let this money not be with us unto perdition.”

What more need be said? So that avarice—the service of idols—and greed, the root of all evils, might be banished from the Christian commonwealth, your Apostolic concern decreed by a singular ordinance that henceforth the tribunals of judges should not be for sale, but should be assigned freely to upright men who, appointed according to the command of the Lawgiver and Prophet, judge the people with righteous judgment and do not incline to either side by accepting gifts, which blind the eyes of the wise and pervert the words of the just (Deut. 16).

In this way you bestow the greatest gifts of generosity and munificence. Scarcely could deeds more worthy of a supreme Pontiff be desired, except perhaps in Innocent XII, who, by a kind of prophecy of future blessings, received the name of the twelfth in number, so that we might hope to find in him something like the fullness of apostolic virtue.

Who now lives more temperately than he who, having wholly excluded the noble Pignatelli family from the revenues of the Church, arranged by decree to transfer the affection of love owed to his parents wholly to the poor? He had been persuaded by Jerome that the glory of a bishop consists chiefly in providing for the poverty of the poor and not striving after his own riches (Letter 2).

Thus in you, most blessed Father, all the things that the distinguished Doctor, inspired by a divine rather than a rhetorical spirit, earnestly urged his closest friends in letters concerning the renunciation of nephews or Nepotians for Christ and the rejection of worldly profits in God’s service are visibly expressed in corresponding deeds (Letters 1, 2).

The letters on one side and the decrees on the other testify how well Jerome and Innocent agree. Both wish the sole form of piety to be flight to the banner of the cross over the trampled body of one’s father; both glory in being called cruel because parental affection has been extinguished.

Others may marvel at such harmony of deeds and words in the greatest Doctor and the supreme Pontiff. For us, whatever excels rightly commands veneration; but the ancient and well-attested agreement of holy men has not caused astonishment.

We know that the faith of Innocent XII was familiarly praised by Jerome, when he presented his predecessor of that name as the first to be followed by the virgin Demetrias:

“I think I ought to warn you beforehand, in the pious affection of charity, to hold fast the faith of holy Innocent, who is the successor and son of the man mentioned above in the apostolic chair; and do not accept a foreign doctrine, even though you may seem prudent and clever” (Letter 8).

Nor is it surprising that Innocent’s faith was praised by one who is declared his son in the Council of Milevis, where that new and exceedingly pernicious heresy, the foreign doctrine of Pelagius, was condemned forever. Nevertheless, the Council of Milevis writes in its letter to Pope Innocent:

“Many more, who have been able to investigate his views more carefully, are struggling against him for the grace of Christ and the truth of the Catholic faith; but above all your holy son, our brother and fellow presbyter Jerome.”

Much more could have been gathered, most holy Father, so that Jerome might be held especially dear to you on account of his faith, the praise of your predecessors, and his perpetual reverence for the Roman See. But why linger longer over these matters, when those present see you exult at the mere sound of the holy Doctor’s name?

You received the new edition of Jerome’s works, prepared by our labor, with such kindness and gratitude that we greatly rejoice to have found Damasus reborn in Your Holiness together with the Jerome restored by us.

Receive, therefore, this most precious monument of sacred antiquity, the previously unpublished Divine Library of Eusebius Jerome; and embrace with a joyful countenance the most learned man returning from Gaul to Rome, as though he were still in the flower of his age. He brings with him a great store of interpretations of sacred Scripture, which the injury of time had led us to believe had perished altogether.

Nor did it happen without divine direction that these works did not emerge from darkness into light until our own age. It was fitting, surely, that under so great a Pontiff the customary services of Jerome, the greatest interpreter of the Scriptures, should be renewed (*Distinction* 15, chapter “The Holy Roman Church”).

He will gladly teach Israel commandment and judgment, if he deserves to have you as helper and patron, approved and confirmed by the oracle of your Pontifical voice. Nor will the aforementioned son of Innocent be delayed by certain followers of Rufinus now rising in this age, if he hears you, his most holy Father, proclaiming with Gelasius and the Roman Council:

“We hold the opinions that we know blessed Jerome to have held”—

and this not only concerning Rufinus, but also concerning all those whom that often-mentioned man rebuked out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

[Col. 0031]

After the great labor we have devoted to obscure and difficult matters, it belongs to you, most blessed Father, to grant Jerome, who proclaims the Gospel, great influence in the Church (Letter 58). May you therefore sit upon the throne to judge with the Twelve; may you obtain with Paul the citizenship of heaven.

We shall regard our literary labor as altogether happy and providential if our progress also becomes your glory, and if Your Holiness, who loves us all as sons because of our priestly office, continues to accompany us with your Apostolic blessing.

To Your Holiness

The most humble monks of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur offer this work.

[Col. 0031]

PROLEGOMENA TO THE DIVINE LIBRARY OF SAINT JEROME, FROM THE BENEDICTINE EDITION

PREFACE

Those who undertake new editions of ancient writers can explain briefly to the reader the work they have undertaken. Since their principal labor consists in restoring the integrity of the books’ text and elucidating certain more obscure passages, one or another discussion devoted to that subject is sufficient for learned people.

For us, however, who have undertaken to prepare for the public benefit the previously unpublished Divine Library of Saint Jerome, so many and such weighty matters of the greatest importance lie upon us that the magnitude of the task imposed not only presses upon our shoulders but requires us to fall beneath the burden before we can lift it.

Who would not fear to examine the principal work of the greatest interpreter of the divine Scriptures; to investigate the Hebrew language, whose knowledge he attained; to assign dates to his writings and translations; to distinguish doubtful and spurious compositions from true and genuine works; to make clear to the reader what use Jerome’s versions had in the Church of Christ; and to demonstrate many similar matters, which could not easily even be listed under their proper names?

I confess that we shudder at that immense and profound sea of discussion into which we are compelled by necessity, being devoted and consecrated to the publication of Jerome’s works. Yet we are sustained by the great hope that a fair-minded reader will more readily grant us pardon if, in matters obscure in themselves and not previously attempted by anyone, we have not satisfied his desire in every respect—or at least if something has occasionally escaped us in writing that more watchful and diligent eyes would not have missed.

Moved especially by this expectation, we publish certain Prolegomena for the elucidation of this Divine Library of Saint Jerome. It will bring to light many things that had remained closed and unknown before our time, remove errors concerning writers and books from the minds of readers, and enrich the Church of Christ with the sacred volumes translated into Latin by Eusebius Jerome, both from Greek and from Hebrew.

FIRST PROLEGOMENON

On the Name “Divine Library” and the Manner in Which It Has Been Published by Us

I. What “Divine Library” signifies.  
II. Jerome’s purpose in translating the sacred Scriptures.  
III. His diligence in thoroughly learning the Hebrew language.  
IV. Who encouraged him, and who opposed his translations from Hebrew.  
V. In his translations he avoided excessive novelty and the *κακοζηλία*—the bad taste or misguided imitation—of interpretation.

[Col. 0031A] Among the ancients, the sacred Volumes that we now call the Bible were known by the name *Divine Library*. Thus, in Jerome’s *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, Eusebius of Caesarea is praised as the most diligent investigator of the Divine Library together with the martyr Pamphilus. For both were exceedingly devoted to the divine Scriptures, to such a degree that they undertook to publish throughout the churches of the East the Palestinian biblical codices prepared by Origen.

In antiquity, not only the copies of the Old and New Testament that were worn out in the hands of Christians enjoyed the name *Library*; [Col. 0032A] the volumes of the Hebrews, too, are designated by the holy Fathers with the same title. Jerome, in his preface to the book of Esther addressed to Paula the younger and Eustochium, virgins of Christ, wrote as follows:

> But you, Paula and Eustochium, since you have also endeavored to enter the libraries of the Hebrews and have examined the contests of the translators, take the Hebrew book of Esther and inspect our translation word by word, so that you may recognize that I have added nothing even by way of augmentation, but have simply handed over the Hebrew history to the Latin language with faithful testimony, exactly as it is found in Hebrew.

Here, therefore, he calls the Hebrew volumes of the Old Testament “the libraries of the Hebrews”—the volumes in which Paula and Eustochium had been instructed under Jerome himself.

The Old Testament is likewise designated even more clearly by this title in Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 3, and in a manuscript codex of the Colbert Library that contains glosses on the divine books and bears the numerical mark 2852. For near the middle of the book these words of Isidore are found, written by an anonymous author:

> Ezra the scribe, after the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans, when the Jews had entered Jerusalem (Isidore: “had returned”), restored the library of the Old Testament, inspired by the divine Spirit. He corrected all the volumes of the Law and the Prophets that had been corrupted by the nations, and established the whole Old Testament in twenty-two books, so that there might be as many books in the Law as there were letters.

Thus wrote that ancient author, whoever he may have been.

In the same sense Jerome, in his letter to Augustine, calls the Old Testament, or its volumes, the libraries of the churches:

> Do you wish, he says, to be a true lover of the Seventy Translators? Do not read what is under the asterisks; indeed, erase it from the volumes, so that you may prove yourself a supporter of the ancients. But if you do this, you will be forced to condemn all the libraries of the churches; for scarcely one or two books can be found that do not contain these things.

That copies of the New Testament were also called by this name is attested by Letter 52, addressed to Pammachius. There the holy Doctor, referring to that *pericope*—that is, passage—of the Apostle in which he discusses virginity and marriage, 1 Corinthians 7, advises that the commentaries of the Fathers be read and that the libraries of the churches be used, so that, after the Apostle’s words have been carefully considered, it may clearly appear that he was much more lenient toward husbands than Paul intended, in order to avoid calumny. [Col. 0033C]

It is therefore said:

> Read through the commentaries of all those whom I mentioned above, and make use of the libraries of the churches; and you will reach what you desire and have undertaken with a more rapid step.

Finally, some manuscript codices preserved among the Celestines and the Avignon Dominicans give the following title to Jerome’s letter to Paulinus, placed at the beginning of the sacred Bible:

> Here begins Jerome’s Prologue to the Library.

We have prefaced so many testimonies, drawn especially from Jerome himself, so that it might be plain to everyone that the volumes of the Old and New Testament [Col. 0033D] translated into Latin by the same interpreter may appropriately be called Jerome’s Divine Library.

Learned men will more readily grant this to us when they know that ancient writers used the name “Jerome’s Library” to designate his Latin translations of the sacred Scriptures. In our library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés there is a codex of venerable antiquity, number 15, in which the scribe added the following at the end of the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> Read in peace the Library of Jerome, priest of Bethlehem.

Imitating this scribe’s zeal and adhering wholly to the words of the holy Doctor, we have arranged for the present volume to be inscribed with the title *Jerome’s Divine Library*, since it contains all the volumes of the Old and New Testament [Col. 0034A] rendered into Latin by him.

We could add more concerning this terminology, were not Jerome alone sufficient for us as proof of the designation by which we have chosen to call the first volume of our edition.

## II

Prompted by the zeal and example of Origen, Jerome first undertook to provide his Latin readers with a most carefully corrected edition of the sacred Scripture, based on the text of the *Hexapla*. He judged that something more useful would come to the churches from this leisure—which he calls such—than from the business of others.

He himself must be heard in the preface to the book of Job, translated from the Greek:

> If I were weaving a little basket from rushes, he says, or folding palm leaves . . . no one would bite at me, no one would criticize me. But now, because, in accordance with the Savior’s saying, I wish to work for food that does not perish, and to clear the ancient path of the divine volumes of thorns and brushwood, a thorn is driven into me; I am called a falsifier, a corrector of faults, and accused not of removing errors but of sowing them. For the force of ancient custom is so great that even acknowledged faults please most people, since they prefer to have beautiful books rather than corrected ones.

Jerome therefore labored to restore the sacred volumes to their integrity and authenticity. With this purpose he supplied many omissions and did not hesitate to remove acknowledged faults, although they pleased most people. Returning to the Greek original, he diligently corrected what had either been badly rendered by faulty translators, perversely amended by ignorant presumptuous men, or added or altered by inattentive copyists.

In this way he worked for food that [Col. 0034C] does not perish, and instead of the fans and baskets of other monks he offered these spiritual and lasting gifts to the Church of God.

Thus, opening his mind to the holy women, he wrote in the preface to Daniel:

> I beseech you, Paula and Eustochium, pour out prayers to the Lord for me, so that, as long as I am in this little body, I may write something pleasing to you, useful to the Church, and worthy of posterity. For I am not greatly moved by the judgments of the present age, since people err on either side, whether through love or through hatred.

What, indeed, is more useful to the Church, what more worthy of posterity, than the path of the divine volumes cleansed of the thorns and brushwood of errors? What is more acceptable to all the faithful in Christ than complete and unblemished codices of the divine Scripture?

Accordingly, out of regard for this public benefit, Jerome undertook the task [Col. 0034D] of correcting whatever, through the carelessness of copyists, the injury of time, or the ignorance of translators, had entered corruptly into the copies of the sacred Bibles translated from the Greek into Latin.

After rendering such great service to the Church of Christ from the interpretation of the Seventy Translators, he turned to more perfect things and undertook a new edition of the Scriptures from the Hebrew, so that thereafter Latins might not follow streams but see the sources of things, and might pierce the eyes of the crows—that is, of the Jews—with the very Hebrew truth.

The holy Doctor testifies in many places in his writings that he had this intention when translating the sacred volumes from the Hebrew source. Particularly memorable is the following statement in book III of his *Apology against Rufinus*:

> You will correct the Latin Scriptures from the Greek, he says, and give the churches something different to read from what they once received from the apostles. Will it not be permitted to me, after the edition of the Seventy, which many years ago I most carefully corrected and gave to the people of my language, also to translate, for the refutation of the Jews, the very copies that they themselves acknowledge to be most accurate? Thus, whenever there is a dispute between Christians and them, they will have no evasive byways, but will be struck most especially by their own sword.

The Jews mocked Christians and insulted the churches of God on account of the alleged falsity of the Scriptures, because of the Seventy Translators, whom they maintained had erred in many places. To repel the accusation of these enemies, Jerome declares in his preface to Isaiah that he had labored in the study of a foreign language, [Col. 0035B] so that the Jews would no longer insult the churches of God over the alleged falsity of the Scriptures.

And in his preface to Chromatius on Chronicles he says:

> Do you think it was a matter of my own choice either to decide from several versions what is true, or to forge a new work upon an old one, and, as the saying goes, to pierce the eyes of the crows while the Jews mock?

No one is unaware that Sophronius was once mocked by the Jews during a disputation. Jerome taught this in the preface to his Psalter translated from Hebrew into Latin, writing to Sophronius as follows:

> Since recently, while disputing with a Hebrew, you brought forward from the Psalms certain testimonies concerning the Lord, and the man, wishing to mock you, maintained in nearly every phrase that the Hebrew did not contain what you were arguing from the Seventy Translators, you earnestly requested me to translate a new edition into Latin after Aquila, Symmachus, [Col. 0035C] and Theodotion.

From this it is clear to us that all those who accused Jerome of having interpreted the holy Scriptures in condemnation of the Seventy Translators were utterly ungrateful and unjust toward him. Nor did he deserve to be blamed for supplying the churches with weapons against the enemies of the Christian faith through his translation.

He therefore justly complains of this at the end of the second book of his *Apology against Rufinus*:

> From the point at which I thought I was deserving well of my Latins and encouraging our people to study—something which even the Greeks do not disdain when a Latin is translated after so many translators—from that point I am accused and force food upon a nauseated stomach. What, then, is safe in a human being, if innocence is criminal?

Finally, he wished to persuade even malicious readers of his zeal by this argument:

> If among the Greeks, after the edition of the Seventy, when the Gospel of Christ was already shining forth, the Jewish Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—heretics who Judaized and concealed many mysteries of the Savior through their deceitful translation—were nevertheless received, and yet are found in the *Hexapla* among the churches and explained by ecclesiastical men, how much more should I, a Christian born of Christian parents and bearing the standard of the cross upon my forehead, whose concern has been to restore what was omitted, correct what was corrupted, and disclose the mysteries of the Church in pure and faithful language, not be rejected either by fastidious or malicious readers?

He himself wrote this in the preface to the book of Job, rendered from Hebrew into Latin.

He proves the same point in Letter 89 to Augustine, to whom he commended his work in these words:

> For I have not so much attempted to abolish the old versions, which I translated from Greek into Latin, corrected for all who speak my language, as to bring forward the testimonies that had been omitted or corrupted by the Jews, so that our people might know what the Hebrew truth contained. If anyone does not wish to read it, no one compels him against his will.
