Let him drink the old wine with pleasure and despise our new wine, which has been produced to explain the earlier versions, so that wherever those are not understood, our versions may make them clearer.

Saint Augustine replied to Jerome, entirely persuaded that this was indeed the case:

> You have already persuaded me concerning the usefulness with which you wished to translate the Scriptures from Hebrew: namely, that you might bring forward what had been omitted or corrupted by the Jews.

For the rest, see Letter 97 among the letters of Jerome.

It therefore remains clear from what has already been set forth that Jerome issued the new translation from the Hebrew source not as an attack on the Seventy Translators, but for every benefit of the Church.

## III

Since Jerome knew that he could interpret only what he had previously understood, and since he had been trained in all the disciplines of the Greeks and Latins, he began to frequent the thresholds of Hebrew teachers and to study their language.

He testified to this abundantly in Letter 4 to the monk Rusticus, teaching that vices must be overcome through love of virtue:

> When I was young, he says, and the wilderness of solitude surrounded me, I could not endure the incitements of vice and the heat of nature. Though I broke this force through frequent fasts, my mind nevertheless seethed with thoughts. To subdue it, I placed myself under the instruction of a certain brother who had come to believe from among the Hebrews, so that after the refinements of Quintilian, the streams of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto, and the gentleness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practice uttering hissing, breathy words. My conscience bears witness to how much labor I expended there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired, how often I stopped, and how, through the determination to learn, I began again—both my own conscience, since I suffered these things, and the conscience of those who shared my life. And I give thanks to the Lord that from the bitter seed of letters I am gathering sweet fruits.

He calls this difficulty in learning the Hebrew language a “mill,” as he says in his preface to Daniel:

> Finally, when I was a young man, after reading Quintilian and Tully and the flowers of rhetoric, I shut myself up in the mill of this language. After much sweat and much time I had scarcely begun to sound out its breathy and hissing words, and, as though walking through a tunnel and seeing only a scant light above, I finally stumbled upon Daniel. I was so wearied that, in a sudden despair, I wanted to abandon all my former labor. But when a certain Hebrew encouraged me and repeatedly impressed upon me in his language the saying, “Hard work conquers all,” I, who had seemed to myself a little learned among them, began once again to be a Chaldaean pupil. And, to speak truthfully, even to the present day I can read and understand the Chaldaean language better than I can pronounce it.

The holy Jerome experienced such great effort and labor in learning Hebrew because of those breathy and hissing words which, even when understood by Latins, we can scarcely pronounce in the manner of the Jews, for whom this barbarous kind of speech is native.

For this reason Jerome himself explains the cause of such difficulty in book I of his *Commentary on chapter 3 of the Epistle to Titus*, saying:

> When he says, “Avoid genealogies and disputes and quarrels that arise from the law,” he is specifically attacking the Jews, who boast about this and think that they possess knowledge of the law if they know the names of each individual. Since these names are barbarous, and we do not know their etymologies, we often pronounce them incorrectly. If by chance we make a mistake in accent, in the lengthening or shortening of a syllable, either lengthening short syllables or shortening long ones, they customarily mock our ignorance—especially in the aspirates and in pronouncing certain letters with a scraping of the throat . . . .

> If, therefore, these features of the names and the language are not expressed by us in the way they are expressed by the Hebrews, precisely because they are barbarous, they customarily burst into laughter and swear that they have no idea what we are saying. For this reason we took care to correct all the books of the Old Law that the learned Adamantius had arranged in the *Hexapla*, having copied them from the Caesarean Library from the authentic texts. In these books the Hebrew words themselves are written in their proper characters and represented in Greek letters by a closely corresponding transcription . . . . so that we need not greatly fear the disdain of the Jews, who delight in loose lips, twisted tongues, hissing, and scraped throats.

That the holy Doctor was assiduous in the Hebrew language is plainly declared by the following words written in the epitaph of Paula, his mother:

> I shall mention another matter, which may perhaps seem unbelievable to my rivals. She wished to learn the Hebrew language, which I myself had partly learned from youth through much labor and sweat and which I do not abandon through tireless practice, lest I myself be abandoned by it; and she learned it, and succeeded, etc.

It was not enough for this exceptionally studious man, who ardently desired understanding of the sacred Bibles, to have learned Hebrew with much sweat, unless he also tested his resources in that undertaking. For a complete understanding of the extremely obscure book of Job, he employed a Hebrew teacher, whom he says did not come to him without payment but was hired for money. In his preface to the same book of Job he writes:

> I remember that, for an understanding of this volume, I purchased at no small price a certain teacher from Lydda, who was considered foremost among the Hebrews. Whether I made any progress through his instruction, I do not know. I know only this: I could not interpret what I had not first understood.

Sparing neither labor nor his purse, therefore, he acquired no ordinary knowledge of the Hebrew language, so that he was able immediately to explain in Latin whatever the Jews themselves uttered in Hebrew.

We have testimony to this in the preface to Tobit, where he taught us the method by which he produced his Latin version:

> And because the language of the Chaldeans is close to the Hebrew language, I found a very eloquent man thoroughly skilled in both languages, undertook a single day’s labor, and whatever he expressed to me in Hebrew words I, having summoned a secretary, rendered in Latin speech.

He certainly could never have accomplished this by himself unless he had known Hebrew accurately and thoroughly. For what half-trained or unskilled man in Hebrew could convert with equal ease into Latin the dictated words of a speaking Hebrew? It is therefore sufficiently evident that Jerome possessed a perfect knowledge of Hebrew speech, even though elsewhere, out of modesty, he said that he had learned the language of the Hebrews only in part, while in Latin he had been worn down from childhood among grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers.

Nor could he deny, in Letter 142 to Pope Damasus, that he had learned much from the Hebrews:

> There is a certain man, he says, from whom I am glad to have learned many things, and who has so polished the Hebrew language that among their scribes he is considered a Chaldaean.

To Marcella, too, in Letter 130, he admits that he had lost something of purer Latin because of his familiarity with the usage of Hebrew idiom:

> As you know, we have been occupied with reading the Hebrews and have allowed rust to gather over our Latin language, to such an extent that even when we speak, a certain non-Latin harshness intrudes. Therefore forgive my dryness, etc.

At the end of his *Commentaries on the Prophet Haggai*, he says that he had lost all elegance of expression through his devotion to the Hebrew language:

> I beseech you, reader, to forgive a rapid dictation, and do not demand the elegance of expression that I lost through long study of the Hebrew language, etc.

Jerome’s zeal is also proved by the Hebrew volumes that he copied or collated with the Greek translators, as well as by the province of Palestine, which he traversed and explored for a fuller understanding of Hebrew names, taking with him as companions the most learned of the Jews.

Let us pursue these matters in order.

While at Rome, the holy man excuses his delay to Saint Damasus in Letter 125, because he had been detained by another work and could not immediately reply to his questions. What that work was he explains in these words at the beginning of the same letter:

> In the meantime, however, he and I were moving our tongues and our stylus, when suddenly a Hebrew arrived, bringing a considerable number of volumes, which he had received from the synagogue as though he intended to read them.

And immediately afterward:

> You have, he said, what you had requested.

Then, leaving me uncertain and not knowing what to do, he so alarmed me in his haste that, setting everything else aside, I flew to copy them—and this is what I am still doing to the present day.

Similarly detained by Hebrew letters and by his continual comparison of books, he wrote a shorter Letter 74 to Marcella:

> There were two reasons why I wrote such a short letter: the courier was in a hurry, and I, detained by another work, was occupying myself with this as a kind of *parerga*—a secondary task. You ask what that work is, so great and so necessary that it has displaced the duty of an epistolary conversation. For a long time now I have been comparing the edition of Aquila with the Hebrew volumes, lest perhaps the synagogue has altered anything out of hatred for Christ. And, to confess frankly to a friendly mind, I find more material that supports our faith. Now, after examining in detail the Prophets, Solomon, the Psalter, and the books of the Kings, I am holding Exodus, which they call *Ellesmoth*, and am about to proceed to Leviticus. You see, therefore, that no duty should be placed before this work.

Occupied with these studies at Rome, the holy man also wished to contemplate Judaea with his own eyes. For just as those who have seen Athens understand the histories of the Greeks better, so the person who has observed Judaea with his own eyes will perceive the sacred Scripture more clearly, having learned the memories of ancient cities, the places, and the same names, whether preserved or altered.

Thus Jerome also took care to undertake this labor with the most learned Hebrews, so that they might travel around the province whose name resounds throughout the universal Church of Christ.

He states this explicitly in his preface to the book of Chronicles, addressed to Domnion and Rogatianus. There he also confessed that he had never relied upon his own powers in the divine volumes, nor treated his own opinion as a teacher, but had been accustomed to inquire even about matters that he thought he knew—and all the more about those concerning which he was uncertain.

He confirms this with the following argument:

> Finally, when you recently demanded by letter that I translate Chronicles for you into Latin, I took on a certain teacher from Tiberias who was held in admiration among the Hebrews, and I examined it with him from beginning to end, as they say, from the crown to the last fingernail. Thus strengthened, I dared to do what you commanded.

I certainly do not see what more could be desired in a devoted scholar. He expends every effort on Hebrew matters, spares no expense, undertakes arduous journeys, continually converses with the most learned Jews, copies books with his own hand, and compares the Greek with the Hebrew. In short, what did he not do to attain an understanding of the holy language?

He therefore rightly said above:

> And I give thanks to the Lord that from the bitter seed of letters I gather sweet fruits—

that is, knowledge of the divine Scriptures and mastery of the Hebrew language.

## IV

Jerome, therefore, distinguished by his knowledge of many languages and celebrated among all for his learning, soon began to be asked by many people to translate the sacred books from the Hebrew sources into Latin. All the little prefaces to the Old Testament, examples of which we shall present in part, bear witness to this matter. It would be superfluous to write otherwise what is found expressed in them. Let us begin, therefore, with Genesis, whose prologue is as follows:

> I have received the letters of Desiderius, the object of my desire, who, by a kind of foreknowledge of things to come, received his name together with Daniel, and who begs that I hand over to our ears the Pentateuch translated from the Hebrew language into Latin.

This Desiderius may perhaps have been that holy presbyter in Vasconia who, together with Riparius, was the author of the splendid work published by Jerome concerning the holy relics of the martyrs against Vigilantius. Jerome says:

> The authors of this little treatise of mine are the holy presbyters Riparius and Desiderius, who write that their parishes have been stained by the proximity of this man, and who sent books through the brother Sisinnius, etc.

Unless we should believe that there was another Desiderius, an honorable and eloquent man to whom the holy Doctor wrote Letter 154. That letter also shows that Jerome’s little works were earnestly requested by a man who, together with Daniel, had received a prophetic name.

But whoever this Desiderius was who demanded that the Pentateuch be translated into Latin from Hebrew, he certainly appears to have been a holy man, and not a person of insignificant merit in the Church.

After completing the Pentateuch, Jerome applied himself to Jesus the son of Nun—that is, Joshua—and to the book of Judges, as well as to Ruth and Esther, because he could not refuse these books to Eustochium, virgin of Christ.

He translated them into Latin from Hebrew after the death of the holy Paula. It is a strong conjecture that the four books of Kings had previously been translated into Latin at Paula’s request, based on these final words of the preface:

> But I also ask you, handmaids of Christ, who anoint the head of the Lord reclining at table with the most precious myrrh of faith . . . to set against the barking dogs who rage against me with rabid mouths . . . the shields of your prayers.

By “handmaids of Christ,” I think he means none other than Paula and Eustochium, who lived out their days with Jerome at Bethlehem.

[Col. 0040B] At the request of the most holy bishop Chromatius, he rendered Chronicles from the Hebrew source in Latin speech:

> If the pure edition of the Seventy Translators, exactly as it was translated by them into Greek, had remained, you would be urging me in vain, Chromatius, most holy and learned of bishops, to translate the Hebrew volumes into Latin speech.

The most holy and learned bishop was therefore urging Jerome to set aside the paths of the streams and hand over the sacred books to Latin readers from the very Hebrew truth.

The following words in the preface prove that Domnion and Rogatianus likewise pressed Jerome to translate the book of Ezra and Nehemiah:

> For three years now you have continually written and written again, asking me to translate the book of Ezra from Hebrew, [Col. 0040C] as though you did not possess Greek and Latin volumes, or as though whatever is translated by us would not immediately be spat upon by everyone.

Certainly, at that time no man in the Church of Christ was more distinguished than Domnion for the glory of holiness, as is attested by numerous letters of Jerome, Augustine, and Paulinus, as well as by the writings of Rufinus and Palladius.

Rogatianus, meanwhile, is believed to have been the brother of that same most holy Father and presbyter Domnion, who, venerable in his white hair, was held in the highest honor by all Christians and, through his practice of hospitality, deserved to be called the Lot of his age.

Such, then, were Jerome’s encouragers of his translations from Hebrew.

He also dedicated the books of Solomon, translated from the Hebrew truth, to the holy bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus. Later, yielding to their requests, he translated into Latin the book of Tobit, written in the Chaldaean language:

> I never cease to marvel, he says, at the urgency of your demands. For you require me to bring into Latin style a book written in the Chaldaean language . . . . I have satisfied your desire, though not my own inclination. For the studies of the Hebrews accuse us and charge us with transferring these things to Latin ears contrary to their canon. But judging it better to displease the judgment of the Pharisees and to serve the commands of bishops, I persisted as best I could, etc.

Sophronius, a highly learned man, must also be counted among those who urged Jerome by letter to undertake such Latin translations.

Thus, when writing to Sophronius about the occasion of his translation of the Psalter [Col. 0041A] from Hebrew, he imagines the following in the preface:

> Since recently, while disputing with a Hebrew, you brought forward from the Psalms certain testimonies concerning the Lord and Savior, and the man, wishing to mock you, maintained in nearly every phrase that the Hebrew did not contain what you were arguing from the Seventy Translators, you earnestly requested me to translate a new edition into Latin after Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion.

> For you said that you were more confused by the variety of the translators and that, because of the affection in which you are bound to me, you would be satisfied either with my translation or with my judgment. Therefore, compelled by you, to whom I cannot refuse whatever I can provide, I once again delivered myself to the barking of my detractors. I preferred that you seek my abilities rather than my willingness in friendship.

> At least I shall say confidently, and shall call many witnesses to this work, that I have knowingly changed nothing at all from the Hebrew truth.

Finally, unwillingly and under compulsion from the daily demands of Paula the mother and the virgin Eustochium, he bestowed Latin form upon the volumes of the prophets, both the major and the minor. He explicitly complains of this in the preface to Jeremiah, which he wished to conclude with these words:

> In return for all these things we await the curses of our rivals, to whom I must reply in each individual work. And I endure this because you compel me. Otherwise, to shorten the evil, it would have been better to put an end to their madness through my silence than, by writing something new every day, to provoke the insanity of the envious.

It is enough to have said this much about the many and such demanding patrons of Jerome’s translations, so that it may be established for everyone that the Hebrew volumes of the Old Testament always possessed the highest authority in the Church of God, and that, translated into Latin, they were dedicated to the churches through the efforts of a company of Christ’s handmaids, learned men, and most holy bishops.

As for the opponents of these same translations, if Augustine is excepted, there was no one among them who did not, provoked by envy, strive to attack the holy work and detract from Jerome.

Thus, in his preface to Ezra, he said of his rivals:

> To this are added the efforts of the envious, who think that everything we write must be criticized, and who sometimes publicly tear apart, against their own conscience, what they secretly read. So much so that I am compelled to cry out and say: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

Nothing exposed the madness of those envious men more clearly than the things read at the end of the second book of his *Apology against Rufinus*, where he discusses at sufficient length a letter falsely attributed to Jerome:

> Brother Eusebius writes, says Saint Jerome, that among the African bishops who had come to the imperial court on ecclesiastical business, he found a letter written as though in my name, in which I was doing penance and confessing that I had been induced by the Jews in my youth to translate the Hebrew volumes into Latin, in which there is no truth. When I heard this, I was astonished . . . . The man who dared to do this—what else would he not dare? It is fortunate that malice does not possess as much power as it has determination. Innocence would have perished if wickedness were always joined to power, and calumny would prevail in everything it desires.

[Col. 0042A] And again:

> What is safe in a human being, if innocence is criminal? While the master of the household slept, an enemy sowed weeds over the seed. The boar from the forest destroyed the vineyard, and a solitary wild beast devoured it. I remain silent, and writings that are not mine speak against me. I am unaware of the crime, and throughout the whole world I confess the crime. Alas for me, my mother, why did you give birth to me—a man judged and discerned by the whole earth?

Inflamed by these torches of envy and equipped with the arts of wickedness, certain scoundrels attacked Jerome’s Hebrew translations. Their standard-bearer was Rufinus, although he swore that he had not written to the Africans under Jerome’s name a letter in which Jerome confessed that he had been induced by the Jews to translate falsehoods.

Among Rufinus’s associates Jerome also had Palladius as an opponent. Jerome himself mentions him in the prologue to his *Dialogues against the Pelagians*, saying:

> Palladius, with servile wickedness, attempted to revive the same heresy and to fabricate a new accusation against me concerning the Hebrew translation, etc.

O happy labors of the holy Doctor, who, never sparing the heretics, acted with every effort so that the enemies of the Church might also become his enemies!

Nor would the Origenists have devised so many calumnies for the destruction of the holy man if he had not previously rebuked their errors publicly and broken their pride through his writings.

But although the hydra hissed and the victorious Sinon hurled firebrands, he was more strongly provoked to study by the charity of holy men than deterred by the detraction and hatred of the envious.

The Jews and malicious Christians alike were tortured by such great jealousy on account of the Hebrew translation that they wished to remove Jerome from their midst. Hence Bede, recalling this kind of envy in his apologetic letter, says:

> For in so necessary a translation of the divine Scripture he was almost overwhelmed with stones by Latins and Hebrews alike. By the Hebrews, because the opportunity to ridicule and calumniate Christians on the basis of allegedly false codices had been removed from them; by the Latins, because new and unfamiliar things, although better, were being forced upon them in place of the old and customary ones.

These words correspond to what is read in Jerome himself, in the preface to the book of Joshua:

> For what benefit is there to the hearer or reader if we sweat through our labor while others labor by their detraction; if the Jews grieve because the opportunity to calumniate and ridicule Christians has been taken away from them; and if members of the Church despise—or rather tear apart—the very thing by which their adversaries are tormented?

[Col. 0042D] Saint Augustine was moved by an altogether different concern when he at one point dissuaded Jerome from interpreting the Hebrew books—namely, by a motive that is not displeasing in the sight of God because it arose from brotherly charity. What reason, then, did that same Augustine most amicably suggest for deterring Jerome from the work of translating the Hebrew Scriptures? He did so in Letter 71, where he says:

“I would certainly prefer you to interpret for us the canonical Scriptures that are Greek and are attributed to the Seventy Interpreters. For it will be exceedingly difficult if your translation begins to be read more frequently throughout many churches, and the Latin churches thereby differ from the Greek churches—especially since a challenger is easily refuted by producing a Greek book, that is, in a language known to all. But whoever is disturbed by something unusual in what has been translated from Hebrew, and brings an accusation of falsity, will scarcely, or never, reach the Hebrew testimonies by which the charge could be defended. And even if he does reach them, who would tolerate the condemnation of so many Latin and Greek authorities? To this is added the fact that even consulted Hebrews may give another answer, so that you alone may appear necessary, since you could even refute them themselves; yet it would be surprising if you could find a judge in whose judgment this might be established.”

These were the arguments by which one saint urged another toward translating the Greek books of the Septuagint, while setting aside the sources of the Hebrew books, because access to Hebrew testimonies for verification was difficult or entirely unavailable to Latin readers. But Augustine soon recognized the usefulness of a Hebrew translation after receiving Jerome’s response to the difficulties that had been raised. Thus, although he scarcely approved its use in the churches, out of fear of disturbing the Christian multitude, he nevertheless admits that in many places the version of the Scriptures from Hebrew is more useful and more excellent than the one first published from the Greek books:

“Concerning your translation,” he says to Jerome in Letter 82, “you have now convinced me of the usefulness with which you wished to translate the Scriptures from the Hebrews: namely, so that you might bring into the open what had been omitted or corrupted by the Jews. . . . I therefore desire your interpretation of the Septuagint, so that we may be freed, as far as possible, both from the incompetence of so many Latin interpreters—whatever their quality—who have ventured upon this task, and so that those who think I begrudge your useful labors may finally understand, if possible, why I do not wish your translation from Hebrew to be read in the churches: namely, lest, by introducing something new against the authority of the Septuagint, we disturb with great scandal the peoples of Christ, whose ears and hearts have become accustomed to hearing that translation, which was also approved by the apostles.”

Jerome himself held the same view. In his letter to Sunnia and Fretela he is found agreeing with Augustine’s words already quoted, when he says:

“From this it is clear that the psalm must be sung as we have interpreted it. Nevertheless, one must know what the Hebrew truth contains. For what the Septuagint translated must, because of its antiquity, be sung in the churches; but the other must be known by the learned for the sake of knowledge of the Scriptures.”

And in the preface to Sophronius on the Hebrew Psalter he says:

“Nor do I say this because I am attacking my predecessors, or because I think anything should be taken away from them, to whom I once gave a translation most carefully corrected for the people of my language; but because it is one thing to read the psalms in the churches of those who believe in Christ, and another to answer Jews who calumniate every individual word.”

Jerome therefore rightly agreed with Augustine that the translation of the Seventy Elders was to be read and sung in the churches of Christ because of its ancient usage, by which the faith of the nascent Church had been strengthened. They knew, however, that the Hebrew translation was superior for understanding the Scriptures. Thus Augustine, replying to Audax in Letter 261, calls it more perfect:

“I do not possess the Psalter translated from Hebrew by Saint Jerome. We, however, did not translate it, but corrected certain corruptions in the Latin books from Greek copies. Hence perhaps we made it somewhat more serviceable than it was, though not such as it ought to have been. For even now, if anything we then overlooked disturbs readers, we correct it by comparing the books. Thus we too, together with you, are seeking that which is perfect.”

He confesses this still more clearly in Book IV, chapter 7, number 15, of *On Christian Doctrine*, where, speaking of the excellence of Jerome’s interpretation, he is found saying:

“Not according to the Septuagint Interpreters, who themselves also interpreted by the divine Spirit, and for that reason seem to have expressed certain things differently, so that the reader’s attention might be more strongly urged to search out the spiritual meaning—for some of their expressions are also more obscure because they are more figurative—but as they were translated from Hebrew into Latin speech by the presbyter Jerome, a man skilled in both languages.”

You see that, according to Augustine’s testimony, the version of the Septuagint Interpreters is more obscure, whereas the one published for us by Jerome, which we call Hebrew because it derives from the Hebrew source, is clearer and better suited to understanding. If you now examine Augustine’s books of *Questions on the Heptateuch*, you will encounter some six hundred passages in which he prefers the version from Hebrew to the Septuagint Interpreters, either because it possesses greater clarity or because of the purer text of Scripture, which the Septuagint had interpolated with numerous additions.

For example, in Question 19 on Judges, after he had cited many things from the LXX translation concerning Pharaoh that are manifestly recognizable as interpolated, he attempted to resolve the difficulty as follows:

“What we must understand to have been said concerning Pharaoh the king, when this history is believed to have been written at the time when those events were still recent. What important thing could have been chosen to be spoken prophetically when past events were being narrated, while greater and especially necessary future events were left unmentioned? We should therefore rather suppose that the Septuagint Interpreters, who are said to have interpreted with prophetic authority through that marvelous agreement itself, added these things—not as announcing what was still future, but because they themselves lived at the time when they remembered that these things had happened and had read them in the books of Kings. For the event took place in the time of the Kings. This seemed more credible to us because we examined the interpretation that is from Hebrew and did not find it there, just as we did not find there what was said concerning Jericho, and so forth.”

Thus it is evident that the Septuagint inserted this material because they knew that it had happened. He prudently excuses such insertions and disturbances of the sacred text in the Septuagint, but frankly admits that they added many things which they had seen fulfilled in their own time, even though they were not found to have been written by the hagiographical authors. Accordingly, whenever he resolves whatever questions are proposed to him from the canonical books, he everywhere brings forward Jerome’s interpretation, which is from Hebrew, as a witness. Thus you will often hear him arguing in this way:

“Yet this question is not resolved by any Hebrew truth”; and again, in Question 152 on Genesis:

“All of whom are counted as sixty-six persons, with whom Jacob is said, according to the Hebrew truth, to have entered Egypt.”

With Jerome, he calls the Latin translation arranged according to the books of the Hebrews the “Hebrew truth.” Augustine followed this translation with such fidelity in his *Speculum* that he inserted nothing whatsoever into it except the very words that are read in the Latin interpretation of the Old Testament published by Jerome according to the Hebrew truth.

On this matter Dom Thomas Blampin should be heard—we gratefully acknowledge to him the new edition of the works of Saint Augustine. In his preliminary notice to the reader of the *Speculum*, he says:

“Moreover, when the holy Doctor prepared this pious work for the use of the common people, he wished it to contain only precepts that were easier to understand. We therefore also believe that for this reason he used a version not from the Greek LXX, which he ordinarily followed, but from Hebrew, since he had finally discovered that this was clearer in many places. For he praises it by this name several times in his later books of *Questions on the Heptateuch*, and so forth.”

Who now, if contentious and raising his eyebrows, will deny that Saint Jerome’s Hebrew translation was praised by Augustine and finally preferred to the Septuagint Interpreters? But concerning the use of Jerome’s version among the Africans, and concerning Augustine’s *Speculum*, we shall speak again later and add nothing more here.

**V.** “It is difficult,” says Jerome, “for an old man to change his language, and to lead a world already grown gray back to the beginnings of childhood. For what learned or unlearned person, when he has taken a volume of Scripture into his hands and sees that what he reads differs from the saliva with which he once imbibed it, will not immediately burst out, crying that the new translator is a falsifier and sacrilegious man, who dares to remove, add, change, or correct anything in the ancient books?”

Jerome therefore took care to guard himself against this hostility in the new Latin edition of the sacred Scriptures. And, so as not to depart too far from the customary Latin reading, he moderated his pen in such a way that, after correcting only those things that seemed to alter the meaning, he often allowed the rest to remain as it had been before.

He himself declares this in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, when he begins to speak of the ancient Latin translator:

“But it must be known,” he says, “that wherever the Greek has written *glorificate*, the Latin translator rendered it *magnificate*, in accordance with what is said in Exodus: ‘Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified.’ In Greek, instead, it is written, ‘He has been glorified’; but if this is translated into Latin speech, the rendering becomes inelegant. And when we formerly corrected the Psalter, wherever the meaning was the same, we did not wish to alter the custom of the ancient translators, lest excessive novelty frighten away the reader’s zeal.”

A little farther on he repeats the same point concerning the word *honorificabit*, or *glorificabit*:

“We therefore did not wish to change what was read by the ancients, because the meaning was the same. . . . But here too there is no change of meaning; and, following the ancient interpretation, we did not wish to change what did no harm.”

When explaining the more difficult and obscure passages of Ecclesiastes in the manner of a brief commentary, he was likewise anxious to avoid the hostility caused by excessive novelty. Thus, in the prologue to that same Commentary, he says:

“I briefly give this warning: I have followed the authority of no one; but, in translating from Hebrew, I have adapted myself more closely to the custom of the Septuagint Interpreters, only in those matters that did not differ greatly from the Hebrew. At times I have also recalled Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, so that I might neither frighten away the reader’s zeal through excessive novelty nor, again, against my conscience, abandon the source of truth and pursue the little streams of opinions.”

In the preface to the book of Job, however, translated from Hebrew into Latin speech, he asserts that he followed none of the ancient translators:

“This translation,” he says, “follows none of the ancients, but will sometimes reproduce words, sometimes sense, and sometimes both together, from the Hebrew and Arabic speech, and at times from the Syriac.”

Whoever wishes to compare Jerome’s Hebrew translation of Job with the one he himself published according to the Greek books will find them so different from one another that he will often be forced to ask himself whether the narrative of Scripture is the same in both copies, or whether there is one and the same account of sacred history.

In the book of Psalms, although many things are different, nevertheless very many passages are found borrowed from the ancient Latin translator—that is, left unchanged in Jerome’s Hebrew Psalter. The attentive reader will recognize that the same practice was observed in the other books, both of the Law and of the prophets, if he wishes to compare the surviving portions of the ancient Latin, or Italic, version with Jerome’s new translation.

A collection of such readings is supplied by the compilation of the sacred Scriptural canticles which the learned Carus published at the end of Jerome’s Psalter from the new and old Latin editions. This distinguished man had, a few years ago at Rome, diligently searched out and arranged for printing many monuments of sacred antiquity.

Jerome therefore adapted himself to the custom of the ancient translators, while nevertheless not abandoning the source of truth in pursuit of the streams. That is, wherever there was no loss of meaning or understanding, he readily followed the ancient Latin translation, lest the reader’s zeal be continually frightened away by novelty of wording.

Moreover, he always avoided inelegant renderings of the Scriptures, and in this respect he did not agree very well with Augustine. Saint Augustine wished solecisms, barbarisms, and the other defects of Latin expression to be disregarded when they detracted nothing from sound understanding. For this reason, in Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, he preferred the reading, with its barbarism, “My bone is not hidden from you” (*ossum meum*), to “my bone” (*os meum*), which is more open but more Latin.

Saint Jerome, by contrast, warns that such obvious defects of expression must be avoided where the Scripture has one meaning. “We follow this principle,” he says in Letter 135, “that wherever there is no change of meaning, we preserve the elegance of Latin speech.”

A little later he repeats:

“The same rule of interpretation must therefore be followed, which we have often stated: wherever there is no loss of meaning, the *euphōnia* (εὐφωνία, pleasantness of sound) and propriety of the language into which we translate must be preserved.”

What rule of interpretation he teaches here must be followed, he demonstrated fully at the beginning of the same letter, saying:

“And it must be known that if we wish to say, ‘Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?’ . . . we shall destroy the *euphōnia*; and while pursuing the *kakozēlia* (κακοζηλία, affected literalism) of interpretation, we shall lose all the beauty of the translation.”

He also shows that the rule of a good translator is to express the *idiōmata* (ἰδιώματα, idioms) of another language through the propriety of his own language. We prove that Cicero did this in Plato’s *Protagoras*, in Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*, and in Demosthenes’ speech against Aeschines, as did Plautus, Terence, and Caecilius, highly learned men, in translating Greek comedies.

Nor should anyone therefore think the Latin language extremely narrow because it cannot translate word for word, since the Greeks themselves render many of our expressions by circumlocution, and rely on the properties of their own language—not on the literal fidelity of interpretation—to express Hebrew words.

Finally, repeating the same point in Letter 101, to Pammachius, he calls translations excessively bound to the words dull and *kakozēloi* (κακοζήλοι, affectedly literal):

“Horace, an acute and learned man, gave the same instruction to the educated translator in the *Art of Poetry*: ‘You will not strive, as a faithful interpreter, to render word for word.’ Terence translated Menander, and Plautus and Caecilius the ancient comic poets. Do they cling to the words, rather than preserve beauty and elegance in translation? What you call the truth of interpretation, the learned call *kakozēlia*.”

In the same place he praises Saint Hilary, who translated many homilies on Job and treatises on the Psalms from Greek into Latin:

“He did not sit down before the drowsy letter, nor twist himself into the dull rusticity of translation; rather, as though they were captives, he transferred the meanings into his own language by the right of a conqueror.”

But he rejects Aquila, a proselyte and contentious translator, who attempted to translate not only the words but also their etymologies. Jerome exposes the faults and *kakozēlia* of his interpretation through several examples, refusing to tolerate that importunate diligence by which the Jewish translator thought that he ought not to weigh the words for the reader but to count them.

Nor should anyone be led by this to believe that Jerome despised every care and precision concerning the words of translators, or that he thought they contributed nothing toward expressing the native meanings of authors. Saint Jerome chiefly censures those whom he knew to pervert the actual sense through excessive devotion to the words.

“We must not,” he says to Sunnia and Fretela, “express word for word in such a way that, while following a syllable, we lose the understanding.”

Then, in the already mentioned Letter 101 to Pammachius:

“Let others hunt for syllables and letters; you seek the meanings.”

Saint Jerome attacks only this servile manner of translating. He did not wish to condemn those who render word for word, but those who translate violently, abandoning the author’s meaning. All learned men, and the supreme pontiffs in their letters, plainly reject this fault of interpretation together with Jerome.

For Gregory the Great says very well in Book VIII, Letter 42:

“We further report that here we suffer serious difficulty from translators. For since there are none who express sense from sense, but they always wish to transfer the exact form, they confuse the entire meaning of what has been said. Consequently, what has been translated can in no way be understood except with great labor.”

Pope Nicholas likewise says in his letter to the emperor Michael:

“If you call the Latin language barbarous because, when changed by translators into Greek diction, it produces barbarisms, the fault belongs not to the Latin language but, as I think, to the translators, who, when necessity demands it, do not attempt to render sense from sense but violently produce word from word.”

Jerome was so attentive and conscientious in expressing the meanings of divine Scripture that he very often released himself from the rules that I have mentioned. Thus, in Book XII of his Commentary on chapter 40 of Ezekiel, he warned us that he had not avoided every fault of expression, although he knew them well:

“It is sufficient to have warned once that I know *cubitus* and *cubita* to be used in the neuter gender; but, for simplicity, ease of understanding, and common usage, I use them in the masculine gender. For it is not our concern to avoid defects of expression, but to explain the obscurity of Holy Scripture by whatever words may serve.”

He also calls the arrangement of words and the flowers of speech “pods” in Letter 146 to Pope Damasus:

“I do not doubt that our speech may seem uncultivated to you, considering the smallness of our ability; but I have often complained that expression cannot be polished unless the writer’s own hand has smoothed it. Therefore forgive my suffering eyes—that is, forgive my dictation—especially since in ecclesiastical matters words are not sought but meanings: life must be sustained by bread, not pods.”

Finally, when encouraging Paulinus in Letter 103 to devote himself to the study of divine literature, he did not wish the eloquent man to be offended by the simplicity of the Scriptures’ style:

“I do not want you to be offended in the Holy Scriptures by the simplicity and, as it were, poverty of their words. This has arisen either from the fault of translators or by deliberate design, so that they might more easily instruct a rustic congregation, and so that one and the same meaning might be heard differently by the learned and the unlearned.”

From these remarks, if I am not mistaken, it is clear that Jerome preserved the elegance and beauty of Latin speech in his translations wherever there was no change of meaning. Yet he did not prohibit every defect of expression when, for ease of understanding and in accordance with common usage, something uncultivated had to be retained.

He therefore attacks the fastidious severity of incompetent translators and their faulty adherence to the words, calling it *kakozēlia* in many places. But he often imitated a simple style because he wished the simple hearts of the faithful to be taught in the sacred Scriptures, not the ears of the curious to be entertained. But enough on this subject.

## PROLEGOMENON II. On the Date of Jerome’s Translations and Their Use in the Church

[Col. 0047]

Jerome published his versions at different times and without following the order of the sacred books. II. Among the Greeks and Latins they immediately began to be read. III. Contemporary writers made use of Jerome’s translations. IV. In the time of Gregory the Great, the Roman Church used both the new edition from Hebrew and the ancient edition from Greek. V. The churches of Gaul especially preferred Jerome’s versions to the others. VI. The Catholic Church declared Jerome’s Latin version authentic by public decree and decreed that it should be used for its own purposes.

[Col. 0049A] I. No learned person is unaware that the Latin translations of the sacred books were composed by Jerome at different times and in something like a haphazard order. For he did not interpret the books of Scripture rashly or on his own initiative, but as he was asked by friends or commanded by holy bishops.

There were those who urged the holy Doctor to undertake a translation of the prophets before he had rendered the books of the Pentateuch into Latin. There were also those who arranged for the volumes of Samuel and Malachim—that is, the four books of Kings—to be translated into Latin before any other interpretations of Holy Scripture. Hence it came about that Jerome translated everything into Roman speech indiscriminately, without preserving the sequence of the sacred canon.

As for his translation according to the Septuagint Interpreters, it must be known that he first corrected the Psalter while he was stationed at Rome in the time of Pope Damasus. Much later, during his retreat at Bethlehem, after Paula and Eustochium had warned him that the ancient error was stronger than the new correction, he undertook, in a second revision, to eradicate the thorns that were growing again from that same Psalter.

In this later revision he also added obeli and asterisks, by which the reader was alerted that the Septuagint sometimes had more and sometimes less than the Hebrew text.

We believe that the first correction of the Psalms was undertaken around the year 382 or 383 after Christ. At that time knowledge of the divine Scriptures was highly esteemed by everyone at Rome, and, since Jerome was accustomed to converse familiarly with the holy pontiff Damasus, he could easily have been asked by him to purge the Psalter of its errors. Although he made the correction hastily, he nevertheless corrected it to a considerable extent.

Later, while living out his days at Bethlehem, some years after the death of Saint Damasus, he undertook a second and more careful revision of the Psalter. This could not have occurred before the year 384 after Christ. We shall briefly demonstrate this from Letter 99, written to Asella at the Roman port.

The holy Doctor lived with the Romans for nearly three years, frequently explaining the divine books to some of them as he was able. He left them to return to Jerusalem after the death of Pope Saint Damasus. Since that death occurred in October of the year 384, while Jerome departed from Rome in August, as he himself testifies in Book III of his *Apology against Rufinus*, it follows that the later revision of the Psalter was undertaken not only after the year 384 and the death of Saint Damasus, but also after several years had elapsed from the time when he safely boarded ship at the Roman port with the presbyter Saint Vincent, his young brother, and other monks, who are said later to have remained at Jerusalem.

For at the beginning of his preface to this later correction of the Psalms from the LXX, recalling the earlier revision, he says that he had completed it long before:

“I corrected the Psalter long ago while I was stationed at Rome,” and so forth.

The word “long ago” is used both of a short period and of a distant one. If we understand it of a distant period, anyone who returns to the date of the first revision and fixes upon the year 383 after Christ—the year in which it is probable that Jerome first corrected the Psalter at Rome—will readily suppose that the work was completed six or eight years later.

For the first correction of the Latin Psalms, which is said to have been carried out hastily by the holy Doctor, the year 383 or 384 after Christ should therefore be assigned. For the second, which contained asterisks (+) and obeli (÷), the year 389 or 390 may be assigned.

Certainly this later correction cannot have been delayed beyond the year 390, because Jerome completed his Latin translation of the Hebrew Psalter in the year 390 or 391. The version, or correction, derived from the Greek books always preceded the other, which we call Hebrew because it arose from the Hebrew truth.

I would therefore have the reader know that the chronological notes we have placed at the beginning of each correction of the Psalter, both the Roman and the Gallican, indicate nothing more than an indefinite period. For when we say that the Roman Psalter was corrected by Jerome around the year 382 after Christ, this must be understood to mean that such a correction was not undertaken before that year, since Jerome came to Rome with the holy bishops Paulinus and Epiphanius toward the end of that same year 382.

The same must be concluded concerning the later correction: it could not have been prepared before the year 384, that is, after the death of Pope Saint Damasus, when the holy man Jerome had returned to Jerusalem and hastened back to his Bethlehem retreat. Whether it was completed sooner or later after Jerome’s return must be judged by those who perhaps do not approve the conjectures we have offered above.

In any event, Jerome says the following about this Psalter corrected by himself at the end of Book II of his *Apology against Rufinus*:

“The Psalter also, which, certainly most carefully corrected according to the Septuagint Interpreters by our labor, Rome received long ago, I fortified with a preface when I translated it again according to the Hebrew,” and so forth.

For more, see our notice concerning both Psalters of Jerome, the one now called Roman and the one called Gallican.

Saint Jerome also gave other books of Holy Scripture to the Latin language according to the Septuagint interpretation, distinguishing them with obeli and asterisks. Whether he translated every individual volume of the Old Testament in this manner into Latin, or rather corrected it from Origen’s Hexapla, remains somewhat uncertain.

The evidence most strongly favoring this view consists in what is read in many places in his writings, where the distinguished Doctor himself seems to affirm this generally concerning all the books of the LXX version. For in Book II of his *Apology against Rufinus*, defending himself against Rufinus’ criticism and accusations, he says:

“Have I spoken against the Septuagint Interpreters, whom many years ago I gave to the students of my language, most carefully corrected; whose exposition I give daily in the gathering of the brethren, and whose Psalms I sing in continual meditation?” and so forth.

We read the same in the preface to the books of Chronicles. In Letter 28 to Lucinius he likewise writes concerning the Septuagint Interpreters rendered into Latin:

“I do not doubt that you possess the edition of the Septuagint Interpreters, which many years ago I gave to students, most carefully corrected.”

Here he says only that he had delivered a corrected edition to the Latins. But in Letter 135 to Sunnia and Fretela he calls it a version:

“Now this *koinē* (Κοινή), that is, the common edition, is the one that is also called the Septuagint. But this is the difference between them: the *koinē*, according to places and times and the will of the scribes, is an old and corrupted edition. The edition found in the *Hexapla* (ἑξαπλοῖ), however, and which we translate, is the very translation of the Septuagint Interpreters preserved incorrupt and immaculate in the books of the learned.”

But again, in Book III of his *Apology against Rufinus*, he is heard using the term “correction”:

“I was not permitted, after the Septuagint edition, which many years ago I gave to the people of my language most carefully corrected,” and so forth.

These and other passages may be used to prove from Jerome himself that all the volumes of the Greek edition were translated or corrected by him into Latin according to the truth of the Hexapla.

Against this view, however, stand numerous and very powerful arguments. The first is drawn from the silence of Saint Jerome, who, leaving everything else aside, mentions only six books corrected according to the Septuagint with the greatest care—for he had already lost the remaining books through the fraud of someone—and refers to them in his controversy with Rufinus and in several prefaces to his edition from Hebrew.

The six volumes specifically listed by him are the book of Job, the book of Psalms, the three books of Solomon—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs—and the book of Chronicles. Apart from these, as far as I know, he says in no preface that he delivered any other book of Holy Scripture to the Latins corrected according to the LXX with obeli and asterisks.

Furthermore, this seems plainly demonstrated by the only four brief prefaces that survive for the books mentioned above. The collection of all the prefaces of Blessed Jerome, which we possess separately in certain very ancient monuments and in the body of both printed and manuscript Bibles, retains only four sets of paired prologues for the sacred volumes: for the books of Job, David, Solomon, and Chronicles.

The rest had perished during Jerome’s lifetime, or at least remained unknown to him. Why would scribes omit the remaining prefaces of Jerome if they had been published together with books translated or corrected according to the LXX? No other reason can be assigned than the one that leads us to believe that only four were found among the papers of the holy Doctor.

Cassiodorus alone, above all others, mentions them all. Third, the ancient writers whom I have read down to the present day do not remember other books published by Jerome according to the LXX. Indeed, Saint Augustine, admiring Jerome’s diligence in producing an edition of the book of Job according to the same LXX—for Augustine did not know that Jerome had already completed this labor—urges him to interpret for the Latin Church the Greek canonical Scriptures attributed to the authority of the Septuagint Interpreters:

“By this,” he says, “you will render the greatest service if you restore to Latin truth that Greek Scripture which the Septuagint produced. It is so varied in different copies that it can scarcely be tolerated, and so suspect that one fears something different may be found in the Greek, so that one hesitates to bring anything forward or prove anything from it.”

Augustine wrote this in Letter 71 when the year 403 after Christ was already drawing to a close. From this we may infer, by no implausible conjecture, that only certain books of the Greek Scripture, or of the Septuagint Interpreters, were translated into Latin and restored to the Greek text by Jerome.

Yet, after examining more carefully the letters exchanged between Augustine and Jerome, we have determined that Jerome delivered to the Latins all the volumes of the Old Testament Scriptures, corrected according to the authority of the Hexapla, even though very few of them reached posterity because of the fraud of some scoundrel or other injuries inflicted by time.

In the year 404 after Christ, Jerome informed Augustine that he had translated old copies of the Septuagint Interpreters’ edition, corrected from Greek into the language of his people. Augustine therefore requested that this translation of Jerome’s—or correction of the Septuagint edition—be sent to him in the following year:

“Then, I beg you,” he says in Letter 82, “send us your interpretation of the Septuagint, which I did not know you had published,” and so forth.

To this Jerome replies in Letter 94, cited by Augustine as Letter 172:

“We suffer in this province from a great shortage of notaries capable of writing Latin; and for this reason we cannot obey your instructions, especially in the edition of the Septuagint, which is distinguished by asterisks and spits. For we have lost most of our earlier labor through the fraud of someone.”

Saint Jerome wrote this only a few years before his death, namely at the beginning of the year 416. It is therefore easy to believe that he did not restore those volumes which fraud had stolen from him in the Septuagint edition.

If matters stood thus, it is not surprising that, from so many volumes translated from Greek into Latin speech, only six have survived for us. In any event, an edition of books of this kind, with asterisks and obeli, must have been completed within five years, from the end of the year 385 after Christ to the beginning of the year 390 or 391. For in the year 391 Jerome completed his later translation of Job and Solomon, as will be stated below.

In an equally disorderly and confused sequence, as we noted earlier, he began to translate the Canon of Hebrew truth into Latin and, with Christ’s help, completed it. He did not proceed from the first book to the last in the order in which they are read there; rather, he translated the books of the Hebrews into Latin speech as he was able and as he was requested.

First, he addressed the volumes of Samuel and Malachim to the most industrious Paula and her daughter Eustochium. Second, he entrusted all the prophets, major and minor—sixteen in number—to the same women. Third, around the same time, he gave the Psalter translated from Hebrew to Sophronius, who had requested that it be rendered into Greek. Fourth, at the request of the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus, he translated the books of Solomon from the Hebrew truth into Latin. Fifth, returning to the beginning of the Canon, he interpreted the book of Genesis and the remaining books of the Pentateuch at the earnest request of his Desiderius.

Finally, he could not refuse Eustochium, the virgin, the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, and Esther, nor could he refuse Chromatius the books of Chronicles. But so that the time assigned to each volume, as far as we are able to know it, might be established, we have taken care to indicate it with the following chronological notes and markers.

Before the other books of the Hebrew Canon, therefore, he first published in Latin the books of Samuel and Malachim, which today we call the four Books of Kings. This will immediately be clear to the diligent reader who wishes to read through the preface placed at the beginning of this edition. For this prologue to the Books of Kings is called the “helmeted beginning” (*Principium galeatum*), a title that could apply to all the books that Jerome translated from Hebrew into Latin:

> This prologue to the Scriptures, he says, like a helmeted beginning, can apply to all the books that we have translated from Hebrew into Latin.

He calls it a “helmeted beginning” because it defended the head of his translations against his critics; or because it was prefixed to his earlier translation from Hebrew and placed before the Scriptures translated by him as a general prologue. The following words of that same prologue plainly declare this:

> Read, therefore, first my Samuel and Malachim—I say, *my* books. For whatever, through more frequent translating and correcting, we have learned and hold more carefully is ours.

He wished the Books of Kings to be read first because he had translated them from Hebrew into Latin before the others; otherwise he would have said so differently if any other translations of the Old Testament had preceded them.

Copies of this earlier translation were found at Rome in the possession of Domnio before [Col. 0053D] the year of Christ 393, when Letter 52 to Pammachius is said to have been written. There Jerome expressly affirmed this:

> I had sent, he says, certain portions of the commentaries on the twelve prophets to the holy Father Domnio, and also Samuel and Malachim, that is, the four Books of Kings, etc.

And, so that we do not wander too far afield, it will not be out of place briefly to cite what we read in that letter concerning Job and the sixteen prophets. Concerning Job, the same Letter to Pammachius says:

> I recently translated Job into our language; you will be able to borrow a copy from your cousin, the holy Marcella. Read it in Greek and Latin, and compare the old edition with our translation; you will clearly see how great the difference is between truth and falsehood.

[Col. 0054A] He had previously mentioned the books of the prophets in these words:

> If you read the sixteen books of the prophets, which I translated into Latin from the Hebrew language, and I discover that you take pleasure in this work, you will urge us not to keep the other books, still closed in the cabinet, any longer.

At that time, besides the translations already mentioned, he kept locked away in his cabinet the translation of the Psalms dedicated to Sophronius and the Books of Solomon, which we said he had dedicated to Chromatius and Heliodorus. The remaining books of the Old Testament had not yet been translated into Latin from Hebrew, although he himself wrote in the year of Christ 392, when he composed his catalogue *On Illustrious Men*, that he had translated the Old Testament according to the Hebrew text.

If someone has thought that this statement should be understood of each individual book, he must necessarily be far from the truth, because from the letter to Lucinius [Col. 0054B] and from the preface to the Book of Joshua we know that the translation of the Pentateuch and of three other books, which he mentions in that same prologue, had not been completed before the death of Saint Paula the mother—that is, before the year of Christ 404.

The Book of Ezra, likewise, is said in its preface to have been published some time after copies of the prophets. Jerome delayed this translation, for the distinguished Domnio and Rogatianus had requested it by writing and writing again for three continuous years.

The Books of Samuel and Malachim are therefore immediately followed by the translation of Job; Job is followed by the translation of the sixteen prophets. Next come the Psalter and the Books of Solomon. Jerome had translated all these books of Scripture from Hebrew into Latin by the year of Christ 392, when he published [Col. 0054C] his book *On Illustrious Men*.

At the same time Sophronius, his associate, translated some of these works from Latin into Greek. Sophronius, a man of outstanding learning, says the holy Doctor in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, “translated my minor works into Greek in elegant language, as well as the Psalter and the prophets whom we translated from Hebrew into Latin.”

These, then, are the works that, up to the fourteenth year of the reign of the emperor Theodosius and the year of Christ 392, had been translated from Hebrew into Latin and from Latin into Greek by Jerome and Sophronius.

From the year 392 to the year of Christ 394, the Book of Ezra and the Book of Genesis appear to have been published. He gave Ezra a Latin form shortly after the publication of the books of the prophets, as the preface addressed to Domnio and Rogatianus testifies. [Col. 0054D] He clearly gave the Book of Genesis to Desiderius after the fourteenth year of the reign of the emperor Theodosius, as is evident from Letter 154, provided that we agree that this is the same Desiderius whom he congratulates on account of the prophetic significance of his name both in that letter and in the preface to Genesis.

Moreover, he translated Genesis from Hebrew before he had published his book *On the Best Kind of Translation*, in which he collected many passages from the Old Testament that are not found in the Septuagint. Finally, many statements repeated from, or at least similar to, Jerome’s minor works are found in Letters 154 and 52, the latter of which, as we have said, was written to Pammachius in the year of Christ 393.

Distracted by various occupations, he could not complete the other four books of the Pentateuch before the year of Christ [Col. 0055A] 404 or 405. He himself taught us this in the preface to Joshua, saying:

> At last, having finished the Pentateuch of Moses, as though released from a great debt, we extend our hand to Jesus the son of Nave.

And below:

> Moreover, after the repose of the holy Paula, whose life is an example of virtue, we resolved to publish these books as well, which I could not deny to the virgin Eustochium, etc.

Jerome wrote this after the death of Saint Paula. It is therefore clear that the translation of the whole Pentateuch was not completed until after the year of Christ 404, because this holy widow departed this life on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the sixth time and Aristaenetus—that is, on 26 January of the year 404.

Jerome was so harassed and exhausted by grief and mourning that, apart from translating the Paschal Book published by Theophilus, he was unable to write anything else of divine literature for a long period. From this it is made fairly clear that the translation of the Octateuch, which he mentions in Letter 28 to Lucinius, was completed at the end of the year of Christ 404 or during the year 405.

Finally, he published the Book of Chronicles according to the Hebrew text in the year of Christ 396. An earlier date cannot be assigned to this translation, because in the preface it is said that the completed version followed Letter 10, *On the Best Kind of Translation*:

> I recently wrote, says Jerome, a book on the best kind of translation, showing that the words from the Gospel, “Out of Egypt I called my son,” etc.

The book addressed to Pammachius on the best kind of interpretation is there said to have been published approximately twenty years after he had translated the *Chronicle* of Eusebius of Caesarea into Latin. Having properly weighed these matters, [Col. 0055C] we have agreed with more learned men that Letter 101 was written in the year 396, and that, after only a short interval—which is sufficiently expressed by the adverb “recently”—the Book of Chronicles was translated from Hebrew.

We could prolong the reader’s stay among these chronological notes, were we not convinced that many such points of time could scarcely, or not at all, be fixed with certainty; and even if we were to discover them through great study and labor, we have recognized that they would be of little practical benefit. Let what we have therefore touched upon briefly be sufficient for the curious reader.

## II

We affirmed, as the second point, that Jerome’s edition of the Scriptures immediately began to be read among Greeks and Latins. And rightly so, since both translations of the same holy Doctor—the earlier one published from the Greek copies of the Septuagint and the later one prepared from the Hebrew source—were regarded as the most complete of all Latin versions.

Writing to Jerome about the translation derived from the Seventy Interpreters, Augustine says in Letter 82 that he desires it so that he may discard the other Latin translations and be free from the incompetence of so many other translators:

> For this reason, he says, I desire your translation from the Septuagint, so that, as far as we can, we may also escape the incompetence of so many Latin translators, whoever they may have been who ventured upon the task.

Sophronius, likewise a man of outstanding learning among the Greeks, and equally dissatisfied with the Greek translations, earnestly requested a new Latin edition from Jerome. [Col. 0056A] Jerome recalls this in the preface to the Hebrew Psalter—that is, to the Psalter rendered into Latin from Hebrew:

> You earnestly requested that, following Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, I translate a new edition into the Latin language. For you said that you were more confused by the variety of translators and that, because of the love with which you cling to me, you would be satisfied either with my translation or with my judgment.

Since more learned men, both among the Greeks and among the Latins, rejected the translations of the many interpreters and were greatly confused by their variety and incompetence, it naturally followed that they sought Jerome’s versions, which everyone knew to be free from similar faults.

For this reason Jerome congratulates himself in Book II of his *Apology against Rufinus* that the Roman Church had accepted his Psalter, most carefully corrected according to the Septuagint Interpreters. And in the preface to the Book of Chronicles—which, urged by the prayers of the celebrated Domnio and Rogatianus, he rendered into Latin—he does not doubt that his translation would please those who welcomed it and would be worn smooth by continual reading at Rome, especially among those who at that time were the lights of the Christian Senate.

How familiar Jerome’s Latin translation according to the Septuagint Interpreters was in the African Church is sufficiently established from Augustine’s book of *Annotations on Job*. In that volume Augustine follows none of the ancient interpreters, but derives the whole work from the translation published by Jerome, with obeli and asterisks added.

I shall scarcely ever be persuaded that the highly learned author of the book *On Famous Interpreters* was correct in saying that Jerome’s earlier edition, derived from the translation of the Seventy Elders, was translated again from Latin into Greek and eagerly received by the Greeks. Why would it have been necessary to translate into Greek once more what was contained in the Hexapla, taking it from Jerome’s Latin, and to repeat an already completed task in an edition of the Scriptures?

What Jerome says, therefore, in Book II *Against Rufinus* about his edition having been received among the Greeks must without doubt be understood of the later translation, which was called Hebrew:

> Hence, I thought I was doing a service to my Latins and encouraging the minds of our people to learn, because the Greeks too did not disdain a translation from Latin after so many translators; for this I am brought under accusation, and I force food upon a nauseated stomach.

Sophronius, Jerome’s close associate, as is widely known, rendered into Greek the Psalter that Jerome had translated from the Hebrew truth, as well as all sixteen prophets. The Greeks eagerly received this edition, not disdaining to borrow something from Latin men.

This is what Jerome wished to teach us—not only in the testimony from the already mentioned *Apology against Rufinus*, but also in the preface to Ezra, where, commending the zeal and goodwill of the Greeks, he complains in the following manner of the insults of his detractors among the Latins and of the charge that they were ungrateful toward him:

> It is another matter if, as they say, with their eyes closed, they wish to curse me, and do not imitate the zeal and goodwill of the Greeks, who, after the Seventy Translators, when the Gospel of Christ was already shining forth, carefully read the Jews and Hebionites, the interpreters of the ancient Law—namely, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—and through Origen’s labor dedicated them to the Churches in the *Hexapla*.

How much more grateful the Latins ought to be, when they see Greece rejoicing that it has borrowed something from them! Greece could not have rejoiced at borrowing from the Latins, after so many translators, unless it had received Jerome’s translation from Hebrew into Latin, which Sophronius rendered into Greek in accordance with the promise by which he was bound to Jerome, as the preface to the Book of Psalms itself confirms.

Jerome’s translations derived from the Hebrew were received and used among the Latins with still greater enthusiasm. For they were celebrated in the daily practice of all the Churches, as is testified by Rufinus’s consuming envy. Because of his hatred for the author, Rufinus not only rejected them, but even wished to claim that crimes and sacrileges had been committed in the new edition of the holy Doctor. The notoriously criminal orator himself says in Book II of his invective against Jerome:

> But those books that you are now translating and sending throughout churches and monasteries, through towns and villages—how shall we receive them? As divine or as human? And what shall we do when you assert that the books bearing the names of the prophets or legislators are more truthful as translated by you than those that the Apostles approved? Tell me how this offense is to be corrected—or rather, how is this impiety to be expiated? For if, in explaining the Law, to have understood something differently is considered blameworthy by you, how often must it be judged blameworthy to pervert the Law itself into something other than what the Apostles handed down?

Thus Jerome’s translations were carried in every direction, sent through churches and monasteries, towns and villages. Copies of them were found at Rome both among the most learned men and among those most celebrated in the city for the reputation of their holiness.

Pammachius, a man of the highest rank, whose zeal for sacred literature Jerome once preferred even to his own, possessed the sixteen books of the prophets. Saint Marcella had a copy of the Book of Job. The holy Father Domnio handled daily the books of Samuel and Malachim translated into Latin from Hebrew, as is abundantly attested in Letter 52 written to Pammachius.

That the same practice was approved among Latin bishops, especially in Italy, can be shown by certain brief prefaces to the Old Testament; several of Augustine’s letters and minor works plainly demonstrate it as well.

Augustine relates in Letter 71—Letter 88 in Jerome’s collection—how a bishop of a certain African Church had arranged for Jerome’s new translation of the prophets to be read in the Church over which he presided. He tells the story as follows:

> A certain brother of ours, a bishop, when he had begun to have your translation read in the Church over which he presides, caused a disturbance over something rendered by you quite differently in the prophet Jonah from what had become fixed in everyone’s understanding and memory and had been sung through the succession of so many generations, etc.

From this passage of Augustine it is perfectly clear that certain bishops in the regions of Africa, far from being satisfied with private reading, had arranged for Jerome’s new translation to be read publicly in their Churches, and that this happened before the year of Christ 403, when Augustine’s already mentioned Letter 71 is said to have been written.

The same holy Doctor writes in Letter 261 to Audax that he did not possess the Psalter translated from Hebrew by Saint Jerome. Yet both men appear to seek it as a completed Latin edition of the Psalms, if we understand these words as referring to that same Psalter:

> Thus, what is complete, we too seek together with you.

More remains to be said below from Augustine; for this reason I shall now pass over these matters.

Jerome especially praises Lucinius of Baetica for his fervor and zeal for the Scriptures. Lucinius had all the minor works that the holy Doctor had dictated from his youth until approximately the year of Christ 394 copied for himself. Jerome’s reputation and that of his scholarly labors had spread throughout Spain. Lucinius, therefore, inflamed by an intense desire, sent six scribes to Jerome, so that they might bring him copies of the monuments of this immortal intellect.

In his reply to him, Jerome mentions his editions of Scripture in these words:

> I have given the Canon of Hebrew Truth, except for the Octateuch, which I now have in hand, to your boys and scribes to copy. I do not doubt that you also possess the edition of the Seventy Interpreters, which many years ago I carefully corrected and gave to students. I revised the New Testament according to the Greek authority. For just as the authenticity of the ancient books must be tested against the Hebrew volumes, so the authenticity of the new books requires the standard of the Greek language.

With the exception, therefore, of the Octateuch, the Churches of Spain received Jerome’s new translation from Hebrew around the year 395. It is equally reasonable to believe that his earlier edition, carefully corrected according to the authority of the *Hexapla*, had been widely circulated among the Spaniards and used by their learned men several years before Lucinius’s scribes arrived in Palestine.

The following words seem clearly to indicate this:

> I do not doubt that you possess the edition of the Seventy Interpreters, etc.

Otherwise Jerome would have sent this edition, copied along with the other minor works, to Lucinius.

## III

The arguments of the preceding chapter are confirmed again by what we have undertaken to discuss throughout the whole section of this article. For whoever among Jerome’s contemporaries employed his translations for his own purposes unquestionably supplies abundant testimony toward establishing the earlier proposition, by which we determined that Jerome’s Latin translations of sacred Scripture soon became celebrated through the reading of learned men.

Hesychius—said to have been a disciple of that great saint Gregory of Nazianzus—a presbyter of Jerusalem, should first be counted among those who quote testimonies from Scripture according to Jerome’s edition derived from the Hebrew sources.

In Book I of his *Commentary on Leviticus*, after citing, according to the Septuagint Interpreters, verse 30 of chapter 4:

> And the priest shall take and place with his finger the blood of the sin offering upon the horns of the altar of burnt offering,

he immediately added the following from the Hebrew translation: [Col. 0059A]

> What Jerome published in a similar sense, saying: “And the priest shall take some of the blood, touching the horns of the altar with his finger.”

Again, in chapter 19 of the same Leviticus, he recalls Jerome’s translation in this way:

> Therefore, when it says, “You shall not lift up the name in injustice,” it added, “and you shall not profane the name of the Lord your God.” Jerome’s translation reads: “You shall not pollute the name of your God.”
