The same Hesychius appears to have published the Book of the Twelve Minor Prophets divided into verses following the example of Saint Jerome, who, in order to serve the needs of his readers, set out his new edition from Hebrew by cola and commas, as is attested at the beginning of the preface to the prophet Isaiah.

Hesychius also mentions the usefulness and advantages of this kind of division of verses at the beginning of his own work, which we read under the following title in Volume VIII of the *Sacred Critics*:

> *The στιχηρόν* [*stichēron*] of Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem, of the twelve prophets;

that is:

> The division of the twelve prophets into verse-like units by Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem.

Those who draw the Greek term *στιχηρόν* or *στιχηδόν* out to mean division into chapters and paragraphs depart considerably from the truth. This division is very different from the one Hesychius intended and says he observed in the hagiographical writers, in the Psalter, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Job, and the Song of Songs.

These books, indeed, were written in meter and verses under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, but were not divided into chapters and paragraphs, as all the most devoted students and careful investigators of the divine Scriptures concede. Hesychius therefore wished to preserve this division of verses in the Book of the Twelve Prophets because he knew that it had been used in ancient times by holy men and hoped, with Jerome, that it would be useful to both learned and unlearned for understanding the prophetic oracles:

> For the division of the verses makes many obscure and uncertain things clear.

Thus Hesychius of Jerusalem, himself a careful writer, preserved in the Twelve Prophets the divisions into members that had been made in Jerome’s edition.

This use by Hesychius contributes no small praise to Jerome’s edition of the Scriptures. But it surpasses every commendation that material concerning it, or drawn from the same Hebrew translation, is found in Augustine’s commentaries.

Sometimes Augustine cites it with an honorable mention of its author; at other times he praises its usefulness and ease, rejecting the more obscure and intricate edition of the Septuagint Interpreters. Finally, from this Jerome’s edition he composed entire books of considerable benefit to Christian piety.

When, in Book IV, chapter 7, sections 15 and following, of *On Christian Doctrine*, he replies to poorly educated men who think that our sacred authors should be despised—not because they lack eloquence, but because they do not display the kind of eloquence these men value excessively—he proves the eloquence of the other prophets especially from the book of that prophet who says that he was a shepherd or herdsman.

He says:

> I shall not do this according to the Septuagint Interpreters, but as the words of Amos were translated from Hebrew into Latin speech by the presbyter Jerome, skilled in both languages.

In Augustine’s sound judgment, Jerome’s translation was therefore more direct and convenient for demonstrating the eloquence of the holy prophets than the other old and Vulgate version derived from the Septuagint Interpreters.

I have often marveled at the great agreement between our present edition of the prophets and the passage from Amos quoted by Augustine. There is no difference either in the wording or in the division of the commas. The three cola of the prophet Amos are set out in this way:

> You who are set apart for the evil day,
>
> [Col. 0060B]  
> And who draw near to the seat of iniquity.
>
> You who sleep on ivory beds;
>
> And live wantonly upon your couches;
>
> You who eat lambs from the flock,
>
> And calves from the midst of the herd.

Concerning these same words, Saint Augustine says in section 18 of the same chapter 7 of *On Christian Doctrine*:

> These six members produced three two-membered periods. For he does not say: “You who are set apart for the evil day, who draw near to the seat of iniquity, who sleep on ivory beds, who live wantonly upon your couches, who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd.” If it were said in this way, that too would indeed be beautiful, so that each of the six members would proceed from the repetition of a single pronoun and each would be brought to an end by the speaker’s voice. But it was made more beautiful that the same pronoun should have two members attached to it, expressing three sentences: one concerning captivity—“you who are set apart for the evil day, and draw near to the seat of iniquity”; another concerning lust—“you who sleep on ivory beds and live wantonly upon your couches”; and a third concerning gluttony—“you who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd.” Thus it lies within the power of the speaker either to end each member separately, making six members, or to suspend his voice after the first, third, and fifth, and, joining the second to the first, the fourth to the third, and the sixth to the fifth, produce three most elegant two-membered periods, etc.

What could have been said more clearly to confirm the division of verses used in our edition? In the material quoted above you have three cola and six commas of the prophecy of Amos. Augustine likewise recognizes six members and three two-membered periods, expressing the same number of sentences.

If, then, any critic wishes to find fault with something in this edition of the Canon of Hebrew Truth, let him consult the minor works of Jerome and Augustine, recall his own conscience, examine the order and texture of the discourse, and then, if he can, detract from our labor.

There are also many other passages in which Augustine reviews Jerome’s Hebrew translation. If I am not mistaken, fifteen occur in the books of the *Questions on the Heptateuch*. In them, scarcely any ambiguous matter is proposed that is not resolved by some Hebrew truth—to use Augustine’s own words, which are found in Question 152 on Genesis.

It would be long and tedious for the diligent reader if I were to repeat each of these in order. I shall nevertheless briefly indicate Questions 20 and 54 on Deuteronomy; Questions 7, 15, 19, 24, and 25 on the Book of Joshua; and Questions 16, 37, 47, and 56 on Judges. In these passages Saint Augustine seeks the assistance of the translation from Hebrew, as though it provided greater light for understanding the Scriptures.

Let one testimony stand for all: the passage taken from Deuteronomy, chapter 14, verses 28 and 29, which Augustine proposes for solution in Book V, Question 20 on the same book.

After reciting the sacred text of the Septuagint Interpreters, he adds some remarks about the tithes that gave rise to the question concerning this passage, and then proceeds to solve the difficulty:

> But it is obscurely stated, because this tithe is not distinguished from that which he wished to be eaten with the Levites in the place that the Lord had chosen for his temple. But in the translation that is from Hebrew, we find this distinction expressed more clearly. For it says: “In the third year you shall set apart another tithe from all that is produced for you at that time, and you shall store it within your gates. Then the Levite, who has no other portion or inheritance with you, and the stranger, the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates shall come, eat, and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands that you perform.”

First, this is clearer in saying “in the third year”: it is understood that one year has intervened. But in the Septuagint, since it says “after three years,” it is uncertain whether it intended those years to intervene, so that the practice would occur every fifth year.

Then, by saying “and you shall set apart another tithe,” it sufficiently shows that it is distinct from the tithe which he wished the offerer himself to eat with his household and the Levites in the place that the Lord had chosen. For he also commanded him to place this other tithe within his gates, not to carry it to the place where the Lord wished himself to be invoked, etc.

That single passage most clearly demonstrates that Augustine held Jerome’s translation in the highest esteem. He cites it as clearer and especially suited to attaining the meaning of Scripture. In the Septuagint, on the other hand, he recognizes much obscurity and considerable perplexity, for the clarification of which Jerome’s interpretation is necessarily required.

We have passed over these matters briefly in order to obtain from Saint Augustine’s *Speculum* a more brilliant confirmation of our argument, since nothing is more suitable to the case of Jerome’s version.

What Augustine’s *Speculum* is, Possidius clearly explained in chapter 28 of his life of Augustine, saying:

> Wishing to benefit everyone—those who wished to read many books but could not—he extracted from both Testaments of God, the Old and the New, after placing a preface before them, divine commands and prohibitions pertaining to the regulation of life, and made one book from them. Thus anyone who wished could read it and recognize in it whether he was obedient or disobedient to God. He wished to call this work the *Speculum*.

Later, commending the reading of this work in Book of the *Institutions of Divine Literature*, chapter 16, Cassiodorus wrote about it as follows:

> The book of the same Augustine, resembling moral philosophy, which he collected from divine authority for the instruction and correction of morals and called the *Speculum*, should be read with great attention.

From where, then, do you suppose Augustine excerpted such a book of moral philosophy, which he wished to benefit all Christians? From the Septuagint, or from Jerome’s Hebrew translation?

Certainly Augustine was at times an advocate of the Septuagint Interpreters, even against Jerome, whom he wished to deter from the study of Hebrew interpretation on the grounds that it would cause future disturbance in the Church. But at length, struck by the splendor, fidelity, clarity, and usefulness of Jerome’s translation, he understood that Christians should be instructed with the greatest benefit from that translation rather than disturbed with great scandal among the peoples of Christ.

For this reason he published the distinguished work of the *Speculum*, which deserved above all to be preserved in memory, composed entirely from Jerome’s new translation, for the Latin Churches and especially for those in Africa. He no longer feared the priesthood, even if he were to present to the faithful many passages expressed by Jerome in a manner quite different from what had become fixed in everyone’s understanding and memory and had been sung through the succession of so many generations.

Who would believe that the Psalter derived from the Hebrew texts would be granted a place in Augustine’s *Speculum*, and that the old man’s language would there have to be changed? For the ears of Christians, accustomed to the old edition of the Psalms and indeed to its chant, and the Latin Churches everywhere, while enduring the novelty of another version, seem in a certain sense to have changed their language.

Thus, in Psalm 2, verses 23 and 24—in the Vulgate edition, verse 12—instead of:

> “Seize discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way,”

the people of the African Church and of the Latin-speaking Churches read in the *Speculum*:

> “Worship purely, lest he perhaps become angry and you perish from the way.”

Similarly, those who wished to commit to memory the divine commandments from Psalm 14:5, where the Septuagint Interpreters read “he swears to his neighbor and does not deceive,” as though they had completely forgotten the old wording, absorbed into their minds this new reading derived from the Hebrew source:

> “He swears so as to afflict himself, and does not change.”

To include all the protocanonical books of the Old Testament in a single statement: after entirely rejecting the Septuagint Interpreters, the Latin Churches accepted the Canon of Hebrew Truth together with the *Speculum* of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo.

The holy Bishop placed nothing in this work that did not come from Jerome’s pure Hebrew translation—that is, from the Canon of Hebrew Truth—apart from certain scribal errors that can now be corrected in the *Speculum* from our edition of the Canon, just as we have corrected certain matters in the Canon after being instructed by Saint Augustine’s *Speculum*.

You therefore have, Christian reader, very many sentences of sacred Scripture quoted from Jerome’s translation by Saint Augustine. You also have an entire work composed according to that same translation, in which the greater part of the Canon of Hebrew Truth has been preserved.

Finally, anyone who wishes to restore from the Canon of Hebrew Truth the number of verses expressed so corruptly in the ancient editions of the *Speculum* at countless points will derive another considerable benefit.

In the new edition of the *Speculum*, it will likewise be possible to correct the differing numbers marked in the manuscript codices and restore the proper number—the number, namely, that Saint Augustine established, following Jerome’s version divided by cola and commas.

Let us take examples from the Psalms. There Dom Blampin first informs us in his notes how he has undertaken to restore, on the authority of the manuscript codices, the number of verses corruptly expressed in the earlier editions of the *Speculum*.

In column 694 of this work we read:

> “In Psalm 26: ‘The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the strength of my life; whom shall I dread?’ And after four verses: ‘If armies should stand against me,’ etc.”

In the notes, under the letter *e*, this is correctly observed:

> “In the earlier editions: ‘And after the third verse.’ We restore from the manuscripts: ‘And after four verses.’”

[Col. 0063B] The new edition of the *Speculum* therefore restores the order and number of the verses as they were read among the ancients. But certain scribal errors in the *Speculum* still require correction, as the following text of our Canon clearly demonstrates.

In Psalm 27 according to the Hebrews, the words cited above appear in our edition as follows:

> The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?
>
> The Lord is the strength of my life; whom shall I dread?
>
> When the wicked draw near me,
>
> to devour my flesh,
>
> my enemies and my foes,
>
> they themselves stumbled and fell.
>
> If armies should stand against me,
>
> my heart will not fear.

[Col. 0063C] Accordingly, the reading “whom shall I fear?” is followed by four verses, up to the words “If armies should encamp,” etc. The Louvain theologians, failing entirely to grasp this, thought that the division of the verses indicated in the *Speculum* of St. Augustine was the one now received in the Latin Vulgate. Hence, supposing that the third verse of Psalm XXVI or XXVII among the Hebrews had been written in Augustine’s copies in the same order, they printed: “And after the third verse: If armies should encamp,” etc., although among the ancient Fathers it was not the third verse, but rather counted as the seventh, as is confirmed by the manuscript books of the Canon of Hebrew Truth.

Moreover, in the new edition of the *Speculum*, the first two verses of this same psalm should have no question mark, because it is perfectly clear that the sense of this passage of Scripture is not that of a prophet asking a question, but affirming that the Lord is his light and the strength of his life, and declaring that he fears him. The beginning of the psalm has also been disordered in the *Speculum*, where the words “My light” precede the word “Lord.”

Nor is the *Speculum* to be corrected from the Canon of Hebrew Truth only in its statements, but also in the numbers of the verses indicated by Augustine. Most improperly, in the printed editions, after the fifteenth verse of Psalm XXXIII one read: “And after the fourth verse”; the new edition changes this, on the authority of the manuscript codices, to: “And after seven verses.” Yet, to tell the truth, the reading still remains somewhat corrupt: for there are six, not seven, verses from the verse “Seek peace and pursue it” up to “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted.” [Col. 0064A] Therefore the *Speculum* must read: “And after six verses.”

Since there is no ambiguity in the division of the verses of Psalm CXI, which ought to retain its individual verses divided according to the number of the Hebrew letters, I am surprised that in the work of the *Speculum* only five verses are counted from the words “he will greatly delight” up to “A good man is gracious and lends.” For six verses proceed with their letters of the Hebrew alphabet, namely gimel, daleth, he, waw, zayin, and heth, and no writer can count fewer. Here, therefore, our new edition of the works of St. Augustine must be corrected; whoever compares the *Speculum* with the published Canon of Hebrew Truth will discover six hundred matters still requiring correction. But let us proceed [Col. 0064B] to those matters that belong to the present undertaking.

After Augustine, who could have served alone as the third witness for proving the assertion we have proposed, we could not, without injustice, remain silent about Philip, that distinguished disciple of Jerome. This contemporary writer added special honor to his teacher when, in his *Commentaries on Job*, he expounded only Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew. Lest anyone call Philip’s *Commentaries* into question on account of the work that circulates under Bede’s name, let him remember what Gennadius transmitted in writing and to memory in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men* concerning Philip:

“Philip, a priest and excellent disciple of Jerome, wrote and published, in simple speech, books commenting on Job,” etc.

The genuine *Commentaries* of Philip, preserved in part by transcription, are held in our monastery of Corbie. They were written nine hundred years ago on very sturdy, or rather extremely dense, parchment; in the library of Saint-Germain they bear the numerical designation 660. The entire sacred text of the Book of Job is written in this copy in uncial letters, while Philip’s interlinear commentary has been added in Lombard characters. If I am not mistaken, this gives us sufficiently certain evidence of the manuscript’s age. In the same hand and in the same Lombard characters, the following words are found at the end of the commentary:

“This interpretation is excerpted from Philip’s exposition.”

In these excerpts and in the *Epitome of the Exposition of Philip the Priest on Job*, the entire sacred text flows in a pure form, without those additions of interpretation that frequently occur in the printed books under Jerome’s name. There are, for example, two additions in Job 1:21–22, namely: “As it pleased the Lord, so it was done,” and, consequently, “with his lips.” That all these words are superfluous and interpolated is clearly demonstrated by the manuscript *Commentaries* of Philip the priest, as will appear from our notes below, col. 799.

Furthermore, that notable addition, “For even bitter things seem sweet to a hungry soul,” which occurs in the printed *Commentaries* on Job under Jerome’s name in chapter 6, does not appear in Philip, Jerome’s excellent disciple. Hence one may conclude that this contemporary of Jerome proposed to expound in his own little works no other Latin translation than that new one by Jerome which, as we said above, has been preserved in the *Speculum* [Col. 0065A] of St. Augustine.

Besides the complete text of Job, Philip cites many scriptural sayings and prophetic passages according to the new edition of his master. One example is the clause omitted by the Septuagint translators at the end of Isaiah the prophet’s second chapter:

“Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is regarded as exalted.”

Philip uses this saying in all the printed *Commentaries* when he interprets those words of Job 27:3: “For as long as my breath remains in me, and the Spirit of God is in my nostrils.” It would have been easy to accumulate further examples from Procopius of Gaza as well, but I am avoiding length in a matter demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently.

IV. I said that in the Roman Church, in the time of Gregory the Great, both editions of Scripture were received [Col. 0065B]—the old one and the new Hieronymian edition. Although all the Churches of Christ gave first place to that translation which they knew to have been derived from the Hebrew sources, nevertheless, because of the antiquity of the Vulgate Italic version, they did not entirely abandon their devotion to it. They proceeded cautiously and gradually in all things, so that what was growing old might of its own accord come to an end.

Gregory the Great himself taught us about the use of both Latin interpretations in the dedicatory letter, or preface, to his *Expositions of the Moralia on Job*. At the end he says:

“I expound the new translation; but, as the purpose of proof requires, I now employ the new and now the old in my citations, so that, since the Apostolic See—which by God’s authority I preside over—uses both, my labor also may be supported by both.”

He regarded the new translation, that is, Jerome’s translation, as the text; the other, old translation was employed by him only for confirmation. How much authority he attributed to the Hieronymian version over the Itala he made perfectly clear in Book XX of the *Moralia*, chapter 23, where he illuminates this passage of Job with his exposition:

“You have changed into cruelty toward me, and with the harshness of your hand you oppose me.”

He says:

“The ancient translation differs widely from this wording, because what is said here of God is spoken there of adversaries and persecutors. Nevertheless, because this new translation is said to have transferred everything more accurately for us from the Hebrew and Arabic language, whatever is said in it must be believed; and our exposition ought carefully to examine its words. Thus he says: ‘You have changed,’ etc.”

So spoke that great Gregory, the light of the Catholic Church and the glory and model of the supreme pontiffs. If I had occasionally imitated him in praising the Hieronymian translation, saying that it had transferred everything to us more accurately and that whatever was written in it ought to be believed—good heavens!—what attacks and furious outbursts I would have had to endure from the know-it-alls of our time, who have dared in some places to accuse me of rashness because I said that the Roman Church had never departed from the Latin Vulgate, even in chronological matters. But away with such writers, who prefer Iberian fables to authoritative books and refuse to follow with us the judgment of the Church of God and of its pontiffs.

All the other Latin Churches followed the mother of all the Churches, over which Gregory presided by God’s authority, accepting the new edition of Scripture from the Hebrew because it was by far superior to all others. No one among the ancients seems to have denied that it was clearer in wording and more truthful in meaning. Thus we read in Isidore of Seville, *On the Offices of the Church*, Book I, chapter 12:

“Of the Hebrew tongue into Latin speech, only Jerome the priest translated the sacred Scriptures. All the Churches everywhere generally use his edition, because it is more truthful in meaning and clearer in wording.”

Since Jerome’s interpretation was such, as Isidore definitively declares, is it surprising that all the Churches rejected the older version as more obscure in wording and not equally truthful in meaning? Concerning the established use of Jerome’s translation [Col. 0066B] among all the Churches, Gregory’s and Isidore’s testimony is so consistent that, as regards the Italians and Spaniards, it would be pointless to affirm the same thing through the opinions of other writers. We must therefore hasten to our own people, since the following section also requires testimony concerning the Gauls.

V. The name “Gallican Psalter” was given to the Book of Psalms revised a second time by Jerome and published with obeli and asterisks. This name came to be applied to that later edition according to the Septuagint, because the Churches of Gaul were the first of all to depart from the use of the Roman Psalter, that is, from the old Latin edition which Jerome, while residing at Rome, had corrected in large part.

This adds to the glory of our Churches not only because they retained the more perfect of the two Psalters, but especially because that Book of Psalms was celebrated from ancient times in the practice of psalm-singing in the Gallican Churches—the same book that the ecumenical Council of Trent eventually approved by public decree together with the other canonical books.

How great was the diligence of our countrymen in copying this Psalter with its asterisks and obeli, we wish to demonstrate by no other evidence than the immense abundance of manuscript codices that still survive in Gallican libraries with such markings. They are not nearly so plentiful in Italy. The learned theologian Carus, a priest, who began for us an edition of Jerome’s Psalter with the aforesaid signs of obeli and asterisks, admits that he found very few copies in his own country. We, having obtained excellent and very numerous manuscripts of this kind, took care to supply what seemed to be lacking in Carus’s Roman edition. But on these matters see below our notice concerning both the Roman and Gallican Psalters.

We may infer that the Churches of Gaul attributed the highest authority to the new translation from the Hebrew from the practice that they consistently maintained in the Psalter according to the Septuagint, revised by Jerome’s later efforts. For why would they not accept in its entirety what they had embraced so zealously in part? That is, if our countrymen received with such great enthusiasm copies corrected according to the Greek interpretations that approached more closely to the Hebrew codices, how eagerly must we suppose that they adhered to the Hebrew Truth, and with what delight must they have drunk water drawn from the purest fountain!

But lest we support our opinion concerning the use of Jerome’s translation among the Gauls merely by conjecture, let a suitable witness be added: Stephen, the second Cistercian abbot, who will settle the matter for us completely. By both his words and his example he shows that the old Latin interpretation was neglected among our people on account of the new one that Jerome had set against the Itala.

When he had copied exemplars of the sacred Bible for the use of his congregation and found in several places material that was redundant and insufficiently consonant with Jerome’s version, he was immediately offended by such discrepancies. After comparing the Latin codices with the Hebrew, he wished everything that was said to be absent from the Hebrew source and that he did not find placed in Jerome to be erased and obliterated in his copy of the *History of the Divine [Scriptures]*. [Col. 0067B] The passage is too important to be omitted or to allow the reader to lose anything from it. I shall therefore transcribe it in full, exactly as it was recently published by Dom Jean Mabillon at the end of volume IV of the works of St. Bernard, cols. XI and XII.

### CENSURE OF STEPHEN, SECOND ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX, CONCERNING SEVERAL PASSAGES OF THE BIBLES

Brother Stephen, abbot of New Monastery, sends greetings to the servants of God, present and future.

Intending to write this History, we encountered among the many books that we had gathered from various Churches, in order that we might follow the more truthful account, one that differed greatly from almost all the others. And because we found it fuller than the rest, [Col. 0067C] trusting it, we wrote this History according to what we found in that book.

When it had been arranged, we were greatly disturbed by the disagreement among the Histories. For sound reasoning teaches fully that what was translated from one interpreter—namely, blessed Jerome, whom our people had recently begun to accept while setting aside the other interpreters—from the single source of Hebrew Truth ought to have a single wording.

There are, however, certain books of the Old Testament that were translated by our same interpreter not from Hebrew but from the Chaldean language, because he found them among the Jews in that form, as he himself writes in the Prologue to Daniel. We likewise accepted them, as we did the other books, according to his translation.

Therefore, greatly wondering at the disagreement among our books, which we had received from one interpreter, we approached certain Jews skilled in their Scriptures. Through the Roman language we diligently inquired about all those passages of Scripture in which the sections and verses that we found in the aforementioned copy—and had already inserted into our own work—occurred, but which we did not find in many other Latin Histories.

They examined several of their books in our presence and, at the passages about which we questioned them, explained to us in Roman words the Hebrew or Chaldean text. Yet they found none of the sections or verses that had troubled us. Consequently, trusting the Hebrew and Chaldean Truth and the many Latin books that did not contain those passages but agreed in every respect with those two languages, we erased all those additions as entirely superfluous, as is apparent in many places in this book, especially in the Books of Kings, where the greater part of the error was found.

Now we ask all who will read this volume not in any way to add the aforesaid sections or superfluous verses to this work again. It is sufficiently evident where they had stood, since the erasure in the parchment does not conceal those places. We also prohibit, by the authority of God and of our Congregation, anyone from presuming to handle dishonorably this book, prepared with great labor, or to mark anything in its writing or margins with a fingernail.

[Col. 0068B] Such a lucid testimony from this holy man leaves us no need to proceed to other proofs. He has explained the matter at issue explicitly: namely, that our Gauls had recently accepted Jerome’s Latin edition from the Hebrew, while rejecting all the other interpreters.

The Churches of Gaul therefore accepted Jerome as their own interpreter. Since they knew that the holy Doctor’s translation had been prepared according to the Hebrew codices, they trusted entirely in the Hebrew and Chaldean Truth and obliterated with the deepest erasures from the sacred codices of the Bible whatever had been derived from other interpretations as superfluous.

Hence we have such a large supply of copies of the Canon of Hebrew Truth that still survive in the libraries of the Franks. Five or six such extremely ancient codices of the Hebrew Canon, rendered into Latin by Jerome, were supplied to us by the Gallican libraries for the present edition, whereas not even a single copy could be found in other regions, although countless codices of the Latin Vulgate are said to survive there. For although the Vulgate had Jerome as its author, it nevertheless retains much material mixed in from other editions, and Stephen, the Cistercian abbot, arranged for all of this to be erased as superfluous in the codices of Jerome’s translation.

For the rest, this is not the place to blunt the language and arguments of a certain critical writer who, envious of the useful labors of ancient and modern monks, devised an accusation against Abbot Stephen because he had approached Jewish teachers in order to judge from the Hebrew codices what ought to be retained in Latin copies of the sacred Bible and what ought instead to be corrected or removed.

As though Jerome himself had not given warning in this kind of correction: he repeatedly insists that the Jews are to be consulted and that the teachers of different cities are to be asked for advice if anything should arise requiring alteration in his new translation from the Hebrew. Thus that author did not hesitate to accuse of rashness the praiseworthy labor and diligence of holy men, when he ought rather to have reverently honored Stephen’s piety than to exercise his eloquence so freely against him.

For what fault did Stephen of Cîteaux commit in cleansing the sacred volumes of errors introduced by copyists, if he followed Cassiodorus’s rules? Cassiodorus, that most learned man, when teaching in Book 15 of *On the Institution of Divine Letters* “with what caution heavenly authority should be reread,” gives this express command:

“Those who are able should not refuse to seek out the Hebrew Scripture or its teachers. For it is fitting that the beautiful correction should return from the place whence the saving translation came to us.”

It is therefore clear that no one should condemn the diligence of the Cistercian abbot; rather, everyone should praise it, since he wished various errors in his codices to be corrected according to the rules established by Jerome himself. But more appropriately on these matters elsewhere.

VI. All who are even moderately learned agree that the Catholic Church declared Jerome’s Latin translation authentic by public decree and claimed its use for itself. Although several complete books in the Latin edition of the sacred Bible commonly called the Vulgate were retained from that ancient version which [Col. 0069B] was in use before Jerome, nevertheless the greatest part of the Old Testament is entirely the translation that that outstanding Doctor produced for us from the Hebrew sources.

To this Hieronymian translation, then, certain portions of the Itala having been added and the two having been joined together into something like a single body, that Vulgate blossomed forth which is now in everyone’s hands and which the perpetual and constant usage of so many centuries has transmitted to us.

Thus the author of the learned book *On Illustrious Interpreters* wrote before us. Sixtus V likewise taught the same thing in the preface placed before his Bibles. There, while proclaiming the authority of the Vulgate edition, he discussed the books contained in it as follows:

“For the books contained in it—as it has been handed down to us by our forebears, as though from hand to hand—were retained partly [Col. 0069C] from a certain common and most ancient Latin edition, which St. Jerome calls the Vulgate edition, blessed Augustine the Itala, and St. Gregory the old translation; this edition the same blessed Augustine judged preferable even to the others that were then in very wide use, because it adhered more closely to the words while preserving clarity of meaning. Partly they were taken from the translation of St. Jerome, and consequently anyone who recognizes the dignity of their translator can readily understand how much honor ought to be accorded them,” etc.

To understand the mind of the supreme pontiff, observe carefully that the entire Canon of Hebrew Truth, with the exception of one Psalter, is found in the Latin Vulgate, together with the two additional books of Tobit and Judith, translated from Chaldean into Latin by that same supreme interpreter of the Catholic Church.

Moreover, in the Book of Psalms you have Jerome’s later revision, which he published with the signs of asterisks and obeli—the very one that we too have restored in the second part of this Divine Library.

All the remaining books of the Old Testament were retained from that ancient Vulgate which is said to have been called the Common or Italic version. These are the Book of Baruch, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, and the First and Second Books of Maccabees.

We also found certain sayings and entire verses from that old edition transferred especially into the Books of Kings and into Solomon’s Proverbs. Although we did not admit these into our edition of the Canon, we nevertheless marked them in their proper places with the marginal obel sign ÷, so that the attentive reader may understand from those signs that the Vulgate contains something more there than is found in Jerome’s pure and unmixed Hebrew translation.

The decree of the Council of Trent concerning the edition and use of the sacred books, promulgated in the fourth session, therefore applies chiefly to the Hieronymian translation, because the greatest part of the Old and New Testaments, as it has been published in Latin in the present Vulgate, has St. Jerome as its author.

Nothing detracts from the authority of this interpretation merely because certain portions of the Itala version are also held as authentic in the Catholic Church, which employs the ancient Latin interpreter for its own purposes wherever Jerome, the Church’s greatest teacher in the interpretation of sacred Scripture, is silent.

We shall now append the decree by which we say that the authority of Jerome’s version was sanctioned at the Council of Trent:

“Furthermore, this same Most Holy Synod, considering that no little benefit may accrue to the Church of God if it becomes known which of all the Latin editions of the sacred books in circulation is to be held as authentic, establishes and declares that this same old and Vulgate edition, which has been approved in the Church itself through such long usage over so many centuries in public readings, disputations, preaching, and exposition, is to be held as authentic; and that no one may dare or presume to reject it under any pretext.”

With the authority of Jerome’s translation thus confirmed by this sanction of the Catholic Church, the minds of all devout people were so moved that we would seek in vain for a longer proof in its commendation.

# PROLEGOMENON III  
## On the Canon of Hebrew Truth and Its Marginal Scholia

[Col. 0069]

I. What the Canon of Hebrew Truth is.  
II. Jerome himself frequently mentions this Canon.  
III. Greek and Latin Fathers acknowledge the Hebrew Truth.  
IV. On the individual parts, or divisions, of this Canon.  
V. The additions to Daniel and Esther received into Jerome’s translation with the signs of obeli.  
VI. Who was the author of the marginal scholia of the Canon, and what is the usefulness and excellence of such annotations.

[Col. 0069D] By the name “Canon of Hebrew Truth” we are to understand the twenty-two books of the Old Testament, which are regarded as canonical both by Jews and by Christians and which were translated into Latin speech by Jerome according to the authority of the Hebrew sources. They were finally joined together into something like a single body, while preserving the threefold order of the books in which the matter was arranged in the codices of the Hebrews in the time of St. Jerome. [Col. 0070D]

The Canon, therefore, is a catalogue of the divine Scriptures that are called canonical because they have been received into the canon and have attained the highest level of authority, not only for the holy formation of morals but also for confirming any ecclesiastical doctrines whatsoever.

We have borrowed this notion of the sacred Canon from the second book of Jerome’s *Apology against Rufinus* and from the preface of the same holy Doctor to the Books of Solomon. At the end of the later *Apology*, he recalls the *Galeate Prologue*, in which he explained the canon of the Hebrews, in these words:

“In the Books of Samuel and Malachim, which we call the four Books of Kings, after the catalogue of divine Scripture I added the following,” etc.

From this one may see that Jerome here called the Canon of the sacred books of the Old Testament the “catalogue of divine Scripture.”

He established this distinction between canonical and noncanonical Scriptures: the latter were read only in the Church for the edification of the people, whereas the canonical were also used to confirm the doctrines of the faith. Thus, he says in the already mentioned preface to the Books of Solomon:

“Just as the Church indeed reads the books of Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees, but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, so also let it read these two books—Ecclesiasticus and Wisdom—for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines.”

Rufinus agrees with Jerome in this part of Scripture. In his Creed he too expressly teaches that no books other than those listed in Jerome’s *Galeate Prologue* were regarded as canonical in his time. After the catalogue of the books of the Old and New Testaments he adds:

“These are the books which the Fathers included within the Canon, and from which they wished the affirmations of our faith to be established. It must nevertheless be known that there are also other books which are not canonical but have been called Ecclesiastical by our predecessors: namely, Wisdom, which is called Solomon’s, and another Wisdom, which is called that of the son of Sirach. Among the Latins this book is called Ecclesiasticus by that general title—not because of the author of the little book, but because of the quality of the Scripture. Books of the same order are Tobit, Judith, and the Books of Maccabees.”

That after the time of Jerome and Rufinus those books called Ecclesiastical were not immediately received into the canon of the sacred Bible is confirmed for us by a manuscript copy. Although it appears extremely ancient, no one denies that it was written at least four hundred years after the death of Rufinus.

This manuscript codex of the Bible, numbered 15 in our library at Saint-Germain, appended the following to the Book of Esther:

“Here ends Esther. Thanks be to God. Amen. Up to this point the Old Testament has been completed, that is, all the canonical Scriptures which Jerome the priest translated from the Hebrew Truth into the Latin language. The remaining Scriptures, which are not canonical but are called Ecclesiastical, are these: namely, the Book of Judith, Tobit, the two Books of Maccabees, Wisdom, which is called Solomon’s, the Book of Jesus son of Sirach, and the Book of the Shepherd.”

I omit several matters that may be seen at the end of column 1152 of this edition. It is therefore perfectly clear from the foregoing what rank of authority the canonical Scriptures possessed in the Church. These are the books that constitute the Canon of Hebrew Truth, in which books called Apocryphal or Ecclesiastical never existed according to the ancient Fathers.

Today, having been received into the Ecclesiastical Canon without any distinction of authority, they deserve equal veneration with the others among all who are truly devout and who glory in adhering to the decree of the Council of Trent concerning the canonical Scriptures.

Cassiodorus likewise mentions the Canon of Hebrew Truth in Book 12 of *On the Institution of Divine Letters*, where he calls it “the division of divine Scripture according to Jerome”:

“According to St. Jerome, divine authority is divided into two Testaments, namely, the Old and the New; into the Law, that is, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy; into the Prophets, which are Joshua son of Nun, Judges, Ruth, Samuel, Malachim, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the twelve Books of the Prophets. Into the Hagiographa, which are Job, David, Solomon’s Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Daniel, the Words of the Days, that is, Paralipomena, Ezra, and Esther.”

Cassiodorus cited this from Jerome’s *Galeate Prologue*, but the division is altogether corrupt, both in the printed and in the manuscript books:

1. The word *Malachim* is everywhere omitted after the word *Samuel*.

2. Quite a few manuscript codices omit Daniel; others, together with the printed editions, count it among the Major Prophets after Ezekiel, preserving the customary order of the sacred Bibles.

3. In place of the name *Ecclesiastes*, they put [Col. 0072C] *Ecclesiasticus*, which is not Solomon’s but the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and which Jerome nowhere admitted into the Canon.

4. Finally, several manuscript copies add the Book of Judith after the volume of Esther, although in many places in Jerome Judith’s book is separated from the number of the canonical Scriptures.

Our Garetius should not, however, be accused of negligence or ignorance because he did not correct these errors of the codices, whether printed or manuscript, in the latest edition of Cassiodorus’s works. Like others who labor to publish the works of the holy Fathers, he faithfully reported what was found in books of better quality, written in an excellent and very ancient hand, and did not regard it as his responsibility or office to correct what was consistently read in codices of such venerable antiquity.

Nevertheless, we think it will be neither unwelcome nor disagreeable to anyone if, in fulfillment of the task we have undertaken of explaining the Hebrew Canon, we point out that all these slips and errors can easily be corrected by those who, imbued with sacred learning in divine letters, undertake to wash and wipe them away with the water of that consecrated source.

Isidore of Seville represents the same Canon of the Hebrews in *Etymologies*, Book VI, chapter 1. We would transcribe it in full here if it were not printed below together with the beginning of the *Galeate Scriptures*, or the preface to the Books of Kings.

It should nevertheless be noted that certain Hebrew words are read differently in Isidore from the way they are read in Jerome. The editors of Isidore more often imitate the modern practice of Hebrew grammarians, and, through the ignorance either of the editors themselves or of copyists, certain words appear in more corrupt forms. Such is the passage:

“Some, however, add Ruth and Rimoth, which in Latin is called the Lamentation of Jeremiah, to the Hagiographa.”

Whoever put the barbarous word *Rimoth* in place of *Kinoth*, or *Cinoth*, which means “lamentations,” must have been utterly ignorant of the Hebrew language. This is what tends to happen among those who presume to restore the works of ancient writers without sufficient knowledge of the many matters with which they deal.

## II.

Jerome himself calls the books of the Old Testament that he rendered into Latin the Canon of Hebrew truth. If this had been otherwise, we would certainly not have marked the first part of this divine library with that title [Col. 0073B]. But since we learned this nomenclature from the holy Doctor, we would act foolishly if we attached a foreign and spurious title to the Hebrew translation of the Old Testament. A fuller and more explicit passage concerning this designation is found in Letter 28, to Lucinius. So that not the smallest part of it may escape us, I quote it in full, chiefly in praise of the Hebrew volumes, against whose authority a certain defender of Egyptian fables in our own time has raged. But let him now hear Jerome responding to Lucinius according to the wisdom granted him:

“I have given the Canon of Hebrew truth, except for the Octateuch, which I now have in hand, to your boys and copyists to write out. I do not doubt that you also possess the Septuagint translation, and I gave it, most carefully corrected many years ago, to diligent students. I rendered the New Testament according to the authority of the Greek. For just as the reliability of the ancient books must be examined from the Hebrew volumes, so the new books require the standard of the Greek language.”

Blessed Jerome could not have declared more clearly or briefly whatever he provided for us in the Divine Library. He very plainly demonstrates the first part when he says, “I have given the Canon of Hebrew truth, except for the Octateuch, which I now have in hand, to your boys and copyists to write out”; the second in these words: “I do not doubt that you also possess the Septuagint translation, and I gave it, most carefully corrected many years ago, to diligent students.” Finally, he indicates the third part of the Divine Library by saying, “I rendered the New Testament according to the authority of the Greek” [Col. 0073D]. What more is needed? So that it might be known upon what foundations he wished his translations of the sacred Scriptures to rest, he suitably and conclusively adds: “For just as the reliability of the ancient books must be examined from the Hebrew volumes, so the new books require the standard of the Greek language.”

This definition of the correction of the Scriptures acquired such authority in the Church that, following Jerome’s prescription, the canon law in Gratian’s *Decree* decrees that the same standard of correction must be followed. Jerome therefore gave the Canon of Hebrew truth to be written out by Lucinius’s six boys and copyists. Praising especially his zeal and devotion to the Scriptures, he writes thus to Theodora in Letter 29:

“Not content with the generosity of his homeland, he sent to the Church of Jerusalem and to the Alexandrian Church as much gold as could relieve the poverty of many. Although many people marvel at and praise this, I shall praise in him rather his zeal and devotion to the Scriptures. Moved by this desire, he urgently requested our little works; and, having sent six copyists, because in this province there is a scarcity of writers and of the Latin language, he had everything that we had dictated from our youth up to the present time copied for him” [Col. 0074A].

Jerome wrote this around the year of Christ 394, when he still had the Octateuch in hand, to be given in translation at the appropriate time. But what that Octateuch was is sufficiently clear from the preface to the book of Joshua, where he says that, once the Pentateuch of Moses had at last been completed, he would set his hand to the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, and Esther.

This can be understood in two or three ways. First, if we combine the book of Judges and Ruth into one, we shall make an Octateuch out of the five books of Moses, one book of Joshua, one of Judges, and finally one of Esther. This will be the Octateuch that Jerome completed after the year of Christ 404, as may be seen in our preceding prolegomenon, where the date of Jerome’s translations was discussed [Col. 0074B].

Second, there is nothing to prevent this Octateuch from being reckoned as Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, and Esther. For when Jerome was writing to Lucinius, it can scarcely be doubted that he had already translated Genesis into Latin. Nor did he render all the books of Moses into Latin at one time, as we have said in its proper place. Rather, he began to interpret Genesis around the year 394, dedicating it to Desiderius, while reserving the remaining books of the Mosaic Pentateuch for greater leisure in writing.

Finally, if the book of Genesis is removed from the reckoning and Ruth is joined to Judges, there will nevertheless still be a complete Octateuch in Jerome’s hands, to be translated into Latin in due time: namely, four books of Moses, one of Joshua, one of Judges and Ruth, one of Esther, and one of Chronicles. For it is certain that the books of Chronicles were not translated from the Hebrew before the year 396, by which time Lucinius had already died [Col. 0074C].

From this the reader may understand that Marianus erred in more than one way in his notes on Letter 28 of St. Jerome. His error lies first in having read *Heptateuch* instead of *Octateuch*, and secondly in thinking Erasmus worthy of criticism for adhering to the correct reading. We therefore warn the scholarly reader that Gravius’s notes, with which he illustrated Jerome’s letters, are better and more learned than those published by Marianus Victorius with the works of the same holy Doctor [Col. 0074D].

Jerome mentions the Canon again in other places. For in the preface to the books of Kings, after explaining it part by part, he wrote as follows:

“Therefore Wisdom, which is commonly entitled ‘of Solomon,’ and the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and Judith and Tobit, and the Shepherd are not in the Canon.”

Likewise, in Book One *Against Jovinianus*, after speaking of the *περίοδοι* (*periodoi*)—a wholly apocryphal volume—he returns to the canonical Scriptures, saying:

“But now our entire dispute concerns the Canon.”

He recalls the same matter in the prologue to his Commentaries on the prophet Jonah:

“The book of Tobit also,” he says, “although it is not held in the Canon, nevertheless, because it is used by ecclesiastical men, records something of this sort,” and so forth.

He also distributed it into its parts in the preface to Daniel translated from the Hebrew, though without expressly naming the Canon. I should point out that Daniel is not counted among the prophets by the Hebrews, but among those who wrote the *Hagiographa*. For they divide all Scripture into three parts: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa—that is, into five, eight, and eleven books. It is not the time to discuss this matter here.

Just as Jerome mentions the Canon without adding the name “Hebrew truth,” so in six hundred places he cites Hebrew truth while omitting any reference to the Canon. He understands the same thing by “the Canon of the Hebrews” as by “Hebrew truth,” because for Jerome “Hebrew truth” always means the canonical Scriptures of the Hebrews—that is, only those Scriptures that are read in the Hebrew source [Col. 0075B].

It would be foolish, then, for anyone to wish to enumerate every place in which Jerome repeats “Hebrew truth.” Scarcely will you turn over any letter or any commentary in which expressions of this kind do not immediately occur: “According to Hebrew truth”; “The Hebrew truth has it otherwise”; “This disagrees with Hebrew truth.” And so with the rest—though to invent examples would be the occupation of an idle writer.

## III.

The Greek and Latin Fathers acknowledged the authority of the Hebrew volumes in many ways; and the more learned they were than others, the more clearly you will see that they devoted themselves to Hebrew truth. When Jerome testifies in Book One of his *Apology Against Rufinus* that he read Origen because of his learning, not in order to follow his faith, he weaves together this distinguished testimony, by which he made the Greeks’ interest in the Hebrew Scripture clear and certain to us:

“Origen himself, and Clement, and Eusebius, and many others, whenever they discuss something from the Scriptures and wish to establish what they say, customarily write in this way: ‘A Hebrew reported to me’; ‘I heard it from a Hebrew’; ‘This is the opinion of the Hebrews.’”

Origen also certainly names the patriarch Huillus, who lived in his time, and in the thirtieth tome on Isaiah, at whose end he explains “Woe to you, city of Ariel, which David conquered,” he concludes with that man’s interpretation. Although he says that he had previously understood the passage differently, he confesses that, having been instructed by Huillus, he now accepts what is truer [Col. 0075C].

He likewise considers the eighty-ninth psalm, entitled “A Prayer of Moses, the man of God,” and the remaining eleven psalms that lack titles, to belong to the same Moses according to Huillus’s interpretation. Nor does he disdain, when interpreting the Hebrew Scripture passage by passage, to insert what seems right to the Hebrews.

At the end of Book Two of the same *Apology*, he again asserts of Origen, Didymus, and Eusebius that they explained the translations of the Jews throughout all their books. He adds the following, which is especially important in praise of Hebrew truth:

“Apostolic men use the Hebrew Scriptures; it is evident that the apostles and evangelists themselves did this. The Lord and Savior, whenever he mentions the Old Scripture, takes his examples from the Hebrew volumes,” and so forth [Col. 0075D].

What, then, is surprising if, after the Lord and Savior, after the apostles and evangelists, and finally after apostolic men, the more celebrated Greek Fathers used the Hebrew Scriptures, acknowledged their authority, and searched out divine meanings from the books of the Jews?

Eusebius of Caesarea likewise commends the same devotion to Hebrew Scripture in Adamantius in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 16, where he says at the very beginning:

“Origen devoted such care and diligence to searching the divine Scriptures that he even learned the Hebrew language and acquired for himself the authentic books of the Scriptures, written in Hebrew characters, which are held among the Jews: τάς τε παρὰ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις ἐμφερομένας προτοτύπους αὐτοῖς Ἑβραίων στοιχείοις γραφάς, κτῆμα ἴδιον ποιήσασθαι”—“and to make his own possession the original writings current among the Jews, written in Hebrew letters” [Col. 0076A].

Eusebius calls the Jewish codices “authentic,” according to Valesius’s translation, in relation to all translations, including comparison with the version of the Seventy-Two Translators. Jerome very frequently adorns these same books with this designation, as in Letter 132, to Vitalis:

“If the Septuagint had one reading in the histories and Hebrew truth another, we could have recourse to our customary defenses and hold to the stronghold of our native language. But now, since both the Authentic and the other interpreters agree with equal authority, the difficulty lies not in the Scripture but in the meaning.”

Similarly, in Letter 135, when bringing forward certain verses of Psalm 67, he applies this correction to them “according to the faith of the authentic books”:

“This verse,” he says, “ought rather to read according to Hebrew truth, ‘Sing to God, sing praises to the Lord’; and what follows at the beginning of the other verse, ‘Sing praises to God,’ is not in the Authentic books but is marked beforehand with an obelus” [Col. 0076C].

Finally, in Book Seventeen of his Commentaries on the Prophet Isaiah, he calls the exemplars of the Hebrews nothing other than authentic books. Thus he writes concerning the Apostle:

“The apostle Paul, as a Hebrew from Hebrews, takes a paraphrase of this testimony from the authentic books in the letter that he writes to the Corinthians.”

Origen therefore acquired for himself those original Hebrew Scriptures—*πρωτότυποι* (*prototypoi*)—or authentic books, and valued them so highly that in the tenth book of his *Stromata* he thought that nothing should be accepted except what was read in the Hebrew books.

Thus, concerning the story of Susanna, he said through Jerome at the end of the Commentaries on Daniel:

“Since the Hebrews reject the story of Susanna, saying that it is not contained in the book of Daniel, we must carefully investigate the names σχίνου καὶ πρίνου, which the Latins translate as holm-oak and mastic, to see whether they exist among the Hebrews and what etymology they have, so that in their language it may be said to derive from σχίνῳ, ‘splitting,’ and from πρίνῳ, ‘cutting’ or ‘sawing.’ If this is not found, necessity will compel us also to agree with those who wish this passage to belong only to the Greek language, possessing a Greek etymology but not a Hebrew one. But if someone proves that the etymology of these two trees—of splitting and cutting—stands in Hebrew, then we shall also be able to accept this Scripture.”

In the same place, while explaining certain matters concerning the words of the king of Babylon and the idol Bel among the Babylonians, he elegantly defends his position by this subtle qualification:

“This which Scripture now says, ‘He cried out with a loud voice,’ because it is spoken of an idolater and one ignorant of God, seems to overturn our observation, by which we previously asserted that a loud voice is found only among the holy. The matter can easily be resolved by one who says that this story is not contained in the book of Daniel among the Hebrews. But if someone can prove that it belongs to the Canon, then we must ask what answer we ought to give him” [Col. 0077A].

From this it is clear to us that Origen adhered to Hebrew truth so closely that he wished to accept nothing outside the Canon of the Hebrews and to defend nothing that was not Hebrew. This is not contradicted by what we read in his Letter to Africanus: for with prudent judgment he did not wish Christians to reject the codices customarily used in the Church, and the Vulgate reading of Scripture, for the edification of the people as adulterine additions or compositions woven by the art of actors.

In his homilies, therefore, which he addresses to the common people, he follows the common edition and customary readings. In his tomes, however—that is, in his more extensive discussions—he is supported by Hebrew truth and surrounded by his own forces, while at times he seeks the assistance of a foreign language. Jerome attests this in the preface to his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* [Col. 0077B].

It should nevertheless be understood that Hebrew truth is also heard clearly in Origen’s homilies and is often preferred to the translations of the Seventy Elders. In the second homily on the *Song of Songs*, after Origen had recited these words of Proverbs 27:10, “Do not enter the house of your brother, unfortunate one,” he wished the final word, “unfortunate,” to be noted in this way:

Where the Septuagint translated “unfortunate,” Aquila, expressing the Hebrew truth, used ἀγροικὸν, “rustic” or “boorish.”

The eleventh homily on Jeremiah is also an unmistakable defender of the Hebrew volumes, to such an extent that it calls those exemplars more certain and more truthful, even in comparison with the version of the Seventy Translators. He says:

“There are two forms of the Scripture. For in many exemplars it reads: ‘I did not profit, nor did anyone profit me.’ But in those exemplars that are more truthful and agree with the Hebrews, it reads: ‘I ought not, nor ought anyone to have done so for me.’ Therefore we must explain both what is in use and read in the churches, and what is found in the Hebrew codices must not be passed over untouched.”

And shortly afterward:

“Since another explanation remains for us because of the more certain exemplars, in which it reads, ‘I ought not, nor ought anyone to have done so for me,’ let us also consider this passage” [Col. 0077C–D].

Anyone who desires more, so as to be persuaded that Origen acknowledged the authority of the Hebrew volumes in everything, should read his books *Against Celsus* and the tomes of his Commentaries on Matthew.

Let Procopius of Gaza, the sophist, now come forward as one witness in place of all the other Greek Fathers to prove our assertion. He most carefully composed his Commentaries on the Octateuch from the expositions of the most ancient orthodox Fathers and other writers, gathering their opinions into one body and one continuous fabric of interpretation.

This Greek writer therefore acknowledges Hebrew truth at the first word of Genesis and comes very near to expressing indignation against the Seventy Translators because of the opportunity for error that they provide in their translation of the Scriptures. He says:

“But if we wish to observe Hebrew truth, we must know that the word for ‘beginning’ signifies ‘head.’ Thus it will be possible to assign this meaning: Moses calls heaven and earth, which are the first of visible beings, the head,” and so forth [Col. 0078A].

Then, examining each point, especially concerning the verb “created” in the first verse of Genesis, he sought to note the following:

“But if we wish to examine the Hebrew expression more carefully, we shall find that the word does not simply mean ‘made,’ but ‘founded,’ ‘brought into our sight,’ and ‘displayed.’ All these things in some way teach that, since it did not previously exist, he established it and displayed it for viewing, not from pre-existing matter. For when the Seventy Translators say ‘made,’ they certainly offered some people an opportunity for serious error.”

For “making” is predicated of things produced from some material, such as a sickle from iron and other objects that craftsmen make for us. Hence some were swept into this error, shouting that Moses, having been taught by the Egyptians, believed that the universe had been founded from pre-existing matter, and that he inculcated this opinion upon us at the very beginning of his work by using the verb “made.”

Because the Seventy Translators did not recognize the shamelessness of these men, they explained the present passage through the word “made,” when it would have been better for it to be explained otherwise, by a word corresponding in every respect to the Hebrew, as Moses is known to have done. By the word he uses, he resists with the greatest force those who introduced matter, clearly showing that matter had not pre-existed. Indeed, he demonstrates that heaven, earth, and the abyss preceded matter, while he teaches the people entrusted to his faith that the adornment of the world proceeded from them [Col. 0078B–C].

How much there is in this Procopian exposition that commends the truth of the Hebrew volumes, and how much, by contrast, that rejects the translation of the Seventy Translators! Yet lest some champion of the LXX Translators, learned in his own eyes but very ignorant in ours, should suppose that Procopius attributed authority to Hebrew exemplars of the sacred Bible only in this one place, let him read his Commentaries on the eleventh chapter of Genesis, where he will find written:

“Shem was one hundred years old and begot Arphaxad two years after the Flood. Hebrew truth has it that Shelah was begotten by Arphaxad.”

The words that are subsequently placed in the middle are seen marked with an obelus. The genealogy of the younger man, called Cainan, was therefore struck through with an obelus, because there was no mention of this patriarch in Hebrew truth. Among the Greeks, those things marked with obeli received no exposition, since in prophetic passages they were regarded as foreign to the source of Scripture and as additions [Col. 0078D].

Time would fail me if I were to repeat everything that appears abundantly in Procopius of Gaza’s collection to demonstrate the authority that Greek writers attributed to Hebrew truth. Yet it would be wrong to omit what Procopius writes concerning the chronological years of the early patriarchs before the Flood, as though speaking on behalf of all the interpreters of Greece:

“It should be noted that the Hebrew consistently revolves around the number one hundred in composing the genealogy. For example: ‘Adam, having lived 230 years, begot Seth,’ who is regarded as the firstborn. But the Hebrew writes: ‘Adam, having lived 130 years, begot Seth’ ... ‘Enosh lived ninety years and begot Kenan’ ... ‘Kenan lived seventy years and begot Mahalalel,’ and so forth.”

Thus he proceeds consecutively up to the patriarch Enoch, who, walking with God, was taken away, lest wickedness alter his understanding.

After presenting in this way the smaller number found in the Hebrew codices, Procopius acknowledges that Moses recorded this chronology with the greatest care:

“See with what care the time preceding the generation of children, and that which followed it, was recorded.”

Here, in chapter 5 of Genesis, he proves the Hebrew Scripture. But in his Commentaries on verse 8 of Deuteronomy 32 he plainly rebukes the error of the Septuagint in these words:

“From Adam to Noah, who was the tenth from him, there were approximately 2,042 years; history reports that no one wandered off onto a broad detour. This is the error of the Seventy Translators” [Col. 0079A–B].

Lest a mass of many similar testimonies overwhelm the reader, I pass over further examples from what I have read in Procopius’s Commentaries. If what has already been presented is insufficient for anyone, let him consult the Commentaries on the Octateuch himself, and he will confirm that I speak the truth.

As for the age of Procopius of Gaza the sophist, learned men do not hold a single opinion. But if the letter of Procopius himself to Jerome is genuine—the letter that Isaac Vossius cited in his response to Simon’s third objections, p. 117—then Jerome and Procopius must have been contemporaries [Col. 0079C].

John Curterius, the interpreter of Procopius on the prophet Isaiah, proves that our sophist of Gaza reached the age of Theodosius I; indeed, that he began somewhat earlier, since he testifies that he saw many people eagerly undergoing martyrdoms, which are found to have ceased under Julian. From Julian’s reign until the second overthrow of the idols, the lifetime of Procopius may therefore be extended. See Curterius’s preface to the *Epitome of Various Commentaries on the Prophet Isaiah*.

Whatever may be the date of Procopius of Gaza, it is certain from him that all the Greek ecclesiastical writers, together with Jerome, clung firmly to Hebrew truth, while the Septuagint Translators were often rejected by them. Hebrew truth is indeed splendidly commended by the matters we have just reviewed. Yet what is especially important and distinctive for adding to its praise is that, in matters of the greatest importance and concerning the Catholic faith, orthodox Greeks and Latins are compelled to return to the Hebrew source and seek the assistance of a foreign language [Col. 0079D].

We have already seen Procopius rejecting the Seventy Translators, who offered an opportunity for error in the first verse of Genesis because of the word “made,” leading many to say that Moses believed the whole structure of heaven and earth to have been founded from pre-existing matter. Procopius refutes the ignorance of this opinion from nowhere else than the Hebrew context, where Moses expressly testifies that God created—*bara*, that is, founded from nothing—heaven and earth [Col. 0080A].

Since the Seventy Translators in some way exclude belief in the creation of the world from nothing, they introduce an even worse creation into the eternal generation of God’s Wisdom, and thereby supply the Arian heresy with the basis for its doctrine. For this reason the holy Fathers appeal to Hebrew truth, by which the error of the Arians is most powerfully refuted.

Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 68, p. 320, responded to the Arians, who pressed the passage badly rendered by the LXX, ὁ Κύριος ἔκτισέ με, “The Lord created me,” as follows:

“These men, who have neither touched nor understood the Hebrew expressions, and who are not in a position to grasp their force, have insolently and wantonly insulted us, those grievous enemies, seeking an opportunity by which to mutilate the faith—or rather themselves, for they cannot overcome the truth. And because they found the words ‘The Lord created me,’ they dangerously imagine and dream, bringing into life things useful for nothing and disturbing the world. But the Hebrew language does not have it so. Hence Aquila also says, ‘The Lord possessed me,’” and so forth [Col. 0080B].

Jerome says the following concerning the same testimony in Book Two of his Commentaries on chapter 4 of the Letter to the Ephesians:

“Hence also the heresy that calumniates Christ’s birth appropriates Solomon’s example: ‘The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways.’”

He corrects this in Book Two of his Commentaries on chapter 4 of Micah, saying:

“Or, as it is written in Hebrew, ‘The Lord possessed me.’ For *CANANI* does not mean ‘created me,’ but signifies ‘possessed me’ and ‘had me.’”

He states the matter even more clearly in his letter to Cyprian, where he explains Psalm 89. He says, not far from the beginning:

“A similar thing is also read in Proverbs from the person of Wisdom, who is Christ: ‘The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, in his works; before the ages he established me in the beginning; before he made the earth and the abysses, before he brought forth the springs of waters, before the mountains were made firm, before all the hills he begot me.’

“No word of creation ought to trouble anyone, since in Hebrew there is not the creation called *BARA* (), but possession. For thus it is written: *ADONAI CANANI RESITH DERCHO* (), which in our language is expressed, ‘The Lord possessed me as the beginning of his ways.’

“There is a great difference between possession and creation. Possession signifies that the Son was always in the Father and the Father in the Son. Creation, however, signifies the beginning of the condition of one who previously did not exist” [Col. 0080C].

The same Jerome, in the book of *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* and in Book One *Against Jovinianus*, presses the doctrine of the immaculate birth of the Virgin Mary, both against the Jews and against heretics, from the Hebrew word *aalma*, which is read in Isaiah 7:14, where the virgin who was to bear our Emmanuel had been foretold.

“Let Isaiah speak,” says the holy Doctor in Book One *Against Jovinianus*, “the mystery of our hope and faith: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel.’

“I know that the Jews customarily object that in Hebrew the word *AALMA* does not mean ‘virgin’ but ‘young woman.’ And in fact a virgin is properly called *BETHULA*, while a young woman or girl is not called *AALMA* but *NAARA*.

“What, then, does *AALMA* signify? A hidden virgin—that is, not merely a virgin, but a virgin with emphasis (*ἐπίτασις*), because not every virgin is hidden or removed from the casual sight of men ... In the passage where it says, ‘The virgin who goes out to draw water,’ *AALMA* is written in Hebrew, that is, ‘a secluded virgin,’ carefully guarded by the excessive diligence of her parents. Or let him show me where married women are called by this word, and I shall confess my ignorance” [Col. 0080D–0081A].

While defending the purest honor of virginity and chastity against the same Jovinianus, Jerome, in the book already mentioned, struck down the heresy with this verse of Zechariah:

“And the prophecy of Zechariah is fulfilled, at least according to Hebrew truth, when he prophesies concerning the virgins of the Church: ‘Its streets shall be filled with boys and girls playing.’ For what is its good, and what is its beauty, except the grain of the elect and the wine producing virgins? These are the virgins,” and so forth [Col. 0081B].

You see, prudent reader, that the defenses of the mysteries of our hope and faith, both against the Jews and against heretics, were sought from the codices of the Hebrews, and that the unconquerable champions of the Catholic Church, whenever the question concerned the faith of Christ’s birth or the eternal generation of the Word, always appealed to Hebrew truth. This would certainly have been pointless unless the authority of the Hebrew volumes had been held constant and perpetual among all.

Jerome therefore rightly said in Letter 74, to Marcella:

“For a long time now I have been comparing the edition of Aquila with the Hebrew volumes, lest perhaps the synagogue may have altered something out of hatred for Christ; and, to confess honestly what concerns the strengthening of our faith, I find more rather than less.”

The holy man suspected that Aquila had altered something in the sacred Scriptures through a deceptive interpretation. Yet when he compared Aquila’s edition with the Hebrew source, he found more in accordance with Hebrew truth for confirming our faith. Elsewhere, therefore, he was ashamed of the contentiousness of our own shallow scholars who criticized Hebrew truth—that is, his own translation from the Hebrew:

“The Jews read against themselves, and the Church does not know what is in her own favor.”

What was read in the Hebrew volumes of the prophets was especially in the Church’s interest, so that Christian faith might possess unshaken testimony even among its enemies. God wished the Jewish people to be scattered throughout the lands with the instruments of the divine Scriptures, by which it is demonstrated that the mysteries of our religion were not fabricated but promised and fulfilled by the true God [Col. 0081D].

Thus St. Augustine says in *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 46:

“For us, those prophecies that are brought forth from the books of our enemies are sufficient. We recognize that they themselves, because of the testimony that they unwillingly bear to us, by possessing and preserving the same books, have been scattered among all nations wherever the Church of Christ is spread ... For if, together with that testimony of the Scriptures, they had remained only in their own land and were not everywhere, the Church, which is everywhere, could not have them as witnesses among all nations to the prophecies that were foretold concerning Christ.”

He taught the same thing on Psalm 56, saying:

“So that the Jews might carry our books about like our book-bearers, so that when the pagans do not believe what we say was foretold concerning Christ, as though it had been fabricated by us, we may send them to the Jews, the enemies of our faith, who carry our books about and in them possess the same things that we proclaim” [Col. 0082A].

These statements agree with what is read in Justin Martyr’s *First Oration to the Greeks*, where he declares that the books of the Christian religion were preserved together with the sacred exemplars of the Jews—not by chance, but through the admirable plan of divine providence:

“For the fact that even now the books of our religion are preserved among the Jews is a work of divine wisdom concerning us.”

Tertullian must also be heard on this subject. He most plainly demonstrates that the Hebrew volumes possessed supreme authority in the Church of Christ for confirming the truth of ineffable matters and for making the pagans believe in the worship of our Christian religion. Thus he addresses and challenges the worshipers of empty gods in *Apology*, chapters 18 and 19:

“We too once laughed at these things. We were of your number: Christians are made, not born. Those whom we have called preachers are called prophets because of their office of proclaiming beforehand. Their words, and likewise the powers that they displayed for establishing belief in their divinity, remain in the treasuries of literature, nor are they now hidden ... Today they are displayed at the Serapeum, in the library of Ptolemy, together with the Hebrew writings themselves. The Jews also read them publicly. Every Sabbath the freedom of access to the tax-paying populace is granted. Whoever listens will find God; whoever strives to understand will be compelled also to believe.

“The highest antiquity claims the first authority for these documents ... Your gods, their temples, oracles, and sacred rites are meanwhile surpassed through the ages by the archive of a single prophet, in which the treasury of the entire Jewish mystery, and therefore also of ours, appears to have been deposited” [Col. 0082B–C].

No prudent and sober person will deny that Tertullian was speaking of the Hebrew volumes in this passage of the *Apology*. If there are people with necks stiff enough to dare twist so plain a testimony of the most ancient writer to suit their own opinions, those who write controversies or undertake lengthy disputations can easily refute their obstinacy from the text itself and the order of the discourse. We are content to have written these things for fair-minded readers, not contentious ones, and we shall proceed to other proofs.

We derive the supreme authority of the Hebrew volumes from another consideration.
