For since Hilary and Ambrose, among the most celebrated of the holy Fathers, always adhered to exemplars corrected and emended according to the Hebrew, they provide us with the clearest indication of how great was the dignity of the Hebrew codices in their eyes [Col. 0082D].

Peter our Coutant observes this reverence for the Hebrew source in St. Hilary, in numbers 19 and 20 of his admonition in the *Commentary on the Psalms*, or in Hilary’s treatises on the Psalms. Although he perhaps did not wish to enter into the controversy that had arisen concerning the age of the world, he removes from himself every suspicion of a preconceived opinion in favor of the Hebrew volumes and offers himself as a substantial witness for explaining the opinion of St. Hilary, whom he published for us.

He therefore examines several passages from the works that he recently edited:

“How highly Hilary valued the book of Psalms corrected according to the Hebrews among the Greeks, he left attested at the beginning of letter 8, on Psalm 118, where he departs from the preconceived opinion confirmed by the Latin codices, and by certain Greek ones, because of the authority of that one reading. In the correction of the same book, as in the explanation of the whole of Psalm 118, Ambrose agreed with him at the same passage.”

You may suitably relate the words of both men to that work of Lucian the martyr, concerning which Euthymius testifies:

“Having examined all the editions and compared them most carefully with Hebrew truth, he gave Christians his own edition, containing nothing defective and nothing superfluous,” and so forth.

He made his view of the Hebrew text clear both by this passage, in which he values so highly the book corrected according to the Hebrews, and by another, in which he implies that the Greek codices, because they are closer to the Hebrew source, possess somewhat greater authority than the Latin ones. Yet he does not impugn the integrity of this text; he merely warns that one must guard against its ambiguity. Indeed, if we correctly understand his words on Psalm II, no. 3, the Hebrew books were collated after the Lord’s resurrection with those which the translators of the Septuagint had produced; and when they were found to agree faithfully, the authority of both was established as indissoluble, by the privilege of their doctrine and antiquity.

Certainly, when he admits in the same place that the translations of the Seventy Elders were not necessary for the Hebrews, and when in no. 4 he shows that Paul, a Hebrew among Hebrews, was permitted to use the Hebrew text among the Hebrews, he plainly indicates that he did not at all suspect this text of corruption. So far was Hilary from thinking the codices of the Hebrews corrupted that, on the contrary, he assigned them indissoluble authority, teaching that those books had been preserved with diligent and religious care, collated after Christ’s passion and resurrection with the version of the Seventy interpreters, and used daily among the Hebrews and by the apostle Paul.

Zealous readers would scarcely allow me to quote this notable passage incompletely. I therefore reproduce it in full, as it was published by our Coutant:

> The translations of these men, therefore, were not necessary for the Hebrews, who at that time used only their own language. Yet, when all these things had been observed with diligent and religious care, and, after the Lord had fulfilled the whole Law through the sacrament of his incarnation, passion, and resurrection, had been collated with those books which the same translators had produced for the king and had been found to agree faithfully, the authority of both was established as indissoluble, by the privilege of their doctrine and antiquity. Blessed, therefore, was the apostle Paul, a Hebrew according to his profession, a Hebrew among Hebrews, who, also according to Hebrew knowledge and faith, called this the first psalm, without using the translators’ distinction. His greatest zeal in preaching to the rulers of the synagogue was to demonstrate from the teaching of the Law that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, had been born, had suffered, had risen, and would reign forever. Thus he maintained this practice: being himself a Hebrew and preaching to Hebrews, he used the custom of the Hebrews.

Our aforesaid editor of Hilary rightly observes that these words of the treatise on Psalm II strongly favor the Hebrew text, and that Hilary granted it unquestioned authority on the grounds both of antiquity and of doctrine. Yet I cannot agree with him when he supposes that Hilary reviewed the canon of the sacred books according to the Hebrews, rather than according to the usage received in the Church in his own time.

For, until the age of this holy Doctor, Jews and Christians had followed one and the same practice in receiving the canonical Scriptures, so that the churches of Christ admitted no more books into the canon than the twenty-two which were held in the Jewish canon. Witnesses to this assertion are Melito of Sardis’s catalogue, preserved by Eusebius in book IV, chapter 26, of the *Ecclesiastical History*; Origen, in Homily 7 on Joshua, in his commentary on Psalm I, and in the same Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 25; canon 60 of the Council of Laodicea; the *Synopsis* commonly attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria, together with his Festal Epistle; Cyril of Jerusalem, in Catechesis 4; Gregory Nazianzen, in his poem on the Authentic Books; Amphilochius, in his letter to Seleucus on the same Scriptures; and many others, whom I do not list here.

Among the Latins, the two principal witnesses are Jerome and Rufinus of Aquileia, who expressly testified that the books of Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees were customarily read in the Church for the edification of the people, but had not yet been admitted among the canonical Scriptures. Consult Jerome’s preface to the books of Solomon and the Creed of the aforementioned Rufinus.

Moreover, it can be gathered from Hilary’s own words, when he lists the canon of the divine books, that he was speaking of the usage received in the Church. For after listing the twenty-two books, he adds:

> Some, however, have thought that, with Tobit and Judith added, twenty-four books should be counted according to the number of the Greek letters, etc.

This clearly shows that Christians are meant in this enumeration. For who among the circumcised is said to have admitted the book of Judith or Tobit into the canon of the sacred Scriptures? It was Christians, therefore, both those who accepted only twenty-two canonical books and those who counted twenty-four according to the number of the Greek letters.

These arguments seem to me so weighty and compelling that they have forced me to depart from the earlier opinion of our colleague, however much I approve his zeal in other matters. Yet even among friends and brothers, this diversity of opinion causes no harm.

How great, finally, was the authority of the Hebrew codices among Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Eucherius of Lyons, and the other later writers of the Latin tongue would be superfluous to note here. I know no learned man who does not admit that the Fathers mentioned above always assigned the first place in authority among the divine books to the Hebrew truth. And unless I am mistaken, the matter has been demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently in our little works, recently published in defense of the Latin Vulgate and the Hebrew truth. To these works we gladly refer all who delight in the sight of simple and pure truth, rather than in the painted face of falsehood and the seductions of eloquence.

I would also have the reader consult what we explained above in the second prolegomenon, nos. 4 and 5. For there the very great authority enjoyed by the sacred Hebrew codices among Gregory the Great and in the Gallican churches is made entirely clear.

As we conclude this brief inquiry, we should warn the learned reader that the Hebrew text was expressly called “the Hebrew truth” by both Greek authors and Latin Fathers. Thus Origen, in the passage cited above; likewise Procopius; and Euthymius in his preface to the Psalms. Among the Latins, Jerome everywhere holds the citadel of the Hebrew truth; Augustine, in book XVIII, chapter 44, of *The City of God*, and in his *Questions on the Heptateuch*, of which we spoke earlier; Bede; Albinus; Joseph, abbot and his disciple; Rabanus Maurus; Agobard; Claudius of Turin; Stephen of Civerci; and countless others more recent than these.

## IV.

The exposition of the individual divisions of the canon is easy and straightforward, because Jerome distinctly and fully described its three constituent orders in the *Galeate Prologue* to the Scriptures, which he prefixed to the four books of Kings and which we have also published at the head of those books. Nevertheless, lest we seem merely to repeat what has already been done, we shall discuss certain matters concerning this canon that have not yet been treated in our disputations, notes, or prolegomena.

The Jews therefore divided all Scripture into three parts: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa. The first class, or first order, which they call *Thora*, that is, the Law, contains the five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

Among the Jews all these books take their names from their beginnings. Thus Genesis is called *Bresith*, because the first word of this book in the Hebrew text is *Beresith*, meaning “In the beginning.” Likewise they call Exodus *Elle-smoth*, or Οὐελλεσμὼθ, *Vellesmoth*, as Origen reads it in his commentary on Psalm I. For the first words in the book of Exodus are אלה שמות, *Vellesmoth*, which is interpreted, “And these are the names,” or “These are the names.”

Leviticus is called *Vajicra*; in Origen, Οὐικρὰ, *Vikra*; in Jerome, *Vajecra*. In Hebrew it is written ויקרא. This means, “And he called.”

The fourth book of Moses, which we call Numbers, begins with the word וידבר, *Vajedabber*, and is called by the Hebrews by the same name. For what Origen noted concerning the book of Numbers in Psalm I does not concern its first word, but rather the subject treated in it, as we said in the notes to the *Galeate Prologue*, column 318.

Finally, the fifth book of the Mosaic Law is called *Elle addabarim*, or, according to Origen, Ἕλλε ἁδδεβαρὶμ, *Helle haddebarim*. For in Hebrew it begins with אלה הדברים, *Elle haddebarim*, that is, “These are the words.”

This is the first part of the canon of the Hebrew truth, constituted by the Pentateuch of Moses.

The second part, or second order, of the books of the canon embraces all the prophets, namely the Former and the Latter Prophets, as they are called by the Jews: נביאים ראשונים, *Neviim rischonim*, and נביאים אחרונים, *Neviim ahharonim*.

The Former Prophets are four: the books bearing the titles Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and *Malachim*, that is, Kings. The Latter Prophets likewise constitute four volumes: I, Isaiah; II, Jeremiah; III, Ezekiel; IV, the Twelve Minor Prophets together.

The second class therefore contains eight books in the canon of the Hebrew truth. Yet the book of Ruth is included in a single volume together with the book of Judges, which among the Hebrews is called שופטים, *Sophtim*, or, according to Origen, Σωφετἰμ, *Sophetim*.

The third and final order contains the Hagiographa, which the Hebrews call כתובים, *Kethuvim*, that is, “Writings”—not common writings, but sacred writings, and , *beruahh haccodesch*, “by the Holy Spirit,” committed to writing through the immediate breathing of the Holy Spirit. Consult Maimonides, *More Nevochim*, part II, chapter 45.

The Hagiographa are counted as nine: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Daniel, Paralipomena, Ezra, and Esther. In Origen, the book of Psalms is entitled σέφερ θιλλὶμ, *Sepher thillim*, and Proverbs bears the title μισλὼθ, *Misloth*. We note this so that the varying forms in which these names are read among ancient writers may not escape us. For in Jerome they are read differently, namely *Sephar tallim* and *Masaloth*, or *Masloth*. For the rest, see the scholia on the *Galeate Prologue*.

Our Savior Christ the Lord mentions this division of sacred Scripture into three principal parts in Luke 24:44: “For it is necessary,” he says, “that all things be fulfilled which are written in the Law of Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms, concerning me.” Here “the Psalms” stands for all the Hagiographa, which constitute the third class of the books of the canon. For the greater part of the prophecies and the clearer oracles concerning Christ are read in advance in the Psalms. Therefore Christ named the book of Psalms as the nobler part of the order of the Hagiographa.

Elsewhere, in Luke 16:16, he names only two parts, saying: “The Law and the Prophets were until John.” Just as we see the Psalms omitted in this passage, so it should not seem strange that Christ referred to the series of the Hagiographa by naming only one book of that order.

It should also be noted that elsewhere, by synecdoche, an entire part of Scripture is put for one book belonging to that part. Thus in John 6:45 it is said: “It is written in the Prophets,” although the testimony quoted by John is found in a single volume of Isaiah, chapter 54, verse 13. By saying “in the Prophets,” the evangelist understands the second class of the books of the canon—namely, the part containing the Prophets.

The same occurs in Acts 13:40: “See, therefore, lest what is spoken in the Prophets come upon you.” For the passage cited there is taken from Habakkuk, chapter 1, verse 5, not from all the prophets. Yet he said “in the Prophets” because he was referring to that part of Scripture which comprises all the prophetic books and is called the order of the Prophets.

We shall add nothing further here, for the purpose of proving that ancient division of the Scriptures into three principal parts, from Josephus, the vernacular Jewish writer, or from the Masoretic commentaries. We believe it sufficient to have brought forward authorities deriving from Christ and the apostles. Whoever wishes to learn more about this subject should consult the Buxtorfs, Bonfrère, and many other commentators who have written introductory essays toward the understanding of the sacred Scriptures.

## V.

The hatred with which Rufinus pursued Jerome at one point persuaded that calumniator that certain parts of Scripture had been cut out of the book of Daniel and cast aside by the holy Doctor. Thus he accuses him in *Against Jerome*, book II:

> That entire story of Susanna, which offered the churches of God an example of chastity, was cut out, cast aside, and disregarded by this man.

He makes similar complaints about the song of the Hebrew youths in the furnace of blazing fire:

> The hymn of the three youths, which is sung above all on solemn days in the Church of God, was completely erased by this man from its proper place.

A recent writer not only imitated this ignorant criticism of Rufinus but, piling calumny upon calumny, dared to assert that the Church of Christ had corrected Jerome’s version and restored to the canon those parts of Daniel which Jerome, under a Jewish understanding and rabbinic influence, had cut away.

To these and similar insults the holy translator replies:

> As for what I report concerning what the Hebrews customarily say against the story of Susanna, the hymn of the three youths, and the tales of Bel and the dragon—which are not found in the Hebrew volume—the man who accuses me proves himself a foolish sycophant. For I did not explain what I myself thought, but what they customarily say against us.

And further:

> I ask you, dearest friend, who are so curious that you know even my dreams, and who summon as evidence against me everything I wrote over so many years without fear of future slander: how can you respond without knowing the prefaces to the books which you accuse? Those prefaces, by a kind of prophecy, answered the future slander, fulfilling the proverb: “The antidote before the poison.”

Certainly, from Jerome’s own preface to Daniel, translated from Hebrew into Latin, it is plainly evident that Rufinus and his modern followers had not read the prologues of the books which they invoke in condemnation. Does Jerome not testify there that he had placed those parts which are not found in Hebrew beneath obelus marks?

> I report this, he says, to show you the difficulty of Daniel, who among the Hebrews has neither the story of Susanna, nor the hymn of the three youths, nor the tales of Bel and the dragon. Since these are dispersed throughout the whole world, we appended them, setting an obelus before them to mark them as slain, lest among the unlearned we might seem to have mutilated a large part of the volume.

Whoever therefore imputes a Jewish disposition to Jerome proves himself a foolish sycophant, since he does not know that in his Latin translation of Daniel, as well as in the hymn of the three youths and the story of Susanna, the holy Doctor assigned those parts their proper place, and mutilated nothing belonging to them—not even in his commentaries on Daniel.

Let those detractors therefore hear the most learned man elegantly descending into the defense of his own case in the preface to the commentaries just mentioned:

> Thus, many years ago, when we translated Daniel, we marked these visions beforehand with an obelus, indicating that they are not found in Hebrew. And I am astonished that certain faultfinders should grow indignant with me, as though I had shortened the book, etc.

Thus Rufinus and his Amasius now prove themselves faultfinders indeed when they assert that the story of Susanna was cut out and disregarded by Jerome, and that the Church of Christ consequently came to the aid of that defect when it gave the faithful the Latin Vulgate for use.

For the pious and properly educated, however, I should like it observed that the hymn of the three youths, the story of Susanna, and the other story of Bel and the dragon were taken not from the Septuagint translators—whose version, by the Church’s sound judgment, was rejected throughout the whole book of Daniel—but from Theodotion, although he was an Ebionite and semi-Jew, because his translation was found to agree with the truth, whereas the version circulating under the name of the Seventy Translators differed greatly from the truth.

And so that everyone may be convinced that the Catholic Church adheres in every respect to Jerome in its Latin edition of Daniel, whoever wishes may compare, in Carus the theologian, the variant readings of the Song of Azariah from verse 26 through verse 45. There he will find many differences in the old edition from what is read in the Vulgate and in the canon of the Hebrew truth published by us.

Furthermore, the annotations of Jerome inserted within the text of Daniel provide the clearest evidence that the Roman Church follows no other version in the book of Daniel than Jerome’s, expressed partly from Hebrew and partly from Theodotion.

The obelus marks with which Jerome prefixed signs to all those deuterocanonical portions of Daniel must now be considered carefully in the book of Daniel. First, it must be understood that through the negligence of scribes those signs were removed from many manuscript books. This carelessness of copyists is so old that Jerome complains of it two or three times in Letter 135:

> When those signs, through the negligence of copyists, are left by most people as though they were superfluous, great error arises in reading.

Nevertheless, several codices remain that retain obeli prefixed both to the earlier additions to Daniel and to the appendices of Esther.

The Royal manuscript of the sacred Bibles, commonly called the Codex of Saint-Maur, numbered 3561 and CCXXII, carefully retains all these obelus marks in the hymn of the three youths in the book of Daniel. Likewise, the splendid exemplar of the Colbert Library, no. 1, formerly given to Charles the Bald by the monks of Saint-Martin of Tours, has those little strokes marked in the same place in Daniel, and indeed at the head of every line.

This is not the case with the exemplars of the canon of the Hebrew truth, in which the negligence of copyists and scribes has caused such signs to be omitted. An exception is the Royal exemplar numbered 3564, which did not completely discard all the obelus marks. It has four or five of them written at the head, middle, and end of the columns, beneath which it intended to include individual lines of these portions of Daniel.

As for the story of Susanna and that of Bel, I have so far been unable to find any manuscript codex in which the obelus marks had not been omitted, although Jerome explicitly testified that these visions had been marked with obeli so that the reader might be warned that they are not found in Hebrew. Why these sections were called “visions” by ancient writers, whereas we today call them “chapters,” will be explained more conveniently below.

Second, it should be noted that the form of the obeli is not uniform merely in different manuscript codices, but even within the same codices. Thus the Colbert manuscript mentioned above retains these signs throughout Jerome’s Psalter with two dots, one above and the other below, in this form: ÷. In the additions to Daniel and Esther, however, it represents the same mark as a transverse stroke—without any dot: —.

The Royal manuscript no. 3561 likewise has an obelus decorated with dots in the hymn of Daniel: ÷. But at the end of Esther it displays only a lying stroke—without accompanying dots—a practice imitated by the Corbie manuscript no. 1. The other manuscripts of Saint-Germain in our possession and the Memmian canon mark the final portions of Esther with obeli furnished with a double dot, upper and lower: ÷. The same obelus signs provided with two dots are seen in the Origenian edition of the book of Esther produced from the Arundel Library.

The prudent reader must take care not to confuse with the obelus the abbreviated mark commonly used in manuscripts, since the two have exactly the same shape. Ancient copyists and scribes use this character, ÷, for the word *est*, the third-person singular of the substantive verb *sum*. Thus we often read:

> Et ÷ sensus,

meaning:

> Et est sensus—“And the meaning is.”

Likewise:

> Quis ÷ in vobis,

for:

> Quis est in vobis—“Who is among you?”

And so in countless other places, according to the preference of ancient scribes, who for roughly seven hundred years, more or less, took care to copy books.

Moreover, the obelus signs in the additions to Daniel and Esther could not everywhere occupy their proper places in this present edition of ours, because the practice of modern scribes or printers does not allow the same arrangement of pages and columns that is represented in manuscript codices.

In manuscripts the obeli are always prefixed to the heads of verses or individual lines of the sacred text, both in the second column of a page and in the first. They leave sufficient space between the columns, and in that space they write the obeli continuously. In printed books, by contrast, there is nothing between the columns except capital letters distinguishing the columns or divisions of the text. The laws of modern typography would permit nothing else to be placed in the middle except the letters just mentioned or a line descending from the top to the bottom of the page.

Therefore, compelled by necessity, and unwilling to introduce a new arrangement among printers, we judged it preferable always to write the obelus signs in the outer margin: in the first column at the head of each line of Scripture, and in the second column at the end of the lines. In each case the point of the obelus is turned toward the text, signifying, in Jerome’s usage, that such portions—which are absent from Hebrew exemplars—are to be struck through.

Finally, concerning the obelus signs, we should also warn the reader that the signs which we have placed in the margins of the books of Samuel and Solomon’s Proverbs differ from the Hieronymian signs discussed above.

For our obelus signs do not signify that anything additional or superfluous exists in the text which we have published in the books of Kings and Proverbs. Rather, they indicate to all learned readers that in these places the Latin Vulgate contains something redundant and borrowed from the Septuagint translators, something not found either in Jerome’s pure version or in the Hebrew source.

No one should therefore understand the use of our obeli indiscriminately, supposing it to be the same as that which Jerome uses in the translation of Daniel and Esther. For our obeli indicate certain verses that are absent; the others point out present sentences of Scripture that have been, as it were, struck through by a spear placed before them, and they serve as a reminder of this.

## VI.

In this present section we raise a question of no small importance, asking who was the first author of the marginal scholia which we find placed in copies of the canon of the Hebrew truth, and what usefulness and excellence such annotations possess.

I considered that nothing should be done before confessing that I had once been mistaken about the author of the scholia, whom I supposed to have been Jerome himself—not without some resemblance to the truth. I knew that the same holy Doctor, in Letter 135, had warned that annotations were sometimes added beside the text for the instruction of readers, but that through the rashness or ignorance of copyists they had been placed in the body of the text.

When, therefore, I discovered learned marginal scholia consonant with the Hebrew truth that had been transferred into the sacred text of Scripture, I readily persuaded myself that the same thing had happened repeatedly as Jerome complains in the letter already mentioned, concerning Psalm 73, verse 8, where he says:

> In the Greek it is written καταπαύσωμεν, and we translated it in this way: “Let us cause all the feast days of God to cease from the earth.” And I am astonished that some rash person thought that our annotation, which we wrote beside the text for the instruction of the reader, should be written into the body of the text. We wrote it in this form: “It does not have καταπαύσωμεν, as some think, but κατακαύσωμεν, that is, ‘Let us burn.’”

And again, in the same place:

> Therefore, if anything has been added beside the text for the sake of study, it ought not to be placed in the body, lest it disturb the earlier translation according to the will of the scribes.

Moreover, I noticed another example of the same rashness of copyists—or perhaps rather of their ignorance—in Letter 142, addressed to Pope Damasus. For in one very ancient Colbert manuscript of the Letters of Saint Jerome I found a certain marginal annotation added beside the text, which in another manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Cyran is found inserted into the body of the text.

Jerome was instructing the Roman pontiff concerning the ineffable name of God, which among the Hebrews is the tetragrammaton, יהוה. He observed the matter in this way:

> The Lord himself is also here a name of four letters, which is properly used of God: JOD, HE, JOD, HE; that is, two JAs, which when doubled produce that ineffable and glorious name of God.

But, having imitated the error of the Greeks, who read the four-letter name יהוה as ΠΙΠΙ, *Pipi*, Jerome immediately corrected both himself and them by adding this annotation beside the text:

> In place of the second JOD, VAV is better read, so that it is JAO.

The Colbert manuscript therefore retains this marginal scholion in its proper place, written in a very small character, and places the sign of correction after the words “that is, two JAs.” But the Saint-Cyran manuscript confuses the cited passage with the annotation in this manner:

> The Lord himself is also here a name of four letters, which is properly used of God: JOD, HE, JOD, HE. In place of the second JOD, VAV is better read, so that it is JAO; that is, two JAs, which when doubled produce that ineffable and glorious name of God.

These words have no meaning because, through the rashness of some copyist, the annotation was placed in the body of the text.

If anyone should nevertheless form the opinion that the erroneous reading of God’s name, יהוה, *Jehova*, or *Adonai*, proceeded from Jerome, while the correction of that same error was supplied by another writer, let him remember that Jerome himself correctly expressed the name with its letters in Letter 136 to Marcella:

> The ninth name of God, τετραγράμματον, which they considered ἀνεκφώνητον, that is, ineffable, is written with these letters: JOD, HE, VAV, HE. Some, not understanding this because of the similarity of the elements, when they find it in Greek books, have become accustomed to reading it *pipi*.

You see that Jerome was not ignorant that the tetragrammaton, the name of God, was composed of *jod* and *vav* with a double *he*, not of two JAs, as he said above—that is, of a double *jod* together with a double *he*.

Nor should you doubt about the reading *Jao*: it is Jerome’s own. For in his commentaries on the prophets he sometimes read the tetragrammaton יהוה as *Jao*—if I remember correctly what, in my own negligence at the time, I failed to note on my papers.

In the commentary on the Psalms, which learned men attribute to the same Jerome, we read the following concerning God’s name, at Psalm VIII, “O Lord, our Lord”:

> The first name of the Lord among the Hebrews consists of four letters: JOD, HE, VAV, HE. It properly signifies the name of God and can be read JAHO; and the Hebrews think it ἄῤῥητον, that is, ineffable. The second, ADONAI, is common to all; it is often used even of human beings.

I took this passage from four very ancient manuscript codices of our Corbie monastery, two numbered 135 and 136, one from Cluny, and another from the Sorbonne. All of them write the Greek word ἄῤῥητον with Latin characters, namely *arreton*, which means “ineffable.”

Moreover, they do not read corruptly, as the printed editions do, that name יהוה, *Jehova*, but *Jaho*, according to the usage of the ancients—or rather *Jao*, without aspiration in the middle, so that it is Ἰαῶ, the Greek form found in Diodorus, book I of the *Bibliotheca Historica*:

> παρὰ δὲ Ἰουδαίοις Μωσῆν τὸντοῖς ἐπικαλούμενον Θεὸν

“Among the Jews, Moses calls God Jao,” etc.

Hence you may see that Drusius rightly observed in chapter 21, concerning the name *Jehova*:

> In the Frobenian edition, which is better in every respect, it is read not *Jehova* but *Jao*. I have no doubt, he says, that this reading is genuine. Ignorant rashness has substituted a recent form for the ancient one—that is, a corrupt form for the true one.

For the same tetragrammaton, יהוה, *Jehova*, *Jaho*, or *Jao*, consult the *Disputation* of the aforementioned Drusius.

But beware, I ask, of the most foolish reading of that same glorious name, which appears in this form in the commentaries of Procopius of Gaza on Exodus 6:

> Moreover, you have gained a greater knowledge of me, since I demonstrated to you my tetragrammaton name, which is ineffable to all others except priests and which was inscribed upon the golden mitre. These are the four letters from which that name is formed: *jod*, *aleph*, *fau*, *thet*. This name signifies the perpetual life and eternity of God.

Whoever produced this reading of the four-letter name יהוה, which is called ineffable, was utterly ignorant of the Hebrew language, presenting it so corruptly as to say that the second letter was *aleph* and the fourth *thet*, although both are *he*, even among those who possess the slightest knowledge of Hebrew letters.

But let us now return to the point from which we digressed.

I regarded Jerome himself as the author of the scholia of the canon in the annotations to my *Prodromus*, page 83, and also in the notes to this divine Library, columns 160 and 164. The cause of this error now seems to me to have been the rashness of ancient copyists, who did not hesitate to place in the body of the text several brief annotations by that holy Doctor which he himself had added beside it.

When I saw that the same thing had also been done in the scholia just mentioned, it was easy for me to believe that those scholia had proceeded from Jerome, especially because they had been added by a man highly skilled in the Hebrew language beside the translations of Saint Jerome.

Furthermore, a similar degree of learning in several places, together with precisely the same style, suggested a single author. For writings that preserve the same form of letters everywhere are believed to have been written by one and the same hand.

Whatever excuse I may have for my error, however, it is still an error, and I must now correct it chiefly on the basis of the arguments that follow.

All learned men will acknowledge that the scholiast of the Canon of Hebrew Truth is a different person from Saint Jerome, once they have established that the scholia of the Canon and the *Hebrew Questions* on the Books of Kings and Chronicles have one and the same author—works published among Jerome’s writings by Erasmus and Mariano Victorio. For since Rabanus Maurus makes it entirely clear that the writer of the *Questions* or *Traditions* on the Books of Kings is someone other than Saint Jerome, who published the *Hebrew Traditions* on Genesis for us, it will follow that Jerome and the anonymous scholiast are different men, provided that we demonstrate that the scholiast of the Canon is the same person who wrote the *Hebrew Traditions* on the Books of Kings.

To prove this, we need only compare the scholia with the aforementioned *Hebrew Questions*: in both places there is the same learning, the same phrases, and precisely the same words in the observations. We might reasonably suppose that these observations were transferred either from the *Hebrew Questions* to the margins of copies of the Canon, or from those margins into the books of the *Hebrew Questions*. One circumstance somewhat opposes this view: there are many scholia that do not occur in the *Hebrew Traditions*, although they do occur in copies of the Canon of Hebrew Truth.

The first point that the author of the *Questions* or *Traditions* on the Books of Samuel observes from the Hebrew concerns the variant reading at 1 Kings [1 Samuel] 1:5: “But to Hannah he gave one portion, being sad.” “In Hebrew,” he says, “it is read thus: ‘But to Hannah he gave one double portion, because he loved Hannah.’” The scholia of the Canon, placed beside the same verse in column 326 of our edition, have the same reading.

Again, at verse 24 of this chapter he attacks the reading of the Latin manuscripts—that is, Jerome’s translation—and attempts to show that it is corrupt, saying:

> In Hebrew it is read not “three measures of flour,” but “a measure of flour”; this passage is evidently corrupted among the Latins through the fault of the scribes. For if he offered three measures of flour together with three calves, he acted contrary to the precept of the Law . . . . From this it is understood that Elkanah did not offer three measures of flour with three calves, but nine-tenths, which, according to the Hebrew measure, make one *ephah*.

In the scholia of the Canon the same author had written: “and a measure of flour.” But the person who copied these scholia into our Saint-Germain manuscript erased the word “three” from the sacred text and thought that the annotation should be placed within the text, leaving the letter *h* in the margin, so that from it the reader might be reminded that the Hebrew has: “and a measure of flour.”

From this it is demonstrated most clearly that the author of the scholia of the Canon and of the *Hebrew Traditions* in the Books of Kings was one and the same. He was plainly different, however, from Saint Jerome, who always translates the Hebrew word *ephah* as “three measures,” “three *seahs*,” and so forth, as is evident from Ruth 2:17 and from Book XIV of his *Commentaries on Ezekiel*. I quoted the relevant words below in our notes on this passage in Samuel, column 327.

In chapter 2 of the First Book of Kings [1 Samuel], at verse 5, this marginal scholion, “*h.* seven,” is placed beside the words “she bore many.” Similarly, beside the eighth verse, next to the words “the foundations of the earth,” the following is written: “*h.* For the afflicted of the earth belong to the Lord.” The author of the *Traditions* on the Books of Kings therefore by no means omitted such marginal scholia. He accordingly informed the diligent reader:

> In Hebrew and in the Septuagint translation it is read not “many,” but “seven.”

And shortly afterward:

> In Hebrew it is thus: “For the afflicted of the earth belong to the Lord.” By “the afflicted of the earth,” the Hebrews understand the poor in spirit and the humble in heart, over whom they say that the Lord has established the world; for they believe that through their merits the earth stands.

I do not doubt that very many people can be found who would judge Jerome’s Latin translation worthy of correction on the basis of such observations by the anonymous Hebrew. But if they remember that it is the rule of a good translator to express the *idiomata* of another language through the distinctive usage of his own language, they will rather marvel at our greatest interpreter of Scripture, who rendered “seven” as “many” in accordance with Latin usage. “For the number seven,” says Procopius of Gaza in commenting on this passage, “denotes multitude.”

Furthermore, when our Hebrew scholiast claims that the source has “For the afflicted of the earth belong to the Lord,” I do not know whether the Hebrew words *metsuqe eres* signify “the afflicted of the earth” more than “the foundations and supports of the earth.” Whatever the grammatical meaning of those words may be, it is certain that the Jews, together with the scholiast, agree—at least in their mystical interpretation—with Jerome’s meaning. For if the world stands through the merits of the humble and afflicted, then without doubt those people are the supports on which the whole world rests.

Now, if you seek the very same words in the scholiast and in the author of the *Traditions*, you should consult this passage, 1 Kings [1 Samuel] 10:25:

> Samuel spoke to the people the law of the kingdom.

There both have: “the Hebrew has ‘the judgment of the kingdom,’” observing nothing beyond the grammatical meaning of the word *mishpat* [*misphat*]. The same should be understood of the linen ephod below, chapter 22, verse 18, and of the city of Maon, chapter 25, verse 2, as well as of very many other passages. In them the scholiast does not depart from himself even by a finger’s breadth—that is, he does not depart from the author of the *Hebrew Traditions*.

And so that the scholiast may become known to you not merely from more beautiful features, but also from his own blemishes, observe carefully what is read below in column 363, where we corrected that author and our scholiast in the notes because he did not approve Jerome’s interpretation at 1 Samuel 30:10 and 21. For that Hebrew writer thinks that the word *piggeru* should be rendered in Latin “they had been ordered,” not “they had stopped because they were weary.” In this he has no supporter among the modern Hebrew grammarians, nor in the seven-language lexicon of the Oriental languages. Here, then, we have manifest evidence that the Hebrew author assigns a special and proper meaning to that word, both in the scholia and in his own *Hebrew Questions*. The same person, therefore, must be regarded as the author who placed the scholia in the margins of Jerome’s translation and who published the *Hebrew Questions* on the Books of Kings and Chronicles.

Let us now inquire when he flourished in the study of Scripture, and from where he derived his lineage.

Only a few days ago I learned from Rabanus Maurus that the author of the *Hebrew Questions* on the Books of Kings and Chronicles was a certain Hebrew who, in the eighth or ninth century, was especially celebrated for his use and understanding of the Holy Scriptures. Whether he was Hebrew by birth and descended from the Jewish people, however, is not sufficiently clear from Rabanus’s prefaces. For, according to the custom of those times, the basis of the name may remain uncertain: many people were not called by their proper names, but others often assigned them fictitious designations derived from their character or intellect.

Thus our John Mabillon, in volume I of the *Ancient Analecta*, page 370, admits that Cuculus, Menalcas, and Daphnis are substitute names rather than their real names, of the sort customarily used by Alcuin and Theodulf, bishop of Orléans. He says that it was impossible to know who Menalcas, Daphnis, or Cuculus had been, except that he thinks Cuculus was that prodigal son whose excesses and downfall Alcuin laments in letters 103 and 114.

In this way a learned man in the Hebrew language could be called a “Hebrew,” even though by origin he was a Gaul or a German. Certainly, if he was Jewish by nation, it is nevertheless clear to us from the words quoted below that he believed in Christ.

Concerning the author of the *Hebrew Questions*, or *Traditions*, on the Books of Kings and Chronicles, Rabanus Maurus says the following in the preface to his *Commentaries on the Four Books of Kings*:

> There he will find what Father Augustine, what Jerome, the distinguished interpreter of the divine books, thought; what the blessed pope and most gentle teacher Gregory thought; what Isidore, bishop of Seville, thought; and what Bede, that noble teacher, and the other Fathers rightly understood—whose names it would take too long to list . . . . Moreover, in many places I have inserted the tradition of the Hebrews concerning the Law, belonging to a certain Hebrew who flourished in our own times in knowledge of the Law, together with a note of his name—not as though I were imposing his authority on anyone, but simply reporting what I found written, leaving its verification to the judgment of the reader.

I wished to restore this passage, which is altogether corrupt, on the authority of Rabanus’s manuscript copies. But no book of this kind has been found in our Saint-Germain Library, if what our associate assured me is true—he is the person who keeps such monuments under lock and key and preserves them. Nevertheless, the difficulty of restoring the text or grasping the meaning of Maurus’s words is not insuperable here, because what he wrote about the Hebrew in this passage he taught again in the preface to his *Commentaries on the Books of Chronicles*, saying:

> For I have decided to write not long and florid treatises, in which eloquent discourse plays attractively, but commentaries on the divine Histories, whose function is to pass over what is obvious and discuss what is obscure. Some years ago, at the request of Abbot Hildon, I published four books of commentaries on the Books of Kings, according to the understanding of the Catholic Fathers. I personally presented them in our monastery to your most sacred father, the Emperor Louis. In them, as in the present work, I inserted in many places the account of Josephus, the Jewish historian, and the opinions of a certain Hebrew who flourished in our own times in knowledge of the Law—not in such a way as to force an unwilling reader to assent to their traditions, but rather leaving these matters to his judgment and examination.

From these statements it is clear that Rabanus Maurus is to be understood in the first testimony as saying that he inserted in many places of his commentaries on the Books of Kings chapters belonging to a certain Hebrew who flourished in his own time in knowledge of the Law and whose chapters contained Hebrew tradition.

Anyone who notices the opinions and entire sections of the *Hebrew Questions* on the Books of Kings and Chronicles placed in Rabanus’s expositions and commentaries, and compares the commentaries of Maurus with the traditions of the Hebrew, will find this indisputable.

Who, then, the scholiast of the Canon was, and at what time he lived, is established with certainty by the two testimonies of Rabanus Maurus cited above. He was called by Rabanus a Hebrew who was considerably celebrated in knowledge of the Law, whose commentaries and *Hebrew Questions* deserved to take their place among the judgments of Jerome, Augustine, and other most distinguished teachers in the Church of Christ.

He flourished in the study of the divine Scriptures at the same time as Alcuin and Rabanus Maurus. For by “our own times” Maurus means the period in which he himself was living, as is shown by the preface, or dedicatory letter, to his *Commentaries on the Book of Genesis*. There he calls the age of Freculphus—the man to whom he writes and offers his preface—the present time:

> It was formerly the endeavor of great men, by writing to one another, to provoke their studies and exercise their intellects. Although you have decided in the present age to act after their example, you are nevertheless to be admired in this respect: you have not sought a suitable person for this endeavor.

By “the present age,” therefore, Maurus understands the very period in which he was writing his commentaries on Genesis at the request of Bishop Freculphus. Accordingly, similar phrases occurring in the prefaces to the commentaries on the Books of Kings and Chronicles are likewise to be understood of the age of the Hebrew who published the marginal scholia of the Canon of Hebrew Truth and the *Hebrew Traditions*: the end of the eighth century or the beginning of the ninth.

These, then, are the “present times” of Rabanus Maurus, in which he testifies that the writer flourished whose material he borrows and inserts so extensively into his commentaries.

However familiar the period of that Hebrew scholiast and commentator may be to us, his origin nevertheless remains uncertain. When Maurus joins him with Josephus the Jewish historian in the preface to his commentaries on Chronicles, he may perhaps have wished to list the two writers together in order to teach us that both were Jews.

But the marginal scholion of the Canon of Hebrew Truth in column 170 strongly opposes this view. There the author of these annotations, following the custom of the Latins, says that in the Hebrew text, at Numbers 17:6, it reads:

> “And there were twelve rods, with Aaron’s rod.”

But in the Latin manuscripts—which he calls “ours,” following the custom of Jerome and Augustine—it is written:

> “And there were twelve rods, apart from Aaron’s rod.”

“The Hebrew,” he says, “has ‘with’; ours, ‘apart from’”—that is, the Hebrew text reads “with Aaron’s rod,” while our Latin manuscripts read “apart from Aaron’s rod.”

Anyone who examines the works of the holy Fathers knows well that men of the Latin language used no other expressions when reporting variant readings of the divine Scriptures. It would be superfluous to gather examples here for a matter certain and obvious to every diligent reader.

It remains, then, for us to say that the Hebrew scholiast called the Latin manuscripts “ours” either because he was descended from Latin-speaking people, or because, believing in Christ, he thereafter wished to call the books of the Roman Church “ours,” together with the other faithful.

“But how do you know,” some reader may ask, “that this scholiast and author of the *Hebrew Traditions* gave his allegiance to Christ?”

The Hebrew writer himself supplied the clearest proof of his religious and Christian faith. In his *Hebrew Questions* on 1 Kings [1 Samuel], chapter 21, he reveals his faith in these words:

> The Hebrews relate that David certainly did not eat those loaves; but the Lord says otherwise in the Gospel.

He therefore acknowledges Christ as his Lord, and the Gospel as his authority, even when it contradicts the traditions of the Jews.

Moreover, when he mentions certain matters concerning the Hebrews in chapter 16 of the First Book of Kings [1 Samuel], he treats them as foreigners and strangers to himself. “In Hebrew,” he says, “it is thus: ‘And you shall visit your brothers, to see whether they are doing well, and you shall take their pledges.’” In this passage the Hebrews understand “pledges” to mean bills of repudiation [divorce documents].

For they say that it was the custom of that people, when their men went to war, to give their wives bills of repudiation, so that if the husband happened to be captured in battle and led away into captivity, his wife, after waiting three years, could take another husband if her own husband did not return.

Let the prudent reader now observe how clearly the Hebrew scholiast, the author of the *Hebrew Questions* on the Books of Kings, presents the Jewish people as alien to himself. He did not say, “For it was the custom of our people,” which a Jewish man would certainly have said. Rather, speaking as though of foreigners, he says: “For they say that it was the custom of that people.”

He acknowledges nothing belonging to his own nation, nothing domestic, in the traditions of the Jews—even though those traditions concern Hebrew women in the matter of the bill of repudiation.

I could also make it clear to the reader, from other chapters of the same *Hebrew Questions* on the Books of Kings and Chronicles, that the scholiast of the Canon of Hebrew Truth was a Christian. But as I hasten to the end of these Prolegomena, a few examples may suffice in place of many, especially since the same difficulty will return for discussion in the other volume.

Nevertheless, before we remove our hand from this tablet, let us briefly touch upon the usefulness of the marginal scholia of the Canon.

Among the chief benefits of the marginal scholia of the Canon of Hebrew Truth, I count first the fact that they furnish us with weapons for refuting the heterodox of our own age, who have repeatedly insulted the Church of God on account of her alleged ignorance of the Hebrew language. They say that no Roman after Jerome’s time was found to know Hebrew, and that all Catholics therefore adhered to the Vulgate version as though with their eyes closed, lacking the ability to expose and correct its “errors,” as they call them.

Let those detractors learn, then, that the Roman Church has never lacked men learned in Hebrew who, handling the Latin manuscripts of the Vulgate every day, could have publicly reproved and corrected it if anything contrary to sound doctrine or holy morals had been found there.

How carefully, do you suppose, did the scholiast of the Canon examine Jerome’s translation? There was no little word, syllable, or letter that escaped the judgment of that learned writer. Yet he always preserved the honor of the Vulgate, or Jerome’s version, which he had decided merely to illuminate with critical notes, not to corrupt or efface through hostility or censorious arrogance.

Everywhere our Hebrew Christian observes that this or that expression is not present in the Hebrew. Yet for that reason he does not remove from the sacred text such redundant Latin words, which he knew had been added by the Latin translator in order to complete the idiomatic requirements of the Latin language in Scripture.

If you judge this opinion trivial, listen to the scholiast himself writing in his brief commentary on the Song of Deborah:

> But where it says, “O Amalek,” this is not read in Hebrew; the Latin translator added it for the sake of the meaning.

He had doubtless read Jerome’s letter to Sunnia and Fretela, in which the holy man discusses verse 38 of Psalm 77 [78] in the following way:

> Likewise: “And he was merciful toward their sins, and did not destroy them.” You say that the Greek does not have “them,” and this is true. But we completed the Latin expression according to its own idiom, so that the sentence would not remain suspended.

And indeed, what could sound more obscure throughout the volumes of the Latin biblical manuscripts than those suspended sentences in which certain words—such as nouns or the substantive verb—were omitted?

For example, the scholiast notes at Leviticus 19:14 that the Hebrew does not have “because” or “I am.” Nevertheless, these words complete the idiom of our language, for the sentence is beautifully expressed: “But you shall fear your God, because I am the Lord.” The meaning is not equally complete if we read: “But you shall fear your God, I the Lord.” The sentence is in some sense suspended because of the absence of the causal particle “because” and of the substantive verb “am.”

Thus those words that are said to be absent from the Hebrew books throughout the entire Canon are not known to have been added superfluously in the Latin version, since without them the sentence would remain obscure or mutilated. This will become clear to the attentive reader whenever, having been alerted by the marginal scholion “the Hebrew does not have,” he directs his attention to the surrounding discourse.

I also consider the scholia of the Canon to possess another considerable benefit: through them we can silence those who have dared to misuse numerous testimonies of Scripture and twist them to their own meaning, to their own destruction and that of others.

Certain writers of this age claim so much for themselves that they hope to overthrow the Church’s most widely received and celebrated tradition through frivolous interpretations of Scripture. They expect readers to believe their own inventions rather than the oracle of Christ who bears witness.

Thus one may see pernicious works written both in Latin and in French, in which the authors obstinately deny that Moses was the author of the books of the Pentateuch. To prove this against the authority of Christ and his apostles, they cite several passages, especially from Deuteronomy, by which they wish to support the opinion of their perverse and hitherto unheard-of doctrine.

“It is written,” they say, “at Deuteronomy 1:1: ‘These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan’; and again at 3:8: ‘At that time we took from the hand of the two kings of the Amorites the land that was beyond the Jordan.’”

But it is inconsistent with these words having been written by Moses himself, since he never crossed the Jordan, and the Amorite kings, with respect to him, lived not beyond but on this side of the Jordan.

If we object that the Hebrew text reads *be-ever* [*be‘ever*], a word that is altogether ambiguous and can, depending on the context, be applied either to the nearer or to the farther side, they press their argument further, saying that all the ancients who knew the Hebrew language always translate it “beyond.”

Yet whether they wish it or not, the author of Deuteronomy was Moses himself. And the modern critics have no further room for their rashness, since the marginal scholia of the Canon of Hebrew Truth demonstrate most clearly that the Hebrew word *be‘ever* should not be rendered “beyond,” but “in the crossing” or “at the passage.”

Read and understood in this way, the passage agrees perfectly with Moses speaking and writing: he was preparing to cross the Jordan when he spoke these words of Deuteronomy to all Israel.

See how easily, through the correct interpretation of a single little word, the terrifying and apparently insuperable machinery of that objection is dismantled—the objection which certain recent critics bring against Moses as the legitimate author of the Pentateuch.

Indeed, by this one passage alone those who deny that Moses was the author of the sacred books of the Pentateuch can be overthrown—and, if only they could also be convinced. Yet there is reason to fear that they will not yield even to this learned and Catholic scholiast, since they do not yield to the testimony of Christ the Lord himself.

But if they refuse to repent, at least all sincere Catholics, as we hope, will be grateful to our scholiast, who vindicates the authority of the divine books against the immoderate censures of these critics.

This one example also teaches us how little confidence we should place in such flimsy arguments, advanced daily against the sacred tradition of the Church to the great harm of simple Christians, whose faith is weakened or often corrupted by these illusions—although they can be dispersed almost with a single breath. Once these matters are recognized, people are ashamed of their error, when simple and devout faith ought to have kept them in their duty.

Who could adequately say how great a benefit those marginal scholia are to us for the learning and understanding of Scripture? There is nothing ambiguous or somewhat obscure in Jerome’s version that they do not bring into the light; nothing expressed in it too loosely or *paraphrastically* that the scholia do not confine within the proper limits and native meanings of the words.

Here they breathe the deepest piety; there they reveal meanings of Hebrew words that are either unusual and unheard-of, or at least extremely rare. They preserve numerous variant readings of the Hebrew text, commend the scholiast’s remarkable faithfulness everywhere, and, if we except a few places in which we believe him to have made a mistake, antiquity could have transmitted to posterity nothing superior to these critical notes.

I will not linger over the enumeration of these benefits, since they are clearer than daylight and perfectly evident to every curious reader. Yet I will display the fruits and usefulness of the scholia on a single page, so that from one passage we may form a judgment concerning their countless other benefits.

In columns 99 and 100 the following marginal scholia occur. First, beside this sacred text:

> “And your people, whom you brought out,” etc.

The scholiast notes: “The Hebrew does not have ‘your.’” In this observation his faithfulness and diligence shine forth most clearly.

Then, beside the words “I know you by name,” he teaches once and again that the Hebrew has: “I shall make myself known to you by name.” I sought this interpretation in vain in other Hebrew writers and in very many Latin commentaries.

We also learn, if I am not mistaken, how pious and religious our scholiast was from the way he explains this passage of Exodus:

> “I will show you all good, and I will call upon the name of the Lord,” etc.

For he does not refer these words to the vision of the divine Essence, as many scholastics of our time do. Rather, he seems to place all the good of a mortal human life in knowing how to entreat God and move him to mercy.

> “I will show you all good.” That is, says the scholiast, “I will show you how you ought to entreat me and move me to mercy.”

O singular and admirable exposition of divine Scripture! The crowded schools did not teach me this, nor the continual reading of commentators. In the meantime, a single marginal scholion of the Canon surpasses the immense volumes of interpreters.

To add something that the reader might have found difficult to believe: the scholiast was so perceptive in resolving the ambiguities of the sacred books that at times he comes closer to the meaning of the hagiographer than Jerome himself, that phoenix—or easily the prince—of interpreters.

For example, so that no obscurity or ambiguity might remain in verses 5 and 6 of chapter 34 of Exodus, he placed several scholia in the margin after the text had been corrected. These remove every shadow of difficulty, and the words read there should no longer be directly referred to Moses as the speaker, but to God as the one teaching Moses how to pray and entreat him.

We shall speak below of the alteration or correction made to the text of this passage in Jerome’s version. For now we merely inform diligent readers that the translation of this passage produced through the scholiast’s correction and notes is superior to the one originally composed by Jerome himself, as we shall shortly attempt to demonstrate by the authority of sacred Scripture.

As a further testimony to our faithfulness in publishing these marginal scholia, we wish to inform the prudent reader that whatever could be read in the manuscript was printed by us in Roman type. The rest—what had been erased and corrupted by age, or eaten away and mutilated—we supplied from the Hebrew text, but in italic type. We did this only where we clearly saw what had been missing and could be restored. In more obscure places we added only dots in place of words and syllables whose exact content we could not sufficiently determine.

Thus, in column 118, you will find written in a different type: “which ought to be offered as a sacrifice,” and afterward, “in all your dwellings,” because part of these words is read in the manuscript and part has been supplied by us, as I have just explained.

But in column 190 we presented the marginal scholion in this form:

> “and the stone . . . of the size . . . its grea . . . . [an uncertain subject] shall have died; the striker shall surely die, etc.”

For we could extract no meaning from the surviving words or syllables. We therefore thought it preferable to leave these matters to the conjectures of diligent readers rather than determine and supplement what is uncertain by our own conjectures.

Finally, in place of the two dots placed in the manuscript at the head of the scholia and above the text opposite the corresponding passage, we represent little stars, which are used in all printed books, since the rules of modern typography do not permit the position of the aforementioned dots.

**[Note: The reader will find neither marginal notes in our edition nor, a fortiori, stars. We insert the scholia into the text, distinguished by brackets. — EDITOR.]**

Concerning the author of the scholia of the Canon, one further point must be noted: we possess many manuscript codices containing several works by the same writer that have not yet been printed. They are listed, both published and unpublished, in the following order after Saint Jerome’s *Hebrew Traditions on Genesis*:

- *The Book on the Ten Temptations*.
- *The Book of Questions on Kings and Chronicles*.
- *The Song of Deborah*.
- *The Lamentations of Jeremiah*.
- *The Letter to Dardanus*.

All these little works bear the name of Saint Jerome as their title in the manuscript codices. With two exceptions, they were published by Erasmus and Mariano together with the works of the same holy Doctor.

The following remain unpublished:

- A commentary on the *Song of Deborah*, which is read in chapter 5 of the Book of Judges.
- Another commentary on the First Lamentation of Jeremiah.

Regarding this last work, I still would not dare to affirm definitively that it is the work of our Hebrew scholiast. But concerning the brief commentary on the *Song of Deborah*, no difficulty remains for us, because its style, learning, opinions, and everything else that can convey knowledge of an author all proclaim it to be the scholiast of the Canon of Hebrew Truth. Learned men will bear witness to this when those little works are issued in print.

# PROLEGOMENON IV  
## On the Titles and Chapters, Verses and Meters of the Sacred Books

I. Ancient writers divided the sacred Bible into specific parts, but in many different ways.  
II. Those sections were indiscriminately called Titles, Briefs, and Chapters.  
III. What divisions of verses were used by the ancients in Sacred Scripture.  
IV. Whether there are meters in the sacred books, and especially in David’s Psalms.  
V. Jerome’s opinion concerning the meters of Scripture explained and defended.

**[Col. 0101]**

**I.** It is not the purpose of the present section, nor of our undertaking, to conduct an exceedingly long discussion of all the sections and divisions of the sacred books. It is enough that the editors of Jerome have fulfilled their task in this Prolegomenon and have explained, with no little care, the various and numerous divisions of the Latin manuscripts, both the major and the minor ones.

For we would now be treating a matter already completed if I undertook here to discuss the divisions, chapters, and verses of Hebrew or Greek copies, since not a few men distinguished for their learning have preceded us in this study.

Our task, then, is to discuss the sections and ancient divisions of the Latin Bibles, both of chapters and of verses, so that nothing may appear in the edition of this divine Library from which the diligent reader cannot derive abundant benefit.

The entire work on the ancient titles, or chapters, sections, and stichometry of the sacred books, composed by the learned priest and theologian Joseph M. Caro, is known to everyone. Yet because he omitted many examples of this kind of division and, as he himself admits, treated the antiquity of these distinctions rather narrowly, we shall endeavor to supply not a few matters that I have observed to have escaped his diligence.

I would first have it observed that the same statement must be made about the ancient chapters and sections of the sacred books as Jerome and Augustine made about the Latin translations of Scripture [Col. 0102C]: namely, that there are as many kinds of such divisions, or capitulations, as there are codices. Just as in Jerome’s and Augustine’s time there were as many different Latin exemplars of the interpretations as there were sacred codices. “Those who translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek,” says St. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 19, “can be counted; but the Latin translators cannot possibly be counted. For whenever, in the earliest times of faith, a Greek codex came into someone’s hands, and he seemed to possess even a little ability in both languages, he dared to translate it.” From those translators whose incompetence Augustine wished to remedy by the assistance of Jerome’s translations, we have, if I am not mistaken, as many methods of division and capitulation in the Old and New Testament [Col. 0102D]. Nor can I persuade myself that the many foolish headings found in the oldest manuscript codices of the sacred books were derived from any writers other than those incompetent Latin translators.

For ancient writers and translators customarily prefixed to their books a table of chapters, so that readers might recognize, almost at a glance, what was treated in the body of the books. Both ecclesiastical and non-ecclesiastical writers had several ways of doing this. Sometimes they placed the chapters of all the books together at the beginning of the entire work, as Pliny the Elder did in the books of his *Natural History* [Col. 0103A], and likewise ecclesiastical writers, who prefixed the chapters of the four Gospels together at the beginning of Matthew, as they are found in our very ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain, no. 15. Sometimes they attempted to prefix the chapter titles to each individual book, as Eusebius of Caesarea did in his *Ecclesiastical History*: he prefaced his books of Histories with tables, or titles, as they are read today in his works. Or else they briefly noted in the margin what meaning each chapter contained within, as Jerome did in his translation of Saint Epiphanius’s letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem, as is clear from Jerome’s own letter to Pammachius, entitled *On the Best Kind of Translation*.

[Col. 0103B] From this ancient practice of prefacing chapters to the beginning of books, it is an easy conjecture that every Latin translator of the Old Testament prefixed his own tables or titles to the sacred books, so that readers might be informed what they would find written in Genesis, what in Exodus, what in Leviticus, and what finally in all the other volumes of sacred Scripture. Since such titles and capitulations were also prepared for the edition of the Septuagint translators, as the ancient barbarism of their names and terms proves, there can scarcely be any doubt that such tables are older than Jerome.

The ancient titles and chapters therefore had the same parents as the various Latin interpretations of the sacred books had authors. I know that Hesychius, a most learned presbyter, composed *argumenta* and κεφάλαια (*kephalaia*, chapters) on the twelve minor prophets [Col. 0103C]; but I am now speaking of the chapters of the Latin Bibles, which differ greatly from the elegance and clarity of the Hesychian ones.

Hesychius composed the first of the twenty chapters of the prophet Hosea in the following manner, in volume VIII of the *Sacred Critics*:

> Εἰκὼν τῆς τῶν Ἰουδαίων συναγωγῇς, ἐξ ἧς ὁ Χριστὸς τὸ κατὰ σάρκα τίκτεται· καὶ λαοῦ τὸ μὲν ἐν ἀπιστίᾳ ἔμεινεν, τὸ δὲ ὕστερον ἐπιστρέφει καὶ σώζεται.

That is:

> An image of the synagogue of the Jews, from which Christ is born according to the flesh; and of the people, one part of whom remained in unbelief, while the other later turns back and is saved.

Thus I render in Latin the meaning of Hesychius’s chapter. How far it differs from the inept composition of the Latin chapters may be shown from the same first chapter of the prophet Hosea, as expressed in the aforementioned Caro [Col. 0103D]:

> I. Go and take for yourself a wife of prostitution.

The present chapter in the Latin manuscript codices contains nothing beyond these words.

> II. And the number of the children of Israel was like the sand of the sea.
>
> III. She made vessels of silver and gold.

What do those three tables have in common with Hesychius’s single κεφάλαιον (*kephalaion*, chapter)? And what do such obscure words contribute to learning, when you cannot understand their meaning at all except by reading the prophetic context?

It remains, therefore, that such foolish chapters, and others like them, in the Latin Bibles were composed by incompetent ancient writers and translators, who prefixed these titles to their copies according to their own understanding and inclination.

I consider those titles extremely ancient, though not those of every book of the Old Testament. For I am not unaware that some were added by our Cassiodorus, as is clear to us from the testimony of that most illustrious man reproduced below. In book I Cassiodorus makes the following observation about these titles:

> But so that the text of the aforesaid Octateuch might be disclosed to us in a kind of abbreviated form, at the beginnings of the books we judged that titles drawn from the entire sequence of the reading should be impressed, titles written down in due order by our ancestors, so that the reader, usefully warned, might be rendered attentively receptive and might easily find each matter while seeking it, since he knows that it has been briefly indicated for him.

Cassiodorus acknowledges that the titles of the Octateuch—that is, of the five books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, and Ruth—had been written down in due order by his ancestors. But he says that he did not find the same thing in the books of Chronicles:

> But in the two books of Chronicles mentioned above [Col. 0104B] … because I did not find the ancient titles, I have, as I think, suitably impressed new ones in the individual places, following the likeness of the preceding titles, so that by whatever service of language the quality of our devotion might be recognized.

He did the same in the books prefixed under Solomon’s name, calling them *chapters* in chapter 5, whereas in the passages already cited he calls them *titles*. He says:

> With the Lord’s help, we have taken care to mark these books—that is, Solomon’s—with chapters, so that, as has often been said, the inexperienced beginner might not be left amid confusion in such necessary reading.

From this we know with certainty that titles or chapters had been prefixed to several books of Scripture before Cassiodorus’s time. For he calls them “ancient titles,” written down “in due order by our ancestors”; this could not be so unless they had been found in ancient [Col. 0104C] codices, written long before in the period when Cassiodorus recorded these words.

Therefore the more recent titles prefixed to copies of the sacred Bible acknowledge Cassiodorus as their author, and they cannot be assigned to a period earlier than the sixth century. Other, more ancient titles may have appeared in the earliest times of faith together with those Latin interpretations of Scripture which Augustine above called innumerable.

Whatever may be the antiquity and authorship of the chapters prefixed to the divine volumes, it is certain that Jerome was not their parent. Such barbarous and foolish headings everywhere reveal a wholly incompetent author—someone whom it would be impious even to imagine in connection with Jerome. Moreover, no trace appears in [Col. 0104D] the works of the holy Doctor from which one could recognize that the use of these titles was accepted by him. The chapters he mentions so often are parts of the very text of the books, not titles placed externally or prefixed at the beginning to represent in summary the same parts found in the text.

To prove this with examples, I shall review several passages from the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, where Jerome mentions chapters three or four times as sections of Scripture that he undertook to explain. For example, he calls the passage in Genesis 25, from verse 13 to verse 18, a chapter:

> “But what we read at the end of this chapter according to the Septuagint—‘He dwelt opposite all his brothers’—is more correctly rendered in the version we have set down: ‘He fell before all his brothers,’ that is, he died in the hands of all his sons, with his children surviving and none having been taken by death before him.”

Here Jerome understands “chapter” to mean only the six verses I have mentioned. Those verses are also contained in chapter 46 of our edition, columns 25 and 26. But the other passages that follow show that the agreement of this chapter with ours is accidental. For the chapter that Jerome later mentions is a single *comma*, or one verse, of the more recent division that we follow today.

Genesis 36:14 reads:

> “This is Ana, who found Jamim in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of Zebeon his father.”

Jerome discusses this *comma* as follows:

> “Many and varied matters are debated among the Hebrews concerning this chapter; among the Greeks and our people, however, there is silence about it,” and so forth.

You will find nothing of this sort in the division of the ancient titles. The content of a single verse is too narrow to constitute a complete chapter, which plainly consists of several verses and statements, as is evident from the collection of all the capitulations.

Jerome’s chapters must therefore be said to differ from those that we have published at the beginning of Genesis, following the authority of the manuscript codices. This can be proved again from the *Hebrew Questions*, where Jerome calls two verses of the division used today a chapter—namely, verses 5 and 6 of Genesis 46:

> “And now, behold, your two sons who were born to you in the land of Egypt,” and so forth.

“If anyone doubted,” says Jerome, “that seventy souls entered Egypt, the present chapter confirms it.”

You will not find this present chapter marked in any series of ancient divisions or capitulations that we have published. It follows necessarily that this division and distinction of the chapters in Genesis was Jerome’s own.

Nor should anyone be disturbed by the fact that Jerome’s chapters are sometimes found equal to the titles of ancient manuscript codices. Such agreements occurred almost accidentally, just as they are sometimes known to agree with modern chapters.

In book V of his *Commentaries on Isaiah*, after Jerome had transcribed the whole text of our twentieth chapter, he begins its exposition as follows:

> “We have set down the entire contents of this chapter, so that we may discuss each part separately,” and so forth.

No one would make Jerome the author of the latest division in our Latin Vulgate merely because the boundaries of this chapter are the same. We ought therefore not to attribute the ancient titles or capitulations to him as their author, even if they sometimes agree with the sections of Scripture that the greatest of Latin interpreters elucidates in his commentaries.

Certainly this entire method of dividing the text depended on the discretion of authors and scribes, and each ancient writer divided the sacred text according to his own understanding. Hence learned men agree—and the diverse divisions and distinctions of the same books demonstrate—that no single division was then approved above all others or commonly received.

We have published four different capitulations—that is, four series of titles or chapters—at the beginning of Genesis, as they are found in different manuscript copies of Jerome’s version. None of them, however, was received by common usage. Copyists used one or another indiscriminately. Those who copied the Canon exemplars preferred titles, which were fewer in number than the other divisions. Others preferred to prefix chapters, much more numerous and different in content, judging that the method which divides the text of Scripture into many parts was more convenient than one which gathers different subjects under the same division.

It was therefore a matter of the copyists’ ingenuity and discretion to prefix so many different forms of chapters to copies of Jerome’s translation. None of them is believed to have been prepared by the holy Doctor, as is easily proved by the arguments already presented above.

## II

Among the ancients, these tables and sequences of sections were called indiscriminately and interchangeably *titles*, *briefs*, and *chapters*. We have already briefly observed this in Cassiodorus. In the first two chapters of book I of *On the Institution of Divine Letters*, he calls the summaries and headings prefixed to the sacred books *titles*; yet in chapter 5 he calls them *chapters*.

In manuscript codices such designations are found to be so inconsistent that we often read in them:

> “Here begin the titles of the book,”

or, in another form:

> “Here begin the briefs of the book of Genesis,”

and afterward, at the end:

> “Here end the chapters of the book of Genesis.”

The Canon of the Hebrew Truth, numbered 9 in our library at Saint-Germain, [Col. 0106C] has various inscriptions at the beginning of many books. It entitles the titles of Exodus as follows:

> “Here begin the chapters of the book of Exodus.”

But not so in Leviticus, where we read:

> “Here begin the titles of the book of Leviticus, that is, *Vayyiqra*,”

and at the end of the sections:

> “Here end the titles of Leviticus.”

The same occurs successively in the other books of Moses. In Joshua, however:

> “Here begin the chapters. Here end the chapters?”

Finally, in the books of *Malachim*, that is, in the third and fourth books of Kings, it first says:

> “Here begin the chapters of the book of Malachim,”

and then:

> “Here end the titles of Malachim.”

In the New Testament also, the headings of the sacred books are inscribed in different ways. Many manuscripts follow the more common received form:

> “Here begin the chapters of Matthew.”

But quite a few Vatican and Gallican codices [Col. 0106D] have:

> “Here begins the Breviary of Matthew,”

and at the end:

> “Here ends the Breviary of Matthew.”

They read the same in the other Evangelists.
