Our library at Saint-Germain possesses a manuscript codex of the Bible, of very venerable as well as curious antiquity, containing many sacred books of the Old and New Testaments according to the ancient Latin, or Italic, version. In this codex the ancient titles of the Gospels bear the following inscriptions:

> “Here begins the capitulation of Matthew.”
>
> “Here begins the capitulation of Mark,”

and so forth. At the end of the titles:

> “Here ends the capitulation of Matthew,”

and so forth.

At the beginning of the Acts of the Apostles it has a wholly distinctive title, or rather this annotation and admonition:

> “An index of what the apostles did in their Acts, so that you may easily find what you wish if, running through the chapters by their numbers, you search for it.”

After this annotation it appends fifty-three chapters, followed by:

> “Here end the chapters.”

From all these different names for the headings found prefixed to the beginnings of manuscript Bibles, it plainly appears that everyone was free to call them *titles*, *briefs*, *breviaries*, *chapters*, *capitulations*, and *indexes*, or tables. These names were applied both to shorter and to more extensive tables of the various sections of sacred Scripture.

The editors of the present divine Library have not allowed such wandering and variable names for the headings to remain. We reduce all the different sections of the sacred books used by ancient writers to three kinds and designations. First place is given to the series of titles; second to the briefs; and third to the chapters, however many are listed, whether more or fewer.

Accordingly, at the beginning of Genesis we have published thirty-eight titles, forty-six briefs, eighty-two chapters, and again, in another table, one hundred and fifty-four chapters. In Exodus we have likewise prefixed three tables of sections: eighteen titles, twenty-one briefs, and one hundred and thirty-eight chapters. The same has been done throughout the entire Heptateuch.

In the books of Samuel and Malachim—that is, in the four books of Kings—we have added nothing except the titles written in three copies of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth: the Memmian, the Carcassonian, and our Saint-Germain copy.

As for the prophetic books, we thought that no table of sections at all should be prefixed to the beginning of these books, lest we appear to have published anything contrary to Jerome’s mind and usage. For it is absolutely certain that he recognizes no other sections of the Prophets in general than those which he himself calls *visions*. Nor does he call anything *chapters* except certain headings in the sacred text and the parts that he divided and elucidated in his commentaries according to his own judgment and understanding.

We have shown above that these chapters of Jerome are very different from those prefixed to the sacred books. I do not hesitate to prove this still further with several examples, insofar as the matter requires.

While explaining two verses of the Vulgate division in Hosea 1, Jerome warned the reader as follows:

> “Since we are writing commentaries, not extensive volumes, reserving individual explanations of each chapter in its proper place [Col. 0107D], let us now discuss only the present chapter.”

The present chapter, as he calls it, contains only verses 3 and 4 of Hosea 1, as I have said. In Jerome’s commentaries, however, five or six similar chapters precede it, since he supplied separate explanations for each chapter. Thus the holy Doctor divided the first four verses of the prophet Hosea into six or seven chapters.

But the first chapter of this same prophet in the manuscript codices and in Caro’s edition contains nine complete verses. The second chapter begins:

> “And the number of the children of Israel shall be,”

and so forth. These words are read at the beginning of the tenth verse of the chapter mentioned above.

From this you can see that the sacred Bibles were divided and distinguished in a quite different manner by Jerome and by other ancient writers or translators. To make this still more certain and evident, hear him discussing the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin chapters in chapter 3, verse 14, of Zephaniah:

> “Let it not seem strange,” he says, “as we have often stated, that the Hebrew chapters end in one way, and the Septuagint—that is, the Greek and Latin chapters—in another. Wherever the translation differs in meaning, there must necessarily be different beginnings or endings.”

I certainly do not see what more could be desired for judging Jerome’s chapters and those of others. He most clearly distinguished his own chapters or sections from all the others, both Greek and Latin, saying that in his Hebrew translation the beginnings and endings of the sections differed from those read in the Septuagint interpretation.

The prophecy of Zephaniah contains more than twenty sections or chapters in Jerome’s commentaries, whereas in the edition of the priest Caro only one chapter is seen prefixed to this book. We therefore rightly rejected such headings from the prophetic books, since they are found to differ so greatly from the chapters distinguished and elucidated in Jerome’s commentaries.

Furthermore, in the books of the Prophets sacred Scripture has received special, almost native divisions according to the different subjects. The sense of the text separates them into many distinct parts, which are by no means dependent upon one another. These sections arise together with the books and are called *visions* by ancient writers. Sometimes they even agree with modern chapters.

Following the custom of his age, Jerome calls Isaiah’s first and second visions what we call the first and second chapters of that prophet. Thus we read the following in his *Commentaries on Isaiah* 2:

> “And in the first vision, which we have already explained, where the Septuagint translated, ‘The vision which he saw against Judea and against Jerusalem,’ the Hebrew has written *AL JUDA UJERUSALEM*, that is, ‘concerning Judah and Jerusalem’; and in this, which is the second, the Hebrew likewise contains … And I marvel,” and so forth.

As you see, he calls the first passage a vision, and likewise the second, whereas we call them the first and second chapters.

The order of the sections in Isaiah, therefore, is the same among us as that received in Jerome’s time among the Fathers and leading men of the Church. In the preface to his translation of Jeremiah from the Hebrew, Jerome also mentions such visions, and he rendered no small service to the Church of Christ by striving to restore them to their original order:

> “Moreover,” he says, “we have corrected the order of the visions, which among the Greeks and Latins was altogether confused, restoring it to its original form.”

Finally, he says that Daniel’s visions, absent from the Hebrew source, were marked beforehand with obeli:

> “Therefore, many years ago, when we translated Daniel, we also marked these Visions beforehand with an obelus, indicating that they are not found in the Hebrew.”

See the preface to the *Commentary on Daniel*.

And, so that nothing should be omitted from the reader’s curiosity, the diligent reader should be informed that the ancients divided the book of Daniel into twelve visions. These are faithfully expressed and described in the manuscript codices of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth and in other very ancient codices of better quality, just as we have now published them in this divine Library.

The chapters prefixed to the beginning of Daniel, however, are counted as many more, both in Caro’s edition and in certain manuscript codices, where they extend as far as the number thirty-one. Our present division is smaller by at least half than that division of the chapters. For the Vulgate Version has only fourteen sections in the entire book of Daniel.

Therefore the division distributed according to the Visions agrees neither with the modern divisions nor with those of the ancient writers, but is found in the true copies of Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew.

[Col. 0109B] Moreover, we published the books of Chronicles, Ezra, and Esther without chapters prefixed, because Cassiodorus above taught us that none had been added to these books by Jerome. Very ancient and excellent manuscript codices retain no table of chapters or titles, but only Jerome’s prefaces, together with the sacred text divided and distinguished into many members according to the method in which we have reproduced it, following the authority of the finest royal, Colbertine, Corbie, and Saint-Germain manuscripts.

We shall nevertheless supply the omitted capitulations whose author was Cassiodorus when, with God’s help, we undertake to publish complete many books of the ancient Vulgate, or Italic, version.

For the God who bestows all good things has granted so much to our wishes and studies [Col. 0109C] that he has not only revealed to us the immense treasure of Jerome’s version, hidden in obscure corners of archives and libraries; he has also, by heaping gifts upon us, wished to place in our hands several copies of the Italic version, both of the Old and of the New Testament, so that in due time they might be made public for the greatest benefit of scholars and of the Christian commonwealth.

Moved, therefore, by reverence for this most ancient version and compelled by the urging of distinguished men, we have decided to restore these sacred monuments to life. Accordingly, provision has already been made by a Royal Diploma, specifically granted to us for this edition of the Italic version, so that it should not be published in the kingdom of France by anyone other than ourselves.

We shall begin with the volume of Matthew [Col. 0109D] and commit it to the press. We shall publish that Gospel separately because of the heated controversy between two writers of the present age, who, on the occasion of the Cambridge manuscript, discuss at length the ancient Latin version of the Gospels—namely, the version that prevailed in the Western Church before Jerome’s revision.

Many things are read in our manuscript copies that are far removed from the conjectures of both writers; others, however, confirm as true now the statement of one, now that of the other. Which side our manuscript codices ultimately favor most strongly, you will not learn until they have been printed.

## III

It would be a lengthy undertaking if I wished to insert into this section all the errors of certain critics, refuting one by one their false opinions about the divisions and distinctions of verses used among the ancients and responding to each with the relevant chapters. Therefore, avoiding the tediousness of a sprawling dispute and compressing my words into a narrow compass, I shall briefly warn the reader only of this: no recent writer has yet spoken with sufficient accuracy about the ancient verses or *commata* of the divine Scriptures.

In their notes and observations they bring forward much from Augustine’s *Speculum* which, when tested against the oldest codices, immediately disappears and is shown to be false. A learned man, whom I have always held in the highest veneration, writes that it seemed to him that Augustine distinguished the verses of the Bible in such a way that each verse contained six words. He adds these words:

> “But this seems to have been peculiar to Augustine’s codex, not common to all. Jerome distinguished most, and perhaps all, of the books of Scripture by verses, but no trace of the modern division exists in him.”

Yet, with due respect to this most learned writer, it is permissible to say that in ancient times there were innumerable verses throughout the volumes of the Bible that contained only two or three words. Such verses cannot be confined by any predetermined number of words, since under no fixed law they sometimes run to more words and sometimes to fewer.

Moreover, nothing was peculiar to Augustine’s codex in the distinctions of verses; it shared them entirely with other copies of the Greek and Latin Fathers. Finally, traces of the modern distinction of verses do appear in Jerome [Col. 0110C], as we shall demonstrate below with the examples provided—not in any contentious spirit, but solely in the interest of presenting the truth.

Those who pay attention to Josephus’s *History*, to the testimony of the presbyter Hesychius, and to the very ancient monuments of the sacred Scriptures, written eleven hundred years ago on precious parchment and still surviving, will readily concede that distinctions of verses were extremely common in the books of ancient writers.

Josephus, therefore, a native Jewish writer and a contemporary or near-contemporary of the apostolic age, notes at the end of book XX of his *Antiquities* that there were sixty thousand verses in the twenty books of his *Antiquities*. These could certainly not have been counted in Josephus’s Greek text if they had not been shorter than our present biblical verses; nor could they have been assigned a definite number unless they had been written distinctly and with intervals in the author’s own original copy.

Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem, shows that this custom of writing much in verses was far older than Josephus. In the treatise he calls *Sticheron*—“A Sticheron of the Twelve Prophets”—he refers it to the time of David and Solomon, or even to Job, who was older than those kings. He further adds that he found a similar distinction of verses in several copies of the apostolic books:

> Πλὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ἀποστολικὴν Βίβλον οὕτω τινὶ συγγραφεῖσαν εὑρὼν etc.

> “Moreover, having found the Apostolic Book written in this way by someone,” and so forth.

Thus the distinction of verses in the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments was not something newly introduced in Hesychius’s time; it was already established and customary.

Nor do we know that only one sacred text was divided and written out in verses. Eusebius of Caesarea taught us that all the Greek versions of the Old Testament were divided by Origen into members, or cola of verses, in book VI, chapter 16, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, where he says the following about Origen’s work of the Hexapla:

> “After he had collected all these translations into a single body, divided them by cola and members, and set them opposite one another, together with the Hebrew text, he left us copies of the Hexapla.”

The learned Henry Valesius, interpreter of Eusebius, discussed the Greek words διελὼν τε πρὸς κῶλον (“dividing them according to the colon”) at considerable length, rightly correcting Christopherson for translating the aforesaid words as “he distinguished them from one another by little necks.” For *cola* are verses, or members, that complete an entire sense.

Yet Valesius himself does not seem to have fully grasped the nature of the verses of Scripture, because in Jerome’s prefaces he confuses the *cola* of verses with *commata*, which are parts and members of the *cola* and often do not complete an entire sense.

But let us bring forward Valesius’s annotation on the passage of Eusebius just cited. He says:

> “Among the Latins, Jerome was the first to distinguish his translation by verses, imitating Origen, who had done the same in the Hexapla. Origen had the readers’ convenience especially in mind. For whatever is distinguished by verses is more easily understood and committed to memory. Moreover, such a distinction was entirely necessary for comparing the Greek editions with one another.”

Later, several followed Origen’s example and did in the New Testament what he had first done in the Old, as Hesychius of Jerusalem testifies in the book he entitled *Sticheron*, “A Sticheron of the Twelve Prophets.” He gave it this title because he had added at the margin of each verse an explanation of difficult passages, which he himself calls παρατίθεσθαι and παράθεσις.

Hesychius’s words are these:

> ἔστι μὲν ἀρχαῖον τοῖς θεοφύροις τὸ σπούδασμα, στιχηδὸν ὡς τὰ πολλὰ πρὸς τὴν τῶν μελετωμένων σαφήνειαν, τὰς προφητείας ἐκτίθεσθαι etc.

We have rendered them into Latin as follows:

> Dividing the prophetic books into cola of verses for the sake of greater clarity is an ancient invention of the holy Fathers. At first they were read without any distinction. Later, however, learned men and students of sacred letters, for the sake of greater clarity, as I have said, devised this kind of division into verses. Thus the books of the Prophets were published by them; so were David’s Psalms, the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Thus also the book of Job is found divided into verses. Moreover, I found the Apostolic Book—that is, the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles—written out in this manner by some.

Hesychius then adds these words:

> Ἀλλ᾽ ἐπειδὴ πολλὰ μὲν τῶν ἀσαφῶν ἡ τῶν στίχων σαφηνίζει διαίρεσις.

Here he calls *stichoi* what he ought to have called *cola* [lacuna]. We have explained above what was first accomplished by Origen in the edition of the Hexapla: he distinguished each translation by cola of verses. Therefore, the distinction of verses that we see today in the interpretation of the Seventy Elders is Origen’s invention.

Thus, it is Origen’s invention that he set the Greek translations opposite one another. But I would not readily accept Valesius’s opinion concerning Origen’s earlier invention, by which he says that the distinction of verses was transmitted into the interpretation of the Seventy Elders. It is more credible, if I am not mistaken, that those ancient Greek translators—the Seventy, I mean, as well as Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—observed some sort of division into verses and commata, rather than that they composed their translations in the wholly confused and undivided manner of incompetent writers.

It was also shown above from Josephus that among ancient authors contemporary with the apostles it was an exceedingly common practice to divide works into verses and to note their number at the end of the books. Furthermore, the books called *sticheric*—that is, Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs—were written in verses from the beginning.

Thus an evident argument arises that, at least in those books, the division of verses cannot in any way be regarded as Origen’s invention. There are many other matters in Valesius’s annotation, especially concerning his interpretation of Hesychius’s Greek words, which we leave to the judgment of the learned.

I shall say only that Hesychius appropriately called verses *stichoi*, not *cola*, as Valesius wished. For Jerome uses *colon* for a complete sentence, which in the sacred books often runs through two or three divisions; *stichos*, however, denotes any division of a colon and any subordinate distinction within the periods of discourse.

Examples will make the matter clear. Psalm 1 had the following arrangement and distinction of verses in the most ancient monuments of the Churches:

> Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,
>
> and has not stood in the way of sinners,
>
> and has not sat in the seat of pestilence.
>
> But his delight is in the law of the Lord;
>
> and in his law he will meditate day and night.

There are two *cola* there, that is, two sentences: the first with three members, the second with two. But there are five members and five *stichoi*, or verses, in the Hesychian sense, each consisting of a separate small sentence and line.

In the copies of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, the *cola* always begin with a single capital letter, often illuminated as well. The *stichoi*, or verses, begin indiscriminately with a lower-case or capital letter, according to the custom of whatever writers and periods produced the books.

For example, in the Psalter of the monastery of Saint-Germain, which is said to have been used by the most holy bishop of Paris and our patron, all the initial letters of the little verses are everywhere seen to be equal, because throughout the entire text they are all uncial, or capital, letters. Thus we read Psalm 1:

> THEREFORE THE UNGODLY SHALL NOT RISE IN THE JUDGMENT. NOR SINNERS IN THE ASSEMBLY OF THE JUST. FOR THE LORD KNOWS THE WAY OF THE JUST, AND THE PATH OF THE UNGODLY SHALL PERISH.

Against these four στίχοι—that is, verses—copied in two [Col. 0113A] cola, the exemplars of the Canon retain the following arrangement:

> Therefore the impious shall not rise in judgment,  
> nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.  
> For the Lord knows the way of the righteous,  
> but the way of the impious shall perish.

Valesius ought therefore to have applied the same distinction between στίχοι and κῶλα that we all recognize between a complete circuit of discourse and the members of that same circuit—that is, between a περίοδος and its κῶλα. To make this clearer from Augustine, let us pause briefly over what is read in chapter 7 of Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*. Some light will be added if what is written there about periods, cola, and commas is correctly understood:

“Another elegance is also recognized: after certain individual phrases have been completed by the speaker’s voice—phrases which we call *members* and *sections*, while the Greeks call them κῶλα and κόμματα—there follows an encompassing circuit, which they call a περίοδος, whose members are suspended in the speaker’s voice until the final conclusion. Of the expressions that precede, the first member of the circuit is, ‘tribulation produces endurance’; the second, ‘and endurance, proven character’; the third, ‘and proven character, hope.’ Then the circuit itself follows, which is completed in three members. The first is, ‘and hope does not disappoint’; the second, ‘because God’s love has been poured out in our hearts’; the third, ‘through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.’ But these and similar matters belong to the art of expression.” And a little farther on:

“Moreover, anyone who understands recognizes that those sections which the Greeks call κόμματα, and the members and circuits of which I spoke shortly before,” and so forth.

The sections, then, are what the Greeks call commata; cola are complete and larger members, greater than commata; periods are circuits completed in several members, so that in discourse a circuit is divided into κῶλα and cola into κόμματα, according to the art of expression which Saint Augustine discusses in the same place. He identifies three kinds of distinction by their proper names in a single περικοπή of blessed Paul.

The Hieronymian distinctions of verses do not correspond equally to these. Jerome mentions only two kinds of division in Scripture: one made through complete κῶλα, and the other made through κῶλα and κόμματα. He explicitly recalls the former distinction of verses through complete cola in the preface to the Books of Chronicles, which he translated into Latin from Hebrew:

“And because I have now translated *DABRE AJAMIM*, that is, ‘Words of Days’ [the Chronicles], I did so for this reason: that I might more clearly arrange through verse-cola the interminable delays and the forest of names, which have been confused through the fault of the scribes, as well as the barbarism of the meanings.”

He calls these same verse-cola “members” in the preface to Joshua:

“We also admonish the reader that a diligent copyist preserve the forest of Hebrew names and the distinctions divided into members.”

In the prefaces to Isaiah and Ezekiel, however, he teaches that his new translation from Hebrew was distinguished not only by cola but by cola and commata, following the practice used in the books of Demosthenes and Cicero:

“Let no one,” he says, “when he sees the prophets written in verses, suppose that among the Hebrews they are bound by meter or that they possess anything resembling the Psalms and the Works of Solomon. Rather, the practice is that used in Demosthenes and Tully: they are written in cola and commata, although they composed prose and not verse. We too, taking thought for the benefit of readers, have distinguished our new translation by a new manner of writing.”

Likewise, in the preface to Ezekiel, which he translated from Hebrew, Jerome invites Paula and Eustochium to read that prophet in these words:

“Read this prophet, then, according to our translation, for, being written in cola and commata, it gives readers a clearer sense.”

Jerome’s new translation of the prophets was therefore distinguished by cola and commata, whereas he divided the Books of Chronicles only by cola. For this reason he did not warn the reader in his prefaces to the historical books of Joshua and Chronicles not to suppose that those books contained meter on account of his distinction by cola, as he expressly teaches that such an opinion must be avoided in the prophetic books, because, being written in cola and commata, they have the appearance of metrical composition.

To make this evident and visible to everyone, I shall not hesitate to set down here several sentences both from the Prophets and from Chronicles. Thus, distinguished by cola and commata, we published the following sentences, or periods, of the prophet Isaiah, chapter 1:

> Hear, O heavens,  
> and listen with your ears, O earth,  
> for the Lord has spoken.  
>   
> I nourished and raised sons,  
> but they rejected me.  
>   
> The ox knows its owner,  
> and the donkey its master’s manger;  
> but Israel has not known,  
> my people has not understood.

This manner of dividing the sacred text of the prophets differs in no respect from that by which the Psalms were written in the exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew truth. For example, in Psalm 9 one finds a similar distinction of verses:

> I will confess to the Lord with all my heart;  
> I will recount all your wonders.  
>   
> I will rejoice and exult in you;  
> I will sing to your name, O Most High.  
>   
> When my enemies turn back,  
> they will fall and perish before your face.  
>   
> For you have executed my judgment and my cause;  
> you have sat upon the throne as judge of righteousness.

The writing of the Prophets and of the Psalms was therefore the same in Jerome’s new translation from Hebrew. It was not without reason, then, that the holy Doctor warned in his preface to Isaiah that no one, when seeing the Prophets written in verses, should suppose that among the Hebrews they were bound by meter or that they possessed anything resembling the Psalms and the Works of Solomon. To this must be added the Book of Job. For Job, according to Jerome’s testimony, is bound by meter among the Hebrews and is read in his translation written in verses after the manner of the Psalms and the Works of Solomon.

The Books of Chronicles, however, are not so arranged. As I have said, they are written and distinguished only by cola, to avoid barbarism and confusion of meaning. Accordingly, these cola are found arranged in the following manner in chapter 1 of the First Book:

> The sons of Regma were Sheba and Datan.  
>   
> Cush begot Nimrod; he began to be mighty  
> on the earth.  
>   
> Mesraim begot Ludim, Anamim, and Laabim,  
> and Naphtuhim, Pathrusim also and Casluhim;  
> from these came the Philistines and the Caphtorim.

No prudent person who has considered the examples just given can fail to see how different this distinction of the verses of Chronicles by cola is from that made by cola and commata. Who could be persuaded that the cola written in Chronicles present the appearance of some kind of metrical composition? Conversely, who would deny that the distinction of the Prophets by cola and commata resembles metrical arrangements? In that distinction of the verses one might say that the Prophets proceed in hexameters and pentameters, although they were written in prose and not in verse.

Chronicles, on the other hand, bears no image of a hexameter or pentameter, but only of discourse divided into members—that is, distinguished by its περικοπαί and circuits. Jerome therefore distinguished the Books of Chronicles and Joshua by cola alone, while he wrote all the Prophets by cola and commata, as he himself confirms in his brief prefaces.

You will understand these two kinds of distinction more easily if you know that the same volumes of Scripture were divided and written in different ways in various and differing manuscript codices. The Book of Job and the Book of Psalms are not everywhere distinguished by cola and commata. It is beyond doubt that sometimes they were written in complete verse-cola, and sometimes by cola and commata, according to the preference of each ancient scribe.

The Book of Job was divided by cola in the manuscript codex of our monastery of Majus near Tours; three exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew truth divide it by cola and commata—namely, the Memmian, the Carcassonian, and our San-Germanensis. In chapter 3 of Job we read the following in the codex of Majus Monastery, beautifully written on parchment six hundred years ago:

> May the day perish on which I was born,  
> and the night in which it was said, “A man has been conceived.”  
>   
> May that day be turned into darkness;  
> may God not seek it from above,  
> and may it not be illumined by light.  
>   
> May darkness and the shadow of death obscure it;  
> may gloom seize it,  
> and may it be wrapped in bitterness.

As you see, three verse-cola are written here, all of them corresponding to the present-day division and to the distinctions of the Masoretes. In the exemplars of the Canon, however, the same words have a different division of verses, since they are separated by cola and commata according to the custom of the very ancient scribes who, some time after Jerome, copied the sacred books in the following manner:

> May the day perish on which I was born,  
> and the night in which it was said, “A man has been conceived.”  
>   
> May that day be turned into darkness;  
> may God not seek it from above,  
> and may it not be illumined by light.  
>   
> May darkness and the shadow of death obscure it;  
> may gloom seize it,  
> and may it be wrapped in bitterness.

In many other manuscript books, the Book of Job has neither the first nor the second kind of distinction, but is written in a single continuous flow and in one sustained manner, as the Books of Moses and Kings are written. The verses in those books are not divided in any other way than by points, two or three according to the preference of the ancient scribes, who seem to have followed Cassiodorus in what he taught in chapter 12 of *On the Institutions of Divine Letters*.

For what Jerome wrote at intervals in his translation, Cassiodorus should be believed to have subsequently placed together and joined, on the evidence of the passage cited:

“We judged that this pandect should be written in fifty-three gatherings in a smaller hand, because what abundant reading had spread out, the density of writing, brought together, might contract.”

The reading of Scripture in Jerome’s edition was extremely extensive because of the intervals distinguishing cola and commata. Cassiodorus made it shorter and more compact, both by using smaller letter forms and by compressing into a single dense body the sections previously distinguished and separated.

Countless manuscript exemplars of the sacred books remain in which the verses, both in the Psalms and in the other books, are distinguished only by punctuation. Rarer are those in which the Psalms, and especially the Book of Job, are written in verse-cola. Rarest of all are those codices which still preserve the books arranged in lines (στιχήρεις)—namely, Job together with the Psalms of David and the Works of Solomon—written by cola and commata.

As for the distinction of verses throughout the entire Canon of the Hebrew truth, we have taken it from the most ancient monuments. Deprived of their assistance, we did not permit ourselves to divide the Books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, and so forth by verse-cola. We completed our edition by using only punctuation for the distinction of verses, as far as our modest abilities allowed.

It must especially be noted that the two kinds of distinction which we said were customary in the verses of Job and the Psalms have not yet become obsolete in many Hebrew manuscript volumes. For everything we observed in Latin books concerning the distinction of verses—sometimes by cola, sometimes by cola and commata—occurs in precisely the same way in ancient Hebrew monuments, which we have examined with no little care for the sake of learning.

The Hebrew manuscripts of the Bible preserved in the Library of the Oratory at Paris, marked with the letters and number BB. 33, recognize no other distinction of verses in the Books of Job, David, and Solomon than that established by the Masoretes through the points called *Siluk*, or *Sof Pasuq*. But the royal Hebrew manuscript volumes of the sacred Bible, numbers 5 and 6, preserve those same books written in verse-cola and commata, so that one might say that the Latin exemplars of the Canon had been copied from those Hebrew manuscripts.

There is such great affinity and agreement between the two sets of codices that we were often astonished when comparing the Latin exemplars with the Hebrew ones.

The Book of Job, according to Jerome’s testimony, begins in prose, proceeds in verse, and ends in ordinary prose. That is, from the beginning of the volume up to the words of Job, where he says, “May the day perish,” and so forth, the discourse is prose. From that comma onward to the end of the book it is completed in verses, namely up to the words, “and I repent in dust and ashes.” The short comma, or chapter, which remains is woven together in prose.

We see this entire structure of the Book of Job religiously observed in the royal Hebrew manuscripts just mentioned, and likewise throughout the exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew truth which Jerome made Latin. They differed only in this respect: the commata of the Hebrew verses are separated from one another by empty spaces on the same line, whereas those commata are placed one beneath and after another in the Latin translation because of the greater abundance of Latin words, by which the particular character of that language is completed.

The matter will be easier to understand if we give examples of this difference. In the third chapter of Job, the distinction of commata in the verses is as follows among the Hebrews:

> May the day on which I was born perish, and the night in which it was said, “A man has been conceived.” [Hebrew transliterated: **Jovad jom havaled bo valaela amar hora gaver.**]

These two commata of the same verse are placed one beneath the other in the Latin translation, as we have said, and are written in this manner:

> May the day perish on which I was born;  
> and the night in which it was said, “A man has been conceived.”

Thus throughout the whole of Job, both in the Hebrew manuscript codices and in the Latin exemplars of the Canon, the verse-cola and commata are found written out. Although we see that their distinction is by no means observed in many manuscript codices, this should not disturb anyone on account of such great variation among the exemplars. The variations were introduced by ancient copyists and scribes, who sometimes join several sentences and sometimes separate them, according to the way the material flowed from the pen and according as the mind of the scribe—whether Hebrew or Latin—was attentive to the work or distracted, as commonly happens in great and prolonged labors.

The scribe of the Hebrew codex of the Oratory mentioned above wrote complete verses continuously throughout the entire Psalter and observed no distinction of commata there. Yet he followed that distinction in the First Book of Chronicles, when, in chapter 16 of that book, he carefully wished to copy Psalm 104.

The same judgment should be made concerning the Latin scribe of the manuscript Bible codex which the canons of Le Puy (Anicium) donated to the Colbertine Library. He distinguished the first eight or ten Psalms of David by verse-cola, but wrote the remaining Psalms without a similar distinction of cola, using only punctuation at the ends of the verses.

Several variant distinctions of verses that sometimes occur in the royal Hebrew codices and in the three Latin exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew truth would also have to be added, unless the examples we have prefaced are sufficient for the curious reader to explain the matter.

If we now return to the periods, cola, and commata observed by Augustine in the Epistles of Paul, the answer is straightforward and easy: in Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, the most holy bishop was considering not the distinction of verses customary in sacred books, but the eloquence of the sacred writers, which he endeavored to demonstrate from the text of the Epistles of blessed Paul, where the distinctions of grammatical art and the laws of more elegant speech are shown to have been preserved.

Augustine’s cola and commata, therefore, signify nothing here beyond grammatical gradation, through which words or meanings are connected one with another, as we see in Romans 5:3: from tribulation comes endurance, from endurance proven character, and from proven character hope. Or they signify another elegance of discourse, in which, after several individual phrases have been completed by the speaker’s voice, there follows an encompassing circuit, which they call a περίοδος.

These cola and commata belong to grammarians and orators. The Hieronymian κῶλα and κόμματα mentioned in the holy Doctor’s prefaces, however, are distinctions of Scripture divided into members, which establish the number of verses in the sacred books.

As we said above, these distinctions of verses were sometimes longer and sometimes shorter among ancient writers. Both kinds of distinction were recognized and used by Jerome, as can briefly be demonstrated from his own words.

The distinction of verses used from ancient times in sacred books must undoubtedly be reckoned first as that which prevailed in the Vulgate edition before Jerome and which was more extensive than all other divisions, both ancient and modern. When the Psalms were formerly divided according to this distinction of verses, they contained twice as many small verses, and sometimes three times as many, as they now contain in our Latin Vulgate.

For example, Psalm 13 is now read as divided into ten verses. According to the ancient division in the Roman Psalter, [Col. 0118C] it contained twelve verses, or thirteen if the title of the psalm is counted as one comma. In the common ancient Latin translation, however, twenty-five στίχοι are counted, or twenty-six with the title.

Jerome mentions this extremely extensive division of verses when he replies to the most learned virgin Eustochium in the prologue to Book XVI of his Commentaries on Isaiah:

“You have brought me a considerable little question, namely, why the eight verses read in the churches and absent from the Hebrew text of the thirteenth Psalm were used by the Apostle when he wrote to the Romans:

> Their throat is an open grave;  
> with their tongues they acted deceitfully;  
> the venom of asps is under their lips.  
>   
> Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness;  
> their feet are swift to shed blood.  
>   
> Destruction and misery are in their ways,  
> and they have not known the way of peace;  
> there is no fear of God before their eyes.

“When I heard this, I was as though struck by a mighty boxer. I began to burn inwardly in silence and to mark the astonishment of my mind by the pallor of my face,” and so forth.

Those eight verses, which have only three divisions in our Latin Vulgate and in the Roman Psalter, proceed in the following order and number in the Psalter of Saint-Germain, which contains the old Vulgate and the Common text (Κοινή) and is written in what are called uncial letters of gold and silver:

> Their throat is an open grave;  
>   
> with their tongues they acted deceitfully;  
>   
> the venom of asps is under their lips.  
>   
> Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.  
>   
> Their feet are swift to shed blood;  
>   
> destruction and misery are in their ways;  
>   
> and they have not known the way of peace;  
>   
> there is no fear of God before their eyes.

Those eight verses were read in the churches of the Latins, according to Jerome’s testimony and that of the virgin Eustochium. They were also written in their codices in the form just displayed, with the same number of verse-divisions, which, compared with our present division, have twice or three times as many sections.

Jerome recognizes the same numerous distinction of verses in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, where he says concerning Psalm 17:13:

“‘Hail and coals of fire,’ and so forth. And you ask why the Greek does not have this verse a second time, with two verses inserted between. But it should be understood that it was added from the Hebrew and from the edition of Theodotion among the translators of the Septuagint under an asterisk.”

Thus the Greek text from which the ancient Latin was expressed did not read in the Common text (Κοινή), “hail and coals of fire,” after the words, “and the Most High gave his voice,” but only once before, “and the Lord thundered from heaven.” Jerome therefore restored that verse under an asterisk in the following manner:

> Hail and coals of fire.  
>   
> And the Lord thundered from heaven;  
>   
> and the Most High gave his voice,  
>   
> + hail and coals of fire.

The last three verses of this division constitute a single verse, number 14, in the Latin Vulgate. From this one may infer the great difference between the present and the most ancient distinction of verses used in the sacred books during the earliest times of the faith.

For this numerous division of verses, consult Jerome further in chapter 21 of Ezekiel, chapter 63 of Isaiah, and countless other passages. It is not useful to recite them, since we believe that the testimonies already given are sufficient for the diligent reader.

One matter remains: to show that some traces of the present distinction of verses exist in Jerome, which I promised above to do. It should therefore be known that the words of Job, chapter 42, verse 6, in which he proclaims his repentance, form one verse in Saint Jerome, just as we say that they form one verse according to the present division of small verses borrowed from the Masoretes.

After Jerome had stated in the preface to the Book of Job that, once translated from Hebrew, it proceeds among the Hebrews in hexameter verses—from the words of Job where he says, “May the day perish,” and so forth, [Col. 0119D] up to the place where, before the end of the volume, it is written, “Therefore I condemn myself, and repent in dust and ashes”—he immediately added:

“From the verse mentioned above to the end of the book, the short comma that remains is composed in prose.”

I would have two things observed here. First, the same distinction and the same content of a single verse in the words of Job mentioned above were used by Jerome as are customary in the present verse-division of the Vulgate. It follows that certain traces of the present distinction appear in Jerome.

Second, the comma called by the same holy Doctor in this passage should not be understood indiscriminately together with the cola and commata of the verses whose divisions are being discussed in this section. For the comma that remains from the verse mentioned above in Job to the end of the book is a complete chapter consisting of many sentences—that is, many verses and the commata of verses. The comma mentioned here is therefore the same as the περικοπή among Origen and the other Greek commentators.

I thought that I had found another trace of the present distinction of verses in Book I of Jerome’s Commentaries on Daniel, chapter 3. Concerning the words, “Bless the Lord, you saints and humble in heart; praise and exalt him forever,” Saint Jerome discusses them as follows:

“To have humility of heart, the present little verse also teaches,” and so forth.

But after carefully examining the manuscript codices of the Commentaries on Daniel, I discovered that the published books have no reliable basis. For they describe the text of Daniel as though Jerome were reciting and explaining the whole of verse 87 of chapter 3 in his commentary, whereas it is certain that he placed and expounded only half of our verse, namely:

> Bless the Lord, you saints and humble in heart.

This is what Jerome calls “the present little verse,” according to the ancient, not the present, distinction of verses.

We must therefore turn to other examples. From the most ancient monuments, from not a few of Jerome’s letters, and from Augustine’s excellent *Speculum*, we learn that a twofold distinction of verses was customary among the ancients in Psalm 118.

These most ancient monuments are the much-praised Psalter of Saint-Germain and the three exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew truth. In Psalm 118 they contain sixteen verses under each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, written in the following manner in the old Vulgate contained in the aforementioned Psalter of Saint-Germain:

> **ALEPH.**  
>   
> BLESSED ARE THE UNDEFILED IN THE WAY,  
>   
> WHO WALK IN THE LAW OF THE LORD;  
>   
> BLESSED ARE THOSE WHO SEARCH HIS TESTIMONIES,  
>   
> WITH THEIR WHOLE HEART THEY SEEK HIM, and so forth.

The same text is read in the most ancient exemplar of the Psalms. In the exemplars of the Canon, the number of verses is the same, but they are written somewhat differently:

> **ALEPH.**  
>   
> Blessed are the undefiled in the way,  
> who walk in the law of the Lord.  
>   
> Blessed are those who keep his testimonies;  
> with their whole heart they seek him.  
>   
> For those who work iniquity  
> have not walked in his ways.  
>   
> You commanded your precepts  
> to be kept exceedingly.  
>   
> Would that my ways might be directed  
> toward keeping your precepts.  
>   
> Then I shall not be put to shame  
> when I look upon all your commandments.  
>   
> I will confess to you with an upright heart  
> when I have learned the judgments of your righteousness.  
>   
> I will keep your precepts;  
> do not utterly forsake me.  
>   
> **BETH.**  
>   
> By what means does a young man correct his way? and so forth.

This was the numerous distinction of verses in Psalm 118, which passed directly from the ancient Latin Vulgate translation into Saint Jerome’s new translation, as is readily apparent from Augustine’s *Speculum*. Augustine cited very many verses of this psalm and determines their number, saying that there are two verses from the words, “I have not forgotten your precepts,” up to those read as verse 85: “The proud have dug pits for me, which were not according to your law.”

There are just as many from these words up to: “They nearly destroyed me on the earth,” and so forth. The numbers of verses which Augustine assigns by repeated statements—“And after two verses,” “And after seven verses,” and so forth—correspond perfectly to the distinction just described, which was customary in the ancient monuments of the churches and which displays divisions of sixteen verses under each letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

Many other very ancient and excellent manuscript codices of the Psalms have only eight verses written under each Hebrew letter, both in the old edition according to the Septuagint translators and in the new Hieronymian edition derived from Hebrew volumes.

Such is the threefold Psalter of Saint Jerome, written in a most ancient Carnutian codex in three columns set opposite one another, after the fashion of Origen’s Tetrapla and Hexapla. Such also is another threefold Psalter of the Sorbonne Library, which most carefully preserves the Greek edition of the Seventy Elders, although written in Latin characters, together with the Roman Psalter and Jerome’s Hebrew translation.

The same is true of the Vatican, royal, Colbertine, San-Germanensis, and countless other manuscript codices of the Psalms, in which Jerome’s new edition or the old edition according to the Septuagint translators is found. All those codices are written by verse-cola—that is, in groups of eight verses—according to the present-day distinction and enumeration of verses in Psalm 118.

Concerning this psalm Jerome wrote to Paula of Urbica:

“You have most diligently inquired what the Hebrew letters seemed to signify that were inserted in the psalm we were reading. I replied that it was composed according to the order of the letters: namely, that eight verses began with the first letter, which among them is called ALEPH; then, again, eight verses began with the following letter, BETH; afterward the same number was completed from GIMEL; and so on through TAU, which is their final letter. Thus the psalm was written,” and so forth.

Hilary and Ambrose follow the same distinction of verses in their commentaries on Psalm 118. It is therefore clear to us that traces of the present distinction and enumeration of verses exist not only in Jerome but also in other teachers of the Church and in the most ancient writers.

The same should be understood of the final section of Proverbs as of Psalm 118. For in Jerome the περικοπή that continues the praises of the valiant woman consists of twenty-two verses, according to the number of the Hebrew letters. Jerome says in the letter already mentioned:

“Solomon’s Proverbs closes the alphabet at the end, which he counts in iambic tetrameter from the place where he says: ‘Who will find a strong woman?’”

In the exemplars of the Canon and in several other very ancient manuscript codices, however, that section contains not merely twenty-two verses but forty-four, because the final alphabet is written there by cola and commata:

> Who will find a strong woman?  
> Her price is far from the furthest boundaries.  
>   
> The heart of her husband trusts in her,  
> and he shall not lack spoils, and so forth.

From this one may conclude that the most ancient monuments contained a twofold distinction of verses, and that both were recognized and used by the older ecclesiastical writers.

In Augustine you will always find the distinction by cola and commata in use. In Jerome, however, you will find sometimes the same distinction and sometimes a different one, according to the character of the individual portions of divine Scripture.

In metrical compositions, which have fixed rhythms according to the sequence of the Hebrew letters, he almost always used the distinction of verses that we follow today in the Latin Vulgate. In the other books, however, as we said above, he counts the verses of the Bible according to the extremely extensive distinction received in the churches in his own time—that is, the distinction received in the old Vulgate, which was worn by the hands of the Latins.

Before we propose various indexes of these small verses, it will not be useless to append several distinctions customary in the New Testament.

A certain distinguished man, F. Desmares, communicated to me some manuscript fragments of the Gospel according to Luke in which the ancient distinction of verses survives, together with the ancient Latin version written in uncial letters on very old parchment. In Luke 5:18 we read the following:

> AND BEHOLD, POWERFUL MEN WERE CARRYING ON A BED A MAN WHO WAS PARALYZED; AND THEY WERE SEEKING TO BRING HIM IN AND PLACE HIM BEFORE HIM; AND, NOT FINDING, etc.

The scribe of that codex distinguished two verses there, marking an upper point at the end of each. I observed no other distinction of verses in that manuscript exemplar.

In another fragment of the same Gospel, however, the division of verses is complete, and the distinction of commata is marked by spaces:

> AND BEHOLD, TWO OF THE DISCIPLES OF JESUS,  
> GOING OUT,  
> WERE JOURNEYING THAT SAME DAY  
> TO A VILLAGE  
> WHICH WAS SIXTY STADIA  
> FROM JERUSALEM,  
> NAMED EMMAUS.

These four verses of the ancient distinction constitute a single verse—Luke 24:13—in our Latin Vulgate. The difference in the numbers of biblical verses between us and the ancients will therefore be as great as the relation of one part to four parts.

No one should therefore be troubled by the greatly differing numbers of verses now counted in the sacred volumes when compared with the enumerations of verses read in ancient manuscript exemplars of the sacred Bible, both Greek and Latin.

It seemed incredible to a recent critical writer that seven hundred or eight hundred verses were missing from the Book of Job alone before the edition of that book which Jerome published with asterisks and obeli. But if he had been moderately familiar with the ancient distinctions of verses, and had judged them from the most ancient exemplars of the divine volumes rather than from his own presumption, he would have recognized the absurdity of his conjecture. By it he wished to tamper with the authentic reading of Jerome’s preface to the Book of Job and to alter it in the following manner:

> “Seventy or eighty verses are missing,”

instead of “seven hundred,” or instead of “eight hundred,” “seventy” or “eighty.”

What sort of restorer of Hieronymian readings is this? Would that those who trouble you were cut off.

We have omitted more, lest excessive length become burdensome to the reader and what benefits the writer’s exercise harm his bodily health. To display every possible ancient and recent distinction of biblical verses, we present in fourfold tables the number of verses contained in each book of divine Scripture, so that every diligent student may clearly perceive such differing distinctions at a single glance and need not thereafter be compelled to follow the errors of individual critics.

The Book of Judith, which is not in the Canon of the Hebrews, contains 1,300 verses according to the ancient distinction; 1,100 in the codices of Jerome’s version; and 1,700 according to Nicephorus of Constantinople. Tobit contains 1,000 verses in the ancient division and 800 according to Nicephorus; elsewhere it is omitted.

In the New Testament the enumerations of verses are indeed different, but the distance between the indexes is smaller than it is in the books of the Old Testament, as the following fourfold tables will show.

[Col. 0124A]

The first enumeration of verses, which we call the ancient one, from before Jerome, we have borrowed from the very ancient Catalogue of the manuscript codex of Saint-Germain, which contains the Epistles of Paul in Greek and Latin, written in uncial letters. The scribe of this book [Col. 0124C] appended at the end, before the Epistle to the Hebrews, a Catalogue of all the divine books of the Old and New Testament, recording opposite each the number of its verses. Nevertheless, he omitted several books of the Old Testament and some of the Epistles of the Apostle Paul. We have noted this omission at the appropriate places in the following manner: “omitted here”—supply the verses of the book not listed in that very ancient catalogue of the sacred Scriptures. Under the name of Barnabas he seems to have listed the verses of the Epistle to the Hebrews; yet he should not be thought so absent-minded that he would carelessly omit altogether the Epistle lying before his eyes while he was copying the Catalogue. Let learned judgment decide this matter.

He numbers the verses of each book according to the divisions found in the ancient Latin version received in use before Jerome. This can be clearly proved from the single book of Job, which he says contains sixteen hundred verses. You should note that, before Job was restored among the Greeks by Origen with asterisks, it had 1,600 verses, or *stichoi* (στίχοι, “lines” or “verses”). Once restored, however, it had 2,200 verses—that is, six hundred more than the preceding number. Consult the testimonies of the ancient writers placed at the beginning of the same book of Job, edited by us with asterisks and obeli, in the second part of this Divine Bible.

[Col. 0124D]

We found the second enumeration of verses in manuscript codices of Jerome’s version, and have set that number out here in our fourfold tables just as it appears in those very ancient exemplars. The errors, therefore, of this sort [Col. 0125A]—however many there are—are to be attributed to ancient copyists and unskilled scribes. Furthermore, we said that the third Catalogue of the sacred books, with the number of verses recorded for each book, was that of Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople. The most learned P. Pithou published it for us in his little work *On the Latin Interpreters of the Holy Scriptures*; the curious reader may consult that work. Finally, Robert Estienne took the index of the fourth column from Greek exemplars. If any difficulty arises there, you should consult the Greek edition of the New Testament, produced by that same writer in exceptionally elegant type.

Studious readers could rightly reproach us if I concealed in silence the recent errors [Col. 0125B] of a critical writer who, indulging his customary conjectures, has laid down many assertions about the division and number of the verses of the Bible in which there is no truth. While he repeatedly attempts to correct the faults of others, he has revealed his own.

This man supposed that ancient writers called every division of the text of the books “verses”—what we call *lignes* in French, and what the Greeks call *stichoi* (στίχοι). He further supposed that these lines were fixed at a definite number of words, so that from the number of verses recorded at the end of the books one could easily know how many words each book contained. Finally, he taught that Augustine frequently referred to verses of this kind in the *Speculum*, and that from certain verses quoted by him it could be inferred that every verse contained only six words.

So taught this critic, who congratulates himself on having brought forth among Catholics a knowledge of the divine Scriptures and fears that it will at some time be completely extinguished with him. But it is easy for us to expose the vanity of this opinion from a single book of Ruth. Reading the whole book with great care in numerous manuscript codices, I counted the lines and the individual words, in order to assess the false observations of the aforementioned writer.

I wished to examine the matter and count the words in the book of Ruth because its brevity makes it more suitable for our purpose, and because the same number of verses is recorded at the end of it in the oldest manuscript codices. The book of Ruth in the Royal manuscript codex of the sacred Scriptures, no. 3563, written in two columns in a minute hand or character, contains 335 lines; each column comprises [Col. 0125D] 42 lines. The lines sometimes have three words, some have four complete words together with half a word, and sometimes five, six, or seven.

The Colbert manuscript no. 157 writes out the whole book of Ruth in 216 lines. Its columns contain 43 lines. The lines have five words, or six, or seven with several syllables, and sometimes even eight.

Another Colbert manuscript, no. 74, completes the entire book of Ruth in 363 lines. Its columns have 30 lines. The lines contain at one point two words or three; elsewhere three and a half; at another point four or five.

The Saint-Germain Bible codex, written on parchment eight hundred years ago and marked no. 3, has in the whole book of Ruth only 243 lines. The columns contain 55 lines; the lines have four, five, six, seven, or eight words, sometimes complete, sometimes cut off and unfinished at the end. [Col. 0126A]

To these must be added the Corbie biblical codex, of the same age as the preceding one, in which Ruth has 218 lines. Each column contains 45 lines, and the lines have four, five, six, seven, or eight words, as they are found in the preceding manuscript codices.

Now, if we remember that among ancient ecclesiastical writers the book of Ruth had only 250 verses, both in the ancient division before Jerome and in the codices of Jerome’s version, who could calmly endure all the many and great errors of recent criticism of the Old Testament, which deceives many earnest men with impunity in matters sometimes of little, sometimes of the greatest, importance?

It is false that the ancients called every line of writing a verse; it is also false that those lines consisted of six words; and it is most false of all that readers could learn from the recorded number of verses how many words each book contained. The five most ancient monuments cited by us have neither the same number of lines nor an equal number of words in their lines nor a similar total number of lines throughout the book, although in the book of Ruth the same number of verses—namely, 250—is recorded at the end of each.

Let our critic produce, if he can, some very ancient exemplar of the Bible in which the number of verses recorded at the end is equal to the number of lines in which that exemplar was written. Let him further show that each line in that exemplar has only six words, and that from this prescribed number of words one can immediately recognize how many words there are in this or that book. If he does this, he will be a great Apollo to us, and I, the abortive offspring of the critics, shall bring forward six hundred volumes that exclude belief in this learned man.

### IV

In this present article we briefly ask whether there are meters in the sacred Scriptures, and especially in the Psalms of David. It is indeed a very famous question, but only among those who are unskilled in the sacred language and unable by their own resources to resolve the difficulty. Among the more learned and experienced in the sacred books, however, there is no doubt that the songs of the Bible are composed metrically.

Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, and Josephus, the wisest, explicitly taught this. After those native Jewish writers, Origen, Eusebius, Ambrose, [Col. 0126D] and Jerome likewise testified to it, together with countless other ecclesiastical authors of a later age and with the most learned scholiast on the Canon of the Hebrew truth, who expressly maintains the same opinion in his *Hebrew Questions* on chapter 23 of the Second Book of Samuel:

“These are the last words of David.”

“They are called ‘last,’” says the scholiast, “because after the Psalter and the other meters, he is said to have composed this meter, in which he says: ‘David, son of Jesse, said; the man said, to whom the ladder of the Christ of the God of Jacob was appointed.’”

He recognizes not only meters in David’s Psalter and in his other songs, but also observes a metrical composition and Davidic melody in the words of Scripture just cited, from the first verse of chapter 23 of the Second Book of Kings [Samuel] through the eighth verse.

Whoever examines these matters with greater care will easily abandon the opinion of certain modern writers who think that there are no meters in the sacred books, because they have been taught this by certain modern authorities whose names I omit, lest I seem to injure anyone.

One of them says that it was the common opinion of the ancients that many parts of Scripture, and especially the Psalter and nearly all the Canticles, consisted of verses. But since some more recent writers oppose this opinion and designate the Psalms of David by the term “poem,” their language may be explained as meaning not that the Psalms are bound by metrical feet, but that their diction is elevated, impassioned, and suited to singing.

Those who have written in this way are mistaken. The ancient writers who call the Psalms of David “poems” cannot be explained in this manner. Unless perhaps you say that in Josephus, *Antiquities*, book II, at the end of the chapter, the words “they compose it in hexameter rhythm” (ἐν ἑξαμέτρῳ τόνῳ συντιθήσιν) mean no more than that he sang God’s praises in elevated and impassioned diction.

Likewise, in Philo and Jerome, verses consisting of trimeter and iambic tetrameter would, on this interpretation, be explained as elevated and impassioned diction, if credence is given to the observations just mentioned. Let us not mock the simplicity of our readers in this way, lest learned writers mock us in their books.

The opinion of the ancients concerning the meters and poems of Scripture is therefore true. The principles of these poems must be learned, and diligently investigated, from the most learned of the Hebrews, not from some ignorant person. R. Azariah teaches you this in part 3, chapter 60, of his work entitled *Me’or ʿEnayim*:

“There is no doubt that the sacred songs possess definite measures and proportions. But these do not consist in the number of movements—that is, syllables—or in complete or incomplete feet, according to the form of modern poems. Rather, they consist in the number of things and of their parts: namely, the subject, the predicate, and that which joins them together in each sentence and proposition, or in each verse.

“Thus one verse consists of two measures or parts of a proposition; if a second is added, there are four parts or measures. Another consists of three measures; if another verse is added to it, there are six measures or parts.

“For example, in the Song of Moses, Exodus 15:6, ‘Your right hand, O Lord’ (*yemineka Adonai*) is one verse consisting of two divisions; ‘Your hand is glorious in power’ (*nedari bakkoach*) is similar and connected with it, and together they make four—that is, a tetrameter—and so forth.”

Azariah offers other examples from the sacred songs, by which he proves that those songs consist of tetrameters or hexameters—that is, of four or six parts, which he calls divisions. But you may see these matters in Johann Buxtorf the Younger, in the *Appendix to Several Dissertations* at the end of the book *Kuzari*.

### V

I said that among the learned there is no question whether some parts of the sacred Scripture possess a certain metrical composition. To deny this against the unanimous agreement of all the most celebrated ancient writers would not be to display the good sense one ought to have, but gratuitously to behave foolishly.

The settled opinion of learned men, therefore, is that metrical art and composition occur in certain sacred books. But this is a very famous question: What was once the structure of ancient sacred poetry? It is burdened with such great difficulties that scarcely anything certain can be established about it.

And if we listen to very many earnest scholars, far from what Josephus, Philo, Eusebius, Jerome, Theodoret, and Isidore wrote about the poems of the Bible making the obscure matter clearer and satisfying readers, they have instead made readers’ minds more uncertain and perplexed. For they have nowhere been able to find what those writers transmitted. Hence they either wish their words to be understood and explained in some other way, or accuse them of having sold smoke to their readers and of speaking too boldly about matters they had not sufficiently known or examined.

We have resolved to remove such reproaches from Jerome [Col. 0128B] and to attempt to show that he was not a seller of smoke but a most experienced interpreter of the divine Scriptures. To bring this matter to a successful conclusion, we must first present the passages in which Buxtorf, speaking for other scholars, complains that Jerome sold smoke.

In the preface to the *Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea*, while discussing the difficulty of interpretation, Jerome makes the following incidental observation about the meters of Scripture:

“Finally, what is more melodious than the Psalter, which, in the manner of our Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, now runs in iambics, now resounds in Alcaics, now swells in Sapphics, now advances on a half-foot? What is more beautiful than the song of Deuteronomy and Isaiah? What is more majestic than Solomon? What is more perfect than Job? All these, as Josephus and Origen write, proceed among their own people composed in hexameter and pentameter verses. When we read them in Greek, they sound like something else; in Latin, they do not hold together at all.”

It is not unusual for Jerome first to follow common opinions and afterward to depart from them when he has had time to assign to each matter its due consideration. He himself warned his reader of this inconsistency when he interpreted the name *Daphca* in Letter 127, station 9:

“This name,” he says, “is called *krouma* (κροῦμα), that is, ‘a striking’ or ‘knocking,’ among the Hebrews, in accordance with what the Lord also says: ‘Knock, and it will be opened to you.’ In the book of Hebrew names, however, we translated it as ‘adhesion’ and ‘retention.’ This should not trouble the reader, nor should he think that we write contradictory things. There we published it according to the common reading, if the middle consonant is written with the letter *beth*; here, however, I found it written in the Hebrew volume with *pe*, a letter that signifies knocking more than sticking . . .

“I ask the prudent and diligent reader to know that I translate the names according to the Hebrew truth. Otherwise, in the Greek and Latin codices, apart from a few items, we find everything corrupted, and I marvel that certain learned and ecclesiastical men wished to translate what is not found in Hebrew.”

We shall soon have occasion to recall this admonition. For the Song of Deuteronomy, which above he followed Josephus and Origen in declaring to be composed in hexameter, he testifies in Letter 155, to Paula of Urbica, to consist of iambic tetrameter. In that letter he discusses the Psalms and other metrical compositions at considerable length:

“Before I discuss each matter, you must know that four Psalms, according to the order of the Hebrews, begin with the letters of the alphabet: the hundred and tenth and the hundred and eleventh, this one about which we are now writing, and the hundred and forty-fourth.

“You should know, however, that in the earlier Psalms each letter is followed by a single verse, and that these verses consist of iambic trimeter; the later ones consist of iambic tetrameter, as does the Song of Deuteronomy.

“In Psalm 118, eight verses follow each letter. In Psalm 144, a single verse is assigned to each letter. There are some who think that other Psalms also begin in this order, but their opinion is false.

“You also have four alphabets in the Lamentations of Jeremiah. The first two seem to be written in Sapphic meter, because the three connected verses that begin with one and the same letter are concluded by a heroic colon. The third alphabet is written in trimeter, and begins with three letters, with three verses beginning from each of them. The fourth alphabet resembles the first and second.

“The Proverbs of Solomon also conclude with an alphabet, which is reckoned as iambic tetrameter, beginning at the place where it says: ‘Who will find a strong woman?’

“The works of Solomon and the Song of Deuteronomy, which in the preface to the *Chronicle of Eusebius* he taught run among their own people composed in hexameters and pentameters, he here asserts, in writing to Paula, to consist of iambic tetrameter.

“He is more consistent with himself in the verses of Job. For in the preface to that same book he says:

“‘From the beginning of the book up to the words of Job, there is prose among the Hebrews. But from the words of Job in which he says, “May the day perish on which I was born,” and so forth, up to the place where, near the end of the book, it is written, “Therefore I condemn myself,” and so forth, there are hexameter verses, running in dactyls and spondees. Because of the idiom of the language, other feet must frequently be admitted—not of the same syllables, but of the same temporal quantities. Sometimes the rhythm itself proceeds sweetly and sonorously with metrical numbers released from the law of meter; this is understood by those skilled in meter rather than by the ordinary reader.’”

[lacuna]

“If anyone finds it incredible that there are meters among the Hebrews, and that the Psalter, the Lamentations of Jeremiah, or nearly all the Canticles of Scripture are included in the manner of Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, Alcaeus, and Sappho, let him read Philo, Josephus, Origen, and Eusebius of Caesarea, and by their testimony he will prove that I speak the truth.”

He likewise presents our Psalmist David as a rival of Greek and Latin poets in the letter written to Paulinus about all the books of the divine History:

“David is our Simonides, our Pindar and Alcaeus; Flaccus also, Catullus, and Serenus: with his lyre he makes Christ resound, and on the ten-stringed Psalter he raises the risen one from the underworld.”

He again proclaims this kind of lyric poetry in explicit terms in book 9 of his *Commentaries on chapter 30 of the prophet Ezekiel*:

“But in the Psalms the answer is easy: the poem is lyric, and in such a work the order of history is not sought, but the poems of individual deeds.”

Finally, in his preface to Jeremiah, he mentioned the fourfold alphabet and the measure of meter in these words:

“Thus he prophesied only in Judah and Benjamin, and lamented the ruins of his city in a fourfold alphabet, which we have rendered in metrical measure and verses.”

These, I think, are the more famous passages in which Jerome declared both his own opinion and that of his predecessors concerning the meters of the sacred Bible. If we could explain and present them in the same spirit in which they were written, I should not despair of most vigorously defending Jerome against the earlier charge of selling smoke.

But I fear that, overcome by the difficulty of the subject, after undertaking Jerome’s exposition I may be forced to cry out with him: “Forgive, reader, the difficulty, and grant pardon to poor understanding.” For through slanting windows made in the form of a net, which are always closed, we thrust in our eye as we attempt to investigate the various kinds of poems in the sacred books.

Nevertheless, it is worthwhile to attempt even this much toward completing our *Prolegomena*, which were prepared with no other purpose than to elucidate and defend the greatest interpreter of Scripture.

To make his opinion concerning the meters and verses of the divine books clear, the testimonies cited above seem to be reducible to three or four kinds of poetry. First, the holy Doctor recognizes in the book of Job hexameter verses proceeding in dactyls and spondees. In the Psalms, however, he recognizes iambic trimeters and tetrameters, as in the Song of Deuteronomy, which he declares to consist of iambic tetrameter, although elsewhere he had said that it was composed in hexameter verse.

Finally, he asserts that the Lamentations are written in something like Sapphic verse, because of the heroic colon that concludes three connected verses. What he says about the Lamentations as written in something like Sapphic verse must likewise be understood of the other kinds of poetry.

Nor would the Hebrew language, in which the sacred books were composed by their hagiographical authors, permit feet altogether identical with the hexameters and pentameters of the Greeks and Latins. Therefore, when you hear “hexameters” and “pentameters,” you must understand a certain resemblance to heroic verses; and likewise with the other types of meter, iambic and Alcaic, in which Jerome says that the Psalter runs and resounds.

Thus the heroic, elegiac, and lyric poems in the sacred Scriptures are not identical with Greek or Latin meters, but resemble those meters. Nevertheless, no one should doubt that these images and likenesses of verses surpass by far all the modes of Pindar, Flaccus, Horace, and Homer.

Let us now pursue our proposal by means of some new experiments, beginning with the book of Job and the metrical resemblance that we have said exists in the sacred books. The verses of Job, chapter 3, begin in the following manner in ancient Hebrew exemplars:

*Jobed jom havaled bo valaela amar hora gaber.*

*Ajom ahu jehi hosach al-jadrasu Eloa mimmaal val-thophaa alav nara.*

These have been rendered into Latin in the following order in the Exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth:

May the day perish on which I was born,

and the night in which it was said: “A man has been conceived.”

May that day be turned into darkness;

may God not seek it from above,

and may it not be illumined by light.

Do not be surprised that in the third word of the first verse I have written *havaled* in place of the Hebrew [the preceding reading is materially uncertain]. For, as Jerome testifies, the ancient Hebrews had the custom of reading *aleph* as *he* and *he* as *aleph*. Hence he says in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*:

“Nor is it surprising that, although among the Greeks and among us the letter A appears to have been added in the name Abram, we say that the Hebrew letter HE was added. For it is an idiom of that language to write with HE but read with A; conversely, they often pronounce the letter A as HE.”

It should also be noted that, guided by Jerome’s authority, I have read *gabor* for the modern *gaver*, and *Hosach* for *choschech*. For in his letter to Evagrius on Melchizedek, he teaches that the Hebrew word *Salim* or *Salem* may be read indifferently:

“It makes no difference,” he says, “whether it is called Salem or Salim, since the Hebrews very rarely use vowels among the consonants, and according to the will of readers and the truth of the regions the same words are pronounced with different sounds and accents.”

I also read the letter *heth* with a capital H, to distinguish it from the simple *he*. This is likewise observed in the appendix to the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, which I ask the reader to consult together with the scholia appended to it.

From this preliminary ancient reading of the Hebrew words, it will not be impossible to vindicate Jerome against unjust critics who condemn whatever they see differing from their own saliva.

The verses of the book of Job therefore present something of the appearance of hexameter in the words of which they consist. In the first verse, for example, dactylic and spondaic feet proceed, and a reasonable comparison may be made between the first verse of the *Aeneid* and this Hebrew verse of Job:

*Jobed jom havaled bo valaela amar hora gaber.*

“I sing of arms and the man who first from the shores of Troy . . .”

The Hebrew verse of Job has as many syllables as the Latin verse of Maro. The caesura also corresponds perfectly in the two, and although the dactyls do not agree either in short syllables or in the number of feet, there are nevertheless certain words consisting of three syllables that take the place of the Greek and Latin dactyls.

Moreover, the Hebrew verse has a similar sound, or rhythm, as the French say, at the ends of its cola, since both cola end in *o*, *bo*, and *bor*. In this respect Hebrew poems possess an ornament beyond Greek or Latin meters.

Furthermore, from the same agreement between Hebrew verses and Latin hexameters—an agreement that occurs six hundred times throughout the whole book of Job—it is clearly demonstrated that Jerome did not speak rashly or ignorantly when he declared that the same book contained hexameter verses, nor did he ineptly discern in it the form and image of dactyl and spondee.

Nor does it prevent this that many things often obstruct such correspondence, since Jerome himself gave warning of it when he said that, because of the idiom of the language, the book of Job frequently admits other feet and forms.
