Let this hastily and provisionally stated discussion of the hexameters of Job suffice in defense of the holy Doctor. We may now briefly touch upon Sapphic verse in the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

The first of the Lamentations of Jeremiah has the following beginning in the Hebrew text:

*Echa jasceva vadad hair rabbathi am*

*hajetha kealmana rabbathi baggoim*

*sarathi bammeainoth hajetha lamas.*

Saint Jerome rendered these into Latin in metrical measure and verses as follows:

**ALEPH**

How does the city sit solitary,

that was full of people?

She has become as a widow,

the mistress of the nations;

the princess of provinces

has been made subject to tribute.

These three verses, connected with one another and beginning with the single letter Aleph, bear the likeness of a single hymnic strophe and seem to have been written in something like Sapphic verse, especially in the Hebrew text, where *hajetha lamas*, the complete heroic colon, concludes the final verse.

They also have a similar ending in their verses, which we call *rime* in French. For the first two end in *mem*, and the first and third end in the vowel *a*—namely, *am* and *mas*. Finally, if the syllables of the verses are counted, you will find an equal number in them.

Thus we have seen and established that Jerome wrote nothing rashly when he said:

“You also have four alphabets in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, of which the first two seem to be written in Sapphic meter, because the three connected verses that begin with one and the same letter are concluded by a heroic colon.”

Something must also be added about the Song of Deuteronomy, which is said to consist either of hexameter verses or of iambic tetrameter. That outstanding poem has the appearance of hexameter in the fact that nearly every verse proceeds through six words, as though through an equal number of feet and meters:

*Haazinu haschamaim vaadabbera vethismah haarets imrephi jaaroph kammatar licchi tizzal kattal imrathi.*

Give ear, O heavens, to what I say;

let the earth hear the words of my mouth.

May my teaching gather like rain;

may my speech flow like dew.

Do not the *cola* of those verses of Deuteronomy plainly present the true appearance of heroic poems? Consider the rhythm in this Virgilian distich:

Meanwhile the sky turns, and night rushes from Ocean.

The ox is stretched out, trembling and lifeless, and falls to the ground.

Consider, I say, those metrical patterns in the pagan poet. I shall always praise the sacred poems of the divine prophet: in their rhythm they retain everywhere equality and gravity; in their caesuras, the gentleness of another sonorous rhythm in the broad sense; and in their six-word verses, a majesty that is almost hexametric and plainly divine.

If the curious reader seeks in the Song of Moses another kind of meter consisting of iambic tetrameter, let him remember the imperfect tetrameter that often runs through sacred hymns, to which the verses of Deuteronomy may certainly be compared. For example, the first two verses of the song just mentioned:

*Haazinn aschamaim vaadebbera vethismah haareets imre-phi jaaroph kammatar licchi tizzal kaltal imrathi.*

They bear some resemblance to these iambic tetrameters:

Sing, tongue, the battle of the glorious struggle;

and tell the noble triumph over the trophy of the cross.

Although the later verse of Deuteronomy lacks some syllables required for a perfect tetrameter, and the earlier one has some in excess, those sacred imperfect iambics nevertheless proceed more sweetly than these verses of Terence:

To neglect money in the proper place is sometimes the greatest profit.

Because of their own weakness they always think themselves neglected.

Those who study these Hebrew verses and seek to understand them will readily grant, with Jerome, that Psalms 110 and 111 are almost iambic trimeters. In the Hebrew books Psalm 110 is written as follows:

*Ode Jaho bechol-levav:*

*besod jescarim veeda.*

I shall confess to the Lord with my whole heart,

in the council of the upright and the congregation.

In Psalm 111 the same kind of verse proceeds as follows:

*Ascre-isc jare eth-Jaho:*

*bemitsvothav hhaphets meod.*

Blessed is the man who fears the Lord;

he greatly delights in his commandments.

Let the reader observe that these Hebrew verses have the same vowel sound at their endings. For *levav* and *veeda* have one ending, or rhythm in the broad sense. Likewise, in Psalm 111, *meod*, ending in the vowel *o*, has the same sound as *Jaho*. For this is how the tetragrammaton, the name of God, ought to be read—not as it is corruptly read today: *Jehova*.

Who does not see that these sacred iambic verses contain a greater melody than the meters of Catullus, Horace, and others? They end in words of two syllables; they have six quasi-feet, or, more accurately, images of feet; they usually retain three complete words, and no more, in the same verse. What else can you call this but iambic trimeter?

Let fastidious men therefore admit that the whole Psalter and all the Canticles of Scripture are animated by a certain poetic character, and that Jerome did not sell smoke when he said:

“Finally, what is more melodious than the Psalter, which, in the manner of our Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, now runs in iambics, now resounds in Alcaics, now swells in Sapphics?”

He had read Pindar and knew what iambic, Alcaic, and Sapphic meter were. Living daily in conversation with the most learned of the Hebrews, and himself thoroughly skilled in the Hebrew language, he could not have been ignorant of which works in the sacred books are metrical and by what metrical laws they are bound.

Therefore Jerome must be trusted rather than Scaliger and the followers of his more recondite discipline. By establishing their own opinion about the meters of Scripture, and especially of the Psalter, they completely overturn the order of the words and verses of the sacred Bible, in which the order of the words is very often itself a mystery.

Hence Jerome says in chapter 3 of his *Epistle to the Ephesians*:

“Because this is how it stands in the Greek, and because individual words, syllables, letters, points, and marks in the divine Scriptures are full of meanings, we prefer to risk the composition and structure of the words rather than the sense.”

Not so the recent writer who, at his pleasure, perverts the sacred text in Psalms 2, 171, and 150 in order to discover rhythmic poetry in them.

It would be easy to restrain such great freedom on the part of this learned man from the distinctions of the most ancient Hebrew codices and from the verses written at intervals in the Exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth. But we have reserved this discussion for more leisurely consideration and another time, contenting ourselves here with laying certain foundations for a future structure.

Whatever the value of these observations, let them not seem frivolous to the reader, even if they displease me, the one who makes them, since I feel that I am knocking on a closed door. They should nevertheless be read with indulgence. Otherwise I could simply have confessed my ignorance and cut off all desire among earnest readers.

For although we are far from perfect knowledge, we judge it a lighter fault to say at least a little about the sacred meters than to say nothing at all.

## EPILOGUE

[Col. 0133]

Our *Prolegomena*, therefore, should be read peacefully, and our efforts should be supported more by goodwill and prayers than despised with a malicious ear, since even the unlearned can criticize and disparage. It belongs to the learned, and to those who know the sweat of laborers, either to extend a hand to the weary or to show the way to those who have gone astray.

And what benefit is there in foaming lips and the chatter of dogs barking against us, when a simple and moderate reply can either appease you, if it is true, or, if it is false, gently and peaceably correct you?

I have said this for the sake of our rivals, whom we know to be directing the censor’s rod [Col. 0134D] and many insults against our work. For the rest, we have by no means abandoned the hope we have placed in fair-minded and learned readers. They will readily grant us pardon if we have made any mistakes in this edition of the Divine Bible—especially if they understand that I am disposed not to fear excessively the haughtiness of certain critics, but to rejoice greatly in obeying every benevolent reprover.

Let others beware, those who threaten lightning, lest they turn their weapons against someone other than Brother John Martianay. Whatever has been done incorrectly in this edition [Col. 0135A] of Saint Jerome, I declare, must be charged to me. No weapons of insult should cling to my other associates, since they had no share whatsoever in my ignorance.

I therefore earnestly ask you to return whatever good there may be—and there is truly much good in this work—to the Father of lights. You will not deny the praise due also to the Lord Antonio Pouget, joined to me by fraternal affection and shared studies, when you see the canons of the Gospels restored with marvelous skill to their proper places.

[Col. 0136A]

In the remaining matters, either bring forth better fare and use me as your guest, or be content with our little dinner, whatever it may be.

[Col. 0135]

## PRAISE OF CERTAIN MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MEN, WITH A CATALOGUE OF THE MANUSCRIPT CODICES ON WHOSE AUTHORITY THE DIVINE BIBLE OF JEROME HAS BEEN RESTORED
[Col. 0135B] Jerome taught that what we have received must be returned promptly and with interest, since delay in repaying the principal generates still greater interest. Accordingly, although customary practice might have led us to place at the end of this volume the catalogue of the manuscript books we were able to consult, I wished to set it here at the beginning, so that from this deliberately reversed arrangement everyone might at last understand the sincere and eager gratitude of our heart toward learned and studious men whom we have found especially favorable to the edition of St. Jerome.

I know that I am bound by a promise dating from the time when I composed the prospectus of our edition. In its first part I promised to express our gratitude toward those who would contribute some assistance or learning toward a new edition of St. Jerome’s works. Therefore, wishing to discharge those promises as though repaying so great a debt with interest, I gladly fulfill them here, even though all praise must fall short of the humanity and benevolence by which we are bound to these men.

And who could worthily receive the first return of our praise except the most learned Lord Jacques-Bénigne BOSSUET, bishop of Meaux? He gave us no ordinary assistance in publishing the Divine Library, since he repeatedly deigned to honor our labor so greatly that he said the greatest benefit for the Church of Christ would come from it. Moreover, how often did he encourage us to complete so difficult a work? How often did he wish to examine our most ancient monuments with inquisitive yet kindly eyes, so that he might be an eyewitness to our fidelity and diligence?

He could not, it is true, lend us the manuscript books that he did not possess; but he rendered a benefit scarcely less important by joining himself, before all devout and studious people, as an approver of our codices, which are pre-eminent both in their merited antiquity and in their excellence. Such a patron, after the supreme Maecenas—the Roman pontiff, I mean—our Jerome was seeking: one in whom episcopal dignity joined with learning and piety would be powerful both to exhort people in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it. He refutes them now by overthrowing the enemies of the Church in his most learned studies, now by restraining certain Catholic writers, whose works are swollen with ignorant presumption, from publishing books.

It was necessary to recall these matters briefly, so that we might indicate to posterity that the most wise man mentioned above everywhere displayed benevolence toward us, and likewise a lasting devotion toward our Jerome. [Col. 0136B]

As we now compile the catalogue of the manuscript codices, we begin with the exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, because it was chiefly on the authority of these that we published the first and nobler part of the Divine Library. We found, unless I am mistaken, six exemplars of this kind: four that divide the whole Old Testament into three orders, which in the manuscript codices bear the following inscriptions in these exact words: “Here begins the first order, of the Law”; “Here begins the second order, of the Prophets”; “Here begins the third order, of the Hagiographa.”

Those codices are: one belonging to the distinguished Church of Narbonne; another to the Church of Carcassonne; a third to this monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; and a fourth to the library of the most illustrious Lord de Mesmes, president of the Paris Parlement. [Col. 0136C]

Among those four exemplars, the Memmian codex is the most complete and perfect. Nothing in it is mutilated or damaged, because it has always been preserved with the greatest care, both on account of the dignity of its antiquity and on account of the elegance and value of its golden and silver script, in which very many portions of the book are written.

That codex does not contain the marginal scholia of the ancient Hebrew scholar mentioned above; in their place, however, it preserves innumerable variant readings in Jerome’s prefaces and in the sacred text. The humanity and benevolence of the illustrious president mentioned above are extraordinary: he has always received us most graciously whenever we came to him. Nor does he allow the codex to be carried outside his own house, because of the oath by which, he says, he and his parents are bound—not to allow that manuscript book to be taken elsewhere. [Col. 0136D]

Knowledge of this book reached us rather late. We had already published two complete orders, or two parts, of the Canon when, from reading a certain citation, I learned that the book of Daniel was found written in the Memmian manuscript codex, not with the other prophets but after the books of Solomon. I immediately understood that this exemplar contained the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, since only in the Canon of the Hebrew Truth is the prophet Daniel ordinarily placed after the book of the Song of Songs and before Chronicles.

Nor was my judgment mistaken: in that Memmian codex we found the most complete exemplar of the Canon. Some scholars had thoroughly examined it under another name, but, though they had the Canon before their eyes, they did not recognize it as such. [Col. 0137A]

From the Narbonnese exemplar we collated nothing except Jerome’s prefaces. Its first part is mutilated, for it begins with the prophet Isaiah, whom, unless I am mistaken, they later placed before the book of Judges for use in the choir. The books that follow retain the Canon’s native order, as we have indicated in their proper places.

The highly honorable and equally noble canons of the Church of Narbonne lent that codex to me with great kindness. We have said more than enough about the Carcassonne codex in the prospectus of St. Jerome. But this too should be added: in the prophetic books that Canon contains certain marginal scholia by a Hebrew critic, which are absent from our Saint-Germain Canon; conversely, the Saint-Germain Canon preserves in many places scholia of this kind that are omitted in the Carcassonne codex. [Col. 0137B]

The three exemplars just mentioned—the Memmian, Carcassonne, and Saint-Germain codices—were written at the same time and, if we may trust those experienced in such matters, more than eight hundred years ago. In the case of the Memmian codex there can be no remaining doubt, since it is said to have been written at the command of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans.

Another exemplar of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth was supplied to us by the Royal Library. It is extremely ancient and of the finest quality; and although it does not contain the inscriptions of the three orders, as do the four exemplars just praised, I nevertheless think it should be ranked behind none of them.

That Canon is written in two large volumes. The first volume bears the number 3563 and contains the first two orders, namely the Law [Col. 0137C] and the Prophets. The second volume, number 3564, contains the order of the Hagiographa. In this final order of the Canon, the copyist inserted the books of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus after the volumes of Solomon.

Yet, in order to restore the book of Daniel to the ancient order of the books, after the inserted volumes of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus he copied again a considerable portion of the Song of Songs, and then the prophet Daniel, in the manner in which he is read in the true and genuine exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth.

We had a similar manuscript codex in the Saint-Germain library, but most of it was lost to us. Nothing complete remains except the book of Solomon’s Proverbs, the books of Chronicles and Ezra, and Esther, with obeli at the end of the volume. Moreover, the highly honorable Lord Camille le Tellier, abbot of Saint Peter of Bourgueil and provost of the Royal Library, supplied us with a copy of the Royal Canon of the Hebrew Truth. [Col. 0137D]

For the edition of this same Canon of the Hebrew Truth, we had many other manuscript codices of the sacred Scriptures, which preserve Jerome’s true translation together with his prefaces. In particular, the Psalter translated into Latin from the Hebrew and restored by the Holy Doctor was established from ten outstanding and extremely ancient manuscript exemplars. In addition to the exemplars of the Canon already listed, we were able to use six others: one Vatican codex; another belonging to the Augustinians of Bordeaux; a third from the monastery of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea; a fourth from the Sorbonne Library; a fifth from Corbie; [Col. 0138A] and finally a sixth from the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres.

The variant readings of the Vatican codex were collected and sent to me in Paris by Dom Claude Estiennot, our congregation’s procurator general at the Roman court. He is exceptionally studious and truly φιλόπονος (*philóponos*, “a lover of labor”), and leaves no stone unturned in providing us assistance for the edition of the holy Fathers.

The Augustinian exemplar from Bordeaux was lent to me by the Reverend Fathers Paul and Corneille. The Lord Chevilier, the most diligent custodian of the Sorbonne Library, received us with the greatest kindness on very many occasions. From him we received manuscript Psalters of Jerome, which are exceedingly valuable and contributed no little to our edition, although they appear to have been written only about four hundred years ago.

I acknowledge that I owe much to the benevolence and remarkable kindness of His Eminence Cardinal de BONZI. From his Narbonne library he generously allowed me to take with me into our monastery at Crass all the printed and manuscript books I wished to bring. The same freedom was likewise granted to me by D. Pontelier, prior of the Cistercian monastery of Fontfroide, who was always extremely obliging toward us.

If I thought that I could adequately thank the Reverend Fathers Celestines and Carthusians of Avignon, I would be lacking in judgment. It is impossible to believe how much humanity and friendship they lavished upon us when we requested from them a great many manuscript codices of the sacred Scriptures.

Nor must we omit Nicolas Faber, a most wise and religious man, [Col. 0138C] who gave us a biblical volume from the library of the Jesuit college at Avignon to examine. From it we cited several passages in our notes on Jerome’s prefaces.

But, to return to our Parisian friends and continue our praise, let Francis Desmarès now enter this catalogue. He was the grandson, through Louise, of Antoine Allemand; and of him it is rightly said: “He alone is a friend to his friend.” It is not enough for this sincere heart to share with us most generously everything he possesses, published and unpublished. He seeks out material belonging to others everywhere; he presses his requests at suitable and unsuitable times; and if he finds anything useful to our plans and editions, he immediately reveals his enthusiasm, overflowing with the greatest delight.

We experienced a similar devotion to friendship and service in the Reverend Father Ildefonsus Sarrasin of the Cluniac order. Through his agency, ten manuscript volumes of St. Jerome’s works were brought to Paris from the famous monastery of the abbey of Cluny. These volumes are extremely ancient and outstanding, and they contribute substantially to the restoration of almost all the writings of the Holy Doctor. [Col. 0138D]

Religious and learned priests of the Congregation of the Oratory in Paris also lent us, with great kindness, several Hebrew manuscript codices of the Bible. A considerable number of such books is preserved among them.

These are, if I remember correctly, the people to whom we owed thanks at the beginning of the Divine Library, because they greatly assisted its publication by communicating or lending the manuscript exemplars cited above. [Col. 0139A]

The time will come when, in other volumes, we shall continue the praises of John Hardouin, priest of the Society of Jesus; Father Jacques Hommey, an Augustinian; and other learned men [Col. 0140A] who wished, together with them, to perform some service for our Jerome.

[Col. 0139]

## Selected Testimonies of Ancient Writers Concerning the Latin Versions of the Sacred Scriptures Made by Jerome

### Augustine, from chapter 43 of Book XVIII of *The City of God*

[Col. 0139A]

“Although in our own time there was the presbyter Jerome, a most learned man and skilled in all three languages, who translated these same Scriptures into Latin speech not from the Greek but from the Hebrew. Yet, although the Jews admit that his scholarly labor is truthful, they maintain that the Seventy translators erred in many matters,” and so forth.

### The same author, Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 7, no. 15

“Not according to the Septuagint . . . but as they were translated from the Hebrew into Latin speech by the presbyter Jerome, skilled in both languages.”

### The same author, from Letter 71, formerly numbered 10, to Jerome

“In this letter I add what we learned later: that you translated Job from the Hebrew, although we already possessed a certain translation of yours of the same prophet, rendered into Latin from the Greek. In that translation, however, you marked with asterisks what is in the Hebrew and absent from the Greek, and [Col. 0139C] with obeli what is found in the Greek and not in the Hebrew—with such remarkable diligence that in certain places we see individual stars assigned to individual words, indicating that those words are present in the Hebrew but absent from the Greek.”

### The same author, from Letter 82, formerly numbered 19, to Jerome

“That is why I desire your translation from the Septuagint: so that we may be free both from the ignorance of so many Latin translators, of whatever quality, who have dared to undertake this work, and so that those who think I envy your useful labors may finally, if possible, understand,” and so forth.

### The same author, from Letter 71, formerly numbered 10, to Jerome

“Accordingly, we give no small thanks to God for your work, by which you translated the Gospel from the Greek, because there is almost no offense anywhere when we compare it with the Greek Scripture. Thus, if anyone contentiously favors the old falsity, when the codices are produced and compared, he is either very easily instructed or refuted. And if a few extremely rare matters rightly cause concern, who is so hard-hearted that he would not readily forgive labor so useful, to which it is not enough merely to return praise?”

### Prosper of Aquitaine, *On the Ungrateful*, chapter 2

“Then too the guest of Bethlehem, of illustrious name,

graceful in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin speech,

an example of conduct and teacher of the world,

Jerome, in books of great excellence,

dissected the enemy,” and so forth.

### Bishop Hydatius, in the *Chronicle*

[Col. 0140A]

“Jerome, mentioned above, pre-eminent in all things and also most skilled in the elements of the Hebrews, continually meditating day and night on the law of the Lord, as it is written, left behind countless labors.”

### Marcellinus Comes, in the *Chronicle*

[Col. 0140B]

“Jerome, living near the town of Bethlehem, where he also founded a monastery, wrote many other works, having been instructed in the ecclesiastical writings and in the Hebrew letters . . . . For Catholics he was an impregnable tower of the Church, but for all heretics an indefatigable enemy, fighting both by the discipline of his life and by the assertions of the books he published.”

### Gennadius, in the *Life of St. Jerome*, from volume IV of the old *Analecta* and from numerous manuscript codices

“Indeed, I would call this man fortunate, since I regard the outcome of this flight, which corrected the situation, as arranged by the judgment of Christ and prepared for the persecutions of wicked men. That is, so that the Roman Church, established under Peter’s governance, and having received the revealed truth of all the books of the Old Testament—God Christ willing and Jerome laboring with special dedication—might also possess the Hebrew Truth, and so that the frivolity of certain Greeks, which proudly claimed that the Romans had received all the divinely inspired Scriptures from them, might recognize that they possess what the Romans do not possess.”

“Thus, having obtained faith through the grace of Christ and being learned in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters, Jerome translated into Latin all the Hebrew books contained in the Old Testament Canon, in a true edition, and commented on them all.”

### The same author, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 1, in the Corbie manuscript and volume II of the old *Analecta*

[Col. 0140D]

“Our Jerome, thoroughly educated in Greek and Latin letters at Rome . . . . . . was so instructed in Hebrew and Chaldean letters that he translated all the books of the Old Testament from the Hebrew codices into Latin. He also rendered the prophet Daniel, who spoke in the Chaldean style, and the righteous Job, who spoke in Arabic, into the Roman language, transforming both authors through a perfect translation. He likewise made the Gospel of Matthew Roman from the Hebrew.”

The same is read in the Colbert manuscript codex no. 2807, which, after Jerome’s eulogy—which it calls an epitaph—adds the following: “These are the words of the authors concerning the blessed presbyter Jerome. The epitaph ends.”

### Cassiodorus, *On the Institution of Divine Literature*, chapter 21

[Col. 0141A]

“Blessed Jerome too, the outstanding enlarger of the Latin language, who provided us with so much in the translation of divine Scripture that we scarcely need to approach the Hebrew source, since he is known to have satisfied us with the abundance of his eloquence.”

### The same author, in the same book, chapter 15

“But if other words are found to have been placed absurdly, they should be corrected without hesitation, whether from those codices which blessed Jerome emended in his edition of the Seventy Translators, or from those which he himself translated from the Hebrew.”

### Gregory the Great, Preface to the *Moral Exposition of Job*

“I discuss the new translation; but, as the purpose of proof requires, I now draw testimony from the new and now from the old, because the Apostolic See—which, by God’s authority, I govern—uses both, and therefore my labor too may be supported by both.”

### The same author, Book XX of the *Moralia*, chapter 23

“But since this new translation is said to have rendered everything for us more truly from Hebrew and Arabic speech, whatever is said in it must be believed; and our exposition ought carefully to examine its words.”

### Isidore of Seville, Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3

“The presbyter Jerome, skilled in three languages, also translated these same Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin speech and rendered them eloquently. His translation is rightly preferred to the others, for it adheres more closely to the words and is clearer in the meaning of its statements.”

### The same author, Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 12

[Col. 0141C]

“Only the presbyter Jerome translated the sacred Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin speech. All the Churches everywhere generally use his edition, because it is more truthful in its meanings and clearer in its words.”

### Bede the Venerable, in the *Martyrology*, the day before the Kalends of October

“At Bethlehem in Judea, the burial of the holy presbyter Jerome, whose life and teaching stand praised everywhere in the Churches of Christ; how he translated the divine books from the Hebrew language into Latin,” and so forth.

### The same author, Preface to the book *On the Reckoning of Time*

[Col. 0141D]

“I have firmly adopted an opinion which, I think, none of the prudent can refute: just as the most reverend interpreter of the Hebrew Truth said to the detractors of his work, ‘I do not condemn or criticize the Seventy, but I prefer the apostles to them all,’ so I too confidently declare that I do not criticize the ancient chroniclers . . . but prefer to all of them the complete purity of the Hebrew Truth, since the most eminent of the learned—Jerome in his books of Hebrew Questions, and Augustine in his books *On the City of God*—approve it.”

### The same author, in the same work, chapter 66

[Col. 0142A]

“These matters concerning the course of the past age we have labored to investigate from the Hebrew Truth, as far as we were able, judging it fair that, just as the Greeks, using the edition of the Seventy translators, constructed books of the times for themselves and their own people from it, so we too, who through the labor of blessed Jerome the interpreter drink from the pure fountain of the Hebrew Truth, may also know the reckoning of time according to it . . . . For the rest, we advise everyone in common that, whether someone uses the Hebrew Truth—which, as even the hostile Jews openly admit, has reached us pure through the aforementioned interpreter—or whether,” and so forth.

### Rabanus Maurus, Book II of *On the Instruction of Clergy*, chapter 54

“Only the presbyter Jerome translated the sacred Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin speech; [Col. 0142B] all the Churches everywhere generally use his edition, because it is more venerable in its meanings and clearer in its words.”

Maurus transcribed this from Isidore. See above, and read *veracior* (“more truthful”) for *veneratior* (“more venerable”).

### The same author, Preface to his Commentary on the Books of Kings

“For there he will find what Father Augustine and the distinguished interpreter of the divine Books, Jerome, thought.”

### The same author, Preface to his Commentary on Chronicles

“Therefore it must be known that among the Scriptures of the Old Testament the present history of Chronicles holds no insignificant place. Concerning it blessed Jerome, the most skilled interpreter of the divine Books, speaks as follows,” and so forth.

### Trithemius, Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[Col. 0142C]

“Jerome, presbyter and monk . . . . . a man among all teachers most learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished by his knowledge of many languages, interpreter of the sacred Law, hammer of heretics and their most powerful conqueror. He is the true evangelical steward, faithful and prudent, who, bringing forth from his treasure things new and old, and giving his fellow servants their measure of spiritual wheat at the proper time, stripped the proud Hebrews and enriched the humble Latins.”

“Among all the teachers of the Church, no one benefited it more than Jerome. In addition to countless minor works, he translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin, corrected the New Testament according to the Greek Truth, and faithfully presented it to the Church for reading.”

### Prayer of the Catholic Church for the feast of the Holy Doctor

[Col. 0142D]

“O God, who deigned to provide your Church with blessed Jerome, your confessor and greatest Doctor, for the exposition of the Scriptures: grant, we ask, that, aided by his merits and with your help, we may be able to practice what he taught alike by word and deed. Through the Lord, etc.”

[Col. 0141]

## Synopsis of the Divine Library, Taken from Jerome’s Letter to Paulinus

[Col. 0141]

GENESIS is plainly the clearest of books. In it the history of the creation of the world, the origin of the human race, the division of the earth, the confusion of languages and peoples, and the departure of the Hebrews are written down.

[Col. 0143]

EXODUS is clear, with its ten plagues, its Decalogue, and its mystical and divine commandments.

The book of LEVITICUS is readily understood: in it each sacrifice, indeed almost every syllable, the garments of Aaron, and the entire Levitical order breathe heavenly mysteries.

And does not NUMBERS contain the mysteries of the whole of arithmetic, of Balaam’s prophecy, and of the forty-two encampments through the wilderness?

DEUTERONOMY too is a second law and a prefiguration of the evangelical law. Does it not present the former things in such a way that everything is nevertheless new from the old? Thus far extends Moses; thus far the Pentateuch—five words by which the Apostle boasts that he wishes to speak in the Church.

What mysteries does JOB, the model of patience, not contain in his speech? It begins in prose, flows into verse, and ends in ordinary speech; and it defines all the laws of dialectic through proposition, assumption, confirmation, and conclusion. Every word in it is full of meaning.

And, to say nothing of the rest, it prophesies the resurrection of bodies so clearly that no one has written of it either more openly or more cautiously: “I know,” it says, “that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see; my eyes shall behold him, and not another. This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom.”

I shall come to JESUS SON OF NUN, who bears the type of the Lord not only in his deeds but also in his name. He crosses the Jordan, overthrows the kingdoms of the enemies, divides the land among the victorious people, and through its individual cities, villages, mountains, rivers, streams, and boundaries describes the spiritual kingdoms of the Church and of the heavenly Jerusalem.

In the book of JUDGES, there are as many figures as there are leaders of the people.

RUTH the Moabite fulfills Isaiah’s prophecy, which says: “Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.”

SAMUEL, in the death of Eli and the killing of Saul, shows the old law abolished. In Zadok and David, moreover, he bears witness to the mysteries of a new priesthood and a new sovereignty.

MALACHIM—that is, the third and fourth books of Kings—describes the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel, from Solomon to Jeconiah and from Jeroboam son of Nebat to Hoshea, who was carried away among the Assyrians. If you consider the history, the words are simple; but if you look into the hidden meaning within the letters, the smallness of the Church and the wars of heretics against the Church are narrated.

The Twelve Prophets, compressed into the narrow limits of a single volume, prefigure something very different from what the literal wording seems to say.

HOSEA frequently names Ephraim, Samaria, Joseph, Jezreel, a prostitute wife, children of prostitution, and an adulterous woman shut up in her husband’s chamber, sitting widowed for a long time beneath mourning clothes and awaiting her husband’s return.

JOEL son of Pethuel describes the land of the twelve tribes, consumed and devastated by the locust, the caterpillar, the grasshopper, and the mildew. After the overthrow of the former people, he declares that the Holy Spirit will be poured out upon God’s male and female servants—that is, upon the names of the one hundred and twenty believers—and poured out in the upper room of Zion. These one hundred and twenty, rising gradually from one to fifteen by successive increments, form the number of the fifteen steps mystically contained in the Psalter.

AMOS, a shepherd and a rustic, a gatherer of bramble-berries, cannot be explained in a few words. For who could adequately express the three or four crimes of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Idumea, the children of Ammon and Moab, and, in the seventh and eighth stages, those of Judah and Israel?

He speaks to the fat cows on the mountain of Samaria and declares that the greater and the lesser house will fall. He himself sees the maker of locusts, the Lord standing upon a plastered or adamantine wall, and the hook for fruit, drawing punishments upon sinners and famine upon the land—not famine of bread or thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God.

OBADIAH, whose name means “Servant of God,” thunders against bloody and earthly Edom and strikes with a spiritual spear Jacob’s brother, ever his rival.

JONAH, the most beautiful dove, prefiguring the Lord’s Passion through his own shipwreck, calls the world back to repentance and, under the name of Nineveh, announces salvation to the nations.

MICAH of Moresheth, a fellow heir of Christ, announces the devastation of the daughter of the robber and lays siege against her, because she struck the cheek of the judge of Israel.

NAHUM, the comforter of the world, rebukes the city of bloodshed and, after its overthrow, says: “Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of the evangelizer and of the one announcing peace.”

HABAKKUK, a strong and rigid wrestler, stands at his watch and plants his foot upon the fortification, so that he may contemplate Christ on the cross and say: “His glory covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise. His splendor shall be like light; horns are in his hands. There his strength is hidden.”

ZEPHANIAH, the watchman and knower of God’s secrets, hears a cry from the Fish Gate, wailing from the Second Quarter, and a crashing sound from the hills. He also announces wailing to the inhabitants of the Mortar, because all the people of Canaan have fallen silent and all who were wrapped in silver have perished.

HAGGAI, festive and joyful, who sowed in tears so that he might reap in joy, rebuilds the destroyed temple and introduces God the Father speaking: “Yet a little while, and I shall shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land; and I shall shake all the nations, and the desired one of all the nations shall come.”

ZECHARIAH, mindful of his Lord and abundant in prophecy, sees Jesus clothed in filthy garments, and a stone with seven eyes, and a golden lampstand with as many lamps as eyes. He also sees two olive trees, one to the left and one to the right of the lampstand, so that after the black, red, white, and dappled horses, after the chariots of Ephraim and the horse of Jerusalem have been dispersed, he may prophesy and proclaim a poor king seated upon a colt, the son of a subject she-ass.

MALACHI speaks openly, at the end of all the prophets, of Israel’s rejection and the calling of the nations: “I have no desire for you,” says the Lord of hosts, “and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations; and in every place a sacrifice is made and a pure offering is presented to my name.”

Who can either understand or explain ISAIAH, JEREMIAH, EZEKIEL, and DANIEL? The first of them does not seem to me to weave a prophecy but a Gospel. The second joins together an almond rod and a boiling pot facing the north, and a leopard stripped of its colors, into an alphabet in four different meters. The third has its beginnings and its end wrapped in such great obscurities that among the Hebrews these sections, together with the beginning of Genesis, are not read before the age of thirty. The fourth, who is also the last among the four prophets, aware of the times and a complete φιλίστωρ (*philístōr*, “lover of history”) of the whole world, announces in clear speech the stone cut from the mountain without hands and overturning all kingdoms.

[Col. 0145]

DAVID, our Simonides, Pindar, and Alcaeus, as well as Horace, Catullus, and Serenus, makes Christ resound on the lyre and, on the ten-stringed Psalter, raises from the underworld the one who is rising again.

SOLOMON, peaceful and beloved of the Lord, corrects morals, teaches nature, joins the Church to Christ, and sweetly sings the epithalamium of the sacred marriage.

ESTHER, in the type of the Church, rescues the people from danger; and after Haman, whose name means “iniquity,” has been killed, she transmits the portions of the banquet and the solemn day to later generations.

The book of CHRONICLES, that is, the ἐπιτομή (*epitomē*, “abridgment”) of the old instrument, is so great and so important that if anyone wishes to claim for himself knowledge of the Scriptures without it, he mocks himself. For throughout it, by individual names and combinations of words, the histories omitted from the books of Kings are touched upon, and innumerable questions of the Gospel are set forth.

EZRA and NEHEMIAH—namely, “helper” and “comforter from the Lord”—are compressed into one volume. They restore the temple and rebuild the walls of the city. That entire multitude of the people returning to their homeland, and the listing of the priests, Levites, Israelites, and proselytes, together with the works assigned by individual families to the walls and towers, present one meaning on the surface and retain another in the marrow.

You see that, carried away by love for the Scriptures, I have exceeded the limits of a letter and yet have not fulfilled what I wished. We have merely heard what we ought to know and what we ought to desire, so that we too may be able to say: “My soul has desired to long for your justifications at all times.” For the rest, that Socratic saying is fulfilled in us: “This alone I know: that I know nothing.”

I shall also touch briefly upon the New Testament.

MATTHEW, MARK, LUKE, and JOHN, the Lord’s four-horse chariot and the true Cherubim—which is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge”—have eyes throughout their entire body. Sparks flash, lightning bolts dart about, their feet are straight and directed upward, their backs are winged and fly everywhere. They hold one another, are intertwined with one another, revolve like a wheel within a wheel, and go wherever the breath of the Holy Spirit leads them.

The Apostle PAUL writes to seven Churches, for the eighth, to the HEBREWS, is excluded from the number by most people. He instructs TIMOTHY and TITUS, and pleads with PHILEMON on behalf of a fugitive servant. Concerning this, I think it better to remain silent than to write only a little.

The ACTS OF THE APOSTLES seem indeed to present a plain history and to weave the infancy of the newborn Church. But if we know that their author is Luke the physician, whose praise is found in the Gospel, we shall likewise perceive that all his words are medicine for a sick soul.

JAMES, PETER, JOHN, and JUDE published seven Epistles, as mystical as they are concise, and at once short and long: short in words, long in meaning; so that few people do not stumble in reading them.

The APOCALYPSE OF JOHN contains as many mysteries as words. I have said too little, and all praise falls short of the merit of the book. Multiple meanings lie hidden in each individual word.

I beg you, dearest brother, to live among these writings, to meditate upon them, to know nothing else, and to seek nothing else. Does it not seem to you that the dwelling of the heavenly kingdom is already here on earth?

Do not be offended in the holy Scriptures by the simplicity and apparent lowliness of their words. Whether through the fault of translators or by deliberate design, they have been expressed in such a way as to instruct a rustic congregation more easily, and so that in one and the same statement the educated person might hear one thing and the uneducated another.

I am not so presumptuous and dull as to claim that I know these things and can grasp the fruits whose roots are fixed in heaven; but I confess that I desire to do so. I present myself to you as you sit; while refusing the role of teacher, I promise to be a companion. To the one who asks, it is given; to the one who knocks, it is opened; the one who seeks finds. Let us learn on earth the things whose knowledge will remain with us in heaven.

I shall receive you with open arms and—as I babble something foolish in the inflated style of Hermagoras—whatever you seek, I shall try to know together with you. Here you have Eusebius, your most loving brother, who doubled my appreciation of your letters by reporting your upright character, your contempt for the world, your fidelity in friendship, and your love of Christ. For your prudence and elegance of speech were already displayed by the letter itself, even without his testimony.

Hurry, I beg you, and cut rather than loosen the rope of the little boat clinging to the sandbank. No one who is about to renounce the world can properly sell what he despised in order to sell. Whatever you take from your possessions for expenses, count as profit. There is an ancient saying: “For the miser, what he has is as lacking as what he does not have.” To the believer, the whole world is wealth; but the unbeliever needs even a small coin. Let us live as having nothing and possessing everything.

Food and clothing are the wealth of Christians. If you have control over your property, sell it; if you do not, throw it away. To the one who takes your tunic, you must also leave your cloak. Clearly, unless you, always putting things off and dragging one day after another, sell your little possessions carefully and gradually, Christ will have no means by which to feed his poor.

He gave everything to God who offered himself. The Apostles left only their boat and nets. The widow put two small coins into the treasury and is preferred to the riches of Croesus. A person easily despises everything who always thinks that he is going to die.

## The First Part of the Divine Library of St. Eusebius Jerome, Presbyter of Stridon

Containing the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, together with marginal annotations by a certain Hebrew who was highly renowned in knowledge of the Law in the time of Rabanus Maurus.

## First Order: The Law
[Col. 0147]

[Note: We collated this letter with three manuscript codices: one belonging to the Roman College of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, and two now in the Vatican Library, one Palatine under no. 3, the other Urbinate. In these, it is entitled “Prologue,” or “Preface to the Pentateuch”; Jerome himself suggests this in the very preface, although in Book II Against Rufinus, no. 25, he calls it the “Prologue to Genesis,” and repeats it word for word from beginning to end.]

# Preface of Saint Jerome to the Pentateuch, addressed to Desiderius

[Col. 0147A] [Note: This seems to be the Desiderius to whom Jerome addressed Letter 47 in our recension. You will learn from that letter what rank and importance he held, where he is extolled for learning, piety, and above all eloquence. We have also sometimes thought that he was the same man who held the rank of presbyter at Rome, and to whom Saint Paulinus addressed Letter 43 and Severus dedicated the Life of Saint Martin.]

I have received the letters I had long desired from my Desiderius, who, by a certain [Note: He addresses him in almost the same words in the letter just mentioned to the same man: “By this omen contained in your name you were predestined for this; for we read that the holy Daniel too was called a man of desires and a friend of God, because he desired to know His mysteries.”] omen of things to come, shares with Daniel the name of the one who beseeches (Daniel 9:23): he asks me to deliver to the ears of our people the Pentateuch, translated into Latin from the Hebrew language.

Certainly it is a perilous undertaking, exposed to the barking of my detractors, who claim that, to disparage the Seventy Translators, I am forging new things in place of the old. [Note: He attacks those who judge books by their age rather than by their merits. Wines grow finer with age; books do not. In this sense he wrote to Augustine in Letter 89: “Let him drink old wine with pleasure, and disdain our new wine.” MART.] Thus they test talent as though it were wine, although I have very often testified that I offer in God’s tabernacle what I can according to my strength, [Note: The Memmian Library’s canon reads this way, although in the margin it retains the alternative reading, namely “from my poor share,” as Haimo the monk thought it should be read. He composed commentaries on Genesis and Deuteronomy, which I possess in a very ancient manuscript codex. Explaining each word of the present prologue, this writer discussed that reading as follows: “From my poor share,” that is, “from my poverty.” For in another preface he says that in God’s tabernacle some offer gold, onyx stones, fine linen, scarlet, and purple; but that it is enough for him if he offers at least goats’ hair. He calls this a poor share, humbling himself, although he himself was offering great things in God’s tabernacle, that is, in the Church. The preface Haimo cites here is the Galeate Prologue prefixed to the books of Samuel and Kings. Accordingly, Jerome himself, in Book II of his Apology against Rufinus, rebukes Rufinus’s ignorance in these words: “See with what haughty disdain I exalt myself against the Seventy Translators, claiming that they offered gold, precious stones, and purple in God’s tabernacle, while I offered skins and goats’ hair.” Nevertheless, here we read, with the Memmian canon and certain other more ancient manuscripts, “according to my share of strength,” or “according to my part of strength,” as you will find written below in the preface to Joshua, where Jerome explains himself. MART. — All our codices read “from my poor share,” and this was formerly the common reading; Jerome would thus have excused himself for offering poor things in proportion to his limited strength. Yet the printed reading is more correct, and is also supported by his Commentary on Ezekiel, Book XXIV: “In the tabernacle too we read that, according to the diversity of strength”—that is, “according to one’s share of strength”—“one offers gold, another silver, scarlet, fine linen, and so forth; others offer skins and goats’ hair.”]

nor allow another’s wealth to be defiled by the poverty of others. My courage to undertake this was aroused by Origen’s zeal: he mingled Theodotion’s translation with the ancient edition, marking it with an asterisk +, and with an obelus ÷—that is, [Note: Elsewhere called an obelus. Hear Isidore: “The obelus, that is, a line lying down, is placed beside words or sentences repeated superfluously, or where a reading has been marked as false, so that, like an arrow, it may strike through what is superfluous and pierce what is false”; for an arrow is called ὀβελός in Greek. Hesychius says they are ῥάβδοι περιτεθέμενοι τοῖς Ὁμήρου στίχοις, “rods placed beside the verses of Homer.” If desired, see Cicero’s letter to Dolabella as well.] a star and a spit—distinguishing the whole work: either making what had previously been less clear shine forth [Note: A recent author of Questions on Jerome maintains that *illustria* should here be restored in place of *illucescere*, as Erasmus and Victorius printed in the *Apology against Rufinus*. But they seem to have altered that word on their own initiative, so as to read more elegantly as they pleased. For *illucescere* is otherwise entirely satisfactory and is attested by all the manuscripts; and *illustria*, without changing the text, can conveniently be understood after *fuerant*: that is, “he makes shine forth what had previously been less [illustrious].” This manner of speaking is not unfamiliar to Jerome. In the preface to Chronicles he writes in almost exactly the same words: “Marking with asterisks what had previously been less [present], that is, marked.”] or striking through and piercing whatever was superfluous; [Note: We have restored this reading on the authority of the Palatine and the other codex, and from the reading preserved in the *Apology*, especially since the sense concerning the Evangelists and so forth is now at last both clear and wholly true. Jerome plainly says that Origen’s zeal prompted him to undertake this translation from Hebrew, and especially those things which the authority of the Evangelists and Apostles proclaimed—testimonies which he subsequently cites. The old editions, which read *maximeque evangelistarum*, and Martianay’s emendation, *maxime quae evangelistarum*, yield either no sense or an entirely false sense contrary to the holy Doctor’s intention, as though he had said that Origen struck through as superfluities especially those things which the authority of the Evangelists and Apostles proclaimed and which were absent from the Septuagint translation.] and I was especially prompted by what the authority of the Evangelists and Apostles proclaimed.

In them we read many things from the Old Testament that are not found in our codices, such as: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15); and, “He shall be called a Nazaraean” (ibid., 2:23); and, “They shall look on him whom they pierced” (John 19:37); and, “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38); and, “Things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have ascended into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9); and many other passages that require their own σύνταγμα, that is, composition or connected exposition.

Let us therefore ask them where these things are written; and when they cannot say, let us produce them from the Hebrew books. The first testimony is in Hosea (Hosea 11:1), the second in Isaiah (Isaiah 11:1), the third in Zechariah (Zechariah 12:10), the fourth in Proverbs (Proverbs 18:4), and the fifth likewise in Isaiah (Isaiah 64:4). Many, being ignorant of this, [Note: By “the Assumption,” or “Apocalypse,” of Elijah he means a spurious work, because of the final testimony in Paul’s Epistle. He writes to Pammachius in On the Best Kind of Translation: “At this passage some habitually pursue the ravings of the apocrypha and say that the testimony was taken from the Apocalypse of Elijah, although in Isaiah, according to the Hebrew, it is read thus: ‘From of old they have not heard,’ and so forth. We understand from where the testimony was taken; nevertheless, the Apostle did not express it word for word, but indicated the same sense in other words παραφραστικῶς, that is, paraphrastically.” Understand the same concerning the other scriptural testimonies, especially the one John reports as taken from Proverbs, where the holy Evangelist indicates the sense in other words. MART. [Col. 0149D] He refers to apocryphal books titled The Ascension of Isaiah and The Apocalypse of Elijah, from which the Gnostics and the followers of Basilides thought that Paul’s passage to the Corinthians had been taken. Jerome himself reveals this both in Letter 57 to Pammachius, On the Best Kind of Translation, and more fully in his Commentary on Isaiah 64, where he soon adduces the testimony.] pursue the ravings of apocryphal writings; and they prefer Iberian nonsense to the authentic books. [Note: Jerome wrote similarly: “And to pursue Iberian follies and Egyptian portents.” In his Letter to Hedibia, Question 10, some think that “Iberian follies” means portentous absurdities, because magical marvels are related among the Iberians, as among the Thessalians. Naeniae also means the laments of poor women hired by relatives of the dead to deliver foolish praises over the deceased. This custom still exists among the inhabitants of the Pyrenean mountains; according to Dionysius, the Iberian peoples migrated from there into Asia and settled in Iberia. But here, unless I am mistaken, Jerome meant something else: the fables of apocryphal books, in which much may have been narrated about Gog and Magog. The Chiliasts, both Jews and Christians, believed that Gog and Magog, joined by the Iberians, would fight against the saints and the Holy City. The holy Doctor calls their opinion “Jewish and old-women’s tales.” Those who dreamed that the devil, with all his army, would one day attack the heavenly Jerusalem, he says invented far worse follies, in Book XI of his Commentary on Ezekiel 38. MART. — He calls them “Iberian follies” for no other reason than that the same heretics who pursued the ravings of the apocryphal Ascension of Isaiah and Apocalypse of Elijah spread those tales in Iberia, that is, in the regions of Spain and Lusitania. This is made perfectly clear in his Commentary on Isaiah 64, where, discussing Paul’s passage as taken from the authentic book of Isaiah, he says: “Therefore let the ravings of the apocrypha be silent, which, on the occasion of this testimony, are thrust upon the Churches of Christ … The Ascension of Isaiah and the Apocalypse of Elijah contain this testimony, and through this opportunity many women of Spain and Lusitania have been deceived … concerning whom the apostolic man Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, writes most carefully, explaining the origins of many heresies, especially of the Gnostics, who through Mark the Egyptian first deceived noble women of Gaul around the Rhône and then of Spain.” Jerome repeats the latter point from Irenaeus in his letter to Theodore. Thus the “Iberian follies” are the visions of the Gnostics and Basilides, by which their disciple Mark the Egyptian occupied Spain. He says the same in Letter to Hedibia, Question 10: “It is much better simply to confess ignorance than to defend the heresy of Basilides and pursue Iberian follies and Egyptian portents.” Finally, in his Commentary on Amos 3, he uses the expression in precisely this sense: “And they marvel at the Iberian absurdities concerning Balsamus and Barbelo.” Recall also what we have observed there.]

I do not intend to explain the causes of their error. The Jews say that this was done by deliberate policy, so that Ptolemy, a worshiper of one God, would not discover even among the Hebrews a dual divinity. They seemed to do this especially because it appeared to fall under Plato’s doctrine. [Note: The Palatine Codex reads “they seemed.” Plato’s saying is: Θεοῦ εὑρεῖν τε ἔργον, εὑρόντα τε εἰς πολλοὺς ἐκφέρειν ἀδύνατον, “To find God is difficult, and, having found him, to declare him to many is impossible.”]

Finally, wherever Scripture bears sacred witness concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they either interpreted it otherwise or remained entirely silent, so that they might satisfy the king and not make the mystery of faith public.

And I do not know what first author built Alexandria’s seventy cells through his lie, in which, supposedly separated from one another, they wrote the same things, although Aristeas [also Aristaeus], [Note: The two manuscripts, as well as the Memmian codex in Martianay, add “that is, protector.” Properly, however, ὑπερασπιστής means a bodyguard or attendant, one who protected the king’s body by interposing an ἀσπίς, or shield.] Ptolemy’s ὑπερασπιστής, or shield-bearer, and, much later, Josephus, [Note: An old edition of the Apology has the negative particle: “and not much later Josephus,” and so forth. Josephus’s testimony is found in Book XII, chapter 2, of the Antiquities: συνέδριον ἐποιήσατο ἐν τῷ παρὰ τὴν ἠϊόνα κατεσκευασμένῳ οἴκῳ, “He [Demetrius] gathered them [the seventy elders] in a house constructed near the shore.” A little later Josephus says that, once the translation of the Law had been completed, Demetrius gathered all the Jews there, with the translators also present. Aristeas therefore agrees with Josephus on this point.] report nothing of the kind; rather, they write that the translators were gathered together in one basilica and compared their work, not that they prophesied.

For it is one thing to be a prophet and another to be an interpreter. [Note: Compare the holy Father himself in the other preface to the books of Chronicles translated from Greek, where he says of the Seventy Translators that, being filled with the Holy Spirit, they translated what was true.] There the Spirit foretells what is to come; here learning and abundance of words transfer what the interpreter understands.

Unless, perhaps, Cicero is to be thought to have translated Xenophon’s Oeconomicus and Plato’s Protagoras, [Note: We read “Pythagoras,” in place of “Protagoras,” in all the manuscripts; but it cannot be doubted by any learned person that this arose from scribal ignorance, since copyists write more familiar and obvious words in place of those they do not know. Thus, for example, “Juda” for “Jehu,” and formerly “Isaiah” for “Asaph,” as Jerome notes in his Commentary on Hosea 1 and Matthew 13. MART. — Our manuscripts too falsely read “Pythagoras.” All those translations by Cicero have perished.] and Demosthenes’ speech Against Ctesiphon, with rhetorical inspiration; or that, concerning the same books, the Holy Spirit composed one set of testimonies through the Seventy Translators and another through the Apostles, so that the latter pretended that what the former had omitted had been written.

What then? Do we condemn the ancients? Certainly not. But after the labors of our predecessors, we work in the Lord’s house with what ability we possess. They translated before Christ’s coming, and, not knowing what was to come, they expressed it in uncertain interpretations. We, after his passion and resurrection, write not so much prophecy as history. Things heard are reported in one way, things seen in another. What we understand better, we also express better.

Listen, then, rival and detractor; listen: I do not condemn or rebuke the Seventy, but I confidently prefer the Apostles to all of them. Through the mouths of the Apostles Christ speaks to me; I read that they were placed among the spiritual gifts before the prophets, while interpreters occupy almost the lowest rank among them (1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11).

Why are you tortured by envy? Why do you stir the minds of the ignorant against me? If I seem to err anywhere in my translation, ask the Hebrews; consult the teachers of the various cities. What they possess concerning Christ, your codices do not possess. It would be another matter if they later approved the testimonies used against themselves by the Apostles, [Note: It seems to me that the contrary word should be supplied here, namely, “rejected”: that is, the Hebrews rejected the testimonies used against them by the Apostles and either erased them from their codices or corrupted them by a deceptive reading. This is plainly what the entire context of the holy Doctor intends; I scarcely doubt that he wrote “rejected” in this sense. I am surprised that the editors and critics have not noticed this.] and if Latin copies were more accurate than Greek, Greek more accurate than Hebrew.

But enough against the envious. Now I ask you, dearest Desiderius, since you have made me undertake so great a work and begin with Genesis, to assist me with your prayers, so that I may transfer these books into Latin speech with the same Spirit by which they were written.

[Col. 0151]

# The Book of Genesis

## Chapter Titles of the Book of Genesis

[Note: We copied the series of these titles from the Memmian canon, a considerable time after the publication of the book of Genesis, which in our San-Germain copy is mutilated in its first seven or eight leaves. Hence it happened that we supplied the earlier numbers of the titles by conjecture in the book of Genesis, and were therefore mistaken in certain places. Let no one therefore be troubled if the marginal number sometimes differs from this collection of titles, since we have indicated the cause of the error. MART.]

# Titles of the Book Bresith, that is, Genesis

[Col. 0151C]

I. On the creation of the world and the fashioning of man; on the prohibition concerning the tree, the transgression, and God’s sentence.

II. On Adam and his wife being clothed in tunics of skins, the guardianship of the tree of life, and the birth of Cain and Abel; on their offerings, Cain’s fratricide of Abel, and the catalogue of the lives of the fathers.

III. The earth corrupted by human uncleanness. The Lord tells Noah to build an ark for himself, and, preserving the seed of every living creature, brings the Flood upon the earth.

IV. Noah builds an altar to the Lord, and the Lord promises that he will never again send waters of a flood over the earth. He places the sign of the covenant, the bow, in the cloud; and when Noah plants a vineyard and becomes drunk after gathering its produce, he is uncovered; Ham, wickedly laughing at his father’s nakedness, incurs the yoke of servitude.

[Col. 0152C]

V. A catalogue of Noah’s sons and how they were dispersed throughout the whole earth; on the building of the tower, the confusion of languages, and the birth of Abraham.

VI. God says to Abraham, “Go out from your land and from your kindred.” He descends into Egypt and appears to call Sarah his wife his sister; and on her account the Lord scourges Pharaoh. Also, the separation of Lot and Abraham.

VII. The kings of the nations gather to engage in battle against Sodom. Abraham, together with his household servants, rescues Lot after he has been plundered and returns him with the spoil; Melchizedek, by his sacrifice, foreshadowing future things.

VIII. Abraham says that he is without children and adopts a household servant as heir; and he hears that, within a year, an heir will be born to him from his wife’s womb. After an offering has been made, he again learns that his offspring will be strangers in a land not their own, that they will increase in the fourth generation, ascend, and possess the lands of promise after the nations have been destroyed.

IX. While Sarah remains barren, Abraham goes in to Hagar at her request. On Hagar’s flight and the angel’s appearance to her; on the promises made to Abraham and the change of his name.

X. Abraham is commanded to mark himself and all the males of his household with circumcision; on the change of Sarai’s name, and the promise that a son would be born to the hundred-year-old Abraham from the ninety-year-old woman.

XI. God appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre in the form of three men.

XII. The Lord converses with Abraham about the destruction of Sodom; Abraham asks him step by step about the number of righteous people, and about Lot’s salvation and the overthrow of those cities.

XIII. Lot remained in the mountain, and his two daughters conceived by him.

XIV. Abraham sojourned in Gerar, and Abimelech the king took Sarah; God warned him not to touch her.

XV. Sarah conceived and, at ninety, bore a son, Isaac, to Abraham at a hundred; Sarah says, “Cast out the maidservant and her son.” Also, Abimelech’s oath with Abraham, and the grove planted at Beersheba.

XVI. God tested Abraham so that he might offer his son, and a promise of blessings was made in his offspring.

XVII. Sarah’s death and Ephron’s sale of the field and the double cave.

[Col. 0153C]

XVIII. Abraham adjures his servant and sends him to take a wife for Isaac from Abraham’s kindred; on the union of Isaac and Rebekah.

XIX. Abraham took Keturah as his wife; on his death and burial; on Rebekah’s conception and childbirth; on Jacob’s stew and Esau’s birthright.

XX. Isaac sojourned in Gerar, called Rebekah his wife his sister, sowed in that land, and obtained a hundredfold. The Philistines, jealous of him, filled in the wells he had dug.

XXI. God appeared to Isaac, intending of his own accord to fulfill what he had promised to Abraham. There he made a covenant with Amalek.

XXII. Isaac’s old age, and how Jacob stole Esau’s blessing.

XXIII. Isaac called Jacob and commanded him not to take a Canaanite wife but to go to Mesopotamia, to his uncle Laban; Esau took Canaanite wives.

XXIV. Jacob set out and slept at Bethel; from there he came to Harran, where he served Laban for his daughters, and concerning their union.

XXV. Jacob received sons from Leah and Rachel and from both maidservants; also, concerning the tending of the flocks.

XXVI. Jacob places various rods in the troughs; on his departure when he wished to return to his homeland, Laban’s pursuit, and the oath between them.

XXVII. As Jacob was setting out, angels of God met him. He sends messengers and gifts to Esau his brother; on his struggle with the angel and the change of his name, so that he would be called Israel.

XXVIII. Shechem, son of Hamor, raped Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, and vengeance was taken for her chastity. Jacob’s departure and the rejection of the idols, which he buried beneath the terebinth.

XXIX. In springtime, Rachel died in childbirth at Ephrath and was buried at Bethlehem. Reuben lay with his father’s concubine; and Isaac, worn out by old age, died.

XXX. A catalogue of the generations that arose from Jacob. On the separation of the men.

[Col. 0154B]

XXXI. Joseph is loved by his father above the other sons. On his dreams, and how he visits his brothers while they are occupied in tending sheep, is lowered into a pit, and is sold to Ishmaelite merchants.

XXXII. Judah went down to Hiram the Adullamite and took a wife there; he took Tamar for his son. Having been given to the next son and widowed of both husbands, she sat in her father’s house and fraudulently exposed her body to her father-in-law for impregnation.

XXXIII. Joseph is sold into Egypt and loved by an Egyptian mistress; he refuses adultery.

XXXIV. Two eunuchs, the chief of the cupbearers and the chief of the bakers, see dreams in prison and ask Joseph for their interpretation. Pharaoh sees a dream, and Joseph becomes a foreteller of things to come.

XXXV. After receiving authority over the land of Egypt, Joseph stores the abundance of seven years in the royal granaries. During the famine of an equal number of years, while he distributes grain, he is recognized by his brothers when they return for the second time. After gifts have been given, he urges them to bring their father and sends wagons.

XXXVI. Having heard the news, Jacob proceeds joyfully to Egypt and sends messengers to Joseph. Joseph goes to meet his father, embraces him, and weeps; he presents his brothers and father before Pharaoh and gives them the land of Goshen. The whole land of Egypt, compelled by the need of famine, comes for silver, and pays a fifth part to Pharaoh.

XXXVII. Jacob’s illness and the blessing of Joseph’s two sons; Jacob gave his son Joseph one portion beyond his brothers, which he had taken from the hand of the Amorite.

XXXVIII. As Jacob approaches death, he summons his sons, rewards them with individual blessings, and foreshadows the mysteries of the future. He urges his sons not to place him in Egyptian tombs but to lay him in the tomb of his ancestors. After giving up his spirit, he is treated with spices, and his body is carried to the land of Canaan. Fearing that Joseph might repay their crime, his brothers plead with him; and Joseph, dying, binds his brothers by an oath that, when divine visitation looks upon them, they should carry his bones away with them.

# Brief Chapters of the Book Bresith, that is, Genesis

[Col. 0155]

[Col. 0155A]

I. On the beginning of light, the separation of darkness from light, and the first day.

II. On the separation of the waters, the firmament made between them, and the second day.

III. On the gathering of the waters beneath the sky, the sprouting of the earth, and the third day.

IV. On the lights of heaven, the division of day and night, and the fourth day.

V. On creeping things and flying creatures, and the fifth day.

VI. On the cattle and beasts of the earth, the creation of man, and the sixth day.

VII. On the sanctification of the seventh day, paradise, its rivers, and the man placed there.

VIII. On Adam, when he gave names to all living creatures; on how the woman was made; and on their transgression.

IX. On the sentence imposed upon them by the Lord, the tunics, and the cherubim with the flaming sword. [Note: The Palatine codex, with which we compared these brief chapters, omits the words “with the flaming sword.”]

X. On Cain and Abel, and God’s curse upon the fratricide.

XI. On Seth, who was born to Adam in place of Abel, [Note: The same codex rejects the name “Adam.”] and on his generation down to Noah.

XII. On the giants, Noah, the ark, and the Flood.

XIII. On Noah’s departure from the ark [Note: The Palatine manuscript also omits this and “the building of the altar.”] and the building of the altar.

XIV. On Noah’s nakedness and the curse of Canaan.

XV. On the generations of Noah’s three sons and on Nimrod.

XVI. On the building of the tower, the confusion of languages, and the descent from Shem to Abraham and Lot.

[Col. 0155C]

XVII. On Abraham’s departure from the land of the Chaldeans to Haran in Mesopotamia with his brothers.

XVIII. On God’s promise to Abraham, his journey into the land of Canaan, and God’s second appearance to him.

XIX. On Abraham’s entry into Egypt and return to Bethel, Lot’s departure, and his dwelling in Sodom.

XX. On God’s third promise to Abraham, the three hundred and eighteen household servants, the slaughter of the enemies, and Lot’s recovery. [Note: The Palatine copy is fuller here by one word, “proceeding.”]

XXI. On God’s fourth promise to Abraham in Hebron, God’s prediction that his offspring would be strangers, and the birth of Ishmael.

XXII. On God’s fifth promise to Abraham, the change of the names Abraham and Sarah, and the covenant of circumcision.

XXIII. On how the Lord appeared to Abraham in three men in the valley of Mamre, where he promised that Isaac would be born; and on the fifty righteous people in Sodom. [Note: The number fifty is missing in the Palatine.]

[Col. 0156A]

XXIV. On the overthrow of Sodom and the conception of Lot’s daughters by their father.

XXV. On Abraham’s journey to Gerar and what Abimelech, king of the Philistines, did there.

XXVI. On Isaac’s birth, his play with Ishmael, Hagar’s expulsion with her son, and Abimelech’s covenant with Abraham.

XXVII. On Isaac, when he was offered by his father; on Rebekah’s birth to Bethuel; and on Sarah’s death.

XXVIII. On Rebekah, how Abraham’s servant approached her as a suitor and, having obtained her, joined her to Isaac.

XXIX. On Abraham, when he took Keturah as his wife; on Abraham’s death; on Ishmael’s offspring; and on Rebekah’s conception and childbirth.

XXX. On Esau, when he sold his birthright to Jacob; on God’s promises in Gerar; and on Isaac’s sowing and obtaining a hundredfold.

XXXI. On the promise to Isaac and Beersheba, where the Lord appeared to him a second time; on King Abimelech’s covenant with Isaac; and on Esau and his wives.

XXXII. On Isaac’s blindness, and how he blessed Jacob in place of Esau.

XXXIII. On Esau’s hatred toward Jacob, Jacob’s flight to Laban, the dream, the ladder, and the angels, and the Lord whom he saw speaking to him.

XXXIV. On Jacob’s service for his wives, the conception of the sheep according to the variety of the rods, and the birth of Jacob’s sons.

XXXV. On Jacob’s departure from Mesopotamia, his quarrel and covenant with Laban, the division of the angels, the wrestling, and Jacob’s reconciliation with Esau.

XXXVI. On Jacob’s dwelling in Shechem, the violation of Dinah, the slaughter of the city, and the idols hidden beneath the terebinth.

XXXVII. On Jacob’s return to Bethel, where God appeared to him again and called him Israel; on Ephrath, where Rachel died and was buried after giving birth to Benjamin; on Reuben’s entering his father’s concubine; on the names of the Patriarchs; on Isaac’s death; and on Esau’s generations.

XXXVIII. On Joseph and his dreams, his sale into Egypt, Judah, and the things reported about Tamar. [Note: These matters, as well as those reported about Tamar, are absent from the Palatine manuscript.]

XXXIX. On Joseph, bought by a eunuch and sent into prison, and on Pharaoh’s dreams.

XL. On Joseph’s being brought out of prison, how he interprets the king’s dream, and his being appointed lord of Egypt; also, on his wife and two children.

XLI. On Joseph’s brothers, how they went down into Egypt and returned, leaving Simeon behind, and on the money found in their sacks.

XLII. On Joseph’s brothers’ second journey to Egypt with Benjamin, and their mutual recognition.

XLIII. On the provisions and gifts Joseph gave his brothers, and Jacob’s journey with his entire household into Egypt.

[Col. 0158A]

XLIV. On Jacob’s entrance before Pharaoh and the possession given to him in the land of Goshen.

XLV. On the dimness of Jacob’s eyes, the blessing of Joseph’s sons, and Jacob’s blessing of his twelve sons.

XLVI. On Jacob’s death and burial in Hebron, and Joseph’s death.

# Chapters of the Book Bresith, that is, Genesis

[Col. 0157]

[Col. 0157A]

I. On the first day, on which light was made.

II. On the second day, on which heaven was made.

III. On the third day, on which earth and sea were made.

IV. On the fourth day, on which the sun, moon, and stars were made.

V. On the fifth day, on which the creatures moving in the sea and the birds of heaven were made.

VI. On the sixth day, on which the four-footed animals, serpents, beasts, all cattle, creeping things, and man were made.

VII. On the seventh day, on which God rested after completing every work.

[Col. 0157B]

VIII. On this book, in which he relates all the things that were made, and on the four rivers.

IX. On the man placed in paradise; on the Lord’s command to Adam; on Adam’s giving names to all living creatures; and on the woman formed from his rib.

X. On the serpent’s deceiving the woman.

XI. On their being questioned about the transgression.

XII. On their being led out of paradise so that they might not take from the tree of life.

XIII. Adam’s sons Cain and Abel were born.

XIV. Cain killed his brother.

XV. Seth was born to Adam in place of Abel.

XVI. On the generations of human beings.

[Col. 0157C]

XVII. Enoch pleased God, and God took him; and on Methuselah and Noah.

XVIII. The sons of God took wives for themselves, and God became angry.

XIX. Noah pleased God, and God commanded him to make an ark.

XX. Noah entered the ark, and the Flood took place.

XXI. The Lord remembered Noah and those who were with him, and the water dried up.

XXII. In the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life, he himself and those who were with him went out of the ark.

XXIII. The Lord blessed Noah and his sons.

XXIV. The Lord decreed that a flood would by no means occur again.

XXV. On Noah’s three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and on Noah himself, when he became drunk.

XXVI. On the generations of Noah and his sons.

XXVII. On the mixing of languages, the tower of confusion, and the generations of Shem.

XXVIII. On the generations of Terah, Abraham’s father.

XXIX. The Lord said to Abraham, “Go out from your land.”
