XXX. The Lord God of Abraham appeared at the place of Shechem. How, when Abraham was in Egypt, Pharaoh took Sarai as his wife.

[Col. 0158A]

XXXI. On the promise to Abraham and his offspring.

XXXII. On the four kings’ fighting against five, taking Lot and all the cavalry of the Sodomites, and Melchizedek’s offering tithes to Abraham.

XXXIII. The Lord appeared to Abraham, blessed him, and said to him, “Your offspring will be a stranger”; and Hagar bore Ishmael to him.

XXXIV. The Lord appeared to Abraham, gave him the sign of circumcision, and concerning Isaac.

[Col. 0158B]

XXXV. The Lord appeared to Abraham when he was going to destroy the Sodomites.

XXXVI. Two angels came to Sodom and stayed with Lot.

XXXVII. The Lord rained fire and sulfur from heaven, overthrew Sodom, and Lot’s daughters conceived by their father.

XXXVIII. The Lord spoke to Abimelech concerning Sarah.

XXXIX. Sarah bore a son, and his father called him Isaac.

XL. Sarah said to Abraham, “Cast out the maidservant and her son”; and at Beersheba the angel of the Lord spoke to Hagar.

XLI. Abraham and Abimelech swore to each other.

[Col. 0158C] **XLII.** God tested Abraham concerning Isaac, and concerning the descendants of Nahor.

**XLIII.** Sarah died, and Abraham purchased a burial place from Ephron.

**XLIV.** Abraham gave instructions to his servant; he departed and brought back Rebekah, and Abraham took Keturah as his wife.

**XLV.** Abraham lived 175 years and died.

**XLVI.** Concerning the descendants and death of Ishmael.

**XLVII.** Concerning the descendants of Isaac.

**XLVIII.** There was a famine; the Lord appeared to Isaac and said to him, “Do not go down to Egypt.” And he lived in Gerar, where he sowed and obtained a hundredfold, and he swore an oath with Abimelech.

[Col. 0158D] **XLIX.** Isaac grew old and blessed Jacob instead of Esau, without knowing it.

**L.** Isaac sent away his son Jacob, so that he might go to Mesopotamia.

**LI.** Jacob saw a vision; and the Lord spoke to him and blessed him.

**LII.** Jacob came to the East and took Laban’s daughters as wives for himself.

**LIII.** Leah bore four sons to her husband Jacob and ceased bearing.

[Col. 0159A] **LIV.** Rachel gave her maid Bilhah to Jacob, and she bore him two sons.

**LV.** Leah also gave her maid to Jacob, and she bore him two sons; and concerning the mandrakes, she herself bore two sons and Dinah.

**LVI.** The Lord remembered Rachel, and she bore Joseph; and Jacob made an arrangement with Laban concerning the various sheep.

**LVII.** The Lord said to Jacob, “Return to the land of your father.” Laban pursued him, and they swore an oath to one another.

**LVIII.** Jacob saw the camp of God, sent messengers to his brother, and wrestled with the angel.

**LIX.** Jacob came to the city of the Shechemites, where his sons killed all the inhabitants because of Dinah.

**LX.** The Lord said to Jacob, “Go up to Bethel,” [Col. 0159B] and he cast away all the idols.

**LXI.** The Lord appeared to Jacob himself, blessed him, and gave him the name Israel.

**LXII.** Rachel bore Benjamin, died, and the descendants of Jacob and the death of his father Isaac are recounted.

**LXIII.** Concerning the descendants of Esau.

**LXIV.** Concerning the chiefs of Esau.

**LXV.** Those who reigned in Edom before there was a king in Israel.

**LXVI.** Concerning Joseph and his dreams.

**LXVII.** When he was thrown into the pit and sold to the Ishmaelites.

**LXVIII.** Concerning Judah and Tamar, his son’s wife, who was a widow.

[Col. 0159C] **LXIX.** Concerning Joseph and Potiphar’s wife.

[Col. 0160A] **LXX.** Concerning those who saw dreams in prison, and Joseph interpreted them.

**LXXI.** Pharaoh’s dream, which Joseph interpreted; he became ruler of the land of Egypt, and two sons were born to him.

**LXXII.** When Jacob sent his sons to Egypt, Joseph recognized them and confined one of them until his brother Benjamin should come.

**LXXIII.** The famine grew severe, and his brothers came to Joseph with Benjamin; and he instructed his father to come to him.

**LXXIV.** The Lord appeared to Jacob and said to him, “Go down to Egypt.”

**LXXV.** The names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt.

[Col. 0160B] **LXXVI.** When Joseph came to meet his father Israel.

**LXXVII.** Joseph announced to Pharaoh that his father had come.

**LXXVIII.** Pharaoh said to Joseph that he should choose the land in which his father would dwell.

**LXXIX.** Israel lived in Egypt and told his son Joseph not to bury him there; Jacob lived 147 years.

**LXXX.** When Jacob fell ill, he blessed Joseph’s sons with crossed hands.

**LXXXI.** Jacob summoned all his sons and told them what would happen in the last days; then he died, was carried away, and was buried in his own land.

**LXXXII.** Joseph lived 110 years and made his brothers swear that, when they were visited by the Lord, [Col. 0160C] they would take his bones with them to their own land.

### From the most ancient Vatican manuscript

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The most ancient manuscript codex of the Vatican Library, formerly belonging to the celebrated monastery of Farfa, preserves this series of chapters. We have removed some solecisms and barbarisms of the copyist, since they could not be tolerated. In the remaining passages we reproduce the manuscript as it is read, with its own faults, asking the reader not to attribute acknowledged errors of ancient scribes to our printers or to us, the editors of this volume. It should also be noted that the manuscript copyist omitted [Col. 0160D] the final chapter, in which the last part of Genesis ought to be represented in this or a similar form: “When Joseph had lived 110 years, he made his brothers swear that, when they were visited, they would take his bones with them to their own land.” For the Book of Genesis does not end in chapter 154, where Jacob blesses his twelve sons, but with the death and burial of Joseph, Jacob’s son. MART.]

## The Book Begins

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Saint Jerome teaches that the Hebrews called the Book of Genesis *Bresith* at the beginning of his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, where he writes: “But this too should be known: among the Hebrews this book is called *Bresith*, following their custom of giving volumes their names from their beginnings.” And again in the prologue to the Scriptures, or *Helmeted Prologue*: “The first book among them,” he says, “is called *Bresith*, which we call Genesis.” Today it is written *Beresith*, *Berescith*, and *Bereschith*. MART. —It is well known that the Hebrews designate each book of Scripture by its opening words. Genesis begins with these words, [Hebrew word not printed in the supplied source], which the ancients, customarily omitting the first *shewa*, pronounced in Greek Βρησὶθ and in Latin *Bresith*. See the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.]

**BRESITH**, which in Greek is called **GENESIS**.

[Col. 0163]

[Col. 0163C] [Note: [Col. 0164D] That is: T. I, the first title according to the division by titles; B. I, the first brief according to the division by briefs; C. I, the first chapter according to the division by chapters; and finally Cap. I, the first chapter according to the Vulgate edition. EDIT.]

**T. I, B. I, C. I, Cap. I.** In the beginning God created heaven and earth. But the earth was shapeless and empty, and darkness [the Vulgate adds “were”] was over the face of the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters. And God said, “Let there be light.” And light came to be. And God saw that the light was good; and God divided light and darkness [the Vulgate: “from the darkness”]. And he called the light Day, and the darkness Night. And evening and morning came to be: one day.

**[B. II, C. II.]** And God said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.” And God made the firmament, and divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament. And it was so. And God called the firmament Heaven. And evening and morning came to be: the second day.

**[B. III, C. III.]** And God said, “Let the waters that are beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear.” And it was so. And God called the dry land Earth, and he called the gatherings of waters Seas. And God saw that it was good. And he said, “Let the earth sprout green vegetation and seed-bearing plants, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth.” And it was so. And the earth brought forth green vegetation bearing seed [the Vulgate: “making seed”] according to their kind, and trees producing fruit, each having its seed [the Vulgate: “its seed-crop”] according to its species. And God saw that it was good. And evening and morning came to be: the third day.

**[B. IV, C. IV.]** And God said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, that [the Vulgate: ‘and’] they may divide the day from the night, and let them be for signs, seasons, days, and years, and that [the Vulgate: ‘that’] they may shine in the firmament of heaven and give light to the earth.” And it was so. And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars. And God placed them in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth, to rule the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good. And evening and morning came to be: the fourth day.

**[B. V, C. V.]** And God said, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and winged creatures above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.” And God created the great sea creatures, and every living and moving creature that the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged creature according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. And he blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let the birds multiply upon the earth.” And evening and morning came to be: the fifth day.

**[B. VI, C. VI.]** And God said, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: livestock, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their species.” And it was so. And God made the beasts of the earth according to their species, and livestock and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. And he said, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, [Col. 0165C] the beasts, the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.” And God created the human being in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them and said, “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all living things that move upon the earth.” And God said, “Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant upon the earth, and all trees that have within themselves the seed of their kind, to be your food; and to all the animals of the earth, every bird of heaven, and all things that move upon the earth and possess a living soul, I have given them for food.” And it was so. And God saw all that he had made [the Vulgate: “had made”], and they were very good. And evening and morning came to be: the sixth day.

**[B. VII, C. VII, Cap. II.]** Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment. And God completed on the seventh day the work that he had made, and on the seventh day he rested from all the work that he had done. And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all the work that God created in order to make.

**[C. VIII.]** These are the generations [the Vulgate inserts “are”] of heaven and earth, when they were created, on the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth. And every shrub of the field before it arose upon the earth, and every plant of the region before it sprouted—for the Lord God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was no human being to cultivate the earth; but a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth. Then the Lord God formed the human being from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul. Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the human being whom he had formed. And the Lord God brought forth from the soil every tree beautiful to look at and pleasant for food, and also the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it divides into four heads. The name of one is Pishon: it is the one that circles the whole land of [Note: [Col. 0165D] It is not *Evita* but *Evilat* and *Eveilat* that is read among the Greek interpreters. In very many Latin manuscripts we likewise find *Hevilat* or *Evilath* written erroneously. But we are entirely certain that Jerome read *Evila*, as we have corrected it according to the evidence of copies based on the Hebrew truth; for he discusses this name *Evila* at length in his book *On Hebrew Places*. Our correction is also supported by the Hebrew word *hhvilh* (as printed; reading uncertain), which the ancients read as *Evila*. The same reading is retained by the Hebrew-Samaritan text, and also in certain passages of the version of the Greek interpreters, for example Genesis chapters X and XXV. MART. —One Palatine manuscript has *Evilath*. The printed reading agrees with the Hebrew text and with the testimony of the better manuscripts.] Havilah, where gold is born. And the gold of that land is excellent; and there is found [Note: [Col. 0165D] Before Jerome, the Latins read this passage according to the Greek interpretation: “There is carbuncle and green stone”; but, Jerome says in his *Hebrew Questions*, “in place of carbuncle and green stone, others translated bdellium and onyx.” He thus acknowledges others before him as the authors of this interpretation, which he later followed when translating from Hebrew. MART. —He appears to have taken “bdellium” and “onyx stones” from Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion.] bdellium and onyx stone. And the name of the second river is Gihon [the Vulgate: Gehon]; it is the one that circles the whole land of Ethiopia. The name of the third river is the Tigris; it flows toward the Assyrians. The fourth river is the Euphrates.

**[C. IX.]** Therefore the Lord God took the human being and placed him in the paradise of delight, to cultivate and guard it. And he commanded him, saying, “Eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die.” And the Lord God said, “It is not good for the human being to be alone. [Note: [Col. 0166D] The current Hebrew text has *’e‘eseh*, “I will make.” The Samaritans and the other Eastern peoples likewise read the singular. The Septuagint, however, has ποιήσωμεν (*poiēsōmen*), “let us make,” from which the plural entered Jerome’s Latin translation—unless Saint Jerome happened to read in his Hebrew copy, as above in chapter I, verse 26, *na‘aseh*, that is, “let us make,” in the plural. MART. —Here too he may have followed Aquila, who translated ποιήσωμεν in the plural. The Hebrew, however, has the singular, “I will make.”] Let us make for him a helper like himself” [the Vulgate: “like him”].

**[B. VIII.]** Therefore, after the Lord God had formed from the soil all the animals of the earth and all the birds of heaven, he brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them; for whatever Adam called a living soul, that was its name. And Adam gave names to all the animals, all the birds of heaven, and all the beasts of the earth.

But no helper like him was found for Adam [the Vulgate: “for Adam”]. So the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled its place with flesh. And the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam. And Adam said, “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; she shall be called Woman [*Virago*], because she was taken from man [*vir*].” Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.

**[C. X.]** [Note: [Col. 0167C] All the older and better manuscripts read this way. The following chapter also begins with the same verse, both among the Greek interpreters and in the Latin manuscript codices. MART. —The Vulgate edition reads: “Now both were naked.”]

Now both were naked, namely Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed.

## [Chapter III]

But the serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth that the Lord God had made. He said to the woman, “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” The woman answered him, “We eat from the fruit of the trees that are in paradise [Note: [Col. 0167C] Several biblical manuscripts read *vescamur*, “let us eat”; this reading appears to be supported by *Nochel* (the Hebrew form as printed), “let us eat,” in the Hebrew and Samaritan text. The Greek interpreters likewise have φαγούμεθα (*phagoumetha*), “we shall eat” or “we will eat,” followed by the Chaldean and Syriac versions. But who does not know that in Hebrew the future is customarily used for an indefinite present? MART. —Some manuscripts cited by Martianaeus read *vescemur*, “we shall eat”; he says that this reading receives some support from the Hebrew נֹאכֵל, as well as from the Greek φαγούμεθα and other ancient versions.] from the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat, and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die.” But the serpent said to the woman, “You shall certainly not die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

Therefore the woman saw that the tree was good for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to behold; and she took of its fruit and ate. She also gave it to her husband, and he ate. And the eyes of both were opened; and when they realized that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made loincloths for themselves.

**[C. XI.]** And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the afternoon breeze, Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God among the trees of paradise. And the Lord God called Adam and said to him, “Where are you?” He answered, “I heard your voice in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” And he said to him, “Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I had commanded you not to eat?” And Adam said, “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate.” And the Lord God said to the woman, “Why have you done this?” She answered, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

**[B. IX.]** And the Lord God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all the animals and beasts of the earth. You shall walk upon your breast, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. [Note: [Col. 0167D] Almost all manuscript codices read *ipsa*, “she,” instead of *ipse*, “he.” But Jerome, both from the Hebrew source and from the Septuagint, read *ipse* in his *Hebrew Questions*. The same thing therefore happened here through the error of copyists as occurred in the time of that same holy Doctor, as he himself complains in his Letter to Lucinius: “Therefore, if you find misspellings or if some things have been copied incompletely and impede the reader’s understanding, you should not attribute this to me but to your own people and to the ignorance of the notaries and the carelessness of the copyists, who write not what they find but what they understand; and while they try to correct the errors of others, they reveal their own.” There is also a very ancient manuscript in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in which *ipse* remains written by the first hand, although a later hand added the mark over the letter *e*, making it *ipsa* instead of *ipse*. Finally, we do not conceal from the curious reader that the ancients once wrote pronouns and adverbs ending in *e* with the diphthong *ae*, as in “*ipsae dixit et facta sunt*,” “she herself spoke, and they came to be,” and “*superbae loqueris, stultae egisti*,” “you will speak proudly; you have acted foolishly,” and so forth. From this writing practice *ipsa* could easily have been retained instead of *ipse*, or *ipsae*. The Chaldean interpreter removes the ambiguity of this word and sentence by saying, “Between your son and her son: he himself …” MART. —One Palatine manuscript, together with the Vulgate edition, has *ipsa*. But this is not the place to reopen the old and transmitted controversy concerning the reading of this pronoun. Consult the interpreters, especially Jerome himself in the *Hebrew Questions*.] He himself shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for his heel.”

And to the woman he said, “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions; in pain you shall bear children, and you shall be under the authority of your husband [Note: [Col. 0168D] The Hebrew text adds the pronoun “your,” that is, [Hebrew form not printed in the supplied source].], and he himself shall rule over you.”

And to Adam he said, “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree from which I had commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your work; through hardships you shall eat it [the Vulgate: “from it”] all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth. By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

And Adam called his wife’s name Eve, because she was the mother of all the living.

**[T. II, C. XII.]** And the Lord God made tunics of skins for Adam [the Vulgate: “for Adam”] and his wife, and clothed them. And he said, “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now therefore, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand and also take from the tree of life, eat, and live forever.” And the Lord God sent him out from the paradise of delight [Col. 0168C] to cultivate the earth from which he had been taken. And he expelled Adam and placed before the paradise of delight the cherubim and a flaming, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.

**[B. X, C. XIII, Cap. IV.]** Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, “I have acquired a man through God.” And again she bore his brother Abel. Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain was a farmer. After many days Cain brought an offering to the Lord from the fruits of the earth. Abel also brought from the firstborn of his flock [Col. 0169A] and from their fat portions. And the Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, but he did not look upon Cain and his offerings. Cain was very angry, and his face fell.

And the Lord said to him, “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do badly, sin will immediately be present at the door. Its desire will be beneath you, and you will rule over it.”

**[C. XIV.]** And Cain said to his brother Abel, “[Note: [Col. 0169D] These words are absent from the Hebrew copy, and Jerome declares them superfluous. Nevertheless, because of their antiquity he retains them in his translation, as the phrase familiar to him demonstrates: “Let us go outside.” For in the old Vulgate he read, “Let us cross over into the field.” MART. —See the *Hebrew Questions* on this passage; although he declares it superfluous there, he seems here to have retained it from Aquila.] Let us go outside.” And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.

And the Lord said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” He answered, “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper? [Note: [Col. 0169D] Several manuscripts read, “Am I perhaps my brother’s keeper?” which is found in the Septuagint. MART. —The Palatine manuscript has *numquid*, “perhaps”; others additionally add *ego*, “I.”]”

And he said to him, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth. Now therefore you shall be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. When you cultivate it, it shall not give you its fruits. You shall be a wanderer and a fugitive upon the earth.”

And Cain said to the Lord, “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon. Behold, today you cast me away from the face of the earth, and from your face I shall be hidden; I shall be a wanderer and a fugitive on the earth. Therefore everyone who finds me will kill me.”

And the Lord said to him, “By no means shall this happen; but whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.” And the Lord placed a mark upon Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. [Note: [Col. 0169D] Many manuscripts read otherwise: “And the Lord placed Cain as a sign,” but *as a sign* was added by scribes. For in Hebrew it reads לְקַיִן (*leqayin*), that is, “for Cain” or “upon Cain.” MART. —The Urbinate codex has *in Cain*, “upon Cain,” closer to the Hebrew.]

And Cain went out from the presence of the Lord and dwelt as a fugitive in the land east of Eden. Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. And he built a city and called its name by the name of his son, Enoch. Enoch begot Irad; Irad begot Maujael; Maujael begot Methusael; and Methusael begot Lamech.

Lamech took two wives: the name of one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah. And Adah bore Jabal, who was the father of those who dwell in tents and shepherds. His brother’s name was Jubal; he was the father of those who play the lyre and pipe. Zillah also bore Tubal-cain, who was a hammerer and craftsman in every work of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.

And Lamech said to his wives, Adah and Zillah:

“Listen to my voice, wives of Lamech;  
pay attention to my speech:  
for I have killed a man for my wound,  
and a young man for my bruise.  
Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain,  
but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

**[Col. 0169D] [B. XI, C. XV.]** Adam again knew his wife [the Vulgate omits “again”], and she bore a son and called his name Seth, saying, “God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.” And to Seth also a son was born, whom he called Enosh. He began to call upon the name of the Lord.

### [C. XVI, Cap. V.]

This is the book of the generation of Adam. On the day when God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. He created them male and female, blessed them, and called their name Adam, on the day when they were created.

Adam lived one hundred and thirty years, and begot a son in his own image and likeness, and called his name Seth. And the days of Adam, after he begot Seth, were eight hundred years; and he begot sons and daughters. Thus all the time that Adam lived amounted to nine hundred and thirty years, and he died.

Seth lived one hundred and five years, and begot Enos. Seth lived, after he begot Enos, eight hundred and seven years, and begot sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Seth amounted to nine hundred and twelve years, and he died.

Enos lived ninety years, and begot Cainan. After his birth he lived eight hundred and fifteen years, and begot sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Enos amounted to nine hundred and five years, and he died.

Cainan lived seventy years, and begot Malaleel. Cainan lived, after he begot Malaleel, eight hundred and forty years, and begot sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Cainan amounted to nine hundred and ten years, and he died.

Malaleel lived sixty-five years, and begot Jared. Malaleel lived, after he begot Jared, eight hundred and thirty years, and begot sons and daughters. [Col. 0170C] Thus all the days of Malaleel amounted to eight hundred and ninety-five years, and he died.

Jared lived one hundred and sixty-two years, and begot Enoch. Jared lived, after he begot Enoch, eight hundred years, and begot sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Jared amounted to nine hundred and sixty-two years, and he died. [Col. 0170B]

### [C. XVII.]

Enoch lived sixty-five years and begot Methuselah, and Enoch walked with God [Col. 0170D] [Note: The Vulgate translator inserts “and he lived,” words not recognized by the Hebrew text.] after he begot Methuselah, for three hundred years, and begot sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Enoch amounted to three hundred and sixty-five years. He walked with God, and he was no longer seen, because God took him.

[Note: In the Septuagint we read “one hundred and sixty-seven years.” Jerome refutes this error in the numbers and testifies that he found precisely the same chronology in the Samaritan volume and in the books of the Hebrews. It is therefore clear that the Hebrew-Samaritan text, which today differs entirely from the Hebrew, was disrupted and corrupted in its chronological years after Jerome’s time. Nevertheless, it can be inferred from Eusebius’s chronology, preserved by Syncellus, that some Samaritan copies had already been corrupted before Jerome. MART.]

Methuselah lived one hundred and eighty-seven years, and begot Lamech. Methuselah lived, [Col. 0170D] after he begot Lamech, seven hundred and eighty-two years, and begot sons and daughters. And [Col. 0171A] thus all the days of Methuselah amounted to nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died.

Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years, and begot a son. He called his name Noah, saying: “This one will console us from the works of our hands, in the land which the Lord has cursed.” Lamech lived, after he begot Noah, five hundred and ninety-five years, and begot sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Lamech amounted to seven hundred and seventy-seven years, and he died.

### [T. III, B. XII, C. XVIII, Cap. VI.]

Now Noah, when he was five hundred years old, begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And when human beings had begun to multiply upon the earth and had begotten daughters, the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose. [Col. 0171B]

And God said: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; his days shall be one hundred and twenty years.”

[Note: In the present Hebrew text and in the Samaritan text we read *yadon*, which Saint Jerome, in the *Hebrew Questions*, interprets as “you will judge,” although, following the Septuagint version, he retains the word with the sense “he will remain.” But *yalon*, or *yalin*, meaning “he will spend the night, he will remain,” may perhaps have been written in the Hebrew exemplar of the Septuagint elders. MART. — In the *Questions* he prefers “he will judge” for the Vulgate reading. Nevertheless, the Hebrew text is also given the sense “to remain” by the ancient versions.]

There were giants upon the earth in those days. For after the sons of God had gone in to the daughters of men, and these had borne children, these were the mighty men of old, men of renown.

When God saw that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth, and that every thought of their heart was directed toward evil at all times, he regretted that he had made man upon the earth. And, touched inwardly by grief of heart, he said: “I will wipe out the human being whom I created from the face of the earth, from man to animals, from creeping things to the birds of the air; for I regret that I made them.”

### [C. XIX.]

But Noah found favor before the Lord.

These [the Vulgate adds “are”] are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just and perfect man among his generations; he walked with God. And he begot three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. [Col. 0171C]

But the earth was corrupted before God and was filled with iniquity. When God had seen that the earth was corrupt—for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth—he said to Noah: “The end of all flesh has come before me; the earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them together with the earth.

“Make for yourself an ark from smoothed wood [Note: The Septuagint has ἐκ ξύλων τετραγώνων, “from squared wood.” When Jerome said that “bitumen-coated” was read in Hebrew [Col. 0172D] instead of “squared wood,” some thought that he had been mistaken and had read *copher* for *gopher*. Yet, with due respect to such writers, it is permissible to assert that Jerome read *copher* and translated very well from the Hebrew, “from bitumen-coated wood.” For *gophrith* is a kind of gum and bitumen, or sulfurous material. The rabbis also include *ets-schemen*, “the tree of fatness,” among the varieties of cedar; and many hold that the ark was made of cedar wood. *Gopher*, therefore, is a species of tree coated with bitumen and exuding resin or pitch, such as fir, pine, and the like. MART. — In the *Hebrew Questions* he prefers to interpret it as “bitumen-coated.”]; you shall make compartments in the ark, and coat it with bitumen inside and outside. [Col. 0171D]

“And this is how you shall make it: the length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. You shall make a window in the ark, and finish it within one cubit at the top. You shall place the door of the ark low on its side; you shall make chambers and three stories in it.

“Behold, I will bring the waters of the flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which there is the breath of life under heaven; everything that is on the earth shall perish [the Vulgate adds “and”]. But I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall enter the ark—you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you. [Col. 0172A]

“And from every living creature of all flesh you shall bring two of each kind into the ark, so that they may live with you, male and female. Of the birds according to their kind, of the cattle according to their kind, and of every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind, two of each shall enter with you, so that they may live.

“You shall therefore take with you from every kind of food that can be eaten, and store it with you; it shall be food for you and for them.”

So Noah did everything that God had commanded him.

### [Cap. VII.]

And the Lord said to him: “Enter, you and all your household, into the ark, for I have seen that you are just before me in this generation. From all clean animals take seven pairs, male and female; but from unclean animals, two, male and female. Likewise, from the birds of the air, seven pairs, male and female, so that offspring may be preserved upon the face of the whole earth. [Col. 0172B]

“For after seven more days I will rain upon the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe out every substance that I have made from the surface of the earth.”

So Noah did everything that the Lord had commanded him. He was six hundred years old when the waters of the flood inundated the earth.

### [C. XX.]

Noah entered, and his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives with him, into the ark because of the waters of the flood. Of clean and unclean animals, of birds, and of everything that moves upon the earth, two by two entered Noah in the ark, male and female, as God had commanded Noah. [Col. 0172C]

When seven days had passed, the waters of the flood inundated the earth. In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, all the fountains of the great abyss burst forth, and the floodgates of heaven were opened, and rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.

On that very day Noah, and Shem, Ham, and Japheth, his sons, his wife, and his sons’ three wives with them entered the ark; they, and every animal according to its kind, all cattle according to their kind, everything that moves upon the earth according to its kind, and every flying creature according to its kind—all birds and every winged creature—entered Noah in the ark, two by two of every flesh in which there was the breath of life. [Col. 0172D]

Those that entered were male and female; of every flesh they entered, as God had commanded him. And the Lord shut him in from outside. [Col. 0173A]

The flood was upon the earth for forty days. The waters multiplied and lifted the ark high above the earth. For they rose exceedingly and covered everything upon the surface of the earth, while the ark was carried upon the waters. The waters prevailed greatly over the earth, and all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered. The water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains that it had covered.

Every creature that moved upon the earth perished: birds, animals, beasts, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth; all human beings, and everything in which there was the breath of life on the earth, died. And he wiped out every substance that was upon the earth, from man to cattle, both creeping things and birds of the air; they were wiped out from the earth. Only Noah remained, and those who were with him in the ark. And the waters prevailed over the earth for one hundred and fifty days. [Col. 0173B]

### [T. IV, C. XXI, Cap. VIII.]

God remembered Noah and all the animals and all the cattle that were with him in the ark, and he caused a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters subsided. The fountains of the abyss and the floodgates of heaven were closed, and the rain from heaven was restrained. The waters receded from the earth, going and returning, and they began to diminish after one hundred and fifty days.

And the ark came to rest in the seventh month, [Note: Thus the Septuagint and Jerome have it; but in the Hebrew and Samaritan texts, and in all the Eastern versions, we read “on the seventeenth day.” I have no doubt that this is erroneous and that, through an easy scribal slip among the Hebrews, *esrim*, “twenty,” was changed to *asar jom*, “the seventeenth day.” MART. — Martianay accuses the Hebrew and Samaritan texts and all the Eastern versions of error because, as he says, through the scribes’ mistake they give “the seventeenth day” instead of “the twenty-seventh.” I would not presume to judge which reading is more correct, though I would nevertheless prefer to side with the Hebrew.] on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia. [Col. 0173C]

The waters continued to go and diminish until the tenth month. In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the summits of the mountains appeared.

After forty days had passed, Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made and sent out a raven. It went out [Note: In one Corbie manuscript it reads, “which went out and returned”; others have “it returned.” This passage differs in many ways in the Septuagint: instead of “the window of the ark,” they read “the door of the ark,” and they say of the raven that it went out and did not return. Jerome himself followed this reading in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, where he says: “Thus the raven is sent out from the ark, and did not return.” But there he is using allegories, and at that time he had not yet examined the Hebrew volumes. Consult the book of the *Hebrew Questions* in the manuscript copies. MART. — Our manuscripts read, “and it did not return”; yet the Hebrew has “and it returned,” with which the Chaldean, Josephus, and the Syriac quoted by Didymus agree.] and returned until the waters dried up upon the earth. [Col. 0173D]

He also sent out a dove after it, to see whether the waters had now ceased upon the face of the earth. When it found no place where its foot could rest, it returned to him in the ark, for the waters were over the whole earth. He stretched out his hand, took it, and brought it into the ark.

After waiting another seven days, he again sent the dove out of the ark. It came to him in the evening, carrying in its beak a green olive branch with leaves. Noah therefore understood that the waters had ceased upon the earth. He nevertheless waited another seven days and sent out the dove, which did not return to him again. [Col. 0174A]

### [C. XXII.]

In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the waters had diminished upon the earth. Noah opened the roof of the ark, looked out, and saw that the surface of the earth had dried.

In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry.

### [B. XIII.]

God spoke to Noah, saying: “Go out of the ark, you and your wife, your sons and your sons’ wives with you. Bring out with you all the living creatures that are with you, of every flesh, birds, beasts, and all creeping things that creep upon the earth; let them go out with you and move upon the earth. Let them increase and multiply upon it.” [Col. 0174B]

So Noah went out, and his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives with him. And all the animals, cattle, and creeping things that creep upon the earth went out of the ark according to their kinds.

### [T. V.]

Noah built an altar to the Lord. He took from all the clean cattle and clean birds and offered burnt offerings upon the altar. The Lord smelled the pleasing odor and said [Note: In Hebrew, *el-libbo*, which is ambiguous and can mean “to his heart” or “to his own heart”—that is, Noah’s heart or God’s heart. Hence the Septuagint: Καὶ εἶπε Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς διανοηθεὶς, “And the Lord God said, reflecting,” or “considering”; likewise Symmachus has “to himself,” and Theodotion, “to his heart.” Jerome refers it to Noah: “And he said to him.” MART. — It may be that Jerome, in the Hebrew, although contrary to the character of that language, read “to him” instead of what is now found, “to his heart” or “to his own heart.” Certainly I know no one who has translated it as he did.] to him: [Col. 0174D]

“I will never again curse the earth because of human beings, for the inclination and thought of the human heart are prone to evil from their youth; therefore I will never again strike down every living creature, as I have done.

“All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day, shall not cease.” [Col. 0174C]

### [C. XXIII, Cap. IX.]

God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them: “Increase and multiply, and fill [the Vulgate has ‘refill’] the earth. Let your dread and your terror be upon all the animals of the earth, all the birds of the air, and everything that moves upon the earth [the Vulgate has ‘over the earth’]. All the fish of the sea have been delivered into your hand.

“Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you. Just as I gave you all green plants, so I give you everything—except that you shall eat flesh with blood. For I will require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast, and from the hand of man; from the hand of each man and his brother I will require the life of man. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed, for man was made in the image of God. [Col. 0175A]

“But you, increase and multiply, move upon the earth, and fill it.”

### [C. XXIV.]

God also said this to Noah and to his sons with him:

“Behold, I establish my covenant with you and with your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you, both birds, cattle, and all the beasts of the earth that have come out of the ark, and all the beasts of the earth.

“I establish my covenant with you: never again shall all flesh be destroyed by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to devastate the earth.”

And God said: “This is the sign of the covenant that I make between myself and you, and every living creature that is with you, throughout perpetual generations. I shall place my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. [Col. 0175B]

“When I cover the sky with clouds, my bow will appear in the clouds, and I will remember my covenant with you and with every living creature that animates flesh; never again shall the waters of the flood become a flood to destroy all flesh.

“The bow shall be in the clouds, and I shall see it and remember the everlasting covenant that has been established between God and every living creature of all flesh that is upon the earth.”

And God said to Noah: “This shall be the sign of the covenant that I have established between myself and all flesh upon the earth.”

### [B. XIV, C. XXV.]

The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Ham himself was the father of Canaan. [Col. 0175C]

These three were the sons of Noah, and from them the whole human race was spread over all the earth. Noah, a man of the soil, began to cultivate the ground and planted a vineyard. Drinking wine, he became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent.

When Ham, the father of Canaan, saw that his father’s private parts were exposed, he told his two brothers outside. But Shem and Japheth took a cloak, placed it upon their shoulders, and, walking backward, covered their father’s private parts. Their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father’s genitals.

When Noah awoke from his wine and learned what his younger son had done to him, he said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers.”

And he said: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem; let Canaan be his servant.” [Col. 0175D]

### [C. XXVI.]

Noah lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood. All his days amounted to nine hundred and fifty years, and he died.

### [T. VI, B. XV, Cap. X.]

These are the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth; and sons were born to them after the flood.

The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. From these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each according to its language, its families, and its nations.

The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabtechah. The sons of Raamah were Sheba and Dedan. [Col. 0176A]

Cush begot Nimrod. He began to be mighty upon the earth and was a mighty hunter before the Lord. Hence the proverb arose: “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.”

The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. From that land Asshur went out and built Nineveh, the streets of the city, and Calah. Resen also lay between Nineveh and Calah; this is the great city.

Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim.

Canaan begot Sidon, his firstborn, and the Hittites, Jebusites, Amorites, Girgashites, Hivites, Arkites, Sinites, Arvadites, Zemarites, and Hamathites. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites were dispersed. [Col. 0176B]

The boundary of Canaan extended from Sidon toward Gerar as far as Gaza, until one enters Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.

These were the sons of Ham, according to their families, languages, lands, and nations.

Sons were also born to Shem, the father of all the sons of Eber and the brother of Japheth the elder. The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram. The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.

Arpachshad begot Shelah, from whom Eber arose. Two sons were born to Eber; the name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided, and the name of his brother was Joktan.

Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan. Their dwelling extended from Mesha toward Sephar, the eastern mountain. [Col. 0176C]

These were the sons of Shem according to their families, languages, and regions, in their nations. These were the families of Noah according to their peoples and nations. From them the nations were divided upon the earth after the flood.

### [B. XVI, C. XXVII, Cap. XI.]

The earth had one language and the same words. As they journeyed from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.

One said to his neighbor: “Come, let us make bricks and burn them in the fire.” They used bricks instead of stones and bitumen instead of mortar. And they said: “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose top may reach to heaven, and let us make our name famous before we are scattered throughout all the lands.” [Col. 0176D]

The Lord descended to see the city and the tower that the sons of Adam were building and said: “Behold, they are one people and have one language; they have begun to do this, and they will not cease from their plans until they complete them in deed. Come, therefore, let us descend and confuse their language there, so that each may not understand the voice of his neighbor.”

And so the Lord divided them from that place throughout all the lands, and they ceased building the city. Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the language of the whole earth was confused; and from there the Lord scattered them over the face of all the regions. [Col. 0177A]

These are the generations of Shem. Shem was one hundred years old when he begot Arpachshad, two years after the flood. Shem lived, after he begot Arpachshad, five hundred years, and begot sons and daughters.

Arpachshad lived thirty-five years and begot Shelah. Arpachshad lived, after he begot Shelah, four hundred and three years [Thus Codex Saint-Germain no. 3, the Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic texts. But the Samaritan, the printed Latin texts, and most manuscripts read 303], and begot sons and daughters.

Shelah lived thirty years and begot Eber. Shelah lived, after he begot Eber, four hundred [the Vulgate has “forty”] and three years, and begot sons and daughters.

Eber lived thirty-four years and begot Peleg. Eber lived, after he begot Peleg, four hundred and thirty years, and begot sons and daughters. [Col. 0177B]

Peleg lived thirty years and begot Reu. Peleg lived, after he begot Reu, two hundred and nine years, and begot sons and daughters.

Reu lived thirty-two years and begot Serug. Reu lived, after he begot Serug, two hundred and seven years, and begot sons and daughters.

Serug lived thirty years and begot Nahor. Serug lived, after he begot Nahor, two hundred years, and begot sons and daughters.

Nahor lived twenty-nine years and begot Terah. Nahor lived, after he begot Terah, one hundred and nineteen years, and begot sons and daughters.

Terah lived seventy years and begot Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

### [C. XXV, 121.]

These are the generations of Terah: Terah begot Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran begot Lot. Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans.

Abram and Nahor took wives. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah. Sarai was barren and had no children.

Terah took Abram his son, and Lot, the son of Haran, his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of Abram his son, and led them out of Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. They came as far as Haran and settled there.

The days of Terah amounted to two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran. [Col. 0177C]

### [T. VII, B. XVII, C. XXIX, Cap. XII.]

The Lord said to Abram: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house [the Vulgate adds “and come”] into the land that I will show you. I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you and magnify your name, and you shall be blessed. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you; and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” [Col. 0177D]

Abram therefore went out as the Lord had commanded him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. He took Sarai his wife, Lot his brother’s son, all the possessions they had acquired, and the persons whom they had made in Haran. [Col. 0178A]

### [C. XXX.]

They went out to go to the land of Canaan. When they had entered it, Abram passed through the land as far as the place of Shechem, as far as the renowned valley. At that time the Canaanite was in the land.

### [B. XVIII.]

The Lord appeared to Abram and said to him: “To your offspring I will give this land.” He built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him.

From there he moved toward the mountain that lay east of Bethel and pitched his tent there, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. He also built there an altar to the Lord and called upon his name.

Abram continued on his way, advancing farther toward the south. A famine arose in the land, and Abram went down into Egypt to reside there, for the famine had become severe in the land. [Col. 0178B]

When he was near entering Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife: “I know that you are a beautiful woman. When the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘She is his wife,’ and they will kill me but preserve you. Say, therefore, I beg you, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me because of you, and my life may be spared for your sake.”

When Abram had entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was exceedingly beautiful. The princes reported her to Pharaoh and praised her to him, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.

They treated Abram well because of her, and he acquired sheep, cattle, donkeys, male and female servants, female donkeys, and camels.

But the Lord struck Pharaoh and his household with very great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife. [Col. 0178C] Pharaoh summoned Abram and said to him: “What is this that you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? Why did you say that she was your sister, so that I took her for myself as a wife? Now, then, here is your wife; take her and go.”

Pharaoh gave orders concerning Abram to his men, and they escorted him away, with his wife and everything that he possessed.

### [B. XIX, Cap. XIII.]

Abram therefore went up from Egypt, he and his wife and everything he possessed, and Lot with him, toward the south.

He was very rich in possessions of silver and gold [Note: In the Hebrew truth it is written: “Abram was exceedingly heavy,” that is, βαρὺς σφόδρα, “very heavy.” MART. — This is the old reading, and it moved Jerome to ask how Abraham, leaving Egypt, could have been “very rich.” The answer, he says, is found in that Hebrew truth in which it is written, “Abram was exceedingly heavy,” that is, βαρὺς σφόδρα.] [Col. 0177D]

He returned by the route along which he had come, from the south toward Bethel, as far as the place where he had previously pitched his tent, between Bethel and Ai, at the place of the altar that he had formerly made; and there he called upon the name of the Lord. [Col. 0178D]

Lot also, who was with Abram, had flocks of sheep, herds, and tents. The land could not contain them so that they might dwell together, for their possessions were great, and they could not live together. Hence a quarrel arose between the herdsmen of Abram’s flocks and those of Lot.

At that time the Canaanite and the Perizzite were dwelling in the land. Abram therefore said to Lot: “Please let there be no dispute between me and you, or between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are brothers. Behold, the whole land is before you; withdraw from me, I beg you. If you go to the left, I will hold to the right; if you choose the right, I will go to the left.” [Col. 0179A]

Lot lifted his eyes and saw the whole region around the Jordan, which was all watered—before the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah—like the paradise of the Lord and like Egypt, as one approaches Zoar. Lot chose for himself the region around the Jordan and departed from the east; and they separated from one another.

Abram dwelt in the land of Canaan, while Lot stayed in the towns around the Jordan and dwelt in Sodom. The men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinful before the Lord [Note: [Col. 0179D] In the Hebrew there is only “before God.” Jerome himself, in his *Questions* on this passage, says that “before God” was needlessly added here by the Septuagint interpreters.]

### [B. XX, C. XXXI.]

The Lord said to Abram [Col. 0179B], after Lot had separated from him: “Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward the north and the south, the east and the west. All the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.

“I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth. If anyone can count the dust of the earth, he will also be able to count your offspring. Rise, walk through the land in its length and breadth, for I will give it to you.”

Abram moved his tent and came to dwell beside the valley of Mamre, which is in Hebron. There he built an altar to the Lord.

### [Treatise VIII, Chapter XXXII, Chapter XIV]

Now it came to pass at that time that Amraphel, king of Shinar, Arioch, king of Pontus, Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites, and Tidal, king of the nations, entered into battle against Bera, king of Sodom, Birsah, king of Gomorrah, Shinab, king of Admah, Shemeber, king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela—which is Zoar.

All these assembled in the Valley of Siddim, which is now the Salt Sea. For twelve years they had served Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled against him. Therefore, in the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer came, together with the kings who were with him. They defeated the Rephaim at Ashtaroth-karnaim, and the Zuzim [Note: [Col. 0179D] Thus following the translators of the Septuagint, who read *bahem*, that is, “with them.” But in the *Hebrew Questions* Jerome asserts that the middle letter of this word is not *he* but *heth*, and that it should be read *bahom*, that is, “in Hom.” Thus Hom is the name of the place in which the Zuzim were struck down by the four kings. MART. —Jerome says *baem*, for which the Septuagint gave *ἅμα* (*hama*), “with them”; they supposed it was written with *he*, being led by the similarity of the letters, whereas it was written with *heth*. For *baem*, when written with three letters, means “among them” if its middle letter is *he*; but if it has *heth*, as here, it signifies a place, namely “in Hom.”], with them; the Emim at Shaveh-kiriathaim; the Horites in the mountains of Seir, as far as the Plain of Paran, which is in the wilderness.

Then they turned back and came to the spring of Mishpat, which is Kadesh, and they struck the whole territory of the Amalekites, as well as the Amorite who dwelt in Hazazon-tamar. And the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar, went out and drew up their battle line against them in the Valley of Siddim—that is, against Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites, Tidal, king of the nations, Amraphel, king of Shinar, and Arioch, king of Pontus: four kings against five.

The Valley of Siddim had many wells of bitumen. Therefore the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah turned in flight and fell there, while those who remained fled to the mountain. They seized all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah and everything belonging to their food, and departed. They also took Lot, the son of Abram’s brother, who was dwelling in Sodom, together with his possessions.

And behold, one who had escaped reported this to Abram the Hebrew, who was dwelling in the valley of Mamre the Amorite, the brother of Eshcol and the brother of Aner; for these men had made a covenant with Abram. When Abram heard that his brother Lot had been taken captive, he counted his trained servants, born in his household, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued [Note: [Col. 0180D] In the current Hebrew text we read, without the attached pronoun, *vaiirdoph ad-dan*, “and he pursued as far as Dan.” The Septuagint, however, as also Jerome, the Syriac, and the Arabic in their Hebrew copies, seem to have read *vaiirdoph ahharehem*, “and he pursued after them as far as Dan”; or *vaiirdephem*, “and he pursued them,” as in the following verse. MART. —So too he reads in the *Hebrew Questions*, though he does not mention in that passage the Hebrew reading, which does not admit the pronoun “them” here.] them as far as Dan.

Having divided his forces, he fell upon them by night, struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is on the left of Damascus. He recovered all the possessions, as well as his brother Lot and his possessions, and also the women and the people.

Then the king of Sodom went out to meet him after he had returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, in the Valley of Shaveh, which is the King’s Valley. But Melchizedek, king of Salem, bringing out bread and wine—for he was priest of God Most High—blessed him and said:

“Blessed is Abram by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed is God Most High, through whose protection your enemies are in your hands.”

And he gave him tithes of everything.

Then the king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people; take the rest for yourself.” He answered him:

“I lift my hand to the Lord, God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, that from a thread of the warp to a sandal strap I will take nothing of all that is yours, lest you say, ‘I made Abram rich’—except what the young men have eaten, and the shares belonging to the men who came with me, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre; let them take their shares.”

### [Treatise IX, Book XXI, Chapter XXXIII, Chapter XV]

After these events, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying:

“Do not be afraid, Abram; I am your protector, and your reward is exceedingly great.”

Abram said, “Lord God, what will you give me? I shall depart childless, and the son of the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus.” Abram continued:

“You have not given me offspring, and behold, my household servant will be my heir.”

Immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying:

“This man shall not be your heir; rather, the one who will come forth from your own body—he shall be your heir.”

He led him outside and said to him, “Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you are able.” Then he said to him, “So shall your offspring be.”

He believed the Lord, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. [Note: [Col. 0181D] The Vulgate reads, “Abram believed God,” in disagreement with the Hebrew.]

And he said to him:

“I am the Lord who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land and to possess it.”

But he said, “Lord God, how may I know that I shall possess it?”

The Lord answered, “Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, together with a turtledove and a pigeon.”

He took all these, divided them down the middle, and placed each half opposite the other; but he did not divide the birds. Birds of prey descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.

When the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and a great and dark terror overwhelmed him. And it was said to him:

“Know beforehand that your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own; they will enslave them and oppress them for four hundred years. Yet I will judge the nation to which they will be enslaved, and afterward they will depart with great possessions.

“But you shall go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a good old age. In the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquities of the Amorites have not yet reached their full measure.”

When the sun had set and darkness had come, behold, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between those divided pieces. On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying:

“To your offspring I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates: the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”

### [Treatise X, Chapter XVI]

Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, had borne him no children. But she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar, and she said to her husband:

“Behold, the Lord has closed me off from bearing children. Go in to my maidservant; perhaps at least through her I may receive children.”

When he consented to her request, Sarai took her Egyptian maidservant Hagar, after they had begun to dwell in the land of Canaan ten years earlier, and gave her to her husband as a wife. He went in to her. When she saw that she had conceived, she despised her mistress.

Sarai said to Abram, “You are acting unjustly toward me. I gave my maidservant into your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she has held me in contempt. May the Lord judge between me and you.”

Abram answered her, “Behold, your maidservant is in your hand; deal with her as you please.”

So Sarai afflicted her, and she fled. When the angel of the Lord found her beside a spring of water in the wilderness that [Vulgate: “which”] is on the road to Shur, [Note: [Col. 0181D] The Vulgate translator adds *in deserto*, “in the wilderness,” which appears to be a variant reading; instead of *in solitudine*, “in the solitude,” it seems to have entered the text from the margin of a book.] he said to her:

“Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?”

She answered, “I am fleeing from the presence of Sarai, my mistress.”

The angel of the Lord said to her:

“Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand.”

And again he said:

“I will greatly multiply your offspring, and they shall not be counted because of their multitude.

“Behold, you have conceived and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heard your affliction. He shall be a wild man; his hand shall be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him, and he shall pitch his tents opposite all his brothers.”

She called the name of the Lord who was speaking to her, “You, God, who have seen me.” For she said, “Surely here I have seen the back of the one who sees me.”

Therefore she called that well, “The Well of the Living One who sees me.” It is between Kadesh and Barad.

Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called his name Ishmael. Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him.

### [Book XXII, Chapter XXXIV, Chapter XVII]

When he had begun to be ninety-nine years old, the Lord appeared to him and said:

“I am God Almighty; walk before me and be perfect. I will establish my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly.”

Abram fell face down. God said to him:

“It is I, and my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of many nations. No longer shall your name be called Abram; rather, you shall be called Abraham, because I have appointed you father of many nations.

“I will make you grow exceedingly, and I will establish you among the nations, and kings shall come forth from you. I will establish my covenant between me and you and between your offspring after you throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, so that I may be your God and the God of your offspring after you.

“I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojourning, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession, and I will be their God.”

[Treatise XI.]

Again God said to Abraham:

“And as for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall observe between me and you and your offspring after you: every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, so that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you.

“Every male child among you shall be circumcised at eight days old, throughout your generations; both the household servant and the purchased slave, and everyone who is not of your lineage, shall be circumcised. My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant.

“Any male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

God also said to Abraham:

“You shall not call your wife Sarai Sarai, but Sarah. I will bless her, and from her I will give you a son, whom I will bless; he shall become nations, and kings of peoples shall arise from him.”

Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart:

“Will a son be born to a hundred-year-old man? And will Sarah, at ninety years of age, give birth?”

And he said to God, “If only Ishmael might live before you!”

God said to Abraham:

“Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his offspring after him.

“As for Ishmael, I have heard you. Behold, I will bless him, increase him, and multiply him exceedingly. He shall beget twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation.

“But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time in the following year.”

When he had finished speaking with him, God ascended from Abraham.

Abraham took Ishmael his son, all the household servants born in his house, and everyone whom he had purchased—every male among the men of his household—and circumcised the flesh of their foreskins on that very day, as God had commanded him.

Abraham was ninety-nine years old when the flesh of his foreskin was circumcised. Ishmael his son had completed thirteen years at the time of his circumcision. On the same day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised. All the men of his household, whether household servants, purchased slaves, or foreigners, were circumcised together.

### [Treatise XII, Book XXXIII, Chapter XXXV, Chapter XVIII]

The Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre as he was sitting at the entrance of his tent, in the heat of the day. When he lifted his eyes, three men appeared standing near him [Vulgate: “nearby”]. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the entrance of his tent and bowed to the ground. He said:

“My lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, please do not pass by your servant. Let a little water be brought, wash your feet, and rest beneath the tree. I will set out a morsel of bread, and strengthen your hearts; afterward you may go on. For this is why you have turned aside to your servant.”

They said, “Do as you have said.”

Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah and said to her:

“Quickly, mix three measures of fine flour and make cakes baked under the ashes.”

He himself ran to the herd, took a tender and choice calf, and gave it to the servant, who hurried to cook it. He also took butter and milk and the calf he had prepared, and set them before them. He stood beside them under the tree.

When they had eaten, they said to him, “Where is Sarah your wife?”

He answered, “She is there in the tent.”

One of them said:

“I will return to you at this time, life permitting, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.”

When Sarah heard this, she laughed behind the entrance of the tent. Both were old and advanced in age, and Sarah had ceased to have the way of women. She laughed secretly, saying:

“After I have grown old, and my lord is aged, shall I give myself to pleasure?”

The Lord said to Abraham:

“Why did Sarah laugh, saying, ‘Shall I truly bear a child, old as I am?’ Is anything difficult for God? At the appointed time I will return to you, life permitting, and Sarah shall have a son.”

Sarah denied it, saying, “I did not laugh,” for she was terrified. But the Lord said, “It is not so; you did laugh.”

When the men had risen from there, they directed their eyes toward Sodom, and Abraham went with them, escorting them.

The Lord said:

“Can I conceal from Abraham what I am about to do, since he is destined to become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him? For I know that he will command his sons and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord and to practice justice and judgment, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham everything that he has spoken to him.”

Therefore the Lord said:

“The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me—or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

They turned from there and went toward Sodom, while Abraham still stood before the Lord. Drawing near, he said:

“Will you really destroy the righteous with the wicked? If there are fifty righteous in the city, will they perish together? Will you not spare that place for the sake of the fifty righteous who are in it? Far be it from you to do such a thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be treated like the wicked. This is not fitting for you. Will the judge of all the earth not execute judgment?” [Vulgate adds: “this judgment.”]

The Lord said to him:

“If I find fifty righteous in Sodom, within the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake.”

Abraham answered:

“Since I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes. What if there are five fewer than fifty righteous? Will you destroy the whole city because of the five?” [Note: [Col. 0183D] The Vulgate translator reads “because of the forty-five,” in disagreement with the Hebrew.]

He said, “I will not destroy it if I find there forty-five.”

Again he spoke to him:

“But if forty [Note: [Col. 0184D] The Hebrew text and the Vulgate translator add *there*, “if forty are found there.”] are found there, what will you do?”

He said, “I will not strike it for the sake of the forty.”

“Please,” he said, “do not be angry, Lord, if I speak. What if thirty are found there?”

He answered, “I will not do it if I find thirty there.”

“Since I have once begun,” he said, “I will speak to my Lord. What if twenty are found there?”

He said, “I will not kill them for the sake of the twenty.”

“I beg you,” he said, “do not be angry, Lord, if I speak once more. What if ten are found there?”

He said, “I will not destroy it for the sake of the ten.”

The Lord departed after he had ceased speaking with Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.

### [Chapter XXXVI, Chapter XIX]

Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the city gate. When he saw them, he rose [Vulgate adds: “to meet them”] and went to meet them. He bowed face down to the ground and said:

“I beg you, my lords, turn aside into the house of your servant and stay there. Wash your feet, and in the morning you shall continue on your way.”

They said, “No, we shall spend the night in the street.”

But he urged them strongly, and they turned aside to him. After they entered his house, he prepared a feast for them, baked unleavened bread, and they ate.

Before they went to bed, the men of the city surrounded the house, from boy to old man—all the people together. They called Lot and said to him:

“Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out here, so that we may know them.”

Lot went out to them, shutting the door behind him, and said:

“Please, my brothers, do not do this evil. I have two daughters who have not yet known a man. I will bring them out to you, and you may abuse them as you please, provided that you do no harm to these men, because they have entered beneath the shelter of my roof.”

They said, “Move aside.”

And again they said:

“You came here as an outsider, and now you would act as a judge? We will afflict you more than them.”

They pressed violently against Lot, and they were already close to breaking down the doors [Vulgate: “the door was already close to being broken down”]. Then the men reached out their hands, brought Lot inside to them, and shut the door. They struck the men who were outside with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door.

They said to Lot:

“Do you have anyone else here who belongs to you—a son-in-law, sons, or daughters? Bring out everyone who belongs to you from this city, for we are going to destroy this place, because their outcry has grown great before the Lord, who sent us to destroy it.” [Vulgate: “them.”]

Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, and said:

“Rise, leave this place, for the Lord is going to destroy this city.”

But he appeared to them to be joking.

When morning came, the angels urged him, saying:

“Rise, take your wife and your two daughters whom you have, lest you also perish in the guilt of the city.”

As he delayed, they seized his hand, the hand of his wife, and the hands of his two daughters, because the Lord spared him. They led him out and placed him beyond the city.

There the Lord spoke to him: [Note: [Col. 0185D] Instead of this reading, “There the Lord spoke to him,” the Hebrew has: “And it came to pass, when they had brought them outside, that he said,” and so forth. The Vulgate translator also differs: “And there they spoke to him, saying,” and so forth.]

“Save your life. Do not look behind you, and do not remain anywhere in the surrounding region. Save yourself on the mountain, lest you too perish.”

Lot said to them:

“Please, my lord, because your servant has found favor before you, and you have magnified your mercy, which you have shown me by saving my life, I cannot be saved on the mountain, lest some evil overtake me and I die. Behold, this city is nearby, and I can flee there; it is small, and I shall be saved in it. Is it not a little one? Then my life will live.”

He said to him:

“Behold, I have also accepted your request in this matter, so that I will not overthrow the city about which you have spoken. Hurry and save yourself there, because I cannot do anything until you enter it.”

Therefore the name of that city was called Zoar.

The sun rose over the land, and Lot entered Zoar.

### [Chapter XXXVII]

Then the Lord rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah, from the Lord out of heaven, and overthrew these cities, the entire surrounding region, all the inhabitants of the cities, and everything growing from the ground.

His wife looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt.

### [Book XXIV]

Abraham rose early and went to the place where he had previously stood with the Lord. He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah and over the whole land of that region, and he saw smoke rising from the earth like smoke from a furnace.

When God overthrew the cities of that region, he remembered Abraham and rescued Lot from the overthrow of the cities in which he had lived.

### [Treatise XIII]

Lot went up from Zoar and remained on the mountain, together with his two daughters—for he was afraid to remain in Zoar. He himself and his two daughters stayed in a cave.

The elder said to the younger:

“Our father is old, and no man remains in the land who can come in to us according to the custom of the whole earth. Come, let us give our father wine to drink and sleep with him, so that we may preserve offspring through our father.”
