That night they gave their father wine to drink. The elder went in and slept with her father, but he did not know either when his daughter lay down or when she rose.

The next day the elder said to the younger:

“Behold, I slept yesterday with my father. Let us give him wine to drink this night also, and you shall sleep with him, so that we may preserve offspring through our father.”

They gave their father wine that night as well [Note: [Col. 0185D] The Hebrew text and the Vulgate translator add “his,” that is, “his wine.”], and the younger daughter went in and slept with him. Even then he did not know when she lay down or when she rose.

Thus both daughters of Lot conceived by their father. The elder bore a son and called his name Moab; he is the father of the Moabites to the present day. The younger also bore a son and called his name Ammon—that is, “son of my people”; he is the father of the Ammonites to this day.

[Note: [Col. 0185D] The name “Ammon” appears to have dropped out of the current Hebrew text, for *Ben-ammi*, which stands in the Hebrew, is not the name itself but gives, as it were, the reason why the younger daughter’s son was called Ammon. MART. —This name is not found in the Hebrew archetype; it has only: “And he called his name Ben-ammi; he is the father,” and so forth. The name *Ben-ammi* means “son of my people,” which is Jerome’s interpretation. Hence Martianay supposes that the name Ammon has dropped out of the current Hebrew text. Yet this is so improbable that it conflicts with the sacred text and with the character of the language, which attaches an etymology—though one that does not correspond very well—to the same native word. It is more likely that the reading here derives from the Greek paraphrase: *ἐκάλεσε τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἄμμαν, λέγουσα, Υἱὸς γένου μου*—“she called his name Amman, saying, ‘Son of my people.’” See the *Hebrew Questions*.]

### [Treatise XIV, Book XXV, Chapter XXXVIII, Chapter XX]

From there Abraham journeyed toward the southern land and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur. He sojourned in Gerar. He said of Sarah his wife, “She is my sister.” Therefore Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for her and took her.

But God came to Abimelech in a dream at night and said to him:

“Behold, you are going to die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband.”

Abimelech, however, had not touched her, and he said:

“Lord, will you kill an ignorant and righteous nation? Did he not say to me, ‘She is my sister,’ and did she herself not say, ‘He is my brother’? In the simplicity of my heart and the purity of my hands I have done this.”

God said to him:

“I know that you did this with a simple heart, and therefore I protected you from sinning against me, and I did not permit you to touch her. Now, therefore, return the wife to her husband, for he is a prophet, and he will pray for you and you will live. But if you are unwilling to return her, know that you shall certainly die, you and all that is yours.”

Abimelech rose early in the morning, called all his servants, and told them all these things in their hearing. All the men were greatly afraid.

Abimelech also called Abraham and said to him:

“What have you done to us? How have we sinned against you, that you have brought such a great sin upon me and my kingdom? You have done to us things that ought not to be done.”

Again reproaching him, he said:

“What did you see that made you do this?”

Abraham answered:

“I thought to myself, saying, ‘Perhaps there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.’ Yet in another respect she truly is my sister, the daughter of my father and not the daughter of my mother, and I took her as my wife.

“But after God brought me out from my father’s house, I said to her, ‘You shall show me this kindness: in every place to which we enter, you shall say that I am your brother.’”

Therefore Abimelech took sheep and cattle, male and female servants, and gave them to Abraham. He also returned his wife Sarah to him and said:

“Behold, my land is before you; dwell wherever it pleases you.”

To Sarah he said:

“Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother. Let this be for you a covering of the eyes among all who are with you and wherever you go; and remember that you have been exposed.”

When Abraham prayed, God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants, and they bore children, for the Lord had closed every womb in Abimelech’s household because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.

### [Treatise XV, Book XXVI, Chapter XXXVIII, Chapter XXI]

The Lord visited Sarah, as he had promised, and fulfilled what he had spoken. She conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time that God had foretold to her.

Abraham called the name of his son whom Sarah bore to him Isaac, and he circumcised him on the eighth day, as God had commanded him, when he was one hundred years old; for Isaac was born when his father was that age.

Sarah said:

“God has made laughter for me; whoever hears of it will laugh with me.”

And again she said:

“Who would have believed that Abraham would hear that Sarah was nursing a son whom she bore to him in his old age?”

The child grew and was weaned. Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning.

### [Chapter XL]

When Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing [Note: [Col. 0187D] After the Septuagint, some printed books and several manuscript copies of the Bible add: “with Isaac his son.” Jerome, however, warns the reader in the *Hebrew Questions* that these words are not found in the Hebrew volumes: “What follows,” he says, “with Isaac his son, is not found in the Hebrew.” MART. —The Old Latin version added “with Isaac his son.” Our manuscripts add only “with Isaac,” while in one Palatine manuscript a later hand wrote the words “his son” in the margin.], she said to Abraham:

“Cast out this maidservant and her son, for the son of this maidservant shall not be heir with my son Isaac.”

Abraham was deeply distressed over his son. God said to him:

“Do not let this seem harsh to you concerning the boy and your maidservant. Whatever Sarah has said to you, listen to her voice, because through Isaac your offspring shall be called. But I will also make the son of the maidservant into a great nation, because he is your offspring.”

Abraham rose early, took bread and a skin of water, placed them upon her shoulder, handed over the boy, and sent her away.

When she had departed, she wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. When the water in the skin had been exhausted, she cast the boy beneath one of the trees that were there. She went away and sat opposite him at a distance as far as a bowshot, for she said:

“I shall not see the death of the boy.”

Sitting opposite him, she raised her voice and wept.

God heard the voice of the boy. The angel of God called Hagar from heaven and said:

“What are you doing, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy from the place where he is. Rise, take the boy, and hold his hand, for I will make him into a great nation.”

God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She went, filled the skin, and gave the boy a drink. God was with him. He grew and dwelt in the wilderness and became a young archer. He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.

### [Chapter XLI]

At the same time Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, said to Abraham:

“God is with you in everything that you do. Therefore swear by God that you will not harm me, my descendants, or my lineage. According to the mercy that I have shown you, you shall deal with me and with the land in which you have dwelt as a stranger.”

Abraham said, “I will swear.”

Then Abraham reproached Abimelech concerning the well of water that his servants had seized by force.

Abimelech answered:

“I do not know who did this thing. Moreover, you did not tell me, and I have heard of it only today.”

Abraham then took sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them made a covenant.

Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock apart. Abimelech said to him:

“What do these seven ewe lambs mean, which you have set apart?”

He answered:

“You shall accept these seven ewe lambs from my hand, so that they may be a witness for me that I dug this well.”

Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there the two of them swore an oath. And they made a covenant over the well of the oath.

Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, rose and returned to the land of the Philistines. Abraham planted a grove at Beersheba and invoked there the name of the Lord, the eternal God. And he dwelt as a resident alien in the land of the Philistines for many days.

[T. XVI, B. XXVII, C. XLII, Cap. XXII.] After these things had taken place, God tested Abraham and said to him: “Abraham!” He answered: “Here I am.” He said to him: “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac—

[Note: [Col. 0188D] Where it now reads “into the land of vision,” the Hebrew has “into the land of Moria”; the Samaritan text has Moraa; domouroje, “of the Amorites” [reading uncertain]; the Syriac reading is not supplied; the Seventy translate it as τὴν ὑψηλὴν, “the lofty [land],” deriving it, if I am not mistaken, from [the root] rum; Aquila has τὴν καταφανῆ, that is, “the manifest” or “bright [land]”; Symmachus has τῆς ὀπτασίας, “of vision.” Others say “the land of divine worship” or “of adoration.” For the Hebrews say that Moria is the mountain [Col. 0189C] on which the Temple was later built. It is not without reason that Saint Jerome here admits that it is difficult to render the idiom of the Hebrew language into Latin. Certainly, the difficulty is demonstrated by the many different interpretations of the same word Moria. MART. —Hebrew: “into the land of Moria.” The holy Father agrees with Symmachus, who renders it τῆς ὀπτασίας. The Seventy also, who translated it “the lofty land,” agree in the same sense, deriving the word from the verb [meaning] “to appear” and “to be seen from afar” because of the elevation of the place, not from [the root] rum, as Martianaeus thinks.]

and go into the land of vision; and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall show you.” Accordingly, Abraham rose early, saddled his donkey, and took with him two young men and Isaac, his son. Having cut wood for the burnt offering, he went to the place that God had commanded him. On the third day, raising his eyes, he saw the place from afar. And he said to his young men: “Wait here with the donkey. I and the boy will hurry on as far as that place; after we have worshiped, we shall return to you.”

He also took the wood for the burnt offering and laid it upon Isaac, his son; but he himself carried fire and a sword in his hands. And as the two of them went on together, Isaac said to his father: “My father!” He answered: “What do you want, my son?” He said: “Behold, the fire and the wood; where is the victim for the burnt offering?” Abraham said: “God will provide for himself the victim of the burnt offering, my son.” So they went on together.

And they came to the place that God had shown him, where he built an altar and arranged the wood upon it. Then, having bound Isaac, his son, he placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood. He stretched out his hand and seized the sword, to sacrifice his son. And behold, the angel of the Lord called to him from heaven, saying: “Abraham! Abraham!” He answered: “Here I am.” And he said to him: “Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, nor do anything to him. Now I know that you fear God, and you have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake.”

Abraham raised his eyes and saw behind him a ram caught by its horns among—

[Note: [Col. 0189D] In Hebrew it has bassabech. In order to explain the force of the word sabech in his Hebrew Questions, Jerome used a longer circumlocution; but our compatriots of Saint-Sever, in the district of Gascony, express the significance of the word sabech and Jerome’s entire circumlocution in a single word. For they call a thicket or a thorny growth—dense branches interwoven with one another—pleix, as though one were to say “plaited” or “entangled.” Thus the Hebrew sabech is the same as the Vasconic pleix or pleigs. MART.]

thorns, and he took it and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son. And he called the name of that place, “The Lord sees.” [Col. 0189C] Hence, to this day it is said: “On the mountain the Lord—

[Note: [Col. 0190D] The present reading of the Masoretes is jorae, that is, “will be seen,” in place of jire, that is, “he will see,” as Jerome read it. MART. —The reading of the Hebrew text is the same in both places, although it is now marked differently by the points of the Masoretes. It may be rendered: “The Lord will be seen,” or “The Lord will provide.”]

will be seen.” The angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son [Note: [Col. 0190D] The Vulgate adds “for my sake,” in accordance with the Greek.], I will bless you and multiply your descendants like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore. Your descendants shall possess the gates of their enemies, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your descendant, because you obeyed my voice.”

Abraham returned to his young men, and they went together to Bersabee; and he dwelt there. After these events, Abraham was informed that Melcha also had borne sons to his brother Nahor: Hus, the firstborn, and Buz, his brother, and Camuel, the father of the Syrians, and Chased, and Azau, and also Pheldas and Jedlaph, and Bathuel, from whom Rebecca was born. Melcha bore these eight to Nahor, Abraham’s brother. His concubine, whose name was Roma, bore Tabee, Gaham, Tahas, and Maacha.

[T. XVII, C. XLIII, Cap. XXIII.] Sara lived one hundred and twenty-seven years. And she died in the city of Arbee, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Abraham came to mourn and weep for her. When he had risen from the funeral rites, he spoke to the sons of Heth, saying: “I am an outsider and a sojourner among you. Grant me the right to a burial-place among you, so that I may bury my dead.”

The sons of Heth answered him, saying: [Col. 0190B] “Hear us, my lord. You are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs, and no one will be able to prevent you from burying your dead in his tomb.”

Abraham rose and bowed down before the people of the land, namely, the sons of Heth. And he said to them: “If it pleases you that I bury my dead, hear me and intercede for me with Ephrom, son of Sohar [Vulgate: Seor], that he may give me the double cave which he has at the end of his field. Let him transfer it to me before you, for money worthy of it, as a burial possession.”

Now Ephron dwelt in the midst of the sons of Heth. Ephron [Note: [Col. 0190D] The Vulgate omits “the Hittite,” although it is found in the Hebrew, Greek, and other texts.] the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of all who entered the gate of his city, saying: “By no means, my lord, but [Vulgate adds: “you”] [Col. 0190C] rather listen to what I say. I give you the field and the cave that is in it. In the presence of the sons of my people, bury your dead.”

Abraham bowed before the people of the land. And he spoke to Ephron in the presence of the assembled people: “I ask you to hear me. I will give money for the field; accept it, and then I shall bury my dead there.” Ephron answered: “My lord, hear me. The land you request is worth four hundred silver shekels. That is the price between you and me—but what is that? Bury your dead.”

When Abraham heard this, he weighed out the money that Ephron had requested, in the hearing of the sons of Heth: four hundred shekels of silver [Col. 0191A] and [Vulgate omits: “and”] of approved public currency.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] Our manuscripts have Ephron. See the Hebrew Questions: Ephran, not Ephron as today, was read in Jerome’s time; he himself most clearly testifies to this in these words: “In Hebrew, as we have set it down here, his name is written Ephron the first time, Ephran the second time. After he had been overcome by the price and had sold the tomb for silver, although Abraham compelled him, the letter vau, which among them is read as o, was removed from his name; and instead of Ephron he was called Ephran.” MART.]

And the field formerly belonging to Ephron, in which was the double cave facing Mamre, both the field itself and the cave, together with all its trees within all its surrounding boundaries [Note: [Col. 0191D] The Vulgate adds “of it,” which is also known to the Hebrew text.]—was confirmed to Abraham as a possession, in the sight of the sons of Heth and of all who entered the gate of that city.

And thus Abraham buried Sara, his wife, in the double cave of the field [Note: [Col. 0191D] In the canon of the Hebrew truth we read: “In the cave of the double field, which faced Mamre.” This does not differ greatly from the Hebrew. MART. —The Palatine manuscript has “of the double.” The Urbinate [manuscript has] qui in place of qua.], which faced Mamre. This is Hebron in the land of Canaan. And the field and the cave that was in it were confirmed to Abraham as a burial possession by the sons of Heth.

[T. XVIII, B. XXVIII, C. XLIV, Cap. XXIV.] Abraham was now old and advanced in age, and the Lord had blessed him in all things. And he said to the senior servant of his household, who was in charge of all that he possessed: “Place your hand under my thigh, so that I may bind you by an oath through the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell, but that you will go to my land [Note: [Col. 0191D] The Vulgate omits “my,” although it is found in the Hebrew.] and to my kindred and take a wife for my son Isaac from there.”

The servant answered: “If the woman is unwilling to come with me to this land, must I then bring your son back to the place from which you departed?” Abraham said: “Beware lest you ever bring my son back there. The Lord God of heaven, who took me from my father’s house and from the land of my birth, who spoke to me and swore [Note: [Col. 0191D] Here too the Hebrew and the Vulgate add “to me.”], saying: ‘To your descendants I will give this land’—he himself will send his angel before you, and you will take a wife for my son from there. But if the woman is unwilling to follow you, you will not be bound by the oath; only, do not bring my son back there.”

So the servant placed his hand under the thigh of Abraham, his master, and swore to him concerning this matter. He took ten camels from the herds of his master and departed, carrying with him some of all his master’s goods, and he journeyed to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.

When he had made the camels kneel outside the town beside a well of water in the evening, at the time when women customarily go out to draw water, he said: “Lord, God of my master Abraham, meet me, I pray, today, and show mercy to my master Abraham. Behold, I stand beside the spring of water, and the daughters of the inhabitants of this city will go out to draw water. Let the young woman to whom I say, ‘Incline your jar that I may drink,’ and who answers, ‘Drink—and I will also give your camels water,’ be the one whom you have prepared for your servant Isaac. By this I shall know that you have shown mercy to my master.”

He had not yet finished speaking within himself, and behold, Rebecca was coming out, the daughter of Bathuel, son of Melcha, wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. She had a jar on her shoulder [Vulgate adds, in accordance with the Hebrew: “her shoulder”]. She was exceedingly beautiful, a most beautiful virgin, and unknown to man. She had gone down to the spring, filled her jar, and was returning.

The servant ran to meet her and said: “Give me a little water from your jar to drink.” She answered: “Drink, my lord.” And she quickly lowered the jar onto her arm and gave him a drink. When he had drunk, she added: “I will also draw water for your camels until they have all drunk.” Pouring out her jar into the troughs, she ran back to the well to draw water; and she drew enough for all the camels.

Meanwhile, the man silently watched her, wishing to know whether the Lord had prospered his journey or not. When the camels had finished drinking, the man brought out golden earrings—

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Instead of “weighing two shekels,” it seems that “two half-shekels” should be read. For what else do these words of Jerome himself in the Hebrew Questions teach us? “The man took,” he says, “a golden earring, its weight a didrachm.” BACI, which in this passage is written for “didrachm,” is half an ounce; SECEL, which is incorrectly called a shekel in Latin, has the weight of an ounce. Thus the two earrings did not weigh two ounces, that is, two shekels; rather, each had the weight of half an ounce, or half a shekel, according to Jerome. The Chaldean and Syriac read in the singular: “a golden earring weighing a shekel,” or “with the weight of one shekel.” This supports the reading of the Latins. MART. —Martianaeus seems right that “half-shekels” should be read instead of “shekels,” on the basis of Jerome’s statement in the Questions concerning this passage that the Hebrew has Bace, written for “didrachm,” which is half an ounce; whereas Secel, incorrectly called a shekel in Latin, has the weight of an ounce. We have shown elsewhere that the weight of the shekel was half an ounce, and this from Jerome’s own testimony, since he does not deny that the shekel weighs four drachmas, while eight drachmas make an ounce. In his Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 4, he says: “The shekel, that is, the stater, contains four drachmas, while eight drachmas make a Roman ounce.”]

weighing two shekels, and two bracelets weighing ten shekels. And he said to her: “Whose daughter are you? Tell me. Is there room in your father’s house for us to lodge?” She answered: “I am the daughter of Bathuel, son of Melcha, whom Nahor fathered.” And she added: “We have plenty of straw and hay, and ample room for lodging.”

The man bowed down and worshiped the Lord, saying: “Blessed is the Lord, God of my master Abraham, who has not withdrawn his mercy and truth from my master and has led me by a straight path to the house of my master’s brother.”

The young woman ran and reported in her mother’s household all that she had heard. Rebecca had a brother named Laban, who hurried out to the man at the spring. When he had seen the earrings and bracelets on his sister’s hands and heard all the words she reported—“This is what the man said to me”—he came to the man, who was standing beside the camels near the spring [Vulgate adds: “of water”], and said to him: “Come in, blessed of the Lord. Why are you standing outside? I have prepared the house and a place for the camels.”

And he brought him into the lodging. He unloaded the camels and gave straw and hay to the camels [Vulgate omits: “to the camels”], and water for washing his feet and the feet of the men who had come with him. Bread was set before him. But he said: “I will not eat until I have spoken my words.” Laban answered him: “Speak.”

He said: “I am Abraham’s servant. The Lord has blessed my master greatly, and he has become very wealthy. He has given him sheep and cattle, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and donkeys. And Sara, my master’s wife, bore a son to my master in his old age, and he gave him everything that he had.

“My master adjured me, saying: ‘You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell. Rather, you shall go to my father’s house and take a wife for my son from my kindred.’ I answered my master: ‘What if the woman is unwilling to come with me?’

“He said: ‘The Lord, in whose presence I walk, will send his angel with you and direct your way. You shall take a wife for my son from my kindred and from my father’s house. You will be innocent of my curse when you come to my relatives and they do not give her to you.’

“So today I came to the spring [Vulgate adds: ‘of water’] and said: ‘Lord, God of my master Abraham, if you have directed the way on which I now travel, behold, I stand beside the spring of water. And—

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Saint Jerome presses this passage against the Jews in the books of the Hebrew Questions, and shows that in Hebrew, instead of “virgin,” aalma is written. This also occurs in Isaiah: for where in our codices it reads, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear,” Aquila deceptively translated, “Behold, a young woman shall conceive and bear,” while the Hebrew has, “Behold, aalma shall conceive and bear.” It should further be noted from Jerome that the word aalma is never written except of a virgin. He therefore concludes his discussion of this passage as follows: “Let the Jews show anywhere in the Scriptures aalma used where it means merely a young woman and not a virgin, and we concede to them that what is said among us in Isaiah, ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear,’ signifies not a concealed virgin but an already married young woman.” MART.]

virgin who comes out to draw water and to whom I say, “Give me a little water to drink from your jar,” and who says to me, “You also drink, and I will draw water for your camels,” be the woman whom the Lord has prepared for my master’s son.’

“While I silently revolved these things within myself, Rebecca appeared, coming with a jar that she carried on her shoulder. She went down to the spring and drew water. And I said to her: ‘Give me a little to drink.’ She quickly lowered the jar from her shoulder and said to me: ‘You also drink, and I will give your camels water.’ I drank, and she watered the camels.

“I questioned her and said: ‘Whose daughter are you?’ She answered: ‘I am the daughter of Bathuel, son of Nahor, whom Melcha bore to him.’ So I hung the earrings on her to adorn her face and placed the bracelets on her hands. And I bowed down and worshiped the Lord, blessing the Lord, God of my master Abraham, who led me by a straight path, so that I might take the daughter of my master’s brother for his son.

“Therefore, if you will show mercy and truth toward my master, tell me; but if you prefer otherwise, tell me that also [Col. 0193D] [Vulgate adds: ‘to me’], so that I may go to the right or to the left.”

Laban and Bathuel answered [h.: “answered”]: “This word has come from the Lord; we cannot speak anything else to you contrary to his pleasure. Behold, Rebecca is before you. Take her and depart, and let her be the wife of your master’s son, as the Lord has spoken.”

When Abraham’s servant heard this, he bowed down [Vulgate adds: “falling down”] and worshiped the Lord on the ground. And bringing out vessels of silver and gold and clothing, he gave them to Rebecca as gifts; he also offered presents to her brothers and mother. They held a feast, and eating and drinking together, they remained there.

When he rose in the morning, the servant said: “Send me away, so that I may go to my master.” Her brothers and mother answered: “Let the girl remain with us at least ten days, and afterward she may depart.” He said: “Do not delay me, because the Lord has directed my way. Send me away, so that I may go to my master.” They said: “Let us call the girl and ask her will.”

When she had been called, they asked her: “Do you wish to go with this man?” She said: “I will go.” So they sent her away, together with her nurse, Abraham’s servant, and his companions, invoking prosperity upon their sister and saying: “Our sister, may you increase to thousands upon thousands, and may your descendants possess the gates of their enemies.”

Then Rebecca and her maidservants mounted camels and followed the man, who was returning hurriedly to his master. At that time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the Well of the Living One [Vulgate adds: “and”] Seeing; for he dwelt in the southern land and had gone out into the field to meditate as the day was declining. When he raised his eyes, he saw camels coming from afar.

Rebecca also, when she saw Isaac, dismounted from the camel and said to the servant: “Who is that man who is coming through the field to meet us?” He said to her: “He is my master.” Then she quickly took up her veil and covered herself.

The servant recounted to Isaac everything that he had done. He brought her into the tent of Sara, his mother, and took her as his wife. And he loved her so greatly that he eased the grief that had come upon him from the death of his mother.

[T. XVIII, B. XXIV, Cap. XXX.] Abraham took another wife, named Cetura, who bore him Zamran, Jecsan, Madan, Madian, Jesboc, and Sue. Jecsan also fathered Saba and Dadan. The sons of Dadan were Asurim, Latusim, and Laomim. From Madian came Epha, Epher [Vulgate: Opher], Enoch, Abida, and Eldaa. All these were the sons of Cetura.

Abraham gave everything that he possessed to Isaac [Col. 0194D]; but to the sons of his concubines he gave gifts, and while he was still living he separated them from Isaac, his son, toward the eastern region.

[C. XLV.] The days of Abraham’s life were one hundred and seventy-five years.

[Note: [Col. 0194D] Jerome, in Book of the Hebrew Questions, says that the words “And Abraham, failing, died” were wrongly added in the Septuagint interpreters, because it is not fitting for Abraham to fail and be diminished. But at that point he plays upon allegories and pursues anagogical meanings [Col. 0195D]; here, however, as the best interpreter, he faithfully expressed the words of Scripture. Therefore vajigva vaijamoth, which we now read in Hebrew, is interpreted: “And, failing, he died.” He likewise adds “of days” to the word “full,” although in the text only sabea, that is, “sated” or “full,” is read. Compare these statements with Jerome’s commentaries on chapter 1 of Zephaniah, where he approves the words that he says were wrongly added here. MART. —The Hebrew properly has: “He expired, and he died.” See the Hebrew Questions and our observations there.]

And, failing, he died in a good old age, advanced in years and full of days; and he was gathered to his people. Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the double cave situated in the field of Ephron, son of Sohar [Vulgate: Seor], the Hittite, opposite Mamre, which he had bought from the sons of Heth. There he was buried, and Sara, his wife. After his death, God blessed Isaac, his son, who dwelt beside the well named the Well of the Living One [Vulgate adds: “and”] Seeing.

[C. XLVI.] These are the generations of Ishmael, son of Abraham, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sara’s maidservant, bore to him. These are the names of his sons according to their names and generations: the firstborn of Ishmael was Nabajoth, then Cedar, Adbeel, Mabsam, Masma, Duma, Masa, Hadar, Thema, Itur [Vulgate: Jethur], Naphis, and Cedma. These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names according to their villages and settlements: twelve princes of their tribes.

[Note: [Col. 0195D] In the Vulgate edition: “And the years came to pass,” and so forth. The Hebrew has: “And these are the years,” and so forth.]

The years of Ishmael’s life were one hundred and thirty-seven. And, failing, he died and was gathered to his people. He dwelt from Evila as far as Sur, which faces Egypt as one enters Assyria.

[Note: [Col. 0195D] This passage is noteworthy in Jerome’s Hebrew Questions. There, reciting almost the whole of this chapter XLVI, he seems to follow the same divisions of the sacred text that we present from the manuscript books in this work [Col. 0196D], for he recognizes as the chapter’s final words those that are truly final here. He says: “But what we read at the end of this chapter according to the Septuagint—‘He dwelt opposite the faces of his brothers’—is more correctly rendered as we have set it down: ‘He fell before all his brothers,’ that is, he died in the hands of all his sons, and so forth.” But lest we deceive our candid reader, we frankly admit that Jerome indiscriminately calls “chapters” any verse-lines and clauses of Scripture that he himself inserts into his works and illuminates with commentaries; thus below, in the books of the Hebrew Questions, he calls the verse Genesis 36:24 a chapter. Consult that passage. MART.]

He died before all his brothers.

[C. XLVII.] These also are the generations of Isaac, son of Abraham: Abraham fathered Isaac. When Isaac was forty years old, he took Rebecca as his wife, daughter of Bathuel the Syrian from Mesopotamia, sister of Laban.

Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren. He heard him and granted conception to Rebecca. But the children struggled in her womb, and she said: “If this was to happen to me, why was it necessary to conceive?” And she went to consult the Lord. He answered her, saying: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger.”

The time for giving birth had now come, and behold, twins were found in her womb. The one who came out first was red and entirely hairy, like a pelt; and his name was called Esau. Immediately the other came out, holding his brother’s heel with his hand; therefore he called him Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when the children were born.

When they had grown up, Esau became a man skilled in hunting and a countryman, while Jacob was a simple man who dwelt in tents. Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his hunting, and Rebecca loved Jacob.

[Col. 0196A] [B. XXX.] Jacob cooked a stew. Esau came in from the field, weary, and said to him: “Give me some of this red stew, for I am exceedingly weary.” For this reason his name was called Edom.

Jacob said to him: “Sell me your birthright.” He answered: “Behold, I am dying; of what use is the birthright to me?” Jacob said: “Swear to me, then.”

[Note: [Col. 0196D] This differs somewhat from the Hebrew text, which has: “Swear to me this day”; and he swore to him, and sold his birthright to him.]

Esau swore, and sold his birthright. And so, after receiving bread and a dish of lentils, he ate and drank and departed, thinking little of the fact that he had sold his birthright.

[C. XLVIII, Cap. XXVI.] A famine arose in the land, after the barrenness that had occurred in the days of Abraham, and Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerara.

[T. XX, B. XXX.] The Lord appeared to him and said: “Do not go down into Egypt, but [Col. 0196B] remain in the land that I shall tell you. Sojourn in it, and I shall be with you and bless you; for I will give all these regions to you and to your descendants, fulfilling the oath that I swore to your father Abraham. And I will multiply your descendants like the stars of heaven, and I will give all these regions to your descendants. And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your descendant, because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my precepts and commandments and observed my ceremonies and laws.”

So Isaac remained in Geraris. When the men of that place questioned him about his wife, he answered: “She is my sister”; for he had been afraid to confess that she was joined to him in marriage, fearing that they might kill him on account of her beauty.

When a long time had passed and he was dwelling there, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looked out through a window and saw him sporting with Rebecca, his wife. He summoned him and said: “It is obvious that she is your wife. Why did you lie and say that she was your sister?” He answered: “I was afraid that I might die because of her.”

Abimelech said: “Why have you deceived us? Someone from the people might have lain with your wife, and you would have brought great sin upon us.” And he commanded all the people, saying: “Whoever touches this man’s wife shall surely be put to death.”

Isaac sowed in that land and found a hundredfold in that same year; and the Lord blessed him. The man grew rich, and he continued to prosper and increase until he became exceedingly great. He also possessed flocks of sheep and herds of cattle and a very large household.

Therefore the Philistines, envying him, stopped up all the wells that the servants of his father Abraham had dug at that time, filling them with earth. So much so that Abimelech himself said to Isaac: “Depart from us, for you have become far mightier than we are” [Vulgate: “than us”].

And he departed, intending to go to the torrent of Gerara and dwell there. He dug again the wells that the servants of his father Abraham had dug and that the Philistines had stopped up long ago after his death. And he called them by the same names by which his father had formerly called them.

They dug in the Torrent and found living water. But there too there was a quarrel between the shepherds of Gerara and the shepherds of Isaac, who said: “The water is ours.” For this reason he called the name of the well, from what had happened, “Calumny.”

They dug another well, and they quarreled over that one also; so he called it “Hostility”—

[Note: [Col. 0197D] In place of “hostilities,” Aquila and Symmachus translated τὴν ἀντικειμένην and ἐναντίωσιν, that is, “the opposing” and “the contrary”; in Hebrew it has Satana. [Col. 0198D] From this we understand that Satan means “the adversary” or “the contrary one.” MART. —Hebrew: Satana. See the Hebrew Questions.]

From there he moved on and dug another well, over which they did not contend. Therefore he called its name “Broad Place,” saying: “Now the Lord has enlarged us and made us grow in the land.”

[T. XXI.] From that place he went up to Bersabee, where the Lord appeared to him that same night, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, your father. Do not fear, for I am with you, and I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of my servant Abraham.”

So he built an altar there, invoked the name of the Lord, and stretched out his tent. He commanded his servants to dig a well.

When Abimelech, Ohuzath [Vulgate: Ohozath], his friend, and Phichol, the commander of the soldiers, came to that place from Geraris, Isaac spoke to them: “Why have you come to me, a man whom you hate and whom you expelled from among you?” They answered: [Col. 0197C] “We saw that the Lord was with you, and therefore we said: ‘Let there be an oath between us, and let us enter into a covenant, that you will do us no harm, just as we have touched none of your possessions and have done nothing that would injure you; rather, we sent you away in peace, increased by the Lord’s blessing.’”

So he prepared a feast for them. After eating and drinking, they rose in the morning and swore to one another; and Isaac sent them away in peace to their own place.

And behold, on that very day Isaac’s servants came and reported to him concerning the well that they had dug, saying: “We have found water.” Therefore he called it Abundance, and the name of the city was made Bersabee, to the present day.

Esau, being forty years old, took as wives Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon of the same place. Both of them offended the spirit of Isaac and Rebecca.

[T. XXII, B. XXXII, C. XLVIII, Chapter XXVII.] Isaac had grown old, and his eyes had become dim, so that he could not see. He called Esau, his elder son, and said to him: “My son!” He answered: “Here I am.” His father said to him: “You see that I have grown old and do not know the day of my death. Take your weapons, your quiver and bow, and go out. When you have caught something in the hunt, prepare for me a dish such as you know I like, and bring it to me to eat, so that my soul may bless you [Col. 0198A] before I die.”

When Rebecca heard this, and he had gone into the field to carry out his father’s command, she said to her son Jacob: “I heard your father speaking with Esau, your brother, and saying to him: ‘Bring me some of your game and prepare food for me to eat, and I shall bless you before the Lord before I die.’ Now therefore, my son, heed my advice. Go to the flock and bring me two of the best young goats, so that I may prepare from them food for your father, which he gladly eats. When you bring it to him and he has eaten, he will bless you before he dies.”

He answered her: “You know that Esau my brother is a hairy man, whereas I am smooth. If my father touches me and realizes this, I fear that he will think I intended to mock him, and I shall bring a curse upon myself instead of a blessing.” [Col. 0198B] His mother said to him: “Let that curse be upon me, my son; only listen to my voice, and go bring what I have said.”

He went and brought them to his mother. She prepared food just as she knew his father liked it. Then she dressed him in Esau’s very fine clothes, which she had with her in the house; she wrapped the skins of the young goats around his hands and covered the bare part of his neck. She gave him the dish, and handed him the loaves she had baked.

When he had brought these things in, he said: “My father!” He answered: “I hear. Who are you, my son?” Jacob said: “I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you commanded me. Rise, sit, and eat of my game, so that your soul may bless me.”

Isaac said to his son again: “How were you able to find it so quickly, my son?” He answered: “It was God’s will that what I wanted should meet me so quickly.” [Col. 0198C] Isaac said: “Come here, my son, so that I may touch you and test whether you are really my son Esau or not.”

He approached his father, and when he had touched him Isaac said: “The voice is indeed Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.” He did not recognize him, because the hairy hands had reproduced the appearance of his elder brother.

As he blessed him, he said: “Are you my son Esau?” He answered: “I am.” He said: “Bring me food from your game, my son, so that my soul may bless you.” When he had eaten the food set before him, he also offered him wine. After drinking it, Isaac said to him: “Come close to me and give me a kiss, my son.” He came close and kissed him.

As soon as he had sensed the fragrance of his clothing, he blessed him [Vulgate adds: “him”] and said: “Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field which the Lord has blessed. May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth, abundance of grain and wine. May peoples serve you, and tribes bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may the sons of your mother bow before you. Whoever curses you shall be cursed, and whoever blesses you shall be filled with blessings.”

Isaac had scarcely finished speaking when Jacob went outside, and Esau arrived. He brought cooked food from the hunt to his father, saying: “Rise, my father, and eat from the game of your son, so that your soul may bless me.”

Isaac said to him: “Who are you?” He answered: [Col. 0199A] “I am your firstborn son Esau.”

Isaac was seized with profound astonishment and, marveling beyond belief, said: “Who, then, was the one who just now brought me game, and I ate of everything before you came? I blessed him, and he shall be blessed.”

When Esau heard his father’s words, he roared with a great cry and, overcome, said: “Bless me too, my father.” He replied: “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing.”

He added: “He was rightly called Jacob [‘Supplanter’], for he has supplanted me twice: he took away my birthright before, and now he has stolen my blessing a second time.” Then he said again to his father: “Have you not reserved a blessing for me as well?”

Isaac answered: “I have made him your lord, and I have subjected all his brothers to his service. I have established him with grain and wine; and for you, my son, what more can I do now?”

Esau said: “Do you have only one blessing, father? Bless me too, I beg you.” As he wept with a great lamentation, Isaac was moved and said to him: “Your dwelling shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above. You shall live by the sword, and you shall serve your brother. But the time will come when you will shake off and loose his yoke from your neck.”

[B. XXXIII.] Esau therefore always hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him. He said in his heart: “The days of mourning for my father will come, [Note: [Col. 0199D] The older manuscript codices and the Septuagint read: “The days of mourning for my father will come, so that I may kill Jacob,” and so forth. MART. —The Palatine manuscript has *occidam* (“I shall kill”) instead of *et* (“and”).] and I shall kill Jacob, my brother.”

This was reported to Rebecca. She sent for Jacob, her son, and said to him: “Behold, your brother Esau is threatening to kill you. Now therefore, my son, listen to my voice: rise and flee to Laban, my brother, in Haran. You shall live with him for a few days, until your brother’s fury subsides and his anger ceases, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I shall send for you and bring you back here. Why should I be deprived of both sons on one day?”

Rebecca also said to Isaac: “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the descendants of this land, I do not want to live.”

[T. XXIII, C. L., Chapter XXVIII.] Isaac therefore called Jacob, blessed him, and commanded him, saying: “Do not take a wife from the family of Canaan. Rather go and depart to Mesopotamia of Syria, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father, and take for yourself from there a wife from the daughters of Laban, your maternal uncle.

“May almighty God bless you, make you grow, and multiply you, so that you may become a multitude of peoples. May he give you the blessing of Abraham, and to your offspring after you, so that you may possess the land of your sojourning, which he promised to your grandfather.”

When Isaac had sent him away, Jacob departed and came to Mesopotamia of Syria, to Laban, son of Bethuel the Syrian and brother of Rebecca, his mother.

When Esau saw that his father had blessed Jacob and sent him to Mesopotamia [Col. 0200A] of Syria so that he might take a wife there; and that, after blessing him, he had commanded him, saying, “Do not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan”; and that Jacob, obedient to his parents [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Vulgate adds *suis* (“his”); the Hebrew has “to his father and his mother.” It will be sufficient henceforth to note such minor matters in the margin of the book.], had gone to Syria; and, observing also that his father did not look favorably upon the daughters of Canaan, he went to Ishmael and took as a wife, in addition to those he already had, Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael, son of Abraham, and sister of Nebaioth.

[T. XXIV, C. LI.] Jacob therefore departed from Beersheba and traveled toward Haran. When he came to a certain place and wanted to rest there after sunset, he took one of the stones lying there, placed it beneath his head, and slept in that place.

In a dream he saw a ladder standing on the earth, whose top touched heaven, and angels of God ascending and descending by it. The Lord was leaning upon the ladder and said to him: “I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac. I shall give you and your offspring the land on which you are sleeping. Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth [Note: [Col. 0200D] In the Hebrew canon and in very many manuscript books it reads: “Your germ/offspring shall be like the dust of the earth.” MART. —The Palatine manuscript has *germen* (“germ, offspring”) instead of *semen* (“seed”).]. You shall spread toward the west and the east, the north and the south. All the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in you and in your offspring. I shall be your guardian wherever you go, and I shall bring you back to this land. I shall not leave you until I have fulfilled everything I have told you.”

When Jacob awoke from sleep, he said: “Truly, the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.” In fear he said: “How terrible this place is! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.”

Jacob rose early, took the stone he had placed beneath his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil over it. He called the name of the city Bethel, although it had previously been called Luz.

He also made a vow, saying: “If God is with me, and guards me on the way by which I travel, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and if I return safely to my father’s house, then the Lord shall be my God; and this stone, which I have set up as a pillar, shall be called the House of God. Of everything you give me I shall offer you tithes.”

[B. XXXIV, C. LII, Chapter XXIX.] Jacob therefore set out and came to the eastern land. He saw a well in the field, with three flocks of sheep lying beside it; for the flocks were watered from it, and its mouth was closed by a large stone.

It was customary that, when all the sheep had been gathered, they would roll away the stone, and, after watering the flocks, place it again over the mouth of the well.

He said to the shepherds: “Brothers, where are you from?” They answered: “From Haran.” He asked them: “Do you know Laban, son of Nahor?” They said: “We know him.” He said: “Is he well?” They answered: “He is well; and here is Rachel, his daughter, coming with the flock [Vulgate adds: ‘her flock’].”

Jacob said: “There is still much daylight left, and it is not yet time to bring the flocks back to the folds. Give the sheep water first, and then take them back to pasture.”

They answered: [Col. 0201A] “We cannot, until all the livestock have been gathered and we have removed the stone from the mouth of the well, so that we may water the flocks.”

While they were still speaking, Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she herself tended the flock. When Jacob saw her and recognized his cousin, as well as the sheep of Laban, his maternal uncle, he removed the stone that closed the well.

After watering the flock, he kissed her. Then, raising his voice, he wept and told her that he was her father’s brother and the son of Rebecca. She hurried and announced this to her father.

When he heard that Jacob, the son of his sister, had come, he ran to meet him, embraced him, and, falling upon his neck, kissed him. After hearing the reasons for his journey, he answered: “You are my bone and my flesh.” When a month had passed, he said to him: [Col. 0201B] “Because you are my brother, shall you serve me for nothing? Tell me what wages you wish to receive [Vulgate: ‘will receive’].”

He had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah [Hebrew: Leah]; the younger was called Rachel. Leah’s eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in face and pleasing in appearance.

Jacob loved her and said: “I will serve you for Rachel, your younger daughter, for seven years.” Laban answered: “It is better for me to give her to you than to another man. Stay with me.”

Jacob therefore served for Rachel for seven years, and they seemed to him like a few days because of the greatness of his love.

He said to Laban: “Give me my wife, for the appointed time has been completed, so that I may go in to her.” Laban gathered many crowds of friends for a feast and held the wedding. In the evening he brought his daughter Leah in to him, giving her a maidservant named Zilpah.

When Jacob had gone in to her according to custom, morning came and he saw Leah. He said to his father-in-law [Vulgate omits “his”]: “What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why have you deceived me?”

Laban answered: “It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the elder. Complete the week of this union; I shall also give you this one in return for the service you will render me for another seven years.”

Jacob accepted the arrangement. After the week had passed, he took Rachel as his wife; her father had given her Bilhah as a maidservant. At last, having obtained the marriage he desired, he preferred the love of the younger to that of the first, serving Laban for another seven years.

[T. XXV, C. LIII.] When the Lord saw that Leah was despised, he opened her womb, while her sister remained barren. She conceived and bore a son, and called his name Reuben, saying: “The Lord has seen my humiliation; now my husband will love me.”

Again she conceived and bore a son, and said: “Because the Lord heard that I was despised, he has given me this one also.” She called his name Simeon.

She conceived a third time and bore another son. She said: “Now my husband will also be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore she called his name Levi.

The fourth time she conceived [Col. 0202A] and bore a son, and said: “Now I shall confess to the Lord.” For this reason she called him Judah. Then she ceased bearing children.

[C. LIV, Chapter XXX.] When Rachel saw that she was barren, she envied her sister and said to her husband: “Give me children, or else I shall die.”

Jacob became angry with her and answered: “Am I in the place of God, who has deprived you of the fruit of your womb?”

She replied: “I have Bilhah as a maidservant. Go in to her, so that she may bear upon my knees, and I may have children through her.”

She gave him Bilhah in marriage. When the man had gone in to her, she conceived and bore a son. Rachel said: “God has judged for me, and he has heard my voice and given me a son.” Therefore she called his name Dan.

Bilhah conceived again and bore another son. Rachel said of him: “God has compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed.” She called him Naphtali. [Col. 0202B]

[C. LV.] When Leah realized that she had stopped bearing children, she gave her maidservant Zilpah to her husband. After she had conceived and borne a son, Leah said: “Fortunately!” Therefore she called his name Gad.

Zilpah also bore another son. Leah said: “This is for my happiness, for women will call me happy.” Therefore she called him Asher.

During the wheat harvest, Reuben went out into the field and found mandrakes, which he brought to his mother Leah. Rachel said: “Give me a share of your son’s mandrakes.”

She answered: “Is it not enough that you have taken my husband from me, without also taking my son’s mandrakes?”

Rachel said: “Let him sleep with you tonight in return for your son’s mandrakes.”

When Jacob came back from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said: “You will come in to me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes.”

That night he slept with her. God heard her prayers, and she conceived and bore a fifth son. She said: “God has given me my wages, because I gave my maidservant to my husband.” She called his name [Note: [Col. 0201D] The manuscript codices of our tradition consistently read *Isachar* with a single *s*. In the current Hebrew text the second *shin* seems superfluous, since it has no vowel associated with it. Nevertheless, we learn from Jerome that the name should be read with two *s*’s. He discussed the matter in the *Hebrew Questions*: “The Septuagint translators gave the etymology of this name as ‘there is a reward.’ It should not be thought, as many incorrectly read it by adding a pronoun, that it is written in this way because it means ‘there is a reward’; rather, the whole name is interpreted as ‘there is a reward.’ For *Is* means ‘is,’ and *sachar* means ‘reward.’” MART. —Our manuscripts consistently read *Isachar*. See the *Hebrew Questions*.] Issachar.

Leah conceived again and bore a sixth son. She said: “God has given me a good dowry; even now my husband will remain with me, because I have borne him six sons.” Therefore she called his name Zebulun.

Afterward she bore a daughter named Dinah.

[C. LVI.] God also remembered Rachel, heard her, and opened her womb. She conceived and bore a son, saying: “God has taken away my disgrace.” She called his name Joseph, saying: “May the Lord add another son to me.”

After Joseph was born, Jacob said to his father-in-law: “Release me, so that I may return to my homeland and my land. Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, so that I may go. You know the service with which I have served you.”

Laban said to him: “May I find favor in your sight. I have learned by experience that God has blessed me because of you. Set your wages, and I shall give them to you.”

He answered: “You know how I have served you, and how great your possession has become in my hands. You had little before I came [Vulgate adds: ‘to you’], but now you have become rich; the Lord has blessed you at my arrival. It is therefore right that I should at some time provide also for my own household.”

Laban said: “What shall I give you?”

He answered: “I want nothing. But if you will do what I ask, I shall again pasture and guard your flocks. Go through all your flocks and separate all the sheep that are variegated and fleeced with spots. Whatever is tawny, spotted, or variegated, among both sheep and goats, shall be my wages.

“My righteousness will answer for me tomorrow, when the time of our agreement comes before you: everything that is not variegated, spotted, or reddish [Vulgate: dark], among both sheep and goats, will accuse me of theft.” [Col. 0203B]

Laban said: “I am pleased with what you ask.”

That day he separated the he-goats, sheep, male goats, and rams that were variegated and spotted. But he handed over the entire single-colored flock—that is, those with white and black wool—to his sons. He placed a distance of three days’ journey between himself and his son-in-law [Hebrew: Jacob], who was pasturing the rest of his flocks.

[T. XXVI.] Jacob therefore took green rods of poplar, almond, and plane tree, and partly stripped the bark from them. When the bark had been removed, whiteness appeared in the places that had been stripped, while the parts left intact remained green; thus the color became variegated.

He placed them in the channels where the water flowed, so that when the flocks came to drink, they would have the rods before their eyes and conceive while looking at them. It happened that, during the heat of mating, the sheep looked at the rods and bore spotted and variegated offspring, mottled with different colors.

Jacob separated the flock and placed the rods [Vulgate adds: “in the channels”] before the eyes of the rams. Everything white and black belonged to Laban; the rest belonged to Jacob, with the flocks separated from one another.

Thus, whenever the sheep mated in the early season, Jacob placed the rods in the channels of water before the eyes of the rams and sheep, so that they would conceive while looking at them. But when the late mating took place, and conception was at its end, he did not place them there.

The late-born animals became Laban’s, and those born in the early season became Jacob’s. The man became exceedingly wealthy and possessed many flocks, maidservants and servants, camels and donkeys.

[Col. 0203D] [C. LVII, Chapter XXXI.] When he heard the words of Laban’s sons, who were saying: “Jacob has taken everything that belonged to our father, and from his property he has grown rich and become famous,” and when he also observed Laban’s face, which was not toward him as it had been yesterday and the day before, especially since the Lord had said to him: “Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I shall be with you,” he sent for Rachel and Leah to come into the field where he was pasturing the flocks.

He said to them: “I see that your father’s face is not toward me as it was yesterday and the day before; but the God of my father has been with me. You yourselves know that I have served your father with all my strength. Yet your father has deceived me and changed my wages ten times; nevertheless, God did not allow him to harm me.

“When he said, ‘Your wages will be variegated,’ all the sheep bore variegated offspring. But when, on the contrary, he said, ‘You shall take all the white ones as your wages,’ all the flocks bore white offspring. God has taken your father’s property and given it to me.

“When the time for the sheep to conceive arrived, I raised my eyes and saw in a dream males mounting the females—variegated, spotted, and of different colors. The angel of God said to me in the dream: ‘Jacob!’ And I answered: ‘Here I am.’

“He said: ‘Raise your eyes and see all the males mounting the females, variegated, spotted, and mottled. For I have seen everything Laban has done to you. I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the stone and made a vow to me. Now rise, leave this land, and return to the land of your birth.’”

Rachel and Leah answered: “Do we still have any share in the possessions and inheritance of our father’s house? Has he not regarded us as foreigners, sold us, and consumed the price paid for us? But God has taken our father’s wealth and given it to us and to our children. Therefore do everything God has commanded you.”

[B. XXXV.] Jacob therefore rose, placed his children and wives upon camels, and departed. He took all his property, his flocks, and everything he had acquired in Mesopotamia, and set out toward his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.

At that time Laban had gone to shear his sheep, [Note: [Col. 0203D] Where we now read “idols,” the Hebrew has *theraphim*, which Aquila translates as μορφώματα (*morphōmata*), that is, “figures” or “images.” Saint Jerome points this out so that we may know what *theraphim* means in the Book of Judges. MART.] and Rachel stole her father’s idols.

Jacob did not want to tell his father-in-law that he was fleeing. When he had departed, together with everything belonging to him, and was crossing the river on his way toward Mount Gilead [Note: [Col. 0204D] This mountain is called by anticipation by the name it was later to receive, as Jerome frequently explains. MART.], it was reported to Laban on the third day that Jacob had fled.

He took his brothers with him, pursued Jacob for seven days, and caught up with him on Mount Gilead. In a dream God said to him: “Beware of speaking harshly to Jacob.”

Jacob had already pitched his tent on the mountain. When Laban caught up with him and his brothers, he pitched his tent on the same Mount Gilead.

He said to Jacob: “Why did you act in this way, secretly carrying off my daughters like captives taken by the sword? Why did you want to flee without my knowledge and not tell me, so that I could have sent you away with joy, songs, tambourines, and lyres? You did not allow me to kiss my sons and daughters. You have acted foolishly.

“Now indeed my hand is able to repay you with evil; but the God of your father said to me yesterday: ‘Beware of speaking anything harsh against Jacob.’ Granted, you longed to go to your relatives, and you desired your father’s house; but why did you steal my gods?”

Jacob answered: “I departed without your knowledge because I was afraid you would violently take your daughters away from me. But as for your accusation of theft, with whomever you find your gods, let him be put to death in the presence of our brothers. Search whatever of yours you find with me, and take it away.” In saying this, he did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols.

Laban entered Jacob’s tent, Leah’s tent, and the tents of both maidservants, but found nothing. When he entered Rachel’s tent, she quickly hid the idols beneath the camel’s bedding and sat upon them. When he searched the entire tent and found nothing, she said: “Let my lord not be angry that I cannot rise before you, for what is customary among women has now happened to me.” Thus the searcher’s anxious inquiry was frustrated.

Jacob, swelling with anger, quarreled with him and said: “For what fault of mine, and for what sin of mine, have you become so inflamed against me and searched through all my belongings? What have you found among all the property of your house? Set it here before my brothers and your brothers, and let them judge between me and you.

“Have I been with you for twenty years for this reason? Your sheep and goats have not been barren; I have not eaten the rams of your flock. I did not show you animals seized by wild beasts; I myself made good every loss. Whatever was lost through theft, you demanded from me. By day and by night I was consumed by heat and frost, and sleep fled from my eyes.

“Thus I served you for twenty years in your house: fourteen for your daughters and six for your flocks. You also changed my wages ten times. If the God of my father Abraham and the Fear of Isaac had not been with me, perhaps by now you would have sent me away empty-handed. God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands, and yesterday he rebuked you.”

Laban answered him: “The daughters are mine, the sons are mine, your flocks are mine, and everything you see is mine. What can I do for my daughters and grandchildren? Come, therefore, and let us enter into a covenant, so that it may be a testimony between me and you.”

Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar. He said to his brothers: “Bring stones.” They gathered stones and made a mound, and they ate there upon the mound. Laban called it “The Mound of Witness,” and Jacob called it “The Heap of Testimony.” [Note: [Col. 0205D] These words were added by the translator and are not found in this form in the Hebrew books. Rather, it is written there that Laban called the heap of stones *igar sedutha*, while Jacob called it *Gilead*. Hence Saint Jerome says in the *Hebrew Questions*: “A heap is called *gal* in the Hebrew language, while *‘ad* means testimony. In the Syriac language a heap is called *igar*, and testimony *sedutha*. Jacob therefore called it ‘heap of testimony,’ that is, Gilead, in the Hebrew language; but Laban called the same thing, namely ‘heap of testimony,’ *igar sedutha* in the language of his people, for he was a Syrian and had exchanged the ancient language of his ancestors for the language of the province in which he lived.” MART. —The Latin translator added this final clause in accordance with the propriety of each language. See the *Hebrew Questions*.] Each named it according to the character of his own language.

Laban said: “This mound shall be a witness between me and you today.” Therefore its name was called Gilead, that is, “Mound of Witness.”

“May the Lord look upon and judge between us when we have departed from one another, if you afflict my daughters or take other wives in addition to them. No witness to our agreement is present except God, who looks upon it as he is present.”

He said again to Jacob: “Behold this mound and the stone that I have set up between me and you; they shall be witnesses. This mound, I say, and this stone shall be for testimony, whether I cross past it toward you or you pass beyond it toward me, intending evil.

“May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.”

Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac. After sacrificing victims on the mountain, he called his brothers to eat bread. When they had eaten, they remained there.

Laban rose during the night, kissed his sons and daughters, blessed them, and returned to his own place.

[T. XXVII, C. LVIII, Chapter XXXII.] Jacob also went on his way. Angels of God met him, and when he saw them he said: “These are the camps of God.” He called the name of that place Mahanaim, that is, “Camps.”

He also sent messengers ahead of him to Esau, his brother, in the land [Vulgate: “region”] of Seir, the region of Edom. He commanded them, saying: “Speak in this way to my lord Esau: ‘Thus says your brother Jacob: I have lived as a foreigner with Laban and have remained there until the present [Col. 0206B] day. I have oxen, donkeys, sheep, servants, and maidservants. Now I am sending a delegation to my lord, so that I may find favor in your sight.’”

The messengers returned to Jacob, saying: “We came to your brother Esau, and behold, he is hastening to meet you with four hundred men.”

Jacob was greatly afraid and, terrified, divided the people who were with him, as well as the flocks, sheep, oxen, and camels, into two companies. He said: “If Esau comes upon one company and strikes it, the other company that remains will be saved.”

Jacob said: “God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, Lord, who said to me, ‘Return to your land and to the place of your birth, and I shall do good to you’: I am too insignificant for all the mercies and faithfulness [Vulgate: “your mercies and faithfulness”] that you have shown your servant.

“With only my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies. Deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand [Vulgate omits: ‘from the hand’] of Esau, for I fear him greatly, lest he come and strike the mother together with her children.

“You said that you would do good to me and multiply my offspring like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted because of its multitude.”

After spending that night there, he selected from what he possessed gifts for his brother Esau: two hundred she-goats, twenty he-goats, two hundred ewes, and twenty rams; thirty nursing camels with their young; forty cows and ten bulls [Note: [Col. 0206D] All our manuscripts count twenty, as do the Syriac and Vulgate translators.]; twenty she-donkeys and ten of their young.

He sent the flocks separately by the hands of his servants and said to his servants: “Go ahead of me, and leave a space between one flock and the next.”

He commanded the first, saying: “If you meet my brother Esau and he asks you, ‘Whose are you?’ or ‘Where are you going?’ or ‘Whose are these things following you?’ you shall answer: ‘Your servant Jacob has sent them as gifts to my lord Esau; he himself is also coming behind us.’”

He gave the same instructions to the second, the third, and all those who followed the flocks, saying: “Speak to Esau in these same words when you meet him. And add: ‘Your servant Jacob himself is following behind us.’”

For he said: “I shall appease him with the gifts that go before me; afterward I shall see him, and perhaps he will be reconciled to me.”

The gifts went ahead of him, while he himself remained in the camp that night.

When he rose early, he took his two wives and their two maidservants, together with his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok. After bringing across everything that belonged to him, he remained alone. And behold, a man wrestled with him until morning.

When he saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it immediately withered. He said to him: “Release me, for dawn has now risen.”

He answered: “I will not release you unless you bless me.” He said: “What is your name?” He answered: “Jacob.”

He said: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for if you have been strong against God, how much more will you prevail against men!”

Jacob asked him: “Tell me, by what name are you called?” He answered: “Why do you ask my name?” And he blessed him there.

Jacob called the name of that place Phanuel, saying: “I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved.”

The sun rose for him immediately after he had passed Phanuel, but he was limping on one foot. For this reason the children of Israel do not eat the sinew that withered in Jacob’s thigh to the present day, because he touched the sinew of his thigh and it became numb.

[Col. 0207C] [Chapter XXXIII.] Jacob raised his eyes and saw Esau coming, with four hundred men. He divided the children among Leah and Rachel and both maidservants. He placed each maidservant and her children first; Leah and her children in the second place; and Rachel and Joseph last.

He himself went ahead of them and bowed to the ground seven times, until his brother approached.

Esau ran to meet his brother, embraced him, clasped his neck, kissed him, and wept. When he raised his eyes and saw the women and their little ones, he said: “What do these people mean to you? Do they belong to you?”

He answered: “They are the little ones whom God has given to your servant.”

The maidservants and their children approached and bowed. Leah also came with her children [Vulgate: “boys”], and after they likewise had bowed, Rachel and Joseph, the last, bowed.

Esau said: “What are these companies that I met?” He answered: “So that I might find favor before my lord.”

Esau said: “I have plenty, my brother; let what is yours remain yours.”

Jacob said: “No, I beg you. But if I have found favor in your eyes, accept this little gift from my hands. For I have seen your face as though I had seen the face of God. Be gracious to me and accept the blessing that I have brought you and that God has given me by granting me everything.”

Only after his brother urged him did he accept it, and he said: “Let us travel together, and I shall accompany you.”

Jacob said: “You know, my lord, that I have tender children, and sheep and cattle with young. If I make them labor too much in walking, all the flocks will die in a single day. Let my lord go ahead of his servant, and I shall follow gradually in his footsteps, as I see that my little ones are able, until I come to my lord in Seir.”

Esau answered: “I ask you to leave with you at least some of the people who are with me, as companions on your journey.”

Jacob said: “There is no need. I need only this: to find favor in the sight [Note: [Col. 0207D] The Vulgate reads “in the sight of you, my lord,” which is farther from the Hebrew.] of my lord.”

Esau returned that day by the way he had come to Seir. [Col. 0208B]

[C. LIX.] Jacob came to Succoth, where he built a house and set up tents. He called the name of that place Succoth, that is, “tabernacles.”

[B. XXXVI.] He crossed over to [Note: [Col. 0207D] An error arises here if one believes that this is Salem, namely Jerusalem, which was also previously called Salem and in which Melchizedek reigned. Consult the book of Saint Jerome’s *Hebrew Questions*. MART. [Col. 0208D] —The Urbinas manuscript omits the word *Salem*. Its copyist may have held the view that this was not the proper name of a city; for the Hebrew teachers understand the passage as saying of Jacob that he came to Shechem *salem*, that is, unharmed and safe. The syntax of the Hebrew text, however, seems to oppose this.] Salem, the city of the Shechemites, which is in the land of Canaan, after returning from Mesopotamia of Syria, and he dwelt near the town.

He bought the portion of the field in which he had pitched his tents from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for one hundred lambs. There he erected an altar and invoked upon it the Most Strong God of Israel.

[T. XXVIII, Chapter XXXIV.] Now Dinah, the daughter of Leah, went out to see the women of that region. When Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of that land, saw her, he fell in love with her, seized her, and slept with her, violating the virgin by force. His soul was attached to her, and he sought to soothe her distress with affectionate words. Going to his father Hamor, he said, “Take this girl for me as a wife.”

When Jacob heard this—his sons being absent and occupied with pasturing the flocks—he kept silent until they returned. Hamor, Shechem’s father, went out to speak with Jacob; and behold, his sons were coming in from the field. When they heard what had happened, they were exceedingly angry, because Shechem had done a disgraceful thing in Israel and, having violated Jacob’s daughter, had committed an unlawful act.

Hamor therefore spoke to them and said: “Shechem my son is attached to your daughter’s soul; give her to him as a wife. Let us intermarry: give your daughters to us and take our daughters. Live with us; the land is in your power. Trade in it, conduct business, and possess it.”

Shechem also said to her father and brothers: “May I find favor in your sight; whatever you prescribe, I will give. Increase the bride-price, demand gifts, and I will gladly give whatever you ask; only give me this girl as a wife.”

Jacob’s sons answered Shechem and his father deceitfully, burning with anger over their sister’s violation: “We cannot do what you ask, nor give our sister to an uncircumcised man, for this is unlawful and detestable among us. But we can make a covenant with you on this condition: if you wish to become like us, every male among you must be circumcised. Then we will give and receive one another’s daughters, live with you, and become one people. But if you will not be circumcised, we will take our daughter and depart.”

Their proposal pleased Hamor and his son Shechem. The young man did not delay, but immediately fulfilled what was demanded, for he loved the girl greatly, and he was himself renowned throughout his father’s household. They entered the gate of the city and spoke to the people:

“These men are peaceful, and they wish to live with us. Let them trade in the land and cultivate it, for it is spacious and broad and needs cultivators. We will take their daughters as wives and give them our daughters. There is only one obstacle delaying so great a benefit: we must circumcise our males, imitating the custom of their nation. Then their property, their livestock, and everything they possess will be ours.

[Note: “This and the livestock,” which also occurs in the Hebrew, is unknown to the Vulgate translator.]

Let us agree to this one condition; living together, we shall become one people.”

All agreed, and every male was circumcised. On the third day, when the pain of the wounds is most severe, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, took their swords and entered the city boldly. They killed every male, and together they killed Hamor and his son Shechem, taking their sister Dinah from Shechem’s house.

[Note: Here also the Hebrew has “his son,” but this is missing from the Vulgate editions.]

After they had gone out, Jacob’s other sons attacked the slain and ravaged the city in vengeance for the violation.

[Variant: Here it does not have “Jacob’s other sons,” but “the sons of Jacob came upon the slain.”]

[Col. 0209C] They carried off their sheep, cattle, donkeys, and everything that was in the houses and fields. They also led away their little ones and wives as captives.

After they had boldly carried this out, Jacob said to Simeon and Levi: “You have troubled me and made me hateful to the Canaanites and Perizzites who inhabit this land. We are few; they will gather together, strike me, and I will be destroyed, together with my household.”

They replied: “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?”

[C. LX, Chapter XXXV.] Meanwhile God spoke to Jacob: “Rise, go up to Bethel, and dwell there; make an altar to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.”

Jacob, having summoned his entire household, said: “Cast away the foreign gods that are among you, purify yourselves, and change your garments. Rise, and let us go up to Bethel and make there an altar to the God who heard me in the day of my distress and was my companion on my journey.”

So they all gave him the foreign gods they possessed and the earrings that were in their ears. He buried them beneath the terebinth that stands behind the city of Shechem. When they had departed, the terror of God came upon all the surrounding cities, and they did not dare pursue those who were leaving.

[C. LXI, B. XXXVII.] Thus Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan and is also called Bethel, he and all the people with him. He built an altar there and called the name of the place “House of God,” for there God had appeared to him when he fled from his brother.
