At that same time Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried at the foot of Bethel beneath an oak. The name of the place was called “Oak of Weeping.”

God appeared again to Jacob after he had returned from Mesopotamia of Syria, and blessed him, saying: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.” He called him Israel and said to him:

“I am God Almighty. Grow and multiply. Nations and peoples of nations shall come from you, and kings shall go forth from your loins. The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you and to your offspring after you.”

And he withdrew from him.

[C. LXII.] Jacob erected a stone monument at the place where God had spoken with him, pouring libations over it and pouring oil upon it. He called the name of that place Bethel.

[T. XXIX.] Departing from there in springtime, he came to the land that leads to Ephrath. While Rachel was giving birth there, she began to be in danger because of the difficulty of the delivery. The midwife said to her: “Do not be afraid, for you will have this son also.”

As her soul was departing because of the pain and death was already near, she called the name of her son Benoni, that is, “son of my pain.” But his father called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.”

Rachel therefore died and was buried on the road leading to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Jacob erected a monument over her grave. This is Rachel’s grave monument, to the present day.

Departing from there, he pitched his tent beyond the Tower of the Flock. While he was dwelling in that region, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine; and Israel learned of it.

Jacob had twelve sons. The sons of Leah were: Reuben, the firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin. The sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, were Dan and Naphtali. The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, were Gad and Asher. These were Jacob’s sons, who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria.

He also came to his father Isaac at Mamre, the city of Arba—that is, Hebron—in which Abraham and Isaac had lived as resident foreigners. Isaac’s days amounted to one hundred and eighty years. Consumed by old age, he died; he was gathered to his people, old and full of days. His sons Esau and Jacob buried him.

[Col. 0210D] [T. XXX, C. LXIII, Chapter XXXVI.] These are the generations of Esau, who is Edom. Esau took wives from the daughters of Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite; Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon the Hivite; and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.

Adah bore Eliphaz; Basemath bore Reuel; and Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam [Vulgate: “Jelom”], and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

Esau took his wives, sons, daughters, all the persons of his household, his possessions, livestock, and everything he could have in the land of Canaan, and went to another region, withdrawing from his brother Jacob.

[Note: Neither the Hebrew text nor the Vulgate translator has “another”; but the Chaldean Targum adds it more explicitly.]

For they were exceedingly wealthy, and they could not dwell together; nor could the land of their sojourning support them because of the multitude of their flocks. Esau dwelt on Mount Seir; he is Edom.

These are the generations of Esau, the father of Edom, on Mount Seir, and these are the names of his sons: Eliphaz, son of Adah, Esau’s wife; and Reuel, son of Basemath, his wife.

The sons of Eliphaz were: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz. Now Timna was the concubine of Eliphaz, son of Esau; she bore him Amalek. These are the sons of Adah, Esau’s wife.

The sons of Reuel were: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah [Vulgate: “Samma and Meza”]. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife.

These were also the sons of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon, Esau’s wife: Jeush, Jalam, and Korah, whom she bore to him.

[C. LXIV.] These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn, were: Chief Teman, Chief Omar, Chief Zepho, Chief Kenaz, Chief Korah, Chief Gatam, and Chief Amalek. These are the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom, and these are the sons of Adah.

[Note: The Hebrew likewise has “chiefs”; the Vulgate edition gives “sons.”]

These also were the sons of Reuel, son of Esau: Chief Nahath, Chief Zerah, Chief Shammah, and Chief Mizzah. These were the chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom; they were the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife.

These were the sons of Oholibamah, Esau’s wife: Chief Jeush, Chief Jalam, and Chief Korah. These were the chiefs of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, Esau’s wife.

These are the sons of Esau, and these are their chiefs; he is Edom.

These are the sons of Seir the Horite, inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom.

The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; Lotan had a sister named Timna. These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.

These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found hot springs [Hebrew: “mules in the wilderness”] while he was pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon. He had a son named Dishon and a daughter named Oholibamah.

These are the sons of Dishon: Hamdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. These also are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. Dishan had sons named Uz and Aran.

These are the chiefs of the Horites: Chief Lotan, Chief Shobal, Chief Zibeon, Chief Anah, Chief Dishon, Chief Ezer, and Chief Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites who ruled in the land of Seir.

[C. LXV.] The kings who ruled in the land of Edom before the Israelites had a king were these: Bela, son of Beor; the name of his city was Dinhabah.

Bela died, and Jobab, son of Zerah from Bozrah, reigned in his place. When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.

When he too had died, Hadad, son of Bedad, reigned in his place. He defeated Midian in the region of Moab, and the name of his city was Avith.

When Hadad died, Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place. When he too had died, Saul of Rehoboth by the river reigned in his place.

When he also had died, Baal-hanan, son of Achbor, succeeded to the kingdom. When he too had died, Hadad [Vulgate: “Adar”] reigned in his place. The name of his city was Pau, and his wife was called Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Me-zahab.

These, then, are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their clans, places, and names: Chief Timna, Chief Alvah, Chief Jetheth, Chief Oholibamah, Chief Elah, Chief Pinon, Chief Kenaz, Chief Teman, Chief Mibzar, Chief Magdiel, and Chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, dwelling in the land of their dominion; he is Esau, the father of the Edomites.

[Cap. XXXVII.] Jacob dwelt in the land of Canaan, in which his father had lived as a resident foreigner. These are his generations.

[Note: The Hebrew has “Jacob”; the Vulgate omits it.]

[T. XXXI, B. XXXVIII, C. LXVI.] When Joseph was sixteen years old—

[Note: In Hebrew Joseph is said to have been seventeen years old. The Greeks and all the eastern versions follow this reading. Nevertheless Jerome correctly expressed the sense, because he understood sixteen completed years. MART.

Another note: Perhaps the final numeral sign fell out of the Latin copy, or, as often happens, escaped the copyist’s eye, who wrote XVI instead of XVII. For everything else is so certainly in agreement with the Hebrew and all the versions that seventeen must here also be read instead of sixteen. Therefore Martianay is not to be heeded when he thinks that Jerome meant years already completed and omitted Joseph’s seventeenth year, which he had not yet completed. Nothing could be less true: Jerome neither had permission to alter the text at will, nor did he ever claim such authority for himself.]

Joseph was tending the flock with his brothers while still a boy, and he was with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives. He reported his brothers’ gravest offense to his father.

Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he had begotten him in his old age, and he made him a richly ornamented robe.

[Note: For “variegated” or “many-colored,” Aquila translated ἀστραγάλειον (*astragaleion*), that is, “ankle-length robe.” Symmachus translated it as “sleeved robe”—either because it descended to the ankles and was distinguished by the marvelous variety of the craftsman’s work, or because it had sleeves; for the ancients generally used sleeveless garments. MART.]

When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his sons, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.

It happened also that he reported a dream to his brothers, which became the cause and seed of greater hatred. He said to them:

“Listen to my dream that I dreamed. I thought we were binding sheaves in the field, and that my sheaf rose up, as it were, and stood upright, while your sheaves surrounded it and bowed down to my sheaf.”

His brothers answered him: “Will you perhaps be our king? Or shall we be subjected to your rule?”

Thus this became the cause of the dreams and words that supplied fuel for envy and hatred.

He had another dream, which he related to his brothers, saying: “I saw in a dream the sun and moon and eleven stars bowing down to me.”

When he had related it to his father and brothers, his father rebuked him and said: “What does this dream that you have seen mean? Shall I, your mother, and your brothers bow down to you upon the earth?”

His brothers therefore envied him, but his father silently considered the matter.

When his brothers were staying at Shechem while tending their father’s flocks, Israel said to him: “Your brothers are pasturing the sheep at Shechem. Come; I will send you to them.”

When he replied, “Here I am,” he said to him [Vulgate adds “to him”]: “Go and see whether all is well with your brothers and the livestock, and report to me what is happening.”

Sent from the valley of Hebron, he came to Shechem. He found a man wandering in the field and asked him what he was seeking. The man replied: “I am looking for my brothers. Tell me where they are pasturing their flocks.”

The man said to him: “They have departed from this place, but I heard them saying, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’”

[C. LXVII.] Joseph therefore went after his brothers and found them at Dothan. When they saw him from a distance, before he came near them, they planned to kill him and spoke to one another:

“Behold, the dreamer is coming. Come, let us kill him and throw him into an old cistern. We shall say, ‘A most savage beast has devoured him’; and then it will become clear what his dreams profit him.”

When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue him from their hands and said:

“Let us not kill his life, nor shed blood. Instead, throw him into this cistern, which is in the wilderness, and keep your hands innocent.”

[Note: Thus the canon of Hebrew truth and another biblical manuscript. In the Hebrew and Samaritan texts stands *naccennu*, “let us strike him” or “let us kill him,” a reading followed also by the Septuagint and the other interpreters; but they differ in what follows, for they read in the third person *al-thisphechu*, “do not shed.” The two manuscripts just mentioned have “let us shed,” evidently, I think, through a scribal error. MART. The Vulgate translator has “do not kill.” One Urbinas manuscript consistently has “nor let us shed.”]

He said this, intending to rescue him from their hands and return him to his father.

As soon as he came to his brothers, they stripped him of his ankle-length, richly ornamented robe and cast him into a cistern that had no water.

They sat down to eat bread. Then they saw Ishmaelite travelers coming from Gilead, with their camels carrying spices, resin, and stacte to Egypt.

[Col. 0213C] Judah therefore said to his brothers: “What benefit will there be if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? It is better that he be sold to the Ishmaelites, and that our hands not be defiled; for he is our brother and our flesh.”

His brothers agreed with his words. As the Midianite merchants passed by, they drew him out of the cistern and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. They brought him to Egypt.

When Reuben returned to the cistern and did not find the boy, he tore his garments, went back to his brothers, and said: “The boy is gone! And I—where shall I go?”

They took Joseph’s robe, dipped it in the blood of a kid they had killed, and sent someone to carry it to their father, saying: “We found this; see whether it is your son’s robe or not.”

When the father recognized it, he said: “It is my son’s robe. A most savage beast has eaten him; a wild animal has devoured Joseph.”

He tore his garments, put on sackcloth, and mourned his son for a long time. When all his children gathered to ease their father’s grief, he refused consolation and said:

“I shall go down mourning to my son into the underworld.”

While he persisted in weeping, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and captain of the guard.

[T. XXXII, C. LXVIII, Chapter XXXVIII.] At that time Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to an Adullamite man named Hirah. There he saw the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua. He took her as his wife and went in to her.

She conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er. Conceiving again, she bore a son and named him Onan. She bore a third son and called him Shelah; after his birth, she ceased bearing.

Judah gave Tamar as a wife to his firstborn son Er. Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord killed him.

Judah therefore said to his son Onan: “Go in to your brother’s wife and unite with her, so that you may raise up offspring for your brother.”

But Onan knew that the children would not be his. When he went in to his brother’s wife, he spilled his seed on the ground, so that children would not be born in his brother’s name. Therefore the Lord struck him down, because he had done a detestable thing.

For this reason Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar: “Remain a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up.” For he feared that he too might die like his brothers.

She went away and lived in her father’s house.

After many days had passed, the daughter of Shua, Judah’s wife, died. When Judah had received consolation after mourning, he went up to the shearers of his sheep, he and Hiras, the Adullamite shepherd of the flock, to Timnah.

[Note: For “shepherd,” or “keeper of sheep,” “friend” is read (). But the word is ambiguous, because both nouns are written with the same letters. “Friend” is read *rce*, while “shepherd” is *roe*. Jerome therefore read the Hebrew word differently: *roe* here, but *ree* in the *Hebrew Questions*. We discussed this varying manner of interpretation, which is not unusual in Jerome, in our prolegomena. MART.]

[Note: The Vulgate translator consistently renders the place-name as Thamnas. The Hebrew form is not legible in the supplied text.]

Tamar was told that her father-in-law was going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. She removed the garments of her widowhood, put on a veil, changed her clothing, and sat at the crossroads on the road leading to Timnah, because Shelah had grown up and she had not been given to him as a husband.

When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face so that she would not be recognized. He went in to her and said: “Allow me to lie with you,” for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law.

She replied: “What will you give me so that you may enjoy my intercourse?” He said: “I will send you a kid from the flock.”

Again she said: “I will permit what you wish, if you give me a pledge until you send what you promise.”

Judah said: “What pledge shall I give you?”

She answered: “Your ring, your bracelet, and your staff that you hold in your hand.”

So she conceived from that one act of intercourse and went away. She put off the clothing she had assumed and put on her widow’s garments.

Judah sent the kid by his Adullamite shepherd to recover the pledge he had given the woman. When he did not find her, he asked the men of that place: “Where is the woman who sat at the crossroads?”

When they all replied, “There has been no prostitute in this place,” he returned to Judah and said to him: “I did not find her. The men of that place also told me that no prostitute had ever sat there.”

Judah said: “Let her keep what she has; surely she cannot accuse us of lying. I sent the kid I promised, but you did not find her.”

After about three months, Judah was informed: “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has committed fornication, and behold, her womb is swelling.”

Judah said: “Bring her out, so that she may be burned.”

As she was being led out to punishment, she sent word to her father-in-law, saying: “I conceived by the man to whom these things belong. Recognize whose ring, bracelet, and staff these are.”

When he recognized the objects, he said: “She is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah.”

[Note: The Hebrew has, “She has been declared righteous by me,” not because she was righteous, but because, in comparison with him, she had done the lesser evil—not wandering into shamefulness, but seeking children. MART.

The Urbinas manuscript adds the name Tamar here.]

He did not know her again thereafter.

When the time of her delivery came, twins appeared in her womb. During the actual birth, one extended his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it, saying: “This one will come out first.”

But when he drew back his hand, the other came out. The woman said: “Why has the wall been breached because of you?” For this reason she called his name Perez.

Afterward his brother came out, the one around whose hand was the scarlet thread, and she called him Zerah.

[T. XXXIII, B. XXXIX, C. LXIX, Chapter XXXIX.] Joseph was brought down to Egypt. Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and captain of the army—

[Vulgate adds “his”]—an Egyptian man, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites by whom he had been brought there.

The Lord was with him, and he was a man who prospered in all things. He lived in the house of his master, who knew very well that the Lord was with him and that the Lord directed everything he did through his hand.

Joseph found favor in the sight of his master and served him. His master appointed him over everything, and he governed the house entrusted to him and all that had been placed under his authority.

The Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house because of Joseph and multiplied all his possessions, both in the house and in the fields. He knew nothing about anything except the bread he ate.

Joseph was handsome in face and attractive in appearance.

After many days, his mistress cast her eyes upon Joseph and said: “Sleep with me.”

But he refused the wicked act and said to her: “Behold, my master, with everything entrusted to me, does not know what he has in his house. There is nothing that is not in my power, or that he has not entrusted to me, except you, because you are his wife. How, then, could I do this great evil and sin against God?”

With words of this kind she importuned the young man day after day, but he refused the adultery.

It happened one day that Joseph entered the house to perform some task without anyone else present. She seized the edge of his garment and said: “Sleep with me.”

He left his cloak in her hand, fled, and went outside.

When the woman saw the garment in her hands and realized that she had been scorned, she called the men of her household and said to them: “Look, he has brought us a Hebrew man to mock us. He came in to me to lie with me, but when I cried out and he heard my voice, he left the cloak that I was holding and fled outside.”

As evidence of her charge, she showed the cloak she had retained to her husband when he returned home and said: “The Hebrew slave whom you brought to us came in to me to mock me. When he heard me cry out, he left the cloak [Vulgate adds “that I was holding”] and fled outside.”

[Note: Other manuscript codices and the standard Hebrew text read: “When he saw me crying out.” The sense is the same in either reading. MART. Our manuscripts, and those consulted by Martianay, have *vidisset* (“saw”) in place of *audisset* (“heard”).]

When the master heard this, and was excessively credulous toward his wife’s words, he became very angry. He handed Joseph over to prison, where the king’s prisoners were kept, and there he was confined.

But the Lord was with Joseph. He showed him mercy and gave him favor in the sight of the prison warden, who placed in Joseph’s hand all the prisoners held in custody. Everything that was done was under his authority. He did not concern himself with anything entrusted to Joseph, for the Lord was with him and directed all his works.

[T. XXXIV, C. LXX, Chapter XL.] After these events, it happened that two eunuchs offended their master, the king of Egypt: the royal cupbearer and the baker.

[Note: Saint Jerome notes that in Hebrew the word written here for “eunuch” is *māšeq*, the same word that appears above in the name of Abraham’s servant. In the Hebrew of today, however, the word differs somewhat: above, in chapter 15:2, the servant of Abraham is written *mesheq*; here it is *masheq*. Jerome, following common usage, calls the name *maseq* “cupbearer.” MART.]

Pharaoh was angry with them—for one was in charge of the cupbearers and the other of the bakers—and he put them in the prison of the captain of the guard, where Joseph was confined.

The prison warden handed them over to Joseph, who served them. Some time passed while they remained in custody.

Both men dreamed a dream on the same night, each dream having an interpretation appropriate to him. When Joseph came to them in the morning and saw that they were sad, he asked them: “Why is your face sadder today than usual?”

They answered: “We have had a dream, and there is no one to interpret it for us.”

Joseph said to them: “Does interpretation not belong to God? Tell me what you have seen.”

The chief cupbearer first related his dream: “I saw before me a vine with three branches. It gradually put forth buds, then flowers, and afterward its clusters ripened. Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand. I took the grapes, pressed them into the cup that I held, and gave the cup to Pharaoh.”

Joseph answered: “This is the interpretation of the dream. The three branches are three more days. After them Pharaoh will remember your service and restore you to your former position. You will place the cup in his hand according to your office, as you used to do before.

“Only remember me when it goes well with you, and show me mercy by mentioning me to Pharaoh, so that he may bring me out of this prison. For I was stolen from the land of the Hebrews, and here, though innocent, I was put into a pit.”

When the chief of the bakers saw that he had interpreted the dream wisely, he said: “I too saw a dream: I had three baskets of flour upon my head. In the uppermost basket I carried all the foods made by the baker’s craft, and birds were eating from it.”

Joseph answered: “This is the interpretation of the dream. The three baskets are three more days. After them Pharaoh will take your head from you and hang you on a cross, and birds will tear the flesh from your body.”

On the third day, Pharaoh’s birthday, he prepared a great feast for his servants. During the meal he remembered the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.

He restored one to his position, so that he might hand the cup to the king; the other he hanged on a cross [Vulgate: “gallows”], so that the truth of the interpreter might be proved.

Yet, as prosperity returned, the chief cupbearer forgot his interpreter.

[C. LXXI, Chapter XLI.] After two years Pharaoh had a dream. He thought he was standing beside the river, from which seven cows ascended, exceedingly beautiful and fat, and they were grazing in marshy places. Seven other cows also emerged from the river, ugly and wasted by extreme leanness [Col. 0217C], and they were grazing on the very bank of the stream in green places. They devoured the former cows, whose appearance and bodily condition had been remarkable. Pharaoh awoke, slept again, and saw another dream: Seven ears of grain were sprouting on one stalk, full and beautiful; and seven others, thin ears of grain, blighted by rust, were springing up and devouring all the beauty of the former ones.

When Pharaoh awoke after his sleep and morning came, terrified by fear, he sent for [Vulg. adds: all] the diviners of Egypt and all the wise men. After summoning them, he told them the dream, but there was no one who could interpret it. Then at last the chief cupbearer, remembering, said: “I confess my sin. The king, angry with his servants, ordered me and the chief baker to be put into the prison [Col. 0217D] of the captain of the guard, where one night both of us had a dream, foreshadowing future events. There was there a Hebrew boy, a servant of that same captain of the guard. When we told him our dreams, we heard from him whatever the outcome afterward proved to be true: for I was restored to my office, while he was hanged on a cross.”

[B. XL.] Immediately, at the king’s command, Joseph was brought out of prison; they shaved him, changed his clothing, and brought him before Pharaoh. He said to him: “I have seen dreams, and there is no one who can explain them; but I have heard that you interpret them very wisely [Vulg. most wisely].”

Joseph replied [Col. 0218A]: “Without me, God will answer [Note: [Col. 0217D] In Hebrew, *Salom* is found; therefore Jerome, in the Questions already mentioned a hundred times, interprets it literally as follows: ‘Without me, God will answer peace to Pharaoh.’ Finally, he says, Symmachus, in his customary manner, translated it more clearly: ‘Not I, but God will answer peace to Pharaoh.’ MART. —He prefers that in the Hebrew Questions it be rendered ‘peace,’ in accordance with the Hebrew.] with what is favorable to Pharaoh.”

So Pharaoh told Joseph what he had seen: “I thought I was standing on the bank of the river, and seven cows came up out of the stream, exceedingly beautiful and well-fleshed, grazing on the green growth of the marsh. And behold, seven other cows followed them, so deformed and emaciated that I had never seen their like in all the land of Egypt. After they had devoured and consumed the former cows, they showed no sign of being satisfied, but remained as lean and filthy as before.

“After I awoke, I was again overcome by sleep and saw a dream: seven ears of grain were sprouting on one stalk, full and exceedingly beautiful. Seven other ears, thin and blasted by scorching, were springing up from the stalk; they devoured the beauty of the former ears. I told the interpreters of dreams [Vulg. the dream], [Col. 0218B] but there is no one who can explain it.”

Joseph answered: “The king’s dream is one. God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do. The seven beautiful cows and the seven full ears are seven years of abundance; they have the same meaning in the dream. The seven thin and emaciated cows that came up after them, and the seven thin ears, blasted by the burning wind, are seven coming years of famine. They will be fulfilled in this order:

“Behold, seven years of great fertility are coming throughout the whole land of Egypt. After them will come seven other years of such sterility that all the former abundance will be forgotten. For famine will consume the whole land, and the greatness of the scarcity will destroy the greatness of the abundance. As for the fact that you saw a second dream concerning the same matter [Col. 0218C], it is an indication of certainty, because the word of God will come to pass and will be fulfilled more quickly.

“Now therefore let the king provide a wise and industrious man and place him over the land of Egypt. Let him appoint overseers over each [Vulg. all] region and gather a fifth of the produce during the seven years of fertility [Vulg. sterility] that are now about to come, storing it in the granaries. Let all the grain be gathered and kept under Pharaoh’s authority in the cities. Thus provision will be made for the coming seven years of famine, which will oppress Egypt, and the land will not be consumed by scarcity.”

The advice pleased Pharaoh and all his ministers. He said to them: “Can we find such a man, one in whom the spirit of God is?”

Then Pharaoh said to Joseph: “Since God has shown you all that you have said, can I find anyone wiser than you or your equal? You shall be over my house, and all the people shall obey the command of your mouth. Only in the throne of the kingdom will I be above you.”

Pharaoh said again to Joseph: “Behold, I have appointed you over the whole land of Egypt.” He took the ring from his hand and placed it on Joseph’s hand; he clothed him in a linen robe and put a gold chain around his neck. He made him mount his second chariot, with a herald proclaiming that all should kneel before him, and [Col. 0219A] that he had been appointed over the whole land of Egypt.

The king also said to Joseph: “I am Pharaoh. Without your command no one shall move hand or foot in the whole land of Egypt.”

[Note: [Col. 0219D] Jerome translated this passage paraphrastically: for in Hebrew only the following is read: ‘And Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Saphaneth Phane.’ But, for easier understanding of the meaning of Scripture, we point out that the additions made by Jerome are quite useful. Thus, in the book of Hebrew Traditions, concerning the name given to Joseph, he himself writes: ‘Although in Hebrew this name means “discoverer of hidden things,” nevertheless, since it is given by an Egyptian, it ought to be understood according to that language. Therefore, in the Egyptian language, *Saphaneth phane* is interpreted as “Savior of the world,” or, as the Seventy wished to translate it, [Col. 0220D] ψομσθὸμ φανὴχ, “Savior of the world,” because he freed the whole world from the impending destruction of famine.’ MART. —It differs somewhat from the Hebrew. For the text does not say, ‘and he translated his name,’ much less does it say ‘in the Egyptian language’; it says only, ‘And Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Zaphnat Pantach.’ Nor was Jerome unaware that these words have an appropriate meaning in Hebrew, namely, ‘the revealer of hidden things’; nevertheless, he preferred to think them of Egyptian origin, which other authors do not accept. See the Hebrew Questions.]

He translated his name and called him, in the Egyptian language, “Savior of the world.” He gave him Aseneth, daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis, as a wife.

[T. XXXV.] Joseph therefore went out into the land of Egypt (he was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh the king) and traveled through all the regions of Egypt. The seven years of fertility came, and the grain was gathered into sheaves and stored in the granaries of Egypt. All the abundance of produce was also stored in each city. There was such a great quantity of wheat that it equaled the sand of the sea, and its abundance exceeded measure [Col. 0219B].

Two sons were born to Joseph before the famine came; Aseneth, daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis, bore them to him. He called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, saying: “God has made me forget all my labors and my father’s house.” He also called the second Ephraim, saying: “God has made me grow in the land of my poverty.”

When the seven years of abundance that had occurred in Egypt had ended, the seven years of scarcity that Joseph had foretold began to come. Famine prevailed throughout the whole world, and there was no bread anywhere in the land of Egypt. When it was suffering hunger, the people cried out to Pharaoh, asking for food. He answered them: “Go to Joseph, and whatever he tells you, do.”

The famine grew daily throughout the whole land [Col. 0219C]. Joseph opened all the granaries and sold grain to the Egyptians, for famine had also oppressed them. All the provinces came into Egypt to buy food and lessen the hardship of scarcity.

[B. XLI, C. LXXII, Chapter XLII.] Jacob heard that food was being sold in Egypt and said to his sons: “Why are you negligent? I have heard that wheat is being sold in Egypt. Go down and buy what we need, so that we may live and not be consumed by scarcity.”

So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain in Egypt (Benjamin was kept at home by Jacob, who had said to his brothers: “Lest he suffer some misfortune on the journey”). They entered the land of Egypt with the others who were going to buy. There was famine in the land of Canaan.

Joseph, [Col. 0219D] the ruler [Vulg. adds: was in the land] of Egypt, was the one at whose command grain was sold to the people. When his brothers had bowed down before him and he had recognized them, he spoke harshly to them as though they were strangers, asking them: [Col. 0220A] “Where have you come from?”

They answered: “From the land of Canaan, to buy provisions for food.”

Although Joseph recognized his brothers, he was not recognized by them. Remembering the dreams that he had once seen, he said to them: “You are spies. You have come to observe the weaker parts of the land.”

They said: “It is not so, my lord, but your servants have come to buy food. We are all sons of one man. We have come peaceably, and your servants are plotting no evil.”

He replied: “It is otherwise. You have come to examine the unfortified parts of this land.”

But they said [Vulg. But]: “We, your servants, are twelve brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is with our father, and the other is no more.”

“This is what I said,” he replied. “You are spies. Now I shall test you. By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not leave here until your youngest brother comes. Send one of you to bring him; but you shall remain in bonds until it is proved whether what you have said is true or false. Otherwise, by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies.”

He therefore handed them over to custody for three days. On the third day, after bringing them out of prison, he said: “Do what I have said, and you shall live, for I fear God. If you are peaceable men, let one of your brothers remain bound in prison; but you may go, carry the grain you have bought to your houses, and bring your youngest brother to me, so that I may test your words and you may not die.”

They did as he had said, and said to one another: “We deserve to suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother. When we saw the anguish of his soul [Col. 0220C], as he begged us, we did not listen; therefore this tribulation has come upon us.”

One of them, Reuben, said: “Did I not tell you: ‘Do not sin against the boy’? But you did not listen to me. Behold, his blood is being required.”

They did not know that Joseph understood, because he spoke to them through an interpreter. He turned away for a while and wept; then he returned and spoke to them. He took Simeon and bound him in their presence, and ordered his attendants to fill their sacks with wheat and to put each man’s money back into his sack, along with provisions for the journey. They did so.

They carried the grain on asses [Vulg. adds: their own] and departed. When one of them opened his sack to give fodder to his animal at the lodging place, he saw the money at the mouth of the sack and said to his brothers [Col. 0220D]: “My money [Vulg. omits: my] has been returned; behold, it is here in the sack.”

They were astonished and troubled, and said to one another: “What is this that God has done to us?”

They came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan [Col. 0221A] and told him everything that had happened to them, saying: “The lord of the land spoke harshly to us and thought that we were spies of the province. We answered him: ‘We are peaceable men and are plotting no ambushes. We are twelve brothers, born of one father. One is no more; the youngest is with our father in the land of Canaan.’

“He said to us: ‘This is how I shall test whether you are peaceable men: Leave one of your brothers with me, take provisions necessary for your households, and go. Bring your youngest brother to me, so that I may know that you are not spies and that you may recover the one who is being held in bonds. After that, you shall have permission to buy whatever you wish.’

“When they poured out their grain, each of them found the money tied at the mouth of his sack. Then all were terrified, and their father Jacob said: ‘You have deprived me of my children: Joseph is no more, Simeon is being held in bonds, and you will take Benjamin away. All these evils have fallen upon me.’

“Reuben answered him: ‘Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you. Place him in my hand, and I will restore him to you.’

“But he said: ‘My son shall not go down with you. His brother is dead, and he alone remains. If some misfortune befalls him in the land to which you are going, you will bring my gray hairs down to the underworld in sorrow.’”

[B. LXII, C. LXXIII, Chapter XLIII.] Meanwhile famine pressed hard upon the whole land. When they had consumed the food they had brought from Egypt, Jacob said to his sons: “Return and buy a little food [Vulg. adds: for us].”

Judah replied: “That man solemnly warned us, saying: ‘You shall not see my face unless you bring your youngest brother with you.’ If, therefore, you are willing to send him with us, we shall go together and buy what you need; but if you are unwilling, we shall not go. For the man, as we have often said, warned us: ‘You shall not see my face without your youngest brother.’”

Israel said to them: “Why did you bring this misery upon me by telling him that you had another brother?”

They answered: “The man questioned us carefully about our family: whether our father was alive and whether we had a brother. We answered him according to what he had asked. Could we have known that he would say: ‘Bring your brother with you’?” [Col. 0221D]

Judah also said to his father: “Send the boy with me, so that we may depart and live, lest both we and our little ones die. I take responsibility for the boy; require him from my hand. Unless I bring him back and set him before you, I shall be guilty of sin against you forever. If this delay had not intervened, we would already have come a second time.”

Then Israel, their father, said to them: “If it must be so, do what you wish. Take some of the best [Vulg. adds: fruits] of the land in your vessels and carry gifts to the man: a little resin, honey, storax, *stacte*, terebinth, and almonds. Also take double the money with you, and carry back the money that you found in your sacks, lest it happened by mistake. Take your brother as well and go to the man.

“May almighty God [Vulg. adds: my God] make him favorable to you and send back with you your other brother whom he is holding, and Benjamin. As for me, I shall be like one bereaved, without children.”

So the men took the gifts, the double amount of money, and Benjamin. They went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph. When he saw them, and Benjamin with them, he ordered the steward of his house: “Bring the men into the house, slaughter victims, and prepare a feast, because they are to eat with me at noon [Vulg. adds: today].”

He did what he had been ordered and brought the men into the house. There, terrified, they said to one another: “Because of the money that we previously carried back in our sacks, we have been brought in, so that he may bring an accusation against us, violently subject us to slavery, and enslave both us and our asses.”

Therefore, approaching the steward at the very doors, they said: “We beg you, lord, to hear us [Vulg. adds: us]. We came down previously to buy food. After buying it, when we reached the lodging place, we opened our sacks and found the money at the mouths of the sacks. We have now brought it back in the same weight. We have also brought other silver, so that we may buy what is necessary [Vulg. adds: for us]. We do not know who put the first money in our bags.”

He answered: “Peace be with you; do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father gave you treasure in your sacks. As for the money that you gave me, I have it as tested and accounted for.”

He brought Simeon out to them [Col. 0222C]. After introducing them into the house, he brought water, and they washed their feet. He also gave fodder to their asses. They prepared their gifts while they waited for Joseph to enter at noon, for they had heard that they were to eat bread there.

Joseph entered his house, and they offered him gifts, holding them in their hands [Vulg. adds: their own]; then they bowed prostrate to the ground. He greeted them graciously and asked them [Vulg. adds: them], saying: “Is your aged father well, of whom you spoke to me? Is he still alive?”

They answered: “Your servant our father is well; he is still alive.” Then they bowed and worshiped him.

Joseph lifted his eyes and saw Benjamin, his uterine brother, and said: “Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me?” Then he said again: “May God have mercy on you, my son.” He hurried away, because his inward parts had been stirred over his brother, and tears were breaking forth. He entered a room and wept.

After washing his face again, he came out, controlled himself, and said: “Set out the bread.”

When it had been served, Joseph sat separately, his brothers separately, and the Egyptians, who were likewise eating, separately—for it is unlawful for Egyptians to eat with Hebrews, and they regard such a meal as profane. They sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his age. They marveled greatly at the portions they had received from him, and the larger portion came to Benjamin, exceeding the others fivefold. [Col. 0223A]

[Note: [Col. 0223D] It is an idiom of the Hebrew language to use “drunkenness” for satiety, as in Psalm LXIV, 11: “With its showers the earth will be made drunk as it sprouts”—clearly meaning the earth irrigated by rain. MART.]

They drank and became drunk with him.

[Chapter XLIV.] Joseph commanded the steward of his house, saying: “Fill their sacks with as much grain as they can carry, and put each man’s money at the top of his sack. Put my silver cup, and the price paid for the wheat, in the mouth of the youngest man’s sack.”

[Note: [Col. 0223D] Instead of “sack,” the Hebrew has *peronem* (‘a wallet’) or *follem* (‘a bag’). [Col. 0224D] Thus Saint Jerome. MART.]

And it was done. When morning came, they were sent away with their asses. They had already gone out of the city and proceeded a short distance when Joseph, calling the steward of his house, said: “Rise, pursue the men, and when you have caught them say: ‘Why have you repaid good with evil? The cup that you stole—is it not the very one from which my lord drinks and by which he practices divination? You have done a very wicked thing.’”

He did as he had been ordered. When he had caught them, he spoke to them one by one. They answered [Col. 0223B]: “Why does our lord speak in this way, as though your servants had committed so great a crime? The money that we found at the tops of our sacks we brought back to you from the land of Canaan. How, then, could it be possible that we should have stolen gold or silver from our lord’s house? With whichever of your servants it is found, let him die, and we shall be slaves of our lord.”

He said to them: “Let it be according to your sentence: the one with whom it is found shall be my slave, but you shall be innocent.”

So they quickly lowered their sacks to the ground and opened them one by one. Searching them, beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest, he found the cup in Benjamin’s sack. They tore their garments, loaded their asses again, and returned to the town.

Judah entered first with his brothers [Col. 0223C] to Joseph—for he had not yet left the place—and they all fell together before him to the ground. He said to them: “Why did you wish to act in this way? Do you not know that there is no one like me in the art of divination?”

Judah said: “What shall we answer my lord? What shall we say, or what justification can we rightly offer? God has found the iniquity of your servants. Behold, we are all my lord’s slaves, both we and the one with whom the cup was found.”

Joseph replied: “Far be it from me to act in this way. The one who stole the cup shall be my slave; but you may go free to your father.”

Judah then came closer and said boldly: “I beg you, my lord, let your servant speak a word in your ears, and do not be angry with your servant, for you are my lord after Pharaoh. You previously questioned your servants: ‘Do you have a father or a brother?’ We answered my lord: ‘We have an aged father and a young boy, born in his old age. His uterine brother is dead, and he alone remains to his mother; his father loves him tenderly.’

“You said to your servants: ‘Bring him to me, and I will set my eyes upon him.’ We told my lord: ‘The boy cannot leave his father. If he leaves him, his father will die.’ And you said to your servants: ‘Unless your youngest brother comes with you, you shall not see my face again.’

“So when we went up to your servant our father, we told him everything that my lord had said. Our father said: ‘Return and buy us a little wheat.’ We replied to him: ‘We cannot go. If our youngest brother goes down with us, we shall depart together; otherwise, if he is absent, we do not dare to see the man’s face.’

“To this he answered: ‘You know that my wife bore me two sons. One went out, and you said: “A beast devoured him”; and he has not appeared to this day. If you take this one also from me, and some misfortune befalls him on the journey, you will bring my gray hairs down to the underworld in sorrow.’

“Therefore, if I go to your servant our father and the boy is absent (since his life depends upon this boy’s life), when he sees that he is not with us, he will die; and your servants will bring his gray hairs down to the underworld in sorrow. I, personally, am your servant, for I have taken responsibility for this boy and pledged myself, saying: ‘Unless I bring him back, I shall be guilty of sin against my father forever.’

“Therefore I shall remain your servant instead of the boy, as a servant of my lord, while the boy may go up with his brothers. For I cannot return to my father without the boy, lest I stand as a witness to the calamity that will overwhelm my father.”

[Chapter XLV.] Joseph could no longer restrain himself before the many people standing nearby. Therefore he ordered everyone to leave, so that no outsider might be present at the mutual recognition. He raised his voice with weeping; the Egyptians heard him, and so did all Pharaoh’s household.

He said to his brothers [Col. 0224C]: “I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?”

His brothers could not answer, terrified by extreme fear. He said to them kindly: “Come closer to me.” When they had come near, he said: “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. Do not be afraid, and do not let it seem grievous to you that you sold me into these regions; for God sent me ahead of you for your preservation. It is now two years since the famine began in the land, and five more years remain in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest.

“God sent me ahead so that you might be preserved upon the earth and might have food for survival. I was sent here not by your plan but by God’s will. He has made me like a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his house, and ruler throughout the whole land of Egypt.

“Hurry and go up to my father, and say to him: ‘Your son Joseph commands this: God has made me lord of the whole land of Egypt. Come down to me, lest you die, and dwell [Vulg. you shall dwell] in the land [Note: [Col. 0224D] Saint Jerome reads it in the same way in the Hebrew Questions. MART. —The Palatine manuscript, together with the Vulgate books, has “Gessen.” See the Hebrew Questions.] of Gesen. You shall be near me—you and your sons and your sons’ sons, your sheep, your herds, and everything that you possess. There I shall feed you, for five years of famine still remain, lest you perish, you and your household and everything that you possess.

“Behold, your eyes and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see that it is my mouth speaking to you. Tell my father of all my glory and everything that you have seen in Egypt. Hurry and bring him to me.’”

Then he fell upon the neck of his brother Benjamin and wept; Benjamin also wept upon his neck. He kissed all his brothers and wept over each of them. After this they dared to speak with him.

The news was heard and spread throughout the king’s court in public report: “Joseph’s brothers have come.” Pharaoh and all his household rejoiced. He said to Joseph that he should command his brothers, saying: “Load your beasts, go to the land of Canaan, take from there your father and your family, and come to me. I shall give you all the good things of Egypt, so that you may eat the marrow of the land.

“Also command them to take wagons from the land of Egypt for transporting their little ones and their wives. And say: ‘Take your father and come as quickly as possible. Do not leave [h. lose] anything of your household goods, because all the wealth of Egypt shall be yours.’”

[B. XLIII.] The sons of Israel did as they had been commanded. Joseph gave them wagons according to Pharaoh’s order, and provisions for the journey. He ordered two garments to be brought for each of them; but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five finest garments. He sent the same amount of money and clothing to his father, adding ten asses to carry all the riches of Egypt, and the same number of she-asses carrying wheat and bread for the journey.

He sent his brothers away, and as they departed he said to them: “Do not quarrel on the way.”

They went up from Egypt and came into the land of Canaan to their father Jacob. They announced to him, saying: “Your son Joseph is alive, and he rules over the whole land of Egypt.”

When he heard this [Vulg. adds: Jacob], as though awakening from a deep sleep, he nevertheless did not believe them. But they recounted to him the whole sequence of events. When he saw the wagons and everything that Joseph had sent, his spirit revived, and he said: “It is enough for me if my son Joseph is still alive. I shall go and see him before I die.”

[T. XXXVI, C. LXXIV, Chapter XLVI.] Israel departed with everything he had and came to the Well of the Oath. After sacrificing victims there to the God of his father Isaac, he heard him calling him in a night vision and saying: “Jacob, Jacob.” He answered: “Behold, here I am.”

God said to him: “I am the mighty God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down into Egypt, for there I shall make you into a great nation. I shall go down there with you, and I shall bring you back when you return. Joseph also will place his hand upon your eyes.”

[C. LXXV.] Jacob arose from the Well of the Oath. His sons carried him, together with their little ones and wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to transport the old man and all that they had possessed [In h.: and they took their flocks with them] in the land of Canaan. He came into Egypt with all his offspring: his sons and grandsons, his daughters, and his entire family together.

These are the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt: he himself with his children; the firstborn, [Col. 0226A] Reuben. The sons of Reuben: Enoch, Phallu, Esron, and Charmi. The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad [Vulg. Ahad], Jachin, Soher, and Saul, the son of the Canaanite woman. The sons of Levi: Gerson, Caath, and Merari. The sons of Judah: Her, Onan, Sela, Phares, and Zara; but Her and Onan died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Phares were Esron and Amul.

The sons of Issachar: Thola, Phua, Job, and Simron. The sons of Zabulon: Sared, Elon, and Jahelel. These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore in Mesopotamia of Syria, together with her daughter Dina: all the persons of her sons and daughters, thirty-three.

The sons of Gad: Sephion, Haggi, Suni, Esebon, Heri, Arodi, and Areli. The sons of Aser: Jimna, Jisua, Jisui, and Beria, together with their sister Sara. The sons of Beria: Heber and Melchiel. These are the sons of Zelpha, whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah; and she bore these to Jacob, sixteen persons.

The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife: Joseph and Benjamin. Joseph’s sons were born in the land of Egypt, whom Aseneth, daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis, bore to him: Manasseh and Ephraim.

The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Asbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Ros, Mophim, Ophim, and Ared. These are the sons of Rachel, whom she bore to Jacob: all the persons, fourteen.

The sons of Dan: Husim. The sons of Naphtali: Jaseel, Guni, Jeser, and Sellem. These are the sons of Bala, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel; and she bore these to Jacob: all the persons, seven.

All the persons who entered Egypt with Jacob and who came forth from his loins, apart from the wives of his sons, were sixty-six. The sons of Joseph who were born to him in the land of Egypt were two persons [Col. 0226C]. All the persons of Jacob’s household who entered Egypt were seventy.

[C. LXXVI.] Judah was sent ahead of him to Joseph, so that he might announce his arrival and Joseph might meet him in Gesen. When he reached the place, Joseph harnessed his chariot and went up to meet his father there. When he saw him, he fell upon his neck and wept in his embrace.

The father said to Joseph: “Now I shall die happy, because I have seen your face and shall leave you alive.”

[C. LXXVII.] And [Vulg. leaves: and] he spoke to his brothers and to all his father’s household: “I shall go up and announce it to Pharaoh, and I shall say to him: ‘My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me. They are shepherds, caring for the tending of flocks. They have brought with them their sheep, herds, and everything they were able to possess.

“When he summons you and says: ‘What is your occupation?’ you shall answer: ‘We, your servants, have been shepherds from our childhood until now, both we and our fathers.’

“You shall say this so that you may dwell in the land of Gesen, because all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.”

### [Chapter XLVII]

Joseph therefore entered and reported to Pharaoh, saying: “My father and my brothers, their sheep and cattle, and everything they possess, have come from the land of Canaan; and behold, they are staying in the land of Goshen.” He also selected five of the last of his brothers and set them before the king. The king asked them, “What is your occupation?” They answered: “We are shepherds of sheep, your servants, both we and our fathers. We have come to sojourn in your land, because there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants, since the famine has grown severe in the land of Canaan. Therefore we ask that you order us to be your servants in the land of Goshen.”

### [C. LXXVIII]

The king therefore said to Joseph: “Your father and your brothers have come to you. The land of Egypt is before you; settle them in the best place, and give them the land of Goshen. And if you know that there are capable men among them, appoint them as overseers of my livestock.”

### [B. XLIV]

After this Joseph brought his father before the king and set him in his presence. He blessed him, and when the king asked him, “How many are the days of the years of your life?” he answered:

“The days of the years of my sojourn [Note: In ancient manuscripts and in the Hebrew text as established, one reads, ‘The days of the sojourn of my life’; but *of my life* appears to have been borrowed from the Seventy Interpreters, who read, ‘The days of the years of my life.’ MART. [Col. 0228D]—Our manuscripts also add *of my life*. But the Hebrew, and Aquila as well, has something more than *the days of my sojourn*, namely, *the days of the years of my sojourn*.] are one hundred and thirty years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not reached the days of the lives of my fathers during the days of their sojourning.”

And after blessing the king, he went out.

Joseph gave his father and his brothers a possession in Egypt, in the best soil of the land [Vulgate: *place*], at Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded. He also provided food for them and for his entire father’s household, supplying rations to each person; for bread was lacking throughout the whole world, and famine had oppressed the land, especially Egypt and Canaan.

From them he collected all the money in payment for the grain and brought it into the king’s treasury. When the money of the buyers had run out [Note: Some books put *times* before *ran out*.], all Egypt came to Joseph, saying: “Give us bread. Why should we die in your presence, since our money has failed?”

He answered them: “Bring your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for them, if you have no money.”

When they had brought them, he gave them food in exchange for horses, sheep, cattle, and asses; and he sustained them that year in exchange for their livestock.

They came also in the second year and said to him: “We will not conceal from our lord [Vulgate: *we will not conceal the gift from our lord*] that, since our money has failed, our livestock has also failed. Nor is it hidden from you that, apart from our bodies and our land, we have nothing. Why then should we die while you look on—both we and our land shall belong to you? Buy us into royal slavery, and provide seed, lest the cultivator perish and the land be reduced to a wasteland.”

Joseph therefore bought all the land of Egypt, since each person was selling his possessions because of the severity of the famine. He subjected it to Pharaoh, together with all its peoples, from the farthest boundaries of Egypt to its opposite extremities, except the land of the priests, which had been given to them by the king. They were also supplied with fixed rations from the public storehouses, and for that reason they were not compelled to sell their possessions.

Joseph therefore said to the peoples: “Behold, as you see, both you and your land belong to Pharaoh. Take seed and sow your fields, so that you may have crops. You shall give the king a fifth part; I leave the remaining four parts to you for seed and for food for your households and children.”

They answered: “Our salvation is in your hand. Let only our lord look favorably upon us, and we shall gladly serve the king.”

From that time to the present day, throughout the whole land of Egypt, a fifth part has been paid to the kings, and it became established as a law, except for the priestly land, which was free from this condition.

### [C. LXXIX]

Israel therefore lived in Egypt, that is, in the land of Goshen, and possessed it. He increased and multiplied exceedingly. He lived there seventeen years, and all the days of his life amounted to one hundred and forty-seven years.

When he saw that the day of his death was approaching [Vulgate adds: *his*], he called his son Joseph and said to him: “If I have found favor in your sight, place your hand beneath my thigh and show me mercy and faithfulness: do not bury me in Egypt, but let me sleep with my fathers; take me away from this land and bury me in the tomb of my ancestors.”

Joseph answered him: “I will do what you have commanded.”

He said: “Swear to me, then.”

When Joseph had sworn, Israel worshiped God, turning toward the head of the bed.

### [T. XXVII, C. LXXX, Chapter XLVIII]

After these things had taken place, Joseph was told that his father was ill. He took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and went to him.

Someone told the old man: “Behold, your son Joseph is coming to you.”

Strengthened, he sat up in bed. When Joseph had entered, he said:

“God Almighty appeared to me at Luz, which is in the land of Canaan. He blessed me and said: ‘I will increase you and multiply you, and I will make you into throngs of peoples. I will give this land to you and to your offspring after you as an everlasting possession.’

“Therefore your two sons, who were born to you [Vulgate adds: *to you*] in the land of Egypt before I came here to you, shall be mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be reckoned as Reuben and Simeon are to me. But the children whom you beget after them shall be yours, and in their inheritances they shall be called by the name of their brothers.

“For when I was coming from Mesopotamia, Rachel died in the land of Canaan on the journey itself. It was springtime, and I was entering Ephrathah; I buried her beside the road to Ephrathah, which is otherwise called Bethlehem.”

Seeing his sons, he said to him: “Who are these?”

He answered: “They are my sons, whom God has given me in this place.”

“Bring them to me,” he said, “so that I may bless them.”

### [B. XLV]

Israel’s eyes had grown dim because of his extreme old age, and he could not see clearly. He drew them close to him, kissed them, and embraced them [Vulgate adds: *them*]. Then he said to his son:

“I was not deprived of seeing you; moreover, God has shown me your offspring.”

When Joseph had taken them from his father’s lap, he bowed with his face to the ground. He placed Ephraim at his right hand—that is, at Israel’s left—and Manasseh at his left, that is, at his father’s right, and brought them both close to him.

He stretched out his right hand and placed it on the head of Ephraim, the younger [Vulgate: *the lesser*] brother; and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, who was the elder, crossing his hands.

He blessed Joseph his son and said:

“God, before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked; God who has fed me from my youth until this day; the Angel who has rescued me from every evil—may he bless these boys [Vulgate adds: *these*]. May my name be invoked over them, and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and may they increase into a multitude throughout the earth.”

When Joseph saw that his father had placed his right hand on Ephraim’s head, he was displeased. He grasped his father’s hand and tried to lift it from Ephraim’s head and transfer it to Manasseh’s head.

He said to his father: “It is not fitting, father, for this one is the firstborn. Place your right hand on his head.”

But he refused and said: “I know, my son, I know. This one too shall become a people, and he shall be multiplied; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall increase into nations.”

He blessed them at that time, saying:

“In you Israel shall be blessed, and it shall be said: ‘May God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh.’”

And he placed Ephraim before Manasseh.

Then he said to Joseph his son:

“Behold, I am dying, but God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. I give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow.”

[Note: The Hebrew has *Sichem ahad*, which the Seventy interpret as **Σίκιμα ἐξαίρετον**, that is, “a distinguished Shechem.” Jerome explained this rather obscure passage with considerable learning: “Shechem,” he says, “has been inflected according to Greek and Latin usage. Otherwise it is called *Shechem* in Hebrew, as the evangelist John also testifies, although, through an established error, it is read incorrectly as *Sychar*; and it is now the city of the Samaritans called Neapolis. Since *Shechem* is translated in Hebrew as “shoulder,” he made an apt allusion to the name by saying, ‘I will also give you one shoulder’; for instead of “distinguished,” that is, **ἐξαίρετον**, the Hebrew writes “one.” But when he says that he possessed it with bow and sword, by bow and sword he calls justice, and so forth. See the *Hebrew Questions*. MART. —Our manuscripts read, “I will give in the future”; the Hebrew indicates rather the past, “I gave.” Moreover, where it says “one portion,” the Hebrew prefers “one shoulder,” although the word meaning “portion” is explained as that which is carried on the shoulder. See also the *Hebrew Questions*.]

### [T. XXXVIII, C. LXXXI, Chapter XLIX]

Jacob called his sons and said to them:

“Gather together, so that I may announce to you what will happen to you in the last days.

“Gather together and hear, sons of Jacob; hear Israel your father:

[Note: Jerome does not always interpret the Hebrew words in the same way. In the *Hebrew Questions*, he teaches that in Hebrew the passage concerning Reuben is written as follows: “Reuben, my firstborn, my strength and the beginning of my children. Greater in bearing, and greater in power: you have poured yourself out like water; do not increase. For you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch in the ascent.” Anyone can learn from him what the meaning of these words is. MART. —One Palatine manuscript adds here also, “and he said to them.” For the names of the following patriarchs, compare the *Hebrew Questions*, where the holy Father interprets the Hebrew differently.]

“Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my grief; foremost in gifts, greatest in authority. You have poured yourself out like water; you shall not increase, because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch.

[Note: In this place the same Jerome reads in the Hebrew text as established: “Simeon and Levi are brothers; instruments of iniquity are their weapons. May my soul not enter their secret, and may my glory not be joined to their assembly, because in their anger they killed a man and in their desire they undermined a wall.” MART.]

“Simeon and Levi are brothers; their weapons are instruments of iniquity. May my soul not enter their council, and may my glory not be in their assembly, because in their anger they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall. Cursed be their anger, because it was stubborn, and their indignation, because it was harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub.

[Note: In Hebrew, according to Jerome, it reads: “From captivity, my son, you have gone up.” MART.]

“To the prey, my son, you have gone up; resting, you have lain down like a lion, and like a lioness—who will rouse him? The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs [Vulgate: *thigh*], until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.

[Col. 0230B]

“Tying his colt to the vine,

[Note: Here too it is written in Hebrew: “Tying his colt to the vine, and to Sorek, my son, his she-ass.” *Sorek* is said to mean a choice vine. It should also be known that where we read “tying his colt to the vine,” the Hebrew may read, instead of *colt*, “his city.” MART.]

“and his she-ass to the vine, O my son. He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape. His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea [Alternative: *dwelt*], and, at the anchorage of ships, shall reach as far as Sidon.

[Note: “Issachar is a bony ass, lying down between the boundaries; and seeing that rest is good and the land beautiful, he bent his shoulder to bear, and became a servant under tribute.” Jerome translated this literally. MART.]

“Issachar is a strong ass, lying between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he bent his shoulder to bear; thus he became a servant to tribute.

“Dan shall judge his people, as also the other tribes in Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s heels so that its rider falls backward. I shall await your salvation, Lord.

[Note: “Gad shall plunder him as a bandit, and he himself shall plunder the heel.” Jerome says that he interprets it this way according to the Hebrew, and then adds: where we have placed “bandit,” *GEDUD* is written, alluding to the name Gad; it may be expressed more significantly as **εὔξωνος**, that is, “belted” or “ready for action.” MART.]

“Gad, being armed, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be armed behind.

“Asher—his bread shall be rich, and he shall provide delicacies for kings.

[Note: In Hebrew it is written: “Naphtali is a watered field, giving words of beauty.” The Hebrews, because of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the Law, wish “a watered field” and “words of beauty” to be understood prophetically. Moreover, where we have “a watered field,” and the Seventy rendered it “a released shrub,” the Hebrew reads **AJALA SELUA** (), which may also be translated “a sent deer,” referring to seasonal crops and displaying the speed of a more fertile land. Thus says Saint Jerome. We have taken care to present such variant readings from the Hebrew so that the reader might understand how many different interpretations of the same Hebrew text we possess from one Jerome, and so that no one might be troubled if he seems somewhat inconsistent with himself: for at one time he wished to express word for word, and at another sense for sense. MART.]

“Naphtali is a released deer, giving words of beauty.

“Joseph is a growing son,

[Note: Another reading, “a growing son,” occurs in the Palatine manuscript, contrary to the authority of the sacred text.]

“a growing son and beautiful in appearance; daughters ran along the wall. But they provoked him, quarreled with him, and envied him, those who carried arrows. His bow remained firm in strength, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob. From there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel.

“The God of your father shall be your helper, and the Almighty shall bless you with blessings from heaven above, with blessings of the abyss lying below, with blessings of breasts and womb. The blessings of your father have prevailed over the blessings of his ancestors, until the desire of the eternal hills should come. May they come upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers.

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall eat prey, and in the evening he shall divide spoils.”

All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said to them; he blessed each one with his proper blessings.

He also commanded them, saying:

“I am being gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the double cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mamre in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial possession. There they buried him and Sarah his wife; there Isaac was buried with Rebecca his wife; and there Leah also lies buried.”

When he had finished the commands with which he instructed his sons, he drew up his feet onto the bed, died, and was gathered to his people.

### [B. XLVI, Chapter L]

When Joseph saw this, he fell upon his father’s face, weeping and kissing him. He ordered his physicians, his servants, to embalm his father. While they were carrying out the orders, forty days passed; for this was the customary period for embalming corpses. Egypt mourned him for seventy days.

When the period of mourning had ended, Joseph spoke to Pharaoh’s household:

“If I have found favor in your sight, speak in Pharaoh’s hearing, saying: ‘My father adjured me, saying: Behold, I am dying. You shall bury me in my tomb, which I dug for myself in the land of Canaan. Therefore I shall go up and bury my father, and I shall return.’”

Pharaoh said to him: “Go up and bury your father, as you have been adjured.”

When he went up, all the elders of Pharaoh’s household went with him, together with all the elders of the land of Egypt; Joseph’s household and his brothers also went, except for the little ones and the flocks and herds, which they had left in the land of Goshen.

He also had chariots and horsemen in his company, and a very large procession was formed.

They came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan. There they held a mourning ceremony with great and intense lamentation for seven days.

When the inhabitants of the land of Canaan saw this, they said: “This is a great mourning for the Egyptians.” Therefore they called the name of that place “The Mourning of Egypt.”

The sons of Jacob did as he had commanded them. They carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the double cave that Abraham had bought with the field as a burial possession from Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mamre.

Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and with the entire procession after burying his father.

When he was dead, his brothers were afraid. They spoke among themselves:

“Perhaps he will remember the injury he suffered and repay us for all the evil we did.”

They sent word to him, saying:

“Your father commanded us before he died to say these words to you on his behalf: ‘I ask you to forget the crime of your brothers, and the sin and malice they practiced against you.’ We also ask you to forgive this iniquity to the servants of the God of your father.”

When Joseph heard this, he wept.

His brothers came to him and, bowing to the ground [Vulgate adds: *worshiping*], said: “We are your servants.”

He answered them:

“Do not be afraid. Can we resist the will of God? You intended evil against me, but God turned it into good, in order to exalt me, as you now see, and to save many peoples. Do not be afraid. I will feed you and your little ones.”

He comforted them and spoke to them gently and kindly.

Joseph lived in Egypt with his entire father’s household, and he lived one hundred and ten years. He saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation. The children of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were also born upon Joseph’s knees.

### [C. LXXXII]

After these events he spoke to his brothers:

“After my death God will visit you and bring you up from this land to the land that he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

When he had adjured them and said, “God will visit you; carry my bones with you from this place,” he died, having completed one hundred and ten years of his life.

After being embalmed with spices, he was placed in a coffin in Egypt.

[Col. 0231]

**The Book of Bresith, that is, Genesis, ends here.**

[Col. 0231]

# The Book of Exodus

## Chapters of the Book of Exodus

## Titles of the Book of Exodus

### I

The number of those who entered Egypt; the increase of the people and their oppression by the king. He summons the midwives and orders them to kill the male children. The birth of Moses and his adoption by Pharaoh’s daughter. He strikes Egypt; flees from Pharaoh’s presence; defends the daughter of the priest of Midian from shepherds; and takes Zipporah as his wife.

### II

After the king of Egypt dies, God hears the cry of Israel. Moses sees the Lord on Mount Horeb. He is called and approaches the burning bush. He is commanded to go to Pharaoh. He asks for signs and receives them. He makes excuses and declares himself ineloquent. The Lord becomes angry and orders him to go with Aaron.

### III

As Moses returns to Egypt, the angel of the Lord meets him because of the circumcision of his son and the blood pledge. Aaron is commanded to go out to meet Moses. He hears from him what the Lord had commanded. They perform signs before the people; the people believe, rejoice, and exult, and they report them to Pharaoh. They resist the command of God, and Pharaoh imposes harsher burdens on the people than before. He scourges the leaders of Israel. They invoke God’s judgment against Moses and Aaron and, pressed by greater distress, no longer believe their words.

### IV

The genealogy of the Levite families, and the point at which Moses is appointed by God as God to Pharaoh. They perform signs before Pharaoh: the staff is changed into a dragon; the waters are turned into blood; frogs are produced, contaminating all the household goods. Pharaoh is not restrained by these three plagues but rather becomes hardened.

### V

The Lord commands Pharaoh to be approached again. Aaron is ordered to strike the dust of the earth so that all the dust becomes gnats. Egypt is likewise filled with flies of various kinds, except for the land in which the children of Israel live. He commands that pestilence be brought upon all the animals. Severe wounds and swelling boils arise in human beings from the scattering of ashes. Hail is brought upon them to destroy all growing things. Pharaoh pretends repentance and pleads until relief is granted; when it is granted, he becomes hardened still more.

### VI

Moses is commanded to enter before him, and locusts are brought. Darkness is imposed, and through all these things he is in no way restrained.

### VII

The law of Passover is commanded, and it is announced that Egypt will be struck at midnight. The lintel and doorposts of the Israelites are smeared with blood as a sign. At midnight the firstborn of the Egyptians are killed. Pharaoh rises and compels the people to leave his land without delay.

### VIII

The departure of the people of Israel from Rameses to Succoth. They hear the religious regulations of Passover and learn who may eat it. The Lord tells Moses that Pharaoh will pursue the children of Israel, and Pharaoh does pursue them to the sea. Pressed by fear, they murmur against Moses. Moses is commanded, after the camp has been moved, to strike and divide the sea. The crossing, the death of the Egyptians, and the song of triumph.

### IX

After being led through the Red Sea, they come to Marah. The waters are sweetened and judgments are set forth. They come to Elim, where they find twelve springs and seventy palm trees; afterward they murmur in Sinai, desiring bread and meat. Manna is provided from heaven, and the amount sufficient for them is prescribed.

### X

They come to Rephidim, where there is no water to drink. The rock is struck with the staff, and water flows. The battle between Israel and Amalek. Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, and the judges who are appointed.

### XI

From Rephidim they come to Sinai, where Moses ascends the mountain to God and commands the people to sanctify themselves for the third day. The Decalogue is proclaimed. The people are terrified by the voices of God and ask to hear God’s commands through Moses.

### XII

The Lord commands laws concerning particular matters, including the judgment by which each person is to be punished.

### XIII

After building an altar, Moses offers a whole burnt offering and sprinkles the people and the book with blood. He is commanded to ascend the mountain to receive the stone tablets. He is ordered to accept firstfruits from the people: gold, silver, and other materials for making the tabernacle and all its equipment; priestly and Levitical garments; the order in which sacrifice is to be consecrated; and the regulations of sacrifice.

### XIV

It is commanded that each person offer a price to the Lord for his life; the bronze basin for the sanctuary; the composition of the incense; the holy oil; and the designation of wise men who will complete everything.

### XV

He receives the tablets of the testimony, but while Moses delays, the people make an idol. God announces his anger to Moses, and Moses bows in worship.
