Descending from the mountain, he breaks the tablets. He seizes the calf, burns it, crushes it, and kills as many as he can together with the Levitical family; then he again pleads with the Lord.

### XVI

He places the tent of the covenant outside the camp, where the Lord speaks with Moses face to face. He asks that God’s glory be shown to him. Then he commands that other tablets be prepared. Moses ascends with them to the mountain, where he is given commands concerning what the people must observe, and the ten words of the covenant are written down.

### XVII

With his face glorified, Moses descends from the mountain. With his face veiled, he recounts to the people what the Lord has commanded concerning the construction of the tabernacle. The people offer voluntarily, and wise men, filled with the spirit of wisdom, fulfill the work of making it.

### XVIII

When the tabernacle has been completed, the whole people offer, and after it has been set up by the priest, the glory of the Lord covers it.

## Brief Chapters of the Book of Exodus

[Col. 0233]

### I

Concerning the king who oppressed the children of Israel, the Hebrew midwives, and the birth of Moses.

### II

Concerning the Egyptian struck by Moses, and Moses’ flight to the land of Midian, where he took a wife, fathered two sons, and saw the vision in the bush.

### III

Concerning the staff changed into a serpent and the hand placed in the bosom; his departure to Egypt and entrance before Pharaoh.

### IV

Concerning the recapitulation of the Hebrew genealogies.

### V

Concerning the second entrance of Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh, and the plagues inflicted upon Egypt, through the tenth.

### VI

Concerning the sacrifice of the lamb and the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt at the completion of the tenth plague.

### VII

Concerning the firstborn consecrated to the Lord and Joseph’s bones carried out of Egypt.

### VIII

Concerning the pillar of cloud and fire, the crossing of the Red Sea, and the song.

### IX

Concerning the bitterness of the water at Marah and the manna first falling in the desert.

### X

Concerning the people’s departure to Rephidim, where water flowed from the rock; the war against the Amalekites; and the place where Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, brings Moses’ wife and sons to him and gives advice about appointing commanders of hundreds.

### XI

Concerning the departure into the wilderness of Sinai, where the people, sanctified for the third day, stand ready, see God at the summit of the mountain, and receive the commandments of the Law.

### XII

Concerning Hebrew servants, release, assailants, murderers, thieves, false witnesses, and the remaining judgments.

### XIII

Concerning the remnants of the land in the seventh year, festivals, and tithes.

### XIV

Concerning the seventy elders who, together with the priests, saw the God of Israel.

### XV

Concerning Moses’ ascent of the mountain and his stay there for forty days, where he is instructed about the making of the tabernacle and the ark.

### XVI

Concerning priestly garments.

### XVII

Concerning sacrifices and victims.

### XVIII

Concerning the altar of incense, the priestly anointing oil, Bezalel and Oholiab, and observance of the Sabbath.

### XIX

Concerning Moses’ return after forty days; the breaking of the tablets; the calf cast from gold; the slaughter carried out against the sacrilegious; and Moses’ intercession for the people.

### XX

Concerning Moses’ second ascent of the mountain; the restoration of the tablets; the prohibition against worshiping idols; all the commandments; the recapitulation of the tabernacle’s implements; and Moses’ return after forty days.

### XXI

Concerning the people’s contribution and preparations, and the construction of the tabernacle, when the glory of the Lord appeared.

## Chapters of the Book of Exodus

### I

Concerning the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt, and the Hebrew infants whom Pharaoh ordered to be thrown into the river.

### II

Concerning the child whom Pharaoh’s daughter found and named Moses.

### III

Concerning the Egyptian whom Moses killed and his flight.

### IV

After Pharaoh died, the Lord heard the children of Israel.

### V

Where the angel appeared to Moses in the bush.

### VI

Concerning the sign that the Lord gave Moses through the staff.

### VII

Concerning the second sign.

### VIII

Concerning the third sign.

### IX

Where Moses came to his father-in-law and said to him: “I am going to my brothers.”

### X

After Pharaoh died, the Lord said to Moses: “Go to Egypt,” and Zipporah circumcised her son.

### XI

The Lord said to Aaron: “Go to meet Moses.”

### XII

They tell Pharaoh to let Israel leave his land.

### XIII

The Lord commands Moses to speak to the people.

### XIV

Concerning the leaders of Israel.

### XV

“I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh,” says the Lord.

### XVI

Aaron threw down his staff before Pharaoh, and it became a dragon; the magicians did the same.

## The Plagues of Egypt

1. The water of the river became blood; the magicians did the same.

2. Aaron again struck the waters of Egypt and brought forth frogs; the magicians did the same.

3. Aaron struck the dust of the earth, and gnats appeared on human beings; the magicians were defeated.

4. He sent the dog-fly over the whole land of Egypt.

5. The Lord sent death upon the livestock of the Egyptians.

6. Concerning the ashes that Moses scattered toward heaven, from which boils arose on human beings.

7. Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and the Lord rained fire and hail.

8. Locusts came over all the borders of Egypt.

9. Darkness came over the whole land of Egypt for three days.

10. Concerning the tenth plague, in which the Lord struck every firstborn of the Egyptians.

### XVII

The Lord says to Moses: “I am bringing one more plague upon Pharaoh.”

### XVIII

The Lord speaks to Moses and Aaron concerning the ordinance of Passover.

### XIX

The children of Israel lived in Egypt for 430 years.

### XX

The Lord gives the law of Passover.

### XXI

The Lord says that every firstborn must be sanctified.

### XXII

In the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from Egypt.

### XXIII

Pharaoh pursued the children of Israel, and the sea covered the Egyptians.

### XXIV

The song.

### XXV

Miriam also sang with the women, with tambourines and dances.

### XXVI

The people murmured in the desert because of water.

### XXVII

They also murmured because of meat.

### XXVIII

The Lord gave the people quail and manna.

### XXIX

They ate manna for forty years.

### XXX

They murmured because of water, and he brought water out of the rock.

### XXXI

Amalek came to battle, and Joshua struck him.

### XXXII

Jethro came to Moses in the desert.

### XXXIII

Jethro gave Moses advice to appoint tribunes and commanders of hundreds.

### XXXIV

The Lord testifies through Moses to the people that they should listen to him.

### XXXV

The Lord descended upon Mount Sinai in fire.

### XXXVI

The Lord commands Moses to ascend the mountain alone.

### XXXVII

The ten words of the Law, which the Lord commanded to be observed:

1. You shall have no gods apart from me.
2. You shall not make an idol for yourself or any likeness.
3. You shall not take the name of your God in vain.
4. Keep the Sabbath day in mind.
5. Honor your father and your mother.
6. You shall not kill.
7. You shall not commit adultery.
8. You shall not steal.
9. You shall not give false testimony.
10. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife or anything belonging to him.

### XXXVIII

The people were afraid and said to Moses: “You speak to us.”

### XXXIX

No silver or golden gods are to be made, but an altar to the Lord.

### XL

Concerning a Hebrew boy who has been bought.

### XLI

Concerning a daughter who has been sold.

### XLII

Concerning one who has been struck and killed.

### XLIII

Concerning those who kill by deceit.

### XLIV

Concerning those who strike their father or mother.

### XLV

Concerning one who sells what has been seized by theft.

### XLVI

Concerning those who curse their father or mother.

### XLVII

If someone strikes another in a quarrel with a stone or a fist.

### XLVIII

If someone strikes a male or female slave and they die.

### XLIX

If someone strikes a woman and she miscarries.

### L

An eye is to be extracted for an eye.

### LI

Concerning one who extracts the eye of a male or female slave.

### LII

If a bull strikes someone with its horn.

### LIII

If someone digs a pit.

### LIV

If a bull strikes another bull with its horn.

### LV

If someone steals a calf or a sheep.

### LVI

Concerning a thief who has been struck.

### LVII

Concerning the grazing of another person’s field.

### LVIII

Concerning a burned field or harvest.

### LIX

Concerning something entrusted and stolen by someone.

### LX

Concerning a beast of burden or other animal that has been entrusted and dies.

### LXI

If someone asks for an animal and it dies.

### LXII

Concerning a virgin who has not yet been betrothed.

### LXIII

A sorcerer must be killed.

### LXIV

One who lies with an animal must be killed.

### LXV

One who sacrifices to gods must be eradicated.

### LXVI

No harm is to be done to a resident alien.

### LXVII

No harm is to be done to a widow or orphan.

### LXVIII

Concerning interest and pledges.

### LXIX

Blasphemy is forbidden.

### LXX

Firstfruits are to be offered to the Lord.

### LXXI

Every firstborn is to be offered to the Lord.

### LXXII

Meat first tasted by a wild animal is not to be eaten.

### LXXIII

Do not readily believe everything you hear.

### LXXIV

Do not agree with unjust witnesses.

### LXXV

Do not do evil with the multitude.

### LXXVI

Do not turn aside with the multitude in judgment.

### LXXVII

Do not despise the poor in judgment, nor act on his behalf.

### LXXVIII

A lost animal belonging to an enemy is to be returned.

### LXXIX

An enemy’s animal burdened by weight is to be raised up.

### LXXX

The judgment of the poor is not to be subverted.

### LXXXI

One must turn away from every unjust word.

### LXXXII

An innocent and just person must not be killed.

### LXXXIII

Gifts must not be accepted.

### LXXXIV

Concerning foreigners and the year of remission.

### LXXXV

No work is to be done on the Sabbath.

### LXXXVI

Everything that God has commanded is to be done.

### LXXXVII

Three times in the year a solemn day is to be celebrated.

### LXXXVIII

Concerning the festival of Unleavened Bread.

### LXXXIX

One must not appear before the Lord empty-handed.

### XC

Three times in the year every male is to appear before the Lord.

### XCI

The firstfruits of the land are to be offered.

### XCII

A kid must not be boiled in its mother’s milk.

### XCIII

The Lord promises Moses an angel who will go before him.

### XCIV

Whoever listens to God will be delivered from his enemies.

### XCV

Foreign gods are not to be worshiped.

### XCVI

The Lord will send fear and hornets to drive out the foreigners.

### XCVII

The Lord said to Moses to ascend to him on the mountain with the elders.

### XCVIII

Moses built an altar from twelve stones.

### XCIX

Moses ascended with the elders.

### C

All the chosen men came to the place of God.

### CI

The Lord says to Moses to ascend the mountain to receive the tablets of the covenant.

### CII

Moses ascended, and the majesty of the Lord descended upon him.

### CIII

The Lord says that first offerings are to be brought for making the tabernacle.

### CIV

What things are to be offered.

CV. Concerning the construction of the ark, the table, the tabernacle, and the altar.

CVI. Concerning the oil for the lamp.

CVII. Concerning the priesthood of Aaron and his sons.

CVIII. Concerning the sacred robe.

CIX. Concerning the priestly garment.

CX. Concerning the ordination of the priests and the victim to be sacrificed.

[Col. 0238D] CXI. Concerning the altar of incense.

CXII. Concerning the offering of fragrance.

CXIII. The priests are commanded to wash both their hands and their feet when they ascend to sacrifice to the Lord.

CXIV. Concerning the incense ointment.

CXV. Concerning Bezalel, whom the Lord filled with the spirit of wisdom for every work.

CXVI. Concerning the observance of the Sabbath.

CXVII. Where the Lord gives Moses the tablets of the Testimony.

CXVIII. Where Aaron made the cast calf.

CXIX. The Lord says to Moses: “Go down quickly.”

CXX. Where Moses prayed for the people.

CXXI. Moses saw the calf and broke the tablets.

CXXII. Where Moses rebuked Aaron because of the calf.

[Col. 0239A] CXXIII. Moses ordered the people to kill one another.

CXXIV. Moses asks the Lord on behalf of the people to forgive their sin.

CXXV. The Lord says to Moses: “Go up to the land that I swore to your fathers.”

CXXVI. The Lord rebukes the people and orders Moses to pitch a tabernacle outside; and he speaks with him in the pillar of cloud.

CXXVII. The Lord spoke with Moses as one speaks with his friend.

CXXVIII. Moses asks the Lord to see him, and the Lord says to him: “You cannot see my face.”

CXXIX. Moses went up the mountain with other tablets, where he received the Lord’s law and commandment.

CXXX. The Lord commands every firstling to be offered to him.

CXXXI. Moses did not eat for forty days while he was writing the words of the Testimony.

[Col. 0239B] CXXXII. Moses’ face became radiant, and he covered it before the people, because it appeared to them to be horned.

CXXXIII. Concerning the days of the Sabbaths.

[Col. 0240A] CXXXIV. Moses commanded that the first offerings be presented to the Lord—whatever they had resolved in their hearts to give for the work of the tabernacle, the altar, and the priestly objects.

CXXXV. Bezalel, Oholiab, and every wise craftsman made the sacred robes and all the work of the tabernacle.

CXXXVI. Bezalel made the ark of the Testimony, the table, the lampstand, the seven lamps, the bronze altar, and the oil of anointing; also the bronze altar with its columns and the vessels of the tabernacle; the offerings according to the number of the warriors; the priestly garment, its bells, and every ornament and furnishing of the tabernacle, together with all its vessels.

CXXXVII. On the first day of the first month, the Lord commanded Moses to sanctify everything and to clothe Aaron in his sacred robe.

CXXXVIII. In the first month of the second year after the departure from Egypt, Moses erected the tabernacle of the Testimony.

[Col. 0240B] CXXXIX. When the tabernacle had been completed, the cloud covered it, and the majesty of the Lord filled it.

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK CALLED ELLE SMOTH, WHICH IN GREEK IS CALLED EXODUS

[Col. 0239]

[Col. 0239C] [T. I, B. I, C. I, Cap. I.] These are the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt with Jacob; they entered individually, each with his household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin; Dan and Naphtali; Gad and Asher. Thus all the persons who came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy. Joseph, however, was in Egypt.

[Note: [Col. 0239D] Through the error of scribes, certain things flowed from the Septuagint into the Canon of Hebrew truth. Hence here, together with another manuscript, it reads: “Thus all the persons who came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy-five,” which Saint Jerome explicitly refutes in the books of the *Hebrew Questions*. He teaches that, when they are gradually counted one by one, the Hebrew books contain only seventy persons. “From this,” he says, “it is clear that all the persons who entered Egypt from Jacob’s thighs were seventy: sixty-six entered afterward and found in Egypt three persons—Joseph, namely, with his two sons; the seventieth, however, was Jacob himself.” He then defends his opinion by appeal to the Septuagint translators themselves, who at Deuteronomy 10:22 state that only seventy persons entered Egypt, although here too the Alexandrian manuscript corruptly reads “seventy-five.” MART. —The Urbinas manuscript has it most correctly in this way; the others, including the one that Martianus calls the Canon of Hebrew Truth, count seventy-five according to the Greek. See the *Hebrew Questions* on Genesis 46:26.]

After he died, together with all his brothers and that entire generation,

[Note: [Col. 0240D] For that relationship, the Canon and several manuscript copies read “his relationship.” But everyone can see that this is false. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript likewise wrongly has “his relationship.” The Hebrew has [Hebrew term not legible in the supplied text], “that generation.”]

the children of Israel increased and, as though sprouting, multiplied; they became exceedingly strong and filled the land. Meanwhile a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph. He said to his people: “Behold, the people of the children of Israel are numerous and stronger than we are. Come, let us oppress them wisely, lest they multiply; and, if war should break out against us, they may join our enemies, defeat us, and depart from the land.”

Accordingly, he set taskmasters over them to afflict them with burdens; and they built cities of tents for Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0240D] Saint Jerome may have read [the Hebrew term not legible in the supplied text] instead of [the Hebrew term not legible in the supplied text], “cities of tents” instead of “treasure-cities,” as the Chaldean and the rabbis, along with many other interpreters, prefer.] Pithom and Rameses. But the more they oppressed them, the more they multiplied and grew. The Egyptians hated the children of Israel and afflicted them, mocking them

[Note: [Col. 0240D] Many manuscripts add here “and envying them,” but without justification. MART.]

and embittering their lives with harsh labor in clay and bricks and with every kind of service by which they were oppressed in the works of the land.

The king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives—one of whom was called Sephora [In Hebrew: Siphrah], and the other Puah—giving them this command: “When you serve as midwives for the Hebrew women, and the time of delivery has come, if it is a male child, kill him; if it is a female, preserve her” [Vulgate adds: “it shall be”]. But the midwives feared God and did not act according to the command of the king of Egypt; they preserved the males. When they were summoned before him, the king said: “Why have you wanted to do this, so as to preserve the boys?” They answered: “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women. They themselves possess the skill of midwifery, and before we come to them, they give birth.” Therefore God dealt well with the midwives, and the people grew and became exceedingly strong. And because the midwives feared God, he built houses for them.

Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying: “Whatever male child is born, throw it into the river; whatever is female, preserve.”

[C. II, Cap. II.] After this, a man from the house of Levi went out, having taken a wife from his own lineage. She conceived and bore a son; and when she saw that he was beautiful, she hid him for three months. When she could no longer conceal him, she took a basket of reeds and coated it with bitumen and pitch. She placed the infant inside, set him among the reeds on the bank of the river, and his sister stood at a distance, watching to see what would happen.

Now Pharaoh’s daughter came down to bathe in the river, and her maidens walked along the bank of the channel. When she saw the basket among the papyrus, she sent one of her attendants. The woman brought it and opened it; and when she saw the little child crying inside, she pitied him and said: “This is one of the infants of the Hebrews.”

The child’s sister said to her: “Do you wish me to go and call a Hebrew woman who can nurse the infant for you?” She answered: “Go.” The girl went and called his mother

[Note: [Col. 0241D] In Hebrew it has “the mother of the child,” which removes all ambiguity from the printed books, which read “his mother.” MART. —More correctly, the Hebrew has [Hebrew term not legible in the supplied text], “the mother of the child”; the Vulgate edition has “his mother.”]

The daughter of Pharaoh said to her: “Take this child and nurse him for me; I shall give you your wages.” The woman took the child and nursed him. When he had grown, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter. She adopted him as a son and called his name Moses, saying: “Because I took him from the water.”

[C. III.] In those days, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his brothers and saw their affliction and an Egyptian striking one of his Hebrew brothers. He looked around in every direction and, seeing that no one was present, struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.

The next day, when he had gone out, he saw two Hebrews fighting. He said to the one who was doing the wrong: “Why are you striking your neighbor?” The man replied: “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Do you intend to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?”

Moses was afraid and said: “How has this matter become known?” Pharaoh heard of it and sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from his presence, stayed in the land of Midian, and sat beside a well.

Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came to draw water, filled the troughs, and wanted to water their father’s flocks. The shepherds came and drove them away. Moses arose, defended the girls, and watered their sheep.

When they returned to their father Reuel, he said to them: “Why have you come sooner than usual?” They answered: “An Egyptian delivered us from the hand of the shepherds; moreover, he drew water with us and gave the sheep to drink.”

He said: “Where is he? Why did you leave the man? Call him, so that he may eat bread.” Moses swore that he would live with him. He took Zipporah, his daughter,

[Note: [Col. 0241D] The Palatine manuscript omits “as wife”; shortly afterward, together with the Urbinas manuscript and the printed editions, it reads “Gersan” instead of “Gershom.”]

as his wife. She bore him a son, whom he called Gershom, saying: “I have been a sojourner in a foreign land.”

[T. II, C. IV.]

[Note: [Col. 0241D] Many printed books and manuscripts add the following: “And she bore another, whom he called Eliezer, saying: ‘For the God of my father is my helper and rescued me from the hand of Pharaoh.’” In other Greek and Latin copies it reads as follows: “He called another Eliezer,” and so forth. None of these words exists in the Hebrew text or in the Samaritan text; they are likewise absent from the Roman edition of the Septuagint, the Alexandrian manuscript, and the Chaldean paraphrase. They appear to have been borrowed from chapter 18 of this same book of Exodus, verses 3–4, where nearly the same words are read concerning Eliezer. Furthermore, the manuscript Bible codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, no. 3, displays this entire passage in the margin; the excellent Royal codex, no. 3563, has the same words outside the sequence and numbering of the lines, written in small characters along the lower margin. Finally, in one Corbie manuscript, no. 1, only these words are found within the text: “And he rescued me from the hand of Pharaoh.” A later hand supplied the rest along the lower margin of the book. From this great variety among the copies, it is sufficiently established that what is said about Eliezer was first written in the margin and, over time, was placed by scribes in the body of the text. MART. —Our manuscripts, as well as those consulted by Martianus, and the printed books, add: “And she bore another, whom he called Eliezer, saying: ‘For the God of my father is my helper, and he rescued me from the hand of Pharaoh.’” Although the original texts do not contain these words, the Coislinian manuscript in Montfaucon’s possession confirms that they were nevertheless written under an asterisk in the Hexapla.]

After a long time, the king of Egypt died. The children of Israel groaned because of their labors and cried out; and their cry because of their labors went up to God. He heard their groaning and remembered the covenant that he had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The Lord looked upon the children of Israel and took notice of them [Vulgate adds: “them”].

[C. V, Cap. III.] Moses was pasturing the sheep of Jethro, his kinsman [Vulgate: “father-in-law”], the priest of Midian. When he had led the flock into the interior of the wilderness, he came to the mountain of God, Horeb.

The Lord appeared to him [Hebrew: “the angel of the Lord appeared”] in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush. He saw that the bush was burning but was not consumed. Moses said: “I will go and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned.”

When the Lord saw that he was approaching to look, he called him from the midst of the bush and said: “Moses, Moses.” He answered: “Here I am.” He said: “Do not come near here. Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.”

And he said: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face, for he did not dare to look toward God.

The Lord said to him: “I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt and have heard their cry because of the harshness of those who oversee their labors. Knowing their pain, I have come down to deliver them [Vulgate: “to deliver and bring them out”] from the hands of the Egyptians and to bring them out from that land into a good and spacious land, into a land flowing with milk and honey, to the regions of the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite.

“Therefore the cry of the children of Israel has come to me, and I have seen the affliction with which the Egyptians oppress them. But come, I will send you to Pharaoh, so that you may bring my people, the children of Israel,

[Col. 0243B] out of Egypt.”

Moses said to God: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” He said to him: “I will be with you. And this shall be your sign that I have sent you: when you have brought the people [Vulgate adds: “my people”] out of Egypt, you shall sacrifice to God upon this mountain.”

Moses said to God: “Behold, I shall go to the children of Israel and say to them: ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you.’ If they say to me, ‘What is his name?’ what shall I say to them?”

God said to Moses: “I am who I am.” He said: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

God said again to Moses: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation.

“Go, gather the elders of Israel, and say to them: ‘The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, appeared to me, saying: “I have visited you with a visitation, and I have seen all that has happened to you in Egypt. And I have said that I will bring you up from the affliction of Egypt into the land of the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite, into a land flowing with milk and honey.”’

“And they will hear your voice. Then you and the elders of Israel shall enter before the king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: ‘The Lord God of the Hebrews has called us. We shall go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, to sacrifice to the Lord our God.’

“But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless by a mighty hand. For I shall stretch out my hand

[Col. 0243D] and strike Egypt with all my wonders that I shall perform in its midst; after this he will let you go.

“And I will grant this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. When you depart, you shall not go out empty-handed; but every woman shall ask from her neighbor and from her house guest vessels of silver and gold and clothing. You shall place them upon your sons and daughters, and you shall strip Egypt.”

[Col. 0244A] [Cap. IV.] Moses answered and said: “They will not believe me or listen to my voice, but they will say: ‘The Lord has not appeared to you.’”

[B. III. C. VI.] He said to him: “What is that which you hold in your hand?” He answered: “A staff.” The Lord said: “Throw it on the ground.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent, so that Moses fled from it.

The Lord said: “Stretch out your hand and seize it by the tail.” He stretched out his hand, seized it, and it became a staff again.

“Thus they may believe,” he said, “that the Lord, the God of their fathers,

[Note: [Col. 0243D] In place of “their fathers,” all manuscript copies read “your fathers”; the Latin translation of the Samaritan text incorrectly followed this reading, although the Samaritan and Hebrew books contain *avotham*, that is, “their fathers” or “their own fathers.” MART. —Our manuscripts, and those praised by Martianus, read “your fathers” instead of “their fathers.”]

the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.”

[C. VII.] The Lord said again: “Put your hand into your bosom.” When he had put it into his bosom, he brought it out leprous, like snow. “Put your hand back into your bosom,” he said. He put it back and brought it out again, and it was like the rest of his flesh.

“If they do not believe you,” he said, “or listen to the message of the first sign, they will believe the message of the second sign.”

[C. VIII.] “But if they do not believe even these two signs and do not listen to your voice, take water from the river and pour it upon the dry ground; and whatever you have drawn from the river will be changed into blood.”

Moses said: “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you have spoken to your servant; I am slower and more impeded in speech.”

The Lord said to him: “Who made the human mouth? Or who fashioned the mute, the deaf, the seeing, and the blind? Is it not I? Go, therefore, and I will be with your mouth; I will teach you what you are to say.”

But he said: “I beg you, Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0244D] Jerome teaches that this should be translated from the Hebrew in Book III of his Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 6. After quoting from the Septuagint translators the reading, “I beg you, Lord, I am not worthy; provide another whom you may send,” he adds another, saying: “Or, as it is read in Hebrew, ‘Send whom you are going to send.’” MART.]

“send whom you are going to send.”

The Lord became angry with Moses and said: “Aaron your brother, the Levite—I know that he is eloquent. Behold, he will come out to meet you; when he sees you, he will rejoice in his heart. Speak to him and put my words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will show you what you must do.

“He will speak for you to the people and will be your mouth; but you will be to him in matters that concern God.

“Take this staff also in your hand, with which you shall perform the signs.

[C. IX.] Moses departed and returned to Jethro, his kinsman [Vulgate: “father-in-law”], and said to him: “I will go and return to my brothers in Egypt, to see whether they are still alive.” Jethro said to him: “Go in peace.”

[T. III, C. X.] The Lord said to Moses in Midian: “Go and return to Egypt, for all those who sought your life are dead.”

Moses therefore took his wife and his sons, set them upon a donkey, and returned to Egypt, carrying the staff of God in his hand.

The Lord said to him as he returned to Egypt: “See that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders that I have placed in your hand. I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.

“You shall say to him: ‘Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I have said to you: Let my son go, so that he may serve me; and you have refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your firstborn son.’”

When he was on the journey, the Lord met him at the lodging place and sought to kill him. Immediately Zipporah took a very sharp stone, circumcised the foreskin of her son, touched his feet, and said: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me.”

He released him after she had said: “A bridegroom of blood,”

[Note: [Col. 0245D] The Canon of Hebrew Truth and the older manuscripts add after the word “blood,” as in the preceding verse, “you are to me.” But these words are absent from the Hebrew source, and there is no doubt that they flowed into the manuscripts through the carelessness of copyists. MART. —The Palatine manuscript and several others consulted by Martianus add here, as in the preceding verse, “you are to me.” Some maintain that Jerome judged these words should be repeated, even though they are absent from the Hebrew archetype.]

because of the circumcision.

[C. XI.] The Lord said to Aaron: “Go to meet Moses in the wilderness.” He went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him. Moses told Aaron all the words of the Lord by which he had sent him, and the signs that he had commanded.

They came together and gathered all the elders of the children of Israel. Aaron spoke all the words that the Lord had said to Moses and performed the signs before the people. The people believed. They heard that the Lord had visited the children of Israel and had looked upon their affliction, and they bowed down and worshiped.

[C. XII.] After this Moses and Aaron entered and said to Pharaoh: “Thus says the Lord God

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Instead of “the God of Israel,” the Canon of Hebrew Truth and another manuscript of excellent quality, Saint-Germain-des-Prés no. 3, read “the Lord God of the Hebrews,” as is said several times below throughout Exodus. It should be noted especially that here, in the Canon, the name “Israel” was erased and the word “Hebrews” inserted in its place, with the marginal sign *h*, by which he wished to indicate to us that this was how it was read in Hebrew. It follows from this observation that in at least some Hebrew copies it was formerly written, “the Lord God of the Hebrews.” Nevertheless, the contrary is clearly supported by the one translator among all others who agrees both with the present Hebrew text and with Pharaoh’s ensuing response: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.” Therefore I remain uncertain here. MART.]

of Israel: ‘Let my people go, so that they may sacrifice to me in the wilderness.’”

But he answered: “Who is the Lord, that I should listen to his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.”

They said: “The God of the Hebrews has called us, so that we may go a three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the Lord our God, lest pestilence or the sword fall upon us.”

The king of Egypt said to them: “Why, Moses and Aaron, are you disrupting the people from their labor? Go to your burdens.”

Pharaoh said: “The people of the land are numerous; you see that the crowd has grown. How much more so if

[Note: [Col. 0246D] Several manuscript copies read “if we give them.” This appears to have been borrowed from the Greek, which reads in the first person, *katapausōmen*, that is, “let us give cessation” or “let us make them rest.” MART. —In the Palatine manuscript: “if you give them rest.”]

you give them rest from their labors?”

That same day he commanded the overseers of the works and the taskmasters of the people, saying: “You shall no longer give the people straw for making bricks, as before; let them go and gather straw for themselves. You shall impose upon them the same quota of bricks that they previously made, and you shall not reduce anything from it. They are idle, and therefore they cry out, saying: ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’ Let them be oppressed with labor and complete it, so that they will not pay attention to lying words.”

The overseers of the works and the taskmasters went out and said to the people: “Thus says Pharaoh: ‘I do not give you straw. Go and gather it wherever you can find it, and nothing shall be reduced from your work.’”

[Col. 0246A] The people were scattered throughout the whole land of Egypt to gather straw. The overseers of the works pressed them, saying: “Complete your daily work, as you used to do when straw was given to you.”

Those who were set over the works of the children of Israel were flogged by Pharaoh’s taskmasters, who said: “Why have you not completed the quota of bricks as before, neither yesterday nor today?”

The leaders of the children of Israel came and cried out to Pharaoh, saying: “Why do you act this way against your servants? Straw is not given to us, yet bricks are commanded of us just the same. Behold, your servants are beaten with whips, and your people are treated unjustly.”

He said: “You are idle, and therefore you say: ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord.’ Go, then, and work. Straw shall not be given to you, and you shall deliver the customary number of bricks.”

The leaders of the children of Israel saw that they were in a bad situation, because it was said to them: “Nothing shall be reduced from the bricks for each day.”

They met Moses and Aaron, who were standing opposite them as they came out from Pharaoh,

[Vulgate: “as they were coming out from Pharaoh”]

and said to them: “May the Lord look upon this and judge, because you have made our odor offensive in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and you have placed a sword in his hand to kill us.”

Moses returned to the Lord and said: “Lord, why have you afflicted this people? Why have you sent me? For from the time I entered before Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has afflicted your people, and you have not delivered them.”

[Cap. VI.] The Lord said to Moses: “Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh. For by a strong hand he will let them go, and by a mighty hand he will drive them out of his land.”

[C. XIII.] God spoke to Moses, saying: “I am the Lord, who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty; but my name, Adonai, I did not make known to them. I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land of their sojourning, in which they lived as resident foreigners.

“I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel, whom the Egyptians have oppressed, and I have remembered my covenant. Therefore say to the children of Israel: ‘I am the Lord, and I will bring you out from the prison of the Egyptians. I will rescue you from slavery and redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments.

“‘I will take you as my people, and I will be your God. You shall know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the prison of the Egyptians and brought you into the land over which I raised my hand

[Col. 0246D] to give it to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession.

[Col. 0247A] I am the Lord.’”

[T. IV.] Moses therefore told all this to the children of Israel, but they did not listen to him because of their anguish of spirit and their most arduous labor.

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Enter and speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, so that he may let the children of Israel go out from his land.”

Moses answered before the Lord: “Behold, the children of Israel do not listen to me; how then will Pharaoh listen to me, especially since I am uncircumcised of lips?”

[C. XIV.] The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a command for the children of Israel and for Pharaoh, king of Egypt, that they should bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt.

[B. IV.] These are the heads of the households according to their families.

The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, were Enoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben.

The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad [Vulgate: Ahod], Jachin, Zohar, and Saul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These are the families of Simeon.

These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their clans: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The years of Levi’s life were one hundred thirty-seven.

The sons of Gershon [Hebrew: Libni and Shimei] were according to their clans.

The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The years of Kohath’s life were one hundred thirty-three.

The sons of Merari were Mahli [Hebrew: Mahali] and Mushi. These are the clans of Levi according to their families.

Amram took as his wife Jochebed [Hebrew: Jochebed], his father’s sister; she bore him Aaron and Moses.

[Note: [Col. 0247D] The Urbinas manuscript omits “to him”; then, together with the Palatine manuscript, it adds after “Moses,” “and Miriam,” from the Septuagint.]

[Note: [Col. 0247D] The Septuagint adds here: “and Miriam their sister.” These words are also read in the Hebrew-Samaritan text, into which, according to the settled opinion of learned men, not a few things flowed from the Septuagint translators. The Syriac, together with several Latin manuscript copies, does indeed read “and Miriam,” but does not have “their sister.” The Canon of Hebrew Truth clearly demonstrates that all these additions are extraneous: after such words had been erased from the body of the text, a scholion was placed at the side reading: *h. does not have Miriam*—that is, “the Hebrew does not have Miriam.” To this may be added the Chaldean and Arabic versions, in which nothing concerning Miriam is found; nor is it found in the better-quality Latin copies. MART.]

The years of Amram’s life were one hundred thirty-seven.

The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.

The sons of Uzziel were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.

Aaron took as his wife Elisheba,

[Note: [Col. 0248D] In Hebrew we read [Hebrew term not legible in the supplied text], that is, “Elisheba,” not “Elizabeth,” as the Septuagint translators have it, followed by the printed editions and some more recent manuscript copies. The name Elisheba in the Greek copies can be shown to have been corrupted not only from the Canon of Hebrew Truth and other older, better-quality Latin manuscripts, but also from the books of Hebrew names, where Saint Jerome, listing this name under Exodus, reads “Elisheba,” which is interpreted as “the oath of my God,” and so forth. This would not be the case if “Elizabeth” were read. MART. —The Palatine manuscript has “Helsabee.”]

the daughter of Amminadab, the sister of Nahshon. She bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

The sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the clans of the Korahites.

Eleazar, Aaron’s son, took a wife from the daughters of Putiel; she bore him Phinehas.

These are the heads of the Levitical families according to their clans.

This is Aaron and Moses, to whom the Lord commanded that they bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt according to their divisions.

These are the men who spoke to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring the children of Israel out of Egypt: Moses and Aaron, on the day when the Lord spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt.

[C. XV.] The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “I am the Lord. Speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, everything that I speak to you.”

Moses said before the Lord: “Behold, I am uncircumcised of lips; how will Pharaoh listen to me?”

[Cap. VII.] The Lord said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. You shall speak everything that I command you; he shall speak to Pharaoh, so that he may let the children of Israel go out from his land.

“But I will harden his heart and multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and they will not listen to you. I will stretch out my hand over Egypt and bring out my army and my people, the children of Israel, from the land of Egypt by very great judgments.

“The Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord, who stretched out my hand over Egypt and brought the children of Israel out from their midst.”

Moses and Aaron did just as the Lord had commanded them [Vulgate omits “them”]; so they acted.

[C. XVI.] Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.

The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “When Pharaoh says to you, ‘Show signs,’ say to Aaron: ‘Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh, and it will become a serpent.’”

Moses and Aaron entered before Pharaoh and did as the Lord had commanded. Aaron took up his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent.

Pharaoh summoned the wise men and sorcerers, and they too, by their Egyptian enchantments and certain secret arts, did likewise. Each threw down his staff, and the staffs became dragons; but Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs.

Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord [Hebrew] had said.

[First Plague.] The Lord said to Moses: “Pharaoh’s heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go. Go to him in the morning. Behold, he will go out to the waters, and you shall stand to meet him on the bank of the river. Take in your hand the staff that was changed into a dragon.

“You shall say to him: ‘The Lord God of the Hebrews has sent me to you, saying: “Let my people go, so that they may sacrifice to me in the wilderness”; and until now you have refused to listen.

“‘Thus says the Lord: “By this you shall know that I am the Lord. Behold, I will strike the water of the river with the staff that is in my hand, and it will be changed into blood. The fish that are in the river will die, the waters will become foul, and the Egyptians will suffer when they drink the water of the river.”’

The Lord said to Moses: “Say to Aaron: ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, channels, marshes, and all their pools of water, so that they may be changed into blood. Let there be blood throughout the whole land of Egypt, both in wooden vessels and in stone ones.’”

Moses and Aaron did so, as the Lord had commanded. Aaron lifted up the staff and struck the water of the river before Pharaoh and his servants, and it was changed into blood.

The fish that were in the river died, the river became foul, and the Egyptians could not drink the water of the river. There was blood throughout the whole land of Egypt.

The Egyptian sorcerers did likewise by their enchantments, and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened; he did not listen to them, as the Lord [Hebrew] had said.

He turned away and entered his house, and he did not set his heart even on this occasion.

All the Egyptians dug around the river for water to drink, for they could not drink from the water of the river.

Seven days were completed after the Lord had struck the river.

### [B. V, Chapter VIII, 2nd Plague]

The Lord also said to Moses [Col. 0249B]: “Go in to Pharaoh and say to him: Thus says the Lord: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will strike all your borders with frogs. The river shall swarm with frogs; they shall come up and enter your house, your bedchamber, and your bed, and the houses of your servants and your people, and your ovens and the remains of your food. They shall come upon you, your people, and all your servants.”

And the Lord said to Moses: “Say to Aaron: Stretch out your hand over the rivers, the canals, and the marshes, and bring frogs up over the land of Egypt.” Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up [Hebrew: frog], and covered the land [Col. 0249C] of Egypt. The magicians likewise acted by their enchantments and brought frogs up over the land of Egypt.

Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: “Pray to the Lord, that he may remove the frogs from me and from my people; and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the Lord.” Moses said to Pharaoh: “Appoint a time for me when I should pray for you, for your servants, and for your people, [Note: [Col. 0249D] Here, following the Septuagint, the printed Latin books read: ‘that the frogs may be driven away from you, from your house, from your servants, and from your people—and only in the river, etc.’ But in Hebrew, with which the Hebrew canon of truth agrees [Col. 0250D], it reads as we have published it. MART. —The same manuscript, together with the printed books and following the Greek, adds: ‘and from your servants, and from your people only, etc.’] so that the frogs may be driven away from you and from your house, and remain only in the river.”

He replied: “Tomorrow.” And he said: “I will act according to your word, so that you may know that there is none like the Lord our God. The frogs shall withdraw from you, from your house, from your servants, and from your people; they shall remain only in the river.”

Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the Lord concerning the agreement about the frogs [Col. 0249D] that he had made with Pharaoh. The Lord acted according to Moses’ word, and the frogs died in the houses, the villages, and the fields. They gathered them into enormous heaps, and the land became foul. But when Pharaoh saw that relief had been granted, he hardened his heart and did not listen to them, as the Lord had said [Vulgate: commanded].

### [T. V, 3rd Plague]

The Lord said to Moses: “Speak to Aaron: Stretch out your rod and strike the dust of the earth, and let there be gnats throughout the whole land of Egypt.” They did so. Aaron stretched out his hand, holding the rod [Col. 0250A], and struck the dust of the earth; and gnats came upon human beings and animals. All the dust of the earth throughout the whole land of Egypt became gnats.

The magicians likewise acted by their enchantments to bring forth gnats, but they could not. The gnats were upon human beings and animals. The magicians said to Pharaoh: “This is the finger of God” [Vulgate: “Here is the finger of God”]. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had spoken [Vulgate: commanded].

### [4th Plague]

The Lord also said to Moses: “Rise early and stand before Pharaoh; for he will go out to the waters. Say to him: Thus says the Lord: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. But if you do not let them go, behold, I will send upon you, your servants, your people, and your houses [Col. 0250B] every kind of flies. The houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with flies of various kinds, and likewise the whole land in which they are.

“On that day I will make the land of Goshen, where my people is, wondrous, so that no flies will be there; and you will know that I am the Lord in the midst of the land. I will set a division between my people and your people; tomorrow this sign shall occur.”

The Lord did so. A very grievous swarm of flies came into Pharaoh’s house, into the houses of his servants, and into the whole land of Egypt; and the land was ruined by such flies.

Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: “Go, sacrifice to your God in the land” [Vulgate and the Memphitic manuscript add: “here”].

Moses said: “It cannot be done in this way, for we shall sacrifice to the Lord our God what the Egyptians regard as abominations. If we sacrifice in their presence [Col. 0250C] what the Egyptians worship, they will stone us. We will go a three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the Lord our God, as he has commanded us.”

Pharaoh said: “I will let you go, that you may sacrifice to the Lord your God in the wilderness; only do not go farther away. Pray for me.”

Moses said: “When I go out from you, I will pray to the Lord, and tomorrow the flies will withdraw from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people. Only do not continue to deceive us by refusing to let the people sacrifice to the Lord.”

Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord. He acted according to Moses’ word and removed the flies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people; not one remained. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, so that even on this occasion he did not let the people go.

### [Col. 0250D] [Chapter IX, 5th Plague]

The Lord said to Moses: “Go in to Pharaoh and speak to him: Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. But if you still refuse and retain them, behold, my hand will be upon your fields, upon your horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, and sheep—a very grievous pestilence.

“The Lord will perform a marvelous distinction between the possessions of Israel and the possessions of the Egyptians, so that absolutely nothing of all that belongs to the children of Israel will perish. The Lord appointed a time, saying: Tomorrow the Lord will [Col. 0251A] perform this deed in the land.”

The Lord performed this deed on the following day, and all the livestock of the Egyptians died; but of the animals belonging to the children of Israel, not one died. Pharaoh sent to investigate, and nothing had died of what Israel possessed.

### [6th Plague]

Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not let the people go. The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “Take handfuls of ashes from the furnace, and let Moses scatter them toward heaven in Pharaoh’s presence. Let the dust be over the whole land of Egypt; for there will be wounds and swelling blisters upon human beings and animals throughout the whole land of Egypt” [Vulgate: “ulcers”].

They took ashes from the furnace and stood before Pharaoh, and Moses scattered them toward heaven. Wounds with swelling blisters appeared [Col. 0251B] upon human beings and animals. The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the wounds that were upon them and throughout the whole land of Egypt. The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had spoken to Moses.

### [7th Plague]

The Lord said to Moses: “Rise early and stand before Pharaoh, and say to him: Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. For on this occasion I will send all my plagues upon your heart [Vulgate adds: ‘and’], upon your servants, and upon your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth.

“For now, as I stretch out my hand [Vulgate omits ‘my hand’], I will strike you and your people with pestilence, and you will perish from the earth. But for this reason I have set you in place, that I may show my strength in you and that my name may be proclaimed throughout all the earth [Col. 0251C]. You still retain my people and are unwilling to let them go? Behold, at this very hour tomorrow I will rain down exceedingly heavy hail, such as has never been in Egypt from the day it was founded until the present time.

“Therefore send now and gather your animals and everything that you have in the field. For human beings and animals, and everything found outside and not gathered in from the fields, upon which the hail falls, will die.”

Whoever among Pharaoh’s servants feared the word of the Lord made his servants and his animals flee into the houses; but whoever disregarded the Lord’s word left his servants and his animals in the fields.

The Lord said to Moses: “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that hail may fall throughout the whole land of Egypt upon human beings, animals, and every plant of the field in the land of Egypt” [Col. 0251D].

Moses stretched out his rod toward heaven, and the Lord gave thunder and hail, with lightning flashing across the land. The Lord rained hail upon the land of Egypt. Hail and fire mingled together were carried along; and it was of such great magnitude as had never before appeared throughout the whole land of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0251] The Hebrew canon of truth reads differently, but with the same meaning: it reads as follows, ‘Since the nation was founded in that land.’ MART.].

The hail struck everything that was in the fields throughout the whole land of Egypt, from human beings to animals; the hail struck every plant of the field and shattered every tree of the region. Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, did the hail not fall [Col. 0252A].

Pharaoh sent for and summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them: “I have sinned even now. The Lord is righteous; I and my people are wicked. Pray to the Lord that God’s thunder and the hail may cease, and I will let you go, and you will no longer remain here.”

Moses said: “When I have gone out of the city, I will spread out my hands to the Lord, and the thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth belongs to the Lord. But I know that you and your servants still do not fear the Lord God.”

The flax and the barley were struck, because the barley was green and the flax was already putting forth its capsules; but the wheat and the spelt were not struck, because they were late crops.

Moses went out from Pharaoh, from the city, and stretched out his hands to the Lord. The thunder and the hail ceased, and the rain no longer fell upon the earth [Col. 0252B]. But when Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail, and thunder had ceased, he increased his sin; his heart, and the hearts of his servants, were hardened and exceedingly obstinate. He did not let the children of Israel go, as the Lord had spoken through Moses.

### [T. VI, Chapter X, 8th Plague]

The Lord said to Moses: “Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants, so that I may perform these signs of mine among them, and so that you may tell your son and your grandson how often I have crushed the Egyptians and performed my signs among them; and you will know [Vulgate: ‘you may know’] that I am the Lord.”

Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him: “Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: How long will you refuse to submit to me? Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. [Col. 0252C] But if you resist and refuse to let them go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your territory. They will cover the surface of the earth, so that no part of it will be visible, and they will eat what the hail has left. They will devour every tree that sprouts in the fields. They will fill your houses, the houses of your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians—something your fathers and grandfathers have never seen from the time they came upon the earth until this present day.”

He turned and went out from Pharaoh.

Pharaoh’s servants said to him: “How long shall we endure this as a snare? Let the men go, that they may sacrifice to the Lord their God. Do you not see that Egypt has perished?”

They brought Moses and Aaron back to Pharaoh, and he said to them: “Go, sacrifice to the Lord your God. Who are the ones who will go?” [Col. 0252D]

Moses said: “We will go with our children and our old men [Vulgate: ‘elders’], with our sons and daughters, with our sheep and cattle; for it is the feast of the Lord our God.”

Pharaoh replied: “May the Lord be with you in the same way that I will let you go with your children! It is clear that you are planning something evil. It shall not be so. Go, you men alone, and sacrifice to the Lord; for that is what you yourselves requested.”

And they were immediately driven from Pharaoh’s presence.

The Lord said to Moses: “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locust, so that it may come up over it and devour every plant that the hail has left.”

Moses stretched out his rod over the land of Egypt, and the Lord brought a scorching wind throughout that whole day and night. When morning came, the scorching wind lifted the locusts [Col. 0253A]. They came up over the whole land of Egypt and settled throughout all the territory of Egypt in countless numbers, such as had never existed before and would never exist afterward. They covered the whole surface of the earth, devastating everything.

The vegetation of the land was devoured, as was every fruit on the trees that the hail had left; nothing green remained on the trees or among the plants of the land, throughout all Egypt.

Therefore Pharaoh hastily called Moses and Aaron and said to them: “I have sinned against the Lord your God and against you. But now forgive my sin, even on this occasion, and pray to the Lord your God that he may take this death away from me” [Col. 0253B].

He went out from Pharaoh’s presence and prayed to the Lord. The Lord caused a very powerful west wind to blow, and it seized the locusts and cast them into the Red Sea; not one remained throughout all the territory of Egypt. But the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the children of Israel go.

### [9th Plague]

The Lord said to Moses: “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and let there be darkness over the land of Egypt, so dense that it can be felt.” Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and dreadful darkness came over the whole land of Egypt for three days. No one saw his brother, nor did anyone move from the place where he was; but wherever the children of Israel lived, there was light.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] The printed books, following the reading of the Septuagint interpreters and the Samaritan text, add here after ‘Moses’: ‘and Aaron.’ It should be known, however, that the word ‘Aaron’ is absent from the Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, and the frequently cited canon. MART. —Our manuscripts read: ‘Moses and Aaron, and he said to them,’ together with the printed books and in accordance with the Greek.]

Pharaoh called Moses and said: “Go, sacrifice to the Lord; only your sheep and cattle shall remain; your children may go with you” [Col. 0253C].

Moses said: “You yourself shall also give us sacrifices and burnt offerings to offer to the Lord our God. All our flocks shall go with us; not a hoof shall remain behind. For we do not know what must be offered in the worship of the Lord our God until we reach that place.”

The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he was unwilling to let them go.

Pharaoh said to Moses: “Withdraw from me” [Vulgate adds: “and”]. “Take care that you do not see my face again; on whatever day you appear before me, you will die.”

Moses replied: “It shall be as you have spoken; I will not see your face again” [Note: [Col. 0253D] The Urbinas manuscript and other manuscripts in Martianay’s possession read: ‘Let it be so.’].

### [C. XVII, Chapter XI]

The Lord said to Moses: “One more plague I will bring upon Pharaoh and Egypt [Col. 0253D]; after this he will let you go and compel you to depart. Therefore say to all the people that each man is to ask from his friend, and each woman from her neighbor, silver and gold vessels. The Lord will grant his people favor in the sight of the Egyptians.”

Moses was a very great man in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh’s servants and of all the people.

And he said: “Thus says the Lord: At midnight I will go out [Vulgate: ‘I will enter’] [Col. 0254A] into Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of the Egyptians shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits upon his throne, to the firstborn of the maidservant who is at the mill, and all the firstborn of the animals. There will be a great cry throughout the whole land of Egypt, such as has never been before and will never be again.

“But among all the children of Israel, from human being to animal, not even a dog will bark, so that you may know by what great marvel the Lord distinguishes between the Egyptians and Israel. Then all these servants of yours will come down to me and bow before me, saying: ‘Go out, you and all the people subject to you’; after that, we will go out.”

And he went out from Pharaoh in great anger.

The Lord said to Moses: “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that many signs may be performed in the land of Egypt.” Moses and Aaron performed all the wonders that are written [Col. 0254B] before Pharaoh; but the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the children of Israel go from his land [Vulgate omits “from his land”].

### [T. VII, B. VI, C. XVIII, Chapter XII]

The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. Speak to the entire assembly of the children of Israel and say to them:

“On the tenth day of this month, let each man take a lamb [Note: [Col. 0253D] The Hebrew canon of truth indicates from where the lamb is to be taken, for it adds ‘to their houses,’ and ‘from the sheep and goats’; the Arabic partly expresses this by saying ‘and that head from the sheep.’ It appears to be a marginal gloss placed into the body of the text by copyists. The closest parallel is found in Leviticus, chapter I, verse 10. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript omits the words ‘and houses.’ The Hebrew reads, ‘a lamb by the household of the fathers, a lamb by the household.’] according to their families and houses.

“But if the number is too small to suffice for eating the lamb, he shall take his neighbor who is joined to his house, according to the number of persons sufficient to eat the lamb. The lamb shall be without blemish, a male, one year old. According to the same rite, you shall also take a kid.

“You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the entire multitude of the children of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening. They shall take some of its blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintels of the houses in which they will eat it.

“They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted over the fire, and unleavened bread with wild lettuce. You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted over the fire; you shall consume its head with its feet and entrails. Nothing of it shall remain until morning; if anything is left over, you shall burn it with fire.

“Thus you shall eat it: you shall gird your loins, have sandals on your feet, and hold staffs in your hands; you shall eat in haste, for it is the Passover—that is, the Passing Over—of the Lord.

“I will pass through the land of Egypt on that night [Col. 0254D] and strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from human being to animal; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments. I am the Lord.

“The blood shall be a sign for you in the houses where you are. I will see the blood and pass over you, and there shall not be among you a destroying plague when I strike the land of Egypt.

“You shall have this day as a memorial [Col. 0255A], and you shall celebrate it as a feast to the Lord throughout your generations, as a perpetual observance.

“For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses. Whoever eats leavened food, that person shall perish from Israel, from the first day until the seventh day” [Note: [Col. 0255D] All the manuscripts read ‘fermented food’ instead of ‘leaven’; nevertheless, the reading of the printed editions should be retained, because in the Hebrew source we read ‘leaven,’ not ‘fermented food.’ MART. —Our manuscripts correctly read ‘leaven,’ unlike those used by Martianay, which read ‘fermented food.’ The Memphitic canon has this marginal note: ‘leaven, not, as others have it, fermented food.’].

“The first day shall be holy and solemn, and the seventh day shall likewise be honored with the same festival. No work shall be done on them, except what pertains to food.

“You shall observe the unleavened bread, for on that very day I will bring your army out of the land of Egypt; and you shall keep this day throughout your generations as a perpetual rite.

“In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month toward evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month toward evening. For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses [Col. 0255B]. Whoever eats leavened food, that person shall perish from the assembly of Israel, whether he is a resident alien or a native of the land. You shall eat no leavened food; in all your dwelling places you shall eat unleavened bread.”

Moses called all the elders [Hebrew] of Israel and said to them: “Go and take an animal by your families, and sacrifice the Passover. Dip a bundle of hyssop in the blood that is at the threshold, and sprinkle some of it on the lintel and on both doorposts. Let none of you go out through the door of his house until morning.

“For the Lord will pass through, striking the Egyptians. When he sees the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts, he will pass over the door of the house and will not permit the destroyer to enter your houses and harm you.

“Keep this prescribed word as a law for yourself and your children forever [Col. 0255C]. When you enter the land that the Lord will give you, as he promised, you shall observe these ceremonies.

“When your children say to you, ‘What does this religious observance mean to you?’ you shall say to them: ‘It is the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passing Over, when he passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt, striking the Egyptians and delivering our houses.’”

The people bowed down and worshiped. The children of Israel went and did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron.

### [10th Plague]

It happened at midnight: the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in prison, and every firstborn of the animals.

Pharaoh rose at night, along with all his servants and all Egypt, and a great cry arose in Egypt [Col. 0255D], for there was no house in which someone did not lie dead.

Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron by night [Vulgate adds: “Pharaoh”] and said: “Rise, go out from among my people, both you and the children of Israel. Go and sacrifice to the Lord, as you have said. Take your sheep and cattle, as you requested, and depart; and bless me.”

The Egyptians pressed the people to leave the land quickly, saying: “We are all going to die.”

The people therefore took their dough before it was leavened; tying it up in their cloaks, they placed it upon their shoulders. The children of Israel did as Moses had commanded, and they asked the Egyptians for silver and gold vessels and a great deal of clothing. The Lord granted the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they lent to them; and they despoiled the Egyptians.

### [T. VIII]

The children of Israel set out from Rameses for Succoth, about six hundred thousand foot soldiers who were men, apart from children [Note: [Col. 0256D] Three manuscripts of the Colbertine Library and one of the more recent manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés agree with the reading of the canon. In the others, the final words ‘and women’ appear to have been erased because of the canon’s marginal annotation. MART.] and women [Hebrew does not have “women”].

A mixed multitude, innumerable, also went up with them, together with sheep, cattle, and very many animals of various kinds. They baked the dough that they had brought from Egypt, having previously kneaded it, and made unleavened hearth-cakes; for they had been forced to leave by the Egyptians, who would not allow them to delay, and they had not been able to prepare any provisions [Col. 0256B].

### [C. XVIII]

The time that the children of Israel lived in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years. When these had been completed, on that same day the whole army of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.

This is a night to be observed for the Lord, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt; all the children of Israel must observe it throughout their generations.

### [C. XX]

The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “This is the rite of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it. Every purchased slave shall be circumcised, and then he may eat of it. A resident alien and a hired servant shall not eat of it.

“It shall be eaten in one house. You shall not carry any of its flesh outside, and you shall not break any of its bones. The whole assembly [Col. 0256C] of the children of Israel shall perform it.

“If any foreigner wishes to pass over into your settlement and celebrate the Passover to the Lord, every male belonging to him shall first be circumcised, and then he shall celebrate it properly; he shall be like a native of the land. But if any person has not been circumcised, he shall not eat of it.

“There shall be one law for the native and for the settler who dwells among you.”

All the children of Israel did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron. On that same day the Lord brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their companies.

### [T. VII, C. XXI, Chapter XIII]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Consecrate to me every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, whether of human beings or animals; for everything is mine.”

Moses said to the people: “Remember this day on which you went out from Egypt and from the house of slavery, because the Lord brought you out from this place with a strong hand; therefore you shall not eat leavened bread.

“You are going out today, in the month of new grain. When the Lord brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites, which he swore to your fathers that he would give you—a land flowing with milk and honey—you shall observe this sacred custom in this month [Col. 0257A].

“For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemn feast of the Lord. You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days; nothing leavened shall appear among you, nor within all your borders.

“On that day you shall tell your son, saying: ‘This is what the Lord did for me when I came out of Egypt.’ It shall be like a sign on your hand and like a memorial before your eyes, so that the law of the Lord may always be in your mouth; for the Lord brought you out of Egypt with a strong hand.

“You shall observe this religious practice at the appointed time, from days to days.

“When the Lord brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and to your fathers, and gives it to you, you shall set apart for the Lord everything that opens the womb, and every firstborn among your livestock; whatever male you have, you shall consecrate to the Lord [Col. 0257B].

“The firstborn of a donkey you shall exchange for a sheep; but if you do not redeem it, you shall kill it. Every firstborn of human beings among your sons you shall redeem with a price.

“When your son asks you tomorrow, saying, ‘What is this?’ you shall answer him: ‘The Lord brought us out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery, with a strong hand. For when Pharaoh had hardened his heart and was unwilling to let us go, the Lord killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of human beings to the firstborn of animals. Therefore I sacrifice to the Lord every male that opens the womb, and I redeem every firstborn of my sons.’

“It shall therefore be like a sign on your hand and like something suspended, as a memorial, between your eyes, because the Lord brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand.”

### [C. XXII]

[Col. 0257C] When Pharaoh had sent the people away, God did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, which was nearby, thinking that they might repent when they saw wars rising against them and return to Egypt. Instead, he led them around by the road through the wilderness near the Red Sea. The children of Israel went up armed from the land of Egypt.

Moses also took Joseph’s bones with him, because Joseph had made the children of Israel swear, saying: “God will visit you; take my bones away from here with you.”

They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness.

### [C. VIII]

The Lord went before them to show them the way, by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar [Col. 0257D] of fire, so that he might guide them on their journey at both times. The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night never failed to stand before the people.

### [C. XXIII, Chapter XIV]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel: Let them turn back and camp opposite Pi-hahiroth, which is between Migdol and the sea, facing Baal-zephon. You shall camp before it, beside the sea.

“Pharaoh will say concerning the children of Israel: ‘They are confined in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.’ I will harden his heart, and he will pursue you. I will be glorified in Pharaoh and in all his army, and the Egyptians shall know that I am [Col. 0258A] the Lord.”

They did so.

The king of Egypt was told that the people had fled. The heart of Pharaoh and his servants was changed concerning the people, and they said: “What have we done, letting Israel go so that they would no longer serve us?”

He harnessed his chariot and took all his people with him. He took six hundred chosen chariots, all the chariots that were in Egypt, and the commanders of the entire army.

The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and he pursued the children of Israel. But they had gone out with a raised hand.

When the Egyptians pursued the tracks of those who had gone ahead, they found them encamped beside the sea. All Pharaoh’s cavalry and chariots, and his entire army, were at Pi-hahiroth opposite Baal-zephon [Note: [Col. 0257D] Through the error of copyists, the first syllable, ‘phi,’ is omitted in all the manuscript copies, and only ‘they were at Abireth’ is read. This carelessness of the copyists should not have escaped the reader. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript has Pi-hahiroth correctly; the Palatine manuscript instead has Athiroth. The same Urbinas manuscript then omits the following name of Pharaoh.]

When Pharaoh drew near, [Col. 0258B] the children of Israel lifted their eyes and saw the Egyptians behind them. They were greatly afraid and cried out to the Lord. They said to Moses: “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us out to die in the wilderness? Why did you want to do this to us, bringing us out of Egypt? Is this not the word that we spoke to you in Egypt, saying: ‘Leave us alone, and let us serve the Egyptians’? For it is much better for us to serve them than to die in the wilderness.”

Moses said to the people: “Do not be afraid. Stand firm and see the great things the Lord will do today. For the Egyptians whom you see now, you will never see again, forever. The Lord will fight for you, and you will keep silent.”

The Lord said to Moses: “Why do you cry out to me? Speak to the children of Israel, so that they may set out. But you [Col. 0258C], raise your rod and stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it, so that the children of Israel may walk through the midst of the sea on dry ground.

“I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians, so that they will pursue you; and I will be glorified in Pharaoh, in all his army, in his chariots, and in his horsemen. The Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord, when I am glorified in Pharaoh, in his chariots, and in his horsemen.”

The angel of God who went before the camp of Israel moved and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved with him, leaving its former position and standing behind them, between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel. It was a dark cloud, yet it illuminated the night, so that the two camps could not approach one another throughout the whole night.

When Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, the Lord drove it back by a powerful [Col. 0258D] and scorching wind throughout the whole night and turned it into dry ground; the water was divided. The children of Israel entered through the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water was like a wall for them on their right and on their left.

The Egyptians pursued them and entered after them into the midst of the sea—all Pharaoh’s cavalry, his chariots, and his horsemen.

The morning watch had now arrived, and behold, the Lord looked upon the Egyptian camp through the pillar of fire and cloud. He destroyed their army and overturned the wheels of their chariots, which were carried into the depths [Col. 0259A].
