The Egyptians said: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord is fighting for them against us.”

The Lord said to Moses: “Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the waters may return upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots and horsemen.”

When Moses stretched out his hand toward the sea, at first light it returned to its former place. As the Egyptians fled, the waters met them, and the Lord overwhelmed them in the midst of the waves.

The waters returned and covered the chariots, the horsemen, and the entire army of Pharaoh that had entered the sea in pursuit; not one of them survived.

The children of Israel went through the midst of the dry sea, and the waters were like a wall for them on their right and on their left. On that day the Lord delivered Israel from the hand of the Egyptians.

They saw [Col. 0259B] the Egyptians dead upon the shore of the sea and the great hand that the Lord had exercised against them. The people feared the Lord, believed in the Lord, and believed in Moses his servant.

Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the Lord, saying:

Let us sing to the Lord,

for he has been gloriously exalted;

horse and rider he has cast into the sea.

The Lord is my strength and my praise;

he has become my salvation.

This is my God, and I will glorify him;

the God of my father, and I will exalt him.

The Lord is like a warrior;

the Almighty [Hebrew: “The Lord”] is his name.

[Note: [Col. 0259D] Rabbanus praises the edition that reads: “The Lord is his name.”]

He cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army [Col. 0259C] into the sea.

His chosen commanders were drowned in the Red Sea;

the abysses covered them;

they sank into the depths like a stone.

Your right hand, O Lord, [Note: [Col. 0259D] Manuscript copies read this passage in various ways. The Hebrew canon of truth reads: “I shall magnify your right hand, O Lord, in strength.” Others read: “Your right hand, O Lord, gloriously in strength.” One more recent manuscript reads: “Let it be glorified in strength.” Thus, according to the will of the copyists, many variant readings of a single sentence frequently occur. MART. —In another Latin edition praised by Rabbanus [Col. 0260D] it reads: “Your right hand, O Lord, has been glorified.”]

has been magnified in strength.

Your right hand, O Lord, struck the enemy;

and in the multitude of your glory you cast down

my adversaries [Hebrew: “your adversaries”].

[Note: [Col. 0260D] The printed editions read “your,” in accordance with the Hebrew. But all the older and best-known manuscripts have “my.” Therefore, so that nothing might be changed by our own authority, we have allowed the reading to remain as it is in the canon. MART. —Our manuscripts, and all the others, likewise have “my.” The Hebrew and the Vulgate, however, have “your.”]

You sent forth your anger, which devoured them like stubble;

and at the breath of your fury the waters were gathered together.

The flowing wave stood still;

the abysses were gathered together in the midst of the sea.

The enemy said: “I will pursue and overtake them;

I will divide the spoils;

my soul shall be filled.

[Col. 0259D] I will draw my sword;

my hand shall destroy them.”

Your breath blew, and the sea covered them;

they sank like lead in the mighty waters.

[Col. 0260A] Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord?

Who is like you, glorious in holiness,

terrible and praiseworthy, doing wonders?

You stretched out your hand [Bohairic: “your right hand”],

and the earth devoured them.

In your mercy you were a guide

of the people whom you redeemed.

In your strength you carried it

to your holy dwelling.

[Note: [Col. 0260D] Rabbanus also found in another edition: “The nations heard, and they were angry.”]

The peoples rose up, and they were angry [Heb. “The peoples heard, and they were dismayed”]:

anguish seized the inhabitants of Philistia.

Then the princes of Edom were thrown into confusion;

trembling seized the mighty men of Moab;

all the inhabitants of Canaan grew rigid with fear.

Let terror and dread fall upon them,

[Col. 0260B] through [Note: [Col. 0260D] One Palatine manuscript: “greatnesses.”] the greatness of your arm.

Let them become motionless like a stone,

until your people pass over, O Lord,

until this people of yours passes over, whom you have acquired.

You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance,

in your most secure dwelling-place, which you have made,

O Lord:

the sanctuary [Vulg. adds “your”], O Lord, which your hands have established.

The Lord will reign forever and beyond.

For [Heb. thus] Pharaoh’s horse entered with his chariots

and his horsemen into the sea;

and the Lord brought back upon them the waters of the sea.

But the children of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst

[Col. 0260C] of it.

[C. XXV.] Then Miriam, the prophet [Vulg. “prophetess”], Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dances. She led them in singing:

“Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified;

the horse and its rider he has cast into the sea.”

[T. IX, B. IX, C. XXVI.] Moses then led Israel away from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur. They traveled for three days through the desert and found no water. They came to Marah, but they could not drink the waters of Marah, because they were bitter; therefore he gave the place an appropriate name, calling it Marah, that is, “bitterness.” The people murmured against Moses, saying, “What shall we drink?” But he cried out to the Lord, who showed him a piece of wood. When he had thrown it into the waters, they were turned into sweetness. There he established for him commandments and judgments, and there he tested him [Heb. “and he said”], saying:

“If you will listen to the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is right before him, and obey his commandments, and keep all his precepts, [Col. 0261A] I will not bring upon you any of the sicknesses that I inflicted on Egypt; for I am the Lord, your healer.”

[C. XXVII.] The children of Israel came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped beside the waters.

[Cap. XVI.] They set out from Elim, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel came into the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had gone out from the land of Egypt. The whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. The children of Israel said to them:

“Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat beside pots of meat and ate bread to satiety [Heb. “in abundance”]. Why did you bring us out into this wilderness, [Col. 0261B] to kill this whole multitude with hunger?”

Then the Lord said to Moses:

“Behold, I will rain down bread for you from heaven [Heb. reading]. Let the people go out and gather enough for each day, so that I may test them, whether they will walk according to my law or not. But on the sixth day let them prepare what they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they were accustomed to gather on each day.”

Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel:

“In the evening you shall know that the Lord brought you out from the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord. For he has heard your murmuring against the Lord. But what are we, that you murmur [Vulg. “have murmured”] against us?”

And Moses said:

“The Lord will give you meat to eat in the evening and bread to satiety in the morning, because he has heard your murmurings with which you have murmured against him. For what are we? Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord.”

Then Moses said to Aaron:

“Say to the whole congregation of the children of Israel: Approach before the Lord, for he has heard your murmuring.”

And while Aaron was speaking to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud.

[C. XXVIII.] The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel. Speak to them: In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread [Heb. reading]; and you shall know that I am [Vulg. “I am”] the Lord your God.”

So it happened in the evening that quail came up and covered the camp; and in the morning dew lay all around the camp. When it had covered the surface of the earth, there appeared in the [Col. 0261D] wilderness something fine and flaky, like frost upon the ground. When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, “MANHU?”—which means, “What is this?” For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them:

“This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat. This is the word which the Lord has commanded: Let each person gather as much of it as is sufficient for eating, an omer per head, according to the number of your souls who dwell in the tent; thus you shall take it.”

The children of Israel did so. Some gathered more, others less. They measured it by the omer, and the one who had gathered more had no excess, nor did the one who had prepared less find any lack; each gathered according to what he could eat.

[Col. 0262A] Moses said to them:

“Let no one leave any of it until morning.”

But they did not listen to him; some left part of it until morning, and it began to swarm with worms and became rotten, and Moses was angry with them. They gathered it each morning, each according to what could suffice for eating; and when the sun grew hot, it melted.

On the sixth day they gathered twice as much food, that is, two omers for each person. All the leaders of the multitude came and reported this to Moses. He said to them:

“This is what the Lord has spoken: Tomorrow is a rest, a sabbath sanctified to the Lord. Whatever is to be prepared, prepare it; and whatever is to be cooked, cook it. Whatever remains, store it until morning.”

They did as Moses had commanded, and it did not become rotten, [Col. 0262B] nor was there any worm in it.

Moses said:

“Eat it today, because today is the sabbath of the Lord; it will not be found today in the field. Gather it for six days, but on the seventh day is the sabbath [Vulg. adds “of the Lord”]; therefore it will not be found.”

The seventh day came, and some of the people went out to gather, but they found nothing. The Lord said to Moses:

“How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my law? See that the Lord has given you the sabbath, and for this reason he gives you twice as much food on the sixth day. Let each person remain in his own place; no one is to go out from his place on the seventh day.”

So the people kept sabbath on the seventh day. The house of Israel called its name MAN. It was like white coriander seed, and its taste was like flour with honey.

[Col. 0262C] Moses said:

“This is the word which the Lord has commanded: Fill an omer from it, and let it be kept for future generations [Heb. lacks “future”], so that they may know the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when you were brought out from the land of Egypt.”

Moses said to Aaron:

“Take one vessel and put there as much MAN as an omer can hold, and place it before the Lord, to be preserved for your generations, as the Lord commanded Moses.”

Aaron placed it in the tabernacle for preservation.

[C. XXIX.] The children of Israel ate MAN for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land; they were fed with this food until they touched the borders of the land of Canaan. An omer is a tenth part of an [Heb. reading] ephah.

[T. X, B. X, C. XXX, Cap. XVII.] The whole multitude of the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin by their stages, according to the word of the Lord, and they encamped at Raphidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. They quarreled with Moses, saying:

“Give us water, so that we may drink.”

Moses replied to them:

“Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the Lord?”

The people thirsted there because of the lack of water, and they murmured against Moses, saying:

“Why did you bring us out of Egypt, to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”

Moses cried out to the Lord, saying:

“What shall I do with this people? A little more, and they will stone me.”

The Lord said to Moses:

“Go ahead of the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel. Take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there, upon the rock at Horeb. You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, so that the people may drink.”

Moses did so before the elders of Israel. He called the name of that place Temptation [Heb. “and strife”], because of the quarrel of the children of Israel and because they tested the Lord, saying:

“Is the Lord among us or not?”

[C. XXXI.] Amalek came and fought against Israel at Raphidim. Moses said to Joshua:

“Choose men, go out, and fight against Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill, holding the staff of God in my hand.”

Joshua did as Moses had told him, and he fought against Amalek. Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. When Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but whenever he lowered them slightly, Amalek prevailed.

Moses’ hands were heavy. So they took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat upon it. Aaron and Hur supported his hands on both sides. His hands remained steady until sunset. Joshua routed Amalek and his people by the edge of the sword.

The Lord said to Moses:

“Write this as a memorial in a book, and announce it to Joshua’s ears: I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.”

Moses built an altar and called its name, “The Lord is my exaltation,” saying:

“Because there is a hand upon the throne [Vulg. “throne-seat”] of the Lord, there will be war for the Lord against Amalek from generation to generation.”

[C. XXXII, Cap. XVIII.] When Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ kinsman, heard all that God had done for Moses and for his people Israel, because the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt, he took Zipporah, Moses’ wife whom he had sent away, and her two sons. One of them was called Gershom, because, his father said, “I was a sojourner in a foreign land.” The other was Eliezer, because, he said, “The God of my father was my help and delivered me from Pharaoh’s sword.”

Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, came with Moses’ sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness, where he was encamped beside the mountain of God. He sent word to Moses, saying:

“I, your kinsman Jethro, am coming to you, and your wife and your two sons with her.”

Moses went out to meet his kinsman, bowed down, and kissed him. They greeted one another with words of peace. When Moses had entered the tent, he told his kinsman everything that the Lord had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians [Col. 0263D] for Israel’s sake, all the hardship that had befallen them on the journey, and how [Vulg. “and that”] the Lord had delivered them.

Jethro rejoiced over all the good things that the Lord had done for Israel, because he had rescued him from the hand of the Egyptians, and he said:

“Blessed is the Lord, who delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of Pharaoh, who rescued his people from the hand of Egypt. Now I know that the Lord is great above all gods, because they acted arrogantly against them.”

Moses’ kinsman offered burnt offerings and sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0263D] Our manuscripts likewise read “to God”; Martianus found “to the Lord” in other copies.] to God. Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with him before God.

[Col. 0264A] [C. XXXIII.] On the following day Moses sat to judge the people, who stood before Moses from morning until evening. When his kinsman saw everything he was doing among the people, he said:

“What is this that you are doing among the people? Why do you sit alone while all the people wait from morning until evening?”

Moses replied:

“The people come to me seeking God’s judgment. Whenever some dispute arises among them, they come to me to judge between them, and I show them God’s precepts and his laws.”

But he said:

“You are not doing a good thing. You and this people who are with you are wearing yourselves out with futile labor. The task is beyond your strength; you cannot bear it alone. But listen to my words and advice, and God will be with you.

“Be the people’s representative in matters that concern God, so that you may bring their words before him. Show the people the ceremonies and the rite of worship, the way in which they must walk, and the work that they must do [Vulg. adds “must do”]. But choose from the whole people capable men who fear God, in whom there is truth and who hate avarice. Appoint them as tribunes, centurions, commanders of fifty, and decans, to judge the people at all times. Whatever is more serious, let them refer to you; let them judge only the lesser matters, so that the burden, divided among others, may be lighter for you.

“If you do this, you will fulfill God’s command, and you will be able to bear his precepts; and all this people will return peacefully to their places.”

After hearing this, Moses did everything that he had suggested. He selected capable men from all Israel and appointed them as leaders of the people, tribunes, [Col. 0264C] centurions, commanders of fifty, and decans. They judged the people at all times; whatever was more difficult, they referred to him, judging only the easier cases.

Then he dismissed his kinsman [Vulg. adds “his own”], who returned and went to his own land.

[T. XI, B. XI, C. XXXIV, Cap. XIX.] In the third month after the children of Israel had gone out from the land of Egypt [Heb. reading], on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. For they had set out from Raphidim and reached the wilderness of Sinai, and they encamped in that same place. Israel pitched its tents opposite the mountain.

Moses went up to God, and the Lord called to him from the mountain, saying:

“These are the words you shall say to the house of Jacob and announce to the children of Israel: You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, how I carried you on eagles’ wings [Col. 0264D] and took you to myself. Now, therefore, if you will listen to my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for the whole earth is mine. And you shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation. These are the words that you shall speak to the children of Israel.”

Moses came, summoned the elders of the people, and set before them all the words that the Lord had commanded him. The entire people answered together:

“Everything that the Lord has spoken, we will do.”

When Moses had reported the people’s words to the Lord, the Lord said to him:

“Behold, now I will come to you in the darkness of a cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking with you and may believe you forever.”

[C. XXXV.] Moses therefore announced the people’s words to the Lord. He said to him:

“Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments. Let them be ready for the third day, for on the third day the Lord will descend before the entire people upon Mount Sinai. Establish boundaries around the people and say [Vulg. adds “to them”]: Beware lest you go up the mountain or touch its boundaries. Everyone who touches the mountain shall be put to death. No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or pierced with arrows [Heb. alternatively: “Let no hand touch him, for if he touches it, he shall be stoned”]. Whether it is an animal or a human being, it shall not live. When the trumpet begins to sound, then let them go up the mountain.”

Moses went down from the mountain to the people [Col. 0265B] and sanctified them. When they had washed their garments, he said to them:

“Be ready for the third day; do not approach your wives.”

The third day had arrived, and morning had dawned. Behold, thunder began to be heard, lightning flashed, and a very dense cloud covered the mountain. The sound of the trumpet resounded ever more loudly, and all the people who were in the camp were afraid [Vulg. omits “all”].

When Moses had led them out from the place of the camp to meet God, they stood at the foot of the mountain. Now [Vulg. “Then”] the whole mountain of Sinai was smoking, because the Lord had descended upon it in fire, and smoke rose from it like smoke from a furnace. The entire mountain was terrifying. The sound of the trumpet gradually grew louder and extended for a longer time.

Moses spoke, and God answered him. The Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, upon the very summit of the mountain, and called Moses to its top. When he had ascended, he said to him:

“Go down and warn the people, lest they wish to cross the boundaries in order to see the Lord, and a very great multitude of them perish. The priests also who approach the Lord must sanctify themselves, lest he strike them.”

Moses said to the Lord:

“The people cannot go up Mount Sinai, for you yourself warned us and commanded us: ‘Set boundaries around the mountain and sanctify it.’”

[C. XXXVI.] The Lord said to him:

“Go, go down. Then you shall come up, and Aaron with you; but let neither the priests nor the people cross the boundaries or go up to the Lord, lest he strike them.”

Moses went down to the people and told them everything.

[Col. 0265D] [C. XXXVII, Cap. XX.] God spoke all these words:

[1st Commandment] “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery.

[2nd Commandment] “You shall have no foreign gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth. You shall not worship or serve them; for I am the Lord your God, a strong and jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation [Col. 0266A] of those who hate me, and showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.

[3rd Commandment] “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not hold innocent the one who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain.

[4th Commandment] “Remember to sanctify the sabbath day. For six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it—you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, your animal, or the sojourner who is within your gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the sabbath day and sanctified it.

[5th Commandment] “Honor your father and your mother, so that [Col. 0266B] you may live long upon the land that the Lord your God will give you.

[6th Commandment] “You shall not kill.

[7th Commandment] “You shall not commit adultery.

[8th Commandment] “You shall not steal.

[9th Commandment] “You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor.

[10th Commandment] “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not desire his wife, his male servant, his female servant, his ox, his donkey, or anything that belongs to him.”

[C. XXXVIII.] The entire people saw the voices and the torches, and the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain. Terrified and shaken with fear, they stood far away and said to Moses:

“Speak to us, and we will listen; but let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.”

Moses said to the people:

“Do not be afraid. For God has come in order to test you, and so that the fear of him may be before you and you may not sin.”

The people stood at a distance.

[T. XII, C. XXXIX.] Moses approached the darkness in which God was. The Lord also said to Moses:

“These are the things you shall say to the children of Israel: You yourselves have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make [Note: [Col. 0265D] The word “with me” is absent in the printed editions; nevertheless it occurs in the Hebrew source, in the Hebrew canon of truth, and in other older and better Latin manuscripts. The same reading is found in Augustine’s *Speculum*, where the Scriptures are quoted according to the Latin translation of St. Jerome, which he produced from the Hebrew. MART. —One Palatine manuscript omits the word “with me.”] gods of silver with me, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves.

“You shall make an altar of earth for me, and you shall offer upon it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where there shall be a memorial of my name, I will come to you and bless you.

“But if you make a stone altar for me, you shall not build it from cut stones; for if you lift your knife over it [Vulg. omits “your”], it will be polluted. You shall not go up by steps to my altar, lest your nakedness be exposed [Heb. “upon it”].”

[C. XL, Cap. XXI.] “These are the judgments that you shall set before them.

“If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years; in the seventh he shall go out free, without payment. With whatever garment he entered, with that he shall go out. If he had a wife, his wife shall also go out with him. But if his master gives him a wife, and she bears sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, while he shall go out with his garment.

“But if the servant says, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,’ his master shall bring him before the gods, and he shall be brought to the door and the doorposts. He shall pierce his ear with an awl, [Col. 0267A] and he shall be his servant forever [Note: [Col. 0267D] Thus the Hebrew canon of truth and another manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, no. 3, read. In the printed editions the sense and order of the words are entirely different, since they contain a general command concerning anyone who sells his daughter; here, however, the meaning concerns a servant whose master sells the servant’s daughter as a maidservant. Whoever wishes may compare this edition with the previously published copies. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript reads “a servant forever.” Together with the Palatine, Memmian, and printed editions, it then reads, “if anyone sells his daughter as a maidservant.”].

[C. XLI.] “If he sells his daughter as a maidservant, she shall not go out as maidservants ordinarily go out. If she displeases the eyes of her master to whom she was given, he shall let her go; but he shall not have the power to sell her to a foreign people if he rejects her. But if he betroths her to his son, he shall treat her according to the custom of daughters. If he takes another wife for him, he shall provide the girl with marriage, clothing, and shall not deny her the price of her virginity. If he does not do these three things, she shall go out free, without payment.

[C. XLII.] “Whoever strikes a person intending to kill him shall be put to death. But if he did not lie in wait for him, and God delivered him into his hands, I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.

[C. XLIII.] “If someone deliberately kills his neighbor by ambush, you shall drag him away from my altar, so that he may die.

[C. XLIV.] “Whoever strikes his father or mother shall be put to death.

[C. XLV.] “Whoever steals a person and sells him, when convicted of the offense, shall be put to death.

[C. XLVI.] “Whoever curses his father or mother shall be put to death.

[C. XLVII.] “If men quarrel and one strikes his neighbor with a stone or a fist, and the latter does not die but lies in bed; if he rises and walks outside supported by his staff, the one who struck him shall be innocent, provided that he compensates him for his labor and pays his medical expenses.

[C. XLVIII.] “Whoever strikes his male servant or female servant with a rod, and he dies in his hands [Note: [Col. 0267D] We have restored this passage according to Saint Augustine’s *Speculum*, where we read, as in the Hebrew, ‘and he dies,’ etc. All other books read in the plural, ‘and they die.’ MART. —The same manuscripts and printed books read ‘and they die.’ Martianus took the printed reading from Augustine’s *Speculum*.], shall be guilty of a crime. But if he survives for a day or two, he shall not be subject to punishment, because he is his property.

[C. XLIX.] “If men quarrel and one strikes a pregnant woman, causing a miscarriage, but she herself survives, he shall be subject to a penalty in whatever amount the woman’s husband demands and the arbitrators determine.

[C. L.] “But if her death follows, he shall give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.

[C. LI.] “If someone strikes the eye of his male or female servant and makes them one-eyed, he shall set them free for the eye that he removed. If he knocks out a tooth of his male or female servant, he shall likewise set them free.

[C. LII.] “If an ox gores [Vulg. ‘strikes’] a man or woman with its horn, and they die, it shall be stoned, and its meat shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be innocent.

[Col. 0267D] “But if the ox has been known to be horned from yesterday and the day before, and its owner has been warned but has not shut it up, and it kills a man or woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner shall be put to death. If a ransom is imposed upon him, he shall give for his life whatever is demanded of him. If it gores a son or daughter, the same judgment shall apply. If it attacks a male or female servant, he shall give thirty shekels of silver to the master, while the ox shall be stoned.

[C. LIII.] “If someone opens a cistern, digs one, and does not cover it, and an ox or donkey falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall repay the value of the animals; but the dead animal shall be his.

[C. LIV.] “If one person’s ox wounds another person’s ox, and it dies, they shall sell the living ox and divide the price, and they shall divide the carcass of the dead ox between them. But if it was known that the ox had been horned from yesterday and the day before, [Col. 0268B] and its owner did not keep it under guard, he shall repay an ox for an ox, and he shall receive the entire carcass.

[C. LV, Cap. XXII.] “If someone steals an ox or a sheep and kills or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep.

[C. LVI.] “If a thief is found breaking into a house, whether by forcing it open or by digging through it, and, after receiving a wound, dies, the one who struck him shall not be guilty of bloodshed. But if he does this after sunrise, he has committed murder, and he himself shall die. If he does not have what he can repay for the theft, he shall be sold [Vulg. adds ‘he himself’]. If what he stole is found alive with him, whether an ox, donkey, or sheep, he shall repay double.

[C. LVII.] “If someone damages a field or vineyard and lets his animal loose to graze what belongs to another, he shall repay as compensation for the damage whatever is best in his own field or vineyard.

[C. LVIII.] “If a fire, having broken out, finds [Note: [Col. 0268D] Through an easy scribal error, all the manuscript copies except the Hebrew canon of truth read ‘ears of grain’ here; that canon retains the correct reading, namely ‘thorns.’ The scribes of our copies follow the error in Saint Augustine’s *Speculum*, not from ignorance but out of reverence, because of the unanimous agreement of the manuscript copies they had examined. MART. —The Vulgate copy and Martianus’s Hebrew Canon of Truth likewise correctly read ‘thorns.’ Most other Latin books, and our manuscripts, read ‘ears of grain.’] thorns and catches hold of heaps of grain or standing crops in the fields, the one who kindled the fire shall repay the damage.

[C. LIX.] “If someone entrusts money or a vessel to a friend for safekeeping, and it is stolen from the person who received it, then, if the thief is found, he shall repay double. If the thief is not discovered, the master of the house shall approach the gods and swear that he did not extend his hand against his neighbor’s property to commit fraud, whether concerning an ox, donkey, sheep, garment, or anything else that can cause damage. The matter of both parties shall come before the gods, and if they give judgment against him, he shall repay double to his neighbor.

[C. LX.] “If someone entrusts his neighbor with a donkey, ox, sheep, or any animal for safekeeping, and it dies, is injured, or is captured by enemies, with no one seeing it, there shall be an oath between them that he did not extend his hand against his neighbor’s property. The owner shall accept the oath, and the other shall not be compelled to make restitution. But if it was taken by theft, he shall repay the loss to the owner. If it was devoured by a wild beast, [Note: [Col. 0269C] The punctuation of this passage differs in the current Hebrew text and in the Samaritan text. In Hebrew it reads: “He shall bring it as a witness; what was torn he shall not restore.” But in the Samaritan scroll it is written, *jabi ed hatterepha, velo jesallem*, that is, “He shall bring a witness of the torn animal, and he shall not restore it.” The two texts differ not only in punctuation but also somewhat in wording. The Hebrew reads with the attached pronoun, *jebiehu*, “he shall bring it”; the Samaritan, without any pronoun, *jabi*, “he shall bring.” The Samaritan likewise has *velo* with the connective particle, whereas the Hebrew has no connective conjunction with the negation, *lo*. Moreover, no one should doubt that some things were transposed in the Hebrew text by the punctuation of the Masoretes, since Jerome read in his Hebrew copy as the Samaritans now read. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript reads *deferet*, the Palatine *deferat*. Martianus is perhaps not entirely right in saying that Jerome read in his Hebrew copy as the Samaritans now read. For the words ‘to him’ indicate that he knew the pronoun, which occurs in Hebrew but not in Samaritan; and in what follows, where the text has ‘what was killed,’ he seems to have read the article as a witness to the Samaritan form, approximately *jabihou eth attrephah*.] he shall bring to him what was killed, and he shall not restore it.

[C. LXI.] “If anyone borrows from his neighbor any of these things, and it is injured or dies while the owner is not present, he shall be compelled to make restitution. But if the owner is present, he shall not make restitution, especially if the animal had been hired for payment for his work.

[C. LXII.] “If someone seduces a virgin who is not yet betrothed and sleeps with her, he shall provide her dowry and take her as his wife. If the virgin’s father refuses to give her, he shall pay money according to the amount of the dowry that virgins customarily receive.

[Col. 0269B] [C. LXIII.] “You shall not allow sorceresses to live.

[C. LXIV.] “Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death.

[C. LXV.] “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be killed, except to the Lord alone.

[C. LXVI.] “You shall not grieve or oppress a sojourner, for you yourselves were also sojourners in the land of Egypt.

[C. LXVII.] “You shall not harm a widow or an orphan. If you harm them, they will cry out to me, and I will hear their cry. My anger will be kindled, and I will strike you with the sword; your wives will become widows, and your children orphans.

[C. LVIII.] “If you lend money to my poor people who dwell with you, you shall not press him like a creditor or oppress him with interest. If you take your neighbor’s garment as a pledge, you shall return it to him before sunset. For it is the only thing by which he covers his body [Col. 0269C]; he has nothing else in which to sleep. If he cries out [Heb. ‘And it shall be, if he cries out’] to me, I will hear him, because I am merciful.

[C. LXIX.] “You shall not speak abusively of the gods, and you shall not curse the ruler of your people.

[C. LXX.] “You shall not delay offering your tithes and your firstfruits.

[C. LXXI.] “You shall give me the firstborn of your sons. You shall do likewise with oxen and sheep: let it remain with its mother for seven days; on the eighth day you shall give it to me.

[C. LXXII.] “You shall be holy men for me. You shall not eat meat that has been tasted by wild beasts; instead, you shall throw it to the dogs.”

[Col. 0270A] [C. LXXIII, Cap. XXIII.] You shall not give credence to a lying report. [C. LXXIV.] Nor shall you join your hand with the wicked, so as to give false testimony. [C. LXXV.] You shall not follow the crowd in doing evil. [C. LXXVI.] Nor, in judgment, shall you agree with the opinion of the majority so as to deviate from the truth. [C. LXXVII.] Nor shall you show pity to the poor in his case.

[Note: [Col. 0270C] The ancient manuscript codices of the Bible, as well as Saint Augustine’s *Speculum* in the manuscript of the Church of Chartres, agree with this reading of the canon. In Hebrew it is written *beribo*, which means “in his case,” “in his lawsuit,” or “in his business.” MART. —The Palatine manuscript likewise has *pauperis quoque misereberis in judicio* (“you shall also show pity to the poor in judgment”), without the negative particle. The Urbinas differs from the printed reading by one word, *quoque*, which it omits.] 

[C. LXXVIII.] If you come upon your enemy’s ox or his wandering donkey, bring it back to him. [C. LXXIX.] If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying beneath its burden, you shall not pass by, but shall help him raise it. [C. LXXX.]

[Note: [Col. 0270D] The meaning is: You shall not pervert judgment when a poor man is litigating before you. Saint Augustine’s *Speculum* instructed us that it should be read in this way; for all the other books, both printed and manuscript, read incorrectly: “You shall not turn aside in the judgment of the poor.” The Hebrew has: “You shall not turn aside,” or “you shall not bend the judgment of your poor man in his lawsuit,” a sense that agrees very well with our Latin text. MART.]

You shall not pervert judgment against the poor. [C. LXXXI.] You shall flee from falsehood. [C. LXXXII.] You shall not kill the innocent and the just, because I reject the wicked. [C. LXXXIII.] Nor shall you accept gifts, which blind even the prudent and overturn the words of the just. [C. LXXXIV.] [Col. 0270B] You shall not harass the foreigner, for you know the souls of foreigners, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

[B. XII.] For six years you shall sow your land and gather its produce. But in the seventh year you shall release it and let it rest, so that the poor of your people may eat, and whatever remains the beasts of the field may eat. You shall do the same with your vineyard and your olive grove.

[C. LXXXV.] For six days you shall work; on the seventh day you shall cease, so that your ox and donkey may rest, and the son of your maidservant and the foreigner may be refreshed. [C. LXXXVI.] You shall keep everything that I have said to you. And you shall not swear by the name of the eternal gods, nor shall it be heard from your mouth. [C. LXXXVII.] Three times each year you shall celebrate feasts for me. [C. LXXXVIII.] You shall observe the feast of Unleavened Bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time of the month of new produce, when you came out of Egypt. [C. LXXXIX.] You shall not appear before me empty-handed. And you shall observe the feast of the firstfruits of your work, of whatever you have sown in the field. You shall also observe the feast at the end of the year, when you have gathered all your crops from the field. [C. XC.] Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord God [Vulgate adds: “your God”]. You shall not sacrifice the blood of my victim with leaven, nor shall the fat of my feast remain until morning. [C. XCI.] You shall bring the firstfruits of the produce of your land into the house of the Lord your God. [C. XCII.] You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk. [C. XCIII.] Behold, I shall send an angel before you, to guard you on the way and bring you to the place that I have prepared. Watch over him and listen to his voice, and do not think him contemptible, for he will not pardon when you have sinned, and my name is in him. [C. XCIV.] But if you listen to his voice and do everything that I say, I shall be an enemy to your enemies and shall afflict those who afflict you. My angel shall go before you and bring you to the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, whom I shall crush. [C. XCV.] You shall not worship their gods or serve them; you shall not do what they do, but shall destroy them and smash their statues. You shall serve the Lord your God, and I shall bless your bread and your waters, and remove sickness from your midst. There shall be no barren or sterile woman in your land; I shall complete the number of your days. [C. XCVI.] I shall send my terror ahead of you, and I shall kill every people among whom you enter, and I shall make all your enemies turn their backs before you, sending hornets ahead of you, which will drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite before you enter. I shall not drive them out from before you in a single year, lest the land become a wasteland and the wild beasts multiply against you. Little by little I shall drive them out from your sight, until you increase and possess the land. I shall set your boundaries from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the river. I shall place the inhabitants of the land into your hands and drive them out from before you. You shall not enter into a covenant with them or with their gods. They shall not dwell in your land, lest perhaps they make you sin against me if you serve their gods; for this would certainly become a snare to you.

[Note: [Col. 0271D] We read “of the Philistines,” not “of the Palestinians,” as it appears in the printed and manuscript books, relying on the authority of Jerome himself, who discusses the matter in his commentary on Daniel, chapter eleven: “It should be noted that, since the Hebrew language does not have the letter π but uses פ (*phe*) in its place, whose force is expressed by the Greek φ (*phi*), in this one place among the Hebrews *phe* is indeed written but read as *p*. Therefore, except for the word *Apadno* in Daniel, *ph* is always read in Hebrew words”—as he also frequently observed in the canon of Hebrew truth—“where others have *p*, as above in the name *Putiphar*, and so forth.” MART. —One Palatine manuscript has “of the Palestinians”; the others preserve the reading that Jerome evidently preferred, “of the Philistines.”]

[C. XCVII, Cap. XXIV.] He also said to Moses: “Go up to the Lord—you, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel—and you shall worship from a distance. Moses alone shall go up to the Lord; they shall not approach, nor shall the people go up with him.”

[T. XIII, B. XIII.] So Moses came and recounted to the people all the words and judgments of the Lord, and all the people answered with one voice: “All the words that the Lord has spoken, we shall do.”

[C. XCVIII.] Moses wrote down all the words of the Lord. Rising early in the morning, he built an altar at the foot of the mountain, [Col. 0271D] and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. He sent young men from among the children of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed calves as peace offerings to the Lord. Moses took half of the blood and put it into bowls; the remaining half he poured upon the altar. Then, taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people, who said: “Everything that the Lord has spoken, we shall do, and we shall be obedient.” But he took the blood and sprinkled it upon the people, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you concerning all these words.”

[C. XCIX.] Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up. [C. C.] And they saw the God of Israel, and beneath his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear. Yet he did not stretch out his hand against those who had withdrawn to a distance from the children of Israel. They saw God, and they ate and drank.

[C. CI.] The Lord said to Moses: “Go up to me on the mountain and remain there. I shall give you the stone tablets, and the law and commandments that I have written, so that you may teach them.” Moses rose, with Joshua his servant. As Moses went up the mountain of God, he said to the elders: “Wait here until we return to you. You have Aaron and Hur with you; if any dispute arises, refer it to them.” When Moses had gone up, the cloud covered the mountain, and the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Sinai, covering it with a cloud for six days.

[C. CII.] On the seventh day he called him [Vulgate adds: “the Lord called him”] from the midst of the darkness. The appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a burning fire upon the summit of the mountain, in the sight of the children of Israel. Moses entered into the midst of the cloud and went up the mountain; and he was there for forty days and forty nights.

[C. CIII, Cap. XXV.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, that they may take firstfruits [Hebrew: offerings] for me. From every person who offers willingly, you shall receive them.”

[Note: [Col. 0272D] Without exception, the manuscript codices read *qui offert* (“who offers”). Nevertheless, the editors’ reading seems preferable, because it is closer both to the sense of Scripture and to the Hebrew truth. MART.]

[C. CIV.] These are the things that you shall receive: gold, silver, and bronze; violet material, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, violet-colored skins, acacia wood, oil for preparing the lamps [Hebrew does not have “for preparing”]; spices for anointing oil, and fragrant incense; onyx stones and gems for decorating the ephod and the breastpiece. They shall make me a sanctuary, and I shall dwell in their midst. According to every likeness of the tabernacle that I shall show you, and of all its vessels for its worship, so shall you make it.

[C. CV.] You shall construct an ark of acacia wood, whose length shall be two and a half cubits, its width a cubit and a half, and its height likewise a cubit and a half. You shall overlay it with purest gold, inside and out, and make a gold molding around it. You shall cast four gold rings for it and place them at its four corners: two rings on one side and two on the other. You shall make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. You shall insert them through the rings that are on the sides of the ark, so that it may be carried by them. They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be removed from them. You shall place in the ark the testimony that I shall give you.

You shall also make a mercy seat of purest gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. You shall make two golden Cherubim, hammered out, at the two sides of the oracle. [Note: [Col. 0273D] In one manuscript codex of the monastery of Corbie, and also in the canon of Hebrew truth, the word “oracle” is added here; thus they read: “One Cherub shall be at one side of the oracle.” MART.] Let one Cherub be on one side and the other on the other. They shall cover both sides of the mercy seat, spreading out their wings and covering the oracle; they shall face one another, with their faces turned toward the mercy seat, which is to cover the ark, in which you shall place the testimony that I shall give you. From there I shall command you and speak to you above the mercy seat, [Note: [Col. 0273D] The Vulgate has: “above the mercy seat and from the midst,” and so forth.] namely, from between the two Cherubim that shall be above the ark of the testimony, concerning everything that I shall command you for the children of Israel.

You shall also make a table of acacia wood, two cubits long, one cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. You shall overlay it with purest gold and make a gold rim around it. For the rim you shall make a molding four fingers high, and above it another gold molding [Hebrew does not have “another”]. [Note: [Col. 0273D] This marginal note is certainly not genuine, or must be judged to have been placed in the wrong location. For the words marked with an asterisk, which it says are absent from the Hebrew, are found in all Hebrew books. What this scholion means, therefore, we cannot know. MART.]

You shall also prepare four gold rings and place them at the four corners of the table, by each foot. Beneath the molding there shall be gold rings, so that poles may be inserted through them and the table carried. You shall make these poles also of acacia wood and overlay them with gold, for carrying the table. You shall prepare its dishes, bowls, censers, and cups, in which libations are to be offered, from purest gold. You shall place upon the table the bread of the Presence, before me always.

You shall also make a lampstand of purest gold, hammered out, with its shaft, branches, cups, spheres, and lilies proceeding from it. Six branches shall extend from its sides, three from one side and three from the other. Three cups shaped like almonds, with a sphere and a lily together, shall be on each branch; and likewise three cups shaped like almonds on the other branch, with a sphere and a lily together. This shall be the work of the six branches extending from the shaft. On the lampstand itself there shall be four cups shaped like almonds, with spheres and lilies on each. There shall be a sphere beneath two branches in three places, making six in all, proceeding from the one shaft. Thus the spheres and branches shall be from the lampstand itself, all hammered out of purest gold.

You shall also make seven lamps and place them upon the lampstand, so that they may give light in front of it. The tongs and trays into which the trimmings are to be extinguished shall also be made of purest gold. The entire weight of the lampstand, with all its vessels, shall be one talent of purest gold. See that you make them according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain.

[Cap. XXVI.] As for the tabernacle, you shall make it as follows: You shall make ten curtains of twisted fine linen, violet material, purple, and scarlet twice-dyed, variegated with embroidered work. The length of one curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits and its width four cubits. All the tent-cloths shall be of one measure. Five curtains shall be joined to one another, and the other five shall be joined together in a similar fashion. You shall make violet loops along the sides and tops of the curtains, so that they may be fastened to one another. Each curtain shall have fifty loops on either side, inserted so that the loops face one another and one may be fitted to the other. You shall also make fifty gold clasps by which the curtains are to be joined, so that the whole becomes one tabernacle.

You shall make eleven curtains of goats’ hair, to cover the roof of the tabernacle. The length of one curtain shall be thirty cubits and its width four; all the curtains shall have the same measure. Five of them you shall join separately, and six you shall join together, so that you double the sixth curtain at the front of the roof. You shall make fifty loops at the edge of one curtain, so that it may be joined to the other, and fifty loops at the edge of the other curtain, so that it may be fastened to the other.

[Note: [Col. 0274D] The canon and all the manuscript codices join this passage to what precedes it. Therefore, in none of them do you read “you shall also make”; rather, immediately after “that it may be fastened to the other,” it says: “fifty clasps,” and so forth. Following Jerome’s practice, we do not wish to alter the readings of the printed books where there is no loss of meaning. MART.]

You shall also make fifty bronze clasps, by which the loops shall be joined, so that the whole becomes one covering. Whatever remains of the curtains prepared for the roof—that is, the one curtain that is extra—you shall cover the rear of the tabernacle with half of it. A cubit shall hang over on one side, and another cubit on the other, from what exceeds the length of the curtains, covering both sides of the tabernacle. You shall also make another covering for the roof from rams’ skins dyed red, and above this still another covering from violet-colored skins.

You shall make upright boards for the tabernacle of acacia wood, each ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. On the sides of each board there shall be two tenons, by which one board may be joined to another; in this way all the boards shall be prepared. Twenty of them shall be on the southern side, facing the South. For them you shall cast forty silver bases, so that two bases are placed beneath each board at its two corners. On the second side of the tabernacle, facing the North, there shall also be twenty boards, with forty silver bases. Two bases shall be placed beneath each board.

For the western side of the tabernacle you shall make six boards, and again two others to be erected at the rear corners of the tabernacle. They shall be joined from bottom to top, and one framework shall hold them all together. The same joining shall be maintained for the two boards placed at the corners. Thus there shall be eight boards altogether, with sixteen silver bases, two bases being counted for each board.

You shall also make poles of acacia wood: five for holding the boards together on one side of the tabernacle, five on the other, and the same number for the western side, to be inserted through the middle of the boards from end to end. You shall overlay the boards with gold and cast gold rings in them, through which the poles may hold the boards together; you shall cover the rings with gold plates. You shall erect the tabernacle according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.

You shall also make a veil of violet material, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and twisted fine linen, woven with embroidered work and beautiful variety. You shall hang it before four columns of acacia wood, which shall themselves be overlaid with gold and have gold capitals but silver bases. The veil shall be inserted through rings. Within it you shall place the ark of the testimony, and by it the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies shall be divided. You shall place the mercy seat upon the ark of the testimony in the Holy of Holies; and outside the veil, the table, with the lampstand opposite the table on the southern side of the tabernacle. The table shall stand on the northern side.

You shall also make a curtain for the entrance of the tabernacle, of violet material, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and twisted fine linen, with embroidered work. You shall overlay five columns of acacia wood with gold, before which the curtain shall be hung; their capitals shall be gold and their bases bronze.

[Cap. XXVII.] You shall also make an altar of acacia wood, five cubits long and the same in width—that is, square—and three cubits high. Its horns shall project from its four corners, and you shall overlay it with bronze. You shall make for its use pots for receiving the ashes, tongs, forks, and fire pans. You shall make all its vessels of bronze. You shall make a bronze grating in the form of a net; at its four corners there shall be four bronze rings, which you shall place beneath the ledge of the altar. The grating shall extend to the middle of the altar.

You shall also make two poles for the altar from acacia wood and cover them with bronze plates. You shall insert them through the rings; they shall be on both sides of the altar for carrying it. You shall make it not solid, but empty and hollow inside, as was shown to you on the mountain.

You shall also make the court of the tabernacle. On its southern side, facing south, there shall be curtains of twisted fine linen; one side shall be one hundred cubits long. There shall be twenty columns with an equal number of bronze bases; their capitals, with their moldings, shall be silver. Likewise, on the northern side, along its length, there shall be curtains one hundred cubits long, twenty columns, and the same number of bronze bases, with their capitals and moldings of silver.

In the width of the court, facing west, there shall be curtains for fifty cubits, with ten columns and the same number of bases. In the width of the court facing east there shall also be fifty cubits. Of these, curtains fifteen cubits long shall be assigned to one side, with three columns and three bases; and on the other side there shall be curtains occupying fifteen cubits, with three columns and three bases.

At the entrance of the court there shall be a curtain twenty cubits long, of violet material, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and twisted fine linen, with embroidered work. It shall have four columns with the same number of bases. All the columns of the court around it shall be covered with silver plates, with silver capitals and bronze bases. The court shall occupy one hundred cubits in length and fifty [Vulgate: forty] in width; its height shall be five cubits. It shall be made of twisted fine linen and shall have bronze bases. You shall make all the vessels of the tabernacle for every use and rite, including its pegs and those of the court, of bronze.

(C. CVI.) Command the children of Israel to bring you pure oil of crushed olives, so that the lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle of the testimony, outside the veil that is spread over the testimony. Aaron and his sons shall arrange it so that it may shine before the Lord until morning. It shall be a perpetual observance throughout their generations, maintained by the children of Israel.

[C. CVII, Cap. XXVIII.] Bring Aaron your brother to yourself, together with his sons, from among the children of Israel, so that they may serve me as priests: Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

[C. CVIII.] You shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and adornment. You shall speak to all the wise of heart whom I have filled with the spirit of understanding, so that they may make garments for Aaron, in which he may be sanctified and minister to me.

[C. CIX.] These are the garments that they shall make: the breastpiece, the ephod, the tunic, the close-fitting linen garment, the turban, and the sash. They shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother and his sons, so that they may serve me as priests. They shall take gold, violet material, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and fine linen.

They shall make the ephod of gold, violet material, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and twisted fine linen, with variegated workmanship. It shall have two joined shoulder pieces at its two sides, so that they may be joined together. The fabric itself and all the variety of its workmanship shall be of gold, violet material, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and twisted fine linen.

You shall take two onyx stones and engrave upon them the names of the sons of Israel: six names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, according to the order of their birth. With the work of an engraver and the engraving of a gem cutter you shall engrave them with the names of the sons of Israel, set in gold and surrounded by it. You shall place them on both sides of the ephod as a memorial for the children of Israel. Aaron shall carry their names before the Lord on both shoulders as a reminder.

You shall also make hooks of gold and two chains of purest gold, linked together, which you shall insert into the hooks.

You shall also make the breastpiece of judgment with variegated workmanship, according to the texture of the ephod, of gold, violet material, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and twisted fine linen. It shall be square and doubled; it shall be a span long and a span wide.

[Col. 0277A] [Note: [Col. 0277D] Saint Jerome often mentions the four rows, or courses, of stones in Aaron’s breastpiece, as in Book XV of his Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 54: “These twelve stones,” he says, “are written in order in Exodus and in Ezekiel, that is, in the *λογεῖον* [Greek: breastpiece] of the priest, and in the crown and diadem of the prince of Tyre,” and so forth. He also composed a treatise on the priestly garment in his Letter to Fabiola, whose beginning is: “To this day,” and so forth. MART.]

You shall place in it four rows of stones. In the first row there shall be a sardius, a topaz, and an emerald; in the second, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper; in the third, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst; in the fourth, a chrysolite, an onyx, and a beryl. They shall be set in gold in their rows. They shall bear the names of the sons of Israel: twelve names shall be engraved, each stone bearing the name of one of the twelve tribes.

You shall make chains for the breastpiece, linked together, of purest gold, and two gold rings, which you shall place at each upper end of the breastpiece. You shall join the gold chains to the rings at its edges, and attach the ends of the chains to the two hooks on each side of the ephod facing the breastpiece.

You shall also make two gold rings, which you shall place at the upper ends of the breastpiece, at its edges, opposite the ephod and facing its rear. You shall also make two other gold rings, to be placed on its two lower sides, facing the front of the lower joining of the ephod, so that it may be fitted to the ephod and the breastpiece fastened by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a violet cord, so that the workmanship remains joined and the breastpiece and ephod cannot be separated from one another.

Aaron shall carry the names of the sons of Israel on the breastpiece of judgment over his heart whenever he enters the sanctuary, as a memorial before the Lord forever. You shall place in the breastpiece of judgment the teaching and truth, which shall be upon Aaron’s breast when he enters before the Lord. Thus he shall always carry the judgment of the children of Israel upon his breast in the sight of the Lord.

You shall make the robe of the ephod entirely violet. In its middle above there shall be an opening for the head, with a woven border around it, as is usually made at the edges of garments, so that it may not easily tear. At the bottom of the same robe, all around, you shall make something like pomegranates of violet material, purple, and scarlet twice-dyed, with bells mixed among them, so that there shall be a golden bell and a pomegranate, then another golden bell and a pomegranate.

Aaron shall wear it in the service of his ministry, so that the sound may be heard when he enters and leaves the sanctuary before the Lord, and he may not die. You shall also make a plate of purest gold, on which you shall engrave, with the work of an engraver: “Holy to the Lord.” You shall bind it with a violet cord, and it shall be upon the turban, projecting over the priest’s forehead. Aaron shall bear the iniquities of the offerings that the children of Israel present and sanctify in all their gifts and offerings. The plate shall always be upon his forehead, so that the Lord may be gracious to them.

You shall gird the tunic with fine linen, make a linen turban, and make a sash with embroidered work. For the sons of Aaron you shall prepare linen tunics, sashes, and turbans, for glory and adornment. You shall clothe Aaron your brother and his sons with all these garments. You shall consecrate their hands and sanctify them, so that they may serve me as priests.

You shall also make linen undergarments to cover the nakedness of their flesh, from the loins to the thighs. Aaron and his sons shall wear them whenever they enter the tabernacle of the testimony or approach the altar to minister in the sanctuary, lest they die bearing guilt. This shall be a perpetual ordinance for Aaron and his descendants after him.

[Col. 0278B] [B. XVII, C. CX, Cap. XXIX.] You shall also do this, so that they may be consecrated to me for the priesthood. Take a young bull from the herd, two unblemished rams, unleavened loaves, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil; you shall make everything from fine wheat flour. You shall place them in a basket and bring the bull, the two rams, Aaron, and his sons to the entrance of the tabernacle of the testimony.

When you have washed the father and his sons [Vulgate adds: “his sons”] with water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments—that is, the linen garment, the robe, the ephod, and the breastpiece, which you shall fasten with the sash. You shall place the turban on his head and the holy plate upon the turban, and pour the anointing oil upon his head. In this manner he shall be consecrated.

You shall also bring forward his sons, [Col. 0278C] clothe them in linen tunics, and gird them with sashes. Aaron, that is, and his sons; you shall place turbans upon them, and they shall be priests [Note: [Col. 0277D] This is found in the canon of Hebrew truth and in the older manuscript codices. MART. —The Palatine manuscript, as well as the manuscripts used by Martianay, has “my priests.”] to me by a perpetual ordinance.

[C. CXI.] After you have consecrated their hands, you shall bring the bull before the tabernacle of the testimony. Aaron and his sons shall place their hands upon its head, and you shall slaughter it in the sight of the Lord beside the entrance of the tabernacle of the testimony. You shall take some of the bull’s blood and put it with your finger upon the horns of the altar; you shall pour out the rest of the blood beside its base. You shall take all the fat that covers the entrails, and [Note: The Hebrew is [uncertain], *jothereth*. But Bochart, since he holds that there is nothing net-like in the liver, thinks this reading itself must be corrected, and that *resticulum* should be read instead of *reticulum*; Saint Jerome also used this word, derived from *restis* and *resticula*, at 1 Kings 7:23. But besides the fact that a different Hebrew word occurs there, according to Bochart’s opinion *resticulum* would have to be substituted not only here, but also repeatedly elsewhere in Leviticus—3:4, 10, 15; 4:9; 7:4; 8:16, 25; and 9:10—where in every case the same Hebrew word [uncertain] occurs, and the Latin rendering *reticulum* appears in both the Vulgate and the manuscripts. Without changing the reading, it is more reasonable to believe that the fatty fibres of the liver are denoted.]
and the fatty lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys and the fat that is upon them, and offer them as incense upon the altar. But you shall burn the flesh of the bull, its hide, and its dung outside the camp, because it is a sin offering [Vulgate: “for sins”].

[Col. 0278D] You shall also take one ram, upon whose head Aaron and his sons shall place their hands. When you have slaughtered it, you shall take its blood and pour it around the altar. [Col. 0279A] You shall cut up the ram into pieces, wash its entrails and feet, and place them upon the pieces and upon its head. You shall offer the entire ram as incense upon the altar.

[C. CXII.] It is an offering to the Lord, a most pleasing fragrance, a sacrifice to the Lord.

You shall also take the other ram, upon whose head Aaron and his sons shall place their hands. When you have slaughtered it, you shall take some of its blood and place it upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron and his sons, and upon the thumbs of their hands and the great toes of their right feet; and you shall pour the blood around the altar. When you have taken some of the blood that is upon the altar and some of the anointing oil, you shall sprinkle Aaron and his garments, his sons and their garments. After you have consecrated them and their garments, you shall take the fat from the ram, the tail and the fat that covers the vital organs, the fatty lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys with the fat upon them, and the right shoulder, because it is the ram of consecration; also one round loaf of bread, one cake mixed with oil, and one wafer from the basket of unleavened bread that is placed before the Lord. You shall place everything upon the hands of Aaron and his sons, and sanctify them by raising them before the Lord.

You shall receive all these things from their hands and burn them upon the altar as a burnt offering, a most pleasing fragrance before the Lord, because it is his offering. You shall also take the breast of the ram by which Aaron was initiated, sanctify it by raising it before the Lord, and it shall fall to your share.

You shall sanctify the consecrated breast and the shoulder that you separated from the ram by which Aaron and his sons were initiated; they shall fall to the share of Aaron and his sons as a perpetual right from the children of Israel, because [Hebrew: “they are an offering”] they are the firstfruits and beginnings of the peace offerings that they present to the Lord.

The holy garment that Aaron uses shall belong to his sons after him, so that they may be anointed in it and their hands consecrated. For seven days the one who has been appointed high priest in his place from among his sons shall wear it, and so shall the one who enters the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the sanctuary.

You shall take the ram of consecration and boil its flesh in a holy place; Aaron and his sons shall eat it. They shall also eat the bread that is in the basket at the entrance of the tabernacle of the testimony, so that it may be an acceptable sacrifice and the hands of those who offer it may be sanctified. No outsider shall eat from it, because it is holy.

If any of the consecrated flesh or bread remains until morning, you shall burn the remainder with fire. It shall not be eaten, because it has been sanctified. You shall do for Aaron and his sons everything that I have commanded you. For seven days you shall consecrate their hands, and each day you shall offer a bull as a sin offering for atonement. You shall cleanse the altar when you offer the sacrifice of atonement, and anoint it for sanctification. For seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and sanctify it, and it shall be most holy. Everyone who touches it shall be sanctified.

This is what you shall do upon the altar: two year-old lambs each day continually, one lamb in the morning and the other in the evening; a tenth part of fine flour mixed with crushed oil, measuring a quarter of a hin, and wine for a libation of the same measure with one lamb. You shall offer the other lamb in the evening, according to the rite of the morning offering and according to what we have said, as a pleasing fragrance, a sacrifice to the Lord, a perpetual offering throughout your generations, at the entrance of the tabernacle of the testimony before the Lord, where I shall appoint that I may speak to you.

There I shall command the children of Israel, and the altar shall be sanctified by my glory. I shall also sanctify the tabernacle of the testimony and the altar, and Aaron with his sons, so that they may serve me as priests. I shall dwell in the midst of the children of Israel and shall be their God. They shall know that I am the Lord their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them—I, the Lord their God.

[Chapter XXX.] You shall also make an altar for burning incense, of acacia wood, having a cubit in length and another cubit in width—that is, square—and two cubits in height. Its horns shall project from it. You shall overlay it with pure gold, both its grating and its walls all around, and its horns. You shall also make for it a golden crown around it, and two golden rings beneath the crown on each side, so that poles may be inserted into them and the altar carried. You shall make the poles also of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. You shall place the altar opposite the veil that hangs before the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat by which the testimony is covered, where I shall speak with you. Aaron shall burn fragrant incense upon it in the morning. When he arranges the lamps, he shall burn it; and when he places them in the evening, he shall burn perpetual incense before the Lord throughout your generations. You shall not offer upon it incense of another composition, nor offering or sacrifice, nor pour libations upon it. Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns once a year, with the blood that was offered for sin, and he shall make atonement upon it throughout your generations. It shall be most holy to the Lord.

[T. XIV.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: When you take the census of the Israelites according to their number, each shall give the Lord a ransom for his life, and there shall be no plague among them when they are counted. This is what everyone who passes [h. “goes over”] into the census shall give: half a shekel according to the sanctuary standard. A shekel contains twenty obols. Half a shekel shall be offered to the Lord. Everyone included in the census, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the ransom. The rich shall not add to the half-shekel, and the poor shall not subtract from it. You shall receive the money that has been contributed by the Israelites and assign it to the service of the tent of meeting, so that it may be a memorial for them before the Lord and make atonement for their lives.

[C. CXIII.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: You shall also make a bronze basin with its base for washing, and place it between the tent of meeting and the altar. Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet in it [Vulg. *ea*] when they are about to enter the tent of meeting and when they approach the altar to offer incense to the Lord, lest they die. It shall be a perpetual ordinance for him and for his descendants throughout their generations.

[C. CXIV.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take for yourself spices [h. “choice spices of pure myrrh”], first-quality [Note: All the manuscripts read not *myrrhae* but *smyrnae*, following the Greek word σμύρνης of the Septuagint translators. We too might have followed the old exemplars, had not the customary practice of writing *myrrha*, rather than *smyrna*, prevailed. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript has *myrrhae, et electae*; the Palatine, together with those available to Martianay, has *smyrnae electae*, following the Greek σμύρνης.] pure myrrh, five hundred shekels; cinnamon, half that amount, namely two hundred and fifty; likewise calamus, two hundred and fifty; and cassia, five hundred shekels, according to the sanctuary standard; and olive oil, a measure of one hin. You shall make holy anointing oil, a compound ointment prepared by a perfumer’s art, and with it you shall anoint the tent of meeting, the ark of the covenant, the table and all its vessels, the lampstand and its utensils, the altars of incense and burnt offering, and all their equipment, and every article belonging to their service. You shall consecrate all these, and they shall be most holy; whoever touches them shall be holy. You shall anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them, so that they may serve me as priests.

You shall also say to the Israelites: This shall be my holy anointing oil throughout your generations. It shall not be poured upon human flesh, and you shall not make another of the same composition, because it is consecrated and shall be holy to you. Whoever compounds anything like it and gives some of it to an outsider shall be cut off from his people.

And the Lord said to Moses: Take for yourself spices—stacte, onycha, fragrant galbanum, and the purest frankincense; all shall be of equal weight. You shall make incense, a compound prepared by a perfumer, carefully blended, pure, and most worthy of consecration. When you have crushed everything into the finest powder, you shall place some of it before the testimony in the tent [Vulg. “tent of testimony”], where I shall appear to you. The incense shall be most holy to you. You shall not make such a composition for your own use, because it is holy to the Lord. Whoever makes anything like it in order to enjoy its fragrance shall perish from among his people.

[Note: This Hebrew word is found punctuated in this way in the inner margin of the canon of the Hebrew Truth, opposite the word *thymiama* (“incense”). Many considerations, however, show that it was placed there by a later hand and rashly. First, it is written in Hebrew characters, whereas the Hebrew words in the scholia of that same canon are everywhere expressed in Latin letters, as in the other works of Jerome. Furthermore, the marginal annotations in the canon are always written in the same ink as the text itself; but in this word, *Cetoreth*, the ink appears less black and fades into a yellow color. Finally, it gives the reader no indication, as the other scholia do, of what it corresponds to in the body of the text or what ambiguity it was added to resolve. Whatever may be said of that word, it is certainly not Jerome’s, since he nowhere acknowledged the vowel points of the Masoretes. MART. —We have deleted [the intervening reading is uncertain] the Hebrew word which Martianay repeats from the inner margin of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth opposite the word *thymiama*, and which he himself admits was added both by a later hand and by an ignorant annotator. The true Jerome, in Epistle 106 to Sunnias and Fretela, on Psalm 65, reads *Catoreth* and interprets it as “incense.” See what we have noted there.]

[C. CXV, Chapter XXXI.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Behold, I have called by name Bezalel son of Uri son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every kind of work, to devise skillfully whatever can be made of gold, silver, bronze, marble [h. “marble” is absent], precious stones, and various kinds of wood. And I have given him as a companion Oholiab son [h.] of Ahisamach of [Col. 0282A] the tribe of Dan. And I have placed wisdom in the heart of every skilled person, so that they may make everything that I have commanded you: the tent of meeting, the ark of the testimony, the mercy seat that is above it, and all the vessels of the tent; the table and its vessels; the pure lampstand with its vessels; the altars of incense and burnt offering and all their vessels; the basin with its base; the holy garments for the ministry of Aaron the priest and his sons, so that they may perform their sacred office; the anointing oil and the fragrant incense for the sanctuary. They shall make everything that I have commanded you.

[C. CXVI.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying [h. “And the Lord said”]: Speak to the Israelites and say to them: See that you keep my sabbath, because it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, so that you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you. Keep the sabbath [Vulg. adds “my”], for it is holy to you. Whoever profanes it shall be put to death; whoever does work on it, that person shall perish from the midst of his people. Six days shall work be done; but the seventh day is a sabbath, a holy rest to the Lord. Whoever does work on that day shall be put to death. Let the Israelites keep the sabbath and celebrate it throughout their generations. It is an everlasting covenant between me and the Israelites, a perpetual sign.
