For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he ceased from work.

[T. XV, B. XIX, Chapter CXXVII.] And when the Lord had finished these words on Mount Sinai, he gave Moses two stone tablets of the testimony, written with the finger of God.

[Col. 0282C] [C. CXVIII, Chapter XXXII.] When the people saw that Moses was delaying in coming down from the mountain, they gathered against Aaron and said: Rise, make gods for us who will go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.

And Aaron said to them: Take the golden earrings from the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me. So all the people did as he had commanded, bringing the earrings to Aaron. When he had received them, he formed them by casting and made from them a molten calf. And they said: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it [Note: In Hebrew it has *lephanau*, that is, “before its face.” This marginal note therefore teaches that, according to the sense of the Hebrew Scripture, Aaron built the altar before the mountain, not before the molten calf. But the sacred critics of our time maintain the opposite, and at the words “before it” understand “before the calf.” We too embrace their opinion as the more probable; nor is it reasonable to believe that a scholion of this kind came from Jerome. MART.] [h. “before the mountain”], and proclaimed with a herald’s voice: Tomorrow is a solemnity of the Lord.

They rose early and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.

[C. CXIX.] And the Lord said to Moses: Go down; your people, whom you brought up from the land of Egypt, have sinned. They have quickly departed from the way that you showed them. They have made for themselves a molten calf, worshiped it, sacrificed to it, and said: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

And again the Lord said to Moses: I see that this people is stiff-necked. Leave me, so that my anger may burn against them and I may destroy them; then I will make you into a great nation.

[C. CXX.] But Moses prayed to the Lord his God, saying: Why, Lord, does your anger burn against your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt with great strength and a mighty hand? Please do not let the Egyptians say: “He brought them out deceitfully, in order to kill them in the mountains and wipe them from the earth.” Let your anger cease, and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: “I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven, and I will give all this land, of which I have spoken, to your offspring, and they shall possess it forever.”

And the Lord was appeased and did not do the evil that he had spoken of doing against his people.

[C. CXXI.] And Moses returned from the mountain, carrying the two tablets of the testimony [Note: The Canon of the Hebrew Truth, together with two other manuscript codices—one from the Colbert Library, no. 74, and the other from Saint-Germain, no. 3—reads here: “carrying the two tablets of the testimony written by the hand of God on both sides.” But this is plainly a scribal error, since copyists frequently recast everything according to their own understanding. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript has: “carrying two tablets written by the hand on both sides.” The Palatine differs from the printed reading by one word, omitting *sua* (“his”); other manuscripts have *manu Dei* (“by the hand of God”). The Hebrew literally: “And the two tablets of the testimony were in his hand, tablets written on their two sides, and from this side they were written.”] in his hand, written on both sides and made by the work of God. The writing of God was also engraved on the tablets.

When Joshua heard the tumult of the shouting people, he said to Moses: The sound of battle is heard in the camp. He replied: It is not the cry of those encouraging battle, nor the shouting of those compelling flight; I hear the voice of singers.

When he drew near the camp, he saw the calf and the dancing. Moses became very angry, threw the tablets from his hand, and broke them at the foot of the mountain. He seized the calf that they had made, burned it, ground it to powder, scattered it in the water, and gave the Israelites some of it to drink.

[C. CXXII.] And he said to Aaron: What did this people do to you, that you brought such a great sin upon it?

He replied: Let not my lord be angry. You know this people, that it is inclined to evil. They said to me: “Make gods for us who will go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.” So I said to them: “Who among you has gold?” They took it off and gave it to me. I threw it into the fire, and this calf came out.

When Moses saw that the people had been stripped naked—for Aaron had stripped them because of the disgrace of their defilement and had exposed them naked among their enemies—

[C. CXXIII.] he stood at the gate of the camp and said: Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join me. And all the sons of Levi gathered to him. He said to them: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh. Go back and forth from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.

The sons of Levi did according to Moses’ command, and about [Note: In many printed editions and manuscripts we read “about twenty-three thousand men.” We have corrected this according to the authority of the Hebrew canon and three other manuscripts, also following the authority of the Hebrew books. MART. —The Palatine, together with the printed editions and other manuscripts used by Martianay, has “twenty-three thousand men,” etc. This number appears to have entered the Latin codices through the passage in 1 Corinthians 10:8: “twenty-three thousand fell in one day.”] three thousand men fell that day.

And Moses said: Today you have consecrated your hands to the Lord, each man against his son and his brother, so that a blessing may be given to you.

[C. CXXIV.] On the following day Moses said to the people: You have committed a very great sin. I will go up to the Lord, to see whether I may somehow be able to entreat him for your offense.

Returning to the Lord, he said: I beg you, this people has committed a very great sin; they have made gods of gold for themselves. Either forgive them this offense, or, if you will not, blot me from the book that you have written.

The Lord answered him: Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him from my book. But now go, lead this people where I told you. My angel shall go before you. Yet on the day of vengeance I will also visit this sin of theirs.

So the Lord struck the people because of their guilt concerning the calf that Aaron had made.

[Col. 0284C] [C. CXXV, Chapter XXXIII.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Go up from this place, you and your people [h. “your” is absent], whom you brought out from the land of Egypt, into the land that I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying: “I will give it to your offspring.” And I will send an angel before you, so that I may drive out the Canaanite, Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite, and that you may enter a land flowing with milk and honey. For I will not go up with you, since you are a stiff-necked people, lest I destroy you on the way.

When the people heard this very grievous word, they mourned, and no one put on his customary adornment.

[C. CXXVI.] And the Lord said to Moses: Say to the Israelites: You are a stiff-necked people. If I go up among you even once, I shall destroy you. Now remove your adornment, so that I may know what to do with you.

So the Israelites removed their adornment from Mount Horeb.

[T. XVI.] Moses also took the tent and pitched it outside the camp, far away, and called it the Tent of Meeting. Everyone who had any question went out to the Tent of Meeting, outside the camp. Whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people rose, and each person stood at the entrance of his own tent; they watched Moses’ back until he entered the tent.

When he had entered the Tent of Meeting, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the entrance, and he spoke with Moses. When all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance of the tent, they themselves stood and worshiped at the doors of their tents.

[C. CXXVII.] The Lord spoke with Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend. When he returned to the camp, his attendant Joshua son of Nun, a young man, did not depart from the tent.

Moses said to the Lord: You command me to lead this people, but you have not made known to me whom you will send with me, especially since you have said: “I know you by name” [h. “I will make you known by name”], and “You have found favor before me.”

[C. CXXVIII.] Therefore, if I have found favor in your sight, show me [Note: The printed editions, together with some manuscripts, read “your face.” In the Hebrew is written *deracheca*, or, as Jerome reads elsewhere, *darchach*, that is, “your way.” In the Hebrew-Samaritan text we read the plural *darchecha*, “your ways.” The Septuagint translated, “Show me yourself”; finally, the Chaldee has, “Show me the way of your goodness.” Among these variant readings, we have followed the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, which here flows purely from its source. MART.] your way, so that I may know you and find favor before your eyes. Consider that this nation is your people.

The Lord said: My face shall go before you, and I will give you rest.

Moses said: If you yourself do not go before us, do not lead us away from this place. For how shall I and your people know that we have found favor in your sight, unless you walk with us, so that we may be glorified above all the peoples who dwell upon the earth?

The Lord said to Moses: I will also do this word that you have spoken, because you have found favor before me and I know you by name [h. “I will make you known by name”].

He said: Show me your glory.

He replied: I will show you all my goodness, and I will proclaim the name of the Lord before you; I will have mercy on whom I wish, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me [h. “That is, I will show you how you must entreat me and bend me toward mercy”].

And again he said: You cannot see my face, for no human being shall see me and live.

And again: Behold, he said, there is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock. When my glory passes by, I will place you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my right hand until I pass by. Then I will remove my hand, and you shall see my back; but you cannot see my face.

[B. XX, C. CXXIX, Chapter XXXIV.] And afterward he said: Cut for yourself two stone tablets like the former ones, and I will write upon them the words that were on the tablets that you broke. Be ready in the morning, so that you may immediately go up Mount Sinai, and stand with me on the summit of the mountain. Let no one go up with you, and let no one be seen anywhere on the whole mountain. Let neither sheep nor cattle graze opposite it.

So he cut two stone tablets like the former ones. Rising during the night, he went up Mount Sinai as the Lord had commanded him, carrying the tablets with him. When the Lord descended in the cloud, he stood there with him [Note: The Urbinas manuscript has “Moses stood with him,” in accordance with the Vulgate.] [that is, with Moses, as the Hebrew has], calling upon the name of the Lord.

[Note: Up to this point the Latins have understood this important passage in such a way that Moses stood with God, invoking the name of the Lord and crying out as the Lord passed by: “Sovereign Lord God,” and so forth. But from the Hebrew, or from the canon of the Hebrew Truth, it is clear that everything that follows consists of God’s words, not Moses’. For just as he had said above, “When I pass by, I will proclaim the name of the Lord,” so now, proclaiming in that name—that is, expressing his own great name, *Adonai*—he says: “Sovereign Lord God, merciful,” and so forth.

It should nevertheless be noted that the Latin Vulgate edition has the Jerusalem Targum as a supporter of its reading, for it reads as follows: “And when the glory of the majesty of the Lord passed before him, Moses prayed and said: Lord, Lord God, merciful,” and so forth. We note this after the learned man, lest anyone rashly presume to condemn our Vulgate whenever it appears to differ from the Hebrew Truth; for it has excellent authorities whom it followed, and everywhere it presents meanings worthy of God. MART. —Our manuscripts agree with the Vulgate reading: “when he passed before him, he said: Sovereign Lord,” and so forth, making these Moses’ words, addressing the Lord as he passed before the mouth of the cave. By contrast, the printed reading, which Martianay restored from the Canon, as he calls it, of the Hebrew Truth, is supported by the Hebrew text and indicates that these are God’s words, as he passes before Moses and reveals to him his attributes.

But without discussing here the superiority of either reading, which is no small question, I greatly fear that the words of a Hebrew corrector, long ago inserted from the margin into the text in a single Memmian manuscript, are being improperly imposed by Martianay as Jerome’s translation. I would rather prefer the authority of all the remaining books. See, however, Martianay’s third Prolegomenon near the end, where he discusses this correction by the annotator.]

And as the Lord passed before him, he said: Sovereign Lord God, merciful and gracious, patient and abounding in compassion and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, taking away iniquity, crimes, and sins, yet no one is innocent before you in himself; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon their children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation.

Moses quickly bowed down to the ground and, worshiping, said: If I have found favor in your sight, Lord, I beg you to walk with us—for it is a stiff-necked people—and take away our iniquities and sins, and possess us.

The Lord replied: I will make a covenant in the sight of all. I will perform signs such as have never been seen on earth or among any nations, so that the people among whom you dwell may see the terrible work of the Lord that I am about to do.

Observe everything that he has commanded you today [Vulg. “that I command you”]. I myself will drive out before you the Amorite, Canaanite, Hittite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite.

Beware lest you ever make a friendship with the inhabitants of that land, which would become a ruin for you. Destroy their altars, break their statues, and cut down their sacred groves. Do not worship a foreign god. The Lord is Jealous by name; he is an impassioned God.

Do not make a covenant with the inhabitants of those regions, lest, when they prostitute themselves with their gods and worship their images, someone invite you and you eat of their sacrifices. You shall not take wives for your sons from among their daughters, lest, after they have prostituted themselves, they make your sons prostitute themselves to their gods.

You shall not make molten gods for yourself.

You shall keep the feast of Unleavened Bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time of the month of new things; for in the month of springtime you came out of Egypt.

[Col. 0287B] [C. CXXX.] Everything that opens the womb of the male sex shall be mine; among all living creatures, whether cattle or sheep, it shall be mine. You shall redeem the firstborn of a donkey with a sheep; but if you do not provide a price for it, it shall be killed. You shall redeem the firstborn of your sons, and you shall not appear before me empty-handed.

Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall cease from plowing and harvesting. You shall celebrate the feast of Weeks, with the firstfruits of the wheat harvest, and the feast when the year turns and everything is gathered in.

Three times each year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord God, the Almighty God of Israel. For when I have driven out the nations before you and enlarged your borders, no one shall lie in wait for your land when you go up and appear before the Lord your God three times a year.

You shall not sacrifice the blood of my victim with leaven, nor shall the sacrifice of the feast of Passover remain until morning. You shall offer the firstfruits of the produce of your land in the house of the Lord your God. You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.

[T. XVII, C. CXXXI.] And the Lord said to Moses: Write these words for yourself, for by them I have made a covenant both with you and with Israel.

He remained there with the Lord forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water, and he wrote upon the tablets the ten words of the covenant.

[C. CXXXII.] When Moses descended from Mount Sinai, he held the two tablets of the testimony and did not know that his face had become horned from speaking with God. When Aaron and the Israelites saw that Moses’ face was horned, they were afraid to come near him.

When he called them, both Aaron and the rulers of the assembly returned. After he had spoken, all the Israelites also came to him. He commanded them everything that he had heard from the Lord on Mount Sinai. When he had finished speaking, he placed a veil over his face.

Whenever he entered before the Lord to speak with him, he removed it until he came out; and then he spoke to the Israelites everything that had been commanded him. They saw that Moses’ face was horned when he came out, but he again covered his face whenever he spoke to them.

[Col. 0288A] [C. CXXXIII, Chapter XXXV.] Then, when the whole assembly of the Israelites had gathered, he said to them: These are the things that the Lord has commanded to be done. Six days shall work be done; the seventh day shall be holy for you, a sabbath and rest to the Lord. Whoever does work on it shall be put to death. You shall not kindle fire in any of your dwellings on the sabbath day.

[C. CXXXIV.] And Moses said to the whole company of the Israelites: This is the word that the Lord has commanded, saying: Set aside among yourselves firstfruits [h. “offerings”] for the Lord. Let everyone offer them to the Lord voluntarily and with a willing heart: gold, silver, and bronze; violet-purple, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and fine linen; goats’ hair; rams’ skins dyed red; violet skins; acacia wood; oil for preparing the lamps; for preparing the ointment; and the most fragrant incense; onyx stones [Note: Wherever “shoulder-piece” is read in Exodus or Leviticus, we should know that among the Hebrews it is called *ephod*. That this is the garment of the high priest, and appropriate exclusively to high priests, is attested by all Scripture. Thus Saint Jerome wrote to Fabiola concerning the priestly garments. MART.]; and gems for adorning the ephod and the breastpiece.

Let everyone among you who is wise come and make what the Lord has commanded: the tabernacle, its covering, and its outer covering; its rings and boards with their poles; its pegs and bases; the ark and its poles; the mercy seat; and the veil that is spread before it; the table with its poles and vessels, and the bread of the Presence; the lampstand for supporting the lights, its vessels and lamps, and oil for feeding the flames; the altar of incense and its poles; the anointing oil and the fragrant incense; the screen for the entrance of the tabernacle; the altar of burnt offering, its bronze grating, its poles and vessels; the basin and its base; the curtains of the court with their columns and bases; the screen for the entrance of the vestibule; the pegs of the tabernacle and the court with their cords; and the garments used in the service of the sanctuary, the garments of Aaron the high priest and of his sons, so that they may serve me as priests.

Then the whole multitude of the Israelites departed from Moses’ presence and offered [Vulg. “offered”] with the readiest and most devoted mind their firstfruits [h. “offerings”] to the Lord, for the construction of the tent of meeting.

Whatever was necessary for worship and for the holy garments, men and women supplied: bracelets, earrings, rings, and armlets. Every golden vessel was set apart as a gift for the Lord.

If anyone possessed violet-purple, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, or violet skins, they offered them. They also offered metals of silver and bronze to the Lord, and acacia wood for various uses.

The skilled women also contributed what they had spun: violet-purple, purple, scarlet, fine linen, and goats’ hair, freely giving everything of their own accord.

The leaders offered onyx stones and gems for the ephod and the breastpiece, as well as spices and oil for preparing the lamps, for making the ointment, and for composing the most fragrant incense.

All the men and women, with devoted hearts, offered gifts for the works that the Lord had commanded through Moses’ hand. All the Israelites dedicated voluntary offerings to the Lord.

[C. CXXXV.] And Moses said to the Israelites: Behold, the Lord has called by name Bezalel son of Uri son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. He filled him with the spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and every kind of skill, to devise and make work in gold, silver, and bronze, to carve stones, and to perform carpentry—whatever can be devised skillfully. He placed this in his heart, and likewise in Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. He instructed both of them in wisdom, so that they might perform the work of the fir-wood worker, the maker of variegated textiles, and the embroiderer, in violet-purple, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and fine linen, and weave everything and devise every new design.

[Chapter XXXVI.] Therefore Bezalel, Oholiab, and every wise man to whom the Lord had given wisdom [Col. 0289B] and understanding [Note: “And every wise man to whom the Lord had given wisdom and knowledge”: some manuscript codices and the Canon of the Hebrew Truth read in this way, following the Septuagint translators. Others have “understanding,” or “intellect,” according to what is written in Hebrew, where *thebuna* occurs. MART.] knew how to work skillfully on everything necessary for the service of the sanctuary and what the Lord had commanded.

When Moses called them, together with every skilled man to whom the Lord had given wisdom and who had voluntarily offered themselves for the work, he handed over to them all the gifts of the Israelites. While they applied themselves to the work, the people continued every morning to bring offerings.

Then the craftsmen, compelled to come, said to Moses: The people are bringing more than is necessary. So Moses ordered a proclamation to be made by the herald’s voice: Let neither man nor woman bring anything further for the work of the sanctuary.

Thus the people ceased bringing gifts, because what had been offered was sufficient and more than enough.

All the wise-hearted workers made ten curtains for completing the work of the tabernacle, of twisted fine linen, violet-purple, purple, and scarlet twice-dyed, with varied workmanship and embroidered design. Each curtain was twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide; all the curtains had the same measurement.

He joined five curtains together, one to another, and connected the other five to one another. He made violet loops at the edge of one curtain on both sides, and likewise at the edge of the other curtain, so that the loops would face one another and be joined together. He cast fifty golden rings to catch the loops of the curtains, so that the whole became one tabernacle.

He also made eleven coverings of goats’ hair to cover the roof of the tabernacle. One covering was thirty cubits long and four cubits wide; all the coverings had the same measurement. He joined five separately and the other six separately.

He made fifty loops at the edge of one covering and fifty at the edge of the other, so that they might be joined to one another. He also made fifty bronze clasps by which the roof would be fastened, so that all the coverings might become one cloak.

He made a covering for the tabernacle of rams’ skins dyed red, and above it another covering of violet skins.

He also made the boards of the tabernacle of upright acacia wood. One board was ten cubits long and one and a half cubits wide. There were two tenons on each board, so that one might be joined to another. He did this for all the boards of the tabernacle.

Twenty of them were on the southern side, facing south, with forty silver bases. Two bases were placed beneath each board, one on either side, where the tenons of the sides ended at the corners.

For the side of the tabernacle facing north, he made twenty boards with forty silver bases, two bases for each board.

For the western side—that is, the side of the tabernacle facing the sea—he made six boards, and two additional boards for each corner at the rear of the tabernacle. These were joined from bottom to top and brought together into a single framework.

He made the same on both sides at the corners, so that there were eight boards altogether, with sixteen silver bases, namely two bases beneath each board.

He made poles of acacia wood: five for holding together the boards on one side of the tabernacle, five more for joining the boards on the other side, and, besides these, five more poles for the western side of the tabernacle, facing the sea.

He also made another pole that extended through the middle of the boards from one corner to the other.

He overlaid the boards with gold and made their rings of gold, through which the poles could be inserted; and he covered the poles themselves with plates of gold.

[Note: In the printed editions and in all the manuscript books, the following words are added: “having cast their silver bases,” but the Canon of the Hebrew Truth erased them, indicating by this marginal sign, h., that they are not in the Hebrew. MART. —Our manuscripts also add “having cast their silver bases,” as Martianay found in his own manuscripts, and as the printed books retain. These words have been repeated from the third verse after this one. The Canon of the Hebrew Truth erased them according to the archetype.]

He also made the veil of violet-purple, purple, scarlet, and twisted fine linen, with embroidered and varied workmanship, and four columns of acacia wood. He overlaid their capitals with gold and cast their silver bases.

He also made the screen at the entrance of the tabernacle of violet-purple, purple, scarlet, and twisted fine linen, with embroidered workmanship, and five columns with their capitals. He overlaid them with gold and cast their bases of bronze.

### [C. CXXXVI, Chapter XXXVII]

Now Beseleel also made the ark from acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and also a cubit and a half high. He overlaid it with the purest gold, inside and out. He made a gold molding around it, and cast four gold rings for its four corners: two rings on one side and two on the other. He also made poles from acacia wood, overlaid them with gold, and inserted them into the rings on the sides of the ark, so that it could be carried.

He also made the propitiatory—that is, the oracle—from the purest gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. He made two cherubim of beaten gold, which he placed on the two sides of the propitiatory: one cherub at the summit of one side and the other cherub at the summit of the other side—one cherub at each end of the propitiatory—extending their wings, covering the propitiatory, and looking toward one another and toward it.

He also made the table from acacia wood, two cubits long and one cubit wide; its height was a cubit and a half [Vulgate: its width was a cubit and a half]. He surrounded it with the purest gold and made a gold rim around it. For the rim he made a finely engraved gold molding four fingers wide, and above it another gold molding. He cast four gold rings and placed them at the four corners, one at each foot of the table, below the molding. He inserted poles into them, so that the table could be carried. He also made the poles from acacia wood and overlaid them with gold.

He made vessels for the table’s various uses—plates, bowls, cups, and censers of pure gold, in which libations were to be offered.

He also made the beaten lampstand from the purest gold. From its central shaft proceeded branches, cups, spheres, and lilies: six on each side, three branches on one side and three on the other. There were three cups shaped like almonds on each branch, together with spheres and lilies; and three almond-shaped cups on the other branch, together with spheres and lilies. The work of the six branches proceeding from the lampstand’s shaft was identical. On the shaft itself were four almond-shaped cups, each accompanied by its sphere and lily. There were also spheres beneath the two branches at three places, making six branches in all, proceeding from the single shaft. Thus both the spheres and the branches were part of it, all beaten from the purest gold.

He also made seven lamps, with their tongs and vessels in which the trimmed wicks were to be extinguished, from the purest gold. A talent of gold was used for the lampstand with all its vessels.

He also made the altar of incense from acacia wood, one cubit square and two cubits high [Vulgate: two cubits wide]; horns projected from its corners. He overlaid it with the purest gold, together with its grating, sides, and horns. He made a small gold molding around it and two gold rings beneath the molding on each side, so that poles could be inserted into them and the altar carried. He made the poles from acacia wood and covered them with gold plates.

He also compounded the oil for the anointing of consecration, and the incense from the purest spices, according to the work of a perfumer.

### [Chapter XXXVIII]

He also made the altar of burnt offering from acacia wood, five cubits square and three cubits high. Its horns projected from its corners, and he covered it with bronze plates. For its uses he prepared various bronze vessels: pots, tongs, forks, hooks, and fire-pans. He made its grating in the form of a bronze net, and beneath it, in the middle of the altar, a small altar. He cast four rings at the four corners of the grating, into which poles could be inserted for carrying it. He made the poles from acacia wood and covered them with bronze plates, inserting them into the rings projecting from the sides of the altar.

The altar itself was not solid, but hollow, made of boards and empty inside.

He also made the bronze basin with its base from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle.

He also made the court. On its southern side were curtains of twisted linen, one hundred cubits long, with twenty bronze columns and their bases; the capitals of the columns, together with all the engraved work, were silver. Likewise, on the northern side, the curtains, columns, bases, and capitals were of the same dimensions, workmanship, and metal.

On the side facing west there were curtains fifty cubits long, ten columns with their bronze bases, and the capitals of the columns, together with all the engraved work, were silver.

[Note: Several manuscript books read here, “and the engraved silver capitals of the columns.” But the reading of the printed editions and of the other manuscripts is much preferable, as can be seen from this chapter, verses 10 and 17, where the same words are written. —MART. Another manuscript, the Urbinas, omits the words “and all the engraved work” and instead has “engraved only.” The Hebrew has “toward the ground,” but the capitals of the columns and their bands were of silver.]

Toward the east he prepared curtains fifty cubits long. Of these, curtains fifteen cubits long, with three columns and their bases, occupied one side; and on the other side there were likewise curtains fifteen cubits long, three columns, and the same number of bases.

[Note: Thus read the Hebrew canon of truth and the more accurate manuscript copies. The meaning is that between the two sides of columns and hanging curtains there was an entrance into the tabernacle. —MART. The commonly circulated editions read: “because he made an entrance into the tabernacle between the two sides.”]

All the curtains of the court were woven of twisted linen. The bases of the columns were bronze, but their capitals, together with their engravings, were silver; and he also overlaid the columns of the court with silver.

At its entrance he made a curtain embroidered in needlework, of violet, purple, scarlet, and twisted linen. It was twenty cubits long and five cubits high, corresponding to the measurements of all the court’s curtains. The columns at the entrance were four, with bronze bases; their capitals and engravings were silver.

He also made the tent pegs of the tabernacle and of the court all around from bronze.

These are the furnishings of the tabernacle of testimony, which were counted according to Moses’ command in the service of the Levites, by the hand of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest. Beseleel, son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, had completed them at the Lord’s command through Moses, with Ooliab, son of Ahisamach, from the tribe of Dan, as his associate. He too was an excellent craftsman in wood and a skilled embroiderer and needleworker in violet, purple, scarlet, and linen.

All the gold expended on the work of the sanctuary, and offered in gifts, amounted to twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels, according to the sanctuary’s measure.

[Note: Here we restore the verse in full according to the canon of Hebrew truth and another manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, no. 3. What follows immediately—“But what was offered …”—does not refer to gold but to silver, since every Israelite, when counted, paid half a shekel. Hence it is clear that something is missing from the Scripture in the printed editions, and that the meaning is sometimes disordered and confused. This will become clear to anyone who compares this edition with the commonly circulated biblical copies, where moreover, in verse 28, silver is written instead of gold, and where the reference to the columns concerns things properly belonging to their capitals. —MART. Our manuscripts also preserve this verse in full, as Martianus previously restored it. It is equally reasonable to suppose that, because the same word “sanctuary” recurs, it was accidentally omitted by Latin scribes; for the words following that term at the end of the verse—“half a shekel for each person”—are found in neither the Urbinas nor the Palatinus manuscripts.]

The amount of silver from the people’s gifts was one hundred talents and one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels, according to the sanctuary’s measure: a half-shekel for each person.

It was offered by those who were counted, from twenty years of age and upward, numbering six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty armed men.

There were also one hundred talents of silver, from which were cast the bases of the sanctuary and the entrance where the veil hangs. One hundred bases were made from the one hundred talents, one talent being reckoned for each base.

From the one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels [Vulgate omits “shekels”] he made the capitals of the columns, which he also overlaid with gold [h.: “gilded”].

There were also offered seventy-two talents of bronze and four hundred shekels, from which were cast the bases at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, the bronze altar with its grating, all its vessels, the bases of the court both around it and at its entrance, and the tent pegs of the tabernacle and of the court all around.

### [Chapter XXXIX]

From violet, purple, scarlet, and linen he made the garments for service in the sanctuary, and the holy garments for Aaron to wear (when he ministered in the holy places), as the Lord had commanded Moses.

[Note: The same manuscript copies correct this passage and read as we have printed it. But what follows—“when he ministered in the holy places”—is superfluous, since the entire context of the Hebrew sources is sufficiently expressed without these words. We therefore enclose what seemed superfluous within dashes or brackets, merely warning the reader of this fact and allowing our pen no further alteration in deleting what is written. —MART. The words “for ministering in the sanctuary” and “the holy garments” are absent from the Urbinas and Palatinus manuscripts, as also from the commonly circulated editions. Martianus enclosed the following words, “when he ministered in the holy places,” in brackets as superfluous.]

He therefore made the ephod of gold, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, in embroidered work. He cut sheets of gold and beat them thin into threads, so that they could be twisted together with the threads of the other colors. He made two joined edges on each side of the upper portions, and a belt of the same colors, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

He prepared two onyx stones, set and enclosed in gold, engraved by the art of the jeweler with the names of the sons of Israel. He placed them on the sides of the ephod as a memorial for the sons of Israel, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

He also made the breastpiece in embroidered work, like the workmanship of the ephod, from gold, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen. It was square and double, a span in size.

He placed in it four rows of precious stones. In the first row were a sardius, a topaz, and an emerald. In the second, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper. In the third, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst. In the fourth, a chrysolite, an onyx, and a beryl, set and enclosed in gold according to their rows.

The twelve stones were engraved with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, one name for each stone.

They made for the breastpiece chains joined to one another, of the purest gold, together with two hooks and the same number of gold rings. They placed the rings on both sides of the breastpiece, from which the two gold chains would hang; they inserted these into the hooks projecting from the corners of the ephod.

These pieces, front and back, fitted together so that the ephod and the breastpiece were mutually joined, fastened to the belt and more tightly secured by rings. A violet ribbon joined them, so that they would not hang loose or shift apart, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

They also made the robe of the ephod entirely violet, with an opening at its upper part in the middle, and a woven border around the opening. At its lower edge, around the hem of the robe, were pomegranates of violet, purple, scarlet, and twisted linen, together with bells of the purest gold, which they placed between the pomegranates around the lower edge of the robe. A gold bell and a pomegranate alternated around it; in this ornament the high priest walked when he performed his ministry, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

They also made woven linen tunics for Aaron and his sons, turbans of linen with their circlets, and linen undergarments. The belt was of twisted linen, violet, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, made by needlework, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

[Note: The canon, together with all the manuscript copies, reads “and distinguished with scarlet,” namely, Aaron’s belt and those of his sons. This gives a suitable sense, although in Hebrew we read as in the printed edition, *ve-tolaʿat shani*, that is, “and scarlet crimson,” or “twice-dyed.” —MART. Our manuscripts, and those consulted by Martianus, read: “distinguished with scarlet by artistic work,” and so forth.]

They also made the plate of sacred honor from the purest gold. They wrote on it, in jeweler’s work, “Holy to the Lord,” and fastened it to the turban with a violet ribbon, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

Thus all the work of the tabernacle and the tent of testimony was completed. The children of Israel did everything that the Lord had commanded Moses. They presented the tabernacle, the tent, and all its furnishings: the rings, boards, poles, columns, and bases; the covering of reddened rams’ skins and the other covering of violet skins; the veil; the ark; the poles; the propitiatory; the table with its vessels and the bread of the Presence; the lampstand, its lamps, and its utensils with the oil; the golden altar; the anointing oil; the incense made from spices; and the curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle.

They also presented the bronze altar, its grating, poles, and all its vessels; the basin with its base; the curtains of the court and its columns with their bases; the curtain at the entrance of the court; its cords and its pegs.

Nothing was lacking from the vessels that had been commanded for the service of the tabernacle and the tent of the covenant. The Israelites also presented the garments for service in the sanctuary and the holy garments used by the priests—namely, Aaron and his sons—as the Lord had commanded. When Moses saw that everything had been completed, he blessed them.

### [C. CXXXVII, Chapter XL]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“In the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall erect the tabernacle of testimony. You shall place the ark in it, and hang the veil before it. After bringing in the table, you shall place upon it what has been duly commanded. The lampstand shall stand with its lamps, and the golden altar on which incense is burned shall be before the ark of testimony. You shall place the curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle, and before it the altar of burnt offering. You shall place the basin between the altar and the tabernacle, and fill it with water.

“You shall surround the court with curtains and its entrance. Taking the oil of anointing, you shall anoint the tabernacle and its vessels, so that they may be consecrated; the altar of burnt offering and all its vessels; the basin and its base. You shall consecrate everything with the oil of anointing, so that they may be most holy.

“You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, wash them with water, and clothe them in the holy garments, so that they may minister to me. Their anointing shall serve for an everlasting priesthood.”

Moses did everything that the Lord had commanded.

### [T. XVII, C. CXXXVIII]

Thus, in the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was set up. Moses erected it, placed the boards, bases, and poles, set up the columns, and spread the covering over the tabernacle, placing the outer covering above it, as the Lord had commanded.

He placed the testimony in the ark, inserted the poles beneath it, and placed the oracle above it. When he had brought the ark into the tabernacle, he hung the veil before it, fulfilling the Lord’s command.

He also placed the table in the tabernacle of testimony on the northern side, outside the veil, arranging the bread of the Presence upon it, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

He placed the lampstand in the tabernacle of testimony opposite the table, on the southern side, setting the lamps in order according to the Lord’s command.

He placed the golden altar beneath the covering of testimony, opposite the veil, and burned fragrant incense upon it, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

He placed the curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle [Vulgate adds: “of testimony”], and the altar of burnt offering in the vestibule of the testimony. On it he offered burnt offerings and sacrifices, as the Lord had commanded.

He also set the basin between the tabernacle of testimony and the altar, filling it with water. Moses, Aaron, and his sons washed their hands and feet when they entered the tent of the covenant and approached the altar, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

He also erected the court around the tabernacle and the altar, hanging the curtain at its entrance.

### [C. CXXXIX]

When everything had been completed, the cloud covered the tabernacle of testimony, and the glory of the Lord filled it. Moses could not enter the tent of the covenant, because the cloud covered everything and the majesty of the Lord flashed forth, for the cloud had covered it all.

Whenever the cloud departed from the tabernacle, the children of Israel set out in their companies. If it remained above it, they stayed in the same place. For the cloud of the Lord rested over the tabernacle by day, and fire by night, before the eyes of all the people of Israel throughout all their encampments.

[Col. 0295] The Book of Elle Smoth, that is, Exodus, ends.

[Col. 0295]

## [THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS]

## [TABLE OF CONTENTS OF THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS]

### TITLES OF THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS, THAT IS, VAJECRA

[Col. 0295C]

I. Where the law of burnt offerings to the Lord from animals or birds is promulgated.

II. The sacrifice for sin committed through ignorance. Provision is made for the high priest’s inadvertence, the people’s error, an unclean act, recollection of sin, and those who act rashly.

III. Concerning the sacrifice of those who through error eat consecrated things, and concerning one who denies or swears falsely, and concerning libations.

IV. Concerning the offerings that priests must offer for themselves, or what they may receive from the offerings; concerning fat and blood.

V. How priests are to be initiated and what garments they are to wear. Concerning the anointing of the tabernacle and its vessels. Where Moses, like the high priest, receives the portion of Aaron the priest. Aaron’s sons are struck down when they unlawfully offer fire.

VI. Priests are commanded not to drink wine when they enter the temple. Concerning clean and unclean animals and birds that may be eaten.

VII. Concerning a woman who gives birth and becomes unclean. Concerning the contamination or diagnosis of leprosy. Concerning leprosy of garments. Concerning the cleansing of leprosy. Concerning the leprosy and cleansing of rich and poor, and the cleansing of houses.

VIII. Concerning a man suffering a discharge of semen, or things that commonly occur during sleep. Concerning women’s menstrual periods and discharges.

IX. Concerning the two goats and the two calves to be sacrificed for the people and the high priest.

X. It is prescribed that every victim slaughtered in the field is to be offered to the Lord as firstfruits, and that no one may eat blood, carrion, or anything seized by a wild beast.

XI. The fear of God is commanded: one must fear one’s father; idols are not to be made; and other matters pertaining to the law and its ordinances.

XII. It is prescribed that no Israelite or member of the holy seed is to be consecrated to an idol. Concerning male and female adulterers; and which persons may lawfully be joined in marriage.

XIII. It is prescribed that a priest must mourn no one and may take neither a widow nor a divorced woman as wife; that one blemished by bodily defects must not offer sacrifice; and that no foreigner may touch the holy things.

XIV. Concerning the peace offerings that are to be consecrated to the Lord. Concerning the festival of unleavened bread and the consecration of ears of grain at Pentecost.

XV. Concerning the seventh month, fasting, and the festivals of booths. Oil to be offered for the lamps. And concerning the twelve loaves continually placed upon the altar.

[Col. 0298A]

XVI. Concerning the blasphemer of the law who is stoned, and how those who enter may obtain the promised land. Concerning the impoverished Hebrew who sells his property. Concerning the houses of the Levites; the sale of free persons; and resident aliens. Blessings for those who keep the law and curses for those who despise the law of God. Concerning vows and sacrifices, and the priest’s valuation.

## BRIEF CONTENTS OF THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS

[Col. 0297]

I. Concerning ten kinds of offerings made without leaven, with salt alone to be mixed in.

II. Concerning another ten kinds of offerings for ignorance, forgetfulness, uncleanness, error, and contempt.

III. Concerning the rite of priestly victims and other sacrifices, and concerning the prohibition against eating blood.

IV. Concerning the consecration of Aaron and his sons and of all the vessels, and concerning sacrificed victims.

V. Concerning the presence of the Lord’s glory over the tabernacle and burnt offerings consumed by divine fire, where Nadab and Abihu were killed by fire.

VI. Concerning clean and unclean animals, and the purification of a woman after childbirth.

VII. Concerning the varieties of leprosy and its cleansing.

VIII. Concerning the afflictions or uncleanness of both man and woman.

IX. Concerning the observance required of the high priest who enters the holy places; concerning the two goats separated by lot; concerning the day of affliction; and concerning the prohibition against eating blood.

X. Concerning the abominable uncleannesses and sacrileges of the nations, and the establishment of commandments.

XI. Concerning magicians, adulterers, and abominations. Concerning the avoidance of ventriloquists; and concerning priests and the whole clergy, so that they may be free from every vice and may not eat holy things while unclean.

XII. Concerning sacrifices to be offered without blemish, and the rejection of offerings from foreigners.

XIII. Concerning the five more celebrated festivals of the year, the oil of the lamps, and the bread of the Presence.

XIV. Concerning the son of an Israelite woman who blasphemed the Name; “an eye for an eye”; the land’s keeping sabbath in the seventh year; the remissions of the jubilee year; and the Lord’s words to the Jews: “The land is mine, and you are resident aliens and settlers.”

XV. Concerning the prosperity that the Lord promises if what he commands is done, and concerning sevenfold vengeance for transgression.

XVI. Concerning the various regulations for redeeming vows by a price.

## CHAPTERS OF THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS, THAT IS, VAJECRA

[Col. 0297]

I. The Lord spoke to Moses from the tabernacle of testimony concerning sacrifices.

II. God tells Moses what is to be offered for the sin of ignorance by a priest or by the people.

III. What is to be offered for negligence.

IV. Concerning something entrusted and found: if someone lies or swears falsely.

V. Concerning the burnt offering.

VI. What the anointed priest is to offer.

VII. The sin offering.

VIII. Fat and blood, and what has been eaten by a wild beast, are not to be consumed.

IX. Concerning the sacrifice of well-being.

X. Moses washed Aaron and his sons and clothed him in priestly garments.

[Col. 0297D]

XI. He anointed Aaron and his sons and clothed them; they offered burnt offerings and sacrifices, and fire descended and consumed everything.

XII. Nadab and Abihu, while offering strange fire, were consumed by heavenly fire.

XIII. He commands priests, when they approach [Note: The Palatinus manuscripts add, “the altar.”] God, not to drink wine.

XIV. Concerning the sacrifice that remains: [Note: The same manuscript adds, “with their priests.”] he commanded the priests to eat it with their own household.

[Col. 0298C]

XV. Concerning animals that may be eaten.

XVI. Concerning fish that may be eaten.

XVII. Concerning birds that may not be eaten.

XVIII. Concerning animals that may not be eaten.

XIX. Concerning reptiles that may not be eaten.

XX. Concerning a woman who has given birth to a male child.

XXI. Concerning a woman who has given birth to a girl.

XXII. Concerning the touch of leprosy.

XXIII. One cleansed of leprosy is to be shown to the priest and may then enter the camp.

XXIV. Concerning a leprous spot in a house.

XXV. Concerning a man who has a discharge from his body.

XXVI. Concerning a woman who has a discharge of blood.

XXVII. Aaron must not continually enter the inner sanctuary.

[Col. 0298D]

XXVIII. In the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, one must fast.

XXIX. Sacrifices are to be offered by God’s priests.

XXX. Blood and an animal that has died of itself are not to be eaten.

XXXI. Carrion and what has been seized by a wild beast are not to be eaten.

XXXII. One must not sleep with any woman of one’s own kin.

XXXIII. One must not commit adultery.

[Col. 0299A]

XXXIV. Those who approach God must be holy [Note: The Palatinus manuscript reads, “who belong to God”] and must love their parents.

XXXV. The remnants of the harvest are to be left for the poor.

XXXVI. One must not steal, lie, swear falsely, or act as an informer.

XXXVII. One must not harm one’s neighbor.

XXXVIII. One must not withhold a hired worker’s wages.

XXXIX. You shall not curse the deaf.

XL. You shall not place a stumbling block before the blind.

XLI. You shall fear the Lord your God.

XLII. You shall not judge unjustly.

XLIII. You shall not show partiality.

XLIV. You shall not walk deceitfully.

XLV. You shall not stand against your neighbor’s blood.

XLVI. You shall not hate [Note: The same manuscript reads “you shall not kill,” instead of “hate.”] your brother, nor shall you take vengeance upon yourself.

[Col. 0299B]

XLVII. You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

XLVIII. You shall not allow your animals to mate with a different species.

XLIX. You shall not wear a garment made of different kinds of material.

L. If someone sleeps with a slave woman betrothed to a man.

LI. You shall not practice divination or augury.

LII. You shall not profane your daughter by making her a prostitute.

LIII. Ventriloquists and enchanters are not to be consulted.

LIV. Elders and presbyters are to be honored.

LV. The resident alien is to be loved.

LVI. Weights and measures are to be kept equal.

LVII. Whoever gives his daughter to the prince Molech shall be put to death.

LVIII. Whoever follows ventriloquists or enchanters shall perish from among the people.

[Col. 0299C]

LIX. Whoever curses his father or mother shall be put to death.

LX. Adulterers shall both be put to death.

LXI. Whoever sleeps with his father’s wife shall both be put to death.

LXII. If anyone remains with his daughter-in-law, both shall be put to death.

LXIII. Whoever lies with a male in a woman’s manner shall both be put to death.

LXIV. Whoever takes a woman and her mother shall be burned with fire.

[Col. 0300A]

LXV. Whoever gives his sexual embrace to a quadruped shall be put to death, and you shall kill the quadruped.

LXVI. [Note: The Palatinus manuscript does not contain this entire chapter 66.] Whatever woman approaches any animal for the purpose of intercourse, they shall be killed.

LXVII. Whoever takes his sister as a wife [Note: We retain “wife” from the Palatinus manuscript; the word was missing.] shall be cut off from the people.

LXVIII. If anyone has intercourse with a menstruating woman, or with his father’s, uncle’s, or brother’s wife, they shall be put to death.

LXIX. The ventriloquist and enchanter are to be stoned.

LXX. Priests must not be defiled in anything, but must be holy.

LXXI. If a priest’s daughter prostitutes herself for fornication, she shall be burned with fire.

LXXII. A man in whom there is a blemish shall not approach to offer gifts to God.

[Col. 0300B]

LXXIII. A priest in whom there is uncleanness who nevertheless approaches the holy things is to be exterminated by God; and no outsider is to eat of the holy things.

LXXIV. A blemished or defective animal is not to be offered.

LXXV. Concerning the sacrifice of prayer.

LXXVI. Concerning the observance of the Sabbath.

LXXVII. Concerning Passover and Unleavened Bread.

LXXVIII. Concerning the offering of the firstfruits of the harvest.

LXXIX. Concerning the seventh month.

LXXX. Oil is to be brought for the light of the lamp.

LXXXI. The blasphemer is to be stoned.

LXXXII. Whoever kills is to be killed, and concerning the Jubilee.

LXXXIII. Concerning the poor brother.

LXXXIV. Concerning the brother who is sold and bought.

[Col. 0300C]

LXXXV. Idols are not to be made.

LXXXVI. Sabbaths are to be observed.

LXXXVII. War will be absent if the commandments are kept.

LXXXVIII. In tribulations, famine, and grievous plagues, those who do not keep the commandments are to be punished.

LXXXIX. The vow of a male or female is to be redeemed by a price, but among cattle the animal is not to be exchanged.

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF VAJECRA, WHICH IN GREEK IS CALLED LEVITICUS

[Col. 0299]

### [T. I, B. I, C. I, Chapter I]

He called Moses, and the Lord spoke to him from the tabernacle of testimony, saying:

“Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: If anyone among you offers an offering to the Lord from livestock—that is, offering victims from cattle or sheep—if his offering is a burnt offering, he shall offer a male without blemish from the herd at the door of the tabernacle of testimony, to make the Lord favorable toward him. He shall place his hand upon the head of the victim, and it shall be acceptable and effective for his expiation.

“He shall slaughter the calf before the Lord. The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall offer its blood, pouring it around the altar that is before the door of the tabernacle. After removing the victim’s skin, they shall cut its limbs into pieces and place them upon the altar fire, with a pile of wood already arranged beneath. They shall arrange the cut members above it—namely, the head and everything attached to the liver—after washing the intestines and feet with water. The priest shall burn them upon the altar as a burnt offering and a sweet odor to the Lord.

“But if the offering is from livestock, a burnt offering from sheep or goats, he shall offer a male without blemish:

[Note: The eleven manuscript copies that we compared exactly in this work read this passage in two ways. The canon of Hebrew truth, the Royal Bible manuscript no. 3563, and four others—from Saint-Germain or the monastery of Corbie—read as follows: “But if the offering is from livestock, a burnt offering from sheep or goats, he shall offer a year-old male without blemish.” Three manuscripts of the Colbert Library—nos. 74, 157, and 181—together with one from Corbie, no. 1, and another from Saint-Germain, no. 7, add *lamb*, that is, they read: “he shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish.” But the Hebrew has neither “lamb” nor “year-old”; there we read, as in the printed editions, *zākār tāmîm yaqrîbennû*, meaning “he shall bring or offer a male without blemish.” The Septuagint interpreters and the Samaritan text agree with this reading, but then add different material. The Samaritan text has: “He shall bring it to the door of the tabernacle,” and so forth. The Septuagint has: *καὶ ἐπιθήσει τὴν χεῖρα ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ*, that is, “And he shall place his hand upon its head.” In any case, there is an obvious error in all the Latin manuscript copies, where scribes wrote “lamb” and “year-old” instead of “male,” or “a male.” —MART. Our manuscripts, and nearly all those used by Martianus, read: “a year-old and unblemished burnt offering”; others read: “a year-old lamb,” and so forth. The Hebrew literally reads: “He shall offer a male without blemish.”]

“He shall slaughter it on the side of the altar facing north, before the Lord. The sons of Aaron shall pour its blood around the altar. They shall divide its limbs, its head, and everything attached to the liver, and place them on the wood beneath which the fire is to be laid. They shall wash the intestines and feet with water. The priest shall offer all of it and burn it upon the altar as a burnt offering and a most sweet odor to the Lord.

“But if the offering to the Lord is a burnt offering from birds, he shall offer a turtledove or a young pigeon. The priest shall bring it to the altar, twist back its head at the neck, and, after opening the wound, let its blood run down upon the rim of the altar. He shall throw the crop with its contents and the feathers beside the altar, toward the east, at the place where ashes are usually poured out. He shall break its wings, but shall not cut it apart or divide it with a blade, and shall burn it upon the altar, with wood placed beneath the fire. It is a burnt offering, an offering of a most sweet odor to the Lord.”

### [Chapter II]

When a person offers an offering [Hebrew: a gift] of sacrifice to the Lord, his offering shall be fine flour. He shall pour oil over it, place frankincense on it, and bring it to the sons of Aaron, the priests. One of them shall take a handful of the fine flour and oil, together with all the frankincense, and place it as a memorial portion upon the altar, as a most sweet odor to the Lord. Whatever remains of the sacrifice shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is most holy among the offerings of the Lord.

When you offer a sacrifice cooked in an oven, it shall be made of fine flour: loaves without leaven, mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil.

If your offering is from a griddle, it shall be fine flour mixed with oil and without leaven. You shall divide it into small pieces and pour oil over it.

But if the sacrifice is from a griddle, the fine flour shall likewise be mixed with oil, and you shall offer it to the Lord, handing it over to the priest. When he has offered it, he shall take a memorial portion from the sacrifice and burn it upon the altar as a sweet odor to the Lord. Whatever remains shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is most holy among the offerings of the Lord.

Every offering presented to the Lord shall be made without leaven; nothing leavened or containing honey shall be burned as a sacrifice to the Lord. You shall offer these only as firstfruits and gifts; they shall not be placed upon the altar as a sweet odor.

Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt, and you shall not remove the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice. In every offering [Vulgate adds: “your”] you shall offer salt.

But if you offer the Lord a gift of firstfruits from your crops, from ears of grain that are still green, you shall roast them in fire, crush them in the manner of grain, and thus offer your firstfruits to the Lord, pouring oil over them and placing frankincense upon them, because it is an offering to the Lord. From it the priest shall burn, as a memorial of the gift, a portion of the crushed grain and oil, together with all the frankincense.

### [Chapter III]

But if his offering is a peace offering, and he wishes to offer from the herd, whether male or female, he shall offer an unblemished animal before the Lord. He shall place his hand upon the head of his victim, which shall be slaughtered at the entrance of the Tent of Witness, and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall pour out its blood around the altar.

They shall offer from the peace offering, as an offering to the Lord, the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is within: the two kidneys with the fat covering the loins, and the lobe of the liver with the kidneys. They shall burn these upon the altar as a burnt offering, with wood placed beneath the fire, as an offering of most pleasing fragrance to the Lord.

But if his offering is from the sheep, and [Col. 0302C] is a peace offering, whether he offers a male or a female, it shall be unblemished. If he offers a lamb before the Lord, he shall place his hand upon the head of his victim, which shall be slaughtered in the vestibule of the Tent of Witness; and the sons of Aaron shall pour out its blood around the altar.

They shall offer from the peace offering a sacrifice to the Lord: the fat and the entire tail together with the kidneys, the fat covering the belly and all the entrails, both kidneys with the fat beside the loins, and the lobe of the liver with the kidneys. The priest shall burn these upon the altar as fuel for the fire and as an offering to the Lord.

If his offering is a goat, and he offers it to the Lord, he shall place his hand upon its head and shall slaughter it at the entrance of the Tent of Witness. The sons of Aaron shall pour out its blood around the altar.

They shall take from it, as [Col. 0302D] food for the Lord’s fire, the fat covering the belly, [Col. 0303A] the fat covering all the entrails, the two kidneys with the network over them beside the loins, and the fatty portion of the liver with the kidneys. The priest shall burn these upon the altar as nourishment for the fire and as a most pleasing fragrance.

Every fat shall belong to the Lord by perpetual right throughout your generations and in all your dwellings. You shall eat neither fat nor blood at all.

[T. II, B. II, C. II, Chapter IV]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel: When a person sins inadvertently by doing anything contrary to any of the Lord’s commandments—things which he has commanded not to be done—if the anointed priest has sinned, bringing guilt upon the people, he shall offer to the Lord for his sin an unblemished bull, and shall bring it to the entrance of the Tent of Witness before the Lord. [Col. 0303B]

He shall place his hand upon its head and slaughter it before the Lord. He shall take some of the bull’s blood and carry it into the Tent of Witness. When he has dipped his finger in the blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times before the Lord, toward the veil of the sanctuary.

He shall place some of the same blood upon the horns of the altar of the most pleasing incense before the Lord, which is in the Tent of Witness. All the remaining blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering at the entrance of the Tent.

He shall remove the bull’s fat for the sin offering [Hebrew: “he shall remove all the fat of the bull of the sin offering”], both the fat covering the entrails and all that is within, the two kidneys and the network over them beside the loins, and the fat of the liver with the kidneys, as it is removed from the bull of the peace offering. He shall burn these upon the altar of burnt offering. [Col. 0303C]

But the hide and all the flesh, together with the head, the legs, the entrails, the dung, and the rest of the body, he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place where the ashes are customarily poured out. He shall burn them upon a pile of wood; they shall be burned in the place where the ashes are poured out.

But if the whole congregation of Israel has acted unknowingly and through ignorance has done something contrary to the Lord’s commandment, and afterward comes to know its sin, it shall offer a bull for the sin [Vulgate adds: “its sin”], and shall bring it to the entrance of the Tent.

The elders of the people shall place their hands upon its head before the Lord. When the bull has been slaughtered in the presence of the Lord, the anointed priest shall carry some of its blood into the Tent of Witness and, having dipped his finger in it, shall sprinkle it seven times toward the veil.

He shall place some of the same blood upon the horns of the altar that is before the Lord in the Tent of Witness. The rest of the blood he shall pour out beside the base of the altar of burnt offerings, which is at the entrance of the Tent of Witness.

He shall remove all its fat and burn it upon the altar, doing with this bull as he did with the former one. When the priest has interceded for them, the Lord will be merciful to them. He shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it as he burned the former bull, because it is for the sin of the multitude. [Col. 0303D]

If a ruler sins and, through ignorance, does one of the things forbidden by the law of the Lord [Hebrew: “forbidden by the law of the Lord his God”], and afterward comes to know his sin, he shall offer to the Lord an unblemished male goat. He shall place his hand upon its head and, when he has slaughtered it in the place where the burnt offering is customarily slaughtered before the Lord—for it is a sin offering—the priest shall dip his finger in the blood of the sin offering, touch the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and pour out the rest [Vulgate adds: “of the blood”] at its base. [Col. 0304A]

He shall burn the fat upon it, as is customarily done with the victims of peace offerings. The priest shall intercede for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.

But if a person from the people of the land sins inadvertently by doing any of the things forbidden by the Lord’s law, and thereby incurs guilt, and comes to know his sin, he shall offer an unblemished female goat. He shall place his hand upon the head of the sin offering and slaughter it in the place of the burnt offering.

The priest shall take some of its blood on his finger, touch the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and pour out the rest at its base. Removing all its fat, as the fat is customarily removed from the victims of peace offerings, he shall burn it upon the altar as a pleasing fragrance to the Lord. He shall intercede for him, and it shall be forgiven him. [Col. 0304B]

But if he offers a sheep from the flock as a sin offering, namely an unblemished ewe, he shall place his hand upon its head and slaughter it in the place where the victims of burnt offerings are customarily slaughtered.

The priest shall take some of its blood on his finger, touch the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and pour out the rest at its base. Removing all its fat, as the fat of the ram slaughtered for peace offerings is customarily removed, he shall burn it upon the altar as an offering to the Lord. He shall intercede for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.

[C. III, Chapter V]

If a person sins by hearing the voice of one administering an oath, and is a witness—whether he has seen the matter himself or is aware of it—yet does not declare it, he shall bear his guilt. [Col. 0304C]

A person who touches anything unclean, whether something killed by a beast, an animal that died naturally, or any other creeping creature, and forgets his uncleanness [Hebrew: “a person who touches anything unclean, or the carcass of an unclean beast, or of any unclean quadruped or creeping creature, and forgets”], is guilty and has incurred sin.

If he touches any human uncleanness, whatever impurity by which a person may become defiled, and afterward forgets it but later comes to know it, he shall be liable for his offense.

A person who swears and utters with his lips that he will do either something evil or something good, and confirms it by oath and speech, but afterward forgets and comes to understand his offense, shall do penance for his sin and offer a female lamb from the flock or a female goat. The priest shall intercede for her and for her sin. [Col. 0304D]

But if he cannot offer an animal, he shall offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the Lord, one for a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering. He shall give them to the priest, who shall first offer the one for the sin offering. He shall twist its head back toward the wings [Hebrew: “the neck”], so that it remains attached to the neck and is not completely torn off.

He shall sprinkle some of its blood on the wall of the altar. Whatever remains of it he shall cause to drip at the altar’s foundation, because it is a sin offering. He shall burn the other as a burnt offering, as is customary. The priest shall intercede for him and for his sin [Hebrew: “the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin”], and it shall be forgiven him. [Col. 0305A]

But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he shall offer fine flour as a sin offering, a tenth part of an ephah. He shall put no oil upon it and shall add no frankincense, because it is a sin offering.

He shall hand it to the priest, who shall take a full handful from it and burn it upon the altar as its memorial, on behalf of the one who offered it, interceding for him and making atonement. The remaining portion shall belong to the priest as an offering.

> **Note:** Another reading is found in the Regius manuscript of the Bible, in one Corbie manuscript, and in the Hebrew canon: *plenum ex toto pugillum* (“a full handful from the whole”), whereas the printed editions, following the Hebrew, read *plenum ex ea pugillum* (“a full handful from it”). MART. The Palatine and Urbinas manuscripts read *plenum ex eo pugillum* (“a full handful from it”); others among Martianus’s manuscripts read *ex toto* (“from the whole”) instead of *ex eo* (“from it”). [Col. 0305D; Col. 0306D]

[T. III]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: If a person, through ignorance [Hebrew: “through inadvertence”], violates the rites concerning things consecrated to the Lord, he shall offer for his offense an unblemished ram from the flock, which may be purchased for two shekels according to the sanctuary standard.

He shall make restitution for the loss itself [Hebrew: lacks this clause] and shall add a fifth part, giving it to the priest. The priest shall intercede for him, offering the ram, and it shall be forgiven him. [Col. 0305B]

If a person sins inadvertently and does one of the things forbidden by the Lord’s law, and, having incurred guilt through sin, comes to know his iniquity, he shall offer to the priest an unblemished ram from the flock, according to the measure and valuation of the sin. The priest shall intercede for him because he acted unknowingly, and it shall be forgiven him, because he sinned against the Lord through error.

[C. IV, Chapter VI]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: If a person sins and, despising the Lord, denies to his neighbor a deposit entrusted to his keeping [Hebrew: “or whatever was entrusted to his keeping”], or forcibly extorts something, or commits fraud, or finds a lost thing and, moreover, perjures himself by denying it, or does any other of the many things by which people commonly sin, once convicted of the offense he shall restore in full everything he sought to obtain by fraud, and shall add a fifth part for the owner whom he injured. [Col. 0305C]

For his sin he shall offer an unblemished ram from the flock and give it to the priest, according to the measure and valuation of the offense. The priest shall intercede for him before the Lord, and he shall be forgiven for each of the things by which he sinned.

[B. III, C. V]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command Aaron and his sons: This is the law of the burnt offering. It shall burn upon the altar all night until morning; the fire from that same altar shall burn in it.

The priest shall put on a tunic and linen undergarments. He shall remove the ashes that the consuming fire has expelled and place them beside the altar. Then he shall remove his former garments, put on others, and carry the ashes outside the camp to a completely clean place, where he shall cause them to be consumed to ashes [Hebrew: lacks “to a completely clean place”; “he shall cause it to be consumed to the ashes”]. [Col. 0305D]

The fire on the altar shall always burn; the priest shall maintain it by placing wood upon it every morning. Having laid the burnt offering upon it, he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings above it. This is the perpetual fire, which shall never fail upon the altar.

This is the law of the sacrifice and libations that the sons of Aaron shall offer before the Lord and before the altar [Hebrew: “before the Lord upon the altar”]. [Col. 0306A]

The priest shall take a handful of fine flour mixed with oil and all the frankincense placed upon the flour. He shall burn it upon the altar as a memorial, a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord. The remaining portion of the flour Aaron and his sons shall eat, without leaven, and they shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the Tent.

It shall not be leavened, because a portion of it is offered as incense to the Lord. It shall be most holy, like the sin offering and the offense offering. Only males of Aaron’s lineage shall eat it. It is a perpetual ordinance [Vulgate: “It shall be”] throughout your generations from the sacrifices of the Lord. Everyone who touches them shall be sanctified.

[T. IV, C. VI]

The Lord also spoke to Moses, saying: This is the offering of Aaron and his sons, which they must offer to the Lord on the day of his anointing. [Col. 0306B]

They shall offer a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour as a perpetual sacrifice, half of it in the morning and half in the evening. It shall be fried in a pan mixed with oil. The priest who succeeds his father by hereditary right shall offer it hot, as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, and it shall be wholly burned upon the altar. For every sacrifice of the priests shall be consumed by fire; no one shall eat from it.

[C. VII]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons: This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is offered, it shall be slaughtered before the Lord. It is most holy.

The priest who is to offer it [Vulgate: “who offers”] shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the Tent. Whatever touches its flesh shall be sanctified.

If any of its blood is splashed upon a garment, it shall be washed in a holy place. The earthen vessel in which it was cooked shall be broken; but if it was a bronze vessel, it shall be scrubbed and washed with water. [Col. 0306C]

Every male of the priestly family shall eat its flesh, because it is most holy. The victim slaughtered for sin, whose blood is brought into the Tent of Witness to make atonement in the sanctuary, shall not be eaten; it shall be burned with fire.

[Chapter VII]

This also is the law of the offense offering; it is most holy. Therefore, where the burnt offering is slaughtered, the victim for the offense shall also be slaughtered. Its blood shall be poured around the altar.

They shall offer from it the tail and the fat covering the entrails, the two kidneys and the fat beside the loins, and the lobe of the liver with the kidneys. The priest shall burn these upon the altar; it is an offering by fire to the Lord for the offense. [Col. 0306D]

Every male of the priestly family shall eat this flesh in a holy place, because it is most holy [Vulgate: “because it is most holy,” masculine]. As the sin offering is offered, so also is the offense offering; there shall be one law for both offerings. It shall belong to the priest who offers it.

The priest who offers the victim of the burnt offering shall have its hide. Every offering of fine flour baked in an oven, and whatever is prepared in a griddle or in a pan, shall belong to the priest by whom it is offered [Hebrew adds: “and”]. [Col. 0307A] Whether it is mixed with oil or dry, it shall be divided in equal measure among all the sons of Aaron.

This is the law of the peace offering that is offered to the Lord. If it is offered in thanksgiving, they shall offer loaves without leaven, mixed with oil, unleavened cakes anointed with oil, and fine flour cooked and mixed with oil. They shall also offer leavened loaves with the thanksgiving victim that is sacrificed as a peace offering.

From these, one shall be offered to the Lord as firstfruits, and it shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the victim. Its flesh shall be eaten on the same day; none of it shall remain until morning.
