On the ninth day the leader of the sons of Benjamin, Abidan son of Gideoni, presented a silver basin weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, a silver bowl containing seventy shekels according to the sanctuary weight, both filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice; a golden mortar weighing ten shekels, filled with incense; a bull from the herd, a ram, and a yearling lamb for a burnt offering; a goat for sin; and, as sacrifices of well-being, two oxen, five rams, five goats, and five yearling lambs. This was the offering of Abidan son of Gideoni.

On the tenth day the leader of the sons of Dan, Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai, presented a silver basin weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, a silver bowl containing seventy shekels according to the sanctuary weight, both filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice; a golden mortar weighing ten shekels, filled with incense; a bull from the herd, a ram, and a yearling lamb for a burnt offering; a goat for sin; and, as sacrifices of well-being, two oxen, five rams, five goats, and five yearling lambs. This was the offering of Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai.

On the eleventh day the leader of the sons of Asher, Pagiel son of Ocran, presented a silver basin weighing one hundred and thirty shekels; a silver bowl containing seventy shekels according to the sanctuary weight, both filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice; a golden mortar weighing ten shekels, filled with incense; a bull from the herd, a ram, and a yearling lamb for a burnt offering; a goat for sin; and, as sacrifices of well-being, two oxen, five rams, five goats, and five yearling lambs. This was the offering of Pagiel son of Ocran.

On the twelfth day the leader of the sons of Naphtali, Ahira son of Enan, presented a silver basin weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, a silver bowl containing seventy shekels according to the sanctuary weight, both filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice; a golden mortar weighing ten shekels, filled with incense; a bull from the herd, a ram, and a yearling lamb for a burnt offering; a goat for sin; and, as sacrifices of well-being, two oxen, five rams, five goats, and five yearling lambs. This was the offering of Ahira son of Enan.

[C. XX.] These were offered at the dedication of the altar by the princes of Israel on the day when it was consecrated: twelve silver basins, twelve silver bowls, and twelve golden mortars. Each basin contained one hundred and thirty shekels of silver, and each bowl seventy shekels—that is, the total silver weight of all the vessels was two thousand four hundred shekels according to the sanctuary weight. There were twelve golden mortars full of incense, each weighing ten shekels according to the sanctuary weight—that is, one hundred and twenty shekels of gold in all. There were twelve bulls from the herd for burnt offerings, twelve rams, twelve yearling lambs, and their libations; and twelve goats for sin. As sacrifices of well-being: twenty-four oxen, sixty rams, sixty goats, and sixty yearling lambs. These were offered at the dedication of the altar, when it was anointed [Hebrew: “after it was anointed”].

[B. XVII.] And whenever Moses entered the tent of meeting to consult the oracle, he heard the voice speaking to him from the mercy seat that was over the ark of the testimony, between the two Cherubim; from there it also spoke to him.

[Cap. VIII.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to Aaron, and say to him: When you have set up the seven lamps—[Note: In printed editions and in several manuscripts the following words occur: ‘Let the lampstand be erected on the southern side. Give this command, therefore, so that the lamps may face directly toward the north, toward the table of the bread of the Presence.’ Robert Estienne and the theologians of Louvain marked these words with an obelus in their editions of the Bible, and rightly so, for no trace of this addition exists either in the Hebrew canon of the truth or in many other ancient Latin codices of the finest quality, such as the Royal, Colbertine, Corbie, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and others. Nor will you find anything of the kind in the Hebrew or Samaritan text, or finally among the interpreters—the Septuagint, Chaldean, Syriac, or Arabic. I would believe that it was for the most part borrowed from Exodus 40:22 and transferred here with a few changes and additions made for the sense. This conjecture is supported by the addition itself, which is found in the manuscripts neither in one form nor in the same words. In manuscript no. 3 of Saint-Germain-des-Prés we read: ‘Speak to Aaron, and say to him that, when he has set up the seven lamps, he should erect the lampstand on the southern side. Give this command, therefore, so that the lamps may face directly toward the north, toward the table of the bread of the Presence; they shall shine toward the side opposite it, the side facing the lampstand.’ In another manuscript, no. 5: ‘Speak to Aaron, and say to him: When you have set up the seven lamps of the lampstand, erect them on the southern side. Thus he commanded that the lamps, etc.’ In the canonical text, however, the sense is this: when you have set up the lamps, they shall shine toward the side corresponding to the front of the lampstand; that is, the projecting arms on which the lamps are placed shall face forward. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript adds: ‘Let him erect the lampstand on the southern side. Give this command, so that the lamps may face directly toward the north, toward the table of the bread of the Presence.’ Martianaeus found this addition, in somewhat different words, in other manuscripts as well; the Vulgate books prefer it, although the theologians of Louvain marked it long ago with an obelus.]—they shall shine toward the side that the lampstand faces.” And Aaron did so: he placed the lamps upon the lampstand, as the Lord had commanded Moses. Now this was the workmanship of the lampstand: it was made of beaten gold, both its central shaft and all the parts branching from either side of the rods; according to the pattern that the Lord had shown Moses, so he made the lampstand.

[B. XVIII, C. XXI.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Take the Levites from among the children of Israel, and purify them according to this rite: Let them be sprinkled with the water of purification, and let them shave all the hair of their bodies. When they have washed their garments and have been cleansed, let them take a bull from the herd, with its grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; and you shall take another bull from the herd for sin. You shall bring the Levites before the tent of meeting, after assembling the whole congregation of the children of Israel. When the Levites are before the Lord, the children of Israel shall lay their hands upon them. Aaron shall offer [Hebrew: ‘shall elevate’] the Levites as a gift before the Lord from the children of Israel, so that they may serve in his ministry. The Levites shall also lay their hands upon the heads of the bulls; you shall make one of them for sin and the other as a burnt offering to the Lord, to make atonement for them. You shall set the Levites before Aaron and his sons, and consecrate those offered to the Lord; you shall separate them from among the children of Israel, so that they may be mine. Afterward they shall enter the tent of meeting [Note: A marginal scholion notes here that the Hebrew text always has, in place of ‘tent of meeting,’ ‘tent of appointment.’ In Hebrew we always read *ohel moed*—‘tent of meeting’; but *moed* is interpreted by Jerome as ‘appointment’ in Book I of Samuel, chapter 20, and elsewhere. Hence Martianaeus takes this as a not implausible indication that the author of the marginal scholia on the Hebrew canon of the truth was Jerome himself. MART. —The same manuscript reads *ingrediantur* (‘let them enter’). As for the Scholiast’s note that the Hebrew always has ‘tent of appointment,’ that is, *ohel moed*, Jerome usually translates *moed* as ‘testimony’ or ‘covenant,’ and more rarely as ‘appointment.’ Nevertheless, Martianaeus could have inferred from this very fact that Jerome was the author of the scholia.] so that they may serve me.” Thus you shall purify and consecrate them as an offering to the Lord [Hebrew omits “to the Lord”], because they have been given to me as a gift by the children of Israel.

[C. XXII.] “In place of all the firstborn who open every womb in Israel, I have taken them. Every firstborn of the children of Israel is mine, both human and animal. From the day when I struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I sanctified them to myself; and I took the Levites in place of all the firstborn of the children of Israel. I gave them as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the children of Israel [Note: In the Vulgate: ‘from among the people, so that they may serve me in place of Israel.’], so that they may serve me in place of the children of Israel in the tent of meeting and pray for them, lest there be a plague among the people if they should dare to approach the sanctuary [Hebrew: ‘and pray for the children of Israel, lest there be a plague among the children of Israel when the children of Israel approach the sanctuary’].”

And Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation of the children of Israel did for the Levites what the Lord had commanded Moses. They were purified and washed their garments. Aaron elevated them before the Lord and prayed for them, so that, having been purified, they might enter upon their duties [Hebrew: ‘so that they might be purified. And afterward the Levites entered upon their duties’] in the tent of meeting before Aaron and his sons. As the Lord had commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so it was done.

[B. XIX, C. XXIII.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “This is the law concerning the Levites: From twenty-five years of age and upward they shall enter to minister in the tent of meeting. When they have completed fifty years of age, they shall cease serving; they shall be ministers to their brothers in the tent of meeting, to guard what has been entrusted to them, but they shall not perform the actual work [Hebrew omits “the actual work”]. Thus you shall assign the Levites to their duties of guarding.”

[T. VI, B. XX, C. XIX, Cap. IX.] The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the second year after they had gone out from the land of Egypt, in the first month, saying: “Let the children of Israel celebrate the Passover at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of this month toward evening, according to all its ceremonies and ordinances.” And Moses commanded the children of Israel to celebrate the Passover. They celebrated it at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of the month toward evening, on Mount Sinai [Hebrew: “in the wilderness of Sinai”]. According to everything that the Lord had commanded Moses, so the children of Israel did.

[C. XXV.] But certain men who were unclean because of a human corpse, and therefore could not celebrate the Passover on that day, came to Moses and Aaron and said to them: “We are unclean because of a human corpse. Why should we be deprived, so that we cannot offer an offering to the Lord at its appointed time among the children of Israel?” Moses replied to them: “Wait, and I will consult what the Lord commands concerning you.”

[C. XXVI.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel: If anyone is unclean because of a corpse, or is on a distant journey in your nation, he shall celebrate the Passover for the Lord in the second month, on the fourteenth day of the month toward evening. With unleavened bread and wild lettuce [Hebrew omits this] they shall eat it. They shall leave nothing of it until morning, and they shall not break any of its bones; they shall observe every regulation of the Passover. But if anyone is clean, was not on a journey, and nevertheless did not celebrate the Passover, that person shall be cut off from his people, because he did not offer the sacrifice to the Lord at its appointed time; he shall bear his sin himself. And if a foreigner or resident alien is among you [Hebrew: ‘and also the alien who dwells among you’], he shall celebrate the Passover for the Lord according to its ceremonies and ordinances. There shall be one ordinance among you for both the foreigner and the native.”

[B. XXI.] Therefore, on the day when the tabernacle was erected, a cloud covered it. From evening onward there was something resembling fire over the tent until morning. It happened continually in this way: by day a cloud covered it, and by night something resembling fire. 

[B. XXII, C. XXVII.] When the cloud that protected the tabernacle was lifted, then the children of Israel set out; and wherever the cloud had stood, there they encamped. At the Lord’s command they set out, and at his command they erected the tabernacle [Hebrew: “encamped”]. All the days that the cloud remained over the tabernacle, they stayed in the same place. If it happened that it remained over it for a long time, the children of Israel kept the Lord’s watch and did not set out for as many days as the cloud remained over the tabernacle. At the Lord’s command they erected their tents [Hebrew: “set out, and at the Lord’s command they encamped”], and at his command they took them down. If the cloud was there from evening until morning, and immediately at dawn it left the tabernacle, they set out; and if it departed after a day and a night, they dismantled their tents [Hebrew: “set out”]. If it remained over the tabernacle for two days, or one month, or a longer time, the children of Israel stayed in the same place and did not set out; but as soon as it departed, they moved their camp [Hebrew omits this]. By the word of the Lord they erected their tents [Hebrew: “encamped”], and by his word they set out; and they kept the Lord’s watch according to his command through Moses.

[B. XXIII, C. XXVIII, Cap. X.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Make for yourself two trumpets [Hebrew: ‘flutes’] of beaten silver, by which you may summon the congregation whenever the camps are to be moved. When you sound them [Hebrew: ‘when they sound them’], the whole assembly shall gather to you at the entrance of the tent of meeting. If you sound only one, the leaders and heads of the congregation of Israel shall come to you. But if a prolonged and broken blast is sounded [Hebrew: ‘if one of them is sounded, the leaders and heads of the congregation of Israel shall come to you; but if a broken blast is sounded’], the camps of those who are on the eastern side shall set out first. At the second sound, with an equally broken blast of the trumpet, those who dwell to the south shall raise their tents [Hebrew: ‘camps’]; and the others shall do likewise, when the trumpets sound a broken blast for departure. When the people are to be assembled, the trumpet blast shall be simple, and they shall not sound a broken blast. The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall sound the trumpets; and this shall be a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations.

“When you go out to war in your land against enemies who fight against you, you shall sound a broken blast on the trumpets, and you shall be remembered before the Lord your God, and you shall be delivered from the hands of your enemies. Whenever you have a feast, or festival days, or New Moons, you shall sound the trumpets over your burnt offerings and sacrifices of well-being, so that they may serve as a remembrance of your God [Hebrew: ‘as a remembrance before your God’]. I am the Lord your God.”

[T. VII, B. XXIV, C. XXIX.] In the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud was lifted from the tabernacle of the testimony [Hebrew: “of the testimony”]. And the children of Israel set out by their companies from the wilderness of Sinai, and the cloud came to rest in the wilderness of Paran. They moved camp for the first time at the Lord’s command through Moses.

The sons of Judah set out by their companies, with Naasson son of Amminadab as their leader. In the tribe of the sons of Issachar the leader was Nathanael son of Zuar. In the tribe of Zebulun the leader was Eliab son of Helon. Then the tabernacle was taken down, and the sons of Gershon and Merari went out carrying it. The sons of Reuben also set out by their companies and in their appointed order, with Elizur son of Shedeur as their leader. In the tribe of the sons of Simeon the leader was Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai. In the tribe of Gad the leader was Eliasaph son of Deuel. Then the Kohathites set out carrying the sanctuary [Hebrew: “and they erected the tabernacle until they arrived—that is, the sons of Gershon and Merari erected the tabernacle until the Kohathites arrived”]. The tabernacle was carried until they came to the place where it was to be erected.

The sons of Ephraim also moved camp by their companies; in their army the leader was Elishama son of Ammihud. In the tribe of the sons of Manasseh the leader was Gamaliel son of Pedahzur. In the tribe of Benjamin the leader was Abidan son of Gideoni [Vulgate adds: “was”]. The last of all the camps to set out were the sons of Dan by their companies; in their army the leader was Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai. In the tribe of the sons of Asher the leader was Pagiel son of Ocran. In the tribe of the sons of Naphtali the leader was Ahira son of Enan. These were the camps [Hebrew: “departures”] and the departures of the children of Israel by their companies, whenever they set out.

[B. XXV, C. XXX.] Moses said to Hobab son of Reuel the Midianite, his kinsman: “We are setting out for the place that the Lord is going to give us. Come with us, so that we may do you good, because the Lord has promised good things to Israel.” He replied: “I will not go with you, but I will return to my land, in which I was born.” And he said: “Do not leave us, for you know in what places we ought to encamp in the wilderness, and you will be our guide” [Hebrew: “For you know how we encamped in the wilderness, and you will be to us as eyes”]. “When you come with us, whatever is best among the possessions that the Lord is going to give us [Vulgate: “hand over to us”], we will give you.”

[B. XXVI.] Thus they set out from the mountain of the Lord on a journey of three days, and the ark of the covenant of the Lord went before them for three days, seeking out a place for the camp. The cloud of the Lord was also over them by day as they marched. Whenever the ark was lifted, Moses said: “Arise, Lord, and let your enemies be scattered; let those who hate you flee from your presence.” But when it was set down, he said: “Return, Lord, to the multitude of the army of Israel.”

[B. XXVII, C. XXXI, Cap. XI.] Meanwhile a murmuring arose among the people, as of those suffering from toil, against the Lord. When the Lord heard it, he was angry. And the fire of the Lord, burning against them, devoured the outermost part of the camp. When the people cried out to Moses, Moses prayed to the Lord, and the fire was extinguished. He called the name of that place “Burning,” because the fire of the Lord had burned against them.

[B. XXVIII, C. XXXII.] The mixed multitude that had gone up with them burned with desire [Note: Some manuscript copies, together with the Hebrew canon of the truth, read ‘burned with desire for meat’; but the words ‘for meat’ are a mere marginal addition explaining the object of the multitude’s desire. Through the ignorance of scribes they were transferred into the sacred text, as can be learned from the Royal biblical manuscript no. 3563, in which the word *carn ium* (‘of meat’) had been written in the margin, preceded by two points, which still remain there, although the word *carn ium* has been entirely erased as foreign to the text. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript adds *carn ium* (‘of meat’), a word Martianaeus also found in his manuscripts.], and, sitting and weeping, with the children of Israel gathered together with them, said: “Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish that we ate freely in Egypt; cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic come to mind.” [Hebrew: “But now our soul is dry.”] “Our soul is dry; our eyes look upon nothing but manna.”

[C. XXXIII.] Now the manna was like coriander seed, and its color was like that of bdellium. The people went about, gathered it, crushed it with millstones or ground it in a mortar, cooked it in a pot, and made cakes from it, with a taste like that of bread baked with oil. When the dew fell upon the camp at night, the manna also fell with it.

Moses heard the people weeping by their families, each at the entrance of his tent. The anger of the Lord was greatly kindled, and the matter also seemed intolerable to Moses. He said to the Lord: “Why have you afflicted your servant? Why have I not found favor before you? Why have you laid the burden of this entire people upon me? Have I conceived this whole multitude, or given birth to it, that you should say to me: ‘Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse is accustomed to carry an infant, and bring them into the land that you swore to their fathers’? Where am I to get meat to give to this whole multitude? They weep against me, saying: ‘Give us meat, so that we may eat.’ I cannot bear this entire people alone, because it is too heavy for me. If you intend to treat me in this way [Hebrew: ‘If you are going to do this to me’], I beg you to kill me, so that I may find favor in your eyes and not be afflicted by such great evils.”

[B. XXIX.] And the Lord said to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people. Bring them to the entrance of the tent of meeting [Hebrew: ‘to the tent of meeting’], and make them stand there with you, so that I may come down and speak with you. I will take from your spirit and give it to them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you alone may not be burdened.

“Say also to the people: ‘Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat meat. For I have heard you saying: “Who will give us meat to eat? It was better for us in Egypt.” The Lord will give you meat, and you shall eat [Hebrew: ‘The Lord will also give you meat, and you shall eat’], not for one day, or two, or five, or ten, or even twenty, but for a whole month, until it comes out of your nostrils and turns to nausea, because you rejected the Lord who is in your midst and wept before him, saying: “Why did we ever leave Egypt?”’”

[C. XXXIV.] And Moses said: “There are six hundred thousand foot soldiers among this people, and you say: ‘I will give them meat to eat for a whole month.’ Shall such a multitude of sheep and oxen be slaughtered that it can suffice for food? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together in one place, so that they may be satisfied?” The Lord replied: “Is the Lord’s hand powerless? Now you shall see whether my word is fulfilled in deed.”

[B. XXX, C. XXXV.] Moses came and reported the words of the Lord to the people, gathering seventy men from the elders of the people [Vulgate adds: “of Israel”], whom he made stand around the tabernacle. Then the Lord descended in a cloud and spoke to him, taking from the spirit that was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men. When the spirit had rested upon them, they prophesied and did not cease [Hebrew: “and they did not cease”].

Two men had remained in the camp, one named Eldad and the other Medad, and the spirit rested upon them. They too had been enrolled, but had not gone out to the tabernacle. When they prophesied in the camp, a boy ran and announced to Moses, saying: “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp.” At once Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ attendant, chosen from among many, said: [Note: In Hebrew, *kelaem* or *chelaem*, which the Chaldean translates as *esarinum*, that is, ‘put them in prison’ or ‘shut them up,’ according to the scholion. Moreover, Jerome very often interprets the verb *chala* or *cala* as ‘to restrain’ or ‘to shut,’ and *calu* in his Prophets signifies ‘confinement’ or ‘prison.’ Nothing therefore prevents this scholion from truly being Hieronymian. MART.] “My lord Moses, restrain them” [Hebrew: “shut them up”]. But he said to him: “Are you jealous on my behalf? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord would give them his spirit!”

[B. XXXI.] Moses returned to the camp, he and the elders of Israel. Then a wind went forth from the Lord and, seizing quail from beyond the sea, brought them down into the camp for a distance equivalent to a day’s journey on every side around the camp. They flew in the air at a height of two cubits above the ground [Hebrew: “on every side around the camp, and at a height of two cubits above the face of the earth”].

The people rose throughout that whole day and night and the following day, and gathered quail—the one who gathered least gathered ten *kor* [Hebrew: “the one who gathered least, ten heaps, which in Hebrew are called *hamarim*”]—and spread them out around the camp to dry. The meat was still between their teeth, and this sort of food had not yet failed, when, behold, the anger of the Lord was kindled against the people, and he struck them with a very great plague. That place was called “Graves of Craving,” because there they buried the people who had desired.

[T. VIII.] Setting out from the Graves of Craving, they came to Hazeroth and remained there.

[B. XXXII, C. XXXVI, Cap. XII.] Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman he had taken, and they said: “Has the Lord indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not also spoken through us in the same way?” When the Lord heard this—for Moses was a man exceedingly meek, more than all the people who dwelt upon the earth—he immediately spoke to him, to Aaron, and to Miriam: “Go out, you three alone, to the tent of meeting.”

When they had gone out, the Lord descended in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tent, calling Aaron and Miriam. When they had come, he said to them: “Hear my words. If there is a prophet of the Lord among you, I shall appear to him in a vision, or I shall speak with him in a dream. But my servant Moses is not like that; he is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I speak with him, openly and not through riddles and figures; he sees the Lord” [Hebrew: “and he sees the form of the Lord”]. “Why, then, were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?”

And, being angry with them, he departed. The cloud that had been over the tabernacle also withdrew, and behold, Miriam appeared white with leprosy, like snow. When Aaron looked at her and saw that she was covered with leprosy, he said to Moses: “I beg you, my lord, do not lay this sin upon us, which we foolishly committed. Do not let her become like one dead, and like an untimely birth cast out from its mother’s womb.

“Behold, half of her flesh has already been devoured by leprosy” [Hebrew: “with half her flesh already consumed”].

Moses cried out to the Lord, saying: “God, I beg you, heal her.” The Lord replied to him: “If her father had spat in her face, would she not at least have had to be covered with shame for seven days? Let her be separated outside the camp for seven days, and afterward she shall be brought back” [Hebrew: “gathered”]. Miriam was therefore excluded outside the camp for seven days, and the people did not move from that place until Miriam had been brought back [Hebrew: “gathered”].

[B. XXXIII, Chapter XIII.] The people set out from Hazeroth and pitched their tents [Hebrew: encamped] in the wilderness of Paran. There the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Send men to survey the land of Canaan, which I am going to give to the Israelites—one from each tribe, from among their leaders [Hebrew: from among their ancestral heads].” Moses did what the Lord had commanded, sending leaders from the wilderness of Paran. These are their names:

From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua son of Zaccur. From the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat son of Hori. From the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh. From the tribe of Issachar, Igal son of Joseph. From the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun. From the tribe of Benjamin, Palti son of Raphu. [Col. 0365C] From the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel son of Sodi. From Joseph’s tribe, from the tribe [Vulgate: scepter] of Manasseh, Gaddi son of Susi. From the tribe of Dan, Ammiel son of Gemalli. From the tribe of Asher, Sethur [Vulgate: Sthur] son of Michael. From the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi son of Vophsi. From the tribe of Gad, Geuel son of Machi.

[C. XXXVII.] These are the names of the men whom Moses sent to survey the land. He called Hoshea son of Nun “Joshua.” Moses therefore sent them to survey the land of Canaan and said to them: “Go up through the southern region. When you reach the mountains [Hebrew: the mountain, that is, Jerusalem], examine the land—what it is like—and the people who inhabit it, whether they are strong or weak, few or many; whether the land itself is good or bad; what the cities are like, whether they are fortified or without walls; whether the soil is fertile or barren, wooded or without trees. Be courageous, and bring us some of the land’s fruit.” It was the season when the early grapes could already be eaten.

When they had gone up, they surveyed the land from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob, at the entrance of Hamath. They went up through the south and came to Hebron, where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak, were. Hebron had been founded seven years before Tanis, a city of Egypt.

Proceeding [Col. 0366A] as far as the Valley of Eshcol, they cut off a branch with its cluster of grapes, which two men carried on a pole. They also took pomegranates and figs from that place. It was called Nehel-Eshcol, that is, “Valley of the Cluster,” because the Israelites had carried a cluster away from there.

After forty days the scouts returned from surveying the land, having gone through the whole region [Hebrew: absent], and came to Moses and Aaron and the entire assembly of the Israelites in the wilderness of Paran, which is at Kadesh. They spoke to them and to the whole multitude and displayed the land’s fruit, reporting:

“We came to the land to which you sent us. It truly flows with milk and honey, as these fruits show. But its inhabitants are extremely strong, and its cities are very large [Vulgate omits: very] and fortified. We saw the descendants of Anak there. Amalek inhabits the south; the Hittite, Jebusite, and Amorite inhabit the hill country; while the Canaanite dwells beside the sea and along the streams of the Jordan.”

Meanwhile Caleb, silencing the murmuring of the people that had arisen against Moses, said: “Let us go up and take possession of the land, for we shall certainly be able to conquer it.” But the others who had gone up with him said: “We cannot go up against that people, for they are stronger than we are.” And they disparaged the land they had surveyed before the Israelites, saying: “The land through which we passed devours its inhabitants; and all the people whom we saw there are of towering stature. There we saw certain monstrous descendants of Anak, from the race of giants; compared with them, we seemed like grasshoppers.”

[B. XXXIV, Chapter XIV.] Then the whole assembly cried out and wept that night, and all the Israelites murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying:

“Would that we had died in Egypt, [Note: [Col. 0365D] All the older manuscripts read this passage with the negative particle, and not ‘Would that we perish in this vast wilderness.’ But there is plainly a scribal error here, since the scribes did not grasp the meaning of Scripture. Consult the annotation on the canon. MART. [Col. 0366D] —Our manuscripts, and those consulted by Martianus, read with the negative particle: ‘and not in this vast wilderness.’ So too do the printed editions before the correction of Sixtus V.”] or in this vast wilderness! Why is the Lord bringing us into this land, so that we may fall by the sword and our wives and children may be led away captive? Is it not better for us to return to Egypt?” And they said to one another: “Let us appoint a leader for ourselves and return to Egypt.”

When Moses and Aaron heard this, they fell prostrate on the ground before the whole multitude of the Israelites. But Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, who had also surveyed the land, tore their garments and spoke to the entire assembly of the Israelites:

“The land through which we passed is exceedingly good. If the Lord is favorable toward us, he will bring us into it and give us a land flowing with milk and honey. Do not rebel against the Lord, and do not fear the people of this land, for we can devour them as easily as bread. Their protection has departed from them; the Lord is with us. Do not fear them.”

When the whole multitude cried out and wanted to overwhelm them with stones, the glory of the Lord appeared [Col. 0367A] over the roof of the tent of covenant [Hebrew: in the tent of covenant] to all the Israelites.

[B. XXXV.] And the Lord said to Moses: “How long will this people disparage me? How long will they refuse to believe me, despite all the signs that I have performed among them? Therefore I will strike them with pestilence and consume them; but I will make you the leader of a great nation, stronger than this one” [Hebrew: “I will make you into a great nation, stronger than this one”].

[C. XXXVIII.] Moses said to the Lord:

“The Egyptians will hear—for you brought this people out from among them—and so will the inhabitants of this land, who have heard that you, Lord, are among this people and are seen face to face; that your cloud protects them; that by day you go before them in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire. If you were to destroy this great multitude as one man, they would say: ‘He was unable to bring the people into the land which he had sworn to give them; therefore he slaughtered them in the wilderness.’

“Therefore, let the Lord’s power be magnified, as you swore, saying [Hebrew: ‘as you spoke, saying’]: ‘The Lord is patient and of great mercy, taking away iniquity and crimes, and leaving no one innocent’ [Note: [Col. 0367D] Hebrew: words that may be rendered literally, ‘and by cleansing you will not cleanse.’ Jerome interpreted these same words above, in his commentary on Exodus 34:7, as ‘No one is innocent before you by himself.’ He explains them in his Dialogue against the Pelagians and elsewhere.], visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation. Forgive, I pray, the sin of this people according to the greatness of your mercy, just as you were favorable to them from their departure out of Egypt until this place.”

[B. XXXVI.] And the Lord said: “I have forgiven them according to your word. Yet, as I live, the glory of the Lord shall fill the whole earth. Nevertheless, all the men who saw my majesty and the signs that I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness, and who have now tested me ten times and have not obeyed my voice, shall not see the land concerning which I swore to their fathers. None of those who have disparaged me shall see it.

“But my servant Caleb, who followed me with a different spirit, I will bring into this land that he surveyed, and his descendants shall possess it. For the Amalekites and the Canaanites dwell in the valleys. Tomorrow break camp and return to the wilderness by way of the Red Sea.”

[C. XXXIX.] The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying:

“How long will this evil multitude murmur against me? I have heard the complaints of the Israelites. Say to them: ‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘as you have spoken in my hearing, so I will do to you. In this wilderness your corpses shall lie. All of you who have been numbered, from twenty years old and upward, and who have murmured against me, shall not enter the land over which I raised my hand, swearing that I would make you dwell in it [Hebrew: in it], except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.

“But your little ones, of whom you said that they would become prey to the enemy, I will bring in, so that they may see the land which displeased you. Your corpses [Col. 0368A] shall lie in this wilderness [Hebrew: in this wilderness]. Your sons shall wander [Hebrew: shepherd] in the wilderness for forty years and bear your faithlessness, until your corpses [Hebrew: yours, that is, of your fathers] are consumed in the wilderness, corresponding to the number of the forty days during which you surveyed the land: a year shall be counted for each day. And [Hebrew omits] for forty years you shall bear your iniquities, and you shall know my vengeance; for just as I have spoken, so I will do to this entire evil multitude that has risen against me. In this wilderness they shall fail and die.’”

[C. XL.] All the men whom Moses had sent to explore the land, who had returned and caused the entire multitude to murmur against him by disparaging the land and saying that it was bad, died, struck down before the Lord. [Col. 0368B] But Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh remained alive among all those who had gone to survey the land.

Moses spoke all these words to all the Israelites, and the people mourned greatly. Then, rising early in the morning, they went up to the summit of the mountain and said: “We are ready to go up to the place about which the Lord spoke, for we have sinned.”

Moses said to them: “Why are you transgressing the word of the Lord? It will not prosper for you.”

[C. XLI.] “Do not go up, for the Lord is not with you [Hebrew: in your midst], lest you fall before your enemies. The Amalekites and the Canaanites are there before you; you will fall by their sword, because you refused to obey the Lord, and the Lord will not be with you.”

But they, blinded, went up to the summit of the mountain. The ark of the Lord’s covenant and Moses, however, did not leave the camp. The Amalekite and the Canaanite who dwelt in the mountain came down, struck them, cut them to pieces, and pursued them as far as Hormah.

[T. IX, B. XXXVII, C. XLII, Chapter XV.] The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“Speak to the Israelites and say to them: When you have entered the land of your dwelling, which I will give you, and you make an offering to the Lord as a burnt offering or a sacrifice, fulfilling vows or presenting freewill offerings, or when at your festivals you burn an offering of pleasing fragrance to the Lord, from cattle or sheep, whoever offers a sacrifice shall present with the victim a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour [Hebrew omits], mixed [Col. 0368D] with oil measuring a quarter of a hin; and he shall provide wine of the same measure for libations, with the burnt offering or the sacrifice.

“For each lamb [Note: [Col. 0367D] The current Hebrew text does not have ‘for each ram’; [Col. 0368D] although a scholion calls attention to it, the Syriac likewise reads in the same way, namely, ‘for one ram,’ which means ‘for each ram.’ MART. —Here the Urbinas manuscript places a τελείαν στίγμην (‘a full stop’), connecting the preceding words with ‘for each lamb.’ It reads: ‘And the sacrifice of the ram shall be similar.’ Although this may carry the flavor of the rashness of an antiquarian critic, it is nevertheless worthwhile to know it.], and [Hebrew: and for each] ram, there shall be a grain offering of two-tenths, mixed with oil measuring one-third of a hin; and he shall offer wine for a libation, one-third of a hin [Vulgate omits: hin] of the same measure, as a pleasing fragrance to the Lord.

“When you make a burnt offering or a sacrifice from cattle, to fulfill a vow or as a sacrifice of well-being, you shall give for each ox a grain offering of three-tenths, mixed with oil measuring half a hin; and you shall give wine for libations of the same measure as an offering of most pleasing fragrance to the Lord. You shall do this for each ox, ram, lamb, and young goat. Both the native and the resident alien shall offer sacrifices according to the same rite. There shall be one ordinance and one judgment [Hebrew: one statute and one judgment] for you and for the resident aliens who dwell in the land.

[B. XXXVIII, C. XLIII.] The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“Speak to the Israelites and say to them: When you have entered the land that I will give you and eat the bread of that region, you shall set aside a first portion for the Lord from your food. Just as you set aside a first portion from the threshing floors, so you shall give a first portion to the Lord from your dough [Hebrew: from mixed flour] [Hebrew: from generation to generation].

[C. XLIV.] “But if through ignorance you overlook any of these things that the Lord spoke to Moses and commanded through him for you—from the day on which he began to give the commandment and thereafter—and the whole multitude forgets to do it, you shall offer a young bull from the herd as a burnt offering of most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, with its grain offering and libations as the rite requires, and a male goat for sin. The priest shall make atonement for the entire multitude of the Israelites, and it shall be forgiven them, because they sinned unintentionally; nevertheless, they shall offer incense to the Lord on their own behalf and on behalf of their sin and error. It shall be forgiven the whole congregation of the Israelites and the resident aliens who dwell among you [Col. 0369C] [Vulgate: them], because the fault was committed by the whole people through ignorance.

“But if one person sins unknowingly, he shall offer a year-old female goat for his sin, and the priest shall make supplication for him because he sinned unknowingly before the Lord; he shall obtain forgiveness for him, and it shall be forgiven him. There shall be one law for both the native and the resident alien, for all who sin unknowingly.

[C. XLV.] “But the person who acts presumptuously, whether he is a citizen or a resident alien—for he has rebelled against the Lord—shall be cut off from his people. For he has despised the word of the Lord and made his commandment void; therefore he shall be utterly cut off and bear his iniquity.

[B. XXXIX, C. XLVI.] It happened that, while the Israelites were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath day. They brought him before Moses and Aaron and the entire assembly. They confined him in prison, because they did not know what should be done to him.

The Lord said to Moses: “Let this man be put to death; let the whole multitude stone him outside the camp.” When they had brought him outside, they stoned him, and he died, as the Lord had commanded. [Vulgate adds: him.]

[B. XL, C. XLVII.] The Lord also said to Moses:

“Speak to the Israelites and tell them to make tassels at the corners of their garments, placing [Hebrew: throughout their generations, placing, etc.] violet cords in them. When they see them, they will remember all the commandments of the Lord and will not follow their own thoughts and their eyes, prostituting themselves with various things [Col. 0370A]; rather, remembering the Lord’s commandments, they shall do them and be holy to their God. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt so that I might be your God” [Hebrew: “I am the Lord your God”].

[T. X, B. XLI, Chapter XVI.] Now Korah son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On son of Peleth, from the descendants of Reuben, rose up against Moses. With them were two hundred and fifty other Israelites, leaders of the assembly, men summoned by name at the time of the council.

When they stood against Moses and Aaron, they said: “Let this be enough for you! For the whole multitude is holy, and the Lord is among them [Hebrew: the Lord is in their midst]. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the Lord’s people?”

When Moses heard this, he fell prostrate on his face [Hebrew: he fell upon his faces] and spoke to Korah and the entire multitude:

“Tomorrow the Lord will make known who belong to him, and he will draw the holy ones to himself; those whom he chooses will approach him. Do this: let each one take his censer—you, Korah, and your entire assembly. Tomorrow put fire in them and place incense upon it before the Lord. The one whom he chooses will be the holy one. You have exalted yourselves greatly, sons of Levi.”

He said again to Korah:

“Hear this, sons of Levi. Is it too little for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the rest of the people and joined you to himself, so that you might serve him in the worship of the tabernacle, stand before the assembly of the people, and minister to it [Hebrew: to it, that is, to the people]? He has brought you and all your brothers, the sons of Levi, near to himself; yet you also seek the priesthood. Is that why your entire group stands against the Lord? What is Aaron, that you murmur against him?”

Moses sent for Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab. They answered: “We will not come. Is it too little for you [Hebrew omits] that you brought us out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, unless you also become our ruler? Truly, you have not brought us into a land flowing with streams of milk and honey, nor given us possession of fields and vineyards. Do you also want to gouge out our eyes? We will not come” [Hebrew: “For you have not brought us into a land flowing with streams of milk and honey, nor given us possession of fields and vineyards. Even if the eyes of those men were gouged out, we would not come.”]

Moses became very angry and said to the Lord: “Do not regard their sacrifices. You [Col. 0370D] know that I have never taken even a donkey from them, nor harmed any one of them.”

Then he said to Korah: “You and your entire assembly, stand apart before the Lord—you and Aaron tomorrow, separately. Each of you take your censer, place incense upon it, and offer to the Lord two hundred and fifty censers. Aaron too shall hold his censer.”

When they had done this, while Moses and Aaron stood there and had gathered the whole multitude against them at the entrance of the tabernacle, the glory of the Lord appeared to all.

[B. XLII.] The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “Separate yourselves from the midst of this assembly, so that I may suddenly destroy them.”

They fell prostrate on their faces and said: “Most mighty God of the spirits of all flesh, shall your anger rage against them all because one man has sinned? [Hebrew: will you be angry against them all?]”

The Lord said to Moses: “Command the whole people to separate themselves from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.”

Moses rose and went to Dathan and Abiram. The elders of Israel followed him, and he said to the crowd: “Withdraw from the tents of these impious men [Hebrew: these], and do not touch anything that belongs to them, lest you be involved in their sins.”

When they had withdrawn all around from their tents, Dathan and Abiram came out and stood at the entrance of their tents with their wives, children, and entire household.

Moses said: “By this you shall know that the Lord sent me to do all these things that you see, and that I have not brought them forth from my own heart: if these men die the ordinary death of all men, and if they are visited with the affliction by which the others are ordinarily visited, then the Lord did not send me. But if the Lord does something new—if the earth opens its mouth and swallows them and everything belonging to them, and they descend alive into the underworld—then you shall know that they have blasphemed the Lord.”

Immediately after he finished speaking, the earth split beneath their feet. It opened its mouth and swallowed them with their tents and all their possessions [Vulgate adds: theirs]. They descended alive into the underworld, covered by the earth, and perished from the midst of the assembly.

All Israel who stood around them fled at the cry of those who were perishing, saying: “Perhaps the earth will swallow us too.” Fire also went out from the Lord and killed the two hundred and fifty men who were offering incense.

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Command Eleazar son of Aaron the priest to remove the censers that lie amid the fire and scatter the fire here and there, for they have been sanctified through the deaths of sinners. Let him hammer them into plates [Hebrew: ‘And let him hammer those sinners’ censers into plates’] and attach them to the altar, because incense was offered in them to the Lord and they have been sanctified; they shall serve as a sign and reminder for the Israelites.”

Eleazar the priest took the bronze censers in which those whom the fire had consumed had offered incense, hammered them into plates, and attached them to the altar, so that afterward the Israelites might have a reminder not to let any outsider, anyone who is not of Aaron’s descendants, approach to offer incense to the Lord, lest he suffer as Korah and his entire assembly suffered, as the Lord had spoken to Moses.

The whole multitude of the Israelites murmured against Moses and Aaron on the following day, saying: “You have killed the Lord’s people.”

When [Note: [Col. 0371D] “When the multitude of the people gathered against Moses and Aaron, they looked toward the tent of covenant, and behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the Lord appeared. After Moses and Aaron entered it, the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Withdraw from the midst of this multitude; I will suddenly consume them.’ Moses and Aaron fell prostrate on the ground.” MART. —The Hebrew scholion reads as follows: “When the multitude of the people gathered against Moses and Aaron, they looked toward the tent of covenant, and behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the Lord appeared. After Moses and Aaron entered it, the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Withdraw from the midst of this multitude; I will suddenly consume them.’ Moses and Aaron fell prostrate on the ground.” Martianus also demonstrates from the context of the narrative that here and below “fire” is used in place of “plague.”] a rebellion arose and the tumult increased, Moses and Aaron fled to the tent of covenant.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] The Urbinas manuscript has “after they entered,” and so forth.]

After they entered it, the cloud covered the tabernacle [Vulgate omits: the tabernacle], and the glory of the Lord appeared. The Lord said to Moses [Note: [Col. 0371D] The same manuscript adds, “and Aaron”]: “Withdraw from the midst of this multitude; even now I will destroy them.”

[B. XLIII, C. XLVIII.] While he lay on the ground, Moses said to Aaron: “Take the censer, put fire from the altar into it, and place incense upon it; go quickly to the people to make supplication for them, for anger [Hebrew: indignation] has already gone out from the Lord, and the plague is raging.”

When Aaron had done this and had run into the midst of the multitude, which the fire was already destroying, he offered incense. Standing between the dead and the living, he made supplication for the people, [Note: [Col. 0372D] This marginal annotation informs us that the Hebrew has “fire” in place of “plague.” This is certainly confirmed if one considers the meaning, rather than the words, of the present passage of Scripture. The Hebrew word is מַגֵּפָה, *maggephah*, which signifies any plague or striking; according to the character of this passage, however, it is determined to mean the fire by which the multitude of the Israelites was being destroyed, as is stated in the preceding verse. MART. —All the manuscripts we consulted at this passage have *absque* (“without”) in place of *cum* (“with”). It is also noted that the Hebrew scholion at that time preferred the Latin manuscripts, which it calls “ours.”] and the plague [Hebrew: fire] ceased.

Those who were struck numbered fourteen thousand seven hundred, besides those who had perished in the rebellion of Korah. Aaron returned to Moses at the entrance of the tent of covenant after the destruction had ceased.

[B. XLIV, C. XLIX, Chapter XVII.] The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“Speak to the Israelites and take from them one staff for each ancestral house, from all the leaders of the tribes—twelve staffs [Hebrew: ‘and let there be twelve staffs’]—and write each man’s name on his staff. Aaron’s name shall be on the staff [Hebrew: in the staff] of Levi, and one staff shall contain all their families [Vulgate: separately]. Place them in the tent of covenant before the testimony, where I will speak with you. The staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will restrain from myself the complaints of the Israelites with which they murmur against you.”

Moses spoke to the Israelites, and all their leaders gave him staffs, one for each tribe. There were twelve staffs, including Aaron’s staff [Hebrew: with Aaron’s staff; our manuscripts omit *with*] [Note: [Col. 0372D] From this passage it should be observed that our scholion, following Jerome’s usage, calls the Latin manuscripts “our” manuscripts. “The Hebrew,” it says, “has *with*; ours, that is, the Latin manuscripts, have *without*. See a similar usage in Book II of the Commentary on Galatians, chapter III.” MART.].

When Moses had placed them before the Lord in the tent of testimony, the next day he returned and found that Aaron’s staff, in the house of Levi, had sprouted. Its buds had swollen, flowers had burst forth, and when the leaves expanded, they had been transformed into almonds [Hebrew: which had been formed into almonds]. Moses therefore brought all the staffs out from before the Lord to all the Israelites. They saw them, and each took back his own staff.

The Lord said to Moses: “Return Aaron’s staff to the tent of testimony, so that it may be kept there as a sign for rebellious sons [Vulgate adds: of Israel], and so that their complaints against me may cease, lest they die.”

Moses did as the Lord had commanded him. The Israelites said to Moses: “Behold, we are failing [Vulgate: we are consumed]; we have all perished. Whoever approaches the Lord’s tabernacle dies [Vulgate: is dying]. Are we all to be destroyed to the point of annihilation?”

[T. XI, B. XLV, C. L, Chapter XVIII.] The Lord said to Aaron:

“You, your sons, and your father’s household with you shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary; you and your sons together shall bear the sins connected with your priesthood. Bring your brothers from the tribe of Levi, the tribe of your father, with you, and let them stand ready and minister to you; but you and your sons shall minister at the tent of testimony.

“They shall keep watch according to your commands and over all the work of the tabernacle, but only on this condition: they must not approach the vessels of the sanctuary or the altar, lest both they and you die. Let them be with you, keeping watch over the duties of the tabernacle and all its rites. No outsider shall join himself to you. Keep watch over the sanctuary and the service of the altar, lest indignation arise against the Israelites.

“I have given you your fellow Levites from among the Israelites and have given them as a gift to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0373] It should read ‘as a gift,’ in accordance with the Hebrew and the Vulgate, which additionally has ‘to you.’], so that they may serve in the ministries [Col. 0373C] of his tabernacle. But you and your sons shall guard your priesthood. Everything pertaining to the service of the altar and everything within the veil shall be administered by the priests. If any outsider approaches, he shall be killed [Hebrew: he shall die].”

[B. XLVI, C. LI.] The Lord said to Aaron:

“Behold, I have given you custody of my first fruits. Everything that the Israelites consecrate I have handed over to you and your sons as a perpetual priestly due. Therefore you shall receive these things [Hebrew: ‘these shall be yours’] from what is consecrated and offered to the Lord.

“Every offering, sacrifice, and anything rendered to me for sin and guilt, which belongs to the holy of holies, shall be yours and your sons’. You shall eat it in the sanctuary [Hebrew: in the holy of holies]; only males shall eat of it, because it has been consecrated to you.

“The first fruits that the Israelites vow and offer I have given to you, to your sons and daughters, as a perpetual right. Everyone who is clean in your household may eat them.

“All the finest [Hebrew: fat] of the oil, wine, and grain—everything they offer as first fruits to the Lord—I have given to you. All the first fruits of the produce that the soil yields and that are brought to the Lord shall fall to your use; everyone who is clean in your household may eat them.

“Everything that the Israelites return as a vow shall be yours [Hebrew: everything consecrated by the Israelites shall be yours]. Whatever first opens the womb of all flesh and which they offer to the Lord, whether human or animal, shall be yours, provided that you accept a price for the firstborn of a human being. Every unclean animal you shall have redeemed; its redemption shall take place after one month, for five shekels of silver [Hebrew: its redemption shall take place after one month, at your valuation, for five shekels of silver], according to the sanctuary’s weight. A shekel contains twenty obols.

“But you shall not redeem the firstborn of cattle, sheep, or goats, because they have been consecrated to the Lord. You shall pour their blood upon the altar and burn their fat as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord. Their flesh shall be yours, just as the consecrated breast and the right shoulder shall be yours.

“All the first fruits of the sanctuary that the Israelites offer to the Lord I have given to you, to your sons and daughters, as a perpetual right. It is an everlasting covenant of salt before the Lord, for you and your sons.

[C. LII.] The Lord said to Aaron:

“You shall possess nothing in their land, nor have a share among them. I am your portion and inheritance in the midst of the Israelites. To the sons of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel as a possession, in return for the service by which they serve me in the tent of covenant, so that the Israelites may no longer approach the tabernacle [Hebrew: covenant] and incur a deadly sin, while only the sons of Levi serve me in the tabernacle and bear the sins of the people.

“This shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations. They shall possess nothing else, being content with the offering of the tithes that I have set aside for their use and necessities.

[C. LIII.] The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: [Col. 0374C]

“Command and instruct the Levites: When you receive from the Israelites the tithes that I have given you [Hebrew: that I have given you as an inheritance], offer a first portion from them to the Lord—a tenth part of the tithe—so that it may be reckoned to you as an offering of first fruits, both from the threshing floor and from the winepress. From everything whose first fruits you receive [Hebrew: and it shall be reckoned to you as though you had given first fruits from the threshing floor and the winepress], offer a first portion to the Lord and give it to Aaron the priest.

“Everything that you offer from the tithes and set aside as gifts for the Lord shall be the best and finest. Say to them: When you offer the finest and best things from the tithes [Hebrew: ‘If’], it shall be reckoned to you as though you had given first fruits from the threshing floor and the winepress. You shall eat them in all your settlements, both you and your households, because they are compensation for the service by which you serve in the tent of testimony.

“You shall not incur sin through this if you reserve for yourselves the excellent and rich portions, lest you profane the offerings of the Israelites and die.”

[T. XII, B. XLVII, Chap. XIX.] And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying:

“This is the ordinance of the sacrifice [h. ordinance of the law] which the Lord established. Command the children of Israel to bring you a red heifer, of full age, in which there is no blemish and which has never borne a yoke; and you shall hand it over to Eleazar the priest. He shall lead it outside the camp and slaughter it in the sight of all. Then, dipping his finger in its blood [h. taking some of its blood on his finger], he shall sprinkle it toward the entrance of the tabernacle seven times. He shall burn it while all look on, consigning to the flame its hide, flesh, blood, and dung. The priest shall also cast cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet twice-dyed into the flame that consumes the heifer.

“Then, having washed his clothes and his body, he shall enter the camp, and he shall be unclean until evening. The one who burned it shall also wash his clothes and his body, and he shall be unclean until evening. A clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer and pour them [h. place them] outside the camp in a very clean place, so that they may be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel and used for the water of sprinkling; for the heifer was burned for sin [h. for the heifer is for sin]. When the one who carried the ashes of the heifer has washed his clothes, he shall be unclean until evening.

“The children of Israel and the resident foreigners who live among them shall have this as a holy ordinance in perpetuity [h. an everlasting ordinance].

“Whoever touches the corpse of a human being and is thereby unclean for seven days shall be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days, and so he shall be cleansed. If he is not sprinkled on the third day, he cannot be cleansed on the seventh. Anyone who touches the corpse of a human being and has not been sprinkled with this mixture defiles the Lord’s tabernacle and shall perish from Israel; because he has not been sprinkled with the water of purification, he shall remain unclean, and his impurity shall remain upon him.

“This is the law concerning a person who dies in a tent: all who enter that tent, and all the vessels that are there, shall be unclean for seven days. A vessel that has no covering or cord fastened over it shall be unclean. If anyone in the open country touches the corpse of a man who was killed or died naturally, or his bone or a grave, he shall be unclean for seven days.

“[C. LIV.] They shall take some of the ashes of the burning for sin [h. of the burning of sin] and pour living water over them in a vessel. A clean person shall dip hyssop in it and sprinkle from it over the entire tent, all its furnishings, and the persons polluted by such contact. In this way the clean person shall purify the unclean person on the third and seventh days. After he has been purified on the seventh day, he shall wash both himself and his clothes, and he shall be unclean until evening. If anyone has not been purified by this rite, that person shall perish from the midst of the congregation, because he has defiled the sanctuary of the Lord and has not been sprinkled with the water of purification.

“This shall be an everlasting ordinance [h. He has not been sprinkled with the water of purification; he shall be unclean]. The one who sprinkles the water shall also wash his clothes. Anyone who touches the water of purification shall be unclean until evening. Whatever the unclean person touches shall become unclean, and the person who touches any of these things shall be unclean until evening.”

**Note.** In Hebrew there is [Hebrew term not reproduced in the supplied text], *leḥuqqat ʿolam*, “an everlasting ordinance,” which below, at verse 21, Jerome himself translates as *legitimum sempiternum*, “an everlasting ordinance,” according to the present marginal annotation of the Canon of Hebrew Truth. Compare also the scholion, “And it shall be reckoned,” etc., with the immediately following verse 30. —MART.

[B. XLVIII, C. LV, Chap. XX.] Then the children of Israel and the entire congregation came into the wilderness of Zin in the first month, and the people stayed at Kadesh. Miriam died there and was buried in the same place.

When the people lacked water, they gathered together against Moses and Aaron; and, turning to rebellion, they said: “Would that we had perished among our brothers before the Lord! Why have you brought the Lord’s congregation into this wilderness, so that both we and our animals should die? Why have you made us come up from Egypt and brought us to this wretched place, where nothing can be sown, where there are neither figs, vines, nor pomegranates, and, moreover, no water to drink?”

Moses and Aaron entered, leaving the assembly, into the tent of meeting, and fell prostrate on the ground.

**Note.** Almost all printed books and manuscripts read this passage as follows: “They fell prostrate on the ground, and cried out to the Lord and said: ‘Lord God, hear the cry of this people and open for them your treasury, the spring of living water, so that, when they are satisfied, their murmuring may cease.’ And the glory of the Lord appeared over them.” But the Canon of Hebrew Truth deletes these words from “and cried out” inclusively through “their murmuring may cease.” They may have been added by some Latin translator, among whom, as Jerome and Augustine testify, there were as many different copies as there were manuscripts. Some think that this addition was taken from one of the Chaldaic paraphrases, of which there were formerly more than there are today.

Whatever may be said, it is certain that these words are superfluous in the biblical copies, because they do not occur in the Hebrew or Samaritan text, nor in the translation of the Seventy Elders, nor among the other translators, such as the Chaldaic, Syriac, and Arabic. Finally, there still survive Latin manuscripts of the sacred Scriptures of excellent quality in which the words that appear in excess in the printed editions are absent. The Corbie copy of the Bible, written eight hundred years ago, bears witness to this: in it one finds nothing except what is read in the Hebrew text. Yet later some faulty corrector supplied the entire addition in the margin of the volume, with a sign placed in the text as though these words had been missing there. —MART.

That notable addition, which all the common Latin biblical manuscripts insert here, we found in one Urbinate manuscript, namely: “and they cried out to the Lord and said: ‘Lord God, hear the cry of this people and open for them your treasury, the spring of living water, so that, when they are satisfied, their murmuring may cease.’” The Palatine manuscript is entirely unaware of it, and in the Memmian copy it is said to have been deleted. It is known, however, that it is found neither in the Hebrew, Chaldaic, or Septuagint texts, nor in the versions made directly from those texts.

[C. LVI.] And the glory of the Lord appeared over them [h. And the glory of the Lord appeared to them]. Then the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“Take the staff and gather the people, you and your brother Aaron; and speak to the rock before them, and it shall give its waters. When you have brought water out of the rock, the whole congregation and its animals shall drink.”

So Moses took the staff that was before the Lord, as he had commanded him. When the congregation had been gathered before the rock, he said to them: “Hear, rebels and unbelievers [h. does not have ‘unbelievers’]. Can we bring water out of this rock for you [h. Can I bring water out]?”

**Note.** Our scholiast refers this word to Moses alone as speaker; but in Hebrew the verb is plural in number, “we will bring out” or “we will draw out.” —MART. [Col. 0377D] It was also noted by Martianay, against the opinion of the scholiast, that the Hebrew archetype has the plural: “we will bring out.”

Then Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with the staff, and abundant waters came forth, so that the people and their animals drank.

The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “Because you did not believe in me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land that I will give them.”

This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarreled with the Lord and he was sanctified among them.

[T. XIII, B. XLIX.] Meanwhile Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, to say:

“This is what your brother Israel says [h. commands]. You know all the hardship that has overtaken [h. found] us: how our fathers went down into Egypt, how we lived there for a long time, how the Egyptians afflicted us and our fathers, and how we cried out to the Lord and he heard us and sent an angel who brought us out of Egypt. Now we are at the city of Kadesh, which lies at the edge of your territory. We ask that you allow us to pass through your land. We will not go through fields or vineyards, nor will we drink water from your wells. We shall travel by the public road, turning neither to the right nor to the left, until we have crossed your boundaries.”

[C. LVII.] Edom answered him: “You shall not pass through me; otherwise I will come out against you with weapons.”

The children of Israel said to him: “We will travel along the beaten road; and if we and our cattle drink your water, we will pay what is right. There will be no difficulty concerning the price; only let us pass through quickly.”

But he answered: “You shall not pass.” Immediately he came out to meet them with an immense multitude and a strong force, and he would not yield to their entreaty or grant them passage through his territory. Therefore Israel turned away from him.

When they had departed from Kadesh, they came to Mount Hor, which is on the borders of the land of Edom.

[C. LVIII.] There the Lord spoke to Moses: “Let Aaron go to his people, for he shall not enter the land that I have given to the children of Israel, because he was unbelieving toward my word [h. because you were unbelieving], at the waters of contradiction. Take Aaron and Eleazar his son with him, and lead them up Mount Hor. When you have stripped his father of his vestments, clothe Eleazar his son with them; and Aaron shall be gathered to his people and die there.”

Moses did as the Lord had commanded, and they went up Mount Hor before the whole congregation. When Aaron had stripped himself of his garments, he clothed Eleazar his son with them. When Aaron had died on the summit of the mountain, Moses came down with Eleazar. The whole congregation, seeing that Aaron had died, mourned for him thirty days throughout all their families.

[B. LI, C. LIX, Chap. XXI.] When the king of Arad the Canaanite, who lived in the south, heard that Israel had come by the route of the spies, he fought against Israel and prevailed, taking captives from them.

Then Israel bound itself by a vow to the Lord and said: “If you deliver this people into my hand, I will destroy [h. devote to destruction] their cities.”

The Lord heard Israel’s prayer and delivered the Canaanite. Israel killed him and destroyed his cities, and called the name of that place Hormah, that is, “the ban” or “devoted thing.”

They set out from Mount Hor by the road leading to the Red Sea, in order to go around the land of Edom. The people began to grow weary of the journey and the hardship.

[B. LII.] They spoke against God and Moses, saying: “Why have you brought us out of Egypt, so that we should die in the wilderness? There is no bread and there is no water; our soul is already nauseated by this worthless food.”

Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people; and when many had been bitten and had died, they came to Moses and said: “We have sinned, because we spoke against the Lord and against you. Pray that he take the serpent away from us.”

Moses prayed for the people.

[C. LX.] The Lord said to him: “Make a serpent [Note: The Vulgate books add *aeneum*, ‘bronze,’ but I would prefer *igneum*, ‘fiery’; for the Hebrew here does not have ‘serpent,’ but only [Hebrew term not reproduced in the supplied text], meaning ‘burning’]. Place it as a sign; whoever has been bitten and looks at it shall live.”

Moses therefore made a bronze serpent and placed it as a sign. Whenever those who had been bitten looked at it, they were healed.

The children of Israel set out and camped at Oboth. From there they departed and pitched their tents at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness facing Moab, toward the eastern side. From there they moved on and came to the torrent of Zared.

[B. LIII.] Leaving it, they camped opposite the Arnon, which is in the wilderness and extends along the borders of the Amorites. Indeed, the Arnon is a boundary in Moab, dividing the Moabites from the Amorites.

Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the Lord: “As he did at the Red Sea, so he will do at the torrents of Arnon. The crags of the torrents have inclined so that they might rest in Ar,”

**Note.** In place of *Ar*, the Canon and nearly all other manuscript copies read *Arnon*; but this is a scribal error. The scribes were misled by the immediately preceding *Arnon* and did not understand that, according to Jerome in his book on Hebrew Place-Names, Arnon is a certain rock projecting upward on the borders of the Amorites, between Moab and the Amorites, whereas Ar is a place or town of the Arnon, called by the translators of the Septuagint, with an extended vowel, *Er*. Concerning the name Ar, Jerome himself wished us to observe the following in Book VI of his Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 15: “In place of Ar,” he says, “which only Theodotion rendered as it is read in Hebrew, Aquila and Symmachus translated ‘city,’ failing to notice that between the Hebrew letters *ayin* and *resh* there was no letter *yod*. If it were present, ‘city’ would rightly be read.” —MART.

and they reclined in the territories of the Moabites.

[C. LXI.] From that place the well appeared, concerning which the Lord spoke to Moses: “Gather the people, and I will give them water.”

Then Israel sang [Note: Saint Jerome recites the entire song in his letter to Fabiola concerning the forty-two stations of the Israelites in the wilderness. Since it contains readings notably different from those in our text, it seemed worthwhile to insert Jerome’s own words here. Thus, at Station 39, read: “After this they came to the well, where Israel sang this song: ‘Rise up, well, which the princes dug and the leaders of the peoples opened, in the gift of the lawgiver and with his staff; and from the wilderness to Mattanah, and from Mattanah to the torrent of God, and from the torrent of God to the heights, and from the heights to the valley which is in the region of Moab, at the summit of Pisgah, which looks toward the wilderness.’ Some interpreters of these places, which are in the territory of the Amorites, think that they are not stations but crossings, etc. I ask the prudent and diligent reader to understand that Jerome here translates certain Hebrew names according to their proper meanings, although in the sacred text he set them down as they are read in Hebrew.” —MART.] this song:

“Rise up, well.” They sang together:

“Well, which the princes dug, and which the leaders of the multitude prepared, with the gift of the lawgiver [h. with the teacher of the law], and with their staffs.”

From the wilderness to Mattanah; from Mattanah to Nahaliel; from Nahaliel to Bamoth. From Bamoth there is a valley in the region of Moab, at the summit of Pisgah, which looks toward the wilderness.

**Note.** The Urbinate manuscript has “more extensively and differently”: “They departed from the wilderness to Mattanah; from Mattanah to Nahaliel,” etc., which is nearly more correct. If desired, compare Letter 78, *On the Stations*, to Fabiola, Station 39, where the holy Father recites this entire song in words often different from these.

Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, saying: “I ask that you allow me to pass through your land. We will not turn aside into fields or vineyards, nor drink water from wells. We will travel by the royal road until we have crossed your boundaries.”

**Note.** The Urbinate manuscript omits the word “water”; nevertheless the Hebrew archetype and other books contain it.

He would not permit Israel to pass through his territory. Rather, he gathered his army and came out to meet Israel in the wilderness. He came to Jahaz and fought against Israel. Israel struck him with the edge of the sword and took possession of his land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and as far as the children of Ammon, because the boundaries of the Ammonites were strongly fortified.

[C. LXII.] Israel therefore took all his cities and lived in the cities of the Amorites, namely Heshbon and its villages. Heshbon was the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, who fought against the former king [Note: The Hebrew also adds “first.”] of Moab.

**Note.** The scholiast rightly observes that Sihon, king of the Amorites, conquered the former king of Moab. Scripture here signifies that Sihon conquered the first king of the Moabites, or the one who had reigned before Balak. —MART.

He took all the land that had been under his rule [h. against the former king of Moab], as far as the Arnon. Therefore it is said in the proverb:

“Come to Heshbon; let it be built and established, the city of Sihon. For fire went forth from Heshbon, a flame from the city of Sihon; it devoured Ar of the Moabites and the inhabitants of the heights of Arnon. Woe to you, Moab! You have perished, people of Chemosh! He gave his sons into flight and his daughters into captivity to Sihon, king of the Amorites. Their yoke perished from Heshbon to Dibon; the exhausted reached Nophah and [h. which is opposite] Medeba.”

**Note.** Formerly, in place of [Hebrew term not reproduced in the supplied text], “to,” which is written in the present Hebrew text, they read here [Hebrew term not reproduced in the supplied text], “against,” as is clear from the Samaritan text and from the present marginal annotation of the canon. —MART. —The Scholiast read, like the Samaritan interpreter, [Hebrew term not reproduced in the supplied text], in place of [Hebrew term not reproduced in the supplied text], as Martianay also thinks.

[B. LIV.] Thus Israel lived in the land of the Amorites. Moses sent men to spy out Jazer; they captured its villages and took possession of its inhabitants. They turned and went up by the road to Bashan. Og, king of Bashan, came out to meet them with all his people, intending to fight at Edrei.

The Lord said to Moses: “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him and all his people and his land into your hand. You shall do to him as you did to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon.”

They struck him, his sons, and all his people until none remained, and took possession of his land.

[B. LV, Chap. XXII.] They set out and camped in the plains of Moab, where Jericho is situated beyond the Jordan.

[T. XIV, C. LXIII.] Balak son of Zippor saw everything that Israel had done to the Amorite and that the Moabites feared him and could not withstand his attack. He said to the elders of Midian: “Now this people will consume all those who live around our borders, just as an ox usually crops the grass down to its roots.”

He was king of Moab at that time. Therefore he sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor, the diviner, who lived beside the river of the land of the children of Ammon [h. Therefore he sent messengers to Balaam son of Behor, who lived in Petho beside the river in the land of the children of his people].
