“After seven years, in the year of remission, at the Feast of Booths, when all Israel gathers to appear before the Lord your God in the place that the Lord chooses, you shall read the words of this law before all Israel, while they listen, with the entire people assembled together—men, women, children, and the resident aliens within your gates—so that, hearing, they may learn to fear the Lord your God and keep and perform all the words of this law.

“Their children also, who now do not know, shall hear and fear [Heb. “hear and learn, so that they may fear”] the Lord your God all the days that they live in the land into which you are crossing the Jordan to possess.”

### [T. XVIII, B. CXXXIX]

The Lord said to Moses: “Behold, the days of your death are near. Call Joshua, and stand in the tent of testimony, so that I may command him.” Moses and Joshua went and stood in the tent of testimony, and the Lord appeared there in a pillar of cloud that stood at the entrance of the tent.

### [C. CL]

The Lord said to Moses: “Behold, you will sleep with your fathers, and this people will rise up and prostitute itself after foreign gods in the land into which it is entering and will dwell there. There it will abandon me [Heb. omits “there”] and break the covenant that I made with it.

“My anger will burn against it on that day. I will abandon it and hide my face from it, and it will be given over to destruction. All evils and afflictions will find it [Heb. “Many evils”], so that on that day it will say: ‘Truly, because my God is not with me’ [Heb. “my God is not in my midst”], these evils have found me.

“I will hide and conceal my face on that day because of all the evil that it has done, because it followed foreign gods. Now therefore write this song for yourselves and teach it to the children of Israel, so that they may remember it, recite it with their mouths, and so that this song may serve as a witness for me among the children of Israel.

“For I will bring him into the land for which I swore to his fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey. When they have eaten and are satisfied and grown fat, they will turn to foreign gods, serve them, insult me, and break my covenant.

“When many evils and afflictions have found him, this song will answer him as a witness, for it will not be forgotten from the mouths of their offspring. For I know his thoughts—what he is going to do today—before I bring him into the land that I promised him.”

### [C. CLI]

Moses therefore wrote this song [Heb. “this song on that day”] and taught it to the children of Israel. He commanded Joshua son of Nun, saying: “Be strong and courageous, for you will bring the children of Israel into the land that I promised them, and I will be with you.”

After Moses had written the words of this law in a book and completed it, he commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, saying:

“Take this book” [Note: The Samaritan text correctly reads here , *lichhu*, that is, “take” or “receive.” The present Hebrew text does not contain the servile letter *vau* at the end, but only the three radicals , *lacoahh*, meaning “taking” or “removing”; that is, “taking this book of the law, place it,” and so forth. Hence it is clear that something has fallen out of the present Hebrew text. Although we have already demonstrated this from many examples, it will not be burdensome to observe the same thing in what follows. MART.] [Heb. “this book of the law”], “and place it beside the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, so that it may be there as a witness against you.

“For I know your stubbornness and your exceedingly stiff neck. While I am still alive and going about among you [Heb. omits “and going about”], you have always acted rebelliously against the Lord; how much more after I am dead! Assemble before me all the male elders according to your tribes and your teachers, and I will speak these words in their hearing and call heaven and earth as witnesses against them [Heb. “I will call witnesses”].

“For I know that after my death you will act wickedly and quickly turn aside from the way that I commanded you. Evils will meet you in the latter days, when you do evil in the sight of the Lord, provoking him through the works of your hands.”

### [B. CXL]

Moses therefore spoke the words of this song in the hearing of the entire assembly of Israel and completed it to the end.

### [Chapter XXXII]

Hear, O heavens, what I speak;

let the earth hear the words of my mouth.

Let my teaching gather like rain;

let my speech flow like dew,

like showers upon the grass,

and like drops upon the herbage.

For I will invoke the name of the Lord.

Give greatness to our God.

The works of God are perfect,

and all his ways are judgments.

A faithful God, without any iniquity,

just and upright:

they sinned against him; they are not his children because of their corruption—

a crooked and perverse generation.

Is this how you repay the Lord,

O foolish and senseless people?

Is he not your father, who acquired you,

made you, and created you?

Remember the days of old;

consider the generations, one by one.

Ask your father, and he will tell you;

your elders, and they will say to you:

When the Most High divided the nations,

when he separated the children of Adam,

he established the boundaries of the peoples

according to the number of the children of Israel.

But the Lord’s portion is his people;

Jacob is the cord of his inheritance.

He found him in a desert land,

in a place of horror and vast solitude.

He surrounded him and instructed him,

and guarded him like the pupil of his eye.

As an eagle urging its young to fly

and hovering over them,

he spread his wings and took him up [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads “and took him up”],

and carried him upon his shoulders.

The Lord alone was his guide,

and no foreign god was with him.

He set him upon a lofty land,

so that he might eat the produce of the fields

and suck honey from the rock,

and oil from the hardest stone.

Butter from the herd and milk from the sheep,

with the fat of lambs and rams, the sons of Bashan;

and goats with the marrow of wheat,

and he drank the purest blood of the grape.

The beloved grew fat [Heb. “the upright”] and kicked;

he grew fat, thick, and broad.

He abandoned God his maker

and withdrew from God his salvation.

They provoked him with foreign gods

and stirred him to anger with abominations [Note: Other books insert “their own”].

They sacrificed to demons and not to God,

to gods whom they did not know.

New and recent gods came [Note: Here too other books add “to them”],

whom their fathers had not worshiped.

You abandoned the God who begot you

and forgot the Lord your creator.

The Lord saw and was provoked to anger,

because his sons and daughters provoked him.

And he said: “I will hide my face from them

and consider what their end will be,

for they are a perverse generation,

faithless children.

They provoked me with what was not God

and angered me with their vanities.

So I will provoke them with what is not a people,

and anger them with a foolish nation.

A fire has been kindled in my fury,

and it shall burn to the depths of hell.

It will devour the earth and its produce [Note: Rabbanus reads: “You will consume the earth and what grows from it”],

and burn the foundations of the mountains.

I will gather evils against them

and exhaust my arrows upon them.

They shall be consumed by famine,

and birds shall devour them with the most bitter bite.

I will send the teeth of beasts against them,

with the fury of those that drag themselves upon the earth,

and of serpents.

Outside, the sword shall devastate them;

inside, terror—

young man and maiden alike,

infant together with old man.

I said: ‘Where are they?’

I will erase their memory from among men” [Heb. “I will exterminate them in my fury, and I will erase…”].

But because of the anger of the enemy I delayed,

lest their enemies become arrogant

and say: “Our hand is exalted;

the Lord did not do all this.”

They are a nation without counsel

and without understanding.

Would that they were wise and understood,

and considered their final destiny.

How could one pursue a thousand,

and two put ten thousand to flight?

Is it not because their God sold them,

and the Lord shut them in?

For our God is not like their god [Vulgate: “gods”];

our enemies are judges.

Their vine is from the vine of Sodom,

and from the fields around Gomorrah.

Their grapes are grapes of gall,

and their clusters are most bitter.

Their wine is the gall of dragons

and the incurable poison of asps.

Are not these things stored up with me,

and sealed in my treasuries?

Vengeance is mine, and I will repay in due time,

when their foot slips.

The day of their destruction is near [Heb. “their destruction”],

and the appointed times hasten upon them.

The Lord will judge his people,

and will have compassion on his servants.

He will see that their hand has become powerless,

that the confined also have failed,

and that the remnant has been consumed.

And they will say: “Where are their gods,

in whom they trusted?

Those whose sacrifices they ate the fat of,

and whose drink offerings they drank?

Let them rise and help you;

let them protect you in your need.”

See now that I, I alone, am he [Heb. “I, I”],

and there is no other God besides me.

I kill, and I make alive;

I strike, and I heal,

and there is no one who can rescue from my hand.

I lift my hand to heaven

and say: “As I live forever,

if I sharpen my sword like lightning,

and my hand takes hold of judgment,

I will repay vengeance to my enemies,

and requite those who hate me.

I will intoxicate my arrows with blood,

and my sword shall devour flesh,

with the blood of the slain

and the captivity of the enemy’s uncovered head.”

Praise, nations, his people,

for he will avenge the blood of his servants.

He will repay vengeance upon his enemies,

and will be merciful [Note: Ancient books insert “the Lord”]

to the land of his people.

[B. CXLI.] Moses therefore came and spoke all the words of this Song in the hearing of the people, he and [Note: [Col. 0459D] The Hebrew and Chaldee read [Hosea], that is, Hosea or Osee, in the manner of the ancients; but the Samaritan, the Septuagint, and the Syriac have an initial yod, [Jehoshua] or Joshua. MART.] Joshua [h. Hosea] son of Nun. And he completed all these words, speaking to all Israel. And he said to them:

“Set your hearts on all the words that I testify to you today, so that you may command your sons to observe and perform them, and to fulfill [h. omits “and to fulfill”] everything written in this law. For they are not empty commandments for you, but so that each one of you may live by them; by doing them you will long endure in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to enter and possess.”

[Col. 0459C] [T. XIX, C. CLII.] And the Lord spoke to Moses on that same day, saying:

“Go up this mountain of Abarim, that is, ‘Passage,’ to Mount Nebo [h. “this Abarim, Mount Nebo”], which is in the land of Moab opposite Jericho, and view the land of Canaan, which I am going to give the Israelites as a possession; and die on the mountain. When you have climbed it, you will be joined to your people, just as Aaron your brother died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his people. For you acted treacherously against me in the midst of the Israelites, at the waters of Contradiction at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, and you did not sanctify me among the Israelites. Therefore [h. “For that reason, on the contrary”] you will see the land, but you will not enter it, the land that I am giving to the Israelites.”

[B. CXLII, C. CLIII, Cap. XXXIII.] This is the blessing with which Moses, [Col. 0459D] the [Note: [Col. 0459D] Jerome plainly approves this scholion in his letter to Cyprian: undertaking there an explanation of Psalm 89, he says: “First it must be known that the title of this psalm according to the Hebrews is, ‘A Prayer of Moses, the man of God’; according to the Septuagint, ‘A Prayer of Moses, the human being of God.’ In the Hebrew we read *ish ha-Elohim*, which the Septuagint also translates here as ἄνθρωπος τοῦ Θεοῦ, ‘man of God’; but in the Chaldee, ‘prophet of God.’ In the Syriac version Moses is called ‘servant of God,’ and in the Arabic ‘apostle of God.’” MART.] man of God [h. man of God], blessed the Israelites before his death, and he said:

“The Lord came from Sinai,  
and rose upon us from Seir.  
He appeared from Mount Paran,  
and with him were thousands of holy ones.  
In his right hand was a fiery law.  
He loved the peoples;  
all his holy ones are in his hand,  
and those who draw near to his feet  
receive instruction from him.  
Moses commanded us a law,  
the inheritance of the multitude of Jacob.  
He became king among the upright,  
when the leaders of the people  
were gathered together with the tribes of Israel.

“Let Reuben live and not die,  
and let his number be small.

“And this is Judah’s blessing:

‘Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah,  
and bring him to his people.  
His hands will fight for him,  
and you will be his helper against his adversaries.’

“And to Levi he said:

‘Your perfection and your instruction belong to your holy man, whom you tested in trial and judged at the waters of Contradiction. He said to his father and mother, “I do not know you,” and to his brothers, “I do not acknowledge you” [Note: Eleven of our manuscripts read, “I do not acknowledge them”; nevertheless, the reading of the editors is preferable because it agrees with the Hebrew text. MART.]; and they did not acknowledge [h. “he did not acknowledge”] their sons. They kept your word and preserved your covenant; your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel [h. “May your judgments enlighten Jacob, and your law Israel”]. They will place incense in your wrath and a whole burnt offering upon your altar. Bless, O Lord, his strength, and accept the work of his hands. Strike the backs of his enemies, and may those who hate him not rise again.’

“And to Benjamin he said:

‘The beloved of the Lord will dwell securely in him; he will remain with him all day long as in a bridal chamber, and he will rest between his shoulders.’

“And to Joseph he said:

‘His land is from the blessing of the Lord,  
from the fruits of heaven,  
from the dew and from the abyss lying beneath,  
from the fruits produced by the sun and the moon,  
from the summit of the ancient mountains,  
from the fruits of the everlasting hills,  
and from the produce of the earth and its fullness.  
May the blessing [h. “will of him”] who appeared in the bush  
come upon the head of Joseph  
and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers.  
His beauty is like that of the firstborn bull;  
his horns are the horns of a rhinoceros.  
With them he will drive peoples  
to the ends of the earth.  
These are the multitudes of Ephraim,  
and these are the thousands of Manasseh.’

“And to Zebulun he said:

‘Rejoice, Zebulun, in your departure,  
and Issachar in your tents.  
They will call peoples to the mountain;  
there they will sacrifice sacrifices of righteousness.  
They will suck the abundance of the sea as though it were milk,  
and the hidden treasures of the sands.’

“And to Gad he said:

‘Blessed is he who enlarges Gad.  
Like a lion he rested,  
and he seized the arm [the printed reading “brach­tum” is uncertain] and the crown of the head.  
He saw that his portion was reserved for him  
as a lawgiver;  
he was with the leaders of the people,  
and he carried out the Lord’s righteous acts  
and his judgments with Israel.’

“And to Dan he said:

‘Dan is a lion’s cub;  
he will flow abundantly from Bashan.’

“And to Naphtali he said:

‘Naphtali will enjoy abundance,  
and he will be full of the Lord’s blessings;  
he will possess the sea and the south.’

“And to Asher he said:

‘Blessed among sons is Asher;  
let him be pleasing to his brothers,  
and let him dip his foot in oil.  
Your footwear shall be iron and bronze.  
As your days are, so shall your old age be.’

“There is no other God like the God of the upright,  
who rides upon the heavens as your helper.  
His magnificence [h. “and his judgments”] traverses [h. omits “traverses”] the clouds;  
his dwelling is above,  
and beneath are everlasting arms.  
He will drive out the enemy before you  
and say, ‘Destroy!’

“Israel will dwell securely and alone;  
the eye [h. “spring”] of Jacob  
will be in a land of grain and wine,  
and his heavens will grow dark with dew.

“Blessed are you, Israel!  
Who is like you, people saved by the Lord?  
He is the shield of your help  
and the sword of your glory.  
Your enemies will deny you,  
and you will defecate upon their necks.”

[Cap. XXXIV.] Moses therefore went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the summit of Pisgah opposite Jericho. And the Lord showed him the whole land, [Note: The Canon has, “from Gilead as far as Dan,” which gives the passage a sufficiently suitable sense. MART. [Col. 0461C] —Less correctly with respect to the Hebrew text, whatever Martianay may think, the Hebrew Canon has “from Gilead”; [Col. 0462B] for it is not written [as in the other reading], but [the Hebrew form].] from Gilead as far as Dan, all of Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, and the whole land of Judah as far as the western sea, and the southern region, and the breadth of the plain of Jericho, the city of palms, as far as Zoar.

And the Lord said to him:

“This is the land for which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to your offspring.’ You have seen it with your eyes, but you will not cross over into it.”

[C. CLIV.] Moses, the servant of the Lord, died there in the land of Moab, by command of the Lord. And he buried him in the valley of the land of Moab opposite Phogor; and no one has known his grave to the present day. Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died. His eye was not dim, nor were his teeth moved [h. “nor were his cheeks wrinkled”]. The Israelites wept for him on the plains of Moab for thirty days, and the days of mourning for Moses were completed.

Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom, because Moses had laid his hands upon him. And the Israelites obeyed him and did as the Lord had commanded Moses.

[C. CLV.] And no prophet arose thereafter in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and wonders that he sent him to perform in the land of Egypt against Pharaoh, all his servants, and his entire land; and in all the mighty power and all the great marvels that Moses performed before all Israel.

The book of Deuteronomy ends here.

## THE SECOND ORDER, OF THE PROPHETS

[Col. 0461]

## [THE BOOK OF JOSHUA]

### PREFACE OF JEROME TO THE BOOK OF JOSHUA SON OF NUN

[Note: Many manuscripts read, “Preface of Saint Jerome to the book of Joshua and Judges.” In fact, there is no separate prologue by Jerome to the book of Judges; this Preface should therefore be regarded as common to these two books. MART. —Some manuscripts add “and Judges,” as Martianay also found in his copies. But Ruth too, which was once counted in the Hebrew canon as an appendix to the book of Judges under its single designation, is included by this Preface. [Col. 0462D]]

At last, with Moses’ Pentateuch completed, as though released from a great debt, we extend our hand to Jesus son of Nave, whom the Hebrews call *Josue ben Nun* [Hebrew], that is, “Joshua son of Nun”; and to the book of Judges, which they call *Sophtim* [Hebrew]; and also to Ruth [Col. 0462C] and Esther [Note: [Col. 0462D] This book, however, is not placed here, so far as I know, in any recension or in the order of the Prophets. Indeed, Jerome himself places it among the Hagiographa, both in this very translation of Scripture from the Hebrew and in the Helmeted Prologue, where he enumerates each book according to its proper class.] [Hebrew], which they designate by these same names.

We urge the reader to preserve carefully the forest of Hebrew names and the divisions by cola [Note: Understand “the cola and commas of the verses,” as is clear from the Preface to the book of Chronicles, in which Jerome declares that he undertook the task of translating from the Hebrew so that the inextricable delays and the forest of names, which had been confused through the fault of scribes, as well as the barbarity of the meanings, might be arranged more clearly by the cola of the verses. Here Erasmus, Jerome’s scholiast, attacks Cardinal Hugo bitterly for his many errors; Marianus attacks Erasmus even more bitterly in reply, because he himself did not grasp Jerome’s meaning above when he spoke about the books of Ruth and Esther. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript inserts a slash here in this fashion: “a careful scribe, divided,” and so forth. What this division of the verses is, we have explained elsewhere, and it is also clear from the example given below.] so that both our labor and the reader’s diligence may not be lost.

And above all, as I have often testified, let him know that I am not inventing novelties in order to criticize the ancients, as my friends accuse me [Note: He means Rufinus and his associates, who conspired to slander Jerome. This is plainly evident from the second book of the Apology of the holy Doctor against Rufinus, where he writes: “Therefore he who had fabricated a letter under my name of repentance, because I had translated the Hebrew volumes badly, is said to accuse me of interpreting the holy Scriptures in condemnation of the Seventy.” And at the end of the same book: “I was compelled to answer on my own behalf, awaiting the three volumes of my friend, and wholly intent upon the heap of his accusations.” MART.], but that, to the best of my ability, I am offering the people of my language—who nevertheless take pleasure in our work—an edition in place of the Greek *Hexapla*, which require immense expense and labor.

And if anywhere they have doubts when reading the ancient volumes, let them compare these with them and find what they seek—especially since among the Latins there are as many copies as there are codices, and each person, according to his own whim, has either added or removed whatever seemed appropriate to him. In any case, what disagrees cannot be true.

Therefore let the scorpion cease rising against us with its curved sting, and let that poisonous tongue cease attacking the holy work—either accepting it, if it pleases, or despising it, if it displeases. Let him remember those verses [Ps. 39:19 ff.]:

“Your mouth has abounded in wickedness,  
and your tongue has fashioned deceit.

“Sitting, you spoke against your brother,  
and against your mother’s son you placed a stumbling block.

“These things you did, and I kept silent.

“You thought, wickedly, that I would be like you;  
I shall rebuke you and set you  
[Note: The Palatine manuscript inserts the words “those things” here.]  
before your face.”

For what benefit is there to the listener or reader in our sweating through labor while others labor by slandering? [Col. 0464A] Are the Jews to grieve because the opportunity for them to slander and mock Christians has been removed, while churchmen despise—or rather tear apart—that by which their adversaries are tormented?

If they are pleased only with the old translation—which is not displeasing to me either—and think that nothing beyond it should be accepted, why do they read and disregard what has been added under asterisks or removed under obeli? [Note: Valesius, not understanding this passage at all, wishes to correct it in a letter to Usserius concerning the Seventy Interpreters, reading “they read and do not neglect.” But Jerome’s meaning is different: he wishes only to say that they read what has been added under asterisks while disregarding what has been marked with obeli. Shortly afterward, “Daniel’s” was corrupt in Martianay’s text instead of “Daniel.” MART.]

Why did they accept Daniel according to Theodotion’s translation in the Church? Why do they admire Origen and Eusebius Pamphilus, who discuss all the editions in the same way? Or what folly was it, after speaking the truth, to put forward what is false? And how will they be able to prove in the New Testament the testimonies they have adopted, which are not found in the ancient books?

We say these things so that we may not seem entirely silent in the face of slanderers. As for the rest, [Col. 0464B] after the repose of the holy Paula, whose life is an example of virtue, and these books, which I could not refuse to the virgin of Christ Eustochium, we have decided, while the spirit still governs these limbs, to devote ourselves to the exposition of the Prophets and to resume, as it were by a right of return, the work long left unfinished—especially since the admirable and holy man Pammachius urgently requests the same thing in writing, and since, as we hasten toward our homeland, we must pass by the deadly songs of the Sirens with deaf ears.

## [CHAPTER SUMMARIES OF THE BOOK OF JOSHUA]

### TITLES OF THE BOOK OF JOSHUA

[Col. 0463D] I. After Moses’ death, the Lord speaks to Joshua and urges him to rise, cross the Jordan, and go to possess the land he had promised. “I will be with you,” he says; “be strong and courageous.” “Let the volume of the law not depart from your heart,” and so forth. Then Joshua commands the people for the following day that, after preparing provisions, they should cross the Jordan. He sends two spies secretly to the city of Jericho. They enter the house of Rahab the prostitute and, when sought by the king, are hidden there. After making an agreement, they are lowered over the wall, climb into the hill country, come to Joshua, and disclose what had happened to them.

II. When the camp is moved, Joshua comes to the Jordan. The Lord sanctifies the people for three days, and Joshua says: “Today I will begin to exalt you before the Israelites. Tell the Levites that when they enter the waters of the Jordan they are to stand there.” Then, when the priests descend into the water, the waters flowing down from above swell like mountains and stand in one mass, while those below dry up. The entire people cross over on dry ground. They bring twelve stones from the middle of the river as a testimony.

III. They camp at Gilgal. The Lord tells Joshua to make stone knives and explains the reason for the second circumcision. There they celebrate Passover; they eat unleavened bread made from the produce of the land of promise, and manna is no longer given to them. There Joshua, raising his eyes, sees the prince of the heavenly army holding a sword and hears: “Remove the sandal from your feet,” and so forth. Again he hears: “I have delivered Jericho and its king into your hand. Let everything be under the ban. You shall shout in this manner and that,” and the destruction of the city follows as described above. Rahab is brought out and preserved. The Israelites transgress—that is, Achan son of Carmi. He sends an army against Ai, which turns its back before the enemy. He himself, having torn his garments, entreats the Lord, and the Lord says that the people have sinned. The one who did this is sought out, discovered, and stoned by the people.

IV. The Lord commands him to proceed against the aforementioned city and, with the shield raised, to know that it has been handed over to him. He goes, captures it, kills, and destroys it. The people divide the city’s livestock and spoil among themselves, and, after building an altar, offer sacrifice. He writes Deuteronomy and reads the words of blessing and curse to all the people. When the kings of Canaan are thrown into confusion, the Gibeonites craftily send ambassadors, make a treaty, and are assigned to servitude.

V. When five kings of the Amorites gather against Israel, Joshua pursues them and says: “Let the sun stand still at Gibeon,” and so forth. After the army is slaughtered, the five kings flee into a cave, are captured, and killed. On the same day he strikes Makkedah and Libnah, then Lachish and Gezer, and possesses all the cities in the hill country and on the plain, since the Lord hands them over.

VI. He lists the kings of the Anakim who were killed one by one—that is, thirty-one—and, after they were destroyed, possesses their provinces.

VII. The Lord says to Joshua: “You have grown old and are advanced in years. Divide the land among the Israelites.” Then, sitting with Eleazar the priest, he divides the entire land. Caleb speaks to him, asking that the city of Kiriath-sepher be assigned to him by lot, as the Lord had commanded. What lot was assigned to each tribe follows.

VIII. They fixed the tent of testimony at Shiloh, and from there he sends surveyors into the remaining land that had not yet been subjected.

IX. The Lord commands Joshua that cities be set apart as places of refuge for fugitives, as he spoke to Moses, and gives the law concerning who should enter those cities of refuge. Cities and their suburbs are distributed to the Levites and priests.

X. Joshua calls the Reubenites, the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh, and says to them: “You have fulfilled the command of the Lord. Go to your tents.” As they proceed to the mounds of the Jordan, they build an altar of immense size, which Joshua and Israel think sacrilegious. They send messengers, and, after receiving their explanation, are appeased.

XI. Joshua calls all Israel and admonishes them to serve the Lord. He recounts the succession of ancient generations and how they were delivered from Egypt; how the Amorites, Canaanites, and the rest were handed over into their power. Joshua sets up a stone as a testimony. After this he dies and is buried at Timnath-serah. Joseph’s bones are buried at Shechem, and Eleazar the priest dies.

[Note: In the Palatine codex these are called “chapters.”]

### BRIEF SUMMARIES OF THE BOOK OF JOSHUA

[Col. 0465]

[Col. 0465B] I. God promises Joshua, saying: “As I was with Moses, [Col. 0465C] so I will be with you.”

II. The people are commanded to prepare provisions so that they may cross the Jordan.

III. Joshua sends spies to Jericho.

IV. The Lord promises Joshua, saying: “Today I will begin to exalt you before all Israel, so that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I am with you.”

V. At the Lord’s command, the channel of the Jordan is dried up while Israel crosses.

VI. Twelve stones are selected from the channel of the Jordan for remembrance in the future.

VII. When Israel enters the land of Canaan, all the kings are terrified.

VIII. This is the reason for the second circumcision.

IX. Up to this point they ate manna.

[Col. 0465D] X. The angel of the Lord appears to Joshua and says: “I am the prince of the army of the Lord.”

XI. The siege and destruction of the city of Jericho.

XII. Joshua’s curse.

XIII. The people’s transgression.

XIV. The Lord strengthens Joshua for battle.

XV. The kings’ disturbance.

XVI. The Gibeonites’ deception.

XVII. Five kings gathered and went up against Joshua. Then he commanded the sun, and it stood still for the space of one day.

XVIII. With the Lord’s help, the kings and their army were destroyed.

[Col. 0466B] XIX. Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh ask Moses to give them the land [Col. 0465C] for themselves.

XX. These are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the Israelites struck down.

XXI. The Lord urges Joshua to divide the lands among the peoples.

XXII. Caleb renews his request for the mountain in which Hebron lies; here Adam is said to have been placed according to the law.

XXIII. The lot of Judah.

XXIV. The lot of the sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh.

XXV. The sons of Joseph ask Joshua to enlarge their allotment. He says to them: “Go up into the mountain, cut down the forest, and clear spaces for yourselves to inhabit.”

XXVI. All the Israelites gathered at Shiloh.

XXVII. Men are appointed to survey the land. When they return, they deliver the survey to Joshua, who casts lots before the Lord at Shiloh and divides the land among the Israelites into seven parts.

XXVIII. The cities of refuge.

XXIX. The Levitical cities.

XXX. After the storms of war, rest was given by the Lord.

XXXI. The altar of immense size constructed without consultation by the tribe of Reuben.

XXXII. As the day of his death approaches, Joshua recounts everything to Israel from the beginning and testifies that they must not depart from the Lord’s commands.

XXXIII. Where Abraham was born and where he was led. Likewise, after gathering them under a covenant oath, Joshua addresses them.

## THE BOOK OF JOSHUA SON OF NUN BEGINS

[Col. 0469]

[Col. 0469B] [T. I, B. I, Cap. I.] And it came to pass after the death of Moses, the servant of the Lord, that the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ attendant, and said to him:

“Moses my servant is dead. Rise, cross this Jordan, you and all the people with you, into the land that I am giving to the Israelites. Every place on which the sole of your foot treads I will give you, as I spoke to Moses. From the wilderness and Lebanon as far as the great river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites as far as the Great Sea toward the setting of the sun shall be your boundary. No one will be able to resist you [h. “you”] all the days of your life. As I was with Moses [Vulgate adds “so”], so I will be with you. I will not abandon you or forsake you. Be strong and courageous, for you will divide this land among the people by lot, the land concerning which I swore to your fathers [h. “their fathers”] that I would give it to them.

“Therefore be strong and very courageous, so that you may observe and do all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn away from it to the right or to the left, so that you may understand everything that you do. Let the volume of this law not depart from your mouth; meditate on it day and night, so that you may observe and do everything written in it. Then you will make your way prosperous and understand it. Behold, I command you: be strong and courageous. Do not fear or be afraid, for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go.”

[B. II, C. I.] And Joshua commanded the leaders of the people, saying:

“Cross through the middle of the camp, command the people, and say: ‘Prepare provisions for yourselves, because after three days you will cross the Jordan and enter to possess the land that the Lord your God is going to give you.’”

And he said to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh:

“Remember the word that Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded you, saying: ‘The Lord your God has given you rest and all the land [h. “and this land”].’ Your wives, your sons, and your livestock will remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan. But you shall cross over armed before your brothers, [Note: The Septuagint reads in the singular, “every man strong in hand,” a reading followed by the Hebrew Canon, the Royal manuscript of the Bible, and one Corbie manuscript. Nevertheless, in manuscripts *omnis* and *fortis* could easily have been written for *omnes* and *fortes*, since the ancients frequently wrote *i* for *e*. MART.] all strong-handed men, and fight for them until the Lord gives your brothers rest, as he has given you. Then they too shall possess the land that the Lord your God is going to give them. Afterward you shall return to the land of your possession and dwell in it, the land that Moses, the servant of the Lord, gave you beyond the Jordan toward the rising of the sun.”

And they answered Joshua and said:

“Everything that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in everything, so we will obey you also. Only may the Lord your God be with you, as he was with Moses. Whoever contradicts your word and does not obey all the words that you command him [Vulgate omits “that you command him”] shall be put to death. Only be strong and act courageously.”

### (Book III, Chapter II, Section II)

Joshua son of Nun therefore sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies and said to them: “Go and inspect the land and the city of Jericho.” [Col. 0470C] They went and entered the house of a prostitute named Rahab, and lodged with her.

It was reported to the king of Jericho, and they told him: “Look, men have come here by night from the Israelites, to spy out the land.” The king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying: “Bring out the men who came to you and entered your house, for they are spies; they have come to inspect the whole land” [Hebrew: “for they have come to spy out the whole land”].

The woman took the men and concealed them, and said: “I admit that they came to me, but I did not know where they were from. When the gate was about to be shut in the darkness, they went out together; I do not know where they have gone. Pursue them quickly, and you will catch them.” But she had brought the men up to the roof of her house [Hebrew: “The Hebrew does not have ‘of her house’”] and covered them with stalks of flax that were there. The men who had been sent pursued them along the road leading to the ford of the Jordan. As soon as they had gone out, the gate was shut.

The men in hiding had not yet fallen asleep when, behold, the woman came up to them and said [Hebrew: “came up to them on the roof and said”]: “I know that the Lord has given you the land. For terror of you has fallen upon us, and all the inhabitants of the land have grown faint” [Hebrew: “before you”]. We have heard how the Lord dried up the waters of the Red Sea before your entry, when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, Sihon and Og, whom you killed. When we heard this, we were terrified [Hebrew does not have “and”], and our heart melted, and no spirit remained in us at your entry. For the Lord your God is himself God in heaven above and on earth below.

### Chapter III

“Now therefore swear to me by the Lord that, just as I have shown you mercy, so you will show mercy to my father’s household. Give me a true sign, so that you may save” [Hebrew: “and preserve alive,” etc.; the sense is, “Receive them into the observance of your faith”] “my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and rescue our lives from death.”

They answered her: “May our life be for you unto death, provided that you do not betray us. When the Lord has given us the land, we will show you mercy and faithfulness.”

[Col. 0471B] So she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was attached to the wall. And she said to them: “Climb into the mountains, lest those pursuing you meet you on your return” [Hebrew: “lest those pursuing you overtake you”]. Hide there for three days, until they return; afterward you may go on your way.”

They said to her: “We shall be free from this oath with which you have bound us, provided that, when we enter the land, this scarlet cord is the sign, and you tie it in the window through which you let us down; and provided that you gather your father, mother, brothers, and all your family into your house. Whoever goes out through the door of your house, his blood shall be upon his own head, and we shall be innocent.”

[Note: [Col. 0471D] Only the true Hebrew Canon reads this way, in accordance with what was written above at verse 17. Other manuscripts and printed books read, “and we shall be strangers” [or “free from guilt”]: the meaning of these words does not seem sufficiently clear for ordinary understanding. Let the reader note that the verse numbers here and elsewhere in our annotations are cited according to the divisions found in the Latin Vulgate, although numerical verse markings do not appear in our text, for the reason given in the Prolegomena. See what is said there. MART. —Together with the Urbinate manuscript, most other books, both printed and manuscript, read “strangers” instead of “free from guilt.” The Palatine manuscript, deleting the former word, substituted the latter in a later hand.]

“As for everyone who is with you in the house, their blood shall fall upon our head if anyone lays a hand upon them. But if you betray us and disclose this matter, we shall be free from the oath with which you have bound us.”

She replied: “As you have spoken, so let it be.” She sent them away, and tied the scarlet cord in the window.

They went on and reached the mountains, remaining there for three days, until those who had pursued them returned. They had searched the whole road [the Vulgate adds “the whole”], but did not find them. After the pursuers had entered the city [Hebrew does not have this], the spies came down from the mountain, crossed the Jordan, and came to Joshua son of Nun. They told him everything that had happened to them and said: “The Lord has delivered this whole land into our hands, and all its inhabitants have been prostrated by fear” [Hebrew: “before us”].

[Col. 0471D] [T. II, Chapter III] Joshua therefore rose during the night and moved the camp. He and all the Israelites went out from Shittim and came to the Jordan, where they remained for three days. When these had passed, heralds went through the middle of the camp and began to proclaim:

“When you see the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, and the priests of the Levitical line carrying it, you too must rise [Hebrew: “from your places”] and follow those going ahead. Let there be a distance of two thousand cubits between you and the ark, so that you may see it from afar and know by which way you are to enter, because you have not traveled that way before. And take care not to approach the ark” [Hebrew: “Two thousand by measure; and take care not to approach the ark, so that you may know the way by which you are to enter, since you have not traveled it from yesterday and the day before”].

### Chapter IV

Joshua said to the people: “Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the Lord will perform wonders among you.” And he said to the priests: “Take up the ark of the covenant and go before the people.” They fulfilled his command, took it up, and went before them.

[Book IV, Chapter V] The Lord said to Joshua: “Today I will begin to exalt you before all Israel, so that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I am with you. Now command the priests who carry the ark of the covenant and say to them: ‘When you enter a part of the waters of the Jordan, stand there.’”

Joshua said to the Israelites: “Come here and hear the words of the Lord your God.” And again he said: “By this you shall know that the living God is among you, and that he will drive out before you the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Hivite, the Perizzite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, and the Jebusite. Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth will go before you through the Jordan. Choose twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one from each tribe.”

### Chapter VI

“When the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord of the whole earth have placed the soles of their feet in the waters of the Jordan, the waters flowing below will run off and fail, while those coming from above will stand in one mass” [Hebrew does not have “of the covenant”; the Septuagint, the Canon, and the Arabic Interpreter have the word “covenant,” although it is absent from the present Hebrew and Samaritan. MART. —None of our manuscripts has the word “covenant” here, nor does the Hebrew text itself acknowledge it. The Palatine manuscript further reads *portabunt*—“they will carry”—in the future instead of *portant*—“carry.”]

[Book V] The people therefore went out from their tents [the Vulgate omits “their”] to cross the Jordan, and the priests carrying the ark of the covenant went before them. When they entered the Jordan and their feet were dipped in part of its waters—for the Jordan had filled the banks of its channel during harvest—the waters flowing downward stood in one place and appeared, swelling like a mountain, far away, from the city called Adam to the place of Zarethan. But the waters below flowed into the Sea of the Wilderness, which is now called the Dead Sea, until they completely failed.

The people were advancing toward [Note: [Col. 0472D] We have not wished to alter this reading, although eleven manuscripts all read “opposite the Jordan.” In the Hebrew exemplars and in the Greek we find the name Jericho, not Jordan. The sense would also become more obscure in Scripture if we followed the Latin manuscripts. MART. —All the manuscripts, both ours and those consulted by Martianay, contradict this, having with equal agreement “opposite the Jordan”; but this may be attributed to the carelessness of scribes.] Jericho. The priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord stood on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan, fully prepared, and all the people crossed through the dry channel.

[Book VI, Chapter VII, Section IV] When they had crossed, the Lord said to Joshua: “Choose twelve men, one from each tribe, and command them to take from the middle of the Jordan’s channel, where the priests’ feet stood, twelve very hard stones [Hebrew does not have “very hard”]. Carry them to the place of the camp where you will pitch your tents tonight.”

### Chapter VIII

Joshua called the twelve men whom he had chosen from the Israelites, one from each tribe, and said to them: “Go before the ark of the Lord your God into the middle of the Jordan, and let each of you carry from there one stone upon his shoulders, according to the number of the Israelites, so that it may be a sign among you.”

### Chapter IX

“When your children ask you tomorrow, saying, ‘What do these stones mean?’ you shall answer them: ‘The waters of the Jordan failed before the ark of the covenant of the Lord when it crossed through it. Therefore these stones have been placed as a memorial for the Israelites forever.’”

The Israelites did as Joshua had commanded them. They carried twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan’s channel, as the Lord had ordered Joshua, according to the number of the Israelites, to the place where they encamped, and there they set them down.

Joshua also set twelve other stones in the middle of the Jordan’s channel, where the priests carrying the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to the present day. The priests carrying the ark stood in the middle of the Jordan until everything was completed that the Lord had commanded Joshua to tell the people and that Moses had told him. The people hurried and crossed.

When they had all crossed, the ark of the Lord also crossed, and the priests went before the people. The sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, armed, went before the Israelites, as Moses had commanded them [Hebrew: “They went before the Israelites, as Moses had spoken to them. Forty thousand armed men marched before the Lord”].

### Chapter X

Forty thousand fighting men marched in companies and detachments across the plains and open country of the city of Jericho. On that day the Lord magnified Joshua before all Israel, so that they feared him as they had feared Moses while he lived.

### Chapter XI

The Lord said to him: “Command the priests who carry the ark of the covenant [Hebrew: “testimony”] to come up from the Jordan.”

He commanded them, saying: “Come up from the Jordan.” When they had come up, carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and had begun to tread on dry ground, the waters returned to their channel and flowed as they had formerly done.

The people came up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and encamped at Gilgal [Galgal] on the eastern side of Jericho. Joshua set up at Gilgal the twelve stones that they had taken from the Jordan’s channel, and said to the Israelites:

### Chapter XII

“When your children ask their fathers tomorrow and say to them, ‘What do these stones mean?’ you shall teach them and say: ‘Israel crossed this Jordan through its dry channel, while the Lord your God dried up its waters before you until you crossed, just as he had earlier done at the Red Sea, which he dried until we crossed. This was so that all the peoples of the earth might learn the exceedingly mighty hand of the Lord, and so that you might fear the Lord your God at all times.’”

[Book VII, Chapter XIII, Section V] After all the kings of the Amorites who lived beyond the Jordan on its western side, and all the kings of Canaan who possessed the regions near the Great Sea, had heard that the Lord had dried up the Jordan’s waters before the Israelites until they crossed, their hearts melted, and no spirit remained in them because they feared the Israelites’ entry.

[T. III, Book VIII, Chapter XIV] At that time the Lord said to Joshua: “Make stone knives for yourself and circumcise the Israelites a second time.”

### Chapter XV

Joshua did what the Lord had commanded and circumcised the Israelites at the Hill of the Foreskins.

This was the reason for the second circumcision: all the male population that had come out of Egypt—all the men of military age—had died in the wilderness during the very long wanderings of the journey; all of them had been circumcised. But the people who had been born in the wilderness during the forty years of travel through the vast desert were uncircumcised, until those who had not obeyed the voice of the Lord had perished, those to whom he had sworn that he would not show them the land flowing with milk and honey [Note: [Col. 0473D] Certain words of the sacred text have fallen out here, in my opinion through the customary error of Latin scribes caused by the recurrence of the same word, “land.” The holy Father must have interpreted it in this way: “that he would show them the land which the Lord had sworn to give their fathers, a land,” etc. But the Latin copyist, as we said, when his eye returned to the word “land” occurring later, rashly omitted the words that came after the first occurrence. The Hebrew exemplar repeats them, and the Greek agrees: *τὴν γῆν ἣν ὤμοσε Κύριος τοῖς πατράσιν αὐτῶν δοῦναι, γῆν ῥέουσαν etc.*—“the land which the Lord swore to give their fathers, a land flowing,” etc. It was certainly worthwhile to observe this. MART.]

Their sons succeeded them, and Joshua circumcised them, because they had been born uncircumcised [Hebrew: “because they were uncircumcised”], and no one had circumcised them on the way. After they had all been circumcised, they remained in the same place in the camp until they were healed.

### Chapter XVI

The Lord said to Joshua: “Today I have removed the reproach of Egypt from you.”

The name of that place was called Gilgal [Hebrew: “Gilgal”] to the present day.

### Chapter XVII

The Israelites remained at Gilgal and celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, toward evening, in the plains of Jericho. On the following day they ate the produce of the land: unleavened bread and parched grain of that same year.

[Book IX, Chapter XVIII] The manna ceased after they had eaten the produce of the land. The Israelites no longer used that food, but ate from the produce of the land of Canaan in the current year.

[Book X, Chapter XIX] When Joshua was in the fields of Jericho, he lifted his eyes and saw a man standing opposite him, holding a drawn sword. He went up to him and said: “Are you one of ours or one of our adversaries?”

He replied: “No; rather, I am commander of the army of the Lord, and now I have come.”

Joshua fell facedown upon the ground and, worshiping, said: “What does my lord say to his servant?”

“Remove your sandal from your foot,” he said, “for the place on which you stand is holy.”

Joshua did as he had been commanded.

[Book XI, Section VI] Jericho was shut and fortified because of the Israelites, and no one dared to go out or enter.

### Chapter XX

The Lord said to Joshua: “Behold, I have given Jericho into your hand, together with its king and all its mighty warriors. All the fighting men shall circle the city once each day. You shall do this for six days. On the seventh day the priests shall take seven trumpets” [Hebrew: “You shall do this for six days, and seven priests shall take seven trumpets used at the jubilee, and they shall go before the ark. On the seventh day you shall circle the city seven times, and the priests shall blow”], “the kind used at the jubilee, and they shall go before the ark of the covenant. You shall circle the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets. When the sound of the trumpet has become prolonged and sharply cut off, and it resounds in your ears, the whole people shall raise a very great shout, and the walls of the city shall fall utterly; and each person shall enter by the place opposite which he is standing.”

Joshua son of Nun called the priests and said to them: “Take up the ark of the covenant, and let seven other priests take seven jubilee trumpets and go before the ark of the Lord.”

He also said to the people: “Go and circle the city, armed, going before the ark of the Lord.”

When Joshua had finished speaking, the seven priests blew the seven trumpets before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and the whole armed army went before it; the remaining people followed the ark, and everything resounded with the trumpets.

### Chapter XXI

Joshua had commanded the people, saying: “You shall not shout, nor shall your voice be heard, nor shall any word come from your mouth, until the day comes when I say to you: ‘Shout and raise the war cry.’”

The ark of the Lord therefore circled the city once that day and returned to the camp, where it remained. When Joshua rose during the night, the priests took up the ark of the Lord, and seven of them took the seven trumpets used at the jubilees [the Vulgate has “at the jubilee”]. They went before the ark of the Lord, walking and blowing the trumpets; the armed people went before them, while the rest followed the ark and sounded the trumpets.

They circled the city once on the second day and returned to the camp. They did the same for six days. On the seventh day they rose at dawn and circled the city seven times, as had been arranged. When the priests blew the trumpets during the seventh circuit, Joshua said to all Israel [Hebrew: “to the people”]: “Raise the war cry, for the Lord has delivered the city to you.”

### Chapter XXII

“Let this city and everything in it be devoted to the Lord. Only Rahab the prostitute shall live, together with everyone who is with her in the house, because she hid the messengers whom we sent. But you must beware of touching anything that has been commanded to destruction, lest you become guilty of transgression and bring all the camp of Israel under sin and disturbance. Whatever there is of gold and silver, and of vessels of bronze and iron, shall be consecrated to the Lord and placed in his treasury.”

### Chapter XXIII

When all the people had raised the war cry and the trumpets were sounding, as soon as the sound and noise resounded in the ears of the multitude, the walls immediately fell. Each person went up by the place opposite him, and they captured the city and killed everything in it, from man to woman, from child to old man. They also struck the oxen, sheep, and donkeys with the edge of the sword.

### Chapter XXIV

Joshua said to the two men who had been sent as spies: “Enter the house of the prostitute and bring her out, together with everything that belongs to her, as you swore to her under oath.”

The young men entered and brought out Rahab, her parents, her brothers, all her possessions, and her entire family, and made them remain outside the camp of Israel.

They burned the city and everything in it, except the gold and silver and vessels of bronze and iron, which they consecrated to the treasury of the Lord. Joshua preserved Rahab the prostitute, her father’s household, and everything she possessed; and they lived in the midst of Israel to the present day, because she had hidden the messengers whom he had sent to spy out Jericho.

[Book XII, Chapter XXV] At that time Joshua pronounced this curse, saying: “Cursed before the Lord is the man who rises up and rebuilds this city of Jericho. At the cost of his firstborn let him lay its foundations, and at the cost of his youngest child let him set up its gates.”

So the Lord was with Joshua, and his name became renowned throughout the whole land.

[Book XIII, Chapter XXVI, Section VII] The Israelites transgressed the commandment and appropriated something from what had been devoted to destruction. Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took something from what had been devoted to destruction, and the Lord’s anger burned against the Israelites.

When Joshua sent men from Jericho against Ai, which is near Beth-aven, east of the town of Bethel, he said to them: “Go up and spy out the land.”

They fulfilled his command and spied out Ai. When they returned, they said to him: “Let not all the people go up; let two or three thousand men go and destroy the city. Why should the whole people be troubled uselessly against very few enemies?” [The Vulgate has “will be troubled.”]

### Chapter XXVII

Three thousand fighting men [Hebrew: “men”] therefore went up. They immediately turned their backs and were struck down by the men of Ai; thirty-six of them fell. Their adversaries pursued them from the gate as far as Sabarim, and they fell while fleeing down the slopes. The heart of the people was terrified and melted like water.

Joshua tore his garments and fell facedown upon the ground before the ark of the Lord until evening, he and all the elders of Israel. They put dust upon their heads, and Joshua said:

“Alas, Lord God, why did you wish to bring this people across the Jordan River [Hebrew does not have “river”], in order to deliver us into the hands of the Amorites and destroy us? If only we had been content to remain beyond the Jordan, as we began!

“My Lord God [Hebrew does not have “God”], what shall I say, seeing Israel turn its back before its enemies? The Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear, combine together, surround us, and wipe our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?”

### Chapter XXVIII

The Lord said to Joshua: “Rise! Why are you lying facedown on the ground? Israel has sinned and transgressed my covenant. They have taken from what was devoted to destruction, stolen, lied, and hidden it among their belongings. Israel will not be able to stand before its enemies; it will flee from them, because it has been polluted by what was devoted to destruction” [Hebrew: “it has become devoted to destruction”]. “I will no longer be with you until you destroy the one who is guilty of this crime.

“Rise and consecrate the people, and say to them: ‘Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, for thus says the Lord God of Israel: There is something devoted to destruction in your midst, Israel. You will not be able to stand before your enemies until the one polluted by this crime has been removed from among you.

“‘In the morning you shall draw near tribe by tribe. The tribe selected by lot shall come forward by its clans, the clan by its households, and each household by its men. Whoever is found to have committed this crime shall be burned with fire, together with all that belongs to him, because he has transgressed the covenant of the Lord and committed an abomination in Israel.’”

### Chapter XXIX

Joshua rose early and brought Israel forward tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was found. When he brought it forward by its families, the family of Zerah was found. When he brought it forward man by man [Note: [Col. 0477D] The Vulgate reads “by households,” contrary to the Hebrew], Zabdi was found. Dividing his household man by man, he found [Note: [Col. 0477D] This name has been changed in some Greek and Latin copies to Achar and Achor. Nevertheless, the Alexandrian manuscript correctly reads Achan with the Hebrew. Jerome also teaches that it should be read this way in his book *On Hebrew Place-Names*: “Emek Achor,” he says, “which is interpreted as the Valley of Achor, that is, of tumult and disturbance, where Achan was crushed by stones … . It is a place near Jericho, not far from Gilgal. Some therefore wrongly think that the Valley of Achor was named after the man who was stoned, since he was called Achan, not Achor or Achar.” MART. —The Palatine manuscript reads Achar; the Urbinate reads Achor. If you wish, recall the holy Interpreter, in his book *On Hebrew Place-Names*, under the entry “Emek Achor,” and our observations there.]

Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah.

Joshua said to Achan: “My son, give glory to the Lord God of Israel and confess to him. Tell me what you have done; do not hide it.”

### Chapter XXX

Achan answered Joshua and said to him: “Truly I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel, and I have done this and this. I saw among the spoil a very fine scarlet cloak” [Hebrew: “one good cloak from Shinar”], “two hundred shekels of silver, and a gold bar weighing fifty shekels. I coveted them, took them, and hid them in the ground opposite the middle of my tent. I covered the silver with earth in a pit.”

Joshua therefore sent servants. They ran to his tent and found everything hidden there, together with the silver. They took it from the tent and brought it to Joshua and all the Israelites, and cast it before the Lord.

Joshua then took Achan son of Zerah, the silver, the cloak, the gold bar, his sons and daughters, his oxen, donkeys, and sheep, his tent itself, and all his possessions—and all Israel with him—and brought them to the Valley of Achor.

Joshua said: “Because you have troubled us” [the Vulgate: “who have troubled us”], “the Lord will trouble you this day.”

All Israel stoned him, and everything that belonged to him was consumed by fire. They heaped over him a great pile of stones, which remains to the present day. The Lord’s anger was turned away from them. The name of that place was called the Valley of Achor to this day.

[T. IV, Book XIV, Chapter XXXI, Section VIII] The Lord said to Joshua: “Do not fear or be afraid. Take with you the whole multitude of fighting men, rise, and go up against Ai. Behold, I have delivered its king, people, city, and land into your hand. You shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. But you shall take its spoil and all its livestock for yourselves. Set an ambush for the city behind it.”

Joshua rose, and all the army of warriors with him, to go up against Ai. He chose thirty thousand [Col. 0478B] valiant men and sent them out by night, commanding them:

“Set an ambush behind the city, and do not go far from it. All of you must be ready. I and the rest of the multitude with me will approach the city from the opposite side. When they come out against us, as we did before [Hebrew does not have “we did”], we will flee and turn our backs, until those pursuing us are drawn far away from the city [the Vulgate: “until we are drawn far away”]. For they will think that we are fleeing from them as before.

“When we flee and they pursue us, you shall rise from the ambush and ravage the city. The Lord your God will deliver it into your hands. When you have captured the city [the Vulgate omits “the city”], burn it, and do everything as you have been commanded” [Hebrew: “Do according to the word of the Lord. See, I am commanding you”].

He dismissed them, and they went to the place of the ambush. They sat between Bethel and Ai, west of the city of Ai. Joshua spent that night among the people. Rising at dawn, he reviewed his companions and went up with the elders at the head of the army, surrounded by the support of the fighting men.

When they had come and gone up opposite the city, they stood on the northern side of Ai, with a valley between it and them. He had chosen five thousand men and placed them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, on the western side of the same city. The rest of the army formed its line to the north, so that the rear of the multitude [the Vulgate adds “of it”] reached the western side of the city. Joshua went that night and stood in the middle of the valley.

### Chapter XXXII

When the king of Ai saw this, he hurried out in the morning with the whole army of the city and drew up his line toward the wilderness, unaware that an ambush lay behind him.

Joshua and all Israel yielded ground, pretending fear, and fled along the road of the wilderness. But they all shouted together, encouraging one another, and pursued them.

When they had withdrawn from the city, and not one man remained in Ai or Bethel who did not pursue Israel—for they had burst out through the open gate [the Vulgate omits “the gate”], leaving the towns behind—then the Lord said to Joshua: “Raise the shield that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it to you.”

When he had raised the shield opposite the city, the ambush that was concealed rose immediately. They went to the city, captured it, and burned it.

The men of the city who were pursuing Joshua looked back and saw the smoke of the city rising to heaven. They could no longer flee in one direction or another, especially since those who had pretended to flee toward the wilderness had turned with great force against their pursuers.

When Joshua and all Israel saw that the city had been captured and that its smoke was rising, they turned back and struck down the men of Ai. For those who had captured and burned the city came out from it against their own people and began to strike the enemy in the midst.

When the adversaries were being cut down on both sides, so that not one of so great a multitude survived, they also seized the king of Ai alive and brought him to Joshua.

After all those who had pursued Israel as it went toward the wilderness had been killed and had fallen by the sword in the same place, the Israelites returned and struck down the city. Those who fell that day, from man to woman, numbered twelve thousand people—all the inhabitants of Ai.

Joshua did not withdraw the hand he had stretched upward while holding the shield until all the inhabitants of Ai had been killed. The Israelites divided among themselves the livestock and spoil of the city, as the Lord had commanded Joshua.

He burned the city and made it an everlasting mound. He also hanged its king on a gallows until evening. At sunset Joshua gave the order, and they took his corpse down from the cross. They threw it at the very entrance of the city and heaped over it a great pile of stones, which remains to the present day.

### Chapter XXXIII

Then Joshua built an altar to the Lord God of Israel on Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of the Lord had commanded the Israelites, and as it is written in the book of the law of Moses: “An altar of unhewn stones, untouched by iron.” He offered burnt offerings upon it to the Lord and sacrificed peace offerings.

He wrote upon the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which Moses had set out before the Israelites.

All the people [Hebrew: “and all Israel”], the elders, leaders, and judges stood on both sides of the ark, in the presence of the priests [Hebrew: “the Levitical priests”] who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, the foreigner as well as the native-born. Half of them stood beside Mount Gerizim and half beside Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of the Lord had commanded.

At first he blessed the people of Israel.

### Chapter XXXIV

After this he read all the words of the blessing and the curse, and everything [Hebrew does not have “everything”] that had been written in the book of the law. He left nothing untouched of all that Moses had commanded; rather, he repeated everything before the whole assembly of Israel, including the women, the children, and the foreigners who lived among them.

[Col. 0480A] [B. XV, Chapter IX.] When these things had been heard, all the kings beyond the Jordan—those who lived in the hill country and in the lowlands, along the coast and on the shore of the Great Sea, as well as those who lived near Lebanon—the Hittite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite—gathered together with one accord to fight against Joshua and Israel, with one purpose and the same resolve [h. does not have this].

[B. XVI, C. XXXV.] But those who lived in Gibeon, hearing all that Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai, and devising a stratagem, took provisions for themselves, placed old sacks upon their donkeys, and wine-skins that were torn and stitched together. They put on very old shoes, which had been sewn with patches as evidence of their age, and old garments. The loaves that they carried for the journey were hard and [Col. 0480B] broken into pieces. They set out for Joshua, who was then staying in the camp at Gilgal, and said to him and to all Israel together:

“We have come from a very distant land, wishing to make peace with you.”

The Israelite men answered them [h. “the Hivite”] and said:

“Perhaps you are living in the land that may be assigned to us, and we shall not be able to make a covenant with you.”

But they said to Joshua:

“We are your servants.”

Joshua said to them:

“Who are you, and from where have you come?”

They answered:

“Your servants have come from a very distant land in the name of the Lord your God. For we have heard of his power and of all that he did in Egypt, and to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan: Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, who were in Ashtaroth. Our elders and all the inhabitants of our land said to us: ‘Take provisions in your hands for the very long journey, go to meet them, and say: “We are your servants; make a covenant with us.”’

“Look: when we left our homes to come to you, we took these loaves warm; now they have become dry and have crumbled through extreme age. We filled new wine-skins; now they are torn and burst. The garments and shoes that we wear and have on our feet have been worn out and almost consumed because of the length of the journey.”

[C. XXXVI.] So they accepted some of their provisions, but did not inquire of the word of the Lord. Joshua made peace with them and, having made a covenant, promised that they would not be killed. The princes also swore an oath to them on behalf of the assembly. But three days after they had made the covenant, they heard that these people lived nearby and would be among them. The Israelites broke camp and came to their cities on the third day. Their names were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim. They did not strike them, because the princes of the assembly had sworn to them in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel [h. “in the Lord God of Israel”]. Then all the common people murmured against the princes.

[C. XXXVII.] They answered them:

“We swore to them in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel [h. ‘in the Lord God of Israel’], and therefore we cannot touch them. But this is what we shall do to them: let them be spared so that they may live, lest the Lord’s anger be stirred up against us if we break our oath. Let them live in such a way that they may cut wood for the needs of the whole assembly [Col. 0481A] and carry water.”

While they were saying these things, Joshua summoned the Gibeonites and said to them:

“Why did you wish to deceive us by fraud, saying, ‘We live very far from you,’ when you are living in our midst? Therefore you shall be under a curse, and none of your stock shall cease to be one who cuts wood and carries water into the house of my God.”

They answered:

“It was reported to us [h. does not have ‘to us’], your servants, that the Lord your God had promised Moses his servant to give you the whole land and to destroy all its inhabitants [h. ‘from before you’]. Therefore we were exceedingly afraid and, compelled by dread of you, took thought for our lives and adopted this plan. But now we are in your hand; do to us what seems good and right to you.”

[Col. 0481B] So Joshua did to them as he had said, and rescued them from the hand of the Israelites so that they would not be killed. On that day he decreed that they should serve all the people and the altar of the Lord, cutting wood and carrying water, down to the present time, in the place that the Lord would choose.

[B. XVII, C. XXXVIII, Chapter X.] When Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard that Joshua had captured Ai and overthrown it—for just as he had dealt with Jericho and its king, so he had dealt with Ai and its king—and that the Gibeonites had defected to Israel [h. “had made peace”] and were their allies, he was very much afraid. For Gibeon was a great city, one of the royal cities, larger than Ai, and all its warriors were very strong.

Therefore Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, sent to Hoham, king of Hebron, to Piram, king of Jarmuth, to Japhia, king of Lachish, and to Debir, king of Eglon, saying:

“Come up to me and bring assistance, so that we may attack Gibeon, which has defected [h. ‘has made peace’] to Joshua and the Israelites.”

[T. V.] So the five kings of the Amorites gathered and went up: the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, together with their armies. They encamped around Gibeon and besieged it.

[C. XXXIX.] The inhabitants of the besieged city of Gibeon [h. does not have this] sent to Joshua, who was then staying in the camp at Gilgal, and said to him:

“Do not withdraw your hands from helping your servants. Come up quickly, rescue us, and bring assistance. For all the kings of the Amorites who live in the hill country have gathered against us.”

Joshua went up from Gilgal, and with him came the whole army of warriors and the most valiant men.

[B. XVIII.] The Lord said to Joshua:

“Do not fear them, for I have delivered them into your hands. None of them will be able to withstand you.”

So Joshua suddenly fell upon them, going up from Gilgal throughout the night. The Lord threw them into confusion before Israel. He struck them with a great slaughter at Gibeon and pursued them along the ascent to Beth-horon, striking them as far as Azekah and Makkedah.

[C. XL.] When they were fleeing from the Israelites [h. “from before Israel”] and were on the descent of Beth-horon, the Lord hurled great stones upon them from heaven as far as Azekah. Many more died from the hailstones than those whom the Israelites had struck with the sword.

[Col. 0482B] Then Joshua spoke to the Lord, on the day when he delivered the Amorite into the sight of the Israelites, and said before them:

“Sun, do not move against Gibeon; and moon, against the valley of Aijalon.”

[C. XLI.] And the sun and the moon stood still until the nation had avenged itself upon its enemies. Is this not written in the [Note: [Col. 0481D] This understanding of the Book of the Upright, or of the Just, appears excessively uncertain. For there is no book among the canonical Scriptures that is not, and may not rightly be called, the book of God. It is better, therefore, that Saint Jerome, in Book XII of his *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter XLIV, expressly determined that the Book of Genesis is called the Book of the Just:

“By another name,” he says, “he calls Israel ISURUN (); for it is a Hebrew word, and the others interpreted it as *euthútaton* (εὐθύτατον), or *euthýn* (εὐθὺν), that is, ‘most upright’ and ‘upright’; only the Seventy added from their own interpretation ‘most beloved,’ joining it to ‘Israel.’ Properly, according to the Hebrews and the truth of the letters, Israel is called ‘upright of God.’ But ‘a man who sees God’ is not in the elements but in the sound of the voice. Hence the Book of Genesis is also called *euthéōn* (εὐθέων), that is, ‘of the just,’ namely Abraham, Isaac, and Israel.”

He brings forward the same point in Book VI of his *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter XVIII, quoting the words of Balaam: “May my soul die among the souls of the just” (Numbers XXIII:10):

“If Balaam [lacuna],” he says, “signifies a vain people, it is clear that the formerly vain people of the nations desires to have fellowship with the souls of the just—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—who are called *eutheîs* (εὐθεῖς), that is, ‘upright’ and ‘just.’ Hence the Book of Genesis took its name from them.”

We have noted these passages from Jerome’s *Commentaries* so that modern critics may now see how far from the truth are those who think it an invention of the authors of the *Gemaroth* that the Book of Genesis is called the Book of the Just. Certainly, if it is an invention, it is shown to be older than all the Talmudic writings, and not only among the Hebrews but also among the ancient ecclesiastical writers it was formerly accepted. More will be said about the Book of the Just when we come to the Second Book of Samuel. MART.

—See what we have observed on this subject in our *Commentaries on Isaiah*, chapter XLIV, and on Ezekiel, chapter XVIII.] Book of the Just [h. “of the upright,” that is, “of God”]?

So the sun stood in the middle of the sky and did not hasten to set for the space of one day. There was neither before nor afterward so long a day [Vulg. “nor afterward”]—such a day [h. “such a day”]—with the Lord obeying the voice of a man and fighting for Israel. Joshua then returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal.

[C. XLII.] For the five kings had fled and hidden themselves in a cave at the city of Makkedah. Joshua was told that five kings had been found hiding in the cave [Vulg. adds “of the city”] of Makkedah. He instructed his companions, saying:

“Roll great stones to the mouth of the cave and place diligent men there to guard those shut inside. But you must not remain here; pursue the enemies and strike down the hindmost of the fugitives. Do not allow those whom the Lord God has delivered into your hands to enter the fortifications of their cities.”

After the adversaries had been struck down with a great slaughter and almost completely destroyed, those who were able to escape from Israel entered the fortified cities. The whole army returned to Joshua at Makkedah, where the camp then was, safe and at full strength. No one dared utter a sound against the Israelites.

[C. XLIII.] Joshua ordered:

“Open the mouth of the cave and bring out to me the five kings who are hiding in it.”

The servants did as he had commanded and brought out to him the five kings from the cave: the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.

[C. XLIV.] When they had been brought out to him, he summoned all the men of Israel and said to the commanders of the army who were with him:

“Go and place your feet upon the necks of these kings.”

When they had gone and were trampling the necks of the prostrate men beneath their feet, he said to them again:

“Do not fear or be afraid. Take courage and be strong, for this is what the Lord will do to all your enemies against whom you fight.”

Joshua then struck and killed them and hung them upon five stakes. They remained hanging until evening. When the sun was setting, he commanded his companions to take them down from the gallows. They took them down and threw them into the cave in which they had hidden, and placed great stones over its mouth, which remain to the present time.

[C. XLV.] On that same day Joshua also captured Makkedah and struck it with the edge of the sword. He killed its king and all its inhabitants and left not even a small remnant in it. He did to the king of Makkedah as he had done to the king of Jericho.

Then he passed with all Israel from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against it. The Lord delivered it, together with its king, into the hand of Israel.
