XXXIII. Abimelech, the son of Jerubbaal, was at Shechem with his mother’s brothers.

[Col. 0508A] XXXIV. Jotham told the men of Shechem a parable about the olive tree, the vine, and the bramble.

XXXV. Jotham says to the men of Shechem: “Have you established Abimelech as king over you rightly and without guilt?”

XXXVI. After Abimelech, Tola, son of Puah, arose as leader in Israel.

XXXVII. Jair the Gileadite judged Israel for twenty-two years.

XXXVIII. The Lord says to the Israelites: “I will not continue to deliver you.”

XXXIX. At that time there was Jephthah the Gileadite, a very valiant man and warrior.

XL. Jephthah spoke all his words before the Lord at Mizpah.

XLI. Jephthah made a vow concerning his daughter against the Ammonites.

[Col. 0508B] XLII. “Why, when you went to battle against the Ammonites, did you not call us to go with you?”

XLIII. Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel; he had thirty sons and an equal number of daughters.

XLIV. Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel for ten years; then he died and was buried in Zebulun.

XLV. Abdon, son of Hillel the Pirathonite, judged Israel.

XLVI. There was a certain man from Zorah, of the family of Dan.

XLVII. Samson was born.

XLVIII. Samson said to his father: “Take this woman for me, because she has pleased my eyes.”

XLIX. The Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson, and he tore the lion apart.

L. Samson proposed to his companions a riddle concerning the honeycomb taken from the lion’s mouth.

[Col. 0508C] LI. Concerning the foxes that Samson captured.

LII. Concerning the jawbone, that is, the mandible of a donkey.

LIII. Concerning the gates that Samson carried to the summit of the mountain, together with their posts and bar.

LIV. Concerning Delilah.

LV. The Philistines, rejoicing at their banquets, summon Samson.

LVI. Micah speaks to his mother.

LVII. Concerning the Danites.

LVIII. Concerning Jonathan, son of Gershom.

LIX. Concerning the Levite living on the side of Mount Ephraim.

# THE BOOK OF SOPHTIM, THAT IS, OF JUDGES, BEGINS

[Col. 0507]

[Col. 0507D] [T. I, B. I, Ch. I.] After the death of Joshua, the Israelites consulted the Lord, saying: “Who shall go up before us against the Canaanite and be our commander in war?” And the Lord said: “Judah shall go up. Behold, I have delivered the land into his hand.” And Judah said to Simeon his brother: “Come up with me into my allotted territory and fight against the Canaanite, so that I too may go with you into your allotted territory.” And Simeon went with him. Judah went up, and the Lord delivered the Canaanite and the Perizzite into their hands; and they struck down ten thousand men at Bezek.

[Col. 0508D] [C. I.] They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek and fought against him, striking down the Canaanite and the Perizzite. But Adoni-bezek fled; they pursued and captured him, cutting off the ends of his hands and feet. And Adoni-bezek said: “Seventy kings, with the ends of their hands and feet cut off, gathered the scraps of food beneath my table. As I did, so God has repaid me.” They brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died.

The sons of Judah attacked Jerusalem, captured it, struck it with the edge of the sword, and consigned the entire city to fire. Afterward, going down, they fought against the Canaanite who lived in the hill country, in the south, and in the lowlands.

Judah then went against the Canaanite who lived in Hebron, whose name in ancient times was Kiriath-arba, and struck down Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. From there he went against the inhabitants of Debir, whose ancient name was Kiriath-sepher, that is, “city of books.”

[Col. 0509B] [C. II.] And Caleb said: “Whoever strikes Kiriath-sepher and devastates it, to him I shall give my daughter Achsah as wife.” When Othniel, son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, had captured it, he gave him his daughter Achsah as wife. As she was traveling, [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads, “her husband instructed her.” See what we said about the meaning of this passage a little earlier, in the commentary on Joshua 15.] her husband instructed her to ask her father for a field.

As she sighed while sitting on the donkey, Caleb said to her: “What is the matter?” She replied: “Give me a blessing, for you have given me dry land; give me also land supplied with water.” So Caleb gave her the upper watercourse and the lower watercourse.

[Col. 0509C] [C. III.] The sons of the Kenite, Moses’ kinsman, went up from the city of palms with the sons of Judah into the wilderness of their allotted territory, which is south of Arad, and settled there with them.

Judah went with Simeon his brother, and together they struck down the Canaanite who lived in Zephath and destroyed him. The name of the city was called Hormah, that is, “anathema” or “devoted thing.”

Judah captured Gaza with its territory, Ashkelon, and Ekron with their borders. The Lord was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country; but he could not destroy the inhabitants of the valley, because they had an abundance of chariots fitted with iron blades.

They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said; and he destroyed from it the three sons of Anak.

[C. IV.] But the sons of Benjamin did not destroy the Jebusite, the inhabitant of Jerusalem. The Jebusite lived with the sons of Benjamin in Jerusalem to the present day.

The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the Lord was with them. While they were besieging the city, which had previously been called Luz, they saw a man coming out of the city and said to him: “Show us the entrance to the city, and we will show you mercy.”

When he had shown it to them, they struck the city with the edge of the sword; but they let that man and all his relatives go. After he had been released, he went into the land of the Hittites and built a city there.

[Col. 0509D] [C. V.] He called it Luz; that is what it is called to the present day.

Manasseh also did not destroy Beth-shean, Taanach with its villages, the inhabitants of Dor, Ibleam, or Megiddo with its villages; and the Canaanite began to live among them. But when Israel grew strong, they made them tributaries and did not destroy them.

Ephraim likewise did not kill the Canaanite who lived in Gezer; rather, the Canaanite lived with him.

Zebulun did not destroy the inhabitants of Kitron and Nahalol; instead, the Canaanite lived among them and became subject to tribute.

[C. VI.] Asher also did not destroy the inhabitants of Acco, Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphek, or Rehob. He lived among the Canaanite inhabitants of that land and did not destroy them.

Naphtali [the Vulgate adds “also”] did not destroy the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath. He lived among the Canaanite inhabitants of the land, and the Beth-shemites and Beth-anathites became tributaries to him.

The Amorite hemmed in the sons of Dan in the hill country and did not allow them to descend to the plains. He lived on Mount Heres—which is interpreted as “of brick”—in Aijalon and Shaalbim. The hand of the house of Joseph became heavy upon him, and he became tributary to them.

The boundary of the Amorite extended from the ascent of Akrabbim, from the rock, and upward.

[B. II, Ch. II.] The angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to the place of weeping and said: “I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land for which I swore to your fathers. I promised that I would never annul my covenant with you—provided only that you did not make a covenant with the inhabitants of this land and [the Vulgate: “but”] overthrow their altars. But you did not wish to listen to my voice. Why have you done this?

“Therefore I did not wish to destroy them from before you, so that you might have enemies and their gods might become your ruin.”

[Col. 0510C] [C. VII.] When the angel of the Lord had spoken these words to all the Israelites, they raised [the Vulgate adds “they themselves”] their voices and wept. The name of that place was called Bochim [the Vulgate adds “the place”], or “of tears”; and there they sacrificed offerings to the Lord.

[C. VIII.] Then Joshua dismissed the people, and the Israelites went, each to his own possession, to take possession of it. They served the Lord throughout all his days and throughout the days of the elders who lived long after him and knew all the works that the Lord had done for Israel.

[T. II, B. III.] Joshua, son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of one hundred and ten years. They buried him within the boundaries of his possession at Timnath-heres, in Mount Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.

All that generation was gathered to its ancestors. Another generation arose after them, one that did not know the Lord or the works that he had done for Israel.

The Israelites did evil in the sight of the Lord and served the Baals. They abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They followed foreign gods, the gods of the peoples who lived around them, worshiped them, and provoked the Lord to anger, abandoning him and serving [Note: According to the Hebrew, our manuscripts read “Baal,” although in the Palatine manuscript a later hand rewrote “Baalim.”] Baal and Ashtaroth.

[C. IX.] The Lord became angry with Israel and delivered them into the hands of plunderers, who deceived them and sold them to the enemies who lived all around. They could not withstand their adversaries; wherever they wished to go, the hand of the Lord was against them, as he had spoken and sworn to them, and they were greatly afflicted.

[B. IV.] The Lord raised up judges who would deliver them from the hands of their devastators; but they would not listen even to them, prostituting themselves with foreign gods and worshiping them. They quickly abandoned the way in which their fathers had walked, and, although they heard the Lord’s commandments, they did everything contrary to them.

Whenever the Lord raised up judges, he was moved to compassion during their days, heard the groans of the afflicted, and delivered them from the slaughter of the devastators.

[Col. 0511B] But after the judge had died, they returned [Note: Thus all the manuscripts read; the printed editions have something much worse. But the meaning is the same whether we read “greater” or “worse.” MART.] and did things much greater than their fathers had done, following foreign gods, serving them, and worshiping them. They did not abandon their practices or their stubborn way, in which they were accustomed to walk.

[C. X.] The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he said: “Because this nation has annulled my covenant, which I made with their fathers, and has refused to listen to my voice, I also will not destroy the nations that Joshua left when he died, in order that through them I may test Israel, whether or not they will keep the way of the Lord and walk in it, as their fathers kept it.”

[B. V.] So the Lord left all these nations and did not quickly overthrow them, nor did he deliver them into the hand of Joshua.

[Col. 0511C] [C. XI, Ch. III.] These are the nations that the Lord left, in order to train Israel through them, and all those who did not know the wars of Canaan, so that afterward their children might learn to fight against their enemies and acquire the practice of warfare: the five satraps of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon to the entrance of Hamath.

He left them in order to test Israel through them, whether they would listen to the commandments of the Lord that he had given their fathers through Moses, or not.

[B. VI, C. XII.] Thus the Israelites lived among the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite. They took their daughters as wives and gave their own daughters to their sons, and they served [Col. 0511D] their gods.

They did evil in the sight of the Lord and forgot their God, serving the Baals and the Ashtaroth.

The Lord became angry with Israel and delivered them into the hands of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia; and they served him for eight years.

[C. XIII.] They cried out to the Lord, and he raised up for them a savior and delivered them—namely, Othniel, son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother. The Spirit of the Lord was upon him, and he judged Israel.

He went out to battle, and the Lord delivered into his hand Cushan-rishathaim, king of Syria; and he subdued him. The land had rest for forty years, and Othniel, son of Kenaz, died.

[T. III, B. VII.] The Israelites again began to do evil in the sight of the Lord. He strengthened Eglon, king of Moab, against them, because they had done evil in his sight. He joined the Ammonites and Amalekites to himself, went forth, struck Israel, and took possession of the City of Palms.

The Israelites served Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years.

[C. XIV.] Afterward they cried out to the Lord, and he raised up for them a savior named [Note: Several more recent manuscripts, together with the Hebrew canon of truth, read not merely “Aod” but “Aod the illustrious, son of Gera.” It is certain, however, that “illustrious” is nothing other than an interpretation of the name Aod, which through scribal error passed from the margin into the sacred text. MART. — Manuscripts read Aoth or Haoth. One of our Palatine manuscripts adds “illustrious” in a second hand; this word is an interpretation of the name Aod itself.]

Aod, son of Gera, son of Jemini, who used both hands as though each were his right. The Israelites sent tribute through him to Eglon, king of Moab.

He made himself a double-edged sword, with a hilt in the middle, a handbreadth long, and strapped it beneath his cloak on his right thigh. He presented the tribute to Eglon, king of Moab. Eglon was exceedingly fat.

When he had presented the tribute, he dismissed his companions who had come with him. Returning from Gilgal, where the idols were, he said to the king: “I have a secret word for you, O king.” The king ordered silence, and after everyone around him had gone out, Aod entered to him. He was sitting alone in his summer chamber.

Aod said: “I have a word from God for you.” He immediately rose from his throne. Aod stretched out his left hand, took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly with such force that the hilt followed the iron into the wound and was gripped by the thickest fat.

He did not draw out the sword but left it in the body just as he had struck him. Immediately the fecal matter burst forth through the natural passage of the bowels.

Aod, having carefully closed the doors of the upper chamber and secured them with the bar, went out through the back entrance.

The king’s servants entered and saw that the doors of the upper chamber were locked. They said: “Perhaps he is relieving himself in the summer room.” They waited a long time, until they were ashamed, and, seeing that no one opened, they took the key. When they opened the doors, they found their lord lying dead on the ground.

While they were in confusion, Aod escaped and passed beyond the place of the idols from which he had returned. He came to Seirah, and immediately the trumpet sounded on Mount Ephraim. The Israelites went down with him, with him leading the way.

He said to them: “Follow me, for the Lord has delivered our enemies, the Moabites, into our hands.” They went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan by which one crosses into Moab. They allowed no one to cross, but at that time they struck down about ten thousand Moabites, all sturdy and valiant men. Not one of them could escape.

Moab was humbled on that day under the hand of Israel, and the land had rest for eighty years.

[B. VII, C. XV.] After him came Shamgar, son of Anath, who struck down six hundred Philistines with an ox-goad; he too delivered Israel.

[B. IX, Ch. IV.] The Israelites again began to do evil in the sight of the Lord after the death of Aod, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned at Hazor. He had a commander of his army named Sisera, while he himself lived at Harosheth of the nations.

The Israelites cried out to the Lord, for Jabin had nine hundred chariots fitted with blades and had harshly oppressed them for twenty years.

[C. XVI.] Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging the people at that time. She sat beneath the palm tree that was called by her name, between Ramah and Bethel, in Mount Ephraim. The Israelites went up to her for every judgment.

She sent for Barak, son of Abinoam, from Kedesh of Naphtali, and said to him: “The Lord God of Israel commands you: Go and lead an army to Mount Tabor. Take with you ten thousand fighting men from the sons of Naphtali and from the sons of Zebulun.

“I shall bring Sisera, commander of Jabin’s army, his chariots, and all his multitude to you at the stream of Kishon, and I shall deliver them into your hand.”

Barak said to her: “If you come with me, I will go; if you do not wish to come, I will not go.” She said to him: “I will certainly go with you, but on this occasion the victory will not be credited to you, because Sisera will be delivered into the hand of a woman.”

[C. XVII.] Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh. He summoned Zebulun and Naphtali, went up with ten thousand fighting men, and had Deborah accompanying him.

But Heber the Kenite had previously withdrawn from the rest of his Kenite brothers, the descendants of Hobab, Moses’ kinsman, and had pitched his tents as far as the valley called Zaanannim, which was near Kedesh.

[C. XVIII.] Sisera was told that Barak, son of Abinoam, had gone up to Mount Tabor. He gathered nine hundred chariots fitted with blades and the entire army from Harosheth of the nations to the stream of Kishon.

Deborah said to Barak: “Rise, for this is the day on which the Lord has delivered Sisera into your hand. Behold, the Lord himself is your leader.”

Barak went down from Mount Tabor, with ten thousand fighting men behind him. The Lord threw Sisera, all his chariots, and the entire multitude into panic before Barak’s sword, so that Sisera leapt down from his chariot and fled on foot. Barak pursued the fleeing chariots and army as far as Harosheth of the nations, and the entire multitude of the enemy fell to destruction.

Sisera, fleeing, reached the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. [B. XIX.] There was peace between Jabin, king of Hazor, and the house of Heber the Kenite.

Jael went out to meet Sisera and said to him: “Enter to me, my lord; enter, do not be afraid.” He entered her tent, and she covered him with a cloak. He said to her: “Please give me a little water, for I am very thirsty.” She opened a skin of milk, gave him drink, and covered him.

Sisera said to her: “Stand at the entrance of the tent, and when someone comes and asks you, saying, ‘Is anyone here?’ you shall answer, ‘No one.’”

Jael, wife of Heber, took a tent peg and likewise took a hammer. She entered secretly and silently, placed the peg against the side of his head, struck it with the hammer, and drove it through his brain to the ground. As sleep passed into death, he collapsed and died.

And behold, Barak, pursuing Sisera, was coming. Jael went out to meet him and said: “Come, and I will show you the man whom you seek.” When he entered her, he saw Sisera lying dead, with the peg driven through his temple.

On that day God humbled Jabin, king of Canaan, before the Israelites. They grew stronger each day and oppressed Jabin, king of Canaan, with a strong hand, until they destroyed him.

[C. XX, Ch. V.] Deborah and Barak, son of Abinoam, sang on that day, saying:

You who willingly offered your lives from Israel to danger,

bless the Lord.

Hear, kings; listen, princes:

I am, I am she who will sing to the Lord;

I will make melody to the Lord, the God of Israel.

Lord, when you went out from Seir

and passed through the regions of Edom,

the earth trembled, and the heavens and clouds dripped with water.

The mountains melted before the Lord,

and Sinai before the Lord, the God of Israel.

In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath,

in the days of Jael, the paths were at rest;

and those who entered upon them walked

along crooked byways.

The strong ceased in Israel and rested,

until Deborah arose,

until a mother arose in Israel.

The Lord chose new wars

and himself overthrew the gates of the enemies.

If shield and spear appear

among forty thousand in Israel.

My heart loves the leaders of Israel,

who willingly offered yourselves to danger;

bless the Lord.

You who ride upon shining asses

and sit in judgment,

you who walk along the road, speak.

[Col. 0514D] Where the chariots collided

and the army of the enemy was strangled,

there let the Lord’s righteous deeds

and his mercy toward the strong in Israel be recounted.

Then the people of the Lord went down to the gates

and obtained dominion.

Rise, rise, Deborah;

rise, rise, and speak the song.

Rise, Barak,

and take your captives,

son of Abinoam.

The survivors of the people were saved;

the Lord fought among the strong.

From Ephraim he destroyed them in Amalek,

and after him, from Benjamin, among your peoples, O Amalek.

[Col. 0515A] From Machir leaders came down,

and from Zebulun those who led the army into battle.

The leaders of Issachar were with Deborah,

and they followed in the footsteps of Barak,

who cast himself into danger

like one plunging into a sheer abyss.

When Reuben divided against himself,

a dispute among the great-hearted was found.

Why do you dwell between two boundaries,

so that you may hear the piping of flocks?

When Reuben divided against himself,

a dispute among the great-hearted was found.

Gilead rested beyond the Jordan,

and Dan occupied himself with ships.

Asher dwelt on the seashore

and remained in its harbors.

[Col. 0515B] But Zebulun and Naphtali offered their lives to death

in the region of Merom.

Kings came and fought;

the kings of Canaan fought

at Taanach beside the waters of Megiddo,

yet they took no spoil.

From heaven the battle was waged against them:

the stars, remaining in their order and their courses,

fought against Sisera.

The torrent Kishon dragged away their corpses,

the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon.

Trample down, O my soul, the mighty!

The horses’ hooves fell,

as they rushed in flight,

[Col. 0515C] and as the strongest of the enemy

plunged headlong.

“Curse Meroz,” said the angel of the Lord;

“curse its inhabitants,

because they did not come to the help of the Lord,

to the aid of his strongest warriors.”

Blessed among women be Jael,

the wife of Heber the Kenite;

blessed be she in her tent.

To the one asking for water

she gave milk,

and in a bowl fit for princes

she offered curds.

She put her left hand to the peg

and her right to the craftsmen’s hammers.

She struck Sisera,

seeking a place for the wound in his head,

and piercing his temple forcefully.

Between his feet he collapsed;

he failed and died.

[Col. 0515D] Before his feet he rolled,

and he lay lifeless and wretched.

Looking out through the window,

his mother wailed

and spoke from the upper chamber:

“Why is his chariot delayed in returning?

Why have the feet of his chariots been slow?”

One wife, wiser than his other wives,

answered these words to her mother-in-law:

“Perhaps he is now dividing the spoil,

and the most beautiful of the women

is being chosen for him.

Garments of various colors are being handed over

as spoil for Sisera,

and varied furnishings are being gathered

to adorn the necks.”

So may all your enemies perish, O Lord;

but may those who love you

shine like the sun at its rising.

[C. XXI.] The land had rest for forty years.

[T. IV, B. X, Ch. VI.] The Israelites did evil in the sight of the Lord, and he delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years; they were grievously oppressed by them.

They made for themselves caves and grottoes in the mountains and strongly fortified places from which to resist. Whenever Israel had sown, Midian, Amalek, and the other eastern peoples would come up, pitch their tents among them, as they were among the crops, and devastate everything as far as the entrance of Gaza. They left nothing whatsoever in Israel that was necessary for life—not sheep, not oxen, not donkeys.

For they and all their flocks came with their tents and filled everything like locusts: an innumerable multitude of people and camels. Whatever they touched, they devastated. Israel was greatly humbled before Midian.

[C. XXII.] He cried out to the Lord, seeking help against the Midianites. The Lord sent them a prophetic man, who said:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I caused you to go up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery. I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the enemies who afflicted you. I drove them out before you and gave you their land.

“I said: ‘I am the Lord your God. Do not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell.’ But you did not wish to listen to my voice.”

The angel of the Lord came and sat beneath the oak that was in Ophrah and belonged to Joash, the head of the family of Ezri.

While Gideon, his son, was threshing and cleaning grain in the winepress in order to escape from Midian, the angel of the Lord appeared to him and said: “The Lord is with you, strongest of men.”

Gideon said to him: “Please, my lord, if the Lord is with us, why have all these things overtaken us? Where are his wonders, which our fathers recounted and said, ‘The Lord brought us up from Egypt’? But now the Lord has abandoned us [the Vulgate adds “the Lord”] and delivered us into the hand of Midian.”

The Lord looked upon him and said: “Go in this strength of yours, and you will deliver Israel from the hand of Midian. Know that I have sent you.”

He replied: “Please, my lord, with what shall I deliver Israel? Behold, my clan is the least in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s house.”

The Lord said to him: “I will be with you, and you will strike Midian as one man.”

He said: “If I have found favor before you, give me a sign that you are the one who is speaking with me. Do not depart from here until I return to you, carrying a sacrifice and offering it to you.”

He replied: “I will await your arrival.”

Gideon entered, cooked a young goat, and made unleavened loaves from a measure of flour. Placing the meat in a basket and putting the meat broth in a pot, he brought everything beneath the oak and offered it to him.

The angel of the Lord said to him: “Take the meat and the unleavened loaves, place them upon that rock, and pour the broth over them.”

When he had done so, the angel of the Lord extended the tip of the staff that he held in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened loaves. Fire rose from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened loaves. The angel of the Lord vanished from his sight.

When Gideon saw that he was the angel of the Lord, he said: “Alas, my lord God! For I have seen the angel of the Lord face to face.”

The Lord said to him: “Peace be with you. Do not fear; you will not die.”

Gideon built an altar there to the Lord and called it “The Lord’s Peace,” to the present day.

While he was still in Ophrah, which belonged to the family of Ezri, the Lord said to him that night: “Take your father’s bull and another bull seven years old. Destroy the altar of Baal that belongs to your father, and cut down the sacred grove around the altar.

“You shall build an altar to the Lord your God on the summit of this rock, upon which you previously placed the sacrifice. Then take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering upon the pile of wood that you cut down from the grove.”

Gideon took ten of his servants and did as the Lord had commanded [the Vulgate adds “him”]. Fearing his father’s household and the men of that city, he did not wish to do it by day, but completed everything at night.

When the men of the town rose in the morning, they saw that the altar of Baal had been destroyed, the grove cut down, and the second bull placed upon the altar that had then been built.

They said to one another: “Who did this?” When they investigated the author of the deed, it was reported: “Gideon, son of Joash, did all this.”

They said to Joash: “Bring out your son, so that he may die, because he destroyed the altar of Baal and cut down the grove.”

He replied to them: “Are you Baal’s avengers, that you should fight for him? Let the one who is his adversary die before tomorrow’s light. If he is a god, let him avenge himself upon the one who demolished his altar.”

From that day he was called Gideon Jerubbaal, because Joash had said: “Let Baal avenge himself upon the one who demolished his altar.”

All Midian, Amalek, and the eastern peoples gathered together, crossed the Jordan, and encamped in the valley of Jezreel.

The Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon. He sounded the trumpet and summoned the house of Abiezer to follow him. He sent messengers throughout Manasseh, which also followed him, and other messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, who came out to meet him.

[C. XXIV.] Gideon said to God: “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, behold, I will place this fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone and dryness throughout the land, I shall know that by my hand, as you have said, you will deliver Israel.”

And it happened so. Rising at night, he wrung out the fleece and filled a bowl with its dew.

He said again to God: “Do not let your anger be kindled against me if I test you once more, seeking a sign in the fleece. I ask that the fleece alone be dry and that the whole land be wet with dew.”

God did so that night, as he had asked: there was dryness on the fleece alone, and dew throughout the whole land.

## [Chapter VII]

Thus Jerobaal, who was also Gideon, rose during the night, and all the people with him, and came to the spring called Harod. The camp of Midian was in the valley on the northern side of the high hill. And the Lord said to Gideon: “The people with you are too numerous, and Midian will not be delivered into their hands, lest Israel boast against me and say, ‘I was delivered by my own strength.’ Speak to the people, and proclaim in the hearing of all: ‘Whoever is fearful and timid, let him return.’” And twenty-two thousand men withdrew from Mount Gilead and returned from among the people, while only ten thousand remained.

### [C. XXV]

And the Lord said to Gideon: “The people are still too numerous. Lead them to the water, and there I shall test them. Whoever I tell you is to go with you, let him go; whoever I forbid to go, let him return.” When the people had gone down to the water, the Lord said to Gideon: “Separate those who lap the water with their tongue, as dogs are accustomed to lap, by themselves; but those who drink while bending their knees shall be on the other side.” The number of those who had lapped the water by bringing it to their mouths with their hands was three hundred men; all the rest of the multitude had drunk kneeling.

And the Lord said to Gideon: “By the three hundred men who lapped the water I shall deliver you and give Midian into your hand; but let all the rest of the multitude return to their own place.” So, taking provisions and trumpets according to the number, he ordered all the rest of the multitude to depart to their tents, while he gave himself to the contest with the three hundred men. The camp of Midian was below, in the valley.

That same night the Lord said to him: “Rise and descend into the camp, because I have delivered them into your hand. But if you are afraid to go alone, let Phurah your servant descend with you. When you hear what they are saying, then your hands will be strengthened, and you will descend more confidently against the enemy camp.”

So he and his servant Phurah descended to a part of the camp where the watches of the armed men were stationed. Midian, Amalek, and all the eastern peoples lay spread out in the valley like a multitude of locusts; their camels too were innumerable, like the sand lying on the seashore.

### [C. XXVI]

When Gideon arrived, someone was recounting a dream to his companion and reporting what he had seen in this manner: “I saw a dream, and it seemed to me that a barley loaf, as though baked under ashes, was rolling down, and it came upon the camp of Midian. When it reached the tent, it struck it, overturned it, and leveled it completely to the ground.”

The one to whom he was speaking replied: “This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon, son of Joash, an Israelite man. God has delivered Midian and all his camp into his hand.”

When Gideon heard the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. Then he returned to the camp of Israel and said: “Rise, for the Lord has delivered the camp of Midian into our hands.”

He divided the three hundred men into three companies and put trumpets into their hands, together with empty jars and torches inside the jars. And he said to them: “Do exactly what you see me do. I shall enter the part of the camp, and whatever I do, follow. When the trumpet in my hand sounds, you too shall blow your trumpets around the whole camp and cry out: ‘For the Lord and for Gideon!’”

Gideon and the three hundred men who were with him entered a part of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch of the night. When the guards had been awakened, they began to blow the trumpets and smash the jars against one another.

### [C. XXVII]

When they had sounded at three places around the camp and had broken the jars, they held torches in their left hands and sounding trumpets in their right, and they cried out: “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!” Each man stood in his place around the enemy camp. Then the entire camp was thrown into confusion, and they fled shouting and howling, while the three hundred men nevertheless continued blowing their trumpets.

### [C. XXVIII]

And the Lord sent the sword throughout the whole camp, and they cut one another down in mutual slaughter. They fled as far as Beth-shittah and the ridge of Abel-meholah, as far as Tabbath. The Israelite men of Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh assembled and pursued Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying: “Come down to meet Midian, and seize the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.” All Ephraim assembled and seized the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.

They captured two men of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the Rock of Oreb, and Zeeb at the Winepress of Zeeb.

### [C. XXIX]

They pursued Midian, carrying the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon [Note: In Hebrew there is [the expression], *meever Laijarden*, which the Septuagint translated as ἀπὸ πέραν τοῦ Ἰορδάνου, or, as in the Alexandrian manuscript, ἐκ τοῦ πέραν τοῦ Ἰορδάνου—that is, “from beyond the Jordan.” Canon has “opposite the course of the Jordan.” But Jerome instructed us that the preposition *de* should be supplied in his book *On Hebrew Places*: “Meeber,” he says, “for which Aquila translated ἀπὸ πέραν (“from beyond”), and Symmachus ἐξεναντίας (“opposite” or “from the opposite side”). Other manuscripts of the Bible read ‘across.’” MART. —Our manuscripts too read, “to Gideon, across the fords of the Jordan.” The expression “from opposite” adheres more closely to the Hebrew [term], and Jerome himself seems to have approved it after Aquila and Symmachus in his book *On Places*, under the entry *Meeber*, as Martianus also notes.] on the far side of the Jordan.

## [Chapter VIII]

The men of Ephraim said to him: “What is this that you have done to us, not calling us when you went to fight against Midian?” And they quarreled fiercely with him and nearly used violence.

### [C. XXX]

He answered them: “What could I have done comparable to what you have done? Is not the cluster of Ephraim better than the vintages of Abiezer? God has delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. What could I have done comparable to what you have done?” When he had said this, their spirit, which had been swelling against him, subsided.

When Gideon came to the Jordan, he crossed it with the three hundred men who were with him. They were extremely exhausted and could not pursue those who were fleeing. He said to the men of Succoth: “Please give loaves to the people who are with me, because they are very weary, so that we may pursue Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian.”

The princes of Succoth answered: “Are the palms of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that you ask us to give bread to your army?”

He said to them: “When, then, the Lord has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hands, I shall tear your flesh with the thorns and briars of the wilderness.”

From there he went up to Penuel and spoke similarly to the men of that place. They answered him as the men of Succoth had answered. So he said to them also: “When I return victorious in peace, I shall destroy this tower.”

Zebah and Zalmunna were resting with their entire army. Only fifteen thousand men remained from all the troops of the eastern peoples, while one hundred twenty thousand warriors who drew the sword had been killed.

Gideon went up by the road of those who dwelt in tents, east of Nobah and Jogbehah. He struck the enemy camp, which was secure and suspected no danger. Zebah and Zalmunna fled, but Gideon pursued and captured them, while their entire army was thrown into confusion.

Returning from the battle before sunrise, he captured a young man from the men of Succoth. He questioned him about the names of the princes and elders of Succoth, and the young man wrote down seventy-seven men. Then he came to Succoth and said to them: “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, ‘Perhaps the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna are in your hands, and for that reason you ask us to give bread to men who are exhausted and weary.’”

So he took the elders of the city, together with thorns of the wilderness and briars, and with them he crushed and mangled the men of Succoth. He also demolished the tower of Penuel and killed the inhabitants of the city.

### [C. XXXI]

And he said to Zebah and Zalmunna: “What were the men whom you killed at Tabor like?” They answered: “They were like you, and one of them looked like a king’s son.”

He said to them [Vulgate: “replied”]: “They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the Lord lives, if you had spared them, I would not kill you.”

And he said to Jether his firstborn: “Rise and kill them.” But he did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a boy.

Zebah and Zalmunna said: “Rise yourself and fall upon us, for a man’s strength corresponds to his age.”

Gideon rose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna. He took the ornaments and pendants with which the necks of royal camels are customarily adorned.

All the men of Israel said to Gideon: “Rule over us—you, your son, and your grandson—for you have delivered us from the hand [the Vulgate omits “hand”] of Midian.”

He answered them: “I shall not rule over you, nor shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule over you.”

And he said to them: “I ask one request of you: give me the earrings from your spoil.” For the Ishmaelites were accustomed to have golden earrings.

They answered: “We shall gladly give them.” They spread a cloak over the ground and threw into it the earrings from the spoil. The weight of the earrings requested was one thousand seven hundred gold shekels, apart from the ornaments, necklaces, and purple garments customarily worn by the kings of Midian, and apart from the golden collars of the camels.

Gideon made an ephod from these things and placed it in his city, Ophrah. All Israel prostituted themselves to it, and it became a ruin to Gideon and to his entire household.

Midian was humbled before the Israelites and could no longer lift its head. And the land rested for forty years, during which Gideon ruled.

### [B. XI]

Jerobaal, son of Joash, departed and lived in his own house. He had seventy sons, who came forth from his loins, because he had many wives. His concubine, whom he had in Shechem, bore him a son named Abimelech.

Gideon, son of Joash, died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash at Ophrah, in the family of Ezri.

### [T. V]

After Gideon died, the Israelites turned away and prostituted themselves with the Baals. They made a covenant with Baal and took him as their god. They did not remember the Lord their God, who had rescued them from the hands of all their enemies round about; nor did they show kindness to the household of Jerobaal, that is, Gideon, in return for all the good he had done for Israel.

## [C. XXXII, Chapter IX]

Abimelech, son of Jerobaal, went to Shechem, to his mother’s brothers, and spoke to them and to the entire clan of his maternal grandfather’s household, saying: “Speak to all the men of Shechem: Which is better for you—that seventy men, all sons of Jerobaal, rule over you, or that one man rule over you? Consider also that I am your bone and your flesh.”

His mother’s brothers spoke about him to all the men of Shechem, repeating all these words, and they inclined their hearts toward Abimelech, saying: “He is our brother.”

They gave him seventy pounds of silver from the temple of Baal-berith. With it he hired destitute and wandering men, and they followed him.

He came to his father’s house at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the seventy sons of Jerobaal, upon one stone. Only Jotham, the youngest son of Jerobaal, remained, for he had hidden himself.

All the men of Shechem and all the families of the city of Millo assembled. They went and made Abimelech king beside the oak that stood at Shechem.

### [C. XXXIII]

When this was reported to Jotham, he went and stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim. He raised his voice, cried out, and said: “Listen to me, men of Shechem, so that God may listen to you [the Vulgate omits ‘so that’].

“The trees went to anoint a king over themselves and said to the olive tree, ‘Rule over us.’ It answered: ‘Can I abandon my fatness, which both gods and human beings use, and go to be promoted among the trees?’

“The trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come and reign over us.’ It answered them: ‘Can I abandon my sweetness and my most excellent fruit, and go to be promoted among the other trees?’

“The trees spoke to the vine: ‘Come and rule over us.’ It answered [the Vulgate adds ‘them’]: ‘Can I abandon my wine, which gladdens God and human beings, and be promoted among the other trees?’ [Another reading: ‘be moved among them.’]

“All the trees said to the thornbush: ‘Come and rule over us.’ It answered them: ‘If you truly establish me as king over you, come and rest in my shade. But if you do not wish to do so, let fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’

### [C. XXXIV]

“Now therefore, if you have rightly and without sin made Abimelech king over you, and if you have dealt well with Jerobaal and his household, and repaid his kindnesses—he who fought for you and exposed his life to danger in order to rescue you from the hand of Midian—if, I say, you have now risen against my father’s household and killed his seventy sons upon one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his slave woman, king over the inhabitants of Shechem because he is your brother; if, therefore, you have acted rightly and without fault toward Jerobaal and his household, rejoice today in Abimelech, and let him rejoice in you.

“But if you have acted wickedly, let fire come out from him and consume the inhabitants of Shechem and the city of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem and the city of Millo and consume Abimelech.”

When he had said this, he fled and went to Beer, where he lived for fear of Abimelech his brother.

Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years. Then the Lord sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the inhabitants of Shechem. They began to hate him and to charge Abimelech their brother and the other leaders of Shechem, who had aided him, with the crime of murdering the seventy sons of Jerobaal and with the shedding of their blood.

They set ambushes against him on the summits of the mountains. While waiting for his arrival, they committed robberies and plundered passersby. This was reported to Abimelech.

Gaal son of Ebed came with his brothers and crossed into Shechem. At his arrival the inhabitants of Shechem were emboldened. They went out into the fields, ravaging the vineyards and treading the grapes. After forming choruses of singers, they entered the temple of their god, and amid food and drink they cursed Abimelech.

And Gaal son of Ebed said: “Who is Abimelech, and what is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerobaal? And has he not made Zebul his servant ruler over the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem? Why, then, should we serve him? Would that someone would place this people under my hand, so that I might remove Abimelech from their midst.”

It was reported to Abimelech: “Gather a large army and come.”

Zebul, the city’s ruler, was greatly angered when he heard the words of Gaal son of Ebed. He secretly sent messengers to Abimelech, saying: “Look, Gaal son of Ebed has come to Shechem with his brothers, and he is attacking the city against you. Therefore rise by night with the people who are with you, and lie in ambush in the fields. At daybreak, when the sun rises, fall upon the city. When he comes out against you with his people, do to him whatever you can.”

So Abimelech rose by night with his entire army and set an ambush near Shechem in four places.

Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the entrance of the city gate. Abimelech and all the army with him rose from the place of the ambush.

When Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul: “Look, a multitude is descending from the mountains.”

He answered him: “You are seeing the shadows of the mountains as though they were men’s heads, and you are being deceived by this error.”

Again Gaal said: “Look, people are descending from the center of the land, and one column is coming by the road that faces the oak.”

Zebul said to him: “Where is your mouth now, with which you said, ‘Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?’ Is this not the people whom you despised? Go out and fight against them.”

So Gaal went out, with the people of Shechem watching, and fought against Abimelech. Abimelech pursued him as he fled and drove him into the city. Many of Gaal’s men fell, as far as the city gate.

Abimelech settled at Rumah, while Zebul expelled Gaal and his companions from the city and did not allow them to remain there.

The next day the people went out into the field. When this was reported to Abimelech, he took his army, divided it into three companies, and set ambushes in the fields.

When he saw the people coming out of the city, he rose and fell upon them with his company, attacking and besieging the city. The other two companies scattered through the field and pursued their opponents.

Abimelech attacked the city throughout that entire day. He captured it, killed its inhabitants, and destroyed it, scattering salt over it.

When the inhabitants of the tower of Shechem heard this, they entered the temple of their god Berith, where they had made a covenant with him; from this the place had received its name. It was strongly fortified.

When Abimelech heard that the men of the tower of Shechem had gathered there together, he went up Mount Zalmon with all his people. He seized an ax, cut off a branch from a tree, placed it on his shoulder, and said to his companions: “What you have seen me do [the Vulgate: ‘what you see me do’], do quickly.”

So each of them cut branches from the trees and followed their leader. They surrounded the stronghold, set it on fire, and thus it happened that, through smoke and fire, one thousand people—men and women alike—among the inhabitants of the tower of Shechem were killed.

Abimelech then departed from there and came to the town of Thebez. He surrounded it and besieged it with his army.

There was a high tower in the middle of the city, to which men and women and all the leaders of the city had fled. Its door was shut most securely, and they stood on the roof of the tower behind the battlements.

Abimelech approached the tower and fought fiercely. As he came near the entrance, he was attempting to set it on fire.

### [C. XXXVI]

And behold, one woman threw a fragment of a millstone from above, struck Abimelech on the head, and crushed his skull.

He immediately called his armor-bearer and said to him: “Draw your sword and kill me, lest it be said that I was killed by a woman.” The man carried out his command and killed him.

When he had died, all the Israelites who were with him returned to their homes. Thus God repaid the evil that Abimelech had done against his father by killing his seventy brothers. The men of Shechem too received recompense for what they had done, and the curse of Jotham son of Jerobaal came upon them.

[Col. 0523D] [T. VI, C. XXXVI, Chapter X]

After Abimelech there arose as leader in Israel Tola son of Puah, the uncle of Abimelech, a man of Issachar, who lived in [Note: We read *Sanir*, not *Samir*, in the Canon and in other manuscript codices. The error may have been introduced by scribes who had read above, in Deuteronomy chapter III, col. 206, under the letter B, the name *Sanir*. Besides this, an error became established among Latin copyists, so that they write *m* for *n*, and *n* for *m*. Jerome has *Samir* in his book of Hebrew names. MART. —Our manuscripts too have *Sanir*; in Hebrew, however, the form is [Hebrew term], and in Greek Σαμὶρ, ‘Samir.’] Samir, in Mount Ephraim. He judged Israel for twenty-three years, then died and was buried at Samir.

### [B. XII, C. XXXVII]

Jair the Gileadite succeeded him. He judged Israel for twenty-two years. He had thirty sons who rode upon thirty young donkeys, and they were rulers of thirty towns, which from his name were called Havvoth-jair—that is, “the towns of Jair”—to the present day, in the land of Gilead.

Jair died and was buried at the place called Kamon.

The Israelites, adding new sins to their former ones, did evil in the sight of the Lord. They served idols, the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, the Ammonites, and the Philistines. They abandoned the Lord and did not worship him.

The Lord was angry with them and delivered them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites. They were afflicted and severely oppressed for eighteen years—all those who lived across the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead.

The Ammonites crossed the Jordan and devastated Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim, so that Israel was greatly afflicted.

They cried out to the Lord and said: “We have sinned against you, because we abandoned our God [the Vulgate adds ‘the Lord’] and served the Baals.”

The Lord said to them: “Did not the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, the Philistines, the Sidonians, Amalek, and Canaan oppress you? You cried out to me, and I rescued you from their hand. Yet you abandoned me and worshiped foreign gods.

### [C. XXXVIII]

“Therefore I shall not continue to rescue you. Go and invoke the gods whom you have chosen; let them rescue you in the time of your distress.”

The Israelites said to the Lord: “We have sinned. Do to us whatever seems good to you; only rescue us now.”

As they said this, they cast out from their territories all the idols of foreign gods and served the Lord [the Vulgate adds “God”]. And he grieved over their afflictions.

The Ammonites assembled with a great cry in Gilead and pitched their tents. The Israelites gathered against them and encamped at Mizpah.

The leaders of Gilead said among themselves to one another: “Whoever first begins to fight against the Ammonites shall be leader of the people of Gilead.”

## [B. XIII, C. XXXIX, Chapter XI]

At that time there was Jephthah the Gileadite, a very brave and warlike man, the son of a prostitute, born of Gilead.

Gilead had a wife, from whom he had sons. When they had grown up, they drove Jephthah out, saying: “You cannot be heir in our father’s house, because you were born of another mother.”

He fled from them and avoided them, and lived in the land of Tob. Destitute and predatory men gathered around him and followed him as their leader.

In those days the Ammonites were fighting against Israel. When they pressed them fiercely, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob to their aid. They said to him: “Come and be our leader, and fight against the Ammonites.”

He answered them: “Are you not the very people who hated me, expelled me from my father’s house, and now, driven by necessity, have come to me?”

The leaders of Gilead said to Jephthah: “For this very reason we have now come to you: come with us, fight against the Ammonites, and be leader over all who live in Gilead.”

Jephthah also said to them: “If you have truly come to me so that I may fight for you against the Ammonites, and if the Lord delivers them into my hands, shall I be your leader?”

They answered him: “The Lord, who hears these things, is himself mediator and witness that we shall fulfill our promises.”

So Jephthah went with the leaders of Gilead, and all the people made him their leader.

### [C. XL]

Jephthah spoke all his words before the Lord at Mizpah.

He sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites to say in his name: “What have you and I to do with each other, that you have come against me to devastate my land?”

He answered them: “Because Israel took my land when he came up from Egypt, from the borders of the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan. Therefore now return it to me peacefully.”

Jephthah again sent messengers and instructed them to say to the king of Ammon:

“This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites. When they came up from Egypt, they traveled through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.

“They sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, ‘Allow me to pass through your land.’ But he refused to heed his request.

“They also sent to the king of Moab, but he too refused to grant passage. So Israel remained at Kadesh, went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab, and came toward the eastern side of the land of Moab. He encamped beyond the Arnon and did not wish to enter the boundaries of Moab, for the Arnon is the border of the land of Moab.

“Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon, and said to him: ‘Allow me to pass through your land as far as the river.’ But he too despised Israel’s words and did not allow him to pass through his borders. Instead, gathering an immense multitude, he came out against him at Jahaz and resisted him fiercely.

“The Lord delivered him into the hands of Israel with his entire army. Israel struck him and took possession of all the land of the Amorite who inhabited that region, and all his borders, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.

“Thus the Lord, the God of Israel, overthrew the Amorite, while his people Israel fought against him. And now you wish to possess his land?

“Do you not rightfully possess what Chemosh your god has given you? Whatever the Lord our God has won as victor will become our possession. Unless, perhaps, you are better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab; or can prove that he quarreled with Israel and fought against him when Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, in Aroer and its villages, or in all the cities beside the Jordan for three hundred years.

“Why did you attempt nothing concerning this claim for so long?

“Therefore I am not sinning against you; rather, you are acting wickedly against me by declaring an unjust war. Let the Lord, the judge, decide this day between Israel and the Ammonites.”

The king of the Ammonites refused to heed the words that Jephthah had sent through the messengers.

Then the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh, through Mizpah of Gilead, and from there crossed over to the Ammonites. He made a vow to the Lord, saying:

### [C. XLI]

[Note: Jerome repeats this entire passage in Book I *Against Jovinian*: “Most of the Hebrews,” he says, “blame the author of the rash vow because he said: ‘If you deliver the Ammonites into my hands, whoever comes out of the door of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall belong to the Lord, and I shall offer him as a burnt offering.’ They ask: ‘If a dog or a donkey had come out to meet him, what would you have done?’ and so forth. Let the reader observe that Jerome’s version comes closer to the Hebrew words than the one read in the sacred text itself. MART. —The holy Father recites this passage more closely according to the Hebrew in Book I *Against Jovinian*, section 23, where, according to our recension, he has: “If you deliver the Ammonites into my hands, whoever comes out of the door of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall belong to the Lord, and I shall offer him as a burnt offering.”]

“If you deliver the Ammonites into my hands, whoever first comes out through the doors [another reading: “from the doors”] of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites, that person I shall offer as a burnt offering to the Lord.”

Jephthah crossed over against the Ammonites to fight them, and the Lord delivered them into his hands.

He struck them from Aroer until, as he came to Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel, which is planted with vineyards, with a very great slaughter. Thus the Ammonites were humbled before the Israelites.

When Jephthah returned to his house at Mizpah, his only daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dances. He had no other children.

When he saw her, he tore his garments and said: “Alas [the Vulgate adds ‘for me’], my daughter! You have deceived me, and you yourself have been deceived. I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot do anything else.”

She answered him: “My father, if you have opened your mouth to the Lord, do to me whatever you promised, since the Lord has granted you vengeance and victory over your enemies.”

And she said to her father: “Grant me only this, which I ask of you: let me go for two months and wander through the mountains, and mourn my virginity with my companions.”

He answered her: “Go.” And he dismissed her for two months.

She went with her companions and friends and mourned her virginity in the mountains. At the end of two months she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed. She had not known a man.

From that time a custom arose in Israel and was observed: after the year had come full circle, the daughters of Israel would assemble and mourn the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite for four days.

## [C. XLII, Chapter XII]

Now a sedition arose in Ephraim. They crossed toward the north and said to Jephthah: “Why did you go to fight against the Ammonites without calling us, so that we might go with you? Therefore we shall burn you and your house” [the Vulgate omits “you and”].

He answered them: “There was a fierce dispute between me and my people against the Ammonites. I called you to provide me with aid, but you refused. When I saw this, I placed my life in my own hands, crossed over against the Ammonites, and the Lord delivered them into my hands. What have I done to deserve your rising against me in battle?”

Then he called all the men of Gilead to himself and fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because Ephraim had said: “Gilead is a fugitive from Ephraim and lives in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh.”

The Gileadites seized the fords of the Jordan by which the Ephraimites would return.

When one of the Ephraimites who was fleeing came to them and said, “Please allow me to cross,” the Gileadites said to him: “Are you an Ephraimite?” When he said, “I am not,” they questioned him: “Then say [Note: Among the Hebrews the first form of this name is written with Shin, [Hebrew term], *Shibboleth*; the second has Samekh, [Hebrew term], *Sibboleth*. Our scholiast notes this, calling the Hebrew letter [Hebrew term] *Zamac*, unless the form *Zamach* arose through the pronunciation or ignorance of notaries and scribes in place of Samekh.

“There is considerable controversy among sacred critics about the sound of *Sibboleth* with Sin and the same word with Samekh. Some maintain that the letter Sin was pronounced like our *s* at the beginning of a word, while Samekh was pronounced like *s* between vowels, as though *Zibboleth* were pronounced with *z*. This agrees with the notes of the Canon of Hebrew Truth, as is especially clear from the reading of an old manuscript in our library, numbered 1. In that codex of the monastery of Corbie we read: “Say therefore, *Sebboleth*, which means ‘ear of grain.’” The man answered, “*Zebboleth*,” and so forth.

“This was also formerly found in the Colbertine manuscript of Anizy, no. 157, where an emendator changed *Zebbolet* into *Tebolet*, as the surviving traces of the letters clearly demonstrate.

“Others teach that the Hebrew letter was pronounced as a thick *s*, which the Ephraimites could not pronounce but replaced with a sharp *s*; that is, instead of *Schibboleth*, they said *Sibboleth*. This opinion may be supported by our codex of Saint-Germain, no. 3, since it writes *Sibboleth* in both places, as though there were no distinction between [the Hebrew letters] among Latins except in the sound of the speaker.

“Finally, Rabbi David Kimhi notes that the Ephraimites suffered from the same defect as the French, who cannot pronounce the letter Shin but pronounce it as though it were Thau with a raphatum. Anyone who consults the biblical manuscripts—Royal 3563, Colbertine 181, Corbie 10, Saint-Germain 5 and 7, and especially 164, in which Thau with a raphatum appears, namely *Thoboleth* instead of *Sibboleth* or *Zibboleth—will acknowledge that this is true. The others read *Tebboleth*, with *t* in place of the Hebrew Samekh.

“But concerning these letters and their pronunciation, Jerome himself must be heard. In his book of Hebrew names he did not leave the letter *s* untouched: ‘This too,’ he says, ‘must now be known concerning the letter *s*. Among them—the Hebrews—there are three letters *s*: one called Samekh, which is read simply, as though represented by our letter; another, Sin, in which a certain hiss unlike that of our language is heard; and a third, Sade, which our ears utterly dread. Hence it is clear that the Hebrew Samekh was pronounced simply as *s* or *z*, while Sin had a certain hiss foreign and unfamiliar to Latins.’ MART. —Our manuscripts unanimously prefer *Sebboleth*. Martianus discusses this word’s varied pronunciation and spelling at greater length.]

“Sibboleth”—*Sibboleth* with Sin, *Zibboleth* with Zamach—“which means ‘ear of grain.’” When he answered *Zibboleth*, being unable to express “ear of grain” with the same letter, they immediately seized and slaughtered him at the very crossing of the Jordan.

At that time forty-two thousand men of Ephraim fell.

Jephthah the Gileadite judged Israel for six years. Then he died and was buried in his city, Gilead.

### [B. XIV, C. XLIII]

After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. He had thirty sons and the same number of daughters. He sent the daughters outside and gave them in marriage, while he took wives for his sons of the same number, bringing them into his household. He judged Israel for seven years. Then he died and was buried at Bethlehem.

### [C. XLIV]

Elon the Zebulunite succeeded him. He judged Israel for ten years. Then he died and was buried in Zebulun.

### [C. XLV]

After him Abdon son of Hillel, the Pharathonite, judged Israel. He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode upon seventy young donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years. Then he died and was buried at Pharathon in the land of Ephraim, on Mount Amalek.

### [Chapter XIII]

Again the Israelites did evil [Col. 0528A] in the sight of the Lord, who delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.

[T. VII, B. XV, C. XLVI.] There was a certain man from Zorah, from the stock of Dan, named Manoah, whose wife was barren. The angel of the Lord appeared to her and said: “You are barren and childless, but you shall conceive and bear a son. Therefore beware that you drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, because you shall conceive and bear a son whose head no razor shall touch. For he shall be a Nazirite of God from infancy and from his mother’s womb, and he shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.”

When she came to her husband, she said to him: “A man of God came to me, with an angelic appearance, exceedingly awe-inspiring. When I asked him who he was, where he had come from, and by what name he was called, he would not tell me, but answered this: ‘Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. Beware that you drink no wine or strong drink and eat nothing unclean, for the child shall be a Nazirite of God from infancy and from his mother’s womb until the day of his death.’”

Manoah therefore prayed to the Lord and said: “I beg you, Lord, let the man of God whom you sent come again and teach us what we ought to do concerning the child who is to be born.” The Lord heard Manoah’s prayer, and the angel of God appeared again to his wife while she was sitting in the field. Manoah, her husband, was not with her. When she saw the angel, she hurried and ran to her husband. She announced to him: “Behold, the man who appeared to me earlier has appeared to me again.”

He rose and followed his wife. When he came to the man, he said to him: “Are you the one who spoke to the woman?” He answered: “I am.”

Manoah said to him: “When your word has been fulfilled, what do you wish the child to do? Or from what must he keep himself?” The angel of the Lord said to Manoah: “Let him abstain from everything I told your wife. Let him eat nothing that comes from the vine; let him drink neither wine nor strong drink; let him eat nothing unclean; and let him fulfill and observe what I have commanded him.”

Manoah said to the angel of the Lord: “I beg you to yield to my prayers, and let us prepare for you a young goat.” The angel answered him: “If you compel me, I shall not eat your bread; but if you wish to make a burnt offering, offer it to the Lord.” Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the Lord.

He said to him: “What is your name, so that, when your word has been fulfilled, we may honor you?” He answered him: “Why do you ask my name, which is wondrous?”

Manoah then took a young goat and grain offerings and placed them upon the rock, offering them to the Lord, who performs wonders. He and his wife were watching. When the flame of the altar rose toward heaven, the angel of the Lord ascended in the flame as well. When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell prostrate upon the ground, and the angel of the Lord appeared to them no more.

Immediately Manoah understood that he was the angel of the Lord, and he said to his wife: “We shall surely die, because we have seen God.” His wife answered him: “If the Lord wished to kill us, he would not have received a burnt offering and grain offerings from our hands; nor would he have shown us all these things or told us what is to come.” [The Vulgate omits *but*.]

[C. XLVII.] She therefore bore a son and called his name Samson. The child grew, and the Lord blessed him. The Spirit of the Lord began to be with him in the camp of Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.

### [Chapter XIV]

Samson then went down to Timnah. Seeing there a woman among the daughters of the Philistines, he went up and reported it to his father and mother [the Vulgate adds: *his mother*], saying: “I have seen a woman in Timnah, among the daughters of the Philistines. I ask you to obtain her for me as a wife.”

His father and mother said to him: “Is there no woman among the daughters of your brothers or among all your people [Note: Thus the Canon and many Latin manuscripts; the Syriac likewise retains the second-person pronoun, and so does the Arabic interpreter. The printed editions read, in accordance with the Hebrew, ‘among all my people.’ MART. —The Urbinas manuscript, together with the Vulgate editions, reads ‘my people’ instead of ‘your people’; this is more correct with respect to the Hebrew.] that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?”

[C. XLVIII.] Samson said to his father: “Get this woman for me, because she is pleasing in my eyes.” His parents did not know that this matter was from the Lord, and that he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.

Samson therefore went down with his father and mother to Timnah. When they came to the vineyards of the town, a fierce young lion appeared, roaring, and rushed toward him.

[C. XLIX.] The Spirit of the Lord came upon Samson, and he tore the lion apart as though he were tearing a young goat to pieces [the Vulgate reads: *tearing apart*], having absolutely nothing in his hand. But he did not tell his father or mother.

He went down and spoke with the woman who had pleased his eyes. After some days, when he returned to take her, he turned aside to look at the lion’s carcass, and behold, a swarm of bees was in the lion’s mouth, together with a honeycomb. He took it in his hands and ate as he went. When he came to his father and mother, he gave them some, and they also ate; yet he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the lion’s body.

His father went down to the woman, and Samson held a banquet there. For this was the custom of young men. When the inhabitants of the place saw him, they gave him thirty companions to be with him.

Samson said to them: “I shall propose a riddle to you. If you solve it for me within the seven days of the banquet, I shall give you thirty linen garments and the same number of tunics. But if you cannot solve it, you shall give me thirty linen garments and the same number of tunics.”

[C. L.] They answered him: “Propose your riddle, so that we may hear it.” He said to them:

“Out of the eater came food,
and out of the strong came sweetness.”

For three days they were unable to solve the riddle.

When the seventh day arrived, they said to Samson’s wife: “Coax your husband and persuade him to tell you [Note: In this and the following verse, the Hebrew Canon of Truth has the word *riddle* written in the text in Greek letters, as follows: ΠΡΟΒΛΗΜΑ (*problema*). We likewise find the same word written in Greek in the margin of our manuscript no. 3. It makes little difference, however, whether it is written in Greek or Latin letters, since nothing is changed in the noun. MART.] what the riddle means. If you refuse to do so, we shall burn you and your father’s house. Did you invite us to the wedding for this reason—to strip us?”

She wept before Samson and complained, saying: “You hate me and do not love me. That is why you will not explain to me the riddle you proposed to the sons of my people.”

He answered her: “I did not wish to tell it to my father or mother; should I tell it to you?”

For the seven days of the banquet she wept with him [the Vulgate reads: *before him*]. Finally, on the seventh day, when she pressed him, he explained it to her. She immediately told it to her townsmen.

On the seventh day, before sunset, they said to him: “What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?”

He said to them [Col. 0530C]: “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have discovered my riddle.”

The Spirit of the Lord came upon him. He went down to Ashkelon and struck thirty men there. He took their garments and gave them to those who had solved the riddle. Being exceedingly angry, he went up to his father’s house. His wife was given to one of his companions and wedding attendants.

### [Chapter XV]

After some time, when the days of the wheat harvest were approaching, Samson came, wishing to visit his wife, and brought her a young goat. When he wanted, as usual, to enter her room, her father prevented him, saying: “I thought you hated her, and so I gave her to your companion. But she has a sister who is younger and more beautiful than she; let her be your wife instead.”

Samson answered him: “From this day I shall be blameless with regard to the Philistines, for I shall do you harm.” [C. LI.]

He went away and caught three hundred foxes. He tied their tails together, fastening torches between them. After lighting the torches, he released them to run here and there. They immediately went into the fields of the Philistines. Once the fields had been burned, both the harvested grain that had been gathered and the standing grain were consumed, so that the flames also destroyed the vineyards and olive groves.

The Philistines said: “Who has done this?” They were told: “Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he took his wife and gave her to another; this is what he has done.”

The Philistines went up and burned both the woman and her father. Samson said to them: “Although you have done this, I shall nevertheless exact vengeance from you, and only then shall I cease.”

He struck them with a great blow, so that, stunned, they laid calf against thigh. Then he went down and lived in the cave of the rock of Etam.

The Philistines then went up into the land of Judah and encamped in a place which was later called Lehi, that is, “Jaw,” where their army was defeated.

The men of Judah said to them: “Why have you come up against us?” They answered: “We have come to bind Samson and repay him for what he did to us.”

Three thousand men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam and said to Samson: “Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why did you wish to do this?”

He answered them: “As they did to me, so I have done to them.”

They said: “We have come to bind you and hand you over to the Philistines.”

Samson answered them: “Swear and promise me that you will not kill me.”

They said: “We shall not kill you, but we shall bind you and hand you over.”

They bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock of Etam. When he came to the place of the Jaw and the Philistines met him shouting, the Spirit of the Lord came upon him. As flax is consumed and scattered by the smell of fire, so the ropes with which he was bound were broken apart and came loose.

[C. LII.] Finding a jawbone—that is, an ass’s jawbone—which was lying there, he seized it and killed a thousand men with it. He said:

“With the jawbone of an ass,
with the jaw of a young donkey,
I have wiped them out;
I have struck a thousand men.”

When he had completed these words in song, he threw the jawbone from his hand and called the name of that place Ramath-Lehi, which means “lifting of the jaw.”

Being very thirsty, he cried out to the Lord and said: “You have given this great salvation and victory into the hand of your servant; yet here I am dying of thirst and falling into the hands of the uncircumcised.”

Then the Lord opened the molar tooth in the ass’s jaw, and water came out of it. When he had drunk, his spirit was revived and he recovered his strength. Therefore that place was called, even to the present day, “the spring of the one who called upon the Jaw.”

He judged Israel in the days of the Philistines for twenty years.

### [Chapter XVI]

He also went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute and entered her. When the Philistines heard this and it became known among them that Samson had entered the city, they surrounded him, placing guards at the city gate. There they waited silently throughout the night, intending to kill him when he came out at daybreak.

[C. LIII.] Samson slept until midnight. Then he rose, seized both doors of the gate, together with their posts and bar, placed them upon his shoulders [the Vulgate adds: *his*], and carried them to the top of the mountain that faces Hebron.

[C. LIV.] After this he loved a woman who lived in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.

The rulers of the Philistines came to her and said: “Deceive him and learn from him the source of his great strength and how we can overcome him, bind him, and afflict him. If you do this, we shall each give you eleven hundred silver pieces.”

Delilah therefore said to Samson: “Tell me, I beg you, in what your great strength lies, and by what means you could be bound so that you could not break free.”

Samson answered her: “If I am bound with seven fresh bowstrings that are not yet dry but still moist, I shall become weak and be like other men.”

The Philistine rulers brought her seven bowstrings, as he had said. She bound him with them, while ambushes were hidden with her and they waited in the bedroom for the outcome. She cried out to him: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!”

He broke the bonds as easily as someone might break a thread twisted from flax [Note: The copyist of the Canon of Hebrew Truth, correcting his manuscript, writes *from flax, twisted from the warp*. The other manuscripts read, as do the printed editions, *twisted from husk*. MART. —The Urbinas manuscript not inappropriately reads, *from flax twisted with spittle*, that is, with saliva. “Husk” properly means the refuse of anything, and here may denote the chaff-like refuse of flax. The Palatine manuscript reads: *a thread of flax twisted from the husk of the warp*. This reading is not itself unacceptable in meaning. I am more surprised that, in so small a matter, the Latin interpretation departs so far from the Hebrew text and from the sequence of the proposed comparison. For the sacred text compares the ropes released by Samson in a single stroke to something that has absorbed the smell of fire. It therefore does not mean a thread twisted from husk, or from the husk of flax, but, plainly, as I understand it from the analogy of the noun itself, it means a tuft or wisp of flax. Thus the comparison is most apt: the flaxen wisp, which almost vanishes into smoke merely from the smell of fire, corresponds to Samson’s readiness in breaking the bonds.]

when it has received the smell of fire. His strength was not discovered.

Delilah said to him: “Behold, you have mocked me and spoken falsely. At least now tell me by what means you should be bound.”

He answered her: “If I am bound with new ropes that have never been used, I shall become weak and like other men.”

Delilah again bound him with them and cried: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” while ambushes had been prepared in the bedroom. He broke the ropes as though they were threads of a web.

Delilah said to him again: “How long will you deceive me and speak falsely? Show me by what means you should be bound.” [Note: The Vulgate adds: “Samson answered her.” In the Hebrew there is only: “And he said to her.”]

He said: “If you weave the seven locks of my head together with the warp and fasten them to the ground with a peg, I shall become weak.”

When Delilah had done this, she said to him: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He rose from sleep and pulled out the peg together with the locks and the warp.

Delilah said to him: “How can you say that you love me when your heart is not with me? Three times you have lied to me and refused to tell me in what your great strength lies.”

Since she distressed him and clung to him continually for many days, allowing him no time for rest, his spirit failed, and he was worn down to the point of death.
