Then, revealing the truth, he said to her: “No iron has ever come upon my head, because I have been a Nazirite—that is, consecrated to God—from my mother’s womb. If my head is shaved, my strength will depart from me; I shall become weak and be like other men.”

When she saw that he had revealed his whole mind to her, she sent to the rulers of the Philistines and said: “Come up once more, for now he has opened his heart to me.”

They came up, bringing the money they had promised.

She made him sleep upon her knees and recline with his head in her lap. Then she called a barber. After shaving the seven locks of his hair, she began to weaken him and drive him away from herself, for his strength immediately departed from him. She said: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!”

When he awoke from sleep, he said to himself: “I shall go out as I did before and shake myself free,” not knowing that the Lord had departed from him.

When the Philistines seized him, they immediately tore out his eyes. They brought him bound in chains to Gaza and shut him in prison, where they made him grind.

His hair had already begun to grow again.

The rulers of the Philistines assembled to offer magnificent sacrifices to their god Dagon and to feast, saying: “Our god has delivered our enemy Samson into our hands.”

The people also saw this and praised their god, saying the same thing: “Our god has delivered into our hands the adversary [the Vulgate adds: *our*], who destroyed our land and killed many.”

While they were rejoicing at their banquets and had already taken their meal, they ordered Samson to be summoned so that he might entertain them. Brought from prison, he played before them. They made him stand between two pillars.

He said to the boy who guided his steps: “Let me go, so that I may touch the pillars upon which the whole house rests, lean against them, and rest for a little while.”

The house was full of men and women. All the rulers of the Philistines were there, and on the roof and balcony there were about three thousand people of both sexes watching Samson as he played.

But he invoked the Lord and said: “Lord God, remember me and restore my former strength to me now, my God, so that I may avenge myself upon my enemies and receive one vengeance for the loss of my two eyes.”

Grasping the two pillars upon which the house rested, holding one with his right hand and the other with his left, he said: “Let my soul die with the Philistines.”

When he had shaken the pillars violently, the house fell upon all the rulers and the rest of the multitude who were there. He killed far more people when he died than he had killed during his life.

His brothers and all his relatives then went down, took his body, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. He judged Israel for twenty years.

### [T. VIII, B. VI, C. XVI, Chapter XVII]

At that time there was a man from the mountain country of Ephraim named Micah. He said to his mother: “The eleven hundred silver pieces that you set aside for yourself and over which, in my hearing, you swore—behold, I have them, and they are with me.”

She answered him: “Blessed be my son by the Lord.”

He returned the silver to his mother. She had said to him: “I solemnly consecrated and vowed this silver to the Lord, so that my son might receive it from my hand and make a carved image and a cast image. Now I give it to you.”

He returned it to his mother. She took two hundred silver pieces and gave them to a silversmith, so that he might make from them a carved image and a cast image. These were placed in Micah’s house.

He also set apart a small shrine for God there and made an ephod and teraphim—that is, a priestly garment and idols. He filled the hand of one of his sons, and the son became his priest.

In those days there was no king in Israel, but each person did what seemed right to him.

[B. XVIII.] There was also another young man from Bethlehem in Judah, from the same clan. [Note: Jonathan, son of Gershon, son of Moses. See below, chapter XVIII.] [Note: The Palatine manuscript, and likewise a little later, reads “Where do you come from?” instead of “where he had come from.”] He was a Levite and lived there.

Leaving the city of Bethlehem, he wished to live wherever he might find it convenient. When he came to the mountain country of Ephraim on his journey and turned aside for a short while to Micah’s house, Micah asked him where he had come from.

He answered: “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to live wherever I can and wherever I see that it will be useful to me.” [The Vulgate adds: “Micah said.”]

Micah said: “Stay with me and be a father and priest to me. I shall give you ten silver pieces each year, a double set of clothing, and whatever is necessary for food.”

He agreed and stayed with the man, and he became like one of his sons. Micah filled his hand, and the young man became his priest. “Now I know,” he said, “that God will do good to me, since I have a priest of Levitical descent.”

### [Chapter XVIII]

In those days there was no king in Israel, and the tribe of Dan was seeking an inheritance for itself in which to dwell. Until that day it had not received a portion among the other tribes. [Note: The Hebrew repeats “in those days”; the Vulgate editions additionally omit the words “to dwell in it.”]

[C. LVII.] The Danites therefore sent five very brave men from their stock and family, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to explore the land and inspect it carefully. They said to them: “Go and examine the land.”

As they were traveling, they came to the mountain country of Ephraim and entered Micah’s house, where they rested. Recognizing the voice of the young Levite and making use of his lodging, they said to him: “Who brought you here? What are you doing here? For what reason did you wish to come here?”

He answered them: “Micah has done this and that for me, and he hired me for wages to be his priest.”

They asked him to consult the Lord, so that they might know whether their journey would prosper and whether their undertaking would succeed. He answered them: “Go in peace. The Lord regards the way you are taking and the journey upon which you are going.”

The five men went on and came to Laish. They saw a people living there without fear, secure and quiet according to the custom of the Sidonians, with no one resisting them at all. The people possessed great wealth and were separated by a great distance from Sidon and from all other men.

They returned to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol. When their brothers asked what they had done, they answered: “Rise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen that the land is exceedingly rich and fertile. Do not neglect it; do not delay. Let us go and possess it. There will be no difficulty. We shall enter a spacious region inhabited by a secure people, and the Lord will give us a place in which there is no lack of anything produced by the earth.”

Six hundred men of the clan of Dan therefore set out, from Zorah and Eshtaol, equipped with weapons of war. They went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. From that time the place received the name “the Camp of Dan”; it lies behind Kiriath-jearim.

From there they crossed into the mountain country of Ephraim. When they came to Micah’s house, the five men who had previously been sent to inspect the land of Laish said to their other brothers: “You know that in these houses there are an ephod, teraphim, a carved image, and a cast image. Consider what you wish to do.”

When they had turned aside for a short distance, they entered the house of the young Levite who was in Micah’s house and greeted him with peaceful words. The six hundred armed men stood before the door.

Those who had entered the young man’s house attempted to take the carved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the cast image. The priest stood before the door, while the six hundred very brave men waited nearby.

Those who had entered took the carved image, the ephod, the idols, and the cast image. The priest said to them: “What are you doing?”

They answered him: “Be silent and put your finger over your mouth. Come with us, so that you may be a father and priest for us. What is better for you: to be a priest in the house of one man, or in one tribe and one family in Israel?”

When he heard this, he agreed to their words and took the ephod, the idols, and the carved image, and departed with them.

As they went on, having sent the children, livestock, and everything valuable ahead of them, and when they were already far from Micah’s house, the men who lived in Micah’s dwelling followed them, shouting. They began to cry out behind them.

When they looked back, they said to Micah: “What do you want? Why are you shouting?”

He answered: “You have taken my gods, which I made for myself, together with the priest and everything I possess, and you say to me, ‘What is the matter with you?’”

The Danites said to him: “Be careful not to speak to us any further, lest men become enraged and come against you, and you perish together with your entire household.”

Thus they continued the journey they had begun.

When Micah saw that they were stronger than he was, he returned to his house.

The six hundred men took the priest and the things mentioned above. They came to Laish, against the peaceful and secure people, and struck them with the edge of the sword. They set the city on fire, since no one came to its aid: they lived far from Sidon and had no association or dealings with any other people.

The city was situated in the region of Rehob. They rebuilt it and lived there, calling the city Dan, after the name of their father, whom Israel had begotten. Previously it had been called Laish.

[C. LVIII.] They set up the carved image for themselves. Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Moses, and his sons served as priests for the tribe of Dan until the day of its captivity. [Note: Among the Septuagint we read *Gerson* and *Gersom*; in the Latin manuscripts, *Gersan* and *Gersam*. The Canon of Hebrew Truth has *Gerson* in the marginal note of the preceding chapter and here in the sacred text. But, unless I am mistaken, this is plainly a copyist’s error, arising from the indiscriminate confusion of Gershon, son of Levi, with Gershom, son of Moses.

Moreover, this Gershom is consistently called the son of Manasseh in the Hebrew and Greek volumes, although all the Latin manuscript codices read that he was the son of Moses. Theodoret seems to reconcile the disagreement when he says: “Jonathan, son of Manasseh, son of Gersam, son of Moses.” The Greek scholiast preserved by Nobilius did not omit this, although he does not agree with Theodoret in every respect. He writes: “Jonathan, he says, son of Manasseh, son of Rechab, son of Moses.” Perhaps υἱοῦ Ῥηχὰβ (“of Rechab”) should be read, not υἱὸν (“son”).

The teachers of the Hebrews say that this young man was indeed the son of Gershom, son of Moses, but because he performed the works of Manasseh, he was also called his son, on account of his idolatry. For this reason the name Manasseh in the Hebrew volumes contains a suspended nun, written in this form [no Hebrew character is printed in the supplied text]. They suspended it in order to indicate that this Jonathan was Moses’ grandson and that the nun was suspended in honor of Moses—as though the text said that he performed works as though he were the son of Manasseh and not of Moses.

They elaborate on this at great length in their commentaries. Although many will find these arguments frivolous, we nevertheless clearly infer from them that Jerome’s reading is correct: in all the manuscript codices the name Moses is consistently found, and not Manasseh, as in the Septuagint.

Finally, the author of the *Hebrew Questions on the Books of Chronicles*, commonly attributed to Jerome, discussed this same Jonathan shortly before the end of the first book as follows: “The sons of Gershon, son of Moses: Sebuel, the first.” He says that this is the same man who is called Jonathan in the Book of Judges, who was a priest in the tribe of Dan, and so forth.

Sebuel, therefore, the firstborn of Gershon—or Gershom—the son of Moses, was believed by the ancients to be identical with this Jonathan. From this it is established that he must be counted among the descendants of Moses. MART. —Our manuscripts read *Gersan*; the Vulgate editions read *Gersam*. It is also well known that the Jews are blamed for having made this Gershom, son of Moses, the son of Manasseh by inserting a letter into the name in this fashion [no Hebrew character is printed in the supplied text], as though, not daring to place that little letter among the others, they nevertheless wished to free their lawgiver from the disgrace of a degenerate grandson. Martianaeus discusses the matter at length after the sacred interpreters. It is truly remarkable, since even the Septuagint call him the son of Manasseh according to the Hebrew exemplar, whereas Jerome, as is thought, more anciently and more correctly retained the name Moses.]

Micah’s idol remained among them throughout the entire period that the house of God was at Shiloh. In those days there was no king in Israel.

### [T. IX, B. XVIII, C. LIX, Chapter XIX]

There was a certain Levite living on the side of the mountain country of Ephraim. He took a wife from Bethlehem in Judah. She left him, returned to her father’s house in Bethlehem, and remained with him for four months.

Her husband followed her, wishing to reconcile himself with her, speak kindly to her, and bring her back with him. He had a young servant and two donkeys in his company. She received him and brought him into her father’s house.

When her father-in-law heard of this and saw him [the Vulgate reads: *and saw him*], he ran out happily to meet him and embraced the man.

The son-in-law remained in his father-in-law’s house for three days, eating and drinking familiarly with him. On the fourth day, rising during the night, he wanted to depart. His father-in-law detained him and said: “First taste a little bread and strengthen your stomach; then you may depart.”

They sat together and ate and drank. The girl’s father said to his son-in-law: “I ask you to remain here today, so that we may rejoice together.”

But he rose and began to want to depart. Nevertheless, his father-in-law earnestly detained him and made him remain with him.

When morning came, the Levite prepared for the journey. His father-in-law said to him again: “I beg you to take a little food and, after you have regained your strength, depart once the day has advanced.”

They ate together. The young man rose to continue with his wife and servant.

His father-in-law spoke to him again: “Consider that the day is declining toward sunset and evening is approaching. Remain with me today also, enjoy a day of gladness, and depart tomorrow to go to your home.”

The son-in-law would not agree to his words. He rose immediately [the Vulgate reads: *he proceeded*] and came opposite Jebus, which was also called Jerusalem [the Vulgate reads: *is called*]. He was taking with him two laden donkeys and his concubine.

When they were near Jebus and the day was turning into night, the servant said to his master: “Please, let us turn aside into the city of the Jebusites and remain there.”

His master answered him: “I shall not enter the town of a foreign people who are not among the Israelites. I shall pass on to Gibeah. When I get there, we shall remain there, or at least in the city of Ramah.”

They passed by Jebus and continued on their way. The sun set near Gibeah, which is in the tribe of Benjamin, and they turned aside there to remain.

When they entered, they sat in the city square, but no one wished to receive them as guests [the Vulgate reads: *wished*].

Then behold, an old man appeared, returning in the evening from his field and his work. He too was from the mountain country of Ephraim and was living as a resident alien in Gibeah. The men of that region were descendants of Jemini.

The old man raised his eyes and saw a man with his baggage sitting in the city square. He said to him: “Where do you come from, and where are you going?”

He answered: “We have set out from Bethlehem in Judah and are traveling toward our home, which is on the side of the mountain country of Ephraim. From there we had gone to Bethlehem, and now we are going to the house of God. No one wishes to receive us under his roof. We have straw and hay for fodder for the donkeys, and bread and wine for my needs, for the needs of your maidservant, and for the young man who is with me. We lack nothing except lodging.”

The old man answered him [Col. 0537D]: “Peace be with you. I shall provide everything necessary. Only, I beg you, do not remain in the square.”

He brought him into his house, provided fodder for the donkeys, and, after they had washed their feet, received them into the banquet.

While they were feasting and, after the labor of the journey, refreshing their bodies with food and drink, men of that city—sons of Belial, that is, “without a yoke”—came and surrounded the old man’s house. They began to pound on the door, shouting to the master of the house and saying: “Bring out the man who entered your house, so that we may abuse him.”

The old man went out to them [Col. 0538A] and said: “No, my brothers, do not commit this evil. Since the man has entered my hospitality, stop this madness. I have a virgin daughter, and this man has a concubine. I shall bring them out to you, so that you may humiliate them and satisfy your lust. Only, I beg you, do not commit this unnatural crime against the man.”

They would not agree to his words.

When the man saw this, he brought out his concubine and handed her over to them for them to abuse. After they had abused her throughout the night, they released her in the morning.

As the darkness receded, the woman came to the door of the house where her master was staying, and there she collapsed.

When morning came, the man rose and opened the door, intending to continue the journey he had begun. Behold, his concubine was lying before the door, with her hands spread across the threshold.

Thinking that she was resting, he spoke to her: “Rise, and let us go.”

When she gave no answer, he realized that she was dead. He took her, placed her upon the donkey, and returned to his house.

When he had entered, he seized a sword and, cutting the corpse of his wife together with her bones into twelve parts and pieces, sent them throughout all the territories of Israel.

When each person saw this, they cried out: “Never has such a thing happened in Israel, from the day our ancestors came up from Egypt until the present time. Give your judgment and decide together what ought to be done.”

## Chapter XX

And so all the children of Israel went out and assembled together as one man, from Dan to Beersheba and the land of Gilead, before the Lord at Mizpah. All the corners of the peoples and all the tribes of Israel gathered in the assembly of the people of God: four hundred thousand foot soldiers fit for battle.

[Note: For “four hundred thousand,” the Canon, with several manuscripts, has “forty thousand,” which must be attributed to scribal carelessness and incompetence. MART. — One Palatine manuscript and another manuscript in Martianay’s possession incorrectly have “forty” for “four hundred.”]

(The children of Benjamin were not unaware that the children of Israel had gone up to Mizpah.) When the Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, was asked how such a great crime had been committed, he replied:

“I came to Gibeah of Benjamin with my wife and turned aside there. And behold, the men of that city surrounded the house in which I was staying by night, intending to kill me; and while they were tormenting my wife with an incredible frenzy of lust, she finally died. I seized her, cut her into pieces, and sent the parts throughout all the territory of your possession, because never had such wickedness and so great a sacrilege been committed in Israel. You are all present, children of Israel; decide what you ought to do.”

Then all the people stood and answered as though with one man’s voice:

“We will not return to our tents, nor shall any man enter his house. Instead, we shall act together against Gibeah. Let ten men be chosen from every hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, and one hundred from every thousand, and one thousand from every ten thousand, to carry provisions for the army, so that we may fight against Gibeah of Benjamin and repay it for the crime it deserves.”

And all Israel gathered against the city, as one man, with one mind and one purpose. They sent messengers to the whole tribe of Benjamin to say:

“Why has such wickedness been found among you? Hand over the men of Gibeah who committed this outrage, so that they may die and the evil may be removed from Israel.”

But they refused to listen to the command of their brothers, the children of Israel. Instead, they gathered at Gibeah from all the cities that had fallen to their lot, to bring them aid and fight against the whole people of Israel.

Twenty-five thousand swordsmen were found among Benjamin, apart from the inhabitants of Gibeah, who numbered seven hundred very strong men. They fought with the left hand as well as with the right, and they could sling stones with such accuracy that they could strike even a hair, without the stone’s blow deviating to either side.

Among the men of Israel, apart from the children of Benjamin, four hundred thousand swordsmen were found, prepared for battle. They arose and went to the house of God—that is, to Shiloh—and consulted God [the Vulgate: the Lord], saying:

“Who among our army shall be commander in the battle against the children of Benjamin?”

And the Lord answered: “Let Judah be your leader.”

Then the children of Israel arose in the morning, encamped near Gibeah, and advanced from there to battle against Benjamin. They began to attack the city. The children of Benjamin came out from Gibeah and killed twenty-two thousand men of the children of Israel that day.

Again the children of Israel, trusting both in their courage and in their numbers, drew up their battle line in the same place where they had fought before. Yet first they went up and wept before the Lord until evening; they consulted him and said:

“Should I continue to fight against the children of Benjamin, my brothers, or not?”

He answered them: “Go up against him [the Vulgate: them], and enter into battle.”

When the children of Israel advanced against the children of Benjamin on the second day, the children of Benjamin burst out from the gates of Gibeah. They rushed upon them and slaughtered them so fiercely that they struck down eighteen thousand swordsmen.

Therefore all the children of Israel came to the house of God and sat weeping before the Lord. They fasted that day until evening, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings to him, and inquired concerning their situation. At that time the ark of the covenant of God [the Vulgate: of the Lord] was there, and Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, was in charge of the house.

Then they consulted the Lord and said:

“Shall we go out again to battle against the children of Benjamin, our brothers, or shall we cease?”

The Lord said to them: “Go up, for tomorrow I shall deliver them into your hands.”

The children of Israel set ambushes around the city of Gibeah. For the third time, as on the first and second occasions, they led out their army against Benjamin. But the children of Benjamin boldly burst out of the city and pursued the fleeing enemy farther. They wounded them as on the first and second days and struck their rear as they turned their backs along two roads, one of which led toward Bethel and the other toward Gibeah. They killed about thirty men, for they thought that the Israelites were retreating in their usual manner.

But the Israelites, pretending to flee as a stratagem, had resolved to draw them out of the city and lead them, as though in flight, toward the roads mentioned above. Therefore all the children of Israel arose from their positions and drew up their battle line at the place called Baal-tamar.

The ambushes around the city also gradually began to reveal themselves and advance from the western side of the city. In addition, another ten thousand men from all Israel challenged the inhabitants of the city to battle.

The battle grew fierce against the children of Benjamin, and they did not understand that destruction was pressing upon them from every side. The Lord struck them before the children of Israel, and on that day they killed twenty-five thousand one hundred men among them, all warriors and swordsmen.

When the children of Benjamin saw that they were defeated, they began to flee. The children of Israel, seeing this, gave them room to flee, so that they would reach the ambushes they had placed near the city.

When those lying hidden suddenly arose, and Benjamin turned his back while they were striking him, the Israelites entered the city and put it to the sword. The children of Israel had given a sign to those placed in ambush: after they had captured the city, they were to light a fire, so that the smoke rising high would show that the city had been taken.

When the children of Israel, who were engaged in the battle itself, saw this—for the children of Benjamin thought that they were fleeing and pursued them more fiercely, after killing thirty men from their army—and saw what seemed to be a column of smoke rising from the city, Benjamin also looked behind him. When he saw that the city had been captured and that the flame was rising toward heaven, those who had previously pretended to flee turned their faces and resisted more strongly.

When the children of Benjamin saw this, they turned to flight and began to go toward the wilderness, while their enemies pursued them there as well. Those who had burned the city also came out to meet them. Thus it happened that they were struck by enemies on both sides, and there was no respite for those who were dying.

They fell and were slain on the eastern side of the city of Gibeah. The men killed in that place numbered eighteen thousand, all extremely strong warriors.

When the survivors of Benjamin saw this, they fled into the wilderness and went toward the rock called Rimmon. During that flight, while scattered and heading in different directions, they killed five thousand men. When they continued farther, the Israelites pursued them and killed another two thousand.

Thus all the men of Benjamin who had fallen in different places numbered twenty-five thousand, warriors most ready for battle. Of the entire number of Benjamin, only six hundred men remained who were able to escape and flee into the wilderness. They sat at the rock of Rimmon for four months.

Then the children of Israel returned and struck with the sword all the remaining inhabitants of the city, from men to animals; and consuming fire devoured all the cities and villages of Benjamin.

## Chapter XXI

The children of Israel also swore at Mizpah, saying:

“None of us shall give his daughter in marriage to the children of Benjamin.”

Then they all came to the house of God at Shiloh and sat there before him until evening. They raised their voices and began to weep with a great wail, saying:

“Why, Lord God of Israel, has this evil happened among your people, so that today one tribe has been removed from us?”

On the following day, rising at dawn, they built an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings there. They said:

“Who did not go up with the army of the Lord from all the tribes of Israel?”

For they had bound themselves with a great oath at Mizpah to kill those who had been absent.

But Israel repented over his brother Benjamin, and they began to say:

“One tribe has been taken away from Israel. From where will they obtain wives? For we all swore together that we would not give them our daughters.”

Therefore they said:

“Who is there among all the tribes of Israel who did not go up to the Lord at Mizpah?”

And behold, it was discovered that the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead had not been present in that army. (At that time also, while they were at Shiloh, none of them was found there.)

So they sent ten thousand of the strongest men and commanded them:

“Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword, both their wives and their children. This is what you must observe: kill every male and every woman who has known a man.”

[Note: The printed editions retain here an addition of the Seventy Translators, namely, “but reserve the virgins.” These words are absent from the Hebrew text, from the Canon, and from the older Latin manuscripts. MART. —The addition found in the Vulgate books, “but reserve the virgins,” is also retained by Urbinas among our manuscripts, and by the Palatine manuscript in a second hand.]

They found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred virgins who had not known a man’s bed, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan.

They sent messengers to the children of Benjamin who were at the rock of Rimmon and ordered them to receive them in peace. At that time the children of Benjamin came, and wives were given to them from the daughters of Jabesh-gilead. But they did not find others whom they could give to them in the same manner.

All Israel grieved deeply and repented over the destruction of one tribe of Israel. The elders said:

“What shall we do for the rest, who have not received wives? All the women of Benjamin have perished, and we must provide with great concern and immense effort that one tribe not be destroyed from Israel.

“We cannot give them our daughters, bound as we are by the oath and the curse by which we said: ‘Cursed is the one who gives one of his daughters as a wife to Benjamin.’”

They took counsel and said:

“Behold, there is an annual feast of the Lord at Shiloh, which lies north of the city of Bethel, east of the road that runs from Bethel toward Shechem, and south of the town of Lebonah.”

They commanded the children of Benjamin, saying:

“Go and hide in the vineyards. When you see the daughters of Shiloh come out, according to custom, to lead the dances, suddenly come out from the vineyards and seize them [the Vulgate: “from among them”], each man one wife, and go into the land of Benjamin.

“When their fathers and brothers come and begin to complain against you and quarrel with you, we shall say to them: ‘Show them mercy. They did not seize them by the right of warriors and conquerors; rather, when they asked you to give them, you did not do so, and the fault lies with you.’”

The children of Benjamin did as they had been commanded. According to their number, they seized for themselves one wife apiece from among the women who were leading the dances. Then they departed to their possession, building cities and dwelling in them.

The children of Israel also returned by tribes and families to their tents.

In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what seemed right to him.

[Col. 0541] Here ends the Book of Judges.

[Col. 0541]

# The Book of Ruth

## Chapters of the Book of Ruth

[Note: We have transferred these chapters here from the Palatine manuscript and from the edition of the priest Joseph Maria Casi, who extracted them from three other manuscripts. Martianay placed none of them [Col. 0542D], because he had not found them in his copies.]

[Col. 0541C]

I. When famine occurred in the land of Judah, Elimelech of Bethlehem of Judah went with his wife Naomi and his two sons into the land of Moab for provisions. After he died, his sons also took wives and died.

II. When Naomi returned to her homeland, Ruth, her daughter-in-law, refused to leave her. After arriving in Bethlehem of Judah, she went to the field of Boaz to gather ears of grain.

III. Boaz grants Ruth permission to gather ears of grain from his field and, at mealtime, to eat with the harvesters, because he had heard that she had acted well toward her mother-in-law.

IV. When Naomi inquires, Ruth tells her what work she had done in the field of Boaz.

V. Instructed by her mother-in-law, Ruth again joins the maidservants of Boaz for work.

VI. When Ruth returns again to her mother-in-law, Naomi advises her how she ought to be joined to Boaz in marriage.

VII. Instructed by Naomi, Ruth places herself at night at the feet of Boaz, who refrains from intercourse with her.

VIII. In the presence of ten men at the gate of Bethlehem, Boaz consults the nearer relative concerning the marriage.

IX. The relative removes his sandal according to custom, gives it to Boaz, and relinquishes his right of kinship. Boaz takes Ruth as his wife, and a son is born to him, whom Naomi, his mother-in-law, undertakes to nurse.

X. The son is named Obed. He is the father of Jesse, the father of David. The genealogies from Perez to David then follow.

[Note: The Book of Ruth has no chapters written at its beginning, no division in the sacred text, and no numbered marks placed in the margin. In the Canon and in other older and better manuscripts, it is found written throughout as a single continuous text. We suppose this is because among the Hebrews the Book of Ruth is like an appendix to the Book of Judges. For, according to Jerome’s testimony, they bind both volumes together into the same book. See the beginning of Jerome’s *Prologue to the Scriptures*, which we have now restored in its proper place before the Books of Samuel and Kings. MART.]

## The Book of Ruth Begins

[Col. 0543]

### [C. I, Chapter I]

In the days of one of the judges, when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land. A man from Bethlehem of Judah went to dwell as a foreigner in the country of Moab, with his wife and his two sons. His name was Elimelech, his wife’s name Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem of Judah. They entered the region of Moab and remained there.

Elimelech, the husband of Naomi [Hebrew: Nahmi], died, and she remained with her sons.

[Note: Our scholiast here diverged from Jerome in the reading of the names Naomi and Orpah. For his assertion that the Hebrew has Nahmi for Naomi and that Harpa is read for Orpah is plainly at variance with Jerome’s usage. Since these names in the Hebrew Scripture have the letter Ain, which St Jerome therefore calls a vowel because he himself represented that element by a bare vowel, he writes Naomi and Orpah. In the Book of Hebrew Names, under Gomorrah, he says: “It should be known that the letter G does not occur in Hebrew, but is written by the vowel AIN.” Moreover, our annotations above, col. 88, have established from Jerome that the Hebrew language does not recognize the letter P. The scholiast, or the copyist of the Canon, therefore wrongly read Harpa for Orpah or Arpha. MART. — Martianay himself finally admits that the scholiast here departs far from Jerome’s manner and judgment in proposing Nahmi for Naomi and, shortly afterwards, Harpa for Orpah.]

They took Moabite wives, one of whom was named Orpah [Hebrew: Harpah] and the other Ruth. They remained there for ten years, and both sons died—Mahlon and Chilion—so that the woman was left bereft of her two sons and her husband.

She arose to return to her homeland with both daughters-in-law from the region of Moab, for she had heard that the Lord had looked favorably upon his people and had given them food. Therefore she went out from the place where she had lived as a foreigner, together with both daughters-in-law, and, already on the road returning to the land of Judah, she said to them:

“Go to your mother’s house. May the Lord show mercy to you, as you have done with the dead and with me. May he grant you to find rest in the houses of the husbands whom you are about to marry.”

And she kissed them. They raised their voices and began to weep, saying:

“We shall go with you to your people.”

She answered them:

“Return, my daughters [the Vulgate: my daughters], why are you coming with me? Do I still have sons in my womb, so that you could hope for husbands from me? Return, my daughters, and go away. I am already worn out by old age and not fit for marriage. Even if I could conceive this night and bear sons, if you were willing to wait for them until they grew up and reached the age of puberty, you would become old women before you married. Do not do this, my daughters, I beg you, for your distress weighs upon me more heavily, and the hand of the Lord has gone out against me.”

So they again raised their voices and began to weep. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law and returned; Ruth clung to her mother-in-law.

Naomi said to her:

“Behold, your sister-in-law has returned to her people and to her gods; go with her.”

She replied:

“Do not oppose me by asking me to leave you and go away. Wherever you go, I shall go; wherever you dwell, I too shall dwell. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Wherever the land receives you when you die, there I shall die, and there I shall receive a place of burial. May the Lord do this to me, and add this also, if anything but death separates me and you.”

When Naomi saw that Ruth had firmly resolved to go with her, she did not wish to oppose her or persuade her to return to her own people. So they went together and came to Bethlehem.

When they entered the city, the news quickly spread among everyone. The women said:

“This is that Naomi.”

She said to them:

“Do not call me Naomi”—that is, “pleasant”—“but call me Mara”—that is, “bitter”—“because the Almighty has filled me with great bitterness. I went out full, and the Lord has brought me back empty. Why, then, do you call me Naomi, when the Lord has humbled me and the Almighty has afflicted me?”

Thus Naomi came with Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, from the land where she had lived as a foreigner. She returned to Bethlehem when the barley harvest first began.

### Chapter II

Now there was a relative of Elimelech, a powerful man of great wealth, named Boaz.

Ruth [the Vulgate silently omits “Ruht”] the Moabite said to her mother-in-law:

“If you command me, I shall go to the field and gather the ears of grain that have escaped the hands of the reapers, wherever I find favor in the eyes of a kindly master.”

She answered:

“Go, my daughter.”

So she went and gathered ears of grain behind the reapers.

It happened that the owner of that field was Boaz [the Vulgate adds: by name], who was from the family of Elimelech. And behold, he was coming from Bethlehem and said to the reapers:

“The Lord be with you.”

### [C. III]

They answered him:

“May the Lord bless you.”

Boaz said to the young man who was in charge of the reapers:

“Whose girl is this?”

He answered:

“She is a Moabite woman who came with Naomi from the region of Moab. She asked permission to gather the ears of grain that remained, following the footsteps of the reapers. From morning until now she has remained in the field and has not returned home even for a moment.”

Boaz said to Ruth:

“Listen, daughter. Do not go to another field to gather, and do not leave this place. Join my maidservants, and follow wherever they reap. I have commanded my young men not to trouble you. If you become thirsty, go to the vessels and drink the water from which the young men also drink.”

She fell on her face, bowed to the ground, and said to him:

“Whence is this to me, that I should find [the Vulgate: “I have found”] favor in your eyes, so that you should recognize me, a foreign woman?”

He answered her:

“Everything that you have done for your mother-in-law after the death of your husband has been reported to me, as well as how you left your parents and the land in which you were born and came to a people whom you previously did not know. May the Lord repay you for your work, and may you receive a full reward from the Lord, the God of Israel, to whom you have come and under whose wings you have taken refuge.”

She said:

“I have found favor in your eyes, my lord, because you have comforted me and spoken to the heart of your maidservant, although I am not like one of your maidservants.”

Boaz said to her:

“When it is time to eat, come here, eat bread, and dip your morsel in vinegar.”

So she sat beside the reapers. He heaped roasted grain for her; she ate, was satisfied, and kept what remained. Then she arose to gather ears of grain according to custom.

Boaz commanded his young men:

“Even if she wishes to reap with you, do not hinder her. Deliberately pull some ears from your bundles and leave them behind, so that she may gather them without embarrassment, and do not rebuke her while she gathers.”

So she gathered in the field until evening. When she beat out and winnowed what she had gathered, she found about an ephah [Hebrew: epha] of barley, that is, three measures.

Carrying it, she returned to the city and showed it to her mother-in-law. She also brought out and gave her the remains of the food with which she had been satisfied.

### [C. IV]

Her mother-in-law said to her:

“Where did you gather today, and where did you work? Blessed is he who showed you mercy.”

She told her with whom she had worked and said that the man’s name was Boaz.

Naomi replied:

“Blessed is he by the Lord, because he has preserved for the living and the dead the same kindness that he had shown before.”

And again she said:

“The man is our relative.”

Ruth said:

“He also commanded me to remain with his reapers until they had finished harvesting all the crops.”

### [C. V]

Her mother-in-law said to her:

“It is better, my daughter, for you to go out with his maidservants to reap [the Vulgate: to grind], lest someone oppose you in another field.”

So she joined the maidservants of Boaz and continued reaping with them until the barley and wheat had been stored in the granaries.

### [C. VI, Chapter III]

After she returned to her mother-in-law, Naomi said to her:

“My daughter, I shall seek rest for you and arrange that it may go well with you. This Boaz, whose maidservants you joined in the field, is our relative. Tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor.

“Therefore wash, anoint yourself, put on your finer clothes, and go down to the threshing floor. Do not let the man see you until he has finished eating and drinking. When he goes to sleep, note the place where he lies. Then come, uncover the cloak with which he is covered at his feet, throw yourself down, and lie there. He himself will tell you what you should do.”

She replied:

“Whatever you command, I shall do.”

She went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had commanded.

### [C. VII]

When Boaz had eaten and drunk and had become cheerful, and had gone to lie down beside the heap of sheaves, she came secretly. She uncovered the cloak at his feet and lay down.

And behold, in the middle of the night the man was startled and troubled. He saw a woman lying at his feet and said to her:

“Who are you?”

She replied:

“I am Ruth, your maidservant. Spread your cloak over your servant, because you are a relative.”

He said:

“Blessed are you by the Lord, daughter. You have surpassed your former kindness with your later kindness, because you have not pursued young men, whether poor or rich. Therefore do not be afraid. Whatever you say to me, I shall do for you. For all the people who dwell within the gates of my city know that you are a woman of virtue.

“I do not deny that I am a relative, but there is another relative nearer than I. Stay here tonight. In the morning, if he wishes to retain you by the right of kinship, the matter is well settled. But if he is unwilling, I shall receive you without hesitation, as the Lord lives. Sleep until morning.”

So she slept at his feet until the night had passed. She arose before people could recognize one another, and Boaz said:

“Let no one know that you came here.”

Again he said:

“Spread the cloak with which you are covered and hold it with both hands.”

When she spread it and held it, he measured out six measures of barley and placed them upon her. Carrying them, she entered the city and came to her mother-in-law.

Naomi said to her:

“What happened, my daughter?”

She told her everything the man had done for her and said:

“Behold, he gave me six measures of barley and said: ‘I do not want you to return empty-handed to your mother-in-law.’”

Naomi said:

“Wait, my daughter, until we see how the matter turns out. For the man will not rest until he has completed what he said.”

### [C. VIII, Chapter IV]

So Boaz went up to the gate and sat there. When he saw the relative passing by, the one about whom the earlier conversation had taken place, he said to him:

“Turn aside for a little while and sit here,” calling him by his name.

He turned aside and sat down. Boaz then took ten men from the elders of the city and said to them:

“Sit here.”

When they had sat down, he said to the relative:

“Naomi, who has returned from the region of Moab, is selling the portion of the field belonging to our brother Elimelech. I wished you to hear this and to tell you about it in the presence of all those sitting here and the elders of my people. If you wish to possess it by right of kinship, buy it and possess it. But if it displeases you, tell me, so that I may know what I ought to do. For there is no relative except you, who are first, and me, who am second.”

He replied:

“I shall buy the field.”

Boaz said:

“On the day when you buy the field from the hand of the woman, you must also accept Ruth the Moabite, who was the wife of the deceased, in order to raise up the name of your relative in his inheritance.”

### [Col. 0547A] [C. IX]

He replied:

“I relinquish my right of kinship, for I must not destroy the posterity of my family. Use my privilege, which I willingly declare myself ready to surrender.”

Now this had formerly been the custom in Israel among relatives: whenever one person ceded his right to another, in order to make the concession firm, he removed his sandal and gave it to his relative. This was the testimony of cession in Israel.

Therefore Boaz said to the relative [the Vulgate adds: his]:

“Remove your sandal.”

He immediately removed it from his foot. Then he said to the elders and to all the people:

“You are witnesses today that I have acquired everything that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon, from the hand of Naomi, and that I have taken Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon’s wife, as my wife, in order to raise up the name of the deceased in his inheritance, so that his name may not be erased from his family, from his brothers, or from his people. You are witnesses of this, I say.”

All the people who were at the gate and the elders answered:

“We are witnesses. May the Lord make this woman who is entering your house like Rachel and Leah, who built up the house of Israel. May she be an example of virtue in Ephrathah and have a celebrated name in Bethlehem. May your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, from the offspring that the Lord will give you by this girl.”

So Boaz took Ruth and married her. He went in to her, and the Lord granted her conception, and she bore a son.

The women said to Naomi:

“Blessed is the Lord, who has not allowed a successor of your family to fail, so that his name may be called in Israel. May you have someone to comfort your soul and nourish your old age. For he has been born from your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is much better to you than if you had seven sons.”

Naomi took the child, placed him in her lap, and served as his nurse and caretaker.

The neighboring women congratulated her, saying:

“A son has been born to Naomi.”

They named him Obed. He is the father of Jesse, the father of David.

These are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron; Hezron fathered Ram; Ram fathered Amminadab; Amminadab fathered Nahshon; Nahshon fathered Salmon; Salmon fathered Boaz; Boaz fathered Obed; Obed fathered Jesse; and Jesse fathered David.

[Col. 0547] Here ends the Book of Ruth.

[Col. 0547]

# The Books of Samuel and Kings

## Preface of Jerome

[Note: This is the title of the prologue in the Canon of Hebrew Truth and in certain other older manuscripts. It appears to have been taken from Jerome, who at the end of the same short preface calls it the “Prologue to the Scriptures.” All the other books, both printed editions and manuscripts, title it either “Jerome’s Preface to the Book of Kings” or “Jerome’s Preface in the Book of Kings.” But since this prologue to the Scriptures can apply to all the books that Jerome translated from Hebrew into Latin, it is rightly entitled as concerning all the books of the Old Testament. MART. —This prologue, and, most importantly, the entire text of the books of Samuel and Kings, we have collated after the Urbinas and Palatine manuscripts previously praised, against the extremely ancient manuscript of the library at Verona, written in uncial letters. I would readily place it seven centuries earlier than the others; among all those so far known, it surpasses them by a very long distance in transmitting the genuine reading of Jerome’s translation. As for the fact that age has deprived us of its first page, we were unable to support the title given here by its authority. Nevertheless, we received it from the same codex, where it prefixes the title to the three places of the “Recapitulations,” as they are called, which we shall append below. Previously the title “Jerome’s Preface to the Books of Kings” was used, as in the Urbinas and Palatine codices. Martianay changed the title used for nearly all the books, on the basis of a single manuscript, to “Preface of Jerome the Priest concerning all the books of the Old Testament.” He adds as the reason that it can apply to all the books which Jerome translated from Hebrew into Latin. The holy Father himself says this below: “This prologue to the Scriptures, like a helmeted beginning, can apply to all the books which we have translated from Hebrew into Latin.” Yet this very preface is not thereby less particular to the Books of Kings, nor would it have received from its author any other title concerning these books. It is clear, after the testimony of the oldest exemplar, how well the title as restored by us agrees both with the character of the remaining text and with Jerome’s usage.]

### Into the Books of Samuel and Kings
[Col. 0547B] Among the Hebrews there are twenty-two letters, as is also attested by the language of the Syrians and Chaldeans, which is largely related to Hebrew: for they too have twenty-two characters with the same sounds, but different forms. The Samaritans likewise write the Pentateuch of Moses with the same number of letters, differing only in figures and strokes. And it is certain—

[Note: [Col. 0548C] This too is as certain to us as anything can be. Yet for the sake of those who strive to tear down the memory of so great an antiquity and attach less weight to the testimonies of the ancient Christians—Origen, Eusebius, and others—on this matter, let us set before them examples from the vernacular language itself, and let the ancient Jews themselves serve as witnesses.

The Babylonian Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin, section 2, folio 21, runs as follows in Latin: “At the beginning the Law was given to Israel in the Hebrew script and the holy language. Afterwards it was given to them, in the days of Ezra, in the Assyrian script and the Aramaic language (or Chaldean). But they chose for the Israelites the Assyrian script and the holy language, and left the Hebrew script and the Aramaic language to the ignorant.”

Take care not to understand Mar-Zutra as saying here that Ezra translated the Law into the Chaldean language. Rather, when the common Jewish people had almost learned Hebrew during the Babylonian captivity, while they were more familiar with the dialect of the Chaldeans, to which they had become accustomed, they copied out the exemplars of the Law in that language and script. Ezra abolished this practice with respect to the language, but permitted it with respect to the characters—or even approved by his authority that the Hebrew text be written in Chaldean letters. Conversely, he left the ignorant—namely, the Cuthaeans or Samaritans—with Chaldean and Aramaic versions, whether written in Hebrew letters or in Chaldean letters as well.

Learned men have thought that the Samaritan version of the Pentateuch belonged to this class, since it differs little from the Chaldean dialect. Again, in the same tractate, Sanhedrin, chapter 1, Rabbi Joshua records the following. Comparing Ezra with Moses, he says: “Although the Law was not given through the hand of Ezra, the script was changed through his hand.” He adds: “Why was the script, changed by Ezra, called Assyrian?” “Because it ascended with them from Assyria.” Similar statements are found elsewhere among the Jewish doctors, although they are sometimes interpolated with the dreams of that people.]

that Ezra the scribe and teacher of the Law, after the capture of Jerusalem [Col. 0549A] and the restoration of the Temple under Zerubbabel, discovered other letters, the ones we now use, although until that time the characters of the Samaritans and Hebrews had been identical. The same reckoning is also mystically displayed in the Book of Numbers (chapter III, verse 39), in the census of the Levites [Col. 0550A] and priests.

[Note: [Col. 0549A] Anyone who attends to the sequence of the discourse will plainly detect that this passage is dislocated. For what relevance does the mystical reckoning of the twenty-two letters in the Book of Numbers, in the census of the Levites and priests, have to the characters of the Samaritans? And what relevance to such a number does the fact that, in certain Greek volumes, the tetragrammaton—the name of God—was found expressed in the ancient Hebrew, that is, Samaritan, letters?

Therefore, so that everything may cohere in meaning, the whole of this passage—“And in certain Greek volumes we find the tetragrammaton of the Lord’s name expressed to this day in ancient letters”—seems to have to be read and restored immediately before the words above: “In the Book of Numbers also,” and so forth. Although this restoration is, in our judgment, necessary, we did not wish to impose it, because of the thirty-four manuscript codices which we carefully collated with the printed books, not one at this point differs from another; all consistently read the text in the transmitted, inverted sequence. Let this warning, then, suffice for the inquisitive reader. MART.

—Martianaeus thought that the passage which follows here, “And the tetragrammaton of the Lord’s name,” and so forth, through “we find,” suffered from an obvious dislocation and should be placed immediately before the preceding passage, “In the Book of Numbers also,” through “is displayed.” He then connects to it at once the next sentence: “But also the thirty-sixth Psalm,” and so forth. For, he says, what relevance does the mystical reckoning of the twenty-two letters in the Book of Numbers, in the census of the Levites and priests, have to the characters of the Samaritans? And what relevance to such a number does the fact that in certain Greek volumes the tetragrammaton, the name of God, was found expressed in the ancient letters of the Hebrews, that is, in Samaritan letters?

In the Hieronymian Questions, Clericus, otherwise a man more hostile to him, approves this restoration of the Benedictine editor both here and again later; he says that he praises it for no other reason than that truth, wherever it comes from, is always truth to him. Nevertheless, I am convinced that both men are mistaken and themselves misleading others. I believe that they were deceived by the preconceived opinion commonly held that, when the holy Doctor speaks of the ancient characters in which the name of God was written in Greek codices, he meant the Samaritan characters. They explain the matter in those very words, and it is clear from the sequence of the discourse that, if this passage is placed before the preceding one, the word “ancient” can denote no other than Samaritan letters.

But the holy Father had nothing of the kind in mind, nor can he be drawn into such a meaning. Accordingly, he cannot be thought to have placed the sentence in the contrary sense beside the sequence established by those editors; and there is therefore no dislocation of the text such as learned men imagine. We shall prove in the following annotation, by the clearest arguments, that when he wished to speak of the Chaldean letters, or those substituted by Ezra, rather than the Samaritan letters, he understood them by the term “ancient.”]

And the tetragrammaton of the Lord’s name in certain Greek volumes we find expressed to this day in ancient letters.

[Note: [Col. 0549D] Jerome may seem to introduce this statement abruptly, unless he did so deliberately in order to guard his reader against the error concerning Samaritan letters into which, as we have said, critics of great reputation have fallen. But so that you may know with certainty that by the “ancient letters” in which the tetragrammaton of God’s name was found written in Greek codices he meant the Chaldean letters which we now use, not the Samaritan, he himself elsewhere reveals their form—most clearly in Letter 25 to Marcella. After saying that the name is written in Hebrew letters as Jod, he, vau, he—that is, [Hebrew characters omitted in supplied text]—he adds that some, failing to understand this because of the similarity of the characters, habitually read it as ΠΙΠΙ when they find it in Greek books.

I do not think he could have more clearly called those letters Chaldean, since he said that, because of the similarity of the characters, they were read by the Greeks as ΠΙΠΙ. For unless those ancient letters were [Hebrew characters omitted in supplied text], whose resemblance to ΠΙΠΙ is so great that it immediately catches the reader’s eye, there were and are nowhere in the whole East any others that in any way reproduce the writing of that word. The Samaritan letters, however, differ from those forms to an extent scarcely expressible in words. In Samaritan, the ineffable name of God is represented by these characters: [Hebrew characters omitted in supplied text]. If anyone thinks these resemble ΠΙΠΙ, let those who defend the Samaritan letters decide.

Yet this reading ΠΙΠΙ had become customary among Greek readers—not merely among the common people, whom Jerome notes, but also among the most learned. A chapter or scholion still survives under the name of Evagrius, which we too published after Martianaeus in volume III, column 694, under the title εἰς τὸ ΠΙΠΙ, “On ΠΙΠΙ.” In the exposition itself the name is continually written in this way, yet it is said to consist of τούτοις τοῖς στοιχείοις, Ἰώθ, Ἥπ, Οὐαύ, Ἥπ—“these letters: Jod, he, vau, he”—whose original form the Greek ΠΙΠΙ represents.

Formerly they may have reproduced them even more exactly, as can be seen in ancient books that describe the Hebrew characters, including some in the Vatican collection which we ourselves have examined. The letter he is entirely closed above, like the Greek π; vau and jod, moreover, differ so little that they sometimes deceive even the eyes of experts.

It is therefore certain and evident that in this passage Jerome called the Chaldean letters “ancient”—the letters that, from the time of Ezra onward, had been written over the copied text—not the earlier Samaritan letters, which had almost fallen out of use. Hence he said simply “ancient,” not “ancient Hebrew.” It is equally clear that the point we established in the preceding note is correct: this passage suffers from no dislocation, and there is no transposition of words or meaning of the kind imagined by learned men who have failed to grasp the holy Father’s intention.

It is fitting to bring in here, to shed further light on what we have said, a passage of Origen which Montfaucon brought forth from Royal Codex 2818 and which Jerome himself seems to have had before his eyes. Adamantius speaks of this same tetragrammatmaton name, which, he says, “is pronounced Κύριος by the Greeks, and in the most accurate ancient Hebrew exemplars is written in ancient letters, but not in the letters now current. For they say that Ezra used other letters after the captivity.”

Here the Samaritan letters are certainly designated by the word ἀρχαίων, “ancient.” For no others can be called ancient in Hebrew codices. But, as I understand it, Origen, like Jerome, meant by that term nothing other than the original or archetypal letters. From this we derive a new argument for our position: just as no one denies that the ancient letters of the Hebrew codex are Samaritan, so, when the subject is a Greek copy translated from a Chaldean exemplar, it is evident from this testimony that “ancient,” meaning the original letters of its archetype, indicates none other than the Chaldean letters.]

But also the thirty-sixth Psalm, and the hundred and tenth, and the hundred and eleventh, [Col. 0551A] and the hundred and eighteenth,

[Note: [Col. 0551C] Its groups of eight verses begin with individual letters of the alphabet; hence the Psalm itself is called the Great Alphabet. It should further be noted concerning the following one hundred and forty-fourth Psalm that the verse which begins with nun is no longer found in the Hebrew exemplar. It seems indeed to have dropped out before Jerome’s own time, since manuscripts of better quality omit it also in his translation from the Hebrew, and the Greek interpreters—Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and others—are silent, as the ancient scholiast also reports. See, however, what we observe below on that passage in Jerome’s translation.]

and the hundred and forty-fourth, although they are written in different meters, are nevertheless composed according to the same alphabet. So too the Lamentations of Jeremiah and his Prayer; and at the end of Solomon’s Proverbs, from the passage where he says, “Who can find a strong woman?” (chapter last, verse 10, to the end), the sections are likewise counted according to the same alphabets.

[Note: [Col. 0550D] In his letter beginning “The day before yesterday,” Saint Jerome mentions only four Psalms composed according to the order of the letters of the Hebrew alphabet; there he does not mention the thirty-sixth Psalm or the Prayer of Jeremiah. “Before I discuss each one,” he says to Paula of Urbica, “you should know that four psalms begin according to the order of the Hebrew letters: the hundred and tenth, the hundred and eleventh, this one on which we are now writing, and the hundred and forty-fourth.” Shortly afterward he adds: “Some think that others also begin in this order, but their opinion is false.”

These statements can easily be reconciled if one says that in his Letter to Paula of Urbica Jerome was referring to the beginnings of the verses, which in Psalms 110, 111, 118, and 144 proceed according to the order of the Hebrew letters; whereas here, in the prologue to Scripture, he is discussing the number of the twenty-two characters, in order to prove from it that twenty-two volumes are counted in the Hebrew canon. Anyone wishing to learn more about this kind of Psalm may consult our prolegomena. MART.

—He could have begun with the thirty-third Psalm, whose individual verses, like those of the hundred and tenth and hundred and eleventh which he cites, begin with the individual letters of the alphabet in sequence, except for vau, which is either absent or included with he in verse 6. In fact, however, the holy Father appeared to exclude not only that Psalm but also the thirty-sixth, which he cites here, from this series in Letter 30 to Paul. There he declares that only four Psalms begin according to the order of the Hebrew letters: the hundred and tenth, the hundred and eleventh, the hundred and eighteenth, and the hundred and forty-fourth; conversely, he calls the opinion of those who think that others begin in this order false. In the thirty-sixth Psalm, two verses begin with each letter of the alphabet.]

There are five doubled letters among the Hebrews: CAPH, MEM, NUN, PHE, and SADE. They write the beginnings and middle portions of words with these letters in one form, and the endings in another. Hence many also reckon five books as doubled: Samuel, Malachim, Dabre-Jamim, Ezra, and Jeremiah together with Cinoth, that is, his Lamentations.

How, then, there are twenty-two characters with which we write in Hebrew everything we speak, and in whose beginnings the human voice is contained, so there are counted twenty-two volumes by which, as though by letters and beginnings, the tender and still suckling infancy of the just man is instructed in the teaching of God.

The first book among them is called BRESITH ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), which we call Genesis. The second, ELLE SMOTH ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), is called Exodus. The third is VAJECRA ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), that is, Leviticus. The fourth is VAJEDABBER ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), which we call Numbers.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] Very many manuscripts read the singular, “which we call Numerus,” but this is plainly a scribal error, as is clear from Jerome, who said above of the same volume, “In the Book of Numbers also,” and so forth. When Origen, in his commentary on the first Psalm, lists the canonical Scriptures according to the Hebrews, he does not say that they call Numbers Vajedabber, but ἀμμεσφεκωδεὶμ, Ammesphecodim. Written in Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text], hammephecudim, without any s in the middle of the word, this means “numbers,” or rather “those numbered.” Accordingly, among the Hebrews the Book of Numbers is called Vajedabber from the first word of the volume; Hammephecudim, however, refers to its subject, because it concerns those who were counted. MART.

—The Greeks have Οὐαλεσμώθ or Οὐελλεσμώθ, and Οὐικρά for Vajecra. They call the Book of Numbers not from its opening words but from its subject, Ἀμμεσφεκωωδεὶμ, as Origen and Eusebius have it, or Ἀμεσφεκκπδὶμ, as Nicephorus does. In Hebrew it should correctly be written without the intervening letter [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text], meaning “those numbered.”]

The fifth is ELLEADDABARIM ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), which is entitled Deuteronomy. These are the five books of Moses, which they properly call THORATH ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), that is, “the Law.”

[Note: [Col. 0552B] All thirty-four manuscript codices which we used to collate this prologue read Thorath, as though the name were in the construct state, as when one says Thorath Mose, “the law of Moses.” It should be noted, however, that the corrector of the Canon of Saint-Germain-des-Prés indicated, by dots placed above and below, that the initial aspiration h and the final th should be removed, and that Tora, not Thorath, should be read according to the Hebrews. He also indicated this in his customary fashion by placing the sign h in the margin. MART.

—This is the reading of all the manuscripts whose thirty-four copies Martianaeus numbers; we cite the most ancient Veronese manuscript in place of all the others. In the construct state it is indeed written [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text], but not in the absolute state, as Jerome here seems to take it. There are, however, other names of this sort which he seems to have represented according to common usage rather than the rules of orthography: for example, shortly afterward Malachot for Malachoth, and Masaloth for Maschalim, forms retained both by him and by interpreters older than he.]

They arrange the books according to the order of the Prophets, beginning with Jesus son of Nun, [Note: [Col. 0552C] We said in our observations on the title of Genesis that, according to Jerome, the Hebrews customarily gave their sacred volumes names from their beginnings—for example, Bresith, meaning “in the beginning,” and Elle smoth, meaning “these are the names,” which are the opening words of Genesis and Exodus. From Jerome himself it now appears that this is to be understood only of the five volumes of the Mosaic Law. For the remaining books, both prophetic and hagiographical, do not receive their names from their beginnings, but from their authors, or at least from the subjects or persons about which much is written in them.

We nevertheless remind the curious reader that the First and Second Books of Kings, which according to Jerome were called Malachim by the Hebrews, meaning “Kings,” are called by Origen from their opening words Vammelech David, “And David the king.” It is therefore sufficiently established that the sacred books of the Hebrews had different names from different sources and possessed various designations. MART.] who among them is called JOSUE BEN NUN ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]). Then they append SOPHTIM ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), that is, the Book of Judges; and they join RUTH ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]) to it, because the history it recounts took place in the days of the Judges.

The third is SAMUEL ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), which we call the First and Second Books of Kings. The fourth is MALACHIM ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), that is, Kings, contained in the Third and Fourth Books of Kings.

[Note: [Col. 0553B] The Greeks prefer to title this book from its opening words, Οὐαμμέλεχ Δαβίδ, “And David was king.” Origen calls it so, as does Josephus, the ancient Christian author, in the Hypomnesticon, and finally Nicephorus, although somewhat corruptly. The Hebrew has [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]. Martianaeus incorrectly began a new chapter of the Prologue at this point.]

It is much better to say MALACHIM, that is, “of Kings,” than MALACHOTH ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), “of kingdoms.”

[Note: [Col. 0553B] This name should be written with a doubled mem at the beginning, namely [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text], mamlachoth, which means “kingdoms.” [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text], malachoth, with a single mem, means not “kingdoms” properly speaking, but “queens.” Nevertheless, so as not to introduce anything foreign, we thought it appropriate to place in the margin the Hebrew words of Jerome with exactly as many characters as he wished to express in the text. MART.

—We said above that Mamlachoth should more correctly have been written. The Veronese manuscript reads Malochoth. A little farther below it has Hiezecihel for Jezeciel, just as above it has Samuhel for Samuel, and similar aspirated forms.]

For it does not describe the kingdoms of many nations, but that of the one Israelite people, which consists of twelve tribes. The fifth is ISAIAS ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]). The sixth is JEREMIAS ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]). The seventh is JEZECIEL ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]). The eighth is the Book of the Twelve Prophets, which among them is called THARE ASRA ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]).

[Note: [Col. 0553C] The Canon of Hebrew Truth of Saint-Germain-des-Prés has here, in a second hand, TRE AZRA. The copyist could have borrowed this from other books while correcting his exemplar, as is confirmed for us by a Bible codex of Saint-Germain written eight hundred years ago, in whose margin this variant reading is found: Thare arsa; others have tre azra. Nevertheless, in the text itself he reads Thare, asra. MART.]

The third order contains the Ἁγιόγραφα, the Hagiographa; and the first book begins with JOB ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]). The second begins with DAVID ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), whom they comprise in five divisions and one volume of Psalms.

The third is SALAMON ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), containing three books: Proverbs, which they call Parables, that is, MASALOTH ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]); Ecclesiastes, that is, COELETH ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]); and the Song of Songs, which they title SIR ASSIRIM ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]).

[Note: [Col. 0553C] Both Hebrew Canons of Truth, namely that of Carcassonne and our own of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, have this form. All the other manuscript codices read Masloth; but manuscript no. 3, cited so often already, has Massaloth in the margin, with a doubled s, while in the body it has Maslot in Greek letters. MART.

—The Veronese book has Massaloth, with a doubled s. Eusebius calls it Μισλώθ, Nicephorus Μεσλῶθ.]

[Note: [Col. 0553D] Three of the most ancient manuscripts of our Corbie monastery have ACCOELETH written as though Jerome had read the Hebrew with an initial a, which grammarians call emphatic, doubling the following letter. The Canon of Saint-Germain likewise read ACCOELETH; but the corrector’s hand removed the first syllable ac, and only Coheleth remains today. Among the Hebrews it is consistently read Coheleth, without any initial he; Origen too read Coeleth in his commentary on Psalm 1. MART.

—The same Veronese manuscript has Accoheleth, as Martianaeus also found in the three Corbie manuscripts. This may perhaps be the more accurate form, since the Hebrews of old may have pronounced it with the emphatic [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text].]

The sixth is DANIEL ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]). The seventh is DABRE AJAMIM ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]), that is, “words of days,” which we may more significantly call the Χρονικὸν, “Chronicle,” of the entire divine history. Among us this book is entitled First and Second Chronicles, or Παραλειπομένων, “of the things omitted.”

[Note: [Col. 0554B] It was not DABRE AJAMIN but debre ajomin that was formerly read in Corbie manuscript no. 1. Nearly the same reading also appears in the margin of our manuscript no. 3, where we find dibre ajomin. From this the present dibre ajamim in the Canon of Saint-Germain seems to have arisen; before correction it read dabre jamim. The Carcassonne exemplar of the Canon of Hebrew Truth reads dabre jamin, as do thirty other manuscript books. In Origen we read διβρὴ ἀϊαμὶμ, that is, dibre ajamim, as now in our Canon.

The Hebrew words in the sacred volumes are [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]. According to Jerome in his letter to Evagrius concerning Melchizedek, it makes no difference whether one pronounces the word dabre, dibre, or debre ajamim, since the ancient Hebrews very rarely used vowels among the consonants and, according to the discretion of readers and the variety of regions, pronounced the same words with different sounds and accents. MART.

—Again the Veronese manuscript has Dabrejamin without the intervening letter which they call the construct marker. Nicephorus seems to have approved this reading, for he has δαβρὶ ἰαμίν. The other Greek writers, Origen, Eusebius, and the rest, correctly have διβρὴ ἀϊαμίμ.]

The eighth is EZRAS ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]) [alternative: Elesdras], which likewise among the Greeks and Latins is divided into two books. The ninth is ESTHER ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]).

And thus the books of the Old Law likewise number twenty-two: five belonging to Moses, eight to the Prophets, and nine to the Hagiographa. Yet some include RUTH ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]) and CINOTH ([Hebrew term omitted in supplied text]) among the Hagiographa, and count these books within their number; consequently they make the books of the ancient Law twenty-four.

[Note: [Col. 0554C] Martianaeus cites Victorinus on the Apocalypse. Tertullian, however, in Book IV against Marcion is to be preferred, though I am reluctant to reproduce him here, since this question has been treated at excessive length and with great learning by nearly all sacred critics.]

[Note: [Col. 0554C] Victorinus counts the same number in the Apocalypse: “There are,” he says, “twenty-four books of the Old Testament; you will find twenty-two in the excerpts of Theodore,” and so forth. Some added Tobit and Judith to the twenty-two volumes of the Hebrew canon, making twenty-four. “Some,” says Hilary in his prologue to the Book of Psalms, “thought that, with Tobit and Judith added, twenty-four books should be counted according to the number of the Greek letters.”

Jerome is not referring to them, but rather to those who habitually counted Ruth and Cinoth among the Hagiographa. The Jews of today call the sacred Bible [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text], Esrim vearbaa, that is, “twenty-four,” and count the Book of Ruth and the Lamentations of Jeremiah among the Hagiographa. See our prefaces for more on this subject. MART.]

These are the books which the Apocalypse of John presents under the number of the twenty-four elders, worshiping the Lamb and offering their crowns before him with faces bowed to the ground, standing before the four living creatures, full of eyes before and behind—that is, looking toward both the past and the future—

[Note: [Col. 0554D] The Veronese manuscript does not recognize the word respicientibus, “looking toward”; perhaps the Hieronymian text is more elegant without it.]

and crying out without ceasing: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come” (Revelation IV, 8).

[Note: [Col. 0555A] “And who is to come.” This is how it is read in the Carcassonne Canon and in Saint-Germain manuscript no. 3; it was also written in our Canon before it was purged of errors. MART.

—The Veronese manuscript more correctly has “who is to come,” as do the three older manuscripts cited by Martianaeus.]

This preface to the Scriptures, as it were a helmeted introduction to all the books that we have translated from Hebrew into Latin, may serve here, so that we may know that whatever lies outside these books is to be placed among the *apocrypha* [Note: The same manuscript has *seponendum*, “to be set aside,” which should be put in place of *esse*: a neater reading.]. Thus Wisdom, which is commonly entitled “of Solomon,” and the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and Judith, and Tobit, and the Shepherd [Note: Unless this is the well-known *Shepherd of Hermas*, I certainly do not understand what other book among the apocryphal Scriptures is to be rejected under this name. If it is that very work, then it was inserted altogether rashly, not by Jerome—who here lists apocryphal books of the Old Testament, not of the New—but by some petty scholar who did not sufficiently attend to the holy Father’s text and intention. For a book belonging to apostolic times cannot pertain to the Old Testament, or to the Hebrew canon, nor could the holy Doctor assign it to that series. I therefore judge that the Urbinate manuscript, which is exceptionally well corrected, is entirely without this name; and I wish it were absent from the other manuscripts as well, especially from the very ancient Veronese manuscript, so that it might be removed on the authority of those witnesses. Since, however, it occurs in all the other books, there are learned men who wish the title “Shepherd” to designate the Third Book of Maccabees. Francis Junius, with considerable ingenuity, writes the word in Greek as *Πάστορα* (*Pastora*), deriving it from *ἀπὸ τῆς παστάδος* or *παστίδος*, that is, from the court in which the high priest, with his faithful retinue, interceded lest the king enter the sanctuary.
