Meibomius, on the contrary, in his book *On the Construction of Triremes*, p. 45, insists that it should be read *Philopator*; by this title, however, he understands the Third Book of Maccabees, which is first in sequence and reaches back to times earlier than the Maccabean period. But the most learned Lemoyne, who attacks and ridicules the former conjecture in his letter to Cuperus on the *Melanophori*, p. 258, makes this one also less probable by the same arguments—not to mention that the reading *Philopator* differs far too greatly from that found in all the manuscripts, *Pastor*. At one time it seemed to us that *Esther* could conveniently be substituted, and that Jerome’s statement might be understood as referring to the last six chapters of that book, which are found only in the Greek editions of the Seventy and are absent from the Hebrew copy, and therefore from its canon. Indeed, this seems to be the reason why the book itself is removed from the list of divine books by Melito of Asia, Athanasius, and Gregory of Nazianzus. The sequence of Jerome’s own statement and of the deuterocanonical books seems likewise to require that he should here speak of this interpolation into the book, or of its divergence from the Hebrew exemplar. Finally, the names *Pastor* and *Esther* are quite similar, especially when heard from a reader’s mouth—unless some critic deliberately, rather than accidentally, substituted *Pastor*, having observed shortly before that Esther, as it stands in Hebrew, is admitted into the canon in the third order, among the *Hagiographa*, in ninth place, and having thought that Jerome would otherwise be inconsistent if he removed it here. We leave it to you, reader, to decide which conjecture you approve. See also Cotelerius on this matter in his preface to Hermas.], are not in the canon [Note: This must be understood of the canon of the Hebrews, not of the Church, as Marianus Victorius teaches in his scholia on the present preface of Jerome. Richard Simon likewise asserts, in *Critical History*, book I, chapter 19, that Jerome was speaking not on his own judgment but according to that of the Jews, when he decreed that certain books canonical in the Church—as Simon himself says—were to be placed among the apocryphal volumes.

If, however, this is understood as Jerome’s own judgment, then, provided that Jerome himself is believed, we cannot conceal the fact that those writers depart far from the truth and impose upon their readers an opinion of their own rather than Jerome’s. This is plainly established by these words, which are read in Jerome’s preface to the books of Solomon:

“It is reported that there is also the all-virtuous book of Jesus son of Sirach, and another pseudepigraphal work entitled the Wisdom of Solomon. Of the former I found a Hebrew copy, entitled not Ecclesiasticus, as among the Latins, but Proverbs; and Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs had been joined to it, so that Solomon’s likeness might be matched not only in the number of books but also in the kind of subject matter. The second is nowhere found among the Hebrews; indeed, its style itself has the flavor of Greek eloquence, and some ancient writers assert that it belongs to Philo the Jew. Therefore, just as the Church indeed reads the books of Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees, but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, so let it read these two volumes for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines.”

Let Marianus and Simon now consider in what sense Jerome spoke.

“Thus Wisdom, which is commonly entitled ‘of Solomon,’ and the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and Judith, and Tobit, and the Shepherd are not in the canon.”

We know, of course, that after the decrees of the Council of Trent all these books are to be received by all truly pious and orthodox persons with equal veneration alongside the others. But our present question concerns Jerome’s time, when, as is clear from the same evidence, the Church did indeed read the books just mentioned for the edification of the people, while nevertheless it did not receive them among the canonical Scriptures. MART.

—That the reference is specifically to the Hebrew canon is clear from the whole of Jerome’s context, and from the judgment of the most learned men—Victorius, Morinus, Simon, and others. Martianaeus, who maintains that the holy Doctor was speaking of the Church’s canon, appeals to that very well-known testimony of Jerome in his preface to the books of Solomon: “It is reported that there is also the all-virtuous book of Jesus son of Sirach, and another pseudepigraphal work entitled the Wisdom of Solomon; of the former I found a Hebrew copy, entitled not Ecclesiasticus, as among the Latins, but Proverbs . . . The second is nowhere found among the Hebrews, and its style itself has the flavor of Greek eloquence; and some ancient writers assert that it belongs to Philo the Jew. Therefore, just as the Church indeed reads the books of Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees, but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, so let it read these two volumes for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines.” These words seem, indeed, to show that the holy Father explained not what the Jews did but what the Church thought about these books. Yet Morinus rightly concludes that one should not infer from this passage what Jerome’s opponents intend; rather, Jerome was softening this statement in order to accommodate it to the other books. In truth, an author’s judgment must be weighed against several testimonies, and the surest proof is that the author himself is the interpreter of his own words.

There are, in fact, many testimonies from the holy Doctor himself in which he declares that he was speaking only of the Hebrews’ catalog, and they are so clear that no twisting of words can evade them. Of the book of Tobit, for example, he says in his preface to Chromatius and Heliodorus: “The Hebrews, cutting it away from the catalog of the divine Scriptures, consigned it to those writings which they call apocryphal. I have satisfied your desire, though not my own inclination. For the studies of the Hebrews accuse us and charge us with transferring these things into Latin ears against their canon. But judging it better to displease the judgment of the Pharisees and to serve the commands of bishops, I applied myself as best I could.”

Of Judith he says still more clearly in the same preface: “Among the Hebrews the book of Judith is read among the apocrypha; its authority is judged even less suitable for strengthening matters that are disputed. Yet, because it was written in the Chaldaean language, it is counted among the Histories. But since the Council of Nicaea is said to have counted this book among the holy Scriptures, I yielded to your request—or rather, your demand.”

The same must be said of Ecclesiasticus and the Wisdom of Solomon, which he includes with Tobit and Judith in one series and class. Whoever wants further information on this subject should consult the critics mentioned above, especially Morinus.] The First Book of Maccabees I found in Hebrew [Note: No Hebrew or Syriac exemplar survives today. Josephus Ben Gorion praises the Book of the Hasmoneans; he wrote around the eleventh century, and it is therefore not implausible that the Hebrew archetype survived until that time. Jerome translated none of these books, though the version now extant is very ancient.]. The second is Greek; this can also be proved from its very phrasing [Note: The Veronese manuscript has *ipsa quoque historia* instead of *φράσει*; I think this is an error caused by a Latin copyist who did not know Greek letters. A little farther on it likewise writes *historiographum* for the Greek *παραφραστήν*, “paraphrast.”]. Since this is so, I beg you, reader, not to regard my labor as an attack upon the ancients. Each person offers to God’s tabernacle what he can: some offer gold, silver, and precious stones; others linen, purple, scarlet, and hyacinth (Exodus 25). We shall be treated kindly if we offer skins and goats’ hair. And yet the Apostle judges our more contemptible things to be more necessary (1 Corinthians 12:21). Thus the whole beauty of the tabernacle, and the distinction signified by each of its parts—the Church of the present and of the future—is covered with skins and sackcloth; and the things that are of less value ward off the heat of the sun and the violence of the rains.

Read, therefore, my Samuel and Malachim—mine, I say, mine. For whatever, through more frequent translation and more careful correction, we have both learned and retained belongs to us. When you have understood what you did not previously know, consider me either an interpreter, if you are grateful, or a *παραφραστής* (*paraphrast*), if you are ungrateful. Yet I am wholly unaware of having altered anything from the Hebrew truth [Ms. *quod*; Ms. *sum* for *sim*]. Certainly, if you are incredulous, read the Greek and Latin manuscripts and compare them with these little works [Note: The printed editions add here, “which we recently corrected.” These words should be deleted as superfluous, since nothing of the kind is found in the older and better manuscripts. Only five or six of the more recent manuscripts read, “which we have listed above”; that too is defective. Jerome does not tell the reader to compare Greek and Latin manuscripts with all the little works he had listed above, or with those he had recently corrected, but only with those he had translated from Hebrew into Latin—that is, with the books of Samuel and Malachim. MART.]. Wherever you see them differing among themselves, ask any Hebrew to which reading you ought to give greater credence. If he confirms our reading, I think you will not regard him as a conjecturer, as though he and I had guessed alike in the same place.

And you also, handmaids of Christ—Paula and Eustochium—I ask you, who anoint the head of the Lord reclining at table with the most precious *myron* of faith [Note: All our manuscripts read this way, except that several write *myrro* with a double *r* instead of *myro*. In Greek, *μύρον* means ointment, whereas *μύρρα* signifies the plant myrrh. The error in the printed books is therefore manifest, where we read “with the most precious myrrh of faith.” The head of the reclining Lord was not anointed with myrrh, but with *myro*, that is, the most precious ointment of the sinful woman in the Gospel narrative, to which Saint Jerome is here alluding. MART.

—The author of the *Hieronymian Questions* argues that the ancient reading, “with the most precious myrrh of faith,” should be restored. He also maintains that the holy Doctor was referring much more directly to the women who brought myrrh to Christ’s tomb than to the woman—or women—who poured ointment upon his reclining head. Evidently his excessive zeal for contradiction darkened his eyes, so that he failed to read the two immediately preceding and perfectly clear words, “the reclining Lord.” There is therefore no doubt that Jerome wrote *myro*, or *μύρῳ*, meaning ointment, as Salmasius long ago demonstrated by firm arguments; Martianaeus later restored the reading to the text with the aid of manuscripts. Our codices likewise confirm the restored reading, though one of them writes *myrro* somewhat incorrectly with a double *r*. Other passages of the Fathers confirm it as well, since they used the word in precisely the same sense—especially Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, Sermon 13: “Mary wiped the feet of Christ, anointed with precious *myro*.” More pointedly, Sermon 20: “The other”—that is, Saint Paul—“carries the precious *myron* of faith among the people through his teaching,” and so forth. Soon afterward the Veronese manuscript reads, “because he by no means [sought] the Savior,” instead of “who by no means seek”; in one Avignon manuscript Martianaeus found *seductorem*, “deceiver,” written quite incorrectly for *salvatorem*, “Savior.”], who by no means seek the Savior in the tomb—for Christ has already ascended to the Father—set against the barking dogs who rage against me with rabid mouths and prowl around the city, and who think themselves learned if they disparage others, the shields of your prayers.

I, knowing my own lowliness, shall always remember that saying:

> “I said, ‘I will guard my ways,
>
> so that I do not sin with my tongue.
>
> I placed a guard over my mouth,
>
> while the sinner stood against me.
>
> I was silent and was humbled,
>
> and I kept silence concerning good things.’”
>
> (Psalm 38:1 ff.)

[Col. 0557]

# Chapters of the Book of Samuel and Malachim

## Titles of the Book of Samuel

I. Where Hannah prays in her heart with unmoving lips.

II. The birth of Samuel.

III. Where Samuel is offered to the temple.

IV. Hannah’s song.

V. Where the sin of Eli’s sons is revealed.

VI. Where Eli addresses his sons concerning their sins.

VII. A prophet without a name is sent to Eli.

VIII. The Lord addresses Samuel while he is sleeping.

IX. The first address to Samuel.

X. Israel is defeated by its enemies.

XI. Where the ark of the covenant is carried against the enemies.

XII. Where the people are struck down; Eli’s sons are killed and the ark is captured.

XIII. Eli the priest dies after falling from his chair.

XIV. Where the Philistines place the ark in the temple.

XV. Where the plague of Ashdod and of the other cities is described.

XVI. The Ekronites receive the ark of the Lord.

XVII. The priests determine with what offering the ark is to be sent away.

XVIII. The receiving of the ark of the Lord: a sacrifice is made from the cows that brought it.

XIX. The transfer of the ark to Gibeah, into the house of Abinadab.

XX. Where Samuel prays and sacrifices for the people.

XXI. Concerning the judgment of Samuel’s sons and the people’s request for a king.

XXII. Where the people are instructed concerning the king’s right and power.

XXIII. The anointing of Saul as king.

XXIV. Where Saul is anointed by Samuel and received with a kiss.

XXV. Saul begins to prophesy.

XXVI. The confirmation of King Saul and the description of the law of the kingdom.

XXVII. Saul’s first battle.

XXVIII. Where Samuel addresses the people concerning his own times.

XXIX. The conclusion of Samuel’s address and the people’s repentance.

XXX. Samuel rebukes Saul for offering sacrifice.

XXXI. Jonathan alone advances against the Philistines.

XXXII. Saul imposes a fast.

XXXIII. The people eat animals slaughtered by decree, though they did not belong to them.

XXXIV. Saul promises to kill Jonathan because he did not observe the imposed fast, and the people plead for him.

XXXV. The Lord’s command to Saul concerning the destruction of Amalek.

XXXVI. The Lord becomes angry with Saul because he spared Agag, king of Amalek.

XXXVII. Obedience is better than sacrifice.

XXXVIII. Where Samuel killed Agag the king.

XXXIX. Where Samuel is sent to anoint David king.

XL. Where Jesse’s sons are presented one by one to Samuel.

XLI. Where David is anointed by Samuel.

XLII. Saul is seized, and an evil spirit comes upon him.

XLIII. Where David is brought to Saul.

XLIV. The beginning of Goliath.

XLV. Where David withdraws from Saul.

XLVI. David is sent by his father after his brothers.

XLVII. Where David presents himself against Goliath.

XLVIII. Where David killed Goliath.

XLIX. Jonathan received David in affection.

L. Where Saul, stirred by the song of the maidens, became hostile to David.

LI. Where Saul promises his daughter Merab to David.

LII. Here Merab is given to another, and Michal is promised to him.

LIII. Where Michal becomes David’s wife.

LIV. Saul orders David to be killed.

LV. Where David fights the Philistines again.

LVI. Here David is saved by his wife Michal.

LVII. When David was with Samuel, both he and those sent against him, as well as Saul when he came, began to prophesy.

LVIII. Saul becomes angry with Jonathan because of his defense of David.

LIX. Concerning the sign of the arrows between David and Jonathan.

LX. Where David ate the bread of the Presence.

LXI. Where David pretended before Achish, king of Gath, that he had a demon.

LXII. Where David gathered fugitives around himself.

LXIII. Where the priests of the Lord were killed by Doeg.

LXIV. At the Lord’s command, David goes with his men to the Philistines.

LXV. Here David receives the ephod from Abiathar the priest and prays.

LXVI. The Ziphites promise Saul that they will hand David over to him.

LXVII. While in the cave, David cuts off Saul’s cloak.

LXVIII. David’s speech to Saul, explaining that he had spared him.

LXIX. Saul’s repentance toward David.

LXX. The beginning of Nabal.

LXXI. Nabal refuses David provisions.

LXXII. Nabal dies, and David took his wife.

LXXIII. David has as wives Michal, Saul’s daughter, whom he had taken back, and Abigail, as well as Ahinoam.

LXXIV. Where Saul gave Michal as a wife to another man.

LXXV. While the whole army was sleeping, David took the spear from beside Saul’s head.

LXXVI. Where Saul, awakened, addresses David.

LXXVII. Where Samuel dies.

LXXVIII. Where Saul consults the pythoness.

LXXIX. Where David is forbidden to go to war against Israel.

LXXX. The Amalekites who rose up are defeated by David.

LXXXI. Where David recovers the spoil.

LXXXII. Where Saul is defeated and killed. Here the First Book of Samuel ends.

LXXXIII. Where David killed the messenger who had reported that Saul was dead.

LXXXIV. After Saul’s death, David is anointed and reigns.

LXXXV. Where David recalls that he was anointed by the people of Judah.

LXXXVI. Where war arose between Ish-bosheth and David.

LXXXVII. Where Abner killed Asahel, Joab’s brother, on David’s side.

LXXXVIII. The names of David’s six sons, who were born from different mothers.

LXXXIX. Where Abner is killed by Joab, commander of David’s army.

XC. Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, is found.

XCI. Here Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, is killed.

XCII. Where David kills the murderers of Ish-bosheth.

XCIII. Where David is anointed and established as king by all the people of Israel.

XCIV. Where Hiram the king supplies timber for David’s house.

XCV. The names of David’s sons by different mothers.

XCVI. Here the ark of the covenant is transferred from the house of Aminadab.

XCVII. Here Michal, Saul’s daughter, is shown to be barren.

XCVIII. Where David is warned by the prophet that he himself will not build the Lord’s temple.

XCIX. David’s prayer after the prophet’s address.

C. The conclusion of David’s prayer.

CI. Where it is shown that he consecrated much spoil and many gifts to the Lord.

CII. Where Scripture refers to Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son.

CIII. Where war is begun against Ammon, the son of Ammon.

CIV. Here David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite.

CV. Nathan the prophet addresses David concerning the wife of the Hittite [Col. 0561B].

CVI. Where David acknowledges his sin.

CVII. The son of David born of Bathsheba dies.

CVIII. Solomon is born of Bathsheba.

CIX. Here Amnon began to love his sister.

CX. Where Tamar is driven away by Amnon and received by her brother Absalom.

CXI. Here Amnon is killed by Absalom.

CXII. Where Joab sends a woman pretending to mourn for Absalom.

CXIII. Here David is reconciled to Absalom through the woman of Tekoa.

CXIV. Where Absalom orders Joab’s field of grain to be burned.

CXV. Here Absalom falsely claims that he has a vow of sacrifice, in order to go to Hebron and make himself king.

CXVI. Where David flees from Absalom.

CXVII. Here David sends forces against Absalom.

CXVIII. Where Shimei reviles David.

CXIX. Ahithophel’s counsel that Absalom should go in to his father’s concubines.

CXX. Where Ahithophel promises to pursue David, but Hushai rejects the plan.

CXXI. Where Ahithophel killed himself by hanging.

CXXII. Joab and Abishai go out against Absalom.

CXXIII. Here Absalom is found hanging from an oak.

CXXIV. Where David is informed that Absalom has been killed.

CXXV. Joab, commander of the army, becomes angry because David mourned Absalom.

CXXVI. Where the people desire to return to David.

CXXVII. Here Shimei asks to be forgiven for the injury he inflicted.

CXXVIII. Where Barzillai gives his son Chimham to David the king.

CXXIX. Sheba separated the people of Israel from David.

CXXX. Where Amasa is killed by Joab.

CXXXI. A woman addresses Joab and also brings out Sheba’s head.

CXXXII. Where the Gibeonites ask for seven descendants of Saul as punishment, and receive them.

CXXXIII. Where David gathers the bones of Saul and Jonathan.

CXXXIV. Here Psalm 17 begins.

CXXXV. David orders water to be brought to him from the cistern in Bethlehem.

CXXXVI. Where David orders the people to be counted.

CXXXVII. Through the prophet Gad, the Lord speaks to David concerning three forms of correction.

[Note: We have taken this from the very ancient Veronese manuscript, which we also followed in editing the books themselves. Martianaeus prefixed nothing to these books except the titles. We compared the recapitulations themselves with the edition of Cardinal Tommasi and recorded the variant readings in the margins of the pages.]

# Recapitulation of the First Book of Malachim

I. Concerning Elkanah and his wives, Eli the priest, and the birth of Samuel.

II. Concerning Hannah’s song and the iniquities of Eli’s sons.

III. Concerning Samuel and the divine accusation directed through him against Eli, where he prophesies [Al. “pronounces”] concerning Christ.

IV. Concerning Samuel, where God calls him for the fourth time in a vision; and concerning the war with the Philistines, the capture of the ark, and the death of Eli [Al. “of the priest”].

V. Concerning the idol Dagon, broken in the presence of the ark, and the plagues inflicted upon the Philistines.

VI. Concerning the ark’s return to Beth-shemesh and the plague inflicted there.

VII. Concerning the ark’s migration to Kiriath-jearim, into the house of Aminadab; the battle in which the Philistines were struck down [Col. 0561D]; and Samuel’s deeds.

VIII. Concerning Samuel’s sons and the people’s request for a king; and concerning Saul and the search for the donkeys.

IX. Concerning Saul’s anointing as king, his prophesying among the prophets, and how his kingdom was confirmed at Mizpah.

X. Concerning Nahash, king of Ammon, how he attacked the city of Jabesh, and the confirmation of Saul’s kingdom at Gilgal.

XI. Concerning Samuel’s commands to the people and the signs displayed from heaven.

XII. Concerning Jonathan and Saul, how they struck the Philistines; and concerning Saul, where he rashly attempted to offer burnt offerings.

XIII. Concerning Jonathan, through whom the Lord struck the Philistine camp, and Saul’s attempt to kill him for tasting honey.

XIV. Concerning Saul, how he humbled all the surrounding nations, and which sons or commanders he had; concerning the destruction of Amalek in vengeance for the Hebrews who came from Egypt [Al. “in vengeance upon the Amalekites”], and concerning King Agag.

XV. Concerning Samuel, where he abandoned Saul and anointed David, and concerning the evil spirit that tormented Saul.

XVI. Concerning the Philistines’ war against Saul, where David killed Goliath and was acclaimed among the ten thousands.

XVII. Concerning Jonathan’s and David’s affection, Saul’s hatred of David, and how David received Michal for a hundred foreskins [Al. “where he received Michal for a hundred foreskins”], while she exposed her father’s plot and saved David.

XVIII. Concerning David’s flight to Samuel and the offense [Al. omitted] of those who were sent and prophesied, where Saul also came and prophesied; and concerning the pact and sign between Jonathan and David.

XIX. Concerning David’s flight and the events related about Ahimelech the priest; how David changed his appearance before Achish the king; and how he went with all his men to the king of Moab.

XX. Concerning Gad the prophet, who warned David to flee into the land of Judah, into the forest; and how, when Doeg betrayed him, Ahimelech was killed with the other eighty priests; and how David, after striking the Philistines, saved Keilah.

XXI. Concerning Saul, how he wished to seize David at Keilah, but David fled from him into the wilderness of Ziph; where Jonathan came to him [Col. 0563B], and how David cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak in the cave.

XXII. Concerning Samuel’s death and his tomb at Ramah; and the events related about Nabal of Carmel and Abigail.

XXIII. Concerning David, where he took Abigail and Ahinoam as wives, and where he took away the cup and spear of Saul, who was pursuing him.

XXIV. Concerning David’s flight to Gath, to Achish king of the Philistines, and what he did there; and concerning Saul and the pythoness.

XXV. Concerning the Philistines gathered against Saul; and concerning David, who, after striking Amalek, brought back a man, the captivity [reading uncertain; Al. “the whole captivity”], and his wives to Ziklag.

XXVI. Concerning the Philistines’ battle, in which Saul and his three sons were killed [Al. “fell”], and how David mourned Saul and Jonathan.

XXVII. Concerning David’s return to Hebron, where he was anointed a second time; and concerning Abner, Mephibosheth, and Joab; and the battle in which the young men played, and Asahel fell.

XXVIII. Concerning David’s sons born at Hebron; how he recovered Michal; concerning Abner, killed by Joab; and the death of Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son.

XXIX. Concerning all the tribes, how they surrendered to David [Al. “followed David”]; how he entered Zion; and concerning Hiram, the craftsmen, and the timber; and concerning the wives or sons born to David in Jerusalem [Al. “born only to him”].

XXX. Concerning Nathan the prophet, who forbids David to build the temple and prophesies concerning Christ; and how David humbled all the surrounding nations.

XXXI. Concerning Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, and Hanun [here written “Anon”], king of Ammon; how he insulted David’s servants, and concerning the battles that followed in vengeance.

XXXII. Concerning Bathsheba, Uriah’s [wife; Al. adds “his wife”], Nathan’s parable, and the death of the child born from adultery.

XXXIII. Concerning the city of Rabbah, captured by David; the birth of Solomon; the events mentioned about Ammon and Tamar [Al. the words in parentheses are absent]; and how Absalom killed Amnon.

XXXIV. Concerning Absalom’s flight to Talmai, king of Syria, in Geshur, and the woman of Tekoa who spoke to King David on his behalf.

XXXV. Concerning Absalom’s beauty and the sons he had; and how he drove his father from the kingdom.

XXXVI. Concerning Ahithophel’s counsel, Hushai’s advice to Absalom, and David’s scouts Ahimaaz and Jonathan.

XXXVII. Concerning the battle in which Absalom perished and how David mourned him.

XXXVIII. Concerning David’s return to Jerusalem and the recovery of the kingdom.

XXXIX. Concerning Sheba, who rebelled against David with part of the people; Amasa, whom Joab killed; and the famine that occurred because of the Gibeonites, whom David avenged by crucifying seven men of Saul’s lineage.

XL. Concerning the battle with the Philistines, in which David was placed in danger; the remaining wars; the song that he sang to the Lord [Al. omits “that he sang to the Lord”]; and the prophecy concerning Christ.

XLI. Concerning the men who were very brave in battle with David, and their deeds of valor.

XLII. Concerning the divine indignation at David’s ordering the people to be counted; the choice offered through Nathan [Al. “through Gad”] in three forms; the killing of seventy thousand by an angel [Al. “the killing inflicted”]; and the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite [Al. “the sacrifice offered by David at the threshing floor of Araunah”].

# Here Begin the Two Books of Samuel, Which Are Otherwise Called One Book of Samuel or the First Book of Malachim

## The First Book
### [Col. 0563C] [T. I, Chapter I]

There was a certain man from Ramathaim-Sophim, from the hill-country of Ephraim, whose name was Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of [Note: Some printed editions and numerous manuscripts read *Thau*, evidently from the Hebrew [Hebrew term]. The Septuagint in the Alexandrian manuscript retains Θεοῦ (*Theou*, “of God”), which the Chaldean likewise rendered with a full *hollem*, as the grammarians say, [Hebrew term], *Thoou* or *Thohu*. We have followed the Hebrew Canon of Truth and another manuscript of Corbie; both write *Shou* and thus preserve, as we have discovered, Jerome’s true reading. This is clear from the *Book of Hebrew Names*, and again from the first book *Against Jovinian*, where the holy Doctor consistently read *Thou*, or *Thoou*, in accordance with the Greek manuscripts. MART. —The manuscripts of Verona and Urbino, together with the Vulgate, have *Thau*, which Jerome may have formed from the Hebrew; although in other books he read *Thou* with the Greeks.] Thou, son of Suph, an Ephraimite. He had two wives: the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children [Hebrew: little ones].

That man went up from his city on appointed days, to worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts at Shiloh. There were there the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests of the Lord. The day came, and Elkanah sacrificed; and he gave portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters. But to Hannah he gave one portion [Hebrew: one double portion], being sad, because he loved Hannah. Now the Lord had closed her womb.

Her rival also afflicted her and harassed her greatly, to such an extent that she reproached her for the Lord’s having closed her womb. Thus she acted every year, whenever they went up to the temple of the Lord at the appointed season; and so she provoked her. But Hannah wept and did not take food.

Then her husband Elkanah said to her: “Hannah, why are you weeping, and why do you not [Note: Our manuscript reads *comedes*, “will you eat?” The Hebrew likewise has the future tense [Hebrew term].] eat? And why is your heart afflicted? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”

After she had eaten and drunk at Shiloh, Hannah rose. Eli the priest was sitting on a chair before the doors of the temple of the Lord. Hannah, being bitter in spirit, prayed to the Lord, weeping profusely, and made a vow, saying:

“Lord of hosts, if you will look upon the affliction of your servant and remember me, and do not forget your maidservant, and give your servant a male child, I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head.”

And it happened, as she multiplied her prayers before the Lord, that Eli watched her mouth. Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice could not be heard at all. Therefore Eli thought that she was drunk, and said to her:

“How long will you be drunk? Let the wine with which you are soaked pass from you.”

Hannah answered: “Not so, my lord. I am an exceedingly unhappy woman, and I have drunk neither wine nor anything that can cause drunkenness; rather, I have poured out my soul before the Lord. Do not regard your maidservant as one of the daughters of Belial, for from the abundance of my pain and sorrow I have spoken until now.”

Then Eli said to her: “Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant you the petition that you have asked of him.”

She said: “Would that your maidservant find favor in your eyes!” And the woman went on her way; she ate, and her face was no longer changed with distress.

### [T. II]

They rose early and worshiped before the Lord. Then they returned and came to their house at Ramah. Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the Lord remembered her. After some time had passed, Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son. She called his name Samuel, because she had asked him from the Lord.

Her husband Elkanah went up, and all his household, to sacrifice to the Lord the customary sacrifice and his vow, but Hannah did not go up. For she said to her husband:

“I will not go until the child is weaned; then I will take him, and he shall appear before the presence of the Lord and remain there continually.”

Her husband Elkanah said to her [Vulgate omits *ei*, “to her”]: “Do what seems good to you, and remain until you have weaned him; and I pray that the Lord may fulfill his word.”

The woman therefore remained and nursed her son [Col. 0566C] until she weaned him.

### [T. III]

And after she had weaned him, she brought him with her, with three calves [Note: The corrector of the Hebrew Canon substituted in our copy “and with one measure of flour” for “and with three measures of flour.” In making this alteration he had a false supporter in Jerome, namely the author of the *Hebrew Questions or Traditions on the Books of Kings*. That writer expressly asserts that the Latin copies are faulty and corrupt wherever they read “and with three measures of flour”; in Hebrew, he says, it is not “with three measures of flour,” but “with one measure of flour,” and he claims that the passage has been corrupted among Latin writers.

“If he offered three calves and three measures of flour,” he continues, “he acted contrary to the command of the law. For the law prescribes: ‘The first day of the seventh month shall be venerable and holy for you. You shall do no servile work; it is a day of trumpet-blowing. You shall offer a burnt offering as a sweet odor to the Lord: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven unblemished yearling lambs; and with their offerings, fine flour mingled with oil, three-tenths for each bull, two-tenths for the ram, and one-tenth for each lamb.’ This tenth was the tenth part of an ephah.

“From this it is understood that Elkanah did not offer three measures of flour with three calves, but nine tenths, which according to the Hebrew measure make one ephah. Thus the old writer speaks—not without learning, indeed, if he had remembered that the Hebrew *epha* was equal to three *sata*, or three Roman measures.”

The true Jerome teaches this explicitly in chapter 2 of the book of Ruth, verse 17, where he interprets: “And what she had gathered by cutting and threshing with the staff, she found to be about an ephah of barley,” that is, three measures. Likewise, in the fourteenth book of his *Commentaries on Ezekiel*, explaining measures both of dry and liquid substances, he wrote the following about the Hebrew ephah:

“Among things measured by the measure, a tenth part of a *cor* is called an ephah, that is, three measures; and among liquid substances a tenth part of a cor is called a bath, or *vadus*. Thus the ephah and the bath have the same measure.”

One ephah of flour therefore contained three *sata*, or, which is the same thing, three measures of flour. One measure, however, contained three tenths, which had to be offered for each calf in the sacrifices. From this we conclude that the work entitled *Hebrew Traditions on the Books of Kings* was falsely attributed to the holy Doctor, since it contains opinions entirely contrary to Jerome’s own words.

Nevertheless, we admit that certain written and printed copies agree completely with the text attributed to our author. For they do not read “and with three measures of flour,” but, as we have already said, “and with one measure of flour.” The Syriac translator likewise intended to express this very reading, saying [Syriac], *ousatho hhado decamhho*, that is, “and one measure of flour.”

Let the diligent reader compare this entire passage with what is read in chapter 29 of Numbers and with the marginal scholia of the Hebrew Canon of Truth, column 183, so that he may derive a plausible argument concerning the author of those scholia and concerning the false Jerome, whose words we now quote. MART.]

“And three measures of flour, and a jar of wine.” And he brought him into the house of the Lord at Shiloh. The child was still very young. They sacrificed a calf and presented the child to Eli.

And she said [Vulgate adds: “Hannah”]: “I beg you, my lord—as surely as your soul lives, my lord—I am that woman who stood here before you praying to the Lord. I prayed for this child, and the Lord granted me my petition, which I asked of him. Therefore I too have lent him to the Lord for all the days that he is lent to the Lord.”

And they worshiped the Lord there. Then Hannah prayed and said:

### [T. IV, Chapter II]

“My heart has exulted in the Lord,

and my horn has been exalted [Note: The manuscript of Verona has *cor*, “heart,” instead of *cornu*, “horn.” To show that you should not regard this as the slip of a copyist, we have observed that the same reading occurs in the *Recapitulations*. Moreover, another very ancient manuscript of Verona, containing the Psalter in Greek and Latin, has *cor* instead of *cornu* where it appends this song at the end. The textual evidence, however, is opposed to it, as are all the other books.]

in my God.

My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies,

because I have rejoiced in your salvation.

There is none holy like the Lord;

for there is no other besides you,

and there is none strong like our God.

Do not multiply lofty words,

boasting.

Let old things depart from your mouth,

for the Lord is the God of knowledge,

and thoughts are prepared by him.

The bow of the strong has been overcome,

and the weak have been girded with strength.

Those who were formerly filled have hired themselves out for bread [Hebrew: “Those who were filled with bread”],

and the hungry have been filled.

Until the barren woman has borne many [Hebrew: seven],

she who had many children has grown weak.

The Lord puts to death and gives life;

he leads down to the underworld and brings back.

The Lord makes poor and enriches;

he humbles and lifts up.

He raises the needy from the dust

and lifts the poor from the dung,

so that he may seat him with princes

and give him possession of the throne of glory.

For the foundations of the earth are the Lord’s [Hebrew: “the afflicted of the earth are the Lord’s”],

and he has set the world upon them.

He will guard the feet of his holy ones,

and the wicked will be silent in darkness,

for a man will not prevail by strength.

The adversaries of the Lord will fear him;

over them he will thunder from the heavens.

The Lord will judge the ends of the earth,

and he will give power to his king,

and exalt the horn of his Christ.”

And Elkanah went to Ramah, to his house. The child, however, ministered in the presence of the Lord before Eli the priest.

### [T. V]

Now the sons of Eli, sons of Belial, did not know the Lord or the priestly duty toward the people. Rather, whenever anyone sacrificed a victim, the priest’s servant would come while the meat was boiling. He had a three-pronged fork in his hand, and he would thrust it into the kettle, the cauldron, the pot, or the pan; and everything that the fork brought up the priest took for himself. Thus they acted toward all the Israelites who came to Shiloh.

Even before the fat was burned, the priest’s servant would come and say to the one sacrificing: “Give me meat to cook for the priest; for I will not accept cooked meat from you, but raw.”

The one sacrificing would say to him: “Let the fat first be burned today according to the custom [Note: The manuscript of Verona has the nearby reading “according to the custom.” Neither this reading nor the former is found in the Hebrew.], and then take as much as your soul desires.”

He would answer: “Not at all. You will give it now; otherwise I shall take it by force.” [Col. 0568B]

Thus the sin of the young men was very great before the Lord, because they were drawing people away from the sacrifice of the Lord [Vulgate: “withdrawing people from the sacrifice of the Lord”].

Samuel, however, ministered before the Lord as a boy, girded with a linen ephod.

### [T. VI]

His mother made him a little robe, which she brought to him at the appointed days, going up with her husband to offer the customary sacrifice. Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife and said [Vulgate adds: “to him”]:

“May the Lord give you offspring from this woman in return for the loan that you have lent to the Lord.”

And they went to their place.

The Lord visited Hannah, and she conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. The boy Samuel grew great before the Lord.

Eli was now very old. He heard everything that his sons did to all Israel, and how they slept with the women who waited at the door of the tabernacle. He said to them:

“Why do you do such things, things that I hear from all the people—such very evil things? Do not do this, my sons. For the report that I hear is not good: you are causing the Lord’s people to transgress. If one man sins against another, God may be appeased on his behalf; but if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?”

They did not listen to the voice of their father, because the Lord desired to kill them. But the boy Samuel progressed and grew, and he was pleasing both to the Lord and to men.

### [T. VII]

A man of God came to Eli and said to him:

“Thus says the Lord: Did I not plainly reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh? And I chose him from all the tribes of Israel for myself as priest, so that he might go up to my altar, burn incense for me, wear the ephod before me, and I gave to the house of your father all the sacrifices of the children of Israel.

“Why do you kick away [Vulgate: ‘have you cast away’] my victim and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple? Why have you honored your sons more than me, so that you might eat the first portions of every sacrifice of my people Israel?

“Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel: I plainly declared that your house and the house of your father would minister before me forever. But now, says the Lord, far be this from me. For whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held in contempt.

“Behold, days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will be no old man in your house. And you will see your rival in the temple, amid all the prosperity of Israel, and there will be no old man in your house for all your days.

“Nevertheless, I will not utterly remove a man from my altar; but [Hebrew does not have this] so that your eyes may fail, your soul may waste away, and the greater part of your house may die when it reaches manhood.

“This will be the sign for you of what will happen to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: on one day both will die.

“And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will act according to my heart and my soul; I will build for him a faithful house, and he will walk [Hebrew: ‘I will walk’] before my Christ all his days.

“For it will happen that whoever remains in your house will come to be prayed for, and will offer a silver coin and a round loaf of bread [Hebrew: ‘will come to worship him, and will receive from him a silver coin and a round loaf of bread’], and will say: ‘Please admit me to one priestly portion, so that I may eat a morsel of bread.’”

### [Chapter III]

The boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli. The word of the Lord was precious in those days; there was no open vision.

One day Eli was lying in his place. His eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished [Hebrew: “before the lamp of God was extinguished”]. Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was.

And the Lord called Samuel.

### [T. VIII]

He answered: “Here I am.” He ran to Eli and said: “Here I am, for you called me.”

He said: “I did not call you. Go back and sleep.”

He went and slept. The Lord called Samuel again. Samuel arose, went to Eli, and said: “Here I am, for you called me.”

He answered: “I did not call you, my son. Go back and sleep.”

Samuel did not yet know the Lord, nor had the word of the Lord been revealed to him. The Lord continued and called Samuel yet again [Hebrew does not have “yet”] for the third time.

He arose and went to Eli and said: “Here I am, because you called me.”

Eli understood, therefore, that the Lord was calling the boy, and he said to Samuel:

“Go, sleep; and if he calls you again, say: ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.’”

Samuel went and slept in his place.

### [T. IX]

The Lord came and stood there, and called as he had called the second time: “Samuel, Samuel.”

Samuel said: “Speak [Vulgate adds: “Lord”], for your servant hears.”

The Lord said to Samuel:

“Behold, I am doing a thing in Israel which, whoever hears it, will make both his ears tingle. On that day I will raise against Eli everything that I have spoken concerning his house. I will begin and complete it.

“For I have told him that I would judge his house forever because of the iniquity, since he knew that his sons were acting disgracefully and did not rebuke them. Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that the iniquity of his house will not be expiated by sacrifices or offerings forever.”

Samuel slept until morning, and opened the doors of the house of the Lord. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the vision.

Eli called Samuel and said: “Samuel, my son.”

He answered: “Here I am.”

He questioned him: “What is the word that he spoke to you [Vulgate adds: “the Lord”]? I beg you, do not hide it from me. May God do these things to you, and add these things, if you hide from me any of the words that were spoken to you.”

Samuel therefore told him every word [Note: The manuscript of Verona omits “every word,” although it is found in the Hebrew, Greek, and other books], and did not conceal anything from him.

Eli answered: “It is the Lord. Let him do what is good in his eyes.”

Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and none of his words fell to the ground. All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord.

The Lord continued to appear at Shiloh, because the Lord had revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh according to the word of the Lord. And the word of Samuel came to all Israel.

### [T. X, Chapter IV]

[Note: The entire passage beginning “And it happened in those days: the Philistines gathered for battle” is absent from the manuscript of Verona; and, what is the decisive point, it is likewise lacking in the Hebrew archetype. From this one may conclude that that manuscript exhibits Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew exactly, and that these words entered the Latin manuscripts only from the Greek Septuagint. Lucas of Bruges also cites six Latin copies that lack the addition. Yet he approves it on the basis of the agreement of the ancient versions, while testifying that it belongs to the *epanorthosis*, or correction, of ancient copies.]

It happened in those days that the Philistines gathered for battle. Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle and encamped near the Stone of Help. The Philistines came to Aphek and drew up their line against Israel.

When the battle had begun, Israel turned its back before the Philistines, and in that battle, here and there throughout the fields, about four thousand men were struck down. The people returned to the camp, and the elders of Israel said:

“Why has the Lord struck us today before the Philistines? Let us bring to ourselves from Shiloh the ark of the covenant of the Lord, so that it may come into our midst and save us from the hand of our enemies.”

The people therefore sent to Shiloh, and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, who sits upon the cherubim. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were with the ark of the covenant of God.

When the ark of the covenant of the Lord came into the camp, all Israel shouted with a great cry, and the earth resounded.

### [T. XI]

The Philistines heard the sound of the shouting and said:

“What is this sound of such a great shout in the camp of the Hebrews?”

They learned that the ark of the Lord had come into the camp. The Philistines were afraid and said:

“God has come into the camp.”

And they groaned, saying:

“Woe to us! There was no such rejoicing yesterday or the day before. Woe to us! Who will save us from the hand of those lofty gods? These are the gods who struck Egypt with every plague in the wilderness.

“Be strong and be men, Philistines, lest you serve the Hebrews as they served you [Note: The manuscript of Verona has *nobis*, “us,” in agreement with the Greek ἡμῖν]. Be strong and fight.”

The Philistines fought, and Israel was struck down; each man fled to his tent.

### [T. XII]

There was a very great slaughter, and thirty thousand infantry of Israel fell. The ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.

A man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh that day, with his clothing torn and dust scattered upon his head. When he arrived, Eli was sitting on a chair facing the road and watching, for his heart was anxious about the ark of God.

The man entered, announced the news to the city, and the whole city wailed. Eli heard the sound of the uproar and said:

“What is this sound of such a tumult?”

The man hurried, came, and announced it to Eli. Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyes had grown dim, so that he could not see.

The man said to Eli: “I am the one who has come from the battle; I am the one who fled from the battle line today.”

He said to him: “What has happened, my son?”

The messenger answered: “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people. Moreover, your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, have died, and the ark of God has been captured.”

### [T. XIII]

When he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his chair beside the gate, broke his neck, and died. For he was an old and very aged man, and he had judged Israel for forty years.

His daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and near childbirth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured, that her father-in-law and her husband had died, she bent down and gave birth, for sudden pains had overtaken her [Hebrew: “her pains”].

At the very moment of her death, the women standing around her said: “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son.”

She did not answer them or pay attention. She called the child Ichabod [Note: In the manuscript of Verona the first two letters are marked with an obelus as canceled, so that you may know it should be called *Cabad*, not *Scabod*], saying:

“Glory has departed from Israel, because the ark of God has been captured, and because of her father-in-law and her husband.”

And she said: “Glory has departed from Israel, because the ark of God has been captured.”

### [T. XIV, Chapter V]

The Philistines took the ark of God and carried it from the Stone of Help to Ashdod. The Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside Dagon.

When the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon was lying face downward on the ground before the ark of the Lord. They took Dagon and restored him to his place.

When they rose early the following morning, they found Dagon lying face downward on the ground before the ark of the Lord. The head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands had been cut off upon the threshold; only Dagon’s trunk remained in its place.

For this reason the priests of Dagon and all who enter his temple in Ashdod do not tread upon the threshold of Dagon to this day.

The hand of the Lord weighed heavily upon the people of Ashdod. He devastated them and struck Ashdod and its territory in the secret parts of the buttocks [Note: The words that appear consecutively in the printed editions—“The villages and fields in the midst of that region swelled up, mice were born, and a great confusion of death arose in the city”—were marked with an obelus by R. Stephanus and the theologians of Louvain, because they are absent from the Hebrew text and from the oldest and most carefully corrected Latin manuscripts of Jerome’s version.

They were borrowed from the Septuagint, or from those Latin translations that were in use before Jerome. Since countless additions of this kind occur, especially in the Books of Kings, it will not be irrelevant to explain to the reader how they are found in the oldest manuscripts of the sacred Scriptures in Jerome’s edition.

Three kinds of Latin manuscripts still remain, by which we can discover the causes and origins of these additions. First are the manuscripts that represent Jerome’s proper and genuine text without additions. Of this sort are the Colbertine, the Anician, and the greater Corbie manuscript no. 1. The Hebrew Canon of Truth must also be added to these, since after its correction it contains nothing spurious.

There are other older manuscripts in which the biblical text indeed flows pure, but which retain in their margins complete foreign and inserted words, together with certain signs within the text, indicating that these words were omitted by the scribes yet belong to the sacred text.

The third kind, finally, consists especially of more recent manuscripts, in whose text the various additions to Scripture have been introduced through the error and incompetence of copyists. In these, because no distinction was subsequently observed, it is scarcely possible to determine which readings properly belong to Jerome and which to the other Latin translators.

In this edition of the Hebrew Canon of Truth, desiring both to uphold the truth and to serve the usefulness of readers, we have indicated with obelis in the margin all these passages that had previously been confused and corrupted by foreign additions. We therefore wish the attentive reader to take note of that sign. MART. —The Vulgate adds: “The villages and fields in the midst of that region swelled up, mice were born, and a great confusion of death arose in the city.” These words are found neither in the Hebrew nor in our own or other Latin manuscripts of better quality, and critics long ago marked them as spurious. Nevertheless, passages transferred from the Greek text into the Vulgate occur frequently in the Books of Kings.]

### [T. XV]

When the men of Ashdod saw this kind of plague, they said:

“Let the ark of the God of Israel not remain with us, for his hand is harsh upon us and upon Dagon our god.”

They sent for and gathered all the lords of the Philistines and said:

“What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?”

The people of Gath answered: “Let the ark of the God of Israel be carried around [Hebrew: “Let it be carried around in Gath”].”

And they carried the ark of the God of Israel around.

While they were carrying it around, the hand of the Lord brought a very great slaughter upon each city [Hebrew: “In the city there was a very great slaughter”]. He struck the men of every city, from the least to the greatest [Hebrew: “the men of the city, from the least”], and their protruding tumors festered [Col. 0573A].

The people of Gath held counsel and made themselves leather seats [Note: This is a clear sign of the genuineness of Jerome’s translation, which the manuscript of Verona preserves. That manuscript lacks the addition, “The people of Gath held counsel, and made themselves leather seats,” which is not found in the Hebrew exemplar but was derived entirely from the Greeks: καὶ ἐποίησαν οἱ Γεθαῖοι ἑαυτοῖς ἕδρας, “and the people of Gath made seats for themselves.” In the Latin it was expanded by the words “held counsel” and “leather.”

Although I do not dare remove it from the text, I nevertheless affirm that it does not appear to have proceeded from Jerome’s pen, but should be numbered among the additions that a later hand imported into his translation from the Septuagint and other Latin versions. It is also surprising that the Hebrew scholiast, or Martianus, did not notice this fragment of interpolated text.]

Then they sent the ark of God to Ekron.

### [T. XVI]

When the ark of God came to Ekron, the Ekronites cried out, saying:

“They have brought the ark of the God of Israel to us in order to kill us and our people.”

They sent for and gathered all the lords of the Philistines, who said:

“Send away [Hebrew: ‘send’] the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its place, so that it may not kill us together with our people.”

For there was a deadly terror in every city [Hebrew: “throughout the whole city”], and the hand of God was exceedingly heavy. The men who had not died were struck in the secret parts of the buttocks, and the wailing of each city [Hebrew: “the wailing of the city”] rose to heaven.

### [Col. 0573B] [Chapter VI]

The ark of the Lord was in the region of the Philistines for seven months. [Note: The manuscript of Verona adds: “And their land swelled with mice.” This appears to have been sewn in from the Septuagint, καὶ ἐξέζεσεν ἡ γῆ αὐτῶν μῦας, “and their land boiled over with mice,” for nothing similar is found here in the Hebrew exemplar.

Yet, as we said above concerning the sixth verse of the preceding chapter, this kind of addition—although expressed there in more words—is rejected by everyone, both by the Hebrew text and by the better manuscripts, and finally by the critics.

Nevertheless, it must be admitted that the swarming of mice from the earth must at some point have been mentioned, since a few verses later the sacred text signifies it by reporting that the Philistines placed golden images of the mice on either side of the ark to protect themselves from their infestation.

Although the matter agrees equally well with the truth of the history whether it is placed there or here, this location nevertheless appears much more suitable for recalling the event. The very simplicity of the wording also seems to bear such a mark of authenticity that I would rather believe that this passage fell from the Hebrew archetype after Jerome’s time than that it was brought here by him from the Septuagint.

Indeed, one of the ancients—whether Aquila, Symmachus, or another of the Hexaplaric translators—read it in Hebrew and translated ἐξέβρασεν, “it boiled forth,” in place of the Septuagint’s ἐξέζεσεν, “it foamed up.” Jerome may likewise have read it and followed that translator more closely.]

They called for the priests and diviners of the Philistines and said:

“What shall we do with the ark of the Lord? Tell us how we shall send it back to its place.”

### [T. XVII]

They said:

“If you send back the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty. Rather, return what you owe [Hebrew does not have this] to him for the sin, and then you will be healed, and you will know why his hand does not withdraw from you.”

They said: “What must we return to him as a guilt offering?”

They answered:

“According to the number of the provinces of the Philistines, make five golden tumors and five golden mice, because one plague has fallen upon all of you and upon your lords.

“Make likenesses of your tumors and likenesses [Col. 0573C] of the mice that have devastated the land. And give glory to the God of Israel, in case he may lighten his hand from you, your gods, and your land.

“Why do you harden your hearts as Egypt and Pharaoh hardened his heart? Did they not, after he was struck, send them away [Hebrew: ‘when he mocked them, did he not send them away?’], and they departed?

“Now therefore take action and make one new cart. Take two milch cows that have not had a yoke placed upon them, harness them to the cart, and shut their calves at home.

“Then take the ark of the Lord and place it on the cart, and put the golden vessels that you have paid [manuscript: ‘will pay’] to him for the guilt in a little chest beside it. Then let it go.

“Watch, and if it goes up by the way of its own border toward Beth-shemesh, then he has done us this great evil. But if not, we shall know that his hand has not touched us; it happened by chance.”

They did this. They took two cows that were nursing calves and harnessed them to the cart, but shut up their calves at home. They placed the ark of the Lord on the cart, together with the little chest containing the golden mice and the likenesses of the tumors.

The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh. They traveled along one road, going and lowing; they did not turn aside either to the right or to the left [manuscript: “they did not turn aside”]. The lords of the Philistines followed them as far as the boundaries of Beth-shemesh.

### [T. XVIII]

The people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. When they lifted their eyes, they saw the ark and rejoiced at seeing it.

The cart came into the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite and stopped there. A large stone was there. They cut up the wood of the cart and placed the cows upon it as a burnt offering to the Lord [Hebrew: “and they offered the cows as a burnt offering to the Lord”].

The Levites took down the ark of God [Note: The manuscript of Verona has “the ark of the Lord,” and this is in fact found in the Hebrew: [Hebrew term]. Nevertheless, neither the manuscript nor the Vulgate consistently follows this rule; it is enough to have noted it once], and the little chest that was beside it, in which the golden vessels were, and placed them upon the large stone.

The men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices to the Lord on that day. The five lords of the Philistines saw it and returned to Ekron on that day.

These are the golden tumors that the Philistines returned to the Lord as a guilt offering: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron; and the golden mice according to the number of the cities of the Philistines, the five provinces, from the fortified city to the village without a wall, and as far as the great Abel, upon which they placed the ark of the Lord, which remained to that day in the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite.

The Lord struck among the men of Beth-shemesh because they had looked upon the ark of the Lord. He struck seventy men of the people [Hebrew: “seventy men and fifty thousand men”] and fifty thousand of the common people.

The people mourned because the Lord had struck the people with a great plague [Hebrew: “with a great plague among the people”].

The men of Beth-shemesh said:

“Who can stand in the presence of this holy Lord God? And to whom shall he go up from us?”

They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying:

“The Philistines have returned the ark of the Lord. Come down and take it to yourselves [Vulgate: ‘bring it back’].”

### [Treatise XIX, Chapter VII]

So the men of Kiriath-jearim came and brought back the ark of the Lord, and carried it into the house of Abinadab [Note: [Col. 0575D] Our manuscript calls him Aminadab, contrary to the Hebrew text] at Gibeah. They consecrated Eleazar his son, so that he might guard the ark of the Lord. And from the day on which the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied [Col. 0575B]—for it was already the twentieth year—and all the house of Israel found rest after the Lord.

Then Samuel spoke to all the house of Israel, saying: “If you return to the Lord with all your heart, remove the foreign gods from among you [the Vulgate adds: Baalim], and the Ashtaroth, and prepare your hearts for the Lord, and serve him alone; and he will rescue you from the hand of the Philistines.”

So the Israelites removed the Baalim and the Ashtaroth and served the Lord alone. Samuel said: “Gather all Israel at [Note: [Col. 0575D] Our manuscript consistently calls it Masphat, closer to the Hebrew] Mizpah, so that I may pray to the Lord for you.” And they gathered at Mizpah; they drew water and poured it out before the Lord, and they fasted that day, and said there: “We have sinned against the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0575D] The manuscript reads: “They said, ‘Have we not sinned, Lord?’,” though this is farther from the Hebrew wording.] And Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah.

When the Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. When the Israelites heard this, they were afraid before the Philistines. They said to Samuel: “Do not cease crying out to the Lord our God for us, so that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines.”

### [Treatise XX]

Samuel took one suckling lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord. Samuel cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him. And while Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines entered into battle against Israel. The Lord thundered with a great roar against the Philistines on that day, and terrified them, and they were defeated [Note: [Col. 0575D] Instead of “before Israel,” manuscript copies read “by the Israelites” [Col. 0576D]. But in the Colbertine manuscript of Anjou and in another manuscript of Saint-Germain, “before Israel” had been written by the first hand, which an unskilled corrector changed into “by the Israelites.” MART. —Our manuscript and those consulted in large number by Martianay read “by the Israelites” instead of “before Israel.” In Hebrew, however, the writing of the two expressions is extremely similar, so that one could be taken for the other and the readings confused.]

before Israel. The Israelites went out from Mizpah, pursued the Philistines, and struck them down as far as the place below Beth-car.

[Col. 0575D] Samuel took one stone and placed it between Mizpah and Shen [the manuscript: Senei], and called its name [the Vulgate adds: “of the place”] the Stone of Help. And he said: “Thus far the Lord has helped us.”

And the Philistines were humbled, and did not continue to come into the territory of Israel. Thus the hand of the Lord was upon the Philistines all the days of Samuel. The cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, together with their territories. Israel was delivered from the hand of the Philistines, and there was peace between Israel and the Amorite.

Samuel also judged Israel all the days of his life. Each year he went around Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and judged Israel in those places. Then he returned to Ramah, for his house was there, and there he judged Israel. He also built an altar to the Lord there.

### [Treatise XXI, Chapter VIII]

When Samuel had grown old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel. The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of the second was Abijah [Col. 0576B], judges in Beersheba. But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside after dishonest gain, accepted gifts, and perverted judgment.

So all the elders of Israel gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah. They said to him: “Look, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Appoint a king for us to judge us, as all the nations have.”

The request displeased Samuel, because they had said: “Give us a king to judge us.” And Samuel prayed to the Lord. The Lord said to Samuel: “Listen to the voice of the people in everything they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but me, so that I should not reign over them. In accordance with all the deeds they have done from the day when I brought them up out of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0576D] The Veronese manuscript reads “out of the land of Egypt”] until this day: just as they abandoned me and served foreign gods, so they are also doing to you.

“Now, therefore, listen to their voice. Nevertheless, solemnly warn them and proclaim to them the right of the king who will reign over them.”

### [Treatise XXII]

Samuel spoke all the words of the Lord to the people who had asked a king from him, and said:

“This will be the right of the king who will rule over you: he will take your sons and place them in his chariots; he will make them his horsemen and runners before his chariots; he will appoint them as his tribunes and centurions, as plowers of his fields, reapers of his crops, and makers of his weapons and chariots.

“He will also make your daughters his perfumers, cooks, and bakers. He will take your fields, vineyards, and finest olive groves and give them to his servants. He will also tithe your crops and the produce of your vineyards, to give them to his eunuchs and servants. He will take your male and female slaves, your finest young men, and your donkeys, and put them to his work. He will tithe your flocks, and you will be his servants.

“You will cry out on that day because of your king whom you have chosen for yourselves, and the Lord will not answer you on that day” [Note: [Col. 0577D] The Vulgate books add: “because you asked for a king for yourselves”; the Hieronymian manuscripts do not know this reading, and it had formerly been marked with an obelus in accordance with the Hebrew text.]

But the people refused to listen to Samuel’s voice and said: “No! There shall be a king over us, and we too shall be like all the nations. Our king shall judge us, go out before us, and fight our battles for us” [Hebrew does not have “for us”].

Samuel heard all the words of the people and repeated them in the ears of the Lord. The Lord said to Samuel: “Listen to their voice and appoint a king over them” [Hebrew: “appoint a king for them”]. Samuel said to the men of Israel: “Let each man go to his city.”

### [Chapter IX]

There was a man from Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror [the manuscript: Seor], son of Bechorath [the manuscript: Beoreth], son of Aphiah, son of a Benjaminite, a mighty man of strength. He had a son named Saul, chosen and good, and there was no man among the Israelites better than he. From his shoulders upward he stood taller than all the people.

Now the donkeys of Saul’s father Kish had gone missing. Kish said to his son Saul: “Take one of the servants with you, rise, go, and search for the donkeys.” When they had passed through the hill country of Ephraim, the land of Shalishah, and had not found them, they also passed through the land of Shaalim, but they were not there. They went through the land of Benjamin as well, but they found nothing.

When they had come to the land of Zuph, Saul said to the servant who was with him [Note: [Col. 0577D] The Veronese manuscript adds “his,” in accordance with the Hebrew]: “Come, let us return, lest my father stop worrying about the donkeys and become anxious about us.”

The servant said to him: “Look, there is a man of God in this city, an honored man; everything he says certainly comes to pass. Now let us go there; perhaps he will tell us about the route by which we have come.”

Saul said to his servant: “Look, if we go, what shall we bring the man [Note: [Col. 0577D] Neither the Veronese manuscript nor the Hebrew text adds “of God” here]? The bread in our bags is gone, and we have no gift to give the man of God [Hebrew: “man of God”], nor anything else.”

Again the servant answered Saul and said: “Look, I have in my hand a quarter of a silver shekel. Let us give it to the man of God [Hebrew: “man of God”], so that he may tell us our way.”

(Formerly in Israel, when anyone went to consult God, he spoke in this way: “Come [the manuscript: “Come, let us go] and let us go to the Seer.” For the one who is now called a prophet was formerly called a Seer.)

Saul said to his servant: “Your proposal is good. Come, let us go.” And they went to the city where the man of God was.

As they were going up the slope of the city, they met young women coming out to draw water, and they said to them: “Is the Seer here?” They answered them [Hebrew does not have these words]: “He is. Look, he is ahead of you. Hurry now, for he came into the city today, because there is a sacrifice today for the people at the high place.

“As you enter the city, you will find him immediately, before he goes up to the high place to eat” [the manuscript and the Vulgate omit “to”]. “The people will not eat until he comes, because he blesses the sacrifice [Hebrew: the offering], and afterward those who have been invited eat. Now go up, for today you will find him.”

And they went up into the city.

### [Treatise XXIII]

As they were walking in the middle of the city, Samuel appeared, coming toward them as he was going up to the high place. The Lord had revealed Samuel’s ear one day before Saul’s arrival, saying:

“At this hour tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him as leader over my people Israel. He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines, because I have looked upon my people; for their cry has come to me.”

When Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said to him: “Look, this is the man of whom I told you. He shall rule my people.”

Saul approached Samuel in the middle of the gate and said: “Please tell me where the house of the Seer is.”

Samuel answered Saul, saying: “I am the Seer. Go up before me to the high place, so that you may eat with me today. In the morning I will send you away [Hebrew: “I will send you”], and I will tell you everything that is in your heart. As for the donkeys that went missing from you three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found [the manuscript adds: “the donkeys”]. And to whom shall belong all that is best in Israel? Is it not to you and to all the house of your father?”

Saul answered and said: “Am I not a Benjaminite, from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the last among all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? Why, then, have you spoken this word to me?”

Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the dining room [Hebrew: “into the chamber”], [Col. 0578C] and gave them a place at the head among those who had been invited. There were about thirty men.

Samuel said to the cook: “Bring the portion that I gave you and ordered you to set aside with you.” The cook lifted the shoulder and placed it before Saul.

Samuel said: “Look, what was left has been placed before you; eat, because it was deliberately reserved for you when I invited the people.” And Saul ate with Samuel that day.

They went down from the high place into the town, and he spoke with Saul on the rooftop [Note: [Col. 0578D] The Vulgate adds: “and Saul spread himself out on the rooftop and slept”; neither the Hebrew nor the better Latin manuscripts contain this.]

When they rose early, and day was already breaking, Samuel called Saul on the rooftop, saying: “Rise, so that I may send you away” [Hebrew: “send you”]. Saul rose, and the two of them—he and Samuel—went out.

As they were going down at the outskirts of the city, Samuel said to Saul: “Tell the servant to go on ahead of us and pass by; but you remain here for a little while, so that I may tell you the word of God.”

### [Treatise XXIV, Chapter X]

Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it over his head, kissed him, and said:

“Behold, the Lord has anointed you over his inheritance as prince [Note: [Col. 0578D] I would like to draw from this another proof of the authenticity of the Hieronymian version preserved by the Veronese manuscript: the entire passage—certainly not a short one—‘and you will deliver his people from the hands of their enemies who surround them. And this shall be your sign, that God has anointed you as prince’—is completely absent. [Col. 0579D] The Hebrew text also entirely lacks it. Although it might seem possible that it had once fallen out of the original because of the recurrence of the same word, through the customary scribal error, the very close agreement of the Latin version with the Hebrew exemplar proves that it was religiously derived from that source and contains neither more nor less. This is all the more evident because, had the intention been to supplement the passage, it would have been easy to take the words from the Greek, which reads: καὶ σὺ σώσεις αὐτὸν ἐκ χειρὸς ἐχθρῶν αὐτοῦ κυκλόθεν, καὶ τοῦτό σοι τὸ σημεῖον, ὅτι ἔχρισέ σε Κύριος ἐπὶ κληρονομίαν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἄρχοντα—‘and you will save him from the hand of his enemies round about, and this shall be your sign, that the Lord has anointed you over his inheritance as prince.’ The holy Father rightly prefaced this by saying that he was not conscious of having changed anything in the Hebrew truth. For this reason it is surprising here that neither the Hebrew commentator nor Martianay noticed this addition in the Latin manuscripts.]

“and you will deliver his people from the hands of their enemies who surround them. And this shall be your sign, that God has anointed you as prince.

“When you leave me today, you will find two men near Rachel’s tomb, in the territory of Benjamin, at Zelzah [Hebrew: “at Zelzah,” which is interpreted as “in the shadow,”] and they will say to you: ‘The donkeys that you went to search for have been found. Your father, having abandoned concern for the donkeys, is anxious about you and says: “What shall I do about my son?”’

“When you leave there and go farther and come to the oak of Tabor, three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you: one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine. When they greet you, they will give you two loaves, and you shall accept them from their hand.

“After this you will come to the hill of God, where there is a Philistine garrison. When you enter the city there, you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place, with a psaltery, a tambourine, a flute, and a lyre before them, while they themselves are prophesying.

“The Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them, and you will be changed into another man. When these signs come upon you, do whatever your hand finds to do, because God is with you.

“You shall go down ahead of me to Gilgal—for I shall come down to you—to offer an offering and sacrifice peace offerings [Hebrew: “to offer and sacrifice peace offerings”]. You shall wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”

### [Treatise XXV]

When Saul had turned his shoulder to leave Samuel, God changed his heart into another one, and all these signs came to pass that day.

They came to the aforementioned hill, and behold, a band of prophets met him. The Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied in their midst.

All who had known him yesterday and the day before, when they saw that he was with the prophets and prophesying, said to one another: “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”

One answered another, saying: “And who is their father?” Therefore it became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

When he had ceased prophesying, he came to the high place. Saul’s uncle said to him and to his servant: “Where did you go?”

They answered: “To search for the donkeys. When we did not find them, we went to Samuel.”

His uncle said to him: “Tell me what Samuel said to you.”

Saul said to his uncle: “He told us that the donkeys had been found.” But he did not tell him what Samuel had said concerning the matter of the kingdom.

Samuel summoned the people before the Lord at Mizpah and said to the Israelites:

“Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt [Col. 0580A] and rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you. But today you have rejected your God, who alone saved you from all your evils and tribulations, and you have said: “No, but appoint a king over us”’ [Hebrew: “and you said to him that you would appoint a king over us”].

“Now, therefore, stand before the Lord by your tribes and by your clans.”
