Samuel brought forward all the tribes of Israel, and the lot fell upon the tribe of Benjamin. He brought forward the tribe of Benjamin and its clans, and the lot fell upon the clan of Matri, and it came down to Saul the son of Kish.

They searched for him, but he was not found. After this they consulted the Lord as to whether he would come there [Hebrew: “whether the man would come there”].

The Lord answered: “Look, he is hidden at home” [Hebrew: “among the baggage”].

So they ran and brought him from there. He stood in the midst of the people and was taller than all the people from the shoulder upward.

### [Treatise XXVI]

Samuel said to all the people: “Surely you see the one whom the Lord has chosen, for there is none like him among all the people.”

All the people shouted and said: “Long live the king!”

Samuel spoke the law [Hebrew: “the judgment”] of the kingdom to the people, wrote it in a book, and placed it before the Lord. Then Samuel dismissed all the people, each to his own house.

Saul also went to his house in Gibeah, and with him went part of the army, those whose hearts God had touched. But the worthless men said: “Can this man save us?” They despised him and brought him no gifts; but he pretended not to hear.

### [Chapter XI]

[Note: [Col. 0580D] The Vulgate places before this: “And it happened about a month later.” These words are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the more carefully corrected Latin books.]

Nahash the Ammonite went up and began to fight against Jabesh-gilead [Hebrew: “and encamped against Jabesh-gilead”]. All the men of Jabesh said to Nahash: “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.”

Nahash the Ammonite answered them: “On this condition I will make a treaty with you: that I gouge out the right eyes of all of you and make you a reproach throughout all Israel.”

The elders of Jabesh said to him: “Grant us seven days, so that we may send messengers throughout all the territory of Israel; and if there is no one to defend [Hebrew: “save”] us, we will come out to you.”

The messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and spoke these words [the Vulgate adds: “these”] in the hearing of the people. All the people raised their voices and wept.

And behold, Saul was coming behind the oxen from the field, and he said: “What is wrong with the people that they are weeping?” They told him the words of the men of Jabesh.

When Saul heard these words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and his anger burned fiercely. He took both oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel by the hand of messengers, saying: “Whoever does not come out and follow Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen.”

Fear [Hebrew: “terror”] from the Lord seized the people, and they came out as one man.

### [Treatise XXVII]

He mustered them at Bezek, and the Israelites numbered three hundred thousand; the men of Judah numbered thirty thousand.

They said to the messengers who had come: “Thus shall you say to the men who are in Jabesh-gilead: ‘Tomorrow there will be deliverance for you, when the sun grows hot.’”

The messengers came and announced this to the men of Jabesh, who rejoiced. They said: “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do with us whatever seems good to you.”

When the next day came, Saul divided the people into three parts. He entered the middle of the camp during the morning watch and struck Ammon until the day grew hot. The survivors were scattered, so that not even two of them remained together.

The people said to Samuel: “Who is this man who said, ‘Saul shall reign over us?’ [Note: [Col. 0581D] The Veronese manuscript places the negative particle before “he shall not reign,” in accordance with the Greek οὐ βασιλεύσει, “he shall not reign,” which may perhaps be the more suitable reading. The current Hebrew exemplar, however, does not have the particle. The Vulgate books prefer the form under an interrogative sign.]

“Give us the men, and we will kill them.”

Saul said: “No one shall be killed on this day, because today the Lord has brought salvation in Israel.”

Samuel said to the people: “Come, let us go to Gilgal, and there let us renew the kingdom.”

All the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the Lord at Gilgal, and they sacrificed peace offerings there before the Lord. Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced there exceedingly.

### [Treatise XXVIII, Chapter XII]

Samuel said to all Israel:

“Behold, I have listened to your voice in everything you said to me, and I have appointed a king over you. And now the king walks before you. I have grown old and gray; and behold, my sons are with you. I have lived before you from my youth until this day. Here I am.

“Speak against me before the Lord and before his Anointed: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or donkey; whether I have falsely accused anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have accepted a gift from anyone’s hand. I will disregard it today and restore it to you.”

They said: “You have not falsely accused us, nor oppressed us, nor taken anything from anyone’s hand.”

He said to them: “The Lord is witness against you, and his Anointed is witness on this day, that you have found nothing in my hand.”

They said: “He is witness.”

Samuel said to the people: “The Lord [Hebrew: ‘And he said: “Witness”; the subject ‘the Lord’ is understood], who made Moses and Aaron and brought our ancestors up from the land of Egypt.”

[Col. 0581D] “Now, therefore, stand, [Note: [Col. 0582D] The Veronese manuscript reads “so that I may contend in judgment,” instead of “and”; the Hebrew particle *ve* admits both interpretations. Symmachus, however, preferred “so that,” ἵνα διακριθῶ, “so that I may be judged/contend in judgment.”] and I will contend in judgment against you before the Lord concerning all the mercies of the Lord that he showed to you and to your ancestors:

“How Jacob entered Egypt, and your ancestors cried out to the Lord; and the Lord sent Moses and Aaron, and brought your ancestors out of Egypt, and settled them in this place. But they forgot the Lord their God, and he handed them over [Hebrew: “sold them”] into the hand of Sisera, commander [Hebrew: “prince”] of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the king of Moab; and they fought against them.

“Afterward they cried out to the Lord and said: ‘We have sinned, because we abandoned the Lord and served the Baalim and the Ashtaroth. Now, therefore, rescue us from the hand of our enemies, and we will serve you.’

“The Lord sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel, and rescued you from the hand of your enemies round about, and you lived securely.

“When you saw that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, had come against you, you said to me: ‘No, but a king shall rule over us,’ although the Lord your God was your king.

“Now, therefore, here is your king whom you chose and asked for. Behold, the Lord has given you a king.

“If you fear the Lord, serve him, listen to his voice, and do not provoke the mouth of the Lord, then both you and the king who rules over you will follow the Lord your God.

“But if you do not listen to the voice of the Lord, but provoke the word [Hebrew: “mouth”] of the Lord, then the hand of the Lord will be against you and against your ancestors.

“Even now, stand and see this great thing that the Lord will do before your eyes. Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the Lord, and he will give thunder and rain. Then you will know and see that you have done a great evil in the sight of the Lord by asking a king for yourselves.”

### [Treatise XXIX]

Samuel cried out to the Lord, and the Lord gave thunder and rain on that day. All the people feared the Lord and Samuel exceedingly.

All the people said to Samuel: “Pray for your servants to the Lord your God, so that we may not die. For we have added this evil to all our sins: that we asked for a king for ourselves.”

Samuel said to the people: “Do not be afraid. You have indeed done all this evil; nevertheless, do not turn away from following the Lord, but serve the Lord with all your heart. Do not turn aside after empty things, which will not benefit you or rescue you, because they are empty.

“The Lord will not abandon his people, for the sake of his great name, because the Lord has sworn to make you his people.

“As for me, far be it from me to commit this sin against the Lord, by ceasing to pray for you. I will teach you the good and right way.

“Therefore fear the Lord and serve him in truth and with all your heart. For you have seen the great things that he has done for you.

“But if you persist in wickedness, both you and your king will perish together.”

### [Chapter XIII]

Saul was a son of one year when he began to reign, and he reigned over Israel for two years. Saul chose three thousand men from Israel: two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and on Mount Bethel, while one thousand were with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin. He sent the rest of the people away, each to his own tent.

Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison that was at Gibeah. When the Philistines heard this, Saul sounded the trumpet throughout the land, saying: “Let the Hebrews hear!”

All Israel heard the report: “Saul has struck the Philistine garrison,” and Israel rose up against the Philistines. The people shouted after Saul at Gilgal.

The Philistines gathered to fight against Israel: thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and the remaining common people, as numerous as the sand on the seashore.

They went up and encamped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven [the manuscript: Bathaven]. When the Israelites saw that they were in a strait—for the people were distressed—they hid themselves in caves, thickets, rocks, holes, and cisterns.

The Hebrews crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. While Saul was still at Gilgal, all the people who followed him were terrified.

They waited seven days, according to Samuel’s appointed time, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people scattered from him. Saul said: “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” And he offered the burnt offering.

### [Treatise XXX]

When he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel was coming. Saul went out to meet him and greet him.

Samuel said to him: “What have you done?”

Saul answered: “Because I saw that the people were scattering from me, and you had not come by the appointed days, while the Philistines had gathered at Michmash, I said: ‘Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not appeased the face of the Lord.’ Compelled by necessity, I offered the burnt offering.”

Samuel said to Saul: “You have acted foolishly and have not kept the commandment of the Lord your God [the manuscript omits ‘your God’], which he commanded you. For if you had not done this, the Lord would by now have established your kingdom over Israel forever. But now your kingdom shall certainly not continue.

“The Lord has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and the Lord has commanded him to be leader over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded” [the manuscript: “what the Lord had commanded”].

Samuel rose and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin.

[Note: [Col. 0583C] We also find many additions at this point in the Latin manuscripts of Jerome’s translation. As we have already said, these derive from the Seventy Translators and are placed in the manuscripts according to the system noted above [Col. 571, note c]. In the best manuscript of Corbie, number 11, copied eight hundred years ago, there is this particular feature: each line or verse comprising the addition is preceded by an obelus, indicating that these words are foreign and borrowed from elsewhere. It will not be useless to display this before the eyes of learned readers, who will thereby have a criterion for judging other similar additions. This is how the matter appears in the manuscript:

“÷ Benjamin. And the remaining ÷ people went up ÷ after Saul to meet the people, ÷ who were attacking ÷ them as they came ÷ from Gilgal to Gibeah, ÷ on the hill of Benjamin.”

If these signs were found in their proper places, everyone would immediately recognize what in the Latin copies was Hieronymian and what was borrowed from the Septuagint Translators. But because the negligence of scribes removed such signs, it became impossible for the Latins to avoid using both editions indiscriminately, and to attribute to Jerome what belonged to the Septuagint. Thus he rightly complains about this in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela: “And from this,” he says, “among you and among most people an error arises, because through the negligence of scribes, with the critical marks and asterisks removed, the entire distinction is confused.” [Col. 0584D] MART. —The Vulgate books add: “And the rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the people who were attacking them as they came from Gilgal to Gibeah, on the hill of Benjamin.” Because of the recurrence of the same name, Benjamin, with which the sentence ends, this period might seem to have fallen out of the Hebrew exemplar through the common and easily made error of scribes. Yet, what is important for our purpose, it is missing not only from the Hebrew and Chaldean texts but also from nearly all the manuscripts of Jerome’s version. The Vulgate books that retain it borrowed it from some Greek codices of the Seventy. Martianay found each verse of this addition marked beforehand with an obelus in the Corbie manuscript.]

Saul numbered the people who were found with him, about six hundred men. Saul, Jonathan his son, and the people who were found with them were at Gibeah of Benjamin, while the Philistines had encamped at Michmash.

Three bands went out from the Philistine camp to raid. One band went along the road to Ophrah [the manuscript: Ephra], toward the land of Saul. Another went along the road to Beth-horon. The third turned toward the road of the border that overlooks the valley of Zeboim, toward the wilderness.

Now no blacksmith [Hebrew omits this phrase] was to be found throughout all the land of Israel. For the Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews make a sword or spear.

So all Israel went down to the Philistines, each to sharpen his plowshare, mattock, axe, or hoe. The edges of the plowshares, mattocks, pitchforks, and axes were blunted, even to the point of straightening the goad.

When the day of battle came, no sword or spear was found in the hand of all the people who were with Saul and Jonathan, except Saul and Jonathan his son.

The Philistine garrison went out to cross over toward Michmash.

### [Chapter XIV]

And it happened one day that Jonathan son of Saul said to his young armor-bearer: “Come, and let us cross over to the Philistine garrison, which is beyond that place.” But he did not inform his father of this [the Hebrew does not have this]. Saul, meanwhile, was staying at the far end of Gibeah [Note: The Veronese manuscript is silent here. “Gibeah,” according to the Greek exemplar; shortly afterward, instead of *Magron* it reads “in the field of Gibeah,” contrary to the Hebrew text.], beneath the pomegranate tree that was in Magron; and the people with him numbered about six hundred men.

And Ahijah son of Ahitub, brother of Ichabod, son of Phinehas, who had been born to Eli the priest of the Lord at Shiloh [the Hebrew has: “son of Phinehas, son of Eli the priest of the Lord at Shiloh”], was carrying the ephod. But the people did not know [Note: The Veronese manuscripts read more correctly, “that he had gone,” etc. The Hebrew likewise has “that,” and the Greek has ὅτι.] where Jonathan had gone.

Now between the ascents by which Jonathan was attempting to cross over to the Philistine garrison were jutting rocks, cliffs broken off on both sides in the manner of teeth. The name of one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh. One cliff projected toward the north [Col. 0585A], opposite Michmash, and the other [Note: The same manuscript has “toward the south”; the Hebrew likewise has this.] toward the south, opposite Gibeah.

### [Treatise XXXI]

Jonathan said to his young armor-bearer: “Come, let us cross over to the garrison of these uncircumcised men, if perhaps the Lord may act for [the Hebrew omits “for”] us; for nothing is difficult for the Lord, whether to save by many or by few.”

His armor-bearer said to him: “Do everything that pleases your heart. Go wherever you wish; I shall be with you wherever you want.”

And Jonathan said: “Look, we are crossing over to these men. When we appear to them, if they speak to us in this way: ‘Stay until we come to you,’ let us remain in our position and not go up to them. But if they say: ‘Come up to us,’ let us go up, because the Lord has delivered them into our hands. This shall be our sign.”

So the two of them appeared before the Philistine garrison. And the Philistines said: “Look, Hebrews are coming out of the caves in which they had hidden themselves.”

The men of the garrison spoke to Jonathan and his armor-bearer and said: “Come up to us, and we shall show you something.”

Jonathan said to his armor-bearer: “Let us go up; follow me [the Hebrew has: “Go up behind me”], for the Lord has delivered them into the hand of Israel.”

Jonathan went up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer following him [Note: This agrees almost exactly with the Veronese Vulgate manuscripts: “crawling with hands and feet.” The Hebrew literally has “on his hands and on his feet.”] Some fell before Jonathan, while others were killed by his armor-bearer as he followed him [the Hebrew has: “And they fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer, following him, killed them”].

The first slaughter in which Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men took place within roughly half a *jugerum*, the amount a yoke of oxen normally plows in a day. And a miracle occurred in the camp, throughout the fields. All the people of the garrison, even those who had gone out to plunder, were also terrified; the earth was thrown into confusion, and something like a miracle from God occurred.

Saul’s watchmen, who were in Gibeah of Benjamin, looked, and behold, the multitude was prostrate and scattering here and there. Saul said to the people who were with him: “Search and see who has gone away from us.”

When they searched, it was found that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were absent.

Saul said to Ahijah: “Bring the ark of God.” For the ark of God was there on that day with the children of Israel.

While Saul was speaking to the priest, a great tumult arose in the Philistine camp. It gradually increased and resounded more loudly. Saul said to the priest: “Withdraw your hand.”

Then Saul and all the people who were with him shouted together and came as far as the place of battle. And behold, each man’s sword had been turned against his neighbor, and there was a very great slaughter [the manuscript does not have this clause].

The Hebrews who had formerly been with the Philistines, yesterday and the day before, and who had gone up with them into the camp, returned so that they might be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan. All the Israelites who had hidden themselves in Mount Ephraim, hearing that the Philistines had fled, joined their countrymen in the battle.

[Note: The Vulgate manuscripts add: “And they were with Saul, about ten thousand men.” This clause is found only in the Septuagint, and not here, but three verses later.]

And the Lord saved Israel on that day. The battle reached as far as Beth-aven. And the Israelite man joined himself to his own people on that day.

### [Treatise XXXII]

Saul adjured the people, saying: “Cursed be the man who eats bread before evening, until I have avenged myself on my enemies.”

And none of the people tasted bread. All the common people of the land came into the forest, where there was honey on the surface of the field. The people entered the forest, and behold, honey was flowing; no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.

Jonathan, however, had not heard his father when he adjured the people. He extended the tip of the staff that he held in his hand and dipped it into a honeycomb. Then he brought his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened.

One of the people answered and said: “Your father bound the people by an oath, saying: ‘Cursed be the man who eats bread today’”—and the people had grown faint.

Jonathan said: “My father has troubled the land. You yourselves have seen that my eyes brightened because I tasted a little of this honey. How much more would it have been if the people had eaten from the spoil of their enemies that they found! Would not the slaughter of the Philistines have been greater?”

So on that day they struck the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon [the manuscript has Ahilon].

### [Treatise XXXIII]

The people were exceedingly weary. They turned to the spoil, took sheep, oxen, and calves, and slaughtered them on the ground; and the people ate with the blood.

They reported to Saul, saying that the people had sinned against the Lord by eating with the blood.

He said: “You have acted treacherously. Roll a large stone to me now.”

And Saul said: “Disperse among the common people and tell them: Let each man bring me his ox and his ram, slaughter it upon this stone, and eat; then you will not sin against the Lord by eating with the blood.”

So all the people brought each his ox in his hand until night [the manuscript omits this phrase], and they slaughtered them there.

Saul built an altar to the Lord; then he began for the first time [the Hebrew omits this] to build an altar to the Lord.

Saul said: “Let us attack the Philistines by night and devastate them until morning, leaving none of them alive.”

The people said: “Do whatever seems good in your eyes.”

The priest said: “Let us draw near here to God.”

Saul consulted God: “Shall I pursue the Philistines? Will you deliver them into the hand of Israel?” But he did not answer him on that day.

### [Treatise XXXIV]

Saul said: “Bring here all the corners of the people, and know and see through whom this sin has occurred today. As the Lord, the savior of Israel, lives, even if it has been done through Jonathan my son [the manuscripts and the Vulgate omit “this”], he shall surely die.”

No one among all the people contradicted him.

He said to all Israel: “You shall be on one side, and I and my son Jonathan shall be on the other side.”

[Note: Only the Canon has “on one side,” written in Hebrew *leever ehhad*, that is, “at one crossing,” or, in the same sense, “on the other side,” “from the other flank,” etc. MART. — The Veronese manuscript, together with the manuscript called the Martian Canon, has “on one side,” more closely following the Hebrew.]

The people answered Saul: “Do whatever seems good in your eyes.”

Saul said to the Lord [the Hebrew has: “to the Lord God of Israel”]:

> “Lord God of Israel [the Hebrew has: “God, Lord God of Israel”], give a sign.”

[Note: The Latin manuscripts of Jerome’s version frequently introduce great confusion, with some verses from the edition of the Septuagint interpreters inserted into it. Since the readings of the same context differ in many places, it is scarcely, if at all, possible to recognize which reading is genuine and properly belongs to the holy Doctor. This is demonstrated most clearly by the following variant readings of this verse.

> The larger Corbie manuscript, number 1, reads: “And Saul said to the Lord: God of Israel, give a sign.”
>
> Another manuscript, number 13, reads: “And Saul said to the Lord God of Israel: give a sign.” A second hand altered this to: “And Saul said to the Lord: Lord God of Israel, give a sign.”
>
> In the Royal manuscript, the Colbertine manuscript 181, the Corbie manuscript 11, and Saint-Germain 5, we read: “And Saul said to the Lord God of Israel: Lord God, give a sign.” The printed editions and our manuscript no. 164 have the same reading, adding only the name “Israel” after “Lord God.”
>
> This discrepancy among the readings was caused by one little Hebrew word and by the repetition of the names of God. For in Hebrew it reads: *Vaijomer schaoul el Adonai elohe Israel hava thamim*, which may be interpreted in several ways because of the word *el*, placed before *Adonai*, or “Jehovah.” For *el* is one of the names of God, but it is also a preposition corresponding to our Latin *ad*, “to.” Thus it may be read: “And Saul said to the Lord: God of Israel, give a sign.” Or, taking *el* as a divine name: “And Saul said: God, Lord God of Israel, give a sign.”
>
> In this manner the scholiast of the Canon of Hebrew Truth translated it into Latin, although he had stated in another scholion that the Hebrew reads: “And Saul said to the Lord God of Israel,” etc.
>
> We have printed this passage according to what is read in the actual text of our Canon and in two other very ancient manuscripts, the Colbertine, the Anician, and the great Saint-Germain manuscript no. 3. We do not deny that in the other manuscripts the word “Lord” in the middle is redundant, since nothing occurs in the Hebrew volumes corresponding to this name. Among so many variants, therefore, we declare that reading complete which is represented by the larger Corbie manuscript, first cited above; for in this excellent exemplar nothing is omitted and nothing is superfluous, as experts in the Hebrew language will readily concede. MART.]

And Jonathan and Saul were seized by the lot, while the people went free.

Saul said: “Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan.” And Jonathan was taken.

Saul said to Jonathan: “Tell me what you have done.”

Jonathan disclosed it to him and said: “I tasted a little honey on the tip of the staff that was in my hand; and behold, I am dying.”

Saul said: “May God do this to me, and add this also: you shall surely die, Jonathan.”

The people said to Saul: “Then Jonathan must die—the one who has brought about this great salvation in Israel? This must not be! As the Lord lives, not a hair from his head shall fall to the ground, for he has worked with God today.”

So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.

Saul withdrew and did not pursue the Philistines; and the Philistines went to their own places.

Saul, having established his kingdom over Israel, fought all around against all his enemies: against Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah [the manuscript has Suba], and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he prevailed.

After gathering an army, he struck Amalek and rescued Israel from the hand of its plunderers.

The sons of Saul were Jonathan, Jesui, and Melchishua. The names of his two daughters were: the name of the firstborn, Merab, and the name of the younger, Michal.

The name of Saul’s wife was Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz; and the name of the commander of his army was Abner [the Hebrew has Abiner only here], son of Ner, Saul’s cousin.

Kish had been Saul’s father, and Ner, father of Abner, was son of Abiel.

There was a powerful war against the Philistines throughout all the days of Saul. Whenever Saul saw any strong man suited for battle, he joined him to himself.

### [Treatise XXXV, Chapter XV]

Samuel said to Saul: “The Lord sent me to anoint you as king over his people Israel. Now, therefore, listen to the voice of the Lord. Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have taken account of all that Amalek did to Israel, how he opposed him on the way when he came up from Egypt.

“Now, therefore, go and strike Amalek, and destroy all that belongs to him; do not spare him. [Note: The Vulgate manuscripts add, “and do not covet anything from his possessions,” a phrase found in no original text but only in certain Latin books; it has long been marked for deletion with an obelus.] But kill man and woman, child and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.”

Saul commanded the people and reviewed them like lambs: two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men of Judah.

When Saul came as far as the city of Amalek, he laid an ambush in the torrent.

Saul said to the Kenite: “Go away, withdraw, and descend [Note: Eleven manuscripts read “depart” instead of “descend.” The author of the Questions on the Hebrew Scriptures concerning the Books of Kings agrees with this, as does the Chaldean paraphrast, in whom we read: “Go, withdraw, separate yourself from among,” etc. The Hebrew has *radu*, meaning “descend.” Certainly the scribal error between *discedite*, “depart,” and *descendite*, “descend,” is an easy one. MART.] from among the Amalekites, lest I involve you with them. For you showed kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up from Egypt.”

And the Kenite withdrew from the midst of Amalek.

Saul struck Amalek from Havilah until you come to Shur, which is opposite Egypt. He seized Agag king of Amalek alive, but he put all the common people to the sword.

Saul and the people spared Agag, as well as the best sheep and herds, garments, rams, and everything that was beautiful, and they were unwilling to destroy these. But whatever was worthless and rejected, that they destroyed.

### [Treatise XXXVI]

The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying: “I regret that I made Saul king, because he has abandoned me and has not fulfilled my words in action.”

Samuel was grieved, and he cried out to the Lord all night.

When Samuel rose during the night to go to Saul in the morning, it was reported to him that Saul had come to Carmel, had erected a triumphal arch for himself, and, turning back, had gone down to Gilgal.

Samuel came to Saul [Note: The Vulgate manuscripts also add the words occurring between the two mentions of Saul: “and Saul was offering a burnt offering to the Lord from the first of the spoils which he had brought from Amalek. And when Samuel came to Saul.” These derive from the Greek Septuagint.], and Saul said to him: “Blessed are you by the Lord. I have fulfilled the word of the Lord.”

Samuel said: “Then what is this sound of flocks that resounds in my ears, and of herds that I hear?”

Saul said: “They brought them from Amalek, for the people spared the best sheep and herds in order to sacrifice them to the Lord your God. The rest we killed [the Hebrew has: ‘we destroyed’].”

Samuel said to Saul: “Allow me, and I shall tell you what the Lord said to me during the night.”

He said to him: “Speak.”

Samuel said: “Were you not small in your own eyes, yet made head among the tribes of Israel? The Lord anointed you king over Israel, and the Lord sent you on the way and said: ‘Go and kill [the Hebrew has: “destroy”] the sinners, the Amalekites, and fight against them until they are exterminated [Note: The Veronese manuscript has more correctly, in accordance with the Hebrew text, “and you shall fight.”]’?

“Why, then, did you not listen to the voice of the Lord? Instead, you turned to the spoil and did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord.”

Saul said to Samuel: “Indeed, I have listened to the voice of the Lord. I walked in the way by which the Lord sent me, and I brought back Agag king of Amalek, and I killed Amalek. But the people took sheep and oxen from the spoil, the firstfruits of what had been slaughtered, to sacrifice to the Lord your God [Note: The Veronese manuscript agrees with the Vulgate manuscripts in reading “your.” But the Hebrew also prefers “your” to “your God.”] at Gilgal.”

### [Treatise XXXVII]

Samuel said: “Does the Lord desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, rather than that the voice of the Lord be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices, and listening better than offering the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply like the crime of idolatry.

“Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, he has rejected you from being king.”

Saul said to Samuel: “I have sinned, because I transgressed the word of the Lord and your words, fearing the people and obeying their voice. But now, please bear my sin, and return with me, so that I may worship the Lord.”

Samuel said to Saul: “I will not return with you, because you rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you from being king over Israel.”

Samuel turned to leave, but Saul seized the edge of his cloak, and it was torn.

Samuel said to him: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor, who is better than you.

“Moreover, the victorious one in [the Hebrew omits “in”] Israel will not spare [the Hebrew has: “Moreover, Israel’s victorious one will not lie”], and he will not be turned by repentance, for he is not a man that he should repent.”

Saul said: “I have sinned, but now honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, so that I may worship the Lord your God.”

Samuel returned and followed Saul [Note: Here the Veronese manuscript departs farther from the Hebrew, reading: “And Saul followed him.” The Hebrew literally has: “Samuel returned after Saul.”], and Saul worshiped the Lord.

### [Treatise XXXVIII]

Samuel said: “Bring Agag king of Amalek to me.”

Agag was brought to him, very fat [the Vulgate adds: “and trembling”].

Agag said: “Does bitter death thus separate?”

Samuel said: “As your sword made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women.”

Samuel cut Agag to pieces before the Lord at Gilgal.

Samuel went to Ramah, while Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul [the Vulgate omits “of Saul”].

Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death. Nevertheless, Samuel mourned for Saul, because the Lord regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.

### [Treatise XXXIX, Chapter XVI]

The Lord said to Samuel: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and come; I shall send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.”

Samuel said: “How shall I go? Saul will hear of it and kill me.”

The Lord said: “You shall take a calf [the Hebrew has: ‘a heifer’] from the herd in your hand and say: ‘I have come to sacrifice to the Lord.’ You shall call Jesse to the sacrifice, and I shall show you what you must do; you shall anoint the one whom I point out [the Hebrew has: ‘whom I tell’] to you.”

Samuel did as the Lord had spoken to him [the Hebrew omits this; the scholiast notes that the Veronese manuscript likewise actually omits it].

He came to Bethlehem, and the elders of the city were astonished [the Hebrew has: “were afraid”]. They came to meet him and said: “Is your entrance peaceful?”

He said: “Peaceful. I have come to sacrifice to the Lord. Sanctify yourselves and come with me, so that I may sacrifice.”

He sanctified Jesse and his sons and called them to the sacrifice.

### [Treatise XL]

When they had entered, he saw Eliab and said: “Is his anointed one before the Lord?”

The Lord said to Samuel: “Do not look at his face or at the height of his stature, for I have rejected him. I do not judge according to a man’s appearance; a man sees what is visible, but the Lord looks upon the heart.”

Jesse called Abinadab and brought him before Samuel. He said: “The Lord has not chosen this one either.”

Jesse brought Shamma [the manuscript has Summa], of whom he said: “The Lord has not chosen this one either” [the Hebrew has: “In this one also”].

Jesse brought seven of his sons before Samuel, and Samuel said to Jesse: “The Lord has not chosen any of these.”

Samuel said to Jesse: “Are these all your sons?”

He answered: “There is still one little one left, and he is tending the sheep.”

Samuel said to Jesse: “Send and bring him, for we shall not sit down [the Hebrew has: ‘we shall not surround the table’] until he comes here.”

He sent and brought him in. He was ruddy, handsome in appearance, and beautiful of face.

The Lord said: “Rise and anoint him, for this is he.”

### [Treatise XLI]

Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. The Spirit of the Lord came upon David [Note: Previously it had been written with an erroneous transposition: “and for the remainder from that day.” The Veronese manuscript corrects it.] from that day onward. Samuel rose and went to Ramah.

### [Treatise XLII]

The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord tormented him.

Saul’s servants said to him: “Behold, an evil spirit from God torments you. Let our lord command, and your servants who are before you will seek a man skilled in playing the lyre, so that whenever the evil spirit from God seizes you, he may play with his hand and you may feel better.”

Saul said to his servants: “Find me someone who plays well and bring him to me.”

One of the young men answered and said: “Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite who knows how to play, is extremely strong, a warrior, prudent in speech, and handsome; and the Lord is with him.”

### [Treatise XLIII]

Saul sent messengers to Jesse, saying: “Send me David your son, who is with the flocks.”

Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin [the Hebrew has: “a wineskin”] of wine, and one young goat, and sent them through David his son to Saul.

David came to Saul and stood before him. Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armor-bearer.

Saul sent to Jesse, saying: “Let David stand in my presence, for he has found favor in my eyes.”

Whenever the Spirit of God seized Saul, David took the lyre and played it with his hand; Saul was refreshed and felt better, for the evil spirit departed from him.

[Note: The Vulgate manuscripts have: “Whenever the evil spirit of the Lord seized Saul,” which is farther from the Hebrew text, which here does not add “evil.”]

### [Treatise XLIV, Chapter XVII]

The Philistines gathered their armies for battle and assembled at Soccho [Note: The Veronese manuscript consistently gives *Socchot*, closer to the Hebrew; Symmachus likewise has Σοχχώθ. Shortly afterward, following the same manuscript, we have printed *Dommim* with a double *m*.] in Judah. They camped between Soccho and Azekah, in the borders of Dammim [the Hebrew has: Dammim].

Saul and the men [the Vulgate has: “sons”] of Israel gathered and came into the Valley of the Terebinth. They drew up their battle line to fight against the Philistines.

The Philistines stood on the mountain on one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side, with the valley between them.

A bastard [or illegitimate man] came out from the Philistine camp, named Goliath, from Gath, six cubits and a span tall. He had a bronze helmet on his head and wore hooked mail [the Hebrew has: “scale armor”] [Note: Both readings suit this sentence, since soldiers used both scale armor and hooked armor. Hence Virgil speaks of armor with a double scale, and in Book I of the *Aeneid* of a cuirass fastened with hooks. The scales and hooks of armor were chains arranged and interlinked in the manner of scales and hooks. MART.].

The weight of his coat of mail was five thousand bronze shekels. He had bronze greaves on his legs, and a bronze shield covered his shoulders.

The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam. The iron of his spear weighed six hundred iron shekels, and his armor-bearer went before him.

Standing, he shouted against the ranks of Israel and said to them: “Why have you come prepared for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose a man from among yourselves and let him come down to single combat.

“If he is able to fight with me and strike me, we shall be your servants. But if I prevail and strike him, you shall be servants, and you shall serve us.”

The Philistine said: “Today I have reproached the ranks of Israel. Give me a man, and let him enter single combat with me.”

When Saul and all the Israelite men heard these words of the Philistine, they were terrified and greatly afraid.

David was the son of an Ephrathite man from Bethlehem of Judah, whose name was Jesse. He had eight sons, and in the days of Saul he was an old man, advanced in years among men [the Hebrew has: “and entering among men”].

His three eldest sons had gone after Saul to battle. The names of his three sons who had gone to war were: Eliab the firstborn, Abinadab the second, and Shamma the third. David was the youngest.

### [Treatise XLV]

After the three eldest had followed Saul, David went back and forth from Saul in order to tend his father’s flock at Bethlehem.

The Philistine came out morning and evening and stood there for forty days.

### [Treatise XLVI]

Jesse said to his son David: “Take an ephah [the Hebrew has: ‘an ephah’] of roasted grain for your brothers, these ten loaves of bread, and run to the camp to your brothers. You shall also carry these ten portions of cheese to the commander [manuscript: “carry”], and visit your brothers to see whether they are doing well; and learn with whom they have been stationed.”

Saul, and they, and all the sons of Israel were fighting against the Philistines in the Valley of the Terebinth [the Hebrew has: “If they are doing well, and you shall take their pledge. But Saul…”].

David rose early, entrusted the flock to a keeper, and departed, laden as Jesse had commanded him.

He came to the place of Magala and to the army, which had gone out to battle and was shouting in the engagement. Israel had drawn up its battle line, and the Philistines too were prepared opposite them.

David left the supplies that he had brought under the hand of the keeper of the baggage and ran to the place of battle. He asked whether everything was going well with his brothers.

While he was still speaking with them, behold, that bastard, coming up, appeared: the Philistine named Goliath, from Gath, from the camp [the Hebrew has: “from the battle line”] of the Philistines. As he spoke these same words, David heard him.

When all the Israelites saw the man, they fled from his face, fearing him greatly [the Hebrew omits “him”].

One of the Israelites said: “Have you seen this man who is coming up? He has come up to reproach Israel. The king will enrich the man who strikes him with great wealth, give him his daughter, and make his father’s house free from tribute in Israel [the Hebrew has: ‘make his father’s house free in Israel’].”

### [Treatise XLVII]

David said to the men who were standing with him: “What will be given to the man [the Hebrew has: ‘What will happen to the man’] who strikes this Philistine and removes reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine who has reproached the armies of the living God?”

The people repeated the same statement to him, saying: “This shall be given [the Hebrew has: ‘This shall happen’] to the man who strikes him.”

When Eliab his older brother heard him speaking with the others, he was angry with David and said: “Why have you come, and why have you abandoned those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and the wickedness of your heart, for you came down to see the battle.”

David said: “What have I done? Is it not merely a word?”

He turned away from him slightly toward another and repeated the same statement. The people answered him with the same words as before.

The words David had spoken were heard and reported in Saul’s presence.

When he was brought before Saul, he spoke to him: “Let no one’s heart fail because of him. I, your servant, will go and fight this Philistine.”

Saul said to David: “You cannot resist this Philistine or fight against him, for you are a boy, whereas he has been a warrior from his youth.”

David said to Saul: “Your servant was tending his father’s flock, and a lion or bear would come and carry off a ram from the middle of the flock. I pursued them, struck them, and snatched it from their mouth; when they rose up against me, I seized them by the jaw, strangled them, and killed them.

“I, your servant, killed both the lion and the bear [the Hebrew has: ‘Your servant killed’]. Therefore this uncircumcised Philistine too shall be like one of them, because he dared to curse the army [the Hebrew has: ‘reproach the ranks’] of the living God.”

[Note: The Vulgate manuscripts insert the following addition: “Now I shall go and remove the reproach of the people, for who is this uncircumcised Philistine?” The Hebrew lacks it, as do the Septuagint themselves. Shortly afterward, the Veronese manuscript reads “army” instead of “to the army,” equally well.]

David said: “The Lord, who rescued me from the hand of the lion and from the hand of the bear, will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.”

Saul said to David: “Go, and may the Lord be with you.”

Saul clothed David in his garments, placed a bronze helmet on his head, and clothed him in a coat of mail.

David was girded with Saul’s sword over his garment and began to test whether he could walk while armed, for he had no experience of it.

David said to Saul: “I cannot walk in these, because I am not accustomed to them.”

He removed them, took his staff, which he always carried in his hands, chose five very smooth stones from the torrent, put them into the shepherd’s bag that he had with him, took his sling in his hand, and went out against the Philistine.

The Philistine went forward, walking and drawing near to David, with his armor-bearer before him.

When the Philistine looked and saw David, he despised him, for he was a youth, ruddy and handsome in appearance.

The Philistine said to David: “Am I a dog, that you come against me with a staff [the Hebrew has: ‘with staffs’]?”

The Philistine cursed David by his gods and said to David: “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth [the Hebrew has: ‘of the field’].”

David said to the Philistine: “You come against me with sword, spear, and shield, but I come against you in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have reproached.

“Today [Note: The Veronese manuscript, with the Vulgate manuscripts and the Greek, has “you reproached today, and you shall give,” etc. Shortly afterward it reads more correctly according to the Hebrew, “corpse” in the singular.] the Lord will give [the Hebrew has: ‘deliver’] you into my hand. I shall strike you, take your head from you, and give the corpses of the Philistine camp today to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, so that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.

“And all this assembly shall know that the Lord does not save by sword or spear; for the battle is the Lord’s, and he will deliver you into our hands.”

When the Philistine rose, came, and drew near against David, David hastened and ran toward the battle to meet the Philistine.

He put his hand into the bag, took out one stone, and hurled it with the sling [the Vulgate adds: “whirling it”]. He struck the Philistine on the forehead, and the stone became embedded in his forehead; and he fell face down upon the ground [the manuscript and Vulgate have: “upon the earth”].

David prevailed over the Philistine with sling and stone. He struck the Philistine and killed him.

David had no sword in his hand, so he ran, stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it from its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head.

When the Philistines saw that their champion [the Hebrew has: “their powerful man”] was dead, they fled.

The men of Israel and Judah rose up, shouted, and pursued the Philistines until they came to the valley and to the gates of Ekron. The wounded Philistines fell along the road from Shaaraim as far as Gath and as far as Ekron.

The children of Israel returned after pursuing the Philistines and raided their camp.

David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he placed his armor in his own tent.

At the time when Saul had seen David going out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army: “From what lineage does this youth descend, Abner?” [the Hebrew has: “When Saul saw David going out against the Philistine, he said to Abner the commander of the army: ‘Whose son is this?’”]

Abner said: “As your soul lives, O king, I do not know.”

The king said: “Ask whose son this boy is” [the Hebrew has: “this youth”].

When David returned after striking the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul, with the head of the Philistine in his hand.

Saul said to him: “From what family are you, young man?” [the Hebrew has: “Whose son are you?”]

David said: “I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite” [the Hebrew omits this].

[Col. 0595A] [T. XLVIII, Chapter XVIII.] And it came to pass, when he had finished speaking to Saul, that Jonathan’s soul was bound [Vulgate: “closely joined”] to David’s soul, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. Saul took him on that day and did not permit him to return to his father’s house.

[T. XLIX.] Jonathan and David entered into a covenant, for he loved him as his own soul. Jonathan stripped off the tunic with which he was clothed and gave it to David, together with his other garments, down to his sword, bow, and belt. David went out wherever Saul sent him, and [Hebrew lacks this] conducted himself wisely. Saul appointed him over the men of war, and he was acceptable in the eyes of all the people, and especially in the sight of Saul’s servants [Col. 0595B] [Hebrew: “of all the people and in the eyes of Saul’s servants”].

When David returned after striking down the Philistine, women came out from all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing in choruses to meet King Saul, with tambourines of joy and sistra. The women played and sang responsively:

“Saul has struck down his thousand,  
and David his ten thousand.”

[T. L.] Saul was exceedingly angry, and this saying displeased him [Note: [Col. 0595D] From this point onward, several very ancient leaves of another Veronese codex are available, written in what he calls majuscule letters, containing the Hieronymian version up to Chapter XXII of this book. We have compared them with the greatest care, and below shall cite their testimony under the designation “Capitular Membranes.” Here, meanwhile, they omit the word “this,” which is nevertheless present in the Hebrew.]

He said: “They have given David ten thousand, and to me they have given one thousand. What more can he have except the kingdom?” Thus Saul looked upon David with an evil eye from that day forward.

On the following day, an evil spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he prophesied in the middle of his house [Hebrew: “in the midst of the house”]. David, meanwhile, played with his hand as he did day after day. [Col. 0595C] Saul was holding a spear, and he hurled it, thinking that he could pin David to the wall. David turned aside from him twice.

Saul was afraid of David, because the Lord was with him and had departed from Saul. Therefore Saul removed him from his presence and made him commander over a thousand men [Hebrew lacks “men”]. He went out and came in before the people. David acted wisely in all his ways, and the Lord was with him.

Saul saw that he was exceedingly wise, and began to fear him [Hebrew: “and he feared him”]. All Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in before them.

[T. LI.] Saul said to David: “Behold, my elder daughter Merob [Hebrew: Merab]; I shall give her to you as wife. Only be a brave man [Hebrew: “be a man for me”] and fight the battles of the Lord.”

Saul was thinking: “Let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him.” David said to Saul: “Who am I, or what is my life, or what is my father’s kinship in Israel, that I should become the king’s son-in-law?”

[T. LII.] But when the time came for Merob [Hebrew: Merab], Saul’s daughter, to be given to David, she was given as wife to Adriel the Meholathite. Saul’s other daughter Michol [Hebrew: Michal] loved David. This was reported to Saul, and it pleased him.

Saul said [Note: [Col. 0596D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “Then Saul said”; the other Membranes: “But Saul said,” and so forth]: “I shall give her to him, so that she may become a snare to him and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.”

Saul said to David: “Today you shall be my son-in-law in two ways.” Saul then commanded his servants: “Speak secretly to David, saying: ‘Behold, you please the king, and all his servants love you. Now therefore become the king’s son-in-law.’”

Saul’s servants spoke all these words [Hebrew lacks “all”] in David’s hearing. David said: “Does it seem a small matter to you to become the king’s son-in-law? I am a poor and insignificant man.”

Saul’s servants reported to him, saying: “David spoke these words.” Saul said: “Speak to David in this way: ‘The king does not require a bride-price, except one hundred foreskins of Philistines, so that vengeance may be taken on the king’s enemies.’”

Saul was planning to deliver David into the hands of the Philistines. When his servants reported to David the words that Saul had spoken [Note: [Col. 0596D] The same Veronese manuscript and other detached leaves read: “the words which we spoke,” without adding the name Saul—plainly more correctly according to the Hebrew exemplar, which likewise omits that name and has only “these words”], the proposal pleased David, that he might become the king’s son-in-law.

After a few days David rose [Hebrew: “The days had not yet been completed. David then rose”] and went with the men who were under him [Note: [Col. 0596D] The Capitular Membranes read “with him.” The Hebrew has this in one word, “and his men”]. He struck down two hundred Philistine men, brought their foreskins, and counted them out before the king, so that he might become his son-in-law.

[T. LIII.] Saul therefore gave him his daughter Michol [Hebrew: Michal] as wife. [Col. 0596C] Saul saw and understood that the Lord was with David. Michol, Saul’s daughter, loved him. Saul became still more afraid of David, and Saul was David’s enemy all his days.

And [Note: [Col. 0596D] Perhaps the Capitular Membranes are more correct: “they returned”] the princes of the Philistines went out. From the beginning of their departure, David conducted himself more wisely than all Saul’s servants, and his name became exceedingly famous.

[T. LIV, Chapter XIX.] Saul spoke to his son Jonathan and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul’s son, loved David greatly.

Jonathan informed David, saying: “My father Saul is seeking to kill you. Therefore, please be on your guard in the morning; remain concealed and hide yourself. I shall go out and stand beside my father [Col. 0596D] in the field wherever he may be [Hebrew: “in the field where you are”], and I shall speak [Note: [Col. 0596D] The same Membranes read “I shall speak for you,” and so forth, more correctly; and shortly afterward “I shall inform you” instead of “I shall report”] about you to my father. Whatever I see, I shall report to you.”

Jonathan therefore spoke well of David to Saul his father. He said to him: “Let not the king sin against his servant David, for he has not sinned against you, and his deeds have been very good toward you. He placed his life in his hand, struck down the Philistine, and the Lord brought about a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced. Why then do you sin against innocent blood by killing David, who is without guilt [Manuscript: ‘outside guilt’; Hebrew: ‘killing David, the innocent’]?”

When Saul heard this, he was appeased by Jonathan’s words and swore: “As the Lord lives, he shall not be killed.” Jonathan then summoned David, told him all these words, and brought David to Saul. He was before him as he had been yesterday and the day before.

[T. LV.] War broke out again. David went out, fought against the Philistines, struck them with a great slaughter [Note: [Col. 0597D] The Capitular Membranes read “with a very great slaughter,” and so forth], and they fled from him. An evil spirit from the Lord came upon Saul. He was sitting in his house and holding a spear, while David played with his hand. Saul attempted to pin David to the wall with the spear, but David turned aside from Saul. The spear passed harmlessly into the wall, and David fled and was saved that night.

[T. LVI.] Saul therefore sent his agents to David’s house to guard him, so that he might be killed in the morning [Note: [Col. 0597D] In the same Membranes: “and kill him in the morning,” and so forth]. When David’s wife Michol reported this to him, saying, “Unless you save yourself this night, tomorrow you will die,” she lowered him through the window. He went away, fled, and was saved.

Michol took a statue, placed it on the bed, put a hairy goatskin [Hebrew lacks “hairy”] at its head, and covered it with clothing [Note: [Col. 0597D] Those same Membranes add “its own clothing”]. Saul sent officers to seize David, and it was reported that he was ill. Saul sent messengers again to see David, saying: “Bring him to me in the bed, so that he may be killed.”

When the messengers arrived, a statue was found on the bed, with a goatskin at its head. Saul said to Michol: “Why have you deceived me in this way and let my enemy go, so that he could escape?” Michol answered Saul: “Because he said to me, ‘Let me go [Hebrew: “Send me”], otherwise I shall kill you.’”

David, having fled and been saved, came to Samuel at Ramah and reported to him all that Saul had done to him. He and Samuel went away and stayed at Najoth [Manuscript: Nachjoth]. Saul was informed by people who said: “Behold, David is in Najoth [Col. 0597D] at Ramah.”

[T. LVII.] Saul therefore sent executioners [Hebrew: “messengers,” here and above] to seize David. When they saw the company of prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing over them, the Spirit of God came upon Saul’s messengers [Note: [Col. 0597D] For “over the messengers of Saul,” the Veronese manuscript, with the Vulgate editions, also has “upon them,” although this differs from the Hebrew text], and they too began to prophesy.

When this was reported to Saul, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. Saul sent messengers a third time, and they too prophesied.

Saul himself went to Ramah and came as far as the great cistern that is in Soccho. He asked: “Where are Samuel and David?” He was told: “Behold, they are in Najoth at Ramah.”

He went to Najoth at Ramah, and the Spirit of God came upon him as well. He walked along, entering and prophesying until he came to Najoth at Ramah. He too stripped off his garments and prophesied with the others [Hebrew lacks “with the others”] before Samuel. [Col. 0598B] [Note: [Col. 0597D] For “fell,” eleven of our manuscripts write “sang.” This corruption also crept into the Canon of Hebrew [Col. 0598D] Truth and escaped the diligence of its corrector and scholiasts. Those scribes perhaps believed Saul’s prophecy consisted in singing God’s praises; hence the error took root, so that they wrote “he sang naked,” etc. MART.]

He fell naked all that day and all that night. Hence the proverb also arose: “Is Saul too among the prophets?”

[Chapter XX.] David fled from Najoth, which was at Ramah, and came and spoke before Jonathan: “What have I done? What is my iniquity, and what is my sin against your father, that he seeks my life?”

He said to him: “Far be it from you; you shall not die. For my father does nothing, great or small, without first revealing it to me [Hebrew: “revealing it to my ear”]. Surely my father would not hide this from me alone? It cannot be so.”

David swore again. Jonathan said: “My father certainly knows that I have found favor in your sight [Hebrew: “in your eyes”], and he will say, ‘Let Jonathan not know this, lest he be grieved.’ Indeed, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is only one step, so to speak, between me and death.”

Jonathan said to David: “Whatever your soul says to me, I shall do for you.”

David said to Jonathan: “Behold, tomorrow is the New Moon, and I ordinarily sit beside the king at table. Let me go, therefore, so that I may hide in the field until the evening of the third day. If your father looks for me [Vulgate adds “looking around”], you shall answer him: ‘David urgently asked me to go quickly to Bethlehem, his city, because there is a solemn sacrifice there for all his kinsmen.’

“If he says, ‘Good,’ there will be peace for your servant. But if he becomes angry, know that his wickedness is complete. Therefore show mercy to your servant, for you have made your servant enter into the Lord’s covenant [Col. 0598D] with you. If there is any iniquity in me [Hebrew lacks “any”], kill me yourself, and do not bring me to your father.”

Jonathan said: “Far be this from you. For if I should certainly learn that my father’s wickedness against you is complete, how could I not inform you?”

David answered Jonathan: “Who will tell me if your father should perhaps answer you harshly [Vulgate adds “about me”]?”

Jonathan said to David: “Come, let us go out into the field” [Vulgate adds “outside”]. When the two had gone out into the field, Jonathan said to David:

“Lord God of Israel, if I investigate my father’s intention tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, and if there is something good regarding David, and I do not immediately send to you and make it known to you, may God do these things to Jonathan and add these things. But if my father’s wickedness persists [Note: [Col. 0599D] Together with the Veronese manuscript, the Capitular Membranes read “may it increase”; shortly afterward, “show mercy with me,” in place of “to me”], I shall reveal it to your ear and send you away, so that you may go in peace. May the Lord be with you, as he was with my father.

“If I live, show me the mercy of the Lord; but if I die, do not remove your mercy from my house forever, when the Lord has eradicated David’s enemies, each one from the earth.”

Jonathan therefore made a covenant with David’s house, and the Lord required it at the hands of David’s enemies. Jonathan also made David swear again, because he loved him; for he loved him as his own soul.

Jonathan said to him: “Tomorrow is the New Moon, and you will be missed, for your seat will be empty until the day after tomorrow. Therefore go down quickly and come to the place where you are to hide on the working day, and sit beside the stone called [Hebrew lacks “called”] Ezel.

“I shall shoot three arrows beside it, as though practicing at a target. I shall also send a boy, saying to him: ‘Go and bring me the arrows.’ If I say to the boy, ‘Behold, the arrows are on this side of you; pick them up,’ then come to me, for you are safe and there is no danger—as the Lord lives. But if I speak to the boy in this way: ‘Behold, the arrows are beyond you; go’ [Vulgate adds “in peace”], then the Lord has sent you away [Hebrew: “has sent you”].

“As for the matter about which you and I have spoken, may the Lord be between me and you forever.”

David hid in the field. The New Moon came, and the king sat down to eat bread. When the king had sat upon his chair, according to custom, which was beside the wall, Jonathan rose, and Abner sat beside Saul. David’s place appeared empty. Saul said nothing at all that day, for he thought that perhaps something had happened to him, so that he was not clean or purified.

When the second day after the New Moon dawned [Hebrew: “the day of the New Moon”], David’s place again appeared empty. Saul said to his son Jonathan: “Why has the son of Jesse not come to eat, neither yesterday nor today?”

Jonathan answered Saul: “He earnestly asked me to go to Bethlehem and said: ‘Let me go, because there is a solemn sacrifice in the city [Hebrew: “a family sacrifice is in the city”]. One of my brothers has summoned me now. Therefore, if I have found favor in your eyes, I shall go quickly and see my brothers.’ For this reason he did not come to the king’s table.

[T. LVIII.] Saul became angry with Jonathan and said to him: “Son of a woman who seizes a man at will [Manuscript: “son”], do I not know that you love the son of Jesse, to your own shame and to the shame of your disgraceful mother? For as long as the son of Jesse lives upon the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Therefore send now and bring him to me, for he is a son of death.”

Jonathan answered Saul his father: “Why should he die? What has he done?” Saul seized his spear to strike him. Jonathan understood that his father had determined to kill David.

Jonathan rose from the table in the anger of his fury and did not eat bread on the second day of the New Moon. He was grieved over David, because his father had disgraced him.

[T. LIX.] When morning dawned, Jonathan went into the field according to David’s arrangement, and a small boy was with him. He said to his boy: “Go and bring me the arrows that I shoot.”

When the boy ran, he shot another arrow beyond the boy. The boy came to the place of the arrow that Jonathan had shot. Jonathan called after the boy and said: “Behold, the arrow is beyond you.”

Jonathan called again after the boy [Vulgate adds “again”], saying [Note: [Col. 0599D] The word “saying” is absent from the Veronese manuscript and from the Hebrew exemplar]: “Hurry quickly; do not stand still.”

The boy gathered Jonathan’s arrows and brought them to his master. He knew nothing at all of what was happening, for only Jonathan and David knew the matter. Jonathan gave his weapons to the boy and said to him: “Go, carry them into the city.”

When the boy had gone, David rose from the place that faced south. Falling prostrate upon the ground, he bowed three times. They kissed one another [Manuscript omits “one another”] and wept together, but David wept more.

Jonathan said to David: “Go in peace. Whatever we have both sworn in the name of the Lord, saying, ‘May the Lord be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring forever.’”

He rose and went away, and Jonathan also entered the city.

(T. LX, Chapter XXI.) David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech was astonished that he had come [Note: [Col. 0600D] So reads the Hebrew Canon of Truth, together with several manuscripts of excellent quality. The Royal manuscript, one Corbeiensis, and three other more recent manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés also retain these words, though with a slightly different order. They read as follows: “And Abimelech was astonished that David had come, and he rose to meet him and said to him,” and so forth. The Hebrew text now has: “And Achimelech trembled to meet David,” to which the Greek also agrees. The Vulgate reading, finally, does not contain the words “and he rose to meet him.” Since these words are absent from the very ancient Veronese manuscript, I would rather judge that the manuscripts from which Martianus extracted those words were interpolated copies in which a marginal scholion had been incorporated into the text. For it is equally possible that, because the Latin words “that he had come” did not seem to correspond to the Hebrew, some diligent person wrote in the margin “and he rose to meet him,” which was afterward imported by scribes into the text.]

He rose to meet David and said to him: “Why are you alone, and no one is with you?”

David said to Achimelech the priest: “The king has commanded me concerning a matter and said: ‘Let no one know the matter on account of which I have sent you [Vulgate adds “by me”], nor what instructions I have given you [Manuscript omits “you”].’ For I have also directed the young men to such and such a place. Now therefore, if you have anything at hand—perhaps five loaves of bread—give them to me, or whatever you find.”

The priest answered David: “I have no ordinary bread at hand, but only holy bread—provided that the young men are clean, especially from women” [Manuscript: “from a woman”].

David answered the priest: “Indeed, if women are concerned, we have kept ourselves from them since yesterday and the day before yesterday, when we went out, and the vessels of the young men were holy. Moreover, this journey is profane [Hebrew: “the journey is ordinary”], but even today it will be sanctified in the vessels.”

So the priest gave him consecrated bread. For there was no bread there except the bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the Lord so that hot loaves might be placed there [Hebrew: “So the priest gave him the holy bread. For there was no bread there except the bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the Lord in order to place hot bread there”].

A certain man was there [Manuscript omits “a certain”], one of Saul’s servants, on that day, inside the tabernacle of the Lord—bound [or “detained”] before the Lord. His name was Doeg the Idumean, the most powerful of Saul’s shepherds.

David said to Achimelech: “Do you have a spear or a sword here at hand? For I did not take my sword or my weapons with me, because the king’s command was urgent.”

The priest said: “Behold [Note: [Col. 0602D] The Veronese manuscript does not have “behold,” which is also absent from the Hebrew. The Vulgate editions have more: “Behold, here”]: the sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Terebinth Valley, is wrapped in a cloak behind the ephod. If you wish to take it, take it, for there is no other here except this one.”

David said: “There is none like it. Give it to me.”

David rose and fled that day from Saul’s presence, and came to Achis, king of Gath. The servants of Achis said to him [Note: [Col. 0602D] The Vulgate books add the words “to him, when they saw David,” which neither the Hebrew text nor the manuscripts of the Hieronymian Version acknowledge]:

“Is this not David, the king of the land? Did they not sing of him in dances, saying:

‘Saul has struck down his thousand,  
and David his ten thousand’?”

[T. LXI.] David laid these words to heart and was exceedingly afraid before Achis, king of Gath. He changed his expression before them, collapsed in their hands, beat against the doors of the gate, and let his saliva run down upon his beard.

Achis said to his servants: “You see a madman. Why have you brought him to me? Do we lack madmen, that you have brought this one to rave in my presence? Is this fellow to enter my house?”

[Col. 0601D] [T. LXII, Chapter XXII.] David departed from there and fled [Hebrew: “escaped”] into the cave of Odollam [Hebrew: Adullam]. When his brothers and all his father’s household heard this, they went down to him there.

All who were in distress, oppressed by debt, or bitter in spirit gathered to him, and he became their commander. There were with him about four hundred men.

David departed from there and went to Maspha, which is in Moab [Hebrew lacks “which is”], and said to the king of Moab: “Let my father and mother, I beg you, remain with you until I know what God will do for me.”

He left them before the king of Moab, and they remained with him throughout all the days that David was in the stronghold.

The prophet Gad said to David: “Do not remain in the stronghold. Depart and go into the land of Judah.”

David departed and came to the forest of Hareth.

Saul heard that David had appeared, and that the men who were with him had appeared. Saul was staying in Gibeah and was in the forest that is at Ramah, holding a spear in his hand, while all his servants stood around him. He said to his servants who attended him:

“Hear now [Vulgate adds “now”], sons of Benjamin: Will the son of Jesse give all of you fields and vineyards and make all of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, because you have all conspired against me and there is no one who reports to me—especially since my son has also entered into a covenant [Note: [Col. 0602D] The same manuscripts read “has joined in a covenant,” and so forth] with the son of Jesse? There is no one among you who grieves over my situation, nor who informs me, since my son has stirred up my servant against me, lying in wait for me to this day [Hebrew: “as on this day”].”

Doeg the Idumean answered, the man who attended Saul and was first among Saul’s servants [Hebrew: “who attended with Saul’s servants”]:

“I saw the son of Jesse at Nob, with Achimelech son of Ahitob [Vulgate adds “the priest”]. He consulted the Lord for him and gave him provisions; he also gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”

The king sent to summon Achimelech son of Ahitob the priest, and all his father’s household, the priests who were in Nob. They all came to the king.

Saul said [Vulgate adds “to Achimelech”]: “Listen, son of Ahitob.”

He answered: “Here I am, my lord.”

Saul said to him: “Why have you conspired [Hebrew: “rebelled”] against me—you and the son of Jesse—and given him bread and a sword, and consulted God for him, so that he might rise against me, a plotter who remains to this day [Hebrew: “a plotter as on this day”]?”

Achimelech answered the king: “Who among all your servants is like David, faithful, the king’s son-in-law, obedient to your command, and honored in your house? Did I begin consulting God for him today? Far be this from me. Let not the king suspect such a thing against his servant or against all my father’s house, for your servant knew nothing at all about this matter, either small or great.”

The king said: “You shall surely die, Achimelech—you and all your father’s household.”

The king said to the emissaries who stood around him: “Turn and kill the priests of the Lord, for their hand is with David. They knew that he had fled, and they did not inform me.”

The king’s servants were unwilling to extend their hands against the priests of the Lord. The king said to Doeg: “You turn and fall upon the priests.”

[T. LXIII.] Doeg the Idumean turned and fell upon the priests. He slaughtered eighty-five men on that day, men wearing [Note: [Col. 0603D] In Jerome’s Epistle now numbered 130, which in the new edition will be numbered not 130 but 8, there is the same note that the Scholiast of the Canon presents here. Where we now read “and all bearing the ephod,” the Hebrew has “bearing the linen ephod.” See more about the linen ephod, or ephod bad, in the already mentioned letter to Marcella and in the letter to Fabiola on the priestly garment, Letter 128. MART.] the linen ephod [Hebrew: “bearing the linen ephod”].

He struck Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword—men and women, children and infants, ox and donkey and sheep, all with the edge of the sword.

One son of Achimelech, son of Ahitob, escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to David. He reported to him that Saul had killed the priests of the Lord.

David said to Abiathar: “I knew on that day, when Doeg the Idumean was there, that he would certainly report it to Saul. I am responsible for all the lives of your father’s household” [Note: [Col. 0604D] The Veronese manuscript, like the Vulgate, omits the word “household”].

“Remain with me; do not be afraid. Whoever seeks my life will seek your life also, and you shall be protected with me.”

[Col. 0603B] [T. LXIV, Chapter XXIII.] They reported to David, saying: “Behold, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and plundering the threshing floors.”

David consulted the Lord, saying: “Shall I go and strike these Philistines?”

The Lord said to David: “Go, and you shall strike the Philistines and save Keilah.”

The men who were with David said to him: “Behold, while we are here in Judah we are afraid; how much more if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines!”

David again consulted the Lord. He answered him: “Rise and go [Hebrew: “go down”] to Keilah, for I shall deliver the Philistines into your hand.”

David and his men went to Keilah, fought against the Philistines, drove away their livestock, and struck them with a great slaughter. David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.

At the time when Abiathar son of Achimelech fled to David at Keilah, he had brought the ephod down with him.

Saul was informed that David had come to Keilah. Saul said: “God has delivered him into my hands, for he has entered a city with gates and bars.”

Saul commanded all the people to go down to battle at Keilah, besiege David, and besiege his men.

[T. LXV.] When David learned that Saul was secretly preparing evil against him, he said to Abiathar the priest: “Bring the ephod near.”

David said: “Lord God of Israel, your servant has heard that Saul is planning to come to Keilah in order to destroy the city because of me. Will the men of Keilah deliver me into his hand? And will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? Lord God of Israel, reveal it to your servant.”

The Lord said: “He will come down.”

David said: “Will the men of Keilah deliver me and the men who are with me into Saul’s hand?”

The Lord said: “They will deliver you.”

David and his men, about six hundred, rose and departed from Keilah, wandering here and there without a fixed direction. It was reported to Saul that David had fled from Keilah [Vulgate adds “and had been saved”], and for that reason he refrained from going out.

David remained in the wilderness, in the strongest places, and stayed on Mount Ziph of the wilderness [Vulgate adds “on the shadowed mountain”]. Saul sought him every day, but God did not deliver him into his hand.

David saw that Saul had gone out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph, in the forest.

Jonathan, Saul’s son, rose and went to David in the forest. He strengthened his hands in God and said to him: “Do not be afraid, for the hand of my father Saul shall not find you. You shall reign over Israel, and I shall be second to you. Even my father Saul knows this.”

The two of them made a covenant before the Lord. David remained in the forest, while Jonathan returned to his house [Note: [Col. 0604D] It is false that the Hebrew text reads “he returned to his way.” For the Hebrew source has *halach lebetho*, that is, “he went to his house.” Perhaps our Scholiast was attending to the sense, which is one, rather than to the words, which are different. In any event, the reliability of this annotation rests with him. MART.].

The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah, saying:

[T. LXVI.] “Behold, is not David hiding among us in the strongholds of the forest, on the hill of Hachilah, which is to the right of the wilderness? Now therefore, as your soul has desired [Hebrew: “your soul, O king”] that you should come down, come down; and it shall be our task to deliver him into the hand of the king.”

Saul said: “Blessed are you by the Lord, for you have pitied my situation [Hebrew: “spared me”]. Go, I beg you [Manuscript: “therefore”], make more careful preparations, act more diligently, and investigate the place where his foot is, or who may have seen him there. For he is considering that I am lying in wait for him by cunning.

“Investigate and see all his hiding places in which he conceals himself, and return to me with certainty, so that I may go with you. If he has hidden himself even in the land, I shall search him out throughout all the thousands of Judah.”

They rose and went to Ziph before Saul. David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the plain, to the right of Jesimuth [Alternate: Jesimon].

Saul and his companions went to seek him. David was informed, and he immediately went down to the rock and remained in the wilderness of Maon.

When Saul heard this, he pursued David in the wilderness of Maon. Saul went along one side of the mountain, while David and his men were on the other side. David despaired of being able to escape from Saul’s presence. Saul and his men therefore surrounded David and his men in the manner of a ring, so that they might capture them.
