A messenger came to Saul, saying: “Hurry and come, for the Philistines have poured themselves over the land.” Saul therefore turned back and ceased pursuing David, and went to meet the Philistines.

For this reason they called that place the Dividing Rock.

## [Chapter XXIV]

David went up from there and stayed in the safest places of En-Gedi. When Saul had returned after pursuing the Philistines, they reported to him: “Look, David is in the wilderness of En-Gedi.” Saul therefore took three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went to search for David and his men, even among the most precipitous rocks, which are accessible only to wild goats. And he came to the sheepfolds [manuscript adds: “also”] that stood beside the road.

**[T. LXVII.]** There was a cave there, and Saul entered it to relieve himself [Hebrew: “to cover his feet”]. David and his men, however, were hiding in the innermost part of the cave. David’s servants said to him: “Look, this is the day of which the Lord spoke to you: ‘I will deliver your enemy into your hand’ [Hebrew: ‘your enemy into your hand’], so that you may do to him whatever seems good in your eyes.”

David therefore rose and silently cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak. Afterward David’s heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak. He said to his men: “May the Lord be gracious to me [Hebrew: ‘Far be it from me, from the Lord’], that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, by stretching out my hand against him, for he is the Lord’s anointed.”

**[T. LXVIII.]** And David restrained his men with words and did not permit them to rise against Saul. Saul, however, rose from the cave and continued along the road he had begun. David also rose afterward and, leaving the cave, called after Saul: “My lord the king!” Saul looked behind him, and David, bowing face downward to the ground, prostrated himself and said to Saul:

“Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ‘David seeks evil against you’? Look, today your eyes have seen that the Lord delivered you into my hand in the cave. I considered killing you, but my eye spared you [Hebrew: the Hebrew does not have this]. For I said: ‘I will not stretch out my hand against my lord, because he is the Lord’s anointed.’

“Indeed, my father, see and recognize the edge of your cloak in my hand. For when I cut off the top of your cloak, I did not wish to stretch out my hand against you [Hebrew: ‘I did not wish to kill you’]. Consider and see that there is no evil or injustice in my hand, and that I have not sinned against you. Yet you lie in wait for my life in order to take it.

“May the Lord judge between me and you, and may the Lord avenge me upon you; but may my hand not be against you. As it is also said in the ancient proverb: ‘From the wicked wickedness will go forth’; therefore may my hand not be against you.

“Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? Whom are you pursuing? You are pursuing a dead dog, a single flea. May the Lord be judge and judge between me and you; may he see and judge my cause, and rescue me from your hand.”

When David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said: “Is this your voice, my son David?” Saul raised his voice and wept, and he said to David:

**[T. LXIX.]** “You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me with good, whereas I have repaid you with evil. Today you have shown the good you have done me: how the Lord delivered me into your hand, and you did not kill me. For who, having found his enemy, would let him go on a good road? But may the Lord repay you for this deed, because of what you have done for me today.

“And now, since I know that you will certainly reign and that the kingdom of Israel will be in your hand, swear to me by the Lord that you will not destroy my descendants after me, nor remove my name from my father’s house.”

David swore this to Saul. Saul then went to his house, while David and his men went up to safer places.

## [Chapter XXV]

Samuel died, and all Israel gathered and mourned for him. They buried him in his house at Ramah [Vulgate: Ramatha]. David rose and went down to the wilderness of Paran.

**[T. LXX.]** There was a certain man in Maon [Hebrew: “in Maon,” not “in the wilderness”], whose property was in Carmel. The man was exceedingly wealthy: he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. It happened that his flock was being sheared in Carmel.

The man’s name was Nabal, and his wife’s name was Abigail. The woman was very intelligent and beautiful, but her husband was harsh, exceedingly wicked, and malicious; he was a descendant of Caleb.

When David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his flock, he sent ten young men [Hebrew: “boys”] and said to them: “Go up to Carmel, and you shall come to Nabal. Greet him peacefully in my name, and say [Veronese manuscript and the Vulgate: “you shall say: Let there be peace to my brothers,” etc.; the Hebrew differs, reading “Thus,” with different punctuation]:

‘Peace to my brothers [Hebrew: “And say thus: My brothers”], peace to you, peace to your house, and peace to everything that you have. I have heard that your shepherds are shearing [Hebrew: “your shearers,” now: “the shepherds who were yours”], who were with us in the wilderness [Hebrew does not have this; the reading *were*, preferred by the scholiast, is also that of the Veronese manuscript]. We never troubled them, nor did anything belonging to the flock ever go missing for the whole time they were with us in Carmel.

“Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Now therefore, may the young men [Vulgate adds: “your young men”] find favor in your eyes, for we have come on a good day. Whatever your hand finds, give to your servants and to your son David.”

**[T. LXXI.]** When David’s young men came, they spoke all these words to Nabal in David’s name and then remained silent. Nabal answered David’s young men:

“Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse? Today servants are increasing who flee from their masters. Shall I take my bread, my water, and the meat of the animals that I have slaughtered for my shearers and give them to men whom I do not know, or even where they come from?”

David’s young men turned back along their way, returned, and reported to him all the words that Nabal had spoken [Hebrew: “these words”]. Then David said to his men: “Let everyone gird on his sword.”

**Note:** This passage, “And each of them girded on his sword,” which consists of exactly the same words in Hebrew, is missing from the Veronese manuscript. Although I would prefer to think that it fell out of this copy through the error of a Latin scribe, because of the repetition of the words “his sword,” I nevertheless wish you to note that it is found neither in the Vatican Greek exemplar of the Septuagint nor in other manuscripts of the highest quality, on which the recent Leipzig edition of 1647 and the Franeker edition of 1709 were based.

Each man therefore girded on his sword, and David also girded on his sword. About four hundred men followed David [Vulgate omits: “about”], while two hundred remained with the baggage.

One of the young men reported to Abigail, Nabal’s wife: “Look, David sent messengers from the wilderness to bless our master [manuscript: “your master”], but he rejected them. These men were very good to us, and they did not trouble us. Nothing ever went missing throughout the whole time we lived with them in the wilderness. They were a wall to us both by night and by day, throughout all the days that we pastured our flocks near them.

“Therefore consider and think [Veronese manuscript: “and see,” closer to the Hebrew] about what you should do. For evil has been completed against your husband and against your household [Hebrew: “against our master and against his whole household”], and he is a son of Belial, so that no one can speak to him.”

Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five cooked rams, five measures of parched grain, one hundred bunches of raisins [Hebrew: “one hundred raisin cakes”], and two hundred cakes of pressed figs. She loaded them on donkeys and said to her young men: “Go on ahead of me; I will follow you from behind.” She did not tell her husband Nabal.

When she had mounted the donkey and was descending toward the foot of the mountain [manuscript: “had descended”], David and his men were coming down to meet her, and she met them. David said:

“Truly, I have guarded all that belonged to this man in the wilderness for nothing, and nothing of everything that belonged to him has gone missing; yet he has repaid me evil for good. May God do this to the enemies of David, and may he add this also, if I leave alive anything that belongs to him until morning—anyone who urinates against a wall.”

**Note:** The Veronese manuscript reads “a dog” instead of “in the morning.” Although this reading differs from the Hebrew and from all other books, it is not implausible, nor does it seem to be the gloss of an unlearned commentator. Much scholarly debate has concerned whether the expression “one who urinates against a wall” signifies males or men, for whom the expression is customary, or dogs. The latter is a familiar proverbial phrase used when someone threatens to spare no one—not even a dog, to whom urinating against a wall is natural—alive. Our ancient scribe—for I would not dare contend that this was written by the holy translator—therefore casts his vote for the latter interpretation, to which I freely confess that I have long since inclined. Vopiscus relates something similar about Aurelian. Angry with the people of the city of Tyana, he bound himself by this oath: “I will leave no dog in this town,” thereby swearing that he would utterly destroy all its inhabitants. Later, moved by compassion at the prospect of so great a slaughter, he softened the literal force of his words and ordered that all the dogs encountered in the city be killed.

When Abigail saw David, she hurried, dismounted from the donkey, fell before David on her face, bowed to the ground, fell at his feet, and said:

“Let this iniquity be upon me [Hebrew: ‘It is upon me’], my lord. Please let your servant speak in your ears, and hear the words of your maidservant. Let not my lord, the king [Hebrew does not have this], set his heart against this exceedingly wicked man, Nabal [Hebrew: “against this man, Nabal the son of Belial”]. For as his name is, so is he: Nabal is his name, and folly is with him [Hebrew: “For according to his name, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him”]. But I, your servant, did not see your young men [Hebrew does not have “your”], my lord [Veronese manuscript and Vulgate: “my lord”; Hebrew reading uncertain], whom you sent.

“Now therefore, my lord, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, the Lord who prevented you from coming to bloodshed and saved your hand for you, may your enemies and those who seek evil for my lord become like Nabal.

“Therefore accept this blessing which your servant has brought to you, my lord, and give it to the young men who follow my lord. Forgive the iniquity of your maidservant [Hebrew: “Forget”]. For the Lord will surely make a faithful house for my lord, because you fight the Lord’s battles, my lord, and evil will not be found in you throughout all the days of your life.

“For if a man should ever rise up against you, pursuing you and seeking your life, the life of my lord will be guarded as in the bundle of the living, with the Lord your God. But the lives of your enemies will be whirled about as in the force and circle of a sling.

“And when the Lord has done for my lord all the good things that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you leader over Israel, this will not be for you a cause of grief or a stumbling block to the heart of my lord: that you have shed innocent blood or avenged yourself. And when the Lord has dealt well with my lord, you will remember your maidservant.”

David said to Abigail:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me; blessed is your speech, and blessed are you, who prevented me today from going to bloodshed and avenging myself with my own hand. Otherwise, as the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, who prevented me from doing you evil [Veronese manuscript: “prevented me from doing evil to you”; Hebrew: in one word, “from doing evil”], if you had not come quickly to meet me, Nabal would not have been left alive until morning—anyone who urinates against a wall.”

David received from her hand everything that she had brought him [Hebrew does not have “everything”], and said to her: “Go peacefully [the same manuscript: “in peace”] to your house. Look, I have heard your voice and honored your face [Hebrew: “accepted your face”].”

Abigail came to Nabal, and behold, he had a banquet in his house, like a king’s banquet. Nabal’s heart was cheerful, for he was exceedingly drunk. She did not tell him a small thing or a great thing until morning.

At daybreak, when Nabal’s wine had dissipated, his wife told him these words. His heart died within him, and he became like a stone.

**[T. LXXII.]** When ten days had passed, the Lord struck Nabal, and he died. When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said:

“Blessed is the Lord, who judged the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, who kept his servant from evil, and who repaid Nabal’s wickedness upon his own head.”

**[T. LXXIII.]** David sent word and spoke to Abigail, asking that he might take her as his wife. David’s young men came to Abigail at Carmel and said to her:

“David has sent us to you, so that he may take you for himself as his wife.”

She rose, bowed face downward to the ground, and said: “Behold, your maidservant shall be a servant, to wash the feet of the servants of my lord [manuscript: ‘and wash the feet’].”

Abigail hurried, rose, mounted the donkey, and five young women went with her as her attendants. She followed David’s messengers, and she became his wife.

David also took Ahinoam from Jezreel, and both became his wives.

**[T. LXXIV.]** Saul gave his daughter Michal [Hebrew: Michal], David’s wife, to Phalti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.

## [Chapter XXVI]

The Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah [manuscript: “from Gibeah”], saying: “Look, David [Hebrew: “Is David?”] is hiding on the hill of Hachilah, which is opposite the wilderness.” Saul rose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph, with three thousand chosen men of Israel, to search for David in the wilderness of Ziph.

Saul camped on the hill of Hachilah, which was opposite the wilderness beside the road, while David was living in the wilderness.

**[T. LXXV.]** When David saw that Saul had come after him into the wilderness, he sent scouts and learned with certainty that he had come there [Vulgate adds: “there”]. David rose [Vulgate adds: “secretly”] and came to the place where Saul was [Hebrew: “where Saul had encamped”]. When he saw the place where Saul and Abner son of Ner, the commander of his army, were sleeping, and Saul sleeping in the tent with the rest of the people around him, David said to Achimelech the Hittite [manuscript: “the Chethite”] and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother:

“Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?”

Abishai said: “I will go down with you.”

David and Abishai came to the people by night and found Saul lying asleep in the tent, with his spear fixed in the ground at his head. Abner and the people were sleeping around him [Hebrew: “And behold, Saul was lying asleep in the tent, and the spear was fixed in the ground at his head; Abner and the people were sleeping around him”].

Abishai said to David: “Today God has delivered your enemy into your hands. Now therefore, let me pierce him with the spear into the ground once; a second blow will not be necessary.”

David said to Abishai: “Do not kill him. For who can stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be innocent [Hebrew: ‘and be guiltless’]?”

David also said: “As the Lord lives, unless the Lord strikes him, or his day comes that he dies, or he goes down into battle and perishes, may the Lord be gracious to me [Hebrew: ‘Far be it from me, from the Lord’] if I stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed. Now therefore, take the spear that is at his head and the cup of water, and let us go.”

David took the spear and the cup of water that were at Saul’s head [manuscript: “which was at Saul’s head”], and they went away. No one saw, understood, or awoke; they were all sleeping, because a sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them.

When David had crossed over to the opposite side and stood at the summit of the mountain in the distance, with a great interval between them [Hebrew: “a great space”], David called to the people and to Abner son of Ner:

“Will you not answer, Abner?”

Abner answered: “Who are you, who call out and disturb the king [Hebrew: ‘who call out to the king’]?”

David said to Abner: “Are you not a man? And who is like you in Israel? Why, then, did you not guard your lord the king? For one of the people came in to kill your lord the king. This thing that you have done is not good. As the Lord lives, you are sons of death, because you did not guard your lord, the Lord’s anointed. Now therefore, see where the king’s spear is and where the cup of water was that stood at his head.”

**[T. LXXVI.]** Saul recognized David’s voice and said: “Is this your voice, my son David?” [The Veronese manuscript omits the verb “said” here; conversely, shortly afterward it adds “the king” to the words “my lord,” although the Hebrew does not support this.]

David said: “It is my voice, my lord the king.”

He said: “For what reason is my lord pursuing his servant? What have I done? Or what evil is in my hand? Now therefore, please hear, my lord the king, the words of your servant:

“If the Lord incites you against me, let him smell an offering. But if it is the children of men, cursed are they before the Lord, because they have driven me out today so that I may not dwell in the Lord’s inheritance, saying: ‘Go, serve foreign gods.’

“And now, let not my blood be poured out upon the ground before the Lord, because the king of Israel has gone out to seek a single flea, just as one pursues a partridge in the mountains.”

Saul said: “I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will certainly do you no more harm, because my life has been precious in your eyes today [manuscript omits “today”]. It is clear that I have acted foolishly and have been greatly ignorant.”

David answered: “Here is the king’s spear; let one of the young men [Vulgate adds: “of the king”] cross over and take it. The Lord will repay each person according to his justice and faithfulness. For today the Lord delivered you into my hand, but I did not wish to raise my hand against the Lord’s anointed.

“And just as your life has been magnified today in my eyes [Hebrew: ‘And behold, just as’], so may my life be magnified in the eyes of the Lord, and may he deliver me from every distress.”

Saul said to David: “Blessed are you, my son David. Indeed, you will surely act, and you will surely prevail.”

David went on his way, and Saul returned to his place.

## [Chapter XXVII]

David said in his heart: “One day I shall certainly fall into Saul’s hands. Is it not better for me to flee and be saved in the land of the Philistines, so that Saul may despair and cease seeking me throughout all the borders of Israel? Let me flee from his hand.”

David rose and departed, he and six hundred men with him, to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath. David lived with Achish in Gath, he and his men, each with his household, and David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelite and Abigail, Nabal’s wife of Carmel [Hebrew: “the Carmelite”].

Saul was told that David had fled to Gath, and he no longer continued to seek him.

David said to Achish: “If I have found favor in your eyes, let a place be given to me in one of the cities of this region [Note: A second manuscript reads, “in one of the cities around the fields.” All the other manuscript codices read as printed here; this is preferable to the poorly corrected reading in the text of the Canon. MART.], so that I may dwell there. For why should your servant remain with you in the royal city [Hebrew: “the city of the kingdom”]?”

Achish gave him Ziklag on that day. For this reason Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.

The number of days that David lived in the region of the Philistines was four months [Hebrew: “four, months and days”].

**Note:** The very ancient Corbie manuscript no. 13 adds the word *quasi*, that is, “about four months.” In Hebrew it is written *yamim ve-arba‘ah ḥodashim*, which means “days and four months.” The Syriac and Arabic, however, understand the expression as “a year”; thus they read: “The number of days that David dwelt in the land of the Philistines was a year and four months,” or, as in the Chaldee, “days, a period within a period, and four months.” Recent critics, on the other hand, argue that *days* cannot here be taken to mean a year or years, because David did not descend into the land of the Philistines until after Samuel’s death, and Samuel’s death preceded Saul’s by only seven months. According to those scholars, therefore, David remained in that region for some days and four months. MART.

David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Gezrites [Note: Thus the corrected Canon and the first hand of Corbie manuscript no. 13. Others corruptly read “Gedrites” or “Gethrites.” The current Hebrew text likewise has the letters in the wrong order, writing *Girzi* or *Gerzi* instead of *Gezri*. The Masoretes nevertheless instruct that it should be read as we have printed it, in accordance with the Latin manuscripts. The Veronese manuscript also reads “Gedrites,” as do most others preserved by Martianay, though less correctly. MART.], and the Amalekites. These peoples had inhabited the land from ancient times, extending toward Shur as far as the land of Egypt.

David struck the whole land [Hebrew does not have “the whole”], leaving neither man nor woman alive. He took sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing, then returned and came to Achish.

Achish said to him: “Against whom did you raid today?” [Hebrew: plural, “Against whom did you raid?” The Veronese manuscript agrees with the Hebrew commentator and with the text itself in using the plural.]

David answered: “Against the Negeb of Judah, against the Negeb of Jerahmeel, and against the Negeb of the Kenites.”

David kept neither man nor woman alive, nor did he bring them to Gath, saying: “Lest they speak against us and say, ‘This is what David has done.’” This was his practice throughout all the days that he lived in the region of the Philistines.

Achish therefore trusted David, saying: “He has made himself utterly hateful among his people Israel; therefore he shall be my servant forever.”

## [Chapter XXVIII]

In those days the Philistines gathered their forces to prepare for war against Israel. Achish said to David: “Know for certain that you and your men shall go out with me in the army.”

David said to Achish: “Now you shall know what your servant will do.”

**[T. LXXVII.]** Achish said to David: “And I shall appoint you as guardian of my head for all your days.”

Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned him and buried him in Ramah [Vulgate: Ramatha], his city. Saul had removed the magicians and diviners from the land.

The Philistines gathered and came and encamped at Shunem. Saul also gathered all Israel and came to Gilboa [manuscript: Gelbue]. Saul saw the camp of the Philistines, became afraid, and his heart was exceedingly terrified.

He consulted the Lord, but the Lord did not answer him, either through dreams, or through the priests [Hebrew: “through instruction”], or through the prophets.

**[T. LXXVIII.]** Saul said to his servants: “Seek for me a woman who has a spirit of divination, so that I may go to her and inquire through her.”

His servants said to him: “There is a woman with a spirit of divination at En-Dor.”

Saul changed his appearance, put on different clothing, and went, he and two men with him. They came to the woman by night, and he said: “Divine for me by the spirit of divination, and raise up for me the one whom I shall name to you.”

The woman said to him: “Look, you know what Saul has done and how he has removed the magicians and diviners from the land. Why then are you laying a trap for my life, so that I may be killed?”

Saul swore to her by the Lord, saying: “As the Lord lives, no evil shall come upon you because of this matter.”

The woman said: “Whom shall I raise up for you?”

He said: “Raise up Samuel for me.”

When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice and said to Saul: “Why have you deceived me? [Hebrew: “Why have you deceived me?”] You are Saul!”

The king said to her: “Do not be afraid. What did you see?”

The woman said to Saul: “I saw gods [or divine beings] ascending from the earth.”

He said to her: “What is his appearance?”

She said: “An old man is ascending, and he is wrapped in a cloak.”

Saul understood that it was Samuel. He bowed face downward to the ground and prostrated himself.

Samuel said to Saul: “Why have you disturbed me by raising me up?”

Saul said: “I am in great distress. The Philistines are fighting against me, God has departed from me, and he would not answer me, either through the prophets or through dreams. Therefore I called you, so that you might show me what I should do.”

Samuel said: “Why do you ask me, when the Lord has departed from you and has gone over to your rival? The Lord will do to you as he spoke through me: he will tear the kingdom [Vulgate adds: “your kingdom”] from your hand and give it to your neighbor, David, because you did not obey the voice of the Lord and did not carry out his fierce anger against Amalek. Therefore the Lord has done this to you today because of what you are suffering.

“The Lord will also deliver Israel with you into the hands of the Philistines. Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me; moreover, the Lord will deliver the camp of Israel into the hands of the Philistines.”

Immediately Saul fell stretched out upon the ground. He was exceedingly terrified by Samuel’s words [the manuscript and Vulgate omit “exceedingly”], and there was no strength in him, because he had eaten no bread throughout that day [Hebrew: “that day and throughout the whole night”].

The woman came to Saul and, seeing that he was greatly disturbed, said to him:

**Note:** We have followed the Canon of the Hebrew truth and another excellent manuscript Bible, Corbie no. 1; the same reading occurs in the Hebrew volumes. All the other manuscript codices present a disordered reading and an entirely confused sense: “The woman therefore came to Saul, and said: For he was greatly troubled; and said to him,” etc. MART. The Veronese manuscript reads “throughout that whole night”; the Hebrew has both “throughout that day” and “throughout the whole night.” It also omits “and seeing that,” and immediately reads with the Vulgate, “for he was greatly troubled.”

“Look, your maidservant has obeyed your voice. I have placed my life in my hand, and I have heard the words that you spoke to me. Now therefore, you too listen to the voice of your maidservant. Let me set a morsel of bread before you, so that you may eat and regain your strength [manuscript: “and eat”], and be able to continue your journey.”

He refused and said: “I will not eat.”

But his servants and the woman compelled him, and at last, having listened to their voice, he rose from the ground and sat upon the bed.

The woman had a fatted calf in the house. She hurried, slaughtered it, took flour, kneaded it, baked unleavened bread, and set it before Saul and his servants. When they had eaten, they rose and walked throughout that entire night [Hebrew: “during that night”].

## [Chapter XXIX]

All the forces of the Philistines gathered at Aphek, while Israel was encamped beside the spring that was in Jezreel.

The Philistine commanders marched in units of hundreds and thousands. David and his men were at the rear of the army with Achish.

The princes of the Philistines said [Vulgate adds: “to Achish”]: “What do these Hebrews want?” [Hebrew: “What are these Hebrews?”]

Achish said to the princes of the Philistines: “Do you not know David, who was the servant of Saul, king of Israel, and has been with me for many days or years? [Hebrew: ‘Is this not David, the servant of Saul, king of Israel, who has been with me for days or years?’] I have found nothing in him from the day he deserted to me until this day.”

**[T. LXXXIX.]** The princes of the Philistines became angry with him and said:

“Let the man return and remain in the place where you appointed him. He shall not go down with us into battle, lest he become our adversary when we begin to fight. For how else could he appease his master, except with our heads?

“Is this not David, to whom they sang in choruses [the Veronese manuscript also omits the words “in choruses,” although they are present in the Hebrew], saying:

‘Saul has struck down his thousands,
and David his tens of thousands’?”

Achish called David and said to him:

“As the Lord lives, you are upright, and you are good in my sight. Your going out and your coming in with me in the camp [Hebrew: ‘As the Lord lives, you are upright and good in my sight; your going out and your coming in with me in the camp’]. I have found nothing evil in you from the day you came to me until this day, but you do not please the princes.

“Return, therefore, and go in peace, and do not offend the eyes of the Philistine princes [manuscript: “you will not offend”].”

David said to Achish: “But what have I done, and what have you found in your servant [Hebrew: ‘in your servant’] from the day I came before you until this day, that I should not come and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?” [The Veronese manuscript omits the negative particle, although it is present in the Hebrew.]

Achish answered and said to David:

“I know that you are good in my eyes, like an angel of God. But the princes of the Philistines have said: ‘He shall not go up with us into battle.’ Now therefore, rise early—you and the servants of your lord who came with you—and when you rise during the night and it begins to grow light, depart.”

**[T. LXXX.]** David rose during the night, he and his men [Hebrew does not have “during the night”], to depart in the morning and return to the land of the Philistines. The Philistines, however, went up to Jezreel.

[Col. 0614A] [Chapter XXX.] When David and his men had come to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid into the southern region and against Ziklag [Hebrew: “into the southern region, and into Ziklag”] [Note: [Col. 0614D] The Veronese manuscript has “they attacked,” and consequently “they struck, burned, and led away.”], and had struck Ziklag and burned it with fire. They had taken captive the women who were in it, from the smallest to the greatest; they had killed no one, but had taken them with them and gone on their way.

When David and his men came to the city and found it burned with fire, and their wives, sons, and daughters taken captive, David and the people who were with him raised their voices and wept until they had no more tears. For David’s two wives had also been taken captive: Ahinoam the Jezreelite, and Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.

David was greatly distressed, for the people intended to stone him, because the soul of every man was bitter over his sons and daughters. But David strengthened himself in the Lord his God. And David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech: “Bring me the ephod.” And Abiathar brought [Manuscript: “had brought”] the ephod to David, and David consulted the Lord, saying: “Shall I pursue these raiders, and shall I overtake them, or not?” [Hebrew: the words “or not?” are absent.] And the Lord said to him [Note: [Col. 0614D] The name “the Lord” is absent here both from the Veronese manuscript and from the Hebrew text]: “Pursue them, for you will certainly overtake them and recover the spoil.”

[T. LXXXI.] So David himself went, together with the six hundred men who were with him, and they came as far as the torrent of Besor [Manuscript: Bosor]. Some of the exhausted men remained behind [Hebrew: “the rest … remained behind”]. David himself continued the pursuit with four hundred men, for two hundred had remained behind, being too exhausted to cross the torrent of Besor [Hebrew: “who had been ordered not to cross the torrent of Besor”].

They found an Egyptian man in the field and brought him to David. They gave him bread to eat and water to drink, as well as a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters [Hebrew: “two raisins”] of raisins. When he had eaten, his spirit returned to him and he revived; for he had eaten no bread and drunk no water for three days and three nights.

David then said to him: “Whose man are you, and where are you from? Where are you going?” [Hebrew omits: “Where are you going?”] He replied: “I am an Egyptian boy, the servant of an Amalekite man. My master abandoned me because I began to fall ill three days ago. For we made a raid upon the southern region [Vulgate: “the southern district”] of the Cherethites, and against Judah, and upon the south of Caleb; and we burned Ziklag with fire.”

David said to him: “Can you lead me to this band?” He replied: “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me and will not hand me over to my master, and I will lead you to this band.” [Note: [Col. 0614D] The Vulgate adds: “And David swore to him.”]

When he had led him there, behold, they were scattered over the whole land, eating and drinking and celebrating almost as though it were a festival day [Hebrew omits: “day”], because of all the great spoil and plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah.

[Col. 0615A] David struck them from evening until the evening of the following day, and none of them escaped except four hundred young men who had mounted camels and fled. Thus David recovered everything that the Amalekites had taken, and he rescued his two wives. Nothing was missing, from the smallest to the greatest, whether sons or daughters, or any of the spoil [Manuscript: “anyone”]; everything that they had seized David brought back.

David also took all the flocks and herds, and they drove them before him. And they said: “This is David’s spoil.”

David came to the two hundred men [Note: [Col. 0615C] The author of the work Questions or Hebrew Traditions on the Books of Kings does not approve the Latin version of this passage, which he denies agrees with the Hebrew truth. He says: “Although the Latin books read that some of the exhausted men remained behind with the baggage, while the Hebrew has it that they had been ordered to remain with the baggage, this passage shows that the Hebrew truth must be followed here. It says: ‘The share of the one who went down to battle shall be equal to that of the one who remained with the baggage.’ It does not say, ‘of those who remained with the baggage because they were exhausted’; for if they had remained because they were exhausted, no share of the spoils would be owed them.” [Col. 0615D] Yet, with due respect to this learned writer, one may rightly say that the Latin manuscripts read excellently, in agreement with the Hebrew truth: “those who had remained because they were exhausted,” and so forth. For the verb פגרו, piggeru, is rendered in Latin as “they were exhausted,” or “they became weak,” or even “they were more sluggish”—plainly because of the feigned exhaustion which they pretended in order not to go on with David.

Moreover, since David had ordered them to remain with the equipment, that is, with the baggage, they were rightfully entitled to a share of the spoils as combatants, even though they had remained at the torrent of Besor under the pretext of real or feigned exhaustion. It is, besides, characteristic of the writer just mentioned, and of the scholiast of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, to interpret the verb פגרו, piggeru, as “they were ordered.” No Hebrew or recent Hebraizing writer, so far as we know, has expressed such a meaning from the root פגר, pigger, or phagar; rather, all agree with Jerome’s Latin interpretation.

It is therefore not implausible to conjecture that one and the same author composed both the Questions mentioned above on the Books of Kings and the scholia on the Canon of the Hebrew Truth—especially since the entire work of Questions or Hebrew Traditions is found to have been compiled from the marginal scholia of that same Canon of the Hebrew Truth. Let the Reader recall what we wrote above in our Prolegomena. MART.]

who had remained behind because they had been unable to follow David, and whom he had ordered to remain [Hebrew: “who had been ordered not to go on with David, and whom he had ordered to remain”] at the torrent of Besor. They went out to meet David and the people who were with him.

David approached the people and greeted them peacefully. But every wicked and worthless man among those who had gone with David answered: “Since they did not come with us, we shall give them nothing of the spoil which we have recovered. Let each one be satisfied with his wife and sons; once they have taken them, let them depart.”

David said: “You shall not act in this way, my brothers, with what the Lord has given us and has preserved for us, and with what he has delivered into our hands—the raiders who had attacked us. No one shall listen to you in this matter. The share of the one who went down to battle shall be equal to that of the one who remained with the baggage, and they shall divide equally.” [Hebrew: “they shall divide together.”]

From that day forward this became established and decreed, as though a law in Israel, continuing to this day.

David came to Ziklag and sent gifts from the spoil [Hebrew omits: “gifts”] to the elders of Judah, his neighbors, saying: “Receive a blessing” [Hebrew: “Here is a blessing for you”] “from the spoil of the enemies of the Lord.” He sent them to those who were in Bethel, those in Ramoth to the south, those in Jattir, those in Aroer, those in Sephamoth, those in Eshtemoa, those in Racal, those in the cities of Jerahmeel, those in the cities of the Kenites, those in Arama [Manuscript: Rama], those at the lake of Ashan, those in Athach, those in Hebron, and to the rest who were in all the places where David himself and his men had sojourned.

[Col. 0616A] [Chapter XXXI.] The Philistines were fighting against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines; and the slain fell on Mount Gilboa [Hebrew: “the wounded”]. The Philistines pressed hard upon Saul and his sons, and they struck Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul.

[T. LXXXII.] The whole weight of the battle turned against Saul [Hebrew: “the battle also became heavy against Saul”]. The archers overtook him, and he was severely wounded by the archers. Saul said to his armor-bearer: “Draw your sword and pierce me, lest these uncircumcised men come and kill me while mocking me.” His armor-bearer would not do it, for he was terrified by overwhelming fear. So Saul seized his sword and fell upon it.

When his armor-bearer saw this—namely, that Saul was dead—he too fell upon his sword and died with him. Thus Saul died, and his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together on that day.

When the men of Israel who were on the other side of the valley and beyond the Jordan saw that the Israelites had fled, and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled. The Philistines came and settled there.

On the following day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons lying on Mount Gilboa. They cut off Saul’s head, stripped off his armor, and sent it throughout the land of the Philistines, all around, to proclaim the news in the temple of their idols [Note: [Col. 0616D] The Veronese manuscript omits “their,” although the Hebrew text adds it] and among the people. They placed his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, but they hung his body on the wall of Beth-shean.

When the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul [Hebrew omits: “all that”], all the valiant men arose. They marched throughout the whole night and took the corpse of Saul and the corpses of his sons down from the wall of Beth-shean. They came to Jabesh [Vulgate adds: “Gilead”] and burned them there. They took their bones and buried them in the grove at Jabesh, and they fasted for seven days.

[Note: [Col. 0617B] Our scholiast notes here, so far as may be inferred from these traces of writing, that among the Hebrews the First Book of Samuel was not divided from the Second. Saint Jerome had taught this earlier in his preface to the Books of Samuel and Malachim—that is, to the four Books of Kings—although, as he himself observes there, many people regarded those books as two separate books.

The Canon of the Hebrew Truth counts the two Books of Samuel as one book, as is proved by the numbers of the chapters or titles, which are marked in one continuous sequence. MART. —There is no heading or other sign of distinction from the preceding book in the Veronese manuscript, except that the copyist stained the words of the preceding book with red ink and also noted in the blank space of the book: “In ancient copies the Second Book begins here.”

By “ancient copies” he evidently means the copies of the Greek versions, τῶν LXX, which were in circulation before Jerome’s version. He indicates by the same words that in the new version which Jerome produced from the Hebrew, and which our manuscript presents here, the Book of Samuel is one continuous book in accordance with the archetype.

The scholiast intended to make the same point, as Martianay inferred from the traces of the annotation. The holy Father himself also taught this in his prologue, and there is scarcely any doubt that, after rejecting the old division, he continued the sequence of his exemplar. Yet it is not now our intention to restore that division; it is enough to have informed the Reader of the matter.]

## BOOK II OF SAMUEL

[Col. 0617]

[Col. 0617A] [Chapter I.] After Saul had died, David returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and remained two days at Ziklag. On the third day, a man appeared, coming from Saul’s camp, with his garment torn and dust upon his head. When he came to David, he fell upon his face and bowed down.

David said to him: “Where do you come from?” He replied: “I have fled from the camp of Israel.” David said to him: “What has happened? Tell me.” He replied: “The people fled from the battle, and many of the people fell and died; Saul also and his son Jonathan have perished.”

David said to the young man [Hebrew: “boy”] who brought him the news: “How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?” The young man who told him replied:

“By chance I came upon Mount Gilboa, and Saul was leaning upon his spear. The chariots and horsemen were drawing near him [Note: [Col. 0617D] The Veronese manuscript omits “him,” although it is expressed in the Hebrew]. When he looked behind him and saw me, he called to me. When I answered him, ‘Here I am,’ he said to me, ‘Who are you?’ I answered him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’ He said to me, ‘Stand over me and kill me, for anguish has seized me, while my whole life is still in me.’

“So I stood over him and killed him, because I knew that he could not live after his fall. I took the crown that was upon his head and the bracelet from his arm, and I have brought them here to you, my lord.”

David seized his garments and tore them, as did all the men who were with him. They mourned, wept, and fasted until evening for Saul, for Jonathan his son, for the people of the Lord, and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.

[T. LXXXIII.] David said to the young man who had brought him the news: “Where are you from?” He answered: “I am the son of an Amalekite resident alien.” David said to him: “Why were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to kill the Lord’s anointed?”

David called one of the young men [Vulgate adds: “his men”] and said: “Approach and fall upon him.” He struck him, and he died. David said to him: “Your blood is upon your own head, for your mouth has spoken against you, saying: ‘I killed the Lord’s anointed.’”

David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son:

“And he ordered them to teach the sons of Judah the bow, [Note: [Col. 0617D] We have stated elsewhere (in this edition, col. 481, note a) what Jerome wrote about the Book of Jashar. Since we promised to say more here about the same volume, let us now hear Rabanus Maurus, who argues as follows in chapter I of his Commentary on the Second Book of Kings:

‘As for what follows, he says, “as it is written in the Book of Jashar,” and so forth: they assert that this book cannot now be found anywhere, not even among the Hebrews themselves; just as the Book of the Wars of the Lord, which is mentioned in the Book of Numbers, cannot be found; nor the songs of Solomon, nor his most wise discussions concerning the nature of trees and all herbs, and likewise of beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish.

‘Similarly, what is said in the Book of Chronicles—“The rest of Solomon’s former and later works are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the vision of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam son of Nebat”—and many volumes of this sort: Scripture proves that they once existed in writing, but it is now evident that they do not exist.

‘For when Judea was devastated by the Chaldeans, the library that had been collected in ancient times was consumed by hostile fire along with the other wealth of the province. From it, the few books that are now contained in Holy Scripture were later restored through the diligence of Ezra the priest and prophet.’

Rabanus copied this word for word from Bede’s Book of Thirty Questions on the Book of Kings. Rabanus then continues:

‘There are, however, some who say that this Book of Jashar should be understood as the very Book of Kings, in which the righteous prophets are contained—namely Samuel, Gad, and Nathan. In their book it is written how Saul, having departed from the fear of the Lord, perished through his disobedience.’

This, I say, is found in the Questions or Hebrew Traditions on the Books of Kings, which are commonly attributed to Jerome. The false Jerome says: ‘The Book of Jashar is the Book of Samuel, in which the righteous prophets are contained,’ and so forth.

From this diversity of opinions it is sufficiently clear that ancient ecclesiastical writers held opinions about the Book of Jashar just as diverse as those now held by recent critics. Above all, I wish it to be observed that the scholiast of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth and the author of the Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings differ from Jerome, Bede, and Rabanus Maurus. MART.]

as it is written in the Book of Jashar” [Hebrew: “And he said, to teach the sons of Judah the bow. Behold, it is written in the Book of Jashar”].

[Note: [Col. 0618D] The Vulgate adds: “And he said: Consider, O Israel, those slain and wounded upon your heights”; neither the Hieronymian manuscripts nor the Hebrew text itself contains this.]

“The illustrious men of Israel lie slain upon your mountains [Hebrew: “upon your heights”]. How the mighty have fallen!

“Do not announce it in Gath; do not proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.

“Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you [Manuscript: “come”], nor fields of firstfruits be upon you, for there the shield of the mighty was defiled—the shield of Saul, as though it had not been anointed with oil.

“From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan never turned back, and the sword of Saul did not return empty.

“Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely in life, were not divided in death; swifter than eagles, stronger than lions.

“Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet for your delights, who provided [Note: [Col. 0619D] The Veronese manuscript reads “garments”] golden ornaments for your apparel.

“How the mighty have fallen in battle! Jonathan was slain upon your heights.

“I grieve over you, my brother Jonathan; you were exceedingly beautiful [Hebrew: “Beauty”] and beloved beyond the love of women” [Manuscript: “of a woman”].

[Note: [Col. 0619D] The Vulgate adds: “As a mother loves her only son, so I loved you”; neither the Hieronymian manuscripts according to the Hebrew exemplar nor even the edition of the Seventy, τῶν LXX, knows this passage.]

“How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!”

## [Chapter II.]

After this David consulted the Lord, saying: “Shall I go up to one of the cities of Judah?” The Lord said to him: “Go up.” David said: “Where shall I go up?” He answered him: “To Hebron.”

David went up, together with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelite and Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. David also brought up each of the men who were with him, together with his household, and they dwelt in the towns of Hebron.

[T. LXXXIV.] The men of Judah came and anointed David there to reign over the house of Judah. It was reported to David that the men of Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul. David therefore sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them:

“Blessed are you by the Lord, who have shown this kindness to your lord Saul and have buried him. And now the Lord will indeed repay you with kindness and faithfulness; I too will repay you with gratitude, because you have done this deed.”

[T. LXXXV.] “Let your hands be strengthened, and be sons of strength. Although your lord Saul has died, the house of Judah has anointed me as its king.”

Now Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, and led him around the camp [Hebrew: “to Mahanaim,” which means “camps”], and made him king over Gilead, over Geshur [Hebrew: Asshur], over Jezreel, over Ephraim, over Benjamin, and over all Israel.

Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for two years. Only the house of Judah followed David.

The number of days that David remained reigning in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.

Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from the camp [Hebrew: “from Mahanaim”] to Gibeon. Joab son of Zeruiah and David’s men also went out, and they met them beside the pool of Gibeon. When they had come together, they sat opposite one another, one group on one side of the pool and the other on the opposite side.

Abner said to Joab: “Let the young men rise and play before us.” Joab answered: “Let them rise.”

So twelve men from Benjamin, on the side of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of David’s men rose and crossed over. Each seized the head of his opponent and thrust his sword into the side of his adversary; they fell together. Therefore that place was called the Field of the Mighty, at Gibeon.

[T. LXXXVI.] A very fierce battle arose on that day, and Abner and the men of Israel were routed by David’s men [Hebrew: “by the men of David”].

There were three sons of Zeruiah there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was an exceedingly swift runner [Hebrew: “Asahel was exceedingly swift on his feet”], like one of the gazelles that dwell in the forests [Hebrew: “in the fields”].

Asahel pursued Abner and did not turn aside to the right or to the left [Manuscript: “or”], abandoning his pursuit of Abner. Abner looked behind him and said: “Are you Asahel?” He answered: “I am.”

Abner said to him: “Turn to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men [Hebrew: “boys”], and take his spoil for yourself.” But Asahel refused to stop pursuing him.

Again Abner said to Asahel: “Withdraw; do not follow me, lest I be forced to strike you to the ground, and then I will not be able to lift my face before your brother Joab.” But Asahel refused to listen and would not turn aside.

[T. LXXXVII.] Abner struck him in the groin with the butt of his spear, and pierced him through [Manuscript omits: “him”]; he died in that same place. Everyone who passed by the place where Asahel had fallen and died stopped there.

While Joab and Abishai pursued Abner as he fled [Hebrew: “after Abner”], the sun went down. They came as far as the Hill of the Aqueduct, which is opposite the valley of the road to the wilderness at Gibeon.

The sons of Benjamin gathered around Abner and formed themselves into one band; they stood at the summit of a single hill.

Abner called out to Joab and said: “Will your sword rage unto utter destruction? Or do you not know that despair is dangerous? [Hebrew: “that the end will be bitter?”] How long will you not tell the people to stop pursuing their brothers?”

Joab said: “As God lives, if you had spoken, the people would have withdrawn in the morning from pursuing their brother.”

Joab blew the trumpet, and the whole army [Hebrew: “people”] halted. They pursued Israel no farther, nor did they continue the battle.

Abner and his men went through the plain throughout that entire night. They crossed the Jordan and passed through all Beth-horon; they came to the camp [“to Mahanaim”].

Joab returned, abandoning the pursuit of Abner, and gathered all the people. Nineteen of David’s men were missing, besides Asahel. David’s servants struck down three hundred and sixty men of Benjamin and of those who were with Abner [Note: [Col. 0620D] The Veronese manuscript omits “men,” as does the Vulgate].

They took Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father at Bethlehem. Joab and the men who were with him traveled throughout the night and reached Hebron at the very break of day.

## [Chapter III.]

There was therefore a long conflict between the house of Saul and the house of David. David advanced and grew ever stronger [Vulgate: “David was proceeding”], while the house of Saul grew weaker day by day.

[T. LXXXVIII.] Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam the Jezreelite; after him came Chileab, by Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; the third was Absalom, the son of Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur. The fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah, the son of Abital. The sixth was Ithream, by Eglah, David’s wife. These were born to David in Hebron.

While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner son of Ner [Hebrew omits: “son of Ner”] governed the house of Saul. Saul had had a concubine named Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] Saint Jerome teaches in his book on Hebrew names that Hisboseth should be read with an aspiration. After listing from the Second Book of Kings the four names Hiram, Histob, Hiras, and Hisboseth, he added this observation: “For this reason we have written these names with an aspiration, because among the Hebrews and Greeks they are written with a diphthong.” What will contemporary Hebrew grammarians, who deny that any diphthong exists in the Hebrew language, answer to this annotation? MART.]

Ish-bosheth said to Abner: “Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?”

Abner was exceedingly angry because of Ish-bosheth’s words and said: “Am I a dog’s head belonging to Judah today, that I have shown kindness to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers and relatives, and have not delivered you into David’s hand? And today you are bringing a charge against me concerning this woman?

“May God do these things to Abner, and may he add these and more, unless, just as the Lord swore to David, so I act toward him, transferring the kingdom from the house of Saul and raising David’s throne over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.”

He could not answer him a word, because he feared him.

Abner therefore sent messengers to David on his own behalf, saying: “Whose is the land?” And he added: “Make a covenant of friendship with me [Hebrew: “a covenant”], and my hand will be with you, and I will bring all Israel over to you.”

David said: “Very well; I will make a covenant of friendship with you [Hebrew: “a covenant”]. But I ask one thing of you: you shall not see my face before you bring Michal, the daughter of Saul. Then you may come and see me.”

David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, saying: “Give me back my wife Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines.”

Ish-bosheth sent for her and took her from her husband [manuscript omits: “her husband”] Paltiel, the son of Laish. Her husband followed her, weeping as far as Bahurim. Abner said to him: “Go back.” And he went back.

Abner also addressed the elders of Israel, saying: “Yesterday and the day before you were seeking David to reign over you. Now, therefore, act, for the Lord has spoken to David, saying: ‘By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from all their enemies.’”

Abner also spoke to Benjamin. Then he went to speak to David in Hebron about everything that pleased Israel and all Benjamin.

He came to David in Hebron with twenty men, and David made a feast for Abner and the men who had come with him.

Abner said to David: “I will rise and go, so that I may gather all Israel to my lord the king [Hebrew: “I will rise and go, so that I may gather all Israel to my lord the king”], and that they may make a covenant with you, and you may rule over all according to your heart’s desire.” [Note: [Col. 0622D] The Vulgate and the Greek likewise read: “that I may make a covenant with you.”]

When David had escorted Abner, and Abner had gone away in peace, David’s servants and Joab immediately arrived, having struck down raiders with exceedingly great spoil.

Abner was no longer with David in Hebron, for David had already dismissed him, and he had departed in peace. Joab and the whole army that was with him arrived afterward.

Joab was told by those who brought the report: “Abner son of Ner came to the king, and he dismissed him, and he went away in peace.”

Joab entered the king and said: “What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you. Why did you dismiss him, so that he went away and departed? Do you not know Abner son of Ner, that he came to you for this purpose [Note: [Col. 0622D] The words “to you,” which are absent from the Hebrew, are also absent from the Veronese manuscript], to deceive you, to learn your going out and your coming in, and to know everything that you do?”

Joab went out from David, sent messengers after Abner, and brought him back from the cistern of Sirah [Hebrew: “and they brought him back”], without David’s knowledge.

When Abner had returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside to the middle of the gate to speak with him deceitfully.

[T. LXXXIX.] He struck him there in the groin, and he died in vengeance for the blood of Asahel his brother.

When David heard what had happened [Note: [Col. 0622D] The Veronese manuscript very correctly reads “when the deed had already been done,” which is expressed in the Hebrew by “afterward” and in the Greek by “after these things” (μετὰ ταῦτα)], he said:

“I and my kingdom are innocent before the Lord forever of the blood of Abner son of Ner. May it come upon the head of Joab and upon all the house of his father. May there never fail from the house of Joab one who suffers from a discharge, or is a leper, or holds a spindle, or falls by the sword, or lacks bread.”

Thus Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had killed their brother Asahel at Gibeon in the battle.

David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him: “Tear your garments, gird yourselves with sackcloth, and mourn before the funeral procession of Abner.”

King David followed the bier. When they had buried Abner in Hebron, the king raised his voice and wept [Hebrew: “lamented”] over Abner’s tomb. All the people also wept [Hebrew: “lamented”].

The king mourned and [Note: [Col. 0622D] The Veronese manuscript again omits “and mourned,” which is likewise not expressed in the Hebrew] lamented [Hebrew: “lamenting”] Abner, saying:

“Abner did not die as ignoble men usually die. Your hands were not bound, nor were your feet weighed down with fetters. Rather, as men fall before the sons of iniquity [Vulgate adds: “so”], you fell.”

All the people wept [Hebrew: “lamented”] over him again and again.

When the whole multitude [Hebrew: “all the people”] came to take food with David, while it was still broad daylight [Note: [Col. 0623D] The Veronese manuscript contentiously rejects the words “broad daylight” in accordance with the Hebrew exemplar. In the Hebrew there is only the word “still,” meaning “still in the day”], David swore, saying:

“May God do these things to me, and may he add more, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets.”

All the people heard [Hebrew: “knew”], and everything that the king had done in the sight [Hebrew: “in the eyes”] of all the people pleased them. All the common people and all Israel knew on that day that the king had not caused Abner son of Ner to be killed.

The king also said to his servants: “Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen today in Israel? But I am still delicate and anointed [Hebrew: “Today I am tender and anointed”] as king, while these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too harsh for me. May the Lord repay the one who does evil according to his wickedness.”

## [Chapter IV.]

The son of Saul heard [Vulgate adds: “Ish-bosheth”] that Abner had fallen at Hebron, and his hands grew weak; all Israel was troubled.

[Note: [Col. 0623D] Here the Veronese manuscript omits “men”; shortly afterward it consistently reads Banaa for Baana. Hebrew: uncertain reading.]

There were two men, commanders of raiding bands, belonging to the son of Saul. The name of one was Baana and the name of the other Rechab, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from the sons of Benjamin. For Beeroth also was reckoned [Manuscript: “reported”] as belonging to Benjamin.

The Beerothites fled to Gittaim and lived there as resident aliens until that time.

[T. XC.] Jonathan, the son of Saul, had a son who was disabled in his feet. He was five years old when the report about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse took him and fled. As she hurried to flee, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.

[T. XCI.] The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite—Rechab and Baana—came and entered the house of Ish-bosheth in the heat of the day. He was sleeping on his bed at noon [Note: [Col. 0624D] The Vulgate adds: “And the doorkeeper of the house, cleaning wheat, had fallen asleep”; the manuscript likewise lacks this, in accordance with the Hebrew archetype].

They entered the house carrying ears of wheat, and Rechab and Baana his brother struck him in the groin and fled. When they had entered the house, he was sleeping on his little bed in his chamber. They struck him and killed him. Then they took his head and departed by the wilderness road throughout the night.

They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron and said to the king: “Behold the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who was seeking your life. Today the Lord has given my lord the king vengeance upon Saul and his offspring.”

[T. XCII.] David answered Rechab and Baana his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them:

“As the Lord lives, who has rescued my life from every distress: when the man who brought me the report and said, ‘Saul is dead,’ thinking that he was bringing good news, I seized and killed him at Ziklag. He ought to have received a reward from me for his news.

“How much more now, when wicked men have killed an innocent man in his own house and upon his bed! Shall I not seek his blood from your hand and remove you from the earth?”

David therefore commanded his young men [Vulgate adds: “his own”], and they killed them. They cut off their hands and feet and hung them over the pool at Hebron. But they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron.

[T. XCIII, Chap. V.] Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron, saying: “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh. Moreover, yesterday and the day before, when Saul was king over us, you were the one leading Israel out and bringing it back. And the Lord said to you: ‘You shall shepherd my people Israel, and you shall be leader over [Col. 0624B] Israel.’” The elders [Heb. all the elders] of Israel also came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the Lord; and they anointed David king over Israel.

David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. In Hebron he reigned over Judah for seven years and six months; in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

Then the king and all the men who were with him went to Jerusalem, to the Jebusite inhabitants of the land. And it was said to David by them: “You shall not enter here unless you remove the blind and the lame who say: ‘David shall not enter here.’” But David captured the stronghold of Zion; this is the city of David. For David had proposed a reward on that day for whoever struck down [Col. 0624C] a Jebusite and touched the water-channel of the roofs, and the lame and the blind who hated David’s life [Heb. “And David said on that day: Whoever strikes the Jebusite and touches the water-channel, and the lame and the blind who hate David’s life”]. Therefore it is said in the proverb: “The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple” [Heb. house].

David lived in the stronghold and called it the city of David, and built all around it, from the Millo inward. And he advanced, prospering and growing stronger, and the Lord God of hosts was with him.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] The Veronese manuscript has *proficiscens* (“setting out”) instead of *proficiciens* (“advancing”), perhaps more closely corresponding to the Hebrew.]

[T. XCIV.] Hiram, king of Tyre, sent messengers to David, together with cedar timbers, carpenters, and workers in stone for the walls; and they built a house for David. David knew that the Lord had established him as king over Israel, [Col. 0624D] and that he had exalted his kingdom for [Heb. because of] his people Israel.

So David took still more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he had come from Hebron.

[T. XCV.] Other sons and daughters were born to David [Heb. “and still more”], and these are the names of those born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada [Ms. Elida], and Eliphelet.

When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went up to seek David. When David heard this, he went down to the stronghold. The Philistines, meanwhile, came and spread themselves out in the Valley of Rephaim.

David consulted the Lord, saying: “Shall I go up against the Philistines? And will you give them into my hand?” And the Lord said to David: “Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand.”

So David came to Baal-perazim, struck them there, and said: “The Lord has divided my enemies before me, as waters are divided.” Therefore the name of that place was called Baal-perazim.

And they left their idols there, which David and his men carried away. The Philistines again went up and spread themselves out in the Valley of Rephaim.

David again consulted the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0625D] The Vulgate copies add again: “Shall I go up against the Philistines, and will you give them into my hands?” Neither the Hebrew nor the manuscripts of Jerome’s version have this.]

He answered: [Col. 0625B] “You shall not go up [Vulg. adds: against them], but circle around behind them, and come upon them from the side opposite the pear trees [Heb. weeping trees]. And when you hear the sound of one moving across the tops of the pear trees [Heb. weeping trees], then you shall enter battle; for then the Lord will go out before you, to strike the camp of the Philistines.”

[Note: [Col. 0625D] The Veronese manuscript reads *ut percutias* (“so that you may strike”). The Hebrew has an indefinite construction, “to strike.”]

David did just as the Lord had commanded him, and he struck the Philistines from Geba until you come to Gezer.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] The same manuscript reads: “when you come to Gezer.”]

[T. XCVI, Chap. VI.] David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. He arose [Vulg. adds: David] and went, and all the people who were with him, the men of Judah, in order to bring up the ark of God, over which the name of the Lord of hosts who sits upon the cherubim was invoked, [Col. 0625C] above it.

They placed the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out from the house of Abinadab, who was in Gibeah. Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart. When they had brought it from the house of Abinadab, who was in Gibeah, Ahio, guarding the ark of God, went before the ark.

David and all Israel were playing before the Lord with every kind of crafted wooden instrument, with lyres, harps, tambourines, sistrums, and cymbals. When they came to the threshing floor of Nachon, Uzzah stretched out his hand toward the ark of God and held it, because the oxen were kicking.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] The Vulgate copies add: “and they had nearly overturned it,” a clause unknown to the Hebrew and to Jerome’s manuscript.]

The Lord was greatly angered against Uzzah and struck him because of his rashness; and he died there beside the ark of God. David was grieved because the Lord had struck Uzzah [Heb. “had broken through against Uzzah”], [Col. 0625D] and [Note: [Col. 0626D] The Veronese manuscript reads *Et vocavit* (“And he called”), which is more faithful to the Hebrew.] the name of that place was called “the striking [Heb. breach] of Uzzah,” to this day.

David was afraid of the Lord on that day, saying: “How shall the ark of the Lord come to me?” And David was unwilling to turn the ark of the Lord toward himself, into the city of David; instead, he turned it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.

The ark of the Lord remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household. It was reported to King David: “The Lord has blessed Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God.”

So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom into the city of David with rejoicing.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] The Vulgate copies add: “and there were with David seven choirs, and the sacrifice of a calf”; these words occur neither in the Hebrew nor in the ancient manuscripts of Jerome’s version.]

When those carrying the ark of the Lord had taken six steps, they sacrificed an ox and a ram, and David danced with all his strength before the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] See what Jerome writes concerning the linen ephod in the letter which, as we have said above, he wrote to Marcella, col. 353. MART.]

David was girded with a linen ephod. David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the covenant [Heb. does not have “of the covenant”] of the Lord with jubilation and the sound of the trumpet.

When the ark of the Lord entered the city of David, Michal, the daughter of Saul, looking through the window, saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart.

They brought in the ark of the Lord and placed it in its place, in the middle of the tent that David had pitched for it. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord. When he had finished offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord of hosts.

He distributed to the entire multitude of Israel, to every man and woman, one cake of bread [Heb. one loaf of bread], one portion of roast beef, and a fried cake made with oil. Then all the people went away, each to his own house.

David returned to bless his household, and Michal, the daughter of Saul, came out to meet David and said: “How glorious the king of Israel was today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants [Col. 0626C] and being exposed as one of the buffoons might expose himself!”

David said to Michal: “Before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father and rather than all his household, and commanded me to be leader over the people of the Lord in Israel, I shall play, and I shall become even more contemptible than I have become, and I shall be humble in my own eyes; and with the maidservants of whom you have spoken, I shall appear more glorious.”

[T. XCVII.] Therefore Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no child until the day of her death.

[Chap. VII.] Now it happened, when the king was dwelling in his house and the Lord had given him rest on every side from all his enemies, that he said to Nathan the prophet: “Do you see that I dwell in a cedar house, while the ark of God is placed in the midst of hides?”

Nathan said to the king: “Go and do everything that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you.”

[T. XCVIII.] But it happened that night that the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: “Go and speak to my servant David: Thus says the Lord: ‘Will you build me a house in which I may dwell? For I have not dwelt in a house from the day [Note: [Col. 0626D] The Veronese manuscript reads “from the day on which I brought out”; this is closer to the Hebrew.] when I brought the children of Israel out of the land [Col. 0627A] of Egypt to this day; rather, I have walked in a tabernacle and in a tent.

“‘Throughout all the places where I have traveled with all the children of Israel, did I ever speak a word to one of the tribes of Israel to whom I commanded that they should shepherd my people Israel, saying: “Why have you not built me a cedar house?”

“‘And now you shall say this to my servant David: Thus says the Lord of hosts: “I took you from the pastures, following the flock, so that you would be leader over my people Israel. I was with you everywhere you went, and I destroyed all your enemies from before you. I made your name great, like the name of the great ones who are on the earth.

“‘“I shall appoint a place for my people Israel, plant them there, and they shall dwell in it and shall no longer be disturbed; nor shall the children of iniquity continue to afflict them as before, from the day when I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I shall give you rest from all your enemies.

“‘“The Lord also foretells to you that the Lord will make you a house. When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your body, and I shall establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I shall establish the throne of his kingdom forever.

“‘“I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me. If he does anything wrong, I shall correct him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men. But I shall not remove my mercy from him, as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before [Note: [Col. 0627C] The Veronese manuscript more correctly has “from before you,” in accordance with the Hebrew.] me.

“‘“And your house and your kingdom shall be faithful forever before you, and your throne shall be established forever.”’”

According to all these words and according to this entire vision, Nathan spoke to David.

[T. XCIX.] King David went in and sat before the Lord, and said: “Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far? Yet even this seemed a small thing in your sight [Heb. in your eyes], Lord God, unless you also speak concerning the house of your servant for the distant future. For this is the law of Adam [Heb. man], Lord God.

“What more can David say to you? For you know your servant, Lord God [Heb. [Col. 0628A] “Lord, Lord”]. Because of your word and according to your heart you have done all these great things, making them known to your servant. Therefore you are magnified, Lord God [Heb. [Note: [Col. 0627C] The Septuagint likewise has “Lord, my Lord.” In the Hebrew it is written , which according to the vowel points of the Masoretes is read *Adonai Elohim*, not, as the less learned suppose, *Adonai Jehovah*. *Elohim* always means “God”; therefore Saint Jerome rightly renders it in Latin, “Lord God,” and the Eastern interpreters—the Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic—agree with him. We cannot conceal, however, that the scholiast of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth was mistaken in the immediately following annotation, because the Hebrew does not have there , which, however much we might tolerate its being interpreted “Lord, Lord,” is written in this very place , *Adonai Elohim*, meaning “Lord God.” MART. —Martianay again criticizes the Hebrew scholiast, since the Hebrew here has , which according to the rule of the Masoretes is to be read *Adonai Elohim*; immediately afterward, however, the words themselves appear. We have said that we suspect the scholiast derived these annotations not from a Hebrew archetype but from some Latin manuscript in which certain readings from the old Septuagint version had become embedded.] Lord, Lord], because there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.

“And what nation is like your people Israel, one nation [Heb. one], on earth, for whose sake God went to redeem it for himself as a people, to establish a name for himself, and to do great and fearful things for them upon the earth, before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its god [Heb. nations and their gods]?

“For you established your people Israel for yourself as an everlasting people, and you, Lord [Vulg. adds: God], became their God.

“Now therefore, Lord God [Heb. does not have “God”], [Col. 0628B] establish forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, and do as you have spoken, so that your name may be magnified forever and it may be said: ‘The Lord of hosts is God over Israel.’ And the house of your servant David shall be established before the Lord [Heb. before you], because you, Lord of hosts, God of Israel, have revealed this to your servant’s ear, saying: ‘I shall build you a house.’ Therefore your servant has found his heart to pray to you in this prayer [Ms. omits “to you”].

“Now therefore, Lord God, you are God, and your words shall be true. For you have spoken these good things to your servant. Begin, then, and bless the house of your servant, so that it may endure forever before you; for you, Lord God, have spoken, and by your blessing the house of your servant shall be blessed forever.”

[Note: [Col. 0628C] In this place the Septuagint also lacks the name of God: “Καὶ νῦν κύριέ μου, ῥῆμα etc.”, that is, “And now, my Lord, the word, etc.” Yet in the present Hebrew text there is , *Veatta Adonai Elohim*, which is translated into Latin as “And now, Lord God.” Therefore, unless I am mistaken, it remains that the Septuagint interpreters and the scholiast of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth used Hebrew exemplars in which the word *Elohim* was absent after the name *Adonai*—or, if one prefers, *Jehovah*.
