MART. —From this we may again infer that the scholiast did not consult the Hebrew exemplar itself, for in the Hebrew “God” is present.]

[Col. 0628C] [T. C, Chap. VIII.] After these things David struck the Philistines and humbled them, and David took the bridle of tribute from the hand of the Philistines.

He struck Moab and measured them with a cord, making them lie level with the ground. He measured two cords, one for killing and one for preserving alive [Heb. “He measured two cords for killing, and one cord for preserving alive”]. Thus Moab became subject to David, bearing tribute [Heb. “Moab became subject to David, bearing gifts”].

David also struck [Note: [Col. 0628D] The printed editions read *Adarezer*, a form that came from the Septuagint interpreters, who read Ἀδρααζὰρ, that is, with *resh* in place of *daleth*. The Hebrew, together with all the older and better Latin manuscripts, has *Adadezer*. MART. —The Veronese manuscript has *Addadeazer*; the Vulgate copies have *Adarezer*.] Adadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, when he went to establish his power [Col. 0629A] over the Euphrates River.

David captured from him one thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand infantrymen. He hamstrung all the draft horses of the chariots, but left one hundred chariots among them.

Syria of Damascus came to bring aid to Adadezer, king of Zobah. David struck down twenty-two thousand men of Syria. David placed a garrison in Syria of Damascus, and Syria became subject to David, bearing tribute [Heb. “subject, bearing gifts”]. The Lord preserved [Heb. saved] David wherever he went.

David took the golden collars that belonged to the servants of Adadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. From Betah and Berothai [Ms. Beroth], cities of Adadezer, King David took a very large quantity of bronze.

When Thou [Heb. Toi], king of Hamath, heard that David had struck down [Col. 0629B] all the strength of Adadezer, he sent Joram [Note: [Col. 0629C] On the authority of the Veronese manuscript, and of the Hebrew and Greek texts, we have supplied here the complete verb, which was missing.] his son to King David to greet him, congratulate him, and give thanks because he had defeated [Heb. “and blessed him because he had fought”] Adadezer and struck him down.

[T. CI.] For Thou was an enemy of Adadezer. In his possession were vessels of gold, vessels of silver, and vessels of bronze. King David also consecrated these to the Lord, together with the silver and gold that he had consecrated from all the nations he had subdued: from Syria, Moab, the children of Ammon, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the spoils of Adadezer son of Rehob [Ms. Roboth], king of Zobah.

David made a name for himself when he returned after the capture of Syria in the Valley of Salt, killing eighteen thousand men.

[Note: [Col. 0629C] Instead of eighteen thousand, the manuscript copies of the sacred Scriptures read twelve thousand. The author of the *Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings* discusses this, saying: “If anyone is troubled that in most Latin manuscripts it is found that David struck down not eighteen thousand but twelve thousand in the Valley of Salt, let him know that this was introduced into those manuscripts through scribal error. Yet David truly struck down eighteen thousand in that same Valley of Salt, while Joab struck down twelve thousand, as is written in the title of Psalm fifty-eight.” Let the reader observe that the number is erroneous here both in the printed books and in the manuscripts; instead of “in the title of Psalm fifty-eight,” one should read “in the title of Psalm fifty-nine,” or, according to the Hebrews, Psalm sixty. MART. —The Veronese manuscript, like all the others that Martianay consulted in large number, has only twelve thousand. This error, introduced through scribal fault into the Latin manuscripts, had already been corrected by the author of the *Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings*, whom Martianay himself cites. Lucas Brugensis likewise found the same corrupt reading in his manuscripts and rejected it in favor of the authority of the Hebrew exemplar.]

He placed guards in Edom and established a garrison, and all Edom became subject to David. The Lord preserved [Heb. saved] David wherever he went.

David reigned over all Israel and administered judgment and justice to all his people.

Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder; Zadok son of Ahitub and [Note: [Col. 0630C] The Veronese manuscript again incorrectly reads *Ahimelech* instead of *Achimelech*. This error had already existed in Greek books from the time of Eusebius, who writes as follows on Psalm 33: “The Book of Kingdoms contains *Achimelech*, the letter having been changed; there is no need for anyone to disturb the text. For because of the similarity between the letter called *beth* among the Hebrews and *kaph*, the name was issued in different forms; for the two letters are nearly identical in form, distinguished only by the change of a very short stroke. The Book of Kings has *Achimelech*; let no one be disturbed by the change of a letter, for the name was rendered differently because of the similarity between the letters *beth* and *kaph*, as the Hebrews call them. In fact, the form of the two letters is almost one and the same, distinguished only by a very short stroke.” Yet Eusebius himself is mistaken: the Hebrew does not spell it with , but with , which is the correct spelling. The Veronese manuscript then has “son of Abiathar the priest,” again incorrectly, unless—given the frequent exchange of the letters E and I—it should be understood as written for “the priests,” with the verb *erant* (“were”) more elegantly omitted.] Ahimelech [Col. 0630A] son of Abiathar were priests; Seraiah was secretary; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites [Heb. “Seraiah, secretary; and Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites”]. The sons of David were priests.

[T. CII, Chap. IX.] David said: “Is there perhaps anyone remaining from the house of Saul, that I may show him mercy for Jonathan’s sake?”

There was a servant from the house of Saul named Ziba. When the king called him to himself, he said to him: “Are you Ziba?” He replied: “I am your servant” [Heb. does not have “I am”].

The king said: “Is anyone still surviving from the house of Saul, that I may show him the mercy of God?”

Ziba said to the king: “Jonathan has a son who is disabled in his feet.”

“Where is he?” he asked.

Ziba said to the king: “Behold, he is in the house of Machir son of Ammiel at Lo-debar.” So King David sent for him and brought him from the house of Machir son of Ammiel at Lo-debar [Ms. Lodabar].

When Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David, he fell on his face and bowed down. David said: “Mephibosheth?” He answered: “Here I am, your servant.”

David said to him: “Do not be afraid, for I will certainly show you mercy for the sake of your father Jonathan. I shall restore to you all the fields of Saul your father, and you shall always eat bread at my table.”

He bowed to him and said: “Who am I [Heb. does not have “Who am I”], your servant, that you have looked upon a dead dog such as I am?”

Then the king called Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said to him: “Everything that belonged to Saul and his entire household I have given to the son of your master. Therefore cultivate the land for him—you, your sons, and your servants—and bring food [Heb. bread] for the son of your master, so that he may be fed. Mephibosheth, the son of your master, shall always eat bread at my table.”

Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. Ziba said to the king: “Just as you have commanded, my lord the king, so your servant will do; and Mephibosheth shall eat at your table [Heb. my table], like one of the king’s sons.”

Mephibosheth had a young son named Micah. All the household of Ziba served Mephibosheth.

Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he continually ate from the king’s table; and he was lame in both feet.

[T. CIII, Chap. X.] After these things, the king of the children of Ammon died, [Note: [Col. 0631D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “and Anon reigned.”] and Annon [Heb. Hanun], his son, reigned in his place.

David said: “I shall show mercy to Anon son of Nahash, just as his father showed mercy to me.” So David sent his servants to console him over his father’s death.

When David’s servants came into the land of the children of Ammon, the princes of the children of Ammon said to Anon their lord: “Do you suppose that David has sent comforters to you out of honor for your father, and not in order to investigate, spy out, and overthrow the city? Is that why David has sent his servants to you?”

Anon took David’s servants, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut their garments in half up to the buttocks, and sent them away.

When this was reported to David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly humiliated [Heb. does not have “greatly”], and David commanded them [Heb. the king]: “Remain in Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return.”

When the children of Ammon saw that they had wronged David [Heb. that they had disgraced David], they sent for hire and enlisted the Syrians of Rehob [Heb. the Syrian of the house of Rehob], the Syrians of Zobah—twenty thousand infantrymen—and from the king of Maacah one thousand men, and from Ishtob twelve thousand men.

When David heard this, he sent Joab and the entire army of warriors.

The children of Ammon went out and drew up their battle line before him [Heb. does not have “before him”] at the entrance of the gate. The Syrians of Zobah, Rehob, Ishtob, and Maacah were separately in the field.

When Joab saw that battle had been prepared against him both in front and behind, he selected from all the chosen men of Israel and drew up the battle line against Syria. He handed over the remaining part of the people to his brother Abishai [Heb. Absai], who drew up the battle line against the children of Ammon.

Joab said [Heb. does not have this]: “If the Syrians prevail against me, you shall come to my aid; but if the children of Ammon prevail against you, I shall come to your aid. Be strong, and let us fight for our people and for the city [Heb. cities] of our God; and the Lord will do what is good in his sight [Heb. in his eyes].”

Joab and the people who were with him engaged the Syrians in battle, and they immediately fled before him. When the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians had fled, they too fled before Abishai and entered the city. Joab returned from the children of Ammon and came to Jerusalem.

When the Syrians saw that they had been defeated before Israel, they gathered together. Adadezer sent [Note: [Col. 0631D] The Hebrew text here has , *Adarezer*, whereas above, in chapter eight, it is read with a doubled *daleth*, *Adadezer*, which the Latin manuscripts also retain here. MART. —The Hebrew exemplar cited here gives *Adarezer*, a form produced throughout by the confusion of highly similar letters.] and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the River; and [Heb. “and they came to Helam”] he brought their army. Sobach, the commander of Adadezer’s army, was their leader.

When this was reported to David, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and came to Helam.

[Note: [Col. 0632D] Other manuscripts read *Helema* and *Helama*. The corrector of the Canon removed the final *a* from *Helama*. MART. —The Veronese manuscript has *Helama*, and the Hebrew likewise adds .]

The Syrians drew up their battle line opposite David and fought against him. The Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen of the Syrians. He struck down Sobach, the commander of the army, and he died immediately.

When all the kings who were under the protection of Adadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, [Note: [Col. 0632D] The Vulgate books insert: “they were terrified and fled—fifty-eight thousand before Israel.” Jerome’s manuscripts and the original texts know nothing of these words.] they made peace with Israel, served them, and from then on the Syrians were afraid to give aid to the children of Ammon [Ms. omits “from then on”].

[Col. 0632B] [Chap. XI.] As the year turned, at the time when kings usually go out to war [Heb. “at the time when kings had gone out to war”], David sent Joab, his servants with him, and all Israel. They devastated the children of Ammon and besieged Rabbah, while David remained [Heb. dwelt] in Jerusalem.

[T. CIV.] While these things were taking place, David happened to rise from his bed after midday and walk on the roof terrace of the royal house [Heb. “And it happened in the evening that David rose from his bed, and he walked on the roof terrace”]. He saw a woman bathing opposite [Heb. does not have “opposite”], above his roof terrace [Heb. from above the roof terrace]. The woman was very beautiful.

The king sent and inquired who the woman was. He was told that she was Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite [Heb. “And he said: Is this not Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”].

David sent messengers and took her. When she had entered to him, he slept with her. Immediately she was sanctified from her impurity [Heb. “And she sanctified herself from her impurity”], and she returned to her house having conceived.

She sent word to David and said: “I have conceived.”

David sent to Joab, saying: “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” Joab sent Uriah to David.

Uriah came to David. David asked how Joab was doing, how the people were doing, and how the war was being conducted. David said to Uriah: “Go down to your house and wash your feet.”

Uriah went out from the king’s house, and a royal meal followed him [Heb. “a royal gift followed him”]. But Uriah slept before the gate of the royal house with the other servants of his lord and did not go down to his house.

It was reported to David: “Uriah did not go down to his house.” David said to Uriah: “Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?”

Uriah said to David: “The ark, Israel, and Judah dwell in tents [Heb. tabernacles], while my lord Joab and the servants of my lord remain upon the face of the earth. Shall I enter my house to eat, drink, and sleep with my wife? By your life and by the life of your soul, [Col. 0633A] I shall not do this thing” [Heb. “As you live, and as your soul lives, I shall not do this thing”].

David said to Uriah: “Remain here today also, and tomorrow I shall send you away” [Heb. “send you”]. Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.

David called him to eat and drink before him, and he made him drunk. But Uriah went out in the evening and slept on his bed with the servants of his lord; he did not go down to his house.

In the morning David wrote a letter [Heb. book] to Joab [Note: [Col. 0633D] A more recent hand in the Veronese manuscript adds: “sealed it with his own hand and with his ring.” I do not know whether this gloss appears anywhere else in any manuscript.] and sent it by the hand of Uriah. In the letter [Heb. book] he wrote:

“Place Uriah opposite the fiercest part of the battle, and withdraw from him so that he may be struck down and die.”

When Joab was besieging the city, he stationed Uriah in the place where he knew that the strongest men were. The men of the city went out and fought against Joab; some of the people, the servants of David, fell, and Uriah the Hittite also died.

Joab sent and reported to David everything that had happened in the battle. He commanded the messenger, saying: “When you have finished reporting all the matters of the battle to the king, if you see him become angry and say: ‘Why did you approach the wall to fight? Did you not know that arrows are shot down from the wall? Who struck down Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth [Ms. Hieroboseth; Vulg. Jerobaal]? Was it not a woman who threw a fragment of a millstone upon him from the wall and killed him at Thebez? Why did you approach the wall?’—then you shall say: ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.’”

The messenger went, came, and reported to David everything Joab had commanded him.

The messenger said to David: “The men prevailed against us and went out [Note: [Col. 0634D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “went out against us.” Other versions likewise have “against us.”] into the field. We made a charge against them and pursued them as far as the gate of the city. The archers shot arrows at your servants from above, from the wall, and some of the king’s servants died; indeed, your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.”

David said to the messenger: “You shall say this to Joab: ‘Do not let this matter trouble you, for the outcome of battle is variable [Heb. does not have this], and the sword consumes now one man, now another [Note: [Col. 0634D] The same manuscript reads “will consume.” The Hebrew likewise has this reading]. Strengthen your warriors against the city, so that you may destroy it, and encourage them [Heb. it].’”

When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband had died, she mourned for him [Heb. “she lamented”].

When the mourning had passed, David sent for her and brought her into his house. She became his wife and bore him a son. But the matter that David had done displeased the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord].

## [T. CV, Chapter XII]

So the Lord sent Nathan to David. When he came to him, he said to him:

“There were two men in one city, one rich and the other poor. The rich man had very many sheep and cattle. But the poor man had nothing at all, except one little ewe-lamb, which he had bought and nourished. It had grown up with him and with his children together, eating from his morsel of bread [Hebrew: “piece of bread”], drinking from his cup, and sleeping in his bosom; and it was to him like a daughter [manuscript: “son”].

“Now when a traveler came to the rich man, he was unwilling to take from his own sheep and cattle to prepare a feast for the traveler who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man’s ewe-lamb and prepared food for the man who had come to him.”

David’s anger was greatly kindled against that man, and he said to Nathan: “As the Lord lives, the man who has done this is a son of death. He shall restore the ewe fourfold, because he did this thing and showed no pity.”

Nathan then said to David: “You are that man. Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I anointed you king over Israel, and I rescued you from the hand of Saul. I gave you the house of your lord, and your lord’s wives into your bosom; I gave you the house of Israel and Judah. And if these things are too little, I will add to you far greater things [Hebrew: “twice as much”]. Why, then, have you despised the word of the Lord, so as to do evil in my sight [Hebrew: “in his eyes”]?

“You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword; you took his wife for yourself [manuscript omits “for yourself”], and you killed him with the sword of the sons of Ammon. Therefore the sword shall not depart from your house forever, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite, so that she might be your wife.

“Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will raise up evil against you from your own house. I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall sleep with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you acted secretly, but I will do this thing in the sight of all Israel and in the sight of the sun.”

## [T. CVI]

David said to Nathan: “I have sinned against the Lord.”

Nathan replied to David: “The Lord has also removed your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have caused the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the son also who has been born to you shall surely die” [Hebrew: “By blaspheming, you have blasphemed the enemies of the Lord; therefore even the son…”].

[Note: Consult this passage in the *Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings*. MART.]

Then Nathan returned to his house.

## [T. CVII]

The Lord struck the child whom the wife of Uriah had borne to David, and he became gravely ill. David pleaded with the Lord for the child; David fasted with a fast [manuscript: “a fasting”], and, entering a secluded place, lay on the ground. The elders of his household came to him and urged him to rise from the ground, but he refused and ate no food with them [Hebrew: “bread”].

On the seventh day the infant died [Hebrew: “the little one”]. David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child had died. For they said: “While the child was still alive, we spoke to him and he did not listen to our voice; how much more, if we say, ‘The child is dead,’ will he do himself harm?”

[Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “when he heard”; the printed reading is closer to the Hebrew.]

When David saw his servants whispering, he understood that the child had died. He said to his servants: “Is the child dead?” They answered him: “He is dead.”

So David rose from the ground, washed and anointed himself. After changing his clothes, he entered the house of the Lord, worshiped, and then went to his own house. He asked that bread be set before him, and he ate.

His servants said to him: “What is this action that you have taken? While the child was still alive, you fasted and wept; but when the child died, you rose and ate bread.”

He replied: “While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said: ‘Who knows whether the Lord may perhaps give him to me, and the child may live?’” [Hebrew: “Who knows whether the Lord may perhaps have pity on me, and the child may live?”]

[Note: The same manuscript reads “and he will live”; the Hebrew also has this reading. Shortly afterward it reads *I fast* rather than *I should fast*, more closely following the Hebrew and the other texts.]

“But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.”

Then David consoled Bathsheba his wife.

## [T. CVIII]

He went in to her and slept with her. She bore a son, and called his name Solomon, and the Lord loved him. He sent word through Nathan the prophet, and he called his name Jedidiah, “Beloved of the Lord,” because the Lord loved him [Hebrew: “And he called the name of the Lord, because of the Lord”].

Meanwhile Joab was fighting against Rabbah of the sons of Ammon and was attacking the royal city. Joab sent messengers to David, saying: “I have fought against Rabbah [Hebrew: “Rabba”], and the city of the waters is about to be taken. Now, therefore, gather the rest of the people, besiege the city, and capture it, lest, when the city has been destroyed by me, the victory be attributed to my name.”

So David gathered all the people and went against Rabba.

[Note: In the Hebrew, [reading uncertain]; the Veronese manuscript prefers *Rabbath*.]

When he had fought against it, he captured it. He took the crown of their king from his head—a talent by weight of gold, with extremely precious gems—and it was placed on David’s head. He also carried away a very great amount of spoil from the city. He brought out its people, sawed them apart, and drove them over iron-spiked chariots; he divided them with knives and passed them through the brick molds. He did this to all the cities of the sons of Ammon.

Then David and all the army returned to Jerusalem.

## [T. CIX, Chapter XIII]

[Note: Many variant readings occur in this place in the manuscript books. The canonical text reads as we have printed it. The Royal manuscript, together with one Corbie manuscript, no. 22, and another of Saint-Germain, no. 5, reads:

“Now it happened after this that Absalom son of David had a very beautiful sister named Tamar, and Amnon son of David loved her and loved her exceedingly, so that he became ill because of his love for her.”

This is nearly the reading of the Septuagint interpreters. The major Saint-Germain manuscript, no. 11, expresses the same sense in different words:

“Now it happened after this that Absalon son of David had a very beautiful sister named Tamar; and Amnon son of David loved her and loved her exceedingly, so that…” [and so forth].

Two manuscripts of the Colbert Library and another of Saint-Germain read in accordance with our Vulgate Latin version, except that they have *and he would pine away greatly for her* instead of *and he would pine away for her greatly*. Finally, our Saint-Germain manuscript, no. 7, reads in the sacred text *and he loved her greatly*, while in the margin it has *or, he would pine away for her*.

To these should be added the major Corbie manuscript, no. 1, which alone presents the pure reading of the Vulgate. For of the eleven manuscripts that remain among those collated in this work, one preserves the reading *and he would pine away for her* instead of the others’ *and he would pine away greatly because of her*. The phrase *to pine away for her*, or *to pine away into her*, is by no means unusual in Jerome, as we shall note in its proper places. MART.]

Now it happened after this that Amnon son of David loved Tamar, the beautiful sister of Absalom, and pined away because of her, so that he became ill because of his love for her. For, since she was a virgin, it seemed difficult to him to do anything dishonorable with her.

Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, son of Shammah [manuscript: “Semmai,”] David’s brother, a very prudent man. He said to him: “Why do you grow so thin from day to day, son of the king? Why do you not tell me?”

Amnon answered him: “I love Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom.”

Jonadab replied: “Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. When your father comes to visit you, say to him: ‘Please let my sister Tamar come and give me food [Hebrew: “bread”], and prepare a dish so that I may eat from her hand.’”

So Amnon lay down and began to act as though he were ill. When the king came to visit him, Amnon said to the king: “Please let my sister Tamar come and make two little cakes before my eyes, so that I may take food from her hand.”

David then sent word to Tamar at the house, saying: “Go to the house of your brother Amnon and prepare food for him.”

Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon. He was lying down. She took flour [Hebrew: “kneaded flour”], mixed it, and, melting it, cooked little cakes before his eyes. She took what she had cooked, poured it out, and set it before him, but he refused to eat.

Amnon said: “Send everyone out from me.”

[Note: The same manuscript omits *out*, which is somewhat more concise. The Hebrew literally has “away from above me.”]

When everyone had been sent out, Amnon said to Tamar: “Bring the food into the inner room, so that I may eat from your hand.”

Tamar took the little cakes she had made and brought them into the inner room to her brother Amnon. When she had offered him the food [manuscript omits “him”], he seized her and said: “Come, lie with me, my sister.”

She answered him: “No, my brother, do not violate me! For this must not be done in Israel. Do not commit this disgraceful act. I could not bear my disgrace, and you would be like one of the fools in Israel. Rather, speak to the king, and he will not refuse me to you.”

But he would not listen to her pleas. Since he was stronger than she, he violated her and slept with her. Then Amnon hated her with an exceedingly great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had previously loved her.

## [T. CX]

Amnon said to her: “Rise and go.”

She answered him: “This evil that you are now doing to me is greater than what you did before, when you drove me out” [Note: The same manuscript, with the Vulgate, adds *me*; the Hebrew has the corresponding word.]

But he would not listen to her. Calling the servant who ministered to him, he said: “Drive this woman out from me and shut the door behind her.”

She was wearing a long robe, for virgin daughters of kings wore garments of this kind. His servant drove her out and shut the doors behind her. She sprinkled ashes on her head, tore the long robe she was wearing, placed her hands on her head, and went away, entering and crying out.

Her brother Absalom said to her: “Has your brother Amnon lain with you? [Hebrew: “Aminon,” interpreted ‘exsp…’ (uncertain); but elsewhere “Amnon,” interpreted ‘most faithful.’] But now, sister, be silent; he is your brother. Do not take this matter to heart” [Hebrew: “Do not set this matter in your heart”].

So Tamar remained, wasting away, in the house of her brother Absalom.

When King David heard these things, he was greatly grieved [Hebrew: “angry”].

[Note: The Vulgate adds: “And he did not wish to grieve the spirit of Amnon his son, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn.” This is absent both from the Hebrew text and from the manuscripts of Jerome’s version.]

Absalom spoke neither good nor evil to Amnon, for Absalom hated Amnon because he had violated Tamar his sister [manuscript: “his”].

After a period of two years, Absalom’s sheep were being sheared at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim. Absalom invited all the king’s sons and came to the king, saying: “Behold, your servant’s sheep are being sheared. Please let the king and his servants come to his servant.”

The king said to Absalom: “No, my son, no. Do not ask that we all come and burden you.”

When he pressed him, but he still refused to go, the king blessed him.

Absalom said: “If you will not come, please let my brother Amnon come with us at least.”

The king said to him: “There is no need for him to go with you” [Hebrew: “Why should he go with you?”].

Absalom pressed him, and he sent Amnon and all the king’s sons with him.

[Note: The Vulgate again adds: “And Absalom prepared a feast like a king’s feast.” This is vainly sought in the Hebrew or in Jerome’s manuscripts.]

Absalom had commanded his servants, saying: “Watch for the time when Amnon is drunk with wine. When I say to you, ‘Strike him and kill him,’ do not be afraid. For I am the one who commands you. Be strong and be courageous men” [Hebrew: “men of strength”].

## [T. CXI]

So Absalom’s servants did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded them [Hebrew omits “them”]. All the king’s sons rose, mounted their mules [Hebrew: “males, their”] one by one, and fled.

While they were still on the road, word reached David: “Absalom has struck down all the king’s sons, and not one of them remains.”

The king rose, tore his clothes, and fell to the ground. All his servants who were standing by him also tore their clothes.

Jonadab, son of Shammah [manuscript: “Semmai”], David’s brother, answered and said: “Let not my lord the king suppose that all the king’s sons have been killed. Amnon alone is dead, because this had been determined in Absalom’s mind from the day he violated his sister Tamar.

“Now, therefore, let not my lord the king take this matter to heart, saying: ‘All the king’s sons have been killed.’ For Amnon alone is dead.”

Absalom had fled. The watchman lifted his eyes and looked, and behold, a large crowd was coming along a side road on the slope of the mountain.

Jonadab said to the king: “Behold, the king’s sons are here. It has happened just as your servant said.”

While he was still speaking, the king’s sons appeared. They entered, raised their voices, and wept. The king and all his servants also wept with an exceedingly great lamentation.

But Absalom, fleeing, went to Talmai [Hebrew: “Thalmai”], son of Ammihud [manuscript: “Amiur”], king of Geshur.

David mourned for his son all his days. But after Absalom had fled and come to Geshur, he remained there three years.

[Note: For what should be thought about this cessation of the pursuit, see, if you wish, the *Hebrew Traditions of the False Jerome on the Books of Kings*. MART.]

King David ceased pursuing Absalom, because he had been consoled concerning Amnon’s death.

## [T. CXII, Chapter XIV]

When Joab son of Zeruiah understood that the king’s heart was turned toward Absalom, he sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman. He said to her: “Pretend to be mourning and put on mourning clothes; do not anoint yourself with oil. Be like a woman who has been mourning the dead for a long time. Then go in to the king and speak these words to him.”

So Joab put the words into her mouth.

When the woman of Tekoa had entered the king’s presence, she fell on the ground before him and worshiped [Hebrew: “she fell on her face to the ground and worshiped”]. She said: “Save me, O king.”

The king said to her: “What is the matter with you?”

She answered: “Alas, I am a widow. My husband is dead. And your servant had two sons, who quarreled with each other in the field, and there was no one to separate them. One struck the other and killed him.

“And behold, the whole family has risen against your servant, saying: ‘Hand over the one who struck his brother, so that we may kill him for the life of his brother whom he killed, and destroy the heir.’ They seek to extinguish my remaining spark, so that no name or remnant of my husband may remain upon the earth” [Hebrew: “upon the face of the earth”].

The king said to the woman: “Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you.”

The woman of Tekoa said to the king: “Upon me, my lord the king [the Vulgate adds: “be”], and upon my father’s house, be the iniquity; but let the king and his throne be innocent.”

The king said: “Whoever contradicts you, bring him to me, and he shall no longer touch you.”

She said: “Let the king remember the Lord his God, so that the avengers of blood may not multiply to take revenge and utterly kill my son” [manuscript: “so that they will not kill”].

He said: “As the Lord lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground.”

The woman said: “Let your servant speak a word to my lord the king.”

He said: “Speak.”

The woman said: “Why have you devised such a thing against the people of God? By speaking this word, the king has made himself guilty, since he does not bring back his banished one. We all die, and like waters poured out upon the ground, which do not return, so we disappear. God does not desire the destruction of a soul, but he takes thought, so that the one who has been cast away may not perish completely.

“Now, therefore, I have come to speak this word to my lord the king in the presence of the people. Your servant said: ‘I will speak to the king; perhaps the king will carry out the word of his servant.’ And the king has heard, so as to deliver his servant from the hand of all who wanted to erase me from God’s inheritance [Hebrew: “destroy me”], together with my son.

“Therefore let your servant say that my lord the king’s word may be like a sacrifice [Hebrew: “like repose”]. For as an angel of God, so is my lord the king, so that he is not moved by blessing or cursing [Hebrew: “so that he hears good and evil”]. Therefore the Lord your God is with you” [Hebrew: “and the Lord is with you”].

The king answered and said to the woman: “Do not hide from me the matter about which I question you.”

The woman said: “Speak, my lord the king.”

The king said: “Is the hand of Joab with you in all these things?”

The woman answered and said: “By the life of your soul [Hebrew: “by your life”], my lord the king, neither to the left nor to the right is there any deviation from all that my lord the king has said. For your servant Joab himself commanded me, and he himself put all these words into the mouth of your servant, so that I might alter the form of this speech. Your servant Joab did this [Hebrew: “made this happen”]. But you, my lord, are wise, like an angel of God, so that you understand everything that is on the earth.”

## [T. CXIII]

The king said to Joab: “Behold, I have granted your request [Hebrew: “this request”]. Go, therefore, and bring back the boy Absalom.”

Joab fell on his face to the ground, worshiped, and blessed the king. Joab said: “Today your servant understands that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, because you have carried out the word of your servant.”

So Joab rose and went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.

[Note: Here the Veronese manuscript rightly adds “the king,” in agreement with the Hebrew text and the Vulgates.]

The king said: “Let him return to his house, and let him not see my face.”

So Absalom returned to his house and did not see the king’s face.

In all Israel there was no man so handsome as Absalom, nor so greatly praised for his beauty [Hebrew omits this clause]. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.

When he cut his hair—for he cut it once a year, because his abundant hair weighed him down [Hebrew: “When his head was cut, at the appointed time it was cut”—], he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels by the public weight [Hebrew: “royal weight”].

Three sons and one daughter were born to Absalom. The daughter’s name was Tamar, and she was of elegant appearance.

[Note: This is a noteworthy passage because of an addition made by the Septuagint translators. After the words *of elegant appearance*, they immediately add:

“She became the wife of Rehoboam son of Solomon, and she bore him Abijah.”

These words are also found in certain Latin manuscripts, and they still remain complete in the Hebrew Canon of Truth, but they are struck through with a transverse line as adulterous and imported from Greek copies.

In any event, these words create an inextricable difficulty for the recent defender of the Greek translation of the Seventy. For when the history of the Kings is carefully examined, and the ages of Absalom, the father of Tamar, as well as those of Solomon, Rehoboam, and Abijah are calculated according to the reckoning of that same defender and restorer of ancient chronology—who confidently teaches in chapter 10 of his new restoration that Solomon fathered Rehoboam from an Ammonite woman in the fifty-third year of his life—it necessarily follows that Tamar, daughter of Absalom, married Rehoboam when she had reached approximately her ninetieth year.

That this should be believed would certainly be ridiculous, in my judgment, and exceedingly monstrous in a wife of Rehoboam, since it was Sarah’s unique privilege to give birth at the age of ninety. But this chronological dispute does not belong to the present place; with God’s help I shall treat it elsewhere. The diligent reader must nevertheless be warned that this passage gives rise to an insoluble problem for those who do not hesitate to assert, apart from the authority of the divine Scriptures, that Solomon reigned for a full eighty years, although the sacred writers of the Books of Kings and Chronicles explicitly testify to the contrary. MART.

The Veronese manuscript has *of elegant form* instead. In certain manuscripts Martianus found the Greek addition inserted here:

“She became the wife of Rehoboam son of Solomon, and bore him Abijah,”

but this addition has scarcely any authority.]

Absalom remained in Jerusalem for two years without seeing the king’s face.

## [T. CXIV]

Then Absalom sent for Joab, asking him to send him to the king, but Joab refused to come to him. When he sent a second time and Joab still refused to come [Note: The Veronese manuscript, in agreement with the Hebrew exemplar, also omits *to him*], Absalom said to his servants:

“You know Joab’s field beside my field, where there is a barley crop. Go and set it on fire.”

So Absalom’s servants set the standing grain [Hebrew: “field”] on fire.

[Note: The Vulgate adds: “And Joab’s servants came, tearing their clothes, and said: ‘Absalom’s servants have set part of the field on fire.’” Jerome’s manuscripts, following the Hebrew text, do not contain these words.]

Joab rose and came to Absalom at his house and said: “Why have your servants set my crop [Hebrew: “my field”] on fire?”

Absalom answered Joab: “I sent to you, pleading that you come to me, so that I might send you to the king and say to him: ‘Why did I come from Geshur? It would have been better for me to remain there. Please let me see the king’s face. If he remembers my iniquity [Hebrew omits *my*], let him kill me.’”

Joab went to the king and reported this to him. When Absalom was summoned, he entered before the king [Hebrew: “to the ground before the king’s face”], bowed on his face to the ground before him, and the king kissed Absalom.

## Chapter XV

After this Absalom made himself a chariot, horses, and fifty men to run before him [Hebrew: “to run before him”].

Absalom rose early and stood beside the entrance of the gate [Note: The Veronese manuscript, with the Vulgate, omits *in the road*. The Hebrew phrase is: “He stood at the hand of the gate road.”] Whenever any man who had a legal matter came to the king’s judgment, Absalom called him to himself and said: “From what city are you?”

He answered: “Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel” [Hebrew omits this clause].

Absalom said to him: “Your statements seem good and just to me, but no one has been appointed by the king to hear you.”

Absalom would also say: “Who would appoint me judge over the land, so that all who have a legal matter might come to me and I could judge justly?”

Whenever a man [Hebrew: “a person”] approached him to greet him, he would extend his hand, seize him, and kiss him. Absalom did this to all Israel who came to the king’s judgment to be heard, and he stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

## [T. CXV]

After [Note: There is great disagreement here about the numbers, not only among the manuscript books but also among the editions of the Bibles of Sixtus and Clement. Three ancient and excellent Corbie manuscripts formerly read *after forty years*, which the correctors changed to *after four*, or even *after two years*. The Royal manuscript, no. 3563, and the major Saint-Germain manuscript, no. 3, had *five years* before correction, but now have *four*. In the Hebrew Canon of Truth, a later hand changed *four or five* into *forty*. The Colbert manuscript, no. 181, retains *forty* from the beginning; but the Aniciensis, likewise Colbert, together with three other Saint-Germain manuscripts from the Meadows, has *four*, not *forty*.

The Roman corrections of the Bibles teach that the numbers four, five, and six should be rejected, although four has some probability—and also authority, since we read four similarly in the Syriac and Arabic interpreters. The learned Grotius approves this reading, saying: “There is no doubt that this is a scribal error, caused by two letters being added to the word. Josephus says that four years intervened, and Theodoret likewise.”

The fact itself also demonstrates that this is true. Yet the pseudo-Jerome taught the contrary in the book of *Hebrew Traditions* on the Second Book of Kings: “Beware, reader,” he says, “of the many corrupt copies in which it is written ‘after four,’ not ‘after forty years.’ In the more truthful copies and in the Hebrew truth, not four but forty years are written.”

But if someone obstinately wishes to establish those four years as running from the time when Absalom killed his brother Amnon until the time when he said to his father, “I will go and fulfill the vows I have vowed to the Lord in Hebron,” he will plainly find, if he investigates carefully, that he is mistaken. For after killing Amnon, Absalom remained three years in Geshur with King Talmai; then, having been recalled, he remained two years in Jerusalem without seeing his father; and in the sixth year he saw his father’s face and prepared rebellion against him, and so forth. From what point those forty years are to be reckoned, see the same writer and the sacred critics. MART.

The Veronese manuscripts have *four* instead of *forty*. The older Martianus manuscripts also prefer this reading. Although it disagrees with the Hebrew, it is nevertheless judged more probable and preferred even to the Hebrew text, which learned critics think corrupt here because two letters, *yod* and *mem*, were added to the word. Hebrew manuscripts are also more easily corrupted, as we shall demonstrate with Luke of Bruges, whatever the author of the *Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings* may think.

If four years are written, their beginning can be adequately understood as reckoned from the reconciliation with his father—that is, from Absalom’s admission into Jerusalem—or, two years later, from the time when he was admitted to see his father’s face. But if forty is read, it is impossible to discover conveniently from what point they should be counted.

Moreover, Josephus in Book VII, chapter 9, of the *Antiquities*, and Theodoret in Question 28, count only four years. Nor do we conceal, with regard to the corruption of the Hebrew exemplar, the note found in Coislinian manuscript 2 in Montfaucon:

“In the Hexapla, ‘forty’ stands in all copies; but in the Hebrew there is *Arbareim*.”

*Arbareim* in Hebrew means “forty.”]

After forty years, Absalom said to the king [the Vulgate adds “David”]: “I will go and fulfill the vows that I vowed to the Lord in Hebron. For your servant made a vow when I was staying in Geshur of Syria [Note: More closely following the Hebrew: “while I was dwelling.” The Veronese manuscript has “when I was”], saying: ‘If the Lord brings me back to Jerusalem, I will sacrifice [Hebrew: “serve”] to the Lord.’”

The king said to him [Note: Again, in agreement with the Hebrew, the Veronese manuscript omits the name “David”]: “Go in peace.”

He rose and went to Hebron. Absalom sent spies throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying: “As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, say: ‘Absalom has become king in Hebron.’”

Two hundred men went with Absalom from Jerusalem, summoned and going in simplicity of heart, knowing nothing of the matter.

Absalom also summoned Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, from his city of Giloh, while he was offering sacrifices. The conspiracy grew strong, and the people gathering around Absalom increased.

A messenger came to David, saying: “All Israel is following Absalom with all its heart” [Note: The same manuscript continues: “was following Absalom.” The Hebrew literally says: “was after Absalom.”]

## [T. CXVI]

David said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem: “Rise, let us flee, for we shall have no escape from the face of Absalom. Hurry to leave, lest he come upon us, bring ruin upon us [Hebrew: “evil”], and strike the city with the edge of the sword.”

The king’s servants said to him: “Whatever our lord the king commands [Hebrew: “chooses”], we, your servants, will gladly carry out” [manuscript: “we carry out”].

The king went out on foot, together with all his household. The king left ten concubines to guard the house.

The king and all Israel went out on foot and stood far from the house. All his servants walked beside him, as did the Cherethites and Pelethites, and all the Gittites—six hundred men who had followed him from Gath and had come on foot [Hebrew omits “legions”]—preceded the king.

The king said to Ittai the Gittite: “Why are you coming with us? Return and remain with the king, since you are a foreigner and have left your place. You came yesterday; must you be compelled to go out with us today? I am going wherever I must go. Return and take your brothers back with you,

[Note: The Vulgate preserves two translations of the same sentence here, namely the Hieronymian and the older one called the Itala. We have printed the one corresponding to the Hebrew source. MART.

The Vulgates insert: “And the Lord will show mercy and truth toward you.” The same idea is repeated in other words in the following sentence: “because you have shown grace and faith.” In the Hebrew text, however, only these two words occur: “mercy and truth.” Joined to the preceding word, “with you,” they form the words of a blessing: “With you are mercy and truth,” or, which I do not deny has the same meaning according to Hebrew idiom: “With you are grace and faith.” The printed sentence is found only in the Hieronymian version, since it more concisely reflects the Hebrew and belongs to much more accurate copies. The Veronese manuscript more correctly omits the adverb “because,” a reading also approved by the scholiast.]

because you have shown grace and faith” [Hebrew: “you have shown mercy and truth”].

Ittai answered the king and said: “As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives [manuscript: “and may my lord the king live”], wherever my lord the king may be, whether in death or in life, there your servant shall be.”

David said to Ittai: “Come and cross over.”

So Ittai the Gittite crossed over, together with all the men who were with him and all the rest of the multitude.

Everyone wept with a loud voice, and all the people crossed over. The king also crossed the brook Kidron, and all the people proceeded toward the road that looks toward the wilderness.

Zadok also came [Hebrew: “Zadok too”], the priest, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set down the ark of God, and Abiathar went up until all the people who had come out of the city had finished crossing.

The king said to Zadok: “Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he will bring me back and show me it and his tabernacle [Hebrew: “and I shall glorify him”]. But if he says to me, ‘You do not please me,’ here I am; let him do with me what is good in his sight” [the Vulgate omits “with me”; Hebrew: “what is good in his eyes”].

The king said to Zadok the priest: “O seer, return to the city in peace [Hebrew: “If it seems good to you, return”]. Your son Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar—these two sons of yours—shall be with you.

“Behold, I will hide myself in the plains of the wilderness [Hebrew: “I will remain”] until word comes from you informing me.”

So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they remained there.

David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, going up and weeping, with his head covered and walking barefoot. All the people who were with him also covered their heads and went up, weeping.

David was told that Ahithophel was among the conspiracy [Hebrew: “rebellion”] with Absalom. David said: “Frustrate, I beg you, the counsel of Ahithophel, O Lord.”

As David was ascending the summit of the mountain where he was about to worship God, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him, his garment torn [Hebrew: “tunic”] and his head covered with earth [Hebrew: “scattered with earth”].

## [T. CXVII]

David said to him: “If you come with me, you will be a burden to me. But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, ‘I am your servant, O king. As I was your father’s servant, so I shall be your servant,’ you will frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel.

“You have Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you. Whatever word you hear from the king’s house, report it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests. Their two sons are with them: Ahimaaz son of Zadok [the Vulgate adds “son”], and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Through them you shall send me every word that you hear” [Hebrew: “through their hands”].

So Hushai, David’s friend, entered the city, and Absalom also entered Jerusalem.

## Chapter XVI

When David had gone a little beyond the crest of the hill, Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, appeared to meet him, with two donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves, one hundred bunches of raisins [Hebrew: “one hundred raisin-cakes”], one hundred cakes of figs, and skins of wine [Hebrew: “a wineskin”]. The king said to Ziba, “What do you intend by these?” Ziba replied, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride; the loaves and the fig-cakes are for the servants to eat; [Note: The Veronese manuscript, together with the Vulgate manuscripts, adds “your servants.”] and the wine is for anyone who becomes exhausted in the wilderness to drink.”

The king said, “And where is your master’s son?” Ziba replied to the king, “He has remained in Jerusalem, saying: ‘Today the house of Israel will restore to me my father’s kingdom.’” The king said to Ziba, “All that belonged to Mephibosheth is yours.” Ziba said, “I entreat you [Note: One manuscript, more closely following the Hebrew, reads “I adore”], may I find favor before you [Hebrew: “in your eyes”], my lord the king.”

## [T. CXVIII]

King David came as far as Bahurim, and behold, a man from the family of the house of Saul was coming out from there, named Shimei, son of Gera. He proceeded onward, cursing and throwing stones at David and at all the servants of King David. All the people and all the warriors walked on the king’s right and left.

Thus Shimei spoke while he was cursing [Note: The same manuscript, along with the Vulgate manuscripts, adds “the king,” whereas the Hebrew has “him”; the same manuscript shortly afterward also reads “He will repay” instead of “He repaid”]:

“Depart, man of bloodshed and man of worthlessness! The Lord has repaid you with all the bloodshed of the house of Saul, because you seized the kingdom in his place; and the Lord has given the kingdom into the hand of Absalom your son. And behold, your evils press upon you [Hebrew: “Behold, you are in your evil condition”], because you are a man of bloodshed.”

Abishai, son of Zeruiah, said to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go and cut off his head.” [Note: The reading “dead,” noted by the scholiast, is preferred by the Hebrew, the Veronese manuscript, and finally by the Vulgate books.]

The king said, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, for the Lord has commanded him to curse David; and who is there who would dare say, ‘Why has he done this?’” [Hebrew: “Who will say?”] [Note: In the Veronese manuscript “that” is absent; in the Hebrew both “let him go” and the following clause are lacking, and the words were easily added here from the Greek, ἄφετε αὐτόν, “let him go.” The manuscript reads the singular, “Let him go, that he may curse.”]

The king said to Abishai and to all his servants, “Behold, my son, who came forth from my womb [another reading: “from my entrails”], seeks my life. How much more now this Benjaminite! Leave him, so that he may curse according to the Lord’s command. Perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction [Col. 0644D] and repay me good for this day’s cursing.” [The Vulgate adds “the Lord” in “and the Lord will repay me.”]

David and his companions therefore went along the road with him [Hebrew does not have these words]. But Shimei walked along the mountain ridge opposite him, cursing and throwing stones at him and scattering dust.

The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted, and there they were refreshed [Note: The Veronese manuscript has the plural, “they were refreshed,” which is closer to the Greek, and agrees with the Vulgate manuscripts].

Absalom and all the people of Israel entered Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.

When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, came to Absalom, he said to him, “Long live the king! Long live the king!” [Hebrew: “May the king live! May the king live!”]

Absalom said to him, “Is this your loyalty [Hebrew: “mercy”] to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?”

Hushai replied to Absalom, “By no means; I shall belong to the one whom the Lord has chosen, and to all this people and to all Israel, and I shall remain with him. But, to add this as well: whom shall I serve? Is it not the son of the king? Just as I obeyed your father, so shall I obey you.”

## [T. CXIX]

Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Take counsel as to what we ought to do.”

Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Go in to your father’s concubines, whom he left behind to guard the palace, so that when all Israel hears that you have made your father odious, their hands may be strengthened with you.”

They therefore spread a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom went in to his father’s concubines before all Israel.

The counsel of Ahithophel, which he gave in those days, was as though someone were consulting God. Such was every counsel of Ahithophel, both when he was with David and when he was with Absalom.

## [Col. 0645C] [T. CXX, Chapter XVII]

Ahithophel said to Absalom, “I will choose for myself [Hebrew: ‘now’] twelve thousand men, and I will rise and pursue David this night. I will fall upon him—since he is weary and his hands are weakened—and strike him. When all the people who are with him have fled, I will strike the king when he is left alone. I will bring back all the people, just as everyone [Note: The Veronese manuscript more accurately reads “everyone is accustomed to return,” in accordance with the Hebrew; Eparnothotes likewise notes to Luke that this is the reading, and the better manuscripts prefer it. The Vulgate reads “as one man is accustomed to return.”] is accustomed to return. For you seek only one man, and all the people will be at peace.”

His speech pleased Absalom and all the elders of Israel.

Absalom said, “Call Hushai the Archite as well, and let us hear what he himself says.”

When Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, “This is the sort of speech which Ahithophel has given: should we act upon it or not? What counsel do you give?” [The manuscript adds “which.”]

Hushai said to Absalom, “The counsel Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”

Hushai continued, “You know your father and the men who are with him: they are very brave and bitter in spirit, like a bear raging in the forest after its cubs have been taken. Your father is also a warrior, and he will not remain with the people. Perhaps he is now hiding in pits or in some place he has chosen. When one of them falls at the beginning, whoever hears of it will hear and say: ‘A slaughter has taken place among the people who follow Absalom.’

“And even he, the bravest man, whose heart is like a lion’s, will be overcome with fear. [Note: The Hebrew reads “and he also”; the Veronese manuscript has “also” in place of “he,” and then additionally reads “all Israel,” etc.] For all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man and that all who are with him are strong.

“But this is the counsel that seems right to me: that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as innumerable as the sand of the sea, and that you be in their midst. [The manuscript and the Vulgate omit “that.”] Let us fall upon him wherever he may be found, and let us cover him as dew usually falls upon the earth. We shall not leave even one of the men who are with him.

“If he has entered some city, all Israel will surround that city with ropes, and we shall drag it—and David with it—into the torrent, so that not even a pebble of it will be found.”

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “Every man,” more closely following the Hebrew.]

By the Lord’s command, Ahithophel’s useful counsel was overturned, so that the Lord might bring evil upon Absalom.

Hushai said to the priests Zadok and Abiathar, “Ahithophel gave this and this counsel to Absalom and to the elders of Israel, and I gave this and this counsel. Now therefore send quickly and inform David, saying: ‘Do not remain [Hebrew: “Do not spend the night”] this night in the plains of the wilderness; cross over without delay, lest the king and all the people who are with him be swallowed up.’”

Jonathan and Ahimaaz were standing near the spring of Rogel. A maidservant went and reported it to them, and they set out to bring the message to King David, for they could not be seen entering the city.

A certain boy saw them and informed Absalom. But they entered quickly into the house of a man in Bahurim who had a well in his courtyard, and they descended into it.

The woman took a covering and spread it over the mouth of the well, as though she were drying parched grain, and so the matter remained hidden.

When Absalom’s servants came to the woman at the house, they said, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?”

The woman replied, “They passed on, after tasting a little water.” [The Vulgate adds “hastily.”]

When those who were searching had not found them, they returned to Jerusalem.

After they had gone, the two men came up from the well, proceeded onward, and reported to King David. They said, “Rise and cross the river quickly, for Ahithophel has given such counsel against you.”

David therefore rose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan until dawn. Not even one remained who had not crossed the river [Hebrew: “the Jordan”].

## [T. CXXI]

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel had not been carried out, he saddled his donkey, rose, and went to his house and to his city. After putting his household in order, he hanged himself and died, and he was buried in the tomb of his father.

David came to Castra [Hebrew: Mahanaim]. [Note: Saint Jerome wisely warned us in his book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis that in Scripture the word “camps” often signifies a place, not an army. When he was discussing the angels who met Jacob, he wished us to observe this. Where “Castra” appears here, the Hebrew has Mahanaim, so that we may know what place is meant whenever it is translated in another passage.

“The false Jerome likewise discusses the same place in his Hebrew Traditions on the Second Book of Kings: ‘David came to the camp, which is called Mahanaim in Hebrew; at that place the angels of God met Jacob, as it is written in Genesis: “And Jacob called the name of the place Mahanaim,” that is, “Camps.”’

“Thus the true and the false Jerome agree beautifully here with the scholiast of the Canon of Hebrew Truth, a point that should not be passed over for diligent readers. MART.] Absalom crossed the Jordan, he and all [Note: The same manuscript, again more closely following the Hebrew, reads “every man”] the men of Israel with him.

Absalom appointed Amasa over the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Jether of Jezreel [Hebrew: “an Israelite”; the manuscript reads “a Jezreelite”], who had gone in to Abigail [Hebrew: Abigal], daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, who was Joab’s mother [Hebrew: “the mother of Joab”].

Israel encamped with Absalom in the land of Gilead.

When David came to Castra [Hebrew: Mahanaim], Shobi, son of Nahash, from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir, son of Ammiel, from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim brought him beds, rugs, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, meal, beans, lentils, roasted chickpeas [Hebrew does not have “roasted chickpeas,” but has “meal”], honey, butter, sheep, and fattened calves.

They gave these to David and to the people who were with him for food, for they supposed that the people were exhausted by hunger and thirst in the wilderness.

## [T. CXXII, Chapter XVIII]

After David had counted [Hebrew: “numbered”] his people, he appointed over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds. He placed one-third of the people under the command of Joab, one-third under the command of Abishai, son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and one-third under the command of Ittai, who was from Gath. [The manuscript omits “part.”]

The king said to the people, “I too will go out with you.”

The people replied, “You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not pay much attention to us; and if half of us fall, they will not care much, because you count as ten thousand of us. It is therefore better that you remain in the city as our support.”

The king said to them, “What seems right to you, I will do.”

The king therefore stood beside the gate, while the people went out by their divisions, hundreds and thousands at a time.

The king commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, saying, “Preserve for me the young man Absalom.”

All the people heard the king giving this command to all the commanders concerning Absalom.

The people went out into the field against Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.

The people of Israel were struck down there by David’s army [Hebrew: “by David’s servants”], and there was a great slaughter on that day: twenty thousand men.

The battle there was scattered over the face of the whole land, and the forest consumed far more of the people than the sword devoured on that day.

## [T. CXXIII]

It happened that Absalom encountered David’s servants while he was riding a mule. When the mule went beneath a large, dense oak, his head caught in the oak, and, hanging between heaven and earth, the mule on which he had been riding passed on.

Someone saw this and reported to Joab, saying, “I saw Absalom hanging from an oak.”

Joab said to the man who had reported it to him, “If you saw him, why did you not strike him to the ground? I would have given you ten silver shekels [Hebrew: “ten pieces of silver”] and one belt.”

The man said to Joab, “Even if you were to weigh a thousand silver pieces into my hands, I would never lay my hand upon the king’s son. For we heard the king command you, Abishai, and Ittai, saying: ‘Protect the young man Absalom.’ Even if I had acted rashly at the peril of my own life, this could not have remained hidden from the king, and you would have stood against me.”

Joab said, “Not as you wish.” [The manuscript omits “you.”] “Rather, I will attack him before your eyes.”

He took three spears in his hand and thrust them into Absalom’s heart. While he was still quivering [Hebrew: “while he was still alive”], clinging to the oak, ten young men, Joab’s armor-bearers [Hebrew: “ten servants”], ran up and struck him and killed him.

Joab blew the trumpet and held back the people from pursuing Israel in flight, wishing to spare the multitude [Hebrew: “the people”].

They took Absalom, threw him into the forest, into a great pit, and piled a very large heap of stones over him. All Israel fled to their tents.

While he was still alive, Absalom had erected for himself a monument in the King’s Valley, for he had said, “I have no son, and this will be a memorial to my name.” He called the monument by his own name, and it is called Absalom’s Hand to this day.

Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, said, “I will run and report to the king, because the Lord has judged in his favor against the hand of his enemies.”

Joab said to him, “You shall not be a messenger on this day; you shall report on another day. Today I do not want you to report, because the king’s son is dead.”

Joab said to Cushite, “Go and report to the king what you have seen.”

Cushite bowed down before Joab and ran.

Again Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, said to Joab, “What prevents me from running after Cushite?”

Joab said to him, “Why do you want to run, my son? You will not be the bearer of good news.”

He replied, “But what if I run?” And Joab said to him, “Run.” [The manuscript omits “to him.”]

Ahimaaz ran by the shortcut and passed Cushite.

David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman who was on the roof of the gate, above the wall, raised his eyes and saw a man running alone.

He cried out and reported it to the king. The king said, “If he is alone, good news is in his mouth.” [Hebrew does not have “good.”]

As the man hurried and came nearer, the watchman saw another man running. He called out from the height and said, “It seems to me that another man is running alone.” [Note: The Veronese manuscript omits the word “another,” which is absent from the Hebrew.]

The king said, “This one too is a good messenger.” [Hebrew does not have “good”; Hebrew: “This too is a messenger.”]

The watchman said, “I can make out the running of the first man; it is like the running of Ahimaaz, son of Zadok.”

The king said, “He is a good man, and he is coming with good news.”

Ahimaaz called out and said to the king, “Hail, O king!” [Hebrew: “Peace”] [Note: Here too the same manuscript omits “king,” a title not added by the Hebrew text here.] He bowed down before the king with his face to the ground [Hebrew does not have “before him”] and said, “Blessed be the Lord your God” [the manuscript omits “your God”], who has shut in the men who raised their hands against my lord the king.”

The king said, “Is there peace for the young man Absalom?”

Ahimaaz said, “I saw a great tumult when your servant Joab sent me, your servant, O king. I do not know anything else” [Hebrew: “what”].

The king said, “Pass over and stand here.”

When he had passed over [the manuscript reads “when he passed by”] and was standing, Cushite appeared. He came and said, “I bring good news, my lord the king, for the Lord has judged in your favor this day against the hand of all who rose up against you.”

## [T. CXXIV]

The king said to Cushite, “Is there peace for the young man Absalom?”

Cushite replied, “May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against him for evil become like that young man.” [Note: The Veronese manuscript has the fuller reading, more closely following the Hebrew: “the young man Absalom.”]

The king was deeply distressed, went up to the upper chamber over the gate, and wept. As he went, he spoke thus:

“My son Absalom, my son Absalom! Who will grant that I might die for you, Absalom my son, my son Absalom!” [Note: The Veronese manuscript does not repeat the name “Absalom,” exactly in accordance with the Hebrew.]

## Chapter XIX

Joab was informed that the king was weeping and mourning for his son [Hebrew: “mourning over Absalom”]. On that day victory [Hebrew: “deliverance”] was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard it said that day, “The king is grieving over his son.”

The people slipped away from entering the city that day, just as people usually slip away, turning aside and fleeing from battle. [The manuscript reads “turned away.”]

## [T. CXXV]

The king covered his head and cried out in a loud voice, “My son Absalom! Absalom my son, my son, my son!” [The Vulgate omits the final “my son.”]

Joab entered the king’s house and said, “Today you have shamed the faces of all your servants who have saved [Hebrew: “rescued”] your life, the lives of your sons and daughters, and the lives of your wives and concubines.

“You love those who hate you and hate those who love you. [The manuscript reads, “loving and hating.”] Today you have shown that you care nothing for your commanders and servants [Hebrew: “Today you have declared that you have neither commanders nor servants”]. Indeed, I know now that if Absalom were alive and all of us had fallen, then it would please you [Hebrew: “in your eyes”].

“Now therefore rise, go out, and speak to your servants, satisfying them. For I swear to you by the Lord [Hebrew: “I have sworn by the Lord”] that if you do not go out, not even one man will remain with you this night. This will be worse for you than all the evils that have come upon you from your youth until now.”

The king rose and sat at the gate. It was reported to all the people that the king was sitting at the gate, and the whole multitude [Hebrew: “all the people”] came before the king. Israel, however, fled to its tents.

## [T. CXXVI]

All the people were contending [Hebrew: “deliberating”] throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying:

“The king rescued us from the hand of our enemies; he himself saved us from the hand of the Philistines; and now he has fled from the land because of Absalom. Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in battle. Why are you silent and do not bring back the king?”

King David sent to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, saying, “Speak to the elders of Judah, saying: ‘Why are you the last to bring back the king to his house?’” [The whole speech of all Israel reached the king in his house; the manuscript and the Vulgate read “had reached.”]

“You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why are you the last to bring back the king?

“And say to Amasa: ‘Are you not my bone and my flesh?’” [The Vulgate adds “you are.”] “May God do this to me and add this to it, if you will not be commander of the army before me for all time” [Hebrew: “all the days”], in place of Joab.

He inclined the hearts of all the men of Judah as one man. They sent to the king, saying, “Return, you and all your servants.”

The king returned and came as far as the Jordan. All Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and escort him across the Jordan.

Shimei, son of Gera, son of the Benjaminite, from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David, together with one thousand men from Benjamin. Ziba, the servant of the house of Saul, and his fifteen sons and twenty servants were with him [Hebrew does not have these words]. They crossed the Jordan ford ahead of the king to escort the king’s household across and to do whatever he commanded [Hebrew: “whatever was good in the king’s eyes”].

## [T. CXXVII]

When Shimei, son of Gera, had crossed the Jordan, he fell before the king and said to him: [Note: The same manuscript and the Vulgate read, “when he had already crossed,” etc.]

“Do not charge me, my lord, with iniquity, and do not remember the wrong [the manuscript reads “wrongdoing”] of your servant on the day when you went out, my lord the king, from Jerusalem. Do not hold it in your heart, O king.

“For your servant acknowledges his sin. Therefore I have come today as the first of all the house of Joseph [the manuscript omits “all”], and I have gone down to meet my lord the king.”

Abishai, son of Zeruiah, replied and said, “Shall Shimei not be put to death for these words, because he cursed the Lord’s Anointed?” [Hebrew: “because he cursed the Lord’s anointed.”]

David said, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Why should you become a satan [adversary] to me today? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel today? Do I not know that today I have become king over Israel?” [Hebrew: “For do I not know?”]

The king said to Shimei, “You shall not die.” And the king swore this to him.

Mephibosheth, Saul’s son, also came down to meet the king. [Note: “With unwashed feet,” that is, literally “with feet not made,” according to the Hebrew expression *velo asa raglau*, which means “and he had not made his feet.” Hence the much-praised author of the Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings appropriately said: “It should be noted that in Hebrew it reads not ‘with unwashed feet,’ but ‘with feet not made.’ For this same Mephibosheth had made wooden feet for himself, which he used as though they were natural ones, as the lame customarily do, and he was lame.” MAR. —Martianus compares the scholiast with the Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings, whose author says at this passage: “It should be noted that in Hebrew it reads not ‘with unwashed feet,’ but ‘with feet not made.’ For this same Mephibosheth had made wooden feet for himself, which he used as though they were natural ones,” and so forth. This is a rabbinic tradition.]

He came with unwashed feet [Hebrew: “with feet not made”] and an untrimmed beard. He had not washed his garments from the day the king went out until the day of his return in peace.

When he came to meet the king at Jerusalem, the king said to him, “Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?”

He replied, “My lord the king, my servant despised me. I, your servant, said to him, ‘Saddle a donkey for me, so that I may mount it and go with the king,’ for your servant is lame. Moreover, he accused me, your servant, to you, my lord the king. But you, my lord the king, are like an angel of God [the Vulgate adds “you are”]; do what is pleasing to you [Hebrew: “in your eyes”].

“For my father’s entire house was deserving only of death before my lord the king, but you placed your servant among those who eat at your table. What right, then, do I have to complain, or what further claim can I make before the king?”

The king said to him, “Why do you continue to speak? What I have said is fixed: you and Ziba shall divide the possessions” [Hebrew: “I have said: you and Ziba shall divide the field”].

Mephibosheth said to the king, “Let him take everything, since my lord the king has returned peacefully to his house.”

Barzillai the Gileadite also came down from Rogelim and escorted the king across the Jordan [Hebrew: “crossed over with the king”], prepared also to continue beyond the river in accompanying him [Hebrew: “to escort him across”].

Barzillai the Gileadite was very old, that is, eighty years old. He himself had supplied food to the king while he stayed in the camp, for he was an exceedingly wealthy man.

The king said to Barzillai, “Come across with me, so that you may rest securely [the manuscript reads “securely”] with me in Jerusalem.”

Barzillai said to the king, “How many days of the years of my life remain, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am eighty years old today. Are my senses still vigorous enough to distinguish what is pleasant or bitter [Hebrew: “good or evil”]? Can your servant still take pleasure in food and drink? Or can I still hear the voice of singers and female singers? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?

“I shall go forward a little way with you from the Jordan, and I do not need this exchange. But I ask that your servant return and die in my own city [the Vulgate adds “and be buried”], beside the tomb of my father and my mother.” [Note: The corrected Canon now reads the third person, “let your servant go forward”; formerly it read the first person, “I shall go forward.” Other manuscripts retain the latter, which was not altered because both readings convey one sense. Moreover, the words printed in the immediately following verse, “and be buried beside …,” are marked deleted in the Hebrew source, as in the Septuagint and the Syriac interpreter. The Chaldee and Arabic, however, translate likewise, “and be buried in the tomb …” MART.]

## [T. CXXVIII]

“Behold, your servant is here, Chimham. Let him go with you, my lord the king, and do for him what seems good to you” [Hebrew: “what is good in your eyes”].

The king said, “Let Chimham cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever pleases you; and whatever you ask of me, you shall obtain.”

When all the people and the king had crossed the Jordan, the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own place.

The king crossed over to Gilgal, and Chimham was with him.

All the people of Judah had escorted the king across, while only half of the people of Israel were present.

Then all the men of Israel came running to the king and said to him, “Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and escorted the king and his household across the Jordan, and all David’s men with him?”

Every man of Judah replied to the men of Israel, “Because the king is closer to me. Why are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten anything belonging to the king, or have gifts been given to us?”

The men of Israel replied to the men of Judah and said, “I have ten shares in the king, and I have a greater claim on David than you do” [Hebrew: “I have ten parts in the king, and in David I am greater than you”]. “Why have you treated me with contempt? Why was I not informed first, so that I might bring back my king?” [Hebrew: “Was not my word first, to bring back my king?”]

But the men of Judah answered the men of Israel more harshly.

## Chapter XX

It also happened that there was there a worthless man named Sheba, son of Bichri [Hebrew: Bichri], a Benjaminite. He sounded the trumpet and said:

“We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse. [Note: In the Canon, here and elsewhere, the word *return* or *go* has been erased, and the corrector has adapted the meaning of Scripture to the Hebrew text: ‘Israel, to his tents.’ But, so that the translation would not become awkward, Jerome occasionally adds Latin words, as he himself states in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela.
