Here, too, the verb *return* or *go back* must necessarily be understood; otherwise the sense is either entirely absent or wholly obscure. MART. —The Verona manuscript has, ‘in the house of David,’ although the other books reject this reading. Shortly afterward, in place of *return*, a word which Martianay found erased in other manuscripts, the Verona manuscript most suitably follows the Hebrew text: ‘Every man to his tents, O Israel’—that is, each man, as the other Eastern versions prefer. Martianay himself later observed that the same reading was found in the Memmian Canon.] Return to your tents, O Israel.”

So all Israel withdrew from David and followed Sheba son of Bichri [Hebrew: Bichri]. But the men of Judah remained attached to their king, from the Jordan as far as Jerusalem.

When the king had come to his house in Jerusalem [Hebrew omits *the king*, saying instead *David*], he took the ten concubines whom he had left to guard the house, placed them in confinement, and provided them with food. He did not go in to them, but they remained shut up until the day of their death, living as widows.

The king said to Amasa: “Summon all the men of Judah to me by the third day, and you yourself be present.”

So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the appointed time which the king had fixed for him. [Note: Both the Hebrew and the Verona manuscript omit *the king*. In the Canon which Martianay calls corrected, he later found the reading, ‘which had been appointed for him.’]

David said to Abishai: “Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take, therefore, the servants of your lord and pursue him, lest he find fortified cities and escape us.”

So Joab’s men went out with him, as did the Cherethites and Pelethites; and all the warriors went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.

When they were near the great stone which is in Gibeon, Amasa came and met them [Hebrew: “Amasa, coming, came before them.” **Note:** “Our manuscripts,” as the Scholiast calls them here, do not differ from the printed reading of Jerome. Conversely, above, in chapter XVII of Numbers, verse 6, he praises the same manuscripts by this name in order to indicate that they differ from the exemplar before him. This matter seemed worthy of closer examination.] Our manuscripts read: “Amasa came and met them.”

Now Joab was wearing a close-fitting tunic suited to his build, and over it he was girded with a sword hanging down to his thighs in its sheath. It had been fashioned so that it could easily be drawn with a slight movement and used to strike. [Note: The Verona manuscript reads much more elegantly, “skillfully made.”]

Joab said to Amasa: “Are you well, my brother?” [Hebrew: “Peace to you, brother.”] And with his right hand he took Amasa by the chin, as though to kiss him.

Amasa did not notice the sword which Joab had [Hebrew: “which Joab had in his hand”]. [T. CXXX.] Joab struck him in the side and spilled out his entrails onto the ground; he did not strike him a second time, [Note: The phrase “and he died,” found in all the other books, is omitted by the Verona manuscript.] and he died.

Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri.

Meanwhile, certain men from Joab’s companions, when they had stopped beside Amasa’s corpse, said: “Behold the man who wished to be in place of Joab [Note: Here too the Verona manuscript omits the words “David’s companion.” The Hebrew, on the contrary, expresses the sense at greater length: [Hebrew text]. Literally: “Who is the one who wished to be with Joab, and who is the one who is for David after Joab?” The Greek likewise adheres closely to this wording.] David’s companion [Hebrew: “from Joab’s servants”] [Note: Here too the Verona manuscript omits the words “David’s companion.” The Hebrew, on the contrary, expresses the sense at greater length: [Hebrew text]. Literally: “Who is the one who wished to be with Joab, and who is the one who is for David after Joab?” The Greek likewise adheres closely to this wording.] They said: ‘Whoever favors Joab and wishes to obey David shall follow Joab.’”

Amasa, covered with blood, lay in the middle of the road. A certain man saw that all the people were stopping to look at him, so he moved Amasa from the road into a field and covered him with a garment, lest passers-by stop because of him.

After he had been removed from the road, every man passed on, following Joab in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri.

But Sheba had gone through all the tribes of Israel as far as Abel and Beth-maacah, and all the chosen men had gathered to him. [Note: The Hebrew word [Hebrew text], which most versions take as the proper name Berim, the Latin translator rendered according to its etymology, by which “chosen men” (that is, men selected from the soldiers) are signified, from the root [Hebrew text]. But the Verona manuscript, adhering more closely to the Hebrew, omits the word *men*. Whether this word was added by Saint Jerome or proceeded from the glossator’s pen must be guessed. Again, Martianay observed that the corrected Canon reads: “All the chosen men gathered and came after him,” where not only *men* is omitted, but *came* is written instead of *had been*, and *after him* instead of *to him.*]

So they came and attacked him at Abel and Beth-maacah. They surrounded the city with siegeworks, and the city was under siege. All the crowd [Hebrew: *the people*] that was with Joab was attempting to destroy the walls.

A wise woman from the city cried out: “Listen, listen! Say to Joab, ‘Come here, and I will speak with you.’”

When he had approached her, she said to him: “Are you Joab?” He replied: “I am.”

She said to him: [T. CXXXI.] “Listen to the words of your servant.” He replied: “I am listening.”

Again she said: “A saying used to be uttered in an ancient proverb [Hebrew omits *in a proverb*]: ‘Let them ask in Abel,’ and so they would settle matters. Am I not the one who answers truthfully in Israel, while you are seeking to overthrow the city and destroy [Note: The Verona manuscript reads *you will seek to destroy*.] the mother in Israel? Why are you bringing down the Lord’s inheritance?”

Joab answered: “Far be it, far be it from me! I neither bring down nor destroy it. The matter is not so. A man [Hebrew: *a man*] from the hill country of Ephraim, Sheba son of Bichri by name, has raised his hand against King David. Hand over only him, and we will withdraw from the city.”

The woman said to Joab: “Behold, his head will be thrown [Hebrew: *will be cast*] to you over the wall.”

Then she went to all the people and spoke wisely to them. They threw the severed head of Sheba son of Bichri to Joab. He sounded the trumpet, and they withdrew from the city, each man to his tent. Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.

Joab was therefore over the whole army of Israel; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites [Hebrew] and Pelethites. Adoram was over the tributes; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder. Siva [Hebrew: Serva] was the scribe. Zadok and Abiathar were the priests. Ira the Jairite [Manuscript: Hiajarite] [Note: The same author immediately adds: “Ira the Jairite was David’s priest,” that is, his teacher, as it is written elsewhere: “David’s sons were priests,” that is, teachers of their brothers. MART.] was David’s priest.

## Chapter XXI

There was also a famine in David’s days for three consecutive years. David consulted the oracle [Hebrew: *the face*] of the Lord.

The Lord said: “It is because of Saul, and his house, and the blood [Hebrew: ‘and the house of bloods’], because he killed the Gibeonites.”

The king summoned the Gibeonites and said to them. (The Gibeonites were not among the children of Israel, but were remnants of the Amorites; the children of Israel had sworn an oath to them, and Saul had sought to strike them down out of zeal, as though on behalf of the children of Israel and Judah.)

David said to the Gibeonites: “What shall I do for you, and what shall be your expiation, so that you may bless the Lord’s inheritance?” [Hebrew: “By what shall I make atonement, so that you may bless …”]

The Gibeonites said to him: “We have no claim concerning silver or gold against Saul and his house [Note: The same manuscript omits the little word *concerning*, which is not present in the Hebrew either.]; nor do we want any man [Hebrew: *man*] of Israel to be killed.”

The king said to them: [Note: Here too the Verona manuscript omits *the king*, which the Hebrew also lacks.] “What, then, do you want me to do for you?”

They said to the king: “The man who crushed us and oppressed us unjustly must be destroyed in such a way that not even one survivor remains [Hebrew: “and so destroy them that not one of them is left”] of his lineage throughout all the borders of Israel. Let seven men of his sons be given to us, and let us crucify them before the Lord at Gibeah of Saul, the former chosen one of the Lord.”

The king said: “I will give them.”

The king spared Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan son of Saul, because of the oath of the Lord which had been between David and Jonathan son of Saul.

The king took the two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah, whom she had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Michal daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai, who was from Meholah, and gave them into the hands of the Gibeonites.

They crucified them before the Lord on the mountain. These seven fell together, slain during the first days of harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself upon the rock, from the beginning of the harvest until water dripped upon them from heaven [Hebrew: *until*]. She did not allow the birds to tear them by day, nor the beasts by night.

David was informed of what Rizpah daughter of Aiah [Manuscript: Ahiah], Saul’s concubine, had done. [T. CXXXII.]

David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them after killing Saul at Gilboa.

He brought away from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son. They also gathered the bones of those who had been impaled and buried them with the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son [Hebrew: “and they gathered the bones of those who had been impaled, and buried the bones of Saul and his sons”] in the land of Benjamin, beside him, in the tomb of Kish his father.

They did everything that the king had commanded, and after this God was reconciled to the land.

There was again a battle between the Philistines and Israel. David went down, and his servants with him, and they fought against the Philistines.

When David was exhausted, Jesbibenob [Manuscript: Jesbidenob], who was of the race of Arapha, [Note: In the Canon, “whose spear weighed three hundred …,” a reading which we do not wish to follow because we suspect such corrections to have been produced from the Hebrew text by an overly zealous scholar. For in the first hand the Canon was read in the same way as it is now printed and as it appears in all the other manuscript books. It is therefore plainly evident that readings of this kind were altered in Jerome’s version, even when they came closer to the Hebrew words. MART.] whose spearhead weighed three hundred ounces, and who was girded with a new sword, tried to strike David.

Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid, struck the Philistine, and killed him. [Note: These words were formerly absent from the Verona manuscript, and a later hand supplied them: “Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid.” They are in fact found in all the other books.]

Then David’s men swore, saying: [Note: The word *now*, which follows in the Vulgate, is absent from the Verona manuscript, in accordance with the Hebrew and other texts.] “You shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you extinguish the lamp of Israel.”

There was another battle at Gob against the Philistines. Then Sobochai of Husati struck down Saph [Manuscript: Seph], of the race of Arapha, of [Note: Two interpretations have been joined here: “of the race of Rapha” and “of the race of giants.” The Hebrew has one expression, [Hebrew text], meaning “of the offspring” or “of the race of Asrapha.” If one wishes to interpret *Rapha* according to its etymology, one may say “of the offspring” or “of the race of giants.” This explanation pleased the Syriac, Arabic, and almost also the Chaldean translators; the Greek preferred the reading, ἐν τοῖς ἐγγόνοις τοῦ Ῥαφὰ, “among the descendants of Rapha.” It is certain and evident that Jerome also chose one or the other interpretation, not rashly joined both together, as the Latin Vulgate books represent him. Which of these he preferred is shown by the Verona manuscript, which has only the former, “of the race of Rapha,” and entirely lacks the other, “of the race of giants.” Here he finds a new argument for the genuineness of Jerome’s version, which it presents as purer than all the others and free from the additions of those who interpreted glosses. Concerning the Vulgate books, I think as follows: since the translation “of the race of Rapha” seemed obscure, some glossator wrote in the margin another form derived from the etymology of the name, “of the race of giants,” which a later scribe, without due consideration, inserted into the text. It is remarkable that this addition in the Latin manuscripts escaped not only Martianay and the Hebrew Scholiast whose edition he published, but also the diligence of all those critics of Holy Scripture whose works we possess. MART.] the race of giants.

There was a third battle at Gob against the Philistines. In it Adeodatus son of Saltus, a Bethlehemite weaver of many-colored cloth, struck Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver’s beam.

There was a fourth battle at Geth. In it there was a tall man [the Vulgate adds *was*] who had six fingers on his hands and feet—that is, twenty-four—and who was of the race of Arapha [other texts add *and*]. He blasphemed Israel. Jonathan son of Samaa, David’s brother, struck him down.

These four were born of Arapha at Geth, and they fell by the hand of David and his servants.

## Chapter XXII

[Note: These words, up to the beginning of the Hymn, are placed as a title and written in large red letters in a very ancient royal manuscript of the Bible. MART.]

David spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. And he said:

[T. CXXXIV.]

The Lord is my rock and my strength,

[Note: We find the first distich of this song divided in this way in Hebrew royal manuscript no. 6. Accordingly, in this edition two cola have been set out according to the authority of that excellent manuscript, whereas in other books and in very many Latin manuscripts they are read as one division or line. This psalm is the same as our Psalm XVII in the Psalter, or Psalm XVIII according to the Hebrew numbering; yet the two versions differ somewhat, containing additional matter or different wording, as any diligent reader may easily discover by comparing them. MART.]

and my deliverer.

My God [the Vulgate omits *my*], my strong one, I will hope

in him;

my shield and the horn of my salvation;

my exaltation and my refuge,

my deliverer, you will free me from iniquity.

[Col. 0657A] I will call upon the praiseworthy Lord,

and I shall be saved from my enemies.

For the pangs of death surrounded me;

the torrents of Belial [Note: The Verona manuscript has *they found*, though I do not know from where the scribe produced it.] terrified me [the Vulgate omits *me*].

The cords of the underworld surrounded me;

the snares of death confronted me.

In my distress I will call upon the Lord,

and I will cry out to my God.

He will hear my voice from his temple,

and my cry will come [Hebrew omits *will come*] to his ears.

The earth was shaken and trembled;

the foundations of the mountains [Note: The Canon corrected according to the Hebrew reads, “they were troubled and shaken”; all the others have the reading printed here. MART.]

were shaken,

and they trembled, because he was angry [the Vulgate adds *with them*].

[Col. 0657B] Smoke rose in his nostrils [Note: The same manuscript reads *from his nostrils*. In the following verse it has *he will devour* in the future tense, with the Vulgate, and more closely following the Hebrew [Hebrew text].],

and fire devoured from his mouth;

burning coals blazed from him.

He inclined [Manuscript: *And he inclined*] the heavens and came down,

and darkness was beneath his feet.

He mounted upon the cherubim [Hebrew: *cherub*] and flew;

he glided [Hebrew: *appeared*] upon the wings of the wind.

He made darkness his hiding place all around him,

sifting waters from the clouds of heaven.

Because of the brightness before him,

coals of fire were kindled.

The Lord will thunder from heaven,

and the Most High will give his voice.

[Col. 0657C] He sent arrows and scattered them,

lightning, and consumed them.

The channels of the sea appeared,

and the foundations of the world were exposed,

at the rebuke of the Lord,

at the blast of the breath of his wrath.

He sent from on high and took me,

and drew me out of many waters.

He delivered me from my most powerful enemy,

and from those who hated me, because they were stronger than I.

He confronted me on the day of my affliction,

and the Lord became my support.

He brought me out into a broad place;

[Col. 0657D] he delivered me, because [Note: The Verona manuscript has *he was pleased*. Immediately afterward it has, more correctly according to the Hebrew, *he repaid* instead of *he will repay*.] I pleased him [the Vulgate: *because I was pleasing to him*].

The Lord will repay me according to my righteousness,

and according to the purity of my hands he will reward me.

For I kept the ways of the Lord,

and I did not act wickedly against my God.

For all his judgments were before my eyes;

[Col. 0658A] and I did not remove his commandments from me.

I will be blameless with him,

and I will guard myself from my iniquity.

The Lord will restore to me according to my righteousness,

and according to the purity of my hands [Hebrew: “according to my purity”], in the sight of his eyes.

With the holy you will be holy,

and with the strong you will be perfect [Hebrew: “with the perfect you will be perfect”].

With the chosen you will be chosen,

and with the perverse you will act perversely [Manuscript: *you will overturn*].

You will save the poor people,

and with your eyes you will humble the exalted.

[Col. 0658B] For you are my lamp, O Lord,

and [the Vulgate adds *you*, O Lord] you will enlighten my darkness.

For in you I will run while girded;

in my God I will leap over a wall.

God—his way is blameless;

the word of the Lord is tested by fire [Hebrew: *smelted*];

he is a shield to all who hope in him.

Who is God besides the Lord,

and who is strong besides our God?

God, who girds me with strength,

and makes my perfect way smooth.

He makes my feet like those of deer,

[Col. 0658C] and sets me upon my heights.

He trains my hands for battle,

and fits my arms like a bronze bow.

You have given me the shield of your salvation,

and my gentleness has multiplied me [Hebrew: *your*].

You will enlarge my steps beneath me,

and my ankles will not give way.

I will pursue my enemies and destroy them,

and I will not turn back until I have consumed them.

I will consume them and crush them, so that they cannot rise again;

they will fall beneath my feet.

You have girded me with strength for battle;

you will bend my adversaries beneath me [the Vulgate: *you have bent*].

[Col. 0658D] You have given me the backs of my enemies,

and I will destroy those who hate me.

They will cry out, and there will be no one to save them;

they will cry to the Lord, and he will not hear them.

I will strike them down [Hebrew: *crush them*] as the dust of the earth;

I will pulverize them like the mud of the streets, and

[Note: Eleven of our manuscripts read here *I will compress them*, a reading which would not lack plausibility if the continuation of the sense did not oppose it. For the preceding words, *I will strike down* and *I will pulverize*, require a connection with *I will crush*, or *I will spread out*. The Hebrew word [Hebrew text], *raca*, properly denotes pressing, compressing, and making firm. These meanings correspond equally well to *compress*. Consult Middoch’s *Sacred Criticism*. MART.]

crush them.

[Col. 0659A] You will save me from the disputes of my people;

[Note: In the margin of the Verona manuscript is written, apparently by the same ancient scribe, *you will appoint*.]

you will preserve me as head of the nations;

a people whom I do not know will serve me.

Foreign sons will resist me [Hebrew: *will deny me*];

at the hearing of the ear they will obey me.

Foreign sons will fade away,

and they will be constrained in their narrow places.

The Lord lives, and blessed is my God [Hebrew: *my strength*];

and [Note: The same manuscript has *and God will be exalted*, in agreement with the Vulgate and the Greek.] may the God of my salvation be exalted.

God, who gives me vengeance,

and casts peoples beneath me;

who brings me out from my enemies,

and raises me above those who resist me;

you will deliver me from the unjust man [Hebrew: *the man of iniquity*].

[Col. 0659B] Therefore I will confess you, O Lord, among the nations,

and I will sing to your name.

[Note: So reads a manuscript of excellent quality and great antiquity, as well as the Hebrew Canon of truth. Others read what appears in the printed editions: “magnifying and doing.” MART.]

To him who magnifies the salvations of his king [the Vulgate: “who magnifies and does”],

and who shows mercy to his anointed,

to David and his seed forever.

## Chapter XXIII

These are the last words [Hebrew] [Note: The same manuscript omits *of David* here; then it prefers, “the last things which he said,” and so forth.] of David.

David son of Jesse said:

The man to whom it was appointed concerning the Anointed of the God of Jacob [“to whom the ladder was appointed, the Anointed of the God of Jacob”],

the excellent psalmist [Hebrew and other manuscripts: [Note: In Hebrew, [Hebrew text], *unim zemiroth*, that is, “excellent” or “pleasant in psalms,” which differs in no respect from “excellent psalmist.” It is not sufficiently clear what the Scholiast of the Canon intended when he says that the Hebrew and other Latin manuscripts read *psaltae*. As for the Latin copies, it is certain that several read in this way; but in Hebrew [Hebrew text], *zemiroth*, does not mean “psalmist,” that is, “singer,” but “psalms” and “songs.” We should therefore believe that the scribes made an error when, in response to the variant Latin wording, they rashly added the notation *h.*, which signifies the Hebrew text. MART. —Along with those whom the Scholiast praises, the Verona manuscript also has *psalta*, which is the same reading.] psalmist] of Israel:

The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me [Hebrew: *in me*],

and his word was upon my tongue [Hebrew: *over my tongue*].

The God of Israel spoke;

the strong one of Israel spoke to me,

the ruler of men, just,

the ruler [Hebrew: *he rules*] in the fear of God.

And like the light of dawn when the sun rises,

the morning shines without clouds,

and as by rain grass springs from the earth [Hebrew: “and as rain makes grass spring from the earth”].

My house is not so great before God

that he should make an eternal covenant with me,

firm and secured in every respect.

For all my salvation and all my desire [Note: The Verona manuscript has “my salvation from that which does not sprout,” omitting the intervening words. This agrees beautifully with the Hebrew if it had added at least *will*, the word which appears in the archetype: [Hebrew text]. For the rest, nothing of it is found there either; the word [Hebrew text], meaning *because*, is equally well rendered by *from that which*.]: nothing of it indeed fails to sprout.

But all transgressors will be plucked out like thorns,

which are not removed [Note: The same manuscript reads “from the hands”; [Hebrew text], “into the hands.”] by hand.

And if anyone wishes to touch them [Hebrew: “and the man touching them”],

he will arm himself with iron and the shaft of a spear,

and, once set alight, they will be burned completely.

These are the names of David’s mighty men.

He who sits in the seat, the wisest prince among the three—he is like the tenderest little worm of wood, who killed eight hundred at one assault.

After him was Eleazar son of his uncle Ahohi [Hebrew: “Eleazar son of Dodo, son of Ahohi”], among the three mighty men who were with David when they challenged the Philistines, and they gathered there for battle.

When the men of Israel had gone up, he stood and struck the Philistines until his hand failed and stiffened around the sword. The Lord brought about a great salvation on that day, and the people who had fled [Hebrew omits *who had fled*] returned to strip the slain.

After him was Shammah son of Age the Hararite.

The Philistines gathered at a military post. There was there a field full of lentils. When the people fled from the face of the Philistines, he stood in the middle of the field, defended it, and struck the Philistines. The Lord brought about a great salvation.

And three who were princes among the thirty had gone down [Hebrew: “and three went down”] earlier [Note: The Hebrew does not have the conjunction *and* before *earlier*. The Verona manuscript also omits the first particle.] and came to David at the time of the harvest, to the cave of Adullam. The camp of the Philistines was stationed in the Valley of the Giants. David was then in the stronghold, while the Philistine garrison was at Bethlehem.

[T. CXXXV.] David longed and said: “If only someone would give me a drink of water from the cistern which is at Bethlehem beside the gate!”

So the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines, drew water from the cistern of Bethlehem which was beside the gate, and brought it to David. But he refused to drink it and poured it out to the Lord, saying: “May the Lord be gracious to me; far be it from me, Lord, to do this” [Hebrew: “Far be it from me, Lord, that I should do this”]. “Shall I drink the blood of these men who went at the risk of their lives?” He would not drink it.

The three mightiest men did these things.

Abishai, brother of Joab son of Zeruiah, was also chief of the three [Note: The Verona manuscript omits the name *these*, as does the Hebrew.] He was the one who raised his spear against three hundred, whom he killed. He was renowned among the three and more honored among the three; he was their commander, but he did not attain to the first three [Hebrew omits *first*].

Benaiah son of Jehoiada, a very brave man [Hebrew: “son of a very brave man”], of great deeds [Hebrew: “master”], from Kabzeel [Manuscript: Capsael], struck down the two lions of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in the middle of a cistern on a snowy day.

He also killed an Egyptian, a man worthy of spectacle, who had a spear in his hand. When Benaiah went down against him with a staff, he forcibly wrested the spear from the Egyptian’s hand and killed him with his own spear.

Benaiah son of Jehoiada did these things. He was renowned among the three mighty men who were among the thirty more distinguished men; nevertheless, he did not attain to the three. David made him his counselor, his confidential officer [Hebrew omits *confidential*].

Asahel, brother of Joab, was among the thirty.

Eleanan son of his uncle [Hebrew: “son of Dodo”], from Bethlehem;

Semma of Arodi;

Elica of Arodi;

Heles [Manuscript: “Arari Helas”] of Phelti;

Hira son of Aces of Thekoa;

Abiezer of Anathoth;

[Note: These names of the mighty men are frequently altered by the author of the *Hebrew Questions* on the Books of Kings. Following the Masoretic pointing, he reads Mebunnai, Arari, and Gigaal, in place of Mobonnai, Orori, and Igaal. The corrected Canon of Hebrew truth has the same words as those found in the said *Questions*. Therefore, lest we impose a false Jerome in place of the true one, we have rejected such corrections and taken care to restore these and similar names according to the other manuscript books, in which the original reading of the Canon remains intact. MART.]

Mobonnai of Usati;

Selmon the Aohite;

Maarai the Netophathite;

Heleb son of Baana [Manuscript: Heled and Banaa], himself [Hebrew omits *himself*] a Netophathite;

Ithai son of Ribai of Gabaath of the sons of Benjamin;

Banaiau the Pharathonite [Manuscript: Fraronithes];

[Col. 0661B] Heddai from the torrent [Hebrew: *torrents*] of Gas;

Abialbon the Arbathite;

Azmaveth of Beromi;

Eliaba of Salboni [Manuscript: Alieba and Sabboni];

The sons of Jasen: Jonathan;

Semma of Orori;

Aiam son of Sarar the Ararite;

Eliphelet son of Aasbai son of the Machathite [Manuscript: “Borodi and Ararorites, Elfeleth son of Aaboi son of Maachathi”];

Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gelonite;

Esrai of Charmel;

Pharai of Arbi;

Igaal son of Nathan of Soba;

Bonni of Gadi;

Selec the Amonite;

Naharai the Berothite, armor-bearer of Joab son of Sarvia [Note: The Verona manuscript has *son* in the main text. The Greek likewise has υἱὸς, “son,” in several copies; the Hebrew admits either case.]

Ira the Jethrite;

Gareb, likewise the Jethrite;

Urias the Hethite.

All thirty-seven.

[T. CXXXVI, Chapter XXIV.] And the anger of the Lord continued to burn against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying: “Go, number Israel and Judah.” Then the king said to Joab, commander of his army: “Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and count the people, so that I may know their number.” Joab said to the king: “May the Lord your God increase the people to as many as they now are, and may he multiply them a hundredfold before my lord the king; but why does my lord the king desire such a thing?” Yet the king’s word prevailed over Joab’s words and those of the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the troops went out from the king’s presence to count the people of Israel [Vulgate: “may count”].

When they had crossed the Jordan, they came to Aroer, to the right of the city that is in the valley of Gad [Hebrew: which is in the midst of the torrent of Gad], and they passed through Jazer and came to Gilead and to the lower land of Hodshi; and they came to Dan, the wooded regions [Note: The present Hebrew text has, “to Dan Jahan.” Saint Jerome must have read *resh* for the final *nun*, that is, [Hebrew forms], instead of [Hebrew form]; and this is indeed more correct. For Jahan is either no place-name at all, or at least it occurs nowhere else in Scripture.]. Going around near Sidon, they passed near [Manuscript: “along”] the walls of Tyre, and through the whole land of the Hivites and Canaanites. Then they came southward into Judah, to Beersheba. After surveying the whole land, they arrived in Jerusalem after nine months and twenty days.

So Joab gave the king the number of the census of the people, and there were found in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword, and in Judah five hundred thousand warriors [Hebrew: men] [Note: We had no hesitation in restoring “eight hundred” here, in accordance with the testimony of all the books known to us, both Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, manuscripts as well as printed editions. We know that learned men have debated this matter extensively, and that the author of the book of Chronicles differs considerably from this number. But we do not know where Martianaeus obtained “eighty” instead of “eight hundred”; and we are all the more distressed that he did not even warn the reader with a word that he had introduced a new reading.].

David’s heart struck him after the people had been counted [Manuscript: “had been counted”], and David said to the Lord: “I have sinned greatly in doing this; but [Hebrew: “but now”] I beg you, Lord,” take away the guilt of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.”

[T. CXXXVII.] David rose in the morning, and the word of the Lord came to Gad the prophet and seer of David, saying: “Go and speak to David. Thus says the Lord: Three choices are offered to you; choose one of them, whichever you wish me to do for you.” When Gad came to David, he announced this to him, saying: “Either seven years of famine will come upon your land, or you will flee your enemies for three months, and they will pursue you [Note: Previously the reading was incorrectly *ille*; the Veronese manuscript, together with the Vulgate and the Greek, does not have *te*.], or for three days there will be pestilence in your land. Now, therefore, deliberate and see what answer I shall give him who sent me.”

David said to Gad: “I am in great distress; but it is better that I should fall into the hand of the Lord—for his mercies are many—than into the hand [Manuscript: “hands”] of men.” And the Lord sent pestilence upon Israel, from morning until the appointed time, and seventy thousand men of the people died, from Dan to Beersheba.

When the angel of the Lord [Hebrew: omits “of the Lord”] had stretched out his hand [Vulgate adds: “his own”] over Jerusalem to destroy it, the Lord took pity [Hebrew: the Lord repented] because of the affliction, and said to the angel who was striking the people: “Enough; now restrain your hand.” Now the angel of the Lord was beside the threshing-floor of Araunah the Jebusite [Note: In the present Hebrew volumes the order of the letters in this name has been disturbed, for there it reads [Hebrew form], *haavarna*. But the Masoretic *Qere*, both in the printed books and in the manuscripts cited above, instructs us to read [Hebrew form], *haarauna*. We found the same spelling in our Hebrew codex of Pelissona, which uses no critical notation of the Masoretes; although below, in verse 18, it reads corruptly with the others [Hebrew form], *Arania*. The scholiast of the Hebrew Canon of Truth likewise used such a copy, as is evident not only from the marginal notation *Arania*, but also from the same name, *Areuna*, written above in the text [Col. 0663B], which the corrector of the Canon altered to *Aravena*, shifting the *shewa* beneath the letter *vau*, although after a short vowel, or *pataḥ*, grammarians of more recent times do not ordinarily place a *shewa*. This is mentioned here for the benefit of the diligent and curious reader. MART. —For *Aureuna*, the person who copied the Veronese book noted in the margin that *Ornan* should be read. This spelling of the name is taken from the Greek; in Hebrew it is variously written [Hebrew forms], or certainly from the books of Chronicles, I, chapter XXII, 28, and II, chapter III, 1, where it occurs as the surname of the Jebusite.].

When David saw the angel striking the people, he said to the Lord: “I am the one who sinned; I acted wickedly. These who are sheep [Hebrew: these sheep], what have they done? Let your hand, I beg you, be turned against me and against my father’s house.”

Gad came to David on that day and said to him: “Go up and [Vulgate omits: “and”] erect an altar to the Lord on the threshing-floor of Araunah the Jebusite” [Hebrew: here, *Arania*]. David went up according to Gad’s word, which the Lord had commanded him [Hebrew: omits “him”] [Note: As the scholiast rightly observes, the Hebrew does not add “to him”; the Veronese manuscript also omits it.]. When Araunah looked out and saw the king and his servants crossing over toward him, he went out and bowed before the king with his face to the ground. He said: “For what reason has my lord the king come to his servant?”

David said to him: “To buy the threshing-floor from you and build an altar to the Lord, so that the slaughter raging among the people may cease.”

Araunah said to David: “Let my lord the king take and offer whatever seems good to him. You have oxen for a burnt offering, and the wagon and the yokes of the oxen for wood. Araunah gives everything to the king” [Note: The Canon alone, together with the Vulgate, retains the word “king.” It is indeed found in the Hebrew, but not in the Septuagint. Araunah, therefore, was either a petty king or descended from the kings of the Jebusites. In the books of Chronicles the same Jebusite is called Ornan; this was certainly not something the writer of the Hebrew Questions concerning those books of Chronicles wished to pass over. MART. [Col. 0664B] —The Veronese manuscript removes the title “king” from Araunah; it has only: “Araunah said to the king,” and the word “king” is in fact not added in the other manuscripts, except in one that Martianaeus calls the Canon. As for the fact that it occurs in the Hebrew, distinguished critics attribute it to the fault of a copyist; or, while preserving the integrity of the text, they explain it according to the character of the Hebrew language: “Araunah, O king, gives everything to the king.”].

Araunah said to the king: “May the Lord your God accept your vow.” The king answered him: “No, but I shall buy it from you at a price, for I shall not offer to the Lord my God burnt offerings that cost nothing.” So David bought the threshing-floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, and David built [Veronese manuscript omits: “David”] an altar there to the Lord and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. The Lord was reconciled to the land, and the plague was restrained from Israel.

[Note: In accordance with the Hebrew exemplar, the Veronese manuscript very correctly reads: “Here ends the book of Samuel.” We have also said that Jerome approves this division in the prologue: “Samuel follows as the third book, which we call First and Second of Kings.” And shortly afterward: “Read, therefore, First Samuel, and my *Malachim*.” The Greek translators also agree: Aquila—for the Coislinian codices cited by Montfaucon testify to this—[Greek: “Following the Hebrews, he did not divide it, but made the two into one”].]

The two books of Samuel end here.

# [Chapter Headings of the Book of Malachim]

## Titles of the Book of Malachim

[Col. 0663]

I. Where Solomon is ordered to be anointed.

II. Where Solomon is anointed king.

III. Where David, about to die, addresses Solomon.

IV. Here King David sleeps, having reigned forty years.

V. Adonijah asks as wife the virgin who had been with David.

VI. Where Adonijah is killed.

VII. Where Joab is killed by Benaiah.

VIII. The killing of Shimei.

IX. Where Solomon is visited by the Lord.

X. Solomon is consulted by two women.

XI. Where the names of all the king Solomon’s officials are displayed.

XII. Here the rest of King Solomon’s reign is described.

XIII. Where Hiram, king of Tyre, sends to King Solomon.

XIV. Likewise, the rest of Solomon’s reign and the arrangement of the Temple.

XV. Where King Hiram agrees to the construction of the Temple.

XVI. The beginning of the construction of the Temple.

XVII. Description of the Temple.

XVIII. Completion of the Temple.

XIX. Where the ornaments of the Temple and its services are described.

XX. The transfer of the ark into the Temple.

XXI. The Lord’s descent into the Temple, and Solomon’s prayer, when he blessed the people.

XXII. The suitable place for prayer at the dedication of the Church.

XXIII. Solomon’s prophecy concerning the captivity of the people.

XXIV. Completion of the prayer and blessing of the people.

XXV. The beginning of the sacrifice after the prayer.

XXVI. When everything had been completed, Solomon is blessed by the people.

XXVII. Where the Lord says that he will destroy the Temple if the people sin.

XXVIII. Where people from the nations are appointed to the king’s service.

XXIX. Where Solomon made a fleet for the Red Sea with Hiram’s servants.

XXX. Where the queen of Sheba comes to the king.

XXXI. How much gold is presented to the king each year by weight.

XXXII. Where the king’s weapons and all his equipment are described.

XXXIII. Where Solomon sins with women and serves idols.

XXXIV. After Solomon’s sin, the adversary Hadad rises up against him.

XXXV. Where God raises up another enemy, Rezon, against Solomon.

XXXVI. Jeroboam rebels against Solomon.

XXXVII. Where Ahijah promises the kingdom to Jeroboam.

XXXVIII. Where Solomon dies, having reigned forty years.

XXXIX. Where Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, reigns.

XL. Where Rehoboam discusses the people’s request with the elders.

XLI. Likewise, after the consultation with the elders, he discusses it with the younger men.

XLII. The separation of the people from Rehoboam.

XLIII. Where the tribes make Jeroboam king.

XLIV. Where only two tribes follow Rehoboam in Jerusalem.

XLV. Where Rehoboam and the people are warned not to fight against Jeroboam and the people of Israel.

XLVI. Where Jeroboam is turned away from God and makes calves for the people to worship.

XLVII. On appointing priests only from the tribe of Levi.

XLVIII. Where the unnamed prophet tells Jeroboam that the calves he made will be destroyed by Josiah, who will arise from the seed of David; Josiah found them after two hundred years. This matter is mentioned in chapter CCXII.

XLIX. Where Jeroboam’s hand, which he had raised against the prophet, withers.

L. Likewise, at the prophet’s prayer, his hand is restored.

LI. Where another prophet in Bethel is deceived, the one who had come from Judah.

LII. The same man is condemned for contempt.

LIII. Where he is killed by a lion for disobedience.

LIV. Where Jeroboam appoints priests of the high places from the outlying peoples.

LV. Where Jeroboam’s wife goes to the prophet Ahijah for the recovery of her son.

LVI. The prophet’s announcement of what will happen to Jeroboam.

LVII. Here Jeroboam dies, having reigned twelve years, and his son Nabab reigns in his place.

LVIII. Here Scripture turns to Rehoboam, whom it says reigned seventeen years in Judah.

LIX. The first king of Egypt, Shishak, plunders Jerusalem.

LX. Here Rehoboam dies, and his son Abijah reigns.

LXI. Here Abijah dies, and Asa, king of Judah, succeeds him; he reigned forty years.

LXII. Where Asa, king of Judah, is praised because, among all the images, he overthrew the temple of Priapus.

LXIII. Here Scripture returns to Nadab, son of Jeroboam, who reigned two years after his father.

LXIV. Here Nadab, the second king of Israel, is killed by Asa, the third king of Judah.

LXV. Where Asa, king of Judah, asks for help against Baasha, king of Israel.

LXVI. The transgression of Baasha, king of Israel.

LXVII. Here Baasha dies, and his son Elah reigns; he is the fourth together with Jeroboam.

LXVIII. Here Elah the king is killed by Omri, who reigned in Israel as the fifth together with Jeroboam.

LXIX. Here Omri is made king by the people after Elah, [lacuna] the sixth together with Zimri, who reigned seven days.

LXX. Here it is shown that Omri reigned twelve years.

LXXI. Here Omri dies, and his son reigns in his place.

LXXII. Elijah’s address to Ahab concerning three years of barrenness.

LXXIII. Elijah the prophet is fed twice each day by ravens.

LXXIV. Here Elijah is fed by a widow.

LXXV. Here Elijah raises the widow’s son.

LXXVI. Elijah is ordered to return to Ahab.

LXXVII. Elijah and Obadiah address one another.

LXXVIII. Elijah shows himself to King Ahab.

LXXIX. Where Elijah and the priests of the Baals contend in sacrifice.

LXXX. Concerning the divided fire and the destruction of the priests of Baal.

LXXXI. When Elijah prayed, the Lord gave rain.

LXXXII. Elijah flees from Jezebel’s presence.

LXXXIII. Where Elijah fasts for forty days.

LXXXIV. Where he is ordered to anoint Hazael king of Syria, Jehu in Israel, and Elisha the prophet.

LXXXV. Where Elisha is taken up by Elijah.

LXXXVI. Where Elisha, having followed Elijah, holds a feast.

LXXXVII. Where an unnamed prophet tells Ahab that he will overcome Ben-hadad, king of Syria.

LXXXVIII. Where Ben-hadad fights against Ahab and is defeated a second time.

LXXXIX. Ben-hadad’s satisfaction concerning Ahab.

XC. Ahab is reproached for making peace with Ben-hadad.

XCI. Where a prophet addresses Ahab, announcing the Lord’s anger because he spared Ben-hadad, king of Syria.

XCII. Where Ahab desires Naboth’s vineyard.

XCIII. Jezebel’s plan for killing Naboth.

XCIV. Where Elijah is sent to Ahab after Naboth’s death.

XCV. The prophet Elijah’s address to Ahab concerning Jezebel’s destruction.

XCVI. After Elijah’s warning, Ahab turns to repentance.

XCVII. Ahab and Jehoshaphat conspire against the king of Syria.

XCVIII. Where the prophet Micaiah is brought to Ahab.

XCIX. Where the prophet Zedekiah prophesies falsely to Ahab.

C. Where the prophet Micaiah forbids Ahab and Jehoshaphat to go out to war.

CI. A lying spirit offers itself to deceive Ahab.

CII. Where Zedekiah strikes Micaiah on the cheek.

CIII. Here Ahab dies, wounded in battle.

CIV. Where Ahaziah, his son, arises as king; he is the eighth.

CV. Where Scripture returns to Jehoshaphat, whom it says reigned twenty-five years in Judah.

CVI. Here Jehoshaphat dies, and his son Jehoram reigns after him, the fifth king.

CVII. Ahaziah, having fallen from the upper room, orders the idols to be consulted.

CVIII. Where Elijah announces that Ahaziah will die.

CIX. Where Ahaziah orders Elijah to be brought for the third time by a company of fifty soldiers.

CX. Where Elijah announces Ahaziah’s death, after whom Jehoram reigned as the eighth king.

CXI. Where Elijah is carried up into heaven.

CXII. After sending his mantle, Elijah divides the waters of the Jordan.

CXIII. Where Elisha receives Elijah’s spirit, as he had requested.

CXIV. Through Elisha’s miracle the waters begin to become sweet.

CXV. Where boys mock Elisha and are devoured by bears.

CXVI. Where it is shown that Jehoram, son of Ahab, reigned twelve years.

CXVII. Here the king of Moab withdraws from the peace with the king of Israel.

CXVIII. Where three kings going up against the king of Moab suffer from lack of water and consult Elisha.

CXIX. Where Elisha gives water to the kings without rain.

CXX. Where Elisha fills a widow’s empty vessels with oil.

CXXI. Where Elisha is received as a guest by a woman and afterward raises her son.

CXXII. Where Elisha promises a son to the woman who had received him as a guest.

CXXIII. Here the woman’s son dies, the one who had been born because Elisha promised him.

CXXIV. Gehazi’s reminder to Elisha concerning the raising of the boy.

CXXV. Where Elisha raises the boy.

CXXVI. Where the sons of the prophets are freed from poisonous herbs by the addition of flour.

CXXVII. Where Naaman the leper is instructed by Elisha.

CXXVIII. Naaman is cleansed of leprosy in the Jordan.

CXXIX. Elisha does not accept Naaman’s gifts.

CXXX. Where Gehazi, Elisha’s servant, takes gifts from Naaman after he has been healed.

CXXXI. Elisha pronounces a punitive rebuke against Gehazi.

CXXXII. Where Elisha raises iron from the Jordan.

CXXXIII. Elisha announces to the king of Israel the ambushes of the king of Syria.

CXXXIV. Where Elisha blinds those sent by the king of Syria.

CXXXV. King Jehoram is approached by women who, during the famine, had been willing to eat their own children.

CXXXVI. Where Elisha promises abundance to the king after the famine.

CXXXVII. Concerning the four lepers who go to the king of Syria and announce that he has fled.

CXXXVIII. Elisha is consulted by Ben-hadad concerning his illness.

CXXXIX. Where Elisha promises Hazael the kingdom of Syria.

CXL. Here is Ben-hadad, king of Syria.

CXLI. After Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, dies, his son Jehoram reigns eight years; he is the fifth together with Rehoboam.

CXLII. Here Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, dies, and his son Ahaziah reigns after him for one year; he is the seventh together with Rehoboam.

CXLIII. Where Jehoram, son of Ahab, king of Israel, is wounded by Hazael, king of Syria.

CXLIV. Where Elisha is sent to anoint Jehu king of Israel after Jehoram, son of Ahab; he is the tenth king.

CXLV. Where Jehu kills Jehoram, son of Ahab.

CXLVI. Where Jehu rebels against the wounded Jehoram.

CXLVII. Concerning the killing of Ahaziah, king of Judah, by Jehu, king of Israel.

CXLVIII. Where Jezebel is killed and devoured by dogs.

CXLIX. Where Jehu orders Ahab’s sons to be killed.

CL. Where Jehu kills the brothers of Ahaziah, king of Judah.

CLI. Where Jehu orders all the prophets of Baal, all his servants, and all his priests to be summoned.

CLII. Where Jehu, after killing the priests, also burns the statue.

CLIII. Here Jehu dies, having reigned twenty-eight years; his son Jehoahaz succeeds him, and is the eleventh king.

CLIV. Here Joash, seven years old and of royal descent, is anointed king of Judah by Jehoiada the priest.

CLV. After Athaliah’s death, Joash is shown to have reigned eleven years in Judah.

CLVI. Where it is shown that Jehoiada the priest did not fail to advise King Joash.

CLVII. Where three kinds of offerings are shown: offerings made by the vow of pilgrims, offerings made for the sake of health, and offerings made voluntarily.

CLVIII. Where the priests are forbidden to receive money from the Temple because of negligence.

CLIX. Where the fidelity of the treasurers is shown, and what is expended in the Temple is allowed to be released.

CLX. Concerning the offering made for sins, so that it may benefit the priests.

CLXI. Here Joash dies, and Amaziah, his son, reigns in Judah.

CLXII. Scripture returns to the king of Israel.

CLXIII. After Jehoahaz dies, his son Joash receives the kingdom of Israel; he is the twelfth king and reigned sixteen years.

CLXIV. Here Joash, king of Israel, dies, and Jeroboam, the thirteenth king, reigns after him.

CLXV. Elisha dies and prophesies that the people of Israel will overcome the people of Syria.

CLXVI. After Elisha’s death, he raises a dead man.

CLXVII. Joash overcomes Syria according to Elisha’s word.

CLXVIII. Scripture returns to the king of Judah and says that Amaziah reigned twenty-eight years.

CLXIX. Where Amaziah, king of Judah, kills the servants who killed his father, but spares their sons according to the law given through Moses.

CLXX. Where Joash, king of Israel, fights against Amaziah, king of Judah.

CLXXI. After the war against Amaziah has been concluded, Joash dies, and his son Jeroboam succeeds him.

CLXXII. After Amaziah’s death, Azariah is made king by the people; he is the eleventh in Judah.

CLXXIII. Where Scripture returns to King Jeroboam, whom it says reigned forty years in Israel.

CLXXIV. Where the prophet Jonah is shown to have lived in those times.

CLXXV. Here Jeroboam dies, and his son Zechariah reigns fourteen years.

CLXXVI. Where Scripture returns to Zechariah, king of Judah, who reigned fifty-two years; he was a leper.

CLXXVII. Where Zechariah, king of Judah, dies, and Scripture returns to Zechariah, king of Israel.

CLXXVIII. Where Zechariah is killed, and Shallum succeeds him as king in Israel; he is the fifteenth king, the Lord’s promise in the line of Jehu having now ended.

CLXXIX. Concerning the killing of Shallum, who reigned one month; Menahem succeeded him as king in Israel and was the sixteenth.

CLXXX. A levy of silver upon the wealthy by Menahem, to be given to the king of Syria.

CLXXXI. Where Menahem dies, and his son Pekahiah reigns after him; he is the seventeenth king.

CLXXXII. Where Pekahiah is killed by Pekah, who was the eighteenth king in Israel.

CLXXXIII. Where Hoshea, son of Pekahiah, kills Pekah and reigns as the nineteenth king in Israel.

CLXXXIV. Where Scripture returns to Jotham, king of Judah, whom it says reigned sixteen years.

CLXXXV. Where Jotham dies, and Ahaz reigns sixteen years as the twelfth king in Judah.

CLXXXVI. Where Ahaz, king of Judah, consecrates his son to idols.

CLXXXVII. Where King Ahaz orders a new altar to be made by Uriah the priest.

CLXXXVIII. Where King Ahaz arranges with Uriah the priest which sacrifices are to be placed on the new altar.

CLXXXIX. Here Ahaz dies, and Hezekiah, the thirteenth king, reigns in his place.

CXC. Where Scripture returns to the king of Israel and shows that Hoshea reigned nine years.

CXCI. Here, the kings of Israel having been completed—nineteen from Jeroboam through Hoshea—the people of Israel are taken captive by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians.

CXCII. Concerning the peoples transferred by the king of the Assyrians to Samaria and devoured by lions.

CXCIII. A reminder of the commandments of the Law given to the people through Moses.

CXCIV. Where Scripture returns to the king of Judah and says that Hezekiah reigned nineteen years.

CXCV. Here Hezekiah is shown to have crushed both the sacred groves and the bronze serpent that Moses had erected.

CXCVI. Where Shalmaneser, king of Syria, wages war against Samaria during the time of Hezekiah, king of Judah.

CXCVII. Where Hezekiah, king of Judah, consults Isaiah while besieged by the king of the Assyrians.

CXCVIII. Where the prophet Isaiah promises Hezekiah victory.

CXCIX. Where the Rabshakeh returns to his own land.

CC. Where Isaiah prophesies to Hezekiah concerning the king of the Assyrians.

CCI. Where Isaiah announces Hezekiah’s death.

CCII. Where fifteen years are added to Hezekiah’s life.

CCIII. Gifts sent to Hezekiah by the king of Babylon.

CCIV. Isaiah’s prophecy that the people of Judah will come into Babylonian captivity.

CCV. Here Hezekiah dies, and his son Manasseh reigns fifty-five years; he is the fourteenth king in Judah.

CCVI. Where, after the impious decrees of King Manasseh, many prophesy Judah’s captivity.

CCVII. Where Manasseh dies, and his son Amon reigns two years.

CCVIII. Where Amon is killed by his servants, and his son Josiah becomes king; he was the sixteenth and reigned twenty-one years.

CCIX. Where King Josiah is ordered to collect the money of the Temple and spend it on repairing the roofs.

CCX. Where the accounts not rendered by the overseers of the Temple are displayed.

CCXI. Here the book of the Law is delivered to King Josiah; after reading it, he burns all the images and sacred groves.

CCXII. Where the bones of that prophet who had come unnamed to Jeroboam are not touched; he is mentioned in the preceding chapter, XLVIII.

CCXIII. Where it is also shown that, although Josiah king of Judah was upright in heart, the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem was not removed.

CCXIV. Here Josiah is killed, and his son Jehoahaz reigns three months; he is the seventeenth.

CCXV. After King Jehoahaz is removed, his brother Jehoiakim reigns eleven years as the eighteenth.

CCXVI. Here it is shown that God did not wish to be reconciled to the people of Judah because of Manasseh.

CCXVII. Here Jehoiakim dies, and, the people already captive, Jehoiakim his son receives the kingdom; he was afterward called Zedekiah and reigned eleven years.

CCXVIII. Where the people of Judah, together with King Zedekiah, are handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and the Temple of Jerusalem is burned.

CCXIX. After Zedekiah, who is also called Jehoiachin, has been led captive and blind to Babylon, Gedaliah is placed over Jerusalem.

CCXX. Where Jehoiakim, who is also called Jeconiah, is released from prison and fed with established provisions. All the people remained in captivity.

# Contents of the Book of Malachim

[Col. 0669]

I. Concerning David’s old age, Abishag the Shunammite, and Adonijah, David’s son, who desired to succeed to the kingdom, and concerning Solomon’s anointing as king.

II. Concerning David’s commands by which he instructed Solomon, David’s death, and the killing of Adonijah, Abiathar, Joab, and Shimei.

III. Concerning Solomon’s wife, Pharaoh’s daughter; his vision at Gibeon, where he asks the Lord for wisdom [Edition: “the appearance of the Lord, where he asks for wisdom,” etc.]; concerning the judgment concerning two women disputing over a dead infant [Edition omits: “a dead infant, disputing”]; and concerning the commanders and officials.

IV. Concerning Solomon’s daily expenditure, horses and chariots, his wisdom and proverbs, King Hiram, cedar wood, and the expenditure of the workers cutting wood [Edition omits: “cutting wood”].

V. Concerning the construction of the Temple, the divine testimony addressed to Solomon, the altar, and the remaining matters.

VI. Concerning the houses Solomon built for himself and for his Egyptian wife; Hiram’s treasury; the sea, bronze oxen and lions; and the remaining furnishings of the Temple.

VII. Concerning the ark placed in the Temple, the glory that appeared in the cloud, Solomon’s supplication to the Lord, and the blessing of the people.

VIII. Concerning the solemnity celebrated and the number of animals offered in sacrifice; how the Lord appeared to him a second time and spoke; and concerning Pharaoh, who gave the captured city of Gezer as a dowry to his daughter; concerning the other cities [Edition omits: “cities”] that Solomon built, his five hundred and fifty officials, and the fleet he made.

IX. Concerning the queen of Sheba and her gifts; the thyine wood and gold brought by King Hiram; the remaining tribute; the two hundred golden shields; the chariots and horses [Edition: horsemen]; and Solomon’s throne.

X. Concerning Solomon’s wives and concubines, through whom he was corrupted [Edition: transgressed], and, having been rebuked by God, was handed over to Satan; concerning Hadad and Jeroboam’s hatred against him; the prophet Ahijah sent to Jeroboam; and Solomon’s death.

XI. Concerning the division of Rehoboam’s kingdom into two tribes; the prophet Shemaiah sent to him; Jeroboam’s kingdom; and the idols he made.

XII. Concerning the prophet sent to Jeroboam who prophesied about Josiah, who was to be born; where Jeroboam’s hand withered; and the prophet, deceived by another, was killed by a lion.

XIII. Concerning Ahijah’s prophecy to Jeroboam’s wife [Edition adds: “and concerning the death of his son and the death of Jeroboam,” etc.]; his son Nadab succeeding to the kingdom; the people’s wickedness; the king of Egypt, Shishak, who destroyed Jerusalem; and Rehoboam’s death.

XIV. Concerning Abijah, son of Rehoboam, his death, and his son Asa, who reigned in his place; Asa’s successor, his son Jehoshaphat; the death of Nadab; and Baasha, his son, king of Israel.

XV. Concerning the prophet Jehu sent to Baasha; Baasha’s death; his son Elah; Zimri; and Tibni [Edition adds: “and Omri”].

XVI. Concerning Ahab, son of Omri; Jezebel; Elijah’s deeds; the woman of Zarephath, whose son he raised; Obadiah, who hid one hundred prophets; the four hundred fifty prophets of the idols who were killed; Elijah’s flight; and the vision on Mount Horeb.

XVII. Concerning Elijah, who is ordered to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu over Israel, and Elisha the prophet; Ben-hadad, king of Syria; the battle in which one hundred thousand Syrians fell; the prophet who told another, “Strike me” [Edition adds: “the other”]; Naboth and his vineyard; Elijah’s rebuke [Edition adds: “of Ahab only”]; and Ahab’s repentance.

XVIII. Concerning the meeting of Jehoshaphat and Ahab, the kings; the four hundred false prophets; the prophet Micaiah; the battle in which Ahab perished; his son Ahaziah; and Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat [Edition: “The Chapters end. The Chapters of the Fourth Book of Kings begin. Concerning the angel’s address to Elijah about Ahaziah,” etc.]; Elijah’s prophecy concerning Ahaziah; and the fifty-man companies consumed by fire at Elijah’s word.

XIX. Concerning Jehoram, Ahaziah’s brother; Elijah, who divides the Jordan and is carried up into heaven; Elisha’s return and division of the Jordan; Jehoram, Jehoshaphat, and the king of Edom, who fought against Moab; and the waters that filled the land without rain [Edition: “water”].

XX. Concerning the woman whose vessels were filled with oil at Elisha’s word, and the Shunammite woman whose son he raised.

XXI. Concerning Naaman the Syrian leper, healed through Elisha, and Gehazi, Elisha’s servant.

XXII. Concerning the king of Syria who came to besiege Samaria; where Elisha, while praying, struck the enemies with blindness; the siege and famine, during which two women ate a child; and the flight of the Syrians.

XXIII. Concerning the seven-year famine; the Shunammite woman who had lived abroad; Ben-hadad [Edition: Nadab] and Hazael, kings of Syria; and Ahaziah [Edition: Achaziah].

XXIV. Concerning Jehu, anointed king, who killed Joram; Jezebel; Ahab’s seventy sons; and the priests of Baal.

XXV. Concerning how Hazael devastated Gilead; Jehoahaz, son of Jehu; Queen Athaliah; Joash hidden away; Jehoiada the priest; and the restoration of the Temple.

XXVI. Concerning how Hazael, king of Syria, carried away the treasures of Israel; Amaziah, son of Joash; Jehoahaz, son of Jehu; Joash, his son; Elisha’s death; and the man who was raised over Elisha’s grave [Edition omits: “over his grave”].

XXVII. Concerning Amaziah, king of Judah; the war Joash waged against him; Jeroboam, son of Joash; Azariah [Col. 0672C], son of Amaziah; and Zechariah, son of Jeroboam.

XXVIII. Concerning Jotham, son of Azariah; the prophet Jonah; Shallum [Edition: “the prophet Azariah and Shallum,” etc.], who reigned after Zechariah; Anahem after Shallum; Pul, king of the Assyrians; and Pekahiah [Edition: “Pekah and Pekahiah”], after whom came Pekah, son of Remaliah.

XXIX. Concerning Tiglath, king of Assyria, and how he destroyed Galilee and Gilead; Hoshea, who reigned after Pekah; Ahaz, son of Jotham; and what is reported concerning Rezin and Pekah.

XXX. [The Edition omits this entire chapter.] Concerning Hezekiah, son of Ahaz; Hoshea, king of Israel; Shalmaneser; and the capture of Samaria, because Israel perished on account of its wickedness; and the foreigners whom lions ate in Samaria.

XXXI. Concerning how Hezekiah removed the bronze serpent; Sennacherib and the Rabshakeh; the prophet Isaiah; and how the angel killed one hundred [lacuna] twenty thousand [Edition: one hundred eighty-five thousand] Assyrians.

XXXII. Concerning Hezekiah’s illness; the sign in the sun; the servants and the letters of Berodach, king of Babylon; Manasseh and his wickedness; and Amon, son of Manasseh.

XXXIII. Concerning Josiah, son of Amon; the book found in the Temple; the prophet Oldad; the idols of Judah and Samaria that were purged; and the Passover that he celebrated [Edition adds above: “Josiah”].

XXXIV. Concerning Jehoahaz, son of Josiah, and Necho, king of Egypt; how he made Jehoiakim king in place of Jehoahaz [Alternative: Joahaz]; Nebuchadnezzar; Jehoiakim, son of Jehoiakim [Alternative: “and Jehoiakim alone, without ‘son of Jehoiakim’”]; the second captivity, when the people were taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin; and Zedekiah.

XXXV. Concerning the third captivity into Chaldea, with King Zedekiah, and the removal of all the vessels of the Temple; Gedaliah, whether he was appointed governor or killed; and Jehoiachin’s being brought out of prison in Babylon.

# The Two Books of Malachim Begin

[Col. 0673]

## Book [Note: In the Veronese manuscript, in which the Book of Malachim is a single book in accordance with the Hebrew text, “First” is not added. Recall what we noted above on this matter at the end of the Book of Samuel.]

## First.

[Col. 0673B] [Chapter I.] Now King David was old and advanced in years; and although they covered him with garments, he was not warmed. Therefore his servants said: “Let them seek for our lord the king a young virgin, so that she may stand before the king, warm him [Hebrew: cover him], sleep in his bosom, and warm our lord the king.” So they sought a beautiful young woman throughout all the borders of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king. The girl was exceedingly beautiful; she slept with the king [Hebrew: and she was a covering for the king] and ministered to him, but the king did not know her.

Now Adonijah son of Haggith exalted himself, saying: “I shall reign.” He made himself a chariot, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. His father had never rebuked him, saying: “Why have you done this?” He himself was also very handsome, born after Absalom [Hebrew: and she bore him after Absalom]. He conferred with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, who supported Adonijah’s faction. But Zadok the priest, Benaiah [Ms. Banaias] son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David’s mighty men [Hebrew: and David’s strongest men] were not with Adonijah.

After sacrificing rams [Hebrew: sheep], calves, and all the fatlings beside the stone of Zoheleth, which was near the spring of Rogel, Adonijah summoned all his brothers, the king’s sons, and all the men of Judah, the king’s servants. But he did not summon Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, any of the mighty men, or Solomon his brother.

Then Nathan said to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother: “Have you not heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has become king, while our lord David does not know this [Hebrew: does not have it]? Now therefore come, accept my counsel from me, and save your life and that of your son Solomon [Hebrew: does not have this]. Go and enter King David’s presence and say to him: ‘Did you not, my lord the king, swear to me [Hebrew: does not have this], your handmaid, saying: “Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne”? [Note: More correctly, the Verona manuscript reads “has become king,” with the Hebrew and most other books.] Why then does Adonijah reign?’ And while you are still speaking there with the king, I shall come in after you and complete your words.”

So Bathsheba entered the king’s chamber. The king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite ministered to him. Bathsheba bowed and worshiped the king. The king said to her: “What do you want?” She answered: “My lord, you swore by the Lord your God to your handmaid, saying [Vulgate omits “that”]: ‘Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne.’ And now, behold, Adonijah reigns [Note: Again the same manuscript, agreeing with the Hebrew, reads: “has become king,” etc.], while you, my lord the king, do not know it. He has slaughtered oxen, fatlings, and very many rams [sheep], and has summoned all the king’s sons, Abiathar the priest also, and Joab the commander of the army; but he has not summoned Solomon your servant. Nevertheless, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are upon you, so that you may declare to them who ought to sit upon your throne, my lord the king, after you [Hebrew: upon the throne of my lord the king after him]. For when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, I and my son Solomon shall be sinners.”

While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet arrived. They announced to the king: “Nathan the prophet is here.” When he had entered the king’s presence [Vulgate: in the presence of the king] and bowed before him with his face to the ground, Nathan said: “My lord the king, did you say: ‘Let Adonijah reign after me, and let him sit upon my throne’? For today he has gone down and sacrificed oxen, fatlings, and very many rams [sheep], and has summoned all the king’s sons and the commanders of the army, Abiathar the priest also. While they eat and drink before him, they say: ‘Long live King Adonijah!’ But me your servant, Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and Solomon your servant, he has not summoned. Has this word proceeded from my lord the king, and have you not informed your servant who is to sit upon the throne of my lord the king after him?”

King David answered: “Call Bathsheba to me.” When she had entered before the king and stood in his presence, the king swore and said: “As the Lord lives, who has rescued my life from every distress, just as I swore to you by the Lord God of Israel, saying: ‘Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne in my place,’ so I shall do today.”

Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and worshiped the king, saying: “May my lord King David live forever” [Vulgate omits “the king”].

[Title I.] King David also said: “Call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada to me.” When they had entered before the king, he said to them: “Take with you the servants of your lord, set my son Solomon upon my mule, and bring [Hebrew: bring him down] him to Gihon. There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet shall anoint him king over Israel. Then blow the trumpet and say: ‘Long live King Solomon!’ You shall go up after him, and you shall come [Hebrew: and he shall come], and he shall sit upon my throne, and he shall reign in my place. I shall command him to be ruler over Israel and Judah.”

Benaiah son of Jehoiada answered the king: “Amen. May the Lord God of my lord the king speak thus [Note: The same Verona manuscript reads “of my lord the king.”]. As the Lord was with my lord the king, so may he be with Solomon, and may he make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David.”

[T. II.] So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and Pelethites went down. They set Solomon upon King David’s mule and brought him to Gihon. Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon. They blew the trumpet, and all the people said: “Long live King Solomon!” Then all the multitude went up after him, with the people playing pipes and rejoicing with great joy, and the earth resounded with their shouting [Note: Here the same manuscript omits, apparently through the copyist’s negligence, the words “with their shouting”; these words are nevertheless present in the Hebrew and in the other books.].

Adonijah and all who had been invited by him heard this, although the banquet had already ended. Joab too, hearing the sound of the trumpet, said: “What does this shouting of the tumultuous city mean?” While he was still speaking, Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. Adonijah said to him: “Enter, for you are a valiant man and bring good news.”

Jonathan answered Adonijah: “Not at all. Our lord King David has made Solomon king. He sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and Pelethites, and they set him upon the king’s mule. Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed him king at Gihon [Ms. Geon], and they went up from there rejoicing, and the city resounded [Mss. thundered]. This is the voice that you heard. Moreover, Solomon sits upon the throne of the kingdom. The king’s servants also entered and blessed our lord King David, saying: ‘May God make Solomon’s name greater than yours, and may he magnify his throne above your throne.’ And the king worshiped upon his bed. He also spoke these words [Vulgate omits “he also spoke these words”]: ‘Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who has today granted one sitting upon my throne while my eyes see it’ [Note: The Verona manuscript, together with the Vulgate copies, reads: “upon my throne.”].”

Then all who had been invited by Adonijah became terrified and rose, each going his own way. Adonijah, fearing Solomon, rose and went away, and seized the horn of the altar. Solomon was informed: “Behold, Adonijah fears King Solomon and has seized the horns of the altar, saying: ‘Let King Solomon swear to me today that he will not kill his servant with the sword.’”

Solomon said: “If he is a good man [Ms. ‘a son of valor’], not even a single hair of his shall fall to the ground; but if evil is found in him, he shall die.” So King Solomon sent and brought him away from the altar. He entered and bowed to King Solomon, and Solomon said to him [Ms. omits “to him”]: “Go to your house.”

[T. III, Chapter II.] The days of David drew near for him to die, and he commanded Solomon his son: “I am going the way of all the earth. Be strong and be a man. Keep [Ms.: “etc.”] the charge of the Lord your God, so that you may walk in his ways, keep his statutes [Hebrew: ordinances], his commandments, his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, so that you may understand all that you do and wherever you turn, so that the Lord may confirm his words which he spoke concerning me, saying: ‘If your sons keep their way and walk before me in truth, with all their heart and with all their soul, a man shall not be taken from you from the throne of Israel’ [Note: The Royal and Corbie manuscripts, number 11, read “my ways.” Others, with the Latin Vulgate, read “their ways.” Some have “my way.” The reading adopted here is the Canon, as we published it. MART. — The Vulgate copies have “their ways” in the plural. The Verona manuscript agrees with the one Martianay calls the Canon.].

“You also know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me, what he did to the two commanders of the army of Israel, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether: he killed them and shed the blood of war in peace, placing the blood of battle upon his belt, which was around his waist, and upon his sandal, which was on his foot. Therefore act according to your wisdom, and do not bring his gray head down peacefully to the underworld.

“But you shall show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and they shall eat at your table, for they came to meet me when I was fleeing from the presence of your brother Absalom.

“You also have with you [Ms. omits ‘with you’] Shimei son of Gera, son of Jemini [Hebrew: does not have this] from Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse when I was going to the camp [Hebrew: Mahanaim]. But because he came down to meet me as I was crossing the Jordan, and I swore to him by the Lord, saying: ‘I shall not kill you with the sword,’ you must not leave him unpunished. You are a wise man, and you will know what to do to him; you shall bring his gray hairs down to the underworld with blood.”

[T. IV.] Thus David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David. The days that David reigned over Israel were forty years: he reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. Solomon sat upon the throne of David his father, and his kingdom was firmly established indeed.

[Note: The Verona manuscript distinguished the name “Solomon” in red ink, to mark the beginning of his reign.]

[T. V.] Adonijah son of Haggith went to Bathsheba, the mother of Solomon. She said to him: “Is your entrance peaceful?” [Ms. omits “is.”] He answered: “Peaceful.” He added: “I have a word for you.” She said to him: “Speak.” He said: “You know that the kingdom was mine, and all Israel had set me over themselves as king” [Ms. “had proposed me”]. “But the kingdom was transferred and became my brother’s, for it was appointed to him by the Lord. Now therefore I ask one request of you: do not put me to shame.”

She said to him: “Speak.” He said: “I ask you to speak to King Solomon—for he cannot refuse you anything [Hebrew: for he will not turn your face away]—so that he may give me Abishag the Shunammite as wife” [Vulgate: “the Shunammite woman,” here and below]. Bathsheba said: “Good; I shall speak to the king on your behalf.”

Bathsheba therefore came to King Solomon to speak to him for Adonijah. The king rose to meet her, bowed to her, and sat upon his throne. A throne was placed for the king’s mother, and she sat at his right hand. He said to her: “I ask one small request of you; do not put me to shame” [Hebrew: “do not turn away my face”].

The king said to her [Ms. omits “and”]: “Ask, my mother [Ms. “my mother”], for it is not right that I should turn your face away” [Hebrew: “Ask, my mother. I shall not turn your face away”]. She said: “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given as wife to your brother Adonijah.”

King Solomon answered his mother: “Why do you ask for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for the kingdom for him as well, for he is my older brother, and he has Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah [Hebrew: ‘for him, Abiathar the priest, and Joab son of Zeruiah’].”

Then King Solomon swore by the Lord, saying: “May God do these things to me, and may he add more, for Adonijah has spoken this word against his own life. And now, as the Lord lives, who established me and placed me upon the throne of David my father, who made me a house as he spoke, Adonijah shall be killed today.”

[T. VI.] King Solomon sent by the hand of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who struck him, and he died.

The king also said to Abiathar the priest: “Go to Anathoth, to your field; indeed, you are a man condemned to death. But I shall not kill you today, because you carried the ark of the Lord God [Hebrew: “Lord Lord”] before David my father and shared in all the labor in which my father labored.”

So Solomon expelled Abiathar, so that he would no longer be priest of the Lord, to fulfill the word of the Lord which he spoke concerning the house of Eli at Shiloh.

A messenger came to Joab because Joab had turned aside after Adonijah but had not turned aside after Solomon [Note: With the single exception of the Canon of Hebrew Truth, all the manuscripts of the scribes and copyists have been corrupted in this way: “A messenger came to Solomon,” etc. For, not understanding the sense of Scripture, they thought it an error if one read “A messenger came to Joab.” Jerome therefore rightly warned in his letter to Lucinius that it is the custom of copyists to write not what they find but what they understand; and while they attempt to correct the errors of others, they reveal their own. MART. — The Verona manuscript again agrees most exactly with Martianay’s Canon. In other copies, instead of “to Joab,” that reading has “he found Solomon.”]. So Joab fled to the tabernacle of the Lord and seized the horn of the altar.

It was reported to King Solomon that Joab had fled to the tabernacle of the Lord and was beside the altar. Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, saying: “Go, kill him.”

Benaiah came to the tabernacle of the Lord and said to him: “The king says: ‘Come out.’” He answered: “I shall not come out, but I shall die here.” Benaiah reported to the king what Joab had said and how he had answered him. The king said to him [Ms. omits “to him”]: “Do as he has said; kill him and bury him, and remove from me and from my father’s house the innocent blood which Joab shed. May the Lord return his blood upon his head, because he killed two men better than himself and struck them down with the sword, without my father David’s knowledge: Abner son of Ner, commander of the army of Israel, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah. Their blood shall therefore return upon the head of Joab and upon the head of his offspring forever. But may there be peace from the Lord for David, his offspring, his house, and his throne forever.”

[T. VII.] Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up, attacked him, and killed him. He was buried in his own house in the wilderness.

The king appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the army in his place, and he appointed Zadok priest in place of Abiathar.

The king sent for Shimei and said to him: “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem, dwell there, and do not go out from there anywhere. On whatever day you go out and cross the torrent of Kidron, know that you shall surely be killed; your blood shall be upon your own head.”

Shimei said to the king: “The word is good” [Ms. omits “is”]. “As my lord the king has spoken, so your servant shall act.” So Shimei dwelt in Jerusalem for many days.

But after three years it happened that Shimei’s servants [Hebrew: two servants] fled to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath.
