Shimei was informed that his servants were in Gath [Vulgate: “had gone to Gath”]. Shimei rose, saddled his donkey, and went to Gath, to Achish, to seek his servants; and he brought them back from Gath.

Solomon was informed that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had returned. He sent for him and said to him: “Did I not adjure you by the Lord and warn you [Hebrew: ‘Did I not adjure you by the Lord, and was grieved: “On whatever day you go out and go here or there, know that you shall die”’]?” And you answered me: “The word is good,” which I heard [Note: In accordance with the Hebrew idiom, the Verona manuscript omits “which.” The Chaldean and the other Eastern versions also read and punctuate it thus: “The word is good; I have heard,” etc.]. Why then did you not keep the oath of the Lord and the commandment which I commanded you?”

The king said to Shimei: “You know all the evil of which your heart is conscious, what you did to David my father. The Lord has returned your wickedness upon your own head. But King Solomon is blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the Lord forever.”

The king commanded Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who went out, struck him, and he died.

[T. VIII, Chapter III.] So the kingdom was established in Solomon’s hand. He became related by marriage to Pharaoh king of Egypt, for he took Pharaoh’s daughter and brought her into the city of David, until he had finished building his own house, the house of the Lord, and the wall around Jerusalem.

Nevertheless, the people sacrificed on the high places, for the temple had not yet been built for the name of the Lord. Solomon loved the Lord, walking in the commandments of David his father, except that he sacrificed on the high places and burned incense.

He went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the greatest high place. Solomon offered a thousand offerings as burnt offerings upon that altar at Gibeon [Hebrew: a thousand burnt offerings].

[T. IX.] The Lord [Ms. omits “now”] appeared to Solomon in a dream by night and said: “Ask what you wish me to give you.”

Solomon said: “You showed great mercy to your servant David my father, just as he walked before you in truth, righteousness, and uprightness of heart with you. You preserved great mercy for him [Note: The Verona manuscript inserts “your,” while the other books omit it], and you gave him a son sitting upon his throne, as it is today.

“And now, Lord my God [Ms. and Vulgate omit “my”], you have made your servant king in place of David my father. But I am a little child, not knowing my going out or my coming in [Hebrew omits this]. Your servant is in the midst of the people [Hebrew: your people] whom you have chosen, an innumerable people who cannot be counted or numbered because of their multitude. Therefore give your servant an understanding heart, so that he may judge your people and discern between good and evil. For who can judge this great people of yours?”

The request pleased the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], because Solomon had asked for such a thing. The Lord said to Solomon: “Because you have asked for this, and have not asked for many days, or riches, or the life [Ms. and Vulgate: lives] of your enemies, but have asked for wisdom to discern judgment, behold, I have done according to your words. I have given you a wise and understanding heart, so that no one like you has existed before you, nor shall anyone like you arise after you.

“But I have also given you what you did not ask for: riches and glory, so that no one like you shall have existed among all the kings of former days [Hebrew: ‘among all the kings in all your days’]. If you walk in my ways, keep my commandments and my ordinances [Note: Here too the Verona manuscript, contrary to the Hebrew text, omits “your commandments,” and shortly afterward also omits the name “David”], as David your father walked, I shall lengthen your days.”

Then Solomon awoke and understood that it had been a dream [Hebrew: “Then Solomon awoke—and behold, it was a dream”]. When he came to Jerusalem, he stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and held a great feast for all his servants [Hebrew omits “great”].

[T. X.] Then two prostitute women came to the king and stood before him. One of them said: “I beg you, my lord [Hebrew omits this]. I and this woman lived in one house, and I gave birth while she was there in the room. On the third day after I had given birth, this woman also gave birth. We were together, and no one else was in the house with us except the two of us.

“This woman’s son died during the night, for she had lain upon him. Rising in the dead of night in silence [Hebrew omits this], she took my son from beside me, your handmaid, while I slept, and placed him in her bosom. But her son, who was dead, she placed in my bosom.

“When I rose in the morning to give milk to my son, behold, he was dead. Examining him carefully in the clear light, I discovered that he was not my son whom I had borne.”

The other woman answered: “It is not so [Vulgate adds ‘as you say’]; your son is dead, but my son is alive.” To the contrary, the first woman said: “You are lying; my son is alive, and your son is dead.” And in this way they contended before the king.

Then the king said: “This woman says, ‘My son is alive, and your son is dead’; and that woman says, ‘No, your son is dead, and my son is alive.’”

The king therefore said: “Bring me a sword.” When they had brought a sword before the king, he said: “Divide the living child into two parts, and give half to one and half to the other.”

The woman whose son was alive said to the king—for her inward parts were stirred over her son: “I beg you, my lord [Hebrew omits ‘my lord’], give her the living child, and do not kill him.” But the other woman said: “Let him be neither mine nor yours [Note: The Verona manuscript also omits the word “but,” which is found neither in the Hebrew nor in most of the other books.]; divide him.”

The king answered: “Give the living child to this woman, and do not kill him, for she is his mother.”

All Israel heard of the judgment which the king had judged, and they feared the king, seeing that the wisdom of God was in him to administer judgment.

[T. XI, Chapter IV.] King Solomon reigned over all Israel, and these were the officials whom he had:

Azariah son of Zadok the priest [Note: The Hebrew has a term which several Greek books correctly render in the nominative as ἱερεύς, “priest”; the Verona manuscript agrees with them, reading “priest” instead of “of the priest”];

Elioreph and Ahiah, sons of Shisha, scribes;

Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud, recorder [Note: In the margin of the Verona codex is written, in the Septuagint: “from memory.” There can be no doubt that this denotes the old Latin version translated from the Greek];

Benaiah son of Jehoiada, over the army;

Zadok and Abiathar, priests;

Azariah son of Nathan, over those who attended the king [Hebrew: over the officials];

Zabud son of Nathan, priest, the king’s friend;

Ahishar, superintendent of the palace;

Adoniram son of Abda, over the forced labor.

Solomon had twelve prefects over all Israel, who supplied provisions for the king and his household. Each one supplied the necessities during one month of the year.

These were their names:

Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim;

Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, Elon, and Beth-hanan;

Ben-hesed, in Arubboth; to him belonged Socoh and all the land of Hepher;

Ben-abinadab, to whom belonged all Naphath-dor; he had Taphath, Solomon’s daughter, as wife;

Baana son of Ahilud ruled over Taanach and Megiddo, and all Beth-shean, which is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah [Note: We have not altered these words, in accordance with the Canon of Hebrew Truth, where we read: “as far as Abel-meholah, and as far as the region of Jokmeam.” As I stated earlier, it is not sufficiently clear from what source the frequent corrections visible in that Canon have flowed: whether from more carefully corrected copies of Jerome’s version, or from the deliberate work of some exceptionally skilled corrector who revised much in Jerome’s translation according to Hebrew manuscripts. Let the learned reader therefore know that we have always added such corrected readings, whenever they seemed of some importance, in our marginal notes, lest anything of scholarly interest should be lost to diligent students if these readings remained untouched and were despised. MART.] opposite Jokmeam;

Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead; he had the settlements of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead, and he was over the whole region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty large and fortified cities with bronze bars;

Ahinadab son of Iddo was over Mahanaim;

Ahimaaz in Naphtali; he too had Basmath daughter of Solomon as wife;

Baana son of Hushai, in Asher and in Baaloth [Ms. “Banaa and Asar”];

Jehoshaphat son of Paruah, in Issachar;

Shimei son of Ela, in Benjamin;

Geber son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, in the land of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, over everything that was in that land [Hebrew: and he was the only prefect over the land].

Judah and Israel were innumerable [Hebrew: very numerous], like the sand of the sea in multitude, eating, drinking, and rejoicing.

[T. XII, Chapter IV.] Solomon was ruler over all the kingdoms [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “all the kingdoms from the River,” etc. Learned men have debated which river is meant: some interpret it as the Euphrates, others as the torrent of Gaza or Besor. But what the word “as” means here, or from what source the copyist produced it, we do not know. Compare the following annotation.] from the River to the land of the Philistines and to the boundary of Egypt. They brought him gifts and served him throughout all the days of his life.

Solomon’s daily provision was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal, ten fattened cattle, twenty pasture-fed cattle, and one hundred rams [Hebrew: sheep], besides deer, gazelles, and buffalo, and fattened birds [Hebrew omits “deer, gazelles, buffalo, and fattened birds”].

For he ruled over the entire region beyond the River [Note: The same manuscript inserts here a word meaning “as if,” apparently a gloss added by some industrious person, just as it did earlier with “as”], from Tiphsah to Gaza, and over all the kings of those regions; and he had peace on every side all around.

Judah and Israel dwelt without any fear [Hebrew: confidently], each under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba, throughout all the days of Solomon.

Solomon had forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen. The aforementioned prefects fed them and also supplied, with great care and at the appointed time, whatever was necessary for King Solomon’s table [Hebrew: “The aforementioned prefects fed King Solomon and all Solomon’s guests with great care at the appointed time.”].

They brought barley and straw for the horses and pack animals to the place where the king was, according to the arrangement assigned to them [Hebrew: “where it was assigned to them”].

God gave Solomon wisdom and exceedingly great understanding, and breadth of heart like the sand on the seashore.

Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the East and of Egypt, and he was wiser than all men: wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Chalcol [Ms. Calcas], and Darda, the sons of Mahol. He was renowned among all the nations round about.

Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered one thousand and five. He discoursed about trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; and he discussed animals, birds, reptiles, and fish.

People came from all nations to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and from all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom [Ms. omits “and”].

[T. XIII, Chapter V.] King Hiram of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon, for he had heard that they had anointed him king in place of his father, because Hiram had always been a friend of David.

Solomon also sent to Hiram, saying: “You know the desire of David my father, and that he could not build a house for the name of the Lord his God because of the wars pressing in on every side, until the Lord placed them beneath the soles of his feet [Hebrew: ‘You know that David my father could not build a house’].”

[T. XIV.] “But now the Lord my God has given me rest on every side [Note: Here the manuscript omits the name “Lord,” which is nevertheless in the Hebrew, and also a particle which the Hebrew likewise lacks], and there is neither adversary nor harmful opposition. Therefore I intend to build a temple for the name of the Lord my God [Ms. omits “of the Lord”], as the Lord spoke to David my father, saying: ‘Your son, whom I shall set upon your throne in your place, shall build the house for my name.’

“Now therefore command that they cut cedars for me from Lebanon, and let my servants be with your servants. I shall give you whatever wages you stipulate for your servants [Hebrew: ‘whatever you say’; Vulgate: ‘whatever you request’]. For you know that there is no man among my people [Hebrew: ‘among us’] who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians.”

When Hiram heard Solomon’s words, he rejoiced greatly and said: “Blessed is the Lord [Note: The Verona manuscript, together with the Hebrew, omits the name “God”] God today, who has given David a very wise son over this great people.”

[T. XV.] Hiram sent to Solomon, saying: “I have heard everything that you commanded me. I shall fulfill all your wishes concerning cedar and fir timber. My servants shall bring them down from Lebanon to the sea, and I shall place them in rafts on the sea until the place which you designate. There I shall unload them, and you shall take them away. You shall provide what I need, so that food may be given to my household.”

Thus Hiram gave Solomon cedar and fir timber, according to all his wishes [Hebrew: here it has “Hiron”].

Solomon supplied Hiram with twenty thousand cors of wheat for food for his household [Note: The Hebrew and the Vulgate, together with the Verona manuscript, prefer “for his household”] and twenty cors of the finest oil. Solomon supplied this to Hiram every year.

The Lord gave Solomon wisdom, as he had spoken to him [Ms. omits “to him”]. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a covenant.

King Solomon selected forced laborers from all Israel, and the levy consisted of thirty thousand men. He sent them to Lebanon, ten thousand each month in rotation, so that they spent two months at home; and Adoniram was over this levy.

Solomon had seventy thousand men who carried burdens [Note: The same Verona manuscript reads “horses,” through the invention of an unlearned glossator], and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountain, apart from the officials supervising each work, numbering three thousand three hundred, who directed the people and those performing the work [Hebrew omits “and”].

The king commanded them to quarry large stones, precious stones, for the foundation of the temple, and to dress them. Solomon’s masons and Hiram’s masons dressed them. The Byblians prepared [Hebrew: “the Giblites also prepared”] the timber and stones for building the house [Note: The Hebrew really expresses this name by “Giblites”; but “Giblos” and “Byblos” are understood as the same Phoenician city at the foot of Lebanon. See Ezekiel 27:9.].

### [C. V. Chapter VI]

It came to pass, therefore, in the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites had gone out from the land of Egypt, in the fourth year, in the month Ziv [the Verona manuscript reads *Zoi*] (that is, the second month), of King Solomon [Vulgate: “of Solomon’s kingdom”] over Israel, that he began to build [Vulgate: “the house began to be built”] the house of the Lord. The house that King Solomon was building for the Lord was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.

There was a portico in front of the temple [Hebrew: “in front of the house of the temple”] twenty cubits long, corresponding to the width of the temple, and it was ten cubits wide in front of the temple façade. He made in the temple slanting windows.

[Note: In the Verona manuscript’s blank space this note is added: “In the Septuagint, concealed latticework doors.” By “the Septuagint” he means the Latin version that preceded Jerome’s, since it was rendered according to their exemplar; others preferred to call it the Old Latin. The Septuagint translators rendered the phrase as Θυρίδας διακυπτομένας (or παρακυπτομένας, or δεδικτυωμένας) κρυπτάς—that is, “windows looking outward” (or “looking obliquely outward,” or “latticed”), “concealed.” Saint Jerome himself, in his Commentary on Ezekiel, book XII, reports that the Septuagint translated it as “concealed windows.” “The windows,” he says, “were oblique; the Septuagint calls them concealed, while Symmachus calls them τοξικάς.” And in chapter XLI he says: “The windows, according to the Septuagint, were made in the form of a net, like latticework … whereas the Hebrew has ‘oblique windows.’”]

He built an upper structure against the wall of the temple all around, along the walls of the house surrounding the temple and the inner sanctuary, and he made side chambers all around. The lower story was five cubits wide, the middle story six cubits wide, and the third story seven cubits wide. He placed beams around the outside of the house so that they would not be fastened into the walls of the temple.

When the house was being built, it was built of dressed and finished stones; neither hammer, axe, nor any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built. The entrance to the middle side-chamber was on the right side of the house; by a spiral staircase they went up to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third.

He built the house and completed it. He also covered the house with cedar ceilings. He built an upper story over the entire house, five cubits high, and covered the house with cedar wood.

### [T. XVI]

The word of the Lord came to Solomon, saying: “As for this house that you are building, if you walk in my statutes, perform my judgments, and keep all my commandments, walking in them, I will establish with you the word that I spoke to David your father. I will dwell among the Israelites and will not abandon my people Israel.”

So Solomon built the house and completed it.

### [T. XVII]

He [the manuscript adds “Solomon”] panelled the inner walls of the house with cedar boards, from the floor of the house to the tops of the walls and up to the ceilings; he covered the interior with wood and covered the floor of the house with fir boards. He built, at the rear of the temple, a cedar-panelled structure twenty cubits long, from the floor to the upper part, and made the inner chamber of the sanctuary—the Holy of Holies.

The temple itself, in front of the inner sanctuary, was forty cubits long. The entire interior of the house was clad in cedar, with its mouldings and expertly fashioned joints and projecting carvings; everything was covered with cedar boards, and no stone at all could be seen in the wall [Hebrew omits this].

In the middle of the house, toward the interior, he made [Hebrew: “prepared”] the inner sanctuary in order to place there the ark of the covenant of the Lord. The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high. He covered and overlaid it with the purest gold [Hebrew: “refined gold”]. He also covered the altar with cedar. He overlaid with the purest gold the house in front of the inner sanctuary and fastened gold sheets to it with golden nails. Nothing in the temple was left uncovered with gold; he also covered the entire altar belonging to the inner sanctuary with gold.

[Note: The name *Cherub* in the singular and *Cherubim* in the plural is treated by interpreters as belonging to two genders, masculine and neuter. Hence in manuscript codices we read both *cherub secundus* and *cherub secundum*. Writing to Damasus about the Seraphim, Jerome said: “There is also a difference of gender. The Septuagint, Aquila, and Theodotion translated *Seraphim* in the neuter gender, while Symmachus used the masculine. Nor should one think that there is sex among the powers of God, since even the Holy Spirit, according to the properties of the Hebrew language, is expressed in the feminine gender, *ruaḥ* (רוּחַ); in Greek it is neuter, τὸ πνεῦμα, and in Latin masculine, *spiritus*. From this it may be understood that when superior matters are discussed and something is expressed as masculine or feminine, it is not so much sex that is signified as the idiom of the language. Indeed, the invisible and incorruptible God is expressed in the masculine gender in nearly all languages, although sex does not apply to him.” MART.]

In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high. One wing of the cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits—that is, together they measured ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other wing [the manuscript omits “of the wing”]. The cherub was also ten cubits high [Note: “the second cherub”]. They were of equal dimensions, and the two cherubim were a single work: one cherub was ten cubits high, and likewise the second cherub.

He placed the cherubim in the inner part of the temple. The cherubim spread out their wings: one wing touched one wall, and the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall; their other wings touched one another in the middle of the temple. He overlaid the cherubim with gold.

He carved all the walls of the temple around with various carvings and with a turning tool.

[Note: The Verona manuscript consistently reads *scalpo* instead of *sculpo*. The former is indeed more elegant, since the grammarians—including Diomedes—deny that the latter is Latin.]

[Note: In the Canon, the words “and he made in them” have been erased because they are not found in the Hebrew; nevertheless they occur in Latin manuscripts. Concerning the following word *cherubim*, what Jerome says in Letter 130 to Marcella should be noted: “In Exodus and the other places where garments woven by embroidery are described, it is stated that *opus Cherubim*, that is, a variegated and painted work, was made. Yet the letter *vav* is not present in *Cherubim*, because wherever it is written with that letter it signifies animals rather than works.” We have found this to be true by carefully examining published and manuscript Hebrew volumes, especially Exodus 26 and Ezekiel 10, where a few variant readings occur, but they are of very little importance. MART.]

He made in them cherubim, palm trees, and various paintings, appearing to project from the wall and to emerge [Hebrew: “inside and outside”]. He also covered the floor of the house with gold, inside and outside.

At the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olive wood, with five-sided cornerposts [Hebrew omits this]. He made two doors of olive wood and carved on them figures of cherubim, representations of palm trees [Hebrew omits this], and very prominent relief work [the manuscript reads “very forcefully prominent”]. He overlaid them with gold and covered with gold both the cherubim and the palm trees and the rest [Hebrew omits this].

At the entrance of the temple he made four-sided doorposts of olive wood, and two doors of fir wood on either side. Each door was double, and the two leaves opened while holding one another.

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads *tenentes aperiebantur* in the plural, namely, “the doorposts opened while holding one another.”]

He carved cherubim, palm trees, and very prominent relief work [Hebrew: “various paintings”]. He covered everything with gold sheets, worked squarely and according to a rule [Hebrew: “he overlaid the carvings evenly with gold”].

He built the inner court with three courses of dressed stones and one course of cedar wood.

### [T. XVII]

In the fourth year the house of the Lord was founded, in the month Ziv; and in the eleventh year, in the month Bul (that is, the eighth month), the house was completed in all its work and all its furnishings [the manuscript omits “its furnishings”]. He built it over seven years.

### [Chapter VII]

Solomon built his own house over thirteen years and brought it to completion. He also built the House of the Forest of Lebanon, one hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high, with four covered walks between cedar columns. For he had cut cedar wood into columns [Hebrew: “above four rows of columns, with cedar wood above the columns”].

He covered the entire chamber with cedar panelling; it was supported by forty-five columns [the manuscript reads “sustained”]. One [Hebrew omits “one”] row had fifteen columns set opposite one another and facing one another, with equal spacing between the columns; and above the columns were squared timbers, all of equal size.

He made a portico of columns fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide, and another portico in front of the larger portico, with columns and beams above the columns. He also made and covered with cedar wood the portico of the throne, where the tribunal was [Hebrew: “where he judged,”] from the floor to the top.

The small chamber [Hebrew: “house”] in which one sat for judging [Hebrew omits “for judging”] was in the middle of the portico [Hebrew: “in another court”], made in the same manner.

He also made a house for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom Solomon had married, in the same manner as this portico. Everything consisted of precious stones, sawn according to a certain rule and measurement, both inside and outside, from the foundation to the top of the walls, and outside [the manuscript reads “inside”] as far as the great court.

The foundations were of precious stones, large stones eight or ten cubits in size. Above them were precious stones cut to equal measurements, and likewise cedar [Hebrew: “and cedar wood”].

The great court was circular, with three courses of cut stones and one course of hewn cedar [the manuscript reads “hewn cedar” in the feminine]. The same applied to the inner court of the house of the Lord and to the portico of the house.

King Solomon sent for Hiram of Tyre. He was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, while his father was a Tyrian; he was a worker in bronze, full of wisdom, understanding, and skill, for carrying out every kind of work in bronze. When he came to King Solomon, he performed all his work.

He cast two bronze columns, one column eighteen cubits high; a line of twelve cubits encircled each column. He also made two capitals to be placed on the tops of the columns, cast in bronze.

[Note: The royal manuscript and the Hebrew Canon of Truth read “cast bronze.” MART. The Verona manuscript agrees almost entirely with Martianay’s Canon: “cast in bronze.”]

One capital was five cubits high, and the other capital was five cubits high. They were woven in a marvelous work, as though in the form of a net and chains intertwined with one another.

[Note: The Verona manuscript more correctly reads *opere* instead of *opera*; the Hebrew has only *opere*. The same word is used immediately afterward, where the Latin has “in the form of,” so that one may see that nothing unusual is being said here in the Hebrew text.]

Both capitals of the columns were cast; there were seven latticeworks of rows on one capital and seven latticeworks on the other. He completed the columns and two rows around each latticework, to cover the capitals that were above the tops of the pomegranates; he did the same for the second capital.

The capitals that were above the tops of the columns were fashioned like lily work in the portico, four cubits high. There were also other capitals at the top of the columns, above, beside the latticework, corresponding to the measurement of the column. There were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital.

He set up two columns in the portico of the temple. When he had set up the column on the right, he called it by the name Jachin; likewise he raised the second column and called its name Booz.

[Note: “He called it by the name Jachin,” that is, “stability” … “and he called its name Booz,” that is, “in strength.” Two codices, the Royal and Corbeiensis no. 13, read these words within the text itself. We have placed them before the reader’s eyes so that it may be clear that many marginal scholia of this kind were transferred into the sacred text through the carelessness and error of scribes or correctors. MART.]

Above the tops of the columns he placed work in the form of a lily, and the work of the columns was completed.

He also made a cast-metal basin ten cubits from rim to rim, circular all around. Its height was five cubits, and a cord thirty cubits long encircled it.

Under its rim, carving surrounded it, encompassing the basin for ten cubits. There were two rows of cast, striated designs.

[Note: The same manuscript reads *historiarum*, which amounts to the same thing as *striarum*. In ancient books, *b* or *y* is commonly added to words beginning with *st*; Luca of Bruges is therefore mistaken when he thinks *histriatum* is the opposite of *striated*. It is also well known that a *stria* is a slightly projecting part of a column.]

It stood on twelve oxen: three faced north, three west, three south, and three east. The basin was above them, and all their hindquarters were turned inward.

The thickness of the basin’s side [the manuscript reads “the side”] was three inches. Its rim was like the rim of a cup and like the leaf of an open lily. It held two thousand baths.

He made ten bronze bases, each base four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “bronze” here. A little later it reads “width” instead of “height,” contrary to the Hebrew text.]

The construction of the bases was inlaid work, with carvings between the joints. Between the wreaths and garlands were lions, oxen, and cherubim; and likewise above, at the joints; and beneath were lions and oxen, like bronze straps hanging down.

Each base had four wheels and bronze axles, and beneath the basin, on its four sides, were cast supports facing one another. The opening of the basin was within, at the top of the headpiece; what appeared on the outside was one cubit, entirely round, and it also had a cubit and a half. At the corners of the columns were various carvings, and the spaces between the columns were square, not round.

The four wheels at the four corners of each base were attached beneath the base; each wheel was a cubit and a half high. The wheels were like those ordinarily made for a chariot, and their axles, spokes, rims, and hubs were all cast.

Those four supports, one at each corner of each base, were cast together with and attached to the base itself. At the top of the base was a rounded structure one and a half cubits in size, fashioned so that the basin could be placed upon it. It had its own carvings and various designs arising from itself [the manuscript reads “from itself” in the masculine].

He carved on the panels that were of bronze, and on the corners, cherubim, lions, and palm trees, as though in the likeness of a standing human being, so that they appeared to be not engraved but applied around the surface.

In this manner he made the ten bases, all from a single casting, with the same measurements and similar carvings.

He also made ten bronze basins. Each basin held forty baths and was four cubits in size; he placed one basin on each of the ten bases.

[Note: Again the same manuscript reads *aereos* for *aeneos*; more significantly, it reads “cubits” for “baths.”]

He placed five bases on the right side of the temple and five on the left. He placed the basin on the right side of the temple, toward the southeast [Hebrew: “toward the east, to the south”].

So Hiram [Hebrew: “Hirom”] made the pots, shovels, and bowls, and completed all the work of King Solomon in the temple [Hebrew: “in the house”] of the Lord.

He made the two columns and the two cords of the capitals above the columns [the manuscript reads “of the capitals”], and the two latticeworks to cover the two cords that were above the tops of the columns [Hebrew: “the two cords of the capitals”].

There were four hundred pomegranates [Note: The Verona manuscript mistakenly reads “forty.”] on the two latticeworks: two rows of pomegranates on each latticework, to cover the cords of the capitals that were above the tops of the columns.

He made ten bases and ten basins upon the bases, one basin on each base. He made one sea and twelve oxen beneath the sea.

The pots, shovels, and bowls—all these vessels [Hebrew: “all these vessels”] that Hiram made for King Solomon in the house of the Lord—were made of orichalcum. The king cast them in the plain [Hebrew omits this] of the Jordan, in clay soil, between Succoth and Zarethan.

Solomon placed all the vessels. Because their number was exceedingly great, the weight of the bronze could not be determined.

### [T. XIX]

Solomon made all the vessels in the house of the Lord: the golden altar and the table on which the bread of the Presence was to be placed, made of gold [Note: The Hebrew does not have the word “golden”; for this reason it was erased by the corrector of the Canon, who in the same verse also changes “of pure gold” to “of first gold.” But among the Hebrews “pure” and “first” have the same meaning when applied to metals. MART.]; the golden lampstands, five on the right and five on the left, opposite the inner sanctuary, of pure gold [Note: The same manuscript reads “first” instead of “pure,” and this too was replaced by another hand in Martianay’s Canon.]; like flowers of lilies, with golden lamps above; the golden tongs [Hebrew omits this], basins, forks, bowls, mortars, and censers, made of the purest gold.

The hinges of the doors of the inner house of the Holy of Holies and of the doors of the temple house were of gold.

Solomon completed all the work that King Solomon was doing in the house of the Lord.

[Note: The Verona manuscript, agreeing with the Vulgate and the Greek, omits “the king.”]

Then he brought in the things that David his father had consecrated: silver and gold and vessels, and placed them in the treasuries of the house of the Lord.

### [T. XX, Chapter VIII]

Then all the elders of Israel, the chiefs of the tribes, and the leaders of the ancestral families of the Israelites gathered before King Solomon in Jerusalem [Hebrew: “Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel, all the chiefs of the tribes, and the leaders of the ancestral families of the Israelites in Jerusalem, in order to bring”].

They were to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the City of David, that is, from Zion. All Israel assembled before King Solomon in the month Ethanim, on the festival day; that is, the seventh month.

All the elders of Israel came, and the priests carried the ark. They carried the ark of the Lord, the tent of meeting, and all the sacred vessels that were in the tent; the priests and Levites carried them.

King Solomon and the entire assembly of Israel that had gathered with him walked before the ark. They sacrificed sheep and oxen beyond counting or number.

The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord into its place, into the inner sanctuary of the temple [Hebrew: “house”], into the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim. The cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and covered the ark and its poles from above.

The poles projected, and their ends could be seen outside the sanctuary before the inner sanctuary; but they could not be seen farther outside. They have remained there to the present day.

In the ark there was nothing else except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed there at Horeb, when the Lord made the covenant with the Israelites as they came out of the land of Egypt.

[Note: Thus reads the Hebrew Canon of Truth together with the Colbertine, Anician, and our Corbeiensis manuscript no. 13. The Royal and San-Germain manuscript 3 read, as does our Vulgate, “there was nothing.” MART. The Verona manuscript reads “Horeb,” which is closer to the Hebrew.]

### [T. XXI]

When the priests had come out of the sanctuary, a mist [Hebrew: “a cloud”] filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand and minister because of the mist [Hebrew: “the cloud”]; for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord.

Then Solomon said: “The Lord said that he would dwell in the cloud. I have built a house for you to dwell in, a most firm throne for you forever.”

The king turned his face and blessed the entire assembly of Israel, for the whole assembly of Israel was standing.

And Solomon said:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David my father and fulfilled it with his hand,

[Note: The corrected Canon reads “and with his hand.” MART.]

saying: ‘From the day when I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I did not choose a city from all the tribes of Israel in which a house should be built and my name should be there; but I chose David to be over my people Israel.’

David my father desired to build a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel. But the Lord said to David my father: ‘Because you conceived in your heart the desire to build a house for my name, you did well to have this intention. Nevertheless, you shall not build the house for me, but your son, who will come forth from your loins, he shall build the house for my name.’

The Lord has confirmed his word that he spoke. I have taken the place of David my father and have sat upon the throne of Israel, as the Lord spoke, and I have built the house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.

I have appointed there a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the Lord that he made with our fathers when they came out of the land of Egypt [Hebrew: “when he brought them out”].”

Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord in the presence of the assembly of Israel [Hebrew: “before the whole assembly”]. He spread out his hands toward heaven and said:

“Lord God of Israel, there is none like you, God, in heaven above or on earth below, who keep covenant and mercy with your servants who walk before you with all their heart [the Vulgate reads “who walked”].

You have kept for your servant David my father what you spoke to him. You spoke with your mouth and fulfilled it with your hands [Hebrew: “You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand you made it; as on this day”], as this day proves.

Now therefore, Lord God of Israel, preserve for your servant David my father what you spoke to him, saying: ‘A man shall not fail to stand before me, one who sits upon the throne of Israel’—provided that your sons keep their way, walking before me as [Note: Together with the Vulgate, the Verona manuscript adds “you” here. It soon omits “Lord,” a name that the Hebrew text adds.] you walked in my sight.

And now, Lord God of Israel, let your words be confirmed that you spoke to your servant David my father.

[Note: Once again, in accordance with the Hebrew exemplar, the Verona manuscript omits the small words “to you.”]

But can it really be thought that God dwells upon the earth?

### [T. XXII]

If heaven and the highest heavens cannot contain you [Hebrew: “Behold, the heavens”], how much less this house that I have built?

Yet look upon the prayer and supplication of your servant, Lord my God. Hear the hymn and the prayer that your servant prays before you today, so that your eyes may be open over this house night and day—over the house of which you said, ‘My name shall be there’—that you may hear the prayer [Hebrew: “over the place of which you said, ‘My name shall be there,’ to hear the prayer”] that your servant prays to you in this place.

Hear the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, whatever they pray for in this place. Hear in the place of your dwelling, in heaven; and when you hear, be merciful.

If a man sins against his neighbor and takes an oath by which he becomes bound, and if he comes because of the oath before your altar, in your house [Hebrew: “this house”], hear in heaven. Act and judge your servants, condemning the wicked and bringing his way back upon his own head, while justifying the righteous and repaying him according to his righteousness.

If your people Israel flee from their enemies [Hebrew: “enemy”] because it will sin against you [Note: This manuscript, more closely following the Hebrew, has “because they will have sinned,” in the plural.], and, having repented and confessed your name, come and [Hebrew omits this] pray and entreat you in this house, hear in heaven. Forgive the sin of your people Israel and restore them to the land that you gave to their fathers.

If the heavens are shut and there is no rain because of their sins, and if they pray in this place, repent before your name [Hebrew: “and confessing your name”], and turn from their sins because of their affliction, hear them in heaven. Forgive the sins of your servants and of your people Israel, and show them the good way in which they should walk.

[Note: The Verona manuscript more correctly has the future “you will show,” with the Hebrew, “you will teach.”] Give rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as their inheritance.

If famine arises in the land, or pestilence, blighted air, mildew, locust, or rust, and if their enemy afflicts them by besieging their gates—whatever plague, whatever sickness, whatever devastation, and whatever curse may befall any person among your people Israel—if anyone recognizes the plague of his heart [Hebrew: “every prayer and supplication that may be made by any person among your people Israel, when each recognizes the plague of his heart”] and spreads out his hands in this house, hear in heaven, the place of your dwelling. Forgive and act, giving to each according to all his ways, as you see [the manuscript reads “as you see” in the participle] his heart—for you alone know the hearts of all human beings—so that they may fear you all the days that they live upon the face of the land that you gave to our fathers.

Moreover, when a foreigner who is not of your people Israel comes from a distant land because of your name—for your great name and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm will be heard of everywhere [Hebrew omits this]—when he comes and prays in this place [Hebrew: “in this house”], hear in heaven, the firmament of your dwelling place, and do everything for which the foreigner calls upon you. Thus all the peoples of the earth may learn to fear your name, as does your people Israel, and may know that your name has been invoked over this house that I have built.

If your people go out to battle against their enemies [Hebrew: “enemy”] by the way, wherever you send them, they will pray to you toward the direction of the city that you have chosen and toward the house that I have built for your name. Hear in heaven their prayer and supplication, and execute judgment for them.”

### [T. XXIII]

“But if they sin against you—for there is no human being who does not sin—and you become angry and deliver them to their enemies, and they are taken captive to the land of their enemies [Hebrew: “enemy”], whether far or near; and if, in the land of their captivity, they repent in their heart [Hebrew: “in the land of those who took them captive”], and, having turned back, entreat you in the land of their captivity, saying, ‘We have sinned, we have acted unjustly, we have behaved impiously’; and if they return to you with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their enemies to which they were taken captive [the Vulgate reads “will be taken captive”], and pray to you toward the direction of their land that you gave to their fathers, and of the city that you chose, and of the temple [Hebrew: “house”] that I built for your name:

Hear their prayers and supplications in heaven, the firmament of your throne, and execute judgment for them. Be merciful to your people who have sinned against you and to all their iniquities by which they have transgressed against you. Grant them mercy before those who took them captive, so that they may have compassion on them.

For they are your people and your inheritance, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt [Hebrew: “out of Egypt”], from the midst [the manuscript reads “from the house”] of the iron furnace.

Let your eyes be open to the supplication of your servant and of your people [the manuscript omits “your people”] Israel, and hear them in everything for which they call upon you.

For you separated them for yourself as an inheritance from all the peoples of the earth, as you spoke through Moses your servant [Hebrew: “through the hand of Moses your servant”], when you brought our fathers out of Egypt, Lord God.”

### [T. XXIV]

When Solomon had finished praying to the Lord this entire prayer and supplication, he rose from before the altar of the Lord, for he had fixed both knees upon the ground and had spread out his hands toward heaven.

He stood and blessed the entire assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying:

“Blessed is the Lord, who has given rest to his people Israel, according to everything that he spoke. Not one word has failed of all the good things that he spoke through Moses his servant [Hebrew: “through the hand of Moses his servant”].

May the Lord our God be with us as he was with our fathers, not abandoning us or rejecting us. May he incline our hearts toward himself, so that we may walk in all his ways and keep his commandments, his statutes [the manuscript omits “his”], and his judgments, whatever he commanded our fathers.

And may these words of mine, with which I have pleaded before the Lord, draw near to the Lord our God day and night, so that he may execute judgment for his servant and his people [the manuscript omits “his people”] Israel day by day.

May all the peoples of the earth know that the Lord himself is God, and that there is no other besides him.

May our heart also be perfect with the Lord our God [Hebrew: “May your heart be perfect with the Lord our God, for walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments”], so that we may walk in his statutes and keep his commandments, as on this day.

Then the king and all Israel with him sacrificed victims before the Lord. Solomon slaughtered as peace offerings to the Lord twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. The king and the Israelites dedicated the house of the Lord.

### [T. XXV]

On that day the king sanctified the middle of the court that was before the house of the Lord. For he offered there the burnt offering, the sacrifice, and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that stood before the Lord was too small and could not contain the burnt offering [the manuscript reads “burnt offerings”], the sacrifice, and the fat of the peace offerings.

At that time Solomon celebrated a great festival, and all Israel with him—a very great assembly—from the entrance of Hamath to the Wadi of Egypt, before the Lord our God, for seven days and seven days, that is, fourteen days.

### [T. XXXVI]

On the eighth day [the manuscript omits “and”] he dismissed the people. They blessed the king and departed to their tents, rejoicing and cheerful of heart over all the good things that the Lord had done for David his servant and for Israel his people.

[Column 0693B] [Chapter IX.] Now when Solomon had finished building the house of the Lord, the royal palace [Hebrew: “and the royal house”], and everything that he had desired and [Note: [Column 0693D] The Verona manuscript has *voverat* (“had vowed”), which I consider a copyist’s error; for the Hebrew has …] intended to make, the Lord appeared to him a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon. And the Lord said to him:

“I have heard your prayer and your supplication, which you have offered before me. I have sanctified this house, which you have built, so that I may place my name there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall be there always. You also, if you walk before me as your father walked, in integrity of heart and uprightness, and do everything that I have commanded you, and keep my statutes and judgments, I will establish [Hebrew: “make firm”] the throne of your kingdom over Israel forever, just as I promised David your father, saying: [Column 0693C] ‘A man of your descendants shall not be removed from the throne of Israel.’

“But if you and your sons turn away altogether from following me, neither keeping my commandments and ordinances [the Vulgate adds: “my”] that I have set before you, but go away, serve foreign gods, and worship them, I will remove Israel from the face of the land that I gave them; and the temple [Hebrew: “house”] that I have sanctified for my name I will cast away from my sight. [T. XXXVII.] Israel shall become a proverb and a byword among all peoples. And this house shall become an example: everyone who passes by it will be astonished and hiss, and will say, ‘Why has the Lord dealt thus with this land and this house?’ And they will answer: ‘Because they abandoned the Lord their God, who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and followed foreign gods, worshiped them, and served them [the Vulgate adds: “them”]; therefore the Lord has brought upon them all this evil.’”

When the twenty years had been completed after Solomon had built the two houses—that is, the house of the Lord and the royal palace—while Hiram, king of Tyre, supplied Solomon with cedar and fir timber and gold according to all that he needed, then King Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee. Hiram went out from Tyre to see the towns that Solomon had given him, but they did not please him. He said: “Are these the towns that you have given me, brother [Hebrew: “my brother”]?” And he called them the land of Chabul, as they are called to this day.

Hiram also sent King [Note: [Column 0693D] Here again, more correctly in agreement with the Hebrew, the same manuscript omits the name “Solomon.”] Solomon one hundred and twenty talents of gold.

This is the total of the expenditures that King Solomon made for building the house of the Lord, his own house, the Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, [Note: [Column 0693D] The ancient manuscripts read in this way; it was likewise found in the canon of the Hebrew truth before its correction. It now reads *Hazor* there, according to the pointing of the Hebrew text; yet not according to the present pronunciation of the letter …, which has a double aspiration and is called *Hheth* or *Cheth*, …, whence *Hhatsor* or *Chasor. MART.] and Ezer, and Megiddo, and Gezer.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, went up and captured Gezer, burned it with fire, killed the Canaanite who lived in the city, and gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon’s wife. So Solomon rebuilt Gezer, Lower Beth-horon, and Baalath, [Note: [Column 0693D] A letter has fallen out of the middle of this word—Daleth, if we are to trust the current copies of the Masoretic tradition, where the space that the letter Daleth would occupy is left blank in the printed editions, with the marginal note *Qere*, to indicate that it should be read …, *Tadmor*. The ancient manuscripts that we have examined all read within the text …, *Thamor*; but the Royal and Oratorian manuscripts cited above also give *Qere* in the margin. Our Pelissonaean manuscript has nothing apart from the pure reading …, *Thamor*. Thus it was written in the Hebrew copy of Saint Jerome, which very clearly proves the word *Palmyra* in the sacred text: for *Thamar* means Palmyra or palm. But the scholiast of the Canon had read in Hebrew codices …, *Thadmor* or *Tadmor*, according to his annotation added in the margin. MART.] and Palmyra [Hebrew: *Tadmor*] in the wilderness.

He fortified all the villages belonging to him that were unwalled [Hebrew: “does not have”], as well as the chariot cities and the cavalry cities, and everything that he desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout the land under his rule. [T. XXVIII.]

All the people who remained of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, who were not of the children of Israel—their descendants who remained in the land, whom the children of Israel had not been able to exterminate—Solomon made tributary to this day. But of the children of Israel Solomon appointed no one to forced labor; they were warriors, his servants, commanders, officers, and officials of chariots and horses [Hebrew: “cavalry”]. There were five hundred and fifty chief officials over all Solomon’s works, who had the people subject to them and commanded them in the assigned tasks.

Pharaoh’s daughter went up from the city of David to her house that Solomon had built for her [the Vulgate adds: “Solomon”]. Then he built the Millo.

King Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings three times each year on the altar that he had built for the Lord, and he burned incense before the Lord. Thus the temple [Hebrew: “house”] was completed. [Column 0694D] [T. XXIX.]

King Solomon also built a fleet at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth [Hebrew: “Elath”] on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom. Hiram sent his servants in that fleet—men who were sailors and knowledgeable about the sea—with Solomon’s servants. When they came to Ophir, they brought from there four hundred and twenty talents of gold to King Solomon.

[T. XXX, Chapter X.] The queen of Sheba also, having heard of Solomon’s fame in the name of the Lord, came to test him with riddles. Entering Jerusalem with a very large retinue and with riches, camels carrying spices, exceedingly great quantities of gold, and precious stones, she came to [Note: [Column 0695D] Again, in accordance with the Hebrew text, the Verona manuscript omits “the king.”] King Solomon. She spoke to him about everything that was in her heart, and Solomon explained to her all the words that she had proposed [Column 0695B]. There was no matter hidden from the king, so that he could not answer her [Note: [Column 0695D] The same manuscript reads *et non responderat* (“and he had not answered”); *responderet* (“could answer”) should be read.].

When the queen of Sheba saw all Solomon’s wisdom, the house that he had built, the food [Hebrew: “food”] of his table, the dwelling places of his servants, the order of his ministers, their clothing, his cupbearers, and his burnt offerings that he offered in the house of the Lord, she was utterly overwhelmed. She said to the king:

“The report that I heard in my land about your words and your wisdom is true. I did not believe those who told me until I came myself and saw with my own eyes and discovered that I had not even been told half of it. Your wisdom and your works are greater than the report that I heard. Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants, who stand before you continually and hear your wisdom. Blessed be the Lord your God, in whom you have found favor [the Vulgate: “with whom you have found favor”], who has set you upon the throne of Israel, because the Lord loved Israel forever and appointed you king to administer judgment and justice.”

So she gave the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold, a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. Never again were such quantities of spices brought as those that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.

(And Hiram’s fleet, which carried gold from Ophir, also brought from Ophir an exceedingly large quantity of *thyine* wood and precious stones. [Note: [Column 0695D] The same manuscript reads “pine wood, thyine wood.” Robert of Sorbonne, in his *Glosses on the Divine Books*, says concerning this passage: “The wood called *thiigna* is unknown, for another edition also has ‘pine wood.’” From this it may be suspected that a double interpretation has been rashly introduced here: the word *thyine* denotes yellow or fragrant wood, while the Hebrew word is *almugim*, which the Septuagint elsewhere translated as “pine,” and Saint Jerome himself followed them in the books of Chronicles.]) The king made from the thyine wood supports for the house of the Lord and for the royal palace, and lyres and harps for the singers. Such thyine wood had never again been brought or seen to the present day [the manuscript omits “seen”].)

King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she desired and requested from him, apart from what he had freely given her as a royal gift. She returned and went to her own land with her servants.

[T. XXXI.] The weight of gold that was brought [the Vulgate: “offered”] to Solomon each year was six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold, apart from what was brought [the manuscript: “offered”] by the men who were in charge of the revenues, by the merchants, by all those selling shields, and by all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land.

[Column 0696A] [T. XXXII.] King Solomon also made two hundred shields [Hebrew: “two hundred spears”] of pure gold; six hundred shekels of gold [Hebrew: “six hundred gold pieces”] were used for the plating of one shield. And three hundred smaller shields [Hebrew: “three hundred shields”] of refined gold; three hundred *minae* [“three mnae”] of gold covered one smaller shield. The king placed them in the house [Note: [Column 0696D] The Verona manuscript reads, more closely following the Hebrew, “forest.”] of the Forest of Lebanon.

King Solomon also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with exceedingly pure gold [Hebrew: “refined gold”]. It had six steps; the top of the throne was rounded at the back; two armrests were on either side holding the seat; and two [Hebrew: “does not have”] lions stood beside each armrest [Hebrew: “does not have”]. Twelve lion cubs stood upon the six steps, on either side. No such work had been made in any kingdom.

All the vessels from which King Solomon drank [Column 0696B] were of gold, and all the furnishings of the house of the Forest of Lebanon were of the purest gold [Hebrew: “gold”]. Silver was considered nothing and was not valued in Solomon’s days. For the king’s fleet went with Hiram’s fleet to Tarshish once every three years, bringing from there gold, silver, ivory tusks, monkeys, and peacocks.

So King Solomon was greater than all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. The whole earth desired to see Solomon’s face, to hear the wisdom that God had placed in his heart. Each person brought him gifts: vessels of gold and silver, garments and weapons of war, spices, horses, and mules, every year.

Solomon gathered chariots and cavalry, and he had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. [Column 0696C] He stationed them in fortified cities [Hebrew: “chariot cities”] and with the king in Jerusalem. He made silver as abundant in Jerusalem as stones, and he provided cedar in abundance like the sycamores that grow in the lowlands.

Horses were brought to Solomon from Egypt and from Kue. The king’s merchants bought them from Kue and brought them at a fixed price. A chariot came up from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver [Hebrew: “six hundred silver pieces”], and a horse for one hundred and fifty. In this way all the kings of the Hittites and of Syria sold horses.

[T. XXXIII, Chapter XI.] King Solomon loved many foreign women, including Pharaoh’s daughter and Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women [the manuscript: “Kittite”], from the nations concerning which the Lord had said to the children of Israel:

“You shall not enter into relations with them, nor shall they enter into relations with you, for they will certainly turn your hearts away so that you follow their gods.”

Solomon was joined to these women in exceedingly ardent love [Hebrew: “does not have”]. He had seven hundred wives who were queens and three hundred concubines; and the women turned his heart away [“his women, his heart”].

When he was already old, his heart was corrupted by the women so that he followed foreign gods. His heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as the heart of David his father had been. Solomon worshiped Astarte [Hebrew: “Astoreth, goddess of the Sidonians”], the goddess of the Sidonians, and Molech, the idol of the Ammonites [Hebrew: “here, Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites”]. [Note: [Column 0697D] Some manuscript copies add here: “and Chemosh, the god of the Moabites.” These words are not found in the Hebrew books, but only in the Septuagint, followed by the Syriac and Arabic versions. They appear to have been transferred here from the following verse, 33. Compare the two passages, but do not follow the disordered sequence of the verses in this chapter in the Septuagint. MART.]

Solomon did what was displeasing before the Lord [Hebrew: “Solomon did evil in the eyes of the Lord”], and he did not fully follow the Lord as David [the manuscript omits “David”] his father had done. Then Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the idol of Moab [Hebrew: “a high place for Chemosh, the idol of Moab”], on the mountain opposite Jerusalem, and for Molech, the idol [Hebrew: “defilement”] of the children of Ammon. [Column 0697B] He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.

Therefore the Lord was angry with Solomon, because his mind [“heart”] had turned away from the Lord God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice and had commanded him concerning this matter not to follow foreign gods; but he did not keep what the Lord had commanded him.

So the Lord said to Solomon:

“Because this has been with you, and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I commanded you, I will utterly tear your kingdom away and give it to your servant. Nevertheless, I will not do this in your days, for the sake of David your father. I will tear it from the hand of your son. Yet I will not take away the entire kingdom [“tear it away”]; I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of my servant David and Jerusalem, which I have chosen.”

[Column 0697C] [T. XXXIV.] The Lord raised up an adversary against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, of royal descent, who was in Edom. When David was in Edom and Joab, the commander of the army, had gone up to bury those who had been killed, and had killed every male in Edom—[Note: [Column 0697D] The Verona manuscript reads: “when they had killed every male,” more closely following the Hebrew.] for Joab and all Israel had remained there six months, until they had killed every male in Edom—Hadad himself and some Edomite men, servants of his father, fled in order to enter Egypt. Hadad was still a very young child.

When they had set out from Midian, they came to Paran, took men from Paran with them, and entered Egypt, going to Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He gave them a house, appointed food [Hebrew: “bread”] for them, and assigned them land.

Hadad found great favor before Pharaoh, so much so that Pharaoh gave him as a wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Queen Tahpenes. Tahpenes’s sister bore him a son, Genubath [the manuscript: “Genebat”], and Tahpenes raised him in Pharaoh’s house. Genubath lived in Pharaoh’s household among his sons.

When Hadad heard in Egypt that David had slept with his fathers and that Joab, the commander of the army, had died, he said to Pharaoh: “Send me away, so that I may go [Hebrew: “Send me, and I will go”] to my own land.”

Pharaoh said to him: “What do you lack with me, that you seek to go to your own land?”

He answered: “Nothing; but I beg [Note: [Column 0697D] The same manuscript does not add “you.” The Hebrew text omits not only that word but also the preceding verb “I beg.”] you to send me away [Hebrew: “send me”].”

[T. XXXV.] God also raised up against him as an adversary Rezon son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer, king of Zobah. He gathered men against him and became the leader of a band of raiders when David was killing them. They went to Damascus, lived there, and made him king in Damascus. He was an adversary of Israel throughout all Solomon’s days. This was the evil caused by Hadad: he hated Israel, and he reigned over Syria.

[T. XXXVI.] Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah, whose mother was named Zeruah, a widow, and who was a servant of Solomon, also raised his hand against the king.

The reason for his rebellion against him was that Solomon had built the Millo and had filled in the depression of the city of David his father. Jeroboam was a strong and capable man. When Solomon saw that the young man was of good character and industrious, he appointed him overseer of all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.

[T. XXXVII.] At that time Jeroboam went out from Jerusalem, and the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him on the road, covered with a new cloak. They were alone in the countryside. Ahijah seized the new cloak with which he was covered and tore it into twelve pieces. He said to Jeroboam:

“Take ten pieces for yourself, for thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘Behold, I will tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and give you ten tribes. One tribe shall remain to him, for the sake of my servant David and Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel, because he has abandoned [Note: [Column 0698D] The Verona manuscript, more correctly following the Hebrew codex, reads in the plural: “they abandoned me and worshiped.” It also reads *Ashtaroth* rather than *Astarte*, a reading likewise preferred by the Arabic version. Shortly afterward it has *Molech* rather than *Milcom*, though this is farther from the Hebrew. Finally, consistently with the preceding parallel clause, and again with the Hebrew, it reads in the plural: “and they did not walk in my ways, to do,” and so forth.] me and worshiped Astarte [Hebrew: “Astoreth”], the goddess of the Sidonians, and Chemosh, the god of Moab, and Milcom, the god of the children of Ammon, and has not walked in my ways to do what is right before me, nor kept my statutes and judgments, as David his father did.

“Yet I will not take the whole kingdom from his hand. I will make him a ruler throughout all the days of his life, for the sake of David my servant, whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes. But I will take the kingdom from the hand of his son and give you ten tribes. To his son I will give one tribe, so that a lamp may remain for David my servant always before me in Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen for my name to be there.

“But I will take you, and you shall reign over everything that your soul desires [Note: [Column 0699C] We have restored “your” from the Verona manuscript, in agreement with the Hebrew text … . All the other versions, including the Vulgate itself, read in the same way. No one, therefore, can now justly blame Martianus, who both arbitrarily changed the more correct reading and did not even mention this change to his reader.]. You shall be king over Israel. If you listen to everything that I command you, walk in my ways, do what is right before me [Hebrew: “in my eyes”], and keep my commandments and statutes as David my servant did, I will be with you. I will build you a faithful house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you. I will afflict the descendants of David because of this, though not forever.’”

Solomon therefore sought to kill Jeroboam. He arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak [the manuscript: “Susac”], king of Egypt, and remained in Egypt until Solomon’s death.

The rest of Solomon’s acts, and everything that he did, and his wisdom—behold, all are written in the book of the acts of Solomon.

[T. [Column 0699B] XXXVIII.] The days that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel were forty years. [Note: [Column 0699D] Reader, beware the opinion of a certain recent chronologer concerning the years of Solomon’s reign. It was not enough for this writer to disparage that outstanding monument of learning, Saint Jerome’s letter to Bishop Vitalis concerning Solomon and Ahaz; he also rose alone against the explicit and most evident testimony of all the Scriptures and against the unanimous agreement of the Greek and Latin Fathers, teaching that Solomon held the empire not merely for forty years but for a full eighty. More remarkably still, he claims that he alone has embraced this opinion, relying upon the unique authority of Josephus the Jew, whom he nevertheless says was mistaken in the years of the kings of Tyre and Israel. What more is there to say? He accuses Isaac Vossius, who hesitated over this difficulty, as does Vossius’s persistent defender, so that at last he might prove himself somewhat superior to his master in resolving ambiguities and riddles of Sacred Scripture. Let him cling, as he wishes, to Josephus and his Vossius; but let us be permitted to cling to the hagiographical writers, to the unanimous judgment of the holy Fathers, and to the greatest interpreter of the divine Scriptures, Jerome. The aforementioned chronologer considers Jerome so inconsistent that he claims Jerome, in the *Hebrew Traditions* on the Second Book of Chronicles, indicated forty years of Solomon’s reign before he transgressed, and another forty during which he retained the kingdom after abandoning the Lord. Yet he is as far from the true meaning as the author of the *Questions on the Hebrews* in Chronicles, who lived in the fourth century and flourished in the Church of God, is distant in time from the true Jerome, while the aforementioned writer lived in the age of Rabanus Maurus. See above, the third prologue. MART.]

Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father. His son Rehoboam [Hebrew: “Rehabam”] reigned in his place.

[T. XXXIX, Chapter XII.] Rehoboam came to Shechem, for all Israel had gathered there to make him king. Jeroboam son of Nebat, while still a fugitive in Egypt from the presence of King Solomon, heard of Solomon’s death and returned from Egypt. They sent for him and summoned him. Jeroboam came, and the whole assembly of Israel, and they spoke to Rehoboam, saying:

“Your father placed a very harsh yoke upon us. Therefore now lighten somewhat the rule [Hebrew: “servitude”] of your father, which was exceedingly harsh, and the heavy yoke that he placed upon us, and we will serve you.”

He said to them: “Go away until the third day, and return to me.”

[T. XL.] When the people had departed, King Rehoboam consulted the elders who had stood before his father Solomon [Note: [Column 0700D] The Verona manuscript has in one word: “while he was still alive.”] while he was alive. He said: “What counsel do you give me, so that I may answer this people?” [The manuscript omits “this.”]

They said to him: “If today you obey this people, serve them, yield to their request, and speak gentle words to them, they will be your servants always.”

[T. XLI.] But he abandoned the counsel of the elders that they had given him. [Column 0700A] He consulted the young men [Hebrew: “children”] who had grown up with him and stood before him, and said to them:

“What counsel do you give me, so that I may answer this people who have said to me, ‘Lighten the yoke that your father placed upon us’?”

The young men [Hebrew: “children”] who had grown up with him said to him:

“Thus you shall speak to this people who have said to you, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us.’ Thus you shall say to them: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s back [Hebrew: “loins”]. And now my father placed a heavy yoke upon you, but I will add to your yoke. My father scourged you with whips, but I will scourge you with scorpions.’”

Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam on the third day, as the king had said: “Return to me on the third day.” The king answered the people harshly, rejecting the counsel of the elders that they had given him, and spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men [Hebrew: “children”], saying:

“My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father scourged you with whips, but I will scourge you with scorpions.”

The king did not listen to the people, because the Lord had turned him aside, in order to establish his word that he had spoken through Ahijah [the manuscript: “Abijah”] the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

[T. XLII.] When all the people [Hebrew: “all Israel”] saw that the king was unwilling to listen to them, they answered him:

“What portion have we in David? What inheritance have we in the son of Jesse? [Note: [Column 0700D] The Verona manuscript omits *vade* (“go away”), which is also absent from the Hebrew through a feature of its language.] Go to your tents, Israel; now look after your own house, David.”

Israel went to its tents. But over the children of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned.

King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him, and he died. But King Rehoboam [Note: [Column 0700D] From such a nearly obsolete annotation we were unable to extract anything further; therefore we do not place much confidence here in our conjecture or reading. MART. [Column 0701D] The Verona manuscript reads in the singular, in agreement with the Hebrew: “the tribute.” The scholiast’s note that follows, its letters worn away by age, has been printed conjecturally by Martianus, who has warned us of this.] hurriedly [Hebrew: “reluctantly”] mounted his chariot and fled to Jerusalem. Israel withdrew from the house of David to the present day.

[T. XLIII.] When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent for him and summoned him. Having assembled the congregation, they made him king over all Israel. No one followed the house of David except the tribe of Judah alone.

[T. XLIV.] Rehoboam came to Jerusalem and gathered the entire house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin—one hundred and eighty thousand chosen men [Hebrew: “does not have”] of warriors—in order to fight against the house of Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam son of Solomon.

[T. XLV.] The word of God [the Vulgate: “of the Lord”] came to Shemaiah, the man of God:

“Say to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin and the rest of the people: ‘Thus says the Lord: You shall not go up, nor shall you fight against your brothers, the children of Israel. Let each man return to his house, for this word has come from me.’”

They obeyed the word of the Lord [Column 0701B] and returned from their journey, as the Lord had commanded them [Hebrew: “according to the word of the Lord”].

Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. From there he went out and built Penuel.

[T. XLVI.] Jeroboam said in his heart:

“Now the kingdom will return to the house of David if this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord in Jerusalem. The heart of this people will turn to their lord Rehoboam, king of Judah; they will kill me and return to him.”

After taking counsel, he made two golden calves and said to them:

“You shall no longer go up to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

He placed one in Bethel and the other in Dan. This became a sin, for the people went to worship the calf as far as Dan.

[T. XLVII.] He made shrines on the high places and appointed priests from the lowest of the people, who were not of the children of Levi. He established a solemn feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, in imitation of the feast that was celebrated in Judah. [Note: [Column 0701D] The same manuscript reads *celebratur* (“is celebrated”). The Hebrew phrase entirely omits this verb.] He went up to the altar that he had made in Bethel to sacrifice to the calves that he had fashioned, and he appointed priests of the high places that he had made in Bethel. He went up to the altar that he had built in Bethel on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, which he had devised from his own heart, and he held a feast for the children of Israel. He went up to the altar to burn incense [the manuscript: “so that incense might be burned”].

[T. XLVIII, Chapter XIII.] And behold, a man of God came from Judah to Bethel by the word of the Lord, while Jeroboam stood beside the altar and was throwing incense [the Vulgate: “making”]. He cried out against the altar by the word of the Lord and said:

“Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places who now burn incense upon you, and he shall burn human bones upon you.”

That day he gave a sign, saying:

“This shall be the sign that the Lord has spoken: Behold, the altar shall be split apart, and the ashes that are upon it shall be poured out.”

When the king heard the word of the man of God, who had cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar, saying: “Seize him.”

[T. XLIX.] His hand, which he had stretched out against him, withered, and he could not draw it back to himself. The altar also split apart, and the ashes were poured out from the altar, according to the sign that the man of God had foretold [Hebrew: “given”] by the word of the Lord.

The king said to the man of God:

“Entreat the face of the Lord your God and pray for me, so that my hand may be restored to me.”

The man of God entreated the face of the Lord, and the king’s hand was restored to him and became as it had been before.

[T. L.] The king said to the man of God:

“Come home with me and eat [the manuscript: “let us eat”], and I will give you gifts.”

The man of God answered the king:

“Even if you gave me half your house, I would not come with you, nor would I eat bread or drink water in this place. For thus I was commanded by the word of the Lord, who instructed me: ‘You shall not eat bread or drink water, nor shall you return by the road on which you came.’”

So he departed by another road and did not return by the way by which he had come to Bethel.

[T. LI.] A certain old prophet lived in Bethel. His son came to him [Note: [Column 0702D] The Vulgate reads: “his sons came and told him,” and so forth.] and told him all the deeds that the man of God had performed that day in Bethel, and the words that he had spoken to the king. They told their father, and their father said to them:

“By what road did he go?”

His sons showed him the road by which the man of God who had come from Judah had gone. He said to his sons:

“Saddle my donkey.”

When they had saddled it, he mounted and went after the man of God. He found him sitting beneath a terebinth and said to him:

“Are you the man of God who [the Vulgate omits “who”] came from Judah?” [Note: [Column 0702D] The Verona manuscript reads *venit* (“came”); shortly afterward, together with the Vulgate, it reads “He answered.” Both readings are farther from the Hebrew.]

He answered: “I am.”

He said to him: “Come home with me and eat bread.”

He said: “I cannot return or come with you. I shall not eat bread or drink water in this place, because the Lord [Hebrew: “does not have”] spoke to me by the word of the Lord, saying: ‘You shall not eat bread or drink water there, nor return by the road by which you came.’”

He said to him: “I too am a prophet like you, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the Lord, saying: ‘Bring him back with you to your house, so that he may eat bread and drink water.’”
