But he deceived him and brought him back with him. So he ate bread in his house and drank water. [Column 0702D]

[T. LII.] While they were sitting at table, the word of the Lord came to the prophet who had brought him back. He cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah:

“Thus says the Lord: Because you were disobedient to the mouth of the Lord and did not keep the command that the Lord your God gave you [the manuscript omits “you”], but returned and ate bread and drank water in the place concerning which he commanded you [the manuscript: “I commanded”] not to eat bread or drink water, your corpse shall not enter the tomb of your fathers.”

When he had eaten and drunk, the prophet who had brought him back saddled his donkey. When he had departed, a lion found him on the road and killed him. His corpse lay thrown upon the road, while the donkey stood beside him and the lion stood beside the corpse.

Some men passing by saw the corpse lying on the road and the lion standing beside the corpse. They came and announced it in the city where that old prophet lived.

When the prophet who had brought him back from the road heard this, he said:

“He is the man of God who was disobedient to the mouth of the Lord. The Lord handed him over to the lion, which crushed him and killed him according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken to him.”

He said to his sons:

“Saddle my donkey.”

When they had saddled it and he had gone, he found the corpse lying on the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside the corpse. The lion had not eaten the corpse and had not harmed the donkey.

So the prophet took the corpse of the man of God, placed it upon the donkey, and returned. The old prophet brought it into the city [Note: [Column 0703D] The Verona manuscript, more correctly following the Hebrew, reads in the genitive: “of the prophet,” so that they might mourn. The Vulgate differs from this reading only in having the singular, “that he might mourn.” Immediately afterward the same manuscript has *heu* once, in agreement with the Hebrew.] so that he might mourn for him.

He placed his corpse in his own tomb, and they mourned over him:

“Alas, alas [Hebrew: “Alas, my brother”], brother!”

When they had mourned [Hebrew: “buried”] him, he said to his sons:

“When I die, bury me in the tomb in which the man of God has been buried; place my bones beside his bones. For surely the word that he foretold [Hebrew: “called”] by the word of the Lord against the altar that is in Bethel and against all the shrines of the high places that are in the cities of Samaria will come to pass.”

[T. LIV.] [Column 0703C] After these words [Hebrew: “after this word”] Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way. On the contrary, he made priests of the high places from the lowest of the people; whoever wished to do so filled his hand and became a priest of the high places. Because of this the house of Jeroboam sinned, was overthrown, and was destroyed from the face of the earth.

[T. LV, Chapter XIV.] At that time Abijah, the son of Jeroboam, fell ill. Jeroboam said to his wife: “Arise, and disguise yourself, so that it will not be known that you are Jeroboam’s wife, and go to Shiloh, where the prophet Ahijah is, who told me that I would reign over this people. Take also in your hand ten loaves, a cake, and a jar of honey, and go to him; he will tell you what will happen to this child.” [Col. 0703D]

Jeroboam’s wife did as he had said. She arose, went to Shiloh, and came to Ahijah’s house. But he could not see, because his eyes had grown dim with age. The Lord said to Ahijah [Hebrew: here it has “Ahian”]: “Behold, Jeroboam’s wife is entering to consult you about her son, who is ill. You shall say such and such things to her.”

When she entered and pretended to be someone other than who she was, Ahijah heard the sound of her feet entering through the doorway and said: “Come in, wife of Jeroboam. [T. LVI.] Why do you pretend to be someone else? I, however, have been sent to you with a harsh message” [Hebrew does not have this]. “Go and say to Jeroboam: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel; because I tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you; and because you were not like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with his whole heart, doing what was pleasing in my sight [Hebrew: in my eyes]; but you have done evil beyond all who were before you, and have made for yourself foreign and molten gods, provoking me to anger, while you have cast me behind your body: therefore [Note: The same manuscript omits *behold*, which only some Greek copies and the Arabic version also omit.] behold, I will bring evil upon the house of Jeroboam, and I will cut off from Jeroboam everyone who urinates against the wall, the confined and the last in Israel [Hebrew: the confined and the abandoned]; and I will cleanse away the remnants of the house of Jeroboam, as dung is customarily cleansed away until it is entirely removed.

“Those of Jeroboam who die in the city, dogs shall eat; and those who die in the countryside, the birds of the sky shall devour, because the Lord has spoken. You, therefore, arise and go to your house; and as soon as your feet enter the city, the child will die [Hebrew: the little one]. [Note: According to the Hebrew, the Veronese manuscript has the plural *they will mourn and bury*.] All Israel will mourn for him and bury him. For he alone of Jeroboam’s family will be brought into a grave, because a good word concerning him has been found [Note: The same manuscript reads: “A good word concerning him has been found with the Lord God of Israel,” following the traces of the Hebrew text.] before the Lord God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam. [Note: The Veronese manuscript, more correctly, reads in the future tense, in agreement with the original texts and the Latin Vulgates.]

“Now the Lord will appoint a king over Israel who will cut off the house of Jeroboam on this day and at this time. And the Lord will strike Israel, as a reed is accustomed to sway in water, and he will uproot Israel from this good land that he gave to their fathers, and he will scatter them beyond the River, because they made sacred groves for themselves, provoking the Lord. And the Lord will hand Israel over because of the sins of Jeroboam, who sinned and caused Israel to sin.”

Then Jeroboam’s wife arose, departed, and came to Tirzah. As she was entering the threshold of the house, the child died, and they buried him. All Israel mourned for him, according to the word of the Lord that he spoke through his servant Ahijah the prophet [Hebrew: here it has “Ahian”].

[T. LVII.] The rest of the deeds of Jeroboam—how he fought and how he reigned—behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. The days during which Jeroboam reigned were twenty-two years [Hebrew does not have this], and he slept with his fathers; and Nadab his son reigned in his place.

[T. LVIII.] Now Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the Lord chose in order to place his name there, from among all the tribes of Israel. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite [manuscript: “Ammanithes”].

Judah did evil before the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], and they provoked him beyond all that their fathers had done through the sins that they committed. For they too built for themselves altars, pillars, and sacred groves [Hebrew: high places and standing stones] on every high hill and beneath every leafy tree. Moreover, there were effeminate men in the land [Hebrew: an effeminate man], and they committed all the abominations of the nations that the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.

[T. LIX.] In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, Shishak, king of Egypt, came up against Jerusalem and took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the royal palace; he seized everything, including the golden shields that Solomon had made. In their place King Rehoboam made bronze shields and entrusted them to the hands of the commanders of the shield-bearers and of those who kept watch before the doorway of the king’s house. Whenever the king entered the house of the Lord, those whose office was to go before him carried them; afterward they returned them to the armory of the shield-bearers.

The rest of the deeds of Rehoboam and all that he did—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles [Vulgate: Book of the Deeds] of the Kings of Judah? There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout all their days. Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of David. [T. LX.] His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite, and Abijah [Hebrew: Abijam] his son reigned in his place.

[Col. 0705C] [Chapter XV.] In the eighteenth year of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Abijam reigned over Judah. He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah, the daughter of Absalom. [Note: The pseudo-Hieronymus, in his *Hebrew Questions on II Chronicles*, warns that this was not David’s son: “This is not,” he says, “Absalom the son of David, but another, as is demonstrated in the Book of Kings.” He paid attention to this passage because, in the gloss according to the Hebrew, the name is Abishalom, not Absalom. MART. — The same manuscript here and below has *Abessalon*, as do the Vulgates. The Hebrew text itself has the reading noted by the scholiast. Indeed, although Absalom and Abessalom are the same name, as is clear from II Chronicles 2:21, it formerly seemed to the sons of the critics that a different Absalom from David’s son was intended here. Josephus considers it more probable that Maacah was a granddaughter born to him from Tamar, the daughter of Absalom, and that she is called his daughter *καταχρηστικῶς*—loosely or improperly.]

He walked in all the sins of his father, which his father had committed before him, and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, like the heart of David his father. Nevertheless, for David’s sake the Lord his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, raising up his son after him and establishing Jerusalem, because David had done what was right in the eyes of the Lord and had not turned aside from anything that he had commanded him throughout all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.

Yet there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout all the time of his life [Hebrew: all the days of his life]. The rest of the deeds of Abijah and all that he did—are these not written in the Book of the Chronicles [Col. 0705D] of the Kings of Judah? There was also warfare between Abijah and Jeroboam [the manuscript and the Vulgate omit “between”].

[T. LXI.] Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David; and Asa his son reigned in his place.

In the twentieth year of Jeroboam, king of Israel, Asa became king of Judah, and he reigned for forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah, the daughter of Absalom [Hebrew: Abishalom].

[T. LXII.] Asa did what was right before the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], like David his father. He removed the effeminate men from the land and cleansed away all the filth of the idols [Hebrew does not have this] that his fathers had made. Moreover, he removed his mother Maacah, so that she would not be chief in the rites of Priapus; and in her place, which she had consecrated, he overthrew her cave, smashed the most disgraceful image, and burned it at the torrent Kidron. Yet he did not remove the high places.

Nevertheless, Asa’s heart was perfect with [manuscript: before] the Lord throughout all his days. He brought into the house of the Lord the things that his father had consecrated and vowed: silver, gold, and vessels. There was war between Asa and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout all their days.

Baasha, king of Israel, came up against Judah and built Ramah, so that no one could go out or enter from the territory of Asa, king of Judah.

[T. LXIII.] Asa therefore took all the silver and gold that remained in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and in the treasuries of the royal palace, placed it in the hands of his servants, and sent it to Ben-hadad, the son of Tabremmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who lived in Damascus. He said:

“There is a covenant between me and you and between my father and your father. Therefore I have sent you gifts of silver and gold, and I ask you to come and annul the covenant that you have with Baasha, king of Israel, so that he may withdraw from me.”

Ben-hadad consented to King Asa and sent the commanders of his army against the cities of Israel. They struck Aijon, Dan, Abel-beth-Maacah, and all Chinneroth [manuscript: Ceneroth], that is, the whole land of Naphtali.

When Baasha heard this, he ceased building Ramah and returned to Tirzah. King Asa sent a proclamation throughout all Judah [Note: The Veronese manuscript has the word “saying,” in accordance with the Hebrew text, and shortly afterward omits the preposition *de* (“of/from”).] saying: “Let no one be excused.” They took away the stones from Ramah and the timber with which Baasha had built it. King Asa built Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah with them.

The rest of all the deeds of Asa, all his might, everything that he did, and the cities that he built—are these not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? Nevertheless, in the time of his old age his feet became diseased. He slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of David his father. [Col. 0706D] Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.

[T. LXIV.] Now Nadab, the son of Jeroboam, reigned over Israel in the second year of Asa, king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel for two years. He did what was evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes], and walked in the ways of his father and in his sins [manuscript: “in his sin,” Col. 0707A], by which he had caused Israel to sin.

Baasha, the son of Ahijah, from the house of Issachar, conspired against him and struck him at Gibbethon, which is a city of the Philistines, while Nadab and all Israel were besieging Gibbethon.

[T. LXV.] Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa, king of Judah, and reigned in his place. When he had become king, he struck the entire house of Jeroboam; he did not leave even one living person of his offspring [Hebrew: of Jeroboam], until he had destroyed him, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through his servant Ahijah the Shilonite, because of the sins of Jeroboam that he had committed and by which he had caused Israel to sin, and because of the offense by which he had provoked the Lord God of Israel.

The rest of the deeds of Nadab and all that he did—are these not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? There was war between Asa and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout all their days.

In the third year of Asa, king of Judah, Baasha, the son of Ahijah, reigned over all Israel at Tirzah for twenty-four years. He did evil before the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], and walked in the way [manuscript: ways] of Jeroboam and in his sins, by which he had caused Israel to sin.

[T. LXVI, Chapter XVI.] The word of the Lord came to Jehu, the son of Hanani, against Baasha [manuscript: Baasa], saying:

“Because I exalted you from the dust and appointed you leader over my people Israel, but you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and caused my people Israel to sin, provoking me through their sins, behold, I will sweep away the posterity [literally, the rear] of Baasha and the posterity of his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat.

“Whoever belonging to Baasha dies in the city, dogs shall eat; and whoever belonging to him dies in the countryside [Hebrew: in the field], the birds of the sky shall eat.”

The rest of the deeds of Baasha, everything that he did, and his battles [Hebrew: his might]—are these not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

[T. LXVII.] Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried at Tirzah; and Ela his son reigned in his place.

When the word of the Lord had come through Jehu the son of Hanani the prophet against Baasha, against his house, and against all the evil that he had done before the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], provoking him by the works of his hands, so that he might become like the house of Jeroboam, for this reason he killed [Col. 0708A] him [Hebrew: for which reason he had killed him], [Note: These are the words of a glossator, not of the translator: the matter itself clearly indicates that they mean “that is, Jehu the son of Hanani, the prophet.” They are absent not only from the Hebrew archetype but also from the Greek and from the other versions, and since the Latin books alone retain them, the purity of the Veronese manuscript—by far the most excellent of all—is certainly the more highly to be valued. Along with many other additions to the sacred text noted above, it wholly rejects and does not know this one, although we know that Estius was once acquainted with other manuscripts that lacked it. Moreover, we know that the matter itself is viewed unfavorably by very learned critics and that this killing of the prophet Jehu appears least credible. For they say that under Jehoshaphat, who reigned after Baasha, this same prophet Jehu the son of Hanani is recorded in II Chronicles 19:2 as having been sent to rebuke that ruler because he had aided the impious Ahab. As for the words “for this reason he killed him,” they refer either to God, who punished Baasha with death for all his crimes, or to Baasha himself, who killed Nadab, the son of Jeroboam, and destroyed his entire family in order to seize the kingdom. However the matter may stand, it is certainly surprising that Martianay did not notice this addition, nor the “Hebrew” cited by the scholiast, who carefully inserts many exceedingly slight and almost wholly insignificant variant readings from the Hebrew. Unless, perhaps, it must be supposed of him that this addition was not present in the Latin exemplar to which he first attached these scholia.] that is, Jehu the son of Hanani, the prophet.

In the twenty-sixth year of Asa, king of Judah, Ela the son of Baasha reigned over Israel at Tirzah for two years. His servant Zimri, commander of half the cavalry [Hebrew: chariots], rebelled against him. Ela was at Tirzah, drinking and intoxicated, in the house of Arza, the prefect of Tirzah.

Zimri attacked him, struck him, and killed him in the twenty-seventh year of Asa, king of Judah, and reigned in his place.

[T. LXVIII.] When he had become king and had sat upon his throne, he struck the entire house of Baasha and left of him [Vulgate: “of her”] no one who urinated against the wall, nor his relatives or friends. Zimri destroyed the entire house of Baasha, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken to Baasha through the prophet Jehu, and because of all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Ela his son, by which they had sinned and caused Israel to sin, provoking the Lord God of Israel through their vanities.

The rest of the deeds of Ela and all that he did—are these not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

In the twenty-seventh year of Asa, king of Judah, Zimri reigned for seven days at Tirzah. Meanwhile, the army was besieging Gibbethon, a city of the Philistines.

[T. LXIX.] When all Israel heard that Zimri had rebelled and killed the king, they made Omri king for themselves. He was the commander of the army over Israel at that time, in the camp.

Omri therefore went up, and all Israel with him, from Gibbethon, and they besieged Tirzah. When Zimri saw that the city was about to be captured, he entered the palace and burned the royal house over himself. He died in his sins, which he had committed by doing evil before the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], walking in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin by which he had caused Israel to sin.

The rest of the deeds of Zimri, his conspiracies, and his tyranny—are these not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

Then the people of Israel were divided into two parties. Half of the people followed Tibni, the son of Ginath [manuscript: Geneth], in order to make him king; the other half followed Omri. The people who were with Omri prevailed over the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath. Tibni died, and Omri reigned.

[T. LXX.] In the thirty-first year of Asa, king of Judah, Omri reigned over Israel for twelve years; he reigned at Tirzah for six years. He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver. He built upon it and called the name of the city that he had built [Note: “By the name Shemer,” that is, “the hill of the Lord,” or “the hill of Samaria.” We found this ignorant gloss inserted into the sacred text of the manuscript Royal Codex. I considered it worthwhile to note it here, so that everyone may know that many glosses of this kind were introduced into the Greek and Latin biblical texts in ancient times through the ignorance and recklessness of copyists, although the authors of the scholia had placed them in the margins of books for the instruction of readers. MART.] by the name of Shemer, “the hill of the Lord,” of Samaria.

Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], and acted wickedly beyond all who had been before him. He walked in every way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat and in his sins, by which he had caused Israel to sin, provoking the Lord God of Israel through his vanities.

The rest of the deeds of Omri and his battles [Hebrew: his might] that he waged—are these not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

[T. LXXI.] Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria; and Ahab his son reigned in his place.

Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel in the thirty-eighth year of Asa, king of Judah. Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria for twenty-two years [Note: We still do not know where our scholiast obtained the claim that Ahab, or Achab, reigned for twenty-four years in Samaria. In the Polyglots, all the witnesses agree on the number twenty-two. Three Hebrew manuscripts that we compared with the printed editions likewise report twenty-two years. Finally, the chronological tables among the historians differ in no respect concerning the years of Ahab’s reign. Thus we remain uncertain, lest, by charging the very diligent scholiast with a lapse of memory, we rashly criticize a variant reading that may perhaps have existed in some ancient Hebrew manuscripts. MART. — From this passage too it may be inferred that the scholiast is citing not the Hebrew archetype but some Latin copy. Yet not only the Hebrew but also all the other surviving books assign only twenty-two years of reign to Ahab.] [Hebrew: twenty-four years].

Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord, beyond all who had been before him. It was not enough for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat; moreover, he took as his wife Jezebel [Hebrew: Isabel], the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians. [Note: Thus the corrected Canon reads. All the other manuscripts have *Methhaal* or *Methabaal*, certainly through an easy error caused by the *m* immediately preceding in the word *filiam* (“daughter”). Who does not know that copyists have hundreds and thousands of times joined the letters of preceding words to the words that follow? MART. — The Veronese manuscript has *Methbaal*, as Martianay found in most of the others, through the obvious error of Latin scribes, who double the final *m* of the preceding word *filiam* and transfer it to the following word.]

He went and served Baal and worshiped him. He set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built in Samaria, and he planted a sacred grove. Ahab did still more in his work, provoking the Lord God of Israel beyond all the kings of Israel who had been before him.

In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundations in Abiram his firstborn [Hebrew: his firstborn son], and set up its gates in Segub, his youngest [Hebrew: his youngest son], according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through Joshua the son of Nun.

[T. LXX, Chapter XVII.] Elijah the Tishbite [Hebrew: the sojourner], from the inhabitants [Hebrew: from the sojourners] of Gilead, said to Ahab: “As the Lord God of Israel lives, before whose presence I stand [Hebrew: stood], during these years there shall be neither dew nor rain except at my word.”

The word of the Lord came to him, saying: “Go away from here, turn eastward, and hide in the brook Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan. There you shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”

He went and did according to the word of the Lord. When he had gone, he sat by the brook Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan.

[T. LXXIII.] The ravens brought him bread and meat [the manuscript omits “to him”] in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook. After some days the brook dried up, for there had been no rain upon the land.

Then the word of the Lord came to him, saying: “Arise and go to Zarephath [Hebrew: Sarephatha] of the Sidonians, and remain there. For I have commanded a widow woman there to feed you.”

He arose and went to Zarephath. When he came to the gate of the city, a widow woman appeared to him gathering sticks. He called her and said [Note: The Veronese manuscript omits “to her,” which is also absent from the Hebrew text]: “Give me a little water in a vessel, so that I may drink.”

As she was going to fetch it, he called after her, saying: “Bring me, I beg you, also a morsel of bread in your hand.”

She replied: “As the Lord your God lives, I have no bread, except as much flour as a handful can contain in a jar, and a little oil in a flask. Behold, I am gathering two sticks [Col. 0710B], so that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, so that we may eat and die.”

[T. LXXIV.] Elijah said to her: “Do not be afraid, but go and do as you have said. Nevertheless, first make me from that little flour a small cake baked under the ashes, and bring it to me; afterward you shall make something for yourself and your son. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: The jar of flour shall not fail, and the flask of oil shall not diminish until the day on which the Lord gives rain upon the face of the earth.”

She went and did according to the word of Elijah. He, the woman, and her household ate; and from that day the jar of flour did not fail [Hebrew: “and her household day by day; the jar of flour…”], nor did the flask of oil diminish, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through Elijah.

[T. LXXV.] After these words [the Vulgate omits “words”], the son of the woman, the mistress of the household, fell ill, and his illness was exceedingly severe [the manuscript and the Vulgate omit “his”; the Vulgate has “very severe” instead of “exceedingly severe”], so that no breath remained in him.

She said to Elijah: “What have I to do with you, man of God? You came to me so that my iniquities might be delayed and that you might kill my son.”

He said to her [the Vulgate adds “Elijah”]: “Give me your son.” He took him from her lap, carried him up to the upper room where he lived, and laid him upon his bed [manuscript: “his couch”].

He cried to the Lord and said: “My Lord God, have you also afflicted the widow with whom I am being sustained in some way [Note: The Veronese manuscript has the slightly corrupt reading *huccumque*, which I would prefer to understand as *hucusque* (“until now”), not *utcumque* (“in some way”). Although nothing in the Hebrew corresponds precisely to either word, the former agrees better with the sacred text and is supported by some translator of the Greek Hexapla, who has ἔτι, “still” or “up to this point.” A later copyist corrected the manuscript to *utcumque*.] so that you might kill her son?”

He stretched himself over the child and measured himself upon the child three times. He cried to the Lord and said: “My Lord God, I beg you, let the soul of this child [Hebrew: little one] return into his inward parts.”

The Lord heard Elijah’s voice, and the soul of the child [Hebrew: little one] returned within him, and he revived. Elijah took the child [Hebrew: little one], brought him down from the upper room to the lower part of the house, handed him to his mother, and said to her: “Behold, your son lives” [Hebrew: “See, your son lives”].

The woman said to Elijah: “Now by this I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true” [Hebrew does not have this].

(T. LXXVI, Chapter XVIII.) After many days, the word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year, saying: [Col. 0711B] “Go and show yourself to Ahab, so that I may give rain upon the face of the earth.”

Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. There was a severe famine in Samaria. Ahab called Obadiah, the steward of his household. Obadiah feared the Lord greatly. For when Jezebel [Hebrew: Isabel] was killing the prophets of the Lord, he took one hundred prophets and hid them by fifties in caves [Note: The same manuscript, in agreement with the Hebrew, has the singular “in a cave”; the Vulgates have “by fifties” twice], and fed them with bread and water.

Ahab said to Obadiah: “Go through the land to all the springs of water and to every valley, if perhaps we can find grass and preserve the horses and mules [Hebrew: horse and mule], so that the animals may not perish completely.”

They divided the regions [Hebrew: the land] between themselves in order to pass through them [Hebrew: it]. Ahab went by one road, and Obadiah went separately by another [Hebrew: alone by one road, and Obadiah separately and alone by another].

[T. LXXVI.] When Obadiah was on the road, Elijah met him. When he recognized him, he fell on his face and said: “Are you my lord Elijah?”

He answered him: “I am. Go and tell your lord: ‘Elijah is here.’”

He said: “What have I done wrong, that you are handing your servant over to the hand of Ahab, so that he may kill me? As the Lord your God lives [the Vulgate adds “because”], there is no nation or kingdom to which my lord has not sent to search for you. When all replied, ‘He is not here,’ he made each kingdom and nation swear an oath, because you could nowhere be found.

“And now you say to me: ‘Go and tell your lord: Elijah is here.’ When I leave you, the Spirit of the Lord will carry you to a place that I do not know. I shall go in and report to Ahab, and when he does not find you [Note: The Veronese manuscript has: “and he will not find you, and he will kill me”], he will kill me. Yet your servant has feared the Lord from his infancy.

“Has it not been reported to you, my lord, what I did when Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord—how I hid one hundred of the prophets of the Lord, by fifties in caves, and fed them with bread and water? And now you say: ‘Go and tell your lord: Elijah is here,’ so that he may kill me?”

Elijah said: “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whose face I stand [Hebrew: stood], today I will appear to him.”

Obadiah went to meet Ahab and told him. Ahab came to meet Elijah.

[T. LXXVIII.] When he saw him, he said: “Are you the one who troubles [Hebrew: troubling] Israel?”

He answered: “I have not troubled [the Vulgate adds “I”] Israel; but you and your father’s house have, because you abandoned the commandments of the Lord. [Note: The same manuscript adds “of your God,” which is not in the present Hebrew text. Nevertheless, the Septuagint translators seem once to have read something similar, since they render it τὸν Κύριον Θεὸν ὑμῶν, “the Lord your God.”] You followed the Baals.

“Nevertheless, now send and gather all Israel to me on Mount Carmel, and the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the sacred groves, who eat at Jezebel’s table.”

Ahab sent word to all the Israelites and gathered the prophets on Mount Carmel.

[T. XXIX.] Elijah approached all the people and said: “How long will you limp between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal is God, follow him.”

The people did not answer him a word.

Elijah said again to the people: “I alone have remained a prophet of the Lord, while the prophets of Baal number four hundred and fifty men. Let two bulls be given to us. Let them choose one bull for themselves, cut it into pieces, and place it upon the wood, but let them not put fire beneath it. I will prepare the other bull and place it upon the wood, but I will not put fire beneath it.

“Invoke the names of your gods [Hebrew: in the name of your gods], and I will invoke the name of the Lord [the Vulgate adds “my”]. The god who answers by fire—he shall be God.”

All the people answered: “Excellent proposal” [Hebrew: “A good word”].

Elijah said to the prophets of Baal: “Choose one bull for yourselves and prepare it first, because you are more numerous. Invoke the names of your gods [Hebrew: in the name of your gods], but do not put fire beneath it.”

When they had taken the bull that he had given them [Note: Again the Veronese manuscript has more, adding here the word “one”; we do not know from what text it derived this word], they prepared it. They invoked the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying: “Baal, hear us!”

There was neither voice nor anyone who answered. They leaped around the altar that they had made.

When it was already noon, Elijah mocked them, saying: “Cry out with a louder voice. For he is a god, and perhaps he is speaking, or is staying in an inn, or is on a journey, or perhaps he is certainly sleeping, so that he may be awakened.”

They cried out with a loud voice and cut themselves with knives and spears according to their custom, until they were covered with blood.

After midday had passed, while they were prophesying and the time had come when the sacrifice is customarily offered, there was no voice heard, no one answered, and no one paid attention to them as they prayed.

Elijah said to all the people: “Come to me.”

When the people approached him, he repaired the altar of the Lord that had been destroyed. He took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the Lord came, saying: “Israel shall be your name.”

He built an altar from the stones in the name of the Lord. He made a channel around the altar, about the size of two furrows, and arranged the wood. He divided the bull into its limbs, placed it upon the wood, and said: “Fill four jars with water and pour it over the burnt offering and over the wood.”

Again he said: “Do this a second time.”

When they had done it a second time, he said: “Do the same thing a third time.”

They did it a third time, and the water ran around the altar, and the channel was filled with water.

When it was already the time for the burnt offering to be presented, the prophet Elijah approached and said: “Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, show today that you are God in Israel [Hebrew: in Israel], that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things according to your command [Hebrew: word]. Hear me, Lord, hear me, so that this people may learn that you are the Lord God, and that you have turned their heart back again [Hebrew: backward].”

Then the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and even the dust, and it licked up the water that was in the channel.

[T. LXXX.] When all the people saw this, they fell on their faces and said: “The Lord himself is God! The Lord himself is God!”

Elijah said to them: “Seize the prophets of Baal, and let not one of them escape [manuscript: flee].”

When they had seized them, Elijah led them down to the brook Kishon and killed them there.

Elijah said to Ahab: “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of abundant rain.”

[T. LXXXI.] Ahab went up to eat and drink, but Elijah went up to the summit of Carmel. He bowed down to the ground, placed his face between his knees, and said to his servant: “Go up and look toward the sea.”

When he had gone up and looked, he said: “There is nothing.”

Again he said to him: “Return seven times.”

On the seventh occasion, behold, a small cloud, like a man’s footprint [Hebrew: a man’s palm], was rising from the sea.

He said: “Go up and tell Ahab: ‘Harness [the Vulgate adds: your chariot] and go down, lest the rain overtake you.’”

While he turned this way and that, behold, the heavens grew dark with clouds [Hebrew: clouds], wind arose, and a great rain fell.

Ahab mounted and went to Jezreel. The hand of the Lord came upon Elijah, and, girding his loins, he ran before Ahab until he came to Jezreel.

### Chapter XIX

Ahab reported to Jezebel everything that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword. Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying: “May the gods do this to me, and add this also, unless by this hour tomorrow I have made your life like the life of one of them.” [T. LXXXII.]

So Elijah was afraid, and, rising, went wherever his inclination carried him. He came to Beersheba [Hebrew: “Elijah was afraid … and rising … and he came to Beersheba”] of Judah, left his servant there, and went on into the wilderness, a day’s journey. When he had arrived and sat beneath a single broom tree, he asked that he might die, and said: “It is enough for me, Lord; take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.”

He threw himself down and fell asleep beneath the shade of the broom tree [Hebrew: “beneath a single broom tree”]. And behold, an angel [Note: More correctly, the Veronese manuscript omits “of the Lord”; that name is not added in the Hebrew.] of the Lord touched him and said: “Rise and eat.” He looked, and behold, at his head was a cake baked under ashes and a vessel of water. So he ate and drank, and again fell asleep. The angel of the Lord returned a second time, touched him, and said to him: “Rise, eat, for a great journey remains before you.” [T. LXXXIII.]

When he had risen, he ate and drank, and walked in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights, as far as Horeb, the mountain of God. When he had arrived there [Col. 0714B], he remained in a cave. And behold, the word of the Lord came to him, and he said: “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He answered: “I have been exceedingly zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have abandoned your covenant [Note: The same manuscript has “the covenant of the Lord,” which is farther from the Hebrew.], demolished your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone have been left, and they are seeking my life to take it away.”

And he said to him: “Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord.” And behold, the Lord passes by, and a great and mighty wind overturns mountains and shattered rocks before the Lord. The Lord was not in the wind. And after the wind, an earthquake: the Lord was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake, fire: the Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze.

When Elijah heard this, he covered his face with his cloak, went out, and stood at the entrance of the cave. And behold, a voice came to him, saying: “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He answered: “I have been exceedingly zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have abandoned your covenant. They have demolished your altars and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone have been left, and they are seeking my life to take it away.” [T. XXXIV.]

And the Lord said to him: “Go and return on your way [Note: The corrected Canon now reads “through the wilderness of Damascus”; formerly it read as we published it, following the evidence of other manuscript copies. MART.] through the wilderness to Damascus. When you arrive [the Vulgate adds: “there”], you shall anoint Hazael as king over Syria; and Jehu son of Nimshi you shall anoint as king over Israel; and Elisha son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, you shall anoint as prophet in your place.

And whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall kill. [Col. 0714D] And I shall leave seven thousand in Israel for myself [Note: This is read word for word in the Hebrew, in our Latin Canon, and in many very ancient manuscripts of Jerome’s version—for example, in the first hand of the Royal manuscript, and in the Corbeiensis manuscripts 11 and 13, and others. The Vulgate has “seven thousand men whose knees have not …” MART.].—all the knees that have not bent to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him [Hebrew: “and every mouth that has not kissed him,”] kissing the hand.”

[T. LXXXV.] So he departed from there [the Vulgate adds: “Elijah”] and found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, and he himself was one of the twelve plowmen. When Elijah came to him, he threw his cloak over him.

Immediately he left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and said: “Let me kiss, I beg you [the manuscript adds: “you”], my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.”

He said to him: “Go and return, for what was mine I have done for you.”

When he had returned from him, he took a yoke of oxen, slaughtered them, cooked the meat with the plow’s wood [Hebrew: “in the vessels of the oxen”], and gave it to the people, who ate. Then he arose, departed, followed Elijah, and ministered to him. [T. LXXXVI.]

### Chapter XX

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered his entire army, together with thirty-two kings, horses, and chariots. He went up and fought against Samaria, and besieged it. Sending messengers to Ahab king of Israel in the city, he said: “Thus says Ben-hadad: Your silver and your gold are mine [Col. 0715B], and your wives and your best sons are mine.”

The king of Israel answered: “According to your word, my lord the king, I am yours, and all that I have.”

The messengers returned and said: “Thus says Ben-hadad, who sent us to you: You shall give me your silver, your gold, your wives, and your sons. Tomorrow at this same hour I shall send my servants to you. They will search your house and the houses of your servants, and whatever pleases them they will place in their hands and carry away.” [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads the plural “houses,” in agreement with the Hebrew.]

The king of Israel summoned all the elders of the land and said: “Take note and see that he is plotting against us. He sent to me for my wives, my sons, my silver, and my gold, and I did not refuse.”

All the elders and all the people said to him: “Do not listen to him or consent to him” [Hebrew: absent].

So he answered Ben-hadad’s messengers: “Tell my lord the king: Everything for which you first sent to your servant I will do; but I cannot do this thing.” The messengers returned and reported this to him.

He sent back word and said: “May the gods do this to me and add this also, if the dust of Samaria will suffice by handfuls for all the people who follow me” [the manuscript reads: “who follow”].

The king of Israel answered and said: “Tell him [Hebrew: absent]: ‘Let not the one who girds himself boast as the one who ungirds himself.’”

When he heard this word [the Vulgate adds: “Ben-hadad”], he was drinking with the kings in the shelters, and he said to his servants: “Surround the city.” And they surrounded it. [T. LXXXVII.]

And behold, a certain prophet approached Ahab king of Israel and said to him: “Thus says the Lord: Surely you have seen this enormous multitude? Behold, I shall deliver it into your hand today, so that you may know that I am the Lord.”

Ahab said: “By whom?”

He said to him: “Thus says the Lord: By the attendants of the governors of the provinces” [Hebrew: “by the young men”].

He said: “Who shall begin the battle?”

He answered: “You.”

So he reviewed the attendants of the governors of the provinces and found their number to be two hundred and thirty-two. After them he reviewed the people, all the Israelites: seven thousand. And they went out at noon.

Ben-hadad was drinking drunk in his shelter [Hebrew: “in the shelters”], together with the thirty-two kings who had come to assist him. The attendants of the governors of the provinces went out in the front rank [Hebrew: “in the first rank”].

Ben-hadad sent men who reported to him, saying: “Men have come out of Samaria.”

He said: “Whether they have come out for peace, seize them alive; whether they have come out to fight, seize them alive.”

So the attendants of the governors of the provinces went out, followed by the rest of the army [Hebrew: “which followed them”]. Each man struck down the man who came against him [the manuscript reads: “who had come”]. The Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them. Ben-hadad, king of Syria, also fled on horseback with the cavalry.

The king of Israel went out, struck the horses and chariots, and inflicted a great defeat on Syria. [T. LXXXVIII.]

A prophet approached the king of Israel and said to him: “Go, strengthen yourself, and understand and see what you should do, for next year the king of Syria will come up against you.”

The servants of the king of Syria said to him: “Their gods are gods of the mountains; therefore they have overcome us. But it would be better for us to fight against them on the plains, and we shall defeat them. Therefore do this: remove each king from his army [the Vulgate reads: “your army”], and appoint governors in their place; restore the number of soldiers who fell from your ranks, and horses equal to the former horses, and chariots equal to the chariots you previously had. Then we shall fight against them on the plains, and you will see that we shall defeat them.” [Hebrew: “And he listened to their voice.”]

He accepted their advice and did so. [Col. 0716C]

When the year had passed, Ben-hadad reviewed the Syrians and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel. The Israelites were reviewed, received provisions, departed to face them, and encamped opposite them like two small flocks of goats, while the Syrians filled the land.

A man of God approached and said to the king of Israel: “Thus says the Lord: Because the Syrians have said, ‘The Lord is a god of the mountains and not a god of the valleys,’ I shall deliver this entire great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

For seven days the two sides drew up their lines opposite each other. On the seventh day the battle began, and the Israelites struck down one hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in a single day.

Those who remained fled to Aphek, into the city, and the wall fell upon twenty-seven thousand men [Hebrew: “warriors”] who remained.

Ben-hadad, fleeing, entered the city and went into a chamber within a chamber. His servants said to him: “Behold, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful. Therefore let us put sackcloth around our waists and cords on our heads [Note: Through the carelessness of copyists, the words “and cords on our heads” have fallen out here in the Veronese manuscript], and go out to the king of Israel; perhaps he will save our lives” [Hebrew: “your life”].

They girded sackcloth around their waists, placed ropes on their heads [the manuscript omits “their”], came to the king of Israel, and said: “Your servant Ben-hadad says: May your life live, I beg you” [Note: The Scholiast notes that this is absent from the Hebrew; the Veronese manuscript likewise omits “I beg you.” Hebrew: absent].

He said: “If he is still alive, he is my brother.”

The men took this as a favorable sign, quickly seized the word from his mouth, and said: “Ben-hadad is your brother.”

He said to them [Hebrew: absent]: “Go and bring him” [the Vulgate adds: “to me”].

Ben-hadad came out to him [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Ben-hadad therefore went out to him, lifted …”] and he lifted him into his chariot [Hebrew: absent].

Ben-hadad said to him: “The cities that my father took from your father I will restore, and you may establish streets for yourself in Damascus, just as my father did in Samaria. And I, having made a treaty, will depart from you.”

So he made a treaty with him and released him [Hebrew: “And I, with the treaty, will send you away. And he made a treaty and sent him away.”] [T. LXXXIX.]

Then a certain man from the sons of the prophets said to his companion by the word of the Lord: “Strike me.”

But he refused to strike him [Hebrew: “to strike him”].

He said to him: “Because you did not listen to the voice of the Lord, behold, when you depart from me, a lion will strike you.”

When he had gone a little way from him, a lion found him and struck him.

He found another man and said to him: “Strike me.”

The man struck him and wounded him. [T. XC.]

The prophet went and met the king on the road. He disguised himself by sprinkling dust over his face and eyes [Note: The Hebrew reads: “and he changed the eyes of his face with dust.” The same is read in the Hebrew Canon of truth, because the word “mouth,” together with the following conjunction “and,” has been erased in it; thus it reads: “And he changed the eyes of his face with a sprinkling of dust.” Nevertheless, the noun “mouth,” which is found in other manuscripts, may have been used by Jerome himself to clarify the meaning, just as elsewhere he frequently adds small explanatory particles. MART.].

When the king passed by, he cried out to the king and said: “Your servant went out to fight at close quarters. When one man fled, someone brought him to me and said: ‘Guard this man; for if he slips away, your life shall be for his life, or you shall weigh out a talent of silver.’ While I, troubled, was turning here and there, suddenly he disappeared.”

The king of Israel said to him: “That is your judgment, which you yourself pronounced.”

Immediately he wiped the dust from his face, and the king of Israel recognized that he was one of the prophets.

He said to him: [T. XCI.] “Thus says the Lord: Because you released from your hand a man worthy of death, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people.”

The king of Israel returned to his house, displeased and furious, and went to Samaria.

### Chapter XXI

After these events [the Vulgate adds: “at that time”], Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.

Ahab spoke to Naboth, saying: “Give me your vineyard, so that I may make it into a vegetable garden, because it is nearby and close to my house. I will give you a better vineyard in exchange for it; or, if you prefer, I will give you its value in silver, as much as it is worth.”

Naboth answered him: “May the Lord be gracious to me [Hebrew: “Far be it from me, from the Lord”], that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.”

So Ahab went into his house angry and chafing over the word that Naboth the Jezreelite had spoken to him: “I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers.”

He threw himself on his bed, turned his face away [Note: The same manuscript, with the Vulgate, has “to the wall” instead of “his face”; this appears to be a gloss inserted by a later hand], and would not eat bread.

Jezebel his wife came to him and said: “Why is your spirit troubled, and why do you not eat bread?”

He answered her: “I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said to him: ‘Give me your vineyard for money; or, if you prefer, I will give you a vineyard in exchange for it’” [the Vulgate adds: “a better one”].

But he said: “I will not give you my vineyard” [the manuscript reads: “I do not give you”].

Jezebel his wife said to him: “You are a man of great authority, and you rule the kingdom of Israel well” [Note: The future tense, “you will rule,” is read in the future-tense Veronese manuscript and in the Hebrew]. “Rise, eat bread, and be of good cheer. I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”

She wrote letters [Hebrew: “books”] in Ahab’s name, sealed them with his ring, and sent them to the elders and nobles who were in his city and lived with Naboth.

This was the substance of the letters [Hebrew: “books”]: “Proclaim a fast, and seat Naboth among the foremost of the people. Set two worthless men opposite him, and let them give false testimony [Hebrew: absent], saying: ‘He has blessed God and the king.’ Then lead him out and stone him, so that he may die.”

His fellow citizens, the elders and nobles who lived with him in the city, did as Jezebel had commanded them and as it was written in the letters [Hebrew: “books”] that she had sent them. They proclaimed a fast and seated Naboth among the foremost of the people.

Two men, sons of the devil [Hebrew: “sons of Belial”], were brought in and seated opposite him. Those devilish men [Hebrew: “men of Belial”] gave testimony against him before the assembly [Hebrew: “before the people”], saying: “Naboth has blessed God and the king.”

Therefore they led him outside the city and killed him with stones.

They sent word to Jezebel, saying: “Naboth has been stoned and is dead.”

When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, she said to Ahab: “Rise and take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, who refused to agree with you and give it to you for money. Naboth is not alive; he is dead.”

When Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he rose and went down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite to take possession of it. [T. XCIV.]

The word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: “Rise, go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria. Behold, he has gone down to Naboth’s vineyard to take possession of it. You shall speak to him, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord: You have killed and, moreover, taken possession.’”

And after this you shall add: “Thus says the Lord: In the place [Note: The Veronese manuscript, with the Vulgate, has “in this place in which …”] where the dogs licked Naboth’s blood, they shall lick your blood also.”

Ahab said to Elijah: “Have you found me, my enemy?”

He said to him [Note: The Veronese manuscript, in agreement with the Hebrew, omits “to him”]: “I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do evil in the sight of the Lord” [Hebrew: “in the eyes”].

“Behold, I shall bring evil upon you, and I shall cut off your posterity [Hebrew: “remove”]. I shall destroy from Ahab every male who urinates against the wall, both the confined and the last [Hebrew: “the abandoned”] in Israel. And I shall make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have acted to provoke me to anger and have caused Israel to sin.” [T. XCV.]

The Lord also spoke concerning Jezebel, saying: “The dogs shall eat Jezebel in the field of Jezreel.”

“If Ahab dies in the city, the dogs shall eat him; but if he dies in the field, the birds of the air shall eat him” [Hebrew: “Whoever of Ahab dies in the city … but whoever dies in the field …”].

Indeed, there was no one like Ahab, who had sold himself to do evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: “in the eyes of the Lord”]. His wife Jezebel had incited him, and he became so abominable that he followed idols [Hebrew: “filth”] made by the Amorites, whom the Lord destroyed from before the Israelites.

[T. XCVI.] When Ahab heard these words, he tore his garments [the manuscript reads: “his garment”], covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with his head bowed.

The word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: “Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring the evil in his days; but in the days of his son I shall bring evil upon his house.”

### Chapter XXII

Three years passed without war between Syria and Israel. In the third year, Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to the king of Israel.

The king of Israel said to his servants: “Do you not know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us, and that we are neglecting to take it from the hand of the king of Syria?” [The manuscript reads: “Ramath.”]

He said to Jehoshaphat: “Will you come with me to fight at Ramoth-gilead?” [T. XCVII.]

Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel [Note: In the Canon certain words are changed in accordance with the Hebrew as follows: “As I am, so are you; and as my people are, so are your people; and as my horses are, so are your horses.” I should suppose that this correction, which is evident in the manuscript codex, flowed into the text from a marginal scholium. We are led to this suspicion by the same phrase being used again in 2 Kings, chapter III, verse 7, where Jerome’s translation remained untouched in the text, while the entire scholium was added in the margin, as it is set here within the text of Scripture. Compare the two passages, if you please. MART.]: “I am as you are, and my people are as your people: we are one, and my horsemen [the manuscript adds: “and”] are your horsemen.”

Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel: “Please inquire today of the word of the Lord” [Hebrew: absent].

So the king of Israel gathered the prophets, about four hundred men, and said to them: “Should I go to battle at Ramoth-gilead, or should I refrain?”

They answered: “Go up, and the Lord will deliver it [the Vulgate adds: “it”] into the hand of the king.”

Jehoshaphat said: “Is there no prophet of the Lord here, so that we may inquire through him?”

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat: “There is still one man through whom we could inquire of the Lord; but I hate him, because he never prophesies good concerning me, but evil: Micaiah son of Imlah.”

Jehoshaphat said: “Let not the king speak so.” [T. XCVIII.]

So the king of Israel summoned a certain eunuch and said to him: “Hurry and bring Micaiah son of Imlah.”

The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah sat, each on his throne, dressed in royal attire, in the open space beside the entrance of the gate of Samaria. All the prophets were prophesying before them. [T. XCIX.]

Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns for himself and said: “Thus says the Lord: With these you shall gore the Syrians until you destroy them” [Hebrew: “consume them”].

All the prophets likewise prophesied, saying: “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and prosper, and the Lord will deliver them into the hands of the king” [Note: The same manuscript reads “into his hand.” The Hebrew has the corresponding expression. Shortly afterward it reads “he had gone to call,” instead of “in order to call.”].

The messenger who had gone to summon Micaiah spoke to him, saying: “Behold, the words of the prophets unanimously promise good to the king. Therefore let your word also be like theirs, and speak good.”

Micaiah said: “As the Lord lives, whatever the Lord says to me, that I shall speak.”

So he came to the king, and the king said to him: “Micaiah, should we go to battle at Ramoth-gilead, or should we refrain?”

He answered him: “Go up and prosper, and the Lord will deliver it [the Vulgate adds: “it”] into the hands of the king.”

The king said to him: “Again and again I adjure you not to speak to me anything except what is true, in the name of the Lord.”

He said: “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. And the Lord said: ‘These have no master’ [Hebrew: “masters”]. Let each return to his house in peace.” [T. C.]

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat: “Did I not tell you that he does not prophesy good concerning me, but always evil?”

Micaiah continued: “Therefore hear the word of the Lord. I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left.

“The Lord said: ‘Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel [Hebrew: absent], so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’

“One spoke in one way, another in another.”

Then a spirit came out and stood before the Lord, saying: “I will deceive him.”

The Lord said to him: “By what means?”

He said: [T. CI.] “I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.”

The Lord said [Hebrew: absent]: “You shall deceive him, and you shall prevail. Go out and do so.”

“Now therefore, behold, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these prophets of yours, and the Lord has spoken evil against you.” [T. CII.]

Zedekiah son of Chenaanah approached and struck Micaiah on the cheek, saying: “Did the spirit of the Lord then depart from me and speak to you?”

Micaiah said: “You shall see on that day, when you enter a chamber within a chamber in order to hide.”

The king of Israel said: “Take Micaiah and let him remain with Amon, governor of the city, and with Joash son of Amalek. Tell them: ‘Thus says the king: Put this man in prison and sustain him with the bread of affliction and the water of distress until I return in peace.’”

Micaiah said: “If you return in peace, the Lord has not spoken through me.”

And he said: “Hear, all peoples.”

The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat: “Take your weapons and enter the battle, and put on your garments.”

The king of Israel changed his clothing [the Vulgate adds: “his own”] and entered the battle.

The king of Syria had commanded the thirty-two commanders of his chariots, saying: “You shall fight against neither small nor great, but only against the king of Israel.”

When the commanders of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they thought that he was the king of Israel. They charged against him, and Jehoshaphat cried out. The commanders of the chariots understood that he was not the king of Israel, and they withdrew from him.

[T. CIII.] A certain man, however, drew his bow and shot an arrow at random; by chance he struck the king of Israel between the lungs and the stomach [Hebrew: “between the shoulders”].

He said to his charioteer: “Turn your hand and carry me out of the army, for I am severely wounded.”

The battle grew fierce that day. The king of Israel remained in his chariot facing the Syrians, and died in the evening. The blood from his wound flowed into the hollow of the chariot.

A herald sounded throughout the army before the sun went down, saying: “Let each man return to his city” [the manuscript and the Vulgate omit “his”] “and to his land” [Hebrew: “in the camp, when the sun was setting, saying: Each man to his city and to his land”].

The king died and was carried to Samaria. They buried the king in Samaria, washed his chariot [Note: Here the Veronese manuscript omits “his,” which is likewise absent from the Hebrew] in the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked his blood; they also washed the reins, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken.

The rest of the deeds of Ahab, all that he did, the ivory house that he built, and all the cities that he constructed—are these not written in the book of the deeds of the days of the kings of Israel? [Note: The same manuscript reads “in the Book of Chronicles,” which is properly the title of the book; it was retained above in continuous form.]

Ahab slept with his fathers, and Ahaziah [Hebrew: “Ahaziah”] his son reigned in his place. [T. CIV.]

[T. CV.] Jehoshaphat son of Asa had begun to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel. He was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Azubah daughter of Shilhi [the manuscript reads: “Salaai”].

He walked in all the way of his father Asa and did not turn aside from it. He did what was right in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: “in the eyes”]. Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.

Jehoshaphat was at peace with the king of Israel.

The rest of the deeds of Jehoshaphat, his works, what he accomplished, and his battles [Hebrew: “strength”]—are these not written in the Book of the Deeds of the Days of the Kings of Judah?

He also removed from the land the remnants of the effeminates who had remained in the days of his father Asa.

At that time there was no king established in Edom.

King Jehoshaphat had made ships on the sea [Hebrew: “ships of Tarshish”] to sail to Ophir for gold, but they could not go, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber.

Then Ahaziah son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat: “Let my servants go with your servants in the ships.”

But Jehoshaphat was unwilling.

[T. CVI.] Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of David his father. His son Jehoram reigned in his place.

Ahaziah son of Ahab had begun to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel for two years.

He did evil in the sight of the Lord, walked in the way of his father and his mother, and in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.

He also served Baal, worshiped him, and provoked the Lord God of Israel, according to everything his father had done.

## The Second Book of Kings

[Note: The Veronese manuscript continues the sequence of the preceding book without adding the title of this second one, since, following the Hebrew exemplar, it treats the Book of Kings as a single book and does not divide it into two. This has been noted above more than once. See nevertheless below, note c at column 723, at the beginning of the following chapter.]

[T. CVII, Chapter I.]

Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab. Ahaziah [Hebrew: “Ahaziah”] fell through the lattice of his upper chamber in Samaria and became ill. He sent messengers, saying to them: “Go and consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I may survive this illness.”

But the angel of the Lord spoke to Elijah the Tishbite [the Vulgate adds: “saying”]: “Rise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say to them: ‘Is there no God in Israel, that you are going to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?’” [T. CVIII.]

Therefore thus says the Lord: “You shall not come down from the bed on which you have climbed; you shall surely die.”

And Elijah departed.

The messengers returned to Ahaziah [Hebrew: “Ahaziah”], who said to them: “Why have you returned?”

They answered him: “A man met us and said to us: ‘Go, return to the king who sent you, and say to him: Thus says the Lord: Is it because there was no God in Israel that you are sending to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you shall not come down from the bed on which you have climbed; you shall surely die.’”

He said to them: “What was the appearance and dress of the man who met you and spoke these words?” [Note: The Veronese manuscript omits “that man”; the word is likewise absent from the Hebrew.]

They said: “He was a hairy man [Hebrew: “hairy”], and he was girded at the waist with a leather belt” [the manuscript reads: “girded”].

He said: “It is Elijah the Tishbite.”

He sent to him a commander of fifty, together with his fifty men. He went up to him, and while Elijah was sitting on the top of the mountain, he said to him: “Man of God [Hebrew: “man of God”], the king commands you to come down.”

Elijah answered and said to the commander of fifty: “If I am a man of God [Hebrew: “man”], let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty.”

Fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty men who were with him.

Again he sent another commander of fifty, with his fifty men. He spoke to him: “Man of God [Hebrew: “man of God”], thus says the king: Hurry and come down.”

Elijah answered: “If I am a man of God [Hebrew: “man of God”], let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty.”

The fire of God [the Vulgate omits “of God”] came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty men. [T. CIX.]

Again he sent a third commander of fifty, with his fifty men. When he came, he bent his knees before Elijah, pleaded with him, and said: “Man of God [Hebrew: “man of God”], do not despise my life or the lives of these servants of yours who are with me.

“Behold, fire has come down from heaven and consumed the first two commanders of fifty and the fifty men who were with them. But now I beg you to have mercy on my life.”

The angel of the Lord spoke to Elijah, saying [Hebrew: absent]: “Go down with him; do not be afraid.”

So he rose, went down with him to the king, and spoke to him: [T. CX.] “Thus says the Lord: Because you sent messengers to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, as though there were no God in Israel from whom you could inquire of his word [Col. 0724A], therefore you shall not come down from the bed on which you have climbed; you shall surely die.”

Thus he died according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken. Jehoram his brother [Hebrew: absent] reigned in his place, in the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, for Ahaziah had no son.

The rest of the deeds of Ahaziah [Hebrew: “Ahaziah”], which he performed—are these not written in the Book of the Deeds of the Days of the Kings of Israel?

[T. CXI, Chapter II.] [Note: [Col. 0723D] Here, in the margin of the Veronese manuscript, the same hand that copied the entire book added this note: “Here ends Book III according to the Septuagint.” [Col. 0724D] I would rather think that the note concerning the beginning of the preceding chapter was not placed in its proper location; for I know of no text that begins Book IV at this point.]

Now when the Lord wished to take Elijah up into heaven in a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were going from Gilgal. Elijah said to Elisha: “Stay here, because the Lord has sent me as far as Bethel.” He replied: “As the Lord lives, and as your life lives, I will not abandon you.” When they had gone down to Bethel [Ms. had gone down], the sons of the prophets who were at Bethel came out to Elisha and said to him: “Do you know that today the Lord will take your master away from you?” He replied: “I know it too; be silent.”

Then Elijah said to Elisha: “Stay here, because the Lord has sent me to Jericho.” He said: “As the Lord lives, and as your life lives, I will not abandon you.” When they had come to Jericho, the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho approached Elisha and said to him: “Do you know that today the Lord will take your master away from you?” And he said: “I know it too; be silent.”

Then Elijah said to him: “Stay here, because the Lord has sent me [Vulg. ‘as far as’] to the Jordan.” He said: “As the Lord lives, and as your life lives, I will not abandon you.” So the two went on together, and fifty men from the sons of the prophets followed them [Vulg. ‘followed them’]. They also stood opposite, at a distance [Note: [Col. 0724D] The Veronese manuscript reads, “stood opposite, far away”—almost more elegantly.] But the two were standing beside the Jordan.

[T. CXII.] Elijah took his mantle, wrapped it up, and struck the waters. They were divided in both directions, and the two crossed over on dry ground. When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha: “Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken away from you [h. ‘ask what I should do for you before I am taken away from you’].” Elisha said: “I ask that a double portion of your spirit be upon me.”

He replied: “You have asked for a difficult thing. Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken away from you, it shall be granted to you as you have asked [h. ‘if you see me being taken away from you, it shall be as you have asked’]; but if you do not see me, it shall not be.” As they continued on, walking and talking, behold, a fiery chariot and fiery horses separated the two, and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind [h. ‘in the whirlwind’]. Elisha saw him and cried out: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” And he did not see him again. Then he seized his garments and tore them into two pieces.

He lifted up Elijah’s mantle, which had fallen from him [h. “which had fallen upon him”], and, returning, stood on the bank of the Jordan. With Elijah’s mantle, which had fallen from him [Note: [Col. 0725D] The Canon text is pure here and corresponds directly to its source. The other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, add “and the waters were not divided”; a marginal obelus indicates that this addition should be rejected. MART. — Here too the Veronese manuscript omits “from him.” The Vulgate manuscripts next have “he struck the waters, and they were not divided, and he said,” etc. Finally, the same manuscript omits the name “Lord,” as do the older Vulgate and Greek books.] [h. “upon him”], he struck the waters and said: “Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah, even now?” He struck the waters, and they were divided this way and that, and Elisha crossed over.

When the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho, opposite him, saw him, they said: “The spirit of Elijah has come to rest upon Elisha” [Ms. and Vulg. omit “him”]. [T. CXIII.] They came to meet him, bowed down before him with their faces to the ground, and said to him: “Behold, there are fifty strong men among your servants, who can go and search for your master [Ms. and Vulg. ‘seek’] [h. ‘go and seek your master’], lest perhaps the spirit of the Lord has taken him and cast him upon one of the mountains or into one of the valleys.”

He said: “Do not send them.” But they pressed him until he yielded and said: “Send them.” So they sent fifty men. After they had searched for three days, they did not find him. They returned to him; meanwhile he was staying in Jericho, and he said to them: “Did I not tell you, ‘Do not send them’?” [Note: [Col. 0725D] The Veronese codex reads, “Do not go,” which agrees more correctly with the Hebrew and with most other texts.]

The men of the city said to Elisha: “Behold, the situation of this city is excellent, as you yourself, lord, can see; but the waters are bad, and [Note: [Col. 0726D] The same manuscript reads “and barren,” with the intervening word “land” omitted; this is plainly the antiquarian’s error.] the land is barren.”

[T. CXIV.] He said: “Bring me a new vessel and put salt in it.” When she had brought it [Ms. “who”], he went out to the spring of the waters, cast salt into it, and said: “Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters, and there shall no longer be death or barrenness in them.” So the waters were healed to this day, according to the word of Elisha that he spoke.

[T. CXV.] From there he went up to Bethel. As he was going up by the road, little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead!” When he looked behind him [Ms. and Vulg. omit “behind him”], he saw them and cursed them in the name of the Lord. Then two bears came out of the woodland and tore forty-two of the boys to pieces [Ms. omits “of them”] [h. “little ones”]. From there he went to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.

[T. CXVI, Chapter III.] Joram, son of Ahab, became king over Israel in Samaria in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. He reigned twelve years. He did evil before the Lord [h. “in the eyes of the Lord”], but not like his father and mother, for he removed the statues [h. “the pillar”] of Baal that his father had made. Nevertheless, he clung to the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin, and did not depart from them.

Now Mesha, king of Moab [Ms. Mesa], kept many flocks [h. omits this] and paid the king of Israel one hundred thousand lambs and one hundred thousand rams, together with their wool. When Ahab died, he broke the covenant that he had with the king of Israel [h. “the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel”]. Therefore King Joram went out from Samaria on that day and mustered all Israel. [Note: [Col. 0726D] The same manuscript reads, “So he went out, therefore … and mustered.” Shortly afterward it has “against Moab” instead of “against him,” together with the Vulgate and the Hebrew text.]

[T. CXVII.] He sent to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, saying: “The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you come with me against him to battle?” He replied: “I will go up. What is mine is yours; my people are your people; my horses are your horses” [h. “As I am, so are you; and as my people are, so are your people; and as my horses are, so are your horses”].

He said: “By which road shall we go up?” He replied: “By the wilderness of Edom” [h. “by the road of the wilderness of Edom”].

[T. CXVIII.] So the king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom set out and went around by the road [h. omits this] for seven days. There was no water for the army or for the animals that followed them [h. “on which they rode”]. The king of Israel said: [Note: [Col. 0726D] Here too the Veronese manuscript repeats “Alas!” three times, as do the Vulgate manuscripts, less well.] “Alas! The Lord has assembled these three kings in order to hand them over to Moab.”

Jehoshaphat said: “Is there no prophet of the Lord here, so that we may entreat the Lord through him?” [h. “so that we may consult the Lord”] One of the servants of the king of Israel answered: “Here is Elisha son of Shaphat, who poured water over the hands of Elijah.” Jehoshaphat said: “The word of the Lord is with him.”

So the king of Israel, Jehoshaphat [Note: [Col. 0726D] The Vulgate adds “king of Judah,” words that the Hebrew and the manuscripts of Jerome’s version lack], and the king of Edom went down to him. Elisha said to the king of Israel: “What have I to do with you? Go to the prophets of your father and your mother.” The king of Israel said to him: “Why has the Lord assembled these three kings in order to hand them over into the hands of Moab?” [Col. 0726C] Elisha said to him: “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand [h. ‘stood’], if I did not respect the face of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, I would certainly not have paid attention to you or looked at you.

“But now bring me a musician.” While the musician was playing, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and he said: “Thus says the Lord: Make this torrent-bed [h. ‘this torrent’] full of ditches and ditches” [h. omits the second “ditches”]. For thus says the Lord: “You shall see neither wind nor rain, yet this torrent-bed [h. “torrent”] shall be filled with water, and you shall drink—you, your households, and your animals. And this is a small thing [h. “a light thing”] in the sight [h. “in the eyes”] of the Lord; moreover, he will also deliver Moab into your hands [Ms. “into your hand”]. You shall strike every fortified city and every choice city, cut down every fruit-bearing tree, stop up all the springs of water, and cover every excellent field with stones.”

[T. CXIX.] In the morning, at the time when the sacrifice is customarily offered, behold, waters were coming by way of Edom, and the land was filled with water. All the Moabites, hearing that the kings had come up to fight against them, summoned everyone who was girded with a belt, and took up their positions at the frontier.

They rose early, and when the sun had already risen opposite the waters, the Moabites saw the waters from a distance, red like blood, and said: “This is blood. The kings have fought against one another [h. omits this] and have slaughtered one another. Now, Moab, proceed to the plunder!”

They went to the camp of Israel. Israel rose up and struck Moab, but they fled before them [Ms. “and they”]. The victors came and struck Moab, destroying the cities.
