They filled every excellent field by throwing stones into it individually, stopped up all the springs of water, and cut down every fruit-bearing tree, until only the clay walls remained. The city was surrounded by slingers and was struck to a great extent.

When the king of Moab saw that the enemy had prevailed, he took with him seven hundred men who drew the sword, intending to break through to the king of Edom [Ms. “so that he might break through”; Vulg. “to break through”], but they could not. Then he seized his firstborn son, who was to reign in his place, and offered him as a burnt offering upon the wall. Great indignation came upon Israel, and they immediately withdrew from him and returned to their own land [h. omits this].

(Chapter IV.) A certain woman, one of the wives of the prophets, cried out to Elisha, saying: “Your servant, my husband, is dead, and you know that your servant was one who feared the Lord. And behold, the creditor has come to take my two sons to serve him.”

Elisha said to her: “What do you want me to do for you? Tell me, what do you have in your house?” She replied: “Your handmaid has nothing at all in her house, except a little oil” [h. “except a flask of oil”], with which I may anoint myself.

(T. CXX.) He said to her: “Go and [Ms. and Vulg. omit “and”] borrow from all your neighbors empty vessels—not a few. Enter, shut your door [Note: [Col. 0727D] The Veronese manuscript omits “your,” in accordance with the Hebrew exemplar and other books] when you and your sons are inside, and pour into all these vessels; and when they are full, take them away.”

So the woman went and shut the door upon herself and her sons. They brought the vessels to her, and she poured. When the vessels were full, she said to her son: “Bring me another vessel.” He replied: “I have none.” And the oil stopped.

She came and reported this to the man [h. “the man”] of God. [Col. 0727D] He said: “Go [Ms. adds ‘and’], sell the oil and pay your creditor; but you and your sons live on what remains.”

(T. CXXI.) One day Elisha was passing through Shunem. There was a prominent woman there, and she urged him to eat bread. Whenever he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread. She said to her husband: “I perceive that this is a holy man of God who frequently passes by us. Let us make a small upper room, put a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand there for him, so that whenever he comes to us, he may stay there.”

One day he came and turned into the upper room and rested there. He said to Gehazi, his servant: “Call this Shunammite.” When he had called her and she had stood before him, he said to his servant [Ms. omits “his”]: “Speak to her: ‘Behold, you have diligently served us in every way. What do you want me to do for you? Do you have some matter, and do you want me to speak to the king or to the commander of the army?’”

She replied: “I dwell among my own people.”

He said: “What then should I do for her?” Gehazi said: “Do not ask her, for she has no son, and her husband is old.” He therefore ordered that she be called. When she had been called and was standing at the door (Vulg. “before the door”), he said to her:

(T. CXXII.) “At this time, at this very hour, [Note: [Col. 0727D] Perhaps the marginal scholium originally read “at the time of life.” For, explaining the same scriptural expression in his notes on the Hebrew Questions, Saint Jerome, after quoting the verse according to the Septuagint, adds: “In place of ‘hour,’ we read ‘life’ in the Hebrew, so that the order or sense is: ‘I will return to you at the time of life,’ as though he had said, ‘if I live, if life accompanies me.’” MART.] if life accompanies it [h. “according to the time of life”], you shall have a son in your womb.”

She replied: “Do not, I beg you, my lord, man of God; do not lie to your handmaid.” The woman conceived and gave birth to a son at the time and in the same hour [Note: [Col. 0728D] The Veronese manuscript omits “which Elisha had told her,” along with the Vulgate’s intervening “to her,” although this is expressed in the Hebrew. More correctly, it next reads “he went out” instead of “he had gone out,” in accordance with the Hebrew text.] that Elisha had told her. The boy grew [h. “the little one grew”].

One day, when he had gone out to his father among the reapers, he said to his father: “My head! [Note: [Col. 0728D] The Vulgate has more: “My head aches, my head aches.”] My head!” His father said to the boy: “Take him and lead him to his mother.”

[T. CXXIII.] When he had taken him and brought him to his mother, she placed him on her knees until noon, and he died. She went up, laid him on the bed of the man [h. “man”] of God, shut the door, went out, called her husband, and said: “Send with me, I beg you, one of the boys and a donkey, so that I may hurry to the man [h. “man”] of God and return.”

He said [Ms., with the Vulgate, adds “to her”]: “Why are you going to him today? It is neither the new moon nor the sabbath.” She replied: [Note: [Col. 0728D] The same manuscript reads “Farewell” instead of “Peace.” Indeed, what is found in the Hebrew the Arabic interpreter also rendered as “Farewell.” The Vulgate manuscripts read less appropriately “I will go” instead of “Farewell,” or read “Peace.”] “Peace.”

She saddled the donkey and commanded the boy: “Lead on and hurry; do not delay me on the way, and do what I command you.” She set out and came to the man of God on Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her from a distance, he said to Gehazi his servant: “Look, there is that Shunammite. Go to meet her and say to her: ‘Is everything well with you, with your husband, and with your son [h. “little one”]?’”

She replied: “It is well” [h. “Peace”]. When she came to the man of God on the mountain, she seized his feet, and Gehazi approached to remove her. The man of God said: “Leave her alone, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden it from me [Vulg. “from my knowledge”] and has not told me.”

She said to him: “Did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not say to you, ‘Do not deceive me’?”

[T. CXXIV.] He said to Gehazi: “Gird your loins, take my staff in your hand, and go. If a man [h. “man”] meets you, do not greet him; and if anyone greets you, do not answer him. Place my staff upon the boy’s face.”

But the boy’s mother said: “As the Lord lives, and as your life lives, I will not leave you.” So he arose and followed her. Gehazi had gone ahead of them [Vulg. “ahead of them”] and had placed the staff upon the boy’s face, but there was neither voice nor consciousness. He returned to meet him and reported to him, saying: “The boy has not arisen.”

Elisha entered the house, and behold, the dead boy was lying on his bed. He entered, shut the door upon himself and [Vulg. “and upon”] the boy, and prayed to the Lord. Then he went up and lay upon the boy [Ms. “him”]; he placed his mouth upon his mouth, his eyes upon his eyes, and his hands upon his hands. He bent over him, and the boy’s flesh grew warm.

Then he returned and walked through the house, once back and once forth. He went up again and lay upon him. The boy yawned seven times and opened his eyes [Note: [Col. 0729D] The same manuscript adds “his,” very appropriately in accordance with the Hebrew text. It also reads “And he,” instead of “But he,” and so forth.]

(T. CXXV.) He called Gehazi and said: “Call this Shunammite.” When she had been called, she entered to him. He said: “Take your son.” She came, fell at his feet, and bowed to the ground. She took her son and went out. Elisha returned to Gilgal.

There was a famine in the land, and the sons of the prophets were dwelling before him. He said to one of his servants [h. “to his servant”]: “Set on the large pot and cook stew for the sons of the prophets.”

(T. CXXVI.) One of them went out into the field to gather wild herbs. He found what seemed to be a wild vine [h. “mallows”; “he found a wild vine”], gathered from it gourds of the field, filled his cloak, and returned and cut them into the pot of stew, for he did not know what they were.

They poured it out for their companions to eat. When they had tasted the cooked food, they cried out, saying: “Death is in the pot, man of God!” And they could not eat.

But he said: “Bring flour.” [Note: [Col. 0729D] The Vulgate manuscripts add: “When he had taken it, he put it into the pot.”] He put it into the pot and said: “Pour it out for the people [h. “the populace”], so that they may eat.” And there was no longer anything bitter [h. “anything evil”] in the pot.

A certain man came from Baal-shalisha [Ms. BalsaIsa], bringing the man of God the firstfruits—twenty barley loaves [Ms. adds “and”] and fresh grain in his sack [h. “and roasted ears of grain”]. He said: “Give it to the people, so that they may eat.”

His servant replied: [Note: [Col. 0729D] Again, in accordance with the Hebrew, the Veronese manuscript omits “to him.”] “How can I set this before one hundred men?” [Vulg. omits “before”] Again he said: “Give it to the people, so that they may eat; for thus says the Lord: ‘They shall eat, and there shall be some left over.’”

So he set it before them. They ate, and some was left over, according to the word of the Lord.

[Col. 0730A] [Chapter V.] Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his lord and highly honored, for through him the Lord had given deliverance to Syria. He was a mighty and wealthy man, but [h. omits this] a leper.

Now raiders had gone out from Syria and had taken captive from the land of Israel a little girl who was serving the wife of Naaman. She said to her mistress: “If only my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Surely he would cure him of his leprosy.”

Naaman went in to his lord and reported to him, saying: “This and this is what the girl from the land of Israel said.” The king of Syria said to him: “Go, and I will send a letter [h. “a document”] to the king of Israel.”

When he had departed, he took with him ten talents of silver, six thousand gold pieces, and ten changes of clothing. He brought the letter [h. “document”] to the king of Israel, which said:

“When you receive this letter, know that I have sent my servant Naaman to you, so that you may cure him of his leprosy.”

When the king of Israel had read the letter [Note: [Col. 0730D] Here the Veronese manuscript differs from the Hebrew archetype by omitting the name “Israel” and, shortly afterward, “I.”] [h. “document”], he tore his garments and said: “Am I God, so that I can kill and give life [h. omits this], that this man has sent to me to cure a man [h. “man”] of his leprosy? Consider and see that he is seeking an occasion against me.”

When Elisha, the man of God, heard that the king of Israel had torn his garments, he sent to him, saying: “Why have you torn your garments? Let him come to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel.”

[T. CXXVII.] Naaman came with horses and chariots [h. “his chariot”] and stood at the door of Elisha’s house. Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying: “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh shall recover, and you shall be clean.”

Naaman became angry and went away, saying: “I thought that he would come out to me, stand, call upon the name of the Lord his God, touch the place of the leprosy with his hand, and cure me. Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel [Note: [Col. 0730D] The same manuscript reads “all that are in Israel,” supplying the understood word “rivers,” so that the sense is correct, although this is an antiquarian’s error visible at a glance], so that I may wash in them and be cleansed?”

When he had turned and was going away in anger, his servants approached him and said: “Father [h. ‘my father’], if the prophet had told you to do something difficult, surely you ought to have done it. How much more, since he has now said to you, ‘Wash, and you shall be clean’!”

[CXXVIII.] He went down and washed in the Jordan seven times, according to the word of the man of God. His flesh was restored like the flesh of a little boy, and he was cleansed.

He returned to the man of God with his entire retinue, came and stood before him, and said: “Truly I know that there is no God [Vulg. “no other God”] throughout the whole earth except in Israel.”

[T. CXXIX.] “Therefore, I ask you to accept a blessing from your servant.” But he replied: “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand [h. ‘stood’], I will not accept it.” Though he urged him, he absolutely refused.

Naaman said: “As you wish. But I ask you to grant your servant this: let me take as much earth as two mules can carry [h. “a load for two mules”]. For your servant will no longer offer a burnt offering or sacrifice to foreign gods, but only to the Lord.

“Yet may the Lord pardon your servant in this one matter: when my lord enters the temple of Rimmon to worship, and he leans on my hand, if I worship in the temple of Rimmon while he worships in the same place, may the Lord pardon your servant for this matter [Ms. omits “him”] [h. “Only in this matter may the Lord pardon your servant: when my lord enters the house of Rimmon to worship there, and he leans upon my hand, if I worship in the house of Rimmon while I worship in the same place, may the Lord pardon your servant for this matter”].”

He said to him: “Go in peace.” So he departed from him for a chosen stretch of ground [i.e. some distance; wording uncertain].

[T. CXXX.] Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, said: “My lord has spared this Syrian Naaman by not accepting from him what he brought. As the Lord lives, I will run after him and take something from him.”

Gehazi followed behind Naaman. When Naaman saw him running toward him [Note: [Col. 0731D] The Veronese manuscript, together with the Vulgate, has only “he.” The Hebrew repeats the name itself, Naaman.], he leapt down from his chariot to meet him and said: “Is everything well [h. ‘Is there peace’]?” He replied: “It is well. My lord has sent me [Note: [Col. 0731D] The Veronese manuscript omits the words “to you,” which are not expressed in the Hebrew.] to say: ‘Just now two young men [h. “boys”] from Mount Ephraim, from the sons of the prophets, have come to me. Give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothing.’”

Naaman said: “It is better that you take two talents.” He pressed him and tied two talents of silver in two sacks, together with the two changes of clothing, and placed them upon two of his servants, who carried them before him.

When he had already arrived in the evening [Ms. “also”], Gehazi took them from their hands and stored them in the house. He dismissed the men, and they departed. He himself entered and stood before his master.

[T. CXXXI.] Elisha said: “Where have you come from [h. omits this], Gehazi?” He replied: “Your servant did not go anywhere [Ms. “to anywhere”].” He said: “Was not my heart present when the man [h. “man”] turned from his chariot to meet you? Now you have received silver and received clothing in order to buy olive groves and vineyards [Vulg. “vineyards”], sheep, oxen, male servants, and female servants. But the leprosy of Naaman shall also cling to you and to your offspring forever.”

And he went out from him leprous, like snow.

[Chapter VI.] The sons of the prophets said to Elisha: “Behold, the place where we dwell before you is too small for us. Let us go as far as the Jordan, and let each of us take one piece of timber from the forest, so that we may build ourselves a place to dwell there.”

He said: “Go.” One of them said: “Come, then, you too, with your servants.” He replied: “I will come.” And he went with them. When they had come to the Jordan, they were cutting wood.

It happened that, when one of them had cut down a piece of timber, the iron of the axe fell into the water. He cried out and said: [Note: [Col. 0732D] This same manuscript repeats “Alas!” three times here, as in the Vulgate, and twice below; in the other books it correctly appears only once.] “Alas, my lord! And I had borrowed that very thing.”

The man of God [h. “the man of God”] said: “Where did it fall?” He showed him the place. [T. CXXXII.] He cut a piece of wood, threw it there [h. “cast it”], and the iron floated. He said: “Take it.” He stretched out his hand and took it [Ms. “brought it”].

The king of Syria was waging war against Israel and took counsel with his servants, saying: “Let us set an ambush in such-and-such a place.”

[T. CXXXIII.] The man of God sent to the king of Israel, saying: “Beware of passing through that place, because the Syrians are lying in ambush there.” The king of Israel sent to the place that the man of God had told him about, and took precautions there [h. “captured him”]—not once or twice.

The heart of the king of Syria was troubled over this matter. He summoned his servants and said: “Why do you not tell me who among us is betraying me to the king of Israel?” One of his servants said: “Not at all, my lord king; but Elisha the prophet who is in Israel tells the king of Israel every word that you speak in your bedchamber.”

He said to them: “Go and see where he is, so that I may send and capture him.” They reported to him, saying: “Behold, he is in Dothan.”

So he sent horses and chariots [h. “a chariot”] there, together with a strong force of the army. When they came by night, they surrounded the city.

The servant of the man of God rose early and went out. He saw the army surrounding the city, with horses and chariots [h. “a chariot”], and reported to him [Ms. omits “to him”], saying: “Alas, my lord, what shall we do?”

He replied: “Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them.” When Elisha had prayed, he said: “Lord, open this man’s eyes, so that he may see.” The Lord opened the boy’s eyes, and he saw; and behold, the mountain was full of horses and fiery chariots surrounding Elisha.

The enemies came down toward him [h. omits “the enemies, however” and has only “came down”]. [T. CXXXIV.] Elisha prayed to the Lord [Ms. omits “to”], saying: “Strike this people, I beg you, with blindness.” The Lord struck them with blindness, according to the word of Elisha.

Elisha said to them: “This is not the road, nor is this the city. Follow me, and I will show you the man whom you seek.” He led them into Samaria. When they had entered Samaria, Elisha said: “Lord, open the eyes of these men, so that they may see.” The Lord opened their eyes, and they saw that they were in the midst of Samaria.

When the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha: “Shall I strike them, my father?” He replied: “You shall not strike them. For you did not capture them with your sword and bow, so as to strike them. Set bread and water before them, so that they may eat and drink and go to their master.”

A great preparation of food was set before them. They ate and drank, and he sent them away [h. “sent them”]. They went to their master, and the raiding parties of Syria no longer came into the land of Israel.

After this, Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered his entire army, went up, and besieged Samaria. There was a great famine [Note: [Col. 0733C] The same manuscript omits the word “great,” contrary to the Hebrew.] in Samaria. It was besieged for so long that a donkey’s head sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a quarter of a kab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver.

[T. CXXXV.] When the king of Israel was passing along the wall, a woman [Vulg. adds “a certain”] cried out to him, saying: “Save me [h. omits this], my lord king.” He said: “If the Lord does not save you, from where can I save you—from the threshing floor or from the winepress?”

The king said to her: “What is troubling you?” She replied: “This woman said to me: ‘Give your son, and we shall eat him today; tomorrow we shall eat my son.’ So we cooked my son and ate him. The next day I said to her: ‘Give your son, and we shall eat him.’ But she hid her son.”

When the king heard this, he tore his garments and was passing along the wall. All the people saw the sackcloth that he wore next to his flesh underneath [h. omits “all”]. He said [Vulg. adds “the king”]: “May God do this to me, and may he add this, if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat remains upon him today.”

Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. He sent a man ahead. Before that messenger arrived, he said to the elders: “Do you know that this son of a murderer has sent someone to cut off my head? Therefore, watch: when the messenger comes, shut the door [Note: [Col. 0733C] The first hand added this scholium in the following form: “And hold him at the door”; later, another hand—or the same scribe—added “strike him down” above “hold him.” It may be believed that this was done by the corrector of the Canon, a man whom we suppose to have been skilled in the Hebrew language. MART.] and do not let him enter [h. “and strike him down at the door”]. For the sound of his master’s feet is already behind him.”

While he was still speaking with them, the messenger appeared, coming to him. The messenger said: “Behold, this great evil is from the Lord. Why should I wait for the Lord any longer [h. ‘Why should I entreat the Lord any longer’]?”

### [T. CXXXI, Chapter VII]

But Elisha said: “Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: At this time tomorrow, a measure of fine flour will be sold for one stater [Hebrew: *shekel*], and two measures of barley for one stater [Hebrew: *shekel*], at the gate of Samaria.”

[Note: [Col. 0733D] The same hand that copied the entire codex noted in the blank space at this passage: “Septuagint: shekel.” Then another, much more recent, hand added: “But in the Septuagint we have ‘measure.’ A shekel denotes the price. For their translation reads: ‘two measures of barley for one shekel.’ But Josephus, *Antiquities* IX, ch. 3, says: ‘two *sata* of barley for one shekel, one *satum* of fine flour for one shekel.’ A *satum*, therefore, contains one and a half Italian modii. As regards the earlier ancient annotation, we acknowledge that it observed quite correctly that the Septuagint used *shekel* for *stater*: *metron semidaleōs siklou, kai dimetron krithōn siklou*—“a measure of fine flour for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel.” Indeed, the Hebrew text itself has [Hebrew omitted in the supplied source]; and this is the same thing that our antiquary from the old version and the scholiast from Hebrew record. As regards the second annotation, it is false that Josephus reckons a *satum* of fine flour at two shekels; for his words are sufficiently clear: *hōsper siklou duo krithēs sata, houtō ōnēsesthai semidaleōs saton siklou*—“just as two *sata* of barley may be bought for a shekel, so one *satum* of fine flour may be bought for a shekel.” Now it is well known that the stater, the term used by our translator [Col. 0734C], is equivalent to the shekel.]

One of the officers, upon whose hand the king leaned, answering the man of God [Hebrew: “man of God”], said: “Even if the Lord should make sluices in heaven, could what you say come to pass?” [Hebrew: “Behold, the Lord will make sluices in heaven. Can what I say come to pass?”]

He replied: “You shall see it with your eyes, but you shall not eat of it.”

### [T. CXXXVII]

There were therefore four leprous men near the entrance of the gate. They said to one another: “Why should we remain here until we die? If we decide to enter the city, we shall die of hunger; if we remain here, we must die. Come, then [manuscript: “and”], let us desert to the camp of the Syrians. If they spare us, we shall live; but if they wish to kill us, we shall nevertheless die.”

So they rose at evening [Hebrew: “in the morning”] to go to the camp of the Syrians. When they had reached the beginning of the Syrian camp, they found no one there. For the Lord had caused the Syrians to hear in their camp the sound of chariots, horses, and a very large army. They said to one another: “Behold, the king of Israel has hired against us the kings of the Hittites and the Egyptians, and they have come against us.”

So they rose and fled in the darkness. They abandoned their tents, horses, and donkeys in the camp, and fled, seeking only to save their lives.

When those lepers reached the beginning of the camp, they entered one tent, ate, and drank. They took silver, gold, and clothing from it, went away, and hid them. Then they returned [Hebrew: absent] and entered another tent, carrying things away from it in the same manner and hiding them.

They said to one another: “We are not doing right. This is a day of good news. If we remain silent and refuse to announce it until morning, we shall be charged with a crime. Come, let us go and report it in the king’s palace.”

When they came to the gate of the city, they told them: “We went to the camp of the Syrians, and found no one there [Vulgate: ‘no men’], except horses and donkeys tied up, and tents standing.”

The gatekeepers went and reported this inside the king’s palace. He rose during the night and said to his servants: “I will tell you what the Syrians have done to us [manuscript: ‘did to us’]. They know that we are suffering from hunger, and therefore they have gone out of the camp and are hiding in the fields, saying: ‘When they come out of the city, we shall seize them alive; then we shall be able to enter the city.’”

One of his servants replied: “Let us take five horses that remain in the city—for they alone remain among the entire multitude of Israel, since the others have been consumed—and, sending them out, we shall be able to reconnoiter.”

So they brought two horses, and the king sent them to the Syrian camp [Vulgate: “into the camp of the Syrians”], saying: “Go and see.”

They went after them as far as the Jordan. Behold, the whole road was full of clothing and vessels which the Syrians had thrown away when they were thrown into confusion. The messengers returned and reported this [Note: The Veronese manuscript adds “to the king,” which is found not only in the Hebrew text but also in the Vulgate manuscripts].

The people went out and plundered the camp of the Syrians. Thus a measure of fine flour was sold for one stater [Hebrew: *shekel*], and two measures of barley for one stater [Hebrew: *shekel*], according to the word of the Lord.

The king appointed that officer, upon whose hand he leaned [manuscript: “had leaned”], at the gate. The crowd trampled him at the entrance of the gate [Hebrew: “the people at the gate”], and he died, in accordance with what the man of God had said when the king had come down to him.

It happened according to the word of the man of God which he had spoken to the king when he said: “Two measures of barley will be sold for one stater [Hebrew: *shekel*], and a measure of fine flour for one stater [Hebrew: *shekel*], at this same time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria”—when that officer had answered the man of God and said: “Even if the Lord should make sluices in heaven, could what you say come to pass?” [Hebrew: “Behold, the Lord will make sluices in heaven. Can what I say come to pass?”]

He had said to him: “You shall see it with your eyes, but you shall not eat of it.” And so it happened to him as had been foretold: the people trampled him at the gate, and he died.

### [Chapter VIII]

Elisha spoke to the woman whose son he had restored to life, saying: “Rise, go—you and your household—and reside wherever you can find a place, for the Lord has summoned a famine, and it will come upon the land for seven years.”

[Note: [Col. 0735D] The Hebrew words *seba sanim* signify both “seven years” and “many years”; for *seba*, or *sabee*, means “seven,” “oath,” or “abundance.” An abundance of years, which is not expressed in the Latin wording [Col. 0736D], denotes spans of many days. Jerome therefore rendered *seba sanim* well here in Latin both as “many days” and as “seven years.” MART.]

She rose and acted according to the word of the man of God [Hebrew: “man of God”]. She went with her household and resided in the land of the Philistines for many days [Hebrew: “seven years”].

When the seven years had ended, the woman returned from the land of the Philistines and went out to appeal to the king on behalf of her house and her fields [Hebrew: “her field”]. The king was speaking with Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, and said: “Tell me all the great things that Elisha has done.”

While he was telling the king how he had raised the dead man [variant: “how he raised the dead man”], the woman whose son he had restored to life appeared, crying out to the king on behalf of her house and her fields [Hebrew: “her field”].

Gehazi said: “My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is her son, whom Elisha restored to life.” The king questioned the woman, and she related everything to him.

The king gave her one eunuch and said: “Restore to her everything that is hers, and all the revenues of the fields [Hebrew: “the field”], from the day on which she left the land until the present.”

### [T. CXXXVIII]

Elisha also came to Damascus. Ben-hadad, king of Syria, was ill. They reported to him, saying: “The man of God has come here.”

The king said to Hazael: “Take gifts with you [Hebrew: ‘in your hand’], go to meet the man of God, and consult the Lord through him, saying: ‘Can I recover [Hebrew: ‘Can I live’] from this illness of mine?’”

So Hazael went to meet him, carrying gifts with him [Hebrew: “in his hand”], all the good things of Damascus, forty camel-loads. When he stood before him, he said: “Your son Ben-hadad, king of Syria, has sent me to you, saying: ‘Can I recover [Hebrew: ‘Can I live’] from this illness of mine?’”

Elisha said to him: “Go and tell him: ‘You will recover [Hebrew: ‘You will live’].’ But the Lord has shown me that he will certainly die.”

He remained with him, and his face became flushed with agitation; and the man of God wept. Hazael said: “Why is my lord weeping?”

He replied: “Because I know what evils you will do to the children of Israel. You will burn their fortified cities [Hebrew: “fortresses”] with fire; you will kill their young men with the sword [manuscript: “their beasts”]; you will dash their little ones to pieces; and you will rip open their pregnant women.”

Hazael said: “What indeed is your servant—a dog—that I should do this great thing?”

### [T. CXXXIX]

Elisha said: “The Lord has shown me that you will be king of Syria.”

When he had departed from Elisha, he came to his lord. The latter said to him: “What did Elisha say to you?”

He replied: “He said to me: ‘You will recover your health’ [Hebrew: ‘You will live’].”

[Note: The Veronese manuscript reads *recipies* (“you will recover”), closer to the Greek *zēse* (“you will live”). The Hebrew has the second person, as do the printed Latin editions. The same manuscript soon reads *sagulum* instead of *stragulum*, a reading I do not reject. An old marginal note adds *opertorium* (“covering”); a much more recent hand adds: “Others read *stragulum*, that is, a covering for a royal bed, woven with remarkable variety; or *sagulum*, a short covering made of coarse wool.”]

### [T. CXL]

On the following day, Hazael took a covering, soaked it with water, and spread it over his face. When he died, Hazael reigned in his place.

### [T. CXLI]

In the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, and of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, Joram son of Jehoshaphat became king of Judah.

He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. He walked in the ways of the kings [manuscript: “king”] of Israel, as the house of Ahab had walked, for Ahab’s daughter was his wife. He did what was evil before the Lord [Hebrew: “in the eyes of the Lord”].

But the Lord did not wish to destroy Judah, because of David his servant, just as he had promised him, to give him a lamp and to give one to his sons for all days.

In his days Edom rebelled [Hebrew: “transgressed”] against Judah, so as not to remain under Judah, and appointed a king for itself. Joram went to Seir, and all the chariots were with him. He rose by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him, as well as the commanders of the chariots; but the people fled to their tents.

Thus Edom rebelled [Hebrew: “transgressed”] against Judah, so as not to remain under Judah, to this day. At that time Libnah also rebelled [Hebrew: “transgressed”].

### [T. CXLII]

The rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

Joram slept with his ancestors and was buried with them in the city of David. His son Ahaziah reigned in his place.

In the twelfth year of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah son of Joram, king of Judah, became king. Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Athaliah, daughter of Omri, king of Israel.

He walked in the ways of the house of Ahab and did what was evil before the Lord [Hebrew: “in the eyes of the Lord”], like the house of Ahab, for he was related by marriage to the house of Ahab.

### [T. CXLIII]

He went with Joram son of Ahab to fight against Hazael, king of Syria, at Ramoth-gilead [manuscript: “Ramath-gilead”]. The Syrians wounded Joram, and he returned to be treated at Jezreel, because the Syrians had wounded him while he was fighting against Hazael, king of Syria, at Ramah [Vulgate: “Ramoth”].

Ahaziah son of Joram, king of Judah, went down to visit Joram son of Ahab at Jezreel, because he was ill there [Note: The Veronese manuscript omits “there.” The Hebrew has “he himself.”]

### [T. CXLIV, Chapter IX]

Elisha the prophet summoned one of the sons of the prophets and said to him: “Gird your loins, take this small flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead.

“When you arrive there, you will see Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi [Hebrew: “Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi”]. Go in, rouse him from among his brothers, and bring him into an inner room.

“Take the small flask of oil, pour it over his head, and say: ‘Thus says the Lord: I have anointed you king over Israel.’

“Then open the door and flee; do not remain there.”

So the young man, the prophet’s boy [Hebrew: “the boy, the boy of the prophet”], went to Ramoth-gilead and entered there [Note: The corrector of the standard text deletes *there* and restores the reading according to the Hebrew: “and he entered, and behold, the commanders of the army …” We have not followed these corrections for the reason given above. The Veronese manuscript also omits *there*. The word is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the other books, except the Vulgate Latin manuscripts. The corrector of the standard text, whom Martianaeus calls the “corrector,” also removed it from his copy].

Behold, the commanders of the army were sitting there. The prophet’s boy said: “I have a word for you, commander.”

Jehu said: “For which one of all of us?”

He said: “For you, commander.”

Jehu rose and entered the room [Hebrew: “house”]. The prophet’s boy poured the oil over his head and said: “Thus says the Lord, God of Israel: I have anointed you king over the people of the Lord, over Israel. You shall strike down the house of Ahab your lord, so that I may avenge upon Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets and the blood of all the servants of the Lord.

“I shall destroy the entire house of Ahab. I shall cut off from Ahab everyone who urinates against the wall, and the confined and the abandoned [Hebrew: “the forsaken”] in Israel. I shall make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah.

“Dogs shall eat Jezebel in the field of Jezreel, and no one shall bury her [Hebrew: absent].”

He opened the door and fled.

Jehu went out to the servants of his lord, who said to him: “Is everything all right [Hebrew: ‘Is there peace’]? Why did this madman come to you?”

He said to them: “You know the man and what he said, do you not?”

They replied: “That is false; tell us instead.”

He said to them: “He said this and that to me, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord: I have anointed you king over Israel.’”

Then each of them hurriedly took his cloak and placed it beneath his feet, making a kind of tribunal, and they sounded the trumpet and said: “Jehu has become king.”

### [T. CXLV]

Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi conspired [Hebrew: “rebelled”] against Joram. Joram had been besieging Ramoth-gilead—he and all Israel—against Hazael, king of Syria. He had returned to be treated at Jezreel because of his wounds, since the Syrians had struck him while he was fighting against Hazael, king of Syria.

Jehu said: “If this is your will, let no one escape from the city as a fugitive, lest he go and report it in Jezreel.”

He mounted his chariot and set out for Jezreel. Joram was ill there, and Ahaziah, king of Judah, had gone down to visit Joram.

The watchman who stood on the tower of Jezreel saw Jehu’s company approaching and said: “I see a company.”

Joram said: “Take a chariot and send it to meet them, and let the man who goes say: ‘Is everything all right?’ [Hebrew: ‘Is there peace?’]”

The man who had mounted the chariot [Hebrew: “horse”] went to meet him and said: “Thus says the king: ‘Is everything peaceful?’ [Hebrew: ‘Is there peace?’]”

Jehu said: “What have you to do with peace? Turn around and follow me.”

The watchman reported: “The messenger reached them, but he is not returning.”

He sent a second chariot with horses. It reached them and said: “Thus says the king: ‘Is there peace?’”

Jehu said: “What have you to do with peace? Turn around and follow me.”

The watchman reported: “He reached them, but he is not returning. The manner of driving is like the driving of Jehu son of Nimshi, for he drives furiously.”

Joram said: “Harness the chariot” [Hebrew: absent].

They harnessed his chariot [manuscript: “they harnessed the chariot”], and Joram, king of Israel, and Ahaziah, king of Judah, went out, each in his own chariot. They went out to meet Jehu and found him in the field of Naboth the Jezreelite.

When Joram saw Jehu, he said: “Is there peace, Jehu?”

He replied: “What peace? The fornications of Jezebel your mother and her many sorceries still flourish.”

Joram turned his hand [Hebrew: “hands”], and as he fled said to Ahaziah: “Treachery, Ahaziah!” [Note: The Veronese manuscript repeats the word “treachery,” which all the other books omit.]

### [T. CXLVI]

Jehu drew his bow and struck Joram between the shoulders [Hebrew: “arms”]. The arrow went out through his heart, and he immediately collapsed in his chariot.

Jehu said to Badacer the commander: “Take him and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite. For I remember that when you and I were sitting in the chariot [Hebrew: “in the coupled chariots”] and following Ahab his father, the Lord pronounced this burden upon him, saying: ‘Surely I will repay you in this field for the blood of Naboth and for the blood of his sons, whom I saw yesterday, says the Lord.’ Now therefore take him and throw him into the field, according to the word of the Lord.”

[Note: This name is written *Bedear* in the Canon, corrected according to the punctuation closest to the Masoretic tradition. All the other manuscript copies retain the original reading, namely *Badacer* or *Badacar*. It is likewise written in this way by Jerome in the *Book of Hebrew Names.]

### [T. CXLVII]

Ahaziah, king of Judah, seeing this [Hebrew: absent], fled by the road of the garden house. Jehu pursued him and said: “Strike this man also [manuscript: ‘strike’] in his chariot.”

They struck him on the ascent of Gur [Hebrew: “Gur”], which is beside Ibleam. He fled to Megiddo and died there.

[Note: [Col. 0739C] The words “and they struck him” are absent from the Veronese manuscript; this is further evidence of the distinctive character of its text, or of the Jerome translation which it presents. For neither the Hebrew text nor the closely adhering Chaldean has this sentence, which is derived entirely from the paraphrase of the Greek Septuagint: *Kai ge auton, kai epataxen auton pros tō harmati*, etc.—“This one also, and he struck him by the chariot,” etc. Moreover, we know that this passage scarcely, if at all, agrees with the very clear testimony of 2 Chronicles 22:9, which says that Ochozias was not killed here on the ascent of Gaber, but, after escaping as a fugitive to Megiddo and being secretly carried thence to Samaria, was finally found there by Jehu and killed. “And seeking Ochozias,” it says, “he seized him while he was hiding in Samaria, brought him to himself, and killed him.” Yet neither Martianaeus nor the scholiast edited by him noticed this addition in the Latin manuscripts.]

His servants placed him on his chariot [Hebrew: absent] and carried him to Jerusalem. They buried [Vulgate adds: “him”] him in his tomb with his ancestors in the city of David.

In the eleventh year of Joram son of Ahab [Note: In place of “reigned,” the Veronese manuscript reads “of the king.” In the margin of the manuscript a letter *R* is added, a mark used by ancient scribes for a reading regarded as doubtful or suspect; it advises that its authenticity be investigated in other copies. At first sight the reading seems indeed abnormal, merely a scribal error. Yet Lucas of Bruges attests that it belongs to older and better manuscripts, and that it is uniquely defensible by sufficiently good arguments, both in relation to itself and to the *Epanorthota*. Nor does it depart from the Hebrew text if one supposes that in Jerome’s time the text still lacked the Masoretic vowel-points, which he certainly did not know, and that other vowels were placed beneath the consonants than those now in use: read *Melech*, with a double segol, instead of qamets and pataḥ, or read *malach*. As for the name Ahaziah that follows, accept it as indeclinable, as it is in Hebrew: *Ahaziah*. Finally, take the conjunction “and he came,” either, with the aforementioned Lucas of Bruges, as serving only to turn the sentence, or as a temporal particle or adverb, as it frequently occurs. The meaning will be entirely clear and will differ in no respect from the historical truth presented by the Vulgate Latin books. The sense is that in the eleventh year of Joram son of Ahab, while Ahaziah was king of Judah, Jehu came to Jezreel. For it is the settled opinion of the interpreters that Ahaziah was brought into the partnership of the kingdom in this year of Joram, although he did not take possession of the government until the following, the twelfth year, as is clear from verse 25 of the preceding chapter.]

Ahaziah reigned over Judah, and Jehu came to Jezreel.

When Jezebel heard of his arrival, she painted her eyes with stibium [Note: In the margin of the Veronese manuscript, opposite this word, the same hand that copied the entire manuscript has written *callibles*. I believe this word, its letters worn away and partly truncated by age, should be restored by the scribe as *Calliblepharon*. This is the Greek *kalliblépharon* (καλλιβλέφαρον), an eye ointment which Pliny mentions in Book XXIII, chapter 6. Perhaps an ancient Latin translator before Jerome used this term for stibium].

She adorned her head, looked through the window as Jehu entered the gate, and said: “Can there be peace for Zimri, who killed his lord?” [Hebrew: “Is there peace for Zimri, who killed his lord?”]

### [T. CXLVIII]

Jehu raised his face toward the window and said [Note: The Hebrew expression *mi itti*, “who is with me? who?” is rendered by Jerome according to the sense of Scripture: “Who is that?” The Septuagint adhered to the words at this point: “Who are you?” (Τίς εἶ σύ), “Who are you?”—as though the Hebrew read *mi att*. Yet it has the form used by the Syrians. Moreover, *itti* is often used in place of *immi*, “with me”; hence the scholiast’s reading: “Who is with me?”]:

“Who is that?” [Hebrew: “Who is mine?”]

Two or three eunuchs leaned toward him. He said to them: “Throw her down.”

They threw her down, and the wall was spattered with blood; the horses’ hooves [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “the hooves of the horses which trampled her,” a reading closer to the Arabic interpreter than the others] trampled her.

When he had entered and eaten and drunk [Note: The same manuscript reads: “and when he had drunk, he said: Go, look …”], he said: “Go and see that accursed woman and bury her, for she is a king’s daughter.”

When they went to bury her, they found nothing except her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands. They returned and reported to him [manuscript omits “to him”].

Jehu said: “This is the word of the Lord which he spoke through his servant Elijah, saying: ‘In the field of Jezreel, dogs shall eat the flesh of Jezebel, and the flesh of Jezebel shall be like dung upon the face of the ground [Hebrew: “field”] in the field of Jezreel, so that passersby will say: Is this that Jezebel?’” [Hebrew: “so that they will not say: ‘This is Jezebel.’”]

[Note: Jerome expressed the sense, but the scholiast, with all the other interpreters, clings closely to the wording and consistently renders it: “so that they will not say, ‘This is Jezebel.’” The Hebrew reads *aser lo jemeru zoth Jezabel*, “so that they will not say: ‘This is Jezebel.’” These words must be understood in the sense that in French one might say: “And will those who pass by not say, ‘Is that Jezebel?’”]

### (Chapter XX)

Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. Therefore Jehu wrote letters [Hebrew: “a book”] and sent them to the nobles of the city [Hebrew: “Jezreel”], to the elders, and to the guardians of Ahab’s children, saying:

“As soon as you receive this letter [Hebrew: “book”], since you have your lord’s sons, chariots, horses, fortified cities, and weapons, choose the best and the one who pleases you from among your lord’s sons [Vulgate adds: “and him”], place him on his father’s throne, and fight for the house of your lord.”

They were exceedingly afraid and said: “Behold, two kings could not stand before him; how then will we be able to resist?”

So they sent the steward of the palace, the prefect of the city [Vulgate: “the stewards and prefects”], the elders, and the guardians to Jehu, saying: “We are your servants. Whatever you command, we shall do. We shall not appoint a king for ourselves [Hebrew: ‘a man for ourselves’]. Do whatever pleases you.” [T. CXLIX]

He wrote them a second letter [Hebrew: “book”], saying: “If you are mine and obey me, take the heads of your lord’s sons and come to me at this same hour tomorrow in Jezreel.”

The king’s sons, seventy men, were being raised in the homes of the city’s nobles. When the letter [Hebrew: “book”] reached them, they took the king’s sons, killed the seventy men, placed their heads in baskets, and sent them to him in Jezreel.

A messenger came and reported to him: “They have brought the heads of the king’s sons.”

He replied: “Place them in two heaps beside the entrance of the gate until morning.”

When it became light, he went out, stood, and said to all the people: “You are righteous. If I conspired [Hebrew: ‘rebelled’] against my lord and killed him, who struck down all these?

“Know now that none of the words of the Lord has fallen to the ground, which the Lord spoke concerning the house of Ahab; the Lord has done what he spoke through his servant Elijah.”

Jehu struck down all who remained of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, as well as all his nobles, acquaintances, and priests, until no remnant of him remained.

He rose and went to Samaria.

### [T. CL]

When he came to the shepherds’ enclosure [Hebrew: “folds”] on the road, he found the brothers of Ahaziah, king of Judah. He said to them: “Who are you?”

They replied: “We are the brothers of Ahaziah, and we have come down to greet the sons of the king and the sons of the queen” [manuscript omits “the sons”].

He said: “Seize them alive.”

When they had seized them alive, they slaughtered them in the cistern beside the enclosure [Hebrew: “folds”], forty-two men, and he left none of them alive [manuscript: “they left none”].

When he had gone from there, he met Jehonadab son of Rechab coming to meet him and blessed him. He said to him: “Is your heart right, as my heart is with your heart?”

Jehonadab said: “It is.”

“If it is,” he said, “give me your hand.”

He gave him his hand [Note: The Veronese manuscript, like the Hebrew, omits the particle “to him”]. Jehu lifted him up to himself into the chariot and said to him: “Come with me and see my zeal for the Lord.”

He had him placed in his chariot and brought him to Samaria. He struck down everyone who remained of Ahab in Samaria, down to the last [Hebrew: “to destruction”], according to the word of the Lord which he had spoken through Elijah.

Jehu gathered all the people and said to them [manuscript: “to him”]: “Ahab served Baal little; Jehu shall serve him more.”

### [T. CLI]

“Now therefore summon to me all the prophets of Baal, all his servants, and all his priests. Let no one fail to come, for I have a great sacrifice for Baal; whoever is absent shall not live.”

Jehu acted deceitfully in this way, in order to destroy the worshipers of Baal [manuscript and Vulgate: “to disperse”]. He said: “Sanctify a solemn day [Hebrew: ‘an assembly’] for Baal.”

He summoned and sent throughout all the borders of Israel, and all the servants of Baal came. Not one was left who did not come.

They entered the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of Baal, and the house of Baal was filled from end to end.

He said to those who were over the garments [Note: The Hebrew and the Veronese manuscript have the singular: “to the one who was over the garments”]: “Bring out garments for all the servants of Baal.”

They brought garments out to them [manuscript: “to him”].

Jehu and Jehonadab son of Rechab entered the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of Baal and said to the worshipers of Baal: “Search and see that no one among you is a servant of the Lord, but that only servants of Baal are here.”

They entered to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Jehu had stationed eighty men outside and had said to them: “Whoever lets one of these men whom I have delivered into your hands escape—his life shall answer for that man’s life.”

### [T. CLII]

When the burnt offering had been completed, Jehu commanded his soldiers and commanders: “Enter and strike them down, so that no one escapes” [Note: The Veronese manuscript and the other Vulgate books, together with the Hebrew text, do not have the word “so that.”]

They struck them with the sword. The soldiers and commanders threw them out, went into the city of the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of Baal, brought out the statue [Hebrew: “the pillars”] from Baal’s shrine, burned it, and smashed it.

They also demolished the shrine of Baal and made latrines in it, as they remain to this day.

Thus Jehu eradicated Baal from Israel.

Nevertheless, he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin; he did not abandon the golden calves that were in Bethel and Dan.

The Lord said to Jehu: “Because you have acted diligently in doing what was right and pleasing in my eyes, and have done everything that was in my heart against the house of Ahab, your sons shall sit upon the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.”

But Jehu did not take care to walk with all his heart in the law of the Lord, the God of Israel. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam, who had caused Israel to sin.

In those days the Lord began to grow weary of Israel. Hazael struck them throughout all the borders of Israel, from the Jordan toward the eastern region: the whole land of Gilead, Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh, from Aroer, which is above the torrent [Col. 0743A] of the Arnon, and Gilead and Bashan.

### [T. CLIII]

The rest of the acts of Jehu, all that he did, and his valor, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

Jehu slept with his ancestors, and they buried him in Samaria. His son Jehoahaz [manuscript: “Joachaz”] reigned in his place.

The days during which Jehu reigned over Israel were twenty-eight years, in Samaria.

## [Chapter XI]

But Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah, seeing that her son was dead, arose and killed all the royal offspring. Jehosheba, however, the daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash, the son of Ahaziah, and stole him away from among the king’s sons who were being killed, together with his nurse, from the bedchamber; and she hid him from Athaliah’s presence, so that he would not be killed. He remained with her secretly in the house of the Lord for six years; meanwhile Athaliah reigned over the land. [Col. 0743B]

[T. CLIV.] In the seventh year Jehoiada sent for the commanders of hundreds [Note: The Verona manuscript has “the commanders of hundreds and the soldiers,” omitting the words “and the officers,” which the other Latin Vulgate books likewise do not retain. The Hebrew has words meaning “the leaders of the commanders of hundreds, the officers, and the runners,” although the first circumlocution of the three words signifies “commanders of hundreds” in a single word. Thus the ancient Greek translators: Aquila, τοὺς ἄρχοντας τῶν ἑκατοντάδων, “the leaders of the hundreds”; Symmachus, τοὺς ἑκατοντάρχους, “the commanders of hundreds,” rendering the three words with one word.] and the officers and the soldiers, and brought them to himself in the house of the Lord [Note: Again, with the Vulgate, the same manuscript reads “into the temple of the Lord”; the Hebrew has an unreadable or omitted form in the supplied text.]. He made a covenant with them, and adjuring them in the house of the Lord, he showed them the king’s son. He instructed them, saying:

“This is what you must do: One third of you shall enter on the Sabbath and guard the watch of the king’s house. Another third shall be at the Gate of Sur [Ms. Sir], and another third shall be at the gate behind the quarters of the shield-bearers [Heb. runners]; and you shall guard the watch of the house [Heb. the watch of the Lord …] of Messa. But two parts of you, all who go out on the Sabbath, shall guard the watches of the house of the Lord around the king. You shall surround him, each with weapons in his hand; and if anyone enters within the temple enclosure, let him be killed. You shall remain with the king as he enters and leaves.”

The commanders of hundreds did everything that Jehoiada the priest had commanded them [Heb. does not have this]; and each took his men, those who entered on the Sabbath together with those who went out on the Sabbath, and they came to Jehoiada the priest. He gave them the spears and the weapons of King David that were in the house of the Lord. Each stood with his weapon in his hand, from the right side of the temple to the left side of the altar and the building, around the king.

Then he brought out the king’s son and placed the diadem and the testimony upon his head [Note: More closely following the Hebrew, the Verona manuscript and the Vulgate books read “upon him.”]. They made him king and anointed him; and, clapping their hands, they said: “Long live the king!”

Athaliah heard the sound of the running [Col. 0743D] people. She went out to the crowds [Heb. to the people] in the house of the Lord and saw the king standing upon the tribunal according to custom, with the singers and trumpets [Heb. flutes] [Col. 0744A] beside him [Note: The Verona copyist, placing an obelus in the margin, strikes out this word and substitutes “beside.”], and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing the trumpets [Heb. flutes]. She tore her garments and cried out: “Conspiracy, conspiracy” [Heb. “Rebellion, rebellion”!]

Jehoiada the priest [Note: The same manuscript and the Vulgate copies omit “the priest,” although the name is added in the Hebrew.] commanded the commanders of hundreds who were over the army and said to them: “Lead her outside the temple enclosures, and whoever follows her shall be struck with the sword.” For the priest had said: “She must not be killed in the temple [Heb. house] of the Lord.”

They laid hands on her and drove her along the way by which the horses entered, beside the palace [Heb. house]; and she was killed there. Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people, that the people should be the Lord’s, and also between the king and the people.

All the people of the land entered the temple [Heb. house] of Baal and demolished his altars and shattered his images completely. They also killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, before the altar [Heb. altars]. And the priest appointed guards over the house of the Lord.

He took the commanders of hundreds, the Cherethites and Pelethites, the troops, and all the people of the land [Heb. “He took the commanders of hundreds, the runners, the officers, and all the people of the land”]; and they led the king down from the house of the Lord. They came by way of the gate of the shield-bearers [Heb. runners] into the palace [Heb. house of the king], and he sat upon the throne of the kings.

All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. [T. CLV.] Athaliah, however, was killed by the sword in the king’s house. Joash was seven years old when he began to reign.

## [Chapter XII]

In the seventh year of Jehu, Joash became king; he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah [Ms. Sebai], from Beersheba.

[T. CLVI.] Joash did what was right before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord] all the days during which Jehoiada the priest instructed him. Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places; for the people were still sacrificing and burning incense on the high places.

Joash said to the priests: “All the money of the sanctuary [Note: Again, the Verona manuscript agrees with the Vulgate books in reading “of the holy things” instead of “of the sanctuary.” The Hebrew literally has “of holy things.”], which is brought into the temple [Heb. house] of the Lord by those who pass by, the money offered for the price of a person, and all the money which they voluntarily and freely bring into the temple [Heb. house] of the Lord, let the priests receive according to their order, and let them repair whatever damage to the house they see to be in need of repair [Note: Following the Verona manuscript and the Vulgate books, we have removed the preposition which Martianus had placed here. The Hebrew idiom and Symmachus’ Greek version, δεόμενον ἐπισκευῆς, “that which needs repair,” support this reading.].”

[T. CLVII.] Yet until the twenty-third year of King Joash the priests did not repair the damage to the temple. King Joash summoned Jehoiada the high priest and the priests and said to them: “Why are you not repairing the damage to the temple [Heb. house]? Therefore do not take any more money according to your order, but hand it over for the repair of the temple [Heb. house].”

[T. CLVIII.] So the priests were forbidden to receive money from the people any longer [Note: The Scholiast is mistaken. The Hebrew does not have that exception; rather, the connective particle should be read as follows: “And the priests were forbidden to receive money from the people and to repair the damage to the house.” All the other translators agree with this reading against our Scholiast, who likewise did not sufficiently attend to the sequence of the discourse. For from the preceding verse it is clear, if I am not mistaken, that the priests were forbidden both to receive the money and to carry out the repair already mentioned—or rather, they were forbidden the duty of this repair, which they seemed to have discharged with no little negligence. MART. [Col. 0746D] —Martianus himself corrects the Scholiast for failing to attend to the sequence of the discourse and for wanting that exception to be a merely connective particle. We have said above at greater length what we think of his readings. For the meaning of this passage, consult the interpreters, if you wish.] and to repair the damage to the house [Heb. unless for repairing the damage to the house].

Then Jehoiada the high priest took one chest, opened an opening in its top, and placed it beside the altar, on the right side of those entering the house of the Lord. The priests who guarded the doors put into it all the money brought into the temple [Heb. house] of the Lord.

When they saw that there was a great amount of money in the chest, the king’s scribe and the high priest went up, poured out, and counted the money found in the house of the Lord. They delivered it by number and measure into the hands of those who supervised the masons of the house of the Lord. They spent it on the woodworkers and masons who worked in the house of the Lord and repaired its damage; on those who cut stones; and on the purchase of timber and quarried stones. Thus the repair of the house of the Lord was completed in every matter requiring expenditure to strengthen the house.

Nevertheless, basins for the temple [Heb. house] of the Lord, forks, censers, trumpets [Heb. flutes], and every vessel of gold and silver were not made from the money brought into the temple of the Lord. For it was given to those who carried out the work, so that they might repair the temple [Heb. house] of the Lord.

[T. CLIX.] No account was rendered to those men who received the money to distribute it to the craftsmen, because they dealt with it in good faith [Heb. because they acted faithfully].

[T. CLX.] The money for guilt offerings and the money for sin offerings was not brought into the temple [Heb. house] of the Lord, because it belonged to the priests.

Then Hazael, king of Syria, went up and fought against Gath, and captured it. He turned his face to go up against Jerusalem. Therefore Joash, king of Judah, took all the consecrated things which Jehoshaphat, Joram, and Ahaziah, his fathers, kings of Judah, had consecrated, and those which he himself had offered; all the gold [Heb. silver] that could be found in the treasuries of the temple [Heb. house] of the Lord and in the palace of the king [Heb. house of the king]; and he sent them to Hazael, king of Syria. Then he withdrew from Jerusalem.

The rest of the deeds of Joash and all that he did—is it not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

[T. CLXI.] His servants arose, conspired [Heb. rebelled] among themselves, and struck Joash in the house of Millo, at the descent toward Sela. For Jozachar, son of Shimeath, and Jozabad, son of Shomer, his servants, struck him; and he died. They buried him with his fathers in the City of David, and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.

## [T. CLXII, Chapter XIII]

In the twenty-third year of Joash, son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned seventeen years. He did evil before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord] and followed the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin; he did not turn away from them.

The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he delivered them into the hand of Hazael, king of Syria, and into the hand of Ben-hadad, son of Hazael, throughout all the days.

Jehoahaz entreated the face of the Lord, and the Lord heard him; for he saw the distress of Israel, because the king of Syria had oppressed them. The Lord gave Israel a savior, and they were delivered from the hand of Syria. The children of Israel dwelt in their tents as yesterday and the day before.

Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin; they walked in them [Vulg. “but they walked in them”; Heb. “he walked in them”]. Indeed, the sacred grove also remained in Samaria.

Only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand infantry remained to Jehoahaz from the people [Note: The Verona manuscript counts two hundred instead of ten chariots. I do not know, however, from what text or authority it did this; for the Arabic version, which has more than the others, adds only another ten and counts twenty.]. For the king of Syria had destroyed them and reduced them like dust on the threshing floor [Heb. does not have this].

The rest of the deeds of Jehoahaz and all that he did, as well as his strength [Vulg. omits “as well as”], are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

[T. CLXIII.] Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria; and Joash his son reigned in his place.

In the thirty-seventh year of Joash, king of Judah, Joash, son of Jehoahaz, became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned sixteen years. He did what was evil [Ms. and Vulg. “is evil”] in the sight of the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord]; he did not turn away from all the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin, but walked in them.

[T. CLXIV.] The rest of the deeds of Joash and all that he did, including his strength and how he fought against Amaziah, king of Judah—is it not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

Joash slept with his fathers, and Jeroboam sat upon his throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.

[T. CLXV.] Now Elisha was suffering from the illness by which he also died. Joash, king of Israel, went down to him and wept before him, saying: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!”

Elisha said to him: “Bring a bow and arrows.” When he had brought him a bow and arrows, Elisha said to the king of Israel: “Place your hand upon the bow.” When he had placed his hand there, Elisha laid his hands upon the king’s hands and said: “Open the eastern window.” When he had opened it, Elisha said: “Shoot.” And he shot.

Elisha said: “The arrow of the Lord’s salvation, the arrow of salvation against Syria! You shall strike Syria at Aphek until you destroy it [Heb. until its destruction].”

Then he said: “Take the arrows.” When he had taken them, he said to him again: “Strike the ground with an arrow” [Heb. does not have “with an arrow”]. When he had struck it three times and stopped, the man of God became angry with him and said: “If you had struck five or six or seven times, you would have struck Syria until its destruction. But now you will strike it only three times.”

[T. CLXVI.] Thus Elisha died, and they buried him. In that same year bands of Moabites entered the land. As some men were burying a man [Heb. a man], they saw the raiders and threw the corpse [Heb. the man] into the tomb of Elisha.

It went [Heb. “And it went”] and touched the bones of Elisha; and the man came back to life [Heb. the man] and stood upon his feet.

So Hazael, king of Syria, oppressed [Heb. crushed] Israel throughout all the days of Jehoahaz. But the Lord had mercy on them and turned back toward them because of his covenant which he had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He did not wish to destroy them or cast them away completely, even to the present time.

Hazael, king of Syria, died, and Ben-hadad his son reigned in his place. Joash, son of Jehoahaz, took from the hand of Ben-hadad, son of Hazael, the cities which he had taken from the hand of Joash’s father Jehoahaz by right of war. Joash struck him three times and restored the cities of Israel.

## [T. CLXVII, Chapter XIV]

In the second year of Joash, son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah, became king.

[T. CLXVIII.] He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jehoaddan, from Jerusalem.

He did what was right before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord], though not like David his father. He did everything that Joash his father had done, except that he did not remove the high places [Heb. nevertheless the high places were not removed]. For the people were still sacrificing and burning incense [Vulg. adds “incense”] on the high places.

[T. CLXIX.] When he had secured the kingdom, he struck down his servants who had killed his father the king. But he did not kill the sons of those who had killed him, in accordance with what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, as the Lord commanded, saying: “Fathers shall not die for sons, nor sons die for fathers; but each person shall die for his own sin.”

He struck Edom in the Valley of Salt—ten thousand men—and captured Sela in battle; and he called its name Joktheel [Ms. Jecethel], even to the present day.

Then Amaziah sent messengers to Joash, son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying: “Come, and let us look one another in the face.”

Joash, king of Israel, sent back to Amaziah, king of Judah, saying:

“The thornbush of Lebanon sent to the cedar that is in Lebanon, saying: ‘Give your daughter to my son as a wife.’ But the beasts of the forest that are in Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thornbush” [Heb. “The beast of the field that is in Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thornbush”].

“Because you struck Edom, you have prevailed, and your heart has lifted you up. Be content with your glory and remain in your house. Why provoke evil, so that you may fall, you and Judah with you?”

Amaziah did not listen.

[T. CLXX.] Joash, king of Israel, went up, and he and Amaziah, king of Judah, saw one another at Beth-shemesh, a town of Judah. Judah was struck down before Israel, and everyone fled to his tent.

Joash, king of Israel, captured Amaziah, king of Judah, son of Joash, son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh. He brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem, from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate, four hundred cubits.

He took all the gold, silver, and all the vessels found in the house of the Lord, in the treasuries of the king [Heb. and in the treasuries of the king’s house], and hostages; and he returned to Samaria.

The rest of the deeds of Joash, which he did, and his strength with which he fought against Amaziah, king of Judah—is it not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

[T. CLXXI.] Joash slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel; and Jeroboam his son reigned in his place.

Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after Joash, son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, had died [Note: Here too the Verona manuscript greatly increases the number, assigning twenty-five years to Amaziah instead of Joash’s fifteen. All the other books contradict it. A similar exaggeration of years occurs below; there we investigate its cause.].

The rest of the deeds of Amaziah—is it not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

A conspiracy [Heb. rebellion] was formed against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish.

[T. CLXXII.] They sent after him to Lachish and killed him there. They carried him back on horses, and he was buried in Jerusalem with his fathers in the City of David.

All the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah. He built Elath [Ms. Achilam] and restored it to Judah after the king had slept with his fathers.

[T. CLXXIII.] In the fifteenth year of Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam, son of Joash, king of Israel, became king in Samaria and reigned forty-one years. He did what was evil before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord]. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.

[T. CLXXIV.] He restored the borders of Israel, from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the Lord, the God of Israel, which he spoke through his servant Jonah, son of Amittai [Note: The word , hannabi, “the prophet,” in Hebrew is ambiguous and can be referred either to Jonah or to his father Amittai. All the Latin manuscripts read “the son of Amittai the prophet.” The corrector of the Canon placed in the text “the son of Amittai the prophet,” which clearly shows that he took it from the Scholiast and that a corruption exists in Jerome’s translation. The Hebrews report that Jonah was the son of the widow of Zarephath, whom the prophet Elijah raised from the dead. If that is true, Jonah was not the son of a prophet—unless, perhaps, he became the son of a prophet when he came back to life at Elijah’s prayer. Consult the preface to St. Jerome’s Commentary on Jonah, where he repeats this entire passage according to the Old Latin translation, which differs considerably in wording from the one Nobilius published with the Greek text of the Septuagint. MART. —The Scholiast, and the corrector of the Canon who follows his footsteps, as Martianus calls him, depart still farther from the truth. Here the famous prophet Jonah is designated, the son of Amittai from Galilee, of the tribe of Zebulun, from the city of Gath-hepher. If no prophecies concerning Jeroboam’s victories are mentioned in his prophecy, it is equally reasonable to believe that not everything he wrote has come down to us.].

He was from Gath [Heb. from Gath-hepher], which is in Ophrah. The Lord saw that the affliction of Israel was exceedingly bitter, and that they had been consumed down to the confined and imprisoned and last man, with no one to help Israel [Heb. down to the imprisoned and abandoned]. The Lord had not said that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven; therefore he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam, son of Joash.

The rest of the deeds of Jeroboam, all that he did, and his strength with which he fought, and how he restored Damascus and Hamath to Israel [Heb. to Judah in Israel]—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

[T. CLXXV.] Jeroboam slept with his fathers, the kings of Israel, and Zechariah his son reigned in his place.

## [T. CLXXVI, Chapter XV]

In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam, king of Israel, Azariah, son of Amaziah, king of Judah, became king. He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jecholiah [Ms. Jecelia], from Jerusalem.

He did what was pleasing before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord], according to all that Amaziah his father had done. Nevertheless, he did not demolish the high places [Heb. the high places were not demolished]; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.

The Lord struck [Heb. afflicted] the king, and he was leprous until the day of his death. He lived in a separate house, while Jotham, the king’s son, governed the palace [Heb. house] and judged the people of the land.

The rest of the deeds of Azariah and all that he did—is it not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

[T. CLXXVII.] Azariah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his ancestors in the City of David; and Jotham his son reigned in his place.

In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah, king of Judah, Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, became king over Israel in Samaria for six months. He did what was evil before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord], as his fathers had done; he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.

Shallum, son of Jabesh, conspired [Heb. rebelled] against him.

[T. CLXXVIII.] He struck him [Note: The Hebrew does not have “in Cablaam” with the preposition, but reads: va-yakkēhu Cabal am, that is, “And he struck him before the people,” or “publicly,” as Jerome translated very well; the Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic agree with him. The Septuagint has καὶ ἐπάταξαν αὐτόν Κεβλαάμ, “and they struck him at Ceblaam.” This gave the Canon’s Scholiast an opportunity for error: he supposed that Zechariah, king of Israel, had been struck in a place called Cablaam. But Cabal-am among the Hebrews means “with the people watching,” “before the people,” and so forth. MART.], publicly [Heb. at Cablaam], killed him, and reigned in his place.

The rest of the deeds of Zechariah—is it not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

This is the word of the Lord which he spoke to Jehu, saying: “Your sons shall sit upon the throne of Israel to the fourth generation” [Note: More correctly, in agreement with the Hebrew exemplar, the Verona manuscript omits “your.” It then has more: “shall sit upon the throne of Israel from you,” where again the Hebrew more closely reads “for you,” or “from you,” since it adds the word meaning “to you” or “of you.”].

And so it happened. Shallum, son of Jabesh, became king in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah, king of Judah, and reigned one month in Samaria.

[T. CLXXIX.] Manahem, son of Gaddi, went up from Tirzah, came to Samaria, and struck Shallum, son of Jabesh, in Samaria. He killed him and reigned in his place.

The rest of the deeds of Shallum and his conspiracy [Heb. rebellion], by which he laid an ambush [Heb. rebelled]—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

Then Manahem struck Tiphsah [Heb. Thiphsah] and all who were in it, as well as its territory from Tirzah. For they had refused to open [Note: In accordance with the Hebrew, the Verona manuscript omits “to him” here. It likewise omits “its” shortly afterward.]; he killed all its pregnant women and ripped them open [Heb. he killed everyone and ripped open its pregnant women].

In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah, king of Judah, Manahem, son of Gaddi, became king over Israel and reigned ten years in Samaria. He did what was evil before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord]; he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin, throughout all his days.

Pul, king of Assyria, came against Tirzah [Vulg. “the land”], and Manahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, so that he might be his ally and establish his kingdom [Heb. establish the kingdom in his hand]. Manahem imposed [Vulg. adds “upon him”] the silver upon all the powerful and wealthy men of Israel, so that each should give the king of Assyria fifty shekels of silver. Then the king of Assyria turned back and did not remain in the land [Note: The same manuscript reads “in Tirzah,” wrongly through the arbitrary choice of an ignorant copyist.].

The rest of the deeds of Manahem and all that he did—is it not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

[T. CLXXXI.] Manahem slept with his fathers, and Pekahiah [Heb. Pekahiah] his son reigned in his place.

In the fiftieth year of Azariah, king of Judah, Pekahiah, son of Manahem, became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned two years. He did what was evil before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord]; he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.

[T. CLXXXII.] Pekah, son of Remaliah, his officer, conspired [Heb. rebelled] against him, struck him in Samaria in the tower of the royal house, beside Argob and beside Arieh, together with fifty men [Heb. “men”] of the sons of the Gileadites, and killed him; and he reigned in his place.

The rest of the deeds of Pekahiah and all that he did—is it not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

In the fifty-second year of Azariah, king of Judah, Pekah, son of Remaliah, became king over Israel in Samaria and reigned twenty years. He did what was evil before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord]; he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.

In the days of Pekah, king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee—the whole land of Naphtali [Ms. Naphtalim]—and carried them away to Assyria.

[T. CLXXXIII.] Hoshea, son of Elah, conspired and laid an ambush [Heb.
