Hoshea, son of Elah, rebelled] against Pekah, son of Remaliah; he struck him and killed him, and reigned in his place in the twentieth year of Jotham, son of Uzziah [Note: A later hand in the Verona manuscript, here and below, altered “of Uzziah” to “of Azariah,” following the Greek exemplar.].

The rest of the deeds of Pekah and all that he did—is it not written [Heb. “behold, written”] in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

[T. CLXXXIV.] In the second year of Pekah, son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, became king. He was twenty-five years old [Heb. “a son of twenty-five years”] when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok.

He did what was pleasing before the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord]; he acted according to all that Uzziah his father had done. Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places [Heb. the high places were not removed]; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places. He built the highest gate of the house of the Lord.

The rest of the deeds of Jotham and all that he did [Heb. does not have “all”]—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

In those days the Lord began to send against Judah Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, son of Remaliah.

[T. CLXXXV.] Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David his father; and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.

## [Chapter XVI]

In the seventeenth year of Pekah, son of Remaliah, Ahaz, son of Jotham, king of Judah, became king. [Heb. “son”] Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was pleasing in the sight of the Lord [Heb. in the eyes of the Lord] his God [Vulg. adds “his”], as David his father had done.

But he walked in the way of the kings of Israel.

[T. CLXXXVI.] Moreover, he consecrated his own son, passing him through the fire according to the idols [Heb. abominations] of the nations which the Lord had destroyed before the children of Israel. He also sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every leafy tree.

Then Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to fight. When they besieged Ahaz, they were unable to overcome him.

At that time Rezin, king of Syria, restored Aila [Heb. Eleth] to Syria and drove the Jews out of Aila [Note: The Verona manuscript reads dejecit (“cast down”), though disjecit (“scattered”) would be preferable.]. The Edomites [Note: The Verona manuscript does not have “and the Syrians.” Not only the Hebrew text but all the other books omit this people here. Lucas Brugensis notes that this is a variant reading in the Hebrew archetype, arising from the similarity of the letters; hence the Hebrews write here “Aramim” but read “Edomim.” The latter word signifies Edomites; the former can in some fashion denote Syrians, although Syriac is usually written without the intervening waw. It is not likely, however, that Jerome approved both interpretations at once; the fidelity of our principal manuscript is therefore especially commendable, since it rejects the glossator’s addition.] and the Syrians came to Elath and dwelt there to the present day.

Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria [Ms. Syria], saying: “I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who have risen against me.”

When Ahaz had gathered the silver and gold that he could find in the house of the Lord and in the treasuries of the king, he sent gifts to the king of Assyria [Heb. “and in the treasuries of the king’s house, and he sent”]. He consented to his request. The king of Assyria went up against Damascus, devastated it, and carried its inhabitants away to Kir [Heb. Chira]; but he killed Rezin.

Ahaz went to meet Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria [Ms. “the king of Assyria”], at Damascus. When King Ahaz saw the altar at Damascus, he sent to Uriah the priest a model of it and a likeness according to all its workmanship.

[T. CLXXXVII.] Uriah the priest built the altar. According to everything that King Ahaz had commanded from Damascus, Uriah the priest did so until King Ahaz came from Damascus.

When the king came from Damascus, he saw the altar and venerated it. He went up and offered his burnt offerings and his sacrifice; he poured out his drink offerings and poured the blood of the peace offerings which he had offered upon the altar.

He moved the bronze altar, which stood before the Lord, away from the front of the temple, from the place of the altar and from the place of the temple of the Lord; and he placed it beside the altar, on the north [Heb. “The bronze altar, which stood before the Lord between the altar and the house of the Lord, he moved away from the front of the house; and he placed it beside the altar, on the north”].

[T. CLXXXVIII.] King Ahaz also commanded Uriah the priest, saying: “Offer upon the greater altar the morning burnt offering, the evening sacrifice, the king’s burnt offering and his sacrifice, the burnt offering of all the people of the land, their sacrifices and their drink offerings. Pour out upon it all the blood of the burnt offering and all the blood of the sacrifice. The bronze altar shall be ready for my decision.”

Uriah the priest did everything that King Ahaz had commanded.

King Ahaz removed [Heb. cut off] the carved bases and the basin that was upon them, and he took the Sea down from the bronze oxen that supported it; he placed it upon a pavement of stone.

He also changed the covered passage of the Sabbath which he had built in the temple [Note: In the plural, in agreement with the Hebrew text, the Verona manuscript reads “which they had built”] and the king’s outer entrance into the temple [Heb. house] of the Lord, because of the king of Assyria.

[T. CLXXXIX.] The rest of the deeds of Ahaz which he did—is it not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David; and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.

## [T. CXC, Chapter XVII]

In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned nine years. He did evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], but not as the kings of Israel who had been before him. Against him came Shalmaneser [Col. 0753B], king of the Assyrians, and Hoshea became his servant and paid him tribute [Hebrew: gifts]. But when the king of the Assyrians discovered that Hoshea, while attempting to rebel, had sent messengers to So [Note: [Col. 0753D] The Scholiast of the Canon here, in his customary manner, pronounces Samech with a z, which you will find nowhere in Jerome, who always wished the letter Samech to be pronounced as s. Thus he has *sua* for the Hebrew [term], which the Scholiast corruptly reads as *zo*. The Latin translator of the Chaldean paraphrase imitates the corrupt pronunciation of our Scholiasts; for he writes *zzo* for the Chaldean [form]. In several copies the Septuagint translated it as Segor, and in the Alexandrian [copy] as Soa. The Syriac has Sou or Sau, [Col. 0754D] and the Arabic has Saou. MART.] [Hebrew: to Zo], king of Egypt, so that he would no longer pay tribute [Hebrew: gifts] [Note: [Col. 0754D] Here, however, the Hebrew and the Veronese manuscript have the singular “tribute.”] to the king of the Assyrians, as he had been accustomed to do every year, he besieged him and sent him bound to prison. Then he overran the whole land, and, advancing against Samaria, besieged it for three years. In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of the Assyrians captured Samaria and transported Israel to Assyria. He settled them in Halah and in Habor, by the river [Hebrew: by the River] of Gozan, in the cities of the Medes.

## [T. CXCI]

Now this happened because the Israelites had sinned against the Lord their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt: they had worshiped foreign gods. They had walked according to the practices of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites and the kings of Israel, because they had acted in the same way.

And the Israelites covered over [Note: [Col. 0754D] Thus the Hebrew Canon of truth and the Veronese manuscript, as well as the very ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, no. 3, although it is read corruptly as having been corrected by an unskilled emendator. The others read “offended” or “provoked,” although the Hebrew has [the word] meaning “covered” and “concealed.” MART.] their Lord God with improper words, and built high places for themselves in all their cities, from the Tower of the Watchmen to the fortified city. They made for themselves statues [Hebrew: pillars] and sacred groves on every high hill and beneath every leafy tree. They burned incense there on the altars [Hebrew: high places], following the practice of the nations whom the Lord had removed from before them. They did very evil things, provoking the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0754D] The same manuscript omits these words.] They worshiped abominations concerning which the Lord had commanded [Manuscript: commanded] them not to do this thing.

The Lord testified against Israel and Judah through all the prophets and seers, saying: “Turn back from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and statutes, according to the whole law that I commanded your fathers, and as I sent it to you through the hand of my servants the prophets.” But they did not listen; they stiffened their necks like the necks of their fathers, who did not wish to obey [Hebrew: did not believe] the Lord their God.

They rejected his statutes and the covenant that he had made with their fathers, and the testimonies with which he had testified against them [Manuscript: admonished them]. They followed vanities [Hebrew: vanity], acted vainly, and followed the nations around them, concerning whom the Lord had commanded them not to act as those nations did.

They abandoned all the commandments of the Lord their God. They made for themselves two molten calves, sacred groves, and worshiped the entire host of heaven. They served Baal, consecrated [Manuscript adds: to him] their sons and daughters through fire, practiced divination [Col. 0754B] and augury, and gave themselves over to doing evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: sold themselves to do evil in the eyes of the Lord], in order to provoke him [Manuscript: they provoked him].

The Lord was exceedingly angry with Israel, and removed them from his sight; only the tribe of Judah remained. Yet Judah itself did not keep the commandments of the Lord its God, but walked in the errors of Israel, which Israel had committed. Therefore the Lord rejected all the descendants of Israel, afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of plunderers, until he had cast them away from his sight.

This began from the time when Israel was torn away from the house of David and they appointed Jeroboam son of Nebat as king. For Jeroboam separated Israel from the Lord and caused them to commit a great sin. The Israelites walked in all the sins of Jeroboam [Col. 0754C] that he had committed; they did not withdraw from them until the Lord removed Israel from his sight, as he had spoken through all his servants the prophets. Thus Israel was transported from its land to Assyria, even to this day.

## [T. CXCII]

The king of the Assyrians brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, and Avva [Manuscript: Havath], Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the Israelites. They took possession of Samaria and lived in its cities.

When they had begun to live there, they did not fear the Lord, and the Lord sent lions among them, which killed them. This was reported to the king of the Assyrians, and it was said: “The nations whom you transported and settled in the cities of Samaria do not know the statutes of the god of the land; therefore the Lord has sent lions among them [Col. 0754D] [Hebrew: does not have ‘the Lord’], and behold, they are killing them because they do not know the practice of the god of the land.”

The king of the Assyrians therefore commanded: “Take there one of the priests whom you brought away captive from that place, and let him go and live with them, and teach them the statutes of the god of the land.” So one of the priests who had been taken captive from Samaria came and lived in Bethel, and taught them how they should worship the Lord.

Each nation made its own god, and placed these gods in the shrines of the high places that the Samaritans had made, each nation in its own cities where they lived. The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth; the men of Cuth made Nergal; the men of Hamath made Ashima. The Avvites [Manuscript: Eveites] made Nibhaz and Tartak [Manuscript: Therthak]. Those from Sepharvaim burned their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim; nevertheless, they also worshiped the Lord.

They appointed from among the lowest people priests of the high places [Col. 0755B], and placed them in the shrines of the high places [Manuscript: boundaries]. Though they worshiped the Lord, they also served their own gods according to the custom of the nations from whom they had been transported to Samaria. To the present day they follow their former practice.

## [T. CXCIII]

They do not fear the Lord, nor do they observe his statutes, judgments, law, and commandment, which the Lord commanded the sons of Jacob, whom he named Israel, with whom he made a covenant [Note: [Col. 0755D] In the Veronese manuscript the verb is in the first person, “I made,” as also in the Hebrew.] and to whom he gave this command:

“Do not fear foreign gods, and do not worship them or serve them [Manuscript omits ‘them’], and do not sacrifice to them. But fear the Lord your God [Hebrew omits this phrase], who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great strength and an outstretched arm. Fear him, worship him, and sacrifice to him. Observe the statutes, judgments, law, and commandment that he wrote for you, so that you may carry them out all your days, and do not fear foreign gods.

“Do not forget the covenant that he made with you. Do not worship foreign gods, but fear the Lord your God [Hebrew: and do not fear foreign gods, but fear the Lord your God], and he will rescue you from the hand of all your enemies.”

But they did not listen; instead, according to their former custom, they continued to act. Thus these nations feared the Lord, but nevertheless served their idols [Manuscript: served their idols]; for their children and grandchildren also act as their fathers [Manuscript: ancestors] had acted, even to the present day.

## [T. CXCIV, Chapter XVIII]

In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah, became king. He was twenty-five years old [Hebrew: a son of twenty-five] when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abi, daughter of Zechariah. He did what was good in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], according to all that David [Col. 0756A] his father had done [Manuscript: his ancestor had done].

## [T. CXCV]

He destroyed the high places, smashed the statues [Hebrew: pillars], cut down the sacred groves, and broke in pieces the bronze serpent [Manuscript: bronze], which Moses had made. For until that time the Israelites had burned incense to it. He called its name [Note: [Col. 0755D] The corrected Canon, according to the Masoretic pointing, has written *Nehushtan*, differing by only one vowel from the modern *Nehushtan*, where the Masoretes read a shewa beneath the letter Nun, whereas the Scholiast or corrector of the Canon read a patah or qamets. The other manuscripts retain *Naasthan*, as we have printed it. In the *Book of Hebrew Names* we find *Noesthan*, which supports the reading of the Latin Vulgate, *Nohestan*. MART. —The same manuscript very correctly has “and he called it” instead of “its name.” The Hebrew archetype likewise has [the form] “he called it,” not “its name.”] Naasthan.

He placed his hope in the Lord God of Israel. After him there was no one like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those who had been before him. He clung to the Lord and did not depart from following him. He kept [Hebrew: observed] the commandments that the Lord had commanded Moses. Therefore the Lord was with him, and in everything he undertook he acted wisely.

He rebelled against the king of the Assyrians and did not serve him. He struck the Philistines as far as Gaza and all their territory, from the Tower of the Watchmen [Col. 0756B] to the fortified city [Manuscript: walled city].

In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians came against [Manuscript omits “against”] Samaria, attacked it, and captured it. Three years later, in the sixth year of Hezekiah—that is, the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel—Samaria was captured. The king of the Assyrians transported Israel to Assyria, and settled them in Halah and in Habor, the rivers of Gozan [Manuscript: Gazan], in the cities [Hebrew: and in the cities] of the Medes, because they had not listened to the voice of the Lord their God. They had violated his covenant: they had not listened to or carried out everything that Moses, the servant of the Lord, had commanded.

## [T. CXCVI]

In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib [Note: [Col. 0756D] We do not conceal that, according to the Greek manuscripts, the Veronese manuscript here reads *Sennacherim*, but we attribute this to scribal error.] king of the Assyrians came against all the fortified cities of Judah [Col. 0756C] and captured them.

Then Hezekiah king of Judah sent messengers to the king of the Assyrians at Lachish [Manuscript omits “at”], saying: “I have sinned; withdraw from me, and I will bear everything that you impose upon me.” The king of the Assyrians therefore imposed upon Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.

Hezekiah gave all the silver that was found in the temple of the Lord and in the treasuries of the king [Hebrew: and in the treasuries of the royal palace]. At that time Hezekiah broke off the doors of the temple of the Lord and the gold plates [Hebrew omits this], which he himself had attached, and gave them to the king of the Assyrians.

The king of the Assyrians sent Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh [Manuscript: Rabsachen] from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem with a strong force. When they had gone up, they came to Jerusalem [Col. 0756D] and stood beside the conduit of the upper pool, which is on the road to the Fuller’s Field.

They called for the king. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the governor of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, came out to them. [Note: [Col. 0756D] In place of Joah, the corrected Canon now has Joha. MART.]

Rabshakeh said to them: “Say to Hezekiah: ‘Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians: What is this confidence on which you rely? Perhaps you have made a plan to prepare yourself for battle. In what do you trust, that you dare to rebel? Or do you hope in Egypt, that broken reed, upon which, if a man leans, it will enter his hand, broken, and pierce it? Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him [Manuscript and Vulgate: trust in Egypt].

“But if you say to me, ‘We have confidence in the Lord our God,’ is he not the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed, while he commanded Judah and Jerusalem: ‘You shall worship before this altar in Jerusalem’?

“Now therefore come over to my lord, the king of the Assyrians, and I will give you two thousand horses, and see whether you will be able to provide riders for them. How then can you resist even one satrap [Hebrew: one of the satraps] among the least servants of my lord? Or do you trust in Egypt because of chariots and horsemen?

“Have I come up to this place without the Lord’s will, in order to destroy it? The Lord said to me: ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’”

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna [Hebrew: Sebna], and Joah said to Rabshakeh: “We beg you to speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand that language. Do not speak to us in Judean in the hearing of the people who are on the wall.”

Rabshakeh replied: “Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you to speak these words, and not rather to the men [Col. 0757C] who sit on the wall, so that they may eat their own dung and drink their own urine together with you?” [Note: [Col. 0757D] The adverb is more likely absent in accordance with the Hebrew exemplar; it is also absent from the Veronese manuscript.]

Rabshakeh then stood and shouted in a loud voice in Judean, saying: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians. Thus says the king: ‘Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to rescue you from my hand. Nor let him give you confidence in the Lord, saying: “The Lord will surely rescue us, and this city will not be delivered into the hand of the king of the Assyrians.”

“‘Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of the Assyrians: Do with me what is advantageous to you and come out to me, and each of you shall eat from his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink water from his own cistern, until I come and transport you to a land like your own land, a land fruitful and rich in wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees, oil, and honey. Then you will live and not die.

“‘Do not listen to Hezekiah, who deceives you by saying: “The Lord will rescue us.” Have the gods of the nations rescued their lands from the hand of the king of the Assyrians? Where is the god of Hamath and Arpad? Where is the god of Sepharvaim, [Note: [Col. 0757D] “Hena and Ivah?” The corrector’s hand inserted this form in the Canon; but in the following chapter, verse 33, it has “Hena and Heva.” MART.] Ana and Avva? Have they rescued Samaria [Note: [Col. 0757D] The same manuscript has “from my hand,” more closely following the Hebrew.] from my hand?

“‘Who among all the gods of the lands has rescued his land from my hand, so that the Lord could rescue Jerusalem from my hand?’”

The people remained silent and did not answer him a word, for they had received the king’s command that they should not answer him. Eliakim [Manuscript: Eliachim] son of Hilkiah, the governor of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and reported to him the words of Rabshakeh.

## [C. CXCVII, Chapter XIX]

When King Hezekiah [Manuscript omits “king”] heard this, he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and entered the temple of the Lord. He sent Eliakim the governor of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz.

They said: “Thus says Hezekiah: ‘This is a day of tribulation, reproach, and blasphemy; for the children have come to the point of birth, but the woman in labor has no strength. Perhaps the Lord your God will hear all the words of Rabshakeh, [Col. 0758B] whom his master, the king of the Assyrians, sent to reproach the living God and to rebuke him with the words that the Lord your God has heard. Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that has been found.’”

So the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah.

## [T. CXCVIII]

Isaiah said to them: “Say this to your lord: Thus says the Lord: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of the Assyrians have blasphemed me. Behold, I will send a spirit into him [Hebrew: I will give him one], and he will hear a report and return to his own land; and I will strike him down with the sword in his own land.”

## [T. CXCIX]

Rabshakeh returned and found the king of the Assyrians attacking Libnah [Hebrew: Libna], for he had heard that he had withdrawn from Lachish. When he heard concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, “Behold, he has gone out to fight against you,” and was going against him, he sent messengers [Hebrew: he turned back and sent messengers] to Hezekiah, saying:

“Say this to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you, nor say: “Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of the Assyrians.” For you yourself have heard what the kings of the Assyrians have done to all the lands, how they devastated them. Will you alone be rescued?

“‘Have the gods rescued the individual peoples whom my fathers devastated—Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the sons of Eden who were in Telassar [Manuscript: Thalassar]? Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Ana and Avva?’”

When Hezekiah received the letters [Hebrew: books] from the hand of the messengers and had read them, [Col. 0758D] he went up to the temple of the Lord and spread them out before the Lord. He prayed in his presence, saying:

“Lord God of Israel, who sit above the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth. Incline your ear, and hear. Open your eyes, Lord [Manuscript omits “Lord”], and see; hear all the words of Sennacherib, who sent [them] to reproach the living God in our presence [Hebrew omits this phrase].

“Truly, Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have devastated the nations and the lands of them all. They have cast their gods into the fire, for they were not gods, but the works of human hands, made of wood and stone, and they destroyed them. Now therefore, Lord our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord God.”

## [T. CC]

Isaiah son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I have heard the prayer that you have made to me concerning Sennacherib king of the Assyrians.

“This is the word that the Lord has spoken concerning him:

“‘The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head behind you. Whom have you reproached, and whom have you blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel.

“‘Through the hand of your servants you have reproached the Lord, and you have said: “With the multitude of my chariots I have gone up to the heights of the mountains, to the summit of Lebanon; I have cut down its lofty cedars and its choice fir trees. I have entered as far as its boundaries [Hebrew: I will enter the dwelling of its boundary], and its forest of Carmel, and I have cut it down [Hebrew: I dug].” [Note: [Col. 0759D] This verse has a complete sense in the present form not only in the Canon but also in all the other interpreters, who begin the following verse in this way: “I dug, and drank,” or “I dried up, and drank,” and so forth. Consult the Polyglot, if you have the opportunity. MART.]

“‘I have drunk foreign waters, and I have dried up with the soles of my feet all the enclosed waters. Have you not heard what I did long ago? From ancient days I fashioned it, and now I have brought it about; fortified cities will become ruins of embattled hills. Their inhabitants, weak of hand, trembled and were confounded; they became like the grass of the field and the green herb of the housetops, which dries up before it reaches maturity.

“‘I know your dwelling, your going out, and your [Note: [Col. 0759D] One or the other of these readings—“your entering” and “your way”—is superfluous and is the fault of scribes who transferred it from the book’s margin into the text. The Scholiast rejects the last; the Veronese manuscript omits the first. Each is meaningful in its own way. From this it is clear that this passage has not been subjected to the hand of later glossators, but presents the pure translation of Jerome, expressed according to the Hebrew exemplar, which mentions only these three things: sitting, going out, and entering. “Your way” also renders the Hebrew sufficiently well.] entering, and your way [Hebrew omits “your way”]. I have known your rage against me. You have raged against me [Hebrew: Because you have raged against me], and your arrogance has risen to my ears, I will put my ring in your nose and my bit [Hebrew: bridle] in your lips, and I will lead you back by the way by which you came.

“‘For you, Hezekiah [Hebrew omits “Hezekiah”], this will be the sign: Eat this year what you find; in the second year, what grows spontaneously; but in the third year sow and reap [Hebrew: Eat this year what grows spontaneously, and in the second year feed on fruits; but in the third year sow and reap]. Plant vineyards and eat their fruit.

“‘Whatever remains of the house of Judah will send roots downward and produce fruit upward. For a remnant will go out from Jerusalem, and what is saved will come from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this.

“‘Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the king of the Assyrians: He will not enter this city, nor shoot an arrow into it, nor occupy it with a shield, nor surround it with a rampart. By the way he came, he will return, and he will not enter this city, says the Lord. I will protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.’”

That night the angel of the Lord came and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the camp of the Assyrians. When he rose at dawn, he saw all the bodies of the dead [Hebrew: when they rose at dawn, behold, all the bodies of the dead]. He withdrew and departed. Sennacherib king of the Assyrians returned and remained in Nineveh.

When he was worshiping in the temple [Hebrew: house] of Nesroch [Manuscript: Neserath], his god, Adrammelech [Manuscript: Adarmelech] and Sharezer, his sons, struck him with the sword. They fled to the land of Armenia, and Esarhaddon [Manuscript: Aseraddon] his son reigned in his place.

## [T. CCI, Chapter XX]

In those days Hezekiah became sick to the point of death. Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet came to him and said: “Thus says the Lord [Manuscript and Vulgate add: God]: Give orders to your household, for you will die [Manuscript omits “you”] and will not live.”

He turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying: “I beg you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is pleasing in your sight [Hebrew: in your eyes].” And Hezekiah wept with great weeping.

## [T. CCII]

Before Isaiah had gone out from the middle of the court, the word of the Lord came to him, saying: “Return and say to Hezekiah, the leader of my people: Thus says the Lord God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears [Note: [Col. 0760D] The Veronese manuscript, more contentiously following the Hebrew singular, has “your tear”]; and behold, I have healed you. On the third day you will go up to the temple [Hebrew: house] of the Lord.

“I will add fifteen years to your days. I will also rescue you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and I will protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.”

Isaiah said: “Bring a cake of figs.” When they had brought it and placed it on his ulcer, he was healed.

Hezekiah had said [Hebrew: He said] to Isaiah: “What will be the sign that the Lord will heal me and that I shall go up on the third day [Manuscript adds “into”] to the temple [Hebrew: house] of the Lord?”

Isaiah said to him: “This will be the sign from the Lord that the Lord will fulfill the word which he has spoken: Shall the shadow advance ten lines [Hebrew: steps], or shall it return the same number of steps?”

Hezekiah said: “It is easy for the shadow to extend ten lines [Col. 0760D] [Hebrew: steps]. I do not want that; let it return backward ten steps.”

The prophet Isaiah called upon the Lord, and he brought the shadow backward by the lines [Hebrew: steps] through which it had already descended on the stairway [Hebrew: steps] of Ahaz—ten steps backward.

## [T. CCIII]

At that time Berodach-baladan [Manuscript omits “Baladan”], son of Baladan, king of the Babylonians, sent letters [Hebrew: books] and gifts to Hezekiah, for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick.

Hezekiah rejoiced at their arrival and showed them the house of spices, the gold and silver, the various spices [Hebrew omits this], the perfumes [Hebrew: the finest perfume], the house of his vessels, and everything that he had in his treasuries. There was nothing that Hezekiah did not show them in his house and throughout his entire dominion.

Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah and said to him: “What did these men say? Or from where did they come to you?”

Hezekiah replied: “They came to me from a distant land [Vulgate adds: to me], from Babylon.”

He answered: “What did they see in your house?”

Hezekiah said: “They saw everything that is in my house. There is nothing that I did not show them in my treasuries.”

## [T. CCIV]

Isaiah therefore said to Hezekiah: “Hear the word of the Lord. Behold, days are coming, and everything that is in your house, and what your fathers stored up [Note: [Col. 0761D] The Veronese manuscript omits the words “to this day,” which all the other books nevertheless contain.] to this day, will be carried away to Babylon. Nothing will remain, says the Lord.

“Your sons who will come from you, whom you will beget, will also be taken away [Manuscript and Vulgate: will be taken away], and they will be eunuchs in the palace [Hebrew: temple] of the king of Babylon.”

Hezekiah said to Isaiah: “The word of the Lord that you have spoken is good. Let there be peace and truth in my days.”

The rest of the deeds of Hezekiah, all his strength, how he made the pool and the conduit and brought water into the city—are these not written in the book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

## [T. CCV]

Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place.

## Chapter XXI

Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hephzibah [Manuscript: Absiba]. He did evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], according to the idols [Hebrew: abominations] of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.

He turned back and rebuilt the high places that Hezekiah his father had destroyed [Manuscript: destroyed], erected altars to Baal, made a sacred grove [Hebrew: a sacred grove] as Ahab king of Israel had made, and worshiped and served the entire host of heaven.

He built altars in the temple of the Lord, concerning which the Lord had said: “In Jerusalem I will place my name.” He built altars for the entire host of heaven in the two courts of the temple [Hebrew: house] of the Lord.

He led his son through fire, practiced divination, observed omens, made spirit-mediums, and multiplied soothsayers, in order to do evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord] and provoke him.

He also placed the idol of the sacred grove that he had made in the temple [Hebrew: house] of the Lord [Hebrew omits this phrase], concerning which the Lord had spoken to David and to Solomon his son: “In this temple [Hebrew: in this house] and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel, I will place my name forever.

“I will no longer cause the foot of Israel to wander from the land that I gave to their fathers, provided that they observe in deed [Vulgate: works] [Col. 0762B] all that I have commanded them and the whole law that my servant Moses commanded them.” [Note: [Col. 0761D] The same manuscript, like the Vulgate, has “provided that they observe,” and so forth. The Hebrew likewise has only “provided that,” and so forth.]

But they did not listen; Manasseh led them astray, so that they did evil beyond the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.

The Lord spoke through his servants the prophets, saying: “Because Manasseh king of Judah has committed these most detestable acts, surpassing all that the Amorites did before him, and has also caused Judah to sin through his abominations—

## [T. CCVI]

“Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I will bring such evils [Manuscript: evil] upon Jerusalem and Judah that everyone who hears of them will have both ears ringing.

“I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria and the plummet of the house of Ahab. I will wipe away Jerusalem as tablets are customarily wiped away [Hebrew: as a flask is wiped clean] [Note: [Col. 0761D] We have different interpretations of this passage because the word [Hebrew term] has different meanings. In many passages of Scripture the word means both “to wipe away” and “to erase.” Accordingly, interpreters have rendered it according to various allusions and metaphors.

“Jerome makes an elegant allusion to wax tablets, on which ancient scribes engraved writing with a stylus and which they could easily erase by turning the stylus, removing the writing down to the bottom. Thus, he says to the monk Chrysogonus: ‘You have entirely forgotten the bond of our relationship, so that you have erased that letter—which the Apostle says is written in the hearts of Christians—not with a slight wiping, but, as they say, down to the lowest wax.’

“Others think that the metaphor here is taken from an oil flask or some vessel that is wiped and cleaned, and that, once wiped, it is turned upside down so that it may not retain any stain. In this way, they say, Jerusalem will be cleansed of its crimes and completely overturned.

“But these interpretations do not fit with the preceding measuring line of Samaria and the plummet of the house of Ahab, in whose likeness Jerusalem is said to be erased. Therefore, since the house of Ahab was completely erased from the face of the earth, Jerome’s interpretation appears the best of all and corresponds to the metaphor once adopted. In the other interpretations the sense does not appear so clear or so easy to understand. Nevertheless, everyone may abound in his own interpretation, provided that the integrity of Scripture and the faith are always preserved. MART.]

“Wiping it away, I will turn it over and repeatedly draw the stylus [Hebrew omits this] across its surface.”

I will abandon the remnant of my inheritance and deliver them into the hand of their enemies. They will become a wasteland and a spoil to all their adversaries, because they have done evil in my sight [Hebrew: in my eyes] and have continued to provoke me from the day their fathers came out of Egypt until this day.

Moreover, Manasseh shed exceedingly much innocent blood, until he filled Jerusalem from end to end, apart from the sins by which he caused Judah to sin, so that it did evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord].

The rest of the deeds of Manasseh, all that he did, and the sin that he committed—are these not written [Col. 0763A] in the book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

## [T. CCVII]

Manasseh slept with his fathers, and was buried in the garden of his house, in the garden of Aza [Manuscripts and Vulgate: Oza] [Note: [Col. 0763D] The Canon, corrected according to the Hebrew, has here and below *Huza* instead of *Aza*, the reading of the earlier hand. MART.], and Amon his son reigned in his place.

Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Messalemeth [Hebrew: Messelemeth], daughter of Harus of Jetaba. He did evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: in the eyes of the Lord], as Manasseh his father had done.

He walked in all the way in which his father had walked. He served the impurities [Hebrew: filth] that his father had served, worshiped them, abandoned the Lord, the God of his fathers, and did not walk in the way of the Lord.

## [T. CCVIII]

His servants plotted against him [Manuscript omits “against him”] [Col. 0763B] [Hebrew: his servants rebelled against him] and killed the king in his own house. But the people of the land struck down all those who had conspired against King Amon, and appointed Josiah his son as king in his place.

The rest of the deeds of Amon, which he did—are these not written in the book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

They buried him [Variant: “He buried him”] in his tomb, in the garden of Uzza, and Josiah his son reigned in his place.

[Chapter XXII.] Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jedidah, daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath. He did what was pleasing in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: “in the eyes of the Lord”], and walked in all the ways of David his father; he did not turn aside to the right or to the left. [T. CCIX.]

In the eighteenth year of King Josiah, the king sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, the secretary of the temple of the Lord, saying to him: “Go to Hilkiah the high priest, so that the money brought into the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of the Lord may be melted down—the money which the doorkeepers [the Vulgate adds: “of the temple”] collected from the people—and let it be given through the overseers to the craftsmen in the house of the Lord. Let them distribute it to those who work in the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of the Lord, to repair the damaged parts of the temple [Hebrew: “house”], namely, to carpenters, masons, and those who repair breaches, and to purchase timber and hewn stones for repairing the temple [Hebrew: “house”]. Yet the money received by them must not be reckoned with them; they shall have it in their keeping and in good faith [Hebrew: “Yet the money shall not be reckoned with those who receive it, because they act in good faith”].” [T. CCX.]

[Note: The Veronese manuscript and the printed Vulgate books have “Aslia”; the Hebrew form is more correct. The same manuscript has “Messullam” with a double *l*. Finally, for the name that follows, it again omits the word corresponding to “son,” in agreement with the Hebrew. MART.]

Then Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the secretary: “I have found the book of the Law in the house of the Lord.” And Hilkiah gave the volume [Hebrew: “book”] to Shaphan, who read it. Shaphan the secretary then came to the king and reported to him what he had been ordered to do, saying: “Your servants have melted down the money found in the house of the Lord [Hebrew omits this], and have given it to the craftsmen through the overseers of the work of the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of the Lord.”

Shaphan the secretary also told the king: “The priest Hilkiah gave me a book.” And Shaphan read it before the king. When the king heard the words of the book of the Law of the Lord [Hebrew omits this], he tore his garments. And he commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying: “Go and consult the Lord for me, for the people, and for all Judah [Hebrew: “for the remnant … and Judah”], concerning the words of this book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the Lord that has been kindled against us, because our fathers did not listen to the words of this book, to do everything written for us.”

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum, son of Thecuah [Hebrew: “Thiteva”], son of Harhas, keeper of the garments, who lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter; and they spoke with her.

[Note: In this word our scholiast follows the reading of the Masoretic text, as also above in the word “Messelemeth,” instead of “Messalemeth.” MART.]

She answered them: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Tell the man who sent you to me: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring evil upon this place and upon its inhabitants—all the words of the Law [Hebrew: “book”] that the king of Judah has read—because they have forsaken me and sacrificed to foreign gods, provoking me by all the works of their hands. Therefore my indignation will be kindled against this place and will not be quenched.

“But to the king of Judah, who sent you to consult the Lord, you shall say this: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you heard the words of the volume [Hebrew omits this], and your heart was terrified, and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard what had been spoken against this place and against its inhabitants—that they would become an object of astonishment and a curse [two manuscripts omit this]—and because you tore your garments and wept before me, I also have heard you, says the Lord. Therefore I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your tomb in peace, so that your eyes may not see all the evil that I am going to bring upon this place.”

[Note: Jerome’s translation expresses the text exactly; therefore the scholiast is wrong whenever he records anything contrary in the margin. MART.]

And they reported to the king what she had said. He sent for them, and all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem gathered to him. The king went up to the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of the Lord, and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with him—the priests, the prophets, and all the people, from the least to the greatest. And he read in the hearing of them all all the words of the book of the covenant that had been found in the house of the Lord.

The king stood upon the step [Hebrew: “pillar”] and made a covenant before the Lord, that they should follow the Lord, keep his commandments, testimonies, and statutes with all their heart and with all their soul, and perform the words of this covenant that were written in that book. And the people consented to the covenant.

The king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, the priests of the second order, and the doorkeepers to remove from the temple of the Lord all the vessels made for Baal, for the sacred grove [the manuscript and the Vulgate: “in the sacred grove”], and for all the host of heaven. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the valley of the Kidron and carried their ashes to Bethel.

He abolished the diviners [Hebrew: “priests”] whom the kings of Judah had appointed to sacrifice on the high places in the cities of Judah and around Jerusalem, and those who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, the moon, the twelve signs, and the whole host of heaven.

He brought the sacred grove out of the house of the Lord, outside Jerusalem, into the valley of the Kidron; he burned it there, reduced it to dust, and cast its dust upon the graves of the common people [the manuscript: “grave”].

He demolished the little houses of the effeminate men that were in the house of the Lord, where women wove little houses as though for the sacred grove [Hebrew omits “as though”].

He gathered all the priests from the cities of Judah and defiled the high places where the priests sacrificed [Hebrew: “burned incense”], from Geba [the manuscript: “Gaba”] to Beersheba. He demolished the altars at the gates, at the entrance of the gate of Joshua, governor of the city, which was on the left side of the city gate.

Nevertheless, the priests of the high places did not go up to the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem; they merely ate unleavened bread among their brothers.

He also defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, so that no one might consecrate his son or daughter through fire to Molech.

[Note: The Veronese manuscript has *Thafeth*, closer to the Greek Ταφὲθ (*Taphéth*), which Symmachus nevertheless also reads from the Hebrew. MART.]

He removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun at the entrance of the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of the Lord, beside the chamber of Nathan-melech the eunuch, which was in [Note: After the correction of the Canon, this name is written *Pharvarim*, with the consonant *vav*, instead of *shureq* or *shourec*, that is, instead of the vowel *u*. MART.] Pharurim. He burned the chariots of the sun with fire.

He demolished the altars on the roofs of the upper chamber of Ahaz, which the kings of Judah had made, and the altars that Manasseh had made in the two courts of the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of the Lord. The king broke them down, ran from there, and scattered their ashes into the torrent of the Kidron.

He also defiled the high places that were opposite Jerusalem, on the right side of the Mount of Offense, which Solomon king of Israel had built for Astarte, the idol of the Sidonians [Hebrew: “their pollution”], for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and for Milcom, the abomination of the sons of Ammon.

He shattered the statues [Hebrew: “inscribed pillars”] and cut down the sacred groves, and filled their places with the bones of the dead.

Moreover, he demolished the altar at Bethel, the high place [the Vulgate adds: “and the high place”] made by Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin. He demolished that altar and high place, burned it, and crushed it to dust; he also burned the sacred grove.

Then Josiah turned and saw the tombs that were on the mountain. He sent for the bones, took them from the tombs, burned them upon the altar, and defiled it, according to the word of the Lord spoken by the man of God who had foretold these things. [T. CCXII.]

And he said: “What is that monument that I see?” The citizens of that city answered him: “It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and foretold these things that you have done against the altar at Bethel.”

He said: “Leave him alone; let no one disturb his bones.” So his bones remained untouched, together with the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria [Hebrew: “They preserved his bones, the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria”].

Josiah also removed all the shrines of the high places that were in the cities of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had made to provoke the Lord, and he dealt with them according to all the deeds he had done at Bethel. He killed all the priests of the high places who were there, upon the altars, and burned human bones upon them. Then he returned to Jerusalem.

[T. CCXIII.] The king commanded all the people, saying: “Celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God, according to what is written in this book of the covenant.” For such a Passover had not been celebrated since the days of the judges who judged Israel, nor throughout all the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah, as this Passover was celebrated to the Lord in Jerusalem in the eighteenth year of King Josiah [the manuscript adds: “to God”].

Josiah also removed the mediums, the diviners, the images of idols, and the abominations and impurities that had been in the land of Judah and Jerusalem, in order to establish the words of the law written in the book that Hilkiah the priest had found in the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of the Lord.

There was no king like him before him who returned to the Lord with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength, according to the whole law of Moses; nor did anyone like him arise after him.

Nevertheless, the Lord did not turn away from the great fury of his wrath with which he was angry against Judah, because of the provocations by which Manasseh had provoked him. [Col. 0766C.]

Therefore the Lord said: “I will also remove Judah from my presence, just as I removed Israel, and I will cast away this city that I chose, Jerusalem, and the house of which I said: ‘My name shall be there.’”

The rest of the deeds of Josiah and everything that he did—is it not written in the book of the Deeds of the Days of the Kings of Judah? [T. CCXIV.]

In his days Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates. King Josiah went to meet him, and he was killed at Megiddo when he saw him. His servants carried him dead from Megiddo, brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his tomb.

The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father. Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Amital [Hebrew: Amutal], daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.

[Note: The Septuagint and Jerome read in their Hebrew copies *Amital*, with a *yod* in the middle. In the present Hebrew text they read *Amutal*, with *shureq*, that is, with the vowel *u*. The scholiast of the Canon followed the latter reading, although he was equal or superior in age to all the Masoretic vowel-points and critical signs. MART.]

He did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done. [T. CCXV.]

Pharaoh Necho bound him at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, so that he would not reign in Jerusalem, and imposed a fine upon the land of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.

Pharaoh Necho made Eliakim son of Josiah king in place of Josiah his father, and changed his name to [Note: Jerome observes in Book I of his Commentary on the first chapter of Matthew that, through scribal error and the passage of time, the names Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin became confused among the Greeks and Latins. “Let us know,” he says, “that the earlier one is the same as Jehoiakim, while the second is his son, not his father. The former is written with *k* and *m*, the latter with *ch* and *n*; this has become confused through scribal error and the passage of time among Greeks and Latins.” Jerome was considering the Greek and Latin forms; yet in his book of Hebrew Names he writes *Joiacim*, following the Hebrew letters and their sound. We also read *Joiachim* in the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, where the *h* was added through scribal error and usage. Relying, therefore, upon Jerome’s authority and example, we may henceforth write *Joaicim* and *Joiachim*. MART. —Compare the holy Doctor’s Commentary on Daniel, chapter 1, where he says: “Let no one think that the Joacim at the beginning of Daniel is the same as the Joachin written at the beginning of Ezekiel. The latter has the final syllable *chin*, the former *cim*. For this reason one generation seems to be missing in the Gospel according to Matthew, because the second group of fourteen ends with Joacim, son of Josiah, and the third begins with Joachin, son of Joacim. Porphyry, ignorant of this, etc.” See also the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 1, and our observations on both passages.] Jehoiakim.

Pharaoh took Jehoahaz and led him into Egypt [Hebrew: “and he died there”; so also the Vulgate]. Jehoiakim gave silver and gold to Pharaoh, after he had imposed a levy upon the land [the manuscript omits “upon the land”], requiring each person to contribute according to Pharaoh’s command. He exacted from the people of the land, according to their ability, both silver and gold, to give to Pharaoh Necho.

Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zebidah, daughter of Pedaiah, from Rumah.

[Note: The Hebrew has *Zabida*. In the current text the *yod* has a point in its interior, that is, in its middle, because they say that it was written in place of *vav shureq*. The scholiast of the Canon found this in his Hebrew copy, for he wrote *Zebuda* in the text. MART.]

He did evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: “in the eyes of the Lord”], according to all that his fathers had done.

[Chapter XXIV.] In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant for three years; then he rebelled against him [the manuscript: “fought against him”]. The Lord sent against him bands of Chaldeans, bands of Syrians, bands of Moabites, and bands of the sons of Ammon. He sent them against Judah to destroy it, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through his servants the prophets. [T. CCXVI.]

This happened by the word of the Lord against Judah, to remove it from his presence because of all the sins of Manasseh that he had committed, and because of the innocent blood that he had shed, filling Jerusalem with the blood of the innocent. For this reason the Lord was unwilling to be reconciled.

[T. CCXVII.] The rest of the deeds of Jehoiakim and everything that he did—is it not written in the book of the Deeds of the Days of the Kings of Judah? And Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place.

[Note: In the Canon of the Hebrew Truth the name is written this way in the first hand, and rightly so, since the Hebrew reads *Jehoiachin*, or *Joiachin*, because among the ancients the *he* was silent. MART. —On the contrary, the Veronese manuscript, in its recapitulations at number XXXIV, has: “Concerning Joachin son of Joiachim.”]

The king of Egypt did not again go out from his land, for the king of Babylon had taken everything that belonged to the king of Egypt, from the Brook of Egypt to the river Euphrates.

Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Nehushta, daughter of Elnathan, from Jerusalem.

[Note: In the corrected Canon we find *Neusta*, according to the Masoretic vowel-points. MART. —A later hand in the Veronese manuscript rewrote it as *Nabesta*.]

He did evil in the sight of the Lord [Hebrew: “in the eyes of the Lord”], according to all that his father had done.

At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against Jerusalem, and the city was surrounded with fortifications. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city while his servants were besieging it. Jehoiachin king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon, he, his mother, his servants, his princes, and his eunuchs; and the king of Babylon received him in the eighth year of his reign.

[Note: The Veronese manuscript adds a decade to this number and reads “the eighteenth year,” though we do not know on whose authority. Perhaps the copyist took a marginal note or asterisk, which some diligent person had placed beside especially notable passages—particularly where the year of an important event was recorded—for the Roman numeral X, and rashly counted it in the text. We have observed the same manuscript adding a decade more than once to the sums of years specified by Scripture, contrary to the testimony of all the books. MART.]

He brought out from there all the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the royal house, and broke into pieces all the golden vessels that Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the Lord, according to the word of the Lord.

He carried away all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the strongest troops—ten thousand into captivity—together with every craftsman and smith; nothing remained except the poorest people of the land.

He also carried Jehoiachin to Babylon, along with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, his eunuchs, and the judges of the land; he led them from Jerusalem into captivity in Babylon. The king of Babylon also led into captivity to Babylon all the strong men, seven thousand, the craftsmen, and the smiths, one thousand—every strong man and warrior.

He appointed Mattaniah, his uncle, in his place and changed his name to Zedekiah. Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Amital, daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.

[Note: The marginal scholion placed above at verse 31 of the preceding chapter was transferred here into the text by the corrector of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth—namely, *Amutal* instead of *Amital*, as we discussed in our first note. MART.]

He did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done. For the Lord was angry with Jerusalem and Judah until he cast them from his presence; and Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

[Col. 0769A] [T. CCXVIII. Chapter XXVI.]

[Note: This final chapter, which had fallen out of the ancient Veronese manuscript through excessive age, was supplied by a later hand. MART.]

In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem. They surrounded it and built fortifications around it.

The city was shut in and besieged until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, on the ninth day of the month. Famine prevailed in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land.

The city was breached, and all the warriors fled by night through the gate-way between the two walls, near the king’s garden (while the Chaldeans were surrounding the city). They fled by the road leading to the open wilderness [Hebrew omits this].

[Note: The Veronese manuscript adds “king,” for which the Vulgate books write the name Zedekiah himself. The Hebrew has neither. Yet the context clearly shows that the reference is to the king, who is immediately said to have been captured. MART.]

The army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and captured him in the plain of Jericho. All the warriors who were with him were scattered and abandoned him. They seized the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where he pronounced judgment upon him.

He killed the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, put out his eyes, bound him with chains, and brought him to Babylon.

In the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month—which was the nineteenth year of the king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan, commander of the army [Hebrew: “chief of the cooks”], a servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.

[Note: The Hebrew reads *rab tabahhim*, “chief” or “master of the slaughterers.” Jerome discusses this name and office in his Hebrew Questions on Genesis 37: “In many places Scripture mentions *archimagiros*, that is, chiefs of cooks, instead of commanders of the army; for in Greek *mageireuein* means ‘to kill.’ Joseph, therefore, was sold to the commander of the army and the warriors—not to Potiphar, as it is written in Latin, but to the eunuch Poti-phar,” etc. The Hebrews therefore call soldiers slaughterers because of the killing of men; and we French say of a great slaughter, *On a fait une grande boucherie*—“A great slaughter has been made.” MART. —For the benefit of the scholiast, who says that “chief of cooks” in Hebrew means commander of the army, compare the genuine Jerome in the Hebrew Questions on Genesis 37:36, a passage also cited by Martianay. “In many places,” he says, “Scripture mentions *archimagiros*, that is, chiefs of cooks, instead of commanders of the army; for in Greek *mageireuein* means ‘to kill.’ Saint Augustine, however, says specifically of this passage: Some do not wish to interpret him as chief of cooks, who in Greek is called *archimageiros*, but as commander of the army, who possessed the power of killing. For that is what the man whom Nebuchadnezzar sent was called, and in him the primacy of military command is more properly found.”]

He burned the house of the Lord and the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, together with every great house, he burned with fire.

[Note: Along with the printed Vulgates, the Veronese manuscript here omits the word “all,” and shortly afterward omits “great.” MART.]

The entire army of the Chaldeans that was with the commander of the army [Hebrew: “chief of the cooks”] demolished the walls of Jerusalem all around.

Nebuzaradan, commander of the army [Hebrew: “chief of the cooks”], carried away the remaining part of the people who had remained in the city, the deserters who had defected to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the common people [Hebrew: “the remnant of the people”].

He left some of the poor of the land as vinedressers and farmers.

The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars that were in the temple [Hebrew: “house”] of the Lord, the bases, and the bronze sea that was in the house of the Lord, and carried all the bronze to Babylon.

[Note: The same manuscript has “all their bronze” instead of “all the bronze,” which is more correct and closer to the Hebrew *their bronze* and to the Greek *their bronze*. MART.]

They also took the bronze pots [Hebrew omits this], shovels, [Note: The Veronese manuscript does not recognize *mortariola* here; nor does the Hebrew text itself mention more than four kinds of instruments: pots, brooms, psalteries, and bowls. The ancient versions and other books preserve the same number. Therefore the fifth kind, “mortars,” was incorrectly added here after the Vulgate. Jerome never dared to add anything to the Hebrew exemplar; nor does this word seem to be anything other than a gloss for another word, perhaps “bowls,” transferred by scribes from the margin into the text. MART.] mortars, forks, bowls, and all the bronze vessels used in the service. He also took the censers and bowls: those that were gold, gold; those that were silver, silver—the commander of the army [Hebrew: “chief of the cooks”] took them.

That is, the two pillars, the one sea, and the bases that Solomon had made in the temple [Hebrew omits this] of the Lord. The weight of the bronze of all the vessels could not be determined.

One pillar was eighteen cubits high, and the bronze capital upon it was three cubits high; the latticework and pomegranates upon the capital of the pillar were all bronze. The second pillar had a similar ornament.

The commander of the army [Hebrew: “chief of the cooks”] took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and three doorkeepers.

From the city he took one eunuch who was overseer of the fighting men, and five men of those who had stood before the king [Hebrew: “seen the king’s face”], whom he found in the city. He also took Sopher, commander of the army, who examined the recruits among the people of the land, and sixty men of the common people [Hebrew: “of the people of the land”] who were found in the city.

[Note: A more recent scribe, who supplied the final page of the Veronese manuscript, failed to decipher the worn letters of the very ancient exemplar and wrote “six” here instead of the complete word “sixty.” MART.]

Nebuzaradan, commander of the army [Hebrew: “chief of the cooks”], seized them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. The king of Babylon struck them and killed them at Riblah in the land of Hamath. Thus Judah was carried away from its land.

The people who remained in the land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left, he placed under the authority of Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan.

When all the commanders of the army and the men who were with them heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah, they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jezonias son of Maacath, together with their companions.

[Note: The same manuscript calls the latter *Machati*, closer to the Greek *Machathi ho*. MART.]

Gedaliah swore to them and to their companions, saying: “Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans [Hebrew: “servants of the Chaldeans”]. Remain in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.”

In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama [the manuscript: “Elimasa”], of royal descent, came with ten men. They struck Gedaliah, and he died, as well as the Jews and Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah.

Then all the people, from the least to the greatest, and the commanders of the army arose and went to Egypt, fearing the Chaldeans.

In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin [the manuscript: “Joachin”], king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month [Hebrew omits this], Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year in which he began to reign, raised the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison.

He spoke kindly to him and set his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon. He changed the garments that he had worn in prison, and Jehoiachin ate bread continually in the king’s presence all the days of his life.

He also assigned him a continual allowance, which was given to him by the king day by day, throughout all the days of his life.

[Col. 0771] Here end the two books of *Malachim*.

[Col. 0771]

[THE BOOK OF ISAIAH.]

JEROME’S PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF ISAIAH

[Col. 0771B] When anyone sees that the Prophets have been set out in verses, let him not suppose that among the Hebrews they are bound by meter, or that they bear some resemblance to the Psalms or the works of Solomon. Rather, it is like what is customary in Demosthenes and Cicero, where writings that are prose, not verse, are arranged in cola and commas. Therefore, seeking the usefulness of readers, we too have distinguished this new translation by a new manner of writing.

[Note: We have discussed the meters and verses of Scripture at length in the Prolegomena to this divine Library. The diligent reader may therefore refer there, so that we do not repeat a discussion of the same subject. We merely note that we have printed the books of the prophets in verse-cola and commas because Saint Jerome himself, taking thought for the unity of his readers, distinguished his new translation by this new manner of writing, as this preface bears witness. In order to restore such divisions into separate members, the Corbie manuscript was of great assistance to us, since it contains almost all the verse-cola in the Prophets, divided and arranged. The *Speculum* of Saint Augustine was no less useful. In that excellent work Augustine followed Jerome’s version and very often records how many verses there are from one section to another. We therefore took care to print the Prophets in verse form according to the evidence of Italian manuscripts, lest both Jerome’s labor and our own effort should perish. MART.]

First, it must be understood concerning Isaiah that he is eloquent in his speech, being a noble man of refined eloquence, with nothing rustic mixed into his language. Hence it has happened that, more than with the other prophets, the translation has been unable to preserve the flower of his speech.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript has a more elegant form, “for he was a noble man of urbane refinement.” This closely resembles Quintilian’s statement about Messala Corvinus: “Polished and pure, and in a certain way displaying in his speech the nobility of his birth.” MART.]

Furthermore, it must be added that he should be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist.

[Note: Saint Augustine also reports this judgment in *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 29: Isaiah seemed to some to be called an evangelist rather than a prophet. Our Jerome says the same in his preface to his Commentaries on this prophet. MART.]

For he has unfolded all the mysteries of Christ and of the Church so completely that you would think he was not prophesying about the future but weaving a history of past events.

[Note: Jerome himself explains in his earlier prologue on Genesis the places in which the Septuagint interpreters especially did this. The Jews, he says, claim that it was done by prudent design, lest Ptolemy, a worshiper of one God, should discover among the Hebrews a plurality of divinity; and shortly afterward: “Wherever Scripture bears sacred witness concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they either interpreted it differently or remained entirely silent, so that they might satisfy the king and not make the mystery of faith public.” See also our observations on this passage. MART.]

For this reason I infer that the Seventy Translators did not wish at that time to disclose openly to the Gentiles the mysteries of their faith, lest they should give what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine. When you read this translation, you will notice that these matters have been concealed by them.

Nor am I unaware how difficult it is to understand the Prophets, nor how easily anyone can judge a translation unless he has first understood what he has read. We too are exposed to the attacks of many who, urged on by envy, despise what they cannot attain.

Knowing this, and knowingly, I thrust my hand into the flames. Nevertheless, I ask this of fastidious readers: just as the Greeks read, after the Seventy Translators, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, either from devotion to their learning or so that they may understand the Septuagint more fully by comparison with them, so let these readers at least grant that after the earlier translators there should be one additional interpreter.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “interpreters,” without altering the sense. MART.]

Let them read first and despise afterward, lest they seem to condemn what they do not understand, not by judgment but through the presumption of hatred.

Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem and Judea before the ten tribes had been led into captivity. Concerning both kingdoms, sometimes together and sometimes separately, he composed his oracle.

Although he sometimes looks to the history of the present and indicates the people’s return to Judea after the Babylonian captivity, all his concern is with the calling of the nations and the coming of Christ.

The more you love him, Paula and Eustochium, the more earnestly ask him to repay me in the future for the present abuse by which my rivals ceaselessly tear me apart—for he knows that I have labored in the learning of a foreign language for this purpose: that the Jews might no longer insult his Churches over the falsity of the Scriptures.

[Note: For this, refer to what Jerome says about Jews mocking and calumniating the Scriptures of Christians in his prefaces to Joshua, Chronicles, and the Psalter translated from Hebrew into Latin at the request of Sophronius. MART.]

[Note: No series of chapters exists for the Prophets, at least one adapted to Jerome’s version. MART.]

THE BOOK OF THE PROPHET ISAIAH BEGINS

[Chapter I.]

The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah

and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham,

Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

Hear, O heavens,

and listen, O earth,

for the Lord has spoken.

I have nourished and raised children,

but they have despised me.

The ox knows its owner,

and the donkey its master’s manger;

but Israel does not know,

my people does not understand.

Woe to the sinful nation,

a people weighed down with iniquity,

a wicked seed,

depraved children!

They have forsaken the Lord,

they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel,

they have turned backward,

estranged from him.

Why should I strike you again,

as you continue to add transgression?

Every head is sick,

and every heart is faint.

From the sole of the foot to the crown,

there is no soundness in it:

wound, bruise,

and swollen sore.
not
is bound up,

and has not been dressed with medicine or softened with oil.

Your land is desolate;

[Col. 0774B] your cities are burned with fire;

before your eyes foreigners devour your countryside,

and it will be desolated as in a hostile devastation.

And the daughter of Zion will be left like a shelter in a vineyard,

and like a hut in a cucumber field,

like a city that is laid waste.

Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed,

we would have been like Sodom,

and would have become like Gomorrah.

Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom;

give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah.

“What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?” says

the Lord.

“I am full:

[Note: [Col. 0773C] Thus read the manuscript codices of the Bible: the Colbertine, Anician, one Corbie manuscript no. 12, and the two of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, nos. 5 and 164; the Regius codex is also found corrected according to their standard. Moreover, the same reading is retained by five older manuscript copies of Saint Jerome’s Commentary on the Prophet Isaiah. These codices are: the first Corbie manuscript, written in Lombard letters; the second, elegantly copied at the Abbey of Cluny and of excellent quality; the third, the Sorbonne manuscript no. 674; the Colbertine no. 186; and, finally, the fifth, from the Great Forest near Bordeaux. In the Sorbonne manuscript, however, the copyist wrote adipae for adipe, with the abbreviated upper stroke of the accusative case. All the rest are alike. We record this because in both Canons of the Hebrew truth—the Carcassonne and our Saint-Germain—another reading is found, namely: “I am full of the burnt offering of rams and the fat of fattened animals; and I did not desire the blood of calves, lambs, and goats.” The present Hebrew text and all the Oriental versions agree with this, as does Saint Jerome’s sacred text in printed books. Yet in this matter nothing outweighs Jerome’s authority, [Col. 0774C] by which the reading of the preceding manuscript codices and of our Latin Vulgate is most clearly confirmed. For when the holy Doctor explains this passage in Book I of the Commentary, he plainly declares why God is said to be “full”: “The whole content of this chapter,” he says, “up to the passage where it says, ‘Judge the orphan,’ and so forth, rejects the sacrifices of victims and teaches that obedience to the Gospel is superior to sacrifice.” And what he added—“I am full”—must be understood in this sense: “I lack nothing; the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness. Hence we too have all received from his fullness.” See, then, that according to Saint Jerome’s judgment God is here called full, not of burnt offerings and the fat of fattened animals, but of majesty, grace, sufficiency, and truth. Furthermore, from this passage you can easily see how useful to readers are distinctions divided by members; for when such divisions are removed, the meaning and order of the matter are completely confused. This has demonstrably occurred in many printed and manuscript books, as is sufficiently clear from what we have just presented. MART.] The burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fattened animals,

and the blood of calves, lambs, and goats

I did not desire.

When you came before my sight,

[Col. 0774C] who asked these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts?

Do not bring sacrifice any longer in vain:

incense is an abomination to me.

[Note: [Col. 0774D] In his Commentaries, the holy Father appears to prefer this reading: “Your new moons and sabbaths.”] New moon, and sabbath, and other festivals I will not endure;

your assemblies are wicked:

[Col. 0775A] your new moons and solemnities my soul has hated;

they have become burdensome to me; I am weary of enduring them.

And when you stretch out your hands,

I will turn my eyes away from you;

and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear:

your hands are full of blood.

Wash yourselves; be clean.

Remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes:

cease to act perversely,

learn to do good:

seek justice,

aid the oppressed,

judge the orphan;

defend the widow.

And come, and argue with me, says the Lord:

If your sins should be like scarlet,

they will be made white like snow;

and if they should be red like crimson, they will become like wool

[Col. 0775B] white.

If you are willing and listen to me,

you will eat the good things of the land.

But if you are unwilling and provoke me

to anger,

the sword will devour you, because the mouth of the Lord has spoken.

How has the faithful city become a harlot, full of judgment?

Justice [Note: [Col. 0775D] In the Commentary he prefers “seeks.”] dwelt in her, but now there are murderers.

Your silver has become dross;

your wine has been mixed with water.

Your princes are faithless [Alternative: disobedient], companions of thieves:

all love gifts and pursue rewards.
