And I said:

“No, my lord.”

And he answered and said to me:

[Col. 1065C] “This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying:

[Note: [Col. 1065D] This entire verse, “Not by an army, nor by strength,” was missing from Martianus’s edition. I readily think it was a printer’s error; although many of this kind occurred, we indicated almost none of them, so as not to expose the reputation of that name to envy, since it was enough for the reader that we corrected them. We note this one, however, so that, if typographical errors have likewise crept into our edition, the reader may be indulgent, knowing that the Parisian printer sometimes committed more serious faults.]  
‘Not by an army, nor by strength,  
but by my spirit,’ says the Lord of hosts.

“Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel?  
You shall become a plain.  
And he shall bring out the chief stone,  
and shall make equal the grace of its grace.”

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“The hands of Zerubbabel founded this house,  
and his hands shall complete it;  
and you shall know that the Lord of hosts  
has sent me to you.

“For who has despised the days of small things?  
They shall rejoice and see the tin stone  
in the hand of Zerubbabel.

“These seven are the eyes [Alternative: there are seven] of the Lord,  
which range over the whole earth.”

And I answered and said to him:

“What are these two olive trees  
on the right of the lampstand  
and on its left?”

And I answered a second time  
and said to him:

“What are the two olive branches  
beside the two golden beaks,  
in which are the golden receptacles?”

And he said to me:

“Do you not know what these are?”

And I said:

[Col. 1066A] “No, my lord.”

And he said:

“These are the two sons of oil  
who stand beside the Ruler of the whole earth.”

[Chapter V.] And I turned and lifted my eyes,  
and I saw,  
and behold, a flying scroll.

And he said to me:

“What do you see?”

And I said:

“I see a flying scroll:  
its length is twenty cubits,  
and its width is ten cubits.”

And he said to me:

“This is the curse that goes out  
over the face of the whole earth.

“For every thief, as it is written there,  
shall be judged;  
and every one who swears,  
from this point onward,  
shall likewise be judged.

“I will bring it forth,” says the Lord of hosts,  
“and it shall enter the house of the thief  
and the house of the one who falsely swears by my name.

“It shall lodge in the midst of his house  
and consume it,  
its wood and its stones.”

And the angel who spoke with me went out  
and said to me:

“Lift your eyes  
and see what this is that is going out.”

And I said:

“What is it?”

And he said:

“This is the ephah [amphora] going out.”

And he said:

“This is their eye throughout the whole earth.”

And behold, a talent of lead was carried,  
and behold, one woman sitting in the midst of the ephah.

And he said:

“This is wickedness.”

And he threw her into the midst of the ephah  
and cast the mass of lead over its opening.

[Col. 1066C] And I lifted my eyes and saw,  
and behold, two women going out,  
with the wind in their wings;  
and they had wings like the wings of a kite.

And they lifted the ephah  
between earth and heaven.

And I said to the angel who spoke with me:

“Where are these taking the ephah?”

And he said to me:

“To build a house for it in the land of Shinar,  
and to establish it  
and set it there upon its base.”

[Chapter VI.] And I turned and lifted my eyes,  
and I saw,  
and behold, four chariots going out  
from [Alternative: in] between two mountains;  
and the mountains were mountains of bronze.

In the first chariot were red horses,  
in the second chariot black horses,  
in the third chariot white horses,  
and in the fourth chariot mottled, powerful horses.

[Col. 1066D] And I answered and said to the angel  
who spoke with me:

“What are these, my lord?”

And the angel answered and said to me:

“These are the four winds of heaven,  
which go out to stand  
before the Ruler of the whole earth.

“Those in which were the black horses  
were going out to the land of the north;  
[Col. 1067A] and the white ones went out after them;  
and the mottled ones went out toward the land of the south.

“But the most powerful ones went out  
and sought to go and patrol throughout the whole earth.”

And he said:

“Go, patrol the earth.”

And they patrolled the earth.

And he called me and spoke to me, saying:

“Behold, those going out to the land of the north  
have given rest to my spirit  
in the land of the north.”

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Take from the exiles, from Holdai,  
from Tobijah, and from Idaiah;  
and you shall come on that day  
and enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah,  
who came from Babylon.

“Then take silver and gold,  
make crowns,  
and put them upon the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak,  
the high priest.

“And you shall speak to him, saying:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts:

“‘Behold, a man whose name is Branch;  
under him he shall branch out,  
and he shall build the temple of the Lord.

“‘He himself shall build the temple of the Lord;  
he himself shall bear glory;  
he shall sit and rule upon his throne.

“‘And he shall be a priest upon his throne,  
and a counsel of peace shall be between the two of them.

“And the crowns shall be for [Note: [Col. 1067C] These are proper names: Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and so forth. The Septuagint translators, following the Hebrew etymology, render them “to those who await him,” “and to the useful things of it,” “and to those who understand it,” and so forth. Therefore, what Martianus found added in one or another manuscript—“to those who sustain,” and so forth—is a gloss on the name Helem derived from the Septuagint, apparently written long ago in the margin and then rashly introduced into the text.] Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and Hen,  
for the son of Zephaniah,  
as a memorial in the temple of the Lord.

“And those who are far away shall come  
and build in the temple of the Lord;  
and you shall know that the Lord of hosts  
has sent me to you.

“And this shall happen  
if you carefully listen to the voice of the Lord your God.”

[Chapter VII.] And it came to pass in the fourth year of King Darius:  
the word of the Lord came to Zechariah  
on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Kislev.

[Col. 1067C] And Sarasar and Rogommelech,  
and the men who were with him,  
sent to the house of God  
to entreat the face of the Lord,  
saying to the priests of the house of the Lord of hosts  
and to the prophets:

“Must I weep in the fifth month,  
or must I sanctify myself,  
as I have already done for many years?”

And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying:

Speak to all the people of the land  
and to the priests, saying:

“When you fasted and mourned  
in the fifth and seventh months  
for these seventy years,  
did you fast for me?

“And when you ate and drank,  
did you not eat for yourselves  
and drink for yourselves?

“Are these not the words  
that the Lord spoke through the former prophets,  
when Jerusalem was still inhabited  
and prosperous,  
both it and its cities [Alternative: its is added] around it,  
and when the south and the lowland were inhabited?”

And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying:

Thus says the Lord of hosts:

“Judge with true judgment,  
and practice mercy and compassion,  
each one toward his brother.

“Do not oppress the widow, the orphan,  
the stranger, or the poor;  
and let no man devise evil against his brother in his heart.”

But they refused to pay attention,  
and they turned a retreating shoulder [Note: [Col. 1067D] Thus our Saint-Germain Canon, together with all the other manuscript copies of the sacred Scriptures except the Carcassonne copy, which reads “they turned away.” Against this St. Jerome taught in Book II of the Commentary on Zechariah: “When, therefore, I had commanded these things, they refused to pay attention and turned the shoulder away, or the back that shows contempt; by the posture of their bodies rejecting my commands. For when, with wrinkled brow and contracted nostril, we despise those admonishing us, we are accustomed to turn our backs, according to what is written: ‘They turned their backs to me and not their faces,’ and so forth.” MART.]  
and made their ears heavy,  
so that they would not hear.

And they made their hearts like adamant,  
so that they would not hear the law,

[Col. 1068B] and the words that the Lord of hosts sent  
by his spirit through the hand of the former prophets.

And great indignation came from the Lord of hosts.

And it happened as he had spoken:  
they did not listen.  
So they shall cry out,  
and I will not hear, says the Lord of hosts.

And I scattered them through all the kingdoms  
that they did not know;  
and the land was desolated by them,  
because there was no one passing through or returning;  
and they made the desirable land a desert.

[Chapter VIII.] And the word of the Lord of hosts came, saying:

Thus says the Lord of hosts:

“I have been zealous for Zion  
with great zeal,  
and with great indignation  
I have been zealous for her.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts:

“I have returned to Zion  
and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem.

[Col. 1068C] “And Jerusalem shall be called  
the city of truth,  
and the mountain of the Lord of hosts  
the holy mountain.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts:

“Old men and old women shall yet dwell  
in the streets of Jerusalem;  
and a man [Note: [Col. 1068C] The Hebrew phrase, retained by the Canon of the Carcassonne Church and by the manuscript copy of St. Jerome’s Commentaries on the Minor Prophets—which was copied with such remarkable diligence that at the beginning of the books it presents the entire sacred text of the Minor Prophets it contains, first according to the Hebrew truth and then according to the translation of the Septuagint translators—is: “and a man, a staff in his hand because of the multitude of days.” This distinguished manuscript exemplar was sent to us from our monastery of Saint-Albinus at Angers, where there still remains a considerable supply of manuscript volumes, revealing both the labors of the ancient monks and the envy of their present-day detractors. But to return to the foregoing: the sense seems clearer in the other manuscript copies, for they read: “And a man’s staff in his hand because of the multitude of days.” This is less faithful to the Hebrew idiom than “this man, a staff in his hand,” and so forth. According to the proper force of the Latin language, this means that each person will hold a staff in his hand because of the multitude of days. MART.] with a staff in his hand  
because of the multitude of days.

“And the streets of the city shall be filled  
with boys and girls  
playing in its streets.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts:

“If it should seem difficult in the eyes  
of the remnant of this people  
in those days,  
would it also be difficult in my eyes?”  
says the Lord of hosts.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts:

“Behold, I will save my people  
from the land of the east  
and from the land of the setting sun.

“And I will bring them,  
and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem;  
and they shall be my people,  
and I will be their God,  
in truth and righteousness.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts:

“Let your hands be strengthened,  
you who hear in these days  
these words from the mouth of the prophets,  
on the day when the house of the Lord of hosts was founded,  
so that the temple might be built.

“For before those days  
there was no wage for human beings,  
nor any wage for animals;  
and there was no peace  
for one entering or going out  
because of the tribulation;  
and I set every man  
against his neighbor.

“But now I will not act toward the remnant of this people  
as in former days,” says the Lord of hosts.

“But there shall be a seed of peace:  
the vine shall give its fruit,  
the earth shall give its produce,  
[Col. 1069B] and the heavens shall give their dew;  
and I will cause the remnant of this people  
to possess all these things.

“And it shall come to pass:

“Just as you were a curse among the nations,  
house of Judah and house of Israel,  
so I will save you,  
and you shall be a blessing.

“Do not fear;  
let your hands be strengthened.

“For thus says the Lord of hosts:

“Just as I planned to afflict you when [sentence incomplete in the supplied text: “to anger”].
your fathers had provoked me, says the Lord,

and I did not show pity.

So I turned and resolved in those days to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah:

do not fear.

These, then, are the words that you shall do:

Speak the truth, each one with his neighbor;

judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates.

[Col. 1069C] And let none of you devise evil against his friend in your hearts;

and do not love a false oath;

for all these are things that I hate, says the Lord.

And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying:

Thus says the Lord of hosts:

The fast of the fourth month,

and the fast of the fifth,

and the fast of the seventh,

and the fast of the tenth,

shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness,

and splendid festivals:

Only love truth and peace.

Thus says the Lord of hosts:

Until peoples come

and dwell in many cities,

and the inhabitants go, one to another, saying:

“Let us go and entreat the face of the Lord,

[Col. 1069D] and seek the Lord of hosts;

I too will go.”

And many peoples and strong nations shall come

to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem,

and to entreat the face of the Lord.

Thus says the Lord of hosts:

In those days, ten men from all the languages of the nations

shall take hold of the hem of a Jewish man, saying:

“We will go with you,

for we have heard that God is with you.”

[Cap. IX.] The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach,

and Damascus shall be its resting place;

for the eye of the Lord is upon man and upon all the tribes of Israel.

[Col. 1070A] Hamath also shall be within its borders, as shall Tyre and Sidon,

for they have acquired great wisdom for themselves.

Tyre built a stronghold for herself

and heaped up silver like dust, and gold

like the mud of the streets.

Behold, the Lord shall dispossess her,

and shall strike down her strength in the sea,

and she herself shall be devoured by fire.

Ashkelon shall see and fear,

and Gaza shall grieve exceedingly,

and Ekron, because her hope has been put to shame.

The king shall perish from Gaza,

and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited.

A divider shall sit in Ashdod,

and I shall destroy the pride of the Philistines.

I shall remove his blood from his mouth,

and his abominations from between his teeth.

He too shall be left for our God,

and shall be like a leader in Judah,

and Ekron like a Jebusite.

[Col. 1070B] And I shall encamp around my house against those who march to and fro,

and no oppressor shall pass over them any longer;

for now I have seen with my own eyes.

Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion;

shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem.

Behold, your king shall come to you,

righteous and a savior;

he is poor and rides upon a donkey,

upon a colt, the foal of a donkey.

I shall destroy the chariot from Ephraim,

and the horse from Jerusalem,

and the bow of war shall be shattered.

He shall speak peace to the nations,

and his dominion shall be from sea to sea,

and from the rivers to the ends of the earth.

You also, by the blood of your covenant,

have sent out your prisoners from the pit [alternative: into the pit],

in which there is no water [alternative: was no water].

[Note: The Colbertinus codex of Anjou reads, with the opposite meaning, “you have sent your prisoners into the pit.” Several manuscripts correspondingly read, “in which there was no water.” MART.]

Return to the stronghold, prisoners of hope;

today also I announce that I will repay you twofold.

[Col. 1070C] For I have stretched Judah for myself like a bow;

I have filled it with Ephraim.

And I shall raise up your sons, Zion,

against your sons, Greece,

and I shall make you like the sword of mighty men.

And the Lord God shall appear over them,

and his arrow shall go forth like lightning.

And the Lord God shall sound the trumpet,

and shall advance in the whirlwind of the south.

The Lord of hosts shall protect them;

they shall devour and subdue with slingstones.

They shall drink and become drunk as with wine,

and shall be filled like bowls,

and like the horns of the altar.

And the Lord their God shall save them on that day as the flock of his people,

for holy stones shall be raised up over his land.

For what is his goodness, and what is his beauty,

if not the grain of the chosen and the wine that makes virgins flourish?

[Col. 1070D]

[Cap. X.] Ask the Lord for rain in the season of the latter rain,

and the Lord will make snow,

and will give them rain in abundance,

grass to each one in the field.

For the idols have spoken uselessly,

and the diviners have seen falsehood,

and the dreamers have spoken in vain.

They offered empty consolation;

therefore they were led away like a flock.

They shall be afflicted, because there is no shepherd for them.

My anger is kindled against the shepherds,

and I shall visit the goats.

For the Lord of hosts has visited his flock,

[Col. 1071A] the house of Judah,

and has made them like the horse of his glory in battle.

From him shall come the corner,

from him the peg,

from him the bow of battle,

from him every oppressor shall go forth together.

And they shall be like mighty men trampling the mud of the roads in battle;

they shall fight, because the Lord is with them,

and the riders of horses shall be put to shame.

I shall strengthen the house of Judah,

and save the house of Joseph,

and I shall restore them, because I shall have mercy on them.

They shall be as they were when I had not cast them away;

for I am the Lord their God, and I shall answer them.

They shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim,

and their heart shall rejoice as with wine.

Their children shall see and rejoice,

and their heart shall exult in the Lord.

I shall whistle for them and gather them,

because I have redeemed them,

[Col. 1071B] and I shall multiply them as they had formerly multiplied.

I shall sow them among the peoples,

and from afar they shall remember me.

They shall live with their children and return.

I shall bring them back from the land of Egypt,

and I shall gather them from Assyria.

I shall bring them to the land of Gilead and Lebanon,

and no place shall be found for them.

He shall pass through the strait of the sea

and strike the waves in the sea.

All the depths of the river shall be confounded,

the pride of Assyria shall be humbled,

and the scepter of Egypt shall withdraw.

I shall strengthen them in the Lord,

and they shall walk in his name, says the Lord.

[Cap. XI.] Open your gates, Lebanon,

and let fire devour your cedars.

Howl, fir tree, for the cedar has fallen,

because the mighty have been laid waste.

[Col. 1071C] Howl, oaks of Bashan,

for the fortified forest has been cut down.

The sound of the shepherds’ howling,

because their magnificence has been laid waste.

The sound of the roaring of lions,

because the pride of the Jordan has been laid waste.

Thus says the Lord my God:

Feed the flock destined for slaughter,

whose owners slaughtered them and did not grieve,

and sold them, saying:

“Blessed be the Lord,

we have become rich.”

And their shepherds did not spare them.

And I shall no longer spare the inhabitants of the land,

says the Lord.

Behold, I shall hand human beings over,

each one into the hand of his neighbor and into the hand of his king.

They shall cut down the land,

and I shall not rescue it from their hand.

[Col. 1071D] And I fed the flock destined for slaughter for this reason,

O poor ones of the flock.

And I took two staffs for myself:

one I called Favor,

and the other I called Bond.

[Note: Saint Jerome himself, the Interpreter, reads the plural *Funiculi* (“Bonds”) in his Commentary. The Hebrew likewise has it.]

And I fed the flock.

And I cut off three shepherds in one month,

and my soul grew weary of them;

for their soul also turned against me.

And I said: “I shall not feed you.

What is dying, let it die;

what is being cut off, let it be cut off;

and let the rest devour each one the flesh of his neighbor.”

[Col. 1072A] And I took my staff, which was called Favor,

and cut it apart, to annul my covenant

which I had made with all the peoples.

And it was annulled on that day.

And the poor of the flock who kept watch over me knew

that it was the word of the Lord.

And I said to them:

“If it is good in your eyes, bring me my wage;

and if not, leave it.”

And they weighed out my wage: thirty pieces of silver.

And the Lord said to me:

“Throw it to the metalworker—

the splendid price at which I was priced by them.”

And I took the thirty pieces of silver

and threw them into the house of the Lord, to the metalworker.

And I cut apart my second staff, which was called Bond,

to dissolve the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.

[Col. 1072B] And the Lord said to me:

“Take for yourself once more the implements of a foolish shepherd.

For behold, I shall raise up a shepherd in the land

who will not visit what has been abandoned,

will not seek what has been scattered,

will not heal what has been crushed,

will not nourish what stands,

will eat the flesh of the fat ones,

and will break their hooves.”

O shepherd and idol, abandoning the flock:

a sword upon his arm

and upon his right eye.

His arm shall wither and dry up,

and his right eye shall grow dim and be darkened.

[Cap. XII.] The burden of the word of the Lord concerning Israel.

Thus says the Lord, who stretches out the heavens,

lays the foundations of the earth,

and forms the spirit of man within it.

Behold, I shall make Jerusalem a threshold of drunkenness

[Col. 1072C] for all the peoples around;

and Judah also shall be in the siege against Jerusalem.

And it shall be:

On that day I shall make Jerusalem a burdensome stone

for all the peoples.

All who lift it shall be torn apart with laceration,

and all the kingdoms [alternative: all the nations] of the earth shall gather against it.

On that day, says the Lord, I shall strike every horse with terror,

and its rider with madness.

But over the house of Judah I shall open my eyes,

and I shall strike every horse of the peoples with blindness.

And the leaders of Judah shall say in their hearts:

“The inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be strengthened for me

by the Lord of hosts, their God.”

On that day I shall make the leaders of Judah like a furnace of fire among wood,

[Col. 1072D] and like a torch of fire among hay.

[Note: The printers apparently previously read “famine” instead of “torch.”]

And they shall devour all the peoples around,

to the right and to the left.

And Jerusalem shall again be inhabited in its own place,

in Jerusalem.

And the Lord shall save the tents of Judah as at the beginning,

so that the house of David may not boast greatly,

nor the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem against Judah.

On that day the Lord shall protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem,

and whoever among them stumbles on that day shall be like David.

And the house of David shall be like God,

[Col. 1073A] like the angel of the Lord [alternative reading in copies of the Canon: “before them”].

And it shall be on that day:

I shall seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.

And I shall pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem

a spirit of grace and prayers.

And they shall look upon me whom they pierced,

and they shall mourn over him with a mourning like that for an only son,

and they shall grieve over him as one grieves

over the death of a firstborn.

On that day there shall be great mourning in Jerusalem,

like the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo.

And the land shall mourn:

each family separately,

the family of the house of David separately,

and their women separately;

the family of the house of Nathan separately,

and their women separately;

the family of the house of Levi separately,

[Col. 1073B] and their women separately;

the family of Shimei separately,

and their women separately;

all the remaining families,

each family separately,

and their women separately.

[Cap. XIII.] On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David

and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem,

for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman.

And it shall be on that day, says the Lord of hosts:

I shall destroy the names of the idols from the land,

and they shall no longer be remembered.

And the false prophets—

[Note: In his Commentary he simply calls them “prophets” (*ἁπλῶς*, “simply”), explaining the name from the Greek: “In place of false prophets,” he says, “the Hebrew has simply prophets, that is, *NEBIN*, which themselves signify false prophets; nevertheless, among the gentiles priests of idols are also called prophets.”]

and I shall remove the unclean spirit from the land.

And it shall be, when someone prophesies thereafter,

that his father and mother who begot him shall say to him:

“You shall not live, for you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord.”

[Col. 1073C] And his father and mother, his begetters [alternative: “who begot him”], shall pierce him

when he prophesies.

And it shall be:

On that day the prophets shall be put to shame,

each one because of his vision when he prophesies.

They shall not cover themselves with a sackcloth cloak in order to lie.

Rather, he shall say:

“I am not a prophet;

I am a farmer,

for Adam has been my model from my youth.”

And it shall be said to him:

“What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?”

And he shall say:

“With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.”

Sword, arise against my shepherd

and against the man who is joined to me, says the Lord of hosts.

Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered;

and I shall turn my hand toward the little ones.

[Col. 1073D] And it shall be throughout all the land, says the Lord:

two parts in it shall be scattered and perish,

and a third part shall remain in it.

And I shall lead the third part through fire,

and I shall refine them as silver is refined,

and test them as gold is tested.

He shall call upon my name,

and I shall answer him.

I shall say: “You are my people”;

and he shall say: “The Lord is my God.”

[Cap. XIV.] Behold, the days of the Lord are coming [alternative: “come”],

[Col. 1074A] and your spoil shall be divided in your midst.

And I shall gather all the nations against Jerusalem for battle.

The city shall be captured,

the houses shall be ravaged,

and the women shall be violated.

Half of the city shall go out into captivity,

but the rest of the people shall not be removed from the city.

And the Lord shall go forth and fight against those nations,

as he fought on the day of battle.

And his feet shall stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives,

which is opposite Jerusalem toward the east.

And the Mount of Olives shall be split from its middle

toward the east and toward the west,

a very great precipice.

And the mountain shall be separated toward the north,

and its middle toward the south.

[Note: The published text reads more correctly, and apparently Saint Jerome himself preferred it in his Commentary, “the middle of the mountain,” instead of “the mountain.” Certainly the Hebrew archetype also has “the middle of the mountain.”]

And you shall flee to the valley of their mountains,

for the valley of the mountains shall be joined to the nearest place.

[Col. 1074B] And you shall flee as you fled from the face of the earthquake

in the days of Uzziah king of Judah.

And the Lord my God shall come,

and all the holy ones with him.

And it shall be on that day:

There shall be no light, but cold and frost.

And there shall be one day, known to the Lord,

neither day nor night;

and at evening there shall be light.

And it shall be on that day:

Living waters shall go forth from Jerusalem.

Half of them toward the eastern sea,

and half of them toward the western sea;

they shall flow in summer and in winter.

And the Lord shall be king over all the earth.

On that day the Lord shall be one,

and his name one.

And all the land shall return as far as the wilderness,

from the hill of Rimmon to the south of Jerusalem.

[Col. 1074C] It shall be exalted and shall dwell in its place,

from the Gate of Benjamin to the site of the former gate,

and as far as the Corner Gate,

and from the Tower of Hananel to the king’s winepresses.

And they shall dwell in it,

and there shall no longer be a ban of destruction.

Jerusalem shall dwell securely.

And this shall be the plague with which the Lord shall strike all the nations

that fought against Jerusalem:

the flesh of each one standing upon his feet shall waste away,

his eyes shall waste away in their sockets,

and their tongue shall waste away in their mouths.

On that day there shall be great confusion from the Lord among them,

and each man shall seize the hand of his neighbor,

and his hand shall be fastened upon the hand of his neighbor.

But Judah also shall fight against Jerusalem.

And the wealth of all the nations around shall be gathered,

gold, silver, and very abundant garments.

[Col. 1074D] And the destruction of the horse and the mule,

the camel and the donkey,

and of all the livestock that shall be in those camps,

shall be like this destruction.

And all who remain of all the nations

that came against Jerusalem

shall go up from year to year

to worship the king, the Lord of hosts,

and to celebrate the Feast of Booths.

[Col. 1075A] And it shall be:

Whoever does not go up from the families of the earth to Jerusalem

to worship the king, the Lord of hosts,

there shall be no rain upon them.

And if the family of Egypt does not go up and does not come,

neither shall rain be upon them.

Rather, there shall be destruction,

because the Lord shall strike all the nations

that do not go up to celebrate the Feast of Booths.

This shall be the sin of Egypt,

and this the sin of all the nations

[Col. 1076A] that do not go up to celebrate the Feast of Booths.

On that day what is upon the horse’s bridle shall be holy to the Lord,

and the cooking pots in the house of the Lord shall be like bowls before the altar.

And every cooking pot in Jerusalem and in Judah shall be sanctified

to the Lord of hosts.

All who sacrifice shall come and take from them,

and shall cook in them.

And there shall no longer be a merchant in the house of the Lord of hosts

on that day.

[Col. 1075] Here ends the Book of the Prophet Zechariah.

THE BOOK OF THE PROPHET MALACHI BEGINS.

[Col. 1075B] [Cap. I.] The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by the hand of Malachi.

“I have loved you,” says the Lord.

And you said: “In what way have you loved us?”

“Was not Esau Jacob’s brother?” says the Lord.

“And I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau.

And I made his mountains a desolation,

and his inheritance the dragons of the wilderness.

But if Edom says: ‘We have been destroyed,

but we shall return and rebuild what has been destroyed’—

thus says the Lord of hosts:

‘They shall build, and I shall destroy.

And they shall be called the borders of wickedness,

and the people with whom the Lord is angry forever.’

And your eyes shall see,

and you shall say:

‘May the Lord be magnified over the border of Israel.’

A son honors his father,

and a servant his master.

[Col. 1075C] If I am a father, where is my honor?

And if I am a master, where is my fear?

says the Lord of hosts to you, O priests,

who despise my name.

And you said: ‘In what have we despised your name?’

You offer polluted bread upon my altar,

and you say: ‘In what have we polluted you?’

In this, when you say:

‘The table of the Lord is despised.’

If you offer a blind animal for sacrifice, is that not evil?

And if you offer a lame and sick animal, is that not evil?

Offer it to your governor:

will he be pleased with it,

or will he receive your person?

says the Lord of hosts.

And now entreat the face of God, that he may have mercy on you

(for this has been done by your hand),

if somehow he will receive your persons,

says the Lord of hosts.

[Col. 1075D] Who is there among you who would shut the doors

and kindle my altar for nothing?

I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts,

and I shall not accept an offering from your hand.

For from the rising of the sun to its setting,

my name is great among the nations,

and in every place an offering is sacrificed and presented to my name,

[Col. 1076B] a pure offering,

because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts.

And you have polluted it by saying:

‘The table of the Lord is contaminated,

and what is placed upon it is contemptible, together with the fire

which devours it.’

And you said: ‘Behold, it is from labor,’

and you puffed it away, says the Lord of hosts.

And you brought what was taken by robbery:

the lame and the sick;

and you brought an offering.

Shall I accept it from your hand? says the Lord.

[Note: In the Commentaries he begins a second chapter with this verse; other original texts, however, disagree with that division.]

Cursed is the deceitful man

who has a male in his flock,

but when making a vow sacrifices what is weak to the Lord.

For I am a great king, says the Lord of hosts,

and my name is fearful among the nations.

[Cap. II.] And now, for you priests, this command:

[Col. 1076C] If you will not hear,

and if you will not take it to heart

to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts,

I shall send poverty upon you,

and I shall curse your blessings,

and I shall curse them,

because you have not taken it to heart.

Behold, I shall cast the arm upon you,

and scatter upon your faces

the dung of your festivals,

and it shall carry you away with it.

And you shall know that I sent this command to you,

so that my covenant might be with Levi,

says the Lord of hosts.

My covenant was with him of life and peace.

I gave him fear, and he feared me,

and he was terrified before my name.

The law of truth was in his mouth,

[Col. 1076D] and iniquity was not found upon his lips.

He walked with me in peace and uprightness,

and turned many away from iniquity.

For the lips of a priest shall guard knowledge,

and they shall seek the law from his mouth,

because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.

But you have departed from the way,

and have caused many to stumble in the law.

You have invalidated the covenant of Levi,

says the Lord of hosts.

[Col. 1077A] Therefore I also have made you contemptible and lowly

before all the peoples,

since you did not keep my ways,

and showed partiality in the law.

Have we not all one father?

Has not one God created us?

Why, then, does each of us despise his brother,

violating the covenant of our fathers?

Judah has transgressed,

and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem,

because Judah has polluted the sanctuary of the Lord,

which he loved,

and has taken the daughter of a foreign god.

The Lord shall destroy the man who does this,

master and disciple from the tents of Jacob,

and the one who offers an offering to the Lord of hosts.

And this you have done again:

you covered the altar of the Lord with tears,

with weeping and groaning.

[Note: Alternatively, “with wailing.” The Hebrew has [the Hebrew term], which conveys more than groaning and properly means the cry of one dying, or a roar.]

[Col. 1077B] Thus I shall no longer regard the sacrifice,

nor accept anything appeasing from your hand.

And you said: “For what reason?”

Because the Lord has testified between you

and the wife of your youth,

whom you have despised.

She is your companion

and the wife of your covenant.

Did not one make her,

and is not the remnant of his spirit his?

And what does that one seek except the offspring of God?

Therefore guard your spirit,

and do not despise the wife of your youth.

“When you hate her, send her away,”

says the Lord, the God of Israel.

“But iniquity will cover his garment,”

says the Lord of hosts.

Guard your spirit,

and do not despise her.

You have wearied the Lord with your words,

and you said: “In what have we wearied him?”

[Col. 1077C] In this, when you say [alternative: “because you say”]:

“Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord,

and such people please him”;

or else:

“Where is the God of judgment?”

[Cap. III.] Behold, I send my angel,

and he shall prepare the way before my face.

And suddenly the Ruler whom you seek

shall come to his temple,

and the angel of the covenant whom you desire.

Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts.

And who will be able to conceive the day of his coming?

And who will stand to see him?

For he is like a refiner’s fire

and like fuller’s herb.

And he shall sit refining and cleansing [alternative: add “as”]

silver,

and he shall purify the sons of Levi,

and shall refine them like gold and like silver.

And they shall be offerings to the Lord in righteousness.

[Col. 1077D] And the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem shall please the Lord,

as in the days of old and as in ancient years.

And I shall draw near to you in judgment,

and I shall be a swift witness against sorcerers,

adulterers,

perjurers,

those who defraud the hired laborer of his wages,

widows,

orphans,

and those who oppress the sojourner,

and who did not fear me,

says the Lord of hosts.

For I am the Lord, and I do not change;

and you, sons of Jacob, have not been consumed.

For from the days of your fathers you have departed from my ordinances,

and have not kept them.

[Col. 1078A] Return to me,

and I shall return to you, says the Lord of hosts.

And you said: “In what shall we return?”

Can a man pierce God, that you pierce me?

And you said: “In what have we pierced you?”

In tithes and firstfruits.

And you are cursed with want,

and you have pierced me,

the whole nation.

Bring every tithe into the storehouse,

so that there may be food in my house,

and test me in this, says the Lord.

If I do not open for you the floodgates of heaven,

and pour out for you a blessing in abundance,

I shall rebuke the devourer for your sake,

and he shall not corrupt the fruit of your land.

Nor shall the vine in the field be barren,

says the Lord of hosts.

And all the nations shall call you blessed,

[Col. 1078B] for you shall be a desirable land,

says the Lord of hosts.

Your words have prevailed against me, says the Lord.

And you said:

“What have we spoken against you?”

You said:

“It is futile to serve God.

And what profit is there in keeping his commandments,

and in walking mournfully before the Lord of hosts?

Therefore now we call the arrogant blessed:

for those who practice wickedness have been built up;

they have tested God and have been saved.”

Then those who fear the Lord spoke,

each one with his neighbor,

and the Lord attended and heard.

And a book of remembrance was written before him

for those who fear the Lord

and think upon his name.

[Col. 1078C] And they shall be mine, says the Lord of hosts,

on the day when I act,

as a treasured possession.

And I shall spare them

as a man spares his son who serves him.

And you shall return,

and you shall see what is between the righteous and the wicked,

between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.

[Cap. IV.] For behold, the day is coming,

burning like a furnace.

And all the arrogant

and all who practice wickedness shall be stubble.

And the coming day shall set them ablaze,

says the Lord of hosts,

and shall leave them neither root nor shoot.

And for you who fear my name

the Sun of righteousness shall rise,

and healing shall be in his wings.

And you shall go out and leap like calves from the herd.

[Col. 1078D] And you shall trample the wicked,

when they are ashes beneath the soles of your feet,

on the day when I act,

says the Lord of hosts.

Remember the law of Moses my servant,

which I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel:

precepts and judgments.

Behold, I shall send you Elijah the prophet,

before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.

And he shall turn the heart of the fathers toward the sons,

and the heart of the sons toward their fathers,

lest I come

and strike the land with a ban.

[Col. 1077] Here ends the Book of the Prophet Malachi.

THE THIRD ORDER, OF THE HAGIOGRAPHA.

[Col. 1079]

[THE BOOK OF JOB.]

PREFACE OF SAINT JEROME TO THE BOOK OF JOB.

[Note: We have compared the Book of Job, as well as the following Book of Esther, with another Palatine-Vatican manuscript marked with the number 24. It is written entirely in what are called capital letters and displays such evidence of antiquity and sound quality that, except for the Veronese manuscript, which contains the Books of Kings, it could occupy the foremost place among nearly all the other biblical codices I have seen. For this reason we treat it somewhat more carefully than the others, and do not omit to record even variant readings of occasionally lesser importance, or even errors.]

[Col. 1079A] I am compelled, book by book, to answer the curses of my opponents [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads: “in divine Scripture.”] in divine Scripture.

They accuse my translation of criticizing the Septuagint translators, as though among the Greeks Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion [Note: The same manuscript reads: “and Theodotion, either word for word, sense for sense, or from both,” etc.; this reading, however, I would reject. A little later it also has “Testament” instead of “Instrument.”] had not likewise produced a mode of translation expressed either word for word, sense for sense, or by a mixture of both, suitably moderated;

and as though Origen had not marked all the volumes of the Old Instrument with obeli and asterisks, inserting into the ancient translation what had either been added or taken from Theodotion, thereby showing that what was added had been missing.

Let my detractors, then, learn to accept in the whole what they accepted in part,

[Col. 1080A] or else let them erase my translation together with its asterisks.

[Note: Martianaeus wrongly printed *susceperint*, which yields no sense, or at least an unsuitable one. In Book II, no. 29, of the Holy Father’s *Apology against Rufinus*, where he repeats this preface almost word for word, we previously restored *perspexerint*, which is both the correct word and is found with this sense in the manuscripts consulted by the Benedictine editor. Nevertheless, I would now prefer, on the authority of the very ancient Palatine manuscript, that whatever that word may be should be wholly absent from this passage, so that *fatentur* (“they acknowledge”) may be understood more elegantly from the following balanced clause. The sense then is that it cannot be that those whom they acknowledge to have omitted many things should not also be acknowledged to have erred in some respects.]

For it is impossible that, having recognized that those translators omitted many things, they should refuse to acknowledge that they also erred in certain matters, especially in Job.

If what has been added under the asterisks is removed from it, the greater part [Note: The Palatine manuscript lacks *τὸ* (“the”) before “volume,” without injury to the sense. Shortly afterward it also reads “before the edition” instead of “before that translation.”] of the volume will be mutilated—

and this only among the Greeks.

Moreover, among the Latins, before the translation that we recently published with asterisks and obeli,

[Note: This recent writer is mistaken, as in many other places, when he presumes to define the inventions of his own speculation for us as rules of understanding. In Book I, page 6, of his *Critical History of the Old Testament*, he says that one should read here: “Nearly seventy or eighty verses are missing,” not “nearly seven or eight hundred.” Evidently he had read the letter of Usserius of Armagh to Louis Cappel, in which that learned man, discussing the verses—or *στίχοι* (“lines”)—of the Book of Job, appropriately observes the following: Hesychius, or whoever was the author of the unpublished *Hypotheses* on the sacred books, notes here by a distinction that the Book of Job had 1,600 *στίχοι* without asterisks, but 2,200 with asterisks. This agrees perfectly with the most ancient records of antiquity. For the catalogue of the books of Holy Scripture, compiled according to a Latin edition older than Jerome and copied more than a thousand years ago at the end of our volume of the Letters of Saint Paul, assigns the Book of Job the number 1,600 verses. But in copies of the Canon of the Hebrew truth, in which the volume of Job is divided and written out stichometrically, there are counted, by cola and commas, 2,227 verses or more. It is therefore clear that among the Latins the Book of Job was mutilated by nearly seven hundred verses before the translation that Jerome published with asterisks and obeli. Origen also admits defects of this kind in his letter to Africanus, especially when, speaking of the middle of the Book of Job, he says: “Again, many passages placed throughout the middle of the book among the Hebrews are not found likewise among us; often four or three verses are missing, sometimes fourteen, sixteen, and nineteen. And why should I enumerate these matters, which we have collected with much labor, so that the difference between the Jewish and our copies might not remain hidden from us?” Some manuscripts, however, offer the following variant reading at this same point: “There are nearly seven or eight hundred verses by which the book has been shortened, lacerated, and so on.” MART.]

nearly seven or eight hundred verses are missing, so that the book, shortened, lacerated, and gnawed away, displays its disgrace openly to its readers.

This translation follows none of the ancient interpreters;

[Col. 1081A] rather, from the Hebrew and Arabic language, and sometimes the Syriac, it will now reproduce words, now meaning, now both together.

[Note: The word “follows” is absent here in the Palatine manuscript. Shortly afterward it reads “will resound” instead of “will echo.” Saint Gregory the Great likewise states that the Book of Job consists of Hebrew and Arabic speech.]

For the whole book is also said to be oblique and slippery among the Hebrews.

And what [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads: “Greek rhetors.”] Greek rhetors call *ἐσχηματισμένος* (*eschēmatismenos*, “figurative” or “schematized”)—while saying one thing, it does another—

is such that, if you wished to hold an eel or a little *muraenula* [a small eel-like fish] in tightly closed hands,

[Note: We have restored *muraenulam* (“little muraena”), the reading preferred by all the manuscripts and by the older editions. Bede and other medieval writers likewise read it in Jerome. Martianaeus, however, wished to rewrite it as *muraenam* (“muraena”), reasoning that *muraenula* was a diminutive form meaning “little chain,” derived from the fish by resemblance. As though, by the analogy of the name, a diminutive could be applied less to the fish than to such a chain, which is also mentioned in the Song of Songs. In printed editions and in many manuscripts, we read the corrupt form *murenulam* for *muraena*. Who does not know that the muraena is a fish not unlike an eel, while *muraenula* is the gold neck-chain commonly so called, according to Jerome, because the metal, drawn out into pliant rods, is woven into a chain of winding arrangement, the name being formed from the image of the fish? See the letter to Marcella on the praises of Asella. MART.]

the more firmly you pressed it, the more quickly it would slip away.

I remember that, for an understanding of this volume, I purchased at considerable expense the instruction of a certain teacher from Lydda,

[Note: The Palatine manuscript reads “a certain Jewish man,” and this is what we say of the man in Saint Jerome’s Life.]

who was considered foremost among the Hebrews.

Whether I gained anything from his instruction, I do not know.

I know only this: I could not translate anything except what I had first understood.

Accordingly, from the beginning of the volume up to the words of Job, among the Hebrews

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “it is prose discourse.” MART.]

[Col. 1081B] it is prose discourse.

But from Job’s words, in which he says:

“May the day perish on which I was born,

and the night on which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived,’”

down to the place where, near the end of the volume, it is written:

“Therefore I condemn myself,”
and I repent in dust and ashes: these are hexameter verses [Note: On such verses and the meters of the divine Scriptures, a fuller discussion is given in the Prolegomena to this Bibliotheca. MART. —What we think about the meters of the Hebrew text is explained in the preface.], moving in dactyls and spondees; and, because of the idiom of the language, frequently admitting other feet as well—not of the same syllables, but of the same quantities. Sometimes, too, the rhythm itself, sweet and ringing, proceeds in numbers freed from the law of meter [Note: Thus the manuscript of the sacred Scriptures of the Church of Narbonne reads; some others do not have the word *metri* (“of meter”), but only *numeris lege solutis* (“in numbers released from the law”). A manuscript biblical copy of our monastery of Blessed Mary of the Gilded, at Toulouse, preserves a very different reading, in which I found written: “Sometimes, too, the rhythm itself, sweet and ringing, proceeds as a number,” which a reader versed in meter understands better than a plain reader. MART. —The word *metri* is absent from the Palatine manuscript, as also from most of the other codices examined by Martianay. Formerly *pedum* (“of feet”) stood in its place. It was preferable, however, to retain both words: for Saint Jerome clearly alludes to Horace’s remark about Pindar, “he is borne along in rhythms released from the law.”] of meter [Col. 1082A]—something understood more by those versed in meter than by the ordinary reader.

From the verse mentioned above to the end of the book, the small remaining section is composed in prose. If anyone finds it incredible that there are meters among the Hebrews, and that, in the manner of our Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, Alcaeus, and Sappho, either the Psalter, or the Lamentations of Jeremiah, or nearly all the songs of Scripture are composed in verse, let him read [Note: Philo spoke of the meters of hymns or psalms when discussing the Essenes; Josephus, in *The Antiquities of the Jews*, Book II, chapter 7, recognizes hexameters in the Scriptures. I have so far found nothing of this kind in Origen; but in Eusebius of Caesarea these words are expressly written in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book XI, chapter 5. MART. —Recall the Preface to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, especially these words: “What is more perfect than Job?” All these works, as Josephus and [Col. 1082D] Origen write, proceed among their people in hexameter and pentameter verses. The testimonies of the writers whose judgment Saint Jerome follows here are also noted there.] Philo, Josephus, Origen, and Eusebius of Caesarea, and their testimony will prove that I speak the truth.

Let my dogs therefore hear that I labored over this volume not to criticize the ancient translation, but so that those things in it which are obscure, omitted, or at least corrupted through scribal fault might be made clearer in my translation [Col. 1082B]—I who have learned the Hebrew language in part [Al. “so that I, who have learned the language of the Hebrews…”], and who in Latin have been worn down almost from infancy among grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers.

And if among the Greeks, after the edition of the Seventy, when the Gospel of Christ was already shining forth, the Jewish Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—heretics who Judaized—were accepted, though by their deceitful translation they concealed many mysteries of the Savior, and yet are preserved in the *Hexapla* (Ἑξαπλοῖς) among the Churches and explained by ecclesiastical writers, how much more should I, a Christian born of Christian parents [Note: The same manuscript again omits here the word *natus* (“born”). What Saint Jerome says about carrying the standard of the cross on his forehead properly refers to the sign of the Cross, with which, together with the fragrance of chrism, we mark the forehead at baptism, as Justus of Urgell says. He notes the same thing frequently elsewhere, and in his commentary on Ezekiel 9, concerning the sign of the Cross painted on the foreheads of Christians. Ennodius likewise writes in *Epigram* XVII:

“We are believed to belong to God by the sign on our forehead.”], and carrying the standard of the cross on my forehead, whose concern has been to restore what was omitted, correct what was corrupted [Note: These words too, “to correct” and “the mysteries,” are absent from the Palatine codex, apparently through the carelessness of copyists.], and disclose the Church’s sacraments in pure and faithful language, be rejected by fastidious [Note: Only the Saint-Germain manuscript reads “by slanderous readers.” MART.] or malicious readers? Let those who wish have ancient books written on purple parchment in gold and silver [Note: One such codex, written on purple parchment in letters of silver, still survives among us in the library of the Church of Verona; it contains the Latin version of the Gospels from before Jerome, and we shall speak of it and of the following volume in its proper place.], or in uncial letters, as they commonly say, more heavily inscribed than books [Note: Two or three manuscripts read *initialibus* (“initial”) instead of *uncialibus*, with the same meaning. MART. —The uncial letters Jerome calls such are explained by the Gloss in Vatican Codex 135 as “long.” Budaeus, in Book I of *On the As*, holds that they were written with the thickness of a thumb. It is much more plausible, however, that they were so called because they were letters of a certain size, approaching, by some proportion, the magnitude of an ounce; examples of them can be seen in certain more ancient codices. In the same way we commonly call letters “cubit-high” when, on stones placed above and farther from the eye, they are inscribed larger, as it were in the form of a cubit. What some manuscripts offer instead, *initialibus*, is plainly corrupt; both Martianay, who claims that it has the same meaning, and others, who think it denotes letters written larger at the beginning of a sentence or chapter after the introduction of the so-called minuscule script, are mistaken—for those familiar with the writing of Jerome’s age know that this cannot fit the period.], provided they allow me and my poor companions to have little sheets—not books so beautiful as books that are corrected.

Both editions—the Septuagint according to the Greeks and mine according to the Hebrews—have been translated into Latin through my labor [Note: This Latin version of Job, which Jerome notes as having been made from the Greek, we present in the following volume together with his other works in their proper place.]. Let each person choose what he wishes, and let him judge me to be a student rather than a malicious critic [Note: Both copies of the Canon, together with twelve other manuscript codices, read *se pro me*, “let him prove himself on my side,” and *studiosum se magis quam malivolum*, “let him prove himself a student rather than malicious.” Let each person therefore choose what he wishes among these variant readings. MART.].

## THE BOOK OF JOB BEGINS [Note: To the Palatine manuscript praised thus far we now join another from the same Vatican library, once belonging to the Queen of the Swedes and marked with the number 7; it is indeed extremely ancient and carefully corrected.]

[Col. 1083]

### Chapter I

There was a man in the land of Uz, named Job; and that man was simple and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil. Seven sons and three daughters were born to him. His possessions were seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys, together with a very large household; and that man was greater than all the people of the East.

His sons would go and hold feasts in their houses, each on his appointed day. They would send for their three sisters and invite them to eat and drink with them. When the days of the feast had gone round, Job would send for them and sanctify them. Rising at dawn, he offered burnt offerings for each one [Al. “for all of them”]. For he said, “Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts.” Thus Job did all his days.

One day, when the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord, Satan was also present among them. The Lord said to him, “Where have you come from?” He answered, “I have gone around the earth and traveled through it.” The Lord said to him, “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth—a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?” Satan answered the Lord, “Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not fenced him in, and his house, and all his possessions around him? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land. But stretch out your hand a little and touch all that he possesses, unless he blesses you to your face [Al. “your face”].”

Then the Lord said to Satan, “Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him.” And Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.

Now one day, when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother, a messenger came to Job and said, “The oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing beside them, when the Sabeans fell upon them, carried everything away, and struck the servants with the sword. I alone escaped to tell you.”

While he was still speaking, another came and said, “The fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants that it touched. I alone escaped to tell you.”

While he was still speaking, another came and said, “The Chaldeans formed three bands, attacked the camels, and carried them away; they also struck the servants with the sword. I alone escaped to tell you.”

While he was still speaking, behold, another entered and said, “While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother, suddenly a violent wind rushed in from the region of the desert and shook the four corners of the house. When it collapsed, it crushed your children, and they died. I alone escaped to tell you.”

Then Job arose and tore his tunic [Note: The Palatine manuscript, together with the common editions, reads “his garments.”], and, having shaved his head, he fell to the ground and worshiped. He said:

“Naked I came from my mother’s womb,  
and naked I shall return there.  
The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away [Note: Two additions are retained here not only in the printed books and very many manuscripts, but also in the Saint-Germain Canon, where the scholiast added critical notes in his customary manner in the margin: “This is absent: ‘As it pleased the Lord, so it happened,’” and afterward, “This is absent: ‘with his lips.’” In the Carcassonne Canon the final addition, “with his lips,” is absent; in the royal biblical codex these words are written externally and by a second hand. Finally, the Corbie codex, written in uncial letters nine hundred years ago and numbered 660 in the library of Saint-Germain, retains nothing foreign to the Hebrew text, but here presents the pure Hieronymian version as we have published it. The first addition was taken from the Seventy Translators, the second from verse 10 of the following chapter. MART. —That little sentence, “As it pleased the Lord, so it happened,” which the common books and most of the manuscripts cited by Martianay insert here from the Greek, is entirely unknown to the ancient Palatine manuscript in accordance with the Hebrew context; in the later hand it is ascribed to the other manuscript of the Queen of Sweden.]; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

In all this Job did not sin [Note: The common editions also add “with his lips,” words plainly derived from verse 10 of the following chapter, since even the Seventy do not have them. Nevertheless, they occur in one Palatine manuscript.] or speak anything foolish against God.

### Chapter II

Now one day, when the sons of God had come and stood before the Lord, Satan also came among them and stood in his presence. The Lord said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” He answered, “I have gone around the earth and traveled through it.” The Lord said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil, and still holding fast to his innocence? But you have stirred me against him, so that I should afflict him without cause.”

Satan answered, “Skin for skin, and everything a man has he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand and touch his bones and his flesh, and then you will see whether he blesses you to your face [Note: The same Palatine manuscript, together with the Vulgate books, reads “he blesses you to your face.”].”

Then the Lord said to Satan, “Behold, he is in your hand; nevertheless preserve his life.” Satan went out from the presence of the Lord and struck Job with a very grievous ulcer, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. He scraped away the discharge with a potsherd and sat on a dung heap.

His wife said to him, “Do you still remain in your simplicity [Al. “remaining, do you…”]? Bless God and die.” He answered her, “You have spoken as one of the foolish [Note: The Queen’s manuscript, more fully than the common editions, reads “as one of the foolish women”; in Hebrew, however, “women” is not specifically added.]. If we have received good things from the hand of God, why should we not receive evil?” In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

When Job’s three friends heard of all the evil that had happened to him, they came, each from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. For they had agreed to come together to visit and console him. When they lifted their eyes from afar, they did not recognize him. They tore their garments and scattered dust over their heads toward heaven. They sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.

## AFTER THIS JOB OPENED HIS MOUTH, CURSED HIS DAY, AND SPOKE:

### Chapter III

“Perish the day on which I was born,  
and the night on which it was said: ‘A man has been conceived.’

Let that day be turned into darkness;  
let God not seek it from above,  
and let no light shine upon it [Al. “let it not be illumined”].

Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure it;  
let gloom seize it,  
and let it be wrapped in bitterness.

Let a dark whirlwind possess that night;  
let it not be counted among the days of the year,  
nor numbered among the months.

Let that night be solitary  
and unworthy of praise.

Let those who curse the day curse it—  
those who are ready to rouse Leviathan.

Let its stars be darkened by obscurity;  
let it await the light and not see it,  
nor the rising of the dawn.

For it did not shut the doors of the womb that bore me,  
nor remove trouble from my eyes.

Why did I not die in the womb?  
Why, when I came forth from the womb, did I not perish at once?

Why was I received upon knees?  
Why was I suckled at the breasts?

For now I would be lying silent in sleep  
and resting in my slumber,

with the kings and governors of the earth  
who build themselves deserted places,

or with princes who possess gold  
and fill their houses with silver,

or, like a hidden miscarriage, I would not exist,  
like infants conceived who never saw the light [Al. “the sun”].

There the wicked cease from turmoil,  
and there those exhausted in strength find rest.

Together, once imprisoned, they are without distress  
and do not hear the voice of the taskmaster.

Small and great are there,  
and the servant is free from his master [Note: The Colbertine manuscript of Anjou uses here a sixth division, which it entitles “the sixth book,” as though the book of Job had been divided into several books. MART.].

Why is light given to the miserable,  
and life to those whose soul is in bitterness?

To those who await death, and it does not come—  
as though they were digging for a treasure [Note: The Queen’s manuscript improperly reads “and do not find.” The following two verses are rendered rather unusually by the Palatine manuscript, which omits the word “treasure”: “as though those digging rejoice exceedingly,” and so forth. Yet the Hebrew does contain that noun, meaning, if not precisely “treasure,” at least something hidden and concealed.],

who rejoice exceedingly  
when they find the grave;

to the man whose way is hidden,  
and whom God has surrounded with darkness?

Before I eat, I sigh;  
and my roaring is like waters overflowing.

For the fear that I feared has come upon me,  
and what I dreaded has happened to me.

Have I not dissembled?  
Have I not been silent?  
Have I not rested?  
Yet indignation has come upon me.”

## ELIPHAZ THE TEMANITE ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter IV

“If we begin to speak to you [Al. “with you”], perhaps you will take it badly;  
but who can hold back a word once conceived [Al. “who will be able to hold it back”]?

Behold, you have instructed many,  
and strengthened weary hands.

Your words have confirmed those who were wavering,  
and you have strengthened trembling knees [Al. “confirmed”].

But now the affliction has come upon you, and you have failed;  
it has touched you, and you are troubled.

Where is your fear, your strength, your patience [Al. “your patience, your strength”],  
and the perfection of your ways?

Remember, I beg you: who has ever perished while innocent?  
Or when have the upright been destroyed [Al. “been”]?

Rather, I have seen those who work iniquity  
and sow sorrows and reap them,

perish when God blows,  
and be consumed by the breath of his anger [Note: In the same manuscript, “of his mouth” is read instead of “of his anger,” contrary to the Hebrew text.].

The roaring of the lion,  
the voice of the lioness,  
and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken.

The tiger perishes because it has no prey,  
and the lion’s cubs are scattered.

Now a word was secretly spoken to me,  
and my ear received, as though furtively,  
the veins of its whisper.

In the horror of a nocturnal vision,  
when sleep usually overtakes human beings,

fear and trembling seized me,  
and all my bones were terrified.

When a spirit passed before me,  
the hairs of my flesh bristled.

Someone stood there whose face I did not recognize—  
an image before my eyes—  
and I heard a voice like a gentle breeze:

‘Can a man be justified in comparison with God,  
or can a human being be purer than his Maker?

Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast,  
and he found perversity in his angels.

How much more will those who dwell in houses of clay,  
whose foundation is earthly,  
be consumed like a moth?

From morning to evening they will be cut down;  
because no one understands,  
they will perish forever.

And those who remain will be taken away from them;  
they will die, and not in wisdom.’”

### Chapter V

“Call, then, if there is anyone who will answer you,  
and turn to one of the holy ones.

Truly, anger kills the fool,  
and envy slays the simple.

I have seen a fool firmly rooted,  
and I immediately cursed his prosperity.

His children will be far from deliverance;  
they will be crushed at the gate,  
and there will be no one to rescue them.

The hungry will eat his harvest;  
the armed will seize him,  
and the thirsty will drink up his wealth.

Nothing on earth happens without cause,  
and trouble does not spring from the ground.

Human beings are born to labor,  
and birds to flight.

Therefore I will entreat the Lord  
and direct my speech to God—

who does great and inscrutable things,  
and wonders without number;

who gives rain upon the face of the earth  
and waters everything;

who sets the lowly on high  
and raises the sorrowful to safety;

who frustrates the thoughts of the crafty,  
so that their hands cannot accomplish what they have begun;

who catches the wise in their cunning  
and scatters the counsel of the wicked.

By day they encounter darkness,  
and at noon they grope as though in the night.

But he will save [Vulgate editions insert “the needy”] from the sword of their mouth  
and the poor from the hand of the violent [Note: The royal codex adds “the needy,” which is absent from the Hebrew, as also from the Saint-Germain Canon and other manuscripts of better quality. MART.].

The poor will have hope,  
but iniquity will shut its mouth.

Blessed is the man whom God corrects;  
therefore do not reject the rebuke of the Lord.

For he wounds, and he heals;  
he strikes, and his hands will heal.

In six troubles he will deliver you,  
and in the seventh evil will not touch you.

In famine he will rescue you from death [Note: The words “from death,” and “in war,” are missing through the carelessness of a copyist, who was misled by the recurrence of the same small word.],  
and in war from the power of the sword.

You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue,  
and you will not fear calamity when it comes.

In devastation and famine you will laugh,  
and you will not fear the beasts of the earth [Al. “the beast”].

You will have a covenant with the stones of the region,  
and the beasts of the earth will be at peace with you.

You will know that your tent is at peace,  
and when you visit your dwelling, you will not sin.

You will know also that your seed will be numerous,  
and your offspring like the grass of the earth [Note: The same manuscript reads “like the sand,” instead of “like the grass”—incorrectly.].

You will enter the grave in abundance,  
as a heap [Note: Some Vulgate books add “of grain,” and it is indeed present in the Hebrew.] is brought in at its time.

Behold, this is so, as we have investigated it;  
having heard it, consider it carefully.”

## JOB ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter VI

“Would that my sins, by which I deserved anger,  
were weighed,  
and the calamity that I suffer were placed in the balance;  
it would appear heavier than the sand of the sea.

Therefore my words are full of pain [Note: The Palatine manuscript has “with deceit” instead of “with pain”; I attribute this to scribal error, unless someone deliberately altered the word after observing that among the Seventy these words are rendered as *phaula*, that is, “evil,” rather than “full of pain.” The Hebrew calls them “swallowed up.”];

for the arrows of the Lord are in me.  
Their indignation drinks up my spirit,  
and the terrors of the Lord wage war against me.

Does the wild donkey bray when it has grass?  
Or does the ox low when it stands before a full manger?

Can what is tasteless, what is not seasoned with salt, be eaten?  
Or can anyone taste what brings death when tasted [Note: In both copies of the Canon, the following verse is inserted after these words: “For even bitter things seem sweet to the hungry soul.” The corrector of the Saint-Germain codex erased the words with a deletion. They appear to have been transferred here from Proverbs 27, where the same thought occurs in verse 7: “Even the bitter will be taken as sweet.” The ancient Concordances of the Bible note that this verse already existed at Job 6:6. MART. —Saint Jerome indicates by this very translation that he had read the wording of the text differently, namely [Hebrew reading omitted in the supplied text], which he renders as “brings death.” Although the Hebrew reading is rendered variously by interpreters, and some hold that *chalamuth* means the white of an egg, it is generally explained more suitably as the saliva of someone sleeping, since *chalamoth* properly means “dreams.” The resulting sense would be: “Can anyone taste the saliva of dreams,” that is, saliva while sleeping? Moreover, among our manuscripts the Palatine adds the verse, “For even bitter things seem sweet to the hungry soul,” which Martianay also found in one or another of his copies and noted as taken from Proverbs 27:7 and transferred here, although the Concordances of the Bible commend it as genuine at this passage in Job.]?

What my soul formerly refused to touch  
is now, because of anguish, my food.

Who will grant that my request may come,  
and that God may give me what I await?

Would that he who began would himself crush me,  
loose his hand, and cut me off.

Let this be my consolation:  
that, though afflicting me with pain, he does not spare me,  
and that I do not contradict the words of the Holy One.

For what is my strength, that I should endure?  
Or what is my end, that I should act patiently?

My strength is not the strength of stones,  
nor is my flesh bronze [Al. “brass”].

Behold, there is no help for me in myself,  
and even those close to me have withdrawn from me.

Whoever removes mercy from his friend  
abandons the fear of the Lord.

My brothers have passed by me  
like a torrent that rushes swiftly through valleys.

Those who fear frost are overtaken by snow;  
when they are scattered, they perish;  
and when it grows warm, they melt away from their place.

The paths of their steps are entangled;  
they walk into emptiness and perish.

Consider the paths of Tema [Al. “Teman”],  
the roads of Sheba [Al. “the Sabeans”],  
and wait a little.

They are confounded because they hoped [Al. “I hoped”];  
they came even to me,  
and were covered with shame.

Now you have come,  
and merely seeing my wound, you are afraid.

Did I ever say, ‘Bring me something,  
and give me a gift from your possessions’?

Or, ‘Deliver me from the hand of the enemy,  
and rescue me from the hand of the strong’?

Teach me, and I will be silent;  
and if I have perhaps been ignorant of something, instruct me.

Why have you detracted from words of truth,  
when there is no one among you who can refute [Al. “refute me”]?

You compose speeches merely for reproof  
and cast words into the wind.

You fall upon the orphan  
and try to overthrow your friend.

Nevertheless, complete what you have begun;  
lend an ear and see whether I am lying.

Answer, I beg you, without contention;  
and, speaking what is just, judge.

You will find no iniquity on my tongue,  
nor will folly sound in my throat.”

### Chapter VII

“Is not human life a campaign upon the earth,  
and are not his days like the days of a hired laborer?

As a servant longs for the shade,  
and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work,

so I have had empty months,  
and I have counted laborious nights for myself.

If I lie down to sleep, I say [Al. “I shall say”], ‘When shall I rise?’  
And again I await the evening [Note: The Queen’s manuscript has “until evening,” which the Palatine itself soon prefers instead of “until darkness.”],  
and I am filled with pains until darkness.

My flesh is clothed with rottenness and clods of dust;  
my skin has dried up and contracted.

My days have passed more swiftly  
than a thread is cut by a weaver,  
and they have been consumed without any hope.

Remember that my life is wind,  
and that my eye will not return to see good.

The sight of a human being will not look upon me;  
your eyes are upon me, and I shall not remain.

As a cloud is consumed and passes away,  
so one who descends to the underworld will not ascend.

He will not return again to his house,  
nor will his place know him any longer.

Therefore I will not spare my mouth;  
I will speak in the tribulation of my spirit;  
I will converse in the bitterness of my soul [Note: The Palatine codex has “I converse in the bitterness.”].

Am I the sea, or a sea monster,  
that you have surrounded me with a prison?

If I say, ‘My bed will comfort me,  
and I shall be relieved while speaking with myself in my couch,’

you will terrify me through dreams,  
and shake me with visions of horror.

Therefore my soul chose hanging,  
and my bones chose death.

I have despaired; I shall no longer live.  
Spare me, for my days are nothing.

What is man, that you magnify him?  
Or why do you set your heart upon him [Al. “why do you add to him”] [Note: The same manuscript has “why do you set around him,” and shortly afterward, “you will not spare me, nor release me, so that…”]?

You visit him at dawn  
and suddenly test him.

How long will you not spare me,  
nor release me so that I may swallow my saliva?

I have sinned; what shall I do to you, O guardian of humanity?  
Why have you set me against you,  
and have I become a burden to myself?

Why do you not take away my sin,  
and why do you not remove my iniquity?

Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust;  
and if you seek me in the morning, I shall not remain.”

## BALDAD THE SHUHITE ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter VIII

“How long will you speak such things,  
and will the many words of your mouth be a mighty wind?

Does God pervert judgment,  
or does the Almighty subvert what is just?

Even if your children sinned against him,  
he abandoned them to the power of their iniquity.

But if you rise early and turn to God,  
and entreat the Almighty,

if you walk pure and upright [Note: Again, whether through scribal carelessness or misguided correction, the Palatine manuscript lacks this entire verse: “If you walk pure and upright.” The Vulgate books read “if he walks.”],

he will immediately awaken on your behalf  
and restore peace to the dwelling of your righteousness,

so that your former state will have been small,  
and your final state will increase greatly.

For ask about the former generation,  
and diligently investigate the memory of the fathers—

for we are of yesterday and do not know,  
because our days upon the earth are like a shadow.

They themselves will teach you;  
they will speak to you  
and bring forth words from their heart.”

Can the rush grow green without moisture?  
Or can the papyrus grow without water [Note: Hebrew *ahu*, or *achou*, which Jerome in Genesis 41 interprets as marshy places; here, however, he translates it as *biblos* according to the Hebrew truth of both copies of the Canon. The Seventy, having read *ahi* in the book of Genesis, translated it here as “meadow.” Jerome must again be heard concerning *ahu* in his *Hebrew Questions*: “Twice in Genesis *achi* is written, and it is neither Greek nor Latin. But the Hebrew itself is corrupt; for it is said *in ahu*, that is, ‘in the marsh.’ But because among the Hebrews the letters VAV and YOD are similar and differ in size, the Seventy Translators rendered *achi* for *ahu* and, according to their custom, joined the Greek letter χ to express the double aspiration of HETH in Hebrew.” MART.]?

While it is still in flower and has not been cut by hand,  
it withers before all other grasses.

So are the ways of all who forget God,  
and the hope of the hypocrite will perish.

His folly will not please him,  
and his confidence is like a spider’s web.

He will lean upon his house, and it will not stand;  
he will support it, and it will not rise.
