He appears moist before the sun comes,  
and at its rising his shoot comes forth [Al. “will come forth”].

His roots will thicken upon a heap of stones  
and will remain among the rocks.

If it is swallowed up from its place,  
it will deny him and say, ‘I do not know you’ [Al. “I did not see you”].

For this is the joy of its way:  
that others may again sprout from the earth [Al. “upward”].

God will not cast away the simple,  
nor will he stretch out his hand against the wicked.

Until your mouth is filled with laughter  
and your lips with rejoicing.

Those who hate you will be clothed with confusion,  
and the tent of the wicked will not remain.”

## AND HE ANSWERED [Note: The Queen’s manuscript adds the name “Job,” which also appears here in the Hebrew copy.] AND SAID:

### Chapter IX

“Truly I know that this is so,  
and that a human being cannot be justified when compared with God [Al. “cannot be justified before God”].

If he wishes to contend with him,  
he will not be able to answer him one thing out of a thousand.

He is wise in heart and mighty in strength;  
who has resisted him and had peace?

He moves mountains, and they do not know it,  
when he overturns them in his anger.

He shakes the earth from its place,  
and its pillars tremble.

He commands the sun, and it does not rise [Al. “will not rise”],  
and he seals up the stars as though beneath a seal.

He alone stretches out the heavens  
and walks upon the waves of the sea.

He makes the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades,  
and the inner regions of the south.

He does great and incomprehensible things,  
and wonders without number.

If he comes to me, I shall not see him;  
if he departs, I shall not understand him.

If he suddenly questions me, who will answer him?  
Or who can say, ‘Why do you do this?’ [Al. adds “thus”]

God, against whose anger no one can stand,  
and beneath whom those who bear up the world bend [Al. “are troubled”].

How then am I, that I should answer him  
and speak with him in my words?

Even if I possessed something just, I would not answer;  
I would entreat my judge.

And when he hears me calling,  
I do not believe that he has heard [Al. “will have heard”] my voice.

For he will crush me in a whirlwind  
and multiply my wounds even without cause.

He does not allow my spirit to rest  
and fills me with bitterness.

If strength is sought, he is most powerful;  
if fairness of judgment, no one dares testify for me.

If I wish to justify myself, my mouth will condemn me;  
if I declare myself innocent, he will prove me perverse.

Even if I am simple, my soul will not know this,  
and my life will weary me.

There is one thing I have said:  
he himself consumes both the innocent and the wicked.

If he scourges, let him kill once for all,  
and let him not laugh at the punishments of the innocent.

The earth has been given into the hand of the wicked;  
he covers the face of its judges.

But if it is not he, who then is it?

My days were swifter than a runner;  
they fled and saw no good.

They passed like ships carrying apples,  
like an eagle flying toward food.

When I say, ‘I will no longer speak thus,’  
I change my face and am tortured with grief.

I feared all my works,  
knowing that you would not spare the transgressor.

But if I am wicked even in this way,  
why have I labored in vain?

If I wash myself as with snow-water,  
and my hands shine like the purest things,

you will nevertheless plunge me into filth,  
and my garments will abhor me.

For I will not answer a man who is like me,  
nor one who can be heard with me on equal terms in judgment.

There is no one who can rebuke us both  
and place his hand upon us both.

Let him remove his rod from me,  
and let his terror not frighten me.

I will speak, and I will not fear him;  
for I cannot answer while afraid.

### Chapter X

“My soul is weary of my life.  
I will let my complaint speak against myself;  
I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.

I will say to God: Do not condemn me;  
show me why you judge me thus.”

Does it seem good to you that you should slander me [Alternative: add “me”],  
and oppress me, the work of your hands,  
and assist the plans of the wicked?

Do you have eyes of flesh,  
or do you see as a human being sees [Note: [Col. 1092D] The Carcassonne Canon has “and you see”; likewise, seven verses later, “and they made me entirely round.” MART.], and will you see [Alternative: “do you see”]?

Are your days like human days,  
and your years like the times of a human being,  
that you should seek out my iniquity  
and investigate my sin?

And should you know that I have done nothing wicked,  
when there is no one who can escape [Alternative: “evade”] from your hand?

Your hands fashioned me  
and made me entirely round [Alternative: “in a circle”];  
and yet you suddenly cast me down?

Remember, I beg you, that you made me like clay,  
and that you will return me to dust.

Did you not milk me like milk,  
[Col. 1092D] and curdle me like cheese?

You clothed me with skin and flesh,  
and fitted me together with bones and sinews.

You granted me life and mercy,  
and your visitation guarded my spirit.

Although you conceal these things in your heart,  
I know nevertheless that you remember everything.

If I sinned, and for a time you spared me,  
[Col. 1093A] why do you not permit me to be clean from my iniquity?

And if I am wicked, woe is me;  
and if I am righteous, I shall not lift up my head,  
being filled with affliction and misery.

And because of my pride you will seize me like a lioness,  
and, turning back, you will torment me wondrously.

You renew your witnesses against me,  
and multiply your anger against me,  
and punishments wage war against me.

Why did you bring me out from the womb?  
Would that I had been consumed,  
so that no eye might have seen me!

I would have been as though I had never existed,  
carried from the womb to the grave.

Will not the small number of my days soon come to an end?  
Leave me, then, so that I may mourn my sorrow a little,  
before I go—and do not return—to the land of darkness  
[Col. 1093B] and covered with the gloom of death:

A land of misery and darkness,  
[Note: [Col. 1093D] The Palatine manuscript has “under the shadow of death.”]  
where the shadow of death and no order are found,  
and everlasting horror dwells [Alternative: “dwells there”].

## SOPHAR THE NAAMATHITE ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter XI

Will one who speaks much not also hear?  
Or will a talkative man be justified?

Will men be silent for you alone?  
And when you mock the others, will no one refute you?

For you said: “My speech is pure,  
and I am clean in your sight.”

Would that God himself would speak with you  
and open his lips to you,  
to show you the secrets of wisdom  
and that his law is manifold!

Then you would understand that far less is demanded of you by God  
[Alternative: “by him”]  
than your iniquity deserves.

[Col. 1093C] Perhaps you will grasp the footprints of God  
and find the Almighty in his perfection?

[Hebrew reading: “Will you grasp the footprints of God, or will you find the Almighty in his perfection?”]

He is higher than heaven—what can you do?  
Deeper than hell—how will you know?  
His measure is longer than the earth  
and broader than the sea.

If he overturns everything, or confines it into one place,  
who will oppose him?

For he knows human vanity;  
and when he sees iniquity, does he not consider it?

A vain man is lifted up in pride  
and thinks himself born free, like a wild donkey’s colt.

But you have made your heart firm  
and spread out your hands toward him.

If you remove from yourself the iniquity that is in your hand,  
[Note: [Col. 1093D] In the Regina manuscript, with the opposite meaning, this is read with a negative particle: “which is not in your hand.” That reading is entirely erroneous.]  
and do not let injustice remain in your tabernacle,  
then you will be able to lift up your face without blemish,  
and you will be steadfast and will not fear.

[Col. 1093D] You will also forget misery  
and remember it like waters that have passed away.

A brightness like midday [Alternative: “midmorning”] will rise for you at evening,  
and when you think yourself consumed, you will rise like the morning star.

[Col. 1094A] You will have confidence, with hope set before you,  
and, having been buried, you will sleep securely.

You will rest, and there will be no one to terrify you;  
and many will entreat your face.

But the eyes of the wicked will fail,  
and refuge will perish from them,  
and their hope will be an abhorrence to their soul.

## JOB ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter XII

So you alone are human beings,  
and wisdom will die with you [Note: [Col. 1093D] The same manuscript has “will dwell with you”; the Hebrew, however, disagrees.].

I too have a heart, as you do,  
and I am not inferior to you.  
For who does not know these things that you know?

One who is mocked by his friend, as I am,  
will call upon God, and he will answer him [Alternative: “answers him”];  
the simplicity of the righteous is mocked.

A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich,  
prepared for the appointed time [Alternative: “the fixed time”].

The tents of robbers abound,  
[Col. 1094B] and they boldly provoke God,  
since he himself has given everything into their hands.

Indeed, ask the beasts, and they will teach you;  
and the birds of heaven, and they will tell you.

Speak to the earth, and it will answer you;  
and the fish of the sea will recount [Note: [Col. 1093D] The Palatine manuscript inserts “to you,” a word that is also present in the Hebrew text.].

Who does not know that the hand of the Lord made all these things?  
In whose hand is the soul of every living thing  
and the spirit of all human flesh.

Does not the ear discern words,  
and the palate of the eater, taste?

With the aged is wisdom,  
and with length of time, understanding.

With him are wisdom and strength;  
he possesses counsel and understanding.

If he destroys, no one can build;  
and if he shuts someone in, no one can open.

If he restrains the waters, everything dries up;  
and if he releases them, they overturn the earth.

[Col. 1094C] With him are strength and [Note: [Col. 1093D] The Hebrew word *tushiyyah* is interpreted by Jerome in many ways. Sometimes he renders it as “wisdom” [Col. 1094D] and “prudence,” as here in Job and below, chapter XXVI, verse 6—or verse 3 in the Latin Vulgate. At times he translates it as “salvation,” “justice,” or “equity.” Finally, above, chapter XI, verse 11—or verse 6 in the Vulgate—he interprets it as “law”: “and that his law is manifold.” Thus the scholiast may have borrowed this present annotation from Jerome himself, or from the Hebrew teachers, who wish *tushiyyah* to signify wisdom, law, and strength. MART.] wisdom [Hebrew: “law”].

He knows both the deceiver  
and the one who is deceived.

He leads counselors to a foolish end  
and judges into stupor.

He loosens the belt of kings  
and girds their loins with a cord.

He leads priests away without honor  
and overturns the mighty.

He changes the speech of the truthful  
and takes away the teaching of the elders.

He pours contempt upon princes  
and raises up those who had been oppressed.

He reveals deep things from darkness  
and brings the shadow [Alternative: “shadows”] of death into the light.

He multiplies nations and destroys them,  
and restores the overthrown to wholeness [Alternative: “will restore”].

He changes the heart of the rulers of the earth  
and misleads them so that they walk aimlessly along a trackless path.

They will grope as in darkness and not in light,  
[Col. 1094D] and he will make them wander like drunkards [Hebrew: “like a drunkard”].

### Chapter XIII

Behold, my eye has seen all these things [Alternative: add “these”],  
and my ear has heard them, and I have understood each one.

According to your knowledge, I too know;  
I am not inferior to you.

[Col. 1095A] Nevertheless, I will speak to the Almighty,  
and I desire to argue with God,  
first showing you to be fabricators of lies  
and defenders of perverse doctrines.

Would that you were silent,  
so that you might be thought wise.

Hear, then, my reproofs,  
and attend to the judgment of my lips.

Does God need your lie,  
so that you may speak deceitfully on his behalf?

Do you show partiality to him [Alternative: “have shown partiality”]  
and attempt to judge on behalf of God?

Or will he be pleased, from whom nothing can be concealed?  
Will he be deceived like a human being by your frauds?

He himself will rebuke you,  
because you show partiality to him secretly.

As soon as he moves, he will disturb you,  
and his terror will fall upon you.

Your memory will be compared to ashes,  
[Col. 1095B] and your necks will be reduced to clay.

Be silent for a little while, so that I may speak  
whatever my mind suggests [Alternative: “suggested”].

Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth  
and carry my soul in my hands?

Even if he kills me, I will hope in him;  
nevertheless, I will argue my ways before him  
[Alternative: “I will argue” omitted].

And he himself will be my savior,  
for no hypocrite will come into his presence.

Hear my speech  
and receive the riddles with your ears.

If I am judged,  
I know that I will be found righteous.

Who is he who will be judged with me? [Note: [Col. 1095D] The Colbertine Anicianus manuscript and another from the monastery of Marmoutier near Tours have only *veniat* (“let him come”). Several other ancient copies added *in judicio* (“in judgment”) in the first hand, but correctors erased it. We have followed the copies of the Canon, as was proper. MART. —In my view, the words *veniat in judicio*, as the scholiast notes, are not found in the Hebrew text. In our manuscripts also, as in the printed books, only the one word *veniat* is found. The Regina manuscript differs here too: “Who is he who will judge me when he comes? Why…”] Let him come into judgment.

[Hebrew: “It does not have ‘let him come into judgment.’”]

Why am I consumed while remaining silent?

Do not do only two things to me,  
[Col. 1095C] and then I shall not hide from your face:

Keep your hand far from me,  
and do not let your dread terrify me.

Call me, and I will answer you [Alternative: add “I”];  
or else I will speak, and you answer me.

How many iniquities and sins do I have?  
Show me my crimes and offenses.

Why do you hide your face  
and consider me your enemy?

Against a leaf driven by the wind you display your power,  
and you pursue a dry straw.

For you write bitter things against me  
and wish to consume me with the sins  
[Hebrew: “and make me inherit the sins”] of my youth.

You have placed my foot in the stocks,  
and watched all my paths,  
and considered the tracks of my feet.

I am consumed like something rotten,  
and like a garment eaten by moths.

[Col. 1095D] ### Chapter XIV

A human being, born of woman,  
lives for a short time and is filled with many miseries.

He comes forth like a flower and is crushed;  
he flees like a shadow [Alternative: “will flee”]  
and never remains in the same condition.

Yet you consider it worthwhile to open your eyes over such a one  
and bring him with you into judgment?  
[Note: [Col. 1096D] The Regina manuscript has “to bring him with you into judgment,” omitting the word “with you,” although it is present in the archetype.]

[Col. 1096A] Who can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed?  
Is it not you, who alone are?

The days of a human being are short;  
the number of his months is known to you.  
You have fixed his limits, which cannot be passed.

Withdraw from him a little, so that he may rest,  
until his desired day comes, like a hired laborer’s days  
[Alternative: “like the day of a hired laborer”].

A tree has hope:  
if it is cut down, it grows green again,  
and its branches sprout.

If its root has grown old in the earth  
and its trunk has died in the dust,  
at the scent of water it will bud  
and produce a crown of foliage as when it was first planted.

But when a human being dies,  
and is stripped and consumed, where, I ask, is he?

As waters depart from the sea,  
[Col. 1096B] and a river, emptied, dries up,  
so a human being, when he has slept, will not rise again.  
Until the heavens are worn away, he will not awaken,  
nor rise from his sleep.

Who will grant me this: that you protect me in hell  
and hide me until your wrath passes,  
and appoint me a time [Note: [Col. 1096D] The Palatine manuscript reads “until you remember me,” and shortly afterward “he will live” instead of “let him live”; finally, it omits the word “I await.”] in which you will remember me?

Do you think that a dead human being will live again?  
All the days of my warfare I wait  
until my change comes.

You will call me, and I will answer you;  
you will extend your right hand to the work of your hands.

Indeed, you have counted my steps,  
but you will spare my sins [Alternative: “spare”].

You have sealed my offenses as in a bag,  
but you have healed my iniquity.

A mountain falling crumbles,  
and a rock is moved from its place.

[Col. 1096C] The waters hollow out stones,  
and by their flooding the earth is gradually worn away;  
so you also destroy a human being in the same way.

You strengthen him for a little while, so that he may pass away forever;  
you change his appearance and send him away [Alternative: “so as to send him away”].

Whether his children are noble  
or ignoble, he will not know.

Nevertheless, while his flesh lives, it will suffer,  
and his soul will mourn over itself [Alternative: “over himself”].

## ELIPHAZ THE TEMANITE ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter XV

Will a wise man answer as though speaking into the wind  
and fill his stomach with heat?

You rebuke one who is not your equal [Alternative: “inferior to you”],  
and speak what is not useful to you.

As far as you can, you have emptied out fear  
and removed prayers from before God.

[Col. 1096D] For your iniquity has taught your mouth [Alternative: omit “your”],  
and you imitate the tongue [Alternative: “words”] of blasphemers.

Your mouth will condemn you, and not I;  
your lips will answer you.

Were you born the first human being,  
and were you formed before the hills?

Have you heard God’s secret counsel,  
and will his wisdom be inferior to you?

[Col. 1097A] What do you know that we do not know?  
What do you understand that we do not?

There are among us both the aged and the ancient,  
much [Alternative: “many”] older than your fathers.

Is it a great thing that God should comfort you?  
But your perverse words prevent it.

What lifts up your heart,  
and, as though thinking great thoughts, makes your eyes stare?

Why does your spirit swell against God,  
so that you utter such words from your mouth?

What is a human being, that he should be without blemish,  
or that one born of woman should appear righteous?

Behold, among his holy ones none is immutable,  
and the heavens are not clean in his sight.

How much more abominable and worthless is a human being,  
who drinks iniquity like water!

I will show you; [Note: [Col. 1097D] The Regina manuscript has: “I will show you what I have seen; hear me, and I will tell you.”] hear me:  
what I have seen, I will tell you.

The wise acknowledge it  
and do not conceal it from their fathers.

[Col. 1097B] To them alone the land was given,  
and no stranger passed among them.

All his days the wicked man is proud,  
and the number of his years is uncertain for his tyranny.

The sound of terror is always in his ears;  
and when there is peace, he always suspects ambushes [Alternative: omit “always”].

He does not believe that he can return from darkness [Note: [Col. 1097D] The words “to the light,” which are not in the Hebrew text, are most correctly omitted by the Palatine manuscript.] to the light,  
looking around on every side for the sword.

When he moves to seek bread,  
he knows that the day of darkness is ready in his hand.

Tribulation will terrify him,  
and anguish will surround him,  
like a king prepared for battle.

For he stretched out his hand against God  
and strengthened himself against the Almighty.

He ran against him with his neck held high  
and armed with a fattened neck.

[Col. 1097C] Fatness covered his face,  
and lard hung from his sides.

He will dwell in devastated cities  
and in deserted houses reduced to heaps.

He will not grow rich,  
nor will his wealth endure,  
nor will he send his root into the earth.

He will not depart from darkness;  
flame will dry up his branches,  
and the breath of his mouth will be taken away.

Let him not trust, deceived by error,  
that he can be redeemed at any price.

Before his days are fulfilled, he will perish,  
and his hands will wither.

His cluster will be injured like a vine in its first flowering,  
and like an olive tree casting away [Alternative: “casting”] its blossom.

For the assembly of the hypocrite is barren,  
and fire will devour the tents of those  
[Col. 1097D] who willingly accept gifts.

He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity,  
and his womb prepares deceit.

## JOB ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter XVI

I have often heard such things;  
all of you are burdensome comforters.

Will windy words ever end?  
Or does anything trouble you, that you speak?

[Col. 1098A] I too could speak things like yours;  
would that your soul were in place of my soul!

I too would comfort you with words  
and shake my head over you.

I would strengthen you with my mouth  
and move my lips as though sparing you.

But what shall I do?  
If I speak, my pain will not be quiet;  
and if I am silent, it will not leave me.

Now, however, my pain has oppressed me,  
and all my limbs have been reduced to nothing [Note: [Col. 1097D] The Palatine manuscript reads “steps” instead of “limbs”; the reading is not itself inappropriate.].

My wrinkles testify against me,  
and a liar rises up before my face,  
contradicting me.

He gathered his fury against me  
and, threatening me, gnawed at me with his teeth.

My enemy looked upon me with terrifying eyes.

They opened their mouths against me  
and, reproaching me, struck my cheek.

[Col. 1098B] They have been filled with my punishments.

God has shut me up with a wicked man  
and delivered me into the hands of the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 1097D] All our manuscripts, as well as the printed books, have: “I, once prosperous,” and so forth.]

So I, once prosperous,  
have suddenly been crushed?

He seized me by the neck and broke me  
and set me up for himself as though for a target.

He surrounded me with his spears,  
pierced my kidneys again and again, and did not spare me,  
and poured out my entrails upon the ground [Hebrew: “my bile”].

He cut me down with wound upon wound;  
he rushed upon me like a giant.

I sewed sackcloth over my skin  
and covered my flesh with ashes.

My face swelled from weeping,  
and my eyelids grew dark.

I have suffered these things without iniquity in my hands,  
while my prayers to God were pure.

Earth, do not cover my blood,  
[Col. 1098C] and let my cry find no place in you to hide.

For behold, my witness is in heaven,  
and my knower is in the heights.

My verbose friends [Note: [Col. 1098D] The Palatine manuscript adds “again” after “my.” At the end it reads: “I will walk the path from which I shall not return.”],  
my eye drips tears to God.

Would that a man might be judged with God  
as a son of man is judged with his companion.

For behold, the short [Alternative: “shortly passing”] years are passing,  
and I shall walk the path by which I will not return.

### Chapter XVII

My spirit will be weakened,  
my days will be shortened,  
and the grave alone remains for me.

I have not sinned,  
yet my eye dwells in bitterness.

Deliver me, Lord, and set me beside you,  
and let anyone’s hand fight against me.

You have made their heart far from discipline;  
therefore they will not be exalted.

[Col. 1098D] He promises prey to his companions,  
and the eyes of his children will fail.

He has made me like a proverb of the people,  
and [Note: [Col. 1098D] In the Saint-Germain Canon, the copyists transferred here the first verse of the following chapter, chapter 30: “But now younger men in age mock me, whose fathers I would not have deemed worthy to be placed with the dogs of my flock.” The same words appear in the margin of the Colbertine Anicianus manuscript, but in a later hand. MART.] I have become an example before them.

My eye has grown dim from indignation [Alternative: “has become darkened”],  
and my limbs have been reduced almost to nothing.

[Col. 1099A] The righteous will be astonished at this,  
and the innocent will rise up against the hypocrite.

The righteous will hold to his way,  
and he whose hands are clean will add strength [Alternative: “the clean-handed man will add strength”].

Therefore, all of you, turn and come,  
and I shall find no wise man among you.

My days have passed;  
my thoughts have been scattered, tormenting my heart.

They have turned night into day,  
and again, after darkness, I hope for light.

If I endure, hell is my house;  
in darkness I have made my bed.

I said to corruption: “You are my father,”  
and to worms: “My mother and my sister.”

Where, then, is my expectation now?  
And who will consider my patience?

All that I have will descend into the deepest hell.  
Do you think that at least there I shall have rest?

## BALDAD THE SUHITE ANSWERED AND SAID:

[Col. 1099B] ### Chapter XVIII

How long will you keep throwing out words [Alternative: “throw out words”]?  
Understand first, and then let us speak.

Why are we regarded as beasts  
and have become filthy before you?

You who destroy your soul in your anger,  
will the earth be abandoned because of you,  
or will the rocks be moved from their place?

Will not the light of the wicked be extinguished,  
and the flame of his fire fail to shine?

Light will grow dark in his tabernacle,  
and the lamp above him will be extinguished.

The steps of his strength will be restricted,  
and his own counsel will cast him down.

For he has put his feet into a net  
and walks in its meshes.

His sole will be caught in a snare,  
and thirst will burn against him.

His trap is hidden in the ground,  
and his pitfall is on the path.

Fears will terrify him on every side,  
and they will entangle his feet [Alternative: omit “his feet”].

His strength will be weakened by hunger,  
and starvation will invade his ribs.

Let death, the firstborn, devour the beauty of his skin  
and consume his arms.

His confidence will be torn from his tent,  
and destruction will trample him as a king.

Let the companions of the one who is not be in his tent;  
let sulfur be scattered over his dwelling.

Below, his roots will dry up;  
above, his harvest will be destroyed.

His memory will perish from the earth,  
and his name will not be celebrated in the streets.

He will drive him from light into darkness  
and remove him from the inhabited world [Alternative: “from the city”].

He will have neither seed nor offspring among his people,  
nor any remnant [Alternative: “rest”] in his regions.

On his day, those who come afterward will be astonished,  
[Col. 1099D] and horror will seize those who came before.

These, then, are the dwellings of the wicked,  
[Col. 1100A] and this is the place of the one who does not know God.

## JOB ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter XIX

How long will you afflict my soul  
and wear me down with words?

Behold, ten times you have humiliated me,  
and you are not ashamed to oppress me.

Indeed, even if I have been ignorant,  
my ignorance will remain with me [Alternative: “is with me”].

But you rise up against me  
and reproach me for my reproaches [Alternative: “for your reproaches”].

At least now understand  
that God has afflicted me with an unequal judgment  
and surrounded me with his scourges.

Behold, I cry out, suffering violence, and no one hears;  
I shout, and there is no one to judge.

He has fenced in my path, and I cannot pass;  
he has placed darkness on my road.

He has stripped me of my glory  
[Col. 1100B] and taken the crown from my head.

He has destroyed me on every side, and I perish;  
and, like a tree torn up by the roots [Alternative: “like a tree”],  
he has taken away my hope.

His fury has grown angry against me,  
and he has treated me as though I were his enemy.

His raiders came together,  
made a road through me,  
and surrounded my tent in a circle.

He has put my brothers far from me,  
and my acquaintances have withdrawn from me like strangers.

My relatives [Alternative: “neighbors”] have abandoned me,  
and those who knew me have forgotten me.

The inhabitants of my house and my maidservants  
have regarded me as a stranger,  
and I have become like a foreigner in their eyes.

I called my servant, and he did not answer [Alternative: add “me”];  
with my own mouth I pleaded with him.

My wife recoiled from my breath [Alternative: “appearance”],  
[Col. 1100C] and I pleaded with the children of my womb.

Even fools despised me,  
and when I had withdrawn from them, they spoke against me.

My counselors once abhorred me [Alternative: omit “once”],  
and the one whom I loved most has turned away from me.

My bone clings to my skin and flesh,  
and only my lips remain around my teeth.

Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends,  
because the hand of the Lord has touched me.

Why do you pursue me like God  
and gorge yourselves on my flesh?

Who will grant that my words may be written?  
Who will grant that they may be inscribed in a book  
with an iron stylus and a sheet of lead,  
or carved with a chisel [Note: [Col. 1099D] The Palatine manuscript has *certe* (“certainly”) here instead of *celte* (“with a chisel”), as do innumerable other manuscripts, both printed and handwritten. More than forty of these were consulted by Father Calmet in the libraries of Gaul, and critics and interpreters of great reputation also support that reading. Those who read *celte* are somewhat more recent and of inferior quality, although there are others that have *scelte* or *scelpte*. Yet although those who retain *certe* may perhaps exceed the others in number and age, anyone can easily persuade himself that scribal carelessness could more readily have substituted *certe* for the unknown word *celte* or *scelpte* than the reverse. Moreover, Jerome himself, in *Against John of Jerusalem*, book 30, prefers *celte* when he cites this testimony from Job. Whether he himself coined the name, or—as is more likely—retained it from the old Latin translator, it is neither without a Latin etymology nor without a plausible analogy from the verb *caelo*, from which comes *caelum*, the engraving instrument used to cut something into bronze or marble. And although it is commonly believed that this name is found nowhere else, in an old Glossary, or in the Labbe Excerpts, I find *celte* translated as Greek *γλυφεῖον*, or *γλυφεῖον* as *celte*. Thus there can be no doubt that, according to the Greek meaning, it denotes an iron engraving stylus. Others who defend this reading, to prove that it occurs in a Latin author, cite the famous passage in Gruter’s *Inscriptions*, p. 329, where we read: “MALLET AND CHISEL, THE INSCRIBED FLINT.” Yet I do not know how much trust should be placed in that testimony.] on flint?

For I know that my Redeemer lives,  
and on the last day I shall rise from the earth.

[Col. 1100D] And again I shall be clothed with my skin,  
and in my flesh I shall see God.

[Col. 1101A] Whom I myself shall see [Note: [Col. 1101D] The Palatine manuscript adds the words “and not another,” which, more correctly according to the original books, belong to the following verse.],  
and my eyes shall behold him, and not another.  
This hope has been stored up in my breast.

Why, then, do you now say:  
“Let us pursue him, and find the root of his word against him”?

Flee, then, from the face of the sword,  
for the sword is the avenger of iniquities;  
and know that there is judgment.

## SOPHAR THE NAAMATHITE ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter XX

Therefore my varied thoughts follow one another,  
and [Note: [Col. 1101D] Perhaps the same Palatine manuscript is more correct: “and my mind is different.” The Hebrew likewise has a word meaning “my sense” or “my readiness.”] my divided mind is carried away.

I will hear the teaching with which you rebuke me,  
and the spirit of my understanding will answer me.

This I know from the beginning,  
from the time when the human being was placed upon the earth:  
the praise of the wicked is brief,  
and the joy of the hypocrite lasts only a moment.

If his pride rises as high as heaven  
[Col. 1101B] and his head touches the clouds,  
he will be destroyed in the end like refuse;  
and those who saw him will say: “Where is he?”

Like a dream flying away, he will not be found;  
he will pass like a vision of the night.

The eye that saw him will not see him,  
nor will his place look upon him again.

His children will be crushed by poverty,  
and his hands will repay him with pain.

His bones will be filled with the sins of his youth,  
and they will sleep with him in the dust.

For when evil is sweet in his mouth,  
he hides it beneath his tongue.

He spares it and does not abandon it;  
he conceals it in his throat.

His bread will be changed inside his belly  
into the gall of asps.

He will vomit up the riches he devoured,  
and God will draw them out of his belly.

[Col. 1101C] He will suck the head of asps [Alternative: “the head of the asp will rise”],  
and the viper’s tongue will kill him.

(He will not see streams of the river,  
torrents of honey and butter.)

He will pay for everything he has done,  
yet he will not be consumed;  
according to the multitude of his schemes,  
so also will he endure.

For by crushing the poor he stripped them naked;  
he seized a house and did not build it.

His belly was not satisfied;  
and when he has what he desired,  
he will not be able to possess it.

Nothing of his food remained,  
and therefore none of his goods will remain.

When he is satisfied, he will be confined;  
he will burn, and every pain will rush upon him [Alternative: “against him”].

May his belly be filled,  
so that He may send against him the wrath of His fury  
and rain down His battle upon him!

He will flee iron weapons  
[Col. 1101D] and rush into a bronze bow.

Drawn out, emerging from its sheath and flashing,  
it advances in bitterness [Note: [Col. 1101D] All our manuscripts and the printed books have the plural *vadent* (“they advance”); moreover, they begin with this verb the isocolon that follows, or the next verse. The Hebrew does not use this circumlocution and properly has no equivalent for that verb.],

and terrible things will come upon him.

All darkness is hidden in his secret places;  
fire that is not kindled will devour him;  
what remains in his tent will be afflicted.

The heavens will reveal his iniquity,  
[Col. 1102A] and the earth will rise up against him.

The offspring of his house will be exposed;  
it will be removed on the day of God’s wrath.

This is the portion of the wicked man from God,  
and the inheritance of his words from the Lord.

## JOB ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter XXI

Hear, I beg you, my words,  
and repent.

Bear with me, and I will speak;  
and afterward, if it seems appropriate, mock my words.

Is my dispute with a human being,  
so that I should not rightly be saddened?

Look at me and be astonished,  
and place your finger upon your mouth.

And when I remember, I am terrified,  
and trembling shakes my flesh.

Why, then, do the wicked live,  
are lifted up, and strengthened by riches?

Their offspring remain before them,  
a crowd of relatives and descendants in their sight.

Their houses are secure and peaceful,  
and there is no rod of God upon them.

Their ox conceives and does not miscarry;  
their cow gives birth and is not deprived of its offspring.

Their little ones go out like flocks,  
and their children leap about in play.

They hold tambourine and lyre  
and rejoice at the sound of the organ.

They spend their days in prosperity  
and in a moment descend to hell.

They say to God: “Depart from us;  
we do not wish to know your ways.”

What is the Almighty, that we should serve him?  
And what profit is there for us if we pray to him?

Yet, since their prosperity is not in their own hand,  
let the counsel of the wicked be far from me.

How often will the lamp of the wicked be extinguished,  
[Col. 1102C] and a flood come upon them,  
and the pains of his wrath be apportioned?

They will be like straw before the face of the wind,  
and like chaff that the whirlwind scatters.

God will store up the father’s pain for his children;  
and when he repays him, then he will know.

His eyes will see his own destruction,  
and he will drink from the wrath of the Almighty.

For what does he care about his house after him? [Note: [Col. 1102D] The Regina manuscript has, corruptly and contrary to the text itself, “He will ask him for the number,” and so forth.]

And what if the number of his months is cut in half? [Note: [Col. 1102D] Several manuscripts read in the same sense: “And if the number of his days is halved.” The scholiast, or another corrector, erased the particle *si* (“if”) in the Saint-Germain manuscript and placed the letter *b* in the margin to indicate that the Hebrew reads without any “if.” MART.]

Can anyone teach God knowledge,  
who judges those on high?

One man dies strong and healthy,  
rich [Alternative: “divided”] and prosperous.

His inner parts are full of fat,  
and his bones are moistened with marrow.

Another dies in bitterness of soul [Note: [Col. 1102D] The Palatine manuscript adds *suae* (“his own”), a pronoun that the Hebrew exemplar omits],  
without any possessions.

Yet they sleep together in the dust,  
and worms cover them.

[Col. 1102D] Certainly I know your thoughts  
and the unjust arguments you bring against me.

For you say: “Where is the house of the prince?  
And where are the tents of the wicked?”

Ask any traveler,  
and you will discover that he understands these same things.

For the wicked man is kept for the day of destruction [Alternative: “will be kept”]  
and led to the day of wrath.

Who will declare his way before him,  
and who will repay him for what he has done?

He will be led to the graves  
and will keep watch in the heap of the dead.

He was sweet to the gravel [Alternative: “the swords”] of Cocytus,  
and behind him he will drag every human being,  
and before him innumerable others.

How, then, do you comfort me in vain,  
when your answer has been shown to contradict the truth?

## ELIPHAZ THE TEMANITE ANSWERED AND SAID:

### Chapter XXII

Can a human being be compared with God,  
even when he is perfect in knowledge?

What does it profit God if you are righteous?  
Or what do you contribute to him if your ways are blameless?  
[Note: [Col. 1103D] The minor manuscript, together with the printed books, has “if your way has been blameless.” In the following verse it has “fearing, he will rebuke,” without the intervening “you.”]

Will he rebuke you because he fears you,  
and come with you into judgment,  
and not because of your great wickedness  
and your countless iniquities?

[Col. 1103B] For you took your brothers’ pledge without cause  
and stripped the naked of their clothing.

You did not give water to the weary,  
and you withheld bread from the hungry.

By the strength of your arm you possessed the land,  
and, being very powerful, you held it.

You sent widows away empty  
and crushed the arms of orphans.

Therefore you are surrounded by snares,  
and sudden fear troubles you.

You thought you would not see darkness  
and would not be overwhelmed by the flood of surging waters [Alternative: “would not overwhelm”].

Do you not think that God is higher than heaven  
and exalted above the summit of the stars?

And you say: “What does God know?  
He judges as though through darkness.”

Clouds are his hiding place, and he does not consider us;  
he walks around the poles of heaven.

[Col. 1103C] Do you wish [Alternative: “does he wish”] to keep to the path of ancient times,  
which wicked men trod?

They were carried away before their time,  
and a river overturned their foundation.

They said to God: “Depart from us,”  
and they regarded the Almighty as though he could do nothing.

Yet he had filled their houses with good things;  
may their counsel be far from me.

The righteous will see and rejoice,  
and the innocent will mock them.

Has not their uprising been cut down,  
and has not fire devoured their remnant?

Submit, then, to him [Alternative: omit “to him”] and have peace;  
through this you will gain excellent fruits.

Receive instruction from his mouth,

and place his words in your heart.

If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up,

and you will remove iniquity far from your tent.

[Col. 1103D] He will give flint in place of earth,

and streams of gold in place of flint.

And the Almighty will be against your enemies,

and silver [Note: [Col. 1103D] The Regin. manuscript adds “your,” which the Hebrew nevertheless does not have.] will be heaped up for you.

Then you will overflow with delights in the Almighty,

and you will lift your face toward God.

You will entreat him, and he will hear you,

and you will fulfill your vows.

You will decree a matter, and it will come to pass for you,

and light will shine upon your ways.

For whoever has been humbled will be in glory,

and whoever has lowered his eyes will himself be saved.

The innocent will be saved;

[Col. 1104A] but he will be saved by the purity of his hands [Al. “by” omitted].

RESPONDING, JOB SAID:

[Chapter XXIII] Even now my speech is in bitterness,

and the hand of my plague is heavier than my groaning.

Who will grant me that I might know and find him,

and come even to his throne?

I would set judgment before him,

and fill my mouth with accusations,

so that he might know the words with which he would answer me,

and I might understand what he would say to me.

I do not want him to contend with me with great strength,

nor press me down with the weight of his greatness.

Let him set equity against me,

and [Note: [Col. 1104D] The Palatin. manuscript has “and let my judgment prevail.” The Hebrew has literally, “and my judgment will favor me.”] let my judgment reach victory.

If I go to the east, he does not appear;

if to the west, I will not understand him.

[Col. 1104B] If to the left, what shall I do? I will not apprehend him;

if I turn to the right, I will not see him.

Yet he himself knows my way,

and has tested me like gold that passes through fire.

My foot has followed his footsteps;

I have guarded his way and have not turned aside from it.

I have not departed from the commands of his lips,

and I have hidden the words of his mouth in my breast.

For he alone is; no one can turn aside his purpose,

and whatever his soul has willed,

that he has done [Note: [Col. 1104D] The same manuscript reads, “whatever he may will, this he does”; the Royal manuscript has “may do,” a single word that differs from the Palatin. manuscript.].

When he has fulfilled his will in me,

many other things of the same kind are also ready at hand for him.

Therefore I am troubled before his face,

and, considering him, I am anxious with fear [Al. “I make anxious”].

God has softened my heart,

and the Almighty has troubled me.

For I have not perished because of the darkness that threatens,

nor has gloom covered my face.

[Chapter XXIV] Times are not hidden from the Almighty;

but those who know him [Al. “God”] do not know his day.

Some have moved boundary stones,

have seized flocks and pastured them.

They drove away the orphan’s donkey,

and took the widow’s ox as a pledge.

They overturned the poor’s way,

and together oppressed the meek of the earth.

Others, like wild asses in the desert, go out to their work;

keeping watch for prey, they prepare bread for their children.

They reap a field that is not theirs,

and harvest the vineyard of the one whom they have oppressed by force [Note: [Col. 1104D] The Palatin. manuscript reads “whom they have oppressed”; “they will harvest” is more literally in keeping with the Hebrew.].

They leave people naked, taking away their clothing,

those who have no covering against the cold.

Those whom the rains of the mountains drench,

[Col. 1104D] and who have no shelter, embrace the rocks.

They used violence, plundering orphans,

and stripped the mass of the poor.

From the naked and those walking without clothing,

and from the hungry, they took away the sheaves.

Among their heaps they rested at noon;

those who thirst after treading the winepresses.

They made men groan from the cities,

and the soul of the wounded cried out;

and God does not permit this to go unavenged [Al. “may not permit it”].

They were rebels against the light;

they did not know its ways,

nor did they return by its paths.

[Col. 1105A] At first light the murderer rises;

he has killed the needy and the poor;

but at night he is like a thief [Note: [Col. 1105D] The Queen’s manuscript incorrectly reads, “he will be like the adulterer’s eye,” etc., omitting the word “thief.”].

The adulterer’s eye watches for darkness,

saying, “No eye will see me,”

and he covers his face.

In darkness he breaks into houses,

as they had agreed among themselves by day,

and they did not know the light.

If dawn suddenly appears,

they regard it as the shadow of death;

and so in darkness they walk as though in light.

He is swift upon the face of the water;

let his portion on the earth be cursed,

and let him not walk by the way of the vineyards.

Let him pass from the waters of the snow to excessive heat,

and let his sin descend even to the underworld.

Let mercy forget him;

let his sweetness become worms.

Let there be no remembrance of him,

but let him be crushed like a fruitless tree.

[Col. 1105B] For he fed the barren woman who [Al. “and who”] does not give birth,

and did no good to the widow.

He struck down the strong by his strength,

and when he stands, he will not trust [Al. “does not trust”] his own life.

God gave him a place for repentance,

but he abuses it in arrogance;

yet his eyes are upon his ways.

They have been lifted up for a little while, and will not endure;

they will be humbled like all things and removed,

and like the tops of ears of grain they will be crushed.

But if this is not so, who can prove me to be a liar,

and set my words before God?

RESPONDING, BALDAD THE SHUHITE SAID:

[Chapter XXV] Power and terror belong to him,

who makes peace in his heights.

Is there any number to his armies?

And upon whom does his light not arise?

Can a human being be justified when compared with God,

or can one born of a woman appear clean?

Behold, even the moon does not shine,

and the stars are not clean in his sight.

How much less a human being, mere decay,

and a son of man, a worm!

RESPONDING, JOB SAID:

[Chapter XXVI] Whose helper are you? Is it the weak [Al. “the weak man”],

and do you sustain the arm of one who is not strong?

To whom have you given counsel?

Perhaps to one who has no wisdom,

and you have displayed your abundant prudence.

Whom did you wish to teach—

was it not the one who made the breath?

Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters,

and those who dwell with them [Hebrew: “those dwelling in them”].

The underworld is naked before him,

and there is no covering for perdition.

[Col. 1105D] He stretches the north over the void,

and hangs the earth upon nothing.

He binds the waters in his clouds,

so that they do not burst forth together below [Hebrew: “and do not burst forth together”].

He holds back the face of his throne,

and spreads his cloud over it.

He has encircled the waters with a boundary,

until light [Note: [Col. 1105D] The Palatin. manuscript reads “so that there may be darkness.” The Hebrew has “with darkness.”] and darkness come to an end.

The pillars of heaven tremble,

and are terrified at his command.

By his strength the seas suddenly gathered together,

and by his wisdom he struck down the proud.

[Col. 1106A] His spirit adorned the heavens,

and by his hand, acting as midwife, the twisting serpent was brought forth [Hebrew: “the bar”].

Behold, these things have been spoken only in part concerning his ways;

and when we have scarcely heard a small drop of his words,

who can contemplate the thunder of his greatness?

JOB ALSO ADDED [Note: [Col. 1105D] The Palatin. manuscript omits here the word “taking up,” which is nevertheless in the Hebrew.], TAKING UP HIS PARABLE, AND SAID:

[Chapter XXVII] As God lives, who has taken away my judgment,

and the Almighty, who has brought my soul to bitterness,

for as long as my breath remains in me,

and the spirit of God is in my nostrils,

my lips will not speak iniquity,

nor will my tongue meditate deceit.

Far be it from me to judge you righteous;

until I perish, I will not depart from my innocence.

I will not abandon my justification, which I have begun to hold fast,

for my heart does not reproach [Al. “seize”] me throughout my life.

Let my enemy be like the wicked,

and my adversary like the unjust.

For what hope does the hypocrite have if he greedily seizes,

and God does not deliver his soul [Hebrew: “Will God deliver his soul?”]?

Will God hear his cry

when distress comes upon him?

Or can he delight in the Almighty

and call upon God at every time?

I will teach you concerning the hand of God [Note: [Col. 1105D] The same manuscript reads, “I will teach you the word of God,” which I would not venture to reject. For although the Hebrew has [reading not reproduced in the source], [Col. 1106D] “in the hand of God,” it nevertheless denotes the works and things of God—what God has done or is able to accomplish—which in the idiom of Scripture are called “words.”]

what the Almighty possesses;

I will not hide it.

Behold, all of you know,

and why do you speak vainly without cause?

This is the portion of the wicked person with God,

and the inheritance of the violent,

which they will receive from the Almighty.

If his children become numerous, they will be for the sword,

and his descendants will not be filled with bread.

Those who survive him will be buried in destruction,

and his widows will not [Note: [Col. 1106D] The Palatin. manuscript reads “will not be mourned.” In this sense the Septuagint also appears to have understood the Hebrew: “no one will pity their widows” (χήρας δὲ αὐτῶν οὐδεὶς ἐλεήσει).] weep.

If he heaps up silver like earth [Hebrew: “like dust”],

and prepares garments like clay,

he will indeed prepare them,

but the just will wear them,

and the innocent will divide the silver.

He built his house like a moth,

and made a shelter like a watchman.

When the rich man sleeps, he will take nothing with him;

he will open his eyes, and find nothing.

Poverty will seize him like water;

at night a storm will overwhelm him.

A burning wind will take him [Hebrew: “it has no”] and carry him away,

and a whirlwind will snatch him from his place.

It will hurl itself upon him and not spare him;

fleeing from his hand, he will flee [Al. “fleeing” omitted].

He will clap his hands over him,

and hiss at him while looking upon his place.

[Chapter XXVIII] There is a source for silver,

and a place where gold is refined.

Iron is taken from the earth,

and stone melted by heat is turned into bronze.

He has set an end for darkness,

and he himself examines the limit of all things,

the stone of darkness and the shadow of death.

He divides [Hebrew: “divided”] the torrent from the migrating people,

[Col. 1107A] those whom the foot of the needy person has forgotten [Note: [Col. 1107D] Our manuscripts read “of people,” closer to the Hebrew “from a person” or “from people.” The Queen’s manuscript further has “and mute” in place of “and trackless.” Consult the interpreters of this exceedingly difficult passage.],

and the trackless.

The earth from which bread came forth—

in its place it has been overturned by fire.

The place of sapphires is its stones,

and its clods are gold.

The bird has not known its path,

nor has the vulture’s eye looked upon it [Note: [Col. 1107D] In the Canon manuscripts and in the Royal manuscript that pronoun is absent. In the excellent volume of the Monastery of Saint-Maur it has the following marginal scholion: “In place of ‘it,’ the Hebrew has ‘him.’ This is confirmed as correct because the masculine suffixes or pronouns agreeing with the masculine noun form occur with the word נָתִיב (nathib), which means ‘path.’” MART. The Regin. manuscript also lacks “it,” as do the two manuscripts cited by Martian.].

The sons of the merchants [Hebrew: “the proud”] have not trodden it,

nor has the lioness passed through it [Al. “passed through it” omitted].

He stretches his hand to the flint;

he overturns mountains from their roots.

In the rocks he cuts channels,

and his eye sees every precious thing.

He searches even the depths of rivers,

and brings hidden things into the light.

But where is wisdom found,

and what is the place of understanding?

A human being does not know its price,

nor is it found in the land of those who live in delight [Hebrew: “not found in the land of the living”].

The abyss says, “It is not in me,”

and the sea says, “It is not with me.”

Pure gold will not be given for it,

nor will silver be weighed in exchange for it.

It will not be compared with the dyed colors of India,

nor with the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire.

Gold or glass will not equal it,

nor will vessels of gold be exchanged for it.

High and eminent things will not be mentioned in comparison with it,

but wisdom is drawn from hidden places.

Topaz from Ethiopia will not equal it [Note: [Col. 1108D] The manuscript codices read *topazium*, the neuter form. One Corbeiensis manuscript has *topazion*, in keeping with what we read in Revelation 21:20 and Exodus 28:17, where the Greek manuscripts retain *τοπάζιον*, the neuter gender. MART.],

nor will the purest dyes [Hebrew: “pure gold”] be combined with it.

From where, then, will wisdom come [Al. “comes”],

and what is the place of understanding?

It is hidden from the eyes of all the living,

and it is concealed even from the birds of heaven.

[Col. 1107C] Destruction and death said:

“We have heard the report of it with our ears.”

God understands its way,

and he himself knows its place.

For he looks upon the ends of the world,

and sees all that is beneath heaven.

He who made a weight for the winds,

and weighed the waters by measure,

when he appointed a law for the rains,

and a way for the sounding storms,

then he saw it and declared it;

he prepared it and searched it out.

And he said to the human being [Hebrew: “Adam”]:

“Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom;

and to turn away from evil is understanding.”

JOB ALSO ADDED, TAKING UP HIS PARABLE, AND SAID:

[Chapter XXIX] Who will grant me that I might be as in former months,

[Col. 1107D] as in the days when God guarded me?

When his lamp shone over my head,

and I walked by his light in darkness;

as I was in the days of my youth,

when God’s secret [Hebrew: “the secret of God”] was in my tent;

[Col. 1108A] when the Almighty was with me,

and my children were around me;

when I washed my feet with butter,

and the rock poured out streams of oil for me;

when I went out to the gate of the city,

and they prepared a chair for me in the square.

Young men saw me and hid themselves;

and old men, rising, stood.

Princes stopped speaking,

and placed a finger over their mouths.

Leaders restrained their voice,

and their tongues clung to their throats.

The ear that heard blessed me,

and the eye that saw bore witness for me.

Because [Al. “Because”] I delivered the poor who cried out,

and the orphan who had no helper [Note: [Col. 1108D] The Queen’s manuscript reads “the needy,” less well in relation to the Hebrew.].

The blessing of the perishing came upon me,

and I comforted the widow’s heart.

I clothed myself with justice,

and it clothed [Al. “I clothed”] me, like a garment and a diadem,

with my judgment.

I was an eye to the blind,

and a foot to the lame.

I was a father to the poor,

and I investigated with the greatest care the case I did not know.

I crushed the jaws of the wicked,

and snatched the prey from his teeth.

And I said:

“I will die in my little nest,

and multiply my days like the palm [Hebrew: “like sand”].

My root is spread out beside the waters,

and dew will remain upon my harvest.

My glory will always be renewed,

and my bow will be restored in my hand.”

Those who heard me awaited a verdict,

and listened silently to my counsel.

They did not dare add anything to my words,

and my eloquence dripped down upon them.

They awaited me like rain,

[Col. 1108C] and opened their mouths as for the late rain.

Whenever I smiled at them, they did not believe it,

and the light of my face did not fall to the ground.

If I wished to go to them, I sat first;

and when I sat like a king, with an army surrounding me [Note: [Col. 1108D] The same manuscript adds “my,” contrary to the Hebrew text.],

I was nevertheless a comforter of the mourners.

[Chapter XXX] But now those younger in age mock me,

whose fathers I would not have considered worthy to be placed with the dogs of my flock.

The strength of whose hands was nothing to me,

and who were thought unworthy even of life itself.

Sterile through poverty and hunger,

they gnawed in the wilderness,

filthy with calamity and misery.

They ate herbs and tree bark,

and the root of juniper was their food.

Those who, snatching these things from the valleys,

whenever they found anything at all,

ran to it with a cry.

[Col. 1108D] They lived in the deserts of the torrents,

in caves of the earth or upon gravel.

Those who rejoiced among such things [Hebrew: “among the shrubs they rejoiced”],

and considered it a delight to be under thornbushes—

sons of fools and of people without renown,

[Col. 1109A] who were not counted at all on the earth.

Now I have become their song,

and I have become their byword [Al. adds “among”].

They abominate me and flee far from me,

and are not afraid to spit in my face.

For he opened his quiver and afflicted me,

and put a bridle in my mouth.

At the right hand of the rising sun my calamities immediately arose;

they overturned my feet,

and overwhelmed me like waves along their paths.

They destroyed my roads,

lay in wait for me and prevailed,

and there was no one to bring help.

Like a broken wall and an opened gate [Hebrew: “a broken gate”],

they rushed upon me,

and rolled down upon my miseries.

I have been reduced to nothing.

You have taken away my desire like the wind,

and like a cloud my salvation has passed away.

[Col. 1109B] Now my soul withers within me,

and days of affliction possess me.

At night pain pierces my bones,

and those who consume me do not sleep.

By their multitude my garment is worn away,

and they girded me like the collar of a tunic.

I have been compared to mud,

and made like dust and ashes.

I cry to you, and you do not hear me;

I stand, and you do not look upon me.

You have changed toward me into cruelty,

and in the hardness of your hand you oppose me.

You have lifted me up,

and, setting me as though upon the wind,

you have dashed me down violently.

For I know that you will hand me over to death,

where the house appointed for every living thing is.

Yet you do not send your hand against my destruction [Note: [Col. 1109D] Together with the common editions, the Queen’s manuscript has “their” in place of “my,” although the Hebrew has the corresponding form of “my.” But immediately afterward “you send your hand” is more correct, since the Hebrew likewise does not add “your.”],

[Col. 1109C] and if they fall, you yourself will save them.

Once I wept over the one who was afflicted,

and my soul had compassion on the poor.

I awaited good things, and evil came to me;

I looked for light, and darkness burst upon me.

My inward parts boiled without any rest;

days of affliction came before me.

I went about mourning, without anger;

I rose and cried out in the assembly.

I was a brother to dragons,

and a companion to ostriches.

My skin has become black upon me,

and my bones have dried out from heat.

My harp has turned to mourning,

and my organ to the voice of weepers.

[Chapter XXXI] I made a covenant with my eyes

not even to think about a virgin.

For what portion would God have in me from above [Note: [Col. 1109D] The same manuscript adds a second “me,” which the Hebrew does not have.],

and what inheritance would the Almighty have from the heights?

Is not destruction for the unjust,

and alienation for those who practice injustice?

Does he not himself consider my ways,

and number all my steps?

If I have walked in vanity,

and my foot has hastened into deceit,

let him weigh me in a just balance,

and let God know my simplicity.

If my steps have turned aside from the way,

and if my heart has followed my eyes [Hebrew: omitted; Note: [Col. 1109D] The same manuscript reads in a nearly different sense, “my eye has followed my mouth.” The edition of Sixtus V and the Complutensian edition likewise read “heart” in place of “mouth.” The printed reading is more consonant with the Hebrew text.],

and a stain has clung to my hands.

Let me sow, and let another eat;

let my offspring be uprooted.

If my heart has been deceived concerning a woman,

and if I have lain in wait at my friend’s door,

let my wife be a prostitute for another,

and let other men bend over her.

For this is wickedness,

and a very great iniquity.

It is a fire consuming even to destruction,

and uprooting all produce.

If I have refused to enter into judgment with my male servant

and my female servant,

when they contended against me,

what then shall I do when God rises for judgment?

And when he inquires, what shall I answer him?

Did not the one who made him make me also in the womb,

and did not one God form me in the womb?

[Col. 1110B] If I denied the poor what they desired,

and made the eyes of the widow wait,

if I ate my morsel alone,

and the orphan did not eat from it,

because from my infancy compassion grew with me [Hebrew: “he made me grow like a father”],

and it came out with me from my mother’s womb;

if I looked down upon one who was perishing because he had no clothing,

and upon the poor without a covering,

if his sides did not bless me,

and he was not warmed by the fleeces of my sheep;

if I raised my hand against an orphan,

even when I saw myself superior in the gate [Hebrew: “above”],

let my shoulder fall from its joint,

and let my arm be broken together with its bones.

For I always feared God like swelling waves over me,

[Col. 1110C] and I could not bear his weight.

If I thought gold was my strength,

and said to pure gold, “My trust,”

if I rejoiced over my many riches,

and because my hand had found very much;

if I looked upon the sun [Hebrew: “light”] when it shone,

and the moon proceeding brightly,

and my heart rejoiced in secret,

and I kissed my hand with my mouth,

this too is a very great iniquity,

and a denial against the Most High God.

If I rejoiced at the ruin of the one who hated me,

and exulted because evil had found him,

for I did not give my throat over to sin

by seeking the cursing of his soul;

if the men of my tent did not say:

“Who will give us some of his flesh, so that we may be filled?” [Note: [Col. 1110D] The particle of negation has been deleted. The same manuscript reads “if the men say,” etc., closer to the Greek of the Septuagint, τῶν LXX; for the Hebrew text has “if they did not say,” etc.],

if no stranger remained outside,

and my door was open to the traveler [Hebrew: “doors”];

if I hid my sin like a human being [Hebrew: “Adam”],

[Col. 1110D] and concealed my iniquity in my breast;

if I was terrified by the great multitude,

and the contempt of relatives frightened me,

and I did not remain silent because of it,

nor go out of the door;

who will grant me a hearer,

so that the Almighty may hear my desire,

and that he himself who judges may write a book,

so that I may carry it on my shoulder,

and place it around me like a crown?

At every one of my steps I would proclaim it,

and offer it like a prince.

[Col. 1111A] If my land cries out against me,

and its furrows weep with it,

if I ate its produce without money,

and afflicted the souls of its farmers,

let thistles arise for me instead of wheat,

and thorns instead of barley.

THE WORDS OF JOB ARE ENDED [Note: [Col. 1111D] These words are absent from some Latin editions. They seem not to have been read—or at least were neglected—by the holy Fathers who commented on Job: Gregory, Philip, Bede, the author of the Commentary under Jerome’s name, and others thereafter. In the old Vulgate, however, they stood in the manner of a heading: “And the words of Job ceased.”].

[Chapter XXXII] These three men ceased answering Job,

because he seemed righteous to himself.

But Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram,

became angry and indignant [Note: [Col. 1111D] The Palatinus manuscript consistently reads “Helius and Baraciel.”]—

he was angry with Job

because he said that he was righteous before God.

He was also indignant against his friends,

because they had found no reasonable answer,

but had merely condemned Job [Hebrew: “because of which they had condemned Job”].

[Col. 1111B] Therefore Elihu waited while Job was speaking,

because those who were speaking were older than he [Note: [Col. 1111D] The Palatinus manuscript omits the word “he,” which nevertheless is expressed in the Hebrew.].

But when he saw that the three could not answer [Al. “could not have answered”],

he became exceedingly angry.

AND ELIHU, SON OF BARACHEL THE BUZITE, RESPONDING, SAID:

I am younger in age,

but you are older;

therefore, lowering my head,

I was afraid to declare my opinion to you [Al. adds “I”].

For I hoped that greater age would speak,

and that a multitude of years would teach wisdom.

But, as I see, there is a spirit in human beings,

and the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding.

The long-lived are not necessarily wise,

nor do the aged understand judgment.

Therefore I will speak: hear me;

I too will show you my knowledge [Al. “wisdom”].

For I waited for your words,

I heard your prudence,

until you debated one another in words.

And while I thought you would say something, I paid attention;

but, as I see, there is no one who can convict Job

and answer his words among you.

Lest you should say [Hebrew: “lest perhaps you say”]:

“We have found wisdom;

God has cast him down, not a human being.”

He said nothing to me,

and I will not answer him according to your words.

They were afraid [Al. “and not”] and no longer answered,

and they withdrew their speeches from themselves.

Since, then, I waited and they did not speak,

they stood and did not answer any longer,

I too will answer for my part,

and show my knowledge.

[Col. 1111D] For I am full of words,

and the spirit of my womb constrains me.

Behold, my belly is like wine without a vent,

which bursts new wineskins.

I will speak and breathe a little;

I will open my lips and answer.

I will not show partiality to a man,

nor will I equate God with a human being.

[Col. 1112A] For I do not know how long I will endure,

or whether my Maker will take me away after a short while.

[Chapter XXXIII] Hear now, Job, my speeches,

and listen to all my words.

Behold, I have opened my mouth;

let my tongue speak in my throat.

My words come from my sincere heart,

and my lips will speak pure judgment [Hebrew: “knowledge”].

The Spirit of God made me,

and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.

If you can, answer me,

and stand before my face.

Behold, God made me as he made you,

and I too was formed from the same clay.

Yet let not my wonder [Hebrew: “my fear”] terrify you,

and let not my eloquence [Note: [Col. 1112D] The Hebrew has “and my hand,” but Saint Jerome seems to have read two distinct words, which mean “my eloquence,” or literally “and altogether my mouth.”] be heavy upon you.

You said, then, in my ears,

and I heard the sound of your words [Note: [Col. 1112D] The pronoun “your,” which is not added in the Hebrew text, is rightly absent from the Palatinus manuscript.]:

[Col. 1112B] “I am clean, without transgression, blameless,

and there is no iniquity in me.

Because he found complaints against me,

he therefore considered me his enemy.

He put my feet in fetters,

he guarded all my paths.”

This, then, is the matter in which you are not justified:

I will answer you, because God is greater than a human being.

Why do you contend against him [Hebrew: “Why contend against him?”],

because he has not answered you concerning all your words?

God speaks once,

and he does not repeat the same thing a second time.

In a dream, in a vision of the night,

when sleep falls upon human beings,

and they sleep in their bed,

then he opens the ears of men,

and, instructing them, disciplines them,

to turn a person away from what he does,

and to free him from pride;

[Col. 1112C] rescuing his soul from corruption,

and his life, so that it may not pass into the sword.

He also rebukes him through pain in his bed,

and makes all his bones waste away.

Bread becomes abominable to him in his life,

and the food of his soul, formerly desirable.

His flesh will waste away,

and his bones, which had been straight, will be exposed.

His soul has drawn near to corruption,

and his life to things deadly [Note: [Col. 1112D] The same manuscript, somewhat more correctly, reads in the future: “It will draw near.”].

If there is for him an angel speaking,

one among a thousand [Note: [Col. 1112D] The Queen’s manuscript, together with the Colbertinus and Aniciensis manuscripts cited by Martianus, reads “one of thousands.”]

[Hebrew: “one of a thousand”],

to declare the person’s righteousness,

he will have mercy on him and say:

“Deliver him,

so that [Al. “and”] he does not descend into corruption.

I have found a means by which I may be gracious to him.”

His flesh has been consumed by afflictions;

let him return to the days of his youth.

He will entreat God, and God will be favorable to him;

[Col. 1112D] he will see his face with rejoicing,

and restore his righteousness to the person.

He will look upon human beings [Al. “the human being”] and say:

“I have sinned,

and truly I have transgressed,

and I have not received what I deserved.”

He has delivered his soul from going into destruction,

so that, while alive, it might see the light.

Behold, God does all these things

[Col. 1113A] three times for each person,

to recall their souls [Hebrew: “his soul”] from corruption,

and to enlighten the light of the living.

Pay attention, Job, and hear me;

and [Al. “and” omitted] be silent while I speak [Al. “while I am speaking”].

But if you have something to say, answer me;

speak, for I want you to appear righteous.

But if you do not, hear me;

be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.

THEREFORE ELIHU PRONOUNCED THIS AND ALSO SPOKE:

[Chapter XXXIV] Hear my words, wise men,

and listen to me, learned men.

For the ear tests words,

and the throat distinguishes foods by taste.

Let us choose judgment for ourselves,

and among ourselves let us see [Al. “choose”] what is better.

For Job said:

“I am righteous,

and God has overturned my judgment.

For in judging me there is falsehood;

my arrow is violent, without any sin.”

What man is like Job,

who drinks mockery like water,

who walks with those who practice iniquity,

and goes with wicked men?

For he said:

“Man will not please God,

even if he runs with him.”

Therefore, men of understanding, hear me:

far be impiety from God,

and iniquity from the Almighty.

For he will repay a person according to his work,

and according to the ways of each he will restore [Al. adds “to them”].

For truly God does not condemn without cause,

nor does the Almighty overturn judgment.

Whom has he appointed over the earth besides himself?

Or whom has he placed over the world that he fashioned?

If he directs his heart toward him,

he will draw his spirit and breath back to himself.

All flesh will perish together,

and the human being will return to ashes.

If, then, you have understanding, hear what is said,

and listen to the voice of my eloquence.

Can one who does not love judgment be healed?

And how can you condemn so greatly

the one who is righteous?

The one who says to a king, “Apostate,”

who calls leaders wicked,

who does not show partiality to princes,

and does not recognize a tyrant when he disputes against a poor person—

for all are the work of his hands [Al. “all things”].

They will die suddenly,

and in the middle of the night peoples will be shaken and pass away,

and he will remove the violent person without a hand.

For his eyes are upon the ways of human beings,

[Col. 1113D] and he considers all their steps.

There are no darknesses and no shadow of death

in which those who practice iniquity might be hidden [Note: [Col. 1113D] A marginal scholion in the manuscript of the Monastery of Saint-Maur notes that this verse is absent from the Hebrew. But the annotator is mistaken, or at least used a mutilated and imperfect Hebrew copy. MART.].

For it is no longer in human power

to come before God for judgment.

He will crush many beyond number,

and set others in their place.

For he knows their works,

and therefore he will bring night, and they will be crushed.

He struck them like the wicked in the sight of those who see.

They deliberately withdrew from him,

and refused to understand all his ways,

so that they might bring to him the cry of the needy,

[Col. 1114A] and that he might hear the voice of the poor.

When he grants peace, who is there to condemn?

When he hides his face, who is there to contemplate him,

both over a nation and over all human beings?

He makes a hypocritical person reign because of the sins of the people.

Therefore, since I have spoken to God,

I will not forbid you also.

If I have gone astray, teach me;

if I have spoken iniquity, I will not add to it.

Will God demand it from you because it displeased you?

For you began to speak, not I;

but if you know something better, speak.

Let men of understanding speak to me,

and let the wise man hear me.

But Job has spoken foolishly [Al. omits “but”],

and his words do not sound like discipline.

My father, let Job be tested to the end;

do not cease among [Note: [Col. 1114D] Together with the common editions, the Queen’s manuscript reads “do not cease from the man of iniquity.” The Hebrew has literally “to answer men of iniquity.”] men of iniquity [Hebrew: “iniquity”].

For he adds blasphemy to his sins;

let him meanwhile be constrained among us,

and then let him challenge God to judgment with his words [Hebrew: “then let him multiply his words to God”].

THEREFORE ELIHU SPOKE THESE THINGS AGAIN:

[Chapter XXXV] Does your thought seem right to you,

when you say:

“I am more righteous than God”?

For you said:

“What is right does not please you,”

or:

“What will it benefit you if I sin?”

Therefore I will answer your words,

and those of your friends with you.

Look up to heaven and see,

and contemplate the sky, which is higher than you.

If you sin, what harm will you do to him [Al. “to it”]?

And if your iniquities are multiplied [Hebrew: “your errors”],

what will you do against him?

Moreover, if you act righteously,

what will you give him,

or what will he receive from your hand?

Your impiety will harm a person [Hebrew: “a man”] like you,

and your righteousness will help a son of man [Al. “the son of man”].

Because of the multitude of oppressors they will cry out,

and they will wail because of the violence of tyrants’ arms.

Yet he did not say:

“Where is God, who made me,

who gives songs in the night?”

Who teaches us more than the animals of the earth,

and instructs us concerning the birds of heaven [Al. “will instruct us”].

There they will cry out, and he will not hear,

because of the pride of the wicked.

Yet God will not hear in vain [Hebrew: “nevertheless”],

and the Almighty will look upon the causes of each person,

even when you say:

“He does not consider.”

Present your case before him, and wait for him.

[Col. 1114D] For now he does not bring his fury [Al. “judgment”],

nor does he take vengeance on a very great crime.

Therefore Job opens his mouth in vain,

and multiplies words without knowledge.

ELIHU ALSO ADDED THESE WORDS:

[Chapter XXXVI] Bear with me a little,

and I will show you;

for I still have something to say on God’s behalf [Al. “I will speak while revealing”].

I will repeat my knowledge [Hebrew: “my knowledge”] from the beginning,

and prove my Maker righteous.

For truly my words are without falsehood,

[Col. 1115A] and complete knowledge will be demonstrated to you.

God does not reject the mighty [Hebrew: those who are mighty in heart],

since he himself is mighty.

But he does not save the wicked, and he grants judgment to the poor

[Variant: “he will grant”].

He will not remove his eyes from the righteous,

[Note: [Col. 1115D] The reading in the present tense, *takes away*, preferred by the scholiast, is also preferred by the Palatine manuscript.]

and he sets kings upon the throne forever,

and they are raised up [Hebrew: “he does not remove his eyes from the righteous, and from kings; he sets them upon the throne forever, and others are raised up”].

And if they are in chains and bound with the cords of poverty,

he will declare to them their deeds

and their crimes, because they have acted violently.

He will also uncover their ear, to rebuke them,

and he will speak so that they may turn back from iniquity.

If they listen and observe, they will complete their days in goodness

and their years in glory.

But if they do not listen, they will pass away by the sword

[Col. 1115B]

and be consumed in folly.

Hypocrites and the cunning provoke the anger of God,

nor will they cry out when they are bound.

Their soul will die in the storm,

and their life among the effeminate.

He will rescue [Variant: “raise up”] the poor from his distress,

and in tribulation he will uncover his ear to him.

Therefore he will save you from the narrow mouth,

into a very broad place [Note: We have followed the San-Germanus Canon in this division. Other manuscript codices read, “from the narrow mouth into a very broad place,” and do not have “and one without a foundation beneath it.”],

and from one that has [Hebrew: “has”] no foundation beneath it.

Your table, however, will be full of richness.

Your cause has been judged as that of a wicked man;

you will receive the cause and the judgment.

Therefore, do not let anger overcome you so that you oppress anyone [Hebrew: “yourself”],

nor let the multitude of gifts incline you.

Lay aside your greatness [Hebrew: “tyranny”] without distress,

and all the strong by their strength.

Do not prolong the night,

[Col. 1115C]

so that peoples may rise up on their behalf.

Beware lest you turn toward iniquity;

for you began to follow this after [Variant: omitted] your misery.

Behold, God is exalted in his strength,

and no one among the lawgivers is like him.
