Who can search out his way [Variant: “his ways”?]?

Or who can say to him, “You have committed iniquity” [Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads, “Who ÷ can ÷ say,” with the word *potest* (“can”), which the printed books likewise prefer, struck through on both sides by obeli. The Palatine manuscript has: “Who could say to him: You have acted,” and so forth. But the Hebrew has neither reading, and that word is rightly marked beforehand with an obelus.]?

Remember that you do not know his work,

of which men have sung [Variant: “fallen”?].

All people see him

[Hebrew: “have seen him”];

everyone looks upon him from afar [Hebrew: “and a man will look from afar”].

Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge;

the number of his years is beyond reckoning.

He removes the drops of rain

and pours down showers like torrents.

From the clouds flow those things that cover everything above.

[Note: [Col. 1116D] In the Queen’s manuscript: “Those who rain from the clouds, the waters cover,” and so forth. It ought to have read, “which [flow] from the clouds,” and so forth; for the Hebrew too continues to speak of the clouds: “Which distil rains,” and so forth.]

If he wishes to spread out the clouds like his tent,

and to flash above with his light,

[Col. 1115D]

he will also cover the hinges of the sea.

Through these things [Hebrew: “Through these …”] he judges peoples

and gives food to many mortals.

He hides the light in his hands [Hebrew: “nearby”],

and commands it to come again.

He announces concerning it to his friend

that it is his possession and that he can ascend to it.

[Cap. XXXVII]

At this my heart trembled,

[Col. 1116A]

and it was moved from its place.

Listen to the hearing in the terror of his voice,

and to the sound [Hebrew: “meditation”] proceeding from his mouth.

It looks upon everything beneath the heavens,

and its light is over the boundaries [Hebrew: “height”] of the earth.

After him the roar will thunder;

he will thunder with a voice of majesty,

and he will not be investigated when his voice has been heard.

God will thunder wondrously with his voice,

he who does great and unsearchable things.

He commands the snow to descend upon the earth,

and the winter rains, and the rain of his strength.

He seals the hand of every human being,

so that each may know his own works.

The beast enters its hiding place

and remains in its den.

From the inner regions the storm will come forth,

and from Arcturus [Variant: “the South”], cold.

When God blows, the ice congeals,

[Col. 1116B]

and again the very broad waters are poured out.

The grain desires the clouds,

and the clouds scatter their light.

They travel around,

wherever the will of the one who guides them leads them,

to everything that he has commanded them

upon the face of the earth.

Whether in one tribe, or in their own land,

or in whatever place of his mercy

he has commanded them to be found.

Listen to these things, Job;

stand and consider the wonders of God.

Do you know when God commands the rains,

so that they might display the light of his clouds?

Do you know the paths of the clouds,

the great and perfect knowledge [Variant: “knowledge,” singular]?

Are your garments warm

when the earth has been blown through by the South?

Did you perhaps construct the heavens with him,

which are exceedingly solid, as though cast from bronze?

Show us what we should say to him,

for we are enveloped in darkness.

Who will recount to him what I say?

Even if a man speaks, he will be swallowed up.

But now they do not see the light;

suddenly the air will be compressed into clouds,

and the passing wind will drive them away.

From the north comes gold,

and fearful praise to God.

We cannot find him worthily [Hebrew: “The Almighty; we cannot find him worthily”]:

great in strength, judgment, and righteousness,

and he cannot be described.

Therefore men will fear him,

and all who seem wise to themselves will not dare to contemplate him

[Hebrew: “and he will not contemplate all who seem wise in heart”].

[Col. 1116D]

BUT THE LORD, ANSWERING JOB FROM THE WHIRLWIND, SAID:

[Cap. XXXVIII]

Who is this who wraps up judgments

in words without knowledge?

Gird your loins like a man:

I will question you, and you answer me.

Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?

Tell me, if you have understanding.

[Col. 1117A]

Who established its measurements, if you know?

Or who stretched the measuring line over it?

Upon what were its bases strengthened?

Or who set its cornerstone,

when the morning stars praised me together

and all the sons of God shouted for joy?

Who enclosed the sea with doors,

when it burst forth as though proceeding from the womb,

when I made the cloud its garment

and wrapped it in darkness as in the swaddling clothes of infancy?

I surrounded it with my boundaries,

and set a bar and doors.

And I said: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall go no farther,

and here you shall break your swelling waves.”

Have you, after your rising, commanded the dawn

and shown the morning its place?

Have you taken hold of the earth’s extremities while they were shaking,

and shaken the wicked out of it?

It will be restored [Hebrew: “turned”] like clay beneath a seal,

and it will stand like a garment.

[Col. 1117B]

Its light will be taken away from the wicked,

and the uplifted arm will be broken.

Have you entered the depths of the sea,

and walked about in the farthest parts of the abyss?

Have the gates of death been opened to you,

and have you seen the dark doors?

Have you considered the breadth [Variant: “breadth,” singular] of the earth?

Tell me, if you know everything.

What is the way in which the light dwells,

and where is the place of darkness,

so that you may lead each one to its boundaries

and understand the paths of its house?

Did you know then that you would be born,

and did you know the number of your days [Hebrew: “do you know”]?

Have you entered the treasuries of snow,

or looked upon the treasuries of hail,

which I have prepared for the time of the enemy [Variant: “for the enemy”],

[Col. 1117C]

for the day of battle and war?

By what way is the light distributed,

and the heat [Hebrew: “burning,” that is, “wind”] divided over the earth?

Who gave the most violent rain its course,

and a way for the resounding thunder,

so that it might rain upon the earth without a man,

in the desert, where no mortal dwells,

so that it might fill the impassable and desolate place [Variant: omitted “and desolate”]

and produce green grass?

Who is the father of rain?

Or who fathered the drops of dew?

[Col. 1118A]

From whose womb did the ice come forth?

And who fathered the frost from heaven?

The waters harden like stone,

and the surface of the abyss is congealed.

[Note: [Col. 1117C] All our manuscripts read “and the surface,” and so forth, in place of “and the face.”]

Can you bind together the shining stars of the Pleiades [Variant: “Plyades”],

or can you scatter the circle of Arcturus?

Do you bring forth [Variant: “will you bring forth”] Lucifer [Hebrew: “the stars”]

in its season,

and cause the evening star to rise over the sons of earth?

Do you know the order of heaven,

and can you establish its reasoning upon the earth?

Will you lift up your voice in the cloud [Hebrew: “to the cloud”],

[Note: [Col. 1117C] The San-Germanus exemplar of the Canon has already been corrected to read “to the cloud”; formerly, with all the other manuscripts, it read “in the cloud.” MART.]

and will the rush of waters cover you?

Will you send forth lightning, and will it go,

and, returning, say to you, “Here we are”?

Who placed wisdom in the inward parts of man [Hebrew: “of eggs”],

[Note: [Col. 1117D] This marginal scholion is particularly noteworthy, since I have been unable to find this meaning of the Hebrew word *tuhhoth* anywhere, either in lexicons or among interpreters. Critics indeed maintain that the word [term illegible in the supplied text], or [term illegible in the supplied text], means the inward parts and kidneys, things hidden and concealed; but concerning the inner parts of eggs there is profound silence among them, just as among Jewish teachers. Therefore, just as the kidneys are called *tuhhoth* or *tuchoth* because they are covered with fat as with a plastering, so the marrow and yolk of eggs can rightly be called *tuhhoth* in Hebrew from their concealment and the superimposition of coverings; for the name *tuhhoth* is derived from the root *tuahh*, which means to smear over, cover, and encrust. Let the curious reader now rejoice that this very ancient scholiast has restored to him a particular meaning of a Hebrew word, unheard of until the present time. MART. — What the scholiast notes, namely that instead of “in the inward parts of man” the Hebrew has “in the inward parts of eggs,” is expressed by the text in this single word [word illegible in the supplied text], which here, with Aben Ezra, it would be more pleasing to translate “inward parts” than, as elsewhere, “kidneys,” since wisdom dwells in the heart, not in the kidneys. Moreover, it denotes whatever is covered and hidden, and thus even these innermost parts of the body; and only by analogy with that meaning, I think, can it be extended to signify the inner parts of eggs.]

or who gave the rooster understanding?

[Col. 1118B]

Who can recount the order of the heavens,

and who can make the harmony of heaven sleep?

When dust was poured upon the earth,

and the clods were compacted [Hebrew: “are compacted”]?

[Note: [Col. 1118D] In the Hebrew, *urgabim jedubacu*, that is, “and the clods were compacted,” as Jerome translated it excellently. The scholiast is therefore mistaken here in taking pains to substitute a verb in the singular person for the plural. MART.]

Can you seize the prey of the lioness

and satisfy the life of her cubs,

when they lie in their dens

and lie in wait in their lairs [Variant: “mirrors”]?

Who prepares food for the raven,

when its young cry out to God, wandering,

because they have no food?

[Note: It might seem more correct to read, with the Sixtine edition and a few other printed books, “wandering” rather than “roaming,” as featherless raven chicks, abandoned to their parents’ care, can in some fashion cry out, but certainly cannot wander about. Nevertheless, both the Hebrew *melot* and the Greek *planōmenoi*—“wandering”—show that the holy translator wrote *vagantes*. I suppose that “wandering” is said of them in the nest itself.]

[Cap. XXXIX]

Do you know the time when the mountain goats give birth among the rocks,

or have you watched the does as they bear?

Their young separate from them,

[Col. 1118C]

and go away to pasture;

Who released the wild ass,

and who loosed its bonds [Hebrew: “its …”]?

[Note: The Septuagint and Jerome take *phere* and *arod* indiscriminately, as though they were two names for the same wild beast and animal. The Scholiast, however, seems to indicate a different species, observing that in place of the relative “its,” which refers to the wild ass, the Hebrew has *eteberes*, that is, *arod* or *garod*, a word which he renders in Latin as *eteberus*. What *eteberus* is, we cannot conjecture, since no trace of this name has appeared to us in the great multitude of books that we have fruitlessly searched through. Nor is there any reason to doubt that this reading may have come down to us corrupted by scribal error; perhaps instead of *eteberi* one should read *id est feri* (“that is, of the wild one”), or something similar. Let the judgment of the more learned decide this.]

To whom I gave a dwelling in the wilderness,

Will you bind the rhinoceros to the plow with your rope?

[Col. 1119A]

See below on Psalm 104. Hence it is clear that the Hebrew words were not interpreted into Latin by the holy Doctor in only one manner.]

AFTER THE LORD HAD SPOKEN THESE WORDS TO JOB, HE SAID TO ELIPHAZ THE TEMANITE [Note: It is marked in the Regina manuscript in large letters, in red ink: “HERE THE PROSE DISCOURSE BEGINS”]:

My anger and fury are kindled against you and against your two friends, because you have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job did. Jerome rejects this addition in his *Questions on Genesis*, chiefly because it is not found in the Hebrew codices.].

[Col. 1123]

# THE BOOK OF PSALMS

## PREFACE OF SAINT JEROME TO THE BOOK OF PSALMS ACCORDING TO THE HEBREW TRUTH

[Note: We collated this book against four very ancient and excellent-quality manuscript codices. Two of them were formerly designated in the collection of Queen Christina of Sweden by the numbers II and 1286; the third bears the number 134 in the Vatican Library itself; the fourth, and in fact generally superior to the others, is a Cistercian manuscript formerly belonging to the monastery of Nonantula, now of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem at Rome, under number 104. As for this very preface of Jerome, or letter to Sophronius, we also consulted many others from the libraries of Italy.]

Eusebius Jerome sends greetings to his Sophronius.

[Col. 1123A] I know [Note: [Col. 1123C] The copyists of the Canon of Hebrew Truth substitute another preface to the book of Psalms. Knowing that these psalms were translated from Hebrew into Latin by Jerome, they also considered it the genuine prologue of this Edition—the one beginning: “In the Hebrew book of Psalms,” etc. Our Saint-Germain exemplar likewise attributes this spurious and wholly supposititious work to Jerome. But on these matters elsewhere. MART.] that some people think the Psalter is divided into five books [Note: [Col. 1123C] We have learned both from the testimonies of the ancient Fathers and from the division of the Hebrew codex itself that it was chiefly the custom of the Hebrews to distribute the Psalter into five parts or books. In the Hebrew manuscript, the second book is inscribed in smaller letters after Psalm XLII, the third after Psalm LXXII, the fourth from Psalm XC, and the fifth from Psalm CVII. But since Jerome, who rejects this division, soon says that he has the Hebrews themselves as his authorities, I do not think that he meant the Hebrew people indiscriminately, or the teachers of the synagogue—as has hitherto commonly been believed—but rather the ancient interpreters descended from the Hebrews whom he had at hand in the Hexapla, namely Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and others, who interpreted the Hebrew text with greater insistence, and whom therefore he wished to oppose to the Septuagint. He may also have had in mind the Hebrew exemplar of the Hexapla, in which there was no mark of division, as Origen testifies in the Fragment preserved by Montfaucon among the Hexapla: “Yet in the Hebrew [text] no number is placed beside any of the Psalms.” Otherwise the ancient Fathers derive that division so certainly from the Hebrews and their codex—Gregory of Nyssa, Epiphanius, Ambrose, and many others—that nothing concerning it seems doubtful; and Eusebius testifies in his preface to the Psalms that it was preserved in the Hebrew exemplars of his own time. And although the opinion of those who maintain that the matter was formerly disputed among the Hebrews, with some rejecting the division, is not without probability, nevertheless they will not rightly suppose that the holy Doctor appealed to the authority of a people whose judgment was either largely contrary to his own or at least uncertain. Finally, I do not know by what other means the holy Father could both agree with the truth of the matter and be defended from the charge of open contradiction, such as appears in Epistle 26 to Marcella, no. 3: “Among the Hebrews the Psalter is divided into five volumes”; and in Epistle 140 to Cyprian, no. 4: “The Hebrews say that one volume of the Psalms contains five books,” and so forth. But he will be entirely consistent with himself if the word is understood in the different sense mentioned above; and if one supposes that “the Hebrews” here means the interpreters opposed to the Septuagint interpreters, and that their authority is preferred, both statements remain intact. From this it is also apparent how far Cassiodorus is from the truth when he attributes this division of the Psalms into five books to Jerome as its author.], so that wherever γένοιτο, γένοιτο is written among the Septuagint interpreters—that is, “Let it be, let it be”—there the end of a book occurs; [Note: [Col. 1124C] The Vatican manuscript reads “etc.” in place of what is printed.] whereas in the Hebrew it reads: AMEN, AMEN ().

We, however, following the authority of the Hebrews, and especially that of the apostles, who always call the book “the Psalms” in the New Testament, [Note: [Col. 1124C] In explaining Psalm CXXXIX in his letter to Cyprian, Jerome acknowledged the same point as follows: “The Hebrews say that one volume of the Psalms contains five books.” In the letter written to Marcella, beginning “Recently, when we were together,” he expressed the same opinion in other words: “For among the Hebrews,” he says, “the Psalter is divided into five volumes.” For further discussion of this division of the Psalter, the authors of the Psalms, and the Hebrew , see the letters just cited. MART.] affirm that they constitute one volume.

We also testify that all the Psalms [another reading: “and the Psalms”] belong to the authors named in their titles: David, Asaph, and Jeduthun; the sons of Korah; Heman the Ezrahite [another reading: Israelite]; Moses and Solomon; and the others whom Ezra included in one volume.

For if AMEN (), which Aquila translated πεπιστωμένως [“faithfully”], [Note: [Col. 1124D] The Vatican manuscript inserts corrupt words here, which do not seem to me to have any meaning, unless it was attempting to represent *pepistōmenos* again in Latin letters. It also reads *legit* (“he reads”) for *poneretur* (“would be placed”).] were placed only at the end of books, and not also sometimes at the beginning or end of a speech or sentence, neither would the Savior ever say in the Gospel, “Amen, amen, I say to you,” nor would Paul’s letters contain it in the middle of their argument. Moses, Jeremiah, and the others likewise would have many books in this form, since they frequently insert AMEN () in the middle of their volumes.

Moreover, the number of the twenty-two Hebrew books, and the mystery of that same number, would be altered. For the Hebrew title itself, SEPHAR THALLIM (), which means “the volume of hymns,” corresponding to apostolic authority, indicates not several books but one volume. [Note: [Col. 1124D] The Sorbonne manuscript reads *Sepheratalim*. MART.]

Since, then, recently, while arguing with a Hebrew, you brought forward from the Psalms certain testimonies concerning the Lord and Savior, and he, wishing to mock you, [Note: [Col. 1124D] One Royal manuscript, together with the Vatican manuscript, reads “to mock.”] asserted in nearly every passage that the Hebrew did not read as you maintained against the Septuagint interpreters, you very earnestly asked me to translate a new edition into Latin after Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion.

[Col. 1123B] For you said that you were more disturbed by the variety of interpreters, and that you were content either with my translation or with my judgment because of the affection with which you are attached to me. [Col. 1125A] Thus, urged on by you, [Note: [Col. 1125B] We have restored this passage on the authority of another very ancient Royal manuscript and of the old edition of 1496. The other books, including Martianay’s edition, had read a passage almost entirely devoid of sense: “to whom I cannot deny what I can.” The Vatican manuscript also recognizes the word *debeo* (“I owe”), although it reads only: “to whom I cannot deny, I owe,” omitting “what I can.” On the other hand, two other manuscripts of ours, together with the printed books, read *negare* (“deny”) in the sense stated above in place of *debeo* and *quae*. I would therefore prefer the passage to be restored more fully, with the individual manuscripts contributing their share: “to whom I owe what I can, and what I cannot deny, I cannot deny.” It is easy to suspect that the copyists, deceived by the recurrence of the same words, omitted the second parallel clause through a common error. Nevertheless, with an equally appropriate meaning and retaining both verbs, the passage reads in the second book of the *Apology against Rufinus*, no. 30, where the holy Father reviews the final section of his Preface: “to whom I must not deny what I cannot,” and that reading may perhaps be preferred to the others. Finally, the most ancient Royal book also reads: “to whom I cannot deny what I cannot,” and so forth.] I owe you what I can, and what I cannot, I again handed myself over to the barking of my detractors; and I preferred that in our friendship you should seek my ability rather than my willingness.

I shall certainly say with confidence, and shall summon many witnesses to this work, that I knowingly changed nothing at all [Note: [Col. 1125C] In the old edition cited earlier, the reading is “nothing at all of the meaning,” rather than “knowingly.” That reading is itself not unsuitable; indeed, it may seem more correct to some who wish to understand Jerome’s method and manner of translating—namely, not word for word but sense for sense—as being indicated here. But a parallel passage in the *Galeate Prologue* stands against it, where Jerome speaks of his own conscience: “I am altogether conscious of no such thing,” he says, “as having changed anything of the Hebrew truth.”] from the Hebrew truth.

If, therefore, my edition differs anywhere from the ancient ones, ask any Hebrew, and you will clearly see that I am unjustly torn apart by rivals who prefer to seem to despise [Note: [Col. 1125C] It may be more correctly read “to despise and envy” rather than “to seem.” The holy Father has similar wording in his prologues to the translation of the Psalms from the Greek and to the book of Chronicles. He may have taken the sentiment from Pliny. MART.] what is excellent rather than to learn.

[Col. 1126A] [Note: [Col. 1125C] The manuscript of Saint Michael “in the peril of the sea” has many additions and changes, as follows: “I am unjustly torn apart by rivals who, whether through envy or arrogance, prefer to appear to despise what is excellent rather than to learn. Most perverse men—and to drink from a turbid stream rather than from the purest spring. For when…” MART.] Most perverse men! For since they are always seeking new pleasures, and the seas near their appetites are not enough for them, why are they content with the old flavor in the study of Scripture alone?

Nor do I say this in order to bite my predecessors [Note: [Col. 1125D] The manuscripts read *praecessores* (“predecessors”), not *praedecessores*. MART. — We have restored *praecessores*, which all the manuscripts and the older printed editions prefer. Earlier the reading was *praedecessores*.], or because I think anything should be taken away from them. Their translation, corrected with the greatest care, I formerly gave to the people of my language. I say it because it is one thing to read the Psalms in the churches of those who believe in Christ, and another to answer Jews who slander every individual word.

If you translate this little work of mine into Greek—as you promise—[Note: [Col. 1125D] Older exemplars add certain Greek words at this point, from which I could extract no meaning: ΑΝΤΙΦΑΟΝΙΚΩΝ ΤΟΒΑΙΑ ϹΥΡΟΥϹΙΝ, unless they should be read as ἀντὶ φοινίκων τὰ βαία σύρουσιν, that is, “before the palm trees they drag palm branches.” The sense would be that, if you translate my little work into Greek and wish to make the most learned men witnesses to my ignorance, you will act no differently from those who bring twigs before trees; hence I shall rightly say to you the Horatian maxim: “Do not carry wood into the forest.” Although these words may appear to cohere, they do not greatly please me, both because the sentence is complete without them and because manuscripts exist in which such words are absent: the Sorbonne manuscript is one, and Vatican manuscript no. 344 another. Finally, neither Erasmus nor Marianus mention this Greek proverb in their editions. I do not know whether they were defeated by the difficulty of the matter or, rather, whether the deficiency of older manuscript exemplars—which we possess in abundance—explains the omission. MART.

It is scarcely possible to say how greatly learned men, each according to his own ability, have labored to restore this passage, from the Greek manuscript reading first published by the Benedictine editor down to the present day. The earlier editors and critics, unable to understand what the slightly corrupt Greek letters meant or intended, omitted them entirely. After Martianay had read them as best he could and had finally given them some Latin sense, since they were still not correct Greek, others likewise attempted to translate them into Latin unsuccessfully; so that, after much dispute, what they signified became almost less certain than before.

He says that he found the following written in older manuscripts: ΑΝΤΙΦΑΟΝΙΚΩΝ ΤΟΒΑΙΑ ϹΥΡΟΥϹΙΝ, which, he says, could be read ἀντὶ φοινίκων τὰ βαία σύρουκιν and rendered “before the palms they drag palm branches.” The sense would be that, if you translate my little work into Greek and wish to make the most learned men witnesses to my ignorance, you will act no differently from those who bring twigs before trees; hence I shall rightly say to you the Horatian maxim, “Do not carry wood into the forest.”

But how false that reading is, and how incongruous and absurd the resulting meaning, will plainly appear from what must shortly be explained; we need not waste time refuting it here. In this matter I would rather say that Martianay’s error is a minor one, and we readily pardon him if he was deceived while joining and explaining an exceedingly difficult sentence. What is more blameworthy is that he prohibited those very words—which seemed to him to cohere perfectly—from being admitted into the text, on rather slight grounds: namely, that the sense of the sentence was complete without them, and that two manuscripts, one Sorbonne and one Vatican, lacked them. He therefore rashly rejected them.

For if certain manuscripts lack them, everyone understands that this was the fault of some Latin copyist who omitted Greek words unknown to him. It is scarcely possible that someone should have added them falsely from his own invention in most of the other exemplars, especially exemplars both much older and of better quality. Moreover, the fact that the sentence is complete even without those words gave an ignorant scribe a reason to omit what he understood less safely; and on the other hand it more strongly proves that the words did not arise from the invention of a glossator, since there was no need to supply anything. They are therefore as genuinely Hieronymian as possible, and after the authority of so many exemplars they could not rightly be rejected.

But their correct reading and meaning must be investigated. Recently Martin, another member of the Benedictine group, read the Greek in such a way that he wanted it to say something about a Syrian mosquito-net, and tried to persuade many people generally—and, I might say, according to the man’s character, to charge us with ignorance. We examined his book nearly ten years ago; since we did not regard it as worth even a farthing, we omitted to note the stupidity of its contents.

Clericus, in Part III of his *Ars Critica*, section 1, chapter 14, confidently declares that he will teach the matter and interpret in a single word what the Parisian Benedictines could not understand. Yet, although it would have been worthwhile, he changed not even a single letter of their Greek reading. He merely says that it should be translated: “dragging branches instead of date clusters.” He insists that this gives an excellent sense in the passage, since Jerome is subtly and elegantly mocking the Greeks who read only the Septuagint translation of this book. He silently compares that translation to branches deprived of fruit, such as palm branches, while the Hebrew truth is compared to the fruit which the Greeks thought they were plucking but were mistaken, tearing away only barren branches.

This is his entire argument, which he embellishes by appealing to Pliny’s testimony in Book XII, chapter 4, concerning the nature of the palm, which bears its fruit at the summit rather than among the leaves. Martianay, attempting to defend his interpretation, replied at length, certainly with as much vehemence and insult toward his opponent as he could muster. Then the affair became increasingly trifling and, to put it plainly, they fought among themselves like blind men. Others who joined the quarrel out of partisan zeal—especially the writers of literary journals, too numerous to list individually—tried to drag and explain the Latin meaning toward their preconceived opinion by substituting now one word, now another.

No one thought of restoring the Greek reading, although they themselves admitted that, as it had long been received, it produced an obscure meaning. Indeed, if they had paid closer attention to the holy Doctor’s context and intention, they would have found it almost absurd and entirely incoherent. The Greek writing therefore had to be tested, and the true reading investigated in the older manuscripts among the corrupt and variously joined letters.

If we have succeeded in this according to our intention, you, reader, will judge; and if by your single judgment you approve our restoration, you will reject the conjectures of the others, so that we need not spend more time refuting them.

Of the fifteen manuscripts that we consulted, all of which retain those Greek letters with equal agreement, although somewhat more corruptly, two have the following readings. One, the Royal manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, cited above and written in uncial script, has: Ι ΙϹ ΑΝΤΙΦλΟΝΙΚωΝΤΟ ΒλΙλ ϹΥΡΟΥϹΙΝ. The other, the manuscript mentioned above from Santa Croce in Jerusalem of the City, not much later in age or inferior in quality, has: ΑΝΤΙΦΙΛΟΝΙΚΟΝ. ΤΟΙϹΛΙΛ ϹΥΡΟΥϹΙΝ.

These readings immediately shed light on the meaning, and that meaning is clear and exceedingly elegant—the very meaning intended by the holy Father. We therefore took the first expression, ἀντιφιλονείκων, as one word, departing from the manuscript tradition by scarcely a single letter. The same manuscripts supplied the other little word, τοῖς; we merely separated the article from the remaining letters. What remained was ΛΙΛ or ΒΛΙΛ and σύρουσιν, which we understood must again be joined into one word, κατασύρουσιν.

We changed the letters ΒΛΙΛ into ΚΑΤΑ, both because the sense requires it and because of the similarity and form of the letters. Those who have handled ancient books know that Latin scribes frequently confused Β with Κ and Λ with Α, and also Ι with Τ, when the short transverse line above escaped the eye.

Thus the Latin meaning emerges: “rejoining, through contention—or in rivalry with the exemplars—those who detract.” For ἀντιφιλονείκειν means to withstand and oppose an adversary by contending over something; and κατασύρειν means “to drag down” or “to detract,” as everyone knows and as the examples commonly found in the lexicographers prove. If you wish, see the holy Doctor himself in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter V, verse 21.

The sense according to the sequence of the sentence is this: “If you translate my little work, Sophronius, into Greek, so that by means of its rivalry with the Hebrew translation you may answer the Greeks and those who, under the pretext of the Greek Septuagint interpreters, detract from me; and if you wish to make even the most learned of them witnesses to my ignorance, I shall say to you that Horatian saying: ‘Do not carry wood into the forest.’” Since there are already more than enough Greek interpreters, there is no need to rework this translation in that language.

Indeed, when the Roman poet was attempting to compose verses in Greek, Romulus appeared to him in a dream and dissuaded him, in Satire 10, because there were more than enough poets among the Greeks:

“Do not carry wood into the forest more foolishly than if

[Col. 1128C] you wished to fill the great ranks of the Greeks.”

There is nothing here about palms, dates, branches, or fruits; nor is there any mention in Jerome of a proverb that never existed.] ἀντιφιλονείκων τοῖς κατασύρουσιν—“contending against those who detract”—and if you wish to make the most learned men also witnesses to my ignorance, I shall say to you that Horatian saying: [Note: [Col. 1128C] Horace, Book 1 of the *Satires*, Satire 10. MART.] “Do not carry wood into the forest.”

Except that I shall have this consolation: if, in our shared labor, I understand that praise and blame are shared between you and me.

I wish you health in the Lord Jesus [another reading omits “Jesus”], and that you remember me. [Note: [Col. 1128C] The Royal and Corbie manuscripts read: “Farewell in the Lord Jesus; I ask you to remember me.” The Vatican manuscript mentioned immediately above reads: “Live in the Lord Jesus,” and so forth. MART.]

[Col. 1127C] [I.] Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the impious,

[Col. 1127D] nor stood in the way of sinners,

[Col. 1128C] But his delight is in the law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1127D] The Cistercian manuscript inserts *fuit* (“was”), a word absent from the Hebrew text.],

[Col. 1128D] and he will meditate on his law day and night.

And he will be like a tree transplanted beside [Note: [Col. 1127D] The marginal scholia marked with *h* that occur from this point onward were copied by Martianay from his manuscripts of what he calls the Canon of the Hebrew Truth.] [Note: [Col. 1127D] We advise the diligent reader that all these marginal scholia, which occur throughout the Psalter, are found in the exemplars of the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, where the text of Jerome’s Version is preserved almost uncorrupted, together with such annotations in the margin. Through the ignorance of copyists, these same scholia were transferred into the sacred text of the Psalms, so that in three ancient manuscript codices the text is found altered by marginal annotations throughout the Psalter. Those manuscripts are the Vatican biblical codex no. 5729; the biblical codex of the Augustinians of Bordeaux; and another from the monastery of Saint Michael “in the peril of the sea.” We also found part of the scholia in other manuscript exemplars, from which they could easily have passed into the printed books. On the authority of the oldest and best manuscripts, we have taken care to restore everything to its proper place. MART.] streams

[Note: The copies of the Canon write this verse in the middle of the column, evidently to distinguish it from Psalm X, which in the Hebrew begins with these words. The other codices write continuously and join these two psalms into one. Hence the error in the subsequent numbering: Psalm X is marked as XI, and Psalm XII as XIII, and so on. MART.—Martianaeus transcribed it in this manner from both copies of the Canon, as he calls them, in capital letters, to indicate the beginning of a new psalm in the Hebrew archetype. Our manuscripts, however, write continuously, without any mark of division or number.]

WHY, O LORD, DO YOU STAND FAR OFF?

your strong ones are left to you [Al. are forsaken],

[Col. 1135A] you have become [Note: Several manuscripts read: “You will be made an assistant”; some others: “You will be an assistant.” MART.] the helper of the orphan.

the nations have perished from his land.

The Lord has heard the desire of the poor [h. You have heard, O Lord].

You have prepared their heart [Note: Three of our manuscripts read: “You have prepared their heart, so that your ear may hear,” etc.], so that your ear may hear,

to judge the orphan and the oppressed,

so that man may no longer be arrogant

upon the earth.

FOR THE DIRECTOR. OF DAVID.

[XI.] In the Lord I have hoped;

how can you say to my soul,

[Note: Our manuscripts read: “Fly over the mountain like a bird.”]

“Fly like a sparrow to the mountain”?

For behold, the impious have bent the bow;

they have placed their arrow upon the string,

to shoot in secret at the upright in heart.

For the laws have been destroyed;

what has the righteous man done?

[Col. 1135B] The Lord is in his holy temple;

the Lord has his throne in heaven.

His eyes see;

his eyelids test the sons of men.

The Lord tests the righteous,

but the impious and the one who loves iniquity

his soul hates.

He will rain snares [Al. He rains snares] upon sinners [h. the impious],

fire and brimstone, and a storm wind will be the portion of their cup.

For the Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness;

the upright will see his face [Al. have seen his face].

FOR THE DIRECTOR. FOR THE EIGHTH. A SONG [h. Psalm] OF DAVID.

[XII.] Save, O Lord [Note: The Cistercian reads “Save me, O God”; and immediately afterward the Regius, joined to it, reads “a deceitful lip” instead of “deceitful.”], for the holy man [h. the merciful] has failed;

for the faithful have been diminished among the sons of men.

Each speaks vainly [Al. He speaks vainly] to his neighbor;

with a deceitful heart and a double heart they have spoken.

May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips,

and the tongue that speaks great things.

They said, “Let us strengthen our tongue;

our lips are with us: who is our lord [h. ruler]?” [Note: Two manuscripts add the verb “is.”]

“Because of the desolation of the needy and the groaning of the poor,

now I will arise,” says the Lord;

“I will place their help in salvation.”

The words of the Lord are pure words:

silver [Note: These same manuscripts, and others examined by Martianaeus, read “silver tested by fire.”] tested,

separated from the earth, refined sevenfold.

You, O Lord, will guard them;

you will preserve us from this generation forever.

The impious will walk around [Al. walk],

when the vilest of the sons of men have been exalted.

FOR THE DIRECTOR. A SONG [h. Psalm] OF DAVID.

[XIII.] How long, O Lord, will you forget me [Al. of me]

utterly?

How long will you hide your face from me?

How long shall I place counsels [Al. counsel] in my soul,

and sorrow in my heart by day?

How long will my enemy be exalted over me?

[Note: The Cistercian reads: “Attend and hear me,” etc.] Turn [h. Look], hear me, O Lord my God;

enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death.

Lest at some time my enemy say, “I have prevailed against him”;

my enemies will exult when I am shaken.

But I trust in your mercy;

my heart will exult in your salvation;

I will sing to the Lord, who has repaid me.

FOR THE DIRECTOR. OF DAVID.

[XIV.] The fool said in his heart,

“There is no God.”

They have been corrupted and have deliberately become detestable;

there is no one who does good.

[Col. 1136B] The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men,

to see whether there was anyone intelligent [Note: The Regina manuscript reads: “whether you were intelligent”; the Cistercian follows with “or seeking.”], seeking God.

All have turned aside; together they have become stuck fast;

there is no one who does good, [Note: The copies of the Hebrew Canon of truth, and the Carnutian and Sorbonian manuscripts, which are written in three columns and contain a threefold version of the Psalm, leave a blank space here. By this they indicate the absence of eight verses, which the Apostle appears to recall in his Letter to the Romans. [Col. 1136D] No such verses, however, exist in the Hebrew source or among the Septuagint translators, but only in the Vulgate edition, which in Greek is called *koine* (κοινή) and was different throughout the world in Jerome’s time, as he himself testifies in the preface to Book XVI of his Commentary on Isaiah the Prophet. See, in the same place, Eustochium the virgin and Jerome, doctor of the Church, disputing about these verses. Consult also John Isaac, the German Levite, *Defense of the Truth of the Hebrew Text against Lindanus*, Book I, p. 40. MART.] not even one.

Will all those who work iniquity not understand,

who devour my people like a morsel of bread?

They have not called upon the Lord.

There [Note: The same Cistercian reads: “They will fear terror.”] they will tremble with fear,

for God is with the righteous generation.

You have confounded the counsel of the poor,

for the Lord is his hope.

Who will grant salvation to Israel from Zion?

When the Lord restores the captivity of his people,

Jacob will exult and Israel will rejoice.

A SONG [h. Psalm] OF DAVID.

[XV.] O Lord, [Note: The copyist of the Vatican manuscript here read not what he found but what he understood: “Who will dwell in your territory?” MART.] who will dwell in your tent,

or who [Al. and who] has dwelt upon your holy mountain?

He who enters without blemish and practices justice,

and speaks truth in his heart.

[Col. 1136C] He who is not quick with his tongue,

who has not done [Al. does not do] evil to his friend [h. companion],

and has not endured reproach against his neighbor [h. fellow].

The wicked man is despised in his eyes,

but he glorifies [Al. glorifies] those who fear the Lord.

He swears an oath to his own harm and does not change it.

He has not lent his money at interest,

and has not accepted gifts against the innocent.

He who does these things

will not be moved forever.

OF DAVID, THE HUMBLE AND SIMPLE.

[XVI.] Guard me, O God, for I have hoped in you.

[Note: The current Hebrew text has the corrupt reading “you said” instead of “I said”—*amarta* or *amartha* instead of *amarthi*. Some Latin manuscripts read “saying to God” instead of “I said to the Lord.” MART.—Some manuscripts read “saying to God.” For the Hebrew reading, which can be rendered in various ways, consult the sacred critics.]

I said to the Lord, “You are my Lord;

I have no good apart from you.”

For the holy ones who are in the land, and the illustrious,

all my desire is in them.

[Col. 1137A] Their idols will be multiplied, following behind [Note: The Cistercian manuscript departs much farther: “Their pains will be multiplied, and afterward they will follow you; I will not pour out their libations” [Col. 1137D]—another manuscript reads “I will not offer”—“because it is more grievous than the pouring out of blood; nor will I take,” etc. These words have more the character of a glossator and paraphraser than of a translator. Nevertheless, the earlier meaning, concerning multiplied pains rather than idols, can equally well be drawn from the Hebrew text.];

I will not pour out their libations from blood,

nor will I take their names upon my lips.

The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and [Note: The same manuscript has in the recto: “and my cup.”] of my cup;

you are the possessor [h. restorer] of my lot.

The lines [Al. linen things] have fallen to me in beautiful places,

and my inheritance is most splendid.

I will bless the Lord who has given me counsel;

moreover, even by night my kidneys have instructed me.

I set the Lord [Al. omits “the Lord”] always in my sight [h. before me],

for he is at my right hand [Al. you are], so that I may not be shaken.

Therefore my heart rejoiced, and my glory exulted;

my flesh also will dwell securely.

For you will not abandon my soul in hell,

nor will you allow your holy one [h. merciful one] to see corruption.

You will show me the path of life;

fullness [h. satiety] [Note: The Canon of Carcassonne reads: “fullness of riches.” MART.] of joys before your face;

delights at your right hand forever.

PRAYER OF DAVID.

[XVII.] Hear, O God, the just man [h. “Hear, O Lord, justice”];

attend to my petition;

listen with your ears to my prayer,

which is without deceitful lips [Al. of deceit].

Let my judgment proceed from your face [h. from your presence];

let your eyes see equity.

You have tested my heart; you have visited me by night;

you have smelted me, [Note: This passage has been notably altered and corrupted both in the printed editions and in the manuscript books. The Canon of Saint-Germain and the Vatican manuscript, together with the Corbeian, read as we have printed it. Two others read as follows: “You have smelted me, and have not found my thoughts. Would that my mouth had not passed into the work of men! Because of the word of your lips,” etc. The Regius manuscript reads: “You have smelted me, and have not found my understandings pass into the works of men. Because of the word of your lips,” etc. Likewise the Carcassonne Canon and the Sorbonian manuscript, except for “in the work of men.” MART.] and you have not found:

would that my thought had not passed through my mouth.

In the work of Adam,

in the word of your lips,

I have observed the ways [h. paths] of the robber.

Support my steps on your tracks,

[Col. 1137C] and let my footsteps not slip [Al. not slide].

I have called upon you, [Note: Three manuscripts read: “You have heard me, O God.” MART.] for you will hear me, O God;

incline your ear to me; hear my speech.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript has the singular: “Make your mercy wonderful”; immediately afterward, it reads “in the eye” instead of “within the eye.”] Make your mercies wonderful, O savior of those who hope,

from those who resist your right hand.

Guard me as the pupil [h. daughter] within the eye;

protect me in the shadow of your wings.

From the face of the impious who devastate me.

My enemies have surrounded my soul;

they have enclosed me in their fat;

they have spoken proudly with their mouths.

Advancing against me, they have now surrounded me;

they have set their eyes to incline toward the earth.

[Col. 1138A] His likeness is like that of a lion desiring prey,

and like that of a cub [Note: The Regina manuscript inserts “of a lion.”] sitting in hiding.

Rise up, O Lord; go before his face; bend him down.

Save my soul from the impious, who is your sword.

From the men of your hand, O Lord,

who are dead in the depths;

whose portion is in life,

and whose belly you have filled from your hidden treasures;

they will be satisfied with sons,

and will leave their remnants to their little ones.

But I will see your face in righteousness;

I will be filled [h. satisfied] when I awake with your likeness.

FOR THE DIRECTOR. OF DAVID, SERVANT OF THE LORD, WHO SPOKE TO THE LORD THE WORDS OF THIS SONG, ON THE DAY WHEN THE LORD DELIVERED HIM FROM THE HAND OF ALL HIS ENEMIES [Note: The Cistercian manuscript has “his own,” and does not have “as he says” at the end.] AND FROM THE HAND OF SAUL. AND HE SAID:

[XVIII.] I will love you, O Lord, my strength;

The Lord [Al. O Lord], [Note: The Regius, Corbeian, Carnutian, and Sorbonian manuscripts read: “O Lord, my rock.” MART.] is my rock and my strength,

and my savior.

[Col. 1138B] My strong God, and I will hope in him;

my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my protector.

Praising him, I will call upon the Lord,

and I shall be saved from my enemies.

The cords of death surrounded me,

and the torrents of the devil [Belial] terrified me.

The cords of hell surrounded me;

the snares of death overtook me.

In my tribulation I will call upon [Al. I called upon] the Lord,

and I will cry out to my God.

He will hear my voice from his holy temple [Note: All our manuscripts omit “holy.” MART.];

and my cry will come before his face into his ears.

The earth was shaken and trembled;

the foundations of the mountains were disturbed

and shaken, because he was angry.

Smoke rose from [Al. out of] his anger,

and fire devoured from his mouth;

[Col. 1138C] burning coals were kindled by him.

He inclined the heavens and came down,

and darkness was beneath his feet.

He mounted upon a cherub [Al. cherubim] and flew;

he flew upon the wings of the wind.

He made darkness his hiding place;

his tabernacle was around him,

[Note: These same manuscripts of ours, and others examined by Martianaeus, read: “dark water in the clouds of the air.”] dark waters in the clouds of the air.

From the brightness before his face the clouds passed by,

hail and burning coals.

And the Lord thundered in the heavens [Al. from heaven],

and the Most High [Note: The copies of the Canon join this verse to the preceding one, contrary to the teaching of Saint Jerome in his Letter to Sunnia and Fretela: “And you ask why the Greek does not have this verse a second time, with two verses interposed,” etc. The question concerned the verse “hail and burning coals,” which was read only once in the Greek text, but appears again in the Hebrew after two verses. This clause was also added from the Hebrew and from Theodotion’s edition to the Septuagint interpreters under an asterisk. MART.] gave his voice:

hail and burning coals.

He sent his arrows and scattered them;

he multiplied lightning and threw them into confusion.

And the outpourings of waters appeared,

and the foundations of the world were uncovered,

at your rebuke, O Lord,

at the blast of the breath of your anger.

He sent from on high and took me;

[Note: Two manuscripts read “he drew me out”; then, in the immediately following verse, most of the others examined by Martianaeus read “from my most powerful enemies.”] he will draw me out of many waters.

He delivered me from my most powerful enemy,

and from those who hated me, for they were stronger

than I.

They overtook me on the day of my affliction,

and the Lord became my support.

He led me out into a broad place,

[Note: One Cistercian manuscript reads “he delivered me”; the Regina manuscript follows with “because he was pleased with me.”] he delivered me because he was pleased with me.

The Lord repaid me according to my justice;

according to the purity of my hands he repaid

me.

For I kept the ways of the Lord,

and did not act impiously against my God.

For all his judgments were before my eyes,

[Col. 1139B] and I did not remove his commands from me.

And I was blameless with him,

and guarded myself from my iniquity.

And the Lord will repay [Al. repaid] me according to

my justice,

according to the purity of my hands in the sight

of his eyes.

With the holy one you will be holy;

with the innocent man you will act innocently.

With the chosen one you will be chosen,

and with the perverse you will be perverted [Al. you will pervert].

For you will save the poor people,

and you will humble haughty eyes.

For [Note: Two manuscripts read: “For you enlighten”; and consequently some other codices read “he will illuminate my darkness.” MART.] you will illuminate my lamp;

O Lord my God, you will illuminate my darkness

[Al. my darknesses].

For in you I run [Note: The Hebrew commentator prefers “I will run”; two of our manuscripts likewise prefer it.] girded [h. “I will run after the girded”],

and in my God I will leap over [Al. leap upon] a wall.

[Col. 1139C] God—his way is blameless;

the word of the Lord is tested [Note: These same manuscripts add “by fire.”]:

he is a shield to all who hope in him.

[Note: Our three manuscripts, and three others examined by Martianaeus, do not acknowledge the adverb “for.”] For who is God besides the Lord,

and who is strong besides our God?

The God who girds me with strength,

and has made my way blameless.

He makes my feet equal to those of deer,

and sets me upon my high places [Note: Two of our manuscripts omit “my.”].

He teaches my hands for battle,

and makes my arms like a bronze bow.

You have given me the shield of your salvation [Al. my salvation],

and your right hand has strengthened [Al. confirmed] me;

and your gentleness has multiplied me.

You will enlarge my step [Al. my steps] beneath

me,

and my ankles will not fail [Al. my ankles].

I will pursue my enemies and overtake them,

and I will not turn back until I consume them.

[Col. 1139D] I will strike them, and they will not be able to rise;

they will fall beneath my feet.

And you girded me with strength for battle;

you will bend those who resist me beneath me.

You gave me the backs of my enemies,

and you destroyed those who hate me.

They will cry out, and there will be no one to save them;

they will cry to the Lord, and he will not hear them.

[Col. 1140A] I will crush them like dust before the face

of the wind;

I will cast them away like mud in the streets.

You will save me from the disputes of the people;

you will set me at the head of the nations.

The people whom I did not know will serve me;

at the report of the ear they will obey me.

The sons of strangers will lie to me;

the sons of strangers will flow away

and will shrink back in their afflictions.

The Lord lives, and blessed is my God [h. my strong one];

and the God of my salvation will be exalted [Al. may the God of my salvation be exalted].

God, who gives me vengeance,

and gathers peoples beneath me,

who saves me from my enemies

and raises me above those who resist me:

you will deliver [Al. deliver] me from the unjust man.

Therefore I will confess to you among the nations, O Lord,

and I will sing [h. play psalms] to your name.

[Col. 1140B] To the one who magnifies the salvations of his king,

and shows mercy to his anointed [Note: The Regina manuscript reads: “They magnify the salvations,” and consistently afterward: “They will show mercy.”],

to David and his seed forever [h. for the age].

FOR THE DIRECTOR. A SONG [h. Psalm] OF DAVID.

[XIX.] The heavens declare the glory of God,

and the firmament announces the work of his hands.

Day pours forth the word to day,

and night reveals knowledge to night.

There is no speech, and there are no words,

whose voice is not heard.

Their sound has gone out through all the earth,

and their words to the end of the world.

He set up a tent for the sun among them.

And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber,

rejoiced like a strong man to run the course [h. path].

His going forth is from the summit of heaven,

and his course [Al. return] reaches to its summit;

[Col. 1140C] there is no one who can hide from his heat.

The law of the Lord is blameless,

restoring the soul.

The testimony of the Lord is trustworthy,

giving wisdom to the little one [Al. little ones].

The precepts of the Lord are right,

gladdening the heart.

The commandment of the Lord is bright,

enlightening the eyes.

The fear of the Lord is pure,

enduring forever [h. for eternity].

The judgments of the Lord are true,

justified in themselves.

They are more desirable than gold

and much precious stone [h. refined gold],

and sweeter than honey and the dripping honeycomb.

Therefore your servant also will teach them;

in keeping them there is great reward.

Who understands errors?

Cleanse me from hidden faults.

[Col. 1140D] And from the arrogant free your servant;

if they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless,

and I shall be cleansed from the greatest offense.

May the words of my mouth be pleasing,

and the meditation of my heart in your sight,

[Col. 1141A] O Lord, my strength and my redeemer.

FOR THE DIRECTOR. A SONG [h. Psalm] OF DAVID.

XX. May the Lord hear you on the day of tribulation;

may the name of the God of Jacob protect you.

May he send you help from the sanctuary,

and strengthen you from Zion.

May he remember all your sacrifice,

and may your burnt offering [Al. your burnt offering is omitted] become fat.

ALWAYS.

May he grant you according to your heart,

and fulfill all your desire [h. all your counsel].

We will praise [Note: Several manuscripts read: “We will be praised in your salvation, and in the name of our God we will lead choirs.” MART.] in your salvation,

and in the name of our God we will lead [Note: The same, joined to the Cistercian manuscript, and several others examined by Martianaeus, read: “we will lead choirs”; perhaps this is more accurate.].

May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.

Now I know that the Lord will save his anointed.

He will hear him from his holy heaven,

with the strength of the salvation of his right hand [Note: These same manuscripts read: “in strength.”].

Some trust in chariots and some in horses;

[Col. 1141B] but we will remember the name of the Lord our God [Note: The printed books and three manuscripts read: “But we will remember the name of the Lord our God.” MART.].

They have been bent down and have fallen;

but we have risen and stand upright.

O Lord, save!

[Note: The Regius, Augustinian Burdigalian, and Saint Michael’s manuscripts read otherwise: “The king will hear us on the day when we call upon you.” The Corbeian and Carnutian codices read: “On the day when we call.” In accordance with the current Hebrew: “On the day when we cry out.” We have followed the copies of the Canon and the Vatican codex. Finally, the Sorbonian has: “King, hear us on the day when we call upon you.” MART.—The Cistercian manuscript reads: “The king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you,” without the addition “him.”] The king will hear us on the day when we call upon him.

FOR THE DIRECTOR. A SONG [h. Psalm] OF DAVID.

[XXI.] O Lord, the king will rejoice in your strength,

and in your salvation he will exult greatly.

You granted him the desire of his heart,

and did not withhold from him the wish of his lips. [Note: Some manuscripts add “him”; others also always erase the mark of the diapsalm. MART.] ALWAYS.

For you will go before him with blessings of goodness;

you will place upon his head a crown [Note: In place of “refined gold,” our manuscripts have “of a precious stone.” Immediately afterward the Cistercian has “from you” instead of “a crown.”] of refined gold [Note: The Corbeian, Vatican, and Sorbonian read: “For you went before him with blessings of goodness.” Then these same manuscripts, the Sorbonian and Corbeian, together with two others, read “a crown of a precious stone.” MART.].

He asked life of you, and you gave it to him;

length of days forever and ever.

Great is his glory in your salvation;

you will place glory and beauty upon him.

For you will set him [Note: All our manuscripts, and others examined by Martianaeus, again read “an everlasting blessing.”] as blessings forever;

you will gladden him with joy before your face.

[Col. 1141C] For the king trusts in the Lord,

and through the mercy of the Most High he will not be deceived.

May your hand find all your enemies;

may your right hand find those who hate you.

You will set them like a fiery oven

at the time of your presence.

The Lord in his anger will cast them down [Al. has cast them down],

and fire will devour [Al. has devoured] them.

You will destroy their fruit [Al. their fruit is omitted] from the earth,

and their seed from among the sons of men,

for they have inclined evil against you;

they have devised a crime which they could not accomplish.

For [Al. because] you will set them as a shoulder,

you will strengthen your cords [h. sinews] against their faces.

Be exalted, O Lord [Al. O God], in your strength;

we will sing and play psalms to your strength [Al. strengths].

FOR THE DIRECTOR [Note: The expression is corrupt in both copies of the Canon and in the Vatican codex: “For the hind of the morning.” Since Jerome himself taught in Book II of his Commentary on the Prophet Hosea that it should be read in the masculine gender, “for the stag of the morning,” he says: “He himself [Christ], and no other, is prepared for us like morning and dawn.” The title of the twentieth psalm also concerns this: “For the assumption of the morning,” although in Hebrew it is written “For the stag of the morning.” He also mentions the same title in his Letter to Marcella, whose beginning is: “Recently, when we were together,” where he says: “I would like to write something to you also about the diapsalm, which is written in Hebrew *SELA* . . . and about what appears in the title of a certain Psalm, ‘FOR AJELETH.’” Although the name *ajeleth* and *ajala* has a feminine form among the Hebrews, Jerome interprets it in the masculine gender in Genesis XLIX.19, Proverbs LIX.19, this Psalm XXI (or XXII according to the Hebrew), and elsewhere. Hence it is apparent that some things were altered by the Canon’s commentator in the manuscript copies of Jerome’s version. [Col. 1142D] MART.—The Regina manuscript omits the name David; the Cistercian also omits “song.”] FOR THE STAG OF THE MORNING, SONG [h. Psalm] OF DAVID.

[XXII.] My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?

The words of my roaring are far from my salvation.

My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear;

and by night, and there is no silence for me.

Yet you are holy, dwelling in the praise [h. praises] of Israel.

In you our fathers trusted;

they trusted, and you saved them.

[Col. 1142B] To you they cried out, and they were saved;

in you they trusted, and they were not confounded.

But I am a worm and not a man [h. adult male];

the reproach of men and the contempt of the people [h. populace].

All who see me mock [Al. mocked] me;

they thrust out the lip and shake the head.

He has fled to the Lord [h. reveals to the Lord]; let him save

him;

let him deliver him, since he wants him.

But you are my defender from the womb;

my trust from my mother’s breasts.

Upon you I was cast from the womb;

from my mother’s belly, my God [Note: Here our manuscripts insert the verb “you are”; then some read “may you make” instead of “may you become,” and again, where the verb “is” appears, they have “there” immediately before.] you are.

Do not be far from me, for tribulation is near,

and there is no helper.

Many calves have surrounded me;

fat bulls [h. of Bashan] have encircled me.

They opened their mouths against me,

[Col. 1142C] a lion seizing and roaring.

[Note: Three manuscripts add “like a lion”; in the following verse they read “it has been poured out” instead of “I have been poured out.”]

I have been poured out like water,

and all my bones have been separated.

My heart has become like wax,

melting in the midst of my belly.

My strength has dried up like a potsherd,

and my tongue has clung [Note: The Cistercian and Regius manuscripts read “to my palate”; and, a reading which also pleases the commentator below, “dogs” instead of “hunters,” omitting the adverb “because.”] to my jaws;

and you have brought me down into the dust of death.

For hunters [h. dogs] have surrounded me,

[Col. 1143A] the assembly of the wicked has encircled me.

They fastened [Note: [Col. 1143B] Several variant readings occur in manuscript copies for this verse. Five older copies, among them the exemplars of the Canon, read as follows: “They bound my hands,” etc. The Codex of the Augustinians of Bordeaux has “They encircled my hands.” The Sorbonicus, more corrupt here than the others, has “They said my hands,” instead of “They fastened my hands,” as found in the printed editions and in two manuscripts, namely the Vatican manuscript and another of Saint Michael’s. Moreover, the present Hebrew text is corrupt and damaged through the error of more recent scribes, who, instead of *kaaru*, wrote *kaari*, deceived by the similarity of the letters *vav* and *yod*, which differ only in their size. But the curious reader must be warned against the confusion caused by certain modern writers, who chatter much nonsense, claiming that this passage was corrupted through the malice of the Jews. In the Colbert Library there is still found manuscript Hebrew no. 627, which preserves the pure and primitive reading: for in it we read not the modern copyists’ *kaari*, but the ancient prophetic *karu*. It has been corrected with such care that the *aleph*, which in this word is servile and superfluous when vowel-points are used, is killed and pierced through with an obelus or some mark above, and is given no point below. Thus we are plainly taught that the verb *caru* or *karu* consists of these three elements alone and can mean nothing other than “they dug.” Jerome read this; so too did the Scholiast, later than Jerome, of the Canon. Finally, this was always written in the ancient and more reliable Hebrew volumes, as the already mentioned manuscript exemplar in the Colbert Library makes clear: it is written with *qamets* under *kaph* and with *shureq* inside *vav*. This completely silences the mouths of the objectors. MART. — The same manuscripts add “me”; they also read “They bound” instead of “They fastened.” This, then, is that much-debated Hebrew reading *kaari*, which learned men have demonstrated—through published disputations on the matter—to have been fabricated or corrupted by the deceit of later Hebrews in place of *karu*, in order to evade the mystery of the Lord’s Passion. Certainly, even if the innumerable other arguments were lacking, this very testimony drawn from Jerome seems quite decisive against the fraud. For he would not have interpreted the word as “they fastened,” “they dug,” or anything similar if he had found the noun meaning “like a lion” written in the Hebrew copies of his age. That he did not in any way alter that word is most clearly established by the reading itself of the Septuagint, as well as of Aquila, Symmachus, and the other interpreters, and by the most explicit testimonies of Justin Martyr, Origen, Eusebius, and other Fathers older than our own time. There are also those who testify that they read Hebrew copies which presented *Caaru* in the text, without any indication of a variant reading, while others noted *Caari* in the margin. But Simonius maintains that Colbert 626, which Martianus cites, originally had *Caari*, then was corrected to *Caaru* by extending the stroke of the *yod*, and was altered and corrected by a certain Christian. Martianus appealed to the judgment of the rabbis, who, after weighing the matter more carefully, declared that this correction was made by the same Hebrew copyist who wrote the codex for Jewish use in the thirteenth century.] my hands and my feet.

I have counted all my bones;

they themselves look on and see me.

They divided my garments among themselves,

and over my clothing they cast lots.

But you, Lord, do not be far away [Another reading: do not act]:

my strength, hasten to my aid.

Deliver my soul from the sword,

and my solitary one from the hand of the dog.

Save me from the mouth of the lion,

and hear me from the horns of the unicorns.

I shall proclaim your name to my brothers;

in the midst of the assembly I shall praise you.

[Note: [Col. 1144C] Three of our manuscripts read “you who fear.”]

You who fear the Lord, praise him;

all the offspring of Jacob, glorify him,

and let all the offspring of Israel stand in awe of him.

For he did not despise or disdain the humility

of the poor,

nor hide his face from him;

and when he cried out to him, he heard him.

[Col. 1143B] With you is my praise in the great assembly;

I shall fulfill my vows in the presence of those who fear him.

The humble shall eat and be satisfied;

those who seek him shall praise the Lord.

Your heart shall live for ever.

All the ends of the earth shall remember

and turn to the Lord;

and all the families of the nations shall worship before you [Note: [Col. 1144C] The same manuscripts read “before him” instead of “before you”; and immediately afterward, “The kingdom belongs to the Lord.”]

For the kingdom belongs to the Lord,

and he shall rule the nations.

[Col. 1144A] All the fat ones [Another reading: princes] of the earth have eaten and worshiped;

before his face all who descend

into the dust shall bow [Note: [Col. 1144C] The Cistercian and Regina manuscripts read: “All shall bend the knee, who,” etc.].

And his soul [Note: [Col. 1144C] In the manuscripts just cited, *ipsi* occurs instead of the negative particle; this gives a somewhat better sense and may itself derive from the Hebrew, since “and not” and “to him” sound exactly alike in pronunciation, and one could easily have been substituted for the other in the Hebrew text.] shall not live.

A seed shall serve him;

it shall be told to the Lord for a generation.

They shall come and proclaim his righteousness [Note: [Col. 1144D] Several manuscripts read “his righteous deeds … which the Lord has done.” MART. — Some of our manuscripts have “righteous deeds” in the plural here, but in the following verse read “which,” referring it to the people; others have “which,” while nevertheless retaining “righteousness.”],

to the people who shall be born, which he has done.

## A SONG [Hebrew: psalm] OF DAVID

### [XXIII]

The Lord feeds me [Hebrew: My shepherd]; I shall lack nothing.

He made me lie down in grassy pastures [Note: [Col. 1144D] Three manuscripts have “he reclined.”];

he nourished me beside waters of refreshment.

He restored my soul;

he led me along paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.

And even if I walk in the valley [Note: [Col. 1144D] In the same manuscripts: “in the valley of death,” with the word “shadow,” which also occurs in the Hebrew, omitted.] of the shadow of death,

I shall fear no evil, for you are with me;

your rod and your staff—they themselves shall comfort me.

[Col. 1144B] You shall set a table before me

in opposition to my enemies;

you have fattened my head with oil [Another reading omits “with”];

my cup is intoxicating.

Indeed, goodness and mercy shall follow me [Another reading: may they follow me]

all the days of my life;

and my dwelling shall be in the house of the Lord

for length of days.

## A SONG [Hebrew: psalm] OF DAVID

### [XXIV]

The earth belongs to the Lord, and its fullness;

the world and those who dwell in it.

[Col. 1145A] For he founded it upon the seas [Note: [Col. 1145C] Several manuscripts retain the masculine form: “he founded it … he established it.” MART. — The Cistercian manuscript has “it” here and shortly afterward; two other manuscripts, retaining the later gender, read “he established him” in the following clause.],

and established it upon the rivers.

Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord,

and who [Another reading: or who] shall stand in his holy place [Note: [Col. 1145C] Greek and Latin codices vary in this word. The Septuagint in the Roman edition has καὶ τίς, that is, “and who”; but in the Sorbonicus manuscript, where the Greek text is written in Latin letters, the reading is ἢ τίς, “or who.” Some Latin copies likewise read “or who,” as does Saint Augustine in the *Speculum*: “or who shall stand,” etc. MART.]?

One innocent in hands and pure in heart,

who has not lifted up his soul in vain,

and has not sworn deceitfully.

He shall receive blessing from the Lord,

and righteousness from God his savior.

This is the generation of those who seek him,

of those who seek your face, Jacob.

Forever.

Lift up your heads, O gates,

and be lifted up, O everlasting doors,

and the King of glory shall enter.

Who is this King of glory?

The Lord, strong and mighty;

the Lord, mighty in battle.

Lift up your heads, O gates,

and lift yourselves up [Note: [Col. 1145D] All our manuscripts read this way, in accordance with the Hebrew. The printed editions read “and be raised up.” MART.], O everlasting doors,

and the King of glory shall enter.

Who is this King of glory?

The Lord of hosts: he is the King of glory.

Forever.

DAVID.

### [XXV]

To you, Lord, I raise my soul [Note: [Col. 1145D] In very many manuscripts this psalm has the letters of the Hebrew alphabet prefixed to its verses, as though it were an acrostic. Some letters are nevertheless missing, and the alphabet is not complete; hence Jerome does not mention this psalm when listing those reckoned by such alphabets or divisions. See the prologue to the Books of Kings and Jerome’s letter to Paula of Urbica; it will also be useful to consult Cassiodorus’s Commentary on Psalm XXIV. MART. — In several of our manuscripts this psalm likewise has the letters of the alphabet prefixed to each verse, as Martianus also observed in his copies. Since, however, this order of letters is absent from the second, fifth, eighteenth, and final verses, and since the holy Father himself nowhere else lists this psalm among the acrostics, no account has been taken of its incomplete alphabet. Others, however, explain very learnedly that the defect can easily be supplied by assigning the first verse to two, the second beginning with “in you I trust”; and thus the fifth begins with “and teach me.” For the eighteenth they place “Rise and see,” etc., and finally combine verses 21 and 22 into one—or rather remove the last from the series, since it concludes the psalm. We have noted this so that the prescribed order of letters in the Latin manuscripts may not seem pointless. Our manuscripts, moreover, read “I shall raise” instead of “I raise,” and shortly afterward “having trusted in you,” etc.].

My God, in you I have trusted; let me not be put to shame;

let not my enemies rejoice over me [Hebrew: and let them not exult over me].

Indeed, let all who hope in you not be put to shame;

let those who act wickedly in vain be put to shame.

Show me your ways, Lord;

teach me your paths.

Lead me [Note: [Col. 1146D] Only the Vatican manuscript reads “lead me in your truth.” MART.] in your truth and teach me,

for you are God my savior [Another reading adds “are”];

I have waited for you all day long.

Remember your mercies, Lord,

and your compassions [Note: [Col. 1146D] One Cistercian manuscript has “which are from eternity.”],

for they are from eternity.

Do not remember the sins of my youth

or my transgressions;

according to your mercy remember me [Another reading omits “you”],

because of your goodness, Lord.

The Lord is good and upright;

therefore he will teach sinners the way.

He will guide the meek in judgment,

and teach the humble his way.

All the paths of the Lord are mercy and truth

for those who keep his covenant and his testimonies.

For your name’s sake, Lord,

be gracious to my iniquity, for it is great.

[Col. 1146A] Who is the man who fears the Lord?

He will teach him the way he should choose.

His soul shall dwell in goodness,

and his offspring shall inherit the earth.

The secret [Another reading: decree] of the Lord is for those who fear him,

and he reveals his covenant to them.

My eyes are always toward the Lord,

for he will draw my feet out of the snare.

Look upon me and have mercy on me,

for I am alone and poor [Hebrew: “I am,” added].

The troubles of my heart have multiplied [Note: [Col. 1146D] Our manuscripts, as do four of Martianus’s, have “have been multiplied.”];

deliver me from my distresses.

See my affliction and my toil,

and forgive all my sins.

See my enemies, for they have multiplied,

and they hate me with unjust hatred.

Guard my soul and deliver me;

let me not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you.

Simplicity and uprightness shall preserve me,

for I have waited for you.

[Col. 1146B] Redeem Israel, O God,

from all its troubles.

DAVID.

### [XXVI]

Judge me, Lord [Another reading: God], for I have walked in my innocence,

and, trusting in the Lord, I shall not falter.

Test me, Lord [Another reading: God], and examine me;

refine [Hebrew: smelt] my kidneys and my heart.

For your mercy is before my eyes [Another reading adds “is”],

and I shall walk in your truth.

I have not sat with men of vanity,

nor shall I enter with the proud.

I have hated the assembly of the wicked,

and I shall not sit with the unjust [Hebrew: impious].

I shall wash my hands [Hebrew: palms] in innocence,

and I shall go around your altar, Lord [Note: [Col. 1146D] Three manuscripts, following the Old Latin interpretation, have “I shall surround the altar.”],

so that I may proclaim praise with a clear voice

and recount all your wonders.

[Col. 1146C] Lord, I have loved the dwelling of your house,

and the place of the tabernacle of your glory.

Do not take [Hebrew: do not place; Note: [Col. 1146D] One Vatican manuscript has, closer to the Hebrew and the Scholiast, “Do not gather.”] my soul away with sinners,

or my life with men of bloodshed.

In whose hands is wickedness [Another reading adds “is”],

and whose right hand is filled with gifts.

But I shall walk in my innocence; redeem me

and have mercy on me.

For my foot has stood on level ground;

in the assemblies I shall bless the Lord.

[Col. 1147A] DAVID.

### [XXVII]

The Lord is my light and my salvation;

whom shall I fear?

The Lord is the strength of my life; whom shall I dread?

When the wicked drew near me

to eat my flesh,

my enemies and my foes—

they themselves stumbled and fell.

Though an army encamp against me,

my heart shall not fear;

though war rise against me,

in this I shall trust.

One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek:

that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life,

and see the beauty of the Lord,

and attend in his temple.

For he shall hide me in his shade on the evil day;

he shall conceal me in the secret place of his tabernacle;

he shall exalt me upon a rock.

[Col. 1147B] Even now he has exalted [Another reading: will exalt] my head

above my enemies who surround me.

And I shall sacrifice in his tabernacle sacrifices of jubilation;

I shall sing and make melody to the Lord.

Hear, Lord, the voice of me calling,

and have mercy on me, and hear me.

My heart has said to you, “My face has sought you”;

your face, Lord, I shall seek.

Do not hide your face from me [Note: [Col. 1147D] The Cistercian manuscript does not have the words “from me.” The Regina codex has, shortly afterward, “in your anger.”],

do not turn away in anger from your servant.

You have been my helper; do not abandon me,

and do not forsake me, God my savior.

For my father and my mother have abandoned me,

but the Lord gathers me in.

Show [Hebrew: enlighten] me, Lord, your way,

and lead me on a straight path

because of those who lie in wait for me [Hebrew: those who chant].

Do not hand me over [Note: [Col. 1147D] The Cistercian and Regina manuscripts insert “Lord.”] to the soul of those who afflict me,

for false witnesses have risen against me, and open falsehood.

[Col. 1147C] But I believe [Another reading: I believed] that I shall see the good things

of the Lord [Hebrew: Unless I had believed that I would see

the good things of the Lord]

in the land of the living.

Wait for the Lord, be strong, and let your heart be strengthened,

and endure for the Lord.

DAVID.

### [XXVIII]

To you, Lord, I shall cry;

my strength, do not become deaf to me,

lest, if you remain silent to me,

I become like those who descend into the pit.

Hear [Note: [Col. 1147D] In the same manuscripts: “Hear, Lord, my supplication.”] the voice of my supplications when I cry to you,

when I lift up my hands toward your holy oracle.

Do not drag [Another reading: hand] me away with the impious and those who practice iniquity,

who speak peace with their friends [Hebrew: companions],

while evil is in their hearts.

Give them according to their work

and according to the evil of their devices;

[Col. 1147D] Give them according to the work of their hands;

repay them their recompense.

For they do not understand the works of the Lord

or the work of his hands;

you shall destroy them and not build them up.

Blessed is the Lord,

for he has heard the voice of my supplication.

The Lord is my strength and my shield;

in him my heart has trusted, and I have received help.

My heart rejoiced,

and in my song I shall give thanks to him.

The Lord is their strength [Note: [Col. 1147D] The Cistercian and Regina manuscripts have “my strength,” instead of “their.”],

and the strength of salvation for his anointed one.

Save your people

and bless your inheritance;
