feed them and lift them up for ever

[Hebrew: age].

## A SONG [Hebrew: psalm] OF DAVID

### [XXIX]

Bring to the Lord the sons of rams;

[Col. 1148B] bring to the Lord glory and dominion [Hebrew: strength].

Bring to the Lord glory for his name;

worship the Lord in holy splendor.

The voice of the Lord is over the waters;

the God of glory thundered;

the Lord is over many waters.

The voice of the Lord is in strength;

the voice of the Lord is in splendor.

The voice of the Lord breaks cedars,

and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.

And he will scatter them [Note: [Col. 1147D] All our manuscripts and two examined by Martianus have “like a calf of Lebanon, and Sirion like the son [Another reading: a son] of a rhinoceros.” The author of the *Breviary on the Psalms*, under Jerome’s name, also says that the Hebrew has “and like a calf of Lebanon.” The Hebrew does indeed have this; but the name “Lebanon” does not seem to belong with these words, since it is not in the grammatical construction, and more properly belongs with what follows. The sense is: “He will make them leap like a calf: Lebanon and Sirion, etc.”] like a calf;

Lebanon and Sirion like the son of a rhinoceros.

The voice of the Lord divides flames of fire.

The voice of the Lord causes the wilderness to give birth [Note: [Col. 1148D] The Cistercian manuscript is confused here, reading “causing to give birth” and shortly afterward “he will cause” in both places. The Hebrew sense is as follows, and Jerome guarantees the accuracy of this interpretation in his Commentary on Isaiah, chapter LXVI: “In the twenty-eighth psalm, where we read ‘the voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness,’ the Hebrew has written ‘the voice of the Lord causing the wilderness to give birth.’”];

the Lord will cause the wilderness of Kadesh to give birth.

The voice of the Lord makes the does calve [Another reading: the hinds],

and strips the forests bare;

and in his temple everyone speaks of glory.

The Lord inhabits the flood,

and the Lord shall sit as king for ever.

[Col. 1148C] The Lord will give strength [Another reading: law] to his people;

the Lord will bless his people with peace.

## PSALM OF A SONG FOR THE DEDICATION OF THE HOUSE, OF DAVID

### [XXX]

I will exalt you, Lord, for you have saved me,

and have not delighted [Hebrew: gladdened] my enemies over me,

Lord my God.

I cried to you, and you healed me.

Lord, you brought my soul up from the underworld;

you gave me life, so that I would not descend into the pit.

Sing to the Lord, you his holy ones [Hebrew: merciful ones],

and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.

For his anger is momentary,

but life comes through his appeasement.

In the evening weeping shall remain,

but in the morning, praise.

But I said in my abundance,

“I shall not be shaken for ever” [Hebrew: age].

Lord, by your will you established [Another reading: placed] strength for my mountain;

you hid your face,

and I became troubled. [Note: [Col. 1147D] Three manuscripts do not understand “the works”; in others only “in” is omitted. The author of the Commentary on the Seventy-Fifth Psalm, formerly called Rufinus, says: “The Hebrews have, ‘They did not look upon the works of his hands.’”]

[Col. 1149A] To you, Lord, I shall cry,

and to the Lord I shall plead.

What profit is there in my blood

when I descend [Another reading: descend] into corruption?

Will dust give you thanks,

or proclaim your truth?

Hear, Lord, and have mercy on me;

Lord, be my helper [Another reading: my helper].

You turned my mourning into dancing for me;

you loosened my sackcloth and girded me with gladness,

so that glory may praise you [Hebrew: sing praise to you] and not be silent.

Lord my God,

I shall give you thanks for ever [Hebrew: age].

## TO THE VICTOR: A SONG OF DAVID [Hebrew: psalm]

### [XXXI]

In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me not be put to shame for ever [Hebrew: age];

in your righteousness save [Hebrew: rescue] me.

Incline your ear to me;

hasten to deliver me.

Be for me a most steadfast stone,

[Col. 1149B] a fortified house, so that you may save me.

For you are my rock and my fortress [Another reading adds “are”];

and for your name’s sake you will lead me and nourish me [Note: [Col. 1149D] The same manuscript has “you will be my guide,” instead of “you will lead me.”].

You will draw me out of the snare that they secretly laid for me,

for you are my strength.

Into your hand I commend [Another reading: commend] my spirit;

you have redeemed me, Lord God of truth.

[Note: [Col. 1149D] Our manuscripts and several cited by Martianus have “You have hated.”] I have hated those who guard vanities in vain;

but I have trusted in the Lord.

I shall exult and rejoice in your mercy,

for you have seen [Another reading: heard] my affliction;

you have known the troubles of my soul.

You have not shut me up in the hand of the enemy [Note: [Col. 1149D] Two manuscripts have “in the hands”; the Cistercian has “you placed,” instead of “you established.”];

you have set my feet in a broad place.

Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am afflicted.

My eye has grown dim in anger,

as have my soul and my belly.

For my life has been consumed in grief,

and my years in groaning.

[Col. 1149C] My strength has been weakened in my iniquity [Note: [Col. 1149D] Again, the Cistercian manuscript has “My strength has collapsed in iniquity.”];

and my bones have wasted away.

I have become a reproach among all my enemies,

and especially among my neighbors,

and a fear to those who know me.

Those who saw me in the streets fled from me.

I have been handed over to oblivion like one dead from the heart;

I have become like a lost vessel [Another reading: as a lost vessel].

For I heard the reproach of many,

a gathering all around,

when they took counsel against me

and plotted [Another reading: were plotting] to take my life.

But I hoped in you, Lord;

I said, “You are my God.”

[Col. 1150A] My times are in your hand;

deliver me from the hand of my enemies and those who pursue me.

Make your face shine [Note: [Col. 1149D] Our manuscripts and several of Martianus’s have “show,” instead of “make shine.” One Cistercian manuscript omits “me” shortly afterward.] upon your servant;

save me in your mercy.

Lord, let me not [Another reading: lest I] be put to shame, for I have called upon you;

let the impious be put to shame;

let them be silent in the underworld.

Let lying lips become mute,

which speak against the righteous [Note: [Col. 1149D] All manuscript codices read this way; the printed editions, however, have “hard.” Saint Jerome here and below, at Psalm XCIV, 4, interprets the Hebrew word *athac* as “old” and “ancient.” The noun *athac* is singular in place of a plural in many passages of Scripture; when it is rendered “hard,” one should understand “hard,” as though one said “hardened by age.” MART. — I consider the reading offered by the Cistercian manuscript, “upright” instead of “old,” much more accurate. Although the Hebrew verb signifies “to grow old,” in Scripture it is often used metaphorically to mean “to exceed,” “to rise above,” and similar things. When the sense concerns words, it properly denotes words that exceed the limits of their office, raising themselves recklessly and arrogantly—precisely those described by the cited manuscript as “upright.” They may also be interpreted as “abnormal,” or, as the Italians say, *cose o parole strane*, “strange things or words.” Shortly afterward the same manuscript has “because great is the goodness,” etc.],

which speak with arrogance and contempt.

How abundant is your goodness,

which you have stored up for those who fear you;

you have worked it for those who hope in you,

in the presence of the sons of men.

You will hide them in the protection of your face

from the harshness of man;

you will conceal them in the shadow

from the strife of tongues.

Blessed is the Lord,

for he has shown me his wondrous mercy in a fortified city.

But I said in my astonishment,

[Col. 1150B] “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” [Note: [Col. 1150D] Three manuscripts have “from the sight of his eyes.”].

Yet you heard the voice of my supplication

when I cried to you.

Love the Lord, all his holy ones [Hebrew: merciful ones];

the Lord preserves the faithful

and repays [Note: [Col. 1150D] The same manuscripts have “he will repay” and “he has repaid.”] those who act with excessive pride.

Take courage, and let your heart be strengthened,

all you who await the Lord.

DAVID. FOR INSTRUCTION [Note: [Col. 1150D] Both our manuscripts and those cited by Martianus read “learned” instead of “of the learned.”].

### [XXXII]

Blessed is he whose iniquity has been forgiven,

whose sin has been hidden.

Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute [Another reading: has not imputed] iniquity,

and in whose spirit there is no deceit.

For when I was silent, my bones grew weak,

through my groaning all day long.

For day and night your hand was heavy upon me;

I was turned in my misery when summer [Note: [Col. 1150D] Two manuscripts have “when summer burned upon me,” where the corrupt reading “summer” seems to have been written through the carelessness of scribes instead of “harvest.”] burned.

CONTINUALLY.

I make my sin known to you,

and I did not conceal my iniquity [Note: [Col. 1150D] Again, our manuscripts have “I do not conceal.” “I said, I shall confess my wickedness.”].

I said, “I shall confess my transgressions to the Lord,”

and you forgave [Hebrew: removed] the iniquity of my sin.

FOREVER.

For this every holy one [Hebrew: merciful one] prays to you,

at a time when you may be found;

so that, when many waters overflow,

they may not come near him.

You are [Another reading adds “are”] my protection; you will guard me from the enemy;

you are my saving praise; you will surround me.

FOREVER.

[Note: [Col. 1150D] The Cistercian manuscript has “I shall teach you, and I shall show”; most others, with the printed editions, have “I shall teach you, I shall show you.”]

I shall instruct you and enlighten you concerning the way in which you should walk;

I shall take counsel concerning you with my eye.

Do not become like a horse or a mule,

which have no understanding [Another reading: in which there is no understanding];

with bit and bridle you constrain their jaws,

so that they do not approach you [Note: [Col. 1150D] Our manuscripts, with others cited by Martianus and with the printed books, have “Constrain their jaws, so that they do not approach you.” The Cistercian manuscript alludes to this with one word, “approaches.”].

Many are the scourges of the impious,

but mercy shall surround the one who trusts in the Lord.

Rejoice in the Lord and exult, righteous ones,

and praise him, all upright in heart.

### [XXXIII] PRAISE THE LORD, O RIGHTEOUS;

praise is fitting for the upright [Another reading: joint praise].

Give thanks to the Lord on the harp;

sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery [Another reading: chant to him].

Sing to him a new song;

play well with jubilation [Note: [Col. 1151D] Again, our manuscripts and many others cited by Martianus carefully have “well,” instead of “rightly.”].

For the word of the Lord is upright,

and all his work is in faithfulness.

He loves righteousness and judgment;

the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.

By the word of the Lord the heavens were made [Another reading omits “by the word”],

and by the breath of his mouth all their adornment.

Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin,

placing the abysses in storehouses.

[Col. 1151B] Let all the earth fear the Lord [Another reading: from the Lord];

let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him.

For he spoke, and it came to be;

he commanded, and it stood firm.

The Lord brings the counsel of the nations to nothing;

he frustrates the thoughts of the peoples.

The counsel of the Lord shall stand for ever;

the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation.

Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord,

the people whom he chose [Note: [Col. 1151D] The Regina manuscript adds “the Lord” here, and in the third verse after this reads “from his most firm throne,” instead of “from his seat,” etc.] as his inheritance.

The Lord looked down from heaven;

he saw all the sons of Adam.

From his most firm seat he looked down

upon all the inhabitants of the earth.

He formed their hearts alike;

he understands all their works.

A king is not saved by a great army [Note: [Col. 1151D] At this point our manuscripts have “is saved.”];

nor shall a mighty man be delivered by an abundance of strength.

The horse is deceptive for salvation,

and by the abundance of its strength it shall not save.

Behold, the eye of the Lord is upon those who fear him,

and upon those who await his mercy [Another reading: and await].

To rescue their souls from death,

and to give them life in famine.

Our soul has awaited the Lord;

he is our help and our shield.

For in him our heart shall rejoice,

because we have hoped in his holy name.

Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us,

as we have awaited you.

DAVID, WHEN HE CHANGED HIS APPEARANCE [Hebrew: taste] BEFORE ABIMELECH, AND HE DROVE HIM OUT, AND HE DEPARTED.

[Note: [Col. 1151D] This psalm too is alphabetic. In one Cistercian manuscript each verse is prefixed in order with its own letter, not even omitting *vau*, although it is known that the sequence is interrupted in the Hebrew archetype. Nor can it easily be supplied, as a recent interpreter of Scripture thinks, by beginning the seventh verse with the words “and the Lord heard him.” For then the seventh letter, *zayin*, or the verse assigned to it, would be missing—unless one wishes to regard these three words, “this poor man cried,” as a complete verse and to reverse the order of the letters. We note this to indicate that those letters were not added by Jerome to this Latin translation.]

### [XXXIV]

I will bless the Lord at all times;

his praise shall always be in my mouth.

In the Lord my soul shall be praised [Note: [Col. 1152D] The exemplars of the Canon and several manuscript codices read: “In the Lord my soul shall rejoice.” MART.];

let the humble hear and rejoice.

Magnify the Lord with me,

and let us exalt his name together.

I sought the Lord, and he heard me,

[Col. 1151D] and he delivered me from all my troubles.

Look toward him and run together,

[Col. 1152A] and your faces shall not be put to shame.

This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him,

and he saved him from all his tribulations [Note: [Col. 1152D] Our manuscripts do not add “his,” and shortly afterward they read “surrounds,” instead of “will surround.”].

The angel of the Lord shall surround those who fear him,

and he shall rescue them.

Taste and see that the Lord is good;

blessed is the man who hopes in him.

Fear the Lord, you his holy ones,

for there is no want for those who fear him.

Lions have lacked and suffered hunger,

but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.

Come [Another reading: Walk], children, hear me;

I shall teach you the fear of the Lord.

Who is the man who desires life,

loving to see good days?

Guard your tongue from evil,

and let your lips not speak deceit.

Turn away from evil and do good;

seek peace and pursue it.

[Col. 1152B] The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,

and his ears are toward their cries.

The face of the Lord is upon [Hebrew: upon] those who do evil,

to destroy their memory from the earth.

They cried out [Note: [Col. 1152D] One Cistercian manuscript inserts “the righteous.”], and the Lord heard them,

and delivered them from all their tribulations.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted,

and he shall save those crushed in spirit.

Many are the tribulations [Hebrew: many are the evils] of the righteous,

but the Lord shall deliver him from them all [Another reading: delivered him].

He guards all his bones;

not one of them shall be broken.

Evil shall kill the impious,

and those who hate the righteous shall be condemned [Note: [Col. 1152D] All our manuscripts unanimously have “shall be overcome,” instead of “shall be condemned.”].

The Lord shall redeem the souls of his servants,

and none who hope in him shall sin [Hebrew: shall be condemned].

[Col. 1152C] DAVID.

### [XXXV]

Judge, Lord, my adversaries;

fight against those who fight me.

Take up shield and spear [Another reading: staff],

and rise to my aid [Another reading: for me].

Draw the sword and confront

those who pursue me;

say to my soul, “I am your salvation” [Another reading adds “I am”].

Let those who seek my soul be put to shame and disgraced;

let those who devise evil against me

turn back and be put to shame.

Let them be like dust before the face of the wind,

and let the angel of the Lord drive them away.

Let their way be darkness and slippery ground,

and let the angel of the Lord pursue them.

For in vain they secretly hid a net for me;

without cause they dug for my soul.

Let disaster come upon him [Another reading: them] which he does not know,

and let the net which he hid seize him,

and let him fall into the snare [Hebrew: into disaster].

But my soul shall exult in the Lord,

[Col. 1153A] and shall rejoice in his salvation [Another reading: your salvation].

All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you,

rescuing the poor from one stronger,

and the needy and beggar from the violent?

Unjust witnesses rose up;

they questioned me about things I did not know.

They repaid me evil for good,

barrenness to my soul.

But when they were sick [Note: [Col. 1153C] Two of our manuscripts and others cited by Martianus have “when I was sick because of them, I clothed myself,” etc.], I clothed myself in sackcloth;

I humbled my soul with fasting,

and my prayer shall return to my bosom [Another reading: toward my bosom].

As toward a friend [Hebrew: companion], as toward my brother,

so I walked;

as one mourning for a mother, I bowed down in sorrow.

And when I was infirm, they rejoiced and gathered together;

they gathered against me, striking, and I did not know it;

tearing apart [Note: [Col. 1153D] The Carcassonne Canon has “tearing apart and not shedding blood.” The same reading occurs in our Canon of Saint-Germain, but in a second hand. The Chaldean paraphrast agrees with this reading. MART.] and not keeping silent.

With feigned words of pretense

they gnashed their teeth against me.

Lord, how long will you look [Another reading: behold]?

[Col. 1153B] Turn my soul away from their calamities [Another reading: his],

from the lions, my solitary one.

I shall give thanks to you in the great assembly [Another reading: large];

among a strong people I shall praise you.

Let not my deceitful enemies rejoice over me;

those who hate me without cause, winking [Another reading: restraining] the eye,

let them not rejoice.

For they do not speak peace,

but in the plundering of the land they compose deceitful words.

And they opened their mouths wide against me;

they said, “Ha, ha! Our eye has seen it.”

You have seen, Lord; do not be silent.

Lord, do not be far from me.

Rise up [Hebrew: Awaken], and keep watch for my judgment,

my God and my Lord [Another reading: the Lord, my God],

for my cause.

Judge me according to your righteousness, Lord my God,

and let them not exult over me.

[Col. 1153C] And let them not say in their heart, “Ah, our desire!”:

[Note: [Col. 1153D] The Cistercian manuscript repeats the interjection “Ah” twice; the Regina manuscript and others, three times.]

and let them not say, “We have swallowed him.”

Let those who rejoice in my affliction be put to shame and confounded together;

let those who magnify themselves over me be clothed with shame and disgrace.

Let those who desire my vindication rejoice and be glad,

and let them say always, “The Lord is magnified,”

who desires the peace of his servant.

And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness,

and on your praise all day long.

[Note: [Col. 1153D] Thus the corrected Chartres manuscript. The Royal, Corbie, and Sorbonne manuscripts, however, prefer this title: “For victory, of David, servant of the Lord.” Both copies of the Canon have “For victory, David, servant of the Lord”; two others, “Victory of David, servant of the Lord.” MART.]

FOR THE VICTOR, DAVID, SERVANT OF THE LORD.

[XXXVI.] The wicked man’s transgression has spoken within his heart [Note: [Col. 1153D] The Hebrew has *bekereb libbi*, that is, “within my heart,” instead of “within his heart.” MART. —The holy Father apparently read in his Hebrew copy [Hebrew term], as did the Septuagint and other ancient translators, instead of the reading now preferred, [Hebrew term], that is, “my heart.” In our manuscripts the reading follows: “there is no fear of God,” instead of “there is no fear,” etc.],

“There is no fear of God before his eyes.”

For he has acted deceitfully against him in his own eyes,

so that he might discover his iniquity and hate it.

The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit;

[Col. 1154A] he has ceased to consider [Note: [Col. 1154D] These same manuscripts of ours read “to consider doing good.”],

so as to do good.

He devises iniquity upon his bed;

he takes his stand on a way that is not good;

he does not reject evil.

Lord, your mercy is in heaven,

your faithfulness reaches to the clouds.

Your righteousness is like the mountains, O God [Alternatively: Lord];

your judgment is a great abyss.

You save human beings and animals, Lord.

How precious is your mercy, O God [Alternatively: Lord];

and the children of Adam shall hope in the shadow of your wings.

They shall be filled with the abundance of your house,

and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delights.

For with you is the fountain of life;

in your light we shall see light.

Draw out your mercy to those who know you,

and your righteousness to the upright in heart.

Let not the foot of pride come against me,

and let not the hand of the wicked move me.

There the workers of iniquity have fallen;

they have been driven out and have not been able to rise.

DAVID.

[XXXVII. Aleph.] [Note: [Col. 1154D] Saint Jerome, in the prologue to the Scriptures known as the *Galeatus*, lists the present psalm among those whose verses are composed according to the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. For this reason we have placed here the names of those letters opposite the verses to which they correspond. This arrangement is also found in many manuscript codices. MART. —Each pair of verses in this psalm begins with one letter of the alphabet in its proper order; we retain this same sequence of letters, placed after Martianay, in the margin of the book on the authority of several Latin manuscripts. See, however, what we note below at verse 28, under the letter Hain.]

Do not contend with the wicked,

and do not envy those who practice iniquity.

For like grass they shall quickly be cut down,

and like green vegetation they shall wither.

[Beth.] Hope in the Lord, and do good;

sojourn [Hebrew: dwell] in the land, and feed on faithfulness.

And delight in the Lord,

and he will grant you the desires of your heart.

[Gimel.] Roll [Hebrew: reveal] your way onto the Lord,

and trust in him, and he will act.

And he will bring forth your righteousness like the light,

and your judgment like midday.

[Daleth.] Be silent before the Lord and wait for him;

do not contend with one who prospers in his way,

with the man who does what he has devised.

[He.] Abandon anger and forsake wrath;

[Col. 1154C] do not contend so as to do evil.

[Note: [Col. 1154D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “do not hurry,” instead of “do not contend.”]

For those who do evil shall perish;

but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land.

[Vav.] Yet a little while, and the wicked shall be no more;

you will consider his place, and he will not remain.

But the meek shall inherit the land,

and shall delight in an abundance of peace.

[Zain.] The wicked plots against the righteous,

and gnashes his teeth at him.

The Lord will laugh at him,

[Note: [Col. 1154D] The Regina manuscript reads “when he sees,” instead of “because he saw.” The Cistercian manuscript also reads “when it comes,” instead of “because his day has come.”]

because he has seen that his day has come.

[Heth.] The wicked have drawn the sword; they have bent their bow,

to strike down [Hebrew: to cast down] the poor and needy,

and to kill the upright [Note: [Col. 1154D] The Cistercian manuscript inserts “in heart.”] on the way.

[Heth.] Let their sword enter their own heart,

and let their bows be broken.

[Col. 1155A] [Teth.] Better is the little that belongs to the righteous

than the great riches of the wicked.

For the arms of the wicked shall be broken,

but the Lord upholds the righteous.

[Jod.] The Lord knows the days of the blameless,

and their inheritance shall be eternal [Hebrew: for an age].

They shall not be confounded in an evil time,

and in days of famine they shall be satisfied.

[Caph.] For the wicked shall perish,

and the enemies of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1155C] In the same manuscript, apparently from the pen of an over-learned copyist, [Col. 1155D] “they shall be overthrown like mountains,” instead of “they shall glory like unicorns.”]

who glory like unicorns shall be consumed;

they shall be consumed like smoke.

[Lamed.] The wicked borrows and does not repay;

but the righteous gives and distributes.

For those who have been blessed by him shall inherit the land,

but those who have been cursed shall perish.

[Mem.] The steps of a man are made firm by the Lord,

and he will delight in his way.

When he falls, he will not be cast down,

for the Lord supports his hand.

[Nun.] For I was young, and now I am old,

[Col. 1155B] and I have not seen the righteous forsaken,

or his offspring seeking bread.

All day long he gives and lends,

and his offspring is blessed.

[Samekh.] Turn away from evil and do good,

and dwell forever [Hebrew: for an age].

For the Lord loves judgment,

and he will not forsake his holy ones [Hebrew: his merciful ones].

[Note: [Col. 1155D] The letter Hain, which ought to have been assigned to this verse, is absent; nor does this verse in fact begin with it in the present Hebrew copy. It is commonly believed among learned scholars that in the time of the Septuagint translators the archetype did not lack this letter, and this is inferred from their translation, in which they place here the two words Ἄνομοι ἐκδικηθήσονται, “The lawless shall be punished,” which in Hebrew would be [Hebrew term]. Thus they indicate that the copy before them began with the letter Hain. What others think about this matter may be seen among the sacred critics. Since the text has not been interpolated, we may argue from this very interpretation of Jerome, which begins the verse with the words “They are guarded forever”: in Hebrew, [Hebrew term]. The preceding letter, Lamed, being plainly ancillary and servile, was apparently not considered by the Hebrews or by Jerome himself to impair the acrostic arrangement; and since the word itself begins with Hain, the sequence of letters could therefore be continued according to the laws of the meter. Moreover, I do not know whether one may suspect that [the word] “eternal” was written simply by the royal Psalmist himself [Hebrew term].]

They are guarded forever [Hebrew: for an age],

and the offspring of the wicked shall perish [Alternatively: perishes].

The righteous shall inherit the land,

and shall dwell upon it forever [Hebrew: for an age].

[Phe.] The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom,

and his tongue shall speak judgment.

The law of his God is in his heart;

his steps shall not falter.

[Sade.] The wicked watches the righteous

and seeks to kill him.

[Col. 1155C] The Lord will not abandon him into his hand,

and he will not condemn him when he is judged [Alternatively: when he is being judged].

[Coph.] Wait for the Lord and keep his way,

and he will exalt you, so that you may possess the land;

when the wicked perish [Alternatively: perish], you shall see it.

[Res.] I saw the wicked man in power,

and very strong, like a native tree flourishing.

Then I passed by, and behold [Alternatively: omit “behold”], he was not;

I sought him, and he was not found.

[Sin.] Keep integrity and look upon what is upright,

for peace shall be for the man at the end [Alternatively: toward the end].

[Note: [Col. 1156D] Three of our manuscripts and others in Martianay’s possession read instead: “But the transgressors shall be destroyed together.”]

But the transgressors shall perish together,

and the latter end of the wicked shall perish.

[Thav.] But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord;

he is their strength in the time of distress.

And the Lord will help them and save them;

[Col. 1156A] [Note: [Col. 1156D] The words “he will deliver them” are absent from our manuscripts. In the Hebrew the same verb is repeated as was just translated, “he will save them.”]

he will deliver them from the wicked,

and save them, because they have hoped in him.

A SONG OF DAVID, FOR COMMEMORATION.

[XXXVIII.] Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger [Hebrew: indignation],

and do not chastise me in your fury [Hebrew: wrath],

For your arrows have been driven into me,

and your hand has touched [Hebrew: terrified] me.

There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation;

there is no peace [Alternatively: add “in”] in my bones because of my sin.

For my iniquities have passed over my head;

like a heavy burden they have become too heavy upon me.

My wounds have become foul and festering,

because of my folly.

I am afflicted and bowed down exceedingly;

all day long I went about mourning.

For my loins [Alternatively: kidneys; Hebrew: my sides] are filled

with disgrace [Hebrew: worthlessness],

and there is no soundness in my flesh.

[Col. 1156B] I have awakened and am afflicted exceedingly;

I roared because of the groaning of my heart.

Lord, before you is all my desire,

and my groaning is not hidden from you.

My heart was troubled; my strength deserted me,

and even the light of my eyes is not with me.

My loved ones and my friends [Hebrew: companions] [Note: [Col. 1156D] Our manuscripts insert “as it were” here.] stood against my leprosy,

and my neighbors [Hebrew: those near me] stood far away.

And they rushed in, seeking my life;

and those investigating evil against me spoke treachery,

and plotted deceit all day long.

But I, like a deaf man, did not hear,

and like a mute [Note: [Col. 1156D] These same manuscripts of ours read: “like a mute who does not open his mouth”; and shortly afterward one Cistercian manuscript reads “who has nothing in his heart,” instead of “in his mouth.”]

who does not open his mouth.

And I was like a man [Hebrew: a male] who does not hear,

and who has no reproofs in his mouth.

For I waited for you, Lord;

you will hear me, Lord my God.

For I said, “Perhaps they will exult over me,”

and when my foot falters [Note: [Col. 1156D] A larger number of our manuscripts read: “when my feet have faltered.”], they will magnify themselves against me.

For I am ready for blows [Alternatively: wounds],

and my pain is always against me.

For I declare my iniquity [Alternatively: “I declare my iniquity”],

[Note: [Col. 1156D] The printed editions and several manuscripts, including those examined by Martianay, read “I shall be anxious,” instead of “I shall be sorrowful.”]

and I shall be sorrowful for my sin.

But my living enemies have grown strong,

and those who hate me falsely have multiplied.

And those who repay evil for good opposed me,

because I pursued what is good.

Do not abandon me, Lord;

my God, do not depart far from me.

Hasten to my help,

Lord [Alternatively: God], my salvation.

[Col. 1157A] [Note: [Col. 1157D] The Royal codex reads: “For the end, of Jeduthun, a psalm of David”; but this is plainly a copyist’s error, since he dared to transfer several psalm titles from the Septuagint into this Hebrew edition of Jerome. Jerome therefore teaches in the preface to his Commentary on Daniel that the word *lamnatseahh*, as it is read today, is better interpreted as “for victory” than “for the end.” Hence, he says, many psalms contain in their titles the Hebrew word *LAMANASSE*, which the Septuagint translated “for the end,” but which is better understood as “for victory.” Aquila translated it τῷ νικοποιῷ, that is, “to the one who grants victory.” Symmachus has ἐπινίκιον, which properly signifies triumph and the victor’s palm. More will be said about the Hebrew *lamanasse* or *lamnatseahh* when we come to the title of Psalm XLIV, or XLV according to the Hebrew numbering. MART.]

FOR THE VICTOR, OF JEDUTHUN, A SONG OF DAVID.

[XXXIX.] I said, “I will guard my ways,

so that I may not sin with my tongue.

I will guard my mouth with silence,

while the wicked is before me.”

I was mute in silence; I kept silent about what is good,

and my pain was troubled.

My heart grew hot within me;

in my meditation a fire burned,

and I spoke with my tongue.

Show me, Lord, my end,

and let me know what the measure of my days is,

so that I may know what I lack [Alternatively: “so that I may know”].

Behold, you have made my days short,

and my life is as nothing before you;

for every human being who endures is wholly vanity [Note: [Col. 1157D] The Regina manuscript reads: “Vanity is a standing man.” *Diapsalma.*]. ALWAYS.

Only as an image does a man [Hebrew: a person] walk;

only in vain is he troubled.

[Col. 1157B] He gathers, yet does not know for whom he will leave them [Hebrew: gathers].

Now, therefore, what do I await, Lord?

You are my expectation [Hebrew: my expectation is toward you].

Deliver me from all my iniquities [Hebrew: errors];

do not make me a reproach to the fool.

I was mute [Note: [Col. 1157D] The printed books and the Sorbonne manuscript read in the future tense: “I shall be mute; I shall not open my mouth.” MART.],

I did not cover [Alternatively: I shall not open] my mouth,

because you acted.

Take your blows [Hebrew: leprosy] away from me;

I am consumed by the conflict of your hand.

With rebukes

you chastised a man for iniquity [Alternatively: because of iniquity],

and you made his precious things like a moth;

yet every human being is vanity. ALWAYS.

Hear my prayer, Lord,

and heed [Hebrew: perceive with your ears] my cry;

do not be deaf to my tears,

for I am a sojourner with you,

a stranger like all my fathers.

[Col. 1157C] Spare me, so that I may smile,

before I go away and cease to exist.

[Note: [Col. 1158D] Again our manuscripts read “For victory,” which they also consistently retain below in the titles of the remaining psalms instead of “For the victor.” See what we note at the immediately preceding passage.]

FOR THE VICTOR, DAVID, A SONG [Hebrew: Psalm].

[XL.] I waited patiently for the Lord;

and he inclined toward me and heard my cry.

And he brought me up from the pit [Note: [Col. 1158D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “from the famous pit,” instead of “from the pit of sound.”] of tumult,

from the mire of mud;

and he set my feet upon a rock,

and made my steps firm.

And he put a new song in my mouth,

praise to our God.

Many shall see, and fear,

and hope in the Lord.

Blessed is the man who made the Lord his confidence,

and did not turn toward proud vanities and false spectacles [Alternatively: “false things”].

You have done many wonderful things,

Lord my God,

and your thoughts are for us.

[Col. 1158A] I cannot set them in order before you;

if I wished to recount and number them,

they are more than can be told.

You have no need of sacrifice and offering [Hebrew: you did not desire],

but you dug ears for me;

you did not ask for a burnt offering or a sin offering.

Then I said, “Behold, I come;

in the scroll of the book it is written concerning me.

I desired to do your good pleasure [Alternatively: your will],

my God,

and your law is within my inmost being [Alternatively: heart].

I proclaimed your righteousness in a great assembly;

behold, I shall not restrain my lips—you know, Lord.

I did not hide your righteousness within my heart;

I declared your faithfulness and your salvation.

I did not conceal your mercy

and your truth in a great assembly.

You, Lord, will not withhold [Alternatively: you will not withhold] your mercies

[Hebrew: acts of faithful love] from me;

your mercy and your truth will continually preserve

[Col. 1158B] me.

For evils beyond number have surrounded me;

my iniquities have seized me,

and I could not see.

They have become more numerous than the hairs of my head,

and my heart has abandoned me.

May it please you, Lord, to deliver me;

Lord, hasten to help me.

Let those who seek my life in order to take it

be confounded and put to shame together.

Let those who desire evil for me

turn back and be confounded.

Let those who say to me, “Ah! Ah!”

perish in their disgrace.

Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you;

let those who love your salvation say continually,

“Let the Lord be magnified.”

[Col. 1158C] But I am needy and poor;

the Lord will be concerned for me.

You are my help and my salvation,

my God; [Note: [Col. 1158D] The Regina manuscript reads “do not delay.” According to the Hebrew, [Hebrew term].]

do not delay.

FOR THE VICTOR, A SONG [Hebrew: Psalm] OF DAVID.

[XLI.] Blessed is he who considers the poor;

on the evil day the Lord will deliver [Alternatively: save] him.

The Lord will guard him and preserve him alive;

he shall be blessed in the land,

and he will not hand him over [Alternatively: may he not hand him over] to the soul of his enemies.

The Lord strengthened him upon the bed of sickness;

you have transformed his entire bed in his illness.

I said, “Lord, have mercy on me;

heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.”

My enemies speak [Alternatively: are speaking] evil against me:

“When will he die, and his name perish?”

And if he comes in order to see [Note: [Col. 1158D] The Carcassonne Canon and several manuscripts read here: “And if he comes in order to visit”; Erasmus and Marianus followed this reading in this Psalter of Jerome, although the holy Doctor expressly stated in his letter to Sunnias and Fretela that the Septuagint translators rendered it: καὶ εἰ εἰσεπορεύετο τοῦ ἰδεῖν, that is, “And if he entered in order to see.” Yet in this passage “to see” means, unless we are mistaken, “to visit.” MART. [Col. 1159C] Most of our manuscripts and many others cited by Martianay, as well as the printed books, read “to visit” instead of “to see.” See what we observe about this reading in the letter to Sunnias and Fretela.],

he will speak vainly;

his heart will gather iniquity for itself,

and going outside he will slander.

All those who hate me murmured together against me;

they devised evil against me [Alternatively: omit “me”].

They poured into themselves a word [Hebrew: Belial, “worthlessness” or “wickedness”] of the devil:

“Once he has lain down, he will not rise again.”

Even the man at peace with me, in whom I trusted,

who ate my bread,

lifted his heel against me.

But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up,

and I shall repay them.

By this I know that you desire me:

my enemy will not exult over me.

But I have been helped by you in my integrity,

and you will set me before your face forever [Hebrew: for an age].

Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel,

from age to age and forever; amen and amen.

[Note: [Col. 1159D] All manuscript codices except the copies of the Canon have “for victory” in this title, as also frequently elsewhere, instead of “for the victor.” We shall discuss this below at Psalm XLV. MART.]

FOR THE VICTOR, THE MOST LEARNED [Hebrew: instructed] OF THE SONS OF KORAH.

[XLII.] As a prepared garden-bed for channels of water,

[Col. 1159B] so my soul is prepared [Note: [Col. 1159D] This verse is corrupted in the copies of the Canon and in two other manuscripts, where the Vulgate reading, “As a deer longs for springs of water,” etc., has been substituted for Jerome’s version, which we have retained and which the San-German Canon had in its first hand. MART. —The Cistercian manuscript places before Jerome’s interpretation a different version of the first two verses: “As a deer bellowing for springs of water, so my soul roars for you, O God.”] [Hebrew: longs] for you, O God.

My soul thirsts for the living strong God [Alternatively: fountain];

when shall I come and appear before the face of God?

My tears have been my bread day and night,

while it is said to me all day long, “Where is your God?”

I remembered these things,

and poured out my soul within me,

for I shall come to the shelter;

I shall be silent until the house of God,

amid a voice of praise and confession,

of a multitude keeping festival.

Why are you bowed down, my soul, and why do you trouble me?

Wait for God, for I shall yet confess to him

for the salvations of his countenance.

My soul is bowed down within me, my God;

therefore I shall remember you from the land of the Jordan,

and from Hermonim, from the little mountain.

Deep calls to deep

at the sound of your cataracts;

all your whirlpools and your waves

have passed over me [Note: [Col. 1159D] So all the manuscripts read, except the Memmian Library codex and the Carcassonne Canon, which read in the sacred text, “have entered upon me,” adding this marginal note [Col. 1160C]: “Hebrew: have passed over.” MART. —The Cistercian manuscript reads “have passed over me,” without the intervening “me.”].

[Col. 1159C] By day the Lord has commanded his mercy,

and by night his song is with me,

a prayer to the God of my life.

I shall say to God, “You are my rock” [Hebrew: *El zelai*, which is interpreted as “God, my rock,” and is one of the names of God];

why have you forgotten me?

Why do I walk sorrowfully while the enemy afflicts me?

When they were killing me [Alternatively: when they kill me] in my bones,

my enemies reproached me,

saying [Note: [Col. 1160D] Here too the Cistercian manuscript omits the words “to me.”] to me all day long, “Where is your God?”

Why are you bowed down, my soul, and why do you trouble me?

Wait for God, for I shall yet confess to him,

for the salvations of my face and my God.

[Note: [Col. 1160D] The same manuscript places before this the title: “A psalm for those who have obtained faith.” It is untitled among the Hebrews.]

[XLIII.] Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause

from an unholy nation [Hebrew: “without mercy”].

Save me from a deceitful and unjust man.

For you are God, my strength; why have you cast me away?

Why do I walk sorrowfully while the enemy afflicts me?

Send your light and your truth;

[Note: [Col. 1160D] The Regina manuscript reads “they themselves shall lead me,” and introduces me to the mountain, without the intervening “me”; the Cistercian manuscript also omits it. Then it reads “to your tabernacle” and “to your altar,” instead of “to God”; the Cistercian has “to your altar, Lord.”]

they themselves shall lead me;

they shall bring me to your holy mountain

and to your tabernacles.

And I shall enter the altar of God,

to God, the joy of my gladness,

and I shall confess to you on the lyre, God, my God.

Why are you bowed down, my soul,

and why do you trouble me?

Wait for God, for I shall yet confess to him,

for the salvations [Alternatively: salvation] of my face and my God.

[Note: [Col. 1160D] Our manuscripts and those cited by Martianay read: “For victory, of the sons of Korah, instruction,” instead of “For victory, of the sons of Korah, the learned.”]

FOR THE VICTOR, OF THE SONS OF KORAH, INSTRUCTION.

[XLIV.] O God, we have heard with our ears;

our fathers have told us

the work that you worked in their days,

in days of old.

With your hand you destroyed [Hebrew: disinherited] nations,

and planted them [Alternatively: planted them, feminine];

you afflicted peoples [Alternatively: nations],

and drove them out.

For they did not possess the land by their sword,

nor did their arm save them,

but your right hand and your arm,

and the light of your face,

because you were pleased [Note: [Col. 1160D] The Regina manuscript reads “you were pleased with yourself,” instead of “in them”; then, “you are my king,” without “he himself,” which the Cistercian also omits.].

with them.

You are yourself my king, O God;

command salvation [Note: [Col. 1160D] Our manuscripts and several of Martianay’s read “for salvations.”] for Jacob.

Through you we shall scatter our enemies;

in your name we shall trample our adversaries.

For I shall not trust in my bow,

nor shall my sword save me,

because you saved us from our enemies,

and confounded those who hated us.

In God [Note: [Col. 1160D] The same manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “In the Lord we shall rejoice.”] we shall praise all day long,

and we shall confess your name forever. ALWAYS.

Yet you cast us away and confounded us,

and you will not go out with our armies [Note: [Col. 1160D] The Cistercian manuscript inserts the name “God”; shortly afterward, together with two Regina manuscripts, it reads “they plundered us,” instead of “they plundered for themselves.”].

You turned our backs before the enemy,

and those who hated us plundered us.

[Col. 1160C] You gave us like sheep to be devoured,

and scattered us among the nations.

You sold your people for no price,

and there was no great exchange for them [Hebrew: and you did not profit by their exchange].

You made us a reproach to our neighbors,

a mockery and derision to those around us.

You made us a proverb [Hebrew: parable] among the nations,

a shaking of the head among the tribes [Hebrew: peoples].

[Note: [Col. 1160D] Concerning this verse Jerome writes in his letter to Sunnias and Fretela: “Otherwise, in the Hebrew,” he says, “I found it written thus: ‘You made us a proverb among the nations.’” MART. —Two of our manuscripts omit the word “among.” The holy Father likewise says in his letter to Sunnias and Fretela: “In the Hebrew, I found it written thus: ‘You made us a proverb among the nations.’” Martianay also cites this passage.]

All day long my disgrace is before me,

and shame has covered my face,

at the voice of the one reproaching and blaspheming,

at the face of the enemy and avenger.

All these things have come upon us,

yet we have not forgotten you,

nor have we dealt falsely with your covenant.

Our heart has not turned back,

nor have our steps departed from your path.

For you have cast us down in the place of dragons,

and covered us with the shadow of death.

If we have forgotten the name of our God,

and stretched out our hands to a foreign god,

will not God investigate this?

For he knows the secrets of the heart.

For because of you we are put to death all day long;

we are counted as sheep for slaughter.

Rise up [Hebrew: Awake], why do you sleep, Lord?

Awaken; why do you cast us away [Alternatively: have you cast us away] forever?

Why do you hide your face?

Why do you forget [Note: [Col. 1161C] All our manuscripts read: “Why do you forget our afflictions and our distresses.”] our affliction and our poverty?

For our soul is bowed down in the dust;

our belly has clung to the earth [Alternatively: to the ground].

Rise up, help us,

and redeem us for the sake of your mercy.

[Col. 1161B] [Note: [Col. 1161C] We found this entire psalm read in Hebrew in an outstanding manuscript of our monastery at Chartres. We shall present it carefully collated and copied in an appendix to the Canon of Hebrew Truth, together with a substantial portion of the second psalm, which is likewise written in Hebrew but in Latin characters in that Chartres Psalter. Many manuscripts preserve divergent readings in the title. The Vatican codex reads as follows: “For victory, for the lilies of the sons of Korah, instruction, a most beloved song.” In the copies of the Canon and in four other manuscripts: “A most beloved song of instruction.” But there can be no doubt about which is the genuine reading and which readings are corrupted and distorted, since Jerome himself, explaining the psalm in full in his letter to the virgin Principia, immediately observes the following about the title: “When reading the forty-fourth psalm, I found in the title: ‘For the end, for those who shall be changed, of the sons of Korah, a song of understanding, for the beloved.’ In Hebrew it is written, *LAMMANASSE AL SOSANIM LABNE CORE MESCHIL SIR IDIDOT* [Hebrew text], which we translate into Latin: ‘For victory, for the lilies of the sons of Korah, a song of instruction, of the most beloved.’ Symmachus, more explicitly in his usual manner, translated it ‘triumph for the flowers.’ Therefore *SOSANIM* is rendered either ‘for those who are to be changed’ or ‘lilies’ and ‘flowers’; *MESCHIL* likewise signifies both ‘instruction’ and ‘most learned’; *SIR*, ‘song’; *IDIDIA* is Solomon’s name, who in another sense is called ‘Pacific.’ Four psalms, although they differ in the latter part of their titles, are prefaced by this same beginning: the forty-fourth, fifty-ninth, sixty-eighth, and seventy-ninth. Of these, the two middle ones are entitled ‘of David’; the first and last, ‘of the sons of Korah’ and ‘of Asaph.’ Thus far Jerome. We have taken care, in many places in the Psalms, to restore the oblique and corrupted readings in accordance with his words as with a measuring rule. MART.]

FOR THE VICTOR, FOR THE LILIES OF THE SONS OF KORAH, A SONG OF INSTRUCTION, OF THE MOST BELOVED.

[XLV.] My heart has uttered a good word;

I speak my works to the king;

my tongue is the pen of a swift scribe.

You are more beautiful in appearance than the sons of men;

grace has been poured out upon your lips;

therefore God has blessed you forever.

Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty;

your glory and your beauty.

In your beauty ascend prosperously,

because of [Note: [Col. 1162C] Jerome testifies that he read it this way in the letter just mentioned; nevertheless, not a few manuscripts read, with the printed edition, “because of the word of truth.” MART.]

truth,

and meekness of righteousness,

[Note: [Col. 1162C] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “Your right hand shall teach you terribly.” See the cited letter to Principia, no. 11, and our notes there on this passage.]

and your right hand shall teach you terrible things.

Your arrows are sharp;

peoples shall fall beneath you,

[Col. 1162A] in the heart of the king’s enemies.

Your throne, O God, is forever and ever;

the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom.

You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity [Hebrew: impiety];

therefore God, your God, has anointed you

with the oil of gladness above your companions.

[Note: [Col. 1162C] The same manuscripts read “myrrh and aloe,” from the Hebrew [Hebrew term]. Shortly afterward, instead of “from ivory houses,” Jerome wrote “from the temple of teeth.” Some infer this from the Letter to Principia [Col. 1162D], and the Hebrew commentator hints at it; but this is scarcely probable.]

Myrrh, stacte, and cassia are on all your garments,

from [Note: [Col. 1162D] “More correctly,” says the holy Doctor in the same place, “it is written in Hebrew, ‘from the temple of teeth.’” To this the marginal note of a very ancient scribe comes close. MART.]

the ivory chambers [Hebrew: from the temples]

with which the daughters of kings have gladdened you

in your honor.

The queen [Hebrew: bride] stood at your right hand,

in a golden diadem.

Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear;

forget your people and the house [Alternatively: home] of your father.

And the king shall desire your beauty,

because he is your Lord [Alternatively: add “God”], and worship him.

And [Note: [Col. 1162D] Several manuscripts read “And, daughter of the Mighty One”; two read “O daughter of the Mighty One,” instead of “And, O daughter of the Mighty One,” as it is read in the Chartres manuscript. Jerome also teaches that “O daughter of the Mighty One” should be read from the Hebrew. The diligent reader may find several other variant readings of lesser importance in the letter to the virgin Principia. MART.]

O daughter of the Mighty One [Hebrew: of Tyre],

the rich among the peoples shall entreat your face with gifts.

[Col. 1162B] All the glory of the king’s daughter is within;

she is clothed in golden bands [Hebrew: golden borders, her garments].

In embroidered garments she shall be led to the king;

virgins [Note: [Col. 1162D] Martianay incorrectly read, from other manuscripts, “immediately they follow.” Shortly afterward, two Regina manuscripts and the Cistercian read “they shall be led there,” instead of “to you.” Jerome himself appears to have taken this reading from the Hebrew copy in his letter to Principia, no. 20, although there he has “to you.” MART.]

shall follow her;

her companions [Hebrew: friends] shall be led to you.

They shall be led with joy and gladness;

they shall enter the king’s chamber [Hebrew: temple].

In place of your fathers, sons [Alternatively: daughters] shall be yours [Hebrew: yours],

and you shall appoint them princes over all the earth.

I shall remember your name

in every generation and generation;

therefore the peoples shall confess you

forever and ever.

FOR THE VICTOR, OF THE SONS OF KORAH, FOR THE YOUNG WOMEN, A SONG.

[XLVI.] God is our hope [Hebrew: for us] and strength;

you have proved a powerful help in tribulations.

Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is moved,

and mountains are shaken in the heart of the sea.

When its waters roar and swell [Note: [Col. 1163D] Our manuscripts and others cited by Martianay, together with the older printed books, read “when they swell.” Shortly afterward, one Regina manuscript reads “when the mountains are shaken,” without the particle. Finally, the Cistercian also omits the pronoun “its” in the following verse.]

and mountains are shaken in its power. ALWAYS.

Its river branches

make glad [Note: [Col. 1163D] Again our manuscripts and many of Martianay’s read: “makes glad the city of God, the holy tabernacle of the Most High.” Then only our manuscripts read: “The Lord is in its midst,” and afterward, “God is in its dawn.”] the city of God,

the holy tabernacles of the Most High.

God is in its midst; it shall not be moved;

God will help it at the break of dawn.

The nations were troubled, the kingdoms were shaken;

he uttered his voice, and the earth was thrown down.

The Lord of hosts is with us;

the God of Jacob is our protector. ALWAYS.

Come and see the works of the Lord,

how many desolations he has made on the earth.

He brings wars to an end as far as the end of the earth;

he will break the bow and cut down the spear [Alternatively: spears];

he will burn the chariots with fire.

Cease, and know that I am God;

[Col. 1163B] I shall be exalted among the nations,

I shall be exalted on the earth.

The Lord of hosts is with us;

the God of Jacob is our strength [Hebrew: our supporter].

ALWAYS.

[Note: [Col. 1163D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “Victory”; the Regina codex, “Victory” in the accusative; none of ours has “For the victor.”]

FOR THE VICTOR, OF THE SONS OF KORAH, A SONG [Hebrew: PSALM].

[XLVII.] All peoples [Alternatively: nations], clap your hands;

shout to God with a voice of praise.

For the Lord [Alternatively: God] Most High is terrible,

a great king over all the earth.

He gathered [Note: [Col. 1163D] Three copies of the Canon—the Carcassonne, San-German, and Memmian—together with two other manuscripts, read “He subjected the peoples.” MART.] peoples beneath us,

and tribes [Hebrew: peoples] beneath our feet.

He chose our inheritance for us,

the glory [Hebrew: pride] of Jacob, whom he loved. ALWAYS.

God ascended with a shout;

the Lord [Alternatively: God] with the sound of the trumpet.

Sing to God, sing;

sing to our king, sing.

For God is king of all the earth;

[Col. 1163C] sing with understanding.

God has reigned over the nations;

God sits upon his holy throne.

The princes of the peoples have gathered together,

the people of the God of Abraham;

for the gods are the shields of the earth;

they have been greatly exalted.

CANTICLE [Note: [Col. 1163D] In the main text, all our manuscripts read “Psalm.”] OF THE SONS OF KORAH.

[XLVIII.] Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised,

in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.

A beautiful shoot, the joy of the whole earth,

Mount Zion, on the northern sides,

the city of the great King.

God is known in its houses,

as he comes to their aid.

For behold, the kings assembled;

they came [h. passed over] together.

When they saw it, they were astonished;

they were troubled and amazed.

[Col. 1163D] Trembling seized them there;

[Col. 1164A] anguish, as of a woman in labor.

By the wind of scorching heat,

you will shatter [Note: [Col. 1163D] In the Cistercian manuscript, “shattering”; then, with all the rest joined, [Col. 1164D] “ships of the sea” for “of Tarshish”; finally, “God of hosts” for “Lord,” etc.] the ships of Tarshish.

As we have heard, so we have seen,

in the city of the Lord of hosts,

in the city of our God:

God founded it forever [h. for the age].

ALWAYS.

We have considered, O God, your mercy

within your temple.

According to your name, O God,

so is your praise to the ends [Al. as far as the end] of the earth;

your right hand is filled with righteousness.

Let Mount Zion rejoice; let the daughters of Judah exult,

because of your judgments.

Surround Zion and encircle it;

count its towers.

Set your hearts upon its walls [h. upon its strength];

separate its palaces [Al. adds “its”],

so that you may recount it to the final generation.

[Col. 1164B] For this is [Al. “he himself is”] God, our God forever,

and for all eternity;

he himself will be our guide unto death [h. forever].

TO THE VICTOR: A CANTICLE [h. PSALM] OF THE SONS OF KORAH.

[XLIX.] Hear this [Al. “these things”], all peoples;

give ear, all inhabitants of the west [h. of the world].

Both sons of Adam and sons [h. of man], each and every one,

rich together with poor.

My mouth shall speak wisdom [Al. “wisdom” singular],

and the meditation of my heart understanding [Al. “understanding” singular].

I incline my ear to a parable;

I will open my riddle upon the lyre.

Why should I fear in days of evil?

The iniquity of my heel will surround me.

Those who trust in their strength

and boast in the abundance of their riches.

[Note: [Col. 1164D] More correctly, I think, the Regina manuscript reads “Brother” in the main text.]

A man cannot redeem a brother,

nor can he give God a ransom for him,

[Col. 1164C] or the price of the redemption of their souls.

But he will rest for ever and live beyond, eternally,

and will not see destruction [Al. “forever”],

when he sees the wise dying.

Together the foolish and the unlearned will perish,

and they will leave their riches to strangers.

Their inward thoughts are their houses forever,

their tents from generation to generation;

they have called lands by their own names [Al. adds “their own”].

And man, though in honor, will not [Note: [Col. 1164D] Up to this point it has been read “will be moved,” a verb plainly alien both to the sacred writer’s meaning and to the context, and easily substituted by ancient copyists for the genuine “will remain.” We have therefore restored this reading, not on our own judgment, but first on the authority of the ancient Regina and Cistercian codices, and also of two manuscripts cited by Martianay—which, although less accurate elsewhere, could certainly here have put us on the track of the true reading. Finally, the Hebrew text convinced us, where the word means “will not endure,” or literally “will not spend the night”; and this sense is expressed exclusively by “will not remain.”] remain;

he is made like the beasts [Al. adds “he is”], and has been made equal to them.

This is the way of their folly [h. “their way”],

and after them they will run according to their mouth. ALWAYS.

Like a flock [h. “sheep”], they have been placed in hell; death will feed

on them,

and the upright will rule over them in the morning.

Their form will be crushed in hell, after their dwelling.

Yet God will redeem my soul

[Col. 1164D] from the hand of hell, when he takes me. ALWAYS.

[Col. 1165A] Do not fear when a man becomes rich,

when the glory of his house is multiplied.

For when he dies he will take nothing with him,

nor will his glory descend after him.

For in his lifetime he will bless his soul;

they will praise you [Note: [Col. 1165D] One Regina manuscript reads, “he will praise you, saying.” Then, more correctly, it seems, together with the Cistercian manuscript: “when you have dealt well with yourself,” which corresponds precisely to the Hebrew.]

when it goes well with you.

He will enter to the generation of his fathers,

to the end they will not see the light.

When man [Note: [Col. 1165D] In the San-German Canon the corrector of the codex wrote: “When man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with beasts and made like them.” This undoubtedly flowed from the Vulgate edition. The manuscripts of St. Michael and of the Augustinians of Bordeaux retain this reading: “When man was in honor, he would not remain; made like beasts, he was made equal to them.” MART.] was in honor, he did not understand;

he compared himself with beasts, and will be silenced.

CANTICLE [h. PSALM] OF ASAPH.

[L.] The mighty God, the Lord, has spoken,

and summoned the earth,

from the rising of the sun to its setting.

From Zion, perfect in beauty,

God has appeared [Al. omits “God”].

Our God will come, and will not be silent:

fire [Note: [Col. 1165D] In three canons we read, “Fire will burn before him.” In two other manuscripts, “It will burn in his presence.” MART.] will devour before him,

[Col. 1165B] and around him a mighty tempest.

He will summon heaven above,

and the earth, to judge his people.

Gather to me my holy ones [h. “my merciful ones”],

those who strike my covenant in sacrifice.

And the heavens will proclaim his righteousness,

for God himself is judge. ALWAYS.

Hear, my people [Al. “O people”], and I will speak;

Israel, and I will testify against you.

I am God, your God.

I will not rebuke you because of your sacrifices,

and your burnt offerings are before me. ALWAYS.

I will not take a bull [h. “a bullock”] from your house,

nor goats from your flocks.

For all the animals of the forests are mine [h. “of the forest”],

the cattle [h. *behemoth*] on a thousand hills.

I know all the birds of the mountains,

and the whole of the field [h. “*ziz* is said; it is the name of a bird]

is with me.

[Note: [Col. 1165D] Perhaps the pronoun “my” is more correctly omitted by the Regina manuscript; but the Hebrew text admits both readings according to the variation of the vowel-points.]

[Col. 1165C] If I were hungry, I would not tell you,

for the world and its fullness are mine.

Shall I eat the flesh [Al. “fleshes”] of bulls,

or drink the blood of goats?

Offer praise to God,

and pay your vows to the Most High [Al. omits “vows”].

And call upon me in the day of tribulation;

I will deliver you, and you will glorify me.

But to the sinner God said:

“What have you to do with recounting my precepts,

or with taking my covenant upon your lips?

[h. “And you”] You hate discipline,

and have cast my words behind you.

If you saw a thief, you consented with him,

and your portion was with adulterers [Note: [Col. 1165D] Two of our manuscripts add, “your portion was.” Then one Cistercian manuscript reads “you set your mouth,” instead of “you sent,” and “your tongue devises,” instead of “will devise,” which seems more consistent with the tense of the preceding sentence, though it differs from the Hebrew text.]

You sent your mouth toward evil,

and your tongue will devise deceit.

[Col. 1166A] Sitting, you spoke against your brother;

against the son of your mother [Al. “and against”] you fashioned

reproach.

You did these things, and I was silent;

you thought that I would become like you [Al. omits “me”].

I will rebuke you and set [it] before your eyes.

Understand this, you who forget God,

lest I seize you and there be no one to deliver.

He who sacrifices thanksgiving glorifies me,

and to the one who orders his way I will show the salvation of God.”

[Note: [Col. 1166D] The Regina manuscript reads, “To the one who walks in an ordered way I will show,” and so forth.]

TO THE VICTOR: A CANTICLE [h. PSALM] OF DAVID, WHEN NATHAN THE PROPHET CAME TO HIM, WHEN HE HAD ENTERED IN TO BATHSHEBA.

[LI.] Have mercy on me, O God, according to your mercy;

according to the abundance of your compassion

blot out my iniquities.

Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity,

and cleanse me from my sin.

For I know my iniquities [h. “my errors”],

[Col. 1166B] and my sin is always before me.

Against you alone I have sinned, and done what is evil before you [h. “in your eyes”],

so that you may be justified in your words,

and prevail [Note: [Col. 1166D] The Sorbonicus manuscript reads, “when you judge”; in the Canon exemplars, “when you are judged,” and this was followed by the Corbie manuscript and the first hand of the Chartres manuscript. MART.] when [Al. “while”] you judge [h. “when you are judged”].

Behold, I was conceived in iniquity,

and in sin my mother bore me.

For behold [Note: [Col. 1166D] The Carcasson Canon reads: “For behold, you love truth in secret; and in the hidden place of your wisdom you have made it known to me.” The manuscripts of the Augustinians of Bordeaux and of St. Michael similarly have this in the first verse, and consequently read, “you will make wisdom known to me.” MART.] you love truth;

you have made the hidden and secret things of wisdom known to me [h. “we will make wisdom known”].

You will sprinkle [h. “purify”] me with hyssop, and I shall be clean;

you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.

You will make me hear joy and gladness,

[Note: [Col. 1166D] In several manuscripts: “so that the bones may rejoice.”]

and the bones you have crushed will rejoice.

Turn your face away from my sins,

and blot out all my iniquities.

Create in me a clean heart, O God,

and renew a steadfast spirit within me.

[Col. 1166C] Do not cast me away from your presence,

and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.

Restore to me the joy [h. “of Jesus”] [Note: [Col. 1166D] The Scholiast prefers “of Jesus” to “of your salvation”; our manuscripts likewise prefer it.]

of your salvation,

and strengthen me with a powerful spirit.

I will teach the wicked your ways,

and sinners will return to you.

Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, God of my salvation;

my tongue will praise your righteousness.

Lord, you will open my lips,

and my mouth will proclaim your praise.

For you do not desire that I should bring a sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1166D] “I should strike” is nearly always preferable, since all our manuscripts, as well as several others cited by Martianay, have it instead of “I should bring”; the Hebrew agrees literally: “you will not desire a sacrifice.”]

nor are you pleased with a burnt offering.

The sacrifice [h. “sacrifices”] of God is a troubled [h. “crushed”] spirit;

a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.

Do good [h. “deal kindly”] in your good will,

[Al. adds “Lord”] to Zion;

[Col. 1167A] [Al. adds “and”] let the walls of Jerusalem be built.

Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness,

offerings and burnt offerings;

then they will place bulls [h. “bullocks”] upon your altar.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] The Regina manuscript reads “Victoria from *crudito*”; together with most others, it reads the names “Doeg” and “Ahimelech” in this way.]

TO THE VICTOR: THE INSTRUCTION OF DAVID, WHEN DOEG [Al. DOECH] THE EDOMITE CAME AND TOLD SAUL [Al. SAUL], SAYING TO HIM: “DAVID CAME TO THE HOUSE OF AHIMELECH [Al. AHIMELECH].”

[LII.] Why do you boast in evil, mighty man?

The mercy of God is all day long.

Your tongue devises plots,

like a sharp razor, practicing deceit.

You loved evil more than good,

falsehood more than speaking [Al. omits “speaking”] righteousness.

ALWAYS.

You loved every devouring word, deceitful tongue [Note: [Col. 1167D] Three manuscripts, together with the printed text, read “deceitful tongue.” MART.] [Al. “deceitful tongue”].

But God will destroy you;
forever he will terrify you [h. adds “you”],

he will uproot you from your tent,

[Col. 1167B] and root you out of the land of the living. ALWAYS.

The righteous will see and fear,

and they will laugh at him:

“Behold the man who made God his strength,

but trusted in the abundance of his riches

and grew strong in his plots.”

But I, like a flourishing olive tree in the house of God,

have trusted in the mercy of God

forever [Note: [Col. 1167D] Thus the Royal, Corbie, Sorbonicus, and *Speculum* manuscripts. In others we read, “forever and ever.” MART.]

I will give thanks to you forever, because you have acted,

and I will wait for your name, because it is good

in the presence of your holy ones [h. “merciful ones”].

TO THE VICTOR [Note: [Col. 1167D] The Sorbonicus manuscript reads “To the victor” instead of “for the choir, understanding.” Seven other manuscript codices have at the end of the title “the instructed David.” MART. —The Cistercian manuscript has “for the choir, understanding”; the others merely prefer “instructed,” instead of “instruction.” —Here too all our manuscripts read “instructed,” instead of “instruction.”] FOR THE CHOIR: THE INSTRUCTION OF DAVID.

[LIII.] The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.”

They are corrupt and have become abominable in iniquity;

there is no one who does good.

God looked down from heaven upon the sons of men,

[Col. 1167C] to see whether there was anyone who understood and sought God.

All have turned away; together they have clung together;

there is no one who does good, not even one.

Have they not known, those who practice iniquity,

who devour my people as though eating bread?

They have not called upon God.

There they feared with fear

where there was no fear [Al. “is no fear”],

for God scattered the bones of those surrounding you;

you will be put to shame, because God rejected them.

Who will grant from Zion the salvation of Israel? [Note: [Col. 1167D] The Carcasson Canon and the Vatican manuscript read “the salvation of Israel”; all the others read “salvation to Israel.” MART.]

When God restores the captivity of his people,

Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.

TO THE VICTOR: IN PSALMS, THE INSTRUCTION OF DAVID, WHEN THE ZIPHITES CAME AND SAID TO SAUL: “IS NOT DAVID HIDDEN AMONG US?”

[LIV.] O God, save me by your name [Al. “make me safe”],

and vindicate me by your strength.

[Col. 1167D] O God, hear my prayer;

[Col. 1168A] give ear to the words of my mouth.

For strangers have risen up against me,

and the mighty have sought my life.

[Note: [Col. 1168D] The same manuscripts read, “and they did not set God before them,” and so forth.]

They have not set God before them. ALWAYS.

Behold, God is my helper;

the Lord sustains my soul.

He will repay evil to those lying in wait for me [h. “those who sing”];

in your truth [Al. omits “your”] destroy them.

I will sacrifice to you willingly;

I will give thanks to your name, O Lord, because it is good.

For he has delivered me from every tribulation,

and my eye has looked upon my enemies.

TO THE VICTOR [Note: [Col. 1168D] Several manuscripts have here, as above, “the instructed David.” MART. —With equal agreement our manuscripts read “he looked upon,” instead of “he saw.” In the title of the following psalm, some prefer “instructed,” others “canticle,” instead of “instruction.”] IN PSALMS: THE INSTRUCTION OF DAVID.

[LV.] Hear, O God, my prayer,

and do not despise my supplication.

Attend to me and hear me:

I am humbled in my meditation,

[Col. 1168B] and troubled by the voice of the enemy,

by the face of the impious persecutor.

For they have cast iniquity upon me,

and in anger they opposed me.

My heart was troubled within me,

and the terrors of death fell upon me.

Fear and trembling came [Al. “came” plural] upon me,

and darkness covered me.

And I said, “Who will give me the wings of a dove,

so that I may fly away and rest?

So that I may go far away

and dwell in the desert?” ALWAYS.

I will hasten [h. “Hasten”] [Note: [Col. 1168D] St. Jerome discusses these two verses in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, saying that the whole meaning of the present passage is read among the Hebrews as follows: “I will hasten to be delivered from the spirit of storm and tempest.” Here you may see that the Canon’s Scholiast differs from Jerome, the truth of the Hebrew being read and interpreted in a different way with respect to *ahhisa*. MART.] to be delivered

from the spirit of storm and tempest.

Hurl them down, Lord; divide their tongues,

for I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city.

By day and night they go around its walls.

Iniquity and sorrow are in its midst.

Plots are within it,

[Col. 1168C] and damage and deceit do not depart from its streets.

For it was not an enemy who reproached me, so that I could bear it;

nor was it one who hated me who magnified himself against me,

so that I might hide from him.

But it was you, a man of one mind with me [Al. omits “my”],

my leader and my acquaintance,

with whom we shared sweet intimacy,

and walked in the house of God amid fear.

Let death come upon them;

let them descend alive into hell,

for there are wickednesses in their assembly, in their midst.

But I will cry to God,

and the Lord will save me.

Evening, morning, and midday I will speak,

and cry aloud, and he will hear my voice.

[Note: [Col. 1168D] Many manuscripts retain the future tense, “he will redeem in peace.” MART. Other manuscripts among ours read “redeem,” while others read “he will redeem.”]

He has redeemed my soul in peace

from those who draw near to me,

for there were many against me.

[Col. 1168D] God will hear and humble them,

[Col. 1169A] he who is judge from the beginning. ALWAYS.

For they do not change, and they do not fear God.

He has stretched out his hands [Al. “his hand”] toward his peaceful things;

he has violated his covenant.

His mouth is smoother than butter,

but his heart is at war;

[Note: [Col. 1169C] The same manuscript reads, “they have softened their words with oil”; in the others as well the preposition *ab* is absent. Shortly afterward the Cistercian manuscript reads: “Cast your tribulation upon the Lord,” added in the margin: “your thought.”]

his words are softer than oil,

yet they are spears.

Cast your charity upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you;

he will not forever permit the righteous to waver.

But you, O God, will lead them into the pit of destruction;

men of blood and deceit will not halve their days;

but I will trust in you.

TO THE VICTOR: FOR THE SILENT DOVE, BECAUSE DAVID, HUMBLE AND SIMPLE, WENT FAR AWAY, WHEN THE PHILISTINES SEIZED HIM IN GATH.

[LVI.] Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me;

all day long, fighting, he has afflicted me.

[Col. 1169B] Those lying in wait for me [h. “those who sing”] have trampled me

all day long;

for many are those who fight against me, O Most High.

On whatever day I am terrified, I will trust in you [Al. omits “I”].

In God I will praise his word [Al. omits “his”];

in God I have trusted; I will not fear

what flesh can do to me.

All day long they afflicted me with words;

all their thoughts against me were for evil.

They will gather secretly; they themselves [Al. omits “themselves”] will watch my footsteps

[h. “my heels”],

waiting for my life.

There is no deliverance for them;

in anger, bring down the peoples [Note: [Col. 1169C] Two of our manuscripts read “take away,” a reading shown to be corrupt through the carelessness of the scribes by the letter to Sunnia and Fretela.] O God.

You have numbered my secret things [h. “my wandering, you”];

place [Note: [Col. 1169C] This is a notable passage for students curious about sacred and secular antiquity, whose inquiries the Canon’s Scholiast had satisfied a thousand years ago [Col. 1169D], unless the splendid monuments of this intellect had lain forgotten through the neglect of the ages until the present. Thus we read in the Vatican manuscript—in whose text, as we have noted, the marginal scholia of the Canon had been incorporated: “You have counted my wandering; put my tear in your sight [h. ‘in your wineskin’], or in your number.” In the Carcasson Canon the last verse is expressed similarly, “or in your number”; the rest is found, as you see, in the scholia. The San-German Canon, which thereafter has no critical annotations, retains the entire pure text of the psalm, as do four other manuscripts, namely the Royal, Chartres, Corbie, and Sorbonicus manuscripts. The two remaining manuscripts, those of the Augustinians of Bordeaux and of St. Michael in Periculo Maris, which we previously said were everywhere mixed with marginal scholia and corrupted, do not differ from the Vatican manuscript just cited. Moreover, the Septuagint and Jerome here interpret *benodecha* as “in your sight,” or “before you,” although elsewhere they translate *nod* as “wineskin.” In turning over the Hebrew lexicons, we found nothing that supported this interpretation except the word *nidnud*, which among the rabbis means a movement of the eye. Anyone wishing to know about the ancient tear-vessels, or wineskins, in which the tears of mourners of the dead were kept, should consult Th. J. ab Almeloveen, *Specimen of Sacred and Profane Antiquities*, pp. 131 ff. MART.] my tear in your sight [h. “in your wineskin”];

but not in your record.

Then my enemies will turn backward,

on whatever day I call upon you;

I know this, for you are my God [Al. adds “you”].

In God I will praise the word;

[Note: [Col. 1170D] In the Cistercian manuscript: “and in God I will proclaim.”]

in the Lord I will proclaim the saying [h. “I will praise”].

In God I have trusted; I will not fear

what man can do to me.

My vows are upon me, O God;

I will repay you with thanksgivings.

[Col. 1170A] For you have delivered my soul from death,

and my feet from falling,

so that I may walk before God in the light of the living.

[Note: [Col. 1170D] The Royal codex is so corrupt in many psalm titles that it reveals the deterioration and ignorance of public copyists. Here it gives the title as: “To the end, do not destroy; David, with the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.” But the codices contain, instead of “to the victor” or “do not destroy,” and so forth. MART. —The Cistercian manuscript has “for the victor”; the Regina manuscript, together with many others, has “for victory,” and so forth, which I think was also preferred by those whom Martianay cites. For he does not seem to have read correctly, “for the victor or do not,” and so forth.]

TO THE VICTOR: “DO NOT DESTROY”; OF DAVID, HUMBLE AND SIMPLE, WHEN HE FLED FROM THE FACE OF SAUL INTO THE CAVE.

[LVII.] Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me,

for my soul has trusted [Al. “trusts”] in you;

and in the shadow of your wings I will trust,

until the plots pass away.

I will call upon God Most High,

God, my avenger.

He will send from heaven and save me;

[Note: [Col. 1170D] The printed editions and five manuscripts read “your hands,” instead of “your hands’.” MART. —A manuscript reads “he reproached those who trample”; it also omits the following “always.”]

he will reproach those who trample me. ALWAYS.

God will send his mercy and his truth.
