My soul slept among lions, raging fiercely;

the sons of men have teeth like spears and arrows,

and their tongue is a sharp sword.

Be exalted above the heavens, O God;

[Col. 1170B] your glory is over all the earth.

They prepared a net for my steps,

to bend down my soul [h. “my soul was bent down”];

they dug a pit before me;

they fell into its midst. ALWAYS.

My heart is prepared, O God; my heart is prepared;

I will sing and make melody.

Awake [h. “rouse yourself”], my glory;

awake [h. “rouse yourself”], lyre and harp;

I will rise [h. “rouse myself”] at dawn.

I will give thanks to you among the peoples, Lord;

I will sing [h. “make melody”] to you among the nations.

For your mercy is great even to the heavens,

and your truth reaches to the clouds.

Be exalted above the heavens, O God;

your glory is over all the earth.

TO THE VICTOR: “DO NOT DESTROY”; OF DAVID, HUMBLE AND SIMPLE.

[Col. 1170C] [LVIII.] If indeed you speak righteousness,

judge uprightly, sons of men.

For in your heart you practice iniquities [h. “burnt offerings”];

on earth you weigh the iniquities of your hands.

Sinners have been estranged from the womb;

from the womb they have gone astray, speaking falsehood.

Their fury is like the likeness [Note: [Col. 1170D] All our manuscripts read “like the fury of a serpent,” instead of “the likeness of fury,” and so forth.] of a serpent’s fury,

like a deaf adder that stops its ear,

[Col. 1171A] so that it does not hear the voice of charmers,

nor the clever enchantments of the enchanter.

O God, shatter their teeth in their mouth;

break the molars [Al. “grinders”] of the lions, Lord.

Let them melt away like waters that flow off;

he will bend his bow [h. “his arrow”] until they are crushed.

Like a melting worm, let him pass away [Al. “let them pass away”];

like a woman’s miscarriage that does not see [Al. “does not see”]

the sun.

Before your thorns grow into a thornbush,

as living things, as in anger [Note: [Col. 1171D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “In the anger of the tempest he will snatch them away.”] the tempest will sweep them away.

The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance;

he will wash his feet in the blood of the wicked.

And man will say [Al. “let him say”], “Truly there is fruit for the righteous;

truly there is a God judging on earth.”

TO THE VICTOR: “DO NOT DESTROY”; OF DAVID, HUMBLE AND SIMPLE, WHEN SAUL SENT MEN AND THEY GUARDED THE HOUSE TO KILL HIM [Al. “to kill him”].

[Col. 1171B] [LIX.] Deliver me from my enemies, O God [h. “Lord”],

my God,

and protect me from those who resist me.

Free me from the workers of iniquity [Al. “those who work iniquities”],

and save me from men of blood.

For behold, they lay in wait for my soul;

the strongest [h. “most cruel”] gather against me,

without iniquity or sin on my part, Lord.

I have done no wrong, yet they run [Al. “ran”] and prepare themselves.

Rise [h. “rouse yourself”] to meet me and look upon me.

And you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel,

awake to visit all the nations.

Do not have mercy on all

who practice iniquity. ALWAYS.

They return in the evening;

they howl like a dog [Al. “dogs”]

[Col. 1171C] and go around the city.

Behold, they speak with their mouths;

swords are on their lips,

as though no one were listening.

But you, Lord [Al. omits “Lord”], will laugh at them;

you will mock all the nations.

I will keep my strength for you,

for you, God, are my lifter-up.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] The corruption of this verse is perfectly obvious both in the printed editions and in certain manuscripts, where we read: “The mercy of my God will precede me.” Jerome himself expressly taught in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela that the Hebrew reads: “My God, my mercy, will precede me.” MART.]

God, my mercy, will precede me;

God will show me among those lying in wait for me [h. “those who sing”].

Do not kill them, lest my people forget;

scatter them by your strength and overthrow them,

our protector, Lord [Al. “God”].

For the sin of their mouth, by the word [Al. “in sin and in the word”]

of their lips,

let them be caught in their pride,

while recounting cursing and falsehood.

Consume them in fury, consume them so that they do not exist;

and let them know that God rules [Al. “will rule”]

[Col. 1171D] Jacob to the ends of the earth. ALWAYS.

And let them return in the evening,

howl like a dog [Al. “dogs”],

and go around the city.

They will wander about to eat,

and when they are not satisfied, they will murmur.

[Col. 1172A] But I will sing of your dominion,

and in the morning I will praise your mercy,

for you have become my strength [h. “my supporter”]

and refuge in the day of my tribulation.

I will sing my strength to you [Note: [Col. 1172D] The Cistercian manuscript adds “my.” Then, together with the Regina and other manuscripts, it omits the words “my strength”; in the following verse they add “my strength.”] [h. “to you I will sing my strength”],

for God is my helper [h. “supporter”],

God, my mercy.

TO THE VICTOR: FOR THE SONS, THE TESTIMONY OF THE HUMBLE AND [Note: [Col. 1172D] Instead of “simple,” all our manuscripts and others cited by Martianay read “perfect.” Then one Regina manuscript omits the words “Mesopotamia” and “against Syria.”] SIMPLE DAVID, FOR INSTRUCTION, WHEN HE FOUGHT AGAINST MESOPOTAMIAN SYRIA AND AGAINST THE SYRIANS OF ZOBA; AND JOAB RETURNED AND STRUCK EDOM IN THE VALLEY OF THE SALT PITS, TWELVE THOUSAND MEN.

[LX.] O God, you rejected us, you tore us apart;

in anger you turned us back.

You shook the earth and [Note: [Col. 1172D] In one Cistercian manuscript, “you tore it apart.”] shattered it;

heal its fractures, for it has been shaken.

[Col. 1172B] You showed your people hardship;

you gave us wine that stupefies [Note: [Col. 1172D] Some manuscripts read “wine of sorrow.” MART.].

You gave a sign to those who fear [Al. “are afraid of”] you,

so that they might flee from the face of the bow. ALWAYS.

So that your beloved might be delivered,

save with your right hand and hear me.

God has spoken in his sanctuary: “I will rejoice;

I will divide Shechem,

and measure out the valley of Succoth.

Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine;

Ephraim is the strength of my head;

Judah is my lawgiver.

Moab is the basin [Note: [Col. 1172D] The exemplars of the Canon and two or three others read, “Moab is the basin of my washing.” MART.] of my washing.

Over Edom I will cast my sandal;

Philistia has become allied with me.”

Who will lead me to the fortified city?

Who will lead me as far as Edom?

Are you not the God who rejected us,

and who will not go out, O God, with our armies?

[Col. 1172C] Give us help from [Al. “in”] tribulation,

for help from man is vain.

In God we will act valiantly,

and he himself will trample down those who afflict us.

TO THE VICTOR: IN PSALMS, OF DAVID.

[LXI.] Hear, O God, my praise;

attend to my prayer.

From the ends of the earth I will cry to you,

when my heart is sorrowful.

When the mighty man rises up against me,

you will be my guide.

For you have been my hope [Al. omits “for”],

a most strongly fortified tower against the enemy.

I will dwell continually in your tent [h. “I will sojourn”]

[h. “forever”];

I will hope in the protection of your wings. ALWAYS.

For you, O God, have heard my prayer;

you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.

You will add days to the king’s days;

his years from generation to generation.

He will sit forever [h. “for the age”] before God;

mercy and truth will preserve him.

So I will sing [h. “make melody”] to your name continually,

repaying my vows day by day.

[Col. 1173A] TO THE VICTOR [Note: [Col. 1173A] The same manuscript reads “for Jeduthun,” instead of “through Jeduthun.”]: THROUGH JEDUTHUN, A CANTICLE [h. PSALM] OF DAVID.

[LXII.] Yet my soul is silent before God;

from him comes my salvation.

Yet he himself is my shield [h. “my strength”] and my salvation;

my strength [h. “my supporter”], I shall not be moved any more.

How long will you lie in wait for a man and murder him, all of you,

[Note: [Col. 1173C] The Carcasson Canon and its two companions, namely the manuscripts of the Augustinians of Bordeaux and of St. Michael, read: “Like a leaning wall, a collapsing hedge.” MART. —The Cistercian manuscript reads “like a wall,” and so forth. The Royal manuscript omits what follows, “and a collapsing wall.”]

like a leaning wall and a collapsing fence?

For they planned to drive away his portion;

they delighted in falsehood.

With their mouth they bless,

but in their heart [h. “inwardly”] they curse. ALWAYS.

Yet be silent [Al. “be quiet”] before God, my soul,

for my expectation is from him [Note: [Col. 1173D] The Regina codex reads: “For my salvation is from him alone.”].

For he is [Al. “is”] my strength and my salvation;

my supporter, I will not fear [h. “I will not be moved”].

In God are my salvation and my glory;

the rock of my strength and my salvation are in God.

[Col. 1173B] Hope in him at all times, peoples;

pour out your hearts before him;

God is our hope. ALWAYS.

Yet the sons of Adam are vanity,

the sons of man [Al. “of men”] are falsehood;

on deceitful scales they act together fraudulently [h. “placed on scales, vanity altogether”].

Do not trust in oppression

or in robbery, and do not become vain.

If riches increase [Note: [Col. 1173D] Nearly all the manuscripts read: “If wealth flows in.” MART.] [Al. “flow in”], do not set your heart upon them.

God has spoken once;

I have heard these two things: that dominion [h. “strength”] belongs to God,

and to you, Lord, belongs mercy,

for you repay each person according to his work.

A CANTICLE [h. PSALM] OF DAVID, WHEN HE WAS IN THE WILDERNESS OF JUDAH.

[LXIII.] O God [h. “O God, my God, you”], you are my strength;

from dawn I rise to you.

[Col. 1173C] My soul has thirsted for you [Note: [Col. 1173D] All the printed and manuscript books read “my soul has thirsted for you.” St. Jerome discusses it in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela: “My soul has thirsted for you,” whereas in Greek it is “my soul has thirsted for you.” But the Hebrew does not have *ATTHA* (), which means “you,” but *LACH* (), which means “for you,” and all the interpreters translated it so. Therefore it has been rendered into Latin according to the propriety of the language. St. Jerome himself, however, in his Psalter published according to the Hebrew source, translated it according to the propriety of Latin: “I have thirsted for you, I have desired you,” perhaps imitating Cicero’s phrase, “I neither thirst for honors nor desire glory.” MART.],

my flesh has desired you,

in a trackless and parched land, and without water.

Thus I appeared to you in the sanctuary,

to see your strength and your glory.

For your mercy is better than life [Al. “life” singular];

my lips will praise you.

Thus I will bless you [Al. “bless for you”] in my life;

in your name I will raise my hands [h. “palms”].

My soul will be filled [h. “satisfied”] as with fat and richness,

[Col. 1174A] and my mouth will sing [h. “praise”] with lips of praise,

remembering you upon my bed;

during every watch I will meditate on you.

For you have been my help,

and in the shadow of your wings I will praise you [Note: [Col. 1173D] The same manuscript reads “I will sing,” instead of “I will praise”; shortly afterward the Royal manuscript reads “they sought,” instead of “they seek.”].

My soul has clung to you;

your right hand has received me.

But they seek to kill my soul [h. “for calamity”];

let them enter the depths [h. “the lower places”] of the earth.

Let them be gathered into the hands of the sword;

they will become the portion of foxes.

But the king will rejoice in God;

everyone who swears by him will be praised,

for the mouth of those who speak falsehood will be stopped.

[Note: [Col. 1173D] This title is absent from the Cistercian manuscript.]

TO THE VICTOR: A CANTICLE [h. PSALM] OF DAVID.

[LXIV.] Hear, O God, my voice as I speak;

preserve my life from the fear [h. “terror”] of the enemy [Note: [Col. 1173D] In the same manuscript: “preserve my soul.”].

Hide me from the counsel of the wicked;

[Col. 1174B] from the tumult of those who practice iniquity.

For they have sharpened their tongue like a sword;

they have bent their bow: a most bitter word.

To shoot the innocent in secret,

suddenly they will shoot him, and will not fear.

They have strengthened themselves in an evil speech;

they have spoken in order to hide snares.

They said, “Who will see them?” [Note: [Col. 1174C] All our manuscripts read “Who will see us?” instead of “them.”]

They searched out iniquities:

They exhausted themselves searching with scrutiny,

and with the thoughts of each one, and with a deep heart.

Therefore God will shoot them with a sudden arrow [Note: [Col. 1174C] Jerome observes in the same letter that the following is read here among the Hebrews: “God will strike them with a sudden dart, and their wounds will be inflicted.” This certainly has the same sense, although there appears to be some difference in the wording. We restore the present division of the verses on the testimony and authority of Jerome himself, since [Col. 1174D] it has been corrupted in the manuscript codices through scribal error. MART.]:

their wounds will be inflicted.

And they will fall upon themselves [Note: [Col. 1174D] The printed books retain this marginal scholion, and in the Hebrew we read *leschonam*, that is, “their tongue,” or “their tongues.” MART. —The same manuscripts prefer “with their tongues,” which also pleases the scholiast and is closer to the Hebrew text.] by their own wounds [Heb. tongues]:

all who see them will flee.

And all human beings will fear,

and they will proclaim the work of God,

and they will understand his works.

The righteous will rejoice in the Lord and hope in him:

[Col. 1174C] and all upright in heart will exult.

TO THE VICTOR [Note: [Col. 1174D] Only three manuscripts have *Victori carmen David, Canticum*, “To the Victor, a song of David, a canticle”; the interlinear Latin version agrees with this reading. Nevertheless, the alternative seems preferable from the title of the following Psalm 68, in which the same words retain their natural order: *Victori David psalmus Cantici*, “To the Victor, a psalm of David, of the Canticle.” MART. —Again all our manuscripts and two others in Martianay have *silens*, “being silent,” instead of *silet*, “is silent.”] A SONG [Heb. PSALM] OF DAVID, OF THE CANTICLE.

## [LXV.]

Praise is silent for you, O God, in Zion,

and the vow will be paid to you.

Hear [Note: [Col. 1174D] In four manuscripts—namely the Vatican, Canon of Carcassonne, Augustinian of Bordeaux, and Saint Michael—“Hearing prayer; let all flesh come to you.” MART.] my prayer,

until all flesh comes to you.

Words of iniquities have prevailed against me:

you will show mercy to our crimes.

Blessed is the one whom you choose and receive:

for he will dwell in your courts;

[Col. 1175A] we shall be filled with the good things of your house,

with the holiness of your temple.

In awesome deeds, hear us in righteousness,

O God our Savior:

the hope of all the ends of the earth

and of the distant sea.

You prepare [Alt. who prepares] the mountains by your power,

girded with strength.

You restrain the roaring of the sea,

the tumult of its waves,

and the multitude of the nations [Heb. peoples].

And those who dwell at the ends of the earth will fear because of your signs:

the goings forth of morning and evening will praise you [Note: [Col. 1175D] The San-German Canon, with the printed books, reads: “The goings forth of morning and evening,” etc. The Memmian: “The goings forth of morning and evenings.” MART. —The Cistercian and Regina manuscripts read “the morning goings forth and evening”; in the others Martianay found “the going forth of morning.”].

You have visited the earth and watered it;

you enriched it with abundance.

The stream of God is full of water;

you will prepare [Note: [Col. 1175D] Saint Jerome, in the frequently cited letter, says: “You say that in the Greek it does not contain *of it*, whereas in the Hebrew *TECHINA* (), plainly signifies ‘its preparation.’” We repeat this interpretation because of our scholiast’s marginal annotation, which agrees with Jerome’s observation. MART.] their grain, because in this way you established it

[Heb. you will prepare] it.

Water its furrows, multiply its crops [Heb. bring forth its ranks]:

[Col. 1175B] water it with rains; bless its growth.

The year will roll on in your goodness [Heb. You crowned the year],

and your footsteps will drip with abundance.

The pastures of the wilderness will grow rich [Heb. will drip],

and the hills will gird themselves with rejoicing.

The flocks will be clothed with lambs,

and the valleys will be full of grain;

they will be made level and will sing.

TO THE VICTOR, A CANTICLE OF A PSALM.

## [LXVI.]

Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.

Sing [Heb. sing psalms] glory to his name [Alt. the glory of his name].

Give glory to his praise.

Say [Note: [Col. 1175D] Several manuscripts read, “his awesome works.” MART.] to God: How awesome is your work!

Because of the abundance of your power,

your enemies will lie to you.

Let all the earth adore you and sing [Heb. sing psalms] to you;

let it sing [Heb. sing psalms] to your name. SELAH.

[Col. 1175C] Come [Heb. go] and see the works of God,

his awesome [Note: [Col. 1175D] On the other hand, the same manuscripts read here in the singular, “his awesome counsel.” MART.] counsels concerning the sons of men [Heb. Adam].

He turned [Alt. he will turn] the sea into dry land;

they crossed the river on foot;

there we rejoiced in him.

He rules in his power forever;

his eyes observe the nations [Note: One manuscript of the Regina codex has *oculi ejus in gentes*, “his eyes upon the nations,” which is somewhat closer to the Hebrew, .];

those who are unbelieving—

let them not exalt themselves. SELAH.

Bless our God, O peoples,

and make the voice of his praise heard.

He placed our soul in life,

and did not allow our feet to be shaken.

For you tested us, O God;

you refined us by fire [Note: [Col. 1176D] Some manuscripts omit “by fire.” MART.] as silver is refined.

You brought us into a siege [Alt. into a net];

you placed distress upon our back [Heb. loins];

you set men upon our head.

We passed through fire and water,

[Col. 1176A] and you brought us into refreshment.

I will enter [Alt. into] your house with burnt offerings;

I will fulfill my vows to you, which my lips promised [Heb. distinguished] [Note: The same manuscript adds here *tibi*, “to you,” which is also echoed shortly afterward in the Hebrew.],

and my mouth spoke when I was afflicted.

I will offer you burnt offerings rich in marrow,

with the incense of rams [Note: The San-German manuscript and the Memmian retain the corrupted ancient reading, “with incense and rams.” But Jerome says above that this is wrong; for in Hebrew it is written *EM CATOROTH ELIM* (), which is interpreted, “with the incense of rams.” If anyone is troubled that we read *catoroth* instead of *catereth*, let him consult the manuscript codices of the letter to Sunnia and Fretela.],

I will make offerings of oxen with goats. SELAH.

Come [Heb. go], hear, and I will recount it, all you who fear God,

what he has done for my soul.

I called upon him with my mouth,

and exalted him with my tongue.

If I saw iniquity in my heart,

may the Lord not hear me.

Therefore God heard,

and attended to the voice of my supplication [Heb. prayer].

Blessed is God, who did not remove my prayer

and his mercy from me.

[Col. 1176B] TO THE VICTOR IN PSALMS [Heb. SONGS], A CANTICLE [Heb. PSALM] OF A SONG.

## [LXVII.]

May God have mercy on us and bless us [Alt. bless us];

may he make his face shine upon us. SELAH.

So that your way may be known on earth,

your salvation among all nations.

May the peoples confess you, O God;

may all the peoples confess you.

May the nations [Heb. peoples] rejoice and praise you,

because you judge the peoples with equity,

and you are the guide of the nations [Heb. peoples] that are on the earth. [Note: [Col. 1176D] Our manuscripts have, “you are their eternal guide.”] SELAH.

May the peoples confess you, O God;

may all the peoples confess you.

The earth has given its produce [Alt. fruit];

may God, our God, bless us.

May God bless us,

and may all the ends of the earth fear him.

[Col. 1176C] TO THE VICTOR, A PSALM OF DAVID, OF THE CANTICLE.

## [LXVIII.]

Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered [Alt. dispersed],

and let those who hate him flee from his presence.

As smoke vanishes, so may they vanish;

as wax melts before fire,

[Note: [Col. 1176D] The Cistercian manuscript omits the little word *sic*, “so,” which is not properly present in the Hebrew either.] so may the wicked perish before God.

But let the righteous rejoice and exult in God’s presence,

and delight in gladness.

Sing psalms to God, [Note: [Col. 1176D] Instead of *psallite*, “sing psalms,” the Cistercian manuscript has “and bless”; the Regius has “sing.” See Letter 106 to Sunnia and Fretela.] sing to his name;

prepare [Note: [Col. 1176D] In the text of the Canon of Carcassonne and in the Vatican codex we read, “for him who ascends toward the setting sun.” MART.] the way for him who ascends through the deserts [Heb. *araboth*, that is, the upper heaven].

The Lord is his name;

exult before him.

Father [Heb. Judge] of orphans and defender of widows:

God in his holy dwelling.

God makes the solitary dwell in a house;

he brings out prisoners in strength;

[Col. 1177A] but the unbelieving dwell in parched places.

O God, when you went out before your people

and marched through the wilderness. SELAH.

The earth was shaken, and the heavens poured down rain before God,

this Sinai, before God, the God of Israel [Note: [Col. 1177C] This is an intricate and obscure passage. Two manuscripts, together with the printed books, read: “The heavens poured down rain before your face, O God, that is, in Sinai.” The Sorbonicus manuscript likewise retains this, but has “before your face, O God, and Sinai.” The San-German Canon has “before the face of God and Sinai.” Finally, the corrected Chartres manuscript, revised by someone not inexperienced in Hebrew, placed, closer to the Hebrew: “before the face of God, this Sinai.” We shall speak of the Memmian manuscript in the additions. MART. —The Regina manuscript has: “before your face, O God, that is, in Sinai”; the Cistercian follows with a reading closer to the Hebrew: “before God, the God of Israel.”].

You lifted up a voluntary rain, O God;

you strengthened your weary inheritance.

Your animals dwelt in it;

in your goodness you prepared it for the poor, O God.

The Lord will give the word

to the women proclaiming the great power [Heb. great army].

The kings of armies will be allied, they will be allied;

and the beauty of the house will divide the spoils.

If you sleep among the boundaries,

the wings of the dove are silver-plated,

and its hind parts are green with gold.

When the Almighty scattered kings in it [Alt. when he scattered the mighty kings in it],

they were made white as snow in Selmon [Note: [Col. 1177D] Two manuscripts have, “in the green of a jewel.” In four manuscript copies we subsequently read: “When the Almighty separates the kings in it, they will be whitened with snow in Selmon.” MART.].

[Col. 1177B] The mountain of God is a fertile mountain [Heb. Bashan];

a lofty mountain, a fertile mountain [Heb. Bashan].

Why do you contend, lofty mountains,

against the mountain that God chose as his dwelling?

Indeed, the Lord will dwell there forever [Note: [Col. 1177D] In some manuscripts, “he will dwell there confidently.” MART. —Instead of *in aeternum*, “forever,” our manuscripts have *semper*, “always,” which has the same meaning unless you take it as the customary indication of the *diapsalma*. One Cistercian manuscript gives “ten thousand times ten thousand” instead of “thousands of abundance”; and the Hebrew itself counts twenty thousand. Thus I understand it as a doubling of the term , or , which signifies ten thousand. But the other Hebrew word translated here as “abundance” properly means “doubled” or “repeated.”].

The chariots of God are innumerable, thousands upon thousands;

the Lord is among them, Sinai [Alt. in Sinai] in the sanctuary.

You ascended on high;

you led captivity captive;

you received gifts [Note: [Col. 1177D] The Regina manuscript has “gifts for men,” without the preposition *in*.] among men;

moreover [Note: What the holy Father himself says in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela—“We translated, ‘Indeed, those who do not believe to dwell’”—and many other things of this kind, he attributes to his own translation from the Greek.] even those who do not believe in dwelling with the Lord God.

Blessed be the Lord day by day;

God our salvation will carry us. SELAH.

Our God [Heb. to us] is the God of salvation [Heb. salvations],

and the Lord God has the exits from death.

Nevertheless God will crush the heads of his enemies,

the crown of the hair of one who walks in his offenses [Alt. delights].

The Lord said: I will return from Bashan;

I will return from the depths of the sea.

So that your foot may tread in blood,

the tongue of your dogs may have its portion from the enemies, from yourself.

They saw your processions, O God,

the processions of my God, my king, in the sanctuary.

The singers went before them,

followed by those who played psalms,

in the midst of girls beating tambourines.

[Col. 1178A] In the assemblies bless God,

the Lord, from the fountain [Alt. fountains] of Israel.

There Benjamin, the youngest, leads them down [Heb. caused them to descend];

the princes of Judah in their purple [Heb. will stone them];

the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.

Your God has commanded by your strength:

strengthen, O God, what you have wrought in us.

From your temple, which is in Jerusalem,

kings will offer you gifts.

Rebuke the beast of the reed,

the congregation of the strong, with the calves of the peoples

kicking against the wheels [Alt. gates] of silver;

scatter the peoples who desire wars.

Let them offer swiftly [Heb. let envoys come] [Note: [Col. 1178C] Instead of *velociter*, “swiftly,” which Aquila also preferred, the Cistercian manuscript has “richly,” or “with rich gifts.” Some of the older rabbis indeed interpret the gifts mentioned here in the Hebrew as *Chasmanim*. MART.]

from Egypt;

let Ethiopia hasten [Note: [Col. 1178D] Both all our manuscripts and others in Martianay insert here the verb *dare*, “to give”: “let it hasten to give its hands,” and so forth. Perhaps this is the more correct reading; for Symmachus, whose footsteps Saint Jerome usually follows, translates with the verb of giving: *σπευσάτω διδοῦσα χεῖρα*, “let it hasten, giving its hand.” Shortly afterward one Cistercian manuscript has “kings” instead of “kingdoms,” and “sing” instead of “sing psalms.”] to give its hands to God.

Kingdoms [Note: [Col. 1178D] Although the manuscript codices divide these words into two verses, Jerome calls them one verse in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela.] of the earth, sing to God;

sing psalms to the Lord. SELAH.

He who ascends above the heaven of heaven [Note: [Col. 1178D] The Hebrew scholiast prefers “from the beginning” instead of “from the east,” and all our manuscripts likewise prefer it; it is also more harmonious with the Hebrew expression. Shortly afterward, instead of “his voice,” the Cistercian has “of his voice,” and the Regius has “to his voice.”] from the east [Heb. from the beginning]:

behold, he will give his voice, the voice of strength.

[Col. 1178B] Give glory [Heb. strength] to God;

his magnificence is over Israel,

and his strength is in the heavens.

Awesome is God from his sanctuaries [Note: [Col. 1178D] In our manuscripts, “from his sanctuary.”];

the God of Israel himself will give strength

and power to his people. Blessed be God.

TO THE VICTOR, FOR THE LILIES, OF DAVID.

## [LXIX.]

Save me, O God,

for the waters have come up to my soul. [Note: [Col. 1178D] The Cistercian has *introierunt*, “have entered,” as does the Regina manuscript, up to “my soul.”]

I am sunk in deep mud,

and cannot stand;

I have come into the depths of the waters,

and the flood [Heb. wave] has covered me.

I am weary from crying out; my throat is parched;

my eyes fail while waiting for my God.

Those who hate me without cause

are more numerous than the hairs of my head;

those who persecute me unjustly, my enemies,

have grown strong;

what I did not seize, then I repaid.

O God, you know my foolishness,

and my sins are not hidden from you.

Let those who wait for you [Alt. who await you]

not be put to shame because of me,

Lord God of hosts.

Let those who seek you, God of Israel,

not be put to shame because of me.

For on your account I bore reproach;

shame covered my face.

I became a stranger to my brothers

and a foreigner to my mother’s sons [Alt. son].

For zeal for your house consumed me,

and the reproach of those reproaching you fell upon me.

I wept, afflicting my soul with fasting,

and it became a reproach to me.

I put on sackcloth as my garment,

and I became a byword to them.

Those who sat at the gate spoke against me,

and those drinking wine sang [Heb. strong drink].

But my prayer [Note: [Col. 1179D] The Canon of Carcassonne, with its two usual followers—the Augustinian codex of Bordeaux and another of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris—reads differently: “But my prayer is to you, Lord.” MART.] is to you, Lord;

it is a time of reconciliation [Heb. favor].

O God, in the abundance of your mercy,

hear me according to the truth [Note: [Col. 1179D] Our manuscripts unanimously have “according to the truth of your salvation.” MART.] of your salvation.

Rescue me from the mud, so that I do not sink;

deliver me from those who hate me,

and from the depths

[Col. 1179B] of the waters.

Let not the flood of water [Note: [Col. 1179D] Two manuscripts read “the river of water, and let it not swallow,” etc.] cover me,

nor let the deep swallow me;

let the pit not close its mouth over me.

Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is good.

According to the abundance of your mercies, look upon me.

And do not hide your face from your servant,

for I am afflicted; quickly [Heb. hasten], hear me.

Draw near [Note: [Col. 1179D] The Memmian Canon and our San-German manuscript read: “Attend to my soul and redeem it.” Later they have “redeem me” instead of “deliver me.” MART.] to my soul and redeem it;

because of my enemies, deliver me.

You know my reproach,

my shame and my disgrace;

all my enemies are before you.

My heart is broken by reproach,

and I am in despair.

I waited for one who would grieve with me,

but there was none;

and for one who would comfort me,

but I found none.

And they gave gall for my food,

[Col. 1179C] and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “and concerning the wound of your wounded they spoke.” Indeed, the Hebrew itself has this: literally, “and concerning the pain of your wounded they will speak.” But in the manuscript, as also in the printed text, that verse is read and appears, as it seems, to have been added by some scholiast as its gloss.]

Let their table become a snare before them,

and a recompense for their downfall.

Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see,

and always bend their back [Heb. loins].

Pour out your indignation upon them,

and let the fury of your anger seize them.

Let their dwelling become desolate;

let there be no one dwelling in their tents.

For they persecuted the one whom you struck,

and they will speak in order to afflict your wounded [Note: [Col. 1179D] The Cistercian manuscript has, “and concerning the wound of your wounded they spoke.” Indeed, the Hebrew itself has: literally, “and concerning the pain of your wounded they will speak.” But in the manuscript, as also in the printed text, this verse appears, as it seems, to have been added by some scholiast as a gloss.].

Add iniquity upon their iniquity,

and let them not enter into your righteousness.

Let them be erased from the book of the living,

[Col. 1180A] and not be written among the righteous.

But I am poor and sorrowful;

your salvation, O God, has received me. [Note: [Col. 1179D] Our manuscripts have the future, “will receive me.” In the Hebrew it is in the optative sense: “may it receive me, may it lift me up,” and so forth. MART.]

I will praise the name of God in a song,

and magnify him with thanksgiving.

And it will please the Lord more than a young calf [Heb. a bull],

with horns and hooves.

The meek will see and rejoice;

you who seek God, your soul will live [Heb. your heart].

For the Lord has heard the poor,

and has not despised his prisoners.

Let the heavens and the earth praise him,

the seas and everything that moves in them.

For God will save Zion,

and will build the cities of Judah;

they will dwell there and possess it.

And the offspring of his servants will possess it,

and those who love his name will dwell in it.

[Col. 1180B] TO THE VICTOR, OF DAVID, FOR REMEMBRANCE.

## [LXX.]

O God, come to deliver me;

Lord, hasten to help me.

Let those who seek my soul

be confounded and put to shame.

Let those who desire evil for me

turn back and be put to shame.

Let those who say, “Aha! Aha!”

turn back because of the shame they suffer.

Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you,

and let those who love your salvation always say,

“God is magnified.”

But I am needy and poor;

O God, hasten for me.

You are my help and my savior.

Lord, do not delay.

## [LXXI.]

In you, Lord, I have hoped;

let me not be put to shame forever [Heb. for the age].

[Col. 1180C] In your righteousness rescue me and deliver me;

incline your ear to me and save me.

Be for me a strong dwelling, so that I may enter continually.

You commanded that I should be saved;

[Note: [Col. 1180D] The Cistercian manuscript adds another gloss derived almost entirely from the old Latin version: “Be for me in God a protector, so that…” It then has, “command me to be saved,” which is equally acceptable. The printed verses are also retained together.] for you are my rock and my fortress.

My God, save me from the hand of the wicked,

from the hand of the unjust and harmful.

For you are my expectation,

Lord God, my trust since my youth. [Note: [Col. 1180D] The Regius and Corbeiensis manuscripts have, “God the Lord is my trust”; in the Canon of Carcassonne, “Lord, Lord,” and so forth. MART.]

Upon you I have been supported from the womb;

from my mother’s belly you are my protector;

my praise is continually in you. [Note: [Col. 1180D] The Regina manuscript has “always,” incorrectly, if it intended—as it appears—to indicate the *diapsalma*. Shortly afterward the Cistercian and several others in Martianay have “my strongest hope.”]

I have become like a portent to many,

but you are my strongest hope. [Note: [Col. 1180D] Several manuscripts have, “My strongest hope.” MART.]

[Col. 1181A] Let my mouth be filled with your praise,

with your magnificence all day long.

Do not cast me away in the time of old age;

when my strength fails [Alt. is lacking], do not abandon me.

For my enemies have spoken against me,

and those who watched my soul

have taken counsel together,

saying: “God has abandoned him;

pursue him and seize him,

for there is no one to rescue him.” [Note: [Col. 1181D] The Cistercian manuscript adds *eum*, “him.” Joined with the Regius and other manuscripts, it has: “My God, hasten to help me.”]

O God, do not be far from me;

my God, hasten to my help.

Let the adversaries of my soul

be confounded and consumed.

Let those who seek evil for me

be covered with reproach and confusion.

But I will always hope,

and I will add to all [Note: [Col. 1181D] The same manuscripts, in the plural, have “to all your praises.”] your praise.

My mouth will proclaim your righteousness,

your salvation all day long,

for I have not known the letters.

I will enter into the mighty deeds of the Lord God;

I will remember your righteousness alone.

O God, you have taught me from my youth,

and until now I will proclaim your wonders.

And even until old age and gray hairs,

O God, do not abandon me,

until I proclaim your arm to the generation

[Note: [Col. 1181D] The Cistercian manuscript has, “to all who are to come,” and has no more; neither does the Hebrew text. It has “your mighty deeds” in the plural, and “the righteousness of God” instead of “your righteousness, O God,” which is less good.] and to all who are to come your strength.

And your righteousness, O God, reaches to the heights;

how great are the mighty things you have done:

O God, who is like you [Alt. like yours]?

For you have shown us [Note: [Col. 1181D] Our manuscripts have “you have shown me” instead of “us.” A Hebrew exemplar also has *cheri* in the margin instead of , which appears in the text—that is, “you have shown me” instead of “you have shown us.” Consistently, beginning with this verse, it teaches that the singular should be read: “you will revive me” and “you will bring me out.” Likewise, our manuscripts unanimously read “afflictions” instead of “evil things.” Symmachus, whose manner Saint Jerome often followed, also translated substantively *κακώσεις*, “evils” or “afflictions.” It is entirely possible that both Symmachus and the holy Father—for I prefer to regard this as his genuine reading—read in the Hebrew , “afflictions,” instead of the form now containing, with very similar script, “evil things.” MART.] many and evil tribulations;

and turning again, you will revive us,

and once more bring us up from the depths of the earth.

You will increase my greatness,

and turning again, you will comfort me.

[Col. 1181C] But I will give you thanks with the instruments of the psaltery

for your truth, my God;

I will sing to you on the lyre, Holy One of Israel.

My lips will rejoice when I sing [Heb. sing psalms] to you,

and my soul, which you have redeemed.

Moreover, my tongue will meditate on your righteousness all day long,

because those seeking evil for me

have been confounded and disgraced.

[Note: [Col. 1182D] In two manuscripts, those of the Augustinian monks of Bordeaux and of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris, we find this title: “Verses of Solomon.” MART. —Our manuscripts prefer “Of Solomon.” Martianay found “verses” added in others.]

TO SOLOMON.

## [LXXII.]

O God, give your judgment to the king,

and your righteousness to the king’s son.

He will judge your people in righteousness,

and your poor in judgment.

The mountains will take up peace for the people,

[Col. 1182A] and the hills righteousness.

He will judge the poor of the people;

he will save the children of the poor [Alt. the poor],

and crush the oppressor.

And they will fear you as long as the sun endures,

and beyond the moon, throughout generations of generations.

He will descend like rain upon fleece,

like drops that water the earth.

In his days righteousness will spring forth [Heb. the righteous],

and an abundance of peace until the moon is no more.

And he will rule from sea to sea,

and from the river to the ends [Note: [Col. 1182D] The Regina manuscript adds, “to the ends of the world.”] of the earth.

Before him the Ethiopians will fall,

and his enemies will lick the dust.

The kings of Tharsis and the islands will offer gifts;

the kings of Arabia and Saba [Heb. Saba] will bring tribute.

And all kings will adore him;

all nations will serve him.

For he will rescue the poor from the powerful,

and the needy who has no helper.

[Col. 1182B] He will spare the needy and the poor,

and save the souls of the poor.

He will redeem their souls from usury and iniquity [Alt. their soul],

and their blood will be precious in his sight. [Note: [Col. 1182D] The Cistercian omits the pronoun *eorum*, “their,” here, although it is present in the Hebrew text.]

And he will live, and there will be given to him of the gold of Saba;

and they will pray for him continually;

all day long they will bless him.

There will be memorable grain in the land;

it will rise high on the tops of the mountains;

its fruit will be like that of Lebanon,

and they will flourish from the city like the grass of the earth.

His name will endure forever [Heb. for the age];

his name will persist before the sun [Heb. beyond the sun].

And they will be blessed in him;

all nations will call him blessed.

Blessed be the Lord God, the God of Israel,

who [Note: [Col. 1182D] Three of our manuscripts have, “who made,” and so forth. MART.],

[Col. 1182C] and the whole earth will be filled with his glory: amen and amen.

THE PRAYERS OF DAVID, SON OF JESSE, HAVE BEEN COMPLETED [Note: [Col. 1182D] In the printed books these words are wrongly joined to the title of the following Psalm; Jerome explicitly censures this error in his letter to Marcella concerning the death of Lea. He says: “When at about the third hour of the present day we had begun to read the seventy-second Psalm, that is, the beginning of the third book, and were compelled to explain that part of the title itself belonged to the end of the second book and part to the beginning of the third book: namely, that ‘The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have ended’ was the conclusion of the preceding book, while ‘A Psalm of Asaph’ was the beginning of the following one,” and so forth. MART. —These same manuscripts, as Saint Jerome himself elsewhere does, have *Jesse* instead of *Isai*.] A SONG [Heb. PSALM] OF ASAPH.

## [LXXIII.]

Yet God is good to Israel,

to those who are pure in heart.

But my feet nearly stumbled;

my steps almost slipped.

For I was jealous of the wicked,

seeing the peace of sinners.

For they have no concern for their death,

and their foundations are firm.

They are not in human toil,

and they will not be scourged with other people.

[Col. 1183A] Therefore they were nourished unto pride [Note: [Col. 1183C] The Cistercian manuscript, apparently because of the worn condition of the letters, seems here to prefer: “Therefore pride suffocated them.” This interpretation is, in our view, the most satisfactory of all. MART.];

they surrounded themselves with iniquity.

Their eyes proceeded from fatness;

the thoughts of their heart went beyond measure.

They mocked and spoke maliciously of oppression,

speaking from on high.

They set their mouth against heaven,

and their tongue walked through the earth.

Therefore his people will turn here,

and every fullness will be found in them.

And they said: “How does God know,

and is there knowledge in the Most High?”

Behold, these are the wicked;

prospering in the age, they have multiplied riches.

Then have I cleansed my heart in vain,

and washed my hands in innocence?

And I have been scourged all day,

and my correction comes in the mornings.

And I said: If I speak in this way,

behold, I would have abandoned the generation of your children.

[Col. 1183B] And I considered in order to understand this;

it is labor in my eyes.

Until I enter the sanctuaries [Alt. sanctuary] of God,

I will understand their end [Note: [Col. 1183C] The printed and manuscript books read with the connective particle, “and understanding at their end.” This is acceptable, unless Jerome had not taught Sunnia and Fretela that it should be read without the conjunction. Thus he wrote to them: “Regarding what you say you have read in the Greek, ‘and understanding,’ the conjunction here is superfluous.” MART.].

Nevertheless, you placed them on slippery ground;

you cast them down into destruction.

How suddenly they have been devastated;

they have failed and been consumed as though they did not exist. [Note: [Col. 1183D] The Cistercian manuscript has, “as those who do not exist.”]

Like a dream upon waking,

Lord, in the city you will reduce their image to nothing. [Note: [Col. 1183D] The same manuscript, together with the Regina manuscript, inserts *tua*, “your,” here, following the old Latin version.]

For my heart was contracted,

and my kidneys [Note: [Col. 1183D] Our San-German manuscript and the Memmian Canon have, “and my reins were dissolved.” The Canon of Carcassonne and two other copies also read “reins,” and “my reins were like smoking fire.” MART.] were like smoking fire.

But I was foolish and ignorant;

I became like a beast before you. [Alt. I was.]

And I am always with you,

and you hold my right hand.

You will lead me by your counsel,

and afterward receive me into glory.

[Col. 1183C] What is there for me in heaven,

and besides you what did I desire [Alt. did I not desire] on earth?

My flesh and my heart have failed;

the strength of my heart and my portion is God forever [Heb. for the age].

For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish;

you have destroyed every one who commits fornication away from you.

But for me, drawing near to God is good;

I have placed my hope in the Lord God,

that I may proclaim all your announcements [Note: [Col. 1183D] The Canon of Carcassonne and the Vatican codex retain in the text this marginal scholion: “that I may proclaim all your commands.” I had long ago thought that I had read Saint Jerome, the most holy Doctor of the Church, saying this in my notes on his letter to Sunnia and Fretela; but after examining very many manuscripts I have changed my opinion, having found the copyist of the Canon of Carcassonne—who is unreliable and rash in many places—putting annotations of the scholiasts into the body of the text without hesitation. The Corbeiensis manuscript, moreover, reads not “your proclamations” but “your preachings,” although both “announcement” and “preaching” convey the same meaning. MART.].

ERUDITION [Note: [Col. 1184C] Some manuscripts have “The erudition of Asaph”; the Carcassonne manuscript, “The learned Asaph”; that of Saint Michael, “The prayer of Asaph.” MART. —Three of our manuscripts have *eruditiones*, “teachings”; others in Martianay have *eruditionis*, “of teaching.”] OF ASAPH.

## [LXXIV.]

Why, O God, have you rejected us forever?

Will your fury smoke [Alt. smoked] against the flock of your pasture?

Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning,

[Note: [Col. 1184C] Some manuscripts place the conjunction *et*, “and,” before this; then they read *montem*, “the mountain,” instead of *montem* in the other form; finally, one manuscript adds *tuo*, “your,” after “sanctuary” in the second verse.] you redeemed the rod [Heb. scepter] of your inheritance:

Mount Zion, in which you dwelt.

The exaltation of your feet has been destroyed to the end;

the enemy has done every evil in the sanctuary.

Your enemies roared in the midst of your covenant;

they set up their signs as a trophy.

They made their signs known at the entrance above;

in the thicket of the trees, with axes.

[Col. 1184B] And now they have together carved its sculptures [Alt. carvings];

with a double axe and with chisels they scraped them away. [Note: [Col. 1184D] Jerome concludes the frequently cited letter in this way: “*Λαξευτήριον*, for which the Latin translator rendered *asciam*, ‘axe,’ we interpret as a kind of tool with which stones are hewn. Finally, translating from the Hebrew, we said: ‘And now they have together scraped away its carvings, with a double axe and with chiseling tools.’ Thus *λαξευτήριον* can be called a carving tool.” MART.]

They set fire to your sanctuary;

they profaned to the ground the dwelling [Note: [Col. 1184D] All our manuscripts read “dwelling” instead of “tabernacle.”] of your name.

They said in their hearts, their posterity altogether:

“They have burned all the solemn feasts of God in the land.” [Note: [Col. 1184D] Jerome discussed this verse at greater length in his reply to Sunnia and Fretela. See our annotations in the preface to Saint Jerome. MART.]

We have not seen our signs;

there is no longer a prophet,

and there is no one among us who knows how long.

How long, O God, will the adversary reproach [Alt. reproached]?

Will the enemy blaspheme [Alt. blasphemed] your name forever?

Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand?

Bring it forth from the midst of your bosom [Note: [Col. 1184D] The Carnutensis, Regius, and Corbeiensis manuscripts have, “to the midst of the sign, then consume.” Three others read, “consuming.” MART. —The Greek reads most correctly, “to the end,” which agrees well with “unto completion,” “unto the end,” “continually,” “always,” “without interruption,” and similar expressions.];

consume.

But God is our king from the beginning;

he works [Alt. has worked] salvation in the midst of the earth.

You shattered the sea by your strength;

[Col. 1184C] You crushed the heads of dragons in the waters.

You shattered the heads of Leviathan;

you gave him as food [Alternative: for food] to the people of the Ethiopians.

You split open the spring and the torrent [Alternative: springs and torrents];

[Col. 1185A] you dried up mighty rivers.

The day is yours, and the night is yours;

you established the luminary [Alternative: luminaries] and the sun.

You fixed all the boundaries of the earth;

you formed summer and winter.

Remember this:

the enemy has reproached the Lord,

and a foolish people has blasphemed your name.

Do not hand over to beasts the soul instructed in your law;

do not forget the lives of your poor forever.

Look to the covenant,

because the dark places of the earth are filled with habitations of iniquity.

[Note: Two of our manuscripts add here the word *subruptae* (“broken down”), which nevertheless has the appearance of an inept glossator.]

Let the crushed and confounded person not return [Alternative: and not];

the needy and poor will praise your name.

Arise, God; judge your cause.

Remember the reproach brought against you

all day long by the fool.

Do not forget the voices of your enemies;

[Col. 1185B] the tumult of your adversaries rises continually.

**FOR THE VICTOR: DO NOT DESTROY; A PSALM, A SONG OF ASAPH.**

[Note: The same manuscripts, and others in Martianay’s possession, insert the particle *ut* (“that is”): “For the victor, that you may not destroy,” and so forth.]

**[LXXV.]** We will confess you, God;

we will confess you, and, according to your name,

they will proclaim your wonders.

When I receive the appointed time [Hebrew: the decree],

I will judge with equity.

The earth will be dissolved with all its inhabitants;

I weighed its pillars. **EVER.**

I said to those acting wickedly, “Do not act wickedly,”

and to the ungodly, “Do not lift up your horn.”

Do not lift your horn on high;

do not speak with an arrogant neck.

For neither from the east nor from the west,

nor from the desert of the mountains.

But God is judge:

he humbles one and exalts another.

[Col. 1185C] For a cup is in the hand of the Lord [Note: Our manuscripts have more fully: “In the hand of the Lord it is, and mixed with unmixed wine to the full.”],

and it is mixed to the full with unmixed wine,

and he will pour from it;

yet its dregs all the ungodly of the earth will drink.

But I will proclaim forever;

I will sing praise [Hebrew: psalm] to the God of Jacob.

And I will break all the horns of the ungodly;

the horns of the righteous will be exalted.

[Col. 1186A] **FOR THE VICTOR, IN PSALMS [Hebrew: songs]: A PSALM, A SONG OF ASAPH.**

[Note: The manuscripts of the Queen’s collection, Corbie, and the Sorbonne inscribe it differently: “For the victor, in the Psalms, a song, a composition of Asaph.” Four others follow them, except that instead of “For the victor, in the Psalms,” they corruptly read “For the victor, a psalm,” and so forth. MART. —Again, all our manuscripts and others in Martianay’s possession read: “For the victor, in the Psalms, a song, a composition of Asaph.” Then, immediately in the first word of the text, one Cistercian manuscript has *Cognoscetur* (“will be known”) instead of *Cognoscitur* (“is known”).]

**[LXXVI.]** God is known in Judaea;

his name is great in Israel.

And his tabernacle will be in Salem,

and his dwelling place in Zion.

There he shattered the flying things of the bow [Hebrew: the bow of the devil],

[Note: In Hebrew it is *rischphe casceth*, which Jerome aptly renders “the flying things,” that is, the arrows of the bow. Nor is it unsuitable that the scholiast wrote “the bow of the devil,” because in Habakkuk 3:5 or 15 in our edition, *reseph* is rendered “devil.” MART.]

the shield, the sword, and the battle. **EVER.**

You are magnificently radiant

from the mountains of captivity.

The stouthearted have been plundered;

they have slept their sleep,

and none of all the men of strength found their hands.

At your rebuke, God of Jacob,

both chariot [Alternative: and chariot] and horse fell into deep sleep.

You are terrible,

and who can stand before you

from the time of your anger?

From heaven you will proclaim [Hebrew: caused to be heard] judgment.

The earth feared and was silent.

[Col. 1186B] When God rises for judgment,

to save all the meek of the earth. **EVER.**

[Note: Five manuscripts—Memmian, Saint-Germain, the Queen’s, Corbie, and the Sorbonne—have *moerorem* (“sorrow”) instead of *iram* (“anger”): “For the sorrow of man . . . you will be girded with the remnants of sorrow.” MART. —Of our manuscripts, one Cistercian likewise prefers *moeror* here for *ira*, and shortly afterward *moeroris* for *irarum*. The Regius has *irae* (“of anger”) in this latter place only, instead of *irarum*. In Hebrew the word is one that properly signifies fury.]

The anger of man will confess you;

with the remnants of your wrath you will gird yourself.

Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God,

all who surround him;

let them bring gifts to the Terrible One,

to him who removes the breath of princes,

to the Terrible One among the kings of the earth.

**FOR THE VICTOR, OVER JEDUTHUN: A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript has “through Jeduthun”; two Cistercian manuscripts and two others preserved by Martianay have “for Jeduthun.”]

**[LXXVII.]** With my voice I cried to God;

with my voice I cried to God, and he heard me [Hebrew: and gave ear to me].

In the day of my tribulation I sought the Lord;

my hand is stretched out by night and does not cease.

My soul refused consolation;

remembering God, I was troubled.

I spoke within myself,

and my spirit failed. **EVER.**

[Col. 1186C] I restrained the suspicion of my eyes [Hebrew: you seized the vigilance of my eyes].

I was astonished and did not speak.

I considered the ancient days,

the years of the ages.

[Note: Three manuscripts have “and the former years.” Shortly afterward they read *scopebam* (“I swept”) instead of *scrutabar* (“I searched”). Thus, indeed, the holy Father says that he translated in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, with a large number of our manuscripts agreeing at that passage; whatever Martianay later thought, who now wishes *scrutabar* to be restored there. MART.]

I remembered my psalms [Hebrew: my song] in the night;

with my heart I spoke,

and I searched my spirit.

[Note: The printed books and the Corbie manuscript read, “I swept my spirit.” I remember having published this reading in the *Prodromus of Saint Jerome*, and no other reading is firmly retained by the manuscript copies of the letter to Sunnia and Fretela, to which we ought to have adhered until we obtained better Hebrew-Latin Psalters of this kind. In seven older and better manuscripts, however, it is written, “I searched my spirit.” This too is sufficiently indicated as the correct reading by the holy Doctor, when he says in the aforementioned letter that Symmachus and the Fifth Edition translated *anēreunōn*, that is, “I searched thoroughly” or “I sought.” The Regius manuscript of the Psalms alone reads here, “I concealed my spirit.” MART.]

Will the Lord then cast us off forever [Hebrew: for ages],

and will he not again be gracious?

[Col. 1187A] Will he then have completed his mercy to the end?

[Note: One Cistercian manuscript has *complebit* (“he will complete”), and afterward, “he will bring the word to an end for a generation.”]

Will the word be brought to an end from generation to generation?

[Note: All manuscripts except the Sorbonne manuscript have this form; the latter, together with the printed editions, reads “from generation to generation.” MART.]

Has God forgotten to have mercy,

or will he complete his mercies [Hebrew: acts of steadfast love] in anger? **EVER.**

And I said, “This is my weakness:

the change [Hebrew: the years] of the right hand of the Most High.”

I will remember the thoughts of the Lord,

remembering your ancient wonders.

And I will meditate on all your works,

and I will speak of your inventions.

O God, your way is in the holy place.

[Note: All our manuscripts prefer *Sanctuario* (“sanctuary”) here to *Sancto* (“holy place”).]

Who is a great god like God?

You are the God who performs wonders,

making your power known among the peoples.

You redeemed your people by your arm,

the sons of Jacob and Joseph. **EVER.**

[Col. 1187B] The waters saw you, O God;

the waters saw you and writhed [Alternative: omit *te*, “you”],

and the abysses were shaken.

The clouds poured out waters;

the clouds gave forth a voice,

and your arrows sped about.

The voice of your thunder was in the wheel;

your lightning flashes appeared [Hebrew: shone] upon the world.

The earth trembled and was shaken.

[Note: In the Cistercian manuscript: “The earth was shaken and gave birth,” a reading which, if it has ever pleased any interpreter, I do not know. The Hebrew certainly signifies being moved.]

Your way was in the sea,

and your paths in many waters,

and your footprints were not recognized.

You led your people like a flock [Hebrew: sheep],

by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

**OF INSTRUCTION [Alternative: INSTRUCTIONS], OF ASAPH.**

**[LXXVIII.]** Listen, my people, to my law;

incline your ears to the words of my mouth.

I will open my mouth in a parable;

[Col. 1187C] I will speak ancient riddles.

Things that we have heard and known,

which our fathers told us.

They were not hidden from their children,

from the generation that followed,

as they proclaimed the praises of the Lord,

his power, and the wonders that he performed.

He established a testimony in Jacob [Alternative: omit “in”],

and set a law in Israel,

which he commanded our fathers

to teach their children,

so that the succeeding generation might know,

the children yet to be born might rise up,

and tell their own children.

[Col. 1188A] So that they might place their hope in God,

and not forget the kinships [Hebrew: inventions] of God,

and might keep his commandments.

And [Alternative: so that] they would not be like their fathers,

a crooked and provoking generation,

a generation that did not prepare its heart,

and whose spirit did not believe God.

The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow [Alternative: and bending],

turned their backs on the day of battle.

They did not keep God’s covenant [Note: These same manuscripts add “his”; shortly afterward they read *commutationum* (“changes”) instead of *cogitationum* (“thoughts”).],

they refused to walk in his law,

and they forgot his thoughts [Hebrew: inventions],

and his wonders that he had shown them.

Before their fathers he performed wonders,

in the land of Egypt, in the region of Tanis.

He divided [Hebrew: tore open] the sea and led them through;

he made the waters stand like a heap [Hebrew: in a skin].

And he led them in a cloud by day,

[Col. 1188B] and all night in the light of fire.

He split the rock in the wilderness,

and gave them drink as though from great abysses.

And he brought streams out of the rock,

and drew out waters like rivers.

And they continued to sin against him,

so as to provoke the Most High in the trackless place.

[Note: In the Saint-Germain and Memmian Canons: “And they provoked the Most High,” and so forth. MART.]

And they tested God in their hearts,

asking for food for their souls.

And speaking against God,

they said, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?”

[Note: Again these manuscripts read, “Can God set a table in the wilderness?”]

Behold, he struck the rock, and waters flowed,

and torrents overflowed.

“Can he also give bread,

or prepare meat for his people?”

Therefore the Lord heard, and did not delay;

[Note: Three copies of the Canon, as well as the Vatican, Augustinian, Bordeaux, and Saint Michael manuscripts, read without the negation: “Therefore the Lord heard and delayed.” And in Psalm 130—according to the Vulgate, Psalm 59—three of them have: “God heard and delayed.” The Hebrew reads *vaiyith‘abar*, “and he became angry,” but “and he delayed” is not an inappropriate interpretation, since to delay is also to scatter, tear apart, and disturb. Jerome seems to understand that God did not delay his anger, but, having heard the murmuring of the Hebrew people, immediately inflicted punishments and blows upon the unbelievers. MART.]

and fire was kindled against Jacob,

and wrath rose up against Israel.

[Col. 1188C] For they did not believe in God,

[Note: The word *in* is absent in our manuscripts. Shortly afterward, *praecepit* (“he commanded”) is read for *praecipit* (“he commands”).]

nor did they trust in his salvation.

And he commanded the clouds above,

and opened the doors of heaven.

And he rained manna upon them so that they might eat,

[Note: One manuscript of the Queen’s collection has *man* for *manna*, evidently because it is the Hebrew name.]

and gave them the grain of heaven.

Man ate the bread of the mighty;

he sent them food in abundance.

He removed the east wind from heaven,

and brought in the south wind by his strength.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript has “by his force” instead of “by his strength,” and shortly afterward has *carnes* (“meats”) in the plural.]

And he rained flesh upon them like dust,

and winged birds like the sand of the sea.

And they fell in the midst of their camp [Note: More closely following the Hebrew idiom, our manuscripts read in the lesser number, “of his camp” and “of his tents.” The Hebrew has the forms corresponding to these expressions.],

around their tents.

[Col. 1189A] And they ate and were filled exceedingly,

and he brought them what they desired.

They were not deprived of their desire [Hebrew: they had not satisfied their desire],

while their food was still in their mouths.

[Note: This entire clause is found in the Vatican manuscript in the following form: “They had not yet satisfied their desire, while their food was still in their mouths.” The copyist of the Carcassonne Canon therefore left the former verse in a marginal gloss, but inserted the latter into the text. The Saint-Germain Canon, together with the other manuscripts—the Regius, Corbie, Chartres, and Sorbonne—retains Jerome’s pure reading, which we have printed, and the Memmian agrees with them. MART.]

Then the wrath of God rose up against them,

and killed their fat ones,

and struck down the chosen men of Israel.

In all these things they sinned again,

and did not believe in his wonders.

And he consumed their days in vanity,

and their years swiftly.

When he killed them, then they sought him [Alternative: sought after him];

they returned and rose early to God.

And they remembered that God was their strength,

and that God Most High was their redeemer.

And they flattered him with their mouths,

and lied to him with their tongues.

[Col. 1189B] But their heart was not steadfast with him,

nor did they remain in his covenant.

Yet he, being merciful,

would be gracious toward iniquity and would not destroy [Note: It appears that the holy Father added the pronoun *eos* (“them”) here. Thus he answers Sunnia and Fretela: “You say that *eos* is not present in the Greek, and that is true; but we, so that the sentence would not remain incomplete, completed the Latin expression in accordance with its idiom.” Unless, perhaps, he is to be understood as speaking there only of his own translation from the Greek.]

And many times he turned away his anger,

and did not stir up all his fury.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript has: “But he remembered,” and so forth.]

And he remembered that they were flesh,

a breath that goes away and does not return.

How often they provoked him in the wilderness,

and grieved him in the desert.

And they turned back and tested God,

and provoked the Holy One of Israel.

They did not remember his hand,

the day [Alternative: of the day] when he redeemed them from the oppressor.

He performed his signs in Egypt,

and his wonders in the region of Tanis.

He turned their rivers into blood,

and their streams, so that they could not drink.

He sent upon them every kind of fly, to devour them,

[Col. 1189C] and frogs, to destroy them.

He gave their crops to the caterpillar,

and their labor to the locust.

He killed their vineyards with hail,

and their sycamores with frost.

He delivered their pastures to the hail,

and their cattle to winged creatures [Hebrew: demons].

He sent upon them the anger of his fury:

indignation, threat, and distress;

a mission of evil angels.

He made a path for his fury;

[Note: The same manuscript has “the path of your fury,” and “he spared death,” and so forth.]

he did not spare their souls from death,

and he delivered their living creatures to pestilence.

And he struck every firstborn in Egypt,

the beginning of birth-pains [Hebrew: pain]

in the tents of Ham.

And he took away his people like sheep,

and led them like a flock in the wilderness.

[Col. 1190A] And he brought them out in confidence and without fear;

but the sea covered their enemies.

And he brought them to the boundary of his holy place,

this mountain which his right hand possessed.

[Note: See what we observed concerning this passage in the letter to Sunnia and Fretela. The conjecture that we proposed there for supplementing the holy Father’s text appears more probable from this translation.]

And he drove out the nations before them,

and made them possess an inheritance by a measuring line,

and settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.

And they tested and provoked God Most High,

and did not keep his testimonies.

And they turned back and transgressed like their fathers;

they were bent like a useless bow.

And they provoked him in their high places,

and stirred him to jealousy with their carved images.

God heard, and did not delay,

and utterly rejected Israel.

And he abandoned the tabernacle at Shiloh,

the tent that he had placed among human beings.

And he handed over his strength to captivity [Note: Our manuscripts have “his glory” instead of “his strength,” and so forth],

and his beauty into the hand of the enemy.

[Col. 1190B] And he shut up his people under the sword,

and did not delay regarding his inheritance.

Fire devoured their young men,

and their maidens were not mourned.

Their priests fell by the sword,

and their widows were not wept for.

[Note: Four manuscripts corrupted by scholia have: “And their widows, or his widows, did not weep.” MART.]

And the Lord awoke as one sleeping,

like a mighty man after the wine-drinking.

And he struck his enemies backward;

he gave them everlasting reproach [Note: The Queen’s manuscripts have “he gave them” instead of “he gave it to them.”].

And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph,

and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.

But he chose the tribe of Judah,

Mount Zion, which he loved.

And he built his sanctuary like that of a unicorn [Alternative: *monoceroton*],

[Note: Here too it will be worthwhile to hear the holy Doctor discussing the interpretation of this passage in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, although there he says nothing about this particular translation of his from the Hebrew.]

and founded it like the earth forever.

And he chose David his servant,

and took him from the sheepfolds.

[Col. 1190C] He brought him from following the ewes,

to shepherd Jacob his people,

[Note: Three manuscripts read “to shepherd Jacob . . . and Israel,” without the preposition *in*.]

and Israel his inheritance.

He shepherded them with an upright heart,

and by the prudence of his hands he guided them.

[Note: Saint Jerome observes in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela that the Septuagint does not have *en tē synesei* in the singular, as they supposed, but *en tais synesesi(n)*, which means “understandings.” We have especially confirmed this from a threefold Sorbonne manuscript Psalter, where the Greek text of this passage is represented in Latin letters as follows: “Ke en tes sunesesin ton chiron autu odigisen autus,” that is, καὶ ἐν ταῖς συνέσεσιν τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ ὡδήγησεν αὐτούς, “and by the understandings of his hands he guided them.” The Hebrew likewise has the plural number, *bathbunoth*, or *bithbunoth*, meaning “in understandings.” Jerome, however, following Aquila, who reads *kai en phronēsei*, translates here in his Hebrew Psalter “in prudence,” attending to the sense of Scripture rather than slavishly to the words. MART.]

**A SONG [Hebrew: A PSALM] OF ASAPH.**

**[LXXIX.]** God, the nations have entered into your inheritance;

they have defiled your holy temple;

they have made Jerusalem into heaps of stones [Alternative: heaps].

They have given the corpses of your servants

as food [Alternative: foods] to the birds of heaven,

the flesh of your holy ones [Hebrew: merciful ones] to the beasts of the earth.

They have poured out their blood

like water around Jerusalem,

and there was no one to bury them.

[Col. 1191A] We have become a reproach to our neighbors,

a mockery and derision to those who are around us.

How long, Lord, will you be angry forever?

Will your jealousy burn like fire?

Pour out your fury upon the nations that have not known you,

and upon kingdoms that have not called upon your name.

For they have devoured Jacob,

and laid waste his beauty.

Do not remember our former iniquities;

let your mercies quickly [Hebrew: hasten to] overtake us,

for we have become exceedingly weak.

Help us, God our savior,

for the glory of your name [Alternative: add “and”];

deliver us,

and be gracious toward our sins for your name’s sake.

[Note: Four manuscripts have “God our Savior.” The Saint-Germain Canon and the Memmian have: “Jesus our Savior.” Consequently, the marginal gloss is retained in the text at this place in the Carcassonne, Augustinian, Bordeaux, and Saint Michael manuscripts, because of the word “glory,” and so forth. MART.]

Why will the nations say, “Where is their God?”

Let the vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been poured out

become known among the nations before our eyes.

[Col. 1191B] Let the groaning of the prisoners enter before you,

according to the greatness of your arm;

preserve the sons of destruction.

And repay our neighbors sevenfold in their bosom

the reproach with which they reproached you, Lord.

For we are your people,

and the sheep of your pasture;

we will confess you forever,

from generation to generation

we will proclaim your praise.

[Note: These same manuscripts have “and the flock of your pasture,” then “forever” instead of “for an age,” and finally “we will praise your praises.”]

**FOR THE VICTOR, FOR THE LILIES [Note: The Queen’s manuscript has “for the lilies of testimony.” I omit the fact that several manuscripts plainly read *filiis* (“sons”) instead of *liliis* (“lilies”) here and elsewhere, an obvious scribal error.], A TESTIMONY, A SONG OF ASAPH [Hebrew: A PSALM].**

**[LXXX.]** You who shepherd Israel, listen [Hebrew: Shepherd of Israel, give ear],

you who lead Joseph like sheep;

you who sit upon the cherubim, reveal yourself.

Before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh,

stir up your strength,

and come to save us.

[Col. 1191C] God, restore us,

and show your face, and we will be saved.

Lord God of hosts,

how long will you burn against the prayer of your people?

You fed them with bread of tears,

and gave them to drink tears threefold.

[Note: Thus the Carcassonne Canon and the Augustinian-Bordeaux manuscript. The others, following the Septuagint, read “You fed us . . . you gave us to drink,” or “You will feed us,” and so forth. MART.]

You made us a contention [Alternative: contradiction] to our neighbors,

and our enemies mocked us.

God of hosts, restore us,

and show [Hebrew: illumine] your face, and we will be saved.

You brought a vine out of Egypt;

you drove out the nations and planted it.

You prepared a place before it,

and established its roots, and it filled the land.

The mountains were covered by its shadow [Alternative: under its shadow],

and its branches [Alternative: its branch] were like the cedars of God.

It stretched its shoots to the sea,

and its seedlings to the river [Alternative: its seedlings].

Why have you destroyed its wall [Hebrew: hedge]?

All who pass along the way have gleaned it.

The boar from the forest has ravaged it,

and all the beasts of the field have fed upon it.

God of hosts, return, I beg you;

look down from heaven and see,

and visit this vine,

and the root that your right hand planted,

and the son whom you strengthened for yourself.

Burned with fire and ruined,

[Note: Our earlier printed editions also prefer the manuscripts’ reading, “and stripped of branches,” instead of “ruined.” Martianay’s editions and the Corbie manuscript read *diramatam* or *deramatam*, “stripped of branches.”]

at the rebuke of your face let it perish.

Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand,

and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself.

And we will not depart from you;

you will revive us,

[Col. 1192B] and we will be called by your name.

Lord God of hosts, restore us;

show [Hebrew: illumine] your face, and we will be saved.

**FOR THE VICTOR, IN THE WINEPRESSES, OF ASAPH.**

**[LXXXI.]** Praise God, our strength [Hebrew: Sing to God, our strength];

shout joyfully to the God of Jacob.

Take up a song and give the tambourine,

the beautiful lyre with the psaltery.

Blow the trumpet at the new moon,

and in the middle [Hebrew: on the throne] of the table,

on the day of our solemnity.

For it is a statute for Israel,

a judgment for the God of Jacob.

[Note: Again, the Cistercian manuscript has “and a judgment of the God of Jacob.”]

He established a testimony in Joseph [Hebrew: Joseph],

when he went out from the land of Egypt.

I heard a language that I did not know.

[Col. 1192C] I removed his shoulder from the burden;

his hands withdrew from the basket.

In tribulation you called upon me [Alternative: add “me”], and I delivered you.

I answered you in the hidden place of thunder;

I tested you at the waters of contradiction. **EVER.**

Hear, my people, and I will testify against you [Alternative: I testify to you];

Israel, if you will hear me.

Let there be no foreign god among you,

and do not worship an alien god [Hebrew: strange god].

I am the Lord your God [Alternative: omit “your”],

who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

Open wide your mouth,

and I will fill it.

But my people did not hear my voice,

and Israel did not believe [Hebrew: consent to] me.

So I let him go according to the stubbornness of his heart;

they will walk in their own counsels.

If only my people had heard me,

if Israel had walked in my ways.

I would have humbled his enemies to nothing,

and turned my hand against his foes.

Those who hate the Lord will deny him,

and their time will endure forever.

And he fed them with the fat of wheat,

and satisfied them with honey from the rock.

[Note: The Carcassonne Canon reads in the singular: “And he fed him . . . and satisfied him with honey from the rock.” Others likewise read, “with honey from the rock.” MART.]

[Note: Two of our manuscripts have “with honey from the rock.”]

**A SONG [Hebrew: A PSALM] OF ASAPH.**

**[LXXXII.]** God stood in the assembly of God;

in the midst of the gods he judges.

How long will you judge unjustly,

and show favor to the faces of the ungodly? **EVER.**

Judge for the poor and the orphan;

do justice for the needy and the impoverished.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript has the single word “justify.”]

Rescue the needy and the poor;

deliver them from the hand of the ungodly.

[Col. 1193B] They do not know and do not understand;

they walk in darkness.

All the foundations of the earth will be shaken.

I said, “You are gods,

and all of you are sons of the Most High.”

[Note: With the pronoun *vos* (“you”), the Cistercian manuscript begins the next verse: “You, therefore, will die like Adam,” as does the Greek Alexandrian exemplar. The Queen’s manuscript omits this pronoun.]

Therefore you will die like Adam,

and like one of the princes you will fall.

Arise, God; judge the earth,

because you will inherit all the nations.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript has: “because you will inherit all the nations.”]

**A SONG, A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

**[LXXXIII.]** God, do not keep silent for yourself;

do not be silent.

[Note: *Tibi* (“for yourself”) means “let there not be silence for you,” that is, “do not be silent,” simply rendered. The Queen’s manuscript omits *tibi*. The Cistercian has: “Lord, do not keep silent, and do not be silent.”]

And do not rest, God.

For behold, your enemies have made a tumult,

and those who hate you have lifted up their head [Alternative: raised it].

They have plotted wickedly against your people,

and have entered into counsel against your secret place.

They said, “Come, let us wipe them out as a nation,

and let the memory of the name of Israel be no more.”

For they conspired together in their heart.

[Note: All our manuscripts omit *nomen* (“name”) and more closely follow the Greek, which has *ebouleusanto*, and the older translation derived from it, “they thought.”]

[Col. 1193C] Against you they made a covenant.

The tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites,

Moab and the Hagrites,

Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek,

Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre.

Assyria also came [Hebrew: joined] with them;

they became an arm for the sons of Lot. **EVER.**

Do to them as to Midian,

as to Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon.

They were crushed at En-dor;

they became like dung on the ground.

Set their leaders like Oreb and Zeeb,

like Zebah and Zalmunna, all their princes,

who said, “Let us possess for ourselves

the beauty of God.”

[Col. 1194A] My God, make them like a wheel,

like straw before the face of the wind.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript does not have “before the face”; shortly afterward it reads “the forest will burn” instead of “it burns,” and so forth. Finally, when joined with the Queen’s manuscript, it has “pursue them and trouble them.”]

As fire burns the forest,

and as flame consumes the mountains,

so you will pursue them in your storm,

and in your whirlwind you will trouble them.

Fill their faces with disgrace,

and they will seek your name, Lord.

Let them be confounded and troubled forever [Hebrew: eternally];

let them be ashamed and perish.

And let them know that you alone are named Lord,

Most High over all the earth.

**FOR THE VICTOR, FOR THE WINEPRESSES [Note: Our manuscripts read in the singular, “for the winepress.”], A SONG OF THE SONS OF KORAH [Hebrew: A PSALM].**

**[LXXXIV.]** How beloved are your tabernacles,

Lord of hosts!

My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord;

my heart and my flesh will praise God, God living.
