[Note: Thus the two Saint-Germain Canons and the Memmian. This can indeed be read from the Hebrew *yerannenu el el hai*, where the word *el* is doubled, repeating the name of God. Modern interpreters wish the first *el* to be a preposition, supplying the segol vowel beneath the aleph with the Masoretic pointing; hence they translate, “they will rejoice toward the living God.” MART. —The Cistercian manuscript has “God” only once. Martianay also notes that the Hebrew reads the word twice, one of the two, with the segol point beneath it, being taken as the preposition “to” by the modern interpreters, as also by the Septuagint before the Masoretes were born.]

Indeed, the sparrow [Alternative: bird] has found a house,

and the bird [Alternative: sparrow] a nest for itself,

where it may place its young.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, together with the printed books, has *ut reponat* (“that it may place”). Others also have *reponat*; but with *ubi* as an adverb, it is “where it may place.” MART.]

Your altars, Lord of hosts,

my king and my God.

Blessed are those who dwell in your house;

they will still praise you. **EVER.**

Blessed is the man whose strength is in you;

paths are in his heart.

Passing through the valley of weeping,

they will make it a spring;

the teacher will also be clothed with blessing.

They will go from strength to strength;

they will appear before God in Zion.

Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer;

listen [Hebrew: give ear], God of Jacob. **EVER.**

Look upon our shield [Note: The Queen’s manuscript repeats the word *vide* (“look”) twice; shortly afterward, in accordance with the older translation, it adds “one day in your courts.”], O God,

and regard the face of your anointed one.

[Col. 1194C] For one day in your courts is better than thousands.

I chose to be cast down in the house of my God

rather than dwell in the tents of wickedness.

For the Lord God is sun and shield;

the Lord will give grace and glory.

He will not withhold good

from those who walk in integrity.

Lord of hosts,

blessed is the man who trusts in you.

**FOR THE VICTOR, OF THE SONS OF KORAH, A SONG [Hebrew: A PSALM].**

**[LXXXV.]** You have been gracious to your land, Lord;

you have restored the captivity of Jacob.

You have forgiven the iniquity of your people;

you have covered all their sins. **EVER.**

You have restrained all your indignation;

you have turned away from the anger of your fury.

[Col. 1195A] Restore us, God Jesus [Hebrew: our salvation],

and turn away your anger from us.

Will you be angry with us forever,

extending your anger from generation to generation [Alternative: through generation and generation, etc.]?

Will you not, when you return, revive us,

so that your people may rejoice in you?

Show us, Lord, your mercy,

and grant us your salvation.

I will hear what the Lord God will speak.

For he will speak peace to his people and to his holy ones,

so that they do not return to folly.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript has, with a somewhat different sense, “so that they may turn back from folly.”]

Yet his salvation is near those who fear him,

so that glory may dwell in our land.

Mercy and truth have met;

justice and peace have kissed.

Truth has sprung from the earth,

and justice has looked down from heaven.

The Lord also will give goodness,

[Col. 1195B] and our land will give its produce.

Justice will go before him,

and will set his footsteps on the way.

**A PRAYER OF DAVID.**

**[LXXXVI.]** Incline your ear, Lord; hear me,

for I am needy and poor [Alternative: add “I am”].

Guard my soul, for I am holy [Hebrew: merciful].

Save your servant, you [Alternative: omit “you”], my God,

who trusts in you.

Have mercy on me, Lord,

for I will cry to you all day.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript has “for I cried to you.” The Cistercian omits the name “Lord” in the third occurrence from this verse.]

Gladden the soul of your servant,

for to you, Lord, I lift up my soul.

For you, Lord, are good and gracious,

and abundant in mercy to all who call upon you.

Hear [Hebrew: give ear], Lord, my prayer,

and listen to the voice of my supplications.

In the day of my tribulation I will call upon you,

because you will hear me.

There is none like you among the gods, Lord,

and there is none according to your works.

[Note: The Cistercian has *non juxta* (“not according to”), omitting the preceding *priori* (“first”) and the particle *et* (“and”).]

All the nations that you have made

will come and worship before you, Lord,

and will glorify your name [Alternative: add “Lord”].

For you are great and perform wonders;

you alone are God.

Teach me [Hebrew: enlighten me], Lord, your way,

that I may walk in your truth.

Make my heart one,

so that it may fear your name.

I will confess you, Lord my God, with all my heart,

and I will glorify your name forever [Hebrew: for an age].

For your mercy is great toward me,

and you have rescued my soul from the deepest hell [Hebrew: the lower place].

God, the proud have risen up against me,

and an assembly of the strong have sought my life,

and have not set you before them.

[Col. 1196A] But you, Lord God, merciful and gracious,

patient [Hebrew: “slow to anger”],

and abundant in mercy

and true,

look upon me and have mercy on me:

give your strength to your servant,

and save the son of your handmaid.

Give me a sign in your goodness,

so that those who hate me may see it and be confounded:

for you, Lord, have helped me,

and have comforted me.

## A PSALM OF A SONG OF THE SONS OF KORAH

### [LXXXVII]

Its foundations

are in the holy mountains.

The Lord loves the gates of Zion

more than all the dwellings of Jacob.

Glorious things have been spoken of you,

city of God. **Selah.**

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Many manuscripts read *I shall be remembered* (*commemorabor*); others, consistently, *of Babylon, knowing me* (*Babylonis scientis me*), instead of *those who know me* (*scientibus me*). In Hebrew it is written *Rahab and Babylon* (*rahab ubabel*), as it is read in the Vulgate. MART. —The same manuscripts, and many others according to Martianay, read *I shall be remembered* (*commemorabor*), then *knowing* (*scientis*). The Queen’s manuscript retains *I shall remember* (*commemorabo*) and thereafter reads *those who know* (*scientes*).]

I shall remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me:

[Col. 1196B] behold Palestine and Tyre with Ethiopia:

this man was born there.

But to Zion it shall be said:

“A man, indeed a man, was born in her,”

and the Most High himself founded her.

The Lord will count, when he records the peoples:

“This man was born there.” **Selah.**

[Note: [Col. 1196D] Our manuscripts read: “He himself was born in her.” Then the Cistercian manuscript has “and they shall sing,” together with the earlier printed editions; the Queen’s manuscript, with a smaller number of others, reads “and he shall sing, as it were,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 1196D] The printed editions and some manuscripts read, “And they shall sing.” But the Canon of Saint-Germain and the Memmian manuscript read, “And princes,” in accordance with the Hebrew word *satim*, which signifies “princes” or “singers.” MART.]

And singers, as in choruses:

“All my springs are in you.”

## A SONG OF A PSALM OF THE SONS OF KORAH, TO THE VICTOR, FOR THE CHOIR, TO BE SUNG; A SONG OF INSTRUCTION OF EMAN THE EZRAHITE

### [LXXXVIII]

Lord, God of my salvation,

by day I have cried out, and by night before you.

Let my prayer enter before you:

incline your ear to my praise.

For my soul is full of evils,

and my life has descended to the underworld [Hebrew: “has reached”].

[Col. 1196C] I have been reckoned among those descending into the pit:

I have become like a helpless man, free among the dead;

like the slain who lie sleeping in the grave,

whom you remember no longer;

and those who have been cut off from your hand.

[Note: [Col. 1196D] Two manuscripts read: “And they themselves have been cut off by your hand.” MART.]

You have placed me in the lowest pit [Hebrew: “the deepest”],

in darkness and in the depths.

Your anger has been made firm against me,

and with all your waves you have afflicted me. **Selah.**

You have put those known to me far from me.

You have made me an abomination to them,

shut in and unable to go out.

My eye has grown weak from affliction;

I have called upon you, Lord, all day;

I have spread out my palms toward you.

Will you work wonders for the dead?

Or will giants rise [variant: “rise again”] and confess

to you? **Selah.**

[Col. 1196D] Will your mercy be recounted in the grave,

your truth in perdition?

Will your wonders be known in darkness,

and your righteousness in a land given over to oblivion?

[Col. 1197A] But I have cried out to you, Lord [Hebrew: “I have pleaded”],

and in the morning my prayer will come before you.

Why, Lord, do you reject my soul?

Why do you hide your face from me?

I am poor and afflicted from my youth;

I have borne your wrath and have been disturbed.

[Note: [Col. 1197D] In the Cistercian manuscript: “They have passed over me,” and so forth.]

Your angers have passed over me;

your terrors [variant: “and your terrors”] have overwhelmed me.

They have surrounded me like waters all day;

they have hemmed me in together.

You have put friend and companion far from me;

you have taken my acquaintances away [Hebrew: “because of darkness”].

[Note: [Col. 1197D] The same manuscript reads: “The instruction of Ethan,” and so forth.]

## THE INSTRUCTION OF ETHAN THE EZRAHITE

### [LXXXIX]

I shall sing the mercies of the Lord forever [Hebrew: “for an age”];

from generation to generation

I shall announce [Hebrew: “make known”] your truth with my mouth.

[Col. 1197B] For I said: Your everlasting mercy [Hebrew: “an age”]

shall be built up;

you will establish the heavens, and your truth in them.

[Note: [Col. 1197D] All manuscripts except those of Saint-Germain, Memmianus, and the Sorbonne read: “For you said,” and so forth. Then the Canon of Carcassonne together with the Vatican manuscript reads: “As you establish the heavens, you will establish your truth in them.” MART.]

I have made a covenant with my chosen one;

I have sworn to David my servant.

Forever I shall establish your seed,

and from generation to generation I shall build your throne.

**Selah.**

And the heavens shall confess your wonders,

Lord,

and your truth in the assembly of the holy ones.

For who in the cloud [variant: “clouds”] can be compared with the Lord?

Who can be made like the Lord among the sons of God?

God is renowned [Hebrew: “mighty”] in the secret council of the holy ones,

and greatly feared by all who are around him [Hebrew: “above all who surround him”].

[Note: [Col. 1197D] Cistercian manuscripts read “who are with him,” and shortly afterward “like you,” instead of “to you.”]

Lord God of hosts, who is like you?

Most mighty Lord, and your truth is around you.

You rule the pride of the sea,

[Col. 1197C] and you restrain [Hebrew: “magnify”] the swelling of its waves.

You crushed the proud one as though wounded.

[Note: [Col. 1197D] The same manuscript reads, “And with your strong arm you scattered,” and so forth. Then, three verses after this, it omits the final little word.]

With the arm of your strength you scattered your enemies.

The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours;

you founded the world and its fullness.

You created the north [note below] and the right hand:

Thabor and Hermon shall praise your name.

[Note: [Col. 1197D] The Royal and Corbie manuscripts read: “And you created the right.” MART. —The Cistercian manuscript’s reading, “the right” instead of “the right hand,” is not without significance. Anyone who has read the passages in the Holy Father’s commentaries where the north is discussed knows that *Aquilo*, the harshest wind, is called by the name “right.” For those who think that the four quarters of the world are designated by the names north, right hand, Tabor, and Hermon, I do not know by what authority they would wish the names of those mountains to be used for east and west. I do know, however, that Symmachus—whose ingenuity the Holy Father especially admired—rendered the phrase in Greek as: “toward the north and the right.”]

Your arm is with strength;

let your hand be strengthened, and let your right hand be exalted.

Righteousness and judgment are the foundation of your throne;

mercy and truth shall go before your face.

Blessed is the people who knows the joyful shout.

[Note: [Col. 1198D] In Martianay’s edition and in the earlier printed books, and even in some manuscripts, there was a shameful error: *who does not want the jubilation* (*qui nolit jubilum*). The Hebrew text, which gives the wording literally, first taught us that *knows* (*novit*) should be restored instead of *does not want* (*noluit*): “Blessed is the people knowing how to blow the trumpet.” Then a single Cistercian manuscript confirmed the reading we restored by its testimony and authority. The old Latin version also reads: “Blessed is the people that knows the jubilation,” in accordance with the Greek exemplar itself, ὁ γινώσκων ἀλαλαγμόν, “the one who knows the joyful cry.” I fear, however, that this old corruption of *noluit* for *novit* must be attributed to some excessively bold critic rather than to a sleepy antiquarian.]

Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance.

In your name they shall rejoice all day,

and in your righteousness they shall be exalted.

For you are the glory of their strength,

[Col. 1198A] and by your favor [variant: “mercy”] you will raise up our horn.

For protection is from the Lord [Hebrew: “our protector”],

and from the Holy One, our king.

Then you spoke through a vision to your holy ones [Hebrew: “merciful ones”],

and said: “I have placed help upon the mighty;

I have exalted the chosen one from the people.”

[Note: [Col. 1198D] The Cistercian manuscript adds: “from my people.”]

I found David my servant;

with my holy oil I anointed him.

With him my hand shall be firm,

and my arm shall strengthen him.

The enemy shall not deceive him,

and the son of iniquity shall not afflict him.

But I shall crush his enemies before his face,

and those who hate him I shall strike [Hebrew: “strike with lightning”].

My truth and my mercy [variant: “shall be”]

shall be with him,

and in my name his horn shall be exalted.

[Col. 1198B] And I shall set his hand upon the sea,

and his right hand upon the rivers.

He shall call upon me: “You are my father,

my God, and the strength of my salvation.”

But I shall make him my firstborn [Hebrew: “give him”],

highest [variant: “and highest”] among the kings of the earth.

Forever [Hebrew: “for an age”] I shall preserve my mercy for him,

and my faithful covenant [note below] with him.

[Note: [Col. 1198D] Our manuscripts again have more: “His faithfulness shall be with him. And I shall establish forever,” and so forth. Shortly afterward they read: “But if his sons forsake,” and so forth.]

And I shall establish his seed forever,

and his throne like the days of heaven.

If his sons forsake my law,

and do not walk in my judgments;

if they profane my ordinances,

and do not keep my commandments;

I shall visit their crimes [Hebrew: “crime”] with the rod,

and their iniquities [variant: “iniquity”] with blows.

But I shall not take my mercy from him,

nor lie against my truth.

[Col. 1198C] I shall not violate my covenant,

and what has gone forth from my lips I shall not change.

Once I swore by my holiness

[Note: [Col. 1198D] The Queen’s manuscript, together with the Hebrew commentator, reads: “If I should lie to David,” and so forth.]

that I would not lie to David [Hebrew: “if I lie to David”].

His seed shall be forever [Hebrew: “for an age”],

and his throne like the sun before me [Hebrew: “in my presence”];

like the moon it shall be established forever [Hebrew: “for an age”],

and like a faithful witness in heaven [Hebrew: “in the cloud”]. **Selah.**

But you have rejected and cast away;

you have been angry against your anointed one.

You have weakened the covenant of your servant;

you have profaned his crown on the ground.

You have broken down all his walls [Hebrew: “hedges”];

you have made his fortifications a terror.

All who pass along the way have plundered him;

he has become a reproach to his neighbors.

[Col. 1199A] You have exalted the right hand of his enemies;

you have gladdened all his enemies.

[Note: [Col. 1199C] Here the word “all” is present, although elsewhere the Cistercian manuscript omits it.]

For you have turned back the strength of his sword,

and you have not supported him in battle.

You have made his purity cease [Hebrew: “fail”],

and you have cast his throne down to the earth [variant: “the earth”].

You have shortened the days of his youth;

you have covered him with disgrace. [Note: [Col. 1199C] Three manuscripts read “forever,” referring it to “disgrace.”] **Selah.**

How long, Lord, will you hide yourself forever?

Will your indignation burn like fire?

Remember me from the depths.

[Note: [Col. 1199C] The Memmian Canon, the Carcassonne manuscript, and three followers of the same reading have: “Remember me from the earth.” MART.]

Otherwise, why have you created the sons of human beings in vain?

What man is there who will live and not see death,

who will save his soul from the hand of the underworld?

[Note: [Col. 1199C] Instead of “Selah,” the Queen’s manuscript places here the title “Diapsalma.”]

**Selah.**

Where are your former mercies [Hebrew: “ancient mercies”], Lord,

which you swore to David in your truth?

Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] Some manuscripts add what is found in the printed editions: “For I have borne in my bosom,” and so forth. But the Carcassonne Canon and the manuscript of Saint Michael read: “I have borne in my bosom the reproach of many nations.” MART.]

I have borne in my bosom all the iniquities of the peoples.

With which your enemies reproached you, Lord,

with which they reproached the footsteps of your anointed one.

Blessed be the Lord forever [Hebrew: “for an age”];

amen and amen.

## A PRAYER OF MOSES, THE MAN OF GOD

### [XC]

Lord, you have become our dwelling place.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] Saint Jerome expounded this psalm—which among Greeks and Latins is inscribed as the eighty-ninth—to Cyprian, a most devoted priest. We therefore consult his commentaries, where variant readings occur in manuscript copies. MART. —We have supplied from the manuscripts the little word “you,” which is also present in the Hebrew. For the rest, compare Letter 140, to Cyprian, where the Holy Father rereads and explains this entire psalm both from the Hebrew and from the Septuagint.]

From generation to generation.

Before the mountains were born,

and the earth and the world were brought forth,

from age and unto age you are God.

You turn man to destruction,

and say [Hebrew: “say”]: “Return [variant: “turn back”], sons of Adam.”

For a thousand years in your eyes

are like yesterday, which has passed,

and like a watch in the night.

When you strike them, they will be like a dream;

in the morning, like grass passing away.

In the morning it flourished and passed away;

[Col. 1199C] toward evening it will be cut down and withered.

For we have been consumed by your fury,

and by your indignation we have been disturbed.

You have set our iniquities before you,

our hidden faults in the light of your countenance.

For all our days

have passed away in your fury;

[Col. 1200A] we have spent our years like a spoken word.

The days of our years in them are seventy years;

but if there is greater strength, eighty years.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] Five manuscripts read, with the Vulgate, “But if there is strength, eighty years.” The Royal, Corbie, and Sorbonne manuscripts retain Jerome’s true reading: “But if there is more, eighty years,” and so forth. MART.]

And what is more is labor and sorrow.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] The Queen’s manuscript, as does the recently mentioned letter to Cyprian, reads: “And what is more is labor,” and so forth.]

For we have passed swiftly, and we have flown away.

Who knows the power of your anger,

and, according to your fear, your indignation?

So make our days known, that we may gain a wise heart.

Return, Lord—how long?

And be gracious toward your servants.

Fill [Hebrew: “satisfy”] us in the morning with your mercy,

and we shall rejoice and be glad throughout all our days.

Gladden us according to the days [Hebrew: “for the days”] in which you afflicted us,

and according to the years in which we saw evil.

Let your work appear to your servants,

and your glory [Hebrew: “beauty”] upon their children.

And let the beauty [Hebrew: “splendor”] of the Lord our God be upon us.

[Col. 1200B] And establish the work of our hands for us.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “Make firm.”]

And establish the work of our hands.

[Note: [Col. 1200C] Instead of “confirm” in the Canon of Saint-Germain and the Memmian manuscript, we read “direct.” MART.]

### [XCI]

He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High,

shall abide in the shelter of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1200D] The Hebrew has written the name *Shaddai*, which Jerome interprets in Ezekiel as “the exalted God.” Aquila renders it ἄλκιμον, “mighty”; this, Jerome says, we may understand as “strong and sufficient for accomplishing all things.” See the Holy Doctor’s letter to Marcella, whose beginning is: “Reading the ninetieth psalm,” and so forth. MART. —The Holy Doctor himself should also be consulted in Letter 25, to Marcella: “Reading the ninetieth psalm at the place where it is written, ‘He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven,’ I had said that among the Hebrews, instead of ‘God of heaven,’ *Shaddai* is placed, which Aquila translates as ἱκανόν, ‘sufficient’; this we may understand as ‘strong and sufficient for accomplishing all things,’ and so forth.” See also what we observe at this place.]

Saying: “Lord, you are my hope and my strength;

my God, I shall trust in him.”

For he will deliver you [variant: “he has delivered you”] from the snare of the hunters,

from deadly ambushes.

With his shoulders he will overshadow you,

and under his wings you will hope;

his truth is shield [Hebrew: “spear”] and protection.

You will not fear the terror of the night,

or the arrow flying by day,

or the pestilence that walks in darkness,

or the bite of the one lying in wait at noon.

[Note: [Col. 1200D] At this place two copies, those of the Canon of Saint-Germain and the Memmian Canon, preserve the reading: “From the bite of the demon of noon, lying in wait at noon.” The printed editions, together with four manuscripts, read: “From the bite of the raging one at noon.” The Carcassonne Canon and two dependent manuscripts read: “From the bite of the demon of noon.” MART. [Col. 1201C] —The Queen’s manuscript, with the earlier printed editions, reads: “From the bite of the raging one at noon”; the Cistercian manuscript: “From the bite of the demon of noon.” [Col. 1201D] The Holy Father is said elsewhere to have translated it: “From the bite of the one raging at noon.”]

A thousand shall fall at your side,

and ten thousand at your right hand;

but it shall not approach you.

[Col. 1200C] Nevertheless, with your eyes you shall see [Hebrew: “behold”],

and you shall look upon the punishment [Hebrew: “completion”] of the wicked.

For you, Lord, are my hope;

you have made the Most High your dwelling place.

Evil shall not approach you,

and plague shall not come near your dwelling.

For he has commanded his angels concerning you,

[Col. 1201A] to guard you in all your ways.

They shall carry you in their hands [Hebrew: “palms”],

lest your foot strike against a stone.

Upon the asp and the basilisk you shall tread.

[Note: [Col. 1201D] The same Queen’s manuscript reads, “And upon the basilisk you shall walk”; the Cistercian manuscript adds the conjunction “and”: “And you shall trample.”]

You shall trample the lion and the dragon.

Because he has clung to me, I shall deliver him;

I shall exalt him, because he has known my name.

He will call upon me, and I shall answer him;

I shall be with him in tribulation.

I shall rescue him and glorify him.

I shall fill [Hebrew: “satisfy”] him with length of days,

and I shall show him my salvation.

## A SONG OF A PSALM FOR THE SABBATH DAY

### [XCII]

It is good to confess to the Lord,

and to sing psalms to your name, Most High,

to announce your mercy in the morning,

and your faithfulness at night.

Upon the ten-stringed instrument and the psaltery,

with song [Hebrew: “poem”], upon the lyre.

[Col. 1201B] For you have gladdened me, Lord, by your work;

I shall praise you for the works of your hands.

How greatly your works have been magnified, Lord!

Your thoughts have been made exceedingly deep.

The foolish man shall not know,

and the senseless shall not understand this.

The wicked have sprouted like grass,

and all who work iniquity have blossomed,

so that they may be destroyed forever.

But you are Most High,

forever [Hebrew: “for an age”], Lord.

Behold [variant: “for behold”] your enemies, Lord;

behold, your enemies shall perish,

and all who work iniquity shall be scattered [Hebrew: “divided”].

My horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn,

and my old age in abundant oil.

And my eye shall look upon those lying in wait for me;

from among those who rise against me in wickedness

my ear shall hear.

[Note: [Col. 1201D] The same manuscripts read: “And my eye shall despise those who lie in wait for me,” which is closer to the ancient translation.]

[Col. 1201C] The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree;

he shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon.

Planted in the house of the Lord,

they shall flourish in the courts of our God.

They shall still bear fruit in old age;

they shall be fat [variant: “abundant”] and leafy.

[Note: [Col. 1201D] Here too the Cistercian manuscript, closer to the Greek and the ancient translation, reads: “fat.”]

Declaring that the Lord is upright:

he is my strength, and there is no iniquity in him.

### [XCIII]

The Lord has reigned;

he has clothed himself with glory.

The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself.

[Note: [Col. 1201D] The manuscripts of the Canon have a different division. The Carcassonne manuscript reads in the second clause: “He is girded with strength.” The manuscripts of Saint-Germain and Memmianus divide this colon not into three but only into two clauses, as we have published it, in accordance also with the Hebrew manuscripts. MART.]

Moreover, he established the world, which shall not be moved.

Your throne has been firm from that time;

you are from eternity [variant: “from everlasting”].

The rivers have lifted up, Lord;

[Col. 1202A] the rivers have lifted up their voice [variant: “your voices”];

the rivers have lifted up their waves,

at the sound of many waters.

The breakers of the sea are great;

the Lord on high is great.

Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy.

Holiness befits your house,

Lord, for length of days.

### [XCIV]

God of vengeance, Lord;

God of vengeance, reveal yourself.

Rise up, judge of the earth.

[Note: [Col. 1202D] Three of our manuscripts read: “Rise up, you who judge the earth; repay recompense to the proud.”]

Repay the proud according to their deeds.

How long, Lord?

How long shall the wicked exult?

They shall pour forth ancient words;

all who work iniquity shall chatter.

They shall crush your people, Lord,

and afflict your inheritance.

They shall kill the widow and the stranger,

and murder the orphans.

[Col. 1202B] And they said: “The Lord shall not see,

and the God of Jacob shall not understand.”

Understand, you fools among the people,

and learn wisdom at last, you senseless ones.

He who planted the ear, will he not hear?

Or he who formed the eye, will he not see [Hebrew: “look”]?

He who disciplines [Hebrew: “chastises”] the nations, will he not rebuke—

he who teaches human beings knowledge?

The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings,

that they are vain.

Blessed is the man whom you instruct [Hebrew: “chastise”], Lord,

and teach from your law.

So that he may rest from the days of affliction,

until a pit is dug for the wicked.

For the Lord will not abandon his people,

and he will not forsake his inheritance.

For judgment shall return to righteousness,

and all upright in heart shall follow it.

Who will stand for me against the wicked?

Who will stand for me against the workers of iniquity?

[Col. 1202C] Unless the Lord had been my helper,

my soul would almost have dwelt in the underworld.

If I said, “My foot has slipped” [variant: “has been shaken”],

your mercy, Lord, would sustain [variant: “sustained”] me.

Amid the multitude of my thoughts,

which are within me,

your consolations delight my soul.

Will the throne of iniquity have fellowship with you,

fashioning suffering through a command?

[Note: [Col. 1202D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “Fashioning labor,” and so forth.]

They shall join together against the soul of the righteous,

and condemn innocent blood.

But the Lord has become my refuge,

and my God the rock of my hope.

And he shall repay them their iniquity [Hebrew: “suffering”],

[Col. 1203A] and in their wickedness he shall destroy them;

the Lord our God shall destroy them.

### [XCV]

Come, let us praise the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] The Cistercian manuscript again prefixes, from the Vulgate, the title “A Song of David.” Moreover, in the second verse of the psalm it reads “Jesus Christ,” instead of “Jesus our [salvation].”]

Let us make a joyful noise to the rock of Jesus [Hebrew: “our strong salvation”].

Let us come before his face with thanksgiving [Hebrew: “confession”];

let us make a joyful noise to him with songs [Hebrew: “psalms”].

For the Lord is a great God

and a great king above all gods.

In whose hand are the foundations of the earth,

and the heights of the mountains are his.

The sea is his, for he made it,

and his hands formed the dry land.

Come, let us adore and bow down.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] Two of our manuscripts read: “Let us bend and bow the knee,” and so forth. Shortly afterward they likewise read: “For he is God,” and so forth.]

Let us bend the knee before the face of the Lord our maker,

for he is our God;

and we are the people of his pasture,

and the sheep [Hebrew: “flock”] of his hand.

Today, if you hear his voice,

[Col. 1203B] do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion,

as on the day of testing in the wilderness,

where your fathers tested me;

they proved me and saw my work.

For forty years that generation displeased me.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] All our manuscripts add *that* (*illa*), nearly in accordance with the old Vulgate translation.]

And I said: “They are a people wandering in heart,

and they have not known my ways.”

And I swore in my anger

that they would not enter into my rest.

### [XCVI]

Sing to the Lord a new song;

sing to the Lord, all the earth.

Sing to the Lord, bless his name;

announce his salvation from day to day.

Declare his glory among the nations,

his wonders among all peoples.

For the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy;

he is terrible above all gods.

For all the gods of the peoples are carved images [Hebrew: “idols”],

but the Lord made the heavens.

[Col. 1203C] Glory and beauty are before his face;

strength and rejoicing are in his sanctuary.

Bring to the Lord, families of the peoples;

bring to the Lord glory and strength.

Bring to the Lord glory for his name;

lift up offerings and enter his courts.

Adore the Lord in the beauty of the sanctuary;

let all the earth tremble before his face.

Say among the nations: “The Lord has reigned,”

for he will establish the world unmoved.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] Two manuscripts read “in an instant” instead of “for”; then all agree in reading “in equity.”]

He will judge the peoples with equity.

Let the heavens rejoice,

and let the earth exult;

let the sea thunder, and its fullness.

Let my field rejoice, and all that is in it;

then all the trees of the forest shall praise.

Before the face of the Lord, for he has come,

for he has come to judge the earth.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “to judge”; together with the Queen’s manuscript, “in the just,” instead of “with justice.”]

He shall judge the world in justice,

and the peoples in his faithfulness.

### [XCVII]

The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice.

[Note: [Col. 1204D] The same Cistercian manuscript reads in the future tense: “He will reign; it will rejoice.” The Queen’s manuscript has only “it rejoiced,” instead of “let it rejoice.”]

[Col. 1203D] Let the many islands rejoice.

Cloud and darkness surround him;

justice and judgment are the foundation of his throne.

Fire shall go before his face,

and burn his enemies round about.

His lightning has appeared to the world;

[Col. 1204A] the earth saw it and trembled.

The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord,

before the face of the ruler of all the earth [variant: “the whole world”].

The heavens declared his righteousness,

and all peoples saw his glory.

Let all who serve a carved image be confounded,

those who glory in idols.

Adore him, all gods.

Zion heard and rejoiced,

and the daughters of Judah exulted

because of your judgments, Lord.

For you, Lord, are Most High over all the earth;

you are greatly exalted above all [variant: “all”] gods.

You who love the Lord, hate evil.

He guards the souls of his holy ones [Hebrew: “merciful ones”];

he will deliver them from the hand of the wicked.

Light has arisen [Hebrew: “has been sown”] for the righteous,

and joy for the upright in heart.

Rejoice, righteous ones, in the Lord,

[Col. 1204B] and confess the memory of his holiness.

## A SONG [Hebrew: “PSALM”]

### [XCVIII]

Sing to the Lord a new song,

for he has done wonders.

His right hand and his holy arm

have saved him [variant: “will save him”].

The Lord has made his salvation known;

in the sight [Hebrew: “in the eyes”] of the nations

he has revealed [variant: “will reveal”] his righteousness.

He has remembered his mercy

and his truth to the house of Israel.

[Note: [Col. 1204D] All our manuscripts read “Jacob” instead of “Israel.” From this it may be conjectured that what is added in some Greek copies to the preceding verse—τῷ Ἰακώβ, “to Jacob,” where it reads “he remembered his mercy”—does not belong there, but was originally a marginal reading for the variant name “Israel,” and was subsequently, through error, brought into the text.]

All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.

Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth;

break forth, rejoice, and sing.

Sing to the Lord on the lyre,

on the lyre and with the voice of a song [Hebrew: “psalms”].

With trumpets and the sound of the horn,

make a joyful noise before the king, the Lord.

[Col. 1204C] Let the sea thunder, and its fullness;

the world and those who dwell in it.

The rivers shall clap their hands [Hebrew: “palms”];

the mountains shall rejoice together.

Before the Lord, for he has come to judge the earth.

[Note: [Col. 1204D] Again the Cistercian manuscript reads: “To judge the world,” and so forth. See the preceding psalm, XCVI, at its conclusion.]

He shall judge the world in justice,

and the peoples with equity.

### [XCIX]

The Lord shall reign; let the peoples tremble.

He sits upon the cherubim; let the earth be shaken.

The Lord is great in Zion,

and exalted above all peoples.

Let them confess your great,

terrible, and holy name.

[Hebrew: “Great and terrible is his name, and holy; and strength.”]

And the king’s power loves judgment.

You established equity;

you performed judgment and justice in Jacob.

Exalt the Lord our God,

and adore the footstool of his feet, for it is holy [variant: “he is holy”].

[Col. 1204D] Moses and Aaron among his priests,

and Samuel among those who invoke his name.

They invoked the Lord,

and he answered them [variant: “used to answer them”].

He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.

They kept his testimonies

[Col. 1205A] and the commandment that he gave them.

Lord our God, you answered them;

Lord, you were gracious toward them,

yet avenging the inventions [Hebrew: “deeds”] they made.

Exalt the Lord our God,

and adore him on his holy mountain,

for the Lord our God is holy.

## A SONG [Hebrew: “A PSALM FOR CONFESSION”] OF THANKSGIVING

### [C]

Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth;

serve the Lord with gladness.

Enter before him with praise;

know that the Lord himself is God.

He made us, and we are his,

his people and the sheep [Hebrew: “flock”] of his pasture.

Enter his gates with thanksgiving [Hebrew: “confession”],

his courts with praise.

[Col. 1205B] Confess to him; bless his name,

for the Lord is good.

His mercy is forever [Hebrew: “for an age”],

and his faithfulness from generation to generation.

## A SONG OF DAVID [Hebrew: “A PSALM”]

### [CI]

I shall sing mercy and judgment;

to you, Lord, I shall sing psalms.

I shall be instructed in the perfect way:

when will you come to me?

I shall walk in the integrity of my heart

within my house.

I shall not set before my eyes a word of Belial.

[Note: [Col. 1205C] The Memmian Canon reads “the words of Belial.” Some manuscripts have “the words of the devil.” MART. —The Queen’s manuscript reads: “the proud Belial before my eyes.” In the old editions of Saint Augustine’s *Speculum* one formerly read “the words of Belial.”]

I hated the one who practices deviations;

he did not cling to me.

A perverse heart shall depart from me;

I shall know no evil.

The one who speaks [Hebrew: “slanders”] in secret against his neighbor [Hebrew: “companion”],

I shall destroy him.

The one with proud eyes and a lofty heart—

I could not endure being with him.

[Note: [Col. 1205C] The same manuscript reads: “I shall not be able to be with him.”]

My eyes are upon the faithful of the land,

so that they may dwell with me.

The one who walks in a blameless way,

he shall minister to me.

He shall not dwell in the midst of my house,

the one who practices deceit and speaks falsehood;

he shall not be approved in the sight of my eyes.

[Col. 1206A] In the morning I shall destroy all the wicked of the land,

so that I may cut off from the city of the Lord

all who practice iniquity.

## A PRAYER OF THE POOR MAN WHEN HE IS ANXIOUS AND POURS OUT HIS SPEECH BEFORE THE LORD

### [CII]

Lord, hear [variant: “heed”] my prayer,

and let my cry [Hebrew: “pleading”] come to you.

Do not hide your face from me.

On the day of my tribulation incline your ear to me;

on whatever day I call upon you,

quickly [Hebrew: “hasten”] answer me.

For my days have been consumed like smoke,

and my bones have withered like something fried.

My heart has been struck and has dried up like grass,

for I have forgotten to eat my bread.

At the sound of my groaning,

my bone has clung to my flesh.

I have become like a pelican of the wilderness;

[Col. 1206B] I have become like an owl of desolation.

[Note: [Col. 1205C] Jerome appears to interpret this verse differently in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, where he says: “In Hebrew, in place of *nycticorax*, the word *bos* is written; Aquila, the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition translated it as *nycticorax*; Symmachus as *hoopoe*; the Sixth Edition as *owl*, which we too follow more closely. Thus, where our texts and the Greek read, ‘I have become like a *nycticorax* in a dwelling,’ the Hebrews say, ‘I have become like an owl among ruins.’ Most contentiously think that a horned owl is meant.” It should be noted that, instead of the Hebrew *kechos* used today, Jerome read *kebos*, or *chebos*, as all the manuscripts of the aforementioned letter to Sunnia and Fretela attest. In that letter the Holy Doctor translates it, “like an owl among ruins,” whereas here in the Psalter it is interpreted, “like an owl of desolation.” Many further details about *Bos* and *Chos* will be found by the curious reader in the annotations to the *Prodromus*. MART. —In the letter that Martianay also cites, to Sunnia and Fretela, he seems rather to have approved “like an owl among ruins.” Nevertheless, it may be inferred from the same letter that here the Holy Interpreter preferred to conform to the generally received opinion, since he adds: “Most contentiously think that a horned owl is meant.” See, if desired, what we observe at that passage.]

I have kept watch, and have become like a solitary bird upon the roof.

All day my enemies reproached me;

those who exulted over me swore by me [Hebrew: “insulted me”].

For I ate ashes like bread,

and mixed my drink with weeping,

because of the face of your indignation and your wrath;

for you lifted me up [variant: “raised me up”] and dashed me down.

My days have declined like a shadow,

and I have withered like grass.

But you, O Lord, remain forever,

and your memorial from generation to generation.

You will arise and have mercy on Zion,

for it is time to have mercy on her,

for the appointed time has come.

[Note: Three manuscripts—the Carcassonian, Vatican, and St Michael’s—read: “for the appointed time has come, for the pact has come.” The same was written in the Chartres manuscript before its correction. There is nothing in the Hebrew to support this duplication; it must therefore be rejected as superfluous. Unless our judgment deceives us, two Latin renderings of the same Hebrew text occur here. MART. — This second hemistich, “for the pact has come,” is added here both by our manuscripts and by several manuscripts in Martianus’s possession. Since nothing corresponds to it either in the Hebrew or in the ancient translators, it is easy to suppose that it is a gloss on the same sense in the sacred text, or another rendering of it. Indeed, the noun which Jerome renders “time” properly denotes, as I think, the course of years, or a fixed period determined by appointed times, as we gather from Daniel in more than one place. Thus the translator who rendered it here *pactum*, “pact,” rather than *foedus*, “covenant,” intended to indicate not a covenant, but the appointed or fixed time denoted by the Hebrew. It is well known that these words of the Psalm refer to the period of years foretold by Jeremiah, chapter 25, verse 11, and elsewhere: once that period had elapsed, God had promised and decreed the restoration of the city of Zion and the release from captivity. The Hebrew scholiast above, on Psalm LXXV, verse 2, likewise wished this noun to be understood as “appointed.”]

For your servants have taken pleasure in her stones,

and have made her dust pitiable.

[Note: In the Carcassonian Canon and two other manuscripts, the Vatican and St Michael’s, this reads: “For your servants have taken pleasure in her stones, and they have had mercy on her dust.” The Canon, however, reads “your servants” instead of “your servant.” MART.]

And the nations will fear the name of the Lord,

and all the kings of the earth your glory.

[Column 1206C] For the Lord has built Zion:

he has appeared in his glory.

He has regarded the prayer of the destitute [Hebrew: the pierced],

and has not despised their prayer.

Let this be written for the last generation,

[Column 1207A] and the people that will be created will praise the Lord.

For he looked down from his holy sanctuary:

the Lord looked upon the earth from heaven,

to hear the groaning of the prisoner,

to release the children of death,

so that the name of the Lord might be declared in Zion,

and his praise in Jerusalem,

when the peoples are gathered together,

and kingdoms, to serve the Lord.

He weakened my strength on the way;

he shortened my days.

I said, “My God, do not take me away in the middle of my days”;

your years endure through generations of generations.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads, “I shall say, Lord my God,” and the Cistercian manuscript, “in the middle of my days,” and so forth.]

In the beginning you founded the earth,

and the heavens are the work of your hands.

They will perish, but you will remain,

and all things will grow old like a garment.

You will change them like a cloak [Hebrew: a garment], and they will be changed.

[Column 1207B] But you are the same,

and your years will not fail.

The sons of your servants will dwell there,

and their offspring will endure before your face [variant: before their face] [Hebrew: will be established].

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript has “David himself”; and immediately in the first word, “I shall bless” instead of “Bless.”]

## DAVID

### [CIII.]

Bless the Lord, O my soul [variant: my soul, to the Lord],

and all my inward parts, his holy name.

Bless the Lord, O my soul,

and do not forget all his recompenses.

He who is merciful toward all your iniquities,

who heals all your infirmities,

who redeems your life from corruption,

who crowns you with mercy and compassion,

who fills your adornment with good things [Hebrew: satisfies],

your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.

[Note: The Carcassonian, Memmian, and Vatican manuscripts improperly retain the first-person pronoun, “my youth.” Unless Jerome perhaps read *neurai* instead of the present Hebrew *neurajechi*, which has a feminine second-person suffix with an additional *yod*, as elsewhere in the Psalms according to Syrian usage. MART.]

The Lord executes acts of justice

and judgments for all who suffer oppression.

He made his ways known to Moses,

his thoughts [Hebrew: his devices] to the children of Israel.

The Lord is compassionate and gracious,

patient [Hebrew: slow to anger] and of great mercy.

He will not contend forever [Hebrew: he will not litigate],

nor will he remain angry forever [Hebrew: endure for an age].

He has not dealt with us according to our sins,

nor repaid us according to our iniquities.

For as high as heaven is above the earth [variant: from the earth],

so strong is his mercy toward those who fear him [variant: toward those fearing him].

[Column 1208A] As far as the east is from the west,

so far has he removed our crimes from us.

As a father has compassion on his children,

so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him.

For he knows our formation [Hebrew: our thought];

he remembered that we are dust.

Man—his days are like grass;

like a flower of the field, so he will blossom.

[Note: Again the Cistercian manuscript reads, “like a flower of the field he will blossom, because the spirit has passed over him.”]

For the spirit passed over him, and he will not remain,

and his place will know him no more.

But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity [Hebrew: from the age],

and unto eternity [Hebrew: unto the age] upon those who fear him,

and his righteousness upon children’s children,

for those who keep his covenant

and remember his commandments, to perform

[variant: to be performed] them.

The Lord established his throne in heaven,

and his kingdom rules over all.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads, “he will rule in the future.”]

Bless the Lord, his angels,

[Column 1208B] mighty in strength, doing his word,

obedient to the voice of his command.

Bless the Lord, all his armies,

his ministers, who do his pleasure.

Bless the Lord, all his works,

in every place of his dominion.

Bless the Lord, O my soul.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript places the name “David” before the title, though the Hebrew lacks it.]

### [CIV.]

Bless the Lord, O my soul.

O Lord my God, you are exceedingly magnified.

You are clothed with glory and splendor,

wrapped in light as in a garment.

You stretch out the heavens like a skin.

You cover [Hebrew: covered] your upper chambers with waters.

You make [Hebrew: made] the clouds your chariot.

[Note: The holy Father seems to have preferred to conform his rendering to that of the ancient translators, who used the verb “to cover,” as did the Septuagint, ὁ στεγάζων (“the one who covers”), or perhaps he read with them in the Hebrew a word meaning “to cover,” instead of the form now read, which properly means “to plank over,” that is, to construct a boarded or vaulted roof. The Cistercian manuscript shortly afterward reads, “you make the cloud your chariot,” and, with the Royal manuscript, “your chariot.” MART.]

You walk upon the wings of the wind.

You make your angels spirits [Hebrew: he makes his angels spirits],

your ministers a burning fire [Hebrew: his ministers].

You founded the earth upon its bases

[variant: upon its base];

[Column 1208C] it will not be shaken forever and ever [Hebrew: and beyond].

You covered it with the deep as with a garment;

the waters will stand above the mountains.

At your rebuke they will flee;

at the voice of your thunder they will fear.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript omits “your.” The Cistercian manuscript reads, “They ascend the mountains and descend the plains,” and shortly afterward, “that the wild ass may refresh itself.”]

The mountains rise and the valleys descend

to the place that you founded for them.

You set a boundary that they will not cross,

nor will they return to cover the earth.

You send forth springs in the valleys,

so that they may flow [Note: All our manuscripts read “flow” instead of “walk”; and shortly afterward, “that the wild ass may refresh itself,” in the smaller number of manuscripts. MART.] among the mountains.

[Column 1209A] All the animals of the countryside drink,

and the wild asses refresh their thirst.

Above them the birds of heaven dwell;

from among the foliage they give voice.

You water the mountains from your upper chambers.

From the fruit of your works the earth will be filled [Hebrew: satisfied].

You make grass grow for cattle [Hebrew: *san*; uncertain],

[Note: We cannot guess what our scholiast intended to note, since in these verses there is no Hebrew word written or read as *san*. MART.]

and plants for the service of human beings,

to bring forth bread from the earth,

and wine to gladden the human heart.

To brighten the face with oil [Hebrew: above oil],

bread strengthens the human heart.

The trees of the Lord are satisfied,

the cedars of Lebanon which he planted.

[Note: Not only do the manuscripts we use unanimously read in the second person, “which you planted,” but the holy Father himself supports this reading in his Commentaries on Isaiah, chapter 2, column 39, where he says: “In the hundred and third Psalm we read, according to the Hebrew truth: ‘The trees of the Lord will be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon which you planted.’ Nevertheless, since the Hebrew text reads in the third person, I judge that nothing here should be altered.” MART.]

There the birds will build their nests;

the fir tree is the house of the kite.

The high mountains are for the deer;

the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs.

[Note: The printed editions read “a refuge for the porcupine.” The Carcassonian Canon, as well as the Memmian, reads “a refuge for the rabbit.” The Sorbonic and St Michael’s manuscripts read likewise. Consult Jerome’s letter, already cited a hundred times, concerning these variant readings. MART.]

He made the moon for appointed times;

the sun knows its setting.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “its going down.”]

You appointed darkness, and night came;

in it all the beasts of the forest move [Hebrew: creep].

The lions roar for prey

and seek their food from God [variant: foods for themselves].

When the sun rises, they withdraw

and lie down in their dens [Hebrew: lairs].

[Note: The Cistercian book reads “he goes out immediately.”]

Human beings go out to their work

and to their service until evening.

How many are your works, O Lord!

You made them all in wisdom;

the earth is filled with your possession.

This is the great and broad sea,

where there are innumerable creeping creatures,

small animals together with great ones.

There ships pass through.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “Ships will pass through.”]

You formed this Leviathan to play with him.

[Note: The Memmian Canon reads, “to play with him,” with which many manuscripts agree. The Carcassonian Canon and the St Michael’s manuscript read more plainly according to the Hebrew, “that you might play in it.” This appears to have been derived from the scholiast. MART.]

All of them hope in you,

that you may give them food in due season.

[Column 1209C] When you give it to them, they gather it;

when you open your hand, they are filled with good [Hebrew: satisfied].

When you hide your face, they are troubled;

when you take away their spirit, they fail

and return to their dust.

You send forth your spirit, and they are created,

and you renew the face of the earth.

May the glory of the Lord endure forever [Hebrew: for an age];

the Lord will rejoice in his works.

He looks upon the earth, and it trembles [variant: trembles];

he touches the mountains, and they smoke.

I will sing to the Lord throughout my life;

I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist.

May my speech please him;

I, however [variant: but I], will rejoice in the Lord.

May sinners vanish from the earth,

and may the wicked be no more.

Bless the Lord, O my soul [variant: bless the Lord].

Alleluia.

[Column 1210A] ### [CV.]

Give thanks to the Lord; call upon his name.

Make his thoughts [Hebrew: his devices] known among the peoples.

Sing to him and sing psalms to him;

[Note: In the Memmian and Sorbonic manuscripts we read without the preposition: “Speak to all about his wonders.” In the Carcassonian and St Michael’s manuscript: “Speak all his wonderful deeds.” MART.]

speak of all his wonders.

Exult [Hebrew: praise] in his holy name;

let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.

Seek the Lord and his strength;

seek his face continually.

Remember his wonders that he performed,

his signs [Hebrew: marvels] and the judgments of his mouth.

The offspring of Abraham, his servant;

the children of Jacob, his chosen ones.

He himself is the Lord our God;

his judgments are throughout all the earth.

He remembered his covenant forever [Hebrew: for an age],

the word that he commanded [Hebrew: the word he commanded] for a thousand

generations,

the covenant he made with Abraham,

and his oath with Isaac.

[Column 1210B] And he established [Hebrew: appointed] it for Jacob as a law [Hebrew: as a commandment],

for Israel as an everlasting covenant,

saying, “To you I will give the land of Canaan,

the measuring-cord of your inheritance.”

When they were few in number,

few and sojourners in it,

they passed from nation to nation,

and from one kingdom to another people.

He did not allow anyone to harm them [Hebrew: to slander them],

and he rebuked kings for their sake.

“Do not touch my anointed ones,

and do not afflict my prophets.”

And he summoned famine upon the land;

he broke every staff [Hebrew: staff] of bread.

He sent a man before them:

Joseph was sold into slavery.

They afflicted his feet with fetters;

his soul entered iron.

[Column 1210C] Until the time when his word came,

the speech of the Lord tested him.

The king sent and released him,

the ruler [Hebrew: master] of peoples, and dismissed

[Hebrew: released] him.

He appointed him lord [Hebrew: ruler] of his house,

and ruler [Hebrew: master] of all his possession,

to discipline [Hebrew: chastise] his princes according to his will,

and to teach his elders wisdom.

And Israel entered Egypt,

and Jacob was a sojourner in the land of Ham.

And he made his people exceedingly fruitful,

and strengthened them over their enemies.

[Note: Two of our manuscripts read, “and he turned.” Shortly afterward, one of the Queen’s manuscripts reads, “so that they might act deceitfully.”]

He turned their heart so that they hated his people,

so that they might act deceitfully against his servants.

He sent Moses his servant,

[variant: and] Aaron, whom he had chosen for himself.

[Column 1210D] He placed in them the words of his signs,

[Column 1211A] and of his portents in the land of Ham.

He sent darkness, and it became dark,

and they were not disobedient to his words.

He changed their waters into blood,

and killed their fish.

Their land swarmed with frogs,

in the chambers [variant: rooms] of their kings.

He spoke, and every kind of fly came,

gnats [Hebrew: lice] throughout all their borders.

He gave them hail for rain,

flaming fire in their land.

He struck their vine and their fig tree,

and shattered the trees of their borders.

He spoke, and locusts came,

and grasshoppers, whose number was beyond counting.

They consumed all the grass of their land,

and devoured the fruit of their soil.

He struck every firstborn in their land,

the firstfruits of all their offspring [Hebrew: pain].

And he brought them out with silver and gold,

[Column 1211B] and there was no weak person among their tribes.

Egypt rejoiced when they departed,

because dread of them had fallen upon it.

He spread out a cloud as a covering,

and fire to give light by night.

They asked, and he brought them quail [Hebrew: quail],

and he filled them with heavenly bread.

He opened the rock, and waters flowed;

rivers ran through the dry places.

For he remembered his holy word,

with Abraham his servant.

And he brought out his people with joy [Hebrew: with rejoicing],

[Note: These same manuscripts and others cited by Martianus read “praising” instead of “in praise.”]

his chosen ones with praise.

And he gave them the lands of nations [variant: the land of nations],

and they possessed the labor [variant: labors] of peoples [Hebrew: tribes],

so that they might keep his ordinances

and observe his laws.

Alleluia.

[Column 1211C] ALLELUIA.

### [CVI.]

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: for an age].

Who can speak of the mighty deeds of the Lord?

Who can make all his praises heard?

Blessed are those who keep judgment

and practice [variant: and practice] righteousness at all times.

Remember me, O Lord, in the favor shown to your people;

visit me with your salvation,

so that I may see the good things of your chosen ones,

and rejoice in the joy of your nation,

and exult with your inheritance.

We have sinned with our fathers;

we have acted wickedly and impiously.

Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders

[Hebrew: they were not instructed by your wonders];

they did not remember the multitude of your mercies.

And they provoked him to anger by the sea, at the Red Sea.

[Note: Only the Carcassonian manuscript reads here, “and they provoked him to anger at the sea,” and so forth. MART.]

But he saved them for the sake of his name,

[Column 1211D] to make his strength known.

He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up,

and he led them through the depths as through a wilderness.

He saved them from the hand of the one who hated them,

and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.

And the waters covered their enemies;

not one of them survived.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads in the smaller number, “and the water covered,” and so forth.]

And they believed his words,

and sang his praise [variant: praises].

[Column 1212A] They quickly [Hebrew: hastily] forgot his works,

and did not await his counsel [Hebrew: plan].

They desired a desire in the wilderness,

and tested God in the solitude.

So he granted them their request,

and sent leanness into their soul.

And they were jealous of Moses in the camp,

of Aaron, the holy one of the Lord.

The earth opened and swallowed Dathan,

and covered the assembly of Abiram.

And fire was kindled in their assembly;

the flame consumed the wicked [Hebrew: the mountains].

They made a calf at Horeb

and worshiped the molten image.

They exchanged their glory

for the likeness of an ox that eats grass.

They forgot God their savior,

who had done great things in Egypt,

wonders in the land of Ham,

[Column 1212B] terrible deeds at the Red Sea.

Therefore he said that he would destroy [Hebrew: disperse] them,

unless Moses, his chosen one,

had stood in the midst before him,

to turn away his indignation and prevent him from destroying them.

They despised the desirable land

and did not believe his word.

They murmured in their tents;

they did not hear the voice of the Lord.

And he raised his hand against them,

to overthrow them in the wilderness,

and to overthrow their offspring among the nations,

and scatter them throughout the lands.

And they consecrated themselves to Baal-Peor,

and ate sacrifices of the dead.

And they provoked him by their practices,

and a plague struck them.

But Phinehas stood and judged,

and the plague was held back.

[Note: Both copies of the Canon—the Memmian and Carcassonian—as well as two other manuscripts read, “Phinehas stood and interceded.” The Memmian manuscript additionally has the word “but”: “But Phinehas stood,” and so forth. MART.]

[Column 1212C] And it was counted to him as righteousness,

from generation to generation, forever

[Hebrew: for an age].

They provoked him at the waters of Contradiction,

and Moses suffered because of them.

For they provoked his spirit,

and he spoke rashly [Hebrew: brought forth] with his lips.

They did not destroy the peoples

whom the Lord had told them about,

but they mingled with the nations

and learned their works.

They served their carved images [Hebrew: idols],

and it became a stumbling block for them.

They sacrificed their sons

and their daughters to demons.

They poured out innocent blood,

the blood of their sons and daughters,

whom they sacrificed to the carved images [Hebrew: idols] of Canaan.

And the land was polluted [Hebrew: contaminated]

[variant: in] with bloodshed.

[Column 1212D] And they were defiled by their works,

and prostituted themselves in their practices [Hebrew: devices].

Therefore the anger of the Lord was kindled against his people,

and he abhorred his inheritance.

And he gave them into the hand of the nations,

and those who hated them ruled over them.

Their enemies oppressed them,

and they were humbled under their hand.

[Column 1213A] Many times he delivered them,

but they provoked him by their counsels,

and they were humbled because of their iniquity [variant: iniquities].

And he saw their distress

when he heard them crying out.

And he remembered his covenant with them,

and repented [variant: when he repented] according to the multitude

of his mercy.

And he made them objects of pity

before all those who had taken them captive.

Save us, O Lord our God,

and gather us from among the nations,

so that we may give thanks to your holy name

and sing in praise of you.

[Note: The printed editions have, “and let us sing in your praise.” The Memmian Canon does not read “you” at the end: “and let us sing, praising.” MART.]

Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel,

from eternity and unto eternity [Hebrew: from age to age],

and all the people shall say, “Amen.” Alleluia.

### [CVII.]

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: for an age].

Let the redeemed of the Lord say so,

those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy.

And he gathered them from the lands,

from east and west, from north and sea.

They wandered in the wilderness, in a deserted way;

they found no city in which to dwell.

Hungry and thirsty,

their soul fainted within them.

And they cried to the Lord in their tribulation,

and he delivered them from their distress [Hebrew: their angustias].

And he led them by a straight way,

so that they might come to an inhabited city.

[Note: The Memmian Canon reads, “He led them by a straight way into an inhabitable city.” The reading in the printed editions and the other manuscripts is better. The Carcassonian reads “so that they might go” instead of “so that they might come.” MART. —The Cistercian manuscript reads, “And he led them out”; shortly afterward, “so that they may give thanks to the Lord for his mercy.” It retains this reading below as well, where the verse is repeated two or three times.]

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercy

and for his wonders toward the children of men.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and his wonders toward the children of men.” The Sorbonic, together with the printed books, retains the plural “mercies,” whereas the older manuscripts read the singular “mercy,” which we have followed. MART.]

For he satisfied the empty soul,

and filled the hungry soul with good things.

Those who dwelt in darkness and the shadow of death,

bound in poverty and iron,

[Column 1213C] because they had provoked the words of God

and blasphemed the counsel of the Most High.

And he humbled their heart with labor;

they fell, and there was no one to help.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads “they fell” instead of “they collapsed.”]

And they cried to the Lord in their tribulation,

and he saved them from their distress.

[Note: Again the Cistercian manuscript reads, “And he delivered them from their distress.”]

And he brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death,

and broke their bonds.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercy

and for his wonders toward the children [variant: toward the children] of men.

For he shattered bronze gates [Hebrew: bronze doors]

and broke iron bars.

Fools, because of the way of their wickedness [Hebrew: from the way],

and because of their iniquities [Hebrew: from their iniquities],

were afflicted.

Their soul abhorred every kind of food,

and they drew near to the gates of death.

And they cried to the Lord in their tribulation,

and he saved them from [variant: and from] their distress.

He sent his word and healed them,

[Column 1213D] and saved them from their destruction.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercy

and for his wonders toward the children [Hebrew: toward the children] of men.

[Column 1214A] And let them sacrifice sacrifices of thanksgiving [Hebrew: confession],

and declare his works with praise.

Those who go down to the sea in ships,

doing their work [variant: their works] upon many waters,

they saw the works of the Lord

and his wonders in the deep.

He spoke, and a storm-wind arose [Hebrew: established],

and lifted up its waves.

They rose to heaven and descended into the depths;

their soul melted in distress [Hebrew: evil].

They reeled and staggered like a drunken man,

and all their wisdom was swallowed up.

[Note: In the same manuscript, “They will cry,” and shortly afterward, “he led them out of their distress,” with the pronoun “their” omitted.]

But they cried to the Lord in their tribulation,

and he led them out of their distress.

He will turn the storm into calm [Hebrew: will raise the tempest into tranquility],

and its waves are silent.

They rejoice because they have become quiet,

and he leads them to the harbor they desired.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercy

and for his wonders toward the children of men.

[Column 1214B] Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people,

and praise him in the seat of the elders.

He makes rivers into wilderness,

and springs [Hebrew: outlets] of water into thirst.

He makes fruitful land saline,

because of the wickedness of its inhabitants.

He makes wilderness into pools of water,

and parched land into springs [Hebrew: outlets] of water.

And he settled the hungry there,

and they founded a city for habitation.

They sowed fields and planted vineyards,

and produced crops and shoots [variant: plants].

He blessed them, and they multiplied greatly,

and their cattle [Hebrew: livestock] did not decrease.

But they became few and afflicted

because of the distress of evil and sorrow.

He pours contempt upon princes,

and makes them wander in a trackless wilderness [Hebrew: emptiness].

And he raises the poor from poverty,

[Column 1214C] and sets families like a flock [Hebrew: sheep].

The upright will see and rejoice,

and all iniquity will shut its mouth.

Who is wise and will keep these things,

and will understand the mercies of the Lord?

## A SONG OF THE PSALM OF DAVID

### [CVIII.]

My heart is ready, O God;

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads, “I sing”; then the Cistercian, “Rise up, Psalter,” and so forth.]

I will sing and play psalms, and my glory also.

Awake [Hebrew: rouse yourself], O psaltery and lyre;

I will awake early [Hebrew: I will rise at dawn].

I will give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord,

and sing to you among the nations [Hebrew: play psalms to you among the peoples].

For your mercy is great above the heavens,

and your truth reaches to the clouds.

Be exalted above the heavens, O God,

and let your glory be over all the earth.

So that your beloved ones may be delivered,

save with your right hand and answer me.

[Column 1214D] God has spoken in his sanctuary: “I will rejoice;

I will divide Shechem [variant: Sichem], and measure the valley of Succoth.

[Column 1215A] Gilead is mine, Manasseh is mine,

and Ephraim is the strength [Hebrew: inheritance] of my head.

Judah is my leader [Hebrew: lawgiver].

Moab is the basin of my washbowl.

Over Edom I will cast my sandal.

With Philistia I will make a treaty [Hebrew: Philistia will be subject to me].”

Who will lead me into the fortified city?

Who will lead me as far as Edom?

Are you not, O God, who had cast us away,

and had not gone forth, O God, with our armies?

[Note: The Carcassonian Canon and its derivative manuscripts read, “Are you not, O God, who cast us away, and will not go forth,” and so forth. MART. — The Cistercian manuscript reverses the order: “God, Lord, act,” and so forth. In the Hebrew: [unrecoverable in the supplied text].]

Give us help in tribulation,

for human salvation is vain.

In God we shall be strong [we shall perform valor],

and he himself will trample our enemies.

## FOR THE VICTOR: A SONG OF DAVID [Hebrew: A PSALM]

[Note: Many manuscripts have, “A Song of David for victory.” Jerome does not seem to reject this entirely in the preface to his Commentaries on Daniel. Enough has been said about this above. MART. —All our codices, instead of “For victory,” and so forth, have this heading.]

### [CIX.]

O God worthy of my praise, do not be silent,

for the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me.

They have spoken against me with a lying tongue,

and surrounded me with words of hatred,

[Column 1215B] and attacked me without cause.

In return for my love of them, they opposed me,

but I prayed.

They repaid me evil for good,

and hatred for my love.

Appoint a wicked man over him,

and let Satan stand at his right hand.

When he is judged, let him come out condemned,

and let his prayer become sin.

Let his days be few,

and let another receive his office.

Let his children become orphans,

and his wife a widow.

Let his children wander about unstable and beg,

and let them seek [Note: The same manuscripts read “be sought” or “complain.” To the printed reading, which is closer to the Hebrew, supply “food.” MART.] in their ruined places.

Let the creditor search out everything he possesses,

and let strangers plunder his labor.

Let there be no one who shows him mercy,

nor anyone compassionate toward his orphans.

[Column 1215C] Let his end be destruction;

in the next generation let his name be erased.

[Note: The Hebrew has *shemam*, “their name.” This is also read in the Carcassonian Canon and in the manuscripts found to have been corrupted by marginal scholia. MART.]

Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the Lord,

and let the sin [Hebrew: iniquity] of his mother not be erased.

Let them always be before the Lord,

and let their memory perish from the earth.

Because he did not remember to show mercy,

but pursued the poor and needy man

and the brokenhearted, in order to kill him.

He loved cursing, and it will come upon him;

he did not desire blessing, and it will be far from him.

He clothed himself with cursing as with his garment,

and it entered his inward parts like water,

[Column 1216A] and like oil into his bones.

Let it be for him like a cloak [Hebrew: garment] with which he is wrapped,

and like a belt with which he is always girded.

This is the retribution of those who oppose me from the Lord,

and of those who speak evil against my soul.

But you, Lord God, act with me for the sake of your name,

for your mercy is good; deliver me.

For I am needy and poor,

and my heart is wounded within me.

Like a shadow when it declines, I am carried away;

I am shaken off like a locust.

My knees have become weak from fasting,

and my flesh has become altered [Hebrew: emaciated], without oil.

And I have become a reproach to them;

when they saw me, they shook their heads.

Help me, O Lord my God;

save me according to your mercy.

[Column 1216B] And let them know that this is your hand;

you, O Lord, have done it.

They will curse, but you will bless;

they resisted, and they will be confounded [Hebrew: they resisted and were confounded];

but your servant will rejoice.

Let my adversaries be clothed with confusion,

and let them be covered with their confusion as with a cloak.

[Note: The same manuscript adds “their,” and shortly afterward reads “with a garment” instead of “with a cloak.”]

I will give great thanks to the Lord with my mouth,

and I will praise him in the midst of many people [Hebrew: many].

For he will stand at the right hand of the poor [Hebrew: needy],

to save his soul from his judges [Hebrew: from those judging him].

[Note: The same manuscript adds “my soul,” in accordance with the ancient version from the Greek, τὴν ψυχὴν μου (“my soul”).]

## A SONG OF DAVID [Hebrew: A PSALM]

### [CX.]

The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand,

until I make your enemies your footstool.”

The Lord will send from Zion the rod [Hebrew: staff] of your strength;

[Column 1216C] rule in the midst of your enemies.

Your people [Note: We scarcely find two similar manuscripts for this verse. The Memmian Canon reads: “Your people will be judges in the day of your strength.” The Carcassonian reads: “Your people, willing, in the day of your strength.” The Corbeian and Royal manuscripts read: “Your people’s leaders will be willing,” and so forth. The St Michael’s manuscript reads: “Your people’s leaders in the day,” and so forth. We have followed the Sorbonic, because it seems to preserve Jerome’s true reading. The Carcassonian Canon thereafter reads, “on the holy mountains.” It also, together with the St Michael’s manuscript, omits the particle “as,” which nevertheless appears in all the other manuscripts and printed books. Nothing further will be said about the San-Germanus Canon, because it survives for us mutilated from Psalm 94 onward. MART. — Other manuscripts, together with the Cistercian, read “judges” instead of “willing”; others, “willing leaders”; Martianus also found these variant readings in his manuscripts. The Hebrew literally has, “Your people are willing,” and so forth.]

will be willing in the day of your strength,

upon the holy mountains [Hebrew: splendors].

From the womb, like the dew,

your youth will arise for you.

The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent,
you are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.

The Lord at your right hand [Alternatively: at your right]:

he struck kings on the day of his wrath.

He will judge among the nations; he filled [Hebrew: with corpses] the valleys;

he will strike the head over a broad land.

He will drink from the torrent along the way;

therefore he will lift up his head.

[Column 1217A] [CXI.] [Aleph.] [Note: Here and in the following psalm, the acrostic is constructed not so that one alphabetic letter is set before each verse, but so that a successive letter is set before each half-verse. We likewise retain them, marked beforehand in the blank space of the book, after Martianay, on the authority of our manuscripts.] I will praise the Lord with my whole heart:

[Beth.] In the council of the upright [Hebrew: rectitude] and in the congregation.

[Gimel.] Great are the works of the Lord:

[Daleth.] They are to be sought [Note: Thus the copies of the Canon, together with several other manuscripts. But the printed editions and very many manuscripts read: “They are to be sought in accordance with all their desires.” The Hebrew has: “with all who desire them,” that is, his commandments. MART.] by all who desire him.

[He.] Glory and majesty are his work:

[Vau.] And his righteousness endures forever.

[Zain.] He has made a memorial of his wonders:

[Heth.] Gracious and merciful is the Lord [Alternatively: God].

[Teth.] He has given food to those who fear him:

[Jod.] He will remember his covenant forever [Hebrew: for the age].

[Chaph.] He will proclaim the strength of his works

to his people,

[Lamed.] That he may give them the inheritance of the nations.

[Mem.] The work of his hands is truth and judgment:

[Nun.] All his commandments are faithful.

[Samech.] They are established forever [Hebrew: for the age], continually:

[Ain.] They are made in truth and uprightness.

[Phe.] He sent redemption to his people,

[Sade.] He commanded his covenant forever [Hebrew: for the age].

[Column 1217B] [Coph.] Holy and fearsome is his name.

[Res.] The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord,

[Sin.] Good instruction [Hebrew: teaching] belongs to all who do them:

[Thav.] His praise endures continually.

ALLELUIA.

[CXII.] [Aleph.] Blessed is the man who fears the Lord,

[Beth.] He takes very great delight in his commandments.

[Gimel.] His offspring will be mighty in the land:

[Daleth.] The generation [Note: Such scholia are in no way approved by Jerome, who, addressing Sunnia and Fretela before these comments, wisely warned concerning Psalm XLVIII: “You say that you found εὐθεῖς, that is, ‘upright,’ in the Greek; but this was translated into Latin in that form for the sake of euphony. Otherwise, in the place where we read εὐθοὺς in the book, we understand ‘of the upright,’ and we ought not to render word for word in such a way that, while following syllables, we lose the meaning.” MART.] of the upright [Hebrew: rectitude] will be blessed.

[He.] Wealth and riches are in his house,

[Vau.] And his righteousness endures forever.

[Zain.] Light has risen in the darkness for the upright [Hebrew: the straight]:

[Heth.] He is gracious, merciful, and just [Hebrew: pious].

[Teth.] The good man is gracious and lends:

[Jod.] He will distribute [Note: All our manuscripts read “he distributed”; “he will scatter,” which formerly stood in the text, was erroneous.] his words in judgment.

[Chaph.] For he will not be moved forever [Hebrew: for the age]:

[Column 1217C] [Lamed.] The righteous man will be in everlasting memory.

[Mem.] He will not fear an evil report:

[Nun.] His heart is ready, trusting in the Lord.

[Samech.] His heart is firm; he will not fear:

[Ain.] Until he looks upon his enemies.

[Phe.] He scattered; he gave to the poor,

[Sade.] His righteousness remains forever:

[Coph.] His horn will be exalted in glory.

[Res.] The wicked man will see and be angry;

[Sin.] He will gnash with his teeth and waste away:

[Thav.] The desire of the wicked will perish.

ALLELUIA.

[CXIII.] Praise the Lord, servants:

praise the name of the Lord:

May the name of the Lord be blessed:

from this time and forever [Hebrew: for the age].

From the rising of the sun to its setting:

[Column 1218A] the name of the Lord is worthy of praise.

The Lord is exalted above all nations:

his glory is above the heavens.

Who is like the Lord our God,
