who dwells in the heights?

He looks upon the lowly [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads “he will regard”]

in heaven and on earth.

He raises the needy from the earth [Hebrew: dust],

and lifts the poor from the refuse heap,

that he may make him sit with princes,

with the princes of his people.

He gives a home to the barren woman,

a joyful mother of children. [Note: The Cistercian manuscript transfers this word, “Alleluia,” to the heading of the following psalm, in accordance with the Septuagint and the Vulgate.] Alleluia.

[CXIV.] When Israel went out from Egypt,

the house of Jacob from a barbarous people,

Judah became [Note: The Septuagint reads “Judea became,” and so on. The Carcassonne Canon retains this reading, together with its followers. MART.] his sanctuary,

Israel his dominion.

The sea saw and fled;

the Jordan turned back.

The mountains leaped like rams,

[Column 1218B] the hills like the young of the flock [Hebrew: sheep].

What ails you, sea, that you fled?

Jordan [Note: Two of our manuscripts insert “because”; then, instead of “you leaped,” they read “you rejoiced.”], did you turn back?

Mountains, did you leap like rams,

hills, like the young of the flock [Hebrew: sheep]?

At the presence of the Lord [Note: The Regina manuscript reads “let the earth tremble”]

the earth trembles,

at the presence of the God of Jacob,

who turns the rock into pools of water,

the flint into springs of water.

[CXV.] Not to us [Note: Among the Hebrews, Psalm CXV begins here; among the Greeks and Latins, it is written together with the preceding psalm. MART.], O Lord, not to us,

but give glory to your name,

because of your mercy and your truth.

Lest [Hebrew: Why] the nations say,

“Where is their God?”

But our God is in heaven:

he has done all that he willed.

The idols of the nations [Hebrew: their idols] are silver and gold,

the work of human hands.

They have mouths, but they will not speak;

[Column 1218C] they have eyes, but they will not see.

They have ears, but they will not hear;

they have noses, but they will not smell.

They have hands, but they will not touch;

they have feet, but they will not walk;

they will not make a sound in their throat.

May those who make them become like them,

and all who trust in them.

Israel [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads “will trust” here and shortly afterward.] trusts in the Lord:

he is their helper and protector.

The house of Aaron trusts in the Lord:

he is their helper and protector.

Those who fear the Lord trust in the Lord:

he is their helper and protector.

The Lord has remembered [Note: The same manuscript reads “the Lord has remembered us and will bless us.”] us; he will bless us;

he will bless the house of Israel;

he will bless the house of Aaron.

He will bless those who fear the Lord,

[Column 1219A] the small and the great.

May the Lord add to you,

to you and to your children,

You are blessed by the Lord,

who made heaven and earth.

The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord,

but he gave the earth to the children of men.

The dead will not praise the Lord,

nor all those who have descended into silence.

But we bless the Lord,

from this time and forever. [Note: The Regina manuscript omits this final word, “Alleluia”; the Cistercian manuscript, however, prefixes it to the following psalm as a title, in accordance with the Vulgate.] Alleluia.

[CXVI.] I have loved [Note: Three manuscripts read: “I have loved, because you will hear, O Lord.” The Memmianus and the corrected Chartres Canon read: “because the Lord has heard.” MART.] because the Lord will hear [Alternatively: will listen]

the voice of my supplication.

For he has inclined his ear to me,

and in my days [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads “I called.”] I will call upon him.

The cords of death surrounded me,

and the snares of the underworld found me.

I found distress and sorrow,

and I will call upon the name of the Lord:

I beseech you, O Lord, save [Hebrew: rescue] my soul.

[Column 1219B]

The Lord is gracious and just,

and our God is merciful [Hebrew: pious].

The Lord preserves the little ones;

I was brought low, and he saved me.

Return, my soul, to your rest,

for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you.

For he will rescue my soul [Note: The same manuscript omits “my.”] from death,

my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling.

I will walk before the Lord

in the land of the living.

[Note: From this point the same manuscript, following the Septuagint and the Vulgate derived from it, begins Psalm CXV, with the heading “Alleluia” placed before it.] I believed [Note: The Greeks and Latins begin Psalm CXV with these words. MART.] because [Hebrew: that] I spoke:

[CXIX.] [Aleph.] [Note: In the copies of the Canon, this psalm is divided, like the others, into cola and commas, so that sixteen verses are placed under each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Saint Augustine followed this division in his Speculum, because it had already been received by custom, before Jerome, in the common and widespread Latin edition of the psalms. We, however, following the Hebrew manuscript volumes, which assign eight verses to each letter, and especially following Jerome, assign to each letter as many verses as he indicated should be assigned. But you must know, says the holy Doctor to Paula of Urbica, “that in the earlier psalms (CX and CXI), under each letter there are attached individual verses consisting of iambic trimeters … In Psalm CXVIII, eight verses follow each individual letter,” and so forth. MART. —In accordance with the custom of the Vulgate, the Cistercian manuscript prefixes the title “Alleluia.” Concerning the acrostic construction of this psalm in groups of eight verses, recall the holy Interpreter in Letter 30 to Paula.] Blessed are the undefiled in the way,

the torrent would have passed over our soul.

Perhaps the waters would have passed over our soul,

[Col. 1227D] the waters of arrogance.

[Col. 1228A] Blessed be the Lord,

who did not give us as prey to their teeth.

Our soul was rescued like a bird

from the snare of the hunters:

the snare was broken,

and we were set free.

Our help is in the name of the Lord,

who made heaven and earth.

## A SONG OF ASCENTS

### [CXXV]

Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion,

immovable, inhabited forever.

[Note: [Col. 1228D] The reading in the *Speculum* of St. Augustine is defective: “immovable, Jerusalem inhabited forever.” Better is the reading in the Carcassonian manuscript and its copy: “it shall not be moved; it shall dwell forever.” MART.]

Mountains surround Jerusalem,

and the Lord surrounds his people,

from now and forever.

For the rod of wickedness shall not rest

over the portion of the righteous,

lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity.

Do good, Lord,

to those who are good

and upright in heart.

[Col. 1228B] But those who turn aside to their crooked ways,

the Lord will lead away with those who work iniquity.

Peace upon Israel.

## A SONG OF ASCENTS

### [CXXVI]

When the Lord restores the captivity of Zion,

[Note: [Col. 1228D] Three manuscripts, always alike—the Carcassonian, Vatican, and St. Michael’s—read: “When the Lord restores … we shall be like dreamers.” MART.]

we became like dreamers.

Then our mouth will be filled with laughter,

and our tongue with praise.

Then they will say among the nations:

“The Lord has done great things for them.”

The Lord has done great things for us;

we have become like those who rejoice.

Restore our captivity, Lord,

[Note: [Col. 1228D] A smaller number of our manuscripts and others cited by Martianay read “like a stream.”]

like streams in the south.

Those who sow in tears

will reap in exultation.

He who went forth walking and weeping, carrying seed for sowing,

will surely come with exultation,

[Col. 1228C] carrying his sheaves.

## A SONG OF ASCENTS OF SOLOMON

[Note: [Col. 1228D] The Cistercian manuscript omits the name Solomon.]

### [CXXVII]

Unless the Lord builds the house,

those who build it have labored in vain.

Unless the Lord guards the city,

[Note: [Col. 1228D] The manuscript of Regina reads: “the one who guards it will keep watch in vain.”]

the one who guards it keeps watch in vain.

It is vain for you to rise early,

[Al. “to rise”]

to sit down afterward,

you who eat the bread of sorrows;

thus he will give sleep to those who love him.

Behold, children are the inheritance of the Lord;

the fruit of the womb is a reward.

Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man,

so are the children of youth.

Blessed is the man who has filled his quiver with them;

they shall not be put to shame when they speak with their enemies

at the gate.

## A SONG OF ASCENTS

### [CXXVIII]

Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 1228D] According to the Vulgate and the Cistercian manuscript: “Blessed are all who fear …”]

who walks in his ways.

When you eat the labor of your hands,

[Hebrew: “the labor of your palms”]

you are blessed, and it will go well with you.

Your wife will be like a fruitful vine

within the chambers of your house;

your children like olive shoots

around your table.

Behold, thus shall the man be blessed
who fears [Hebrew: “to one who fears”] the Lord.

May the Lord bless you from Zion,
and may you see [Hebrew: “See”] the good of Jerusalem all the days

of your life.

And may you see your children’s children.

Peace [Hebrew: “peace be”] upon Israel.

## A SONG OF ASCENTS

### [CXXIX]

They have often attacked me from my youth—

let Israel now say—

they have often attacked me from my youth,

but they could not prevail against me.

[Col. 1229B] The plowers plowed upon my back;

they prolonged their furrow.

The Lord is righteous:

he will cut the cords of the wicked.

Let all who hate Zion

be put to shame and turned backward.

Let them become like the grass of the rooftops,

which withers as soon as it has sprung up.

Of it the reaper does not fill his hand,

nor the one who gathers sheaves his lap.

Nor do passersby say of it:

“The blessing of the Lord be upon you;

we bless you in the name of the Lord.”

## A SONG OF ASCENTS

### [CXXX]

From the depths I cried to you, Lord;

Lord, hear my voice.

Let your ears be attentive

to the voice of my supplication.

If you observe iniquities, Lord,

Lord, who will endure?

[Col. 1229C] For with you is forgiveness,

since you are fearful.

I waited for the Lord;

my soul waited, and I hoped in his word.

My soul waits for the Lord

from the morning watch until the morning watch.

Let Israel hope in the Lord,

for with the Lord is mercy,

and abundant redemption with him.

And he himself will redeem Israel

from all its iniquities.

## A SONG OF ASCENTS OF DAVID

### [CXXXI]

Lord, my heart has not been exalted,

nor have my eyes been lifted up.

I have not walked among great things

or among things too wonderful for me.

If I have not set it before myself,

[Col. 1229D] and made my soul be silent,

[Col. 1230A] like a weaned child upon its mother,

so let my soul be as a weaned child upon me.

[Note: [Col. 1229D] Thus read the copies of the Canon of Memmianus and of the Carcassonian manuscript, as well as the manuscripts of Chartres, the Sorbonne, and St. Michael’s. Two others read: “As a child weaned from his mother, so my soul is weaned from me.” MART. The manuscript of Regina reads: “Like one weaned toward his mother”; then, together with the Cistercian and others: “so my soul is weaned toward me.”]

Hope in the Lord, Israel,

from now and forever.

## A SONG OF ASCENTS

### [CXXXII]

Remember, Lord, David

and all his affliction.

He swore to the Lord;

he vowed a vow to the God [Hebrew: “the Mighty One”] of Jacob.

“If I enter the tent of my house,

if I sit down [Hebrew: “ascend”] upon the bed of my bedding

[Hebrew: “coverings”],

[Note: [Col. 1229D] The scholiast approves “ascend,” which the Cistercian manuscript also prefers; it also supports the variant reading “covering” for “bedding.”]

if I give sleep to my eyes

and slumber to my eyelids,

until I find a place for the Lord,

dwelling places [Al. “a dwelling place”] for the God [Hebrew: “the Mighty One”]

of Jacob.”

[Note: [Col. 1229D] Blessed Paula had learned that this is the correct reading, as Jerome reports her saying: “Behold, we heard him in Ephrata; we found him in the fields of the forest.” For the Hebrew word *zo*, as you taught me, signifies not Mary, the mother of the Lord—that is, αὐτὴν (“her”)—but him, that is, αὐτόν (“him”). For the rest see the *Epitaph of Mother Paula to the virgin Eustochium*. MART.]

Behold, we heard of him in Ephrata;

we found him in the region of the woodland.

Let us enter his dwelling places [Al. “the dwelling places”];

[Col. 1230B] let us worship at the footstool of his feet.

Rise, Lord, to your resting place,

you and the ark of your strength.

Let your priests be clothed with righteousness,

and let your holy ones [Hebrew: “your merciful ones”] praise you.

For the sake of David your servant,

do not turn away the face of your anointed one.

The Lord swore truth to David,

and he will not turn away from it:

“From the fruit of your womb

I shall set upon your seat

[Hebrew: “your throne”].”

If your children keep my covenant

and my testimonies that I shall teach them,

their children also

[Note: [Col. 1229D] The copies of the Canon and the manuscript of St. Michael’s follow a reversed order: “And their children shall sit upon your throne forever,” and so forth. MART.]

will sit upon your throne forever.

For the Lord chose Zion;

he desired it as his dwelling place [Hebrew: “for himself”].

“This is my resting place forever;

here I shall dwell, for I have desired it.

I shall abundantly bless her hunting.

[Note: [Col. 1230D] Jerome discusses this passage in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: “The word *seda*, he says, which all have unanimously translated as ἐπισιτισμός, that is, provisions or food, also occurs in the Psalter. Where our copies read, ‘Blessing I will bless her widow,’ although in many manuscripts, instead of ‘widow’—that is, χήρα—some read θήρα. In Hebrew it has *seda*, that is, ‘blessing I will bless her provisions.’ Now θήρα can signify hunting more readily than crops, and so on. The ignorance of scribes, moreover, caused some manuscripts to read ‘her sprouting’ or ‘her generation,’ and so forth.” MART.]

I shall satisfy her poor with bread.

I shall clothe her priests with salvation,

and her holy ones [Hebrew: “merciful ones”] will praise with praise.

There I shall cause the horn of David to spring forth;

I have prepared a lamp for my anointed one.

I shall clothe his enemies with shame,

but upon him his crown shall flourish.

[Note: [Col. 1230D] Three manuscripts read: “His sanctification shall flourish.” The Memmian and Sorbonne manuscripts retain the first-person pronoun: “my crown.” MART.]

## A SONG OF ASCENTS OF DAVID

[Note: [Col. 1230D] The Cistercian manuscript does not add the name David.]

### [CXXXIII]

Behold, how good and how pleasant it is

for brothers to dwell together as one.

It is like precious ointment upon the head,

which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron,

which descends upon the edge of his garment.

It is like the dew of Hermon,

which descends upon the mountains [Hebrew: “mountain”] of Zion.

For there the Lord commanded blessing:

[Col. 1230D] [Al. “and”] life forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

[Col. 1231A] ## A SONG OF ASCENTS

### [CXXXIV]

Behold, bless the Lord,

all servants of the Lord,

who stand in the house of the Lord by night.

Lift up your hands to the holy place [Hebrew: “holiness”],

and bless the Lord.

May the Lord bless you from Zion,

the maker of heaven and earth.

[Note: [Col. 1231D] In place of “Alleluia,” the Cistercian manuscript substitutes the title “A Song of Ascents,” incorrectly.]

## ALLELUIA

### [CXXXV]

Praise the name of the Lord;

praise the Lord, servants.

You who stand in the house of the Lord,

in the courts of the house of our God,

praise the Lord, for the Lord is good.

[Note: [Col. 1231D] The same manuscript reads: “for the Lord is kind.”]

Sing [Hebrew: “play psalms”] to his name, for it is fitting.

For the Lord chose Jacob for himself,

Israel as his treasured possession.

For I know that the Lord is great,

and that our Lord [Hebrew: “ruler”] is above all gods.

Whatever the Lord willed, he did

[Col. 1231B] in heaven and on earth,

in [Al. “and in”] the sea and in all the abysses.

He raises clouds from the ends of the earth;

he makes lightning into rain;

he brings forth winds from his treasuries.

He struck the firstborn of Egypt,

from man to beast [Hebrew: “quadruped”].

He sent signs and portents in your midst, Egypt,

against Pharaoh and all his servants.

He struck many nations

and slew mighty kings:

Sihon, king of the Amorites,

and Og, king of Bashan,

and all the kingdoms of Canaan.

And he gave their land as an inheritance,

an inheritance to Israel, his people.

Lord, your name is forever [Hebrew: “for the age”];

Lord, your memorial is from generation to generation.

[Col. 1231C] For the Lord will judge his people,

and toward his servants [Al. “in his servants”] he will be gracious.

The idols of the nations are silver and gold,

the works of human hands.

They have mouths, but they will not speak;

they have eyes, but they will not see.

They have ears, but they will not hear;

nor is there breath in their mouths.

Let those who make them become like them,

and everyone [Note: [Col. 1231D] According to the Vulgate and the Cistercian manuscript: “all who trust in them.”]

who trusts in them.

House of Israel, bless the Lord;

house of Aaron, bless the Lord.

House of Levi, bless the Lord.

You who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.

Blessed be the Lord from Zion,

who dwells in Jerusalem. Alleluia.

### [CXXXVI]

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

Give thanks to the God of gods,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

[Col. 1231D] Give thanks to the Lord of lords,

[Col. 1232A] for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

He alone does great wonders,

[Note: [Col. 1231D] The manuscript of Regina reads: “who does”; the Cistercian: “you do.” MART.]

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

He made the heavens in wisdom

[Hebrew: “with understanding”],

[Note: [Col. 1231D] The Canon of Memmianus reads: “who made the heavens with simplicity.” Likewise the Carcassonian manuscript in the sacred text, but in its marginal note it reads, according to the Hebrew, “with understanding.” MART.]

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

He established the earth upon the waters,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

He made the great lights,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

The sun to rule the day,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

The moon and stars to rule the night,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

He struck Egypt with its firstborn,

[Note: [Col. 1231D] Almost all the manuscripts differ here. The Corbeiensis reads “with their firstborn”; the Regius, “with his first fruits”; the Chartres and Memmian manuscripts, “with his firstborn”; the Sorbonne, “with its firstborn.” Finally, the Carcassonian and Vatican manuscripts read “among their firstborn.” MART.]

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

And he brought Israel out from their midst,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

[Note: [Col. 1232D] Four manuscripts—the Carcassonian, Vatican, St. Michael’s, and corrected Chartres—read: “He led Israel across through the midst of it.” MART.]

With a strong hand and an outstretched arm,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

He divided the Red Sea into sections,

[Col. 1232B] for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

And he brought Israel out from its midst,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

And he overwhelmed Pharaoh and his army

in the Red Sea,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

He led his people through the wilderness,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

He struck great kings,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

And he slew powerful [Hebrew: “glorious”] kings,

[Note: [Col. 1232D] The printed editions and many manuscripts retain the marginal note “magnificent” in the text. Only the Corbeiensis reads “strong kings.” We have followed the copies of the Canon. MART.]

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

Sihon, king of the Amorites,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

And Og, king of Bashan,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

And he gave their land as an inheritance,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

An inheritance to Israel his servant,

[Col. 1232C] for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

For he remembered us in our humiliation,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

And he rescued us from our tribulations

[Hebrew: “and redeemed us from our enemies”],

[Note: [Col. 1232D] The Memmian manuscript reads: “for he rescued,” and so forth. Here too the printed books and many manuscripts retain the marginal annotation of the scholiast. MART.]

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

He gives bread to all flesh,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

Give thanks to the God of heaven,

for his mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”].

### [CXXXVII]

[Note: [Col. 1232D] The Cistercian manuscript prefixes an epigraph derived almost from the Septuagintal translation: “Of David himself, a lamentation of Jeremiah.” But there is none in the Hebrew archetype.]

By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat

and wept,

when we remembered Zion.

Upon the willows in its midst

we hung our lyres.

For there those who led us captive

asked us for words of song [Hebrew: “songs”],

and those who afflicted us asked us joyfully:

“Sing for us one of the songs of Zion.”

[Col. 1232D] How shall we sing the song of the Lord

[Col. 1233A] in a foreign land?

If I forget you, Jerusalem,

let my right hand be forgotten.

Let my tongue cling to my throat,

if I do not remember you,

if I do not set Jerusalem

at the beginning of my joy.

Remember, Lord, the children of Edom

on the day of Jerusalem,

who said: “Lay it waste, lay it waste” [Hebrew: “dig it out, dig it out”],

to its very foundations.

Daughter of Babylon, devastated,

blessed is the one who repays you

with the recompense you paid us.

Blessed is the one who seizes

and dashes your little ones [Al. “his little ones”] against the rock.

## DAVID

### [CXXXVIII]

I will give thanks to you, Lord, with all my heart;

in the presence of the gods I will sing [Hebrew: “play psalms”] to you.

[Col. 1233B] I will worship in your holy temple

[Hebrew: “toward your holy temple”],

and I will give thanks to your name,

for your mercy and your truth,

because you have magnified your word above every name.

On the day I called, you answered me,

[Note: [Col. 1233D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “I will call you, and you will answer,” and so forth.]

you enlarged the strength of my soul.

May all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, Lord,

because they have heard the words of your mouth.

And let them sing in the ways of the Lord,

for great is the glory of the Lord.

For the Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly

[Hebrew: “he sees the humble and knows the exalted”],

and he recognizes the exalted from afar.

If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will revive me;

against the anger of my enemies you will stretch out your hand,

and your right hand will save me.

The Lord will act on my behalf.

[Col. 1233C] Lord, your mercy endures forever [Hebrew: “for the age”];

do not abandon the works of your hands.

## FOR THE VICTOR: A SONG OF DAVID

[Note: [Col. 1233D] The manuscript of Regina and several others in Martianay read: “A song for the victory of David.”]

[Hebrew: PSALM]

### [CXXXIX]

Lord, you have searched me and known me;

you know my sitting down and my rising up.

You have understood my thought from afar.

You have examined my path and my lying down,

and you have understood all my ways.

For there is no word on my tongue.

Behold, Lord, you know all things:

behind and before you formed me,

and you placed your hand [Hebrew: “palm”] upon me.

[Note: [Col. 1233D] Thus read both copies of the Canon and the manuscripts of the Sorbonne and St. Michael’s. Others read, with the printed editions: “Your knowledge is above me, and it is exalted,” and so forth. Three of the manuscripts mentioned above also add the pronoun, absent from the Hebrew: “Your knowledge.” The Vatican reads: “Your knowledge is more wonderful than I,” and so forth. MART. The manuscripts used here, like the earlier printed editions, read: “Your knowledge is above me, and it is exalted,” and so forth. “Above me,” that is, beyond my understanding, would not be objectionable.]

Your knowledge is more wonderful than I;

it is exalted—I cannot reach it.

Where shall I go from your spirit,

[Col. 1233D] and where shall I flee from your face?

[Col. 1234A] If I ascend into heaven, you are there;

if I lie down in the underworld, you are present.

If I take the wings of the dawn,

[Al. “and”] and dwell at the farthest end of the sea,

even there your hand will lead me,

and your right hand will hold me.

If I say, “Perhaps darkness will cover me,”

the night too will be light around me.

Even darkness is not dark to you,

and night shines like day.

[Note: [Col. 1233D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “like light.”]

Darkness and light are alike,

for you possessed my inmost parts,

and you fashioned me in my mother’s womb.

I will give you thanks, for you have magnified me fearfully.

Your works are wonderful,

and my soul knows them exceedingly well.

[Note: [Col. 1233D] The same manuscript reads: “my soul knows them very well.”]

My bones were not hidden from you,

when I was made in secret;

I was formed in the depths of the earth.

Your eyes saw me when I was still unformed,

and in your book they will all be written.

The days were formed

[Note: [Col. 1234D] The manuscript of Regina reads in the feminine: “the day was formed,” which also fits better. The Cistercian manuscript adds: “not one of them is hidden from you.” The Hebrew text itself varies in these words.]

and not one is among them.

But how precious your friends [Hebrew: “companions”] have become to me, God;

how mighty [Hebrew: “how numerous”] are their poor [Hebrew: “their chiefs”].

[Note: [Col. 1234D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “how mighty are their rulers,” which the scholiast also approves. The Hebrew has “their heads.” St. Jerome seems to have read, without the intervening word, “their poor,” from a verb meaning “to become poor”; hence the Vulgate in 1 Kings 18:23 translates it “to become poor.”]

I will count them, and they will be more numerous than sand.

I awoke, and I am still with you.

If you slay the wicked, God,

men of blood, depart from me.

Those who speak wickedly against you,

your enemies have been lifted up in vain.

[Note: [Col. 1234D] The Regius and Corbeiensis read: “Those who wickedly oppose you.” MART.]

Have I not hated those who hate you, Lord,

and opposed [Hebrew: “resisted”] your enemies?

I hated them with perfect hatred;

they became enemies to me.

Search me, God, and know my heart;

test me, and know my thoughts.

And see whether there is a way of deceit within me,

[Note: [Col. 1234D] The manuscript of Regina reads: “whether there is a way of an idol within me.”]

and lead me in the everlasting way.

## FOR THE VICTOR: A SONG OF DAVID

[Note: [Col. 1234D] Several manuscripts and the Memmian Canon title this psalm: “For victory.” MART.]

[Hebrew: PSALM]

[Col. 1234C] ### [CXL]

Rescue me, Lord, from the evil man;

save me from violent men.

They have plotted evil in their heart;

all day long they have engaged in battles.

They have sharpened their tongue like a serpent;

the poison of asps is beneath their lips. ALWAYS.

Guard me, Lord, from the hand of the wicked;

save me from the man of iniquities,

who plotted to trip up my steps.

The proud have hidden a snare for me;

they have stretched out a net with ropes.

Beside the path they have placed a stumbling block for me. ALWAYS.

I said to the Lord, “You are my God;

hear [Hebrew: “listen with your ears”], Lord, the voice of my supplication.”

Lord God, strength of my salvation,

[Col. 1234D] you protected my head on the day of battle.

[Col. 1235A] [Note: [Col. 1235D] The manuscript of Regina again reads “the wicked”; “the wicked man” would be more accurate. Thus the Hebrew is rendered: “Do not grant, Lord, the desires of the sinner.”]

Do not grant, Lord, the desires of the wicked;

do not let his crimes be poured out and exalted. ALWAYS.

[Note: [Col. 1235D] As far as I know, the Hebrew reads differently here.]

The bitterness of my companions:

the labor of their lips will cover them.

[Note: [Col. 1235D] The printed editions and some manuscripts divide this colon differently: “Coals of fire shall fall upon them; you shall cast them into pits, so that they may not rise.” But what we have printed, following the copies of the Canon of the Hebrew truth and two other manuscripts, is better and more accurate. MART. The Cistercian follows the other manuscripts cited by Martianay.]

Coals shall fall upon them;

you shall cast them into fire,

into pits, so that they may not rise.

The talkative man shall not be established upon the earth;
evils shall seize the violent man unto destruction.

I know that the Lord will execute the cause of the poor,

the judgments of the needy.

Yet the righteous will give thanks to your name;

the upright will dwell in your presence.

## A SONG [Hebrew: PSALM] OF DAVID

### [CXLI]

Lord, I cried to you; hasten to me.

Hear [Hebrew: “listen with your ears”] the voice of me crying

to you.

Let my prayer be directed like incense in your presence;

[Col. 1235B] the lifting of my hands [Hebrew: “palms”] like an evening sacrifice.

Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth;

protect the poverty of my lips.

Do not incline my heart toward an evil word,

to turn over wicked thoughts

with men who practice iniquity.

Nor let me eat of their delicacies.

[Note: [Col. 1235D] The manuscript of Regina incorrectly reads “in their offenses.” It then more correctly has *arguat* rather than *arguet*; and, with most others, “my prayer is still against their evils.”]

Let the righteous strike me in mercy and rebuke me;

let not the oil of bitterness fatten my head.

For my prayer is still against their evils.

Their judges have been swept away beside the rock,

and they will hear my words, for they are pleasing.

As when a farmer cuts the earth,

so our bones have been scattered at the mouth of the underworld [Al. “the lower world”].

For my eyes are toward you, Lord God;

in you I have hoped; do not empty my soul.

Guard me from the hands of the snare that they set for me,

[Al. “which they set”]

[Col. 1235C] from the stumbling blocks of those who practice iniquity.

The wicked will fall into his net;

but I shall pass through.

## AN INSTRUCTION OF DAVID, WHEN HE WAS IN THE CAVE: A PRAYER

[Note: [Col. 1236D] The manuscript of Regina reads “of the learned”; the Cistercian prefers “understanding.”]

### [CXLII]

With my voice I cried to the Lord;

with my voice I entreated the Lord.

I pour out my speech before him;

I declare my tribulation before him.

When my spirit grows faint within me,

you know my path.

On this road on which I walk,

they have hidden a snare for me.

Look to the right and see,

for there is no one who knows me.

Flight has perished from me,

and there is no one who seeks my soul.

I cried to you, Lord; I said, “You are my hope,

my portion in the land of the living.”

[Col. 1235D] Listen to my supplication,

[Col. 1236A] for I have become exceedingly weak.

Rescue me from my persecutors,

for they have grown stronger than I.

Bring my soul out of prison,

so that it may give thanks to your name.

The righteous will be crowned in me

when you reward me.

[Note: [Col. 1236D] The Cistercian manuscript titles it simply “Prayer.”]

## A SONG [Hebrew: PSALM] OF DAVID

### [CXLIII]

Lord, hear my prayer;

listen [Hebrew: “hear with your ears”] to my supplication in your truth.

[Note: [Col. 1236D] The same manuscript reads: “You have answered me in your righteousness.”]

Hear me in your righteousness.

And do not enter into judgment with your servant,

for no living person will be justified in your sight.

For the enemy has pursued my soul;

he has crushed my life to the ground.

He has placed me in darkness

[Hebrew: “he has settled me in darkness”]

From this one may conclude that the entire Hebrew text is mutilated in this part, and that the fourteenth verse of this psalm disappeared before Jerome’s time. Nor is it found in the copies of the Canon of the Hebrew truth, although scribes have rashly written it into four manuscripts of this Hieronymian version. The missing words are: “The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works.” MART. The Cistercian manuscript supplies the verse: “The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works.” It is certain that this verse fell out of the Hebrew exemplar from the absence of the letter *nun*, with which it must begin. It seems to have disappeared before Jerome’s own time, since the better manuscripts containing this version from the Hebrew, as well as the versions of the most careful ancient translators—Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—also lack it. Yet the Syriac and Arabic translators from the Oriental languages read it, unless—as may especially be suspected here—they themselves took it from the Septuagint, which long before translated it thus: Πιστὸς Κύριος ἐν πᾶσι λόγοις αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὅσιος ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ, “Faithful is the Lord in all his words, and holy in all his works.” From this it becomes highly probable that it once stood in the Hebrew archetype as well, with the verse beginning with the letter *nun*. ## [BOOKS OF SOLOMON]

[Col. 1241]

[Note: The Canon of the Memmian Library bears this inscription at the beginning of the books of Solomon: “Jerome to the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus, concerning an edition translated fully from the Hebrew.” The Sacred Bible of the Church of Narbonne, which likewise contains the Canon of Hebrew Truth, as explained in its proper place, gives the book of Proverbs this title: “The Book of Solomon, that is, his Parables, translated according to the Hebrew Truth by Eusebius Jerome the presbyter, at the request of Chromatius and Heliodorus the bishop.” The same words, but more clearly, are read in the manuscript Bible of the monastery of Silva Major: “The Book of Solomon, that is, his Parables, translated according to the Hebrew Truth by Jerome the presbyter, at the request of the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus.” We find this title also in the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, no. 6. Hence, unless I am mistaken, it manifestly appears that the present translation of Solomon’s books is precisely the one Jerome indicates against Rufinus in these words: “I also translated from the Hebrew the books of Solomon, which I had formerly rendered into Latin according to the Seventy, adding obeli and asterisks, and dedicated them to the holy bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus. At the end of my brief preface I added this: ‘If anyone prefers the edition of the Seventy translators, he has it corrected by us some time ago,’” etc. Nor do certain additions introduced into the text of our Latin Vulgate from the interpretation of the Seventy Elders invalidate this opinion, since they were inserted into the Hebrew translation long after Jerome’s time—not rashly, as the heterodox accuse, but for clarification of the meaning or the reader’s edification—according to the testimony of the author of such additions, who will shortly emerge from the darkness at the sign of the first obelus ÷ in our annotations on chapter 5 of this edition. MART.]

### PREFACE OF JEROME TO THE BOOKS OF SOLOMON

[Note: At least thirty manuscript codices, including those consulted by Martianay, consistently read **Masloth** in this preface. Yet in the prologue prefixed to the books of Scripture, Samuel and Kings, some have **Masaloth**, while the frequently cited Vatican manuscript has **Misloth**, following Origen’s Commentary on Psalm 1, where Μισλὸθ is read. The same Vatican manuscript consequently writes **Acoheleth** instead of **Coeleth**. Let whoever wishes compare these matters. MART.]

[Note: On the authority of the ancient books, including those consulted by Martianay, we add “bishops,” which is also what Rabanus read in his copy. Indeed, this Chromatius was already bishop of Aquileia, to whom the holy Father himself had not long before dedicated his Commentary on Habakkuk; Heliodorus, as everyone knows, occupied the see of Altinum. Moreover, when the holy Father himself speaks in Book 2, no. 31, against Rufinus, of this translation of his books of Solomon from the Hebrew, he says that he dedicated it to the holy bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus.]

Jerome to the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus.

[Col. 1241A] Let a letter join those whom the priesthood joins; indeed, let parchment [Note: He used almost the same words in letter 7 of our recension, writing to the same Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius: “Parchment ought not to divide those whom mutual love has joined.”] not divide those whom the love of Christ binds together.

I would have written the commentaries on Hosea, Amos, Zechariah, and Malachi that you request, if my health had allowed it. You send assistance for expenses; you support our secretaries and copyists, so that our intellect may labor especially for you. And behold, from the side comes a frequent crowd of various petitioners—as though it were fair that, while you are hungry, I should labor for others, or that in the reckoning of what is given and received I should be indebted to anyone besides you.

And so, broken by a long illness [Note: This seems to us to be the illness into which the holy Father complains in letter 114 of our recension that he had fallen, and from which he indicates not long afterward, in the prologue to the third book of his Commentaries on Amos, that he had recovered. We shall treat this matter more fully in the preface prefixed to this volume and still more clearly in the Life of the holy Doctor.], so that I might not remain entirely silent this year or be mute before you, I devoted a work of three days to your name: namely, a translation of three books of Solomon—[Note: We discussed this reading above, in the prologue to the Galeate Preface. For the fact that the feminine ending is used, although in Scripture this name is consistently masculine, and even the title of the book itself in the so-called construct state bears the masculine form, seems to have arisen from the custom of the rabbis and from the pronunciation and usage of this name commonly received since Jerome’s age.]

**MASLOTH**, which the Hebrews call “Parables,” while the Vulgate edition calls it “Proverbs”;

**COELETH**, which in Greek may be called *Ecclesiastes*, and in Latin “Preacher”;

**SIR ASSIRIM**, which in our language is rendered “Song of Songs.”

There is also the wholly virtuous book of Jesus son of Sirach, **πανάρετος** [“entirely virtuous”], and another **ψευδεπίγραφος** [“pseudepigraphal”], entitled the Wisdom of Solomon. Of the former I found a Hebrew copy. It was not entitled Ecclesiasticus, as among the Latins, but was headed “Parables”; attached to it were Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, so that Solomon’s likeness might be matched not only in the number of books but also in the kind of subject matter.

The second book is nowhere found among the Hebrews, [Note: I would prefer to read *quin* (“since indeed”) instead of *quia* (“because”); or perhaps, “since the very style itself,” etc.] because even its style suggests Greek eloquence. And some ancient writers affirm that it belongs to the Jew Philo. [Note: Those who think that Philo of Alexandria, who lived in the time of Gaius and was a most distinguished imitator of Plato, is intended here are far removed from every appearance of truth. For this Philo, to whom the Book of Wisdom was attributed as author, or at least interpreter, is much older than that one—indeed, he was praised by Alexander Polyhistor, who flourished in the time of Lucius Sulla, as Eusebius records in Book 9 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, where he cites from Polyhistor’s testimony approximately fifteen lines from Philo’s work *Concerning Jerusalem*. He is also praised by Josephus, Book 1 *Against Apion*, no. 23, who calls him “Philo the elder,” Φίλων ὁ πρεσβύτερος, although he seems to have thought him a Gentile rather than a Jew, since he lists him among Gentile writers. Jerome, however, most clearly calls him a Jew; and the subjects of the books he treated persuade us that he belonged to that people, as does his work on the Kings of the Jews, which Clement of Alexandria mentions in the first book of the *Stromata*. Clement also says that the Gentile writer Demetrius of Phalerum had gone further in committing that history to writing. Moreover, Jerome’s claim that the Book of Wisdom was written by this elder Philo is less probable than the commonly accepted view: that he merely collected and copied it, or finally expounded it in a freer interpretation, as Huet prefers.]

Thus, just as the Church reads the books of Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees [Note: See what we noted on this matter in the prologue to the Galeate Preface.], but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, so also let it read these two books for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines.

If anyone truly prefers the edition of the Seventy translators, he has it corrected by us long ago. [Note: Nothing now survives of this revised edition of Solomon’s books according to the Greek except the prologue to Paula and Eustochium—or rather a fragment of its prologue—which we shall discuss in its proper place in a subsequent volume. Some critics, especially Capellus, argue that Jerome was not the author of this very translation from the Hebrew that we print, because it contains Greek additions. We shall answer their arguments in the revision of the work itself, where we shall show that the additions—at most thirteen in the entire book—taken from the Greek translation are absent from the better manuscripts of Jerome and were not read by the ancient writers who used that translation.] For we do not fashion new things in such a way as to destroy the old. Yet, since he has read it with the greatest care, let him know that what is ours is more truly understood when it has not been poured into a third vessel and left to congeal there, but has been entrusted immediately from the press to the purest clay and has preserved its own flavor.

[Col. 1243]

## THE BOOK OF PROVERBS BEGINS

Called in Hebrew **MASLOTH**.

[Col. 1243C] **THE PARABLES OF SOLOMON, SON OF DAVID, KING OF ISRAEL**

### [Chapter I]

For knowing wisdom and discipline;

for understanding the words of prudence;

for receiving instruction in doctrine,

justice, judgment, and equity;

so that cunning may be given to the simple,

knowledge and understanding to the young.

When the wise man hears, he will become wiser,

and the understanding man will possess guidance.

He will discern a parable and its interpretation,

the words of the wise and their riddles.

The fear of the Lord is the beginning [Note: Several manuscripts, including those used by Martianay, read “of wisdom” according to the Vulgate; others shortly afterward read “discipline” instead of “instruction.”] of knowledge;

fools despise wisdom and instruction.

Hear, my son, the discipline of your father,

and do not abandon your mother’s law,

so that grace may be added to your head,

and a necklace to your neck.

My son, if sinners entice you,

do not [Note: All manuscripts except Colbertinus no. 158 and Sangermanensis no. 15 add the pronoun: “do not consent to them.” But it is absent from the Hebrew and is easily understood in this sentence. MART.] consent.

If they say, “Come with us;

let us lie in wait for blood;

let us hide snares without cause against the innocent;

let us swallow him alive like the underworld,

and whole, as one descending into the pit.

We shall find every precious substance;

we shall fill our houses with spoils.

Cast your lot in with us;

let there be one purse for us all.”

My son, do not walk with them;

keep your foot from their paths.

For their feet run toward evil,

and they hasten to shed blood.

[Col. 1244C] But a net is thrown in vain

before the eyes of winged creatures.

They themselves lie in wait against their own blood

and devise deceits against their own lives.

So are the paths of everyone who is greedy:

they seize the lives of those who possess them.

Wisdom cries aloud outside;

she raises her voice in the streets.

At the head of the crowds she cries out;

at the entrances of the city gates

she speaks her words, saying:

“How long, little ones, will you love childishness?

And fools, how long will they desire what harms them?

And the ignorant, how long will they hate knowledge?

Turn back at my reproof;

behold, I shall pour out my spirit for you,

and make my words known to you.

Because I called and you refused;

I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked.

[Col. 1244D] You rejected all my counsel,

and neglected my reproofs,

I also will laugh at your destruction,

and mock when what you feared comes upon you.

When sudden calamity falls upon you,

and destruction rushes upon you like a storm;

when tribulation and distress come upon you,

then they will call upon me, and I will not answer;

they will rise early, and will not find me,

because they hated instruction

and did not receive the fear of the Lord.

[Col. 1245A] They did not consent to my counsel,

and despised all my reproof.

Therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way,

and be filled with their own counsels.

[Note: In one manuscript among ours, *Eversio* (“overthrow”) is read. In Hebrew the word signifies turning away or withdrawal, and it consistently bears a bad sense.]

The turning away of the simple will kill them,

and the prosperity of fools will destroy them.

But whoever listens to me will rest without fear,

and will enjoy abundance,

with the fear of evils removed.”

### [Chapter II]

My son, if you receive my words

and hide my commandments with you,

so that your ear may listen to wisdom,

incline your heart to know prudence.

For if you call upon wisdom

and incline your heart toward prudence;

if you seek her like money

and dig for her as for treasures,

then you will understand the fear of the Lord

and find the knowledge of God.

For the Lord gives wisdom,

[Col. 1245B] and from his mouth come knowledge and prudence.

He will guard the safety of the upright

and protect those who walk simply.

He preserves the paths of justice

and guards the ways of the holy.

Then you will understand justice and judgment,

equity and every good path.

If wisdom enters your heart

and knowledge pleases your soul,

counsel will guard you

and prudence will preserve you,

so that you may be delivered from the evil way,

from the man who speaks perversely;

from those who abandon the straight path

and walk along dark ways;

who rejoice when they have done evil

and exult in the worst things;

whose ways are crooked

and whose footsteps are shameful.

[Col. 1245C] You will be delivered from the foreign woman

and from the stranger who makes her words seductive,

who abandons the guide of her youth

and has forgotten the covenant of her God.

For her house inclines toward death,

and her paths toward the underworld.

All who enter to her will not return,

nor will they grasp the paths of life.

Walk, therefore, in the good way

and keep to the paths of the righteous.

For the upright will dwell in the land,

and the simple will remain in it.

But the wicked will be destroyed from the land,

and those who act unjustly will be removed from it.

### [Chapter III]

My son, do not forget my law,

and let your heart guard my commandments.

For they will add to you length of days,

years of life, and peace.

Let mercy and truth not abandon you;

bind them around your neck,

[Col. 1245D] and write them on the tablets of your heart.

Then you will find grace and good discipline

before God and human beings.

Trust in the Lord with all your heart,

and do not rely on your own prudence.

Acknowledge him in all your ways,

and he himself will direct your steps.

Do not be wise in your own eyes;

fear the Lord and turn away from evil.

For it will be health to your navel

and refreshment to your bones.

Honor the Lord from your substance,

and from the firstfruits of all your produce.

Then your barns will be filled with abundance,

and your winepresses will overflow with wine.

My son, do not reject the Lord’s discipline,

and do not faint when he rebukes you.

For the Lord rebukes the one he loves,

and, like a father with a son, takes pleasure in him.

Blessed is the person who finds wisdom,

and the one who abounds in prudence.

Her acquisition is better than trade in silver,

and her fruits better than the finest and purest gold.

[Note: Here we have followed the Memmian Canon, which agrees with the Hebrew. The Carcassonian Canon and the Corbeian manuscript no. 14 originally had “and gold, and her first fruits,” without “finest”; the manuscript of Saint-Germain no. 15 still retains that reading. The others, together with the printed editions, read “and the finest and purest gold,” etc. MART. —Closer to the Vulgate reading, though formerly read with different punctuation by Rabanus and others, is: “Her acquisition is better than trade in silver and gold: her fruits are first and purest.”]

She is more precious than all riches,

and all that is desired cannot be compared with her.

Length of days is in her right hand;

in her left are riches and glory.

[Col. 1246B] Her ways are ways of beauty,

and all her paths are peaceful.

She is a tree of life to those who grasp her,

and whoever holds her fast is blessed.

The Lord founded the earth by wisdom;

he established the heavens by prudence.

By his wisdom the depths burst forth,

and the clouds gather dew.

My son, do not let these things flow away from your eyes;

guard law and counsel.

Then they will be life for your soul

and grace for your throat.

Then you will walk confidently on your way,

and your foot will not stumble.

If you sleep, you will not fear;

you will rest, and your sleep will be sweet.

Do not fear sudden terror

or the power of the wicked rushing upon you.

For the Lord will be at your side

[Col. 1246C] and will guard your foot, so that you are not caught.

Do not prevent one who can do good;

if you are able, do good yourself.

Do not say to your friend, “Go and come back;

tomorrow I will give it to you,” when you can give it immediately.

Do not plot evil against your friend

when he has confidence in you.

Do not contend with a person without cause

when he has done you no harm.

Do not envy the unjust person,

nor imitate his ways.

For every mocker is an abomination to the Lord,

but his conversation is with the simple.

Poverty from the Lord is in the house of the wicked;

but he blesses the dwellings of the righteous.

He himself will mock the mockers,

but to the meek he will give grace.

The wise will possess glory;

the exaltation of fools [Note: In the manuscripts *exsulatio* (“exile”) is corruptly read instead of *exaltatio* (“exaltation”); for the Hebrew has *meum*, which signifies exaltation. MART.] is disgrace.

### [Chapter IV]

Hear, children, the discipline of your father,

[Col. 1246D] and attend, so that you may know prudence.

I give you a good gift;

do not abandon my law.

For I too was my father’s son,

tender and the only child before my mother.

And he taught me and said:

“Let your heart receive my words;

guard my commandments, and you will live.

Acquire wisdom, acquire prudence.

Do not forget, and do not turn away from the words of my mouth.

Do not abandon her, and she will guard you;

love her, and she will preserve you.

The beginning of wisdom: acquire wisdom;

and in all your possessions acquire prudence.

Seize her, and she will exalt you;

she will glorify you when you have embraced her.

She will give your head an increase of graces,

and a noble crown will protect you.”

Hear, my son, and receive my words,

so that the years of your life may be multiplied.

I shall show you the way of wisdom;

I shall lead you along the paths of equity.

When you enter them, your steps will not be confined,

and when you run, you will not have a stumbling-block.

Hold fast to discipline; do not abandon it;

guard it, because it is your life.

Do not take pleasure in the paths of the wicked,

and do not let the way of evildoers please you.

[Col. 1247B] Flee from it, and do not pass along it;

turn aside and abandon it.

For they do not sleep unless they have done evil,

and sleep is taken from them unless they have overthrown someone.

They eat the bread of wickedness

and drink the wine of iniquity.

But the path of the righteous is like shining light;

it advances and grows until perfect day.

The way of the wicked is dark;

they do not know where they will fall.

My son, listen to my words

and incline your ear to my utterances.

Let them not depart from your eyes;

guard them in the midst of your heart.

For they are life to those who find them,

and health to all flesh.

Guard your heart with every vigilance,

because from it life proceeds.

Remove from yourself a crooked mouth,

and let deceitful lips be far from you.

Let your eyes look straight ahead,

and let your eyelids go before your steps.

Make the path straight for your feet,

and let all your ways be firmly established.

Do not turn aside to the right or to the left;

turn your foot away from evil.

For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right,

but those on the left are crooked.

He himself will make your courses straight,

and will lead your journeys in peace.

### [Chapter V]

My son, attend to my wisdom,

[Col. 1248A] and incline your ear to my prudence,

so that you may guard your thoughts,

and your lips may preserve instruction [Note: This marginal obelus indicates an addition translated from the Seventy and introduced into the Latin Vulgate, as we now read it: “Do not attend to the deceit of a woman.” These words are absent from the Hebrew in the exemplars of the Canon of Hebrew Truth and in all ancient manuscript codices; nor does the *Speculum* of St. Augustine, composed from Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew, mention this addition. But by attending more carefully to such additions, which we mark with obeli, we have discovered their true origin in an ancient anonymous writer who appended the following warning to the end of the preface to the books of Solomon published by Jerome when he first revised these volumes according to the Greek codices of the Seventy translators, distinguishing the whole work with obeli and asterisks. “For this reason,” says our anonymous writer, “the two prefaces prefixed to this book have been supplied from the Hebrew, because certain things from the Greek have been either inserted into the Hebrew translation for clarification of the sense and the reader’s edification or added externally. Therefore, whoever reads, always remember that they are foreign.” This is what he says, whoever he may have been, whether the scholiast of the Canon of Hebrew Truth or another writer of the same age. Everything, therefore, of which he warned the reader is found placed in the Memmian Canon, copied eight hundred years ago. For both prefaces of Jerome—that is, both the first, which he had prefixed to his version from the Seventy translators, and the later one published with the Hebrew translation—are read at the beginning of the books of Solomon in that codex, together with the warning of the same Anonymous appended to the end of the earlier preface. The codex also retains in the body some part of the added sentences; it represents the rest opposite them in the margin, so that one might say that the Memmian codex is the one in which the author first inserted this Greek admixture into the Hebrew translation. The Carcassonian Canon is different: its copyist transferred all the additions, except one or two, into the sacred text. The other manuscript codices omit these extraneous additions or place them externally in the margins. The same thing is therefore plainly shown to have occurred in the Book of Proverbs, as we noted above in the Books of Kings at chapter 5. Let the diligent reader allow this matter to be referred there. Jerome’s preface, at whose end the Anonymous appended his warning, was printed with notes at the end of the first part of this sacred Library. MART.]

÷ For the lips of a prostitute drip like a honeycomb,

and her throat is smoother than oil.

But her end is bitter as wormwood,

and sharp as a two-edged sword.

Her feet descend toward death,

and her steps reach the underworld.

They do not walk along the path of life;

her steps wander and are traceable [Note: Instead of “unsearchable,” as he interprets it elsewhere, from the verb *vestigo*.].

Now therefore, my son, hear me,

and do not depart from the words of my mouth.

Make your way far from her,

and do not approach the doors of her house.

Do not give your honor to strangers,

nor your years to the cruel one.

Otherwise strangers may be filled with your strength,

and your labors may be in a foreign house.

Then you will groan at the end,

when you have consumed your flesh and your body,

and say:

“Why did I hate discipline,

and why did my heart not consent to reproof?

Why did I not hear the voice of those teaching me,

and not incline my ear to my teachers?

I was almost in every evil,

in the midst of the assembly and the congregation.”

Drink water from your own cistern,

and flowing water from your own well.

Let your fountains flow outward,

and divide your waters in the streets.

Keep them for yourself alone,

and let strangers not share in them.

Let your spring be blessed,

and rejoice [Alternative: nourish] with the wife of your youth,

the most beloved doe and most graceful fawn.

Let her breasts intoxicate you at all times;

be continually delighted in her love.

[Col. 1248C] Why are you led astray, my son, by a foreign woman,

and warmed in the bosom of another?

The Lord observes the ways of a person,

and considers all his steps.

His iniquities seize the wicked,

and he is bound with the cords of his sins.

He himself will die, because he did not possess discipline,

and he will be deceived by the multitude of his folly.

### [Chapter VI]

My son, if you have become surety for your friend,

you have given your hand to a stranger.

You have been ensnared by the words of your mouth

and caught by your own utterances.

[Col. 1249A] Do therefore what I tell you, my son, and free yourself,

because you have fallen into the hand of your neighbor.

Run, hurry, rouse your friend.

Do not give sleep to your eyes,

nor let your eyelids slumber.

Free yourself like a doe from the hand,

and like a bird from the snare of the fowler.

Go to the ant, you lazy one;

consider its ways and learn wisdom.

Although it has no leader,

nor instructor nor ruler,

it prepares its food in summer,

and gathers at harvest what it may eat.

How long will you sleep, lazy one?

When will you rise from your sleep?

You will sleep a little,

you will doze a little,

you will fold your hands a little to sleep;

and poverty will come upon you like a traveler,

and want like an armed man [Note: The Memmian Canon retains within the text here the sentence marked by our obelus as an addition to the Latin Vulgate; the Carcassonian Canon places it externally in the lower margin of the codex. MART. —The other addition in the Vulgate, “But if you are diligent, your harvest will come like a spring, and poverty will flee far from you,” is taken from the Greek of the Seventy. It is also read by Rabanus, who nevertheless does not know many other additions of this kind. The older and more genuine manuscripts of Jerome, in accordance with the Hebrew text, entirely lack it.]

÷ An apostate man, a worthless person,

[Col. 1249B] walks with a perverse mouth;

he winks with his eyes, rubs with his foot,

and speaks with his finger.

With a crooked heart he devises evil,

and at all times sows quarrels.

Destruction will come upon him suddenly;

he will immediately be crushed, and will have no remedy.

There are six things that the Lord hates,

and the seventh his soul detests:

haughty eyes, a lying tongue,

hands that shed innocent blood;

A heart devising the worst designs,

feet swift to run toward evil;

a false witness who utters lies,

and one who sows discord among brothers:

Keep, my son, the commands of your father,

and do not forsake the teaching of your mother.

Bind them continually upon your heart,

and fasten them around your throat.

[Col. 1249C] When you walk, let them accompany you;

when you sleep, let them guard you;

and when you awake, speak with them.

For the commandment is a lamp,

and the law is light,

and the reproof of discipline is the way of life:

to guard you from the wicked woman,

and from the flattering tongue of a strange woman.

Let not your heart desire her beauty,

nor let yourself be captured by her glances.

For the price of a prostitute is scarcely that of one loaf of bread;

but a woman captures a man’s precious soul.

Can a man hide fire in his bosom

without his garments being burned?

Or can he walk upon coals

without the soles of his feet being scorched?

So it is with one who goes in to his neighbor’s wife:

he will not be clean when he has touched her.

The guilt is not great when someone has stolen;

for he steals to satisfy his hungry soul.

[Col. 1249D] Yet, when caught, he will repay sevenfold,

and surrender all the property of his household.

But the adulterer, because of the poverty of his heart,

will destroy his own soul.

He gathers disgrace and dishonor for himself,

and his reproach will not be wiped away.

For the jealousy and fury of a husband

will not spare him on the day of vengeance;

[Col. 1250A] he will not yield to anyone’s entreaties,

nor accept many gifts as ransom.

[Cap. VII.] My son, keep my words,

and store up my commands for yourself.

My son, keep my commandments, and you will live;

and my teaching as the apple of your eye.

Bind it upon your fingers;

write it on the tablets of your heart.

Say to Wisdom, “You are my sister,”

and call Prudence your friend,

so that she may guard you from the strange woman,

from the foreign woman who makes her words sweet.

For from the window of my house,

through the lattice, I looked out.

And I saw young people,

I observed an inexperienced young man,

who was passing through the street near the corner,

and walking close to the road by her house,

in the darkness, at the falling of evening,

in the night’s darkness and gloom.

[Col. 1250B] And behold, a woman met him,

dressed as a prostitute and prepared to ensnare souls.

Talkative and restless, unable to keep her feet still at home,

now outside, now in the streets,

now lying in wait near the corners.

She seized the young man and kissed him,

and with a bold face caressed him, saying:

“I have vowed sacrificial offerings for my well-being;

today I have paid my vows.

Therefore I came out to meet you,

desiring to see you, and I have found you.

I have woven my bed with cords;

I have spread Egyptian embroidered coverings.

I have sprinkled my couch with myrrh,

with aloe and cinnamon.

Come, let us drink our fill of love until daybreak,

and let us enjoy the embraces we have desired.

For the man is not at home;

[Col. 1250C] he has gone on a very long journey.

He took a bag of money with him;

he will return home on the day of the full moon.”

She ensnared him with many words

and drew him away with the flatteries of her lips.

At once he follows her,

like an ox led to the sacrifice,

and like a [Note: [Col. 1250D] The Hebrew has a word meaning “fetter”; the sense is therefore, “like a fetter for the chastisement of a fool.” Commonly, however, it is thought that the translator, in his Hebrew exemplar, read *agnus*, “lamb,” in place of [the Hebrew word]. I would rather suppose, with Symmachus, that he adapted the sense more closely; Symmachus translates it as *skirtōn* (σκιρτῶν), that is, “leaping,” and so forth.] frisky lamb,

not knowing that a fool is being dragged to fetters,

until an arrow pierces his liver;

as when a bird hastens to the snare,

not knowing that his life is at stake.

Now therefore, my son, hear me,

and attend to the words of my mouth.

Do not let your mind be drawn into her ways;

do not be deceived by her paths.

For she has struck down many wounded,

and the strongest of all have been slain by her.

Her house is the way to the underworld,

penetrating into the inner chambers of death.

[Cap. VIII.] Does not Wisdom cry out,

and Prudence give forth her voice,

upon the highest and loftiest peaks above the road,

standing in the midst of the paths,

beside the gates of the city,

speaking at the very entrances, saying:

“O men, to you I cry,

and my voice is addressed to the sons of men.

[Col. 1251A] Understand prudence, you simple ones,

and take notice, you fools.

Hear, for I am about to speak of great things;

and my lips will open to proclaim what is right.

My throat will meditate truth,

and my lips will detest the wicked.

All the words of my mouth are just;

there is nothing crooked or perverse in them.

They are straightforward to those who understand,

and right for those who find knowledge.

Receive my discipline, not money;

choose instruction rather than gold.

For Wisdom is better than all the most precious things,

and nothing desirable can be compared with her.

I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel,

and I am present among the learned in their thoughts.

The fear of the Lord hates evil:

arrogance and pride, the crooked way,

and the double-tongued mouth I detest.

Mine are counsel and justice;

[Col. 1251B] mine is prudence, mine is strength.

Through me kings reign,

and lawgivers decree what is just.

Through me rulers govern,

and the powerful determine justice.

I love those who love me,

and those who watch for me early will find me.

With me are riches and glory,

splendid wealth and justice.

My fruit is better than gold and precious stone,

and my produce than refined silver.

I walk in the ways of justice,

in the midst of the paths of judgment,

so that I may enrich those who love me

and fill their treasuries.

The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways,

before he made anything, from the beginning.

From eternity I was ordained,

and from ancient times, before the earth existed.

[Col. 1251C] The abysses did not yet exist, and I had already been conceived;

the springs of water had not yet burst forth;

the mountains had not yet been established with their massive weight.

Before the hills, I was brought forth;

while he had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers,

nor the hinges of the inhabited world.

When he prepared the heavens, I was present;

when, by a fixed law and a circle, he enclosed the abysses;

when he made firm the heavens above

and balanced the springs of water;

when he surrounded the sea with its boundary

and established a law for the waters, lest they pass beyond their limits;

when he suspended the foundations of the earth,

I was with him, arranging all things;

and I delighted day by day,

playing before him at all times,

shining in the inhabited world,

and my delight was to be with the sons of men.

Now therefore, sons, hear me:

blessed are those who keep my ways.

[Col. 1251D] Hear discipline and become wise,

and do not reject it.

Blessed is the man who hears me,

who watches daily at my doors

and keeps guard at the posts of my entrance.

Whoever finds me finds life

and draws salvation from the Lord.

But whoever sins against me injures his own soul.

All who hate me love death.”

[Cap. IX.] Wisdom built herself a house;

she hewed out seven pillars.

She sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine,

and set her table.

[Col. 1252A] She sent her maidens to call from the citadel

and from the battlements of the city:

“Whoever is simple, let him come to me.”

And she spoke to the foolish:

“Come, eat my bread,

and drink the wine I have mixed for you.

Leave childishness and live,

and walk in the ways of prudence.

Whoever instructs a scoffer does himself an injury,

and whoever rebukes the wicked brings a blemish upon himself.

Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you.

Rebuke the wise, and he will love you.

Give an opportunity to the wise, and wisdom will be added to him.

Teach the righteous, and he will hasten to receive instruction.

The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord,

and knowledge of the holy ones is prudence.

For through me your days will be multiplied,

and years of life will be added to you.

If you are wise, you will be wise for yourself;

but if you are a scoffer, you alone will bear the evil.”

[Col. 1252B] The foolish and clamorous woman,

full of seductive allurements and knowing absolutely nothing,

sat at the doors of her house

upon a seat in the high place of the city,

to call to passersby on the road

and to those proceeding on their journey:

“Whoever is simple, let him turn in to me.”

And she said to the foolish:

“Stolen waters are sweeter,

and bread eaten in secret is more pleasant.”

But he did not know that giants are there,

and that her guests are in the depths of the underworld.

## THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON

[Cap. X.] A wise son makes his father glad,

but a foolish son is the sorrow of his mother.

Treasures of wickedness will not profit,

but righteousness will deliver from death.

The Lord will not afflict the soul of the righteous with hunger,

and he will overthrow the snares of the wicked. [Note: [Col. 1251D] Vulgate manuscripts add, “He who relies on lies feeds the winds; he himself also pursues flying birds.” These words are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek, nor in the better-quality Hieronymian manuscripts, nor in the printed Royal Bibles. [Col. 1252D]]

[Col. 1252C] A slack hand produces poverty,

÷ but the hand of the strong prepares riches.

He who gathers during the harvest is a wise son;

but he who sleeps during summer is a son of shame.

The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous,

but the mouth of the wicked conceals iniquity.

The memory of the righteous is accompanied by praises,

but the name of the wicked will rot.

The wise in heart receives commandments,

but the fool is beaten by his lips.

He who walks simply walks securely,

but he who perverts his ways will be exposed.

He who winks with his eye causes pain;

the fool will be struck by his lips.

The mouth of the righteous is a vein of life,

but the mouth of the wicked conceals iniquity.

Hatred stirs up quarrels,

but charity covers all offenses.

Wisdom is found on the lips of the wise,

[Col. 1252D] and a rod on the back of the one who lacks understanding.

The wise conceal knowledge,

but the mouth of the fool is near to confusion.

The wealth of the rich is his fortified city;

the terror of the poor is their poverty.

The work of the righteous leads to life,

but the fruit of the wicked leads to sin.

The way of life belongs to one who keeps discipline,

but whoever abandons reproof goes astray.

Lying lips conceal hatred;

whoever utters insult is a fool.

In much speaking sin will not be absent,

but whoever restrains his lips is most prudent.

Refined silver is the tongue of the righteous,

[Col. 1253A] but the heart of the wicked is worthless.

The lips of the righteous instruct many,

but those who lack learning will die in poverty of heart.

The blessing of the Lord makes rich,

and no affliction will be joined to it.

As though laughing, the fool commits crime;

but wisdom is prudence for a man.

What the wicked fears will come upon him,

and the desire of the righteous will be granted.

As a storm passing by, the wicked will be no more,

but the righteous is like an everlasting foundation.

As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes,

so is the lazy person to those who send him.

The fear of the Lord adds days,

but the years of the wicked will be shortened.

The expectation of the righteous is joy,

but the hope of the wicked will perish.

The strength of the upright is the way of the Lord,

but terror is for those who do evil.

[Col. 1253B] The righteous will never be shaken,

but the wicked will not dwell upon the earth.

The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom,

but the tongue of the perverse will perish.

The lips of the righteous consider what is acceptable,

but the mouth of the wicked what is perverse.

[Cap. XI.] A deceitful balance is an abomination to the Lord,

but a just weight is his will.

Where there is pride, there will also be disgrace;

but where there is humility, there is wisdom.

The simplicity of the righteous will guide them,

but the treachery of the perverse will devastate them.

Riches will not profit on the day of vengeance,

but righteousness will deliver from death.

The righteousness of the simple directs his way,

but the wicked will fall through his own wickedness.

The righteousness of the upright will deliver them,

but the wicked will be caught in their own snares.

When a wicked man dies, there will be no further hope,

[Col. 1253C] and the expectation of the anxious will perish.

The righteous is freed from distress,

and the wicked is handed over in his place.

The hypocrite deceives his neighbor with his mouth,

but the righteous will be delivered by knowledge.

The city will rejoice in the prosperity of the righteous,

and there will be praise at the destruction of the wicked.

Through the blessing of the righteous the city will be exalted,

and through the mouth of the wicked it will be overthrown.

Whoever despises his neighbor lacks understanding,

but a prudent man will remain silent.

He who walks deceitfully reveals secrets,

but whoever is faithful in spirit conceals what his friend has entrusted to him.

Where there is no governor, the people will fall;

but there is safety where there is much counsel.

Misfortune will afflict one who gives surety for a stranger,

but whoever avoids snares will be secure.

A gracious woman [Note: [Col. 1253D] Instead of “will find,” some manuscript codices read “will have.” Canon Memmianus retains both variant readings in the text: “will have,” and in the margin, “will find.” MART.] will find [Alternative: “will have”] glory,

and the strong will possess riches.

A merciful man benefits his own soul,

but the cruel man rejects his relatives.

The wicked performs unstable work,

but for one who sows righteousness the reward is sure.

Kindness prepares life,

but the pursuit of evils, death.

A crooked heart is an abomination to the Lord,

but his will is with those who walk simply.

An evil man will not be innocent, hand in hand.

But the offspring of the righteous will be saved.

A golden ring in her nostrils:

a beautiful but foolish woman.

[Col. 1254A] The desire of the righteous is wholly good,

but the expectation of the wicked is fury.

Some distribute their own possessions and become richer;

others seize what is not theirs and are always in poverty.

The soul that blesses will be enriched,

and whoever gives drink will himself also be given drink.

Whoever hoards grain will be cursed among the peoples,

but blessing will be upon the head of those who sell it.

He who rises early seeking good does well,

but whoever investigates evil will be overwhelmed

by it.

Whoever trusts in riches will fall,

but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.

He who troubles his household will possess winds,

and the fool will serve the wise.

The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life,

and whoever wins souls is wise.

If the righteous is repaid on earth,

how much more the wicked and the sinner?

[Cap. XII.] Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge,

[Col. 1254B] but whoever hates reproof is foolish.

He who is good will obtain favor from the Lord,

but whoever trusts in his own thoughts acts wickedly.

Man will not be strengthened by wickedness,

but the root of the righteous will not be shaken.

An industrious woman is a crown to her husband,

but she who acts shamefully is rottenness in his bones.

The thoughts of the righteous are judgments,

but the counsels of the wicked are deceitful.

The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood,

but the mouth of the righteous will deliver them.

Overturn the wicked, and they will be no more,

but the house of the righteous will remain.

A man will be known by his teaching,

but one who is empty and senseless will be exposed to contempt.

Better is a poor man who is sufficient for himself

than one who is glorious but lacks bread.

The righteous knows the soul of his animals,

[Col. 1254C] but the inward parts of the wicked are cruel.

He who works his land will be satisfied with bread,

but whoever pursues idleness is utterly foolish. [Note: [Col. 1253D] The Vulgate editions add: “He who is fond of lingering over wine leaves disgrace in his fortifications” (some incorrectly read “moderations” instead of “lingerings”). [Col. 1254D] These words, taken from Greek exemplars, are entirely unknown to the Hebrew and to the manuscripts of the Hieronymian version.]

÷ The desire of the wicked is a fortress of the worst things,

but the root of the righteous will prosper.

Because of sins of the lips, ruin approaches the evil man,

but the righteous will escape from distress.

Each person will be filled with good things from the fruit of his mouth,

and he will be repaid according to the works of his hands.

The way of a fool is right in his own eyes,

but the wise man listens to counsel.

The fool immediately reveals his anger,

but whoever conceals an insult is shrewd.

Whoever speaks what he knows [Note: [Col. 1254D] Some printed books, and Latin interpreters, read “judge” instead of “one who makes known,” incorrectly.] is a revealer of justice,

but whoever lies is a deceitful witness.

There is one who promises and is pierced as though by a sword of conscience,

but the tongue of the wise is health.

The lip of truth will remain forever,

but a sudden witness contrives a tongue of deceit.

Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil,

but joy follows those who make plans for peace.

Nothing that happens to the righteous will grieve him,

but the wicked will be filled with evil.

Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord,

but those who act faithfully please him.

A cunning man conceals knowledge,

but the heart of fools provokes foolishness.

The hand of the strong will rule,

[Col. 1255A] but the slack hand will serve under tribute.

Sorrow in a man’s heart will humble him,

but he will be made joyful by a good word.

Whoever disregards loss for the sake of a friend is righteous,

but the way of the wicked will deceive them.

The deceitful will not find profit,

and a man’s wealth will be the price of gold.

In the path of righteousness there is life,
