but the crooked way leads to death.

[Cap. XIII.] A wise son is the teaching of his father,

but a scoffer does not listen when he is reproved.

A man will be satisfied with good things from the fruit of his mouth,

but the soul of transgressors is wicked.

Whoever guards his mouth guards his soul,

but whoever is careless in speaking will experience evil.

The lazy man both wishes and does not wish,

but the soul of those who work will be enriched.

The righteous detests a lying word,

but the wicked brings shame and is put to shame.

[Col. 1255B] Righteousness guards the way of the innocent,

but wickedness trips up the sinner.

There is one who is as though rich, though he has nothing,

and one who is as though poor, though he possesses many riches.

A man’s riches are the redemption of his soul,

but the poor man does not endure reproof.

The light of the righteous gives joy,

but the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished.

Among the proud there are always quarrels,

but those who do everything with counsel are guided by wisdom.

Wealth acquired hastily will diminish,

but what is gradually gathered by hand will increase.

Hope deferred afflicts the soul,

but desire coming to fulfillment is a tree of life.

Whoever disparages a thing binds himself for the future,

but whoever fears the commandment will live in peace. [Note: [Col. 1255D] Manuscript codices have here a certain addition, as we said above—not indeed the same sentence as that found in the Vulgate, but the one occurring below in chapter XIV, verse 15. MART. The Vulgate codices add: “Deceitful souls go astray in sins, but the righteous are merciful and show mercy,” apparently imported into the Greek exemplar from nearly similar sayings in Psalms XXVI and CXI. They are not found in the Hebrew, nor in the Hieronymian codices derived from it.]

÷ The law of the wise is a fountain of life,

so that he may turn away from the ruin of death.

Good teaching gives grace,

but in the way of scorners is an abyss.

The astute acts in everything with counsel,

but the fool reveals his foolishness.

The messenger of the wicked will fall into evil;

a faithful envoy is health.

Poverty and disgrace belong to one who abandons discipline,

but whoever submits to the reprover will be glorified.

When desire is fulfilled, it delights the soul;

fools detest those who flee from evil.

Whoever walks with the wise will be wise,

but the friend of fools will become like them.

Evil pursues sinners,

but good things will be repaid to the righteous.

The good man leaves heirs: sons and grandchildren;

and the sinner’s wealth is stored up for the righteous.

There is abundant food in the fields of the fathers,

but it is gathered by others without judgment.

Whoever spares the rod hates his son,

[Col. 1255D] but whoever loves him diligently instructs him.

The righteous eats and fills his soul,

but the belly of the wicked is insatiable.

[Cap. XIV.] A wise woman builds her house,

but the foolish woman tears down even what has been built, with her hands.

[Col. 1256A] He who walks on the straight way and fears God

is despised by one who walks on an infamous path.

In the mouth of a fool is the rod of pride,

but the lips of the wise guard them.

Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty;

but where there are abundant crops, there is evident strength

in the ox.

A faithful witness does not lie,

but a deceitful witness utters lies.

The scoffer seeks wisdom and will not find it;

instruction is easy for the prudent.

Go away from a foolish man,

for he does not know the lips of prudence.

The wisdom of the cunning is to understand his way,

but the folly of fools is wandering.

The fool mocks sin,

but among the righteous grace will remain.

The heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul

will not admit a stranger into its joy.

The house of the wicked will be destroyed,

[Col. 1256B] but the tents of the righteous will flourish.

There is a way that seems right to a man,

but its end leads to death.

Laughter will be mixed with sorrow,

and mourning will occupy the end of joy.

The fool will be filled with his own ways,

and a good man will be over him.

The innocent believes every word,

but the astute considers his steps. [Note: [Col. 1255D] The addition retained here by the Vulgate is not found in manuscript codices. See our preceding annotation to chapter III, verse 13 [Col. 1256D], according to the numbering of the verses in the printed editions. Again, nearly the same addition occurs in some Vulgate editions: “There will be no good for a deceitful son, but the actions of a wise servant will prosper, and his way will be directed.” These words are borrowed verbatim from verse 13 of the immediately preceding chapter in the Greek.]

The wise fears and turns away from evil;

the fool leaps over it and is confident.

The impatient man will act foolishly,

and the crafty man is hateful.

The simple will possess foolishness,

but the astute will await knowledge.

The wicked will lie before the good,

and the impious before the gates of the righteous.

Even the poor is hated by his neighbor,

but the friends of the rich are many.

[Col. 1256C] Whoever despises his neighbor sins,

but blessed is whoever has mercy on the poor. [Note: [Col. 1256D] The words added here by the Vulgate codices—“whoever trusts in the Lord loves mercy”—are found neither in the Hebrew, nor in the Greek, nor finally in the older Latin manuscripts.]

Those who do evil go astray;

mercy and truth prepare good things.

In every work there will be abundance,

but where there are very many words, there is often poverty.

The crown of the wise is their wealth;

the foolishness of fools is imprudence.

A faithful witness delivers souls,

but the deceitful man utters lies.

In the fear of the Lord is confidence of strength,

and there will be hope for his sons.

The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life,

so that they may turn away from the ruin of death.

In the multitude of the people lies the dignity of a king,

but in the smallness of the populace, the disgrace of a ruler.

Whoever is patient is governed by great prudence,

but whoever is impatient exalts his foolishness.

The life of the flesh is the health of the heart,

[Col. 1256D] but envy is the rottenness of the bones.

Whoever slanders the needy insults his Maker,

but he honors him who has mercy on the poor.

The wicked will be expelled by his wickedness,

but the righteous hopes even in his death.

[Col. 1257A] Wisdom rests in the heart of the prudent,

and it will instruct all the unlearned.

Righteousness exalts a nation,

but sin makes peoples miserable.

An intelligent servant is acceptable to the king,

but the useless servant will endure his anger.

[Cap. XV.] A gentle answer breaks anger,

but a harsh word arouses fury.

The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge,

but the mouth of fools pours forth foolishness.

In every place the eyes of the Lord

observe the evil and the good.

A soothing tongue is a tree of life,

but an unrestrained one will crush the spirit.

The fool mocks the discipline of his father,

but whoever keeps reproofs will become more astute. [Note: [Col. 1257D] Some copies of the Vulgate version add, “In abundant righteousness there is great strength, but the thoughts of the wicked will be uprooted.” These words are absent not only from the Hebrew and the Hieronymian codices derived from it, but also from several Greek editions, and seem to be nothing other than a double interpretation of the following verse, “The house of the righteous,” and so forth.]

The house of the righteous has very great strength,

but in the fruits of the wicked there is disturbance.

The lips of the wise scatter knowledge,

but the heart of fools is unlike it.

[Col. 1257B] The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord,

but the vows of the righteous are acceptable.

The way of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord,

but whoever follows righteousness is loved by him.

Bad discipline is for one who abandons the way. [Note: [Col. 1257D] The Vulgate has “the way of life”; but the Hebrew does not recognize the final word.]

Whoever hates reproof will die.

The underworld and destruction are before the Lord;

how much more the hearts of the sons of men!

The pestilent man does not love one who rebukes him,

nor does he walk with the wise.

A joyful heart makes the face cheerful,

but in sorrow of spirit the spirit is cast down.

The heart of the wise seeks instruction,

but the mouth of fools is fed on ignorance.

All the days of the poor are evil,

but a secure mind is like a continual feast.

Better is a little with the fear of the Lord

than great and insatiable treasures.

Better is [Note: [Col. 1257D] This is the reading of all manuscript copies; the printed books have the passive form “to be called.” MART.] to invite [someone] to vegetables with love [Alternative: “to be called”]

[Col. 1257C] than for a fatted calf with hatred.

An angry man provokes quarrels,

but the patient man calms those that have been stirred up.

The way of the lazy is like a hedge of thorns,

but the way of the righteous is without stumbling.

A wise son makes his father glad,

but a foolish man despises his mother.

Foolishness is joy to a fool,

but a prudent man directs his steps.

Thoughts are scattered where there is no counsel,

but where there are many counselors, they are confirmed.

A man rejoices in the judgment of his mouth,

and a timely word is best.

The path of life lies above the learned,

so that he may turn away from the lowest underworld.

The Lord will demolish the house of the proud,

but he will make firm the boundaries of the widow.

The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord,

but a pure word is most beautiful. [Note: [Col. 1257D] Vulgate codices add in one continuous sequence, “It will be established by him”; this is known neither to the original texts nor to the Greek, nor to most Latin books, both printed and manuscript.]

[Col. 1257D] He who pursues greed troubles his household,

but whoever hates gifts will live. [Note: [Col. 1258D] The Vulgate again adds: “By mercy and faith sins are cleansed, but by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil.” This is the sixth verse of the following chapter; here it occurs only among the Septuagint.]

[Col. 1258A] The mind of the righteous meditates obedience [Note: [Col. 1258D] The San-Germain manuscript no. 15 reads, “meditates wisdom.” The Hebrew has written *jege laanoth*, “he meditates in order to answer.” MART.] [Alternative: “wisdom”];

the mouth of the wicked overflows with evils.

The Lord is far from the wicked,

but he will hear the prayers of the righteous.

Light of the eyes makes the soul joyful,

and a good report makes the bones fat.

An ear that hears the reproofs of life

will dwell in the midst of the wise.

Whoever rejects discipline despises his own soul,

but whoever submits to reproofs is a possessor of a heart

[or: “a wise-hearted person”].

The fear of the Lord is the discipline of wisdom,

and humility precedes glory.

[Cap. XVI.] It belongs to man to prepare his soul,

but it belongs to the Lord to govern the tongue.

All a man’s ways are open to his eyes,

but the Lord weighs the spirits.

Reveal your works to the Lord,

and your thoughts will be directed.

The Lord has made all things for himself,

[Col. 1258B] even the wicked for the evil day.

Everyone arrogant is an abomination to the Lord;

even if hand joins hand, he will not be innocent. [Note: [Col. 1258D] Here too the Vulgate translator adds: “To begin a good way is to practice righteousness; but it is more acceptable to God than offering a sacrifice,” with the Hebrew and most other books contradicting it. See the preceding chapter, verse 7.]

Iniquity is redeemed by mercy and truth,

and by the fear of the Lord one turns away from evil.

When a man’s ways please the Lord,

he will turn even his enemies toward peace.

Better is a little with righteousness

than many fruits with iniquity.

A man’s heart plans his way,

but it belongs to the Lord to direct his steps.

Divination is on the lips of the king;

his mouth will not err in judgment.

Weight and balance are the judgments of the Lord,

and all the stones of the bag are his work. [Note: [Col. 1258D] Most authors after Bede read “the stones of the age.”]

Those who act wickedly are an abomination to the king,

for the throne is established by righteousness.

[Col. 1258C] Just lips are the desire of kings;

whoever speaks what is right will be loved.

The king’s indignation is messengers of death,

but a wise man will appease it.

In the brightness of the king’s face there is life,

and his clemency is like the late rain.

Possess wisdom, for it is better than gold,

and acquire prudence, for it is more precious than silver.

The path of the righteous turns away from evil;

whoever guards his own soul preserves his way.

Pride precedes destruction,

and a spirit is exalted before a fall.

It is better to be humbled with the meek

than to divide spoils with the proud.

One instructed in speech will find good,

and blessed is whoever hopes in the Lord.

Whoever is wise in heart will be called prudent,

and whoever is sweet in speech will receive greater things.

The instruction of its possessor is a fountain of life,

but the teaching of fools is foolishness.

The heart of the wise will instruct his mouth,

[Col. 1259A] and will add grace to his lips.

Well-arranged words are a honeycomb;

sweetness to the soul and health to the bones.

There is a way that seems straight to a man,

but its end leads to death.

The soul of one who labors labors for itself,

because his mouth compels him.

The wicked man digs evil,

and fire burns on his lips.

A perverse man stirs up quarrels,

and a talkative man separates rulers.

An unjust man entices his friend,

and leads him along a bad way.

Whoever thinks perversely with staring eyes,

biting his lips, accomplishes evil.

Old age is a crown of dignity,

which will be found in the ways of righteousness.

The patient man is better than the strong,

and whoever rules his spirit is better than one who captures cities.

[Col. 1259B] Lots are cast into the lap,

but they are governed by the Lord.

[Cap. XVII.] Better is a dry morsel with joy

than a house full of sacrifices with quarrels.

A wise servant will rule over foolish sons,

and he will divide the inheritance among brothers.

As silver is tested in the fire and gold in the furnace,

so the Lord tests hearts.

The wicked man obeys an evil tongue,

and the deceitful man complies with lying lips.

Whoever despises the poor insults his Maker,

and whoever rejoices in another’s ruin will not go unpunished.

The crown of the aged is the children of their children,

and the glory of sons is their fathers.

Polished words do not suit a fool,

nor a lying lip a prince.

A most pleasing gem is the expectation of one who waits;

wherever it turns, it understands prudently.

Whoever conceals an offense seeks friendship,

but whoever repeats the matter in another speech separates allies.

[Col. 1259C] Correction benefits the prudent more

than a hundred blows benefit a fool.

The wicked man is always seeking quarrels,

but a cruel angel will be sent against him.

It is better to meet a bear deprived of its cubs

than a fool confident in his own foolishness.

Whoever repays good with evil,

evil will not depart from his house.

He who lets water loose is the beginning of quarrels,

and before he suffers insult, he abandons judgment.

Whoever justifies the wicked and whoever condemns the righteous

are both abominable to God.

What benefit is it for a fool to possess riches

when he cannot buy wisdom? [Note: [Col. 1259D] The Vulgate translator adds another verse: “He who builds his house high seeks ruin, and whoever avoids learning will fall into evils,” derived solely from the Septuagint.]

At all times the one who is a friend loves,

and a brother is proved in distress.

A foolish man claps his hands

when he has become surety for his friend.

Whoever meditates discord directs quarrels,

[Col. 1259D] and whoever exalts [Note: [Col. 1259D] Some Latin books give “your mouth” instead of “the doorway”; those who read the other word commonly interpret it as “mouth.”] the doorway seeks ruin.

Whoever has a perverse heart will not find good,

and whoever twists his tongue will fall into evil.

A fool is born to his own disgrace,

[Col. 1260A] and even his father will not rejoice in the fool.

A joyful mind makes one’s age flourish,

but a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones.

The wicked man accepts gifts from the bosom

to pervert the paths of judgment.

Wisdom shines on the face of the prudent,

but the eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth.

A foolish son is the anger of his father,

and the grief of the mother who bore him.

It is not good to inflict loss on the righteous,

nor to strike a ruler who judges rightly.

Whoever moderates his words is learned and prudent,

and an educated man is precious in spirit.

Even if a fool remains silent, he will be considered wise,

and if he restrains his lips, intelligent.

[Cap. XVIII.] He who wishes to withdraw from a friend

seeks opportunities [Note: [Col. 1259D] The Hebrew has a word that properly means “desire,” or, as Aquila and Symmachus interpret it, *eis epithymian* (εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν), “for desire.” Jerome, however, may have preferred to retain the reading commonly received from the Septuagint, or may himself have read in his Hebrew exemplar a word not very different in form, meaning “opportunity,” in place of [the Hebrew term].];

he will be reproachable at all times.

A fool does not receive the words of prudence

unless you say what is in his heart.

[Col. 1260B] When the wicked comes into the depths of sins, he acts contemptuously,

but disgrace and reproach follow him.

The words from a man’s mouth are deep waters,

and a flowing torrent, a fountain of wisdom.

To show partiality to the wicked is not good,

so as to turn aside from the truth of judgment.

The lips of a fool involve themselves in quarrels,

and his mouth provokes disputes.

The mouth of a fool is his ruin,

and his lips are the destruction of his soul.

The words of a double-tongued person seem simple,

but they reach the innermost parts of the belly [or: “the body”].

[Note: [Col. 1260D] The Vulgate adds, “Fear casts down the lazy, but the souls of the effeminate will hunger.” This is an old translation from the Septuagint version of the same verse, “The words of a double-tongued person,” and so forth. It is not found in the Complutensian edition or in the Hieronymian codices.]

Whoever is soft and negligent in his work

is a brother to one who dissipates his own work.

The name of the Lord is a most fortified tower;

the righteous runs to it and will be exalted.

The wealth of the rich is his strong city,

and like a solid wall surrounding him.

[Col. 1260C] Before he is crushed, a man’s heart is exalted;

and before he is honored, he is humbled.

Whoever answers before he hears

shows himself to be a fool and worthy of confusion.

A man’s spirit sustains his weakness;

but who can endure a spirit easily provoked to anger?

A prudent heart will acquire knowledge,

and the ear of the wise seeks instruction.

A man’s gift enlarges his path

and makes room for him before princes.

The righteous is the first to accuse himself;

then his friend comes and investigates him.

The lot puts an end to disputes

and decides even among the powerful.

A brother helped by his brother is like a fortified city,

and their judgments are like the bars of cities.

From the fruit of a man’s mouth his belly will be filled,

and the produce of his lips will satisfy him.

Death and life are in the power of the tongue;

[Col. 1260D] those who love it will eat its fruits.

Whoever finds a [Note: [Col. 1260D] Neither the Hebrew nor several Latin editions recognize the added word “good.”] good wife finds what is good

and will draw delight from the Lord [Note: [Col. 1260D] Here again certain manuscripts of the Vulgate add another verse: “Whoever drives away a good wife drives away what is good; but whoever keeps an adulterous woman is a fool and an impious man.” Most Latin manuscripts, following the Hebrew, do not know this verse. See the biblical critics.].

The poor man speaks with entreaties,

[Col. 1261A] but the rich man answers harshly.

A [Note: [Col. 1261D] For *amabilis* (“lovable”), most manuscripts read *amicabilis* (“friendly”): “A friendly man,” and so forth. The word is somewhat inelegant, but it yields a meaning not inconsistent with Scripture. Saint Augustine’s *Speculum* also preserves it. MART.] lovable [Al. friendly] man

will be more of a friend than a brother.

[Chapter XIX.] Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity

than [Note: [Col. 1261D] In copies of the Canon and in certain other manuscripts one reads, “than a rich man twisting his lips, a fool”; but the word “rich” is not found in the Hebrew, nor in several of the oldest and more accurate manuscripts of Jerome’s version. It was added to complete the contrast with the preceding clause, in which “poor” seemed to require the contrary word “rich” after it. MART.—The Vulgate has “rich” here as well, [Col. 1262D] although that word is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek Septuagint or in the better Jerome manuscripts.] a fool who twists his lips.

Where there is no knowledge of the soul, there is no good;

and whoever is hasty with his feet will stumble.

A man’s folly subverts his steps,

and in his heart he rages against God.

Riches add many friends;

but from the poor even those whom he had withdraw.

A false witness will not go unpunished,

and whoever speaks lies will not escape.

Many court the presence of the powerful,

and are friends of the giver of gifts.

The brothers of a poor man hate him;

indeed, his friends have withdrawn far from him.

Whoever pursues only words will have nothing;

but whoever possesses a sound mind loves his life

[Col. 1261B]

and whoever guards prudence will find good things.

A false witness will not go unpunished,

and whoever speaks lies will perish.

Luxury is not fitting for a fool,

nor for a servant to rule over princes.

A man’s understanding is known through patience,

and it is his glory to pass over wrongdoing.

As the roaring of a lion, so is the anger of a king;

and as dew upon grass, so is his cheerfulness.

A foolish son is the grief of his father,

and a quarrelsome wife is like a roof continually dripping.

House and riches are inherited from fathers,

but a prudent wife comes especially from the Lord.

Sloth sends sleep,

and the idle soul will hunger.

Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his soul;

but whoever neglects his ways will be put to death.

Whoever shows mercy to the poor lends to the Lord,

[Col. 1261C] and he will repay him what he has given.

Discipline your son, and do not despair;

but do not set your heart on killing him.

Whoever is impatient will suffer loss;

and when he has seized something, he will add another thing.

Hear counsel and accept discipline,

so that you may be wise in your latter days.

Many are the thoughts in a man’s heart,

but the will of the Lord will endure.

A needy man is merciful,

and a poor man is better than a liar.

The fear of the Lord leads to life;

and in abundance he will dwell, untouched by the visitation of evil [Al. *pessima* (“evil”)].

The sluggard hides his hand beneath his armpit

and does not bring it back to his mouth.

When the scoffer is scourged, the fool becomes wiser;

but if you rebuke the wise, he will understand discipline.

[Col. 1261D] Whoever afflicts his father and drives away his mother

is disgraceful and unhappy.

Do not cease, my son, to hear instruction,

and do not neglect words of knowledge.

An unjust witness mocks judgment,

[Col. 1262A] and the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity.

Judgments are prepared for scoffers,

and hammers for striking the bodies of fools.

[Chapter XX.] Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous;

whoever delights in these will not be wise.

As the roaring of a lion, so is the terror of a king;

whoever provokes him sins against his own life.

It is an honor for a man to withdraw from disputes;

but all fools become involved in insults.

Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow;

therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him.

As deep water, so is counsel in a man’s heart;

but a wise man will draw it out.

Many men are called merciful;

but who will find a faithful man?

The righteous who walks in his integrity

will leave blessed children after him.

A king who sits upon the throne of judgment

scatters all evil with his gaze.

[Col. 1262B] Who can say, “My heart is clean;

I am pure from sin”?

A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure:

both are abominable before God.

A boy is understood by his habits,

whether his deeds are pure and upright.

The Lord made both the hearing ear

and the seeing eye.

Do not love sleep, lest poverty overwhelm you;

open your eyes, and you will be filled with bread.

“It is bad, it is bad,” says every buyer;

but when he has gone away, then he boasts.

There is gold and an abundance of jewels,

but a precious vessel is lips of knowledge.

Take away his garment who became surety for a stranger,

and take a pledge from him on behalf of foreigners.

The bread of deceit is sweet to a man,

but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel.

Plans are strengthened by counsels,

[Col. 1262C] and wars must be directed by guiding-rules.

With one who reveals secrets and walks deceitfully,

and with one who opens his lips wide, do not associate.

Whoever curses his father and mother—

his lamp will be extinguished in the midst of darkness.

An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning

will lack blessing at the end.

Do not [Note: [Col. 1262D] The copyists of the Canon added these two words here, “for evil”; for in them we read, “I will repay evil for evil.” But this is shown to be corrupt. MART.] say, “I will repay evil”;

wait for the Lord, and he will deliver you.

A weight and a weight are an abomination before the Lord;

a deceitful scale is not good.

The steps of a man are directed by the Lord;

but who among men can understand his way?

It is the ruin of a man to devour [Note: [Col. 1262D] Certain Latin editions disagree among themselves: some have “It is ruin for a man to devote the holy ones,” others “to summon” or “to mark out the holy ones.” The reading printed in the German edition is closer to the Hebrew. Shortly afterward, common books read *retractare* (“withdraw”) instead of *tractare* (“deal with”).] the holy ones

and afterward to deal with vows.

A wise king scatters the wicked

and bends a wheel over them.

The Lord’s lamp is the breath of man,

searching all the hidden places of the belly.

[Col. 1262D] Mercy and truth guard the king,

and clemency strengthens his throne.

The glory of young men is their strength;

and the dignity of the old is their gray hair.

The bruise of a wound wipes away evils,

and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly.

[Chapter XXI.] As the divisions of waters, so is the king’s heart

in the hand of the Lord:

he inclines it wherever he wills.

Every way of a man seems right to him,

but the Lord weighs hearts.

To practice mercy and judgment

pleases the Lord more than sacrifice.

The lifting up of the eyes and the enlargement of the heart—

the lamp of the wicked is sin.

The thoughts of the strong are always in abundance,

but every sluggard is always in want.

Whoever gathers treasures by a lying tongue

[Note: [Col. 1263D] The Vulgate and certain manuscripts among Martianay’s copies read, “He is vain and senseless,” from the translation of the Septuagint, τῶν LXX.]

is vain and will stumble into the snares of death.

The spoils of the wicked will drag them away,

because they refused to practice judgment.

The perverse way of a man is alien to him;

but whoever is clean has an upright work.

It is better to sit in a corner of the roof

than with a quarrelsome woman in a common house.

[Col. 1263B] The soul of the wicked desires evil;

he will not spare his neighbor.

When the scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wiser;

and if he follows the wise, he will acquire knowledge.

The righteous devises a plan concerning the house of the wicked,

to remove the wicked from evil.

Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor

will himself cry out and not be heard.

A hidden gift extinguishes anger,

and a gift in the bosom, the greatest indignation.

It is joy to the righteous to practice judgment,

but terror to those who work iniquity.

A man who wanders from the way of instruction

will dwell in the assembly of giants.

Whoever loves feasting will be in poverty;

whoever loves wine and fat things will not grow rich.

An impious man is given in place of the righteous,

and a wicked man in place of the upright.

It is better to dwell in a desert land

[Col. 1263C] than with a quarrelsome and irritable woman.

A desirable treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the righteous,

but a foolish man will squander them.

Whoever pursues righteousness and mercy

will find life, righteousness, and glory.

A wise man climbs the city of the mighty

and destroys the strength of its confidence.

Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue

guards his soul from distress.

A proud and arrogant man is called uneducated,

one who acts in proud anger.

Desires kill the sluggard,

for his hands refused to do anything.

All day long he craves and desires;

but the righteous gives and does not cease.

The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable,

because they are offered from wickedness.

A lying witness will perish;

an obedient man will speak of victory.

An impious man hardens his face insolently,

[Col. 1263D] but whoever is upright corrects his way.

There is no wisdom, no prudence,

no counsel against the Lord.

The horse is prepared for the day of battle,

but the Lord grants salvation.

[Chapter XXII.] A good name is better than abundant riches;

and good favor is better than silver and gold.

Rich and poor meet one another;

the Lord is the maker of them both.

The shrewd man saw the evil and hid himself;

the innocent passed by and suffered harm.

The end of modesty is the fear of the Lord,

riches, glory, and life.

[Col. 1264A] Weapons and swords are on the way of the perverse;

but whoever guards his own soul withdraws far from them.

There is a proverb: “A young man according to his way—

even when he grows old, he will not depart from it.”

The rich rules over the poor,

and whoever receives a loan is the servant of the lender.

Whoever sows iniquity will reap evils,

and the rod of his anger will be consumed.

Whoever is inclined to mercy will be blessed,

for he has given the poor man bread from his own [Note: [Col. 1263D] Certain editions of the Vulgate add, “He who gives gifts will acquire victory and honor, but he takes away the life of those who receive them.” These words are absent from other editions, from the Jerome manuscripts, and also from the Hebrew.].

Cast out the scoffer, and strife will go out with him;

causes and insults will cease.

Whoever loves purity of heart

will have the king as his friend

because of the grace of his lips.

The eyes of the Lord guard knowledge,

but the words of the wicked are overthrown.

The sluggard says, “There is a lion outside;

I will be killed in the midst of the streets.”

The mouth of a foreign woman is a deep pit;

the one with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it.

Folly is bound up in the heart of a child,

but the rod of discipline will drive it away.

Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his riches

will himself give to one richer and will suffer want.

Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise;

apply your heart to my instruction.

It will be beautiful for you when you keep it in your belly

[Al. “in your heart”],

and it will overflow upon your lips,

so that your confidence may be in the Lord;

therefore I have shown it to you today.

Behold, I have written it out for you in three ways,

in counsels and knowledge,

to show you certainty and words of truth,

so that you may answer from them those who sent you.

Do not do violence to the poor because he is poor,

nor crush the needy at the gate,

for the Lord will judge his cause

[Col. 1264C] and will pierce those who pierced his soul.

Do not be a friend to an irascible man,

nor walk with a furious man,

lest you learn his paths

and take a stumbling-block for your soul.

Do not associate with those who put up security,

and who offer themselves as guarantors for debts.

For if you have nothing with which to repay,

why should he take away the covering from your bed?

Do not move the ancient boundaries

that your fathers established.

Have you seen a man swift in his work?

He will stand before kings

and will not be before obscure men.

[Chapter XXIII.] When you sit to eat with a ruler,

pay careful attention to what is placed before you.

And set a knife at your throat,

if indeed you have control over your soul,

[Col. 1264D] lest you desire his delicacies,

in which there is the bread of deceit.

Do not labor to become rich,

but set a limit to your prudence.

Do not raise your eyes to riches that you cannot possess,

for they will make themselves wings like an eagle’s

and fly up into heaven.

Do not eat with an envious man,

and do not desire his foods,

for, like a diviner and an interpreter of omens,

he estimates what he does not know.

“Eat and drink,” he will say to you,

but his heart is not with you.

[Col. 1265A] You will vomit the food that you had eaten

and lose your fine words.

Do not speak in the ears of fools,

for they will despise the instruction of your speech.

Do not touch the boundaries [Note: [Col. 1265D] The Hebrew has *gevulot ʿolam*, “ancient” or “old boundaries.” In its place, the holy Father seems to have read *naʿar*, with the second vowel-point omitted, meaning “young man” or “little child,” differing from the other reading only by the intervening *waw*.] of children,

and do not enter the fields of orphans.

For their near kinsman is strong,

and he himself will judge their cause against you.

Let your heart enter into instruction,

and let your ears attend to words of knowledge.

Do not withdraw discipline from a child;

for if you strike him with the rod, he will not die.

You will strike him with the rod,

and you will deliver his soul from hell.

My son, if your heart is wise,

my heart will rejoice with you.

And my kidneys will exult

when your lips speak what is right.

Let your heart not envy sinners,

but be in the fear of the Lord all day long,

[Col. 1265B] for you will have hope at the end,

and your expectation will not be taken away.

Hear, my son, and be wise,

and direct your heart in the way.

Do not be among those who drink at banquets,

nor among those who provide meat for feasting,

for those who devote themselves to drinking

and contribute their shares will be consumed,

and drowsiness will clothe itself in rags.

Hear your father who begot you,

and do not despise your mother when she grows old.

Buy truth, and do not sell it—

wisdom, instruction, and understanding.

The father of the righteous rejoices with joy;

whoever begets wisdom will rejoice in him.

Let your father and your mother rejoice,

and let her who bore you exult.

Give me your heart, my son,

[Col. 1265C] and let your eyes guard my ways.

For a prostitute is a deep pit,

and a foreign woman is a narrow well.

She lies in wait on the road like a robber,

and kills those whom she sees off guard.

[Note: [Col. 1265D] The Hebrew has literally, “To whom woe? To whose father woe?” In Hebrew: . Learned men think that Jerome read the second isocolon as three separate words, , or, in two words, with another *aleph* added, instead of .]

To whom is there woe? Whose father has woe?

For whom are quarrels? For whom are pits?

For whom are wounds without cause?

For whom is redness of eyes?

Is it not for those who linger over wine

and devote themselves to emptying cups?

Do not look at wine when it glistens,

when its color shines in the glass.

It enters smoothly,

but in the end it will bite like a serpent

and spread poison like a basilisk.

Your eyes will see foreign women,

and your heart will speak perverse things.

And you will be like one sleeping in the midst of the sea,

and like a slumbering helmsman who has lost the tiller.

[Col. 1265D] And you will say:

“They struck me, but I did not feel pain;

they dragged me, and I did not know it.

When will I awake,

and again find wine?”

[Chapter XXIV.] Do not envy evil men,

nor desire to be with them,

for their mind meditates robberies,

and their lips speak deceit.

By wisdom a house will be built,

and by prudence it will be strengthened.

[Col. 1266A] By instruction the storerooms will be filled

with every precious and beautiful possession.

A wise man is strong,

and a learned man is robust and powerful.

For war is undertaken with careful planning,

and there will be safety where there are many counselors.

Wisdom is too high for a fool;

at the gate he will not open his mouth.

Whoever plans to do evil

will be called a fool.

The thought of a fool is sin,

and the detractor is an abomination to men.

If you lose heart when you are weary on the day of distress,

your strength will be diminished.

Rescue those who are being led to death,

and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction.

If you say, “Our strength is insufficient,”

the one who examines the heart understands.

Nothing escapes the guardian of your soul,

and he will repay a man according to his works.

[Col. 1266B] Eat honey, my son, because it is good,

and the honeycomb is sweetest to your throat.

Such is the instruction of wisdom to your soul:

when you have found it, you will possess it at the end [Note: [Col. 1266D] The printed editions and certain manuscripts among Martianay’s copies add, “hope at the end.” The Hebrew has only, “and it will be at the end.”],

and your hope will not perish.

Do not lie in wait or seek impiety in the house of the righteous,

nor destroy his rest,

for the righteous falls seven times and rises again,

but the wicked will fall into evil.

When your enemy falls, do not rejoice,

and when he is ruined, let your heart not exult,

lest the Lord see it and it displease him,

and he turn his anger away from him.

Do not contend with the worst of men,

nor envy the wicked,

for the evil have no hope of what is to come,

and the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished.

Fear the Lord, my son, and the king,

and do not associate with detractors,

[Col. 1266C] for their destruction will rise up suddenly;

and who knows the ruin of them both?

These things also are for the wise:

To recognize a person in judgment is not good.

Those who say to the wicked, “You are righteous,”

will be cursed by peoples,

and tribes will detest them.

Those who rebuke will be praised,

and blessing will come upon them.

Whoever answers with upright words

will kiss the lips.

Prepare your work outside,

and carefully cultivate your field,

so that afterward you may build your house.

Do not be a false witness against your neighbor,

nor deceive anyone with your lips.

Do not say, “As he did to me, so I will do to him;

I will repay each one according to his work.”

I passed by the field of a sluggard

and by the vineyard of a foolish man,

and behold, it was entirely filled with nettles;

[Col. 1266D] thorns had covered its surface,

and its stone wall had been destroyed.

When I saw this, I laid it to heart

and learned discipline from the example.

“A little sleep,” I said, “a little slumber,

a little folding of the hands to rest;

and your poverty will come upon you like a runner,

and your want like an armed man.”

[Col. 1267A] THESE ALSO ARE THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON, WHICH THE MEN OF HEZEKIAH, KING OF JUDAH, TRANSFERRED [Note: [Col. 1267D] In the Memmian Canon, “Diapsalma” is incorrectly read here after the word “Judah.” MART.].

[Chapter XXV.] It is the glory of God to conceal a word,

and the glory of kings to investigate a matter.

Heaven above and earth below,

but the heart of kings is unsearchable.

Remove the dross from silver,

and a most pure vessel will emerge.

Remove wickedness from the face of the king,

and his throne will be established in righteousness.

Do not appear glorious before the king,

nor stand in the place of the great.

For it is better that someone say to you, “Come up here,”

than that you be humbled before a prince.

What your eyes have seen, do not quickly bring out in a quarrel,

lest afterward you be unable to correct it

when you have dishonored your friend.

Discuss your case with your friend,

and do not reveal a secret to a stranger,

[Col. 1267B] lest, when he hears it, he insult you

and never cease reproaching you.

[Note: [Col. 1267D] The Vulgate manuscripts append this other verse: “Grace and friendship deliver; preserve them for yourself, lest you become reproachable.” It is derived solely from the Septuagint; but some further add, ἀλλὰ φύλαξον τὰς ὁδούς σου εὐσυναλλάκτως, “but keep your ways in friendship.” Yet neither the Hebrew, the Jerome manuscripts themselves, nor finally the Complutensian edition contains any of these.]

Golden apples in silver settings:

such is a word spoken at the proper time.

A golden earring and a shining pearl

is one who rebukes a wise man

and an obedient ear.

As the cold of snow on the day of harvest,

so is a faithful messenger to the one who sent him:

he gives rest to his soul.

Clouds and wind, but no following rain:

such is a boastful man who does not fulfill his promises.

Patience will soothe a ruler,

and a gentle tongue will break hardness.

You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you,

lest, when you are filled, you vomit it.

Withdraw your foot from your neighbor’s house,

lest, when he is satisfied, he hate you.

A dart, a sword, and a sharp arrow

is a man who speaks false testimony against his neighbor.

[Col. 1267C] A rotten tooth and a weary foot

is one who trusts in a faithless man on the day of distress,

and one who loses his cloak on a cold day.

Vinegar on soda

is one who sings songs to a most wicked heart. [Note: [Col. 1268D] The same Vulgate manuscripts add, “As a moth to a garment and a worm to wood, so the sadness of a man harms the heart.” These words occur in the Chaldean version but not in the Hebrew, the Jerome manuscripts, or the Complutensian edition.]

If your enemy is hungry, feed him;

if he is thirsty, give him water to drink.

For you will heap burning coals upon his head,

and the Lord will repay you.

The north wind disperses rains,

and a sad face a slandering tongue.

It is better to sit in a corner of the roof

than with a quarrelsome woman in a common house.

Cold water for a thirsty soul,

and good news from a distant land.

A spring muddied by the foot and a corrupted fountain

is the righteous man falling before the wicked.

As it is not good for one who eats too much honey,

[Col. 1267D] so one who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory.

As an open city without a surrounding wall,

so is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking.

[Chapter XXVI.] As snow in summer and rain in harvest,

so glory is unfitting for a fool.

As a bird flying toward [Note: [Col. 1268D] Certain editions, such as that of Sixtus V and the Complutensian edition, as well as interpreters of this passage, read “toward high places” instead of “toward other things.”] other things,

[Col. 1268A] and a sparrow going wherever it pleases,

so a curse uttered without cause against anyone

will come upon him.

A whip for a horse, a bridle for an ass,

and a rod for the back of the foolish.

Do not answer a fool according to his folly,

lest you become like him.

Answer a fool according to his folly,

lest he seem wise to himself.

A lame man with his feet useless,

and one who drinks iniquity,

is the person who sends words by a foolish messenger.

As a lame man has beautiful legs uselessly,

so a proverb is unfitting in the mouth of fools.

As one who throws a stone into a heap of Mercury,

so is one who gives honor to a fool.

As when a thorn grows in the hand of a drunkard,

so is a proverb in the mouth of fools.

Judgment determines cases,

and whoever imposes silence on a fool calms anger.

As a dog that returns to its vomit,

[Col. 1268B] so is the foolish man who repeats his folly.

Have you seen a man who seems wise to himself?

The fool offers more hope than he does.

The sluggard says, “A lion is on the road;

a lion is in the paths.”

As a door turns on its hinge,

so does the sluggard on his bed.

The sluggard hides his hand beneath his armpit

and finds it difficult to bring it back to his mouth.

The sluggard seems wiser to himself

than seven men who speak judgments.

As one who takes a dog by the ears,

so is one who passes by impatiently

and becomes involved in another’s quarrel.

As one who is guilty is he who shoots arrows and spears

toward death,

so is a man who deceitfully harms his friend

and, when he has been caught, says, “I was joking.”

When wood fails, the fire will be extinguished;

[Col. 1268C] and when the whisperer is removed, disputes will cease.

As coals to burning embers and wood to fire,

so an angry man kindles quarrels.

The words of a whisperer are like simple things,

but they reach the innermost parts of the belly.

As if you wished to decorate an earthen vessel

with tarnished silver,

so are swollen lips joined to a wicked heart.

An enemy is understood by his lips

when he has plotted deceit in his heart.

When he makes his voice gentle, do not believe him,

for there are seven evils in his heart.

Whoever deceitfully conceals hatred,

his malice will be revealed in the assembly.

Whoever digs a pit will fall into it,

and whoever rolls a stone, it will return upon him.

A deceitful tongue does not love truth,

and a slippery mouth works ruin.

[Chapter XXVII.] Do not boast about tomorrow,

for you do not know what the coming day will bring.

Let another praise you, and not your own mouth;

a stranger, and not your own lips.

A stone is heavy and sand is burdensome,

but the anger of a fool is heavier than both.

Anger has no mercy, nor does bursting fury;

and who can withstand the assault of an enraged man?

Open rebuke is better

than concealed love.

Better are the wounds of a lover

[Col. 1269A] than the deceitful kisses of one who hates.

A satisfied soul will trample upon a honeycomb;

a hungry soul will take even what is bitter for sweet.

As a bird migrating from its nest,

so is a man who abandons his place.

The heart delights in ointment and various fragrances,

and the soul is sweetened by the good counsels of a friend.

Do not abandon your friend or your father’s friend,

and do not enter your brother’s house on the day of your affliction.

A neighbor who is near is better

than a brother who is far away.

Strive for wisdom, my son, and gladden my heart,

so that you may answer with a word

the one who reproaches you.

The astute man, seeing evil, hid himself;

the simple passed by and suffered loss.

Take away the garment of the one who stood surety for a stranger,

and take a pledge from him on behalf of foreigners.

Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice,

rising at night,

will be like one who curses.

A roof continually dripping on a cold day

and a quarrelsome woman are alike.

Whoever holds her is like one who holds the wind,

and he will call for oil from his right hand.

Iron is sharpened by iron,

and a man sharpens the face of his friend.

Whoever keeps a fig tree will eat its fruit,

and whoever is guardian of his master will be honored.

As faces are reflected in water for those who look,

so the hearts of men are manifest to the prudent.

Sheol and destruction [Note: [Col. 1269D] Several manuscripts read, “are never filled.” MART.] are not [Al. “never”] filled;

so the eyes of men are likewise insatiable.

As silver is tested in the crucible

and gold in the furnace,

so a man is tested by the mouth of the one who praises him. [Note: [Col. 1269D] Not only do the Hebrew and Chaldean texts lack this verse, but so do the Greek text itself and the Latin Complutensian edition; nor do the Jerome manuscripts know the verse that the Vulgate inserts here: “The heart of the wicked searches out evils, but the upright heart searches out knowledge.”]

If you pound a fool in a mortar

like groats, with the pestle striking above,

his folly will not be removed from him.

Know carefully the appearance of your flock,

and consider your herds.

For you will not always possess power;

but a crown is given from generation to generation.

The meadows are open, and green grasses have appeared,

and hay has been gathered from the mountains.

Lambs are for your clothing,

and goats for the price of a field.

Let the milk of goats be sufficient for your food,

for the necessities of your household,

and for the nourishment of your maidservants.

[Chapter XXVIII.] The wicked flees when no one pursues him,

but the righteous, like a lion resting,

will be without fear.

Because of the sins of a land, many are its princes;

but because of a man’s wisdom,

and of his knowledge of the things that are said,

the life of a leader will be prolonged.

[Col. 1269D] A poor man who slanders the poor

is like a violent rain in which famine is prepared.

Those who abandon the law praise the wicked;

those who keep it are inflamed against him.

Evil men do not consider judgment;

but those who seek the Lord pay attention to everything.

Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity

than a rich man on perverse paths.

Whoever keeps the law is a wise son;

but whoever feeds revelers disgraces his father.

[Col. 1270A] Whoever heaps up riches through usury and interest

gathers them for one generous toward the poor.

Whoever turns away his ears so as not to hear the law—

his prayer will be accursed.

Whoever deceives the upright on an evil way

will fall in his own destruction,

and the simple will possess his goods.

A rich man seems wise to himself,

but a prudent poor man will examine him.

In the exultation of the righteous there is much glory;

when the wicked rule, there are the ruins of men.

Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper;

but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy.

Blessed is the man who is always fearful;

but whoever is hard-hearted will fall into evil.

A roaring lion and a hungry bear

is an impious prince over a poor people.

A leader lacking prudence will oppress many through slander;

[Col. 1270B] but whoever hates greed will prolong his days.

A man [Note: [Col. 1270D] Worthy of repetition here is the reading of three manuscripts among Martianay’s copies: “A man who slanders a soul’s blood: if he flees as far as the pit, let no one support him.”] who slanders a person’s blood—

if he flees as far as the pit, no one supports him.

Whoever walks simply will be safe;

whoever walks on perverse ways will fall once.

Whoever works his land will be filled with bread;

but whoever pursues idleness will be filled with poverty.

A faithful man will be greatly praised;

but whoever hastens to become rich will not be innocent.

Whoever shows partiality in judgment does not act well;

he even abandons truth for a morsel of bread.

A man who hastens to become rich and envies others

does not know that poverty will come upon him.

Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find favor with him,

more than the one who deceives through flattering words.

Whoever takes anything from his father or mother

and says, “This is not a sin,”

[Col. 1270C] is a partner of a murderer.

Whoever boasts and enlarges himself stirs up quarrels;

but whoever hopes in the Lord will be healed.

Whoever trusts in his own heart is a fool;

but whoever walks wisely will himself be saved.

Whoever gives to the poor will not lack;

whoever despises the one who begs will suffer want.

When the wicked rise up, men will hide themselves;

when they perish, the righteous will multiply.

[Chapter XXIX.] A man who despises one who rebukes him,

being stiff-necked,

will suddenly meet destruction,

and healing will not follow him.

When the righteous multiply, the people will rejoice;

when the wicked assume power, the people will groan.

A man who loves wisdom gladdens his father;

but whoever nourishes prostitutes will lose his substance.

A righteous king will raise up the land;

a greedy man will destroy it.

[Col. 1270D] A man who speaks to his friend

with smooth and deceptive words

spreads a net for his steps.

An unjust sinner will be caught in a snare,

but the righteous will praise and rejoice.

The righteous knows the cause of the poor;

the wicked does not understand knowledge.

Pestilent men destroy a city,

but the wise turn away fury.

A wise man, if he contends with a fool,

whether he becomes angry or laughs,

will find no rest.

Men of blood hate the simple;

[Col. 1271A] but the righteous seek his life.

The fool pours out his whole spirit;

the wise man delays and reserves it for afterward.

A ruler who willingly listens to lying words

will have wicked ministers.

The poor man and the creditor meet one another;

the Lord illuminates both of them.

A king who judges the poor in truth—

his throne will be established forever.

The rod and correction give wisdom;

but a child left to his own will disgrace his mother.

When the wicked multiply, crimes will multiply;

and the righteous will see their ruins.

Discipline your son, and he will refresh you

and give delights to your soul.

When prophecy fails, the people will be scattered;

but whoever keeps the law is blessed.

A servant cannot be instructed by words,

[Col. 1271B] because he understands what you say

and disdains to answer.

Have you seen a man swift to speak?

Folly is more to be hoped for than his correction.

Whoever nourishes a servant delicately from childhood

will afterward find him rebellious.

An irascible man provokes quarrels;

and whoever is quick to anger will be more prone to sin.

Pride is followed by humility,

and glory will receive the humble in spirit.

Whoever shares with a thief hates his own soul;

he hears the one who adjures him and does not reveal it.

Whoever fears man will quickly fall;

whoever hopes in the Lord will be lifted up.

Many seek the face of a ruler,

but judgment concerning each one proceeds from the Lord.

The righteous abhor an impious man,
[Col. 1271C] And the wicked abhor those who are on the right path.

[Note: [Col. 1271D] The Vulgate edition adds this verse: “The son who keeps the word shall be outside destruction.” Although it was imported into the Latin codices solely from the translation of the Septuagint, those copies do not place it here, but in the preceding chapter, XXIV, after the twenty-second verse. Saint Augustine, in *On Lying* to Consentius, chapter 18, seems to have read still more: “The son who receives the word shall be far from destruction”; and “he who receives it shall take it to himself, and nothing false shall proceed from his mouth.”]

## THE WORDS OF THE CONGREGATOR, THE SON OF VOMITING

### Chapter XXX

The vision that the man spoke, with whom God is,

and who, strengthened by God dwelling with him, said:

I am the most foolish of men,

and the wisdom of men is not with me.

I have not learned wisdom,

and I know the knowledge of the holy.

[Note: [Col. 1272D] Thus read the copies of the Hebrew Canon of Truth, as well as all the manuscript codices; the printed editions add the negative particle, “and I do not know,” etc. This is indeed to be understood in similar Hebraisms, as we have already noted in our annotations on Psalm IX. MART.]

Who has ascended into heaven and descended?

Who has enclosed the wind in his hands?

Who has bound the waters as though in a garment?

Who has raised up all the boundaries of the earth?

What is his name,

and what is the name of his son, if you know?

Every word of God is tested by fire;

he is a shield to those who hope in him.

Do not add anything to his words,

lest you be reproved and found a liar.

Two things I have asked of you; do not deny them to me before I die:

Remove vanity and lying words far from me.

Do not give me poverty or riches;

grant me only what is necessary for my sustenance,

lest, when I am satisfied, I be enticed to deny you

and say, “Who is the Lord?”

or, driven by poverty, steal and profane the name

of my God.

Do not accuse a servant to his master,

lest perhaps he curse you and you fall.

A generation that curses its father

and does not bless its mother;

a generation that seems clean to itself,

yet is not washed from its filth;

a generation whose eyes are exalted

and whose eyelids are raised high;

a generation that has swords for teeth

and devours with its molars, so as to eat the needy from the earth

and the poor from among mankind.

The leech has two daughters

who say, “Give, give.”

There are three things that are never satisfied,

and a fourth that never says, “Enough”:

the underworld, the mouth of the womb,

and the earth, which is not satisfied with water;

but fire never says, “Enough.”

The eye that mocks its father

and despises the birth of its mother—

may the ravens of the torrents dig it out,

and the young of the eagle devour it.

There are three things too difficult for me,

and a fourth I utterly do not know:

the way of an eagle in the sky,

the way of a serpent upon a rock,

the way of a ship in the midst of the sea,

and the way of a man in his youth.

Such also is the way of an adulterous woman:

she eats, wipes her mouth,

and says, “I have done no wrong.”

By three things the earth is shaken,

and a fourth it cannot bear:

by a servant when he has become king;

by a fool when he is filled with food;

by a hateful woman when she is taken in marriage;

and by a maidservant when she becomes heir to her mistress.

[Col. 1272C] There are four things that are least upon the earth,

yet they are wiser than the wise:

ants are a people without strength,

yet they prepare their food in harvest;

the little hare is a feeble people,

yet it makes its dwelling in the rock;

the locust has no king,

yet it goes out in all its companies;

the lizard supports itself with its hands

and dwells in kings’ palaces.

There are three things that walk well,

and a fourth that proceeds happily:

the lion, strongest among beasts,

fears no one’s encounter;

the rooster with girded loins;

and the ram—and there is no king who can resist him.

And he who appeared foolish after he had been raised up on high—

for if he had understood, he would have put his hand over his mouth.

[Col. 1272D] Whoever presses the breasts forcefully to draw out milk

produces butter;

whoever squeezes the nose violently draws out blood;

and whoever provokes anger produces disputes.

## THE WORDS OF KING LEMUEL

### Chapter XXXI

The vision with which his mother instructed him.

What, my beloved? What, beloved son of my womb?

What, beloved child of my vows?

[Col. 1273A] Do not give your wealth to women,

or your ways to those who destroy kings.

[Note: [Col. 1273B] This passage has been corrupted in more than one way through scribal error. The copies of the Canon, and some other manuscript codices, retain this faulty reading: “And your riches to the destruction of kings.” In many copies we read, “And your delights,” etc. But the Corbeiensis manuscript no. 1, of the finest quality and very ancient, corresponds directly to the Hebrew source; in its first hand it has, “And your ways,” etc., which is also found written in the Hebrew volumes, where the word *darchecha*, or *derachecha*, means “your ways.” MART.—Likewise the Complutensian Latin edition, and the better-quality Hieronymian codices according to the Hebrew, prefer “your ways”; while others have “riches,” and others “delights.”]

Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel;

do not give wine to kings,

because where drunkenness reigns there is no secrecy.

Lest they drink and forget judgments,

and pervert the case of the poor man’s children.

Give strong drink to those who grieve,

and wine to those who are bitter in spirit.

Let them drink and forget their poverty,

and remember their sorrow no more.

Open your mouth for the mute,

and for the causes of all the children who pass by.

Open your mouth, decide what is just,

and judge the needy and the poor.

[Aleph.] Who will find a strong woman? Her price is far beyond that of the farthest boundaries.

[Beth.] The heart of her husband trusts in her,

and he shall have no need of spoils.

[Gimel.] She will repay him with good, not evil,

all the days of her life.

[Col. 1273B] [Daleth.] She sought wool and flax,

and worked with the counsel of her hands.

[He.] She became like a merchant’s ship,

bringing her bread from afar.

[Vav.] She rose during the night,

gave food to her household,

and provisions to her maidservants.

[Zain.] She considered a field and bought it;

from the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard.

[Heth.] She girded her loins with strength

and strengthened her arm.

[Col. 1274A] [Teth.] She tasted and saw that her commerce was good;

her lamp shall not be extinguished at night.

[Jod.] She put her hand to strong things,

and her fingers grasped the spindle.

[Chaph.] She opened her hand to the needy

and extended her palms to the poor.

[Lamed.] She shall not fear cold for her household

when there is snow;

for all her household are clothed in double garments.

[Mem.] She made herself a quilted garment;

fine linen and purple are her clothing.

[Nun.] Her husband is noble at the gates,

when he sits with the senators of the land.

[Samech.] She made linen cloth, sold it,

and supplied a belt to the Canaanite.

[Ain.] Strength and beauty are her clothing,

and she shall laugh on the last day.

[Phe.] She opened her mouth with wisdom,

and the law of kindness is on her tongue.

[Sade.] She watches over the paths of her household,

and does not eat idle bread.

[Col. 1274B] [Coph.] Her children rose up and called her most blessed;

her husband also, and he praised her.

[Res.] Many daughters have gathered riches;

you have surpassed them all.

[Sin.] Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain;

the woman who fears the Lord—she shall be praised.

[Thav.] Give her from the fruit of her hands,

and let her works praise her at the gates.

The book of Proverbs ends.

[Col. 1273]

## THE BOOK OF ECCLESIASTES BEGINS, CALLED *COELETH* IN HEBREW

THE WORDS OF ECCLESIASTES, SON OF DAVID, KING OF JERUSALEM

[Note: [Col. 1273C] In all the manuscript codices the scribes wrote “The words of Ecclesiastes,” etc., as though *Ecclesiastes* were an indeclinable name, or Hebrew. MART.]

[Col. 1273C]

### Chapter I

Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes;

vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.

What more does a man have

from all his labor with which he labors under the sun?

One generation passes, and another comes,

but the earth stands forever.

The sun rises and sets,

and returns to its place;

and, rising again there, it circles toward the south

and bends toward the north.

The spirit, surveying everything, proceeds in a circuit,

and returns to its circuits.

All the rivers enter the sea,

yet the sea does not overflow;

to the place from which the rivers flow,

they return, so that they may flow again.

[Col. 1274C] All things are difficult;

man cannot explain them in speech.

The eye is not satisfied with seeing,

nor is the ear filled with hearing.

What is that which has been?

The same as what will be.

What is that which has been done?

The same as what is to be done.

There is nothing new under the sun,

nor can anyone say, “Look, this is new.”

For it has already existed in the ages

that were before us.

There is no memory of former things;

nor will there be remembrance among those

who will exist at the end

of the things that will later come to pass.

I, Ecclesiastes,

was king over Israel in Jerusalem,

and I resolved in my heart to seek

and investigate wisely

all that is done under the sun.

This is the most grievous occupation God has given

to the children of men,

to be occupied with it.

I saw all that is done under the sun,

and behold, everything is vanity and affliction of spirit.

What is crooked is difficult to correct,

and the number of fools is infinite.

I spoke in my heart, saying:

“Behold, I have become great,

and I have surpassed in wisdom all

who were before me in Jerusalem;

my mind also contemplated many things wisely,

and learned.”

I gave my heart to know prudence and learning,

and errors and folly;

and I recognized that in these also there was labor

and affliction of spirit.

[Col. 1275B] For where there is much wisdom,

there is also much indignation;

and whoever adds knowledge adds labor

[Alternative: sorrow].

[Note: [Col. 1275D] The Corbeiensis manuscript no. 1 adds “and sorrow,” which the emenders inserted in many copies, where the first hand had written “adds labor.” Both Canons, namely the Carcassonian and the Memmian, retain the pure text. MART.]

### Chapter II

I said in my heart:

“I will go and abound in delights,

and enjoy good things.”

And I saw that this too was vanity.

I considered laughter an error,

and said of joy, “Why are you deceived in vain?”

I resolved in my heart to withdraw my flesh from wine,

so that I might turn my mind toward wisdom

and avoid folly,

until I should see what is useful for the children of men:

what they ought to do under the sun

during the number of the days of their life.

I magnified my works;

I built houses for myself,

and planted vineyards.

[Col. 1275C] I made gardens and orchards,

and planted them with trees of every kind.

I constructed pools of water for myself,

to irrigate a forest of growing trees.

I acquired male and female slaves,

and had a large household.

I also had herds of cattle

and great flocks of sheep,

more than all who were before me in Jerusalem.

I heaped up silver and gold for myself,

and the treasures of kings and provinces.

I made for myself male and female singers,

and the delights of the children of men,

cups and jugs for the service of pouring out wine.

And I surpassed in wealth all

who were before me in Jerusalem.

Wisdom also remained with me.

Whatever my eyes desired, I did not deny them,

nor did I restrain my heart from enjoying every pleasure

and delighting in the things I had prepared.

[Col. 1275D] And I regarded this as my portion,

if I used my labor.

When I turned to all the works my hands had made,

and to the labors at which I had toiled in vain,

I saw in everything vanity and affliction of mind,

and that nothing endures under the sun.

I turned to contemplate wisdom,

and errors and folly.

[Col. 1276A] “What,” I said, “is man,

that he can follow the King, his Maker?”

And I saw that wisdom surpasses folly

as much as light differs from darkness.

The eyes of the wise man are in his head;

the fool walks in darkness.

And I learned that the same fate awaits them both.

I said in my heart:

“If the end of both the fool and myself will be one,

what profit is there for me in having applied myself

more diligently to wisdom?”

And speaking with my mind,

I perceived that this too was vanity.

For the memory of the wise man will not be like that of the fool forever;

future times will equally cover all things with oblivion.

The learned man dies just like the unlearned.

[Note: [Col. 1275D] Some manuscripts, together with the corrected Carcassonian Canon, read “just like the ignorant.” MART.]

Therefore my life became wearisome to me,

when I saw that all things under the sun were evil,

and all were vanity and affliction of spirit.

[Col. 1276B] Again I detested all my industry

with which I had labored most diligently under the sun,

since I would have an heir after me

whom I do not know, whether he will be wise or foolish;

and he will rule over the labors

for which I had sweated and been anxious.

And is anything so vain?

Therefore I ceased,

and my heart gave up laboring further under the sun.

For when another labors in wisdom, learning, and anxiety,

he leaves what he has acquired to a man who is idle;

and this too is vanity and a great evil.

[Note: [Col. 1276D] Here we have followed the Memmian Canon. The Carcassonian reads interrogatively: “And is this not vanity?” Many manuscript codices agree with it. MART.]

For what benefit will a man have from all his labor

and from the affliction of spirit

with which he has been tormented under the sun?

All his days are full of pains and distress,

and even at night his mind does not rest.

And this too is vanity.

[Note: [Col. 1276D] The Vulgate translator, and certain manuscripts belonging to Martianus, use the interrogative sign: “And is this [or these things] not vanity?”]

[Col. 1276C] Is it not better to eat and drink,

and show his soul good things from his labors?

And this too is from the hand of God.

For who will eat and abound in delights as I do?

God has given wisdom, knowledge, and joy

to the good man in his sight;

but to the sinner he has given affliction and superfluous anxiety,

so that he may add and gather,

and hand it over to one who pleases God.

But this too is vanity and an empty concern of the mind.

### Chapter III

Everything has its season,

and all things pass under heaven in their appointed periods.

A time to be born,

and a time to die.

A time to plant,

and a time to uproot what has been planted.

A time to kill,

[Col. 1276D] and a time to heal.

A time to destroy,

and a time to build.

A time to weep,

and a time to laugh.

A time to mourn,

and a time to dance.

A time to scatter stones,

and a time to gather them.

A time to embrace,

[Col. 1277A] and a time to keep far from embraces.

A time to acquire,

and a time to lose.

A time to keep,

and a time to cast away.

A time to tear,

and a time to sew.

A time to be silent,

and a time to speak.

A time for love,

and a time for hatred.

A time for war,

and a time for peace.

What more does a man have

from his labor?

I saw the affliction that God gave the children of men

to be occupied with it.

He made everything good in its time,

and handed the world over to their disputation,

so that man may not discover the work that God has worked

[Col. 1277B] from beginning to end.

And I learned that there was nothing better

than to rejoice and do good during his life.

For every man who eats and drinks

and sees good from his labor—

this is God’s gift.

I learned that all the works God has made

endure forever.

We cannot add anything to them,

nor take away anything from what God has made,

so that he may be feared.

What has been made remains;

what is to be has already been;

and God restores what has passed away.

I saw under the sun, in the place of judgment, wickedness,

and in the place of justice, iniquity.

And I said in my heart:

God will judge the just and the wicked,

and then there will be a time for every matter.

I said in my heart concerning the children of men

[Col. 1277C] that God was testing them

and showing that they are like beasts.

Therefore the death of man and of animals is one,

and the condition of both is equal.

As man dies, so they die;

all breathe alike,

and man has nothing more than an animal.

All are subject to vanity,

and all go to one place.

They are made from the earth,

and together they return to the earth.

Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam rises upward,

and whether the spirit of animals descends downward?

And I discovered that there is nothing better

than for a man to rejoice in his work,

[Col. 1278A] and that this is his portion.

For who will bring him to know what will happen after him?

### Chapter IV

I turned to other matters,

and saw the oppressions that are done under the sun,

and the tears of the innocent,

with no one to comfort them;

and that, deprived of everyone’s help, they could not resist their violence.

And I praised the dead more than the living,

and judged happier than either the one

who has not yet been born

and has not seen the evils that are done under the sun.

Again I contemplated all the labors and industries of men,

and perceived them to be exposed to a neighbor’s envy.

And in this too there is vanity and superfluous anxiety.

The fool folds his hands

and eats his own flesh, saying:

“Better is one handful with rest

than both hands full with labor and affliction of mind.”

[Col. 1278B] Considering this, I found another vanity under the sun:

there is one person, and he has no second—

neither son nor brother—

yet he does not cease laboring,

nor are his eyes satisfied with riches.

He does not reflect, saying:

“For whom do I labor,

and defraud my soul of good things?”

[Note: [Col. 1277D] The printed books have “in this too there is vanity”; but what we have published, following the testimony of many manuscript copies, is better and closer to the Hebrew. MART.]

And in this too there is vanity

[Alternative: “in this too”],

and a most grievous affliction.

Therefore two are better than one,

for they have the advantage of their companionship.

If one falls, the other will support him.

Woe to the one who is alone;

when he falls, he has no one to lift him up.

And if two sleep together, they will be warmed by one another;

how will one person be warmed?

And if someone prevails against one,

two will resist him.

A threefold cord is not easily broken.

A poor and wise man is better

than an old and foolish king

who does not know how to foresee the future.

For sometimes one goes from prison and chains to kingship,

while another, born in kingship,

is consumed by poverty.

I saw all the living who walk under the sun

with the second youth who will rise in his place.

The number of all the people who were before him is without end,

as are those who will come afterward;

yet they will not rejoice in him.

But this too is vanity

and affliction of spirit.

Guard your foot as you enter the house of God.

[Note: [Col. 1277D] The scribes transferred this entire clause here: “And draw near, so that you may hear.” It is absent from Saint Augustine’s *Speculum*, and in the Colbertine-Anician manuscript it is placed in the margin by a more recent hand. The Regius manuscript too has been corrupted by an emender who inserted these words into the sacred text, although earlier it was pure and lacked such an addition. In the Carcassonian Canon the same words are read, but outside the sequence and placed above the text; in the Memmian they appear as the same verse, undisturbed and in the original lineation. It should nevertheless be understood that this was borrowed from the Greek edition of the Seventy Interpreters, or from Jerome’s *Commentaries on Ecclesiastes*, where he adapted himself more closely to Septuagint usage. For here the Hebrew text, *vocarob lischmoa mi hheth hakkesilim zabahh*, is sufficiently expressed by these Latin words: “For obedience is much better than the sacrifice of fools”; among the Hebrews, being near in order to hear and being obedient are one and the same. MART.—The words that follow this verse in the Hebrew archetype are as follows, and are literally translated: “and draw near to hearing, lest you give—or rather, more than that you give—the sacrifice of fools.” Saint Jerome interpreted the former words, “and draw near to hearing,” from the Hebrew in a phrase with sufficiently suitable meaning: “obedience is much better,” that is, “choose rather to hear, or to obey.” Hence the Benedictine editor rightly concluded before us that Jerome’s words, “and draw near, so that you may hear,” which certain manuscripts and all the printed editions insert, cannot readily be regarded as genuine, since they retain at the same time the following interpretation, “for obedience is much better,” which is another exposition of the same Hebrew sense. It has also been noted that these words are absent from Saint Augustine’s *Speculum*.]

[Col. 1279A] For obedience is much better than the sacrifices of fools,

who do not know what evil they are doing.

### Chapter V

Do not speak rashly,

nor let your heart be quick to utter a word before God.

For God is in heaven, and you are upon earth;

therefore let your words be few.

Dreams follow upon many cares,

and folly is found in many words.

If you have vowed anything to God,

do not delay in fulfilling it.

For an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him;

but whatever you have vowed, fulfill it.

It is much better not to vow

than, after making a vow, not to fulfill the promise.

Do not give your mouth occasion to make your flesh sin,

nor say before the angel, “There is no providence.”

Lest perhaps God, angered by your words,

destroy all the works of your hands.

Where there are many dreams,

there are also many vanities and innumerable words.

But you: fear God.

If you see the oppressions of the needy

and violent judgments,

and justice overturned in the province,

do not be astonished at this matter.

For one who is high is watched by another higher,

and above these there are still others more eminent;

and over all the earth the king rules over the one who serves.

The greedy will not be filled with money,

and whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them.

And this too is vanity.

Where there are many riches,

there are also many who consume them.

And what profit does the possessor have,

except that he sees his riches with his eyes?

Sleep is sweet to the laborer,

whether he eats little or much;

but the abundance of the rich does not permit him to sleep.

[Col. 1279C] There is also another most grievous infirmity

that I saw under the sun:

riches preserved to the harm of their owner.

For they perish in a most grievous affliction.

He begets a son who will be in extreme poverty.

As he came naked from his mother’s womb,

so he will return,

and he will take nothing with him from his labor.

A thoroughly miserable infirmity:

as he came, so he will return.

What then does he gain by laboring for the wind

all the days of his life?

He eats in darkness,

with many cares,

in distress and sorrow.

This, therefore, seemed good to me:

that a person should eat and drink

and enjoy gladness from his labor,

with which he has labored under the sun

during the number of the days of his life

that God has given him;

this is his portion.

[Col. 1279D] And every person to whom God has given riches and possessions,

and has granted power to eat from them,

to enjoy his portion

and rejoice in his labor—

this is God’s gift.

For he will not remember the days of his life at length,

because God occupies his heart with delights.

### Chapter VI

There is another evil that I saw under the sun,

and it is indeed common among men:

a man to whom God has given riches, possessions, and honor,

and whose soul lacks nothing of all that he desires,

yet God does not grant him the power to eat from it;

instead, a stranger will consume it.

This is vanity and a great misery.

If someone begets a hundred children

[Note: [Col. 1279D] The Hebrew does not have the word “children,” which some manuscripts retain here together with the printed editions. MART.—The Vulgate adds “offspring,” and certain manuscripts “children”; but the Hebrew text has neither.]

and lives many years,

and has many days of life,

but his soul does not enjoy the good of his possessions
