and he lacks burial,

I declare that an untimely birth is better than he.

For it comes in vain and departs into darkness,

and its name will be erased by oblivion.

It has not seen the sun,

nor known the difference between good and evil.

Even if he lives for two thousand years

and has not enjoyed good things,

do not all go to one place?

All the labor of man is for his mouth,

yet his soul is not filled.

What more has the wise man than the fool?

And what does the poor man have except to go there

where life is?

It is better to see what you desire

than to desire what you do not know.

But this too is vanity

and presumption of spirit.

What is to be has already been called by its name,

and it is known that he is a man,

and that he cannot contend in judgment

against one stronger than himself.

There are many words

that contain much vanity in disputation.

### Chapter VII

What need has a man to seek things greater than himself,

when he does not know what is useful to him during his life,

[Col. 1280C] during the number of the days of his pilgrimage,

and during the time that passes like a shadow?

Or who can tell him

what will happen after him under the sun?

A good name is better than precious ointments,

and the day of death than the day of birth.

It is better to go to a house of mourning

than to a house of feasting.

For in the former the end of all men is recalled,

and the living considers what the future will be.

[Note: [Col. 1279D] In certain manuscript codices one reads, “what he will become.” Saint Jerome, moreover, recognizes this division of the verses, when he says: “Symmachus interpreted the last verse more clearly, saying, ‘And the one who lives will look toward understanding.’” See Jerome’s *Commentaries on the seventh chapter of Ecclesiastes* and Saint Augustine’s *Speculum*, because they entirely agree below at verses 8 and 10 of our Vulgate, that is, in the division of the verses retained by the copies of the Canon. MART.]

Anger is better than laughter,

because through the sadness of the face

the mind of the offender is corrected.

The heart of the wise is where there is sadness,

and the heart of fools where there is joy.

It is better to be rebuked by a wise man

than deceived by the flattery of fools.

For as the crackling of burning thorns beneath a pot,

so is the laughter of a fool.

But this too is vanity.

[Col. 1280D] Slander troubles the wise man

and destroys the strength of his heart.

The end of a discourse is better than its beginning;

the patient man is better than the arrogant.

Do not be quick to anger,

for anger rests in the bosom of a fool.

Do not say, “Why, do you suppose,

were former times better than these?”

[Col. 1281A] For such a question is foolish.

Wisdom with riches is useful,

and brings greater benefit to those who see the sun.

For just as wisdom protects,

so money protects.

But learning and wisdom have this further advantage:

they give life to their possessor.

Consider the works of God:

no one can correct what he has despised.

On a good day, enjoy good things,

and beware of an evil day.

For God made one as well as the other,

so that man may not find just complaints against him.

This too I saw in the days of my vanity:

the just man perishes in his justice,

and the wicked man lives for a long time in his wickedness.

Do not be excessively just,

nor become wiser than necessary,

lest you become bewildered.

[Col. 1281B] Do not act excessively wickedly,

and do not be a fool,

lest you die before your time.

It is good for you to support the just man,

but do not withdraw your hand from him either;

for whoever fears God neglects nothing.

Wisdom strengthens the wise man

more than ten rulers of the city.

For there is no just man on earth

who does good and does not sin.

Nor should you give your heart

to all the words that are spoken,

lest perhaps you hear your servant cursing you.

For your conscience knows

that you too have often cursed others.

I tested everything through wisdom.

I said, “I will become wise.”

But it withdrew farther from me than before,

and by much.

Deep is the depth;

who will find it?

[Col. 1281C] I surveyed everything in my mind

to know, consider, and seek wisdom and reason,

and to recognize the wickedness of the fool

and the error of the imprudent.

And I found a woman more bitter than death,

whose heart is a hunter’s snare

and a net.

Her hands are bonds.

Whoever pleases God will escape her,

but the sinner will be captured by her.

Behold, this I found, said Ecclesiastes:

[Note: [Col. 1281D] The same Father himself, in the Commentary, having translated “one to one, that I might find,” etc., declares that he adhered more closely to the Hebrew language. See the passage in volume three, col. 448 ff.]

one thing after another,

to discover the reason that my soul still seeks,

but I did not find it.

Among a thousand men I found one man,

but among all women I did not find one.

Only this I found:

God made man upright,

but he himself entangled himself in countless questions.

Who is like the wise man?

And who knows the interpretation of a word?

### Chapter VIII

A man’s wisdom shines in his face,

and the most powerful will change his countenance.

I observe the mouth of the king

and the commands of God’s oath.

Do not hasten to withdraw from his presence,

nor persist in an evil deed;

for he will do whatever he wishes,

and his word is full of power.

No one can say to him,

“Why are you doing this?”

Whoever keeps the commandment

[Col. 1282A] will experience no evil.

The wise heart understands

the time and the answer.

For every matter there is a time and an opportunity,

and man has much affliction,

because he does not know the past,

and no messenger can tell him what is to come.

It is not in man’s power to restrain the spirit,

nor does he have authority over the day of death.

There is no discharge during the outbreak of war,

nor will wickedness save the wicked.

I considered all these things

and gave my heart to all the works done under the sun.

Sometimes one man rules another

to his own harm.

I saw the wicked buried,

who, while they were still alive,

had been in a holy place

and were praised in the city as though they had performed just works.

But this too is vanity.

[Col. 1282B] Indeed, because sentence against evil deeds

is not quickly carried out,

the hearts of the children of men are filled with the determination

to do evil without fear.

Nevertheless, because the sinner commits evil a hundred times

and is sustained by patience,

I knew that it would be well with those who fear God,

who revere his face.

May it not be well with the wicked,

and may his days not be prolonged;

but may those who do not fear God’s face

pass away like a shadow.

There is another vanity that occurs upon the earth:

there are just people to whom many things happen

as though they had done the works of the wicked,

and there are wicked people who are as secure

as though they possessed the deeds of the just.

But this I judge to be the greatest vanity.

Therefore I praised joy,

because there is no good for man under the sun

except to eat, drink, and rejoice.

[Col. 1282C] And this alone he would take with him from his labor

during the days of his life

that God has given him under the sun.

And I applied my heart to know wisdom

and to understand the perplexity

[Note: [Col. 1282D] The Complutensian Latin edition, together with quite a few others, prefers “dissension”; the interlinear gloss has “distraction.”]

that takes place on earth.

There is a man who does not obtain sleep for his eyes

by day or by night.

And I understood that man cannot discover

the reason for any of God’s works,

of the things that are done under the sun.

The more he labors to seek,

the less he finds.

Even if the wise man says that he knows,

he will not be able to discover it.

### Chapter IX

I considered all these things in my heart

so as to understand them carefully.

There are just and wise people,

and their works are in the hand of God.

Yet man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred.

[Col. 1282D] All things in the future remain uncertain.

For everything happens alike

to the just and the wicked,

to the good and the evil,

to the clean and the unclean,

to the one who sacrifices victims

and to the one who despises sacrifices.

The good person is like the sinner,

and the one who swears falsely is like the one who swears truthfully.

This is the worst of all that happens under the sun:

that the same things happen to everyone.

Therefore the hearts of the children of men

are filled with wickedness

and contempt during their life,

and afterward they are led down to the underworld.

There is no one who lives forever

or who has confidence in this matter.

A living dog is better than a dead lion.

For the living know that they will die,

but the dead know nothing more,

nor do they have any further reward,

because their memory has been consigned to oblivion.

Love, hatred, and envy have likewise perished together,

and they have no further share in this world

or in any work done under the sun.

Go, then, eat your bread with gladness

and drink your wine with joy,

for God approves your works.

At all times let your garments be white,

and let oil not fail from your head.

Enjoy life with the wife whom you love

all the days of your unstable life,

which have been given to you under the sun

throughout all the days of your vanity.

[Col. 1283B] For this is your portion in life

and in your labor with which you labor under the sun.

Whatever your hand is able to do,

perform it diligently.

For there is neither work, nor reason,

nor wisdom, nor knowledge

in the underworld, where you are going.

I turned to another matter and saw under the sun

that the race does not belong to the swift,

nor war to the strong,

nor bread to the wise,

nor riches to the learned,

nor favor to the skilled,

but time and chance govern everything.

Man does not know his end.

As fish are caught with a hook

and birds are taken in a snare,

so people are caught in an evil time

when it suddenly falls upon them.

[Col. 1283C] This wisdom too I saw under the sun,

and I considered it very great.

There was a small city with few men in it.

A great king came against it and surrounded it.

He built fortifications around it,

and the siege was completed.

A poor but wise man was found in it,

and by his wisdom he delivered the city.

Yet no one afterward remembered that poor man.

And I said that wisdom is better than strength.

How, then, was the poor man’s wisdom despised,

and his words not heard?

The words of the wise are heard in silence

more than the shouting of a ruler among fools.

Wisdom is better than weapons of war.
and whoever sins in one matter will lose many good things.

## [Chapter X] The dying flies

destroy the sweetness of the perfume.

[Col. 1283D] Wisdom and glory are more precious than a little folly for a time.

The heart of the wise is at his right hand,

and the heart of the fool at his left.

But [Note: [Col. 1283D] Saint Jerome, in his Commentaries on this passage, says that in copies of the Canon this colon, consisting of two complete verses, is a single verse. The words of the following verse, however, he says belong to the holy Doctor himself, where he says: “But even when the fool walks along the road, his heart fails him, and he says: ‘Everyone is foolish.’” This is the sense, and so forth. He therefore acknowledges here the distinction of verses that we call Masoretic, used in Hebrew volumes. On the other hand, in verse 15 of this chapter he says that several verses occur in one sentence or a single verse of our Vulgate: for when he had quoted this Scripture, “The labor of fools will weary them, those who do not know how to go to the city,” he adds: “Join these verses also to the preceding ones.” Thus he did not deny that there were several verses in this sentence. See our conjectures on these matters in the Prolegomena. MART.] while the fool walks along the road,

being himself foolish, he considers everyone foolish.

If the spirit of one who has authority rises against you,

[Col. 1284A] do not leave your place,

because calmness will put a stop to great sins.

There is an evil that I have seen under the sun,

as though arising through an error from the presence of a ruler:

a fool placed in a position of high dignity,

and the rich sitting below.

I have seen slaves on horses,

and princes walking like slaves upon the earth.

Whoever digs a pit will fall into it,

and whoever breaks through a hedge will be bitten by a snake.

Whoever moves stones will be hurt by them,

and whoever splits wood will be wounded by it.

If the iron has become blunt,

and this has not been restored as before, but has grown dull,

it will be sharpened with much labor,

and after industry wisdom will follow.

If a snake bites without making a sound,

the secret slanderer is no less dangerous.

The words of the mouth of the wise bring favor,

but the lips of the fool will bring him to ruin.

[Col. 1284B] The beginning of his words is folly,

and the end of his mouth is the worst error.

The fool multiplies words.

A person does not know what has been before him,

and as for what will happen afterward, who can tell him?

The labor of fools will weary them,

those who do not know how to go to the city.

Woe to you, land whose king is a child,

and whose princes eat in the morning.

Blessed is the land whose king is noble,

and whose princes eat at the proper time,

for refreshment and not for indulgence.

Through laziness the framework sags,

and through weakness of the hands the house leaks.

They make bread for laughter, and wine so that the living may feast [Note: [Col. 1284D] Most manuscript books and printed editions read “drinking” in place of “living.”]

and all things obey money.

Do not revile the king even in your thoughts,

and do not curse the rich in the privacy of your bedroom,

[Col. 1284C] for a bird of the sky will carry your voice,

and the winged creature will report the matter.

## [Chapter XI]

Cast your bread upon the passing

waters,

for after many days you will find it.

Give a portion to seven, and also to eight,

because you do not know what evil may occur upon the earth.

When the clouds are filled,

they pour rain upon the earth.

If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north,

in whatever place it falls, there it will remain.

Whoever watches the wind does not sow,

and whoever observes the clouds will never reap.

Just as you do not know what the way of the spirit is,

or how the bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman,

so you do not know the works of God, who makes everything.

In the morning sow your seed,

and in the evening do not let your hand cease,

[Col. 1284D] for you do not know which will spring up, this or that,

or whether both will spring up together; it will be better.

Light is sweet,

and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun.

If a person lives for many years

and rejoices in them all,

he ought to remember the dark time

and the many days:

[Col. 1285A] when they come, the past will be shown to have been vanity.

Therefore rejoice, young man, in your youth,

and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth.

Walk in the ways of your heart

and in the sight of your eyes.

Know, however, that for all these things

God will bring you into judgment.

Remove anger from your heart,

and put away wickedness from your flesh.

For youth and pleasure are vanity.

## [Chapter XII]

Remember your Creator in the days of your youth,

before the time of affliction comes

and the years draw near of which you will say, “I do not

like them.”

Before the sun grows dark,

and the light, and the moon, and the stars,

and the clouds return after the rain;

when the keepers of the house tremble,

and the strongest men stagger;

[Col. 1285B] when the grinders are idle because their number has become small,

and those who look through the openings grow dark-eyed;

when the doors in the street are closed,

as the sound of the grinding becomes low;

and they rise at the voice of the bird,

[Note: [Col. 1285] Alcuin formerly read “they will become mute”; but he says that the Hebrew has the better reading, “they will become deaf.”]

and all the daughters of song become deaf.

They will also fear the heights,

and be afraid on the way.

The almond tree will blossom,

the locust will grow fat,

[Col. 1286A] and the caperberry will be scattered,

because a person will go to his eternal home,

and mourners will go about in the street.

Before the silver cord is broken,

and the golden ribbon returns;

before the pitcher is shattered at the fountain,

and the wheel is broken above the cistern;

and the dust returns to the earth from which it came,

and the spirit returns to God who gave it.

“Vanity of vanities,” said Ecclesiastes; “all is vanity.”

And although Ecclesiastes was supremely wise,

he taught the people and recounted what he had done;

and, investigating, he composed many proverbs.

He sought useful words,

and wrote upright sayings, full

of truth.

The words of the wise are like goads,

and like nails driven deep,

[Col. 1286B] which were given by one shepherd through the counsel of the teachers.

Beyond these, my son, do not seek anything further.

There is no end to making many books,

and frequent study is a weariness of the flesh.

Let us all hear the conclusion of the matter together:

Fear God and observe his commandments,

for this is the whole of man.

God will bring everything that is done into judgment,

concerning every error, whether it is good or evil.

The Book of Ecclesiastes ends.

[Col. 1285]

# THE SONG OF SONGS BEGINS, which in Hebrew is called SIR ASSIRIM.

[Col. 1285C] [Chapter I] Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,

for your breasts are better than wine,

fragrant with the finest perfumes.

Your name is poured-out oil;

therefore the young women have loved you.

Draw me after you;

we shall run [Note: [Col. 1285C] The words added by the Vulgate, “in the fragrance of your perfumes,” derive from the Septuagint translators and are not found in the Hebrew; the Complutensian Latin edition itself also omits them.].

The king has brought me into his chambers;

we shall exult and rejoice in you,

remembering your breasts more than wine.

The upright love you.

I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem,

like the tents of Kedar,

like the curtains of Solomon.

Do not look at me because I am dark,

because the sun has discolored me.

The sons of my mother fought against me;

they appointed me keeper of the vineyards.

I did not keep my own vineyard.

Tell me, you whom my soul loves,

where you pasture, where you lie down at midday,

lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.

If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women,

go out and follow the tracks of the flocks,

and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents.

[Col. 1286C] I have compared you, my beloved,

to my mare among Pharaoh’s chariots.

Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove,

your neck like necklaces.

We shall make you golden ornaments,

studded with silver.

While the king was on his couch,

my nard gave forth its fragrance.

My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me;

he will lie between my breasts.

My beloved is a cluster of henna to me,

in the vineyards of Engedi.

Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved;

behold, you are beautiful;

your eyes are like those of doves.

Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and handsome.

Our bed is in bloom;

the beams of our houses are cedars,

and our ceilings are cypresses.

## [Chapter II]

I am a flower of the field

and a lily of the valleys.

Like a lily among thorns,

so is my beloved among the daughters.

Like an apple tree [Alternative: apple] [Note: [Col. 1286C] Manuscript codices read “apple,” which does not seem sufficiently suitable to the sense of this passage. MART.] among the trees of the forest,

so is my beloved among the sons.

[Col. 1287A] I sat beneath his shade, whom I had desired,

and his fruit was sweet to my palate.

He brought me into the wine chamber;

he ordered love toward me.

Strengthen me with flowers,

support me with apples,

for I am faint with love.

His left hand is beneath my head,

and his right hand will embrace me.

I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,

by the gazelles and the stags of the fields,

do not arouse or awaken the beloved

until she herself wishes it.

The voice of my beloved—

behold, he comes leaping over the mountains,

bounding over the hills.

My beloved is like a gazelle

and a young stag.

Behold, he stands behind our wall,

looking through the windows,

[Col. 1287B] gazing through the lattice.

Behold, my beloved speaks to me:

“Arise, hurry, my beloved, my dove,

my beautiful one, and come.

For winter has already passed,

the rain has gone away and receded.

Flowers have appeared on the earth;

the time of pruning has come.

The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.

The fig tree has put forth its early figs;

the flowering vines have given their fragrance.

Arise, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come,

my dove in the clefts of the rock,

in the recess of the wall.

Show me your face;

let your voice sound in my ears,

for your voice is sweet

and your face is beautiful.

Catch the little foxes for us,

[Col. 1287C] which destroy the vineyards,

for our vineyard has blossomed.”

My beloved is mine, and I am his,

who pastures among the lilies,

until the day breathes

and the shadows decline.

Return; be like a gazelle, my beloved,

or a young stag upon the mountains of Bether.

## [Chapter III]

On my bed by night I sought him

whom my soul loves.

I sought him and did not find him.

I will rise and go around the city;

through the streets and squares I will seek him

whom my soul loves.

I sought him and did not find him.

The watchmen who guard the city found me.

“Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”

A little while after I had passed them,

I found him whom my soul loves.

I held him and will not let him go

until I bring him into my mother’s house,

[Col. 1287D] and into the chamber of her who bore me.

I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,

by the gazelles and the stags of the fields,

do not arouse or awaken the beloved

until she herself wishes it.

Who is this woman who ascends through the wilderness,

like a column of smoke made from perfumes of myrrh and frankincense,

and every kind of perfumer’s powder?

Behold, Solomon’s couch;

sixty mighty men surround it,

the strongest of Israel.

All hold swords and are highly trained for war;

each man’s sword is upon his thigh

because of the terrors of the night.

King Solomon made for himself a litter

of the wood of Lebanon.

He made its columns of silver,

its backrest of gold,

its seat of purple.

The interior was paved with love

[Col. 1288A] for the daughters of Jerusalem.

Go out and see, daughters of Zion,

King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him

on the day of his betrothal

and on the day of the gladness of his heart.

## [Chapter IV]

How beautiful you are, my beloved,

how beautiful you are!

Your eyes are like those of doves,

apart from what is hidden within.

Your hair is like a flock of goats

that have come up from Mount Gilead.

Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep

that have come up from the washing.

All of them bear twins,

and none among them is barren.

Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon,

and your speech is sweet.

Your cheek is like a slice of pomegranate,

apart from what is hidden within.

Your neck is like the tower of David,

[Col. 1288B] built with battlements.

A thousand shields hang from it,

all the armor of the mighty.

Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle,

which feed among the lilies,

until the day breathes

and the shadows decline.

I will go to the mountain of myrrh

and to the hill of frankincense.

You are wholly beautiful, my beloved,

and there is no blemish in you.

Come from Lebanon, bride,

come from Lebanon, come.

You will be crowned from the summit of Amana,

from the peak of Senir and Hermon,

from the dens of lions,

from the mountains of leopards.

You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride;

you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes,

and with one lock of your neck.

How beautiful are your breasts,

my sister, my bride!

[Col. 1288C] Your breasts are more beautiful than wine,

and the fragrance of your perfumes is above all spices.

Your lips drip honeycomb, bride;

honey and milk are beneath your tongue,

and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.

A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride,

a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.

Your shoots are a paradise

of pomegranates with the fruit of orchards,

with henna and nard,

nard and saffron,

calamus and cinnamon with every tree of Lebanon,

myrrh and aloe with all the finest perfumes.

A fountain of gardens,

a well of living waters,

which flow forcefully from Lebanon.

Rise, north wind, and come, south wind;

blow upon my garden,

and let its perfumes flow.

## [Chapter V]

Let my beloved come into his garden

and eat the fruit of his trees.

I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride;

I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.

[Col. 1288D] I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey;

I have drunk my wine with my milk.

Eat, friends, and drink;

drink deeply, dearest ones.

I sleep,

but my heart is awake.

The voice of my beloved knocking:

“Open to me, my sister, my beloved,

my dove, my undefiled one.

For my head is full of dew,

and my locks with drops of the night.”

I have taken off my tunic;

how shall I put it on again?

I have washed my feet;

how shall I soil them?

My beloved put his hand through the opening,

and my stomach trembled at his touch.

I rose to open to my beloved;

[Col. 1289A] my hands dripped with myrrh,

and my fingers were full of finest myrrh.

I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved,

but he had turned aside and gone away.

My soul melted when he spoke.

I sought him but did not find him;

I called him but he did not answer me.

The watchmen who go around the city found me.

They struck me and wounded me;

the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak.

I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,

if you find my beloved,

tell him that I am faint with love.

What is your beloved more than another beloved,

O most beautiful among women?

What is your beloved more than another beloved,

that you have so adjured us?

My beloved is white and ruddy,

chosen from among thousands.

His head is the finest gold;

[Col. 1289B] his locks are like raised palm branches,

black as a raven.

His eyes are like doves beside streams of water,

washed in milk

and sitting beside overflowing streams.

His cheeks are like beds of spices,

planted by perfumers.

His lips are lilies,

dripping finest myrrh.

His hands are golden cylinders,

full of hyacinths.

His belly is ivory,

inlaid with sapphires.

His legs are marble columns,

founded upon golden bases.

His appearance is like Lebanon,

chosen like the cedars.

His throat is most sweet,

and he is altogether desirable.

[Col. 1289C] Such is my beloved,

and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.

Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women?

Where has your beloved turned aside, and we will seek him

with you?

## [Chapter VI]

My beloved has gone down into his garden,

to the bed of spices,

to pasture in the gardens

and gather lilies.

I belong to my beloved,

and my beloved belongs to me,

who pastures among the lilies.

You are beautiful, my beloved,

sweet and lovely like Jerusalem,

terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.

Turn your eyes away from me,

for they have made me fly away.

Your hair is like a flock of goats

that have appeared from Gilead.

Your teeth are like a flock of sheep

that have come up from the washing.

[Col. 1289D] All of them bear twins,

and none among them is barren.

Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate,

apart from what is hidden within.

There are sixty queens

and eighty concubines,

and there is no number of young women.

One is my dove, my perfect one,

one is her mother’s child,

the chosen one of her who bore her.

The daughters saw her

and proclaimed her most blessed;

the queens and concubines

praised her.

[Col. 1290A] Who is this woman who advances like the rising dawn,

beautiful as the moon,

chosen as the sun,

terrible as an army drawn up in battle array?

I went down to the garden of nut trees

to see the fruits of the valley,

to see whether the vine had blossomed

and the pomegranates had budded.

I did not know; my soul troubled me

because of the chariots of Aminadab.

Return, return, [Note: [Col. 1289D] We read “Shunammite,” not “Shulammite,” in the Latin manuscript codices. In the Greek copies, however, both “Shulammite” and “Shunammite” are found; but this, unless I am mistaken, is due to scribal error. MART. [Col. 1290D] Although this reading is preferable from the Hebrew, nevertheless many manuscripts and printed editions, following the Greek, and the Church itself in the divine Offices, call her “the Shunammite.”] Shulammite;

return, return, that we may look upon you.

## [Chapter VII]

What will you see in the Shulammite,

except the dances of the camps?

How beautiful are your steps

in your sandals, daughter of a prince!

The joints of your thighs are like necklaces,

made by the hand of an artisan.

Your navel is a turned bowl,

never lacking cups.

[Col. 1290B] Your belly is like a heap of wheat,

surrounded with lilies.

Your two breasts

are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.

Your neck

is like an ivory tower.

Your eyes are like the pools of Heshbon,

which are by the gate of the daughter of the multitude.

Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon,

which faces toward Damascus.

Your head is like Carmel,

and the hair of your head like royal purple bound in channels.

How beautiful and how lovely you are,

dearest, in delights!

Your stature is like a palm tree,

and your breasts like clusters of grapes.

I said, “I will climb the palm tree

and take hold of its fruit.”

[Col. 1290C] Your breasts will be like clusters of the vine,

and the fragrance of your mouth like apples.

Your throat is like the finest wine,

worthy of my beloved to drink,

and for his lips and teeth to taste.

I belong to my beloved,

and his turning is toward me.

Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field,

let us stay in the villages.

Let us rise early and go to the vineyards;

let us see whether the vine has blossomed,

whether the flowers are producing fruit,

whether the pomegranates have flowered.

There I will give you my breasts.

The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates.

All new and old fruits,

my beloved,

I have stored up for you.

## [Chapter VIII]

Who will give you to me as my brother,

nursing at my mother’s breasts,

so that I may find you outside

and kiss you,

and no one would despise me?

I would take hold of you

and lead you into my mother’s house.

There you would teach me,

and I would give you a cup of spiced wine

and the juice of my pomegranates.

His left hand is beneath my head,

and his right hand embraces me.

I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,

do not arouse or awaken the beloved

until she herself wishes it.

Who is this woman who comes up from the wilderness,

[Col. 1291A] overflowing with delights,

leaning upon her beloved?

Under the apple tree I awakened you.

There your mother was corrupted;

there she who bore you was violated.

Set me like a seal upon your heart,

like a seal upon your arm,

for love is strong as death,

and jealousy is harsh as hell.

Its lamps are lamps of fire

and flames.

Many waters could not extinguish love,

nor will rivers overwhelm it.

If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love,

they would utterly despise him [Note: [Col. 1291A] Thus read the copies of the Canon and other manuscript codices, in which what we have printed is consistently retained. In the Hebrew also the verb is plural, with the masculine pronoun *bo yābûz lô*, that is, “they will despise him with contempt.” Augustine likewise seems to have read it in the same way, since the manuscript copies of the *Speculum* have the verb in the plural, “they will despise,” not “he will despise.” MART.].

Our sister is small,

and has no breasts.

What shall we do for our sister

[Col. 1292A] on the day when she is to be addressed?

If she is a wall,

let us build battlements of silver upon it.

If she is a door,

let us fit it with cedar boards.

I am a wall,

and my breasts are like towers,

since I have become in his eyes like one who has found peace.

A man of peace had a vineyard

in that which has peoples.

He entrusted it to keepers;

a man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.

My vineyard is before me.

A thousand are yours, O man of peace,

and two hundred for those who guard its fruit.

You who dwell in the gardens,

your companions are listening.

Let me hear your voice.

Flee, my beloved,

and be like a gazelle

or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.

The Song of Songs ends.

[Col. 1291]

# [THE BOOK OF DANIEL]

[Note: [Col. 1291C] We have entirely collated this prologue of Jerome, as well as the whole Latin interpretation of Daniel, against two manuscript codices of the highest quality, one designated Palatine 3, the other Vatican 333.]

## JEROME’S PREFACE TO DANIEL THE PROPHET

The Church of the Lord and Savior does not read the prophet Daniel according to the Septuagint translators, but uses the edition of Theodotion; and why this happened, I do not know. Either because the language is Chaldean and differs from our speech in certain peculiarities, the Septuagint translators did not wish to preserve the same linguistic features in translation [Note: [Col. 1291C] Several manuscripts omit the word “of the language,” and the older ones also read in this way: “The Septuagint translators did not wish to preserve the same lines in translation.” MART. —Perhaps the Palatine manuscript and several others cited by Martianay are more correct: “the same lines,” with the intervening word “of the language” omitted.]; or because the book was published under their name by someone else who did not know the Chaldean language sufficiently; or because some other cause was involved, which I do not know. I can affirm only this: that it greatly departs from the truth and was rejected by sound judgment.

For it must be understood [Note: [Col. 1291C] Daniel was written in Chaldean from verse 2 of chapter II through chapter VIII. Ezra was written from verse 8 of chapter IV through chapter VII, verse 27. Finally, the passage of Jeremiah written in Chaldean is read in chapter X, verse 11—in our edition, verses 32, 33, and 34. MART. —Daniel was written in Chaldean not from the second verse, as Martianay thinks, but from the fourth verse of the second chapter through the beginning of the eighth chapter, as the holy Father himself testifies in his Commentary. Ezra extends from the eighth verse of the fourth chapter to the seventh verse of chapter XXVII, and Jeremiah’s *pericope* [περικοπή], consisting of three verses, from verses 32 to 34 of chapter ten, sounds in the Chaldean language.], that Daniel and Ezra in particular were written in Hebrew letters but in the Chaldean language, and that one *pericope* [περικοπή] of Jeremiah, as well as Job, has very close affinity with the Arabic language.

Finally, when I was a young man, after reading Quintilian and Cicero and the flowers of rhetoric, and when I had shut myself up in the mill of this language, and with much sweat and much time had scarcely begun to utter its panting and hissing words, and, as though walking through a crypt, had glimpsed a rare light from above, I finally stumbled upon Daniel. I was so exhausted that in sudden despair I wanted to cast aside all my former labor.

But when a certain Hebrew encouraged me, repeatedly impressing upon me that saying in his own language [Note: [Col. 1292C] The little word is absent from the Palatine manuscript, as is also the name “a certain” shortly before in several manuscripts cited by Martianay.] [Note: [Col. 1292C] This is borrowed from Virgil, *Georgics* I. MART.], “Unremitting labor conquers all,” I—who had seemed to myself a little scholar among [Note: [Col. 1292C] Here too the Palatine manuscript seems more correct in reading “a little scholar among the Hebrews”; this designation more clearly contrasts with “Chaldean.”] them—began once again to be a Chaldean student. And, to tell the truth, down to the present day I can read and understand the Chaldean language better than I can pronounce it.

I have said this [Note: [Col. 1292C] Two manuscripts add: “I have said this for this reason, so that…”] to show you the difficulty of Daniel, which among the Hebrews has neither the story of Susanna,

nor the hymn of the three youths,

nor the tales of Bel and the dragon [Note: [Col. 1292C] To refute the slanders of Erasmus, Clericus, and others directed against Jerome on this occasion, it is enough to understand from Book II, section 33, *Against Rufinus*, with what intention he said these things and in what sense he wished them understood. “Concerning Daniel,” he says, “I will answer briefly: I did not deny that he was a prophet, for I immediately confessed at the beginning of the prologue that he was a prophet; but I wished to show what the HEBREWS said and by what arguments they tried to prove their position.” And shortly afterward: “But when I report what the HEBREWS commonly say against the story of Susanna, the hymn of the three youths, and the tales of Bel and the dragon—which are not found in the Hebrew volume—the person who accuses me proves himself a foolish slanderer. For I am not explaining what I myself thought, but what they usually say against us,” and so forth. Recall also what we have noted on this passage.],

which, because they are scattered throughout the whole world, we have included after placing a dagger [÷] before them and cutting them down [Col. 1293A] [Note: [Col. 1293C] Consult the annotations of Leander of Saint-Martin on this Preface of Jerome, where the learned man rightly criticizes Erasmus, who recklessly attempts in his scholia to mock the Church’s usage, contrary to the mind of the holy Doctor. Whatever the excessive admirers of Erasmus’s learning and insufficiently impartial judges of matters may wish, Erasmus’s arguments are at times poorly digested. MART.], lest we seem to the uninstructed to have mutilated a large part of the book.

I heard one of the teachers of the Jews, while mocking the story of Susanna and saying that it had been fabricated by some Greek or other, counter the argument that Africanus also brought against Origen: that these etymologies, *apo tou schinou schisai* [ἁπὸ τοῦ σχίνου σχίσαι, “to split from the mastic tree”] and *apo tou prinou prisai* [ἀπὸ τοῦ πρίνου πρῖσαι, “to saw from the holm-oak”], derive from the Greek language.

We can offer this understanding of the matter in our own language. For example, we might say that he spoke from the name of the holm-oak when he said, “May you perish immediately” (*illico*); and from the mastic tree, “May the angel crush you into lentils,” or “may you not perish slowly,” or “may you be led to death slowly”—that is, flexibly—or something else appropriate to the name of the tree.

Then he mocked the three youths, saying that they had so much leisure that in the furnace of blazing fire they could play with meter and summon all the elements one by one to praise God [Note: [Col. 1294C] In the Palatine manuscript, with the negative particle added by a second hand, it reads: “that there was not so much leisure.” For the passage itself, see the holy Doctor’s prologue to his Commentary on this prophet.]. Or what miracle or sign of divine inspiration was there in killing a dragon with a lump of pitch, or in detecting the devices of the priests of Bel—things accomplished more by the prudence of an intelligent man than by the prophetic spirit [Alternative: “were accomplished”]?

When he came to Habakkuk and read that he had been carried from Judea to Chaldea, carrying a dish [Alternative: “carrying food”] [Note: [Col. 1294C] The Vatican codex mentioned above reads the Latin interpretation of this word: “carrying a dish after having been snatched away.” MART.] [Note: [Col. 1294C] The Vatican codex, whose reading we have often mentioned above, has the Latin interpretation of this word: “carrying a dish after having been snatched away.” MART.] he asked for an example of where we had read in the whole Old Testament that any saint had flown with a heavy body and crossed such great distances of the earth in an instant.

When one of our people, rather ready with words, brought forward Ezekiel and said that he had been transported from Chaldea to Judea, he mocked the man and demonstrated from the book itself that Ezekiel saw himself transported in the spirit.

Finally, he said that even our Apostle, evidently as a learned man and one who had learned the law from the Hebrews, had not dared to affirm that he had been caught up in the body, but had said: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Corinthians 12:2).

By such arguments and others like them he attacked the apocryphal stories in the Church’s book. On this matter, leaving the judgment to the reader’s discretion, I merely point out that among the Hebrews Daniel is not counted among the prophets, but among those who wrote the *Hagiographa* [Ἁγιόγραφα, “Sacred Writings”].

For among them all Scripture is divided into three parts:

the Law,

the Prophets,

and the *Hagiographa*,

that is, into five, eight, and eleven books. It is not the time to discuss this matter [Note: [Col. 1294C] See what is written in the Prologue prefixed to the books of Scripture, from Samuel to Malachi. MART.].

As for what Porphyry objects from this prophet—or rather against this book—Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinaris are witnesses. By answering his madness with many thousands of lines, I do not know whether they satisfied the curious reader.

Therefore I beseech you, Paula and Eustochium, to pour out prayers for me to the Lord, so that as long as I remain in this little body I may write something pleasing to you, useful to the Church, and worthy of posterity.

For I am not sufficiently moved by the judgments of those now living, who in either direction are led astray by love or hatred.

# THE BOOK OF THE PROPHET DANIEL BEGINS

[Col. 1293D] [Vision I] In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah,

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against [Alternative: omission; “came to”]

Jerusalem

and besieged it.

And the Lord delivered Jehoiakim, king of Judah,

into his hand,

together with part of the vessels of the house of God [Note: [Col. 1293D] The Vatican manuscript adds here the word “he took,” which is not found in the Hebrew, Greek, or Latin books.].

And he carried them into the land of Shinar,

into the house of his god,

and brought the vessels into the treasury of his god.

And the king said to Ashpenaz, chief of the eunuchs [Note: [Col. 1294D] The same manuscript has the additional pronoun “his,” which also appears in the Hebrew archetype and can suitably be supplied in Latin.],

that he should bring in some of the sons of Israel,

and from the royal stock and from tyrants, young men,

in whom there was no blemish,

handsome in appearance,

trained in every kind of wisdom,

skilled in knowledge,

and learned in discipline,

[Col. 1294D] and able to stand in the king’s palace,

so that he might teach them the writing and language of the Chaldeans.

And the king appointed for them a daily ration

from his own food

and from the wine that he himself drank,

so that, nourished for three years,

they might afterward stand in the presence of the king.

Now among them, from the sons of Judah,

were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

And the chief of the eunuchs gave them names:

to Daniel, Belteshazzar;

to Hananiah, Shadrach;

to Mishael, Meshach;

and to Azariah, Abednego.

But Daniel resolved in his heart

that he would not defile himself with the king’s table,

or with the wine of his drink,

and he asked the chief of the eunuchs not to defile him.

And God gave Daniel grace and mercy

in the sight of the chief of the eunuchs.

And the chief of the eunuchs said to Daniel:

“I fear my lord the king,

who has appointed your food and drink.

For if he sees your faces thinner than those of the other young men of your age,

you will condemn my head to the king.”

And Daniel said to Malassar,

whom the chief of the eunuchs had appointed over

Daniel, Hananiah,

Mishael, and Azariah:

“Test your servants, I beg you, for ten days.

Let vegetables be given us for food

and water for drink.

Then look upon our faces

[Col. 1295B] and the faces of the young men who eat the royal food,

and deal with your servants according to what you see.”

When he heard such words,

he tested them for ten days.

After ten days,

their faces appeared better and fuller than those of all the young men

who ate [Note: [Col. 1295D] These two words, “the royal food,” are omitted by the Vatican manuscript, although the original texts recognize them.] the royal food.

So Malassar removed their portions and the wine of their drink,

and gave them vegetables.

To these young men God gave knowledge and understanding

in every book and in wisdom.

To Daniel he also gave understanding of every vision

and dream.

When the days were completed after which the king had ordered them

to be brought in,

the chief of the eunuchs brought them into the presence of Nebuchadnezzar.

[Col. 1295C] And when the king had spoken with them,

none were found among all the others like Daniel,

Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

And they stood in the presence of the king.

And in every matter of wisdom and understanding

about which the king questioned them,

he found them ten times better than all the diviners

and magicians

who were in his entire kingdom.

Daniel remained until the first year of Cyrus

the king.

## [Vision II]

In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar,

Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream,

and his spirit was terrified,

and his dream fled from him.

Then the king commanded that the diviners, magicians,

sorcerers, and Chaldeans be summoned

to tell the king his dreams.

When they came,

they stood before the king.

And the king said to them:

“I saw a dream,

[Col. 1295D] and my mind is confused; I do not know what I saw.”

And the Chaldeans answered the king in Syriac:

“O king, live forever.

Tell your servants the dream,

and we will declare its interpretation.”

The king answered and said to the Chaldeans:

“The matter has departed from me.

Unless you tell me the dream and its interpretation,

you will perish,

and your houses will be confiscated.

But if you tell the dream and its interpretation,

</source>
rewards, gifts, and great honor from me.

[Col. 1296A] Therefore, tell me the dream and its interpretation.

They answered a second time and said:

“Let the king tell the dream to his servants, and we will declare its interpretation.”

The king replied and said:

“Truly I know that you are buying time, since you know that the word has gone from me. If, therefore, you do not tell me the dream, there is one sentence for all of you: for you have also prepared a false and deceit-filled interpretation, so that you may speak to me until the time passes.

Therefore, tell me the dream, so that I may know that you will also speak its true interpretation.”

Then the Chaldeans, answering before the king, said:

“There is no man upon the earth who can fulfill your word, O king.

[Col. 1296B] Indeed, no great and powerful king has ever asked such a thing of any diviner, magician, or Chaldean.

For the matter that you, O king, seek is difficult, and no one will be found who can disclose it in the presence of the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with human beings.”

When he heard this, the king, in fury and great anger, ordered that all the wise men of Babylon be put to death.

When the sentence had gone forth, the wise men were being killed; and Daniel and his companions were sought so that they too might perish.

Then Daniel inquired about the law and the sentence from Arioch, commander of the king’s army, who had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon.

And he asked him, who had received authority from the king, for what reason so cruel a sentence had gone forth from the king’s presence.

[Col. 1296C] When Arioch had disclosed the matter to Daniel, Daniel went in and asked the king to grant him time to make the interpretation known to the king.

Then he entered his house and informed his companions Ananias, Misael, and Azarias of the matter, so that they might seek mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, and so that Daniel and his companions might not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.

Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision by night, and Daniel blessed the God of heaven and said:

“Blessed be the name of God from age to age and forever, for wisdom and strength belong to him.

He changes times and seasons; he transfers kingdoms and establishes them.

[Col. 1296D] He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who understand instruction.

He reveals deep and hidden things, and he knows what is established in darkness; light is with him.

To you, God of my fathers, I give thanks, and you I praise, because you have given me wisdom and strength.

And now you have shown me what we asked of you, because you have disclosed the king’s word to us.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, as also the Memmian manuscript, according to Martianus, and our Vulgate, reads “my fathers” rather than “our fathers.”]

After this Daniel went to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon, and spoke to him as follows:

“Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon.

[Col. 1297A] Bring me into the presence of the king, and I will declare the interpretation to the king.”

Then Arioch hastily brought Daniel before the king and said to him:

“I have found a man among the sons of the captivity of Judah who will announce the interpretation to the king.”

The king replied and said to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar:

“Are you truly able to tell me the dream that I saw and its interpretation?”

Daniel answered before the king and said:

“The mystery that the king asks about cannot be declared to the king by wise men, magicians, diviners, or soothsayers.

But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and he has shown you, King Nebuchadnezzar, what is to come in the latter days.

Your dream and the visions of your head upon your bed are as follows:

[Col. 1297B] You, O king, began to consider on your bed what would happen after these things; and he who reveals mysteries showed you what is to come.

As for me, this mystery has not been revealed to me through wisdom that is in me, more than in any other living person, but so that the interpretation might be made known to the king and you might know the thoughts of your mind.

You, O king, were looking, and behold, there was a single great statue. That statue was immense and of extraordinary height; it stood before you, and its appearance was terrifying.

The head of that statue was of the finest gold; its chest and arms were of silver; its belly and thighs were of bronze.

Its legs were of iron, while part of its feet was iron and part was clay.

[Col. 1297C] You were looking until a stone was cut from the mountain without hands; it struck the statue on its iron and clay feet and shattered them.

Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold were shattered together and became like the chaff of a summer threshing floor, which the wind carried away. No place was found for them.

But the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

This is the dream. We shall also declare its interpretation before you, O king.

You are the king of kings, and the God of heaven has given you kingdom, power, dominion, and glory.

And everything in which the children of human beings dwell, [Col. 1297D] together with the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven, he has given into your hand and established under your rule. You, therefore, are the head of gold.

After you another kingdom will arise, inferior to you [the Vulgate adds: “of silver”].

Then a third kingdom, another one of bronze, will arise, and it will rule over the whole earth.

And there will be a fourth kingdom, like iron: just as iron crushes and subdues everything, so it will crush and shatter all these things.

But because you saw that part of the feet and toes was potter’s clay and part iron, the kingdom will be divided; yet it will arise from the stock of iron, just as you saw iron mixed with clay from the mud.

[Col. 1298A] And as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so the kingdom will be partly strong and partly shattered.

And because you saw iron mixed with clay from the mud, they will indeed mingle with human seed, but they will not adhere to one another, just as iron cannot be mixed with clay.

In the days of those kingdoms, the God of heaven will raise up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, and its kingdom will not be handed over to another people.

It will crush and consume all these kingdoms, but it itself will stand forever.

Just as you saw that a stone was cut from the mountain without hands and crushed the clay, the iron, the bronze, the silver, and the gold, the great God has shown the king what will happen afterward. The dream is true, [Col. 1298B] and its interpretation is reliable.”

Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and worshiped Daniel, and ordered sacrifices and incense to be offered to him.

Then the king spoke and said to Daniel:

“Truly, your God is God of gods, Lord of kings, and revealer of mysteries, because you were able to disclose this mystery.”

Then the king raised Daniel to a high position and gave him many great gifts.

He appointed him governor over all the provinces of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon.

Daniel, however, made a request of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the administration of the province of Babylon. Daniel himself remained at the king’s gate.

## [Vision III]

King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue, [Col. 1298C] sixty cubits high and six cubits wide, and set it up in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.

Therefore King Nebuchadnezzar sent word to assemble the satraps, magistrates, judges, commanders, tyrants, governors, and all the rulers of the regions, so that they might gather for the dedication of the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

Then the satraps, magistrates, judges, commanders, tyrants, and nobles who had been appointed to positions of authority, together with all the rulers of the regions, assembled to gather for the dedication of the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

They stood before the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had erected, and the herald cried out loudly:

“To you it is proclaimed, peoples, tribes, and languages:

[Col. 1298D] At the moment when you hear the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, symphony, and every kind of music, fall down and worship the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.

But whoever does not fall down and worship will be cast immediately into a furnace of blazing fire.”

Therefore, as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, symphony, and every kind of music, all the peoples, tribes, and languages fell down and worshiped the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

At that very moment, Chaldean men came forward and accused the Jews.

[Col. 1299A] They said to King Nebuchadnezzar:

“O king, live forever.

You, O king, issued a decree that every person who hears the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, symphony, and every kind of music must fall down and worship the golden statue.

But whoever does not fall down and worship must be cast into a furnace of blazing fire.

There are Jewish men whom you appointed over the administration of the province of Babylon—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These men, O king, have despised your decree. They do not worship your gods, and they do not worship the golden statue that you set up.”

Then Nebuchadnezzar, in fury and anger, ordered that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be brought in. They were immediately brought before the king.

King Nebuchadnezzar pronounced judgment and said to them:

[Col. 1299B] “Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you do not worship my gods and do not worship the golden statue that I set up?

Now then, if you are ready, at whatever moment you hear the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, symphony, and every kind of music, fall down and worship the statue that I made.

But if you do not worship, at that same moment you will be cast into a furnace of blazing fire. And what god is there who can rescue you from my hand?”

Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered and said to King Nebuchadnezzar:

[Note: See in what sense the holy Father himself comments on this passage: “In the Hebrew the king does not have the wording found in the Septuagint, lest they should seem to flatter the impious man,” and so forth. For in the present copy we read the matter quite clearly.]

“We have no need to answer you concerning this matter.

Behold, our God, whom we worship, is able to rescue us from the furnace of blazing fire and to deliver us from your hands, O king.

But if he does not wish to, let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods [Col. 1299C] and do not worship the golden statue that you have set up.”

Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the appearance of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered that the furnace be heated seven times more than it was accustomed to be heated.

He commanded the strongest men in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego by their feet and throw them into the furnace of blazing fire.

Immediately those men, bound in their trousers, turbans, sandals, and garments, were thrown into the middle of the furnace of blazing fire.

For the king’s command was urgent, and the furnace had been heated excessively.

The flame of the fire killed the men who had thrown Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego into it.

But these three men—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego— [Col. 1299D] fell bound into the middle of the furnace of blazing fire.

[Note: More clearly in the first book of the Commentary: “What follows is not found in the Hebrew, or rather in the Chaldean, but was added from the edition of Theodotion. For this section, marked with obeli, is placed here among the passages written in Chaldean in Daniel. Moreover, the manuscript copy of the Holy Scriptures that once belonged to the Monastery of Saint-Denis in France still preserves these obelus marks; it is now in the Library of the Most Christian King, no. 3561.”]

What follows was not found in the Hebrew volumes.

And they walked in the midst of the flame, praising God and blessing the Lord.

Azarias stood and prayed as follows; opening his mouth in the midst of the fire, he said:

[Col. 1300A] “Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers, and your name is praiseworthy and glorious forever.

[Note: All the manuscripts, except the codex of Saint-Albin of Angers, divide these verses as follows: “Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers, and praiseworthy, and your glorious name,” and so forth.]

For you are just in all that you have done to us; all your works are true, your ways are straight, and all your judgments are true.

For you have executed true judgments in accordance with all that you have brought upon us and upon the holy city of our fathers, Jerusalem.

For in truth and judgment you have brought all these things upon us because of our sins.

For we have sinned and acted wickedly by turning away from you; we have offended in everything.

We have neither listened to your commandments nor observed them, nor have we done as you commanded us, so that it might be well with us.

Therefore, all that you have brought upon us and all that you have done to us, you have done by true judgment.

You have delivered us into the hands of lawless enemies, most wicked and transgressing, and into the hands of an unjust and exceedingly wicked king, more wicked than the whole earth.

And now we cannot open our mouth. We have become a shame and reproach to your servants and to those who worship you.

Do not, we beg you, deliver us forever because of your name, and do not abolish your covenant.

Nor take your mercy from us, for the sake of Abraham, your beloved, and Isaac, your servant, and Israel, your holy one,

to whom you spoke, promising that you would multiply their offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore.

For, Lord, we have been reduced more than all the nations, and today we are humbled throughout the whole earth because of our sins.

[Col. 1300C] At this time there is neither prince, nor prophet, nor leader, neither burnt offering, nor sacrifice, nor offering, nor incense, nor place for firstfruits before you, so that we might find mercy.

But may we be received with a contrite soul and a spirit of humility.

As with the burnt offerings of rams and bulls and with thousands of fat lambs, so may our sacrifice be in your sight today, and may it please you.

For there is no shame for those who trust in you.

And now we follow you with our whole heart, fear you, and seek your face.

Do not put us to shame, but deal with us according to your gentleness and according to the abundance of your mercy.

Deliver us through your wonders and give glory to your name, O Lord.

[Col. 1300D] Let all who inflict evil upon your servants be put to shame; let them be put to shame in all their power, and let their strength be broken.

Let them know that you alone are the Lord God, glorious throughout the inhabited world.”

And those who had thrown them in—the king’s servants—did not cease feeding the furnace with naphtha, tow, pitch, and bundles of firewood.

[Col. 1301A] The flame rose forty-nine cubits above the furnace.

It burst out and burned the Chaldeans whom it found near the furnace.

But the angel of the Lord descended with Azarias and his companions into the furnace. He drove the flame of the fire out of the furnace and made the middle of the furnace like a blowing wind filled with dew.

The fire did not touch them at all, nor distress them, nor cause them any harm.

Then these three, as if with one mouth, praised, glorified, and blessed God in the furnace, saying:

“Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers; you are praiseworthy and exalted above all forever.

Blessed is your holy name of glory; it is praiseworthy and exalted above all forever.

Blessed are you in the holy temple of your glory; [Col. 1301B] you are supremely praiseworthy and exalted above all forever.

[Note: Here too, as in many other manuscripts cited by Martianus, our manuscripts read “supremely glorious” rather than “exalted above all.”]

Blessed are you upon the throne of your kingdom; you are supremely praiseworthy and exalted above all forever.

Blessed are you who behold the abysses and sit upon the cherubim; you are praiseworthy and exalted above all forever.

Blessed are you in the firmament of heaven; you are praiseworthy and glorious forever.

All works of the Lord, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Angels of the Lord, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Heavens, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

All waters above the heavens, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

All powers of the Lord, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

[Col. 1301C] Sun and moon, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Stars of heaven, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Every rain and dew, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

All spirits of God, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Fire and heat, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

[Note: The royal manuscript reads “fire and burning heat.”]

Cold and heat, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Dews and frost, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Frost and cold, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Ice and snow, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Nights and days, bless the Lord; [Col. 1301D] praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Light and darkness, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Lightning and clouds, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Let the earth bless the Lord; let it praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Mountains and hills, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

All things that sprout upon the earth, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

[Col. 1302A] Springs, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Seas and rivers, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Sea creatures and all that moves in the waters, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

All birds of heaven, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

All beasts and cattle, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Children of human beings, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Let Israel bless the Lord; let it praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Priests of the Lord, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Servants of the Lord, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord; [Col. 1302B] praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Holy and humble in heart, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever.

For he rescued us from the underworld, saved us from the hand of death, delivered us from the midst of the burning flame, and rescued us from the midst of the fire.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.

All the devout, bless the Lord, God of gods; praise him and give thanks to him, for his mercy endures throughout all ages.”

Up to this point these things are not found in the Hebrew, and what we have set down was translated from the edition of Theodotion.

Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished and rose quickly.

[Col. 1302C] He said to his nobles:

“Did we not throw three men, bound, into the midst of the fire?”

They answered and said to the king:

“Certainly, O king.”

He replied and said:

“Behold, I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no corruption in them; the appearance of the fourth is like a son of God.”

Then Nebuchadnezzar approached the door of the furnace of blazing fire and said:

“Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out and come here.”

Immediately Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out from the midst of the fire.

Then the satraps, magistrates, judges, and the king’s powerful men assembled and examined those men, because the fire had had no power over their bodies.

[Col. 1302D] The hair of their heads had not been singed, [Col. 1301D] their *saraballa* had not been altered,

[Note: Almost all manuscripts read *sarabara* in place of *saraballa*, as in the Septuagint. The Memmian Canon has *sarabara* in the text and this variant reading in the margin, elsewhere *sarabarie*. Saint Jerome refutes these errors in Book I of his Commentary on Daniel: “For the trousers,” he says, “which Symmachus translated as ἀναξυρίδας [*anaxyridas*, trousers or leggings], Aquila and Theodotion called *saraballa*, and not, as it is corruptly read, *sarabara*. In the Chaldean language *saraballa* means the legs and shins of human beings; and, by homonymy, their trousers, by which the legs and shins are covered, as though they were called coverings for the legs and shins.”]

and the smell of fire had not passed over them.

Then Nebuchadnezzar exclaimed and said:

“Blessed be their God—the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—who sent his angel and rescued his servants who trusted in him.

They changed the king’s word and surrendered their bodies rather than serve or worship any god except their own God.

Therefore, this decree is established by me: every people, tribe, and language that speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be destroyed, and its house shall be laid waste.

For there is no other god who can save in this way.”

Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

King Nebuchadnezzar to all peoples, nations, and languages who dwell throughout the whole earth:

“May your peace be multiplied.

The Most High God has performed signs and wonders for me.

Therefore it has pleased me to proclaim his signs, because they are great, and his wonders, because they are mighty.

His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, [Col. 1303B] and his dominion endures from generation to generation.”

## [Vision IV]

“I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace.

I saw a dream that terrified me; my thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head disturbed me.

Therefore I issued a decree that all the wise men of Babylon should be brought before me, so that they might declare the interpretation of the dream to me.

Then the diviners, magicians, Chaldeans, and soothsayers entered, and I told the dream before them, but they did not declare its interpretation to me.

[Note: The Hebrew text has a Chaldean word that properly means “another.” For this reason learned men thought that the holy Father had before him a Greek copy, and indeed a defective one, in which he read ἑταῖρον [*hetairon*, “companion”] instead of ἕτερον [*heteron*, “another”]. See, however, what we have noted in the Commentary on this passage.]

Until a companion entered before me—Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar according to the name of my god, and who had within himself the spirit of the holy gods.

[Col. 1303C] And I spoke the dream before him:

“Belteshazzar, chief of the diviners, whom I know to possess within you the spirit of the holy gods, and for whom no mystery is impossible: tell me the visions of my dreams that I saw and their interpretation.

The vision of my head upon my bed was this:

I saw, and behold, a tree in the middle of the earth, and its height was immense.

The tree was great and strong, and its height reached to heaven; its appearance extended to the ends of the whole earth.

Its leaves were exceedingly beautiful and its fruit abundant; there was food for all in it.

Beneath it lived the animals and beasts, and in its branches dwelt the birds of heaven; every living creature fed from it.

[Col. 1303D] I saw in the vision of my head upon my bed, and behold, a watcher and holy one descended from heaven.

He cried out loudly and said:

‘Cut down the tree and prune its branches; shake off its leaves and scatter its fruit.

Let the beasts that are beneath it flee, and the birds from its branches.

Nevertheless, leave the stump of its roots in the earth, and let it be bound with a band of iron and bronze among the grass outside; let it be moistened with the dew of heaven, and let its portion be with the wild beasts in the grass of the earth.

[Col. 1304A] Let its human heart be changed, and let the heart of a beast be given to it; and let seven periods pass over it.

By the decree of the watchers the sentence has been issued, and by the word of the holy ones the request has been made, so that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of human beings and gives it to whomever he wishes, and sets the lowliest of human beings over it.’

This dream I, King Nebuchadnezzar, saw.

Therefore, Belteshazzar, declare its interpretation quickly, because none of the wise men of my kingdom can make its interpretation known to me. But you can, because the spirit of the holy gods is in you.”

Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, began silently to consider within himself for about one hour.

[Col. 1304B] His thoughts troubled him.

The king answered and said:

“Belteshazzar, do not let the dream or its interpretation trouble you.”

Belteshazzar answered and said:

“My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you, and its interpretation for your enemies.

The tree that you saw, lofty and strong, whose height reaches to heaven and whose appearance extends over the whole earth, whose branches are most beautiful and whose fruit is abundant, with food for all in it, beneath which the beasts of the field dwelt and in whose branches the birds of heaven lodged—you are that tree, O king.

You have become great and strong; your greatness has increased and reached to heaven, and your power to the ends of the whole earth.

[Col. 1304C] And as for the king’s seeing a watcher and holy one descending from heaven and saying:

‘Cut down the tree and destroy it; nevertheless, leave its stump of roots in the earth, and let it be bound with iron and bronze among the grass outside, let it be sprinkled with the dew of heaven, and let its food be with the wild beasts until seven periods pass over it’—

this is the interpretation of the sentence of the Most High, which has come upon my lord the king:

They will drive you away from human beings, and your dwelling will be with the wild beasts. You will eat grass like an ox, and you will be drenched with the dew of heaven.

Seven periods will also pass over you until you know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of human beings and gives it to whomever he wishes.

But as for the command to leave the stump of its roots—that is, of the tree—your kingdom will remain yours after you have recognized that heavenly power exists.

Therefore, O king, may my counsel please you: redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by mercy toward the poor. Perhaps he will forgive your offenses.”

All this came upon King Nebuchadnezzar.

Twelve months later, he was walking in the palace of Babylon.

The king answered and said:

“Is this not great Babylon, which I built as a royal house by the strength of my power and for the glory of my splendor?”

[Col. 1305A] While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven:

“To you it is spoken, King Nebuchadnezzar:

The kingdom has passed from you.

They will drive you away from human beings, and your dwelling will be with the wild beasts.

You will eat grass like an ox, and seven periods will pass over you until you know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of human beings and gives it to whomever he wishes.”

At that same moment the word was fulfilled against Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven away from human beings; he ate grass like an ox, and his body was moistened with the dew of heaven, until his hair grew like the feathers of eagles [Col. 1305B] and his nails like those of birds.

After the end of the days, I, Nebuchadnezzar, raised my eyes toward heaven, and my understanding was restored to me.

I blessed the Most High and praised and glorified him who lives forever, because his power is everlasting power and his kingdom endures from generation to generation.

All the inhabitants of the earth are regarded as nothing before him; for he does according to his will among the powers of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth.

There is no one who can resist his hand or say to him, ‘Why have you done this?’

At that time my understanding returned to me, and I came again to the honor and splendor of my kingdom; my appearance also returned to me.

[Col. 1305C] My nobles and magistrates sought me out, and I was restored to my kingdom; still greater magnificence was added to me.

Now, therefore, I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise, exalt, and glorify the King of heaven, for all his works are true and his ways are just, and he is able to humble those who walk in pride.”

## [Vision V]

“King Belteshazzar made a great banquet for a thousand of his nobles, and each one drank according to his age.

Then, already drunk, he ordered that the golden and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar his father had carried away from the temple in Jerusalem be brought, so that the king, his nobles, his wives, and his concubines might drink from them.

[Col. 1305D] Then the golden vessels that he had carried away from the temple in Jerusalem were brought, and the king, his nobles, his wives, and his concubines drank from them.

They drank wine and praised their gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone.

At that very moment fingers appeared, like the hand of a human being writing opposite the lampstand on the plaster of the wall of the royal hall, and the king watched the fingers of the hand that was writing.

Then the king’s face changed, and his thoughts troubled him. The joints of his loins became slack, and his knees knocked against one another.

The king therefore cried out loudly and ordered the magicians, Chaldeans, and soothsayers to be brought in.

[Col. 1306A] And the king declared to the wise men of Babylon:

“Whoever reads this writing and makes its interpretation clear to me shall be clothed in purple, shall have a golden chain around his neck, and shall be third in my kingdom.”

Then all the king’s wise men entered, but they could not read the writing or make its interpretation known to the king.

Therefore King Belteshazzar was greatly troubled, and his face changed; his nobles too were disturbed.

The queen, because of what had happened to the king and his nobles, entered the banquet hall.

She spoke and said:

“O king, live forever. Do not let your thoughts trouble you, and do not let your face be changed.

There is a man in your kingdom who has within him the spirit of the holy gods.

[Col. 1306B] In the days of your father, knowledge and wisdom were found in him.

For King Nebuchadnezzar your father appointed him chief of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and soothsayers—your father, O king—because an extraordinary spirit, prudence, understanding, interpretation of dreams, disclosure of secrets, and the untying of what is bound were found in him, that is, in Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar.

Now, therefore, let Daniel be summoned, and he will declare the interpretation.”

So Daniel was brought before the king.

The king began by saying to him:

“Are you Daniel, one of the sons of the captivity of Judah, whom the king my father brought from Judea?

I have heard about you, that you possess the spirit of the gods, and that exceptional knowledge, understanding, and wisdom have been found in you.

And now the wise men and magicians have entered before me to read this writing and make its interpretation known to me, but they could not declare the meaning of this message.

Moreover, I have heard about you that you can interpret obscure matters and dissolve what is bound.
