Therefore, if you are able to read the writing and make its interpretation known to me, you shall be clothed in purple, shall have a golden chain around your neck, and shall be the third-ranking ruler in my kingdom.”

Daniel answered and said before the king:

“Let your gifts remain with you, and give the presents of your house to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing for you, O king, and will show you its interpretation.

O king, the Most High God gave kingdom, greatness, glory, and honor to Nebuchadnezzar your father.

[Col. 1306D] And because of the greatness that he had given him, all peoples, tribes, and languages trembled and feared him.

Whomever he wished, he killed; whomever he wished, he struck; whomever he wished, he exalted; and whomever he wished, he humbled.

But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened in pride, he was deposed from the throne of his kingdom and his glory was taken away.

He was driven away from the children of human beings; his heart was placed with the beasts, and his dwelling was with the wild asses.

He ate grass like an ox, and his body was moistened with the dew of heaven, until he recognized that the Most High has authority over the kingdom of human beings.

[Col. 1307A] He raises over it whomever he wishes.

But you, his son Belteshazzar, have not humbled your heart, although you knew all these things.

Instead, you have exalted yourself against the Lord of heaven, and the vessels of his house were brought before you.

You and your nobles, your wives, and your concubines drank wine from them.

You praised gods of silver, gold, bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor feel.

But you did not glorify the God who holds your breath in his hand and all your ways.

Therefore, a finger of the hand was sent by him,”

[Note: [Col. 1307D] Several manuscripts read the relative pronoun in the masculine: “who wrote this”; this can refer to the finger. Although in the Chaldaic text the relative pronoun refers to the hand, *di jeda*, that is, “of this hand.” MART.]

which wrote this, which is inscribed.

This is the writing that was set down:

[Col. 1307B] **MENE, TEKEL, PERES.**

And this is the interpretation of the words:

**MENE:** God has numbered your kingdom

and brought it to an end.

**TEKEL:** You have been weighed in the balance,

and have been found wanting.

**PERES:** Your kingdom has been divided,

and given to the Medes and Persians.

Then, at the king’s command, Daniel was clothed in purple,

and a golden chain was placed around his neck;

and it was proclaimed concerning him that he would have authority

as third in his kingdom [Note: [Col. 1307D] The Vatican manuscript omits the pronoun “his”; it is likewise absent from the Hebrew alone.].

That same night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed [Note: [Col. 1307D] The Carcassonne Canon inserted, with the gentilic pronoun, the proper name of the royal city Babylon: “That same night Belshazzar, king of Babylon, was killed. And Darius,” etc. MART.].

And Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom,

being sixty-two years old.

[Vision VI.] It pleased Darius, and he appointed over the kingdom

one hundred and twenty satraps,

so that they might be throughout his entire kingdom.

And over them, three commissioners,

[Col. 1307C] one of whom was Daniel,

so that the satraps might render an account to them,

and the king might not suffer inconvenience.

Now Daniel surpassed all the commissioners and satraps,

because the spirit of God was more abundant in him.

Therefore the king considered appointing him over the whole

kingdom;

whereupon the commissioners and satraps sought an opportunity

to find some charge against Daniel on the king’s side [Note: [Col. 1308D] In the Chaldaic text we read *malchutha*, which signifies “kingdom,” not “king.” Hence we may call the reading of the Royal manuscript no. 3564 genuine, where it has “on the side of the kingdom.” Nevertheless, Jerome interprets it as “king,” as can be demonstrated most clearly both from the manuscript and from his Commentary. MART.].

But they could find no charge or suspicion, because he was faithful,

and no fault or suspicion was found in him.

Then those men said:

“We shall find no charge against this Daniel

unless it concerns the law of his God.”

Then the commissioners and satraps approached the king,

and spoke to him in this manner:

“King Darius, live forever!

All the officials of the kingdom,

[Col. 1307D] the magistrates, satraps, senators, and judges,

have agreed that an imperial decree and edict should be issued:

that anyone who makes a petition of any kind to any

god or human being for thirty days,

except to you, O king,

shall be cast into the lions’ den.

Now, therefore, O king, confirm the sentence and write the decree,

[Col. 1308A] so that what has been established may not be altered by the Medes and

Persians,

and no one may transgress it.”

So King Darius published the edict,

and established it.

When Daniel learned of this—that is, of the law that had been established—

he entered his house.

With the windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem, three times a day he bent his knees

and prayed,

giving thanks before his God,

as he had previously been accustomed to do.

Those men, therefore, investigating more carefully,

found Daniel praying and entreating

his God.

Then they approached and spoke to the king concerning the edict:

“King, did you not establish

that every person who should petition any of the gods or

human beings for thirty days,

[Col. 1308B] except you, O king,

should be cast into the lions’ den?”

The king answered them:

“The word is true, according to the decree of the Medes and Persians,

which may not be violated.”

Then they answered before the king:

“Daniel, one of the children of the captivity of Judah,

has paid no attention to your law or to the edict that you established,

but three times a day he makes his prayer and entreaty.”

When the king heard this,

he was deeply distressed.

And he set his heart on Daniel in order to deliver him,

and until sunset he labored to rescue him.

But those men, understanding the king, said to him:

“Know, O king, that it is the law of the Medes and Persians

that every decree established by the king may not be altered.”

Then the king gave the order,

and they brought Daniel

and cast him into the lions’ den.

The king said to Daniel:

“Your God, whom you continually serve, will himself deliver you.”

Then a stone was brought

and placed over the mouth of the den.

The king sealed it with his own ring and with the rings of his nobles,

so that nothing might be done against Daniel.

Then the king went to his house and spent the night fasting;

food was not brought before him,

and sleep also departed from him.

At first light the king rose

and hurried to the lions’ den.

As he approached the den, he called to Daniel in a voice full of tears,

and addressed him:

[Col. 1308D] “Daniel, servant of the living God,

do you suppose that your God, whom you continually serve, has been able

to deliver you from the lions?”

Daniel answered the king:

“O king, live forever!

My God sent his angel

and shut the mouths of the lions,

and they have not harmed me,

[Col. 1309A] because righteousness was found in me before him;

and before you also, O king, I have committed no offense.”

Then the king rejoiced greatly over him,

and commanded that Daniel be brought up from the den.

Daniel was brought up from the den,

and no injury was found on him,

because he had believed in his God.

At the king’s command, those men who had accused Daniel were brought,

and they were cast into the lions’ den,

they themselves, their children, and their wives.

They had not yet reached the floor of the den

before the lions seized them and crushed all their bones.

Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, tribes,

and languages

dwelling throughout the whole earth:

“May peace be multiplied among you.

By me a decree has been established

that throughout my entire dominion and kingdom

[Col. 1309B] they shall tremble and fear the God of Daniel.

For he is the living God, and he endures forever;

his kingdom shall not be destroyed,

and his power shall endure forever.

He is the deliverer and savior,

performing signs and wonders in heaven and on earth,

who delivered Daniel from the lions’ den.”

Daniel continued until the reign of Darius

and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

[Vision VII.] In the first year of Belshazzar, king of Babylon,

Daniel saw a dream.

The vision of his head was upon his bed,

and, writing down the dream, he summarized it in a brief account;

and, giving its main outline, he said:

“I was looking in my vision by night,

and behold, the four winds of heaven were battling upon the great sea.

And four great beasts were rising from the sea,

[Col. 1309C] different from one another.

The first was like a lioness,

and it had the wings of an eagle.

I watched until its wings were torn away,

and it was lifted from the earth.

Then it stood upon feet like a human being,

and a human heart was given to it.

And behold, another beast, resembling a bear, stood on one side;

and there were three rows in its mouth,

and in its teeth.

And they said to it:

‘Arise, eat very much flesh.’

After this I looked,

and behold, another beast, like a leopard.

It had four wings of a bird upon its back,

and the beast had four heads,

and authority was given to it.

After this I looked in the night vision,

and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and extraordinary,

[Col. 1309D] and exceedingly strong.

It had great iron teeth; it devoured and crushed,

and trampled the remainder under its feet.

It was unlike the other beasts that I had seen before it,

and it had ten horns.

I considered the horns,

and behold, another small horn arose from among them.

And three of the first horns were uprooted from before it.

And behold, eyes like human eyes were in this horn,

[Col. 1310A] and a mouth speaking great things.

I watched until thrones were set in place,

and the Ancient of Days took his seat.

His garment was white as snow,

and the hair of his head like clean wool.

His throne was flames of fire;

its wheels were burning fire.

A stream of fire, swift and rushing,

flowed out from before him.

Thousands of thousands served him,

and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.

The court sat,

and the books were opened.

I watched because of the sound of the great words

that the horn was speaking.

And I saw that the beast was killed,

and its body perished and was handed over to be burned with fire.

The authority of the other beasts was also taken away,

and a term of life was assigned to them until a time and a time.

[Col. 1310B] I continued watching in the night vision,

and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven.

He came up to the Ancient of Days,

and they presented him before him.

And he gave him authority, honor, and a kingdom,

and all peoples, tribes, and languages would serve him.

His authority is an everlasting authority that shall not be taken away,

and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.

My spirit was horrified;

I, Daniel, was terrified by these things,

and the visions of my head troubled me.

I approached one of those who were standing by,

and sought the truth from him concerning all these things.

He told me the interpretation of the words

and instructed me:

‘These four great beasts [Note: [Col. 1309D] Thus the older and better manuscripts read, according to the Hebrew or Chaldaic idiom, in which neither a substantive verb nor a relative pronoun is found. The text of Jerome’s Commentary on Daniel supplies what is lacking here, for there we read: “These four great beasts are four kingdoms that shall arise from the earth.” In the Chaldaic source it is written, *arbea malchim jecumun min araa*, that is, “four kings shall arise from the earth.” MART.] are four;

four kingdoms shall arise from the earth.

[Col. 1310C] But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom,

and they shall possess the kingdom forever and ever.’

After this I wished to learn carefully about the fourth beast,

which was very different from all the others and exceedingly terrifying,

with its iron teeth and claws.

It devoured and crushed,

and trampled the remainder under its feet.

I wished to learn about the ten horns that it had on its head,

and about the other horn that had arisen,

before which three horns had fallen;

and about that horn which had eyes

and a mouth speaking great things,

and which was larger than the others.

I watched,

and behold, that horn was making war against the saints,

and prevailed over them,

until the Ancient of Days came and judgment was given to the saints

of the Most High.

Then the time came, and the saints received the kingdom.

And he said:

‘The fourth beast shall be a fourth kingdom on the earth,

which shall be greater than all the kingdoms.

It shall devour the whole earth, trample it,

and crush it.

The ten horns of that kingdom

shall be ten kings.

Another shall arise after them,

and he shall be more powerful than the former ones,

and he shall humble three kings.

He shall speak words against the Most High,

[Col. 1311A] and shall crush the saints of the Most High.

He shall think that he can change times and laws,

and they shall be delivered into his hand for a time,

times, and half a time.

But the court shall sit,

so that his power may be taken away,

crushed, and destroyed to the end.

The kingdom, the power, and the greatness of the kingdom

under the whole heaven

shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High.

His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom,

and all kings shall serve and obey him.’

**HERE ENDS THE WORD.**

I, Daniel, was greatly troubled by my thoughts,

and my face was changed within me,

but I kept the word in my heart.

[Vision VIII.] In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar,

a vision appeared to me.

I, Daniel, after what I had seen at the beginning,

[Col. 1311B] saw in a vision [Note: [Col. 1311D] Six or seven manuscript codices, together with the copies of the Canon, read this way; others have “the region” instead of “the city”: “which is in the region of Elam.” Jerome did not overlook this in his Commentary on this passage; for he writes: “In the region of Elam, or, as Symmachus interpreted it, in the city; from which the region also received its name, just as Babylon gave its name to Babylonia, and Elam to the Elamites,” etc. MART.],

when I was in Susa the citadel, which is in the city of Elam.

And I saw in the vision

that I was beside the gate of Ulai.

I lifted my eyes and looked,

and behold, a single ram stood before the marsh,

with high horns,

one higher than the other and growing higher.

Afterward I saw the ram butting with its horns toward the west,

toward the north,

and toward the south.

No beast could withstand it,

and no one could be rescued from its hand.

It acted according to its will

and became great.

And I was understanding.

And behold, a male goat was coming from the west,

[Col. 1311C] across the face of the whole earth,

and it did not touch the ground.

The goat had a conspicuous horn between its eyes.

It came up to the horned ram that I had seen standing before the gate,

and ran toward it with the force of its strength.

When it had drawn near the ram, it became furious against it,

and struck the ram.

It shattered its two horns,

and the ram could not withstand it.

When it had thrown it to the ground, it trampled it,

and no one could rescue the ram from its hand.

The male goat became exceedingly great.

But when it had grown strong, the great horn was broken,

and four horns arose beneath it toward the four winds of heaven.

From one of them a small horn came forth.

[Col. 1311D] It became great toward the south,

toward the east,

and toward the power.

It became great up to the power of heaven,

and it cast down some of the host and some of the stars,

and trampled them.

It became great even against the Prince of the host,

and from him it took away the continual sacrifice,

and cast down the place of his sanctuary.

Power was given against the continual sacrifice

because of transgressions.

[Col. 1312A] Truth was cast down upon the earth,

and it acted and prospered.

Then I heard one of the holy ones speaking,

and one holy one said to another—I do not know to whom he was speaking:

‘How long will the vision last,

and the continual sacrifice,

and the sin of desolation that has occurred,

and the sanctuary and the host be trampled?’

And he said to him:

‘Until evening and morning, [Note: [Col. 1312D] Our manuscripts, together with the Vulgate, place the noun “days” here: “two thousand three hundred days,” etc.; the Hebrew, however, omits it.]

two thousand three hundred;

then the sanctuary shall be cleansed.’

Now it happened, when I, Daniel, saw the vision

and sought understanding,

that behold, there stood before me something like the appearance of a man.

And I heard the voice of a man between the banks of Ulai,

and he cried out and said:

‘Gabriel, make this man understand the vision.’

And he came and stood near where I was standing.

When he came, I was afraid and fell upon my face,

and he said to me:

‘Understand, son of man,

[Col. 1312B] that the vision will be fulfilled at the time of the end.’

While he was speaking with me, I fell prostrate upon the ground.

He touched me, raised me to my standing position,

and said to me:

‘I shall show you what is to happen at the final time of the curse,

for the appointed time has its end.

The ram that you saw with horns

is the king of the Medes and Persians.

The male goat is the king of the Greeks,

and the great horn that was between its eyes

is the first king.

As for the horn being broken and four arising in its place,

four kings shall arise from his nation,

but not with his strength.

After their kingdom, when iniquities have increased,

a king shall arise shameless in face and understanding riddles.

[Col. 1312C] His strength shall become powerful,

but not by his own forces.

Beyond what can be believed, he shall lay everything waste,

and he shall prosper and act.

He shall destroy the strong

and the people of the saints according to his will,

and deceit shall be directed by his hand.

He shall magnify his heart,

and in the abundance of possessions he shall kill many.

He shall rise up against the Prince of princes,

and he shall be broken without human hand.

The evening-and-morning vision that was spoken of is true.

Therefore seal up the vision,

for it concerns many days.’

And I, Daniel, languished

and was sick for several days.

When I rose, I performed the king’s business,

and I was astonished at the vision,

and there was no one to interpret it.

[Col. 1312D] [Vision IX.] In the first year of Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of Median descent,

who ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldeans,

in the first year of his reign,

I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of years

concerning which the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah

the prophet,

that the desolations of Jerusalem would be completed in seventy years.

And I set my face toward the Lord God,

[Col. 1313A] to seek and entreat him in fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.

And I prayed to the Lord my God,

and confessed, and said:

“I beseech you, Lord, great and awesome God,

who keeps the covenant and mercy for those who love you

and keep your commandments.

We have sinned,

we have committed iniquity,

we have acted wickedly,

and we have turned away.

We have turned aside from your commandments and judgments.

We have not obeyed your servants the prophets,

who spoke in your name to our kings,

our rulers,

our ancestors,

and all the people of the land.

To you, Lord, belongs righteousness;

but to us, shame of face,

[Col. 1313B] as it is today—to the men of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and all Israel;

to those who are near and those who are far away,

in all the lands to which you have driven them,

because of their iniquities in which they sinned against you.

Lord, to us belongs shame of face—

to our kings,

our rulers,

and our ancestors who sinned.

But to you, Lord our God, belong mercy and forgiveness,

because we have turned away from you.

We have not listened to the voice of the Lord our God,

so as to walk in his law, which he set before us

through his servants the prophets.

All Israel has transgressed your law and turned aside,

refusing to listen to your voice.

Therefore the curse and the oath that are written in the book of Moses,

the servant of God, have been poured out upon us,

[Col. 1313C] because we sinned against him.

He has fulfilled the words that he spoke against us

and against our rulers who ruled over us,

bringing upon us great evil,

such as had never occurred under all heaven,

as has happened in Jerusalem.

As it is written in the law of Moses,

all this evil has come upon us.

Yet we have not entreated your presence, Lord our God,

to turn back from our iniquities

and understand your truth.

The Lord kept watch over the evil

and brought it upon us.

The Lord our God is righteous in all his works

that he has done,

for we have not listened to his voice.

And now, Lord our God,

[Col. 1313D] who brought your people out of the land of Egypt

with a strong hand

and made for yourself a name, as it is today—

we have sinned; we have acted wickedly,

Lord, against all your righteousness.

Let your anger and your wrath, I beseech you,

be turned away from your city Jerusalem

and your holy mountain.

[Col. 1314A] For because of our sins and the iniquities of our ancestors,

Jerusalem and your people have become a reproach to all those around us.

Now therefore, hear, O our God, the prayer of your servant

and his entreaties.

Show your face upon your sanctuary,

which is desolate,

for your own sake.

Incline your ear, my God, and hear.

Open your eyes and see our desolations

and the city upon which your name has been invoked.

For we do not cast our prayers before your presence

on the basis of our righteousness,

but on the basis of your many mercies.

Hear, Lord;

be gracious, Lord;

pay attention and act.

Do not delay for your own sake, my God,

[Col. 1314B] because your name has been invoked over the city

and over your people.”

While I was still speaking and praying,

confessing my sins and the sins of my people Israel,

and laying my prayers before the presence of my God

for the holy mountain of my God,

while I was still speaking in prayer,

behold, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning,

came swiftly and touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice.

And he instructed me,

and spoke with me, saying:

“Daniel, now I have come forth to teach you

and make you understand.

At the beginning of your entreaties the word went forth,

and I have come to declare it to you,

because you are a man of desires.

[Col. 1314C] Therefore pay attention to the word

and understand the vision.

Seventy weeks have been decreed for your people and your holy city,

to finish transgression and bring sin to an end,

to erase iniquity,

to bring everlasting righteousness,

to fulfill the vision and [Note: [Col. 1313D] In the Royal manuscript of the Bible: “and the prophecy may be fulfilled.” In the one we mentioned above from Saint Albinus of Angers, the same reading occurs, but in the plural: “and the visions and prophets may be fulfilled.” The copies of the Canon and many other manuscript codices retain the reading we have published. MART. —The Vatican manuscript reads “and the prophet”; others have “the prophets,” while in Hebrew there is [the supplied text is blank].]

prophecy,

and to anoint the Holy of Holies.

Know, therefore, and understand:

from the issuing of the word to restore and rebuild Jerusalem

until Christ the prince,

there shall be seven weeks,

and sixty-two weeks.

And the street shall be rebuilt again,

and the walls, in the distress of the times.

And after the sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed,

and there shall be nothing belonging to him [Note: [Col. 1314D] Here one should supply what is inserted in printed editions and in several manuscripts, namely: “the people who will deny him.” For in Hebrew you read nothing other than *ve’en lo*, that is, “and not to him,” or “and not his,” which agrees with the Royal codex, which we have followed here as being free from every addition. MAR.].

[Col. 1314D] And the people of the coming prince shall destroy

the city and the sanctuary.

And its end shall be devastation,

and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed.

He shall confirm a covenant with many for one week,

and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall cease.

[Col. 1315A] And in the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation,

and desolation shall continue until the consummation and the end.”

[Vision X.] In the third year of Cyrus, king of the Persians,

a word was revealed to Daniel, whose name was Belshazzar.

The word was true,

and there was great strength in it.

He understood the word,

for understanding is needed in the vision.

In those days I, Daniel, mourned for three weeks.

I did not eat desirable bread,

and neither meat nor wine entered my mouth.

Nor did I anoint myself with oil,

until the three weeks were completed.

On the twenty-fourth day of the first month,

I was beside the great river, which is the Tigris.

I lifted my eyes and looked,

and behold, one man clothed in linen,

his loins girded with refined gold.

His body was like chrysolite,

[Col. 1315B] his face like the appearance of lightning,

his eyes like burning lamps.

His arms and the parts extending downward to his feet

were like the appearance of glowing bronze,

and the sound of his words was like the sound of a multitude.

I, Daniel, alone saw the vision.

The men who were with me did not see it,

but an exceedingly great terror fell upon them,

and they fled into hiding.

I was left alone and saw this great vision,

but no strength remained in me.

My appearance was changed within me,

and I wasted away, having no strength at all.

I heard the sound of his words,

and as I heard, I lay terrified upon my face,

with my face clinging to the ground.

And behold, a hand touched me,

[Col. 1315C] and raised me upon my knees

and upon the joints of my hands.

And he said to me:

“Daniel, man of desires,

understand the words that I speak to you,

and stand upright,

for now I have been sent to you.”

When he had spoken this word to me,

I stood trembling.

And he said to me:

“Do not fear, Daniel,

for from the first day on which you set your heart to understand

and to humble yourself before your God,

your words were heard,

and I came because of your words.

But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days.

And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes,

came to help me,

and I remained there beside the king of the Persians.

I have come to teach you what will happen to your people

[Col. 1315D] in the latter days,

for the vision still concerns days to come.”

While he was speaking these words to me,

I lowered my face toward the ground and was silent.

And behold, something resembling a son of man touched my lips.

I opened my mouth and spoke,

and said to the one standing opposite me:

“My lord, in the vision my joints have come apart,

and no strength remains in me.

And how can the servant of my lord speak with my lord?

For no strength remains in me,

and my breath is failing.”

Again something resembling the appearance of a man touched me,

strengthened me,

and said:

“Do not fear, man of desires.

[Col. 1316A] Peace be with you.

Take courage and be strong.”

When he spoke with me, I recovered,

and I said:

“Speak, my lord, for you have strengthened me.”

And he said:

“Do you know why I have come to you?

And now I shall return to fight against the prince of the Persians.

When I was going out, behold, the prince of the Greeks came.

Nevertheless, I shall announce to you what is expressed

in the writing of truth.

There is no one who helps me in all these matters

except Michael, your prince.

[Chapter XI.] And I, from the first year of Darius the Mede,

stood ready to strengthen and reinforce him.

And now I shall announce the truth to you.

Behold, three more kings shall arise in Persia,

and the fourth shall become exceedingly rich above them all.

When he has grown powerful through his wealth,

[Col. 1316B] he shall stir everyone against the kingdom of Greece.

Then a powerful king shall arise,

and he shall rule with great authority

and do whatever pleases him.

When he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken

and divided toward the four winds of heaven,

but not among his descendants

and not according to the power with which he ruled.

For his kingdom shall be torn apart and given to outsiders,

apart from these.

The king of the south shall grow strong,

and one of his princes shall prevail over him and rule a dominion,

for his dominion shall be great.

After the end of the years they shall form an alliance.

The daughter of the king of the south shall come to the king of the north

to make an agreement.

But she shall not retain the strength of her arm,

nor shall her offspring endure.

[Col. 1316C] She herself shall be handed over,

together with those who brought her,

her young men,

and those who supported her in those times.

A branch from the shoots of her roots shall arise in his place.

He shall come with an army,

enter the province of the king of the north,

and act against them and prevail.

Moreover, he shall carry their gods,

their molten images,

and their precious vessels of silver and gold

as captives into Egypt.

He shall prevail against the king of the north,

and the king of the south shall enter his kingdom

and return to his own land.

His sons shall be provoked,

and they shall gather a very large multitude of armies.

One shall come swiftly, overflowing;

then he shall return, become inflamed,

and engage him in battle with his strength.

[Col. 1316D] The king of the south, being provoked, shall go out

and fight against the king of the north.

He shall prepare a very great multitude,

and the multitude shall be delivered into his hand.

He shall capture the multitude,

and his heart shall be exalted.

He shall bring down many thousands,

but he shall not prevail.

For the king of the north shall return

and prepare a much larger multitude than before.

At the end of the times and years,

he shall come swiftly with a great army

and exceedingly great wealth.

In those times many shall rise against the king of the south.

The sons of the transgressors among your people shall also exalt themselves

to fulfill the vision,

but they shall fall.

[Col. 1317A] The king of the north shall come,

raise a siege ramp,

and capture the most strongly fortified cities.

The forces of the south shall not withstand him.

His chosen forces shall rise up to resist,

but there shall be no strength.

He shall come against him according to his pleasure,

and no one shall stand before him.

He shall stand in the glorious land,

and it shall be consumed by his hand.

He shall set his face to come and seize his entire kingdom,

and he shall make right terms with him.

He shall give him the daughter of women

to overthrow it,

but she shall not stand,

and she shall not belong to him.

He shall turn his face toward the islands

and capture many.

He shall bring to an end the prince of his reproach,

and his reproach shall turn back upon him.

He shall turn his face toward the dominion of his land,

and he shall stumble and fall,

and shall not be found.

In his place shall arise one who is most contemptible

and unworthy of royal dignity.

[Col. 1317B] In a few days he shall be crushed,

not in anger and not in battle.

In his place shall arise one who is despised,

and royal honor shall not be given to him.

He shall come secretly

and obtain the kingdom through deception.

The forces of the fighter shall be swept away before him

and crushed,

together with the prince of the covenant.

After forming an alliance with him, he shall act deceitfully.

He shall go up and prevail with a small people.

He shall enter rich and prosperous cities

and do what neither his fathers nor his ancestors had done:

he shall scatter their plunder, spoil, and riches,

and devise plans against the strongest fortresses.

This shall continue for a time.

His strength shall be stirred up,

[Col. 1317C] and his heart shall be against the king of the south

with a great army.

The king of the south shall be provoked to war

with many and exceedingly strong auxiliaries,

but they shall not stand,

because they will devise plans against him.

Those who eat bread with him shall crush him,

and his army shall be overwhelmed.

Many slain shall fall.

The hearts of both kings shall be bent on doing evil.

At one table they shall speak lies,

but they shall not prosper,

because the end still awaits another time.

He shall return to his land with great wealth.

His heart shall be against the holy covenant,

and he shall act,

and return to his land.

At the appointed time he shall return

and come to the south.

The latter event shall not resemble the former.

Ships and Romans shall come against him,

[Col. 1317D] and he shall be struck and return.

He shall become angry against the covenant of the sanctuary

and shall act.

He shall return and take thought against those

who abandoned the covenant of the sanctuary.

Forces from him shall arise,

and they shall profane the sanctuary of strength,

[Col. 1318A] remove the continual sacrifice,

and set up the abomination of desolation.

The wicked shall feign deceitfully in regard to the covenant.

But the people who know their God shall prevail and act.

The learned among the people shall instruct many.

They shall fall by the sword,

by flame,

by captivity,

and by plunder for many days.

When they fall, they shall receive a little help,

and many shall join themselves to them deceitfully.

Some of the learned shall fall,

so that they may be refined, chosen, and purified

until the appointed time,

for there will still be another time.

The king shall act according to his will.

He shall exalt himself

and magnify himself against every god.

He shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods

and shall prosper

until the wrath is completed,

for the decree has been carried out.

He shall pay no regard to the God of his ancestors.

[Col. 1318B] He shall be devoted to the desires of women,

and shall pay regard to no god,

for he shall rise up against them all.

But he shall honor the god Maozim in his place [Note: [Col. 1317D] The Carcassonne Canon has *Moozim, Memmiam*; the Memmian has *Moozim*. Both can be read from the Hebrew [the supplied text is blank], which the Masoretes read as *Maumyim*. MART. —The Vatican manuscript likewise has *Moozim*, together with the Vulgate copies; others prefer *Moozim*.].

He shall honor a god whom his ancestors did not know

with gold, silver, precious stones, and costly things.

He shall act so as to fortify Maozim with a foreign god whom he has known,

and he shall increase his glory,

give them authority over many,

and distribute land without price.

At the appointed time the king of the south shall fight against him.

The king of the north shall come against him like a storm,

with chariots, horsemen, and a great fleet.

He shall enter the lands,

crush them,

and pass through.

He shall enter the glorious land,

[Col. 1318C] and many shall fall.

But these alone shall be saved from his hand:

Edom, Moab,

and the first part of the children of Ammon.

He shall stretch out his hand over the lands,

and the land of Egypt shall not escape.

He shall rule over the treasures of gold and silver

and over all the precious things of Egypt.

He shall also pass through Libya and Ethiopia.

But a report from the east and from the north shall trouble him,

and he shall come with a great multitude

to crush and kill many.

And he shall pitch his tent [Note: [Col. 1317D] We find this passage marked in the Memmian Canon. For when the copyist had written *Ephedno* in the text, he added this in the margin: “According to the Septuagint, *Ephadanon*.” Jerome says in his Commentary: “It should be noted that, since the Hebrew language has no letter P but uses *phe* in its place, whose force is represented by the Greek sound, in this one passage *phe* is indeed written in Hebrew but pronounced P.” MART.] between the seas,

upon the glorious and holy mountain.

He shall come to its summit,

and no one shall help him.

[Chapter XII.] At that time Michael shall arise,

the great prince

who stands for the children of your people.

And there shall be a time

such as has not been since nations first came into existence,

[Col. 1318D] until that time.

At that time your people shall be saved,

everyone who is found written in the book.

And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake:

some to everlasting life,
and others to disgrace, [Note: [Col. 1318D] In the Hebrew exemplar, instead of *ut videant* there is [Hebrew], that is, “for ignominy,” evidently with the same sense as “to disgrace and to everlasting ignominy,” or “forever.” It is therefore highly probable that the holy Translator read in the copy before him what he saw, with the letter [Hebrew] removed; that letter means “to see,” or “that they may see.” Certainly he did not borrow this reading from the Septuagint, who translate, in accordance with the Hebrew, καὶ εἰς αἰσχύνην (“and to shame”).] that they may see forever.

[Col. 1319A] [Note: [Col. 1319D] To this should be referred the testimony of the holy Translator himself in Epistle 53 to Paulinus, no. 3: “At the end of the most sacred vision, Daniel says that the righteous shine like stars, and the intelligent, that is, the learned, like the firmament . . . Although, according to the Hebrew truth, both statements may be understood of the learned; for thus it reads: ‘But those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many in righteousness, like stars for everlasting ages.’”]

But those who are learned

will shine like the brightness of the firmament;

and those who instruct many in righteousness,

like stars for everlasting ages.

But you, Daniel, close up the words

and seal the book until the appointed time:

Many shall pass through,

and knowledge shall be multiplied.

And I, Daniel, looked,

and behold, two others were standing:

one on this side, on the bank of the river,

and the other on that side, on the opposite bank of the river.

And I said to the man clothed in linen,

who stood above the waters of the river:

How long until the end of these wonders?

And I heard the man clothed in linen,

who stood above the waters of the river,

when he raised his right and left hands toward heaven

and swore by him who lives forever,

[Col. 1319B] that it would be for a time, times, and half a time.

And when the dispersion of the hand of the holy people has been completed,

all these things will be fulfilled.

And I heard, but I did not understand.

And I said: “My lord, what will happen after these things?”

And he said: “Go, Daniel,

for the words are closed up and sealed

until the appointed time.

Many will be chosen, purified,

and tested as though by fire;

the wicked will act wickedly,

and none of the wicked will understand,

but the learned will understand.

And from the time when the continual sacrifice is removed

and the abomination of desolation is set up,

there will be 1,290 days.

Blessed is the one who waits

and reaches 1,335 days.

[Col. 1319C] But you, go on to the appointed end;

you will rest and stand in your allotted place at the end of the days.”

Thus far we have read Daniel in the Hebrew book. The remaining passages that follow, up to the end of the book, have been translated from Theodotion’s edition. [Note: [Col. 1319D] Some infer from these words that the additions that follow, taken from Theodotion’s edition, were not translated into Latin by Jerome, but merely corrected from the Greek in that earlier edition of the Scriptures which he revised against the Greek text. Nor does the following testimony of the holy Father in the preface to his Commentary on this prophet contradict that view: “And so, many years ago, when we were translating Daniel, we marked these visions beforehand with an obelus, indicating that they are not found in the Hebrew.”]

÷ [Vision XI.] And there was a man living in Babylon whose name was Joakim. He took a wife named Susanna, the daughter of Helcias, exceedingly beautiful and God-fearing. For her parents, being righteous, had instructed their daughter according to the law of Moses. Joakim was very wealthy, and he had an orchard adjoining his house; and the Jews gathered there because he was more distinguished than all the others.

Two elders were appointed as judges in that year—those of whom the Lord spoke: “For lawlessness came forth from Babylon, from the elders who appeared to govern the people.” These men regularly visited Joakim’s house, and all who had lawsuits came to them. [Col. 1319D]

[Col. 1320A] When the people had returned at noon, Susanna would enter and walk about in her husband’s orchard. The elders saw her entering and walking about every day, and they became inflamed with desire for her. They perverted their judgment and turned their eyes away, so that they would not look toward heaven or remember the judgments of righteousness. For both were wounded by love for her, yet they did not disclose their distress to each other; they were ashamed to reveal their desire to one another, since they wished to lie with her. Nevertheless, each day they watched more carefully in order to see her.

Then one said to the other: “Let us go home, for it is time for luncheon.” They left and separated from each other. But when they returned, they came together; and, questioning each other about the reason, they confessed their desire. Then together they fixed a time when they might find her alone.

It happened that, while they were watching for a suitable day, she entered as she had the day before and the day before that, with only two maidservants. She wished to bathe in the orchard, for it was hot. [Col. 1320B] There was no one there except the two elders, who were hiding and watching her.

So she said to the maidservants: “Bring me oil and perfumes, and close the doors of the orchard so that I may bathe.” They did as she had ordered: they closed the doors of the orchard and went out by the back entrance to fetch what she had commanded. They did not know that the elders were hiding inside.

When the maidservants had gone out, the two elders rose, hurried to her, and said: “Look, the doors of the orchard are closed, and no one sees us; and we desire you. Therefore consent to us and lie with us. But if you refuse, we will testify against you that a young man was with you, and that for this reason you sent the maidservants away from you.”

Susanna groaned and said: “I am hemmed in on every side. If I do this, death awaits me; but if I do not, I shall not escape your hands. Yet it is better for me to fall into your hands without having done the deed than to sin in the sight of the Lord.”

And Susanna cried out in a loud voice; the elders also cried out against her. One of them ran and [Col. 1320C] opened the doors of the orchard. When the household servants heard the shouting in the orchard, they rushed in through the back entrance to see what had happened.

After the elders had spoken, the servants were deeply ashamed, because nothing of this kind had ever been said about Susanna.

The next day came. When the people had come to her husband Joakim, the two elders also came, full of wicked thoughts against Susanna, in order to put her to death. And they said before the people: “Send for Susanna, the daughter of Helcias, the wife of Joakim.” And immediately they sent for her. She came with her parents, her children, and all her relatives.

Susanna was exceedingly delicate and beautiful in appearance. But those wicked men ordered that she be uncovered—for she was veiled—in order that they might at least in this way satisfy themselves with the sight of her beauty. Her family and all who knew her therefore wept.

Then the two elders rose in the midst of the people and placed their hands upon her head. She, weeping, looked up toward heaven, for her heart trusted in the Lord. [Col. 1320D]

And the elders said: “As we were walking alone in the orchard, this woman entered with two maidservants. She closed the doors of the orchard and sent the maidservants away from her. Then a young man who had been hiding came to her and lay with her.

“Now, while we were in a corner of the orchard, seeing this wickedness, we ran toward them and saw them lying together. We could not seize the young man, because he was stronger than we; and when he opened the doors, he leapt out. But after we had seized this woman, we asked her who the young man was, and she refused to tell us. We are witnesses to this.”

The crowd believed them as judges and elders of the people, and they condemned her to death.

But Susanna cried out in a loud voice and said: “Eternal God, who know the hidden things, who know all things before they happen, you know that they have borne false witness against me. And behold, I am dying, though I have done none of the things that these men have maliciously contrived against me.”

The Lord heard her voice. As she was being led away to execution, the Lord stirred up the holy spirit of a young boy whose name was Daniel, [Col. 1321B] and he cried out in a loud voice: “I am innocent of this woman’s blood.”

The entire people turned toward him and said: “What is this statement that you have made?”

When he stood in their midst, he said: “Are you such fools, sons of Israel? Without judging and without determining what is true, you have condemned a daughter of Israel? Return to judgment, for they have spoken false testimony against her.”

The people therefore returned in haste. And the elders said to him: “Come, sit in our midst and judge us, for God has given you the honor of old age.”

Daniel said to them: “Separate them far from one another, and I will examine them.”

When they had been separated from each other, he called one of them and said to him: “You who have grown old in evil days, now your sins have come upon you, which you formerly committed by rendering unjust judgments, oppressing the innocent, and releasing the guilty, while the Lord says: ‘You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous.’

“Now then, if you saw her, say under what tree you saw them speaking with each other.” [Col. 1321C]

He answered: “Under a mastic tree.”

But Daniel said: “You have lied correctly against your own head. For behold, the angel of God, having received the sentence from him, will cut you in two.”

After removing him, he ordered the other to come and said to him: “Offspring of Canaan, not of Judah, beauty deceived you and desire perverted your heart. This is how you used to treat the daughters of Israel; and they, being afraid, spoke with you. But the daughter of Judah did not endure your wickedness.

“Now tell me: under what tree did you catch them speaking with each other?”

He answered: “Under an evergreen oak.”

But Daniel said to him: “You too have lied correctly against your own head. For the angel of God remains, holding a sword, to cut you in two and put you both to death.”

Then the whole assembly cried out in a loud voice and blessed God, who saves those who hope in him.

And they rose against the elders—for Daniel had convicted them from their own mouths of having given false testimony—and did to them as they had wickedly intended to do to their neighbor, acting according to the law of Moses. They put them to death, and innocent blood was saved on that day.

Helcias [Col. 1321D] and his wife praised God for their daughter Susanna, together with her husband Joakim and all her relatives, because no shameful thing had been found in her.

From that day onward Daniel became great in the sight of the people.

And King Astyages was gathered to his ancestors, and Cyrus the Persian received his kingdom.

[Vision XII.] Daniel was a companion of the king and honored above all his friends. There was also an idol named Bel among the Babylonians. Twelve artabas of fine flour, forty sheep, and six jars of wine were expended for it every day. The king too worshiped it and went every day [Col. 1322A] to adore it. Daniel, however, worshiped his God.

The king said to him: “Why do you not adore Bel?”

He answered him: “Because I do not worship handmade idols, but the living God who created heaven and earth and has authority over all flesh.”

And the king said to him: “Do you not think that Bel is a living god? Do you not see how much he eats and drinks every day?”

Daniel replied with a smile: “Do not be deceived, O king. For this one is clay within and bronze without, and he has never eaten.”

The king became angry, summoned Bel’s priests, and said to them: “Unless you tell me who consumes these expenses, you will die. But if you show that Bel consumes them, Daniel will die, because he has blasphemed against Bel.”

Daniel said to the king: “Let it be according to your word.”

There were seventy priests of Bel, apart from their wives, their little ones, and their children.

The king came with Daniel into the temple of Bel. The priests of Bel said: “Look, we are going outside. You, O king, place the food, mix the wine, and shut the door and seal it with your ring. When you enter in the morning, if you do not find everything consumed by Bel, let us die—or let Daniel die, who has lied against us.”

They were unconcerned because they had made a concealed entrance beneath the table, through which they always entered and devoured the offerings.

After they had gone out, the king placed the food before Bel. Daniel ordered his servants to bring ashes, and he sifted them throughout the entire temple in the presence of the king. Then they went out, shut the door, sealed it with the king’s ring, and departed.

The priests entered at night according to their custom, together with their wives and children, and they ate everything and drank the wine.

The king rose at first light, and Daniel with him. The king said: “Are the seals intact, Daniel?”

He answered: “They are intact, O king.”

Immediately, when he had opened the door, the king looked at the table and cried out in a loud voice: “Great are you, Bel, and there is no deceit in you!”

Daniel laughed and restrained the king from entering. He said: “Look at the floor and notice whose footprints these are.”

The king said: “I see the footprints of men, women, and children.”

The king became angry. Then he seized the priests, their wives, and their children; and they showed him the concealed little doors through which they entered and consumed what was on the table.

So the king put them to death and handed Bel over to Daniel’s power, who destroyed both it and its temple.

There was also a great dragon in that place, and the Babylonians worshiped it.

The king said to Daniel: “Now surely you cannot say that this is not a living god. Therefore worship it.”

Daniel said: “I worship the Lord my God, because he is the living God. [Note: [Col. 1321D] Here and below the printed books contain several additions that are not found in the older manuscripts, especially in the copies representing the Hebrew canon of truth. Whoever wishes may consult our edition alongside those previously published. MART.] But you, O king, give me permission, and I will kill the dragon without sword or club.”

The king said: “I give it to you.”

So Daniel took pitch, fat, and hair, boiled them together, made cakes, and put them into the dragon’s mouth; and the dragon burst open.

And he said: “This is the one you worshiped.”

When the Babylonians heard this, they became extremely angry. They gathered against the king and said: “The king has become a Jew: he has destroyed Bel, killed the dragon, [Col. 1322D] and put the priests to death.”

When they came to the king, they said: “Hand Daniel over to us, or we will kill you and your household.”

The king saw that they were violently attacking him. Compelled by necessity, he handed Daniel over to them.

They threw him into the lions’ den, and he remained there for six days. There were seven lions in the den, and each day they were given two bodies and two sheep; but at that time these were not given to them, so that they might devour Daniel.

Now the prophet Habakkuk was in Judea. He had cooked a stew and crumbled bread into a bowl, and he was going into the field to bring it to the reapers.

The angel of the Lord said to Habakkuk: “Carry the meal that you have to Babylon, to Daniel, who is in the lions’ den.” [Col. 1323A]

Habakkuk said: “Lord, I have not seen Babylon, and I do not know where the den is.”

The angel of the Lord seized him by the crown of his head, carried him by the hair of his head, and by the force of his spirit placed him in Babylon above the den.

Habakkuk cried out, saying: “Daniel, [Note: [Col. 1323A] The same printed books add “servant of God,” which the manuscripts do not contain. The Greek has Daniel’s name twice in its place: Δανιήλ, Δανιήλ, λάβε (“Daniel, Daniel, take …”).] take the meal that God has sent you.”

Daniel said: “For you have remembered me, God, and have not abandoned those who love you.”

Daniel rose and ate.

Then the angel of the Lord immediately restored Habakkuk to his own place. [Col. 1324A]

The king came on the seventh day to mourn for Daniel. He came to the den, looked inside, and behold, Daniel was sitting there.

And [Note: [Col. 1323A] The Vulgate books add here “in the midst of the lions,” which is found neither in the Greek nor in the manuscripts.] the king cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Great are you, Lord, God of Daniel!”

And he drew him out. [Note: [Col. 1323A] One Vatican manuscript adds “from the den”; the Vulgate books add “of the lions.” Immediately afterward, with equal agreement, they add after the word “he threw” the words “into the den.” The Greek and the better manuscripts contain nothing of this kind. [Col. 1324A]]

Then he threw in those who had been responsible for his destruction, and they were devoured in an instant before him. [Note: [Col. 1324A] The Vulgate books crown the book with the following conclusion: “Then the king said: Let all who dwell throughout the whole earth fear the God of Daniel, for he is the Savior who performs signs and wonders on earth, who delivered Daniel from the lions’ den.” Some of Martianay’s manuscripts, as well as our manuscripts and the Greek text itself, know nothing of this conclusion.]

The Book of the Prophet Daniel ends.

[Col. 1323]

[BOOK OF PARALIPOMENON]

JEROME’S PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF PARALIPOMENON. [Hebrew Text]

[Col. 1323B] If the pure edition of the Seventy Translators, exactly as it was translated by them into Greek, had remained, you would not have urged me unnecessarily, [Note: [Col. 1323B] A manuscript codex of the sacred Bible belonging to the most eminent Cardinal Bondi reads thus: “You would have urged me superfluously, my Chromatius,” etc. So also does a manuscript of the monastery of Blessed Mary of the Golden Church at Toulouse. Another, of the Church of Narbonne, reads: “You would have urged me unnecessarily, Chromatius,” etc. The remaining manuscript copies, thirty or more, omit the pronoun “me.” MART. — Some manuscripts here omit the word *mi* (“my”); others shortly afterward add *tibi* (“you”), as it is also read in the cited *Apology*: “that I might [translate] the Hebrew [books] for you,” etc.]

most holy and learned Chromatius, bishop, to transfer the Hebrew volumes into the Latin language. For what had once occupied human ears and strengthened the faith of the nascent Church deserved also to be confirmed by our silence. [Col. 1324B]

But now, since different copies are circulated according to the diversity of regions, and that genuine and ancient translation has been corrupted and violated, you think it belongs to my judgment either to determine from the many what is true, or to forge a new work within the old work, and, as the saying goes, to pierce the eyes of crows, while mocking Jews. [Note: [Col. 1323B] Budaeus and Erasmus offer various interpretations of this proverb; but nothing seems better suited to make Jerome’s meaning clear than what he himself writes in the preface to the book of Joshua: namely, that the Jews grieved because the opportunity to slander and ridicule Christians had been removed from them when the Latin translation was annotated from the Hebrew copies. The adversaries were especially tormented by this, since previously they boasted that they alone possessed knowledge of the divine Scriptures and prophetic oracles.

We have as witness to this Sophronius, otherwise a very learned man but unversed in Hebrew. Once, while disputing with a Hebrew, he brought forward from the Psalms certain testimonies concerning the Lord the Savior. His opponent ridiculed him, asserting almost word by word that the Hebrew text did not read as Sophronius claimed on the basis of the Seventy Translators. Hence he earnestly requested Jerome, after Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, to transfer a new edition into Latin.

Thus an outstanding teacher was found who, as the saying goes, “pierced the eyes of crows,” because by his Hebrew translation he pierced the eyes of the Jews, who wished to appear wiser and to be guides of the blind. See the preface to the book of Psalms. MART.

—Erasmus and Victorius correctly noted long ago that this proverb was used by Latins in order to mock those who think or boast that they can mock everyone. Either this is because the crow is an exceptionally sharp-sighted animal, or because it eagerly and above all seeks the eyes of corpses to which it is said to be drawn, as Bochart observes in *Hierozoicon*, part II, book II, chapter 10. To “pierce the eyes of crows” therefore means proverbially to outwit clever and cunning people by cleverness and cunning, and to deceive the deceivers by their own very craft. The proverb occurs in this sense among the ancients, especially Cicero, from whom Jerome took it: *Pro L. Murena*, chapter 11, and the subsequent *Pro L. Flacco*, chapter 20. Erasmus, Victorius, Clericus, and others successively cite these passages, adding the passage from Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book VII, chapter 5: “Let a Greek steal this applause from a Greek, as a crow plucks out a crow’s eyes.” Yet Martianay does not seem to have grasped Jerome’s allusion or the meaning of this passage.]

Alexandria and Egypt praise Hesychius in their copies of the Seventy; [Note: [Col. 1324C] Those misunderstand this passage who suppose that the Greek editions of the Seventy Translators were used in all the Churches in such a way that, in the assemblies of Alexandria and Egypt, the sacred codices were publicly read to the Christian people according to Hesychius’s recension, while in the Churches of Constantinople as far as Antioch they were read according to the revision of the martyr Lucian. Jerome teaches the contrary in many places. First, in his preface to the four Gospels addressed to Damasus, he expressly testifies that these editions were accepted by few: “I pass over those codices which the perverse contention of a few persons maintains are called after Lucian and Hesychius; for assuredly they were permitted neither to correct anything in the whole Old Instrument after the Seventy Translators, nor did it profit them to have corrected the New,” etc. You see, reader, that within the provinces already mentioned the copies of the Scriptures associated with Hesychius and Lucian were received by a few persons, who were themselves engaged in perverse contention.

The same must not be thought of the codices prepared by Origen, who in the edition of the Seventy mingled Theodotion’s edition, marking with asterisks what had previously been lacking and with obeli what seemed to have been added superfluously. For that edition was so celebrated among all that it was publicly used in all the Churches of Christians. Hence Jerome warned in the prologue to his Commentary on Daniel: “Origen also placed asterisks from Theodotion’s work in the Vulgate edition, showing that the things added had been lacking; and again he marked certain verses with obeli, indicating every superfluity. And since all the Churches of Christ—the Greek, Latin, Syrian, and Egyptian alike—read this edition with its asterisks and obeli, let the envious pardon my labor,” etc. Who would say that this is to be understood of Daniel’s volume alone? For while discussing the matter elsewhere with Augustine, he plainly declares the Church’s practice; and no one can deny that, in the following words, he encompasses all copies of the divine Scriptures: “Do you wish to be a true admirer of the Seventy Translators? Do not read what stands under the asterisks; rather, erase it from the volumes, so that you may prove yourself a partisan of the ancients. If you do this, you will be forced to condemn all the libraries of the Churches; for scarcely one or two books are found which do not contain these things.” See Epistle 89, in Augustine 75. MART. — Yet Martianay denies the very thing that the holy Father states so explicitly, or at least forbids its being understood in the sense that the Hesychian edition is said to have prevailed in the assemblies of Alexandria and Egypt, and the Lucianic edition in those of Constantinople as far as Antioch. He relies on this other testimony of Jerome in the prologue to the Gospels addressed to Damasus: “I pass over those codices which the perverse contention of a few persons maintains are called after Lucian and Hesychius.” And indeed, unless one has a very clear grasp of the holy Doctor’s meaning and the context of the passage, not only might one, as Martianay does, infer from this against the currency of those editions, but the holy Father would be at odds with himself: here he teaches quite clearly enough that Alexandria and Egypt commend Hesychius as their author, and that the remaining provinces from Constantinople to Antioch approve the copies of the martyr Lucian; whereas previously he had written to Damasus that support for Lucian and Hesychius was confined to a few persons and was perverse contention.

But from the whole context and purpose of that other passage it is clear that he is speaking there of Lucianic or Hesychian codices of the New Testament, in whose revision the industry of those authors was less approved; whereas here he speaks of the Old Testament, whose editions the Churches of such great regions accepted. This is so evident that even now passages of Scripture commended by the Alexandrian Fathers may be identified as belonging to Hesychius’s interpretation, just as those which the people of Constantinople commend are immediately recognized as Lucianic. From Chrysostom alone—who first held the see of Antioch and then that of Constantinople, and lived in Jerome’s time—if you make the trial, innumerable testimonies will occur drawn from Lucian’s recension which differ from the codices of the Alexandrian Church; and, conversely, those codices revised by Hesychius differ from the Palestinian copies prepared by Origen. It is not our purpose to explain the matter by examples, of which a great many are available. See what we note elsewhere and in the commentary on the cited prologue to the Gospels.]

Constantinople as far as Antioch approves the copies of Lucian [or Julian], the martyr. The provinces between these read the Palestinian copies, which Eusebius and Pamphilus published after Origen had prepared them. And the whole world contends with itself amid this threefold diversity.

And certainly Origen not only compiled copies of four editions, writing the individual words in parallel columns so that, whenever one differed, it might immediately be exposed by the agreement of the others; but—and this was the bolder undertaking—he mixed Theodotion’s edition into the edition of the Seventy, marking with asterisks what had previously been lacking, and with obeli what seemed to have been added unnecessarily.

[Note: [Col. 1326C] One Vatican manuscript and another of ours read *Hexapla*, but incongruously, since the subject here is four editions—that is, Origen’s *Tetrapla*—not his *Hexapla*. MART.]

If, then, others were permitted not to retain what they had once accepted, and, after opening the seventy chambers—[Col. 1325B] [Note: [Col. 1326D] These individual chambers of the Seventy Translators are popularly asserted without authority. For neither Aristaeus, the *hyparchos* (“champion”) of King Ptolemy, nor Josephus, much later, reports anything of the sort; rather, they write that the translators gathered in the same basilica and compared their work, not that they prophesied. Jerome says this in the preface to Genesis. MART.]—which are popularly proclaimed without an authority, to open the individual chambers, and if what the Seventy did not know is read in the Churches, why should my Latins not accept me, since I have composed a new edition in such a way, without violating the old edition, that I can prove my work by the Hebrews and, what is more, by the authority of the Apostles?

I recently wrote a book on the best kind of translation, showing that the following passages are found in the Hebrew books: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15); “He shall be called a Nazarene” (ibid., 23); “They shall look on him whom they pierced” (John 19:37); and the Apostle’s statement, “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9), along with other passages like these. [Col. 1326A]

Certainly the Apostles and Evangelists knew the Seventy Translators. How, then, could they say these things, which are not found in the Seventy?

Christ our Lord, the author of both Testaments, says in the Gospel according to John: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). Surely what the Savior testifies to have been written is written. Where is it written? The Seventy do not have it; the Church knows no apocrypha. We must therefore return to the Hebrews, from whom the Lord speaks and from whom the disciples take their examples.

I say these things with due regard for the ancients, and I answer only my detractors, who gnaw at me with a dog’s tooth, attacking me publicly, while reading in corners—both accusers and defenders at once—when in others they approve what they condemn in me, as though virtue and vice lay not in the things themselves but changed with their author. [Col. 1326B]

I remember, moreover, that I once attributed to our people an edition of the Seventy Translators corrected from the Greek. [Note: [Col. 1326D] We have said that only a small part of that edition survives; we shall review it in a subsequent volume and discuss it more fully in the preface.] I should not therefore be considered an enemy of those whom I always expound in the assembly of the brethren.

And what I have now translated, *DABRE JAMIM* ([Hebrew]), that is, “Words of Days,” I did so in order to make clearer the interminable delays, the forest of names confused through the fault of copyists, and the barbarism of the meanings, arranging them more openly according to the cola of the verses. I am singing to myself and to my own Ismenias [Note: [Col. 1327A] We read *Hismenius*, not *Ismenias*, in all the manuscript copies except the Canon of Hebrew Truth, in which we find *Hismaenias*. Moreover, *Ismenias* is the name of an excellent Theban flute-player in Apuleius and in Plutarch’s *Life of Pericles*. When he was playing to an audience coldly, his teacher Antigenidas, as Cicero reports in *On the Famous Orators*, said to him: “Play for me and the Muses.” Valerius Maximus also mentions him in book III, chapter 7 of his *Memorable Deeds and Sayings*. Hence “to sing for oneself and the Muses” means to write or say what only the learned, or the singer himself, understand, not the ignorant and ungrateful crowd. This fits Jerome’s thought and meaning exactly, since only the learned, or the author himself, could understand the great benefit that this edition from the Hebrew would bring to the Churches. MART.], if the ears of others are deaf.

THE BOOK OF DABRE JAMIM BEGINS—that is, THE WORDS OF DAYS, which among us is called PARALIPOMENON.

[Col. 1327]

[Col. 1327B] [Chapter I.] Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Malaleel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Mosoch, and Tiras.

The sons of Gomer: Ascenez, Riphath, [Note: [Col. 1327D] In Hebrew it is written with the first letter [Hebrew], *Diphath*. See, however, what is noted concerning the spelling of this name at Genesis 10:3.] and Togarmah.

The sons of Javan: Elisa and Tarshish,

Kittim and Dodanim.

The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.

The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca.

The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.

Cush begot Nimrod; he began to be mighty on the earth.

Mizraim begot the Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, and Casluhim—from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim.

[Col. 1327C] Canaan begot Sidon, his firstborn, and Heth; also the Jebusite, the Amorite, and the Girgashite,

the Hivite, the Arkite, and the Sinite,

the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite.

The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech.

Arphaxad begot Shelah, who himself begot Eber.

Two sons were born to Eber: the name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided; the name of his brother was Joktan.

Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan.

Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah, Abram—he is Abraham.

The sons of Abraham were Isaac and Ishmael.

These are their generations. The firstborn of Ishmael was Nebaioth, then Kedar, Abdeel, Mibsam, [Col. 1327D] Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael.

The sons of Abraham’s concubine Keturah, whom she bore, were Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.

The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan. [Note: [Col. 1327D] The words that the Vulgate books add—“The sons of Dedan: Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim”—appear to have been formerly brought here from Genesis 25:3 and were long ago removed by Martianay in accordance with the Hebrew text and the older, better-quality copies. [Col. 1328D]]

The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Enoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah.

Abraham begot Isaac, whose sons were Esau and Israel.

The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.

The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, Timna, and Amalek.

The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.

The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan.

The sons of Lotan: Hori and Homam. Lotan’s sister was Timna.

The sons of Shobal: Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi, and Onam.

The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah.

The sons of Anah: Dishon.

The sons of Dishon: Amram, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.

The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Jaakan.

The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.

These are the kings who ruled in the land of Edom before there was a king over the Israelites: Bela son of Beor; the name of his city was Dinhabah.

Bela died, and Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah reigned in his place.

When Jobab had died, Husham from the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.

And Husam also died, and Adad son of Badad reigned in his place; he struck down Midian in the land of Moab, and the name of his city was Avith.

When Adad too had died, Semla of Maresca reigned in his place.

Semla also died, and Saul of Rohoboth, which is situated beside the river, reigned in his place. [Col. 1328D]

[Col. 1329A] When Saul had died, Bahalanan son of Achobor reigned in his place.

This man too died, and Adad reigned in his place. The name of his city was [Note: [Col. 1329D] The false Jerome, author of the *Hebrew Questions on the First Book of Chronicles*, notes that this name is written *Phau* in Genesis, but *Phai* in Chronicles. This is confirmed by the Masoretic copies: for in Genesis 36:29 we read *Phau*, whereas here we find *Phai*. But the true Jerome read *Phau*, or *Phou*, in both places in his Hebrew copies, with *vav* at the end, and with *ayin* as the vowel *o* or *d*. Whoever wishes to know more about variant readings in proper names should consult the aforementioned *Questions* of the false Jerome, who was diligent in observing such matters. MART.] Phou; and his wife was called Meetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezaab.

After Adad had died, chiefs began to rule in Edom in place of kings: the chief of Thamna, the chief of Alva, the chief of Jetheth, the chief of Oolibama, the chief of Ela, the chief of Phinon, the chief of Cenez, the chief of Theman, the chief of Mabsar, the chief of Magdiel, and the chief of Hiram. These were the chiefs of Edom.

[Cap. II.] The sons of Israel were Ruben, Simeon, Levi, Juda, Issachar, and Zabulon; Dan, Joseph, and Benjamin; Nephtali, Gad, and Aser.

The sons of Juda were Her, Onan, and Sela. Three were born to him by the daughter of Sue, the Canaanite woman.

Her, Juda’s firstborn, was evil in the sight of the Lord, and He killed him.

Thamar, his daughter-in-law, bore him Phares and Zara.

[Col. 1329B] Thus all the sons of Juda were five.

The sons of Fares were Esron and Amul.

The sons of Zara were Zamri, Ethan, Eman, and also Chalchal and Dara—five in all.

The sons of Charmi were Achar, who troubled Israel and sinned by stealing what had been placed under the ban.

The son of Ethan was Azarias.

The sons of Esron born to him were Jerameel, Ram, and Calubi.

Ram fathered Aminadab.

Aminadab fathered Naasson, prince of the sons of Juda.

Naasson also fathered Salma, from whom Booz arose.

Booz fathered Obed, who himself fathered Isai.

Isai fathered his firstborn Eliab, his second Abinadab, his third Samaa, his fourth Nathanael, his fifth Raddei, his sixth Asom, and his seventh David.

Their sisters were Sarvia and Abigail.

The sons of Sarvia were Abisai, Joab, and Asael—three.

[Col. 1329C] Abigail bore Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite.

Caleb son of Esron took a wife named Azuba, by whom he fathered Jerioth; her sons were Jesar, Sobab, and Ardon.

When Azuba had died, Caleb took Ephrath as his wife, [Note: [Col. 1330D] The Carcassonne Canon has *Ephrata*. The other manuscript codices read *Ephrath*, in accordance with the present Hebrew text: for it is written here *Ephrath*, although below, in verse 24, *Ephratha* is read, with the final letter; Latin manuscripts also retain *Ephratha* there. The false Jerome did not notice this in his *Hebrew Questions on the Books of Chronicles*. MART.] and she bore him Hur.

Hur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Bezeleel.

After this, Esron went in to the daughter of Machir, father of Galaad, and took her when he was sixty years old; she bore him Segub.

Segub also fathered Jair, who possessed twenty-three cities in the land of Galaad. He captured Gessur and Aram, the towns of Jair, and Canath with its villages—sixty towns. All these were sons of Machir, father of Galaad.

When Esron had died, Caleb went in to Ephrata.

Esron also had a wife named Abia, who bore him Assur, father of Thecue.

[Col. 1329D] The sons born to Jerameel, Esron’s firstborn, were Ram, his firstborn, and Buna, Aram, Asom, and Ahia.

Jerameel also took another wife, named Atara, who was the mother of Onam.

The sons of Ram, Jerameel’s firstborn, were Moos, Jamin, and Achar.

Onam had sons, Semei and Jada.

[Col. 1330A] The sons of Semei were Nadab and Abisur. The name of Abisur’s wife was Abiail, who bore him Ahobban and Molid.

The sons of Nadab were Saled and Apphaim. Saled died without children.

The son of Apphaim was Jesi; Jesi fathered Sesan, and Sesan fathered Oholi.

The sons of Jada, the brother of Semei, were Jether and Jonathan. Jether also died without children.

Jonathan fathered Phaleth and Ziza. These were the sons of Jerameel.

Sesan had no sons, but daughters, and an Egyptian servant named Jeraa.

He gave him his daughter as a wife, and she bore him Etthei.

Etthei fathered Nathan, and Nathan fathered Zabad.

Zabad also fathered Ophlal, and Ophlal fathered Obed.

Obed fathered Jeu; Jeu fathered Azariam.

Azarias fathered Helles; Helles fathered Elasa.

[Col. 1330B] Elasa fathered Sisamoi; Sisamoi fathered Sellum.

Sellum fathered Icamiam, and Icamia fathered Elisama.

The sons of Chaleb, the brother of Jerameel, were Mosa, his firstborn; he was the father of Ziph, and the sons of Maresa, the father of Hebron.

The sons of Hebron were Core, Thaphphu, Recem, and Samma.

Samma fathered Raham, father of Jercaam, and Recem fathered Sammai.

The son of Sammai was Maon, and Maon was the father of Bethsur.

Chaleb’s concubine Epha bore Aran, Musa, and Gezez.

Aran fathered Gezez.

The sons of Jadai were Regom, Joathan, Gesan, Phalet, Epha, and Saaph.

Chaleb’s concubine Maacha bore Saber and Tharana.

Saaph, father of Madmena, fathered Sue, father of Machbena and father of Gabaa.

Chaleb’s daughter was Achsa. These were the sons of Chaleb, son of Hur, firstborn of Ephrata: Sobal, father of Cariath-Jarim; Salma, father of Beth-Leem; and Hariph, father of Beth-Gader.

The sons of Sobal, father of Cariath-Jarim, were he who saw half of the resting-places.

From the clan of Cariath-Jarim came Jethrei, Aphuthei, Semathei, and Maserei. From these came the Saraitae and the Esthaolitae.

The sons of Salma were Beth-Leem, the Netophathites, the Crown of the House of Joab, and half of the resting-place of Sarai.

There were also the clans of scribes dwelling in Jabes: the Singers and the Resounders, and those dwelling in tents. These were the Cinaei, who came from Calore, father of the house of Rechab.

[Cap. III.] David had these sons, born to him in Hebron: Amnon, the firstborn, by Ahinaam the Jezraelite; Daniel, the second, by Abigail the Carmelite; Absalon, the third, son of Maacha, daughter of Tholmai, king of Gessur; Adonias, the fourth, son of Aggith; Saphatias, the fifth, by Abital; and Jethraam, the sixth, by his wife Egla.

Six were therefore born to him in Hebron, where he reigned seven years and six months.

He reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.

[Col. 1331A] In Jerusalem sons were born to him: Samaa, Sobab, Nathan, and Salomon—four, by Bethsabee, daughter of Amiel;

Jebaar, Elisama, Eliphaleth, Noge, Nepheg, and Japhie, and also Elisama, Eliade, and Eliphaleth—nine.

All David’s sons, apart from the sons of his concubines, had a sister named Thamar.

Salomon’s son was Roboam; his son Abia fathered Asa.

From him also was born Josaphat, father of Joram.

Joram fathered Ohoziam, from whom Joas arose; and his son Amasias fathered Azariam.

Azaria’s son Joatham fathered Ahaz, father of Ezechias, from whom Manasses was born.

Manasses also fathered Amon, father of Josias.
