The sons of Josias were Johanan, the firstborn; Joiacim, the second; Sedecias, the third; and Sellum, the fourth.

From Joiacim were born Jechonias and Sedecias.

The sons of Jechonias were Asir, Salathiel, Melchiram, Phadaia, Sennaser, Jecemia, Sama, and Nadabia.

From Phadaia arose Zorobabel and Semei.

Zorobabel fathered Mosollam, Ananiam, and their sister Salomith.

Also Asaban, Ool, Barachian, Asadiam, and Josabesed—five.

The son of Anania was Phaltias, father of Jeseia; his son was Raphaia. His son was Arnan, from whom Obdia was born; his son was Sechenia.

The son of Sechenia was Semeia. His sons were Attus, Jegal, Baria, Naaria, and Saphat—six in number.

[Note: [Col. 1331D] Three manuscript codices—the Royal, Corbie 1, and the corrected Colbertinus Aniciensis—read: “And Saphat; Sessa,” making six. Saint-Germain manuscript no. 4 placed *Sessa* in the margin. In Hebrew it is written *Vesaphat sissa*, that is, “and Saphat, six.” Hence the manuscripts mentioned above retained *sissa* or *sessa*, meaning “six,” together with its interpretation; it is reasonable to believe that this came from some scholiast. MART. — Three manuscripts in Martianus, as well as several printed books, such as the Bible of Robert Estienne, the Sixtine edition, the Antwerp Polyglot, and others, insert here the name *Sessa* or *Sesa*, the Hebrew word meaning “six,” apparently repeated as a proper name to complete the number. This is unnecessary, however, since Semeia himself is clearly counted as one of that number.]

The son of Naaria was Elioenai, Ezechias, and Ezricam—three.

The sons of Elioenai were Odvia, Eliasub, Pheleia, Accub, Johanan, Dalaia, and Anani—seven.

[Cap. IV.] The sons of Juda were Phares, Esron, Charmi, Hur, and Subal.

Reaia son of Subal fathered Jeth, from whom Ahimai and Led were born. These were the clans of the Sarathi.

[Col. 1331C] This also was the lineage of Etam: Jezrael, Jesema, and Jedebos. Their sister’s name was Asalelphuni.

Phanuel [Note: [Col. 1332D] In the present Hebrew text, *Phanuel* is found; nevertheless, Latin manuscripts read *Phuniel*. MART.] was the father of Gedor, and Ezer was the father of Hosa. These were the sons of Hur, firstborn of Ephratha, father of Beth-Leem.

Assur, father of Thecue, had two wives, Hala and Naara.

Naara bore him Oozam, Hepher, Themani, and Ahasthari. These were the sons of Naara.

The sons of Halaa were Sereth, Isaar, and Ethnan.

Cos fathered Anob, Soboba, and the clan of Haral son of Arum.

Jabes was more renowned than his brothers. His mother called his name Jabes, saying, “Because I bore him in pain.”

Jabes called upon the God of Israel, saying: “If you will surely bless me, enlarge my boundaries, let your hand be with me, and keep me from being oppressed by evil.” And God granted what he had asked.

Chaleb, brother of Sua, fathered Mahir, who was the father of Esthon.

Esthon fathered Bethrapha, Phesse, and Thena, father of the city of Naas. These were the men of Recha.

[Col. 1332A] The sons of Cenez were Othoniel and Saraia. The sons of Othoniel were Athath and Maonathi.

Maonathi fathered Ophra, and Saraia fathered Joab, father of the Valley of Craftsmen, for craftsmen were there.

The sons of Chaleb son of Jephone were Hir, Ela, and Nahem.

The son of Ela was Cenez.

The sons of Jaleleel were Ziph, Zipha, Thiria, and Asrael.

The sons of Ezra were Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. He fathered Mariam, Sammai, and Jesba, father of Esthamo.

His wife, Judaia, bore Jared, father of Gedor; Heber, father of Socho; and Icuthiel, father of Zano. These were the sons of Bethia, daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took.

The sons of Odaia’s wife, the sister of Naham, father of Ceila, were Garmi and Esthamo, who was from Machathi.

The sons of Simon were Amnon, Renna son of An[n?], and Thilon. The sons of Jesi were Zoeth and Benzoeth.

[Col. 1332B] The sons of Sela, son of Juda, were Her, father of Lecha; Laada, father of Maresa; and the clans of the workers in fine linen in the house of the oath.

Also he who made the sun stand still, and the men of Lies, and Securus, and Incendens, who were chiefs in Moab, and those who returned to Leem. These are ancient words.

These were the potters dwelling in the Plantations and in the Sheepfolds, dwelling there with the king for his work.

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Nearly all editions have *sepes* (“hedges”) instead of *praesepes* (“sheepfolds”). The Hebrew term is one which the Septuagint interpreters themselves took as the proper name Γαδηρὰ (*Gadera*).]

The sons of Simeon were Namuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zara, and Saul.

His son was Sellum; his son was Mapsam; his son was Masma.

The sons of Masma were Amuel his son, Zachur his son, and Semei his son.

The sons of Semei were sixteen, and his daughters six. His brothers did not have many sons, and the whole clan could not equal the number of the sons of Juda.

[Col. 1332C] They dwelt in Bersabee, Molada, Hasarsual, Bala, Asom, Tholad, Bathuel, Horma, Siceleg, Bethmarchaboth, Asarsusim, Bethberai, and Saarim. These were their cities until the reign of King David.

Their villages were Etam, Aen, Remmon, Thochen, and Asan—five cities.

All their villages were around these cities as far as Baal. This was their dwelling-place and the distribution of their settlements.

Also Mosobab, Jemlech, Josa son of Amasia, Joel, and Jeu son of Josabia, son of Saraia, son of Asiel; and Elipenai, Jacoba, Isuaia, Asaia, Adiel, Ismiel, and Banaia;

also Zaza son of Sephei, son of Allon, son of Idaia, son of Semri, son of Samaia.

These were the named chiefs in their clans, and they multiplied greatly in the house of their relatives.

[Col. 1332D] They set out to enter Gador, toward the east of the valley, and to seek pasture for their flocks. They found rich and very good pasture, and a broad, peaceful, and fertile land, in which those descended from Cham had previously dwelt.

These men, whose names we have listed above, [Col. 1333A] came in the days of Ezechias, king of Juda. They struck down their tents and the inhabitants found there, and destroyed them to the present day. They dwelt in their place, because they found exceedingly rich pastures there.

Five hundred men from the sons of Simeon went to Mount Seir, with Phaltias, Naaria, Raphaia, and Oziel, sons of Jesi, as their chiefs. They struck down the remnant of the Amalecites who had escaped, and dwelt there in their place to the present day.

[Cap. V.] The sons of Ruben, Israel’s firstborn—for he was indeed his firstborn; but when he violated his father’s bed, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel, and he was not reckoned as firstborn.

Juda, however, who was strongest among his brothers, produced chiefs from his line; nevertheless, the birthright was reckoned to Joseph.

The sons of Ruben, Israel’s firstborn, were Enoch, [Col. 1333B] Phallu, Esron, and Charmi.

The sons of Joel were Samaia his son, Geg his son, Semei his son, Micha his son, Reela his son, Baal his son, and Beera his son, whom Theglatphalnasar, king of the Assyrians, took captive; and he was a prince in the tribe of Ruben.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Some manuscripts have *Sheglath-Phalassar*; others, *Theglath-Phalnasar*. It is not surprising that it is written differently in Latin codices, since the same variation is found in Hebrew volumes. For in the Second Book of Kings, which we now call the Fourth Book of Kings, chapter 15, verse 29, and chapter 16, verses 7 and 10, we read *Theglath-Phalasar*; here, however, and below in 2 Chronicles 28:20, *Seglath-Phalnasar*. MART.]

His brothers and his entire clan, when counted by their families, had as chiefs Jeiel and Zacharia.

Bala son of Azaz, son of Samma, son of Joel, dwelt in Aroer as far as Nebo and Beelmon.

Toward the eastern side he dwelt as far as the entrance of the wilderness and the river Euphrates. For he possessed a very large number of livestock in the land of Galaad.

In the days of Saul they fought against the Agareans [or Agarenes], killed them, and dwelt in their tents throughout the whole region facing eastward from Galaad.

[Col. 1333C] The sons of Gad dwelt opposite them in the land of Basan as far as Selcha.

Joel was chief, and Saphan second; then Janai and Saphat in Basan.

Their brothers, according to the houses of their clans, were Michael, Mosollam, Sebe, Jori, Jachan, Zie, and Heber—seven.

These were the sons of Abihail, son of Huri, son of Jaro, son of Galaad, son of Michael, son of Jesisi, son of Jeddo, son of Buz.

The brothers of the sons of Abdiel, son of Guni, were also chiefs of their ancestral houses.

They dwelt in Galaad, Basan, its villages, and all the surrounding lands of Saron as far as the boundaries.

All these were counted in the days of Joathan, king of Juda, and in the days of Jeroboam, king of Israel.

The sons of Ruben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasse were fighting men, bearing shields and swords, drawing the bow, and trained for battle: forty-four thousand seven hundred and sixty advancing to war.

They fought against the Agareans. [Note: [Col. 1334D] The manuscripts have *Agarenes*, in accordance with the usage found elsewhere. MART.]

The Ituraeans, the Naphaeans, and Nodab gave them assistance.

The Agareans and all who were with them were delivered into their hands, because they called upon God while fighting; and He heard them because they had trusted in Him.

They took all that these peoples possessed: fifty thousand camels, two hundred fifty thousand sheep, two thousand asses, and one hundred thousand human beings.

[Col. 1334A] Many wounded fell, for it was a war of God.

They dwelt in their place until the time of the captivity.

The sons of half the tribe of Manasse possessed the land from the boundaries of Basan to Baal, Hermon, Sanir, and Mount Hermon, for they were very numerous.

These were the chiefs of the houses of their clans: Epher, Jesi, Eliel, Ezriel, Jeremia, Odoia, and Jediel—men of great valor and power, renowned chiefs in their families.

But they abandoned the God of their fathers and prostituted themselves after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them.

So God stirred up the spirit of Phul, king of the Assyrians, and the spirit of Thelgathphalnasar, king of Assur. He carried away Ruben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasse, bringing them to Lale, Abor, Ara, and the river Gozan, to the present day.

[Col. 1334B] [Cap. VI.] The sons of Levi were Gerson, Caath, and Merari. The sons of Caath were Amram, Isaar, Hebron, and Oziel.

The sons of Amram were Aaron, Moses, and Maria.

The sons of Aaron were Nadab, Abiu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

Eleazar fathered Phinees, and Phinees fathered Abisue.

Abisue fathered Bocci, and Bocci fathered Ozi.

Ozi fathered Zaraiam, and Zaragias fathered Meraioth.

Meraioth fathered Amariam, and Amarias fathered Ahitob.

Ahitob fathered Sadoc, and Sadoc fathered Ahimaas.

Ahimaas fathered Azariam. Azarias fathered Johanan.

Johanan fathered Azariam; he was the one who served as priest in the house that Salomon built in Jerusalem.

Azarias fathered Amariam, and Amarias fathered Ahitob.

Ahitob fathered Sadoc, and Sadoc fathered Sellum.

Sellum fathered Helcias, and Helcias fathered Azarias.

Azarias fathered Saraias, and Saraias fathered Josedec.

[Col. 1334C] Josedec went away when the Lord carried Juda and Jerusalem away by the hand of Nabuchodonosor.

Thus the sons of Levi were Gerson, Caath, and Merari.

These are the names of the sons of Gerson: Lobeni and Semei.

The sons of Caath were Amram, Isaar, Hebron, and Oziel.

The sons of Merari were Mooli and Musi. These were the clans of Levi according to their families.

Gerson: Lobeni his son, Jaath his son, Zamma his son, Joaa his son, Addo his son, Zara his son, and Jethrai his son.

The sons of Caath: Aminadab his son, Core his son, Asir his son, Elcana his son, Abiasaph his son, Asir his son, Thaat his son, Uriel his son, Ozias his son, and Saul his son.

The sons of Elcana were Amasai, Ahimoth, and Elcana.

The sons of Elcana: Sophai his son, Naath his son, Eliab his son, Jeroam his son, and Elcana his son.

[Col. 1334D] The sons of Samuel were Vasseni, the firstborn, and Abia.

The sons of Merari: Mooli, Lobeni his son, Semei his son, Oza his son, Samma his son, Haggia his son, and Asaia his son.

These were the men whom David appointed over the singers in the house of the Lord, from the time the ark was placed there. They ministered before the tabernacle of the testimony with singing until Salomon built the house of the Lord in Jerusalem.

They stood according to their order in the service.

These are those who served with their sons: from the sons of Caath, Eman the singer, son of Joel, son of Samuel;

[Col. 1335A] son of Elcana, son of Jeroam, son of Eliel, son of Thou;

son of Suph, son of Elcana, son of Maath, son of Amasai;

son of Elcana, son of Joel, son of Azariae, son of Sophoniae;

son of Thaath, son of Asir, son of Abiasaph, son of Core;

son of Iser, son of Caet, son of Levi, son of Israel.

His brother was Asaph, who stood at his right hand: Asaph son of Barachia, son of Samaa;

son of Michael, son of Basia, son of Melchia;

son of Athanai, son of Zara, son of Adaia;

son of Ethan, son of Zamma, son of Semei;

son of Jeth, son of Gersom, son of Levi.

The sons of Merari, their brothers, stood on the left: Ethan son of Cusi, son of Abdi, son of Maloch;

son of Asabia, son of Amasia, son of Helcia;

son of Amasai, son of Boni, son of Somer;

son of Mooli, son of Musi, son of Merari, son of Levi.

Their brothers, the Levites, were appointed for all the service of the tabernacle of the house of the Lord.

Aaron and his sons burned incense upon the altar of burnt offering and upon the altar of incense, for every work of the Holy of Holies, and to pray for Israel, according to all that Moses, the servant of God, had commanded.

These were the sons of Aaron: Eleazar his son, Phinees his son, Abisue his son, Boec his son, Ozi his son, Zaraia his son, Merajoth his son, Amaria his son, Ahitob his son, Sadoc his son, and Ahimaas his son.

These were their dwelling-places, with their villages and surrounding territories—that is, the dwelling-places of the sons of Aaron according to the clans of the Caathites, for the lot had fallen to them.

They gave them Hebron in the land of Juda and its surrounding pasturelands.

But the fields of the city and its villages they gave to Chaleb son of Jephone.

To the sons of Aaron they gave cities of refuge: Hebron, Lobna, and its pasturelands; Jether and Esthomo with its pasturelands; Helon and Dabir with their pasturelands; Asan, Beth-Semes, and their pasturelands.

[Note: [Col. 1335D] The Memmian Canon notes that although it reads *Esthom* in the sacred text, elsewhere—that is, in other copies—it is written *Esthamo*. We do not consider these variant readings to be rejected, since they can easily be derived from the Hebrew, although today many read *Eschtemoa* from the Masoretic pointing. In the *Book of Hebrew Names* it is called *Asthemoe*. Such differing readings of proper names are frequent in the Memmian codex, and two or three are often supplied together; for example, the sons of Her are elsewhere called Aer and elsewhere Aser. Likewise Agag is elsewhere Asac and elsewhere Achac, and so forth. MART.]

[Col. 1335C] From the tribe of Benjamin: Gabee and its pasturelands, Almath with its pasturelands, and Anathoth with its pasturelands. All the cities were thirteen, according to their clans.

To the remaining sons of Caath, according to their clan, they gave from half the tribe of Manasse ten cities as a possession.

To the sons of Gerson, according to their clans, they gave from the tribe of Issachar, the tribe of Aser, the tribe of Nephtali, and half the tribe of Manasse in Basan thirteen cities.

To the sons of Merari, according to their clans, they gave by lot from the tribe of Ruben, the tribe of Gad, and the tribe of Zabulon twelve cities.

The sons of Israel also gave the Levites cities and their pasturelands.

By lot they gave from the tribe of the sons of Juda, the tribe of the sons of Simeon, and the tribe of the sons of Benjamin these cities, which they called by their names.

To those who belonged to the clans of the sons of Caath, the cities in their territory were from the tribe of Ephraim.

[Col. 1335D] They gave them cities of refuge: Sichem with its pasturelands on Mount Ephraim, Gazer with its pasturelands, Jecmaan with its pasturelands, Bethoron likewise, Helon with its pasturelands, and Gethremmon in the same manner.

From half the tribe of Manasse: Aner and its pasturelands, and Baalam and its pasturelands; these belonged to the remaining clans of the sons of Caath.

[Col. 1336A] To the sons of Gerson, from the clan of half the tribe of Manasse, they gave Gaulon in Basan and its pasturelands, and Astaroth with its pasturelands.

From the tribe of Issachar: Cedes and its pasturelands, Dabereth with its pasturelands, Ramoth with its pasturelands, and Anem with its pasturelands.

From the tribe of Aser: Masal with its pasturelands, Abdon likewise, Hucac with its pasturelands, and Roob with its pasturelands.

From the tribe of Nephtali: Cedes in Galilee and its pasturelands, Hamon with its pasturelands, and Cariathaim with its pasturelands.

To the remaining sons of Merari, from the tribe of Zabulon: Remmono and its pasturelands, and Thabor with its pasturelands.

Beyond the Jordan, opposite Jericho, toward the east of the Jordan, from the tribe of Ruben: Bosor in the wilderness with its pasturelands, Jasa with its pasturelands, Cademoth with its pasturelands, and Miphaat with its pasturelands.

From the tribe of Gad: Ramoth in Galaad with its pasturelands, Manaim with its pasturelands, Esebon with its pasturelands, and Jezer with its pasturelands.

[Cap. VII.] The sons of Issachar were Thola, Phua, Jasub, and Simeron—four.

The sons of Thola were Ozi, Raphaia, Jeriel, Jemai, Jebsem, and Samuel, chiefs according to the houses of their clans.

From the lineage of Thola, twenty-two thousand six hundred valiant men were counted in the days of David.

The sons of Ozi were Jezraia, from whom were born Michael, Obadia, Joel, and Jesia—five in all, all chiefs. With them, according to their families and peoples, were thirty-six thousand valiant men equipped for battle, for they had many wives and sons.

Their brothers throughout the entire clan of Issachar, strongest in battle, numbered eighty-seven thousand.

The sons of Benjamin were Bale, Bochor, and Jadiel—three.

The sons of Bale were Esbon, Ozi, Oziel, Jerimoth, and Urai—five chiefs of families and very strong in battle.

Their number was twenty-two thousand and thirty-four.

The sons of Bochor were Zamira, Joas, Eliezer, Elioenai, Amri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth, and Almathan. [Note: [Col. 1336D] Martianus reconstructed this from his manuscripts and the Alexandrian Greek; since the Hebrew has only the supplied, unreadable form, he suspects that its final letter has fallen out. Nevertheless, the Greek text he cites reads not *Almathan* but Ἐλμεθὲμ. The Vulgate likewise has *Almath* sufficiently correctly.]

All these were the sons of Bochor.

They were counted according to their families, chiefs of their clans and very strong in war: twenty thousand two hundred.

The sons of Jadiel were Balan.

The sons of Balan were Jeus, Benjamin, Aod, Chanana, Zethan, Tharsis, and Abisahar.

All these were the sons of Jadiel, chiefs of their clans, valiant men—seventeen thousand two hundred advancing to battle.

Sepham and Hapham were the sons of Hir; and Hasim was the son of Aher.

The sons of Nephthali were Jasiel, Guni, Jeser, and Sellum, sons of Bala.

The son of Manasse was Esriel, and his concubine Syra bore Machir, father of Galaad.

Machir took wives for his sons, Apphiam and Sephan, and he had a sister named Maacha.

[Col. 1337A] The name of the second was Salphaad, and Salphaad had daughters.

Maacha, the wife of Machir, bore a son and called his name Phares.

His brother’s name was Sares; his sons were Ulam and Recen.

The son of Ulam was Badan.

These were the sons of Galaad, son of Machir, son of Manasse.

His sister Regina bore a handsome man, Abiezer, and Moola.

The sons of Semida were Ahin, Sechem, Leci, and Aniam.

The sons of Ephraim were Suthula, Bared his son, Thaath his son, Elada his son, Thaath his son, Zabad his son, Suthala his son, Ezer his son, and Elad.

The men of Geth, natives of the land, killed them, because they had gone down to invade their possessions.

Ephraim, their father, mourned for many days, and his brothers came to console him.

[Col. 1337B] He went in to his wife; she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Beria, because he had been born amid misfortune in his household.

His daughter was Sara, who built Lower and Upper Bethoron, and Ozensara.

His son was Rapha, then Reseph, and Thale, from whom Thaan was born; Thaan fathered Laadan; his son Ammiud fathered Elizama; from him Nun arose, who had a son Josue.

Their possession and dwelling were Beth-El with its villages toward the east, Noran; toward the west, Gazer and its villages; also Sichem with its villages as far as Aza with its villages.

Alongside the sons of Manasse were Bethsan and its villages, Thanach and its villages, Mageddo and its villages, and Dor and its villages.

In these places dwelt the sons of Joseph, the sons of Israel.

The sons of Aser were Jemna, Jesua, Jesui, Baria, and their sister Sara.

[Col. 1337C] The sons of Baria were Heber and Melchiel; he was the father of Bersaith.

Heber fathered Jephlat, Somer, Otham, and their sister Suaa.

The sons of Jephlat were Phosech, Chamaal, and Asoth.

The sons of Somer were Ahi, Roaga, Jaba, and Aram.

The sons of Helem, his brother, were Supha, Jemna, Selles, and Amal.

The sons of Supha were Sue, Arnaphed, Sual, Beri, Jamra, Bosor, Od, Samma, Salusa, Jethran, and Bera.

[Note: [Col. 1337D] Instead of *Arnaphed*, we read *Arnapher* in Hebrew, with *resh* at the end. Through the easy error of copyists, *resh* is written in place of *daleth*. MART. — All the original books, not excepting even the Greek and the Vulgate translator, read *Arnapher* with *r*.]

The sons of Jether were Jephone, Phaspha, and Ara.

The sons of Olla were Aree, Aniel, and Resia.

All these were the sons of Aser, chiefs of clans, chosen and valiant leaders of leaders.

Their number, at the age fit for war, was twenty-six thousand.

[Col. 1337D] [Cap. VIII.] Benjamin fathered Bale, his firstborn, and Asbal, the second.

Ahora was the third, Nuhaa the fourth, and Rapha the fifth.

The sons of Bale were Addar, Gera, Abiud, Abisue, Nooman, Ahoe, Gera, Sephuphan, and Uram.

These were the sons of Aod, chiefs of the clans dwelling in Gabaa, who were carried away to Manaath.

Nooman, Achia, and Gera—he carried them away—and he fathered Oza and Ahiud.

[Col. 1338A] Saaraim fathered children in the land of Moab after he had sent away his wives Usim and Bara.

By Hedes his wife he fathered Jobab, Sebia, Mosa, Molchom, Jeus, Sechia, and Marma.

These were his sons, chiefs in their families.

Meusim fathered Ahitob and Elphaal.

The sons of Elphaal were Heber, Misaam, and Samad.

He built Ono, Lod, and its villages.

Baria and Sama were chiefs of the clans dwelling in Aialon; they drove out the inhabitants of Geth.

Also Ahio, Sesac, Jerimoth, Zabadia, Arod, Heder, Michael, Jespha, and John, the sons of Baria;

also Zabadia, Mossollam, Hezeci, Heber, Jesamari, Jezlia, and Jobab, the sons of Elphaal;

also Jacim, Zechri, Zabdi, Elioenai, Selethai, Eliel, Adaia, Baraia, and Samarath, the sons of Semei;

also Jesphan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zechri, Anan, Anania, Abilam, Anathothia, Jephdaia, and Phanuel, the sons of Sesac;

also Samsari, Sooria, Otholia, Jersia, Elia, and Zechri, the sons of Jeroam.

These were the patriarchs and chiefs of clans who dwelt in Jerusalem.

In Gabaon dwelt Abigabaon, whose wife was named Maacha. His firstborn son was Abdon, then Sur, Cis, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher, and Macelloth, who fathered Samaa.

They dwelt opposite their brothers in Jerusalem, with their brothers.

Ner fathered Cis, and Cis fathered Saul.

Saul fathered Jonathan, Melchisue, Abinadab, and Esbaal.

Jonathan’s son was Meribbaal, and Meribbaal fathered Micha.

The sons of Micha were Phiton, Melech, Thara, and Ahaz.

[Col. 1338C] Ahaz fathered Joada, and Joada fathered Almoth [or Alamoth], Azmoth, and Zamri.

[Note: [Col. 1337D] The copies of the Canon inserted the name *Almoth* twice, reading: “Joada fathered Almoth, and Almoth fathered Zamri”; this arose through the error of copyists. MART.]

Zamri fathered Mosa, and Mosa fathered Banaa, whose son was Rapha, from whom Elasa arose, who fathered Asel.

Asel had six sons, named Ezricam, Bocru, Ismael, Saria, Obadia, and Anan. All these were the sons of Asel.

The sons of Esec, his brother, were Ulam, the firstborn; Us, the second; and Eliphalet, the third.

The sons of Ulam were valiant men, mighty in strength and skilled in drawing the bow. They had many sons and grandsons, up to one hundred fifty.

[Note: [Col. 1338D] The same should be said of the word “thousands,” added here in Latin codices: it is absurd and contrary to the sense of Scripture to say that Ulam had grandsons numbering up to one hundred fifty thousand. MART.]

All these were the sons of Benjamin.

### Chapter IX

Thus all Israel was enrolled, and the sum of them was recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

They were transferred to Babylon because of their transgression.

[Col. 1338D] The first to dwell in their possessions and in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants.

In Jerusalem there dwelt people from the sons of Judah, from the sons of Benjamin, and also from the sons of Ephraim and Manasseh.

Othei son of Ammiud, son of Amri, son of Omri, son of Bonni, from the sons of Phares, son of Judah.

And from the Silanites: Asaiah the firstborn and his sons.

From the sons of Zerah: Jeuel and their brothers, six hundred and ninety.

[Col. 1339A] From the sons of Benjamin: Salo son of Mosollam, son of Odvia, son of Asana;

and Jobania son of Jeroam; Ela son of Ozi, son of Mochori; and Mosollam son of Saphatia, son of Rauel, son of Jebania.

Their brothers, according to their families, numbered nine hundred and fifty-six.

All these were heads of ancestral clans according to their fathers’ houses.

Among the priests were Jedaia, Joiarib, and Jachin;

also Azarias son of Helcia, son of Mosollam, son of Sadoc, son of Maraioth, son of Ahitob, chief priest of the house of God.

Moreover, Adaias son of Jeroam, son of Phasur, son of Melchias;

and Masaia son of Adiel, son of Jezra, son of Mosollam, son of Mosollamith, son of Emmer.

Their brothers, heads of their families, numbered one thousand seven hundred and sixty, men of great strength for carrying out the work of the ministry in the house of God.

[Col. 1339B] Among the Levites were Semeia son of Assub, son of Ezricam, son of Asebia, from the sons of Merari;

also Bacbacar the carpenter, Galal, and Mathania son of Micha, son of Zechri, son of Asaph;

and Obdia son of Semeia, son of Gafal, son of Idithun;

and Barachia son of Asa, son of Elcana, who dwelt in the courts of Netophati.

The gatekeepers were Sellum, Accub, Telmon, Ahiman, and their brother Sellum, the chief.

Until that time they kept watch in their appointed turns at the king’s gate on the east, from among the sons of Levi.

Sellum son of Core, son of Abiasaph, son of Core, with his brothers and his father’s household—these were the Korites, assigned to the work of the ministry, guardians of the vestibules of the tabernacle; their families kept watch in the camps of the Lord according to their turns, guarding the entrance.

Phinees son of Eleazar was their leader before the Lord.

Zacharias son of Mosollamia was gatekeeper of the gate of the [Col. 1339C] tabernacle of the testimony.

All these, chosen as gatekeepers at the gates, numbered two hundred and twelve. They were enrolled in their own villages; David and Samuel the Seer appointed them in their faithfulness, both them and their sons, to serve at the doors of the house of the Lord and in the tabernacle, according to their turns.

There were gatekeepers on the four sides—that is, toward the east, west, north, and south.

Their brothers dwelt in the villages and came on their Sabbaths from time to time.

These four Levites were entrusted with the entire number of the gatekeepers, and they were in charge of the chambers and treasuries of the house of the Lord.

They also dwelt around the temple of the Lord at their posts, so that, when the time came, they themselves might open the doors in the morning.

Some of their group were also assigned to the vessels used in the ministry, for they brought the vessels in and carried them out.

Some of them, those entrusted with the utensils of the sanctuary, were in charge of the fine flour, wine, oil, incense, and spices.

The sons of the priests prepared the ointments from the spices.

Mathathias the Levite, the firstborn of Sellum the Korite, was in charge of what was fried in the pan.

From the sons of Caath, their brothers, some were responsible for the bread of the Presence, preparing fresh loaves every Sabbath.

These were the heads of the singers according to the families of the Levites, [Col. 1340A] who dwelt in the chambers so that day and night they might continually perform their ministry.

The heads of the Levites, chiefs according to their families, remained in Jerusalem.

In Gibeon dwelt the father of Gibeon, Jaiel, and the name of his wife was Maacha.

[Note: [Col. 1339D] Some Hebrew manuscripts therefore give less correctly “of his sister” instead of “of his wife,” as Jerome also read it; likewise, nearly all the other translators render it “wife.”]

His firstborn son was Abdon, followed by Sur, Cis, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacharias, and Macelloth.

Macelloth fathered Semma.

These dwelt opposite their brothers in Jerusalem, together with their brothers.

Ner fathered Cis, and Cis fathered Saul; and Saul fathered Jonathan, Melchisue, Abinadab, and Esbaal.

Jonathan’s son was Meribaal, and Meribaal fathered Micha.

Micha’s sons were Phithon, Melech, and Thara.

Ahaz fathered Jara, and Jara fathered Almoth, Azmoth, and Zamri; Zamri fathered Mosa.

Mosa fathered Banaa, whose son was Raphaia; he fathered Elasa, from whom Asel was descended.

Asel had six sons, named Ezricam, Bocru, Ismahel, Saria, Obdia, and Anan. These were the sons of Asel.

### Chapter X

The Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines; the wounded fell on Mount Gelboe.

When the Philistines drew near, pursuing Saul and his sons, they struck Jonathan, Abinadab, and Melchisue, the sons of Saul.

The battle grew heavy against Saul; the archers found him and wounded him with their arrows.

Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and kill me, lest these uncircumcised men come and mock me.”

But his armor-bearer would not do it, terrified with fear.

So Saul seized his sword and fell upon it.

When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell upon his sword and died.

Thus Saul, his three sons, and his whole household perished together.

When the Israelites who lived in the lowlands saw this, they fled. And when Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and scattered here and there.

Then the Philistines came and dwelt in them.

On the following day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his sons lying on Mount Gelboe.

When they had stripped him, cut off his head, and removed his armor, they sent these things throughout their land to be carried around and displayed in the temples of their idols and among the people.

They consecrated his armor in the shrine of their god, and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.

When the men of Jabesh-gilead heard everything that the Philistines had done to Saul, all the brave men arose and carried away the corpses of Saul and his sons.

They brought them to Jabesh and buried their bones beneath the oak that was in Jabesh, and they fasted for seven days.

Saul died because of his iniquities, because he had transgressed the commandment of the Lord that he had given, and had not kept it; moreover, he had consulted a woman who practiced divination and had not hoped in the Lord. Therefore He killed him and transferred his kingdom to David son of Jesse.

### Chapter XI

All Israel therefore gathered to David at Hebron and said:

[Col. 1341A] “We are your bone and your flesh. Yesterday and the day before, when Saul was still king, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back.

For the Lord your God said to you, ‘You shall shepherd my people Israel, and you shall be ruler over them.’”

So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them before the Lord.

They anointed him king over Israel, according to the word of the Lord spoken through Samuel.

David and all Israel then went to Jerusalem. This was Jebus, whose inhabitants were the Jebusites.

The inhabitants of Jebus said to David, “You shall not enter here.”

But David captured the stronghold of Zion, which is the City of David, and said:

“Whoever first strikes a Jebusite shall be chief and commander.”

Joab son of Sarvia went up first and became chief.

David dwelt in the stronghold; therefore it was called the City of David.

He built the city around it, from the Millo to the circuit; Joab rebuilt the rest of the city.

David advanced, going forward and growing stronger, and the Lord of hosts was with him.

These were the chiefs of David’s mighty men, who helped him become king over all Israel, according to the word of the Lord spoken to Israel.

This was the number of David’s warriors:

Jesbaam son of Achamoni, chief among the Thirty; he raised his spear against three hundred wounded at one time.

After him was Eleazar son of his uncle, the Ahohite, who was among the three mighty men. He was with David [Note: [Col. 1341D] All manuscripts read “with David” together with the exemplars of the Hebrew verity. Printed editions, following the Hebrew, have “at Phesdomim,” or “at Baphas-dammim.” MART.] at Aphesdomim [variant: Phesdomi], when the Philistines had gathered there for battle. The field of that region was full of barley, and the people had fled from before the Philistines.

[Note: [Col. 1341D] We have restored the plural—“They stood” and “they defended”—and shortly afterward “they struck,” in accordance with the Hebrew text and the testimony of the Latin manuscripts we have seen. The author of the Hebrew Questions on this book, whom Martianus cites, likewise reads it this way and adds the reason why the Books of Kings have the singular: so that the king’s strength might be displayed. Moreover, it is much more probable that the name Semma was omitted by the scribes in the archetype in the immediately preceding verse. Martianus, however, using some of his manuscripts, printed the singular: “He stood,” “he defended,” and so forth.—Some manuscripts read these words in the singular, while the printed editions have the plural, “They stood ... they defended,” and so forth. The Hebrew likewise retains the plural in this passage; but in 2 Samuel 23:12 it reads the same story, or the same statement, in the singular. Hence the author of the Hebrew Questions on Chronicles teaches as follows: “They stood in the middle of the field and defended it”—namely, David and Eleazar. “In Chronicles it is put in the plural; in the Books of Kings it is put in the singular, so that the king’s strength might be displayed.” In both places we have followed the manuscripts of Jerome’s version. MART.]

They stood in the middle of the field and defended it.

When they had struck the Philistines, the Lord granted a great deliverance to his people.

Three of the Thirty chiefs went down to the rock where David was, to the cave of Odollam, while the Philistines were encamped in the valley of Raphaim.

David was then in the stronghold, while the Philistine garrison was at Bethlehem.

David longed for water and said, “Oh, that someone would give me water from the cistern of Bethlehem, which is by the gate.”

So the three went through the middle of the Philistine camp, drew water from the cistern of Bethlehem by the gate, and brought it to David to drink.

But he would not drink it; rather, he poured it out to the Lord, saying:

[Col. 1342A] “Far be it from me, before my God, to do this and drink the blood of these men, for they brought the water at the risk of their lives.” For this reason he would not drink it.

These things were done by the three mightiest men.

Abisai, brother of Joab, was himself chief of the Three. He raised his spear against three hundred wounded, and he was the most renowned among the Three, [Note: [Col. 1342D] In the Royal manuscript and two manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, as well as in both exemplars of the Hebrew verity, the construction ends here: “second in renown among the Three.” MART.—The Hebrew text does not have the word “first,” but only “Yet as far as the Three,” or “the third,” he did not attain. The Greek likewise has καὶ ἕως τῶν τριῶν οὐκ ἤρχετο, “and he did not reach the Three.”] second in renown among the Three, and their chief.

Nevertheless, he did not reach the first Three.

Banaias son of Joiada was a very brave man who had performed many deeds, from Cabseel.

He struck down two Ariels of Moab; he also went down and killed a lion in the middle of a cistern during snowy weather.

He also struck an Egyptian man of five cubits in height, who had a spear like a weaver’s beam.

He went down against him with a staff, snatched the spear from his hand, [Col. 1342B] and killed him with his own spear.

These things Banaias son of Joiada did. He was among the three mighty men, most renowned; he was first among the Thirty, yet he did not attain the Three.

David appointed him over his bodyguard [literally, “at his ear”; reading uncertain].

The mighty men of the army were Asael brother of Joab; Eleanan son of his uncle from Bethlehem; Semmoth the Harorite; Helles the Phallonite; Ira son of Acces the Tekoite; Abiezer the Anathothite; Sobbochai the Hushathite; Ilai the Ahohite; Marai the Netophathite; Heled son of Baana the Netophathite; Ethai son of Ribai from Gibeah of the sons of Benjamin; Banaia the Pharathonite; Uri from the Torrent of Gaas; Abiel the Arabathite; Azmoth the Bauramite; Eliaba the Salabonite.

The sons of Asom the Genozite; Jonathan son of Sega the Ararite; Ahiam son of Sachar the Hararite; Eliphal son of Ur; Epher the Mecherathite; Ahia the Phelonite; Asro the Carmelite; Noorai son of Azbai; Joel brother of Nathan; Mabar son of Agarai; Selec the Ammonite; Noorai the Berothite, armor-bearer of Joab son of Sarvia; Ira the Jethrite; Gareb the Jethrite; Urias the Hittite; Zabad son of Ooli; Adina son of Seza, a Reubenite and chief of the Reubenites, with thirty men under him; Hanam son of Maacha; Josaphat the Mathanite; Ozia the Astarothite; Samma and Jaiel, sons of Hotham the Arorite; Jediel son of Samri and his brother Joha the Thosaite; Eliel the Maumite; Jeribal; Josaia, sons of Elnaem; Jethma the Moabite; Eliel; Obeb; and Jasiel from Masobia.

### Chapter XII

These men also came to David at Siceleg while he was still fleeing from Saul son of Cis. They were mighty and outstanding warriors, skilled with the bow, able to use both hands to sling stones and shoot and aim arrows; they were from Saul’s kinsmen, from Benjamin.

Their chiefs were Abiezer and Joas, sons of Samaa, Gibeathites; Jaziel and Phallet, sons of Azmoth; Baracha; and Jeu the Anathothite.

Samaias the Gibeonite was also the mightiest among the Thirty and over the Thirty.

[Col. 1342D] Jeremias, Jeziel, Johanan, and Jezbad the Gaderothite; [Col. 1343A] Eluzai, Jerimuth, Baalia, Samaria, and Saphatia the Haruphite; Elcana, Jesia, Azrael, Joezer, and Jesbaam from Carehim.

Joela and Zabadia, sons of Jeroam from Gedor.

Men also defected from Gad to David while he was hiding in the wilderness—mighty men and excellent warriors, holding shield and spear. Their faces were like the faces of lions, and they were swift as gazelles on the mountains:

Ezer the chief; Obdias the second; Eliab the third; Masmana the fourth; Jeremias the fifth; Ethi the sixth; Eliel the seventh; Johanan the eighth; Elzebad the ninth; Jeremias the tenth; Machbanai the eleventh.

These were chiefs of the army from the sons of Gad. The least commanded one hundred soldiers, and the greatest commanded one thousand.

These were the men who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it usually overflowed its banks; and they drove away all who dwelt in the valleys, both toward the eastern and the western side.

[Col. 1343B] Men also came from Benjamin and Judah to the stronghold where David dwelt.

David went out to meet them and said:

“If you have come to me in peace, to help me, let my heart be joined to you. But if you are plotting against me on behalf of my adversaries, although there is no injustice in my hands, may the God of our fathers see and judge.”

Then the spirit clothed Amasai, chief among the Thirty, and he said:

“We are yours, David, and with you, son of Jesse. Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers, for your God helps you.”

David therefore received them and appointed them chiefs of the troops.

Men from Manasseh also defected to David when he came with the Philistines against Saul to fight.

But he did not fight with them, because the Philistine commanders, after deliberation, sent him back, saying:

“Perhaps, at the risk of our heads, he will return to his master Saul.”

When he returned to Siceleg, men from Manasseh defected to him: Ednas and Jozabad, Jediel, [Note: [Col. 1343D] The printed books add here, after the word “Michael,” “and Ednas.” The Colbertine and Anician manuscripts read, “and Michael, and Nas, and Jozabad.” But this—“and Nas,” or “and Ednas”—is absent from the Hebrew and from the other Latin manuscripts. MART.—What the Vulgate manuscripts insert here, or repeat—the name “Ednas”—is found neither in the Hebrew nor Greek text, nor in the ancient manuscripts of Jerome, [Col. 1344D] nor in the manuscripts of better quality.]

and Michael, Jozabad, Eliu, and Salathi, chiefs of thousands in Manasseh.

They gave David assistance against the raiders, for they were all mighty men and became commanders in the army.

Moreover, day by day men came to David to help him, until the number became great, like the army of God.

This is also the number of the army commanders who came to David at Hebron, to transfer Saul’s kingdom to him, according to the word of the Lord.

From the sons of Judah, bearing shield and spear, six thousand eight hundred equipped for battle.

From the sons of Simeon, seven thousand one hundred mighty men prepared for war.

[Col. 1343D] From the sons of Levi, four thousand six hundred.

Joiada, chief of the family of Aaron, with him three thousand seven hundred.

Sadoc also, a young man of outstanding character, and twenty-two chiefs from his father’s house.

From the sons of Benjamin, Saul’s brothers, three thousand; for a large part of them still followed the house of Saul.

From the sons of Ephraim, twenty thousand eight hundred, [Col. 1344A] men of great strength, distinguished in their clans.

From half the tribe of Manasseh, eighteen thousand, each of them coming by name to establish David as king.

From the sons of Issachar, learned men who understood the proper times and knew what Israel ought to do, two hundred chiefs.

All the rest of the tribe followed their counsel.

From Zebulun, those who went out to battle and stood in battle formation equipped with weapons of war, fifty thousand came [Note: [Col. 1344D] The Hebrew text has a term that properly means “to draw up the battle line.” It seems that Jerome, and before Jerome the Seventy, read in the exemplar before them a similar term meaning “for assistance,” one letter having been exchanged for another, and the two letters being extremely similar.]

to give assistance, without a divided heart.

From Naphtali, one thousand chiefs; and with them thirty-seven thousand equipped with shield and spear.

From Dan, twenty-eight thousand six hundred prepared for battle.

From Asher, forty thousand going out to war and advancing in battle formation.

[Col. 1344B] From across the Jordan, from the sons of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, one hundred and twenty thousand equipped with weapons of war.

All these warriors, equipped for battle, came to Hebron with a perfect heart, to establish David as king over all Israel.

All the rest of Israel likewise had one heart, that David should become king.

They remained there with David for three days, eating and drinking, for their brothers had prepared provisions for them.

Even those who lived nearby, as far as Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali, brought food on donkeys, camels, mules, and oxen for them to eat: flour, cakes, raisins, wine, oil, cattle, and rams in abundance. For there was joy in Israel.

### Chapter XIII

David took counsel with the tribunes, centurions, and all the leaders, and said to the whole assembly of Israel:

[Col. 1344C] “If it pleases you, and if the word I speak proceeds from the Lord our God, let us send to our remaining brothers throughout all the regions of Israel, and to the priests and Levites who dwell in the suburbs of the cities, so that they may gather to us; and let us bring back to us the ark of our God, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul.”

The entire multitude answered that this should be done, for the proposal pleased all the people.

So David gathered all Israel, from the Shihor of Egypt to the entrance of Hamath, in order to bring the ark of God from Cariath-jearim.

David and every man of Israel went up to the hill of Cariath-jearim, which is in Judah, to bring from there the ark of the Lord God, who sits upon the cherubim, whose name had been invoked there.

They placed the ark of God on a new cart from the house of Abinadab.

Oza and his brother drove the cart.

[Col. 1344D] David and all Israel played before God with all their might, with songs, lyres, psalteries, tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets.

When they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Oza stretched out his hand to steady the ark, for the ox, having become frisky, had tilted it slightly.

The Lord was therefore angry with Oza and struck him because he had touched the ark; and he died there before the Lord.

[Col. 1345A] David was grieved because the Lord had struck Oza.

He called that place “The Breach of Oza,” to the present day.

At that time he feared God, saying, “How can I bring the ark of God to me?”

For this reason he did not bring it to himself, that is, into the City of David, but turned it aside to the house of Obededom the Gittite.

The ark of God therefore remained in the house of Obededom for three months.

The Lord blessed his household and everything he possessed.

### Chapter XIV

Hiram, king of Tyre, sent messengers to David, along with cedar wood and craftsmen skilled in walls and wood, to build him a house.

David recognized that the Lord had established him as king over Israel and that his kingdom had been exalted over his people Israel.

[Col. 1345B] David took additional wives in Jerusalem and fathered sons and daughters.

These are the names of those born to him in Jerusalem: Samua, Sobab, Nathan, Solomon, Jebar, Elisua, Eliphalet, Noga, Napheg, Japhie, Elisama, Baliada, and Eliphalet.

When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, they all went up to seek him.

When David heard this, he went out to meet them.

The Philistines came and spread themselves through the Valley of Raphaim.

David consulted the Lord, saying, “Shall I go up against the Philistines, and will you deliver them into my hand?”

The Lord said to him, “Go up, and I will deliver them into your hand.”

When they had gone up to Baal-Pharasim, David struck them there and said:

“God has divided my enemies by my hand, as waters are divided.”

Therefore that place was called Baal-Pharasim.

They abandoned their gods there, and David ordered them to be burned.

The Philistines attacked again and spread through the valley.

David again consulted God, and God said to him:

“Do not go up after them; withdraw from them and come against them opposite the pear trees.

When you hear the sound of movement in the tops of the pear trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.”

David did as God had commanded him, and he struck the camp of the Philistines from Gibeon to Gazera.

[Col. 1345D] David’s name became renowned throughout all the regions, and the Lord placed dread of him upon all the nations.

### Chapter XV

David made houses for himself in the City of David, built a place for the ark of God, and spread a tent over it.

Then David said, “It is not permitted for anyone to carry the ark of God except the Levites, whom the Lord chose to carry it and minister to him forever.”

He gathered all Israel to Jerusalem, so that the ark of God might be brought to the place he had prepared for it,

[Col. 1346A] along with the sons of Aaron and the Levites.

From the sons of Merari: Asaia the chief and his brothers, two hundred and twenty.

From the sons of Gershom: Joel the chief and his brothers, one hundred, thirty, twenty [numeral sequence as printed].

From the sons of Gershom: Joel the chief and his brothers, one hundred and thirty.

From the sons of Elisaphan: Semeias the chief and his brothers, two hundred.

From the sons of Hebron: Eliel the chief and his brothers, eighty.

From the sons of Oziel: Aminadab the chief and his brothers, one hundred and twelve.

David summoned the priests Sadoc and Abiathar, and the Levites Uriel, Asaia, Joel, Semeia, Eliel, and Aminadab.

He said to them: “You who are heads of the Levitical families, sanctify yourselves with your brothers and bring up the ark of the Lord God of Israel to the place prepared for it.

[Col. 1346B] Otherwise, because you were not present at the beginning, the Lord struck us; so now also let this happen to us if we do what is forbidden.”

The priests and Levites therefore sanctified themselves to carry the ark of the Lord God of Israel.

The sons of Levi carried the ark of God on their shoulders, with its poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the Lord.

David ordered the chiefs of the Levites to appoint singers from among their brothers, with musical instruments—namely, nablas, lyres, and cymbals—so that the sound of joy might resound on high.

They appointed the Levites: Eman son of Joel and, from among his brothers, Asaph son of Barachias;

from the sons of Merari, their brothers, Ethan son of Casaia.

With them were their brothers in the second order: Zacharias, Ben, Jaziel, Semiramoth, Jahiel, Ani, Eliab, Banaia, Maasia, Mathathia, [Col. 1346C] Eliphalu, Macenia, Obededom, and Jeiel, the gatekeepers.

The singers were Eman, Asaph, and Ethan, striking bronze cymbals.

Zacharias, Oziel, Semiramoth, Jahiel, Ani, Eliab, Maasias, and Banaias sang mysteries on the nablas.

Mathathias, Eliphalu, Macenias, Obededom, Jeiel, and Ozaziu sang on lyres for the octave, [Note: [Col. 1345D] The Hebrew has *lamnatseahh*, which Jerome read as *Lamanasse* in the preface to his Commentaries on Daniel, where he says that Symmachus interprets this word as ἐπινίκιον (*epiníkion*), which properly signifies triumph and the palm of victory. MART.] “the triumphal song.”

Chonenias, chief of the Levites, was in charge of prophecy, to lead the melody, for he was exceedingly wise.

Barachias and Eleana were gatekeepers of the ark.

Sebenias, Josaphat, Nathanael, Amasai, Zacharias, Banaias, and Eliezer, the priests, sounded the trumpets before the ark of God.

Obededom and Jehias were gatekeepers of the ark.

David, all the elders of Israel, and the tribunes went to carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord [Col. 1346D] from the house of Obededom with rejoicing.

When God had helped the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, seven bulls and seven rams were sacrificed.

David wore a robe of fine linen, as did all the Levites who carried the ark, the singers, and Chonenias, chief of prophecy among the singers.

David also wore a linen ephod.

All Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the Lord with jubilation and the sound of the horn, trumpets, cymbals, nablas, and lyres.

When the ark of the covenant of the Lord reached the City of David, Michal daughter of Saul looked out through the [Col. 1347A] window, saw King David dancing and playing, and despised him in her heart.

### Chapter XVI

They brought the ark of God in and placed it in the middle of the tent that David had spread for it, and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God.

When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord.

He distributed to everyone, man and woman alike, a round loaf of bread, a portion of roasted beef, and flour fried in oil.

He appointed before the ark of the Lord Levites to minister, to remember his works, to glorify him, and to praise the Lord God of Israel:

Asaph as chief, and Zacharias second to him;

Jaiel, Semiramoth, Jehiel, Mathathias, Eliab, Banaia, Obededom, and Jeiel over the instruments of the psaltery and lyres;

Asaph to sound the cymbals;

Banaias and Jaziel the priests to sound the trumpet [Col. 1347B] continually before the ark of the covenant of the Lord.

On that day David appointed Asaph and his brothers to give thanks to the Lord.

“Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name; make known [Note: [Col. 1347D] In the Book of Psalms, which we printed above, where Psalm 105 occupies this place, it is often read differently: here, “make known his thoughts among the peoples”; and three verses after this, “speak of all his wonders,” and so forth. “Rejoice in his holy name,” and similar expressions below, may be observed by comparing the passages yourself.] his discoveries among the peoples.

Sing to him and sing psalms to him; recount all his wonders.

Praise his holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.

Seek the Lord and his strength; seek his face continually.

Remember his wonders, which he has done, his signs [variant: omits “his”] and the judgments of his mouth.

O offspring of Israel, his servant,

sons of Jacob, his chosen ones.

He himself is the Lord our God;

his judgments are throughout all the earth.

Remember his covenant forever,

the word that he commanded for a thousand generations,

the covenant he made with Abraham,

and his oath with Isaac.

He established it for Jacob as a commandment,

and for Israel as an everlasting covenant,

saying: “To you I will give the land of Canaan,

the measuring-cord of your inheritance.”

When they were few in number,

few and resident foreigners in it,

they passed from nation to nation,

and from one kingdom to another people.

He did not permit anyone to oppress them,

but rebuked kings for their sake:

“Do not touch my anointed ones,

and do not harm my prophets.”

[Note: [Col. 1347D] This psalm is Psalm 96 in the Psalter according to the Hebrew. It also frequently differs from the version of Jerome that we printed above. The Hebrew text of the two books likewise varies; critics note these passages.]

Sing to the Lord, all the earth;

announce his salvation from day to day.

Declare his glory among the nations,

his wonders among all peoples.

[Col. 1347D] For the Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise,

and fearsome above all gods.

For all the gods of the peoples are idols,

but the Lord made the heavens.

Praise and magnificence are before him;

strength and joy are in his place.

Bring to the Lord, families of the peoples,

bring to the Lord glory and dominion.

Give the Lord glory for his name;

[Col. 1348A] bring an offering and come into his presence,

and worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness.

Let all the earth tremble before him,

for he founded the world immovably.

Let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult,

and let them say among the nations, “The Lord reigns.”

Let the sea thunder, and all that fills it;

let the fields exult, and everything in them.

Then the trees of the forest will praise before the Lord,

for he has come to judge the earth.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,

for his mercy is everlasting.

And say: “Save us, God our savior,

gather us and rescue us from the nations,

that we may give thanks to your holy name

and exult in your praises.”

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel

from eternity to eternity;

and let all the people say:

“Amen,” [Note: [Col. 1348D] Some manuscripts have, “Amen and a hymn to the Lord.” Let the diligent reader compare the psalm at this place with the same Song, which is numbered Psalm 105 in the Psalter, and then with Psalm 96; he will certainly find many differences in both the Hebrew and Latin manuscripts. MART.] and “a hymn” [variant: “hymn”] “to the Lord.”

[Col. 1348B] He left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, to minister continually in the presence of the ark, each day according to their appointed turns.

Obededom and his sixty-eight brothers;

and Obededom son of Idithun and Asa he appointed as gatekeepers.

He appointed Sadoc the priest and his brother priests before the tabernacle of the Lord at the high place that was in Gibeon,

to offer burnt offerings continually to the Lord upon the altar of burnt offering, morning and evening, according to everything written in the law of the Lord, which he commanded Israel.

After him were Eman, Idithun, and the remaining chosen men, each designated by name, to give thanks to the Lord: “For his mercy is everlasting.”

Eman and Idithun also sang, sounding trumpets, striking cymbals, and using all the musical instruments to sing to God.

He appointed the sons of Idithun as gatekeepers.

[Col. 1348C] All the people returned to their homes, and David returned to bless his own household.

### Chapter XVII

When David was living in his house, he said to Nathan the prophet:

“Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, while the ark of the covenant of the Lord is beneath skins.”

Nathan said to David, “Do everything that is in your heart, for God is with you.”

That night the word of God came to Nathan, saying:

“Go and speak to my servant David: Thus says the Lord:

‘You shall not build me a house in which to dwell.

For I have not dwelt in a house from the time when I brought Israel out until this day; rather, I have continually moved from place to place, in a tabernacle and dwelling in a tent with all Israel.

Did I ever speak to even one of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, [Col. 1348D] and say, “Why have you not built me a house of cedar?”

Now therefore say this to my servant David: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I took you from the pasture, where you followed the flock, so that you might be leader of my people Israel.

I was with you wherever you went; I destroyed all your enemies before you and made your name like the name of the great ones who are honored in the earth.

[Col. 1349A] I appointed a place for my people Israel; it shall be planted and shall dwell there, and it shall no longer be disturbed.

The sons of iniquity shall not wear them down as at the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel, and I humbled all your enemies.’”

I therefore announce to you that the Lord will build a house for you.

And when your days are fulfilled, so that you go to your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, one who shall be among your sons, and I will establish his kingdom.

He shall build a house for me, and I will make his throne firm forever.

I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me; and I will not withdraw my mercy from him, as I withdrew it from the one who was before you.

And I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be made exceedingly firm forever.

In accordance with all these words and according to this entire vision, Nathan spoke thus to David.

[Col. 1349B] When King David came and sat before the Lord, he said:

“Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you should grant me such things?

Yet even this seemed little in your sight, and therefore you have spoken concerning the house of your servant also for the future.

And you have regarded me as eminent above all men, Lord God.

What more can David add to you, when you have thus glorified your servant and known him?

Lord, because of your servant and according to your own heart, you have done all this magnificence, and you have wished to make known all these great things.

Lord, there is none like you, and there is no other God besides you, among all whom we have heard with our ears.

For what other nation is like your people Israel, a single nation on earth, to which God went in order to redeem it, and make it a people for himself, and by his greatness and terrors drive out nations from before the face of the people whom he had redeemed from Egypt?

And you have established your people Israel as your people forever, and you, Lord, have become their God.

Now therefore, Lord, let the word that you have spoken to your servant and concerning his house be confirmed forever, and do as you have spoken.

And let your name remain and be magnified forever, and let it be said: ‘The Lord of hosts is God over Israel,’ and ‘the house of David his servant remains before him.’

For you, Lord my God, have revealed this to the ear of your servant, so that you might build him a house; and therefore your servant has found confidence to pray before you.

Now therefore, Lord, you are God, and you have spoken such benefits to your servant. And you have begun to bless the house of your servant, so that it may always be before you; for when you bless, Lord, it shall be blessed forever.”

[Chapter XVIII] After these events, David struck the Philistines, subdued them, and took Gath and its villages from the hand of the Philistines. He also struck Moab, and the Moabites became servants of David, bringing him tribute.

At that time David also struck [Note: [Col. 1349D] Thus the Latin manuscripts read. In the Hebrew we read here *Adarezer*, with *resh* in the middle; whereas in the books of Samuel it is read *Adadezer*, with *daleth*. Consult our annotations. MART.] Adadezer, king of Zobah in the region of Hamath, when he went to extend his dominion as far as the Euphrates River.

David therefore captured a thousand of his chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand foot soldiers; and he hamstrung all the chariot horses, except for one hundred chariots, which he kept for himself.

Then the Syrian of Damascus came to assist Adadezer, king of Zobah; but David also struck down twenty-two thousand of his men.

And he stationed troops in Damascus, so that Syria too might serve him and bring tribute. The Lord helped him in everything he undertook.

David also took the golden quivers that the servants of Adadezer had possessed and brought them to Jerusalem.

And from Tebah and Chun, the cities of Adadezer, he took a great quantity of bronze, from which Solomon made the bronze Sea, the columns, and the bronze vessels.

When Thou, king of Hamath, heard that David had struck the entire army of Adadezer, king of Zobah, he sent his son Adoram to King David to ask peace of him and congratulate him, because he had defeated and struck Adadezer; for Thou was Adadezer’s adversary.

David the king also dedicated to the Lord all the vessels of gold, silver, and bronze, together with the silver and gold he had taken from all the nations—from Edom, Moab, the sons of Ammon, the Philistines, and Amalek.

Abishai, son of Zeruiah, struck Edom in the Valley of Salt—eighteen thousand men.

And he stationed a garrison in Edom, so that Edom might serve David.

The Lord saved David in everything he undertook.

Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered judgment and justice to all his people.

Joab, son of Zeruiah, was over the army; Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the recorder.

Zadok, son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech, son of Abiathar, were priests; Shavsha was the scribe.

Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was over the Cherethites and Pelethites.

And the first sons of David were at the king’s hand.

[Chapter XIX] Now it happened that Nahash, king of the sons of Ammon, died, and his son reigned in his place.

David said: “I will show kindness to Hanun [Col. 1350C], son of Nahash, for his father showed me kindness.”

And David sent messengers to console him concerning the death of his father.

When they reached the land of the sons of Ammon to console Hanun, the princes of the sons of Ammon said to Hanun:

“Perhaps you think that David has sent comforters to you out of honor for your father. Do you not realize that his servants have come to you in order to explore, investigate, and examine your land?”

Then Hanun shaved David’s servants, cut off their garments from the buttocks to the feet, and sent them away.

When they had departed and reported this to David, he sent to meet them—for they had suffered a great insult—and ordered them to remain at Jericho until their beards grew back; then they were to return.

When the sons of Ammon saw that they had wronged David, Hanun and the rest of the people, they sent a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen for themselves from Mesopotamia, from Syria Maacah, and from Zobah.

They hired thirty-two thousand chariots, as well as the king of Maacah with his people. When these arrived, they encamped opposite Medeba.

The sons of Ammon also gathered from their cities and came to battle.

When David heard this, he sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men.

The sons of Ammon came out and drew up their line beside the city gate, while the kings who had come to their aid stood separately in the field.

Joab, realizing that battle was being prepared against him in front and behind [Col. 1351A], selected the bravest men from all Israel and marched against the Syrians.

He placed the rest of the people under the command of his brother Abishai, and they marched against the sons of Ammon.

He said: “If the Syrians prevail against me, you shall come to my aid; but if the sons of Ammon prevail against you, I will be your protection.

Be strong, and let us act bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. The Lord will do what is good in his sight.”

So Joab and the people who were with him advanced against the Syrians for battle, and he routed them.

When the sons of Ammon saw that the Syrians had fled, they too fled before Abishai, Joab’s brother, and entered the city.

Joab also returned to Jerusalem.

When the Syrians saw that they had been defeated before Israel, they sent messengers and brought the Syrians who were beyond the River.

Shophach, commander of Adadezer’s army, was their leader.

When this was reported to David, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, rushed upon them, and drew up his line against them while they fought.

The Syrians fled before Israel.

David killed seven thousand Syrian chariots and forty thousand foot soldiers, as well as Shophach, commander of the army.

When the servants of Adadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they defected to David and served him. Syria was unwilling thereafter to assist the sons of Ammon.

[Chapter XX] After the year had come around, at the time when kings usually go out to war, Joab gathered the army and the military forces, devastated the land of the sons of Ammon, marched on, and besieged Rabbah.

David, however, remained in Jerusalem while Joab struck Rabbah and destroyed it.

David took the crown of Milcom from its head, and found in it a talent’s weight of gold and very precious gems; he made a diadem for himself from it. He also took a great quantity of the city’s plunder.

He led out the people who were in it, and made threshing sledges, drags, and iron carts pass over them, so that they were cut apart and crushed.

Thus he did to all the cities of the sons of Ammon. Then he returned with all his people to Jerusalem.

After this, war broke out at Gezer against the Philistines. In it Sibbecai the Hushathite struck Sippai, who was of the family of the Rephaim, and subdued them.

Another war was waged against the Philistines. In it Adeodatus, son of Saltus the Lehemite, struck the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver’s beam.

[Note: [Col. 1351D] The Memmian Canon reads this passage in this way in the sacred text, with the following variant readings noted in the margin: elsewhere “Bethlehemite,” elsewhere “Helomite.” The false Jerome, in the Hebrew Questions concerning this passage, notes how the present clause is read in Hebrew: “In which he struck Elhanan.” In Hebrew, he says, it is written: “Elhanan son of Jair, the Lehemite, brother.” *Jair*, meaning “watchful,” is written in Kings as *Hur son of Jare*, which means “forest”; in Kings it is written “Bethlehemite,” in Chronicles “Lehemite brother,” and so forth. See II Samuel, chapter XXI, verse 19. Let the reader note that the readings of the Hebrew Questions differ in manuscripts and printed books; if life permits, we shall discuss these at their proper places. MART.]

Another battle took place at Gath, where there was a man of extraordinary height, having six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot—that is, twenty-four altogether. He too was descended from the family of the Rephaim.

[Col. 1352A] He blasphemed Israel, and Jonathan, son of Shimeah, David’s brother, struck him.

These were the descendants of the Rephaim in Gath, who fell by the hand of David and his servants.

[Chapter XXI] Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to number Israel.

David said to Joab and to the leaders of the people: “Go and number Israel from Beersheba to Dan, and bring me the number, so that I may know it.”

Joab replied: “May the Lord increase his people a hundredfold beyond their present number. Are they not all, my lord the king, your servants? Why does my lord seek this, so that it may be counted as a sin against Israel?”

But the king’s word prevailed. Joab went out and traveled through all Israel, then returned to Jerusalem.

David gave the number of those whom he had counted, and the total number of all Israel was found to be one million one hundred thousand men who drew the sword.

Of Judah there were [Note: [Col. 1351D] The copies of the Canon retain this number, as do all the Latin manuscripts that we examined. The printed editions read, in accordance with the Hebrew, “four hundred and seventy thousand.” The Arabic translator, however, has the larger number, namely “five hundred and seventy thousand.” The author of the Hebrew Questions, whom we have often mentioned, attempts to reconcile discrepancies of this kind occurring in the books of Kings and Chronicles. MART.] three hundred and seventy thousand warriors.

[Col. 1352B] He did not number Levi and Benjamin, because Joab unwillingly carried out the king’s command.

But what had been commanded displeased God, and he struck Israel.

David said to God: “I have sinned greatly by doing this. I beg you, take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted foolishly.”

And the Lord spoke to Gad, David’s seer, saying: “Go and speak to David, and say to him:

‘Thus says the Lord: I offer you three choices. Choose whichever one you wish, and I will do it to you.’

When Gad came to David, he said to him: “Thus says the Lord: Choose what you wish:

either three years of famine; or three months of fleeing before your enemies, unable to escape their sword; or three days of the sword of the Lord and death [Alt. pestilence] moving through the land, with the angel of the Lord killing throughout all the territories of Israel.

[Note: [Col. 1352D] The printed editions read “pestilence.” The Hebrew word *deber*, or *dever*, signifies both death and pestilence. MART.]

[Col. 1352C] Now therefore, see what answer I shall give to the one who sent me.”

David said to Gad: “I am greatly distressed on every side. But it is better for me to fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercies are many, than into human hands.”

So the Lord sent pestilence upon Israel, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell.

He also sent an angel to Jerusalem to strike it.

When it was being struck, the Lord saw and relented concerning the magnitude of the evil.

And he commanded the angel who was striking: “Enough; now let your hand cease.”

The angel of the Lord was standing beside the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

[Note: [Col. 1352D] The Memmian Canon has *Areuna* written twice in the body of the text, while the margin has *Ornan*. See what has been noted at the end of II Samuel concerning this name, which there is called *Areuna*. MART.]

David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of the Lord standing between earth and heaven, with his drawn sword in his hand, turned against Jerusalem.

Then he and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces to the ground.

David said to God: “Was it not I who commanded the people to be numbered? I am the one who sinned; I am the one who did evil. What has this flock done? Lord my God, I beg you, let your hand be turned against me and against my father’s house, but let your people not be struck.”

The angel of the Lord commanded Gad to tell David that he should go up and build an altar to the Lord God on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

David therefore went up according to the word Gad had spoken to him in the name of the Lord.

When Ornan looked up and saw the angel, he and his four sons with him hid themselves, for at that time he was threshing wheat on the threshing floor.

When David came to Ornan, Ornan saw him, went out from the threshing floor to meet him, and bowed before him with his face to the ground.

David said to him: “Give me the site of your threshing floor, so that I may build an altar to the Lord on it. Take from me as much silver as it is worth, so that the plague may cease from the people.”

Ornan said to David: “Take it, and let my lord the king do whatever pleases him. I also give the oxen for burnt offerings, the threshing sledges for wood, and the wheat for the offering. I give everything freely.”

King David said to Ornan: “By no means; rather, I will pay you its full value in silver. For I may not take what is yours and offer to the Lord burnt offerings that cost me nothing.”

So David gave Ornan six hundred shekels of gold for the site, according to a very exact weight.

And David built an altar there to the Lord, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called upon the Lord; and he answered him with fire from heaven upon the altar of the burnt offering.

Then the Lord commanded the angel, and he returned his sword to its sheath.

Immediately, when David saw that the Lord had answered him on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed victims there.

The tabernacle of the Lord, which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offerings were at that time on the high place at Gibeon.

David could not go to the altar to entreat God there, because he had been terrified by excessive fear when he saw the sword of the angel of the Lord.

[Chapter XXII] David said: “This is the house of God, and this is the altar for the burnt offering of Israel.”

And he ordered all the foreigners in the land of Israel to be gathered, and appointed them as stonecutters to quarry and dress stones for the building of the house of God.

David also prepared a great quantity of iron for the nails of the doors and for the clamps and joints, as well as an uncountable weight of bronze.

The cedar wood that the Sidonians and Tyrians had brought to David could not be estimated.

David said: “Solomon my son is young and delicate, but the house that I wish to build for the Lord must be such that it is renowned in all the regions. Therefore I will prepare what he needs.”

For this reason, before his death, he prepared all the expenses.

He summoned his son Solomon and commanded him to build a house for the Lord God of Israel.

David said to Solomon: “My son, it was my intention to build a house in honor of the name of the Lord my God, but the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘You have shed much blood and fought very many wars; you cannot build a house in honor of my name, because you have shed so much blood before me.’

The son who will be born to you shall be a man of profound peace. For I will give him rest from all his enemies on every side; therefore he shall be called ‘Peaceful.’ I will give peace and quiet to Israel throughout all his days.

He shall build a house in honor of my name. He shall be a son to me, and I will be a father to him; and I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever.

Now therefore, my son, may the Lord be with you. Prosper and build the house of the Lord your God, as he has spoken concerning you.

May the Lord also give you wisdom and understanding, so that you may govern Israel and keep the law of the Lord your God.

For then you will prosper, if you keep the commandments and judgments that the Lord commanded Moses to teach Israel.

Be strong and act bravely; do not fear or be dismayed.

Behold, with my very limited means I have prepared resources for the house of the Lord: one hundred thousand talents of gold and one million talents of silver. As for bronze and iron, their weight cannot be measured, for their quantity is beyond reckoning. I have prepared wood and stones for all the expenses.

You also have a great many craftsmen: stonecutters, masons, workers in wood, and men highly skilled in every craft [Col. 1354B] needed for the work—in gold, silver, bronze, and iron, beyond number.

Rise, therefore, and act, and the Lord will be with you.”

David also commanded all the leaders of Israel to assist his son Solomon.

“You see,” he said, “that the Lord your God is with you, that he has given you rest on every side, that he has delivered all your enemies into your hands, and that the land has been subjected before the Lord and before his people.

Therefore devote your hearts and souls to seeking the Lord your God.

Rise and build the sanctuary of the Lord God, so that the ark of the covenant of the Lord and the vessels consecrated to the Lord may be brought into the house being built in honor of the Lord’s name.”

[Chapter XXIII] David, now old and full of days, made his son Solomon king over Israel.

He gathered all the leaders of Israel, and the priests [Col. 1354C] and Levites.

The Levites were counted from thirty years of age and above, and thirty-eight thousand men were found.

[Note: [Col. 1353D] Some manuscripts, including certain ones examined by Martianay, have “twenty” instead of “thirty.” A little farther below, in this same chapter, the number of the sons of Levi from twenty years and above will also be reckoned. MART.]

Of these, twenty-four thousand were selected and assigned to the service of the house of the Lord; six thousand were officials and judges.

There were also four thousand gatekeepers, and an equal number of singers praising the Lord with instruments that David had made for singing.

David divided them into the courses of the sons of Levi—namely, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

The sons of Gershon: Ladan and Shimei.

The sons of Ladan: the chief Jahiel, and Zetham and Joel—three.
