The sons of Shimei: Shelomith, Haziel, and Haran—three. These were the heads of the families of Ladan.

The sons of Shimei were Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah—four.

Jahath was the first, Zina the second.

Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, and therefore they were counted as one family and one household.

The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel—four.

The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses.

Aaron was set apart to minister in the Holy of Holies, he and his sons forever, to burn incense before the Lord according to its rite and to bless his name forever.

The sons of Moses, the man of God, were also counted among the tribe of Levi.

The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer.

The son of Gershom: Shubael, the first.

The sons of Eliezer: Rehabiah, the first; and Eliezer had no other sons.

[Col. 1355A] The sons of Rehabiah became exceedingly numerous.

The son of Izhar: Shelomith, the first.

The sons of Hebron: Jeriah, the first; Amariah, the second; Jahaziel, the third; and Jekameam, the fourth.

The sons of Uzziel: Micah, the first, and Isshiah, the second.

The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi.

The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish.

Eleazar died and had no sons, only daughters; and the sons of Kish, their brothers, took them as wives.

The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth—three.

These were the sons of Levi according to their clans and families, heads by their courses, according to the number of each individual head, who performed the service of the house of the Lord from twenty years of age and above.

For David said: “The Lord God of Israel has given rest to his people, and Jerusalem as a dwelling place forever.

The Levites will no longer be required to carry the tabernacle and all its vessels for service.”

According to David’s final instructions, the sons of Levi from twenty years of age and above were to be counted.

They were to serve under the sons of Aaron in the service of the house of the Lord, in the courts, chambers, place of purification, sanctuary, and all the works of service in the temple of the Lord.

The priests were responsible for the showbread, the offering of fine flour, the unleavened cakes, [Note: [Col. 1355D] The Hebrew *velammurbacheth*, which means “for roasting,” is rendered incorrectly by the false Jerome, who says: “What appears in certain books as ‘for boiling fine flour,’ and in others merely as ‘for boiling,’ is an error.” In Hebrew, *fine flour* is not found in this passage, because fine flour has already been mentioned somewhat earlier; instead, “for roasting” is written in Hebrew, with ears of grain understood. For when the firstfruits of the ears were brought, they were roasted and the grains eaten. This kind of food is commonly called *graneae*. He immediately adds: “In certain books it is found as ‘over every weight and measure’; but in Hebrew in this passage ‘weight’ is not present, only ‘measure,’ expressly mentioned twice,” and so forth. This is what he says; but we considered it more appropriate to follow the testimony of all the manuscript copies than to adhere to this writer. MART.] the frying pan, the boiled fine flour, and everything concerning every weight and measure.

The Levites were to stand in the morning to give thanks and sing to the Lord, and likewise in the evening, both at the offering of the burnt offerings of the Lord and on Sabbaths, new moons, and the remaining solemn feasts, according to the number and rites appropriate to each matter, continually before the Lord.

They were to guard the observances of the tabernacle of the covenant, the rite of the sanctuary, and the observances of the sons of Aaron, their brothers, in order to minister in the house of the Lord.

[Chapter XXIV] These were the divisions of the sons of Aaron:

The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

Nadab and Abihu died before their father without children, and Eleazar and Ithamar exercised the priesthood.

David divided them—that is, Zadok from the sons of Eleazar and Ahimelech from the sons of Ithamar—according to their courses and service.

The sons of Eleazar were found to have many more chief men than the sons of Ithamar.

He divided them—that is, the sons of Eleazar—into sixteen chief families, and the sons of Ithamar into eight families and households.

He divided both groups into families by lot, for there were leaders of the sanctuary and leaders of God, both from the sons of Eleazar and from the sons of Ithamar.

Shemaiah, son of Nethanel, the Levite scribe, recorded them in the presence of the king, the leaders, Zadok the priest, [Col. 1355D] Ahimelech son of Abiathar, and the heads of the priestly and Levitical families: one household was assigned to Eleazar, which presided over the others, and another household to Ithamar, which had the rest under it.

The first lot came out for Jehoiarib,

the second for Jedaiah,

the third for Harim,

the fourth for Seorim,

the fifth for Malchijah,

the sixth for Mijamin,

[Col. 1356A] the seventh for Hakkoz,

the eighth for Abijah,

the ninth for Jeshua,

the tenth for Shecaniah,

the eleventh for Eliashib,

the twelfth for Jakim,

the thirteenth for Huppah,

the fourteenth for Jeshebeab,

the fifteenth for Bilgah,

the sixteenth for Immer,

the seventeenth for Hezir,

the eighteenth for Aphses,

the nineteenth for Pethahiah,

the twentieth for Jehezekel,

the twenty-first for Jachin,

the twenty-second for Gamul,

the twenty-third for Delaiah,

the twenty-fourth for Maaziah.

These were their courses according to their services, so that they might enter the house of the Lord according to their rite, under the authority of Aaron their father, as the Lord God of Israel had commanded.

Among the remaining sons of Levi, from the sons of Amram there was Shubael; from the sons of Shubael, Jedaiah.

From the sons of Rehabiah, the chief was Isshiah.

From Izhar, the son was Shelomoth, and the son of Shelomoth was Jahath.

His son was Jeriah; Amariah was the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.

The son of Uzziel was Micah; the son of Micah was Shamir.

Micah’s brother was Isshiah; the son of Isshiah was Zechariah.

The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi.

The son of Uzziah was Beno.

The sons of Merari were Uzziah, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri.

Mahli’s son was Eleazar, who had no children.

The son of Kish was Jerahmeel.

The sons of Mushi were Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth.

[Col. 1356C] These were the sons of Levi according to their household families.

They too cast lots against their brothers, the sons of Aaron, in the presence of King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the priestly and Levitical families, both great and small. The lot divided everyone equally.

[Chapter XXV] David and the commanders of the army set apart for service the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, who were to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals, serving in their appointed office according to their number.

The sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asarelah, sons of Asaph, under the authority of Asaph, who prophesied at the king’s direction.

Jeduthun: the sons of Jeduthun—Gedaliah, Zori, Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah—six, under the authority of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre over those giving thanks and praising the Lord.

Heman: the sons of Heman—Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shubael, Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Othir, and Mahazioth.

All these were the sons of Heman, the king’s seer, in the words of God, to exalt the horn. God gave Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.

All these, under the authority of their father, were assigned to sing in the temple of the Lord with cymbals, harps, and lyres, for the service of the house of the Lord under the direction of the king—namely, Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman.

[Col. 1357A] Their number, together with their brothers who were trained in the song of the Lord—all teachers—was two hundred and eighty-eight.

They cast lots for their courses equally, the elder and the younger alike, the learned together with the unlearned.

The first lot came out for Joseph, who was of Asaph.

The second for Gedaliah, for him, his sons, and his brothers—twelve.

The third for Zaccur, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The fourth for Izri, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The fifth for Nethaniah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The sixth for Bukkiah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The seventh for Jesharelah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The eighth for Jeshaiah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The ninth for Mattaniah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The tenth for Shimei, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The eleventh for Azarel, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

[Col. 1357B] The twelfth for Hashabiah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The thirteenth for Shubael, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The fourteenth for Mattithiah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The fifteenth for Jeremoth, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The sixteenth for Hananiah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The seventeenth for Joshbekashah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The eighteenth for Hanani, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The nineteenth for Mallothi, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The twentieth for Eliathah, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The twenty-first for Othir, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

[Col. 1357C] The twenty-second for Giddalti, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The twenty-third for Mahazioth, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

The twenty-fourth for Romamti-ezer, for his sons and brothers—twelve.

[Chapter XXVI] The divisions of the gatekeepers were as follows: among the Korahites, Meshelemiah, son of Kore, from the sons of Asaph.

The sons of Meshelemiah: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth, Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, and Elioenai the seventh.

The sons of Obed-edom: Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth, Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, and Peullethai the eighth, because the Lord blessed him.

Shemiah’s sons were heads of their families, for they were mighty men.

The sons of Shemaiah were Othni, Raphael, Obed, and Elzabad, his brothers, mighty men; as well as Elihu and Semachiah.

All these were from the sons of Obed-edom: they, their sons, and their brothers, mighty men fit for service—sixty-two from Obed-edom.

The sons and brothers of Meshelemiah, all strong men, numbered eighteen.

From Hosa, that is, from the sons of Merari, there was Shimri as chief. He had not been the firstborn, but his father had appointed him chief. Hilkiah was second, Tebaliah third, and Zechariah fourth. All these were Hosa’s sons and brothers—thirteen.

These were divided among the gatekeepers, so that they and their brothers might serve continually as heads of the guard in the house of the Lord.

Lots were cast equally, for small and great alike, by their families, for each of the gates.

The eastern lot fell to Shelemiah. For his son Zechariah [Col. 1358A], a prudent and learned man, the northern sector fell by lot.

Obed-edom and his sons received the southern sector, where the council of the elders of the house was located.

Shuppim and Hosa received the western sector, beside the gate leading toward the road of ascent, guard opposite guard.

On the east there were six Levites; on the north, four each day, and similarly on the south, four each day; and where the council was located, two by two.

At the gatekeepers’ chambers on the west there were four on the road and two at each chamber.

These were the divisions of the gatekeepers, the sons of Korah and Merari.

Ahijah was over the treasuries of the house of God and the holy vessels.

The sons of Ladan, sons of Gershon: from Ladan, the heads of families were Ladan and the Gershonite Jehieli.

The sons of Jehieli were Zetham, Joel, and their brothers, who were over the treasuries of the house of the Lord.

The Amramites, Izharites, Hebronites, and Uzzielites.

Shubael, son of Gershom and grandson of Moses, was in charge of the treasuries.

His brothers included Eliezer, whose son was Rehabiah, whose son was Isaiah, whose son was Joram, whose son was Zichri, and whose son was Shelomith.

Shelomith himself and his brothers were over the treasuries of the holy things that King David, the heads of families, the tribunes, the centurions, and the commanders of the army had consecrated from the spoils of war and the plunder of battles for the restoration and equipment of the temple of the Lord.

Samuel the seer, Saul son of Kish, Abner son of Ner, and Joab son of Zeruiah had consecrated all these things; everything was entrusted to the care of Shelomith and his brothers.

The Izharites were under the authority of Chenaniah and his sons, for external affairs concerning Israel, to instruct and judge them.

[Col. 1358C] From the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brothers—one thousand seven hundred mighty men—were over Israel west of the Jordan in all the work of the Lord and in the king’s service.

The head of the Hebronites was Jeriah, according to their families and clans.

In the fortieth year of David’s reign they were counted, and mighty men were found in Jazer of Gilead, together with two thousand seven hundred of his brothers, men of mature age, heads of families.

King David appointed them over the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh for every service of God and of the king.

[Chapter XXVII] The sons of Israel, according to their number—the heads of families, tribunes, centurions, and officers who served the king according to their divisions, entering and leaving service each month of the year—each had twenty-four thousand men under them.

[Col. 1358D] Over the first division, for the first month, was Jashobeam, son of Zabdiel, with twenty-four thousand under him.

He was of the sons of Perez and chief of all the commanders of the army in the first month.

The division for the second month was under Dodai the Ahohite, with another named Mikloth after him, who commanded part of the army of twenty-four thousand.

The commander of the third division, for the third month, was Benaiah, son of Jehoiada the priest; his division numbered twenty-four thousand.

This was the Benaiah who was mightiest among the thirty and stood over the thirty; the commander of his division was his son Ammizabad.

The fourth, for the fourth month, was Asahel, Joab’s brother, followed by his son Zebadiah; his division numbered twenty-four thousand.

The fifth, for the fifth month, was the commander Shamhuth the Izrahite; his division numbered twenty-four thousand.

[Col. 1359A] The sixth, for the sixth month, was Ira, son of Ikkesh the Tekoite; his division numbered twenty-four thousand.

The seventh, for the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, from the sons of Ephraim; his division numbered twenty-four thousand.

The eighth, for the eighth month, was Sibbecai the Hushathite, from the family of Zerah; his division numbered twenty-four thousand.

The ninth, for the ninth month, was Abiezer the Anathothite, from the sons of Benjamin; his division numbered twenty-four thousand.

The tenth, in the tenth month, was Marai, himself a Netophathite of the stock of Zarai; and in his division were twenty-four thousand.

The eleventh, in the eleventh month, was Benaiah the Pharathonite, of the sons of Ephraim; and in his division were twenty-four thousand.

The twelfth, in the twelfth month, was Holdai the Netophathite, of the stock of Gothoniel; and in his division were twenty-four thousand.

Now over the tribes were these leaders: over the Reubenites, Eliezer son of Zichri;

over the Simeonites, Shephatiah son of Maacah;

[Col. 1359B] over the Levites, Hashabiah son of Kemuel;

over the Aaronites, Zadok;

over Judah, Elihu, David’s brother;

over Issachar, Omri son of Michael;

over the Zebulunites, Ishmaiah son of Obadiah;

over the Naphtalites, Jeremoth son of Azriel;

over the sons of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Azaziah;

over the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joel son of Pedaiah;

and over the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Jaddo son of Zechariah;

over Benjamin, Jasiel son of Abner;

and over Dan, Azarel son of Jeroham.

These were the leaders of the sons of Israel.

David did not wish to number those who were under twenty years of age, because the Lord had said that he would multiply Israel like the stars of heaven.

Joab son of Zeruiah had begun to number them, but did not finish, because wrath had fallen upon Israel on account of this; and therefore the number of those who had been counted was not entered [Col. 1359C] in the official records of King David.

Over the king’s treasuries was Azmoth son of Adiel. Over the treasuries that were in the cities, villages, and towers was Jonathan son of Uzziah.

Over the agricultural work, and over the farmers who cultivated the land, was Ezri son of Chelub.

Over the cultivators of the vineyards was Shimeiah the Ramathite; and over the wine-cellars was Zabdi [Note: [Col. 1359D] Thus the Regius and Colbertinus Aniciensis manuscripts read in the first hand; others, together with the printed editions, read “Zabdias the Aphonite,” which seems to have arisen from a scribal error: the scribes should have joined the final *s* of *Zabdias* with the beginning of the following *Aphonites*. In the present Hebrew text it is written “[Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], Zabdi Assiphmi,” with some letters altered and intermingled. MART.] the Saphonite.

Over the olive groves and sycamore trees that were in the lowlands was Baal-hanan the Gederite.

Over the oil stores was Joash.

Over the herds that grazed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite.

Over the cattle in the valleys was Shaphat son of Adlai.

Over the camels was Obil the Ishmaelite.

Over the donkeys was Jehdeiah the Meronothite.

Over the sheep also was Jaziz the Hagrite [Alternative reading: Hagarenite].

All these were the officials over King David’s property.

Jonathan, David’s uncle, was a counselor, an intelligent and learned man;

he and Jehiel son of Hachmoni were with the king’s sons.

Ahithophel was also the king’s counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king’s friend.

After Ahithophel came Jehoiada son of Benaiah, and Abiathar.

The commander of the king’s army was Joab.

## Chapter XXVIII

David therefore summoned all the leaders of Israel, the chiefs of the tribes, and the commanders of the divisions [Col. 1360A] who served the king, together with the tribunes and centurions, those who were over the king’s property and possessions, his sons with the eunuchs, and the powerful and strongest men in the army of Jerusalem.

When the king had risen and was standing, he said:

“Hear me, my brothers and my people. I had intended to build a house in which the ark of the covenant of the Lord and the footstool of our God’s feet might rest, and I prepared everything for its construction.

“But God said to me: ‘You shall not build a house for my name, because you are a man of war and have shed blood.’

“Yet the Lord God of Israel chose me from my entire father’s house to be king over Israel forever. For he chose leaders from Judah;

and from the house of Judah, my father’s house; and from my father’s sons, he was pleased to choose me as king over all Israel.

“Moreover, among my sons—for the Lord has given me many sons—he chose my son Solomon to sit [Col. 1360B] on the throne of the kingdom of the Lord over Israel.

“And he said to me: ‘Solomon your son shall build my house and my courts, for I have chosen him as my son, and I will be his father.

“‘I will establish his kingdom forever, if he perseveres in keeping my commandments and judgments, as at this day.’

“Now, therefore, before the whole assembly of Israel, with the Lord our God listening, keep and seek out all the commandments of the Lord our God, so that you may possess the good land and leave it to your sons after you forever.

“And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a perfect heart and a willing spirit.

“For the Lord searches every heart and understands every thought of the mind.

“If you seek him, you will find him; but if you abandon him, he will cast you away forever.

“Now, therefore, since the Lord has chosen you to build [Col. 1360C] a house for the sanctuary, take courage and complete it.”

David then gave Solomon his son the plan of the vestibule, the temple, the storerooms, the upper chambers, the rooms in the inner sanctuary, and the house of the mercy seat;

and likewise the plan of everything he had conceived concerning the courts and the chambers around them, the treasuries of the house of the Lord, and the treasuries of the sacred things;

also the divisions of the priests and Levites, for every service of the house of the Lord, and for all the vessels used in the ministry of the temple of the Lord.

He specified the weight of gold for each vessel used in the ministry, and likewise the weight of silver according to the different kinds of vessels and works.

He also specified gold for the golden lampstands and their lamps, according to the measure of each lampstand and its lamps.

Likewise, for the silver lampstands and their lamps, according to the different measurements, he assigned the weight of silver [Col. 1360D];

and he gave gold for the tables of the presentation-bread, according to the different tables, and likewise silver for the other silver tables.

For the forks, bowls, and censers he assigned a weight of the purest gold; [Note: [Col. 1360D] In the Hebrew exemplar there is read [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], a name more likely of Chaldean than Hebrew origin, which occurs twice in Ezra, in chapters 2 and 8, and is rendered “bowl” by the same translator in the Vulgate. Jerome, however, by changing a single little letter—letters that differ only in size—reads [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text] and interprets it as “little lions.” MART.]

and for the golden “little lions,” according to the required size, he distributed the weight for each little lion.

Similarly, for the silver lions he set apart different weights of silver.

For the altar on which incense was burned he gave the purest gold [Col. 1361A], so that from it a likeness might be made of the chariot of the cherubim, whose wings were outspread and covered the ark of the covenant of the Lord.

“‘All this,’ he said, ‘came to me in writing from the hand of the Lord, so that I might understand all the works of the pattern.’

“David also said to Solomon his son: ‘Act manfully, take courage, and do it. Do not fear or be dismayed.

“For the Lord my God will be with you, and he will not abandon you or forsake you until you complete all the work of the ministry of the house of the Lord.

“‘Behold, the divisions of the priests and Levites are ready to assist you in every ministry of the house of the Lord; and the leaders and the people alike know how to carry out all your commands.’”

## Chapter XXIX

King David then said to the whole assembly:

“God has chosen Solomon my son alone, while he is still a boy and tender; but the work is great, for a dwelling is not being prepared for a human being [Col. 1361B], but for God.

“I have prepared with all my strength the expenses for the house of my God: gold for the golden vessels, silver for the silver ones, bronze for the bronze ones, iron for the iron ones, and wood for the wooden ones; onyx stones, stones like stibium, stones of various colors, every precious stone, and Parian marble in great abundance.

“Moreover, in addition to what I have given for the house of my God from my own property, I give gold and silver for the temple of my God, besides what I have prepared for the holy house.

“Three thousand talents of gold from the gold of Ophir, and seven thousand talents of refined silver, for gilding the walls of the temple.

“Wherever gold is needed, let the work be done with gold; wherever silver is needed, with silver, by the hands of the craftsmen.

“And if anyone offers willingly, let him fill his hand today and offer whatever he wishes to the Lord.”

Then the heads of families, the leaders of the tribes of Israel, the tribunes and centurions, and the officials over the king’s possessions made their promises.

They gave for the work of the house of God five thousand talents of gold and ten thousand gold coins; ten thousand talents of silver, eighteen thousand talents of bronze, and one hundred thousand talents of iron.

And wherever stones were found, they gave them to the treasury of the house of the Lord, through the hand of Jehiel the Gershonite.

The people rejoiced when they made their voluntary promises, because they offered them to the Lord with their whole heart.

King David also rejoiced with great joy and blessed the Lord before the whole multitude, saying:

“Blessed are you, Lord, God of Israel our father, from eternity to eternity.

“Yours, Lord, are greatness, power, glory, victory, and praise.

“For everything in heaven and on earth is yours. Yours, Lord, is the kingdom, and you are above all [Col. 1361D] rulers.

“Riches and glory are yours; you rule over all. In your hand are strength and power; in your hand are greatness and dominion over all.

“Now, therefore, our God, we confess to you and praise your glorious name.

“Who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to promise you all these things?

“All things are yours; and what we have received from your hand, we have given to you.

“For we are strangers before you and sojourners, like all our fathers.

“Our days upon the earth are like a shadow, and there is no delay.

“Lord our God, all this abundance that we have prepared [Col. 1362A] for the building of a house for your holy name is from your hand, and all things are yours.

“I know, my God, that you test hearts and love sincerity; therefore, in the sincerity of my heart I have gladly offered all these things.

“And I have seen your people, who are found here, offer gifts to you with immense joy.

“Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, preserve forever this disposition of their hearts, and may this inclination always remain in their reverence for you.

“Give also to Solomon my son a perfect heart, so that he may keep your commandments, testimonies, and ordinances, and do everything, and build the temple whose expenses I have prepared.”

David then commanded the whole assembly:

“Bless the Lord our God.”

And the whole assembly blessed the Lord, the God of their fathers; they bowed down and worshiped God [Col. 1362B], and afterward the king.

They sacrificed victims to the Lord and offered holocausts on the following day: one thousand bulls, one thousand rams, and one thousand lambs, with their libations, and with great abundance according to the entire rite, for all Israel.

They ate and drank before the Lord on that day with great joy.

They anointed Solomon son of David a second time.

They anointed him before the Lord as ruler, and Zadok as high priest.

Solomon sat upon the throne of the Lord as king in place of David his father, and everyone was pleased; all Israel obeyed him.

All the leaders, powerful men, and all the sons of King David likewise pledged their allegiance and became subject to King Solomon.

Thus the Lord magnified Solomon over all Israel and gave him royal glory such as no king of Israel had possessed before him.

David son of Jesse therefore reigned over all [Col. 1362C] Israel. The days during which he reigned over Israel were forty years:

he reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.

He died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and glory. Solomon his son reigned in his place.

The earlier and later deeds of King David are written in the book of Samuel the Seer, in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the volume of Gad the Seer, together with the records of his entire reign, his valor, and the times that passed under him, whether in Israel or in all the kingdoms of the earth.

## Book II — Chapter I

Solomon son of David was strengthened in his kingdom, [Note: [Col. 1361] In manuscript codices these two words, “his God,” are omitted, although they are found in the Hebrew books. MART.] and the Lord his God was with him and exalted him greatly.

Solomon commanded all Israel—the tribunes, centurions, commanders, judges of all Israel, and heads of families.

He went with the entire assembly to the high place at [Col. 1362D] Gibeon, where the tabernacle of the covenant of God was, which Moses, the servant of God, had made in the wilderness.

David had brought the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place he had prepared for it and where he had set up a tabernacle for it—that is, in Jerusalem.

The bronze altar that Bezalel son of Uri son of Hur had made was there before the tabernacle of the Lord; Solomon and the whole assembly sought it.

Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the tabernacle of the covenant of the Lord and offered a thousand victims upon it.

And behold, that very night God appeared to him and said: “Ask what you wish me to give you.”

Solomon said to God:

“You showed great mercy to David my father [Col. 1363A] and appointed me king in his place.

“Now, therefore, Lord God, let your promise be fulfilled that you made to David my father.

“For you have made me king over your numerous people, who are as innumerable as the dust of the earth.

“Give me wisdom and understanding, so that I may go out before your people and enter among them.

“For who can judge this great people of yours worthily?”

God said to Solomon:

“Because this was pleasing to your heart, and you did not ask for riches, possessions, and glory, nor for the lives of those who hated you, nor did you ask for many days of life, but you asked for wisdom and knowledge so that you might judge my people over whom I have made you king: wisdom and knowledge are granted to you.

“Moreover, I will give you riches, possessions, and glory,

[Col. 1363B] so that no king, either before you or after you, shall be like you.”

Solomon then came from the high place at Gibeon to Jerusalem, before the tabernacle of the covenant, and reigned over Israel.

He gathered chariots and horsemen; he had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed them in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.

The king made silver and gold as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar trees as plentiful as sycamores that grow in great abundance in the lowlands.

Horses were brought to him from Egypt and from Kue by the king’s merchants. They purchased a chariot of horses for six hundred silver coins, and a horse for one hundred fifty.

Likewise, purchases were made from all the kingdoms of the Hittites and from the kings of Syria.

## Chapter II

Solomon resolved to build a house for the name of the Lord [Col. 1363C] and a palace for himself.

He counted seventy thousand men to carry burdens on their shoulders, eighty thousand to quarry stones in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred overseers.

He sent to Huram, king of Tyre, saying:

“As you dealt with David my father and sent him cedar wood so that he could build a house for himself in which he lived, deal likewise with me, so that I may build a house for the name of the Lord my God and dedicate it for burning incense before him, for burning aromatic offerings, for the continual presentation of bread, and for holocausts morning and evening, on Sabbaths, new moons, and festivals of the Lord our God forever, as was commanded Israel.

“The house I wish to build is great, for our God is greater than all gods.

“Who, then, can prevail so as to build him a house worthy of him?

[Col. 1363D] If heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain him, how great am I that I should be able to build him a house?

“But only so that incense may be burned before him.

“Send me, therefore, a skilled man who knows how to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, purple, scarlet, and violet, and who knows how to engrave carvings, together with the craftsmen I have with me in Judah and Jerusalem, whom David my father prepared.

“Send me also cedar, fir, and pine wood from Lebanon; for I know that your servants know how to cut timber from Lebanon.

“My servants will work with your servants, so that a great quantity of timber may be prepared for me.

[Col. 1364A] For the house I wish to build will be exceedingly great and renowned.

“Moreover, I will give your servants who cut the timber, as provisions, twenty thousand kors of wheat, an equal quantity of barley, twenty thousand measures of wine, and twenty thousand measures of oil.”

King Huram of Tyre replied by letter, which he sent to Solomon:

“Because the Lord loved his people, he made you king over them.”

And he added:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who gave King David a wise, learned, sensible, and prudent son, so that he might build a house for the Lord and a palace for himself.

“I am sending you Huram, my wise and most skilled man, my father’s son, the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan, whose father was a Tyrian. He knows how to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, marble, and wood, and in purple, violet, fine linen, and scarlet [Col. 1364B]. He knows how to engrave every kind of sculpture and to devise skillfully whatever may be needed for the work, together with your craftsmen and the craftsmen of my lord David your father.

“Therefore send to your servants the wheat, barley, oil, and wine that you promised, my lord.

“We will cut timber from Lebanon, as much as you require, and bring it by rafts over the sea to Joppa. It will be your responsibility to transport it to Jerusalem.”

Solomon counted all the resident foreigners who were in the land of Israel, after the census that David his father had taken, and they were found to number one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred.

Of these, he appointed seventy thousand to carry burdens on their shoulders and eighty thousand to quarry stones in the mountains; and three thousand six hundred were appointed as overseers of the people’s work.

## Chapter III

Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father, at the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite [Col. 1364C].

He began to build in the second month, in the fourth year of his reign.

These are the foundations Solomon laid for building the house of God: its length, measured in the first standard, was sixty cubits, and its width twenty cubits.

The portico before the front, extending lengthwise along the width of the house, was twenty cubits; its height was one hundred twenty cubits. He overlaid it inside with the purest gold.

He also covered the larger house with panels of fir wood and fastened plates of refined gold throughout. He carved palms and interwoven chainwork in it.

He paved the floor of the temple with the most precious marble, of great beauty.

The gold was of the finest quality; with its plates [Col. 1364D] he covered the house, its beams, posts, walls, and doors, and he carved cherubim on the walls.

He also made the house of the holy of holies: its length, corresponding to the width of the house, was twenty cubits, and its width likewise twenty cubits. He covered it with plates of gold, amounting to about six hundred talents.

He made golden nails as well, each nail weighing fifty shekels, and he covered the upper chambers with gold.

In the house of the holy of holies he also made two cherubim of sculptured work and covered them with gold.

The wings of the cherubim extended twenty cubits, so that one wing was five cubits long and touched the wall of the house, while the other, also five cubits long, touched the wing of the other cherub.

Likewise, the wing of the second cherub was five cubits long [Col. 1365A] and touched the wall, while its other wing, five cubits long, touched the wing of the first cherub.

Thus the wings of both cherubim were outspread and extended twenty cubits. They themselves stood upright on their feet, and their faces were turned toward the outer house.

He also made a veil of violet, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and embroidered cherubim upon it.

Before the doors of the temple he made two pillars thirty-five cubits high.

Their capitals were five cubits high.

He also made something like chainwork in the inner sanctuary and placed it on the capitals of the pillars, together with one hundred pomegranates inserted among the chains.

He set up the pillars in the vestibule of the temple, one on the right and the other on the left. He called the one on the right Jachin and the one on the left Boaz.

## Chapter IV

He also made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high.

[Col. 1365B] He made the cast Sea ten cubits from rim to rim, circular all around; it was five cubits high, and a cord thirty cubits long encircled it.

Below it was a likeness of oxen. Certain external engravings, described as being “ten cubits” [the construction is uncertain], surrounded the belly of the Sea, as it were in two rows. The oxen were cast as part of it.

The Sea rested upon twelve oxen: three faced north, three west, three south, and the remaining three east. The Sea was set upon them, while the hindquarters of the oxen were inward, beneath the Sea.

Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its rim was like the rim of a cup, or like a curved lily. It held three thousand measures.

He also made ten basins and placed five on the right and five on the left, for washing in them everything that was to be offered as a holocaust [Col. 1365C].

The priests washed in the Sea.

He also made ten golden lampstands, according to the pattern in which they had been commanded to be made, and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left.

He also made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left.

He made one hundred golden bowls.

He also made the court of the priests and the great hall, together with doors for the hall, which he overlaid with bronze.

He placed the Sea on the right side, toward the southeast.

Hiram made the cauldrons, shovels, and bowls, and completed all the work of the king in the house of God:

the two pillars, the capitals and moldings, and something like nets to cover the capitals above the moldings;

four hundred pomegranates and two nets, so that two rows of pomegranates were joined to each net [Col. 1365D], covering the moldings and capitals of the pillars;

the bases, and the basins that he placed upon the bases;

one Sea, and twelve oxen beneath the Sea;

the cauldrons, shovels, and bowls.

Hiram his father made all these vessels for Solomon in the house of the Lord, from the purest bronze.

The king cast them in the region of the Jordan, in clay ground, between Succoth and Zeredathah.

There was such a multitude of vessels that the weight of the bronze could not be determined.

Solomon made all the vessels of the house of God: the golden altar, the tables, and the presentation-bread upon them;

the lampstands with their lamps, to give light before the inner sanctuary according to the prescribed rite, from the purest gold;

and certain floral ornaments, lamps, and golden tongs. Everything was made of the purest gold.

[Col. 1366A] He also made incense materials, censers, bowls, and mortars of the purest gold.

He overlaid with gold the doors of the inner temple—that is, of the holy of holies—and the outer doors of the temple.

Thus all the work that Solomon did in the house of the Lord was completed.

## Chapter V

Solomon brought in everything that David his father had dedicated: the silver, gold, and all the vessels, and he placed them in the treasuries of the house of God.

After this he gathered the elders of Israel, all the leaders of the tribes, and the heads of the families of the Israelites in Jerusalem, so that they might bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the city of David, which is Zion.

All the men of Israel came to the king on the festival day of the seventh month.

When all the elders of Israel had come, the Levites carried the ark and brought it in, together with all the furnishings of the tabernacle.

The priests and Levites carried the vessels of the sanctuary that had been in the tabernacle.

[Col. 1366B] King Solomon and the whole assembly of Israel, and all those who had gathered before the ark, sacrificed rams and oxen without number, for the number of victims was immense.

The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord into its place, that is, into the inner sanctuary of the temple, into the holy of holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim. The cherubim spread their wings over the place where the ark had been set and covered the ark and its poles.

The poles by which the ark was carried were somewhat longer, so that their ends were visible before the inner sanctuary; but if someone stood slightly outside, he could not see them.

The ark remained there to the present day.

There was nothing else in the ark except the two tablets that Moses had placed there at Horeb, when the Lord gave the law to the children of Israel as they came out of Egypt.

When the priests came out of the sanctuary—for all the priests who could be found there had sanctified themselves [Col. 1366C]—the divisions and order of their ministries had not yet been distributed among them.

The Levites and the singers, namely those under Asaph, those under Heman, and those under Jeduthun, with their sons and brothers, clothed in fine linen, sounded cymbals, psalteries, and lyres. They stood on the eastern side of the altar, and with them were one hundred twenty priests sounding trumpets.

When all were together—trumpets, voices, cymbals, instruments, and music of every kind—making melody and raising their voices on high, the sound was heard from far away.

When they began to praise the Lord and say, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever,” the house of God was filled with a cloud, and the priests could not stand and minister because of the darkness.

For the glory of the Lord had filled the house of God.

[Col. 1366D] ## Chapter VI

Then Solomon said:

“The Lord promised that he would dwell in darkness. I have built a house for his name, so that he might dwell there forever.”

The king turned his face and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, for the entire crowd stood attentively, and he said:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who has fulfilled by his works what he spoke to David my father, saying:

“‘From the day when I brought my people out of the land of Egypt, I did not choose a city from all the tribes of Israel in which a house would be built for my name.

“‘Nor did I choose any other man to be leader over my people Israel.

“‘But I chose Jerusalem, so that my name might be there, and I chose David to establish him over my people Israel.’

“When it was the desire of David my father to build a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, the Lord said to him:

“‘Because it was your desire to build [Col. 1367A] a house for my name, you have done well to have this desire; but you will not build the house. Rather, your son, who will come forth from your loins, will build the house for my name.’

“Thus the Lord has fulfilled his word that he spoke, and I have risen in place of David my father and sat upon the throne of Israel, as the Lord said; and I have built a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.

“And I have placed there the ark containing the covenant of the Lord, which he made with the children of Israel.”

He then stood before the altar of the Lord, opposite the whole assembly of Israel, and stretched out his hands.

For Solomon had made a bronze platform and placed it in the middle of the hall. It was five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high.

He stood upon it, and then knelt with his knees before the whole assembly of Israel, raising his palms toward heaven, and said:

“Lord God of Israel, there is no God like you in [Col. 1367B] heaven or on earth. You keep the covenant and mercy with your servants who walk before you with their whole heart.

“You have fulfilled for your servant David my father whatever you spoke to him; what you promised with your mouth, you have accomplished by your works, as the present time also proves.

“Now, therefore, Lord God of Israel, fulfill for your servant David my father whatever you spoke, saying: ‘A man shall not fail to be before me, sitting on the throne of Israel,’ provided only that your sons guard their ways and walk in my law, as you have walked before me.

“And now, Lord God of Israel, let the word stand firm that you spoke to your servant David.

“Can it truly be believed that God dwells with human beings on earth? If heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built?

“Yet it was made for this alone: that you might regard the prayer and supplication of your servant, Lord God [Col. 1367C] my God, and hear the prayers that your servant pours out before you; that you might open your eyes over this house by day and by night, over the place in which you promised that your name would be invoked; and that you might hear the prayer which your servant prays in it, and hear the prayers of your servant and your people Israel.

“Whatever person prays in this place, hear him from your dwelling place—from heaven—and be merciful.

“If anyone sins against his neighbor and comes prepared to swear against him, binding himself by a curse before the altar in this house, hear from heaven and judge your servants, so that you repay the wicked by bringing his way upon his own head, and vindicate the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.

“If your people Israel are defeated by their enemies—for they will sin against you—and then, having turned back, repent, implore your name, and pray in this place, hear from heaven, forgive the sin of your people Israel, and restore them to the land [Col. 1367D] that you gave to them and to their fathers.

“If the heavens are shut and rain does not fall because of the sins of the people, and they pray in this place, confess your name, and turn from their sins when you afflict them, hear from heaven, Lord, and forgive the sins of your servants and of your people Israel. Teach them the good way in which they should walk, and give rain to your land, which you gave to your people as a possession.

“If famine arises in the land, or pestilence, blight, mildew, locust, or caterpillar, or if enemies devastate the regions and besiege the gates of the cities, and every plague and sickness afflicts them—if anyone of your people Israel prays, recognizing his plague and sickness, and spreads out his hands in this house, hear from heaven, from your exalted dwelling place, and be merciful. Repay each one according to his ways, for you know what is in his heart.

[Col. 1368A] “For you alone know the hearts of the children of human beings.

“Let them fear you and walk in all your ways throughout all the days that they live upon the face of the land that you gave to our fathers.

“Moreover, if a foreigner who is not of your people Israel comes from a distant land because of your great name, your strong hand, and your outstretched arm, and prays in this place, hear him from heaven, your firm dwelling place, and do everything for which that foreigner calls upon you, so that all the peoples of the earth may know your name, fear you as your people Israel do, and recognize that your name has been invoked over this house that I have built.

“If your people go out to war against their enemies by the way on which you send them, and they worship you facing toward the road on which this city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name stand, hear their prayers and supplication from heaven and vindicate them.

[Col. 1368B] “But if they sin against you—for there is no human being who does not sin—and you become angry with them and deliver them to their enemies, so that their captors carry them away to a distant land or one that is nearby, and if they turn their hearts in the land to which they were taken captive, repent, and pray to you in the land of their captivity, saying, ‘We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have behaved unjustly,’ and if they return to you with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their captivity to which they were carried, and worship you facing toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, and toward the city that you chose and the house that I built for your name,

“then hear their prayers from heaven, from your firm dwelling place; render judgment and forgive your people, though they are sinners.

“For you are my God. Let your eyes, I beg you, be open and your ears attentive to the prayer made in this place.

“Now, therefore, arise, Lord God, into your resting place [Col. 1368C], you and the ark of your strength.

“Let your priests, Lord God, be clothed with salvation, and let your holy ones rejoice in good things.

“Lord God, do not turn away the face of your anointed one; remember the mercies shown to David your servant.”

## Chapter VII

When Solomon had finished pouring out his prayers, fire descended from heaven and consumed the holocausts and victims, and the majesty of the Lord filled the house.

The priests could not enter the temple of the Lord, because the majesty of the Lord had filled the temple of the Lord.

All the children of Israel also saw the fire descending and the glory of the Lord over the house.

They fell prostrate upon the ground, upon the pavement laid with stone, worshiped, and praised the Lord:

“For he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

The king and all the people sacrificed victims before the Lord.

[Col. 1368D] King Solomon then sacrificed twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred twenty thousand rams; and the king and all the people dedicated the house of God.

The priests, meanwhile, stood at their appointed duties, and the Levites with the instruments for the songs of the Lord, which King David had made for praising the Lord: “For his mercy endures forever,” singing David’s hymns with their hands.

Moreover, the priests were sounding the trumpets before them, and all Israel was standing.

Solomon also consecrated the middle of the court before the temple of the Lord, for he had offered there burnt offerings and the fat of peace offerings, because the bronze altar that he had made could not contain the burnt offerings, sacrifices, and fat.

Thus Solomon held the festival at that time for seven days, and all Israel with him—a very great assembly, from the entrance of Hamath to the Torrent of Egypt.

[Col. 1369A] On the eighth day he held an assembly, because he had dedicated the altar for seven days and celebrated the festival for seven days.

Then, on the twenty-third day of the seventh month, he dismissed the people to their tents, rejoicing and glad because of the good that the Lord had done for David, Solomon, and his people Israel.

Solomon completed the house of the Lord and the royal palace, and everything that he had resolved in his heart to do in the house of the Lord and in his own house; and he prospered.

The Lord appeared to him by night and said: “I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice.

“If I shut up the heavens so that rain does not fall, and if I command and order the locust to devour the land, and send pestilence among my people,

“and my people, over whom my name has been invoked, turn back, beseech me, seek my face, and repent of their [Col. 1369B] very evil ways,

“then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sins, and heal their land.

“My eyes also shall be open and my ears attentive to the prayer of the one who prays in this place.

“For I have chosen and sanctified this place, so that my name may be there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall remain there throughout all days.

“You too, if you walk before me as your father David walked, and do everything that I have commanded you, and keep my statutes and judgments,

“then I will establish the throne of your kingdom, as I promised your father David, saying: ‘A man from your line shall not be taken away who is ruler in Israel.’

“But if you turn away and abandon my statutes and commandments, which I have set before you, and go and serve foreign gods and worship them, I shall uproot you from my land, which I gave you,

“and this house, which I have sanctified for my name, I shall cast away from my presence and make it a proverb and an example among all peoples.

“And this house shall become a byword for all who pass by, and they shall say in astonishment: ‘Why has the Lord dealt in this way with this land and this house?’

“And they shall answer: ‘Because they abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of the land of Egypt; they seized foreign gods, worshiped them, and served them.

“‘Therefore all these evils have come upon them.’”

[Chapter VIII] When twenty years had been completed, after Solomon had built the house of the Lord and his own house, he built the cities that Hiram had given to Solomon, and settled the Israelites there.

He also went against Hamath-zobah and captured it.

He built Tadmor in the wilderness and built other very strongly fortified cities in Hamath.

He also built Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon, fortified cities with gates, bars, and bolts.

He built Baalah as well, and all the strongly fortified cities that belonged to Solomon, all the cities for chariots and the cities for cavalry—everything that Solomon desired and planned to build—in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout the land under his authority.

All the people who remained from the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, who were not of Israelite descent—their descendants and those whom the Israelites had not destroyed—Solomon subjected to forced labor as tribute, down to the present day.

But Solomon did not make the Israelites serve in the king’s work, for they were warriors, chief commanders, and commanders of his chariots and cavalry.

All the commanders of King Solomon’s army numbered two hundred fifty; they instructed the people.

He transferred Pharaoh’s daughter from the City of David [Col. 1370A] to the house that he had built for her. For he said:

“My wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, because it is holy, since the ark of the Lord has entered it.”

Then Solomon offered burnt offerings to the Lord on the altar of the Lord that he had built before the portico, so that offerings might be made upon it each day according to the commandment of Moses: on Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days, three times a year—that is, at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Booths.

According to the arrangement of his father David, he appointed the priests to their duties and ministries,

and the Levites to their order, to praise and minister before the priests according to the rite of each day,

and the gatekeepers in their divisions, gate by gate; for this is what David, the man of God, had commanded.

Neither the priests nor the Levites transgressed the king’s commands in anything that he had ordered, [Col. 1370B] including the supervision of the treasuries.

Solomon had all the necessary expenses prepared from the day on which he laid the foundations of the house of the Lord until the day on which he completed it.

Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and Elath, on the shore of the Red Sea, which is in the land of Edom.

Hiram sent him ships through his servants, together with sailors skilled in the sea; and they went with Solomon’s servants to Ophir. From there they brought four hundred fifty talents of gold and delivered it to King Solomon.

[Chapter IX] The queen of Sheba, having heard of Solomon’s fame, came to Jerusalem to test him with riddles, with great wealth, camels bearing spices, a very great quantity of gold, and precious stones.

When she came to Solomon, she spoke with him about everything that was in her heart.

Solomon explained to her everything she had asked; [Col. 1370C] there was nothing that he did not make clear to her.

When she had seen Solomon’s wisdom, the house he had built, the food of his table, the quarters of his servants, the offices of his ministers and their clothing, his cupbearers and their clothing, and the sacrifices that he offered in the house of the Lord, she was utterly overwhelmed with astonishment.

She said to the king: “The report that I heard in my land about your achievements and wisdom is true.

“I did not believe those who told me until I came myself, and my eyes saw and I tested it. Indeed, barely half of your wisdom had been reported to me; you have surpassed the report by your achievements.

“Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants who stand before you continually and hear your wisdom.

“Blessed be the Lord your God, who delighted in setting you upon his throne as king for the Lord your God.

[Col. 1370D] “Because God loves Israel and wishes to preserve it forever, therefore he has made you king over it, so that you may administer judgments and justice.”

She gave the king one hundred twenty talents of gold, an exceedingly great quantity of spices, and very precious stones.

There had never been spices like those that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.

The servants of Hiram, together with Solomon’s servants, also brought gold from Ophir, algum wood, and very precious stones. From the algum wood the king made stairs in the house of the Lord and in the royal palace, as well as lyres and harps for the singers.

Such wood had never before been seen in the land of Judah.

King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she desired and requested, much more than she had brought to him.

Then she returned and went to her own land with her servants.

[Col. 1371A] The weight of the gold that was brought to Solomon each year was six hundred sixty-six talents of gold, apart from the amount brought by the envoys of various nations and by merchants, and by all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the lands who brought gold and silver to Solomon.

King Solomon therefore made two hundred golden spears, using six hundred gold pieces; six hundred gold pieces were spent on each spear.

He also made three hundred golden shields, using three hundred gold pieces for each shield.

The king placed them in the armory that was set among the wooded grounds.

The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with the purest gold. It had six steps by which one ascended to the throne, a golden footstool, two armrests on either side, and two lions standing beside the armrests; there were also twelve other young lions standing upon the six steps, one on each side.

No such throne existed in any kingdom.

[Col. 1371B] All the vessels used at the king’s banquets were gold, and the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold.

For silver was considered worthless in those days.

Indeed, the king’s ships went to Tarshish with Hiram’s servants once every three years, and brought back gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.

Thus Solomon became greater than all the kings of the earth in wealth and glory.

All the kings of the lands desired to see Solomon’s face, to hear the wisdom that God had given him.

They brought him gifts: silver and gold vessels, garments, weapons, spices, horses, and mules, year by year.

Solomon also had forty thousand horses in the stables, and twelve thousand chariots and horsemen; he stationed them in the chariot cities and wherever the king was in Jerusalem.

[Col. 1371C] He exercised authority over all the kings from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines and to the borders of Egypt.

He made silver as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar wood as abundant as the sycamores that grow in the lowlands.

Horses were also brought to him from Egypt and from every region.

The rest of Solomon’s deeds, former and latter, are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the vision of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat.

Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years.

He slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the City of David; and his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.

[Chapter X] Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had gathered there to make him king.

When Jeroboam son of Nebat, who was in Egypt—for he had fled there before Solomon—heard this, he immediately returned.

They summoned him, and he came with all Israel. They spoke to Rehoboam, saying:

“Your father placed a very harsh yoke upon us. Now lighten the harsh service that your father imposed upon us and ease our burden somewhat, so that we may serve you.”

He said to them: “Return to me after three days.”

[Col. 1372A] When the people had departed, he took counsel with the elders who had stood before his father Solomon while he was still alive, saying: “What counsel do you give, so that I may answer this people?”

They said to him: “If you please this people and speak gentle words to them, they will serve you always.”

But he abandoned the counsel of the elders and began to consult the young men who had grown up with him and were in his retinue.

He said to them: “What do you think? What answer should I give this people who said to me: ‘Lighten the yoke that your father imposed upon us’?”

They answered him as young men, having been raised with him in luxury, and said:

“This is what you shall say to the people who said to you: ‘Your father made our yoke heavy; you lighten it.’ This is how you shall answer them:

“‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s loins. My father placed a heavy yoke upon you, but I shall add to your burden. My father scourged you with whips, but I shall scourge you with scorpions.’”

Then Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam on the third day, as he had instructed them.

The king answered harshly, abandoning the counsel of the elders; he spoke according to the young men’s advice: “My father placed a heavy yoke upon you, but I shall make it heavier. My father scourged you with whips, but I shall scourge you with scorpions.”

He did not heed the people’s petitions, for it was God’s will that his word should be fulfilled, the word that he had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

When the king had spoken more harshly to them, all the people answered him:

“We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, Israel! Now look after your own house, David.”

And Israel went to its tents.

[Col. 1372C] Over the Israelites who lived in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned.

King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was in charge of the tribute; but the Israelites stoned him, and he died.

King Rehoboam quickly mounted his chariot and fled to Jerusalem.

Thus Israel revolted from the house of David to this day.

[Note: [Col. 1371D] Certain Bibles printed in the years 1478, 1489, and 1521, as well as others from later times—especially the Nivellian edition printed at Paris in 1573—and also certain manuscripts, according to P. Calmet, append here a passage derived from 3 Kings 12:20: “When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and summoned him. They gathered an assembly and made him king over all Israel; and no one followed the house of David except the tribe of Judah alone.” Lyra also read this in his copy, although the original texts entirely lack it.]

[Chapter XI] Rehoboam came to Jerusalem and summoned the entire house of Judah and Benjamin—one hundred eighty thousand chosen warriors—to fight against Israel and restore the kingdom to himself.

The word of the Lord came to Shemaiah, the man of God, saying: “Speak to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel who are in Judah and Benjamin:

“Thus says the Lord: You shall not go up or fight against your brothers. Let each man return to his house, for this has happened by my will.”

When they heard the word of the Lord, they returned and did not proceed against Jeroboam.

Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem and built fortified cities in Judah. He built Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, Beth-zur, Soco, and Adullam, as well as Gath, Mareshah, and Ziph; he also built Adoraim, Lachish, and Azekah, and Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron, which were in Judah and Benjamin—very strongly fortified cities.

[Col. 1373A] When he had enclosed them with walls, he appointed commanders in them and storehouses for food, that is, for oil and wine.

In every city he also established arsenals of shields and spears, strengthened them with great care, and ruled over Judah and Benjamin.

The priests and Levites who were throughout Israel came to him from all their settlements, abandoning their pasturelands and possessions and moving to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his descendants had expelled them so that they could not serve as priests of the Lord.

Jeroboam had appointed for himself priests of the high places, of demons, and of the calves that he had made.

Moreover, from all the tribes of Israel, everyone who had set his heart on seeking the Lord God of Israel came to Jerusalem to sacrifice their offerings before the Lord, the God of their fathers.

They strengthened the kingdom of Judah and confirmed Rehoboam son of Solomon for three years, for they walked in the ways of David and Solomon for only three years.

Rehoboam took as wife Mahalath, daughter of Jerimoth, son of David; and Abihail, daughter of Eliab, son of Jesse. She bore him Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.

After her he took Maacah, daughter of Absalom, who bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.

Rehoboam loved Maacah daughter of Absalom more than all his wives and concubines.

For he had taken eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.

He appointed Abijah son of Maacah as chief, commander over his brothers, for he intended to make him king, since he was wiser and more powerful than all his sons.

Throughout all the territories of Judah and Benjamin and in all the fortified cities, he provided them with abundant provisions and sought many wives for them.

[Chapter XII] When Rehoboam’s kingdom had been strengthened and fortified, he abandoned the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him.

In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem—because they had sinned against the Lord—with twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen. The common people who came with him from Egypt were beyond number: Libyans, Troglodytes, and Ethiopians. He captured the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem.

The prophet Shemaiah entered before Rehoboam and the princes of Judah, who had gathered in Jerusalem while fleeing from Shishak, and said to them:

“Thus says the Lord: You have abandoned me, and I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak.”

The princes of Israel and the king were humbled and said: “The Lord is just.”

When the Lord saw that they had humbled themselves, the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah, saying:

“Because they have humbled themselves, I will not destroy them. I shall grant them a little help, and my wrath shall not be poured out upon Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.

“Nevertheless, they shall serve him, so that they may know the difference between serving me and serving the kingdoms of the lands.”

Shishak king of Egypt then withdrew from Jerusalem, taking away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the royal palace; he carried everything away, including the golden shields that Solomon had made.

In their place the king made bronze shields and handed them over to the commanders of the shield-bearers who guarded the entrance to the palace.

[Col. 1374A] Whenever the king entered the house of the Lord, the shield-bearers came and carried them away, then returned them to their armory.

Nevertheless, because they had humbled themselves, the Lord’s anger turned away from them, and they were not utterly destroyed; for good works were found in Judah.

King Rehoboam was strengthened in Jerusalem and reigned. He was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the Lord had chosen to establish his name there, from among all the tribes of Israel.

His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite.

He did evil and did not set his heart on seeking the Lord.

The former and latter deeds of Rehoboam are written in the books of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer, and are carefully set forth.

Rehoboam and Jeroboam were at war with one another all their days.

[Col. 1374B] Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried in the City of David. His son Abijah reigned in his place.

[Chapter XIII] In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah became king over Judah. He reigned three years in Jerusalem; his mother’s name was Micaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah.

There was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.

When Abijah entered the conflict, he had four hundred thousand highly warlike and chosen men, while Jeroboam drew up against him eight hundred thousand men, themselves chosen and very strong for battle.

[Note: [Col. 1373D] Martianaeus cites three manuscript codices in which forty thousand is read instead of four hundred thousand, and in the following verse eighty instead of eight hundred. The older editions likewise prefer this reading, including the Venetian edition of 1478, another of 1489, the Nuremberg edition of 1521, the Basel edition of Frobenius in 1538, the Paris edition of Robert Estienne in 1546, and many others. The Hebrew text, however, the Septuagint, Josephus, and the more carefully corrected Latin editions agree in assigning four hundred thousand men to Abijah and eight hundred thousand to Jeroboam. This also agrees with the subsequent context, where five hundred thousand valiant men are said to have fallen from Jeroboam’s army.]

Abijah therefore stood upon Mount Zemaraim, which is in Ephraim, and said:

“Hear me, Jeroboam, and all Israel! Do you not know that the Lord God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, to him and to his sons, by a covenant of salt?

“Jeroboam son of Nebat, servant of David’s son Solomon, rose up and rebelled against his lord.

“Worthless men and sons of Belial gathered around him, and they prevailed against Rehoboam son of Solomon.

“Rehoboam was inexperienced and fainthearted, and he could not withstand them.

“Now you say that you can resist the kingdom of the Lord, which he possesses through the sons of David. You have a great multitude of people, as well as golden calves, which Jeroboam made for you as gods.

“You have expelled the priests of the Lord, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and have made priests for yourselves like all the peoples of the lands. Whoever comes and consecrates his hand with a bull, with oxen, and with seven rams becomes a priest of those who are not gods.

“But our Lord is God, and we do not abandon him.

“The priests, the sons of Aaron, minister to the Lord, and the Levites are in their appointed order.

“They offer burnt offerings to the Lord every morning and evening, incense prepared according to the precepts of the law, and the loaves are set upon the purest table.

“With us there is also a golden lampstand and its lamps, to be lit every evening.

“For we keep the commandments of the Lord our God, whom you have abandoned.

“Therefore God is the commander of our army, and his priests are with us, sounding the trumpets and raising the battle cry against you.

“Children of Israel, do not fight against the Lord, the God of your fathers, for it will not prosper you.”

[Col. 1375A] While he was speaking, Jeroboam was secretly arranging an ambush behind them.

When he stood opposite the enemy, he surrounded the unsuspecting Judah with his army.

Judah looked back and saw that battle threatened both from the front and from the rear, and they cried out to the Lord; and the priests began to blow the trumpets.

All the men of Judah shouted, and as they shouted, God terrified Jeroboam and all Israel who stood opposite Abijah and Judah.

The Israelites fled before Judah, and God delivered them into their hands.

Abijah and his people struck them with a great blow, and five hundred thousand valiant men of Israel fell wounded.

The Israelites were humbled at that time, while the people of Judah grew exceedingly strong because they had placed their hope in the Lord, the God of their fathers.

Abijah pursued Jeroboam as he fled and captured his cities: Bethel and its dependent towns, Jeshanah [Col. 1375B] and its dependent towns, and Ephron and its dependent towns.

Jeroboam could no longer resist during Abijah’s days; the Lord struck him, and he died.

After Abijah had strengthened his rule, he took fourteen wives and fathered twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.

The rest of Abijah’s words, ways, and deeds are written with the greatest care in the book of the prophet Iddo.

[Chapter XIV] Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the City of David.

His son Asa reigned in his place. In his days the land had rest for ten years.

Asa did what was good and pleasing in the sight of his God. He overthrew the altars of foreign worship and the high places, broke the sacred pillars, and cut down the sacred groves.

He commanded Judah to seek the Lord, the God of their fathers, to observe the law and all the commandments.

[Col. 1375C] He removed from all the cities of Judah the altars and shrines, and he reigned in peace.

He also built fortified cities in Judah, because the land was at rest and no wars had arisen in his days, since the Lord had granted peace.

He said to Judah: “Let us build these cities, surround them with walls, and strengthen them with towers, gates, and bolts, while everything is quiet from war, because we have sought the Lord, the God of our fathers, and he has granted us peace on every side.”

They built, and there was no hindrance in the construction.

Asa had in his army three hundred thousand shield- and spear-bearers from Judah, and from Benjamin two hundred eighty thousand shield-bearers and archers; all these were mighty men.

Zerah the Ethiopian came out against them with an army of one million men and three hundred chariots, and he came as far as Mareshah.

[Col. 1375D] Asa marched out to meet him and drew up his battle line in the Valley of Zephathah, near Mareshah. He called upon the Lord God and said:

“Lord, it makes no difference to you whether you help with few or with many. Help us, Lord our God, for we rely on you and on your name, and we have come against this multitude. Lord our God, you are our God; let no human being prevail against you.”

The Lord terrified the Ethiopians before Asa and Judah, and the Ethiopians fled.

Asa and the people who were with him pursued them as far as Gerar. The Ethiopians fell to destruction, for the Lord struck them down and they were crushed, while his army fought.

They took much plunder and struck all the cities around Gerar, for a great terror had seized everyone. They plundered the cities and carried away abundant booty.

[Col. 1376A] They also destroyed the sheepfolds and carried away an immeasurable quantity of livestock and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem.

[Chapter XV] Azariah son of Oded, moved by the spirit of God, went out to meet Asa and said to him: “Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin! The Lord is with you because you are with him. If you seek him, you will find him; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you.

“For many days Israel shall be without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without the law.

“But when they return in their distress to the Lord God of Israel and seek him, they will find him.

“In that time there shall be no peace for those going out or coming in, but terrors on every side among all the inhabitants of the lands. Nation shall fight against nation and city against city, because the Lord will trouble them with every kind of distress.

“Therefore be strong, and do not let your hands [Col. 1376B] grow weak, for your work shall have its reward.”

When Asa heard this—namely, the words and prophecy of the prophet Oded—he was strengthened. He removed the idols from all the land of Judah and Benjamin and from the cities that he had captured in the hill country of Ephraim, and he dedicated the altar of the Lord that stood before the portico of the Lord.

He gathered all Judah and Benjamin, together with the immigrants from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon, for many had fled to him from Israel when they saw that the Lord their God was with him.

When they came to Jerusalem in the third month, in the fifteenth year of Asa’s reign, they sacrificed to the Lord on that day from the spoils and booty they had brought: seven hundred oxen and seven thousand rams.

They entered, according to custom, to strengthen the covenant, so that they might seek the Lord, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and all their soul.

“If anyone,” he said, “does not seek the Lord [Col. 1376C] God of Israel, let him die, from the least to the greatest, from man to woman.”

All Judah swore to the Lord with a loud voice, amid rejoicing, the sound of trumpets, and the blast of horns, with a curse. For they swore with all their heart and sought him with their whole will, and they found him; and the Lord granted them rest on every side.

He also removed Maacah, the mother of King Asa, from her position of authority, because she had made an image of Priapus in a sacred grove. He smashed it completely, crushed it to pieces, and burned it in the Kidron Valley.

The high places, however, were not removed from Israel; nevertheless, Asa’s heart was perfect all his days.

The things that his father had vowed, and that he himself had vowed, he brought into the house of the Lord: silver, gold, and various kinds of vessels and furnishings.

There was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign.

[Col. 1376D] [Chapter XVI] In the thirty-sixth year of his reign, Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah and fortified Ramah, so that no one could safely go out or enter from Asa’s kingdom.

Asa therefore brought out silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the Lord and the treasuries of the king, and sent them to Ben-hadad king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying:

“There is a covenant between me and you, and there was concord between my father and your father. Therefore I have sent you silver and gold, so that you may break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel and make him withdraw from me.”

When Ben-hadad learned this, he sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel. They struck Aijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the fortified cities of Naphtali.

When Baasha heard this, he stopped building Ramah and discontinued his work.

[Col. 1377A] King Asa then took all Judah, and they carried away the stones from Ramah and the timber that Baasha had prepared for the construction. With these he built Geba and Mizpah.

At that time Hanani the prophet came to Asa king of Judah and said to him: “Because you placed your trust in the king of Syria and not in the Lord your God, therefore the army of the king of Syria has escaped from your hand.
