“Were not the Ethiopians and Libyans much more numerous in chariots, horsemen, and an exceedingly great multitude? Yet, because you believed in the Lord, he delivered them into your hand.

“For the eyes of the Lord survey the whole earth and grant strength to those who trust in him with a perfect heart.

“You have acted foolishly in this matter, and from this time onward wars will arise against you.”

Asa became angry with the seer and ordered him to be put in the stocks, for he was exceedingly indignant about this.

He also killed many of the people at that time.

[Col. 1377B] The former and latter deeds of Asa are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.

In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa became ill with an extremely severe disease of the feet. Even in his illness he did not seek the Lord, but instead trusted in the skill of physicians.

He slept with his fathers and died in the forty-first year of his reign.

They buried him in his tomb, which he had hewn for himself in the City of David. They placed him upon his bier, filled with spices and perfumed ointments prepared by the art of the perfumers, and burned a very great quantity over him.

[Chapter XVII] His son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place and prevailed against Israel.

He appointed contingents of soldiers in all the fortified cities of Judah and established garrisons in the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that his father Asa had captured.

[Col. 1377C] The Lord was with Jehoshaphat because he walked in the former ways of his father David [Note: Some ancient Latin codices are said to add “and latter,” but this nevertheless appears to be a scribal error, owing to the occurrence of the subsequent words “and not.”] and did not place his hope in the Baals, but in the God of his father. He followed his commandments and did not act according to the sins of Israel.

The Lord confirmed the kingdom in his hand, and all Judah brought gifts to Jehoshaphat. He acquired immeasurable wealth and great glory.

When his heart had gained courage because of the ways of the Lord, he also removed the high places and sacred groves from Judah.

In the third year of his reign, he sent some of his princes—Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah—to teach in the cities of Judah.

With them were the Levites Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah, and with them Elishama and Jehoram the priests.

They taught in Judah, carrying the Book of the Law of the Lord. They went around all the cities of Judah and instructed the people.

Thus the terror of the Lord came upon all the kingdoms [Col. 1377D] of the lands surrounding Judah, and they did not dare to wage war against Jehoshaphat.

The Philistines also brought gifts and silver tribute to Jehoshaphat, and the Arabs brought him livestock: seven thousand seven hundred rams and the same number of goats.

Jehoshaphat grew and became exceedingly great; he built houses in Judah like towers and fortified cities. He also prepared extensive works in the cities of Judah.

There were also mighty and warlike men in Jerusalem, whose numbers by households and families were as follows:

In Judah, commanders of the army: Ednah the commander, and with him three hundred thousand of the strongest men.

[Col. 1378A] After him, Jehohanan the commander, and with him two hundred eighty thousand.

After him, Amasiah son of Zichri, consecrated to the Lord, and with him two hundred thousand mighty men.

After him came Eliada, strong for battle, and with him two hundred thousand men bearing bows and shields.

After him also came Jehozabad, and with him one hundred eighty thousand equipped soldiers.

All these were at the king’s disposal, apart from the others whom he had stationed in the fortified cities and throughout Judah.

[Chapter XVIII] Jehoshaphat was therefore very rich and renowned, and he became related by marriage to Ahab.

After some years he went down to him in Samaria.

At his arrival Ahab slaughtered very many rams and oxen for him and for the people who had come with him, and persuaded him to go up against Ramoth-gilead.

King Ahab of Israel said to King Jehoshaphat of Judah: “Come with me to Ramoth-gilead.”

He answered him: “I am as you are, and my people as your people; we shall be with you in the war.”

Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel: “Please consult the word of the Lord at this moment.”

The king of Israel gathered four hundred prophets and said to them: “Should we go to fight against Ramoth-gilead, or should we refrain?”

But they said, “Go up, and God will deliver them into the hand of the king.”

And Jehoshaphat said: “Is there no prophet of the Lord here, so that we may also inquire of him?”

And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat: “There is one man from whom we can inquire of the Lord’s will, but I hate him, because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only evil.”

“His name is Micaiah son of Imlah.”

Jehoshaphat said: “Let not the king speak in that manner.”

So the king of Israel summoned one of the eunuchs and said to him: “Call Micaiah son of Imlah quickly.”

Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were each seated on his throne, dressed in royal attire.  
[Col. 1378C] They were seated in the open area beside the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them.

Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made iron horns for himself and said: “Thus says the Lord: With these you shall scatter Syria until you crush it.”

And all the prophets were prophesying similarly, saying: “Go up to Ramoth-gilead, and you will prosper, and the Lord will deliver them into the hand of the king.”

The messenger who had gone to summon Micaiah said to him:

“Look: the words of all the prophets unanimously announce good things to the king. I therefore ask you also not to differ from their message, but to speak of prosperity.”

Micaiah answered him: “As the Lord lives, whatever my God says, that I will speak.”

So he came to the king. And the king said to him: “Micaiah, must we go to Ramoth-gilead to fight, or must we remain at rest?”

He answered: “Go up, for everything will turn out favorably, and the enemy will be delivered into your hands.”  
[Col. 1378D]

And the king said: “Again and again I adjure you not to speak to me anything except what is true, in the name of the Lord.”

But he said: “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd, and the Lord said: ‘These have no masters; let each one return to his house in peace.’”

And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat: “Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy anything good to me, but only things that are evil?”

But he said: “Therefore hear the word of the Lord: I saw the Lord seated on his throne, and the whole army of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left.

“And the Lord said: ‘Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And when one said one thing and another something else, a spirit came forward and stood before the Lord, saying: ‘I will deceive him.’ The Lord said to him: ‘In what way will you deceive him?’

“He answered: ‘I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’

“And the Lord said: ‘You shall deceive him, and you will prevail. Go out and do this.’

“Now therefore, behold, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all your prophets, and the Lord has spoken evil concerning you.”

Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah approached and struck Micaiah on the cheek, saying:

“By what way did the Spirit of the Lord pass from me to speak to you?”

Micaiah said: “You yourself will see on that day, when you enter from room to room in order to hide.”

But the king of Israel commanded: “Take Micaiah and lead him to Amon, the city’s governor, and to Joash son of Amelech.”

[Col. 1379B] “And say: ‘Thus says the king: Put this man in prison, and give him a little bread and a little water, until I return in peace.’”

Micaiah said: “If you return in peace, the Lord has not spoken through me.” And he said: “Hear this, all you peoples.”

So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.

And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat: “I will change my appearance, and thus go into battle; but you, put on your own garments.”

When the king of Israel had changed his appearance, he went into battle.

Now the king of Syria had commanded the commanders of his cavalry, saying: “Do not fight against small or great, but only against the king of Israel.”

Accordingly, when the commanders of the cavalry saw Jehoshaphat, they said: “This is the king of Israel.”

And they surrounded him, fighting against him.

But he cried out to the Lord, and he helped him,  
[Col. 1379C] and turned them away from him.

For when the commanders of the chariots saw that he was not the king of Israel, they withdrew from him.

It happened, however, that one of the people shot an arrow at random and struck the king of Israel between the neck and the shoulders.

And he said to his charioteer: “Turn your hand and take me out of the battle line, for I am wounded.”

The battle ended on that day.

The king of Israel remained in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening, and he died at sunset.

## Chapter XIX

Jehoshaphat king of Judah returned peacefully to his house in Jerusalem.

Jehu son of Hanani the seer met him and said to him: “Are you giving assistance to the wicked, and are you joining yourself in friendship to those who hate the Lord? For this reason you deserved the Lord’s wrath. Yet good works have been found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah and prepared your heart to seek God.”

[Col. 1379D] So Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem.

Again he went out among the people, from Beersheba to Mount Ephraim, and brought them back to the Lord, the God of their ancestors.

He appointed judges throughout all the fortified cities of Judah, in each locality.

And instructing the judges, he said: “Consider carefully what you are doing. For you are not administering judgment on behalf of a human being, but on behalf of the Lord, and whatever judgment you render will rebound upon you.

“Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and act with diligence in all things. For with the Lord our God there is no injustice, no partiality, and no desire for gifts.”

In Jerusalem also Jehoshaphat appointed Levites, priests, and heads of families from Israel, to judge the Lord’s judgment and case for its inhabitants  
[Note: [Col. 1379D] In place of “its inhabitants,” the Hebrew exemplar prefers [the supplied text does not reproduce the Hebrew term], which means “and they returned” (or “dwelt”) in Jerusalem. The reason Jerome, following the Septuagint, translated it in the present sense is only that he read [the supplied text does not reproduce the Hebrew term], or took the final yod in place of waw; these letters differ only in size. This word signifies “inhabitants.” In Greek: κατοικοῦντας, “inhabitants.”]

And he commanded them, saying: “Thus you shall act faithfully and with a perfect heart, in the fear of the Lord.

“Whenever any case comes before you from your brothers who dwell in their cities, between one kinsman and another, wherever there is a dispute concerning the law, a commandment, ceremonies, or ordinances, explain it to them, so that they may not sin against the Lord and wrath may not come upon you or your brothers.

“Thus you shall act, and you will not sin.

“Amariah the priest and your high priest shall preside over matters concerning the Lord.

“Zebadiah son of Ishmael, who is the ruler in the house of Judah, shall be over matters belonging to the king’s office.  
[Col. 1380B] And you have Levites as teachers before you.

“Be strong, act diligently, and the Lord will be with the good.”

## Chapter XX

After this, the sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon, and with them some of the Ammonites  
[Note: [Col. 1380D] Nearly all manuscripts read “Ammanites,” as Martianaeus also notes. But many others, especially the printed editions and those cited in large number by Menochius, prefer “Idumeans” here. P. Calmet, however, testifies that in the copies he himself consulted this reading was placed not in the text but in the margin. Consult the author of *Hebrew Questions* on this book.] came to Jehoshaphat to wage war against him.

Messengers came and reported to Jehoshaphat: “A great multitude is coming against you from the regions beyond the sea, from Syria; and behold, they are stationed at Hazazon-tamar, that is, En-gedi.”

Jehoshaphat, terrified by fear, devoted himself entirely to entreating the Lord, and proclaimed a fast throughout Judah.

Judah gathered to implore the Lord; indeed, people also came from all their cities to beseech him.

And when Jehoshaphat stood in the midst of the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the house of the Lord before the new court, he said:

“Lord God of our ancestors, are you not God in  
[Col. 1380C] heaven, and do you not rule over all the kingdoms of the nations?

“In your hand are strength and power, and no one can resist you.

“Were you not, our God, the one who destroyed all the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and gave it forever to the offspring of Abraham, your friend?

“They dwelt in it and built in it a sanctuary for your name, saying:

“‘If evils come upon us—the sword of judgment, pestilence, and famine—we will stand before this house and in your presence, in which your name has been invoked, and we will cry out to you in our tribulations, and you will hear us and save us.’

“Now therefore, behold, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, through whose land you did not permit Israel to pass when they were leaving Egypt, but from whom they turned aside and did not destroy them—

“on the contrary, they are acting and striving to drive us from the possession that you gave us, our God. Therefore, will you not judge them?

“We have no strength sufficient to resist this multitude that is rushing upon us. But since we do not know what we ought to do, this alone remains to us: to direct our eyes toward you.”

Meanwhile all Judah stood before the Lord, with their little ones, wives, and children.

Now Jahaziel son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite from the sons of Asaph, upon whom the Spirit of the Lord came  
[Col. 1381A] in the midst of the assembly, said:

“Pay attention, all Judah, and you inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you, King Jehoshaphat. Thus says the Lord to you: Do not fear or be terrified by this multitude, for the battle is not yours but God’s.

“Tomorrow you shall go down against them. For they will come up by the ascent called Sis, and you will find them at the end of the ravine opposite the wilderness of Jeruel.

“It will not be you who fight. Only stand confidently, and you will see the Lord’s help for you.

“Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear or be terrified. Tomorrow you shall go out against them, and the Lord will be with you.”

Then Jehoshaphat, Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell prostrate on the ground before the Lord and worshiped him.

The Levites from the sons of Kohath and from the sons of Korah praised the Lord God of Israel with a loud voice, in exaltation.

[Col. 1381B] When they rose early in the morning, they went out through the wilderness of Tekoa. As they set out, Jehoshaphat stood in their midst and said:

“Hear me, Judah and all you inhabitants of Jerusalem. Believe in the Lord your God, and you will be secure; believe his prophets, and everything will turn out favorably.”

He then gave counsel to the people and appointed singers of the Lord to praise him in their companies, to go before the army, and to say with united voice:

“Give thanks to the Lord, for his mercy endures forever.”

And when they began to sing praises, the Lord turned their ambushes against themselves—that is, those of the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, who had come out to fight against Judah—and they were struck down.

For the sons of Ammon and Moab rose up against the inhabitants of Mount Seir to kill and destroy them. When they had completed this work, they also turned against one another  
[Col. 1381C] and fell by mutual wounds.

When Judah came to the lookout that faces the wilderness, they saw from afar the entire broad region filled with corpses, and no one remained who could have escaped death.

So Jehoshaphat and all the people with him came to strip the dead. They found among the corpses various kinds of equipment, clothing, and extremely valuable vessels, and they plundered them, so that they could not carry everything away; for the quantity of spoils was so great that they could not remove it even in three days.

On the fourth day they gathered in the Valley of Blessing, because they had blessed the Lord there; and they called that place the Valley of Blessing to the present day.

Every man of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem returned, with Jehoshaphat at their head, to Jerusalem with great joy, because the Lord had given them joy over their enemies.

They entered Jerusalem with psalteries, harps,  
[Col. 1381D] and trumpets, into the house of the Lord.

The dread of the Lord fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the Lord had fought against the enemies of Israel.

The kingdom of Jehoshaphat was at rest, and God granted him peace on every side.

Jehoshaphat ruled over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem.

His mother’s name was Azubah daughter of Shilhi.

He walked in the way of his father Asa and did not turn aside from it, doing what was pleasing in the sight of the Lord.

[Col. 1382A] Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places, and the people still had not directed their hearts to the Lord God of their ancestors.

The rest of the deeds of Jehoshaphat, the earlier and the later, are written in the words of Jehu son of Hanani, which he compiled in the Book of the Kings of Israel.

After this, Jehoshaphat king of Judah entered into an alliance with Ahaziah king of Israel, whose deeds were extremely wicked.

He became a partner with him in making ships to sail to Tarshish; and they built a fleet at Ezion-geber.

But Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying: “Because you formed an alliance with Ahaziah, the Lord has struck your works, and the ships have been wrecked; they were unable to sail to Tarshish.”

## Chapter XXI

Jehoshaphat slept with his ancestors and was buried with them in the city of David.

His son Jehoram reigned in his place. He had brothers, sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehi’el, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah—all these were sons of Jehoshaphat king  
[Note: [Col. 1381D] The printed books and some manuscripts read “king of Judah.” The Memmian Canon reads “king of Judah” in the text but “Israel” in the margin. More and older Latin manuscripts agree with the Hebrew codices, where the name “Israel” is read, both in printed editions and in manuscripts: *melech Israel*, “king of Israel.” Whoever wishes to investigate this difficulty should consult the volumes of the *Sacred Critics*. MART.]

[Col. 1382B] His father gave them many gifts of silver and gold, together with possessions and strongly fortified cities in Judah; but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn.

When Jehoram had established himself over his father’s kingdom, he killed all his brothers with the sword, as well as some of the princes of Israel.

Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.

He walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done; for Ahab’s daughter was his wife, and he did evil in the sight of the Lord.

The Lord did not wish to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant he had made with him and because he had promised to give him a lamp, and to his sons, forever.

In those days Edom rebelled, so as not to be subject to Judah, and appointed a king for itself.

When Jehoram crossed over with his commanders and all the cavalry that was with him, he rose by night and struck Edom, which had surrounded him, together with all its cavalry commanders.

Nevertheless Edom rebelled, so as not to be under the rule of Judah, to this day.

At that time Libnah also withdrew, so as not to be under his hand.

For he had abandoned the Lord, the God of his ancestors. Moreover, he had built high places in the cities of Judah, made the inhabitants of Jerusalem commit fornication, and led Judah astray.

A letter was brought to him from Elijah the prophet, in which it was written:

“Thus says the Lord God of David your father: Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father and in the ways of Asa king of Judah, but have followed the path of the kings of Israel; because you have made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem commit fornication, imitating the fornication of the house of Ahab; and because, in addition, you have killed your brothers, your father’s house, who were better than you—behold, the Lord will strike you with a great plague,  
[Col. 1382D] together with your people, your sons, your wives, and all your possessions.

“But you yourself will suffer from a terrible disease of the bowels, until your vital organs gradually emerge day by day.”

So the Lord stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and the Arabs who border the Cushites. They came up against the land of Judah, devastated it, and plundered all the possessions found in the king’s house.

They also took his sons and wives; and no son remained to him except Jehoahaz, who was the youngest.

And in addition to all this, the Lord struck him with an incurable disease of the bowels.

[Col. 1383A] As day followed day and periods of time passed, the cycle of two years was completed. Thus, consumed by a prolonged wasting disease, so that even his intestines were expelled, he lost both his health and his life.

He died in a most grievous illness, and the people did not make a funeral burning for him according to the custom of his ancestors, nor did they perform the rites they had performed for his forebears.

He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.

He walked improperly, and they buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

## Chapter XXII

The inhabitants of Jerusalem appointed his youngest son Ahaziah king in his place.

For all the older sons who had preceded him had been killed by the raiders of the Arabs who had invaded the camp.

Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah reigned.

Ahaziah was forty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Athaliah daughter of Omri.

[Col. 1383B] He too walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother urged him to act wickedly.

So he did evil in the sight of the Lord, like the house of Ahab, for they were his counselors after the death of his father, to his destruction.

He followed their counsels. He also went with Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel, to war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead.

The Syrians wounded Jehoram. He returned to Jezreel to be treated, for he had received many wounds in the aforementioned battle.

Therefore Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to visit Jehoram son of Ahab, who was ill at Jezreel.

For it was God’s will against Ahaziah that he should come to Jehoram.

And when he had come out with him against Jehu son of Nimshi, whom the Lord had anointed to destroy the house of Ahab,

[Col. 1383C] when Jehu was overthrowing the house of Ahab, he found the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers, who were attending him, and he killed them.

Then, searching for Ahaziah himself, he found him hiding in Samaria. He brought him to himself and killed him, and they buried him, because he was the son of Jehoshaphat, who had sought the Lord with all his heart. There was no further hope that anyone of the house of Ahaziah would reign.

When Athaliah, his mother, saw that her son was dead, she arose and killed the entire royal offspring of the house of Jehoram.

But Jehoshabeath, the king’s daughter, took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king’s sons while they were being killed. She hid him with his nurse in the bedroom.

Jehoshabeath, who had hidden him, was the daughter of King Jehoram, wife of Jehoiada the high priest, and sister of Ahaziah; for that reason Athaliah did not kill him.

He remained hidden with them in the house of God for six  
[Col. 1383D] years, during which Athaliah ruled over the land.

## Chapter XXIII

In the seventh year, Jehoiada strengthened himself and took the commanders of hundreds—namely, Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Johanan,  
[Note: [Col. 1383D] We have left the name “Obed” unchanged, since it is found written in this way in the printed books, in the Colbertine-Anician manuscript, and in the Hebrew text. The other manuscript codices read “Oded,” with a double d, in accordance with the first verse of the preceding fifteenth chapter, where the name Oded occurs and Azariah is also called the son of Oded. MART.]

Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri—and he made a covenant with them.

They went throughout Judah, gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah, and the heads of the families of Israel, and came to Jerusalem.

So the whole assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God, and Jehoiada said to them:

“Behold, the king’s son shall reign, as the Lord spoke concerning the sons of David.

“This, then, is what you shall do:

“One third of you who come on the Sabbath—the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers—shall be at the gates.

“Another third shall be at the king’s house.

“And another third shall be at the gate called the Foundation.

“But let all the rest of the people remain in the courts of the house of the Lord.

“No one else may enter the house of the Lord except the priests and those Levites who minister there. They alone may enter, because they are consecrated. Let all the rest of the people keep the Lord’s watches.

“The Levites shall surround the king, each with his weapons. If anyone else enters the temple, he shall be killed. They shall remain with the king both when he enters and when he leaves.”

So the Levites and all Judah did according to everything that Jehoiada the high priest had commanded. Each took the men under his authority, and those who came in their weekly rotation came in with those who had completed their Sabbath duty and were about to depart.

For Jehoiada the high priest had not dismissed the companies that customarily succeeded one another each week.

Jehoiada the priest gave the commanders of hundreds spears, shields, and the small shields of King David, which had been consecrated in the house of the Lord.

He stationed all the people carrying daggers around the king, from the right side of the temple to the left side, before the altar and the temple.

And they brought out the king’s son and placed the crown on him,  
[Note: [Col. 1383D] These words—“and they gave into his hand the testimony to hold, the law”—are found neither in the Hebrew text nor in the Greek nor, finally, in the other ancient versions. It may perhaps be suspected—since “testimony” is commonly thought here to signify the precepts of the Law, as the Hebrews assert, or phylacteries, small volumes of parchment to be worn before the eyes—that this entire passage is a gloss belonging to that term, added by some diligent student. For, as Calmet reports, some Latin manuscripts completely omit it.]

and the testimony. They gave into his hand the law to hold, and appointed him king.

Jehoiada the high priest and his sons also anointed him, and they invoked blessings upon him and said: “Long live the king!”

When Athaliah heard the sound of the people running and praising the king, she entered among the people in the temple of the Lord.

When she saw the king standing on the platform at the entrance, with the commanders and companies around him, and all the people of the land rejoicing, blowing trumpets, and singing to the accompaniment of instruments of various kinds, and heard the voices of those praising him, she tore her garments and said: “Conspiracy! Conspiracy!”

Jehoiada the high priest went out to the commanders of hundreds and the army officers and said to them: “Lead her outside the temple precincts, and let her be killed outside with the sword.”

The priest had commanded that she not be killed in the house of the Lord.

So they laid hands on her neck.

When she entered the Horse Gate of the king’s house, they killed her there.

[Col. 1384D] Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, the whole people, and the king, that they should be the Lord’s people.

Then all the people entered the house of Baal and destroyed it. They smashed its altars and images.

They killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, before the altars.

[Col. 1385A] Jehoiada appointed overseers in the house of the Lord under the authority of the priests and Levites whom David had assigned in the house of the Lord, so that they might offer burnt offerings to the Lord, as it is written in the law of Moses, with rejoicing and songs, according to David’s arrangement.

He also appointed gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the Lord, so that no unclean person might enter it in any matter.

He took the commanders of hundreds, the strongest men, the leaders of the people, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the Lord. They entered through the upper gate into the king’s house and placed him on the royal throne.

All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. Athaliah, meanwhile, had been killed with the sword.

## Chapter XXIV

Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah of Beersheba.

He did what was good in the sight of the Lord throughout all the days of Jehoiada the priest.

Jehoiada took two wives for him, and from them he fathered sons and daughters.

After this, Joash decided to restore the house of the Lord. He gathered the priests and Levites and said to them:

“Go out to the cities of Judah and collect money from all Israel for repairing the temple of your God, year by year, and do this quickly.”

But the Levites acted negligently.

The king summoned Jehoiada the chief priest and said to him: “Why have you not taken care to compel the Levites to bring from Judah and Jerusalem the money established by Moses, the servant of the Lord, so that the whole assembly of Israel might bring it into the tabernacle of the testimony?

“For the utterly wicked Athaliah and her sons had destroyed the house of God, and from everything that had been consecrated to the temple of the Lord they had furnished the shrine of the Baals.”

So the king commanded, and they made a chest and placed it outside beside the gate of the house of the Lord.

A proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem that each person should bring to the Lord the payment that Moses, the servant of God, had imposed upon all Israel in the wilderness.

[Col. 1385C] All the princes and all the people rejoiced. They entered and put their contributions into the Lord’s chest until it was full.

Whenever it was time for the chest to be brought before the king by the hands of the Levites—for they saw that there was a great deal of money—the king’s scribe and the officer whom the chief priest had appointed would enter. They emptied the money that was in the chest, then returned the chest to its place. They did this every day, and an immense amount of money was collected.

The king and Jehoiada gave it to those who supervised the work on the house of the Lord.

They hired stonecutters and craftsmen for the various works, to restore the house of the Lord, as well as workers in iron and bronze, so that what had begun to collapse might be strengthened.

Those who worked carried out their task diligently. The damaged places in the walls were repaired by their hands, and they restored the house of the Lord to its former condition and made it stand firmly.

When they had completed all the work, they brought the remaining money before the king and Jehoiada. From it they made vessels for the temple service and for the burnt offerings, as well as bowls and other gold and silver vessels.

Burnt offerings were continually offered in the house of the Lord throughout all the days of Jehoiada.

Jehoiada grew old, full of days, and died when he was one hundred and thirty years old.

They buried him in the city of David with the kings, because he had done good in Israel and for his house.

After Jehoiada died, the princes of Judah entered and paid homage to the king. The king, won over by their acts of submission, listened to them.

They abandoned the temple of the Lord, the God of their ancestors,  
[Col. 1386A] and served the sacred groves and carved images. Because of this sin, wrath came against Judah and Jerusalem.

He sent prophets to them to bring them back to the Lord, but although they testified against them, they refused to listen.

Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest. He stood before the people and said to them:

“Thus says God the Lord: Why are you transgressing the commandment of the Lord, which will not benefit you? You have abandoned the Lord, so that he may abandon you.”

They gathered against him and, at the king’s command, stoned him in the court of the house of the Lord.

King Joash did not remember the mercy that Jehoiada his father had shown him, but killed his son.

As he was dying, Zechariah said: “May the Lord see and avenge!”

When the year had come round, the army of Syria came up against him. It came into Judah and Jerusalem  
[Col. 1386B] and killed all the leaders of the people. They sent all the spoil to the king at Damascus.

Indeed, although only a very small number of Syrians had come, the Lord delivered an immense multitude into their hands, because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their ancestors.

They also carried out shameful judgments against Joash.

When they departed, they left him in great suffering.

Then his servants rose up against him in revenge for the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest. They killed him in his bed, and he died.

They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

Those who plotted against him were Zabad son of Shimeath the Ammonite woman and Jehozabad son of Shimrith the Moabite woman.

His sons, the large amount of money amassed under him, and the restoration of the house of God are recorded more fully in the Book of the Kings.

His son Amaziah reigned in his place.

[Col. 1386C] ## Chapter XXV

Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem.

He did what was good in the sight of the Lord, though not with a perfect heart.

When he saw that his authority had been strengthened, he killed the servants who had murdered his father the king, but he did not kill their sons, as it is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, where the Lord commanded, saying:

“Fathers shall not be put to death for their sons, nor sons for their fathers; each shall die for his own sin.”

So Amaziah gathered Judah and organized them by families, with commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, throughout all Judah and Benjamin.

He counted those twenty years old and above and found three hundred thousand young men who could go out to war and carry spear and shield.

He also hired one hundred thousand strong men from Israel for one hundred talents of silver.

A man of God came to him and said: “O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the Lord is not with Israel and all the sons of Ephraim.”

“But if you think that wars depend upon the strength of the army, God will make you fall before the enemy. For it belongs to God both to help and to turn people to flight.”

Amaziah said to the man of God: “What, then, is to be done about the hundred talents that I gave to the soldiers of Israel?” The man of God answered him: “The Lord has the power to give you much more than these.”

So Amaziah separated the army that had come to him from Ephraim and sent it back to its own place.

But they became extremely angry with Judah and returned to their land.

Amaziah confidently led out his people and went to the Valley of Salt, where he struck down ten thousand of the sons of Seir.

[Col. 1387A] The sons of Judah captured another ten thousand, brought them to the edge of a certain cliff, and threw them from the top into the precipice; they all burst apart.

The army that Amaziah had sent back so that it would not go with him into battle dispersed through the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon. They killed three thousand people and plundered a large amount of spoil.

After the slaughter of the Edomites, Amaziah brought back the gods of the sons of Seir, set them up as gods for himself, worshiped them, and burned incense to them.

Therefore the Lord became angry with Amaziah and sent a prophet to him, who said: “Why have you worshiped gods who did not deliver their own people from your hand?”

While he was speaking these words, Amaziah answered him: “Are you the king’s counselor? Be quiet, or I will kill you.”

As the prophet departed, he said: “I know that God has determined to kill you, because you have done this evil and, in addition, have not listened to my counsel.”

[Col. 1387B] Then Amaziah king of Judah, having taken exceedingly bad counsel, sent a message to Joash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying: “Come, let us look upon one another.”

He sent back a messenger, saying: “The thornbush in Lebanon sent to the cedar in Lebanon, saying: ‘Give your daughter to my son as a wife.’ But the wild beasts that were in the forest of Lebanon passed by and trampled the thornbush.

“You said: ‘I have struck Edom,’ and therefore your heart is lifted up in pride. Stay at home. Why provoke disaster against yourself, so that you may fall, and Judah with you?”

Amaziah refused to listen, because it was the Lord’s will that he be delivered into the hands of his enemies on account of the gods of Edom.

So Joash king of Israel went up, and they confronted one another.

Amaziah king of Judah was at Beth-shemesh, in Judah.

Judah fell before Israel, and they fled to their tents.

Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Joash son of Jehoahaz, at Beth-shemesh, and brought him to Jerusalem. He destroyed its wall from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate, a distance of four hundred cubits.

He also took all the gold, silver, and vessels that he found in the house of God and with Obed-edom, as well as the treasures of the royal house; and he took hostages and returned to Samaria.

Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel.

The rest of the words concerning Amaziah, the earlier and the later, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

After he withdrew from the Lord, they plotted against him in Jerusalem.

When he fled to Lachish, they sent men after him and killed him there.

[Col. 1387D] They carried him back on horses and buried him with his ancestors in the city of  
[Note: [Col. 1387D] The Hebrew does not have “David” here, but “Judah.” Nevertheless, nearly all the other ancient interpreters, as well as the Latin Vulgate books, unanimously prefer “David.”]

David.

## Chapter XXVI

All the people of Judah appointed his son Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, king in place of his father Amaziah.

He built Elath and restored it to the authority of Judah after the king had slept with his ancestors.

Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem.

His mother’s name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.

He did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, according to  
[Col. 1388A] everything that his father Amaziah had done. He sought God in the days of Zechariah, who understood and saw God; and while he sought the Lord, God guided him in all things.

Finally, he went out and fought against the Philistines. He demolished the wall of Gath, the wall of Jabneh, and the wall of Ashdod.

He also built towns in Ashdod and in Philistia.

God helped him against the Philistines, against the Arabs who lived in Gurbaal, and against the Ammonites.

The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah, and his name became known as far as the entrance of Egypt because of his frequent victories.

Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem over the Corner Gate and over the Valley Gate, as well as others along that side of the wall, and he fortified them.

He also constructed towers in the wilderness and dug many cisterns, because he possessed much livestock, both in the [Col. 1388B] lowlands and in the desolate wilderness.

He had vineyards as well, and vinedressers in the mountains and on Carmel, for he was devoted to agriculture.

His army consisted of warriors who went out to battle under the command of Jeiel the secretary, Maaseiah the teacher, and Hananiah, one of the king’s commanders.

The total number of their leaders, according to the families of mighty men, was 2,600.

And under their command was the entire [Note: [Col. 1387D] Thus the Memmian Canon reads in the body of the text; in the margin, however, it gives six hundred instead of three hundred, and eight thousand instead of seven thousand. These variant readings are errors of Latin antiquaries or ancient copyists. MART.] army of 307,500 men, who were fit for war and fought for the king against his enemies.

Uzziah also prepared for them—that is, for the whole army—shields, spears, helmets, breastplates, bows, and slings for throwing stones.

In Jerusalem he made machines of various kinds, which he placed on the towers and at the corners of the walls, so that they could shoot arrows and hurl large stones. [Col. 1388C] His fame spread far abroad, because the Lord helped him and strengthened him.

But when he had become strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction, and he neglected the Lord his God.

He entered the temple of the Lord, intending to burn incense on the altar of incense.

Immediately Azariah the priest entered after him, accompanied by eighty priests of the Lord, men of great courage. They resisted the king and said:

“It is not your office, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord. That is the office of the priests, the sons of Aaron, who have been consecrated for this ministry. Leave the sanctuary; do not despise it. This will not be counted to your glory by the Lord God.”

Uzziah became angry. Holding the censer in his hand and preparing to burn incense, he threatened the priests.

Immediately leprosy broke out on his forehead before the priests in the house of the Lord, above the altar of incense.

When Azariah the high priest and [Col. 1388D] all the other priests looked at him, they saw the leprosy on his forehead and hurriedly expelled him.

He himself, terrified, hastened to leave, because he had immediately felt the Lord’s affliction.

Thus King Uzziah remained a leper until the day of his death. He lived in a separate house, full of leprosy, on account of which he had been expelled from the house of the Lord.

His son Jotham governed the royal household and judged the people of the land.

The rest of the earlier and later acts of Uzziah were written by Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet.

Uzziah slept with his fathers, and they buried [Col. 1389A] him in the field of the royal tombs, because he was a leper. His son Jotham reigned in his place.

## Chapter XXVII

Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem.

His mother’s name was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok.

He did what was right before the Lord, in accordance with everything that his father Uzziah had done, except that he did not enter the temple of the Lord; yet the people continued to sin.

He built the high gate of the house of the Lord and constructed much on the wall of Ophel.

He also built towns in the mountains of Judah, and fortresses and towers in the forests.

He fought against the king of the Ammonites and defeated them. At that time the Ammonites gave him one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and the same number of cors of barley. The Ammonites supplied him with these things in the second and third years.

[Col. 1389B] Jotham grew strong because he ordered his ways rightly before the Lord his God.

The rest of the acts of Jotham, all his battles, and his deeds are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem.

Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. His son Ahaz reigned in his place.

## Chapter XXVIII

Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem.

He did not do what was right in the sight of the Lord, as David his father had done. Instead, he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and even cast images of the Baals.

He was the one who burned incense in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom and passed his sons through the fire, according to the rites of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.

He also sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.

The Lord his God gave him into the hand of the king of Syria, who struck him, took great spoil from his kingdom, and brought it to Damascus.

He was also handed over to the king of Israel, who struck him with a great slaughter.

Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 men in Judah in a single day, all of them fighting men, because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers.

At that time Zichri, a mighty man from Ephraim, killed Maaseiah, the king’s son, Azrikam, the commander of the royal household, and Elkanah, second to the king.

The Israelites took captive from their brothers 200,000 women, boys, and girls, together with enormous spoil, and brought it to Samaria.

At that time there was there a prophet of the Lord named Oded. He went out to meet the army coming to Samaria and said to them:

[Col. 1389D] “Behold, the Lord, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah and gave them into your hands; and you have killed them savagely, so that your cruelty has reached heaven.

Moreover, you intend to subject the sons of Judah and Jerusalem to yourselves as male and female slaves. This must not be done, for by this you have sinned against the Lord your God.

Now listen to my counsel and return the captives whom you have brought from your brothers, because the great fury of the Lord is upon you.”

Then men from among the leaders of the sons of [Col. 1390A] Ephraim—Azariah son of Johanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Hezekiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai—stood against those coming from the battle and said to them:

“You shall not bring the captives in here, lest we sin against the Lord. Why do you intend to add to our sins and heap up our former offenses? For the sin is already great, and the anger of the Lord’s fury hangs over Israel.”

The warriors abandoned the spoil and everything they had taken before the leaders and the whole assembly.

Then the men mentioned above stood up, took the captives, and clothed all those who were naked with the spoil.

After they had clothed them, given them shoes, refreshed them with food and drink, anointed them because of their weariness, and cared for them, they placed on animals all who could not walk and were physically weak. They brought them to Jericho, the city of palms, to their brothers, while they themselves returned to Samaria.

[Col. 1390B] At that time King Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria, asking for help.

The Edomites came and struck many from Judah and took great spoil.

The Philistines also spread through the towns of the lowlands and the south of Judah. They captured Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, and Gederoth, as well as Soco, Timnah, and Gimzo, with their villages, and settled in them.

For the Lord had humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Judah, since he had stripped Judah of support and treated the Lord with contempt.

He brought against him [Note: [Col. 1389D] Certain Latin manuscripts consistently read here “Theglath-Phalasar,” concerning whom enough has already been said. MART.] Thelgath-Phalnasar, king of Assyria, who afflicted him and, with no one resisting, devastated him.

Thus Ahaz, after plundering the house of the Lord and the houses of the kings and princes, gave gifts to the king of Assyria, but it did not benefit him.

Moreover, even in the time of his distress he increased his contempt [Col. 1390C] for the Lord. King Ahaz himself sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, who had struck him, and said:

“The gods of the kings of Syria help them. I will appease them with sacrifices, and they will help me”—whereas they became his downfall and that of all Israel.

Ahaz therefore stripped the house of God of all its vessels, broke them, shut the doors of the temple of God, and made altars for himself in every corner of Jerusalem.

In every city of Judah he also built altars for burning incense and provoked the Lord, the God of his fathers, to anger.

The rest of his acts and all his earlier and later deeds [Note: [Col. 1389D] Other Latin books add “of his own.”] are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried [Note: [Col. 1389D] The Memmian Canon preserves a variant reading here. In the text it reads “in the city of David”; [Col. 1390D] in the margin, however, it gives “Jerusalem” instead of “David.” The Septuagint reads “in the city of David,” which is confirmed as correct by 4 Kings 16:20. The Hebrew reads: “They buried him in the city, in Jerusalem.” MART.] him in the city of Jerusalem. They did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel. His son Hezekiah reigned in his place.

[Col. 1390D] ## Chapter XXIX

Hezekiah began to reign when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem.

His mother’s name was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah.

He did what was pleasing in the sight of the Lord, in accordance with everything that David his father had done.

In the first year and first month of his reign, he opened the doors of the house of the Lord and repaired them.

He brought in the priests and Levites and gathered them in the eastern square.

He said to them: “Listen to me, Levites, and sanctify yourselves. Cleanse the house of the Lord, the God of your fathers, [Col. 1391A] and remove every impurity from the sanctuary.

“Our fathers sinned and did evil in the sight of the Lord our God, abandoning him. They turned their faces away from the dwelling of the Lord and turned their backs.

“They closed the doors that were in the portico, extinguished the lamps, did not burn incense, and did not offer burnt offerings in the sanctuary to the God of Israel.

“Therefore the wrath of the Lord was stirred against Judah and Jerusalem. He gave them over to turmoil, destruction, and derision, as you yourselves see with your eyes.

“Behold, our fathers have fallen by the sword; our sons, daughters, and wives have been taken captive because of this crime.

“Now therefore I desire that we make a covenant with the Lord, the God of Israel, so that he may turn away from us the fury of his wrath.

[Col. 1391B] “My sons, [Note: [Col. 1391D] Manuscript codices read “my son.” The same manuscripts consequently read “son of Amasiah” and “son of Abdai,” rather than “son of Amasai” or “son of Abdi.” MART.] do not be negligent. The Lord has chosen you to stand before him, minister to him, worship him, and burn [Note: [Col. 1391D] These manuscripts also insert the pronoun “to him.”] incense.”

Then the Levites arose: Maath son of Amasai [Al. Amasiah] and Joel son of Azariah, from the sons of Kohath;

from the sons of Merari, Kish son of Abdi [Al. Abdai] and Azariah son of Jahallelel [Al. Jahalleleel];

from the sons of Gershon, Joah son of Zimmah and Eden son of Joah;

from the sons of Elizaphan, Shimri and Jeiel;

from the sons of Asaph, Zechariah and Mattaniah;

also from the sons of Heman, Jehiel and Shimei;

and from the sons of Jeduthun, Shemaiah and Uzziel.

They gathered their brothers, sanctified themselves, and entered according to the king’s command and the Lord’s command, to cleanse the house of God.

The priests entered the temple of the Lord to sanctify it. They removed all the impurity they found inside, in the vestibule of the house of the Lord. The Levites took it out and carried it away to the brook Kidron.

They began to cleanse it on the first day of the first month. On the eighth day of that month they entered the portico of the temple of the Lord; they cleansed the temple for eight days and completed what they had begun on the sixteenth day of the same month.

They then entered King Hezekiah and said to him:

“We have sanctified the entire house of the Lord, the altar of burnt offering and its vessels, the table of the bread of the Presence and all its vessels, and all the furnishings of the temple that King Ahaz had profaned during his reign after his treachery. Behold, everything is set out before the altar of the Lord.”

King Hezekiah rose early, assembled all the leaders of the city, and went up to the house of the Lord.

They offered together seven bulls, seven rams, [Col. 1391D] seven lambs, and seven male goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah.

He ordered the priests, the sons of Aaron, to offer them on the altar of the Lord.

The priests slaughtered the bulls, received the blood, and poured it upon the altar.

They also slaughtered the rams and poured their blood upon the altar.

They slaughtered the lambs and poured the blood upon the altar.

They brought the male goats for the sin offering before the king and the entire assembly, and they laid their hands [Col. 1392A] upon them. The priests slaughtered them and sprinkled their blood before the altar as an expiation for all Israel.

For the king had commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering be made for all Israel.

He appointed the Levites in the house of the Lord with cymbals, psalteries, and lyres, according to the arrangement of David, Gad the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet.

For this command came from the Lord through the hand of his prophets.

The Levites stood holding David’s instruments, and the priests held the trumpets.

Hezekiah commanded that the burnt offerings be offered upon the altar.

When the burnt offerings were being offered, they began to sing praises to the Lord and to sound the trumpets and the various instruments that David, king of Israel, had [Note: [Col. 1391D] The Hebrew and the Greek text likewise have only “the instruments of David king of Israel,” omitting the words that follow, “which he had prepared to sound together.” In several manuscripts Martianaeus found *legit* (“reads”) in place of *concrepaverat* (“had sounded together”).] prepared to sound.

[Col. 1392B] While the whole assembly was worshiping, the singers and those holding the trumpets remained at their duty until the burnt offering was completed.

When the offering had been completed, the king and all who were with him bowed down and worshiped.

Hezekiah and the leaders commanded the Levites to praise the Lord with the words of David and Asaph the seer. They praised him with great joy and worshiped, kneeling.

Hezekiah also added: “You have filled your hands for the Lord. Draw near and offer sacrifices and praises in the house of the Lord.”

The whole assembly therefore offered sacrifices, praises, and burnt offerings with devoted hearts.

The number of burnt offerings offered by the assembly was as follows: seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs.

They consecrated to the Lord six hundred cattle and three thousand sheep.

[Col. 1392C] But the priests were few and unable to skin all the burnt offerings; therefore the Levites, their brothers, helped them until the work was completed and the priests had been sanctified.

For the Levites are sanctified by a simpler rite than the priests.

There were thus many burnt offerings, the fat of the peace offerings, and the libations accompanying the burnt offerings; and the worship of the house of the Lord was completed.

Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because the service of the Lord had been completed, for the matter had been accomplished suddenly.

## Chapter XXX

Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah. He wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh, asking them to come to the house of the Lord in Jerusalem and celebrate the Passover for the Lord, the God of Israel.

After the king, the leaders, and the whole assembly of Jerusalem had taken counsel, they decided to celebrate the Passover in the second month.

They had not been able to celebrate it at its proper time because [Col. 1392D] the priests who could have been sufficient had not been sanctified, and the people had not yet gathered in Jerusalem.

The proposal pleased the king and the whole assembly.

They decided to send messengers throughout Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, inviting them to come and celebrate the Passover for the Lord, the God of Israel, in Jerusalem, for many had not done what was prescribed by the law.

The couriers went out with letters by command of the king and his leaders throughout Israel and Judah, proclaiming according to the king’s order:

[Col. 1393A] “Sons of Israel, return to the Lord, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, and he will return to the remnant that has escaped from the hand of the king of Assyria.

“Do not be like your fathers and your brothers, who departed from the Lord, the God of their fathers, and he gave them over to destruction, as you yourselves see.

“Do not stiffen your necks as your fathers did. Give your hands to the Lord and come to his sanctuary, which he has sanctified forever.

“Serve the Lord, the God of your fathers, and the fury of his wrath will turn away from you.

“For if you return to the Lord, your brothers and sons will find mercy before their masters who took them captive, and they will return to this land.

“For the Lord your God is gracious and merciful, and he will not turn his face away from you if you return to him.”

The couriers went swiftly from city to city through the land of Ephraim and Manasseh as far as [Col. 1393B] Zebulun, but the people mocked and ridiculed them.

Nevertheless, some men from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun accepted the counsel and came to Jerusalem.

In Judah the hand of the Lord was present to give them one heart, so that they would act according to the command of the king and the word of the Lord.

A great number of people gathered in Jerusalem to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month.

They rose and destroyed the altars that were in Jerusalem. They overturned all the places where incense had been burned to idols and threw them into the brook Kidron.

They slaughtered the Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month.

The priests and Levites, at last sanctified, offered burnt offerings in the house of the Lord.

They stood in their appointed order, according to the arrangement and law of Moses, the man of God. The priests received the blood to be poured out from the hands of the Levites, [Col. 1393C] because many in the assembly had not been sanctified. Therefore the Levites slaughtered the Passover for those who had not been able to sanctify themselves to the Lord.

A large part of the people from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, who had not been sanctified, ate the Passover, though not according to what was written.

Hezekiah prayed for them, saying: “The good Lord will show mercy to all who seek the Lord God of their fathers with their whole heart, and he will not charge them with being insufficiently sanctified.”

The Lord heard him and was reconciled to the people.

The Israelites who were found in Jerusalem celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy, praising the Lord each day.

The Levites and priests also praised him with instruments [Note: [Col. 1393D] The Hebrew has “with instruments,” or “with the instruments of the strength of the Lord”: . The Greek is still more concise: ἐν [Col. 1394D] ὀργάνοις τῷ Κυρίῳ, “with instruments for the Lord.” It seems, however, that Jerome read the passage differently in his copy.] appropriate to their office.

Hezekiah spoke to the heart of all the Levites who possessed good understanding concerning the Lord.

They ate for seven days during the festival, offering sacrifices of peace offerings and praising the Lord [Col. 1393D] God of their fathers.

The whole assembly decided to celebrate another seven days as well, and they did so with immense joy.

King Hezekiah of Judah had provided the assembly with one thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep.

The leaders gave the people one thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep. Thus a very great number of priests were sanctified.

All the assembly of Judah was filled with joy, including the priests and Levites, the entire gathering that had come from Israel, the converts from the land of Israel, and those living in Judah.

There was great celebration in Jerusalem, such as had not occurred there since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel.

The priests and Levites rose and blessed the people. Their voice was heard, and their prayer reached the holy dwelling place of heaven.

## Chapter XXXI

After these things had been duly celebrated, all Israel who had been found in the cities of Judah went out. Together they broke the idols, cut down the sacred groves, demolished the high places, and destroyed the altars—not only throughout Judah and Benjamin, but also in Ephraim and Manasseh—until they had utterly destroyed them.

Then all the Israelites returned to their possessions and cities.

Hezekiah established the priestly and Levitical divisions according to their groups, each person in his proper office—priests and Levites alike—for burnt offerings and peace offerings, so that they might minister, give thanks, and sing at the gates of the camps of the Lord.

[Col. 1394B] It was the king’s portion that the burnt offering should be offered from his own substance, every morning and evening, as well as on Sabbaths, new moons, and the other festivals, as it is written in the law of Moses.

He also commanded the people living in Jerusalem to give portions to the priests and Levites, so that they could devote themselves to the law of the Lord.

When this became widely known among the people, the Israelites brought abundant firstfruits of grain, wine, and oil, as well as honey and everything produced by the soil. They brought tithes of all these things.

The Israelites and Judeans who lived in the cities of Judah also brought tithes of oxen and sheep, and tithes of the holy things that they had vowed to the Lord their God. Carrying everything in, they made many heaps.

They began laying the foundations of the heaps in the third month and completed them in the seventh month.

When Hezekiah and his leaders entered and saw the heaps, they blessed the Lord and [Col. 1394C] the people of Israel.

Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites why the heaps lay there in this manner.

Azariah the chief priest, of the family of Zadok, answered him, saying:

“From the time when the firstfruits began to be brought into the house of the Lord, we have eaten and been satisfied, and much remains, because the Lord has blessed his people. This abundance of leftovers is what you see.”

Hezekiah therefore commanded that storerooms be prepared in the house of the Lord.

When this had been done, they faithfully brought in the firstfruits, the tithes, and everything that had been vowed.

Their overseer was the Levite Conaniah, with his brother Shimei as second.

After him came Jehiel, Azariah, Nahath, Asahel, and Jerimoth;

also Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Maath, and Benaiah, overseers under Conaniah and his brother Shimei, by the command of King Hezekiah and Azariah [Col. 1394D] the high priest of the house of God, to whom all these matters belonged.

Kore son of Imnah the Levite, keeper of the eastern gate, was in charge of the freewill offerings made to the Lord, the firstfruits, and the consecrated things in the holy of holies.

Under his care were Eden, Benjamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah, in the cities of the priests, to distribute faithfully the portions to their brothers, both the lesser and the greater:

except for males three years old and above, and all who entered the temple of the Lord, as well as whatever was needed each day for the ministry and for the observances according to their divisions; for the priests by families, and for the Levites from twenty years old and above, according to their orders and [Col. 1395A] groups.

Food was faithfully provided to the whole assembly—to their wives and children of both sexes—as well.

In the fields and suburbs of each city belonging to the sons of Aaron, men were appointed to distribute portions to every male among the priests and Levites.

Thus Hezekiah did all that we have described throughout Judah. He worked what was good, right, and true before the Lord his God in every aspect of the service of the house of the Lord, according to the law and the rites, desiring to seek his God with his whole heart. He acted accordingly, and he prospered.

## Chapter XXXII

After these events and this faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came. He entered Judah and besieged the fortified cities, intending to capture them.

When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come and that the entire force of the war was turning against Jerusalem, he took counsel with the leaders and the strongest men [Col. 1395B] to block the sources of the springs that were outside the city.

With everyone approving this decision, he gathered a very large assembly, and they blocked all the springs and the stream that flowed through the middle of the land, saying:

“Let the kings of Assyria not come and find an abundance of water.”

He also industriously repaired the entire wall that had been breached, built towers upon it, and constructed another wall outside it. He restored the Millo in the city of David and made weapons of every kind and shields.

He appointed commanders over the warriors in the army, summoned everyone to the square at the city gate, and spoke to their hearts, saying:

“Act courageously and be strong. Do not fear or be terrified by the king of Assyria or by the entire multitude that is with him.

“For more are with us than with him.

“With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the Lord our God, who is our helper and fights for us.”

The people were strengthened by these words of Hezekiah king of Judah.

After these things had taken place, Sennacherib king of Assyria sent his servants to Jerusalem—he himself was besieging Lachish with his entire army—to Hezekiah king of Judah and to all the people who were in the city, saying:

“Thus says Sennacherib king of Assyria: In what are you trusting, that you remain besieged in Jerusalem?

“Does Hezekiah deceive you, delivering you over to death by hunger and thirst, while claiming that the Lord your God will rescue you from the hand of the king of Assyria?

“Is this not the same Hezekiah who destroyed his high places and altars and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, saying: ‘You shall worship before one altar, and on it [Col. 1395D] you shall burn incense’?

“Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of the lands?

“Have the gods of the nations, or of all the lands, been able to rescue their regions from my hand?

“Who among all the gods of the nations that my fathers devastated has been able to rescue his people from my hand, so that your god could rescue you from this hand?

“Therefore do not let Hezekiah deceive you or mislead you with empty persuasion, and do not believe him. For if no god of all the nations and kingdoms has been able to rescue his people from my hand and from the hand of my fathers, then certainly your god will not be able to rescue you from my hand.”

His servants also said many other things against the Lord God and against his servant Hezekiah.

[Col. 1396A] He also wrote letters full of blasphemy against the Lord God of Israel and spoke against him:

“As the gods of the other nations were unable to rescue their people from my hand, so the god of Hezekiah will not be able to rescue his people from this hand.”

Moreover, with a loud cry in the language of Judah, he shouted against the people sitting on the walls of Jerusalem, to terrify them and capture the city.

He spoke against the God of Jerusalem as against the gods of the peoples of the earth, the work of human hands.

King Hezekiah and Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet therefore prayed against this blasphemy and cried out to heaven.

The Lord sent an angel, who struck every mighty man, warrior, and commander in the army of the king of Assyria. He returned in disgrace to his own land.

When he entered the house of his god, his sons, who had come forth from his own womb, killed him with the sword.

The Lord saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria and from the hand of everyone else, and he gave them rest on every side.

Many also brought sacrifices and offerings to the Lord in Jerusalem, and gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah, who thereafter was exalted before all the nations.

In those days Hezekiah became sick to the point of death and prayed to the Lord. He heard him and gave him a sign.

But he did not repay according to the benefits he had received, because his heart was lifted up. Therefore wrath came against him, and against Judah and Jerusalem.

Afterward he humbled himself because his heart had been lifted up—both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem—and therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them during the days of Hezekiah.

[Col. 1396C] Hezekiah was very wealthy and highly renowned. He gathered for himself many treasures of silver, gold, precious stones, spices, weapons of every kind, and vessels of great value.

He also had storehouses of grain, wine, and oil, stalls for all kinds of animals, and sheepfolds.

He built cities for himself, for he possessed innumerable flocks of sheep and herds of cattle, because the Lord had given him exceedingly great wealth.

This is the Hezekiah who blocked the upper spring of Gihon and diverted its waters underground toward the west side of the city of David. In all his works he prospered and accomplished whatever he desired.

Nevertheless, when the envoys of the princes of Babylon were sent to him to inquire about the portent that had occurred in the land, God abandoned him in order to test him and to make known everything that was in his heart.

The rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his acts of mercy [Col. 1396D] are written in the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet and in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him above the tombs of the sons of David. All Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem celebrated his funeral rites. His son Manasseh reigned in his place.

## Chapter XXXIII

Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem.

He did evil before the Lord, according to the abominations of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.

He turned back and rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had demolished.

He built altars to the Baals, made sacred groves, worshiped all the host of heaven, and served it.

[Col. 1397A] He also built altars in the house of the Lord, concerning which the Lord had said: “In Jerusalem my name shall be forever.”

He built altars for the entire host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord.

He made his sons pass through the fire in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom.

He observed dreams, pursued omens, practiced magical arts, and kept magicians and enchanters with him.

He committed many evils before the Lord, provoking him to anger.

He also set a carved and cast image in the house of God, concerning which God had spoken to David and to Solomon his son, saying:

“In this house and [Al. the conjunction is omitted] in Jerusalem, which I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever.

“I will no longer make the foot of Israel move from the land that I gave to their fathers—provided only that they take care to do all that I have commanded them, the whole law, rites, and judgments given through Moses.”

Manasseh therefore led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, so that they did more evil than all the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.

The Lord spoke to him and to his people, but they would not listen.

Therefore he brought against them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria. They captured Manasseh, bound him with chains and fetters, and led him to Babylon.

When he was in distress, he prayed to the Lord his God and deeply repented before the God of his fathers.

He entreated him and pleaded earnestly, and God heard his prayer.

He brought him back to Jerusalem and restored him to his kingdom. Then Manasseh recognized that the Lord alone is [Al. “was”] God.

After this he built a wall outside the city of David, [Col. 1397C] west of Gihon in the valley, from the entrance of the Fish Gate around as far as Ophel, and raised it to a great height.

He appointed commanders of the army in all the fortified cities of Judah.

He removed the foreign gods and the image from the house of the Lord.

He also removed the altars that he had built on the mountain of the house of the Lord and in Jerusalem, and threw everything outside the city.

He restored the altar of the Lord, sacrificed upon it victims and peace offerings, and offered praise.

He commanded Judah to serve the Lord, the God of Israel.

Nevertheless, the people continued to sacrifice on the high places to the Lord their God.

The rest of the deeds of Manasseh and his prayer to his God, as well as the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, are contained in the accounts of the kings of Israel.

His prayer and the way he was heard, together with all his sins [Col. 1397D] and acts of contempt, and the places where he built the high places, made sacred groves, and set up images before he repented, are written in the accounts of Hozai.

Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his own house. His son Amon reigned in his place.

Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for two years in Jerusalem.

He did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, as Manasseh his father had done.

He sacrificed to and served all the idols that Manasseh had made.

[Col. 1398A] He did not revere the presence of the Lord, as Manasseh his father had revered it; indeed, he committed far greater offenses.

When his servants conspired against him, they killed him in his own house.

But the remaining people of the land, after killing those who had struck down Amon, made Josiah his son king in his place.

[Chapter XXXIV]

Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem.

He did what was right in the sight of the Lord and walked in the ways of David his father; he did not turn aside either to the right or to the left.

In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still a boy, he began to seek the God of his father David.

And in the twelfth year, after he had begun to reign [Note: [Col. 1397D] The Vulgate manuscripts insert the word “to reign,” which is also to be understood. Nevertheless, on the authority of the ancient manuscripts and the Hebrew text, Martianaeus removed it. In fact, the Hebrew omits not only that word but also the preceding “after,” and has rather a different meaning: “In the twelfth year he began to cleanse Judah,” and so forth. It consequently seems that the Latin text is correct either if that word too is retained, with the Vulgate and the Greek, or if neither word is retained, with the Hebrew.] he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the sacred groves, and the idols and carved images.

They destroyed before him the altars of the Baals, and he demolished the images that had been set above them.

[Col. 1398B] He also cut down and crushed the sacred groves and carved images.

And upon the tombs of those who had been accustomed to sacrifice to them he scattered their fragments.

Moreover, he burned the bones of the priests upon the altars of the idols, and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.

He did the same in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali; he overturned everything.

When he had demolished the altars, the sacred groves, and the carved images, had crushed them into pieces, and had destroyed all the shrines throughout the entire land of Israel, he returned to Jerusalem.

Therefore, in the eighteenth year of his reign, after the land and the temple had been cleansed, he sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz, the recorder, to restore the house of the Lord their God.

They came to Hilkiah the high priest.

They took from him the money that had been brought into the house of the Lord and that the Levites and the gatekeepers had collected from Manasseh, Ephraim, and all the remnant of Israel, as well as from all Judah and Benjamin and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and delivered it into the hands of those who supervised the workers in the house of the Lord, so that they might restore the temple and repair whatever was damaged.

But they gave it to the craftsmen and builders [Note: [Col. 1398D] In the manuscript copies this is consistently read as *lapidicinis* (“stonecutters”); and later, in verse 22, “to Huldah the prophetess.” MART.] to purchase stones from the quarries and timber for the joints of the building and for the flooring of the houses that the kings of Judah had destroyed. And they carried out everything faithfully.

The overseers of the workers were Jahath and Obadiah, descendants of Merari; Zechariah and Meshullam, descendants of Kohath, who supervised the work. All the Levites were skilled in playing musical instruments.

Over those who carried loads for the various tasks were scribes and overseers from among the Levite gatekeepers.

While they were bringing out the money that had been brought into the temple of the Lord, Hilkiah the priest found the book of the Law of the Lord, given through Moses.

Hilkiah said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the book of the Law in the house of the Lord,” and he handed it to him.

Shaphan brought the scroll to the king and reported to him, saying, “Everything that you entrusted to your servants is being carried out.

The silver that was found in the house of the Lord has been melted down, and it has been given to the supervisors of the craftsmen and to those carrying out the various works.”

Then Hilkiah the priest gave me this book.
