When he had read it in the presence of the king, and the king had heard [Col. 1399A] the words of the Law, he tore his garments. And he commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying:

“Go and inquire of the Lord for me, and for the remnant of Israel and Judah, concerning all the words of this book that has been found.

For great is the wrath of the Lord that has been poured out upon us, because our fathers did not keep the word of the Lord by doing everything written in this scroll.”

So Hilkiah and those whom the king had sent with him went to Huldah the prophetess [Alternative reading: prophet], the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem, in the Second Quarter. And they spoke to her the words that we have related above.

She answered them: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Say to the man who sent you to me:

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am bringing disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants, and all the curses written in this book that they read before the king of Judah. For they have forsaken me and sacrificed to foreign gods, provoking me to anger by all the works of their hands.

Therefore my wrath will be poured out upon this place, and it shall not be extinguished.

“But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the Lord, speak as follows:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you have heard the words of the scroll, and your heart was softened, and you humbled yourself before God when you heard what was spoken against this place and its inhabitants, and because you revered my presence, tore your garments, and wept before me, I too have heard you, says the Lord.

“For now I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be brought to your tomb in peace; your eyes shall not see all the evil that I am going to bring upon this place and its inhabitants.”

So they reported to the king everything she had said.

Then he summoned all the elders of Judah [Col. 1399C] and Jerusalem, and went up to the house of the Lord. With him were all the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the priests and the Levites, and all the people, from the least to the greatest.

In their hearing, in the house of the Lord, the king read all the words of the scroll.

Standing upon his platform, he made a covenant before the Lord: that he would follow him, keep his commandments, testimonies, and ordinances with all his heart and with all his soul, and do what was written in that scroll, which he had read.

He also placed under oath all who were found in Jerusalem and Benjamin, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem acted according to the covenant of the Lord, the God of their fathers.

Thus Josiah removed all the abominations from all the regions belonging to the children of Israel, and made all who remained in Israel serve the Lord their God.

Throughout all his days they did not turn away from the Lord [Col. 1399D] the God of their fathers.

[Chapter XXXV]

Josiah celebrated the Passover to the Lord in Jerusalem; it was sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month.

He appointed the priests to their duties and encouraged them to minister in the house of the Lord.

He also spoke to the Levites, through whose instruction all Israel was sanctified to the Lord.

“Place the ark in the sanctuary of the temple that Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built. You shall no longer carry it.

Now serve the Lord your God and his people Israel. Prepare yourselves according to your families and clans, in the divisions of each group, as David king of Israel commanded and as his son Solomon prescribed.

[Col. 1400A] Serve in the sanctuary according to the families and divisions of the Levites, and, having sanctified yourselves, sacrifice the Passover.

Also prepare your brothers, so that they may act according to the words that the Lord spoke through Moses.”

Moreover, Josiah gave all the people who had been found at the Passover celebration lambs and young goats from the flocks, and thirty thousand of the rest of the livestock, together with three thousand cattle. These came from all the king’s possessions.

His officials also freely offered what they had vowed, both to the people and to the priests and Levites.

Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the leaders of the house of the Lord, gave the priests two thousand six hundred animals and three hundred cattle for celebrating the Passover.

Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nathanael, and his brothers, together with Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, the leaders of the Levites, gave the other Levites five thousand animals and five hundred cattle for celebrating the Passover.

[Col. 1400B] The service was prepared, and the priests stood in their places.

The Levites also stood in their divisions, according to the king’s command.

The Passover sacrifice was slaughtered; the priests sprinkled the blood with their hands, and the Levites flayed the burnt offerings. They separated them so that they could be distributed by houses and families and offered to the Lord, as it is written in the book of Moses.

They did the same with the cattle.

They roasted the Passover offerings over the fire, as the Law commanded.

But they boiled the peace offerings in cauldrons, kettles, and pots, and distributed them quickly to all the people.

Afterward they prepared portions for themselves and for the priests.

For the priests were occupied until nightfall with offering the burnt offerings and the fat.

Therefore the Levites prepared portions for themselves and for the priests, the sons of Aaron, last of all.

[Col. 1400C] The singers, the sons of Asaph, stood in their order, according to the command of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, the king’s prophets.

The gatekeepers watched at each gate, so that they did not depart from their service even for a moment.

For this reason their fellow Levites prepared food for them.

Thus all the worship of the Lord was properly completed on that day, so that they might celebrate the Passover and offer burnt offerings upon the altar of the Lord, according to the command of King Josiah.

The children of Israel who were found there celebrated the Passover at that time and kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days.

No Passover like this had been celebrated in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet.

Nor had any of all the kings of Israel celebrated a Passover like Josiah did, together with the priests, the Levites, all Judah, the Israelites who were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

This Passover was celebrated in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign.

After Josiah had restored the temple [Note: [Col. 1399] In the Memmian Canon this variant reading is found: “Necho and Nechato.” MART.], Neco, king of Egypt, went up to fight at Carchemish beside the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to meet him.

But Neco sent messengers to him and said:

“What have I to do with you, king of Judah? I am not coming against you today, but I am fighting against another house, and God has commanded me to go there quickly. Stop opposing God, who is with me, lest he destroy you.”

Josiah would not turn back, but prepared for battle against him, and he did not heed Neco’s words, which came from the mouth of God. Instead, he went forward to fight in the plain of Megiddo.

There he was wounded by the archers and said to his servants, “Take me out of the battle, for I am severely wounded.”

[Col. 1401A] They transferred him from his chariot to another chariot that followed him in royal fashion, carried him to Jerusalem, and he died and was buried in the mausoleum of his fathers.

All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him.

Jeremiah mourned especially; all the male and female singers continue to repeat laments over Josiah to the present day, and it became, as it were, a statute in Israel.

It is said to be written in the Lamentations.

The rest of the acts of Josiah and his acts of mercy, which were prescribed by the Law of the Lord, together with his earlier and later deeds, are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

[Chapter XXXVI]

Then the people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah and made him king in place of his father in Jerusalem.

Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem.

The king of Egypt removed him when he came to Jerusalem, and imposed upon the land a tribute of one hundred talents of silver [Col. 1401B] and one talent of gold.

He made his brother Eliakim king over Judah and Jerusalem and changed his name to Jehoiakim.

He took Jehoahaz with him and led him away to Egypt.

Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil before the Lord his God.

Against him came Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, and he led him bound in chains to Babylon.

He also carried the vessels of the Lord there and placed them in his own temple.

The rest of the words of Jehoiakim and his abominations, which he committed, and whatever was found in him, are contained in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

His son Jehoiachin reigned in his place.

Jehoiachin was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the Lord.

[Col. 1401C] When the year had come around, King Nebuchadnezzar sent for him, and they brought him to Babylon, carrying away with him the most precious vessels of the house of the Lord.

He appointed Zedekiah [Note: [Col. 1401C] In the Hebrew we read *abbiv*, meaning “his brother.” This reading is retained by the older Latin manuscripts—namely, the Regius, Memmian, Colbert, Aniciensis, San-German no. 15, Corbeiensis no. 14, and another, no. 1, in the first hand. It should nevertheless be understood as a Hebraism, by which an uncle is called a brother, just as in Genesis Abraham and Lot are called brothers. For Zedekiah was the brother of Jehoiachin’s father, just as Abraham was the brother of Lot’s father Haran. Thus “brother” here means “uncle,” or kinsman. MART. [Col. 1402C] —The Vulgate of the Fathers, as also the Syriac, prefers this reading, and the Greek states it very clearly: “Zedekiah, the brother of his father” (*Σεδεκίαν, ἀδελφὸν τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ*). Since it is abundantly established that Zedekiah was Jehoiachin’s uncle, not literally his brother, one may suspect that the Hebrew archetype likewise once had a different reading in place of what is now represented by a single word [reading uncertain in the supplied text]. Martianaeus, moreover, who restored the printed reading on the authority of several manuscripts, notes that this is a Hebraism, following the example of Abraham, who called Lot, the son of his brother, his brother.] his brother as king over Judah and Jerusalem.

Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.

He did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord his God, and he did not feel shame before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke to him from the mouth of the Lord.

He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God.

He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart, so that he would not return to the Lord God of Israel.

Moreover, all the chief priests and the people transgressed wickedly, according to all the abominations of the nations, and polluted the house of the Lord, which he had sanctified for himself in Jerusalem.

The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent messengers to them through his messengers, rising early and sending them daily warnings, because he spared his people and his dwelling place.

But they mocked the messengers of God, despised his words, and derided the prophets, until the wrath of the Lord rose against his people and there was no remedy.

For he brought against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of his sanctuary [Col. 1402B].

He spared neither young man nor virgin, neither old man nor even the aged; he delivered them all into his hands.

He carried to Babylon all the vessels of the house of the Lord, both large and small, and the treasures of the temple, of the king, and of the officials.

The enemies burned the house of God, demolished the wall of Jerusalem, burned all its towers, and destroyed everything of value.

If anyone escaped the sword, he was led to Babylon and served the king and his sons until the king of Persia came to power, so that the word of the Lord spoken by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled and the land might observe its sabbaths.

For throughout all the days of its desolation it kept sabbath, until the seventy years were completed.

In the first year of Cyrus, king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the Lord spoken by the mouth of Jeremiah, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of Persia [Col. 1402C], who commanded that this proclamation be made throughout his entire kingdom, even in writing:

“Thus says Cyrus, king of Persia: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judea.

Whoever among you belongs to all his people—may the Lord his God be with him, and let him go up.”

[Col. 1401] Here ends the Book of Chronicles, in Hebrew, *Words of the Days*.

[Col. 1401]

[THE BOOK OF EZRA]

[Note: [Col. 1401D] I collated both this preface and the Book of Ezra itself with the Vatican manuscript formerly belonging to the Queen of the Swedes, no. 7, marked as being of extremely ancient age and especially sound character. [Col. 1402D]]

JEROME’S PREFACE TO EZRA

[Col. 1401D] I have not yet decided whether it is harder to do what you ask or to refuse. For to reject anything when you command is not my way of thinking; and the magnitude of the burden imposed presses so heavily upon my neck that one must fall beneath the load before it can be lifted. Added to this are the efforts of the envious, who think that everything we write ought to be criticized; and sometimes, while their conscience resists them, they publicly tear apart what they read in secret, so much so that I am compelled to cry out and say: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Psalm 119:2).

It is now the third year in which you have continually written and rewritten to ask me to translate the Book of Ezra [Note: [Col. 1403B] The printed books, together with some more recent manuscripts, add “and Esther,” as though Domnio and Rogatianus had been writing and rewriting not only for the translation of Ezra into Latin but also for the Book of Esther. This is shown to be false both by the date at which Esther’s book, long after Ezra, was translated into Latin by Jerome, and by the persons to whom the preface to Esther is said below to have been written. It is established that it was dedicated to the younger Paula and the virgin Eustochium, not to Domnio and Rogatianus. MART. —The Regius manuscript omits “you continually write and rewrite,” which occurs shortly before, and consistently reads *Esdram* rather than *Ezram*.] for you from the Hebrew—as though you did not possess Greek and Latin volumes, or as though whatever is translated by us would not immediately be spat upon by everyone [Alternative reading: by all men].

As someone has said [Note: [Col. 1403C] This is Crispus Sallustius, who expresses the thought in *Jugurtha*, chapter 3: “To strive in vain, and by weariness to seek nothing but hatred, is the height of folly.”], “To strive in vain and by exhausting oneself to seek nothing but hatred is the height of folly.” Therefore I beg you, my dearest Domnio and Rogatianus, to be satisfied with private reading, not to bring the book into public, and not to force food upon the fastidious. Avoid the arrogance of those who know only how to judge others and themselves know how to do nothing.

If there are brothers to whom our work is not displeasing, give them a copy, warning them to transcribe the Hebrew names—of which this volume contains a great abundance—distinctly and with spaces between them. For correcting a book will be of no benefit if the correction is not preserved through the diligence of the scribes.

Nor should anyone be troubled that only one book has been published by us, or take pleasure in the dreams of the third and fourth apocryphal books [Note: [Col. 1403C] The Regius manuscript, together with older printed editions, adds “books.”], since among the Hebrews the books of Ezra and Nehemiah are compressed into a single volume. Whatever is not found among them, nor included among the twenty-four elders [Note: [Col. 1403C] He means the books contained in the canon of Hebrew truth, as is confirmed by the beginning of the *Galeate Preface* prefixed to the books of Samuel and the Kings. MART. —Victorius prefers repeating the verb “are found” here in this form: “Whatever is not found among them, nor is found among the twenty-four elders, must be cast far away.” The Queen’s manuscript reads “elders.” See the *Galeate Preface*, where, according to the opinion of others, not his own, he compares the number of the books of Scripture with the twenty-four elders of Revelation.] must be cast far away.

But if someone should set before you the Seventy Translators, whose copies their very diversity demonstrates to have been torn apart and [Note: [Col. 1403D] I would rather read “overturned,” since it is known that the Greek copies—and among them the most ancient and excellent, the Alexandrian, as we call it, and the Roman—not only admit the third book of Ezra into the series of canonical books but also place it before the others, reversing the order. Thus the book rejected by the Latin Church among the apocrypha is so highly regarded by the Greeks that it occupies the first place in their codices. This is precisely what the holy Father chiefly argues against: measuring the genuine books of Ezra against the Hebrew canon, he was apparently the first of all, even among the Latins, to teach that the third book—entitled in Greek *Ἱερεύς* (“Priest”), rejected by the Hebrews and not written in their language but in Greek—ought to be cast aside with the apocrypha. We say nothing now about the fourth, which the holy Father attacks with still sharper criticism, both here and elsewhere, especially in the book against Vigilantius. Those are mistaken who think that he attributed any authority to that book when, writing against Helvidius, he said: “Whether you wish Moses to be the author of the Pentateuch, or Ezra its restorer, I do not object.” For although this mention of restored sacred books may seem to be drawn from this Book of Ezra, the story was so common and conventional in everyone’s speech that there was no need for him to take it from that author. Since the decrees of the universal Church have followed Jerome’s judgment, only the first two books of Ezra have been received into the canon. It is a piece of utterly reckless falsehood that Clericus, reviving Erasmian calumny against Catholics at this passage of Jerome, prates that we now read the third and fourth books of Ezra without any distinction.], [Col. 1404A] overturned, for what is diverse cannot, of course, be asserted as true, send him to the Gospels. In them many things are presented as coming from the Old Testament that are not found among the Seventy Translators, such as: “For he shall be called a Nazarene”; “Out of Egypt I called my son”; and “They shall look upon him whom they pierced,” along with many other passages that we reserve for a more extensive work [Note: [Col. 1404C] That more extensive work is the book *On the Best Kind of Translation*, which he discussed above in the Preface to Chronicles, where he repeats these same scriptural statements, saying: “I recently wrote a book on the best kind of translation, showing those passages from the Gospel: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son,’ and so forth.” MART. —This is the letter written not long afterward to Pammachius, numbered 57 in our recension, *On the Best Kind of Translation*. See what we said about it shortly above in the Preface to Chronicles.]. Ask him where they are written. And when he cannot produce them, read to him from those copies recently published by us [Note: [Col. 1404D] I think he is speaking of the translation of the Prophets recently prepared by him. See the preface placed before this volume.], which the tongues of slanderers daily stab.

But to come to the point, what I am about to say is certainly most reasonable. Have I published something that is not found in the Greek, or that is found there differently from the way I translated it? Why do they tear the translator apart [Note: [Col. 1404D] The Queen’s manuscript has the equally good reading: “Let those who tear the translator apart ask,” and so forth.]? Let them ask the Hebrews, and on the authority of those very authors let them either grant or deny credibility to my translation.

It is one thing if they wish to slander me, as the saying goes, with closed eyes, and do not imitate the diligence and goodwill of the Greeks. After the Seventy Translators, once the Gospel of Christ was already shining forth, the Greeks carefully read the Jewish and Ebionite interpreters of the ancient Law—namely Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—and through Origen’s labor dedicated them to the Churches in the *Hexapla* (*Ἐξαπλοῖς*).

How much more grateful ought the Latins to be when they see Greece, rejoicing, borrow something from them [Note: [Col. 1404D] Here, I think, he alludes to the Psalter and the Prophets, which he had translated from Hebrew and which Sophronius rendered from Latin into Greek. See chapter 134 of the book *On Illustrious Men*.]?

First, it requires great expense and infinite difficulty to obtain all the copies. Then, even those who possess them, if they are ignorant of the Hebrew language, will err more, not knowing which of the many translators has spoken more accurately.

This also happened recently to a certain very learned man among the Greeks, who sometimes abandoned the meaning of Scripture [Note: [Col. 1405A] This is Apollinaris of Laodicea, whom he names in the second book of his *Apology against Rufinus*, no. 34: “I pass over Apollinaris, who, indeed with good zeal but not according to knowledge, attempted to sew together the patches of all the translations into one garment, and to unravel the coherence of Scripture not according to the rule of truth but according to his own judgment,” and so forth.] and followed the error of each individual translator [Note: [Col. 1405A] Several manuscripts read “the error of any one interpreter.” MART.].

But we, who possess at least a little knowledge of the Hebrew language and are not entirely without command of Latin, can judge more accurately among the others and express in our own language what we ourselves understand.

Therefore, even if the *excetra* [Note: [Col. 1405A] The manuscript copies of the Canon read *excetra* here, and many manuscripts have it written in this way. One Vatican manuscript and another belonging to the Carthusians near Avignon retain the same reading, followed by “and let the hydra hiss.” The sacred Bibles of the Avignon College of the Society of Jesus read in the same sense, “although the serpent may hiss.” In one manuscript of Silva Major the copyist inserted the ridiculous reading, “although outside the citadel it may hiss.” MART.] hisses, and victorious Sinon [Note: [Col. 1406A] This half-line is from Virgil, by which Jerome seems to attack Rufinus. For the notorious traitor Sinon, see Book 2 of the *Aeneid*. MART.] boasts of fires (*Aeneid* 2), my eloquence, with Christ’s help, will never be silent; even with my tongue cut off, it will stammer.

Let those who wish read; let those who do not wish cast it aside. Let them toss the letters about and slander the words. I shall be urged to diligence more by your affection than deterred by their detraction and hatred.

THE BOOK OF EZRA BEGINS

[Col. 1405]

[Chapter I]

In the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians [Note: [Col. 1405D] The Regius codex reads: “And he commanded throughout his entire kingdom in writing, saying,” and so forth. MART.], so that the word of the Lord spoken by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of Persia. He caused a proclamation to be made throughout his entire kingdom, even in writing, saying:

“Thus says Cyrus, king of Persia: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judea. Who among you belongs to all his people? [Col. 1405C] May his God be with him. Let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judea, and build the house of the Lord God of Israel; he is the God who is in Jerusalem. And let all the rest, wherever they live, assist him, each from his own place, with silver and gold, possessions and livestock, in addition to what they freely offer for the temple of God, which is in Jerusalem.”

Then the heads of the ancestral houses of Judah and Benjamin, the priests and Levites, and everyone whose spirit God had stirred up [Note: [Col. 1405D] The Queen’s manuscript adds “the Holy Spirit”; shortly afterward it reads “they might help” instead of “they helped.”] arose to go up and build the temple of the Lord, which was in Jerusalem. And all those who lived around them assisted them with silver and gold vessels, possessions, animals, and furnishings, besides what they had freely offered.

King Cyrus also brought out the vessels of the temple of the Lord that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and placed in the temple of his god.

Cyrus, king of Persia, brought them out through Mithredath son of Gazabar and counted them out to Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah. And this was their number: thirty gold bowls, one thousand silver bowls, twenty-nine knives, thirty gold cups, four hundred and ten second-quality silver cups, and one thousand other vessels. All the gold and silver vessels numbered five thousand four hundred. Sheshbazzar brought all these with those who came up from the Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem.

[Chapter II]

These are the children of the province who came up from the captivity that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried away to Babylon, and who returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own city.

They came with Zerubbabel: Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, [Note: [Col. 1405D] The Queen’s manuscript reads “Belran and Beguiai,” though less correctly.], Bilsan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah.

The number of the men of the people of Israel:

[Col. 1406C] The descendants of Parosh, two thousand one hundred seventy-two; the descendants of Shephatiah, three hundred seventy-two; the descendants of Arah, seven hundred seventy-five; the descendants of Pahath-moab, namely the descendants of Jeshua and Joab, two thousand eight hundred twelve; the descendants of Elam, one thousand two hundred fifty-four; the descendants of Zattu, nine hundred forty-five; the descendants of Zaccai, seven hundred sixty; the descendants of Bani, six hundred forty-two; the descendants of Bebai, six hundred twenty-three; the descendants of Azgad, one thousand two hundred twenty-two; the descendants of Adonikam, six hundred sixty-six; the descendants of Bigvai, two thousand fifty-six; the descendants of Adin, four hundred fifty-four; the descendants of Ater, who were of Hezekiah, ninety-eight; the descendants of Bezai, three hundred twenty-three; the descendants of Jorah, one hundred twelve; the descendants of Hashum, two hundred twenty-three; the descendants of Gibbar, ninety-five; the descendants of Bethlehem, one hundred twenty-three; the men of Netophah, fifty-six; the men of Anathoth, one hundred twenty-eight; the descendants of Azmaveth, forty-two; the descendants of Kirjath-arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, seven hundred forty-three; the descendants of Ramah and Geba, six hundred twenty-one; the men of Michmas, one hundred twenty-two; the men of Bethel and Ai [Note: [Col. 1406D] Since there are both our manuscripts and those cited by Martianaeus that prefer “Gai” to “Ai,” this should not be thought a scribal error but perhaps the learned care of the translator himself, since in Hebrew it is written with the letter represented by *g*, which the older translators commonly render by *g*.], two hundred twenty-three; the descendants of Nebo, fifty-two; the descendants of Magbish, one hundred fifty-six; the descendants of the other Elam, one thousand two hundred fifty-four; the descendants of Harim, three hundred twenty; the descendants of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, seven hundred twenty-five; the descendants of Jericho, three hundred forty-five; the descendants of Senaah, three thousand six hundred thirty.

The priests: [Note: [Col. 1407D] The Vulgate editions read *Jadaia*; the Queen’s manuscript, *Adaia*; but it is tiresome to pursue these matters further.] the descendants of Idaiah, of the house of Jeshua, nine hundred seventy-three; the descendants of Immer, one thousand fifty-two; [Note: [Col. 1407D] In this passage they retain *Paeessur* or *Phesur* without *b*, that is, without the Hebrew *heth*, although it is written *Phesbur*. MART.] the descendants of Pashhur, one thousand two hundred forty-seven; the descendants of Harim, one thousand seventeen.

The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel, descendants of Hodaviah, seventy-four.

The singers: the descendants of Asaph, one hundred twenty-eight.

The descendants of the gatekeepers: the descendants of Shallum, the descendants of Ater, the descendants of Talmon, the descendants of Akkub, the descendants of Hatita, and the descendants of Shobai—one hundred thirty-nine in all.

The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, the descendants of Hasupha, the descendants of Tabbaoth, the descendants of Keros, the descendants of Siaha, the descendants of Padon, the descendants of Lebanah, the descendants of Hagabah, the descendants of Akkub, the descendants of Hagab, the descendants of Shamlai, the descendants of Hanan, the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Gahar, the descendants of Reaiah, the descendants of Rezin, the descendants of Nekoda, the descendants of Gazzam, the descendants of Uzza, the descendants of Paseah, the descendants of Besai, the descendants of Asnah, the descendants of Meunim, the descendants of Nephusim, the descendants of Bakbuk, the descendants of Hakupha, the descendants of Harhur, the descendants of Bazluth, the descendants of Mehida, the descendants of Harsha, the descendants of Barkos, the descendants of Sisera, the descendants of Temah, the descendants of Neziah, and the descendants of Hatipha.

[Col. 1407B] The descendants of Solomon’s servants: the descendants of Sotai, the descendants of Sophereth, the descendants of Peruda, the descendants of Jaala, the descendants of Darkon, the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Shephatiah, the descendants of Hattil, the descendants of Pochereth, who were of Hazzebaim, and the descendants of Ami. All the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon’s servants numbered three hundred ninety-two.

And these were the ones who came up from Tel-melah [Alternative reading: Tel-harsa], Tel-harsha, Cherub, [Note: [Col. 1407D] These names have been confused through scribal error. The manuscript codices read *Arsacherub and Don and Mer*. Through an easy slip they write *Don* for *Eddon* and *Mer* for *Emmer*. MART.] Addon, and Immer, but they could not indicate their ancestral house or their lineage, whether they were Israelites. The descendants of Delaiah, the descendants of Tobiah, and the descendants of Nekoda numbered six hundred fifty-two.

And among the descendants of the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, the descendants of Hakkoz, and the descendants of Barzillai, who took a wife from the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name. These sought the record of their genealogy, but did not find it, and they were excluded from the priesthood.

And Athersatha told them not to eat of the holy of holies until a learned and fully qualified priest should arise. The whole assembly was as one man: forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty, besides their male and female slaves, who numbered seven thousand three hundred and thirty-seven; among them were two hundred singers and female singers. Their horses numbered seven hundred and thirty-six; their mules, two hundred and forty-five; their camels, four hundred and thirty-five; their donkeys, six thousand seven hundred and twenty.

And some of the heads of families, when they entered the temple of the Lord, which is in Jerusalem, freely offered gifts for the house of God, to rebuild it in its proper place. According to their means they contributed toward the expenses of the work: sixty thousand and one gold solidi [Note: Here too there is an error in the number: for sixty they wrote forty, transposing the numerical signs in this way, XL thousand for LX thousand. The Memmian Canon has in the text four hundred thousand solidi and one thousand, but in the margin marks XL for CCCC. MART. —The Reginensis manuscript incorrectly reads “forty and one thousand solidi”; in his own copies Martianaeus seems to have encountered “forty thousand and one thousand,” which is itself also a false reading.] five thousand minas of silver, and one hundred priestly garments. So the priests, Levites, and some of the people, together with the singers, gatekeepers, and Nathinaeans, lived in their own cities, and all Israel in their cities.

## Chapter III

The seventh month had now arrived, and the Israelites were in their cities. Then the people gathered together as one man in Jerusalem, and Jeshua son of Jozadak, together with his brother priests, [Col. 1408A] and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, together with his brothers, arose and built the altar of the God of Israel, in order to offer burnt offerings upon it, as it is written in the law of Moses, the man of God. [Note: “They set up,” etc. The Regius manuscript: “And they set up the altar of the God of Israel upon its bases; but the peoples of the lands around them terrified them.” MART.] They set up the altar [Note: The name of God is omitted here, as in the Reginensis manuscript; the Hebrew and Greek texts likewise omit it.] of God on its bases, while the peoples of the lands around them terrified them, and they offered burnt offerings upon it to the Lord morning and evening. They celebrated the feast of Booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offering in due order, according to the commandment, each day’s work on its day. After this they offered the regular burnt offering, both at the new moons and at all the appointed feasts of the Lord that had been consecrated, and on every occasion when an offering was freely presented to the Lord. From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the Lord, though the foundation of the temple of God had not yet been laid. They gave money to the stonecutters and masons, and also food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and Tyrians, so that they would bring cedar timber from Lebanon to the sea at Joppa, according to what Cyrus king of the Persians had commanded them.

In the second year after their arrival at the temple [Col. 1408B] of God in Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Jeshua son of Jozadak, and the rest of their brother priests and the Levites, together with all who had come from captivity to Jerusalem, began the work and appointed Levites twenty years old and above to supervise the work of the Lord. Jeshua and his sons and his brothers stood there, together with Kadmiel and his sons, [Note: The same Regius manuscript reads differently: “And the sons of Judah unanimously, to supervise those who were doing the work in the house of God . . . and their Levite brothers laid the foundation, building the temple of the Lord, and the priests stood,” etc. Then, at verse 11: “And they answered in praise and thanksgiving to the Lord, for he is good.” All these variant readings are preserved by the above-mentioned manuscript no. 3564 in the library of the Most Christian King. MART.] and the sons of Judah, as one man, to supervise those who were carrying out the work on the temple of God; also the sons of Henadad, their sons, and their brother Levites.

When the temple of the Lord had been founded by the masons, the priests stood in their vestments with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise God through the hands of David king of Israel. They sang responsively in hymns and thanksgiving to the Lord: “For he is good, for his mercy is forever upon Israel.” All the people likewise shouted with a great shout when praising the Lord, because the temple of the Lord had been founded. But many of the priests and Levites and [Col. 1408C] heads of families, the elders who had seen the former temple, when this temple was founded [Note: Thus the outstanding Saint-Germain manuscript reads. Other manuscripts read less correctly, “and this temple,” etc. MART.] before their eyes, wept with a loud voice. Many others shouted for joy and raised their voices. No one could distinguish the sound of the joyful shouting from the sound of the people’s weeping, for the people shouted with a great mixed cry, and the sound was heard from far away.

## Chapter IV

The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the descendants of the captivity were building a temple to the Lord, the God of Israel. They approached Zerubbabel and the heads of families and said to them: “Let us build with you, for we seek your God just as you do. Look, we have been sacrificing victims since the days of Esar-haddon, king of Assyria, who brought us here.” But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of the families of Israel said to them: “It is not for you and us to build a house for our God; we alone will build it for the Lord our God, as Cyrus king of the Persians commanded us.”

Then the people of the land hindered the people of Judah’s efforts [Col. 1409A] and obstructed them in the building. They also hired advisers against them to thwart their plan throughout all the days of Cyrus king of the Persians and until the reign of Darius king of the Persians.

In the reign of Ahasuerus, at the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. In the days of Artaxerxes, Beselam, Mithredath, and Tabeel, together with the rest of their associates, wrote to Artaxerxes king of the Persians. The letter of accusation was written in Syriac and read in the Syrian language. Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote one letter from Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king, as follows:

“Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates—the Dinaites, [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads “Dinai and Pharsethaei,” and shortly afterward “Susanechanaei.”] the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Erechites, the Babylonians, the Susanechites, [Note: The manuscripts have Apharsathaei without the final *chaph*. The Hebrew is inconsistent in writing this name: here it is written with *tau* in the middle, but below, in chapter 5, verse 6, it is written without any *tau*, Apharsachaei. MART.] the Dehaeans, the Elamites, and the rest of the nations whom the great and glorious Asenappar transferred and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the other regions beyond the River, in peace.

[Col. 1409B] This is a copy of the letter that they sent to him:

‘To Artaxerxes the king: Your servants, the men who are beyond the River, send greetings.

Let it be known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have arrived in Jerusalem, that rebellious and wicked city. They are rebuilding it, restoring its walls, and repairing its foundations. Now therefore let it be known to the king that, if that city is rebuilt and its walls restored, they will not pay tribute, tax, or annual revenue, and this offense will reach the kings. Since we remember the salt that we eat in the palace, and since we consider it unlawful to see the king harmed, we have therefore sent and informed the king, so that you may search the records of the histories of your fathers. You will find written in the chronicles and will learn that this city is a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces, and that rebellions have arisen in it from ancient days; for this reason the city itself was destroyed. We inform the king that, if that city is rebuilt [Col. 1409C] and its walls restored, you will have no possession beyond the River.’

The king sent this reply to Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates who lived in Samaria, as well as to the others beyond the River:

‘Greetings and peace.

The accusation that you sent to us has been read clearly before me. I issued an order, and they searched and found that this city has rebelled against kings from ancient times, and that rebellions and battles have arisen in it. Indeed, powerful kings ruled in Jerusalem and dominated the entire region beyond the River; they also received tribute, tax, and revenue. Now therefore hear the decree: prevent those men, and let that city not be built until an order is issued by me. Take care that you do not carry this out negligently, lest the evil gradually increase against the kings.’

Accordingly, a copy of the edict of Artaxerxes the king was read before Rehum, Shimshai the scribe, and their associates. [Col. 1409D] They hastened to Jerusalem to the Jews and stopped them by force and strength. Then the work on the house of the Lord in Jerusalem ceased, and it was not resumed until the second year of the reign of Darius king of the Persians.

## Chapter V

The prophet Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews who were in Judea and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel. Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak arose and began to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, assisting them.

At that time Tattenai [Note: Consistently without aspiration, “Tattannai” is pronounced in the Reginensis manuscript.] came to them, the governor of the region beyond the River, together with Shethar-bozenai and their associates, and said to them: “Who gave you permission to build this house and restore these walls?” To this we replied to them with the names of the men who were responsible for that building. But the eye of their God was upon the elders [Alt. “older men”] of the Jews, and they were unable to stop them. It was decided that the matter should be reported to Darius, and then they would give a response concerning that accusation.

This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai, governor of the region beyond the River, and Shethar-bozenai, together with his associates, the Apharsachites who were beyond the River, sent to Darius the king. The letter that they sent him was written as follows:

“To Darius the king: complete peace.

Let it be known to the king that we went to the province of Judea, to the house of the great God, which is being built with unhewn stones, with timber being placed in the walls. That work is being carefully carried out and is progressing in their hands. We questioned those elders and said to them: ‘Who gave you authority to build this house and restore these walls?’ We also asked them their names, so that we might inform you in writing of the names of the men who are their leaders.

They answered us as follows: ‘We are servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the temple that had been built many years ago, which a great king of Israel had built and completed. [Note: The Reginensis manuscript omits “Israel,” which is nevertheless present in the Hebrew text.] But after our fathers provoked the God of heaven to anger, he delivered them into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, the Chaldean. He destroyed this house as well and carried its people away to Babylon.

‘But in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king issued a decree that this house of God should be built. Moreover, Cyrus the king brought out of the temple of Babylon the golden and silver vessels of the temple of God [Note: Here we have restored the name “God,” which Martianaeus had omitted, from the Reginensis manuscript, in agreement with the Hebrew text and the other printed books.] that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple that was in Jerusalem and had carried away to the temple of Babylon. He gave them to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he also appointed governor, and said to him: “Take these vessels, go, and place them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be built in its place.” Then that Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the temple of God in Jerusalem. From that time until now it has been under construction, and it is not yet finished.

‘Now therefore, if it seems good to the king, let a search be made in the royal library, which is in Babylon, to determine whether it was ordered by King Cyrus that the house of God be built in Jerusalem; and let the king send us his decision concerning this matter.’”

[Col. 1410D] ## Chapter VI

Then King Darius gave the order, and they searched in the library of the books kept in Babylon. It was found in Ecbatana, the fortress in the province of Media [Note: The Regius manuscript reads “in the middle province.” The Memmian Canon has *Medana* in the text, but in the margin *Madana* in one place and *Madena* in another. These differences are certainly of very slight importance, yet they should not be entirely omitted for the sake of those who lie in wait for the labors of scholars. MART.], that one scroll contained this written record:

“In the first year of Cyrus the king: Cyrus the king decreed that the house of God, which is in Jerusalem, should be built as a place where sacrifices are offered, and that its foundations should be laid to support a height of sixty cubits and a width of sixty cubits. [Note: The Reginensis manuscript gives seventy cubits for the height and thirty for the width.] There shall be three courses of unhewn stones, and likewise courses of new timber; the expenses shall be paid from the royal house. Moreover, the golden and silver vessels of the temple of God that Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem and brought to Babylon shall be returned and restored to the temple in Jerusalem, each to its proper place; and they shall be placed in the temple of God.

“Now therefore, Tattenai [Alt. Tannae], governor of the region beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and your associates the Apharsachites who are beyond the River, withdraw far from them and let that house of God [Note: The Reginensis manuscript omits “God,” though it is also expressed in the Hebrew.] be built by the governor of the Jews and their elders. Let those men build that house of God in its place. Moreover, I decree what must be done for those elders of the Jews so that the house of God may be built: namely, that from the royal treasury—that is, from the taxes collected from the region beyond the River—expenses shall be diligently provided for those men, so that the work may not be hindered. And if necessary, let calves, rams, and lambs be given for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, together with wheat, salt, wine, and oil, according to the custom of the priests who are in Jerusalem, each day without fail, so that there may be no complaint in any respect. Let them offer sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons.

“I have therefore issued this decree: whoever alters this command shall have a beam removed from his house, and he shall be raised up and impaled upon it; and his house shall be made a public ruin. May the God who has caused his name to dwell there destroy every kingdom and every people that stretches out its hand to resist or destroy that house of God, which is in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have issued this decree; let it be carried out diligently.”

Then Tattenai, governor of the region beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and his associates diligently carried out what Darius the king had commanded. The elders of the Jews built and prospered [Col. 1411C] according to the prophecy of the prophet Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo. They built and completed it by the command of the God of Israel and by the commands of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of the Persians. They completed this house of God on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.

The Israelites—the priests, the Levites, and the rest of the descendants of the captivity—celebrated the dedication of the house of God with joy. For the dedication of the house of God they offered one hundred calves, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering for all Israel, according to the number of the tribes of Israel. They appointed the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their courses over the service of God in Jerusalem, as it is written in the book of Moses.

The descendants of the captivity celebrated Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. For the priests and Levites had purified themselves as one man; all were clean to sacrifice the Passover for all the descendants of the captivity, for their brother priests, and for themselves. The Israelites who had returned from the captivity ate, together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land and joined them in seeking the Lord God of Israel. They celebrated the feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with joy, because the Lord had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them, so that he assisted them in the work of the house of the Lord, the God of Israel.

## Chapter VII

After these events, during the reign of Artaxerxes king of the Persians, Ezra son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads “son of Ahitub, son of Amariah,” and then “son of Meraioth, son of Azariah,” etc.] Ahitub, son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth, son of Zerahiah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki, son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, [Col. 1412A] son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest from the beginning—this Ezra came up from Babylon. He was a skilled scribe in the law of Moses, which the Lord God of Israel had given. The king granted him everything he requested, according to the hand of the Lord his God upon him.

Some of the Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and Nathinaeans went up to Jerusalem in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king. He came to Jerusalem in the fifth month; that was the seventh year of the king. For he began to go up from Babylon on the first day of the first month, and he arrived in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month, according to the good hand of his God upon him. For Ezra had set his heart to investigate the law of the Lord, to practice it, and to teach in Israel its statutes and judgments.

This is a copy of the letter of the edict that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the learned scribe in the words, commandments, and ordinances of the Lord in Israel:

[Col. 1412B] “Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the most learned scribe of the law of the God of heaven: greetings.

“It is decreed by me that anyone in my kingdom from the people of Israel, their priests, or the Levites who wishes to go to Jerusalem may go with you. You have been sent by the king and his seven counselors to inspect Judea and Jerusalem according to the law of your God, which is in your hand, and to carry the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem. All the silver and gold that you find throughout the province of Babylon, and whatever the people wish to offer, together with what the priests freely offer for the house of their God, which is in Jerusalem, you may freely accept. With this money carefully purchase calves, rams, lambs, their sacrifices and libations, and offer them upon the altar of the temple of your God, which is in Jerusalem.

“Whatever seems good to you and your brothers to do with the remaining silver and gold, do according to the will of your God. The vessels given to you for the service of the house of your God, deliver before the God in Jerusalem. Whatever else is needed for the house of your God, however much it is necessary to spend, [Note: In the first hand of the Reginensis manuscript, *dabis* (“you shall give”) was written.] shall be given from the treasury, the royal fisc, and by me.

“I, Artaxerxes the king, have established and decreed for all the keepers of the public treasury who are beyond the River that whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven, requests from you shall be given without delay, up to one hundred talents of silver, up to one hundred cors of grain, up to one hundred baths of wine, and up to one hundred baths of oil; salt, however, without measure. Whatever pertains to the rite of the God of heaven shall be diligently provided in the house of the God of heaven, lest wrath arise against the kingdom of the king and his sons.

“We also inform you concerning all the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, Nathinaeans, and ministers of this house of God: you shall have no authority to impose tribute, tax, or provisions upon them. You, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God, which is in your hand, appoint judges and magistrates [Col. 1412D] to judge all the people who are beyond the River, namely those who know the law of your God; and teach those who do not know it freely. Whoever does not carefully observe the law of your God and the law of the king shall be subject to judgment, whether death, exile, confiscation of his property, or imprisonment.”

Blessed be the Lord, the God of our fathers, who put this into the heart of the king, to glorify the house of the Lord, which is in Jerusalem, and who inclined his mercy toward me before the king, his counselors, and all the powerful princes of the king.

[Col. 1413A] And I, strengthened by the hand of the Lord my God, which was upon me, gathered from Israel leaders who would go up with me.

## Chapter VIII

These, then, are the heads of the families and their genealogies who went up with me during the reign of Artaxerxes the king, from Babylon. Of the sons of Phinehas: Gershom. Of the sons of Ithamar: Daniel. Of the sons of David: Hattush. Of the sons of Shecaniah, of the sons of Pharosh: Zechariah; and with him one hundred and fifty men were enrolled. Of the sons of Phaath-moab, [Note: The same manuscript reads “Pheth-Moab” and “Azariah” for “Zerah”; it then places the verse “Of the sons of Addin, Ahed” before the following one, “Of the sons of Shecaniah,” etc., which is a scribal error. It likewise soon reads “Hiezechiel” for “Ezekiel,” and a little later “Abedia son of Jechiel”; finally, “Ezead” for “Ezgad” and “Secetan” for “Eccetan.”] Elioenai son of Zerah, and with him two hundred men. Of the sons of Shecaniah, the son of Ezekiel, and with him three hundred men. Of the sons of Addin, Obed son of Jonathan, and with him fifty men. Of the sons of Elam, Isaiah son of Athaliah, and with him seventy men. Of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah son of Michael, and with him eighty men. Of the sons of Joab, Obadiah son of Jehiel, and with him two hundred and eighteen men. Of the sons of Shelomith, the son of Josiphiah, and with him one hundred and sixty men. Of the sons of Bebai, Zechariah son of Bebai, and with him twenty-eight men. Of the sons of Azgad, Johanan [Col. 1413B] son of Eccetan, and with him one hundred and ten men. Of the sons of Adonikam, who were the last: these were their names—Eliphelet, and [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads “Hehihel,” and notes concerning the following name, Shemaiah, that elsewhere it is called Ramiah. It also reads *Zacchur* with a doubled *c*; in the Hebrew and Greek it is written *Zabud*. Jerome, as Martianaeus also observes, read [letters illegible in the supplied text] in place of [letters illegible in the supplied text].] Jeuel, and Shemaiah, and with them sixty men. Of the sons of Bigvai, [Note: In the present Hebrew text we read *Zabud*, which the translators of the Septuagint also read as Ζαβούδ. Jerome, however, read *kaph* rather than *beth* in his Hebrew copies, and *resh* rather than *daleth*: thus *Zachur*, not *Zabud*. MART.] Uthai and Zachur, and with them seventy men.

I gathered them at the river that runs to [Note: Here and below the Reginensis manuscript reads *Havua* for *Aava*, and *Mesolam* for *Mosollam*.] Ahava, and we stayed there three days. I searched among the people and among the priests for descendants of Levi, but found none there. So I sent Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, another Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, the leaders, together with Joiarib and Elnathan, men of understanding. I sent them to Iddo, who was the chief at the place of Casiphia, and I placed in their mouths the words that they should speak to Iddo and his brother Nathinaeans at the place of Casiphia, so that they might bring us ministers for the house of our God.

By the good hand of our God upon us they brought us a very learned man from the sons of Mahli, son of Levi, son of Israel, namely Sherebiah, together with his sons and his brothers, eighteen; and Hashabiah [Note: The same manuscript prefers “Sabiah” for “Hashabiah” and “Saiah” for “Isaiah.”], and with him Isaiah of the sons of Merari, together with his brothers and his sons, twenty. Of the Nathinaeans, whom David and the leaders had given for the service of the Levites, there were two hundred and twenty Nathinaeans; all these were called by their names.

There by the river Ahava I proclaimed a fast, so that we might humble ourselves before the Lord our God and ask from him a straight path for ourselves, our children, and all our possessions. For I was ashamed to ask the king for an escort and horsemen to defend us from the enemy on the road, because we had said to the king: “The hand of our God is upon all who seek him in goodness, but his dominion and strength and wrath are upon all who forsake him.” So we fasted and entreated our God concerning this, and it went well for us.

I set apart twelve of the leading priests: Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers. I weighed out to them the silver, gold, and consecrated vessels of the house of our God [Col. 1413D], which the king, his counselors, his princes, and all Israel who had been found there had offered. I weighed into their hands six hundred and fifty talents of silver, one hundred silver vessels, one hundred talents of gold, twenty golden bowls worth one thousand solidi each, and two vessels of shining, excellent bronze, beautiful like gold.

I said to them: “You are holy to the Lord, and these vessels are holy; the silver and gold have been freely offered to the Lord, the God of our fathers. Watch over them and guard them until you weigh them before the leaders of the priests and Levites and the heads of the families of Israel in Jerusalem, in the treasury of the house of the Lord.” Then the priests and Levites received the weight of the silver, gold, and vessels, to carry them to Jerusalem, to the house of our God.

We departed [Note: The preceding words, “So we departed,” are absent from the Reginensis manuscript.] from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month to travel to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was upon us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and the ambusher on the road. We came to Jerusalem and stayed there three days. On the fourth day the silver, gold, and vessels [Note: Here again the Reginensis manuscript omits the words “and the vessels,” though they are present in the Hebrew. Shortly afterward it reads “Remoth” for “Meremoth.”] were weighed in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth son of Uriah the priest, together with Eleazar son of Phinehas, and with them Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui [Col. 1414B], the Levites, according to the number and weight of everything. The entire weight was recorded at that time.

The descendants of the captivity who had arrived also offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel: twelve calves for all the people of Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering; all as a burnt offering to the Lord. They delivered the king’s edicts to the satraps who were in the king’s presence and to the governors beyond the River, and these officials supported the people and the house of God.

## Chapter IX

When these things had been completed, the leaders approached me and said: “The people of Israel, the priests, and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands and from their abominations—the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites. For they have taken some of their daughters for themselves and for their sons, and have mixed the holy seed with the peoples of the lands. The hand of the leaders and magistrates has also been foremost in this transgression.”

When I heard this, I tore my cloak and tunic, pulled out the hair of my head and beard, and sat mourning. Everyone who feared the word of the God of Israel gathered around me because of the transgression of those who had returned from the captivity. I sat grieving until the evening sacrifice. At the evening sacrifice I rose from my humiliation, and with my cloak and tunic torn, I bent my knees, spread out my hands to the Lord my God, and said:

“My God, I am ashamed and embarrassed to lift my face to you, because our iniquities have multiplied over our heads and our offenses have grown up to heaven. From the days of our fathers until this day we ourselves have sinned greatly, and because of our iniquities we, our kings, and our priests have been handed over to the kings of the lands—to the sword, captivity, plunder, and shame—as it is today.

“And now, as though for a little while and a moment, our supplication has been made before the Lord our God, so that a remnant might be left to us and a peg [Note: The Reginensis manuscript has *pax illius* in two words instead of *paxillus*; other Latin manuscripts make the same error.] might be given to us in his holy place; so that our God might enlighten our eyes and grant us a little life in our servitude. For we are slaves, yet in our servitude our God has not abandoned us. Instead, he has inclined mercy toward us before the king of the Persians, to give us life, raise up the house of our God, rebuild its ruins, and give us a hedge [Note: Again the Reginensis manuscript, together with certain other Latin manuscripts, Lyranus, and Estius, incorrectly prefers *spem* (“hope”) to *sepem* (“hedge”).] in Judah and Jerusalem.

“And now, what shall we say, our God, after this? For we have forsaken your commandments, which you commanded through your servants the prophets, saying: ‘The land into which you are entering to possess it is an unclean land, according to the uncleanness of the peoples of the other lands, because of the abominations of those who have filled it from end to end with their impurity. Now therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take their daughters for your sons. Do not seek their peace or their prosperity forever, so that you may be strong, eat the good things of the land, and leave it as an inheritance to your sons forever.’

“After all that has come upon us because of our most evil deeds and our great offense, since you, our God, have delivered us from our iniquity and granted us deliverance as it is today, shall we again turn away and invalidate your commandments, or enter into marriages with these abominable peoples? Would you be angry with us to the point of destruction, so that you would leave us no remnant or salvation? Lord God of Israel, you are righteous, for we have been left as a remnant, as it is today. Here we are before you in our offense, for no one can stand before you concerning this.”

## Chapter X

While Ezra prayed, pleaded, wept, and lay prostrate before the temple of God, a very great assembly of men, women, and children gathered around him from Israel, and the people wept with much weeping. Shecaniah son of Jeiel, from the sons of Elam, answered [Note: The Reginensis manuscript immediately aspirates the name *Jehiel*.] and said to Ezra:

“We have broken faith with our God and have taken foreign wives from the peoples of the land. But now, if there is repentance in Israel concerning this matter, let us make a covenant with the Lord our God to send away all the wives and those born from them, according to the will of the Lord and of those who fear the commandment of the Lord our God. Let it be done according to the law. Rise, for the matter is yours to decide, and we will be with you. Be strong and act.”

Then Ezra rose and adjured the leaders of the priests and Levites and all Israel to act according to this word, and they swore an oath. Ezra rose before the house of God, went to the chamber of Johanan son of Eliashib, and entered there. He ate no bread and drank no water, for he was mourning over the transgression of those who had returned from the captivity.

A proclamation was sent throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all the descendants of the captivity, ordering them to assemble in Jerusalem. Whoever did not come within three days, according to the decision of the leaders and elders, would have all his property confiscated and would himself be excluded from the assembly of the captivity.

Therefore all the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered in Jerusalem within three days. It was the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month. All the people sat in the square before the house of God, trembling because of the matter and because of the rains. Ezra the priest rose and said to them:

“You have broken faith and taken foreign wives, adding to the guilt of Israel. Now therefore make confession to the Lord, the God of your fathers, and do what pleases him. Separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from the foreign wives.”

The whole assembly answered and said with a loud voice: “According to your word concerning us, so let it be.”

“Nevertheless, the people are numerous, and it is the rainy season, and we cannot remain outside. This is not a matter for one or two days, for we have greatly sinned in this matter. Let leaders be appointed over the entire assembly, and let all those in our cities who have taken foreign wives come at appointed times, together with the elders and judges of each city, until the anger of our God concerning this matter is turned away from us.”

Therefore Jonathan son of Asahel and Jaasiah son of Thecue took charge of this matter, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levites assisted them. And the sons of the captivity did so. Ezra the priest, together with the men and heads of families, went into the house of their fathers, each according to his name, and they sat down on the first day of the tenth month to investigate the matter. And they completed the examination of all the men who had taken foreign wives by the first day of the first month.

Among the sons of the priests, those who had taken foreign wives were found to be these: from the sons of Joshua son of Josedech and his brothers, Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah. They pledged their hands to put away their wives, and for their offense they offered a ram from the sheep. From the sons of Immer: Hanani and Zebediah. From the sons of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah.

[Note: The Regina manuscript reads “from the sons of Jerim: Maaseiah and Elijah.” Immediately afterward it has “Jozabeth and Helesa,” along with other more certain errors, which we deliberately pass over.]

From the sons of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nathanael, Jozabad, and Elasah. From the sons of the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah—that is, Kelita—Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer. From the singers: Eliashib. From the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri.

And from Israel, from the sons of Parosh: Remiah, Jeziah, Malchiah, Miamin, Eliezer, Malchiah, and Benaiah. From the sons of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah. From the sons of Zethah: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza. From the sons of Bebai: Johanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai. From the sons of Bani: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Ramoth.

From the sons of Phaeth-moab:

[Note: The same manuscript here, as noted above, reads Phet-moab for Phaeth; the Vulgate editions read Phahath.]

Edna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh.

From the sons of Erem: Eliezer, Jesue, Melchias, Semeias, Simeon, Benjamin, Maloch, and Samarias.

From the sons of Asom: Mattanai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.

From the sons of Bani: Maadi, Amram, Uel, Baneas, Badaias, Cheliau, Vania, Marimuth, Eliasib, Mathanias, Mathanai, Jasi, Bani, Bennui, Semei, Salmias, Nathan, Adaias, Mecnedabai [another reading: Mechnebedai], Sisai, Sarai, Ezrel, Selemiau, Semeria, Sellum, Amaria, and Joseph.

From the sons of Nebo: Jeiel, Mathathia, Zabad, Zabina,

[Note: The names Jeddu, Joel, and Benaiah are omitted by the Regina manuscript.]

Jeddu, Joel, and Bannaia.

All these had taken foreign wives, and some of them had wives who had borne children.

## The Words of Nehemiah Son of Hechliah

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts of Saint-Germain no. 15 and the Canon Memmianus in its first hand; in the latter, a corrector has incorrectly written “Helchiah” for “Echliah” or “Hechliah.” In Hebrew we read Hachalia; the spelling has kaph before lamed. MART.]

[Note: This reading is more faithful to the Hebrew, and the Regina manuscript likewise prefers it. Others have Haheliah. The oldest Alexandrian Greek copy has Ἀχαλία, “Achalia.” MART.]

### [Book II—Chapter I]

It came to pass in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, while I was in Susa the fortress, that Hanani, one of my brothers, came, together with men from Judah. And I asked them about the Jews who had survived and remained from the captivity, and about Jerusalem. And they said to me:

“The survivors who have been left there in the province from the captivity are in great distress and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem has been broken down, and its gates have been consumed by fire.”

When I heard these words, I sat down and wept, and mourned for many days. I was fasting and praying before the God of heaven. And I said:

“I beg you, Lord, mighty God of heaven, great and terrible, who keeps the covenant and mercy with those who love you and keep your commandments: let your ear be attentive [another reading: let your ears be attentive] and your eyes open, so that you may hear the prayer of your servant, which I pray before you today, night and day, for the sons of Israel, your servants. And I confess concerning the sins of the sons of Israel with which they have sinned against you. Both I and my father’s house have sinned. We have been led astray by vanity, and we have not kept your commandment, statutes, and judgments, which you commanded Moses your servant.

“Remember the word that you commanded Moses your servant, saying: ‘When you transgress, I will scatter you among the peoples. But if you return to me, keep my commandments, and perform them—even if you have been driven to the ends of heaven, from there I will gather you and bring you [another reading: bring you back] to the place that I have chosen, so that my name might dwell there.’

“They are your servants and your people, whom you redeemed by your great strength and by your mighty hand. I beg you, Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant and to the prayer of your servants who desire to fear your name. Direct your servant today, and grant him mercy before this man.”

For I was the king’s cupbearer.

### [Chapter II]

It came to pass in the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, that I took up the wine and gave it to the king. I appeared languid before him. And the king said to me:

“Why is your face sad, when I do not see that you are sick? This is not without cause; surely some evil is in your heart.”

And I was exceedingly afraid. And I said to the king:

“May the king live forever! Why should my face not be sad, since the city, the house of the tombs of my fathers, lies desolate, and its gates have been consumed by fire?”

And the king said to me:

“For what do you ask?”

And I prayed to the God of heaven, and said to the king:

“If it seems good to the king, and if your servant is pleasing before you, send me to Judea, to the city of my fathers’ tombs, and I will rebuild it.”

And the king said to me, while the queen was sitting beside him:

“How long will your journey be, and when will you return?”

And it pleased the king, and he sent me; and I appointed him a time.

And I said to the king:

“If it seems good to the king, let him give me letters to the governors of the region beyond the River, so that they may convey me until I come to Judea, and a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s forest, so that he may give me timber with which I may cover the gates of the tower of the house, the wall of the city, and the house into which I shall enter.”

And the king gave them to me, according to the good hand of my God upon me. And I came to the governors of the region beyond the River and gave them the king’s letters. The king had also sent commanders of the army and horsemen with me.

When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, they were greatly distressed that a man had come seeking the prosperity of the sons of Israel.

And I came to Jerusalem and was there three days. Then I rose at night, I and a few men with me. I had told no one what God had put into my heart to do in Jerusalem, and I had no animal with me except the one on which I was riding.

I went out at night through the Valley Gate, before the Dragon Spring and toward the Dung Gate, and I examined the wall of Jerusalem, which had been broken down, and its gates, which had been consumed by fire. Then I went on to the Spring Gate and to the king’s aqueduct, but there was no place for the animal on which I was riding to pass. I went up by the valley at night and examined the wall; then I returned and came back through the Valley Gate.

The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing. I had told nothing to the Jews, priests, nobles, officials, or the rest who were carrying out the work, until that time.

And I said to them:

“You see the distress in which we are: Jerusalem lies desolate, and its gates have been consumed by fire. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, so that we may no longer be a disgrace.”

And I told them of the good hand of my God that was upon me, and of the king’s words that he had spoken to me. And I said:

“Let us rise and build.”

And they strengthened their hands for the good work.

When Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite servant, and Gosem the Arab heard this, they mocked us and despised us, saying:

“What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?”

And I answered them and said to them:

“The God of heaven himself helps us, and we are his servants. Let us rise and build. But you have no share, right, or memorial in Jerusalem.”

### [Chapter III]

Then Eliashib the high priest rose, together with his priestly brothers, and they built the Sheep Gate. They sanctified it, set up its doors, and sanctified it as far as the Tower of the Hundred, as far as the Tower of Hananel.

Beside him the men of Jericho built. And beside him Zachur son of Amri built.

The Fish Gate was built by the sons of Asnaa. They covered it, set up its doors, bolts, and bars.

Beside them Merimuth son of Uriah, son of Accus, built. Beside them Meshullam son of Barachiah, son of Mesezebel, built.

[Note: In the Regina manuscript, Mesezabal.]

Beside them Zadok son of Baana built. Beside them the Tekoites built, but their nobles did not put their necks to the work of their Lord.

The Old Gate was built by Joiada son of Phasea and Meshullam son of Besodia. They covered it, set up its doors, bolts, and bars.

Beside them Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronathite built, men from Gibeon and Mizpah, for the governor of the region beyond the River.

Beside him Uzziel son of Araia, a goldsmith, built. Beside him Hananiah son of the perfumer built. And they left Jerusalem as far as the wall of the Broad Street.

Beside him Rephaiah son of Ahur,

[Note: Thus the manuscripts read, with an initial a, as though the Hebrew formerly had [Hebrew letters missing in the supplied source], he before heth, [Hebrew letters missing in the supplied source]; the printed editions read “son of Ahur.” MART. —In the Regina manuscript it is “son of Bahur”; the Vulgate editions read “Hur.” Immediately afterward, instead of “Jedaiah son of Aromaph,” the same manuscript prefers “Jojada son of Aromath”; then, along with the Vulgate, “Aseboniah” instead of “Asebeniah”; and immediately afterward “Pahath-moab” instead of “Phaeth,” and so consistently below.]

the ruler of the district of Jerusalem.

Beside him Jedaiah son of Aromaph built opposite his house. Beside him Attus son of Asebeniah built.

Malchiah son of Erem and Asub son of Phaeth-moab built the middle part of the district and the Tower of the Furnaces.

Beside him Shallum son of Alloes, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, built, he and his daughters.

The Valley Gate was built by Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah. They built it, set up its doors, bolts, and bars, and built a thousand cubits of the wall as far as the Dung Gate.

The Dung Gate was built by Malchiah son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccherem. He built it and set up its doors, bolts, and bars.

The Fountain Gate was built by Sellun son of Cholozai, ruler of the district of Mizpah. He built it, covered it, and set up its doors, bolts, and bars, as well as the wall of the Pool of Siloah by the king’s garden, as far as the steps descending from the City of David.

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts read. They consistently retain Cholozai, whereas the present Hebrew reads Choloza without a yod at the end. MART.]

After him Nehemiah son of Azboc, ruler of half the district of Bethzur, built as far as opposite the tombs [another reading: the burial places] of David, as far as the pool constructed with great labor, and as far as the House of the Mighty.

After him the Levites built: Reum son of Benni.

After him Asebias, ruler of half the district of Keilah, built in his district.

After him their brothers built: Bavai son of Enadad, ruler of half the district of Keilah.

[Note: In the Regina manuscript it is Behui instead of Bavai; in Hebrew, [Hebrew text].]

Beside him Azer son of Joshua, ruler of Mizpah, built a second section opposite the ascent to the strongest corner.

After him, on the mountain, Baruch son of Zachai built a second section from the corner as far as the entrance to the house of Eliashib the high priest.

[Note: The Hebrew text instead prefers [Hebrew reading missing in the supplied source], meaning “he stirred himself up,” “took courage,” or “became indignant.” The Septuagint differs in wording, though not in sense, with ἐκράτησε, “he held,” which others also favor.
