It appears that Jerome, who translated “on the mountain,” took one letter for another and read [Hebrew reading missing in the supplied source] instead of [Hebrew reading missing in the supplied source].]

After him Merimuth son of Uriah, son of Accus, built a second section from the entrance of the house of Eliashib until the house of Eliashib was extended.

After him the priests, men from the Jordan plain, built.

After him Benjamin and Asub built opposite their house.

After him Azariah son of Maaseiah, son of Hananiah, built opposite his house.

After him Bennui son of Enadad built a second section from the house of Azariah as far as the bend and as far as the corner.

Phalel son of Ozi built opposite the bend and the tower projecting from the upper royal house—that is, in the court of the prison. After him Phadaia son of Pharos built.

The Nathinaeans lived in Ophel as far as opposite the Water Gate toward the east, and the projecting tower.

After them the Tekoites built a second section opposite, from the great and projecting tower as far as the wall of the Temple.

Above the Horse Gate the priests built, each opposite his own house.

After them Zadok son of Immer built opposite his house.

After him Shemaiah son of Secheniah, keeper of the eastern gate, built.

After him Hananiah son of Shelemiah and Hanun son of Seleph, the sixth, built a second section.

[Note: The Regina manuscript reads “Hanun son of Selo.” Immediately afterward it has Meshullam instead of Mosollam. A little later it reads “of the goldsmith,” as do the Latin Vulgate editions, instead of “of the craftsman,” and this is more correct with respect to the Hebrew word [not reproduced in the supplied source], which more often means a refiner of gold or a goldsmith.]

After him Meshullam son of Barachiah built opposite his treasury.

After him Malchiah son of the goldsmith built as far as the house of the Nathinaeans and the house of the merchants opposite the Judicial Gate, and as far as the upper chamber of the corner.

[Note: The same manuscript has “of the corners at the Sheep Gate.”]

Between the upper chamber of the corner and the Sheep Gate the goldsmiths and merchants built.

### [Chapter IV]

When Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he became very angry. He was greatly stirred up and mocked the Jews. He spoke before his brothers and the multitude of the Samaritans:

“What are these feeble Jews doing? Will the nations leave them alone? Will they sacrifice and finish in a single day? Can they build stones out of heaps of dust that have been burned?”

And Tobiah the Ammonite, who was near him, said:

“Let them build! If a fox climbs up, it will leap over their stone wall.”

“Hear, O our God, for we have become an object of contempt [another reading: contemptible]. Turn their reproach back upon their own heads, and give them over to contempt in the land of their captivity. Do not cover their iniquity, and let their sin not be blotted out from before your face, because they have mocked those who are building.”

So we built the wall, and the whole wall was joined together up to half its height; and the heart of the people was stirred to work.

When Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites heard that the repair of the wall of Jerusalem was progressing and that the breaches had begun to be closed, they were exceedingly angry. And they all conspired together to come and fight against Jerusalem and lay ambushes.

We prayed to our God and stationed guards over the wall day and night against them.

[Note: The Regina manuscript omits the words “and bows,” although they are also present in the Hebrew.]

Then Judah said:

“The strength of the bearer has failed, the rubble is abundant, and we cannot build the wall.”

And our enemies said:

“They will not know or see until we come into their midst, kill them, and stop the work.”

When the Jews who lived near them came and told us ten times, from all the places from which they had come to us, I stationed the people in formation behind the wall all around, with their swords, spears, and bows.

I looked, and rose, and said to the nobles, officials, and the rest of the people:

“Do not fear them. Remember the great and terrible Lord, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your houses.”

When our enemies heard that we had been informed, God frustrated their plan. And we all returned to the wall, each to his own work.

From that day onward, half of their young men did the work, while the other half stood ready for battle, with spears, shields, bows, and breastplates. The officials stood behind all the house of Judah, those building on the wall and those carrying and loading burdens. With one hand each man did the work, and with the other he held a sword. Each of the builders had his sword girded at his loins. They built and sounded the trumpet beside me.

And I said to the nobles, officials, and the rest of the people:

“The work is great and extensive, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another. Wherever you hear the sound of the trumpet, gather there to us. Our God will fight for us.”

And we ourselves continued the work. Half of us held spears from the rising of dawn until the stars came out.

At that time I also said to the people:

“Let everyone remain in the midst of Jerusalem with his servant, and let there be watches for us by night and by day, for the work.”

But I, my brothers, my servants, and the guards who were behind me did not remove our garments. Each man merely took them off for bathing.

### [Chapter V]

There arose a great outcry of the people and their wives against their Jewish brothers. Some were saying:

“Our sons and daughters are many. Let us obtain grain for their price, so that we may eat and live.”

Others were saying:

“Let us pledge our fields, vineyards, and houses, and obtain grain during the famine.”

Others were saying:

“Let us borrow money for the king’s taxes, and give up our fields and vineyards. And now our flesh is like the flesh of our brothers, and our children are like their children. Behold, we are subjecting our sons and daughters to slavery. Some of our daughters are already servants, and we have no means by which they can be redeemed. Our fields and vineyards are possessed by others.”

I became exceedingly angry when I heard their outcry and these words. My heart deliberated within me, and I rebuked the nobles and officials.

[Note: It had previously been written incorrectly, “and he said.”]

And I said to them:

“Are you each exacting interest from your brothers?”

And I convened a great assembly against them, and said to them:

“As you know, we have redeemed our Jewish brothers who had been sold to the nations, as far as we were able. And you, then, are selling your brothers, and we will redeem them?”

[Note: The manuscripts preserve differing readings in this verse. Many read: “And you, then, sell our brothers, and we will buy them.” The Canon Memmianus has in the text: “And you, then, are selling our brothers, and we will redeem them.” In the margin, elsewhere: “Sell your brothers, and we will buy them.” MART. —The Regina manuscript, together with others consulted by Martianay, reads: “Sell our brothers, and we will buy them.”]

They were silent and found nothing to answer. And I said to them:

“What you are doing is not good. Why do you not walk in the fear of our God, lest we be reproached by the nations, our enemies?

“Moreover, I, my brothers, and my servants have lent money and grain to many. Let us not demand this debt in common; let us remit what is owed us. Restore to them today their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses; and, indeed, also the hundredth part of the money, grain, wine, and oil that you are accustomed to exact from them, give back on their behalf.”

And they said:

“We will restore it, and we will demand nothing from them. We will do as you say.”

Then I summoned the priests and adjured them to act according to what I had said.

Moreover, I shook out my garment and said:

“May God shake out from his house and from his possessions every man who does not fulfill this word. May he likewise be shaken out and emptied.”

And the whole assembly said:

“Amen.”

And they praised God. And the people did as had been said.

From the day on which the king commanded me to be governor in the land of Judah—from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes, twelve years—I and my brothers did not eat the allowances due to governors.

The former governors who had been before me burdened the people and received from them, in bread, wine, and money, forty shekels each day. Their servants also oppressed the people. But I did not act in this way, because of the fear of God.

Moreover, I applied myself to the work of the wall. I bought no field, and all my servants were gathered there for the work.

The Jews and officials, one hundred and fifty men, as well as those who came to us from the nations around us, were at my table.

A single ox, six choice rams, besides birds, and every ten days various wines and many other things were prepared for me each day. Yet I did not demand the allowance of my governorship, for the people were heavily burdened.

Remember me, my God, for good, according to all that I have done for this people.

### [Chapter VI]

When Sanballat, Tobiah,

[Note: The same manuscript inserts here the name Maralis, though I do not know from where it was produced.]

Gosem the Arab, and the rest of our enemies heard that I had built the wall and that no breach remained in it—for until that time I had not set up the doors in the gates—Sanballat and Gosem sent to me, saying:

“Come, and let us make a treaty together in the villages [another reading: in the calves; other manuscripts and most pre-Sixtus V Vulgate editions, equally incorrectly, read ‘in bonds’; in some copies ‘one’ is read for Ono] in the plain of Ono.”

They were planning to do me harm. So I sent messengers to them, saying:

“I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work cease when I leave it and come down to you?”

They sent to me according to this word four times, and I answered them according to the former message.

Sanballat sent his servant to me in the same way a fifth time, with a letter in his hand written as follows:

“It has been heard among the nations, and Gosem has said, that you and the Jews are planning to rebel, and that for this reason you are building the wall and intend to set yourself up as king over them. For this reason you have also appointed prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem, saying: ‘There is a king in Judah.’ The king will hear these things. Therefore, now, come, and let us take counsel together.”

And I sent to them, saying:

“No such things as you say have been done. You are inventing them from your own heart.”

For they were all trying to frighten us, thinking that our hands would cease from the work and that we would stop. Therefore I strengthened my hands still more.

Then I entered secretly the house of Shemaiah son of Dalaiah, son of Metabeel. He said:

“Let us meet together in the house of God, in the midst of the Temple, and let us close the doors of the sanctuary, for they are coming to kill you; they will come at night to kill you.”

And I said:

“Should a man like me flee? And who like me would enter the Temple and live? I will not enter.”

And I understood that God had not sent him, but that he had spoken to me as though prophesying, and that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. For he had accepted payment so that I would become frightened, sin, and thereby give them something evil with which to reproach me.

[Note: The same manuscript again incorrectly reads “and not Adaiah.” It is preferable to note that the Hebrew is feminine: Noadiah is called a prophetess, not a prophet.]

Remember me, Lord, concerning Tobiah and Sanballat, according to such deeds as theirs; and also concerning the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who were frightening me.

The wall was completed on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days.

When all our enemies heard this, all the nations around us became afraid and fell into despair within themselves, for they knew that this work had been accomplished by our God.

In those days many letters of the Jewish nobles were being sent to Tobiah, and letters from Tobiah were coming to them. For many in Judah were bound to him by oath, because he was the son-in-law of Secheniah son of Jorei,

[Note: Thus the Canon Memmianus and all the other manuscripts read. The printed editions have “son of Ara,” in accordance with the Hebrew, where no yod appears at the beginning of the name. MART.]

and his son Johanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam son of Barachiah.

They also praised him before me and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to frighten me.

### [Chapter VII]

After the wall had been built and I had set up the doors, and the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites had been appointed, I commanded Hanani my brother and Hananiah, ruler of the house of Jerusalem—for he appeared to be a truthful man and one who feared God more than the others.

And I said to them:

“The gates of Jerusalem shall not be opened until the heat of the sun.”

While they were still standing there, the gates were closed and barred. And I appointed guards from among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, each in his watch and each opposite his own house.

The city was broad and very large, but the people within it were few, and the houses had not been built.

God put it into my heart to gather the nobles, officials, and people, so that I might enroll them. And I found the book of the census of those who had first come up, and I found written in it:

“These are the sons of the province who came up from the captivity of the exiles, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away, and who returned to Jerusalem and to Judah, each to his own city.

“They came with Zorobabel, Josue, Neemias, Azarias, Raamias, Naamani [another reading: Naamanin], Mardochaeus, Belsan, Mespharat, Beggoai, Naum, and Baana.

“The number of the men of the people of Israel:

“The sons of Pharos: two thousand one hundred seventy-two.

“The sons of Saphatia: three hundred seventy-two.

“The sons of Area: six hundred fifty-two.

“The sons of Phaeth-moab, of the sons of Josue and Joab: two thousand eight hundred eighteen.

“The sons of Elam: one thousand two hundred fifty-four [another reading: eighty].

“The sons of Zethua: eight hundred forty-five.

“The sons of Zachai: seven hundred sixty.

“The sons of Bannui: six hundred forty-eight.

“The sons of Bebai: six hundred twenty-eight.

“The sons of Azgad: two thousand three hundred twenty-two.

“The sons of Adonicam: six hundred sixty-seven.

“The sons of Baggoai: two thousand sixty-seven.

[Note: The Regina manuscript has seventy-seven; shortly afterward it likewise has Buggoim instead of Baggoai. The Vulgate has Beguai.]

“The sons of Adin: six hundred fifty-five.

“The sons of Ater, sons of Ezecias: ninety-eight.

“The sons of Asem: three hundred twenty-eight.

“The sons of Besai: three hundred twenty-four.

“The sons of Areph: one hundred twelve.

“The sons of Gabaon: ninety-five.

[Note: Along with the Vulgate and the Greek, the Regina manuscript has “sons” here instead of “men.” The Hebrew has [text not reproduced in the supplied source].]

“The men of Bethlehem and Netupha: one hundred eighty-eight.

“The men of Anathoth: one hundred twenty-eight.

“The men of Beth-azmoth: forty-two.

“The men of Cariath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beroth: seven hundred forty-three.

[Note: The Regina manuscript increases the number by one and reads Goba instead of Geba; shortly afterward it reads Ai instead of Agi. Concerning the other Nebo, learned men have noted that the first Nebo once appeared in the ancient Latin editions. See above, Ezra, chapter XI, verse 32.]

“The men of Rama and Geba: six hundred twenty-one.

“The men of Machmas: one hundred twenty-two.

“The men of Bethel and Ai: one hundred twenty-three.

“The men of the other Nebo: fifty-two.

“The sons of the other Elam: one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

“The sons of Arem: three hundred twenty.

“The sons of Jericho: three hundred forty-five.

“The sons of Lod, Hadid, and Ono: seven hundred twenty-one.

“The sons of Senaa: three thousand nine hundred thirty.

“The priests:

“The sons of Idaia in the house of Josue: nine hundred seventy-three.

“The sons of Emmer: one thousand fifty-two.

“The sons of Phashur: one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

“The sons of Arem: one thousand seventeen.

“The Levites:

“The sons of Josue and Cadmiel [another reading: Cedmiel], sons of Odvia: seventy-four.

“The singers:

“The sons of Asaph: one hundred forty-eight.

“The gatekeepers:

“The sons of Sellum, the sons of Ater, the sons of Telmon, the sons of Accub, the sons of Atita, and the sons of Sobai: one hundred thirty-eight.

“The Nathinaeans:

“The sons of Soa, the sons of Aspha [another reading: Hasupha], the sons of Tebbaoth, the sons of Ceros, the sons of Siaa,

[Note: The Regina manuscript, though not correctly, omitting the word “sons,” has Siaafado as one continuous series. For Selmon, which follows and which is likewise read in our manuscripts, the Latin Vulgates have Selmai, closer to the Hebrew. Shortly afterward, for Gezem the same manuscript has Gezfa; for Munim, Unim; for Nephussim, Neptusim; and below, for Jahala, Gachubada, and so forth.]

“the sons of Phadon, the sons of Lebana, the sons of Agaba,

[Note: In the printed books we read Selmai, following the present Hebrew [text not reproduced in the supplied source]. But the Canon Memmianus, together with all the other Latin manuscripts, has Selmon, as we have printed it. Therefore the Hebrew copies of Saint Jerome must have been written with final nun instead of yod, since the former is plainly identical with the upper part of nun, especially in manuscripts, where scribes could also omit the letter’s lower stroke. MART.]

“the sons of Selmon, the sons of Anan, the sons of Geddel, the sons of Gaer, the sons of Raia, the sons of Rasin, the sons of Necoda, the sons of Gezem, the sons of Aza, the sons of Phasea, the sons of Besai, the sons of Munim, the sons of Nephussim, the sons of Becbuc [another reading: Bachuc], the sons of Acupha, the sons of Arur, the sons of Besloth, the sons of Meida [another reading: Maid], the sons of Arsa, the sons of Bercos, the sons of Sisara, the sons of Thema, the sons of Nasia, the sons of Atipha, the sons of the servants of Solomon: the sons of Sothai, the sons of Sophereth, the sons of Pherida, the sons of Jahala, the sons of Darcon, the sons of Jeddel, the sons of Saphatia, the sons of Atil, the sons of Phochereth, who was descended from Sabaim, son of Amon.

“All the Nathinaeans and the sons of the servants of Solomon numbered three hundred ninety-two.

“These are those who came up from Thelmela, Thelarsa, Cherub, Addon, and Emmer, but they could not identify their ancestral house or their seed, whether they were from Israel.

“The sons of Dalaia, the sons of Tobia, and the sons of Necoda: six hundred forty-two.”

And among the priests were the sons of Abia, the sons of Accos, and the sons of Berzellai, who had taken a wife from the daughters of Berzellai the Gileadite and had been called by their name.

[Note: The Regina manuscript has Gabaaditidis.]

They sought their registration in the census but did not find it, and they were excluded from the priesthood.

And Athersatha told them not to eat from the holy of holies until a learned and instructed priest should arise.

The whole assembly, as one man, numbered forty-two thousand three hundred sixty,

[Note: The Regina manuscript counts six hundred sixty more, and so forth.]

apart from their male and female servants, who numbered seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven. Among them were two hundred forty-five male and female singers.

[Note: After this, the printed editions add the entire verse 68: “Their horses were seven hundred thirty-six; their mules two hundred forty-five.” But the Latin manuscripts are entirely silent about horses and mules, as are the Syriac and Arabic translators, who omit the aforesaid verse. The Masoretic copies and the Alexandrian Greek manuscript still retain what we read in the Latin Vulgate. Hence a considerable suspicion arises that something has fallen out of some Hebrew, Greek, and Latin copies. The same material is read in Ezra, Book I, chapter II, but with many substantial differences. See the Sacred Criticism. MART.]

Their camels numbered four hundred thirty-five, and the donkeys six thousand seven hundred twenty.

[Note: Let the reader note that the annotation placed here in the Vulgate, and in many manuscript books, is entirely absent from the excellent and very ancient Colbertine-Anician manuscript. In our Saint-Germain manuscript no. 15 it is written in the margin, though not at this place, but below, in chapter VIII, opposite the words “Then Ezra brought,” and so, I think, it is sufficiently established that this little annotation did not derive from Jerome but from some other unknown author. It is written as follows: “Up to this point what was written in the Commentary is related; from here onward the history of Nehemiah is woven.” MART. —The Regina manuscript counts nine hundred twenty. Immediately afterward the Vulgate copies append that gloss: “Up to this point what was written in the Commentary is related; from here onward the history of Nehemiah is woven.” That it did not proceed from Jerome’s pen is indicated both by the silence of the original texts and by the Latin manuscripts themselves, which we and Martianay have examined. Moreover, it seemed more correctly to belong not here but somewhat earlier, after verse 64, namely after the words “And Athersatha told them,” and so forth.]

Some also of the heads of families contributed to the work. Athersatha gave to the treasury one thousand drachmas of gold, fifty bowls, and five hundred thirty priestly garments [Note: [Col. 1424D] Not only the Vulgate, but also the Hebrew exemplar itself reckons thirty-five; [the numeral is apparently omitted in the supplied text]. Our manuscripts, however, do not add the five, nor does Martianus seem to have found it in his copies, although he does not alert the reader to this matter.]. And the heads of families gave to the treasury of the work twenty thousand drachmas of gold and two thousand two hundred minas of silver. And what the rest of the people gave was twenty thousand drachmas of gold, two thousand minas of silver, and sixty-seven priestly garments. The priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, and the rest of the people, together with the temple servants and all Israel, lived in their cities.

## Chapter VIII

Now the seventh month had come [Note: [Col. 1424D] The Regina manuscript has here inserted another gloss of its own, in these words: “The Feast of Tabernacles of Saul, Ezra, and Nehemiah.” This was easily first written as a marginal scholion beside the text of the book and then rashly brought into the text.]; and the children of Israel were in their cities. And all the people gathered as one man in the square before the Water Gate. And they said to Ezra the scribe that he should bring the book of the law of Moses, which the Lord had commanded Israel.

Then Ezra the priest brought the law before the assembly of men and women and all who were able to understand, on the first day of the seventh month. And he read from it aloud in the square before the Water Gate, from morning until midday, in the presence of the men and women and those capable of understanding; and the ears of all the people were attentive to the book.

Ezra the scribe stood upon a wooden platform [Col. 1424C] that he had made for speaking. And beside him stood Mattathiah, and [Note: [Col. 1424D] In the Regina manuscript: Semeia and Ahania. The first agrees with the Vulgate reading; the second is more correctly read, in accordance with the Hebrew, as Hanabia. Shortly afterward it has Phaedia instead of Phadaia, and aspirates Misahel.] Shema, and Anaiah, and Uriah, and Hilkiah, and [Col. 1425A] Maaseiah, on his right; and on his left, Pedaiah, Mishael, and Malchiah, and Hashum, and Hashbaddana, Zechariah, and Meshullam. And Ezra opened the book before all the people—for he was above all the people—and when he had opened it, all the people stood. And Ezra blessed the Lord, the great God; and all the people answered, “Amen, amen,” lifting up their hands; then they bowed and worshiped God, prostrate upon the ground. Moreover, Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah—the Levites—made the people keep silence in order to hear the law; and the people stood in their place. And they read distinctly and suitably for understanding in the book of the law of God; and they understood as it was read.

Then Nehemiah (he is Athersatha), and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were interpreting for all the people, said: “This day is holy to the Lord our God. Do not mourn, and do not weep.” For all the people were weeping when they heard the words of the law. And he said [Col. 1425B] to them: “Go, eat rich foods, and drink [Note: [Col. 1425D] In the same manuscript, instead of *mulsum* (“honeyed wine”), there is *mustum* (“new wine”), which some might prefer. In Hebrew, however, the reading means something sweet and pleasant to the taste.] sweet wine, and send portions to him who has prepared nothing for himself; for the day of the Lord is holy, and do not grieve, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.” The Levites also kept silence among all the people, saying: “Be quiet, for the day is holy; do not sorrow.”

So all the people went away to eat and drink, to send portions, and to make great rejoicing, because they had understood the words that had been taught them. On the second day, the heads of all the families of the people, the priests, and the Levites gathered around Ezra the scribe so that he might explain to them the words of the law. And they found written in the law that the Lord had commanded through Moses that the children of Israel should dwell in booths on the feast during the seventh month, and that they should proclaim and publish the message in all their cities and in Jerusalem, saying: “Go out to the mountain and bring branches of olive trees, branches of beautiful trees, branches of myrtle, and palm branches, and branches of leafy trees, to make booths, [Col. 1425C] as it is written.” And the people went out and brought them. And they made booths for themselves, each one on his roof [Note: [Col. 1425D] The Regina manuscript has, instead of “on his roof,” “in his corner.” MART.], and in their courtyards, and in the courtyards of the house of God, and in the square of the Water Gate, and in the square of Ephraim.

So the whole assembly of those who had returned from captivity made booths and lived in the booths; for the children of Israel had not done so from the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day. And there was exceedingly great rejoicing. And he read in the book of the law of God day by day, from the first day to the last. And they kept the feast for seven days, and on the eighth day an assembly, according to the rite.

## Chapter IX

On the twenty-fourth day of this month, the children of Israel assembled in fasting and in sackcloth, with earth upon them. And the offspring of Israel separated themselves from every foreigner; and they stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. And they rose to stand, and they read in the book [Col. 1425D] of the law of the Lord their God four times during the day, and four times they confessed and worshiped the Lord their God.

Then upon the platform of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah [Alt. Sabaniah], Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani; and they cried out with a loud voice to the Lord their God. And the Levites—Jeshua, [Col. 1426A] Kadmiel, Bunni, Hashabniah, [Note: [Col. 1425D] These four names are given thus in the Regina manuscripts: Asebia, Sarechia, Odoia, and Sebna; certainly less correctly.] Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah—said:

“Rise, bless the Lord your God from eternity to eternity; and let them bless your glorious and exalted name with every blessing and praise.

“You alone, Lord, have made heaven and the heaven of heavens, and all their host; the earth and all that is in it; the seas and all that is in them. And you [Note: [Col. 1425D] The same manuscript has, ‘you have given life,’ which is not sufficiently correct.] give life to all these things, and the host of heaven worships you.

“You alone, Lord God, chose Abraham and brought him out [Note: [Col. 1425D] The San-German manuscript no. 15 retains in the margin [Col. 1426D] the variant reading *Hur*. It signifies that God brought Abraham out of Ur of the Chaldeans. Now *Ur*, translated into Latin, is said to mean ‘fire.’ See Genesis XIII, 31, and Jerome’s *Hebrew Questions* on this passage. MART.] of the fire of the Chaldeans, and gave him the name Abraham. And you found his heart faithful before you, and made a covenant with him to give him the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite, to give it to his seed; and you fulfilled your words, because you are righteous.

“And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt, and heard their cry beside the Red Sea. And you gave signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants and [Col. 1426B] all the people of his land, for you knew that they had acted arrogantly against them; and you made for yourself a name, as it is also on this day. And you divided the sea before them, and they passed through the midst of the sea on dry ground; but you cast their pursuers into the depths like a stone into mighty waters [Alt. ‘mighty waters’ in the ablative]. And by day you were their guide in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire, to show them the way by which they were to enter.

“You also came down upon Mount Sinai, and spoke with them from heaven, and gave them right judgments, laws of truth, statutes, and good commandments. And you showed them your sanctified sabbath [Note: [Col. 1426D] The Regina manuscript does not add “your,” although it is present in the Hebrew text.], and commanded them ordinances, statutes, and law through Moses your servant. You gave them bread from heaven in their hunger, and brought water out of the rock for them in their thirst, and told them to enter and possess the land over which you had raised your hand to give it to them.

“But they and our fathers acted arrogantly, hardened their necks, and did not listen to your commandments. They refused to listen and did not remember your wonders that you had performed for them. They hardened their necks and appointed a leader in order to return to their servitude, as though in defiance.

“But you, God, are forgiving, gracious and merciful, patient and rich in compassion; you did not abandon them. Even when they had made for themselves a molten calf and said, ‘This is your god who brought you out of Egypt,’ and had committed great blasphemies, you, in your abundant mercies, did not abandon them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud did not depart from them by day, to lead them on the way, nor the pillar of fire by night, to show them the route by which they were to enter. And you gave them your good spirit [Note: [Col. 1426D] Here the same manuscript has the pronoun “to them,” which the Hebrew omits.], to instruct them; and you did not withhold your manna from their mouths, and you gave them water in their thirst. For forty years you sustained them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their garments did not wear out, and their feet did not become swollen.

“And you gave them kingdoms and peoples, and allotted portions to them; and they possessed the land of Sihon, and the land of the king [Note: [Col. 1426D] The word “king,” which is nevertheless present in the Hebrew archetype, is absent in the Regina manuscript.] of Heshbon, and the land of Og king of Bashan. And you multiplied their children like the stars of heaven, and brought them to the land of which you had told their fathers that they should enter and possess it. And the children came and possessed the land, and you humbled before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites; and you delivered them into their hand, with their kings and the peoples of the land, so that they might do with them as they pleased.

“And they captured fortified cities and fertile soil, and possessed houses full of every good thing, cisterns dug by others, vineyards, olive groves, and many fruit trees. And they ate and were filled, and grew fat, and reveled in the abundance of your great goodness. But they provoked you to anger, withdrew from you, and cast your law behind their backs. They killed your prophets, who testified against them so that they might return to you, and they committed great blasphemies.

“And you delivered them into the hand of their enemies, and they afflicted them. In the time of their distress they cried out to you, and you heard from heaven and, according to your abundant mercies, gave them saviors who saved them from the hand of their enemies. When they had rest, they turned again to do evil in your sight; and you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, and they ruled over them. Then they turned and cried out to you, but you heard from heaven and delivered them according to your many mercies, for a long time.

“And you testified against them, that they should return to your law. But they acted arrogantly and did not listen to your commandments; they sinned against your judgments, by which a person shall do and live. They turned a rebellious shoulder and hardened their neck, and did not listen. You prolonged your patience with them for many years, and testified against them by your spirit through the hand of your prophets; but they did not listen, and you delivered them into the hand of the peoples of the lands. [Note: [Col. 1427D] Someone concerned with scholarship once added in the margin the scholion ‘of the Chaldean king of Babylon’; the Regina manuscript has incorrectly inserted it here into the text.] Yet in your very great mercies you did not make an end of them or abandon them, because you are a God of mercies, and you are gracious.

“And now, our great, mighty, and fearful God, who keeps covenant and mercy, do not let all the hardship that has found us—our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all your people—from the days of the king of Assyria to this day, be turned away from your face. And you are righteous in all that has come upon us, because you have acted faithfully, while we have acted wickedly.

“Our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers did not keep your law, nor heed your commandments and your testimonies by which you testified [Note: [Col. 1427D] Here too the Regina manuscript is not sufficiently correct: ‘by which you testified to us.’ And likewise, in their good kingdoms, and in, etc.] to them. Even while they were in their kingdom, and in the great goodness that you had given them, and in the broad and fertile land that you had placed before them, they did not serve you and did not turn from their evil practices.

“Behold, we ourselves are slaves today; and as for the land that you gave to our fathers, so that they might eat its bread and its good things, we ourselves are slaves in it. Its produce multiplies for the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins; they rule over our bodies and over our beasts according to their will, and we are in great distress.

“Because of all this, we ourselves are making a covenant and writing it; and our princes, our Levites, and our priests are signing it.”

## Chapter X

The signatories were Nehemiah, [Col. 1427D] Athersatha son of Hacaliah, and Zedekiah, Seraiah, Azariah, Jeremiah, Pashhur [Alt. Phasshur], Amariah, Malchijah, Hattush, Shebaniah, Malluch, Harim, Meremoth, Obadiah, Daniel, Ginnethon, Baruch, Meshullam, Abijah, Mijamin, Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah—these were the priests.

[Col. 1428A] The Levites were Jeshua son of [Note: [Col. 1427D] All the manuscripts read thus; the printed editions, however, have Henadad, and consequently Shebaniah and Hodiah instead of Shecaniah and Hodeiah. MART. —The Regina manuscript has Azariah; what follows, Enaddam, is more correct according to the Hebrew, while the Vulgates give Henadad.] Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel, and their brothers: Shecaniah [Alt. Shebaniah], Hodeiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan, Mica, Rehob, Hashabiah, Zaccur, Sherebiah, Shebaniah, Hodiah [Alt. Hodeiah], Bani, and Beninu.

The heads of the people were Parosh, [Note: [Col. 1427D] The Regina manuscript consistently has Pheth-Moab, and shortly afterward Jezekiah instead of Hezekiah. We record the other variant readings alongside the text.] Pahath-Moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani, Bunni, Azgad, Bebai, Adonijah, Bigvai, Adin, Ater, Hezekiah, Azur, Hodeiah [Alt. Hodeiah], Hashum, Besai, Hariph, Anathoth, Nebai, Magpiash, Meshullam, Hezir, Meshezabel, Zadok, Jaddua, Pelatiah, Hanan, Anaiah [Alt. Anaiah], Hoshea, Hananiah, Hashub, Hallohesh, Phaaliah, Shobek, Rehum, Hashabnah, Maaseiah, and Hai [Alt. Echaiah], Hanan, Anan, Malluch, Harim, Baana.

And the rest of the people—the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and all who had separated themselves from the peoples of the lands for the law of God, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, everyone who had understanding—pledging themselves on behalf of their brothers, their nobles, and those who came to make a promise and swear an oath, to walk in the law of God that he had given through Moses, the servant of God, to perform and observe all the commandments of the Lord our God, his judgments and his statutes; and not to give our daughters to the people of the land, nor take their daughters for our sons.

Also, as for the peoples of the land who bring merchandise and every kind of commodity to sell on the sabbath day, we will not buy from them on the sabbath or on a holy day. And we will release the seventh year and every debt.

And we will impose upon ourselves commandments, to give one-third of a shekel each year for the service of the house of our God, for the bread of the Presence, for the continual offering, and for the continual burnt offering on the sabbaths, at the new moons, at the appointed festivals, and at the holy days, and for sin offerings, to make atonement for Israel, and for every use of the house of our God.

We cast lots concerning the offering of wood among the priests, Levites, and people, to bring it into the house of our God according to our ancestral houses, at appointed times, year by year, so that it might burn [Note: [Col. 1428D] The Regina manuscript has, ‘so that it might burn continually before the altar,’ etc.; whereas, together with the printed reading, the Hebrew text omits the following name of Moses.] upon the altar of the Lord our God, as it is written in the law of Moses.

And we would bring the first fruits of our land and the first fruits of every fruit of every tree, year by year, to the house of the Lord; and the firstborn of our sons and of our livestock, as it is written in the law; and the firstborn of our cattle and sheep, to be offered in the house of our God to the priests who minister in the house of our God. We would also bring to the priests, into the treasury of our God, the first fruits of our food and our offerings, the fruit of every tree, and our wine and oil; and the tithe of our land to the Levites. The Levites themselves would receive tithes in all the cities where we work.

The priest, son of Aaron, would be with the Levites over the tithes of the Levites; and the Levites would offer a tenth part of their tithe into the house of our God, into the treasury, in the treasury-house. For the children of Israel and the children of Levi would bring there the first fruits of grain, wine, and oil. There would be the sacred vessels, [Col. 1428D] and the priests, singers, gatekeepers, and ministers; and we would not abandon the house of our God.

## Chapter XI

The princes of the people lived in Jerusalem; but the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of every ten to live in Jerusalem, the holy city, while the other nine parts remained in the cities. And the people blessed all the men who voluntarily offered themselves to live in Jerusalem.

These, then, are the chiefs of the province who lived in Jerusalem and in the cities of Judah. Each lived in his own possession, in his own city: Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the descendants of Solomon’s servants.

In Jerusalem lived some of the children of Judah and of Benjamin. Of the children of Judah: Athaiah son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel; of the children of Perez: Maaseiah son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, son of the Shilonite. All these were descendants of Perez who lived in Jerusalem, four hundred sixty-eight valiant men.

These were the children of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of [Note: [Col. 1429D] The Regina manuscript has ‘son of Asaiah,’ and after him Gabbai, instead of Isaiah and Gebbai. A little earlier it preferred Malehel instead of Mahalalel.] Isaiah; and after him Gebbai and Sallai, nine hundred twenty-eight. And Joel son of Zichri was their overseer, and Judah son of Senua was second over the city.

Of the priests: Jedaiah son of Joiarib, Jachin, Seraiah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub [Alt. Achitob], chief of the house of God, and their brothers who performed the work of the temple, eight hundred twenty-two.

And Adaiah son of Jehoiarib, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah, and his brothers, heads of ancestral houses, two hundred forty-two. And Amassai son of [Note: [Col. 1429D] Here again the manuscript reads Ezriel and Saazi instead of Azarel and Ahazi.] Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer, and their brothers, exceedingly powerful men, one hundred twenty-eight. Their overseer was Zabdiel son of the powerful.

Of the Levites: Shebaniah son of Hashub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni; and Shabbethai and Jozabad, in charge of [Alt. adding “all”] the work outside the house of God, from among the chiefs of the Levites.

And Mattaniah son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of [Col. 1429C] Asaph, [Note: [Col. 1429D] The Hebrew has [Hebrew term omitted in supplied text], which means “leader of prayer,” instead of which Jerome seems to have read *scilicet* (“namely”) for the middle word. Nor did he borrow the reading from the Septuagint, which omits almost the whole of this verse.] chief for giving praise and for thanksgiving in prayer; and Bakbukiah, second among his brothers; and Abda son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun. All the Levites in the holy city numbered two hundred eighty-four.

And the gatekeepers were Akkub, Talmon, and their brothers who guarded the gates, one hundred seventy-two. And the rest of Israel, the priests and Levites, were in all the cities of Judah, each in his own possession [Note: [Col. 1429D] The Regina manuscript has “in his own city.” Shortly afterward it has “Ophel and Siaba” instead of “Ophel and Siaha.”].

The temple servants lived in Ophel: Siaha and Gishpa, from among the temple servants. The overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica. Of the sons of Asaph were the singers in the service of the house of God. For the king’s command concerning them was established, and there was a daily order for the singers. And Pethahiah son of Meshezabel, of the sons of Zerah son of Judah, was at the king’s hand concerning every matter of the people and throughout all their territories.

The children of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba and its villages, and in Dibon and its villages, and in Kabzeel and its hamlets, and in Jeshua, and in Moladah, [Col. 1430A] and in Beth-phelet, and in Hazar-shual, and in Beersheba and its villages, and in Ziklag, [Note: [Col. 1430D] The same manuscript reads Sicileg and Monochona; shortly afterward, Adullam instead of Odollam, and “Azecah and its daughter, and they remained,” instead of “Azecah and its villages,” etc.] and in Meconah and its villages, and in Rimmon, and in Zorah, and in Jarmuth, Zanoah, Adullam and their villages, Lachish and its fields, and Azekah and its villages. And they settled from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom.

The children of Benjamin were from Geba, Michmash, and [Note: [Col. 1430D] The same manuscript has Achia; the Vulgate has Hai; and shortly afterward it has Onna instead of Ono.] Aijah, and Bethel and its villages, Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah, Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim, Hadid, Zeboim, and Neballat, Lod, and Ono, the valley of craftsmen. And the Levites had portions in Judah and Benjamin.

## Chapter XII

These were the priests and Levites who went up with Zerubbabel son of [Note: [Col. 1430D] The words “son of Shealtiel” are absent from the Regina manuscript. Below it reads Semaiah and Joarib instead of Shemaiah and Joiarib, etc.] Shealtiel, and with Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra [Alt. Esdras], Amariah, Malluch, Hattush, Shecaniah, Rehum, Meremoth, Iddo, Ginnethon, Abijah, Mijamin, Moadiah, Bilgah, Shemaiah, and Joiarib, Jedaiah, Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, Jedaiah. These were the chiefs of the priests and their brothers in the days of Jeshua.

The Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, in charge of the hymns, they and their brothers; and Bakbukiah and Anni, and their brothers, each according to his office. Jeshua [Alt. Joshua] begot Joiakim, and Joiakim begot Eliashib, and Eliashib begot Joiada, and Joiada begot [Note: [Col. 1430D] Elsewhere, instead of Jonathan, he reads Johannan; after Josephus and Eusebius, the holy Father himself read this way in his *Commentaries on Daniel*.] Jonathan, and Jonathan begot Jaddua.

In the days of Joiakim there were priests and heads of families: of Seraiah, Amariah [Note: [Col. 1430D] Our manuscripts indeed have Amariah; but, at least according to the Hebrew text, the Vulgates more correctly prefer Meraiah.]; of Jeremiah, Hananiah; of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Johanan; of Millicho, Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph; of Harim, Edna; of Meraioth, Helkai; of Adaiah, Zechariah; of Ginnethon, Meshullam; of Abijah, Zichri; of Mijamin and of Moadiah, Piltai; of Bilgah, Shammua; of Shemaiah, Jonathan; of Joiarib, Mattanai; of Jedaiah [Alt. Joiada], Uzzi; of Sallai, Belai; of Amok, Eber; of Hilkiah, Hashabiah; of Jedaiah, Nethanel.

The Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua were recorded as heads of families, as were the priests, in the reign of Darius the Persian.

The sons of Levi, the heads of families, were recorded in the book of the Chronicles, up to the days of Jonathan son of Eliashib. The chiefs of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua [Alt. Joshua] son of Kadmiel, and their brothers according to their divisions, to praise and give thanks according to the command of David, the man of God, and to observe [Note: [Col. 1430D] The Regina manuscript has, “to observe those things that were according to order,” etc.] equally in due order. Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub were gatekeepers and guardians of the vestibules before the gates.

These served in the days of Joiakim [Alt. Joakim] son of Jeshua, son of Jehozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest and scribe.

At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, they sought the Levites from all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem and celebrate the dedication with thanksgiving, song, cymbals, psalteries, and lyres.

So the sons of the singers gathered from the plains around Jerusalem, from the villages of the Netophathites, and from the house of Gilgal, and from the regions [Note: [Col. 1430D] The same manuscript has Gebba and Azmaveth.] of Geba and Azmaveth, because the singers had built villages for themselves around [Col. 1431A] Jerusalem. And the priests and Levites purified themselves, and purified the people, the gates, and the wall.

Then I brought the princes of Judah up onto the wall [Note: [Col. 1431D] The same manuscript has, “But the princes of Judah went up upon the wall, and he appointed two choirs,” etc.] and appointed two large choirs of those giving praise. One went to the right upon the wall toward the Dung Gate. After them went Hoshaiah, half the princes of Judah, and Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam, Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah. And of the sons of the priests, with trumpets, were Zechariah son of Jonathan, son of Shemaiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Micaiah, son of Zaccur, son of Asaph; and his brothers, Shemaiah, Azarel, Malalai, [Note: [Col. 1431D] The name Galalai is absent from the same manuscript, which also reads Maia instead of Maai.] Galalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani, with the musical instruments of David, the man of God; and Ezra the scribe before them at the Fountain Gate.

Opposite them they went up by the steps of the city of David, by the ascent of the wall above the house of David, and as far as the Water Gate to the east. The second choir of those giving thanks went in the opposite direction, and I followed it, with half of the people upon the wall and upon the Tower of the Ovens, and as far as the Broad Wall, and over the Gate of Ephraim, and over the Old Gate, and over the Fish Gate and the Tower of Hananel, and the Tower of the Hundred, and as far as the Sheep Gate. And they stood at the Gate of the Guard. And the two choirs of those giving praise stood in the house of God, with me and half of the officials with me.

And the priests were Eliakim, Maaseiah, Mijamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets; and Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Johanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang loudly, with Jezrahiah as their overseer. And on that day they offered great sacrifices and rejoiced, for God had given them great joy. Their wives and children also rejoiced, and the joy of Jerusalem was heard from far away.

On that day they appointed men over the treasury chambers, for the offerings, the first fruits, and the tithes, to bring through them the portions of the fields of the cities for the priests and the Levites, in the beauty of thanksgiving [Note: [Col. 1431D] The Hebrew, as it is certainly found now, has a different sentence, namely: “so that through them they might gather from the fields of the cities the portions of the priests.” Jerome, who translates “the rulers of the city,” may easily have read [Hebrew terms omitted in supplied text], *sarei* instead of *sadai*, or instead of [Hebrew term omitted]. Nevertheless, the Syriac version agrees with Jerome: “the prefects of the city,” as do the Septuagint. Again, the holy Father, who translates “in the beauty of thanksgiving,” for which the Syriac has “as it is written in the book of the Law,” seems to have read *Toda* instead of *Tora*—that is, a daleth for a resh.]. For Judah rejoiced in the priests and Levites who were standing by. And they observed the service of their God and the service of purification, as did the singers and gatekeepers, according to the command of David and of Solomon his son. For in the days of David and Asaph, from the beginning, chiefs of the singers had been appointed for the song of praise and thanksgiving to God. And all Israel, in the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah, gave portions day by day to the singers and gatekeepers; and they consecrated the Levites, and the Levites consecrated the sons of Aaron.

## Chapter XIII

On that day, as the people listened, the book of Moses was read; and it was found written in it that the Ammonites and Moabites should never enter the assembly of God, because they had not met the children of Israel with bread and water, and had hired Balaam against them [Alt. “against him”] to curse them; but our God turned the curse into a blessing.

When they heard the law, they separated every foreigner from Israel. Now before this, Eliashib the priest had been appointed over the treasury chamber of the house of our God and was close to Tobiah.

[Col. 1431D] He had made a large treasury chamber for himself, and there, before him, people had been storing the offerings, incense, vessels, the tithe of grain, wine, and oil, the portions of the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, and the priests’ first fruits.

During all this time I was not in Jerusalem, for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, king of Babylon, [Col. 1432A] I came to the king; and at the end of the days I asked [Note: [Col. 1432D] The Regina manuscript has, “I asked him, and I came,” etc.] the king.

And I came to Jerusalem and understood the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, making a treasury chamber for him in the vestibules of the house of God. And it seemed exceedingly evil to me. And I threw Tobiah’s household vessels out of the treasury chamber. I gave orders, and they cleansed the treasury chambers; and I brought back there the vessels of the house of God, the offering, and the incense.

And I learned that the portions of the Levites had not been given, and that each of the Levites, singers, and ministers had fled to his own region. So I brought the officials to trial and said: “Why have we abandoned the house of God?” And I gathered them and stationed them at their posts. And all Judah brought the tithe of grain, wine, and oil into the storehouses. And we appointed over the storehouses Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah of the Levites; and beside them, Hanan son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, because they had been proved faithful, and the portions of their brothers were entrusted to them.

“Remember me, my God, [Note: [Col. 1432D] The Regina manuscript inserts here the words “for good”; someone concerned with scholarship had earlier placed this as a gloss in the margin of the book.] for this, and do not wipe out my mercies, which I performed in the house of my God and in its ceremonies.

“In those days I saw in Judah people treading winepresses on the sabbath [Note: [Col. 1432D] The words “on the sabbath,” although they also occur in the Hebrew, are omitted by the Regina manuscript.], bringing in sheaves, loading wine, grapes, figs, and every burden upon donkeys, and bringing them into Jerusalem on the sabbath day. And I testified against them concerning the day on which they were permitted to sell, that they should sell then.

“And Tyrians lived there, bringing fish and every kind of merchandise; and they sold on the sabbaths to the children of Judah in Jerusalem. And I rebuked the nobles of Judah and said to them: ‘What is this evil thing that you are doing, profaning the sabbath day? Did not our fathers do these things, and did not our God bring all this evil upon us and upon this city? Yet you are adding to Israel’s anger by violating the sabbath.’

“When the gates of Jerusalem were at rest on the sabbath, I spoke; and they shut the doors, and I commanded that they should not open them until after the sabbath. And I stationed some of my young men at the gates, so that no one might bring in a burden on the sabbath day. And the merchants and sellers of every kind of merchandise remained outside Jerusalem once or twice. And I testified against them and said: ‘Why are you remaining opposite the wall? If you do this again, I will lay hands upon you.’ From that time onward they did not come on the sabbath.

“I also told the Levites to purify themselves and come to guard the gates and sanctify the sabbath day. For this also, remember me, my God, and spare me according to the multitude of your mercies.

“In those days I also saw Jews taking wives from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod, and they did not know how to speak Jewish; they spoke according to the language of one people or another. And I rebuked them and cursed them. And I struck some of their men and plucked out their hair, and made them swear by God that they would not give their daughters to their sons, nor take their daughters for their sons or for themselves, saying: ‘Did not Solomon king of Israel sin in precisely this matter? Surely among the many nations there was no king like him; he was beloved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel. Yet foreign women led even him into sin. Shall we then be disobedient and commit all this great evil, transgressing against our God and taking foreign wives?’”

[Col. 1433A] But among the sons of Joiada, son of Eliashib the high priest, one was a son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite; I drove him away from me. Remember, O Lord my God, against those who defile the priesthood and the rights of the priestly and Levitical order. Thus I cleansed them from everything foreign, [Col. 1434A] and established the orders of the priests and Levites, each in his own ministry, and for the offering of wood at the appointed times and for the firstfruits. Remember me, my God, for good. Amen.

> **Note:** [Col. 1433A] The Regina manuscript has *generaret* (“would beget”) by mistake instead of *gener erat* (“was the son-in-law”) of Sanballat the Horonite.

> **Note:** [Col. 1434A] The same manuscript has *primitii*; and it more correctly omits the final word *Amen*, which is not found in the Hebrew.

[Col. 1433] Here ends the Book of Ezra.

[Col. 1433]

# [THE BOOK OF ESTHER]

## Jerome’s Preface to the Book of Esther

> **Note:** [Col. 1433B] We collated this book, together with the Prologue, against two very ancient manuscript codices of the Vatican Library: the first, formerly designated Regina Suecorum no. 7; the second, designated Vatican-Palatinus no. 24, which we found considerably more correct than the former.

[Col. 1433A] The Book of Esther is clearly corrupted by various translators. I, having recovered it from the archives of the Hebrews, translated it more closely, word for word. The Vulgate edition drags the book along here and there with ragged [or: “tattered”] folds of words,

> **Note:** [Col. 1433B] Several manuscripts read “with ropes of words”; some read “with ends of words” instead of “with folds.” How the Book of Esther was dragged along with such ragged folds in copies of the old Latin Vulgate is demonstrated by our manuscript no. 7, which preserves the Vulgate edition commonly used before Jerome. So many and such extensive additions are found there—things that could have been spoken and heard extemporaneously—that we could scarcely have reconstructed them by conjecture, had they not still remained written for us in the aforementioned ancient San-Germanensis monument. Who, indeed, would have believed that, in place of the single verse of chapter fourteen, the following had been inserted by the author of that old Latin edition?

> “I heard in the books of my fathers, Lord, that you preserved Noah in the waters of the Flood. I heard in the books of my fathers, Lord, that you delivered nine kings to Abraham with three hundred and eighteen men. I heard in the books of my fathers, Lord, that you delivered Jonah from the belly of the sea-monster. I heard in the books of my fathers, Lord, that you delivered Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael from the fiery furnace. I heard in the books of my fathers, Lord, that you rescued Daniel from the lions’ den. I heard in the books of my fathers, Lord, that, when Hezekiah king of the Jews had been condemned to death and prayed for life, you took pity on him and granted him fifteen years of life. I heard in the books of my fathers, Lord, that you granted Hannah, when she asked in the desire of her soul, the birth of a son. I heard in the books of my fathers, Lord, that you free those who please you, Lord, to the very end,” and so forth.

> Many other passages occur in this Vulgate edition that confirm Jerome’s words. All learned men will acknowledge this if they read it through in our appendix to the Old Testament. —MART.

adding things that could have been said and heard extemporaneously, as is customary in academic exercises when, after a subject has been proposed, one imagines what words might have been used by the person who suffered an injury or by the one who inflicted it.

> **Note:** [Col. 1433D] The San-Germanensis manuscript no. 4 and the Memmianus Canon read: “as is customary in secular disciplines.” The same Memmianus codex notes another reading in the margin, namely, “scholarly.” —MART.

But you, Paula and Eustochium,

> **Note:** [Col. 1433D] Understand “the younger Paula,” since Paula, the mother of Eustochium, had died before this Latin translation from the Hebrew, as is perfectly clear from what Jerome wrote about the Book of Esther in his Preface to Joshua, which we strongly urge the reader to consult. Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that the name of the younger virgin is found written before the name of Eustochium, whose niece through her brother Paula, the daughter of Laeta, was. For this is how the scribes who daily copied Jerome’s books habitually wrote: “O Paula and Eustochium.” They did not know of the other Paula, nor did they know the chronology of Jerome’s writings. What wonder, then, if they inverted the order in this form of address? —MART.

> Some wish “Paula and Eustochium” to be replaced by “Domnio and Rogatiane.” They argue on two grounds that Jerome addressed this book to them. First, because in the Prologue to Ezra, when saying that he had been asked by them to translate Esther from the Hebrew as well, Saint Jerome is said to have mentioned their request. Second, because Paula, the mother of Eustochium, had died before Jerome prepared this translation. The first argument, however, rests on the presumption of a false reading and can easily be dismissed: some time ago, following Martianay, we removed the name of Esther from that passage of the Prologue in accordance with the testimony of nearly all the manuscripts, and clearly demonstrated that it had been rashly introduced there through scribal error. As for the second argument, Martianay, together with the generality of learned men, replies that the Paula to be understood here is not Paula, the mother of Eustochium, but the younger Paula, the daughter of Laeta and niece through her brother of Eustochium. The inversion—placing the younger before her aunt and elder—should be attributed to the negligence of scribes and to the customary order in which these names were written. What we think about this matter must be stated in the Preface placed at the beginning of this volume, since discussion would lead us too far from the purpose of these notes. —MART.

> **Note:** [Col. 1434C] Among the ancients, the Sacred Scriptures were called “libraries”; therefore, “to enter the libraries of the Hebrews” means nothing other than being sufficiently capable of reading and understanding the volumes of the Hebrew Scriptures. In this respect religious women, virgins and brides of Christ, surpassed many ignorant men of the present age, who, whenever they see certain learned men studying the Hebrew language, immediately burst into laughter and call them “Jews” and “rabbis,” as though it were shameful for freeborn men to learn the sacred language of the prophets, to follow in the footsteps of the teachers of the Church, and to imitate the example of the most noble virgins Eustochium and Paula. —MART.

because you too have sought to enter the Hebrew libraries and have approved the contests among translators, hold the Hebrew Book of Esther in your hands and examine our translation word by word, so that you may recognize that I have added nothing at all,

> **Note:** [Col. 1434D] The royal manuscript of the Bible and our San-Germanensis no. 4 read *umquam* (“ever”) instead of *etiam* (“also”), meaning: “that I have never added anything.” —MART.

> Some manuscripts likewise read *umquam* instead of *etiam*. It seems, however, that another corresponding clause, beginning with the same word, has dropped out—for example, “that I have truncated nothing by being silent,” or something similar.

but, as a faithful witness, have simply handed over the Hebrew history to the Latin language just as it is found in Hebrew. We neither seek human praise nor fear human reproach. For, concerned to please God, we fear human threats not at all, because “God scatters the bones of those who desire to please men” (Psalm 52:6), and, according to the Apostle, “those who are such cannot be servants of Christ” (Galatians 1:10).

> **Note:** [Col. 1435A] In all editions of Saint Jerome’s Preface to the Book of Esther, the following addition is appended after these words:

> “Again, in the Book of Esther we have marked the alphabet in red, from the letter alpha through the letter theta, in various places, wishing by this means to indicate to the diligent reader the order of the Seventy Translators. For our part, following the Hebrew name, we preferred to preserve the order also in the Septuagint edition.”

> So far as we know, this part of the Prologue, which is spurious and falsely attributed, has never been regarded with suspicion by anyone. Consequently, several learned men have illustrated it with notes as though it were a genuine work of Jerome. Yet we know that it is an imposture. We first recognized this with the aid of manuscript codices, but it became still more evident through careful and repeated examination of the same words: no meaning can be extracted from them that suits Jerome’s argument.

> Let us first take the evidence of fraud from the altered opening word of the addition. The older and better manuscripts—namely, the Vatican, Royal, and San-Germanensis copies—do not read “Again, in the Book of Esther,” but “Rufinus’s alphabet in the Book of Esther,” and so forth. It is therefore certain that the artificer of this spurious annotation imitated Rufinus’s example by adding letters of the Greek alphabet to designate the order of the Septuagint translation, although the translator or writer himself was following the sequence of the Hebrew volumes.

> Who does not know that Jerome always stood superior to Rufinus in translating, correcting, and elucidating the Holy Scriptures, and that he never needed to borrow from Rufinus either the origin or arrangement of the Septuagint translation or the elements of the Greek or Hebrew alphabet? Therefore, whoever has borrowed anything from Rufinus in preparing or arranging the divine Scriptures must be regarded as later than Jerome and entirely distinct from him.

> Furthermore, Saint Jerome’s annotations placed in various locations near the final chapters of the Book of Esther agree in no way with the addition to the Preface; nor does the context of the book itself agree with it. For the author of the addition tells the reader that, following Hebrew custom, he has preserved the order even in the edition of the Seventy Translators. Jerome, on the contrary, asserts that this edition of the Book of Esther is purely Hebrew; how, then, could these things be said to have been published nowhere in the Hebrew text? Therefore, it must be admitted that the final part of the Prologue is to be attributed to some unknown writer who, in his Latin edition prepared from Greek manuscripts of the Seventy Translators, followed the order of the Hebrew history.

> We had long been persuaded of this by the meaning of the words of the addition. Now, however, it is most evident and beyond doubt from the Latin manuscript that we mentioned, containing the old Vulgate, or Itala, edition of the Book of Esther. For, after a most careful comparison of that copy with several Greek translations, we discovered that the Latin edition of the Seventy Translators follows the order and practice of the Hebrew history.

> For example, the murderous plot of the two eunuchs Gabatha and Tharra against King Artaxerxes, which the Seventy Translators narrate at the beginning of the Book of Esther, is found in our manuscript, in accordance with the practice of the Hebrew books, after Esther’s marriage to King Artaxerxes. Again, the account of Mordecai’s captivity and deportation to Babylon, which appears in the first chapter of the Septuagint edition, is retained by the Latin manuscript in chapter two, according to the practice of the Hebrew codices.

> These facts clearly establish the truth and reliability of everything we have stated above concerning the final, spurious part of the Preface to the Book of Esther. In addition, there are three very ancient and excellent manuscripts in which nothing is added. They are the Memmianus, the codex of the Church of Narbonne, and another belonging to the Cistercian monastery of Fontfroide. These bring the Preface to an end with the Apostle’s words, “They cannot be servants of Christ,” immediately adding: “Here ends the Preface,” and so forth.

> Nor should the Colbertinus Aniciensis be omitted. In its margin, beside the Apostle’s words just mentioned, the copyist wrote, “Here ends the Prologue,” thereby most clearly indicating that the Preface ends with this scriptural sentence. The remaining material is therefore foreign and added; consequently, it was finally deleted as spurious by some corrector who did not hesitate to obliterate the entire addition at this point.

> In several other Vatican, Royal, and San-Germanensis manuscripts, moreover, the final, spurious part of the Preface does not have the same context as what precedes it, but is written separately and begins with a red initial in the following form: “Rufinus’s alphabet in the Book of Esther,” and so forth. This would be sufficient to prove the novelty and imposture of this suspect passage.

> But enough of this. So that we may omit nothing from which some benefit may be derived, we also set out here the variant readings in the spurious addition to the Preface. The manuscript Bible codex of the most eminent Cardinal Bonzius reads as follows: “We made an alphabet from the Greek letter alpha, in red, through the letter theta, in various places,” and so forth. Another manuscript copy from our monastery at Narbonne has *fecerunt* (“they made”) in the third person instead of *fecimus* (“we made”), as though this alphabet were not attributed to the author of the Prologue or addition, but were said to have been inserted by others.

> These words refute those who thought that Jerome had marked such an alphabet, and indeed in Hebrew letters through theta; both claims are clearly false, as is evident both from these variant readings and from what we said above. Let those malicious critics who sometimes try, with loud outcries, to diminish the authority of manuscript codices now see how much benefit of light they lose through their envious complaints, and how much light and knowledge, by contrast, accrue to all diligent students and defenders of venerable antiquity. —MART.

## The Book of Esther Begins

[Col. 1435]

[Col. 1435D] **Chapter I.** In the days of Ahasuerus, who ruled from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, when he sat on the throne of his kingdom, the city of Susa was the beginning of his kingdom.

> **Note:** [Col. 1435D] In the Vatican-Palatinus manuscript, “Susa” is mentioned immediately.

[Col. 1437A] In the third year of his reign, therefore, he gave a great banquet for all his princes and attendants, the most powerful men of Persia, the distinguished Medes, and the governors of the provinces in his presence, so that he might display the wealth and glory of his kingdom, its greatness, and the magnificence of his power, for a long period—namely, one hundred and eighty days.

When the days of the banquet had been completed, he invited all the people who were found in Susa, from greatest to least. He ordered a banquet to be prepared for seven days in the vestibule of the garden and grove, which had been planted and cultivated with royal care. Tents of sky-blue, linen-colored, and hyacinth-colored fabric hung on every side, supported by cords of fine linen and purple, which were fastened into ivory rings and rested on marble columns. Golden and silver couches had also been arranged on a pavement laid with emerald and Parian stone, which was decorated with a remarkable variety of patterns. Those who had been invited drank from golden cups, and food was served in vessels of many different kinds. [Col. 1437B] Wine too, abundant and excellent, worthy of royal magnificence, was set before them. No one was compelled to drink against his will; rather, as the king had ordered, he appointed the noblemen to preside over the tables, so that each might take whatever he wished.

> **Note:** [Col. 1437D] The Palatinus manuscript has *eis* (“for them”) instead of *mensis* (“tables”).

Queen Vashti also held a banquet for the women in the palace where King Ahasuerus was accustomed to reside.

On the seventh day, when the king was cheerful and, after excessive drinking, had become heated with wine [another reading: “after drinking”], he commanded Mauman, Bazatha, Arbona, Bagatha, Abgatha, Zarath, and Charchas—the seven eunuchs who served in his presence—to bring Queen Vashti before the king, wearing the diadem upon her head, so that she might display her beauty to all the peoples and princes; for she was exceedingly beautiful. But she refused and scorned coming at the king’s command, which had been delivered through the eunuchs.

> **Note:** [Col. 1437D] The same manuscript has “Balatha.” Instead of *Zarath*, which follows, the Vulgate editions, at least in agreement with the Hebrew text, have *Zethar*.

> **Note:** [Col. 1437D] The Memmianus Canon and all the manuscript codices read this way; the printed editions, however, have *Zethar*, following the present Hebrew text. In the course of time, *thau* could easily have been written before *resh*, producing *Zethar* instead of *Zerath* or *Zarath*. —MART.

Therefore the king became angry and, burning with great fury, consulted the wise men who, according to royal custom, were always with him and whose counsel guided all his affairs. They knew the laws and rights of the ancestors. The king’s first and closest advisers were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media who saw the king’s face and customarily sat in the first place after him. He asked what judgment should be passed upon Queen Vashti, who had refused to carry out the command of King Ahasuerus delivered through the eunuchs.

> **Note:** [Col. 1437D] Our manuscripts read: “Memucha, seven princes of the king of Persia,” and so forth; but the word “king” is not added here by the other original books.

Memucan replied in the hearing of the king and the princes: “Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king but also all the peoples and princes who are in every province of King Ahasuerus. For the queen’s conduct will become known to all women, so that they will despise their husbands and say: ‘King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to enter before him, and she would not come.’ By this example, all the wives of the princes of Persia and Media will hold their husbands’ commands in contempt. Thus the king’s anger is justified.

“If it pleases you, let an edict go forth from your presence and be written according to the law of the Persians and Medes, which may not be violated: Vashti may never again enter before King Ahasuerus, and her royal position shall be given to another who is better than she. Let this decree be proclaimed throughout the whole extent of your provinces, so that all wives, both of the great and of the small, may show honor to their husbands.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1438D] The Regina manuscript omits the final word, “honor.” It then adds the pronoun “his” to the word “princes”; both readings are inferior.

The advice pleased the king and the princes. The king acted according to Memucan’s advice and sent letters to all the provinces of his kingdom, in whatever languages and scripts each people could read and understand, in the name of King Ahasuerus. They declared that men were to be princes and masters in their own households, and this was proclaimed among all peoples.

## Chapter II

After these events, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had subsided, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what she had suffered. The king’s attendants and ministers said: “Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king, and let people be appointed to inspect all the provinces for beautiful virgins and bring them to the city of Susa. Let them be entrusted to the house of the women under the authority of Hegai the eunuch, who is in charge of and guards the royal women, and let them be given women’s cosmetics and whatever else is necessary for their use. Whichever among them pleases the king’s eyes shall reign in place of Vashti.” The proposal pleased the king, and he ordered it to be done as they had suggested.

There was a Jewish man in the city of Susa named Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin. He had been carried away from Jerusalem at the time when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon carried away Jeconiah, king of Judah. He had brought up his uncle’s daughter Hadassah, also called Esther. She had lost both parents and was exceedingly beautiful and attractive in appearance. After her father and mother died, Mordecai adopted her as his daughter.

When the king’s command had become known, and many beautiful virgins were brought to Susa according to his order and handed over to the eunuch Hegai, Esther too was delivered to him among the other girls, to be kept among the women. She pleased him and found favor in his sight. The eunuch ordered that her women’s cosmetics be prepared, that her portions be given to her, and that seven exceptionally beautiful young women from the king’s household be assigned to her. He adorned and beautified both her and her attendants. She did not reveal to him her people or her homeland, for Mordecai had commanded her to keep this matter entirely secret. He walked every day before the vestibule of the house where the chosen virgins were kept, concerned for Esther’s welfare and wishing to know what happened to her.

When the time came for each girl in turn to enter the king, after everything required for women’s adornment had been completed, the twelfth month arrived. They were anointed for six months with myrtle oil and for another six months used various cosmetics and perfumes.

> **Note:** [Col. 1438D] The Vulgate editions have “myrrh oil,” as do the Greeks, who call this oil myrrh. It is well known that matrons and virgins used myrrh to anoint their hair, as is clear from Propertius:

> “To drench her hair with Orontian myrrh.”

> The Hebrew text agrees, although the Chaldean translates it as “unripe-grape oil.” Whatever the truth of the matter, both our manuscripts and all those available to Martianay unanimously read *myrtino* (“myrtle oil”), as we have printed it.

When they entered before the king, they received whatever they requested for their adornment; after they had arranged themselves as they wished, they passed from the women’s dining chamber to the king’s bedchamber.
