The girl who entered in the evening went out in the morning and was led from there to the second house, which was under the authority of the eunuch Shaashgaz, who presided over the king’s concubines. She had no power to return to the king unless the king wished it and summoned her by name.

When the time had passed in due order, the day arrived on which Esther, daughter of Abihail, the brother of Mordecai, whom he had adopted as his daughter, was to enter before the king. She did not seek women’s cosmetics, but whatever Hegai the eunuch, guardian of the virgins, wished, he gave her for adornment. For she was exceedingly beautiful, and by her extraordinary loveliness she appeared pleasing and attractive to everyone who saw her.

She was brought to the bedchamber of King Ahasuerus in the tenth month, called Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign. The king loved her more than all the women, and she found favor and mercy before him beyond all the women. He placed the royal diadem on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti. He ordered a magnificent banquet to be prepared for all his princes and servants on the occasion of Esther’s union and marriage. He granted rest to all the provinces and distributed gifts with royal magnificence.

[Col. 1439B] When virgins were again sought and gathered, Mordecai remained at the king’s gate. He had still not revealed Esther’s homeland or people, as he had commanded her. Esther observed everything he ordered and did everything as she had been accustomed to do when he was raising her as a little girl.

At that time, while Mordecai was staying at the king’s gate, Bagathan and Thares, two royal eunuchs who were doorkeepers and presided over the first threshold of the palace, became angry. They planned to rise up against the king and kill him. Mordecai learned of this and immediately informed Queen Esther, who told the king in Mordecai’s name, since he had reported the matter to her. The matter was investigated and found to be true, and both men were hanged on the gallows. The event was recorded in the histories and annals in the king’s presence.

## Chapter III

After these events, King Ahasuerus exalted Haman son of Hammedatha, who was of the lineage of Agag, and set his seat above all the princes whom he had. All the king’s servants who were stationed at the palace doors bent their knees and worshiped Haman, for the emperor had so commanded them. Mordecai alone did not bend his knee or worship him.

The king’s attendants who presided at the palace doors said to him: “Why do you alone, unlike the others, disregard the king’s command?”

When they repeated this to him frequently and he refused to listen, they reported it to Haman, wishing to learn whether he would persist in his position, for he had told them that he was a Jew. When Haman heard this and discovered that Mordecai did not bend his knee to him or worship him, he became exceedingly angry. Yet he considered it beneath him to lay hands on Mordecai alone, since he had learned that Mordecai belonged to the Jewish people. Instead, he resolved to destroy the entire Jewish nation throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus.

In the first month, called Nisan, in the twelfth year of the reign of Ahasuerus, lots were cast into an urn before Haman to determine on what day and in what month the Jewish people should be destroyed. The twelfth month, called Adar, came out.

Haman said to King Ahasuerus: “There is a people scattered and separated from one another throughout all the provinces of your kingdom, using new laws and ceremonies and, moreover, disregarding the king’s decrees. You know very well that it is not expedient for your kingdom to allow them to grow insolent through license. If it pleases you, decree that they perish, and I will weigh ten thousand talents out to the keepers of your treasury.”

The king therefore removed from his hand the ring he used and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha, descendant of Agag and enemy of the Jews. He said to him: “The silver that you promise shall be yours; deal with the people as you please.”

The king’s scribes were summoned in the first month, Nisan, on the thirteenth day of that month. As Haman had commanded, they wrote to all the king’s satraps, the governors of the provinces, and the rulers of the various peoples, in whatever language each people could read and understand, in the name of King Ahasuerus. The letters, sealed with his ring, were sent by the king’s couriers throughout all the provinces, ordering them to kill and destroy all the Jews, from child to old man, children and women alike, on a single day—that is, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called Adar—and to seize their possessions.

The substance of the letters was that all the provinces should know of this and prepare themselves for the appointed day. The couriers who had been sent hastened to carry out the king’s command. The edict was immediately posted in Susa, while the king and Haman celebrated a banquet and all who were in the city wept.

> **Note:** [Col. 1439D] A marginal scholion found in the Memmianus Canon has been transferred into the text of the printed books—namely, the word “Jews.” Thus the sense becomes: “while all the Jews in the city were weeping.” But in the Hebrew, as also in the Latin manuscripts, we read simply, without the word “Jews”: “while all who were in the city were weeping.” —MART.

## Chapter IV

When Mordecai heard this, he tore his garments, put on sackcloth, and scattered ashes on his head. In the middle of the city he cried out with a loud voice, displaying the bitterness of his soul, and continued in this lament as far as the palace gates. For it was not permitted for anyone dressed in sackcloth to enter the king’s court.

In every province, town, and place to which the king’s cruel decree had reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, wailing, and weeping; many used sackcloth and ashes as their bed.

The young women and eunuchs entered and reported this to Esther. When she heard it, she was terrified. She sent clothing so that, after the sackcloth had been removed, Mordecai might put it on, but he refused to accept it. She summoned the eunuch Hathach, whom the king had given her as a servant, and commanded him to go to Mordecai and learn why he was doing this.

> **Note:** [Col. 1440D] The Regina manuscript reads: “having seized Hathach the eunuch,” and so forth.

Hathach went out and approached Mordecai, who was standing in the city square before the palace entrance. Mordecai told him everything that had happened: how Haman had promised to deposit silver in the king’s treasuries in exchange for the slaughter of the Jews. He also gave him a copy of the edict posted in Susa, so that he might show it to the queen and urge her to enter before the king and plead with him for her people.

Hathach returned and reported to Esther everything that Mordecai had said. She replied and ordered him to tell Mordecai: “All the king’s servants and all the provinces under his rule know that any man or woman who enters the king’s inner court without being summoned shall be put to death immediately, without any delay, unless the king extends the golden scepter to that person as a sign of mercy; then the person may live.

“How can I enter before the king, when I have not been summoned to him for thirty days?”

> **Note:** [Col. 1440D] The Palatinus manuscript has the single word “summoned.” Thus, shortly afterward, it also reads “summoned” instead of “not summoned.”

When Mordecai heard this, he again sent word to Esther: “Do not think that you alone will escape with your life because you are in the king’s house, unlike all the Jews. For if you remain silent now, the Jews will be delivered by another means, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows whether you have come to the kingdom precisely so that you might be prepared for a time such as this?”

Esther again sent these words to Mordecai: “Go, gather all the Jews whom you find in Susa, and pray for me. Do not eat or drink for three days and three nights. I too, with my maidservants, will fast in the same way. Then I will enter before the king, contrary to the law, though I have not been summoned, and I will surrender myself to death and danger.” Mordecai went and did everything Esther had commanded him.

## Chapter V

On the third day Esther put on her royal garments and stood in the inner court of the royal house, [Col. 1441A] opposite the king’s hall. He was sitting on his throne in the audience chamber of the palace, opposite the entrance to the house.

> **Note:** [Col. 1441D] Along with the Vulgate editions, the Regina manuscript adds the pronoun “his.”

When the king saw Queen Esther standing there, she pleased his eyes, and he extended toward her the golden scepter that he held in his hand. She approached and kissed the top of his scepter.

The king said to her: “What do you want, Queen Esther? What is your request? Even if you ask for half of the kingdom, it shall be given to you.”

She replied: “If it pleases the king, I ask that you come today with Haman to the banquet that I have prepared.”

Immediately the king said: “Call Haman quickly, so that he may comply with Esther’s request.” Thus the king and Haman came to the banquet that the queen had prepared for them.

After he had drunk wine abundantly, the king said to her: “What do you ask to be given you? What is your request? Even if you ask for half of my kingdom, you shall obtain it.”

Esther replied: “My request and my petition are these: If I have found favor in the king’s sight, and if it pleases the king to give me what I ask and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and tomorrow I will reveal my request to the king.”

Haman went out that day joyful and glad. When he saw Mordecai sitting before the palace gates—and not only had he failed to rise before him, he had not even moved from the place where he was sitting—he became exceedingly indignant. Concealing his anger, he returned to his house and summoned his friends and his wife Zeresh. He displayed to them the greatness of his wealth, the multitude of his sons, and how the king had elevated him in glory above all his princes and servants.

After this he said: “Queen Esther has invited no one else to the banquet with the king except me. Tomorrow too I shall dine with the king. Yet, despite possessing all these things, I consider that I possess nothing as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting before the royal gates.”

His wife Zeresh and the rest of his friends answered: “Have a tall beam prepared, fifty cubits high, and tell the king in the morning that Mordecai is to be hanged on it. Then you will go happily with the king to the banquet.” The advice pleased him, and he ordered a tall cross to be prepared.

## Chapter VI

The king spent that night sleepless and ordered the histories and annals of earlier times to be brought to him. As they were read in his presence, they came to the passage where it was written how Mordecai had reported the plot of the eunuchs Bagathan and Thares, who had sought to assassinate King Ahasuerus.

When the king heard this, he said: “What honor and reward did Mordecai receive for this loyalty?”

His servants and ministers replied: “He received no reward at all.”

Immediately the king said: “Who is in the court?”

Haman had entered the inner court of the royal house to advise the king and order that Mordecai be fastened to the gallows that had been prepared for him.

The attendants replied: “Haman is standing in the court.”

The king said: “Let him enter.”

When Haman had entered, the king said to him: “What should be done for the man whom the king wishes to honor?”

Haman considered in his heart and reckoned that the king wished to honor no one but himself. He answered: “The man whom the king wishes to honor should be clothed in royal garments, placed upon a horse taken from the king’s saddle, and have the royal diadem set upon his head. One of the king’s foremost princes and rulers should lead his horse through the city square, proclaiming and saying: ‘Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king wishes to honor.’”

The king said to him: “Hurry. Take the garment and the horse, and do as you have said to Mordecai the Jew, who sits before the palace gates. Be careful to omit nothing of what you have said.”

Haman therefore took the garment and the horse. He clothed Mordecai, led him on horseback through the city square, and went before him proclaiming: “This is the honor due to the man whom the king wishes to honor.”

Mordecai returned to the palace gate, while Haman hurried home mourning and with his head covered. He told his wife Zeresh and his friends everything that had happened to him.

> **Note:** [Col. 1442A] Some manuscripts omit the final word “his.”

The wise men whom he had in his council and his wife replied: “If Mordecai is of Jewish descent, before whom you have begun to fall, you will not be able to resist him; you will fall before him.”

While they were still speaking, the king’s eunuchs arrived and quickly compelled him to proceed to the banquet that the queen had prepared.

## [Chapter VII]

Then the king and Haman entered to drink with the queen. On the second day also, after he had become warm with wine, the king said to her: “What is your request, Esther, that it may be granted to you? And what do you wish to have done? Even if you should ask for half of my kingdom, you will obtain it.”

She answered him: “If I have found favor in your eyes, O king, and if it pleases you, grant me my life, for which I ask, and my people, for whom I plead. [Col. 1442B] For I and my people have been handed over to be crushed, slaughtered, and destroyed. If only we had been sold into slavery, male and female; the evil would have been bearable, and I would have remained silent, lamenting. But now our enemy is a man whose cruelty rebounds upon the king.”

King Ahasuerus answered and said: “Who is this, and of what power is he, that he should dare to do such things?” Esther said: “This most wicked Haman is our enemy and adversary.” When he heard this, he was immediately dumbfounded, unable to endure the sight of the king and queen.

But the angry king rose and went from the place of the banquet into a garden planted with trees. Haman also rose to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he understood that the king had prepared evil for him. When the king returned from the wooded garden and entered the place of the banquet, he found Haman fallen upon the couch [Note: [Col. 1441D] The Palatine manuscript reads: “fallen upon his own couch,” etc.] on which Esther was reclining, and he said: “Does he even wish to violate the queen in my presence, in my own house?” The word had scarcely left the king’s mouth when they immediately covered [Col. 1442C] Haman’s face.

Arbona, one of the eunuchs who stood in the king’s service, said: “Behold, the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai, who spoke on the king’s behalf, stands in Haman’s house; it is fifty cubits high.” The king said to him: “Hang him on it.” So Haman was hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai, and the king’s anger subsided.

## [Chapter VIII]

On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman, the adversary of the Jews, and Mordecai entered into the presence of the king. For Esther had confessed to him that Mordecai was her uncle.

The king took the ring that he had ordered to be removed from Haman and gave it to Mordecai. Esther, meanwhile, appointed Mordecai over her house. Not content with this, [Note: [Col. 1442D] *Martianaeo* was previously read incorrectly; the text continues.] she fell at the king’s feet, wept, and spoke to him, pleading that he order the evil of Haman the Agagite, and his wicked schemes that he had devised against the Jews, to be annulled. He then, according to custom, extended the golden scepter in his hand, by which a sign of clemency was shown. [Col. 1442D] She rose and stood before him, saying:

“If it pleases the king, and if I have found favor in his eyes, and if my petition does not seem contrary to him, I beg that, by new letters, the former letters of Haman, the plotter and enemy of the Jews, by which he had ordered them to perish throughout all the king’s provinces, be corrected. For how could I endure the death and destruction of my people?”

King Ahasuerus answered Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew: “I have granted Haman’s house to Esther, and I have ordered him to be fastened to the cross, because he dared to lay hands upon the Jews. Write therefore to the Jews as you please, in the king’s name, sealing the letters with my ring. For this was the custom: no one dared contradict letters sent in the king’s name and sealed with his ring.”

[Col. 1443A] The king’s scribes and copyists were summoned. It was the third month, called SIBAN, on its twenty-third day. Letters were written, as Mordecai had desired, to the Jews and to the rulers, governors, and judges who governed the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia—province by province and people by people, according to their languages and scripts—and to the Jews, so that they could read and hear them. The letters themselves, sent in the king’s name, were sealed with his ring and dispatched by mounted couriers, who raced through all the provinces, outstripping the former letters with the new messages.

The king ordered them to assemble the Jews in every city and command them to gather together, so that they might stand up for their lives, attack and kill all their enemies, with their wives, children, and entire households, and destroy them, [Note: [Col. 1443D] Our manuscripts do not recognize this passage—“and seize their spoils.”] and seize their spoils. Throughout all the provinces one day of vengeance was appointed: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, ADAR. The substance of the letter was this: throughout all the lands and peoples subject to the rule of King Ahasuerus, it should be known that the Jews were ready to take revenge upon their enemies. The couriers went out, bearing the swift messages, and the king’s edict was posted in Susa.

Mordecai, leaving the palace and the king’s presence, shone in royal garments—namely, violet and bronze-colored—and wore a golden crown on his head; he was wrapped in a silk and purple cloak. The whole city rejoiced and was glad. For the Jews a new light seemed to have arisen: joy, honor, and festivity. In all the peoples, cities, and provinces, wherever the king’s commands arrived, there was extraordinary rejoicing, feasting, banquets, and celebration, so much so that many of another nation and sect joined themselves to their religion and ceremonies. For a great terror of the Jewish name had seized everyone.

## [Chapter IX]

In the twelfth month, which we have already said is called ADAR, on its thirteenth day, when slaughter had been prepared for all the Jews [Col. 1443C] and their enemies thirsted for their blood, the situation was reversed: the Jews began to prevail and to avenge themselves upon their adversaries. They assembled in every city, town, and place, in order to stretch out their hand against their enemies and persecutors. No one dared resist them, because fear of their greatness had penetrated all peoples. The judges of the provinces, the commanders, the governors, and every official who presided over the various places and offices exalted the Jews out of fear of Mordecai. They had learned that he was chief in the palace and very powerful; the fame of his name also grew daily and flew through everyone’s mouth.

Thus the Jews struck their enemies with a great blow and killed them, repaying them for what they had prepared to do to them. In [Note: [Col. 1443D] Here and below our manuscripts read “in Susa”; then, with a very different sense: “they killed five hundred and ten men, besides Haman’s sons”—but less correctly.] Susa also they killed five hundred men, as well as the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews. Their names were: Pharsandatha, Delphon, Esphatha, [Col. 1443D] Phoratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Phermesta, Arisai, Aridai [Al.: Arisati], and Vaizatha [Al.: Jezatha]. After killing them, they did not wish to touch the spoils of their property.

Immediately the number of those who had been killed in Susa was reported to the king. He said to the queen: “In the city of Susa the Jews have killed five hundred men and the ten other sons of Haman. How great a slaughter do you think they have carried out throughout all the provinces? What more do you request, and what do you wish me to order done?” She answered: “If it pleases the king, let power be given to the Jews so that, just as they have done today in Susa, they may do likewise tomorrow, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on gallows.” The king commanded [Col. 1444A] that it be done. Immediately an edict was posted in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.

When the Jews had assembled on the fourteenth day of the month ADAR, three hundred men were killed in Susa; none of their property was seized by them. Throughout all the provinces subject to the king’s authority, the Jews also stood up for their lives, killing their enemies and persecutors, until the number of those killed reached seventy-five thousand; no one touched any of their property.

The thirteenth day of the month ADAR was the one [Al.: first] day of slaughter for all, and on the fourteenth day they ceased killing. They established it as a solemn day, so that thereafter they might always devote it to feasting, joy, and banquets. But those who had carried out the slaughter in the city of Susa were engaged in killing on the thirteenth and fourteenth days of the same month; on the fifteenth day they ceased striking. Therefore they established that day as a solemn day of feasting and joy. The Jews who lived in unwalled towns and villages, however, decreed the fourteenth day of the month ADAR as a day of banquets and joy, so that they might rejoice on it and send one another portions of feasts and food.

Mordecai wrote down all these things and sent them in a letter to the Jews who lived in all the king’s provinces, both those nearby [Al.: the second *positis* is omitted] and those far away, instructing them to accept the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month ADAR as feast days and to celebrate them every year with solemn honor. For on those days the Jews had avenged themselves upon their enemies, and mourning and sorrow had been turned into gladness and joy. These were to be days of feasting and joy, when they would send portions of food to one another and give small gifts to the poor.

The Jews accepted as a solemn rite all that they had begun to do at that time [Note: [Col. 1444D] The Regina manuscript reads *facere poterant*—“they could do”—instead of *coeperant*—“they had begun.”] and all that Mordecai had commanded them by letter to do. For Haman, son of Amadathus, of the stock of Agag, the enemy and adversary of the Jews, had devised evil against them, intending to kill and destroy them. He had cast PHUR, which in our language is translated as “lot.” Afterwards Esther went in to the king, pleading that his efforts be nullified by the king’s letters, and that the evil he had devised against the Jews return upon his own head. Finally, both he and his sons were fastened to the cross. From that time these days were called PHURIM, that is, “of lots,” because PHUR, that is, a lot, had been cast into an urn.

All that happened is contained in the volume of the letter—that is, of this book. The Jews accepted upon themselves, their descendants, and all who wished to join their religion, both what they had endured and what was thereafter established: that no one should be permitted to pass these two days without solemn observance. Scripture bears witness to this, and fixed times require it as the years continually succeed one another. These are the days that no oblivion will ever erase. Throughout every generation all the provinces of the entire world will celebrate them, and there is no city in which the Jews, and their descendants bound to these ceremonies, will not observe the days of PHURIM, that is, of lots.

Queen Esther, daughter of [Note: [Col. 1444D] The Palatine manuscript reads “Abigail,” but this is not correct. The Hebrew has .] Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew also wrote a second letter, so that this solemn day might be established for the future with every diligence. They sent it to all the Jews who lived in the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces of King Ahasuerus, instructing them to maintain peace and accept the truth. They were to observe the days of Lots and celebrate them joyfully at the appointed time, as Mordecai and [Col. 1445A] Esther had established, and as they had accepted for observance by themselves and their descendants: fasts and cries, the days of Lots, and everything contained in the history of this book called Esther.

## [Chapter X]

King Ahasuerus made the whole land and all the islands of the sea tributary. His strength, power, dignity, and greatness, by which he exalted Mordecai, are written in the books of the Medes and Persians: also how Mordecai, being of Jewish descent, was second to King Ahasuerus, great [Note: [Col. 1445D] The same manuscript reads “great among the Jews.”] among the Jews, and acceptable to the people of his brothers, seeking the good of his people and speaking those things that concerned the peace of his descendants.

I have rendered with complete fidelity what is found in the Hebrew. What follows, however, I found written in the Vulgate edition, which is contained in the Greek language and letters; meanwhile, after the end of the book, this chapter was customarily transmitted. In accordance with our practice, we marked it beforehand with an obelus ÷, that is, a spit. [Note: [Col. 1445D] Many manuscript codices omit these obelus signs. The Memmian manuscript, however, together with the two older manuscripts of ours from Saint-Germain-des-Prés, marked 4 and 15, reproduces them most exactly from this point to the end of the book. MART.]

[Col. 1445B] ÷ Mordecai [Note: [Col. 1445D] The same manuscript adds: “to them.”] said: “These things were done by God. I remembered the dream that I had seen, signifying these very things; not one of them proved false. The small spring that grew into a river, and was transformed into light and sun, and overflowed into many waters: this is Esther, whom the king took as his wife and wished to be queen. The two dragons: I am one, and Haman the other. The nations that assembled are those who attempted to destroy the name of the Jews. My nation is Israel, which cried out to the Lord, and the Lord saved his people. He delivered us from all evils and performed great signs and wonders among the nations. He commanded that there be two lots: one for the people of God, and the other for all the nations. Each lot came on its appointed [Note: [Col. 1446D] The Regina manuscript omits the word *day*.] day before God and all the nations. The Lord remembered his people and had mercy on his inheritance. These days shall be observed in the month ADAR, on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of that same month, with all diligence and joy, by the people gathered into one assembly, throughout all succeeding generations of the people of Israel.”

## [Chapter XI]

In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, [Note: [Col. 1446D] The same manuscript consistently writes *Tholomaeum* with *th*.] Dositheus, who claimed to be a priest and of Levitical descent, and his son Ptolemy brought this letter concerning PHURIM, which they said had been translated by Lysimachus, son of Ptolemy, in Jerusalem.

This too was the beginning found in the Vulgate edition, but it is reported neither in the Hebrew nor as translated by any interpreter.

In the second year of the reign of the great Artaxerxes, on the first day of the month NISAN, Mordecai son of Jair, son of Semel, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, saw a dream. He was a Jewish man living in the city of Susa, a prominent man and one of the foremost in the royal court. He belonged to the number of captives whom King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had transferred from Jerusalem with Jeconiah, king of Judah. This was his dream:

Voices, tumult, thunder, earthquakes, and confusion appeared over the earth. Behold, two great dragons, prepared for battle against each other. At their cry all the nations were stirred up to fight against the nation of the righteous. That day was one of darkness and danger, tribulation and distress, and great fear upon the earth. The nation of the righteous, fearing for its own safety, was thrown into confusion and prepared for death. They cried out to God, and as they cried, a small spring grew into a very great river and overflowed into many waters. Light and the sun rose; the humble were exalted, and they devoured the illustrious.

When Mordecai had seen this and risen from his bed, he pondered what God might intend to do, and fixed in his mind a desire to know what the dream signified.

## [Chapter XII]

At that time he was staying in the king’s court with Bagatha and Thara, the king’s eunuchs who were doorkeepers of the palace. When he understood their thoughts and had carefully observed their concerns, he learned that they were attempting to lay hands upon King Artaxerxes and reported this to the king. After investigating both men, the king ordered them, once they had confessed, to be led to death. The king recorded what had happened in his chronicles, and Mordecai also committed the memory of the event to writing. The king ordered him to remain in the palace court and gave him gifts for his report. Haman, son of Amadathus the Bugaean, was highly honored before the king and wished to harm Mordecai and his people because of the two royal eunuchs who had been killed.

[Col. 1446B] Thus far the Preface.

What follows had been placed in the location where it is written in the volume:

“And they seized their goods, or property.”

This we find only in the Vulgate edition.

The letter, however, had this form.

## [Chapter XIII]

“The great King Artaxerxes sends greetings to the rulers and commanders of the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia who are subject to his authority. [Note: [Col. 1446D] The Regina manuscript adds the word *dicit*, ‘says.’]

Although I ruled over many nations and subjected the entire world to my authority, I wished not at all to abuse the greatness of my power, but to govern my subjects with clemency and gentleness, so that they might pass their lives in quiet without any terror and enjoy the peace desired by all mortals. When I asked my counselors how this could be accomplished, one man, who surpassed the others in wisdom and fidelity and [Col. 1446C] was second to the king, named Haman, informed me that throughout the world there was a people dispersed among the nations that used new laws, acted contrary to the custom of all peoples, despised the commands of kings, and violated the harmony of all nations by its dissension.

When we learned this, seeing that one rebellious people was using perverse laws against the entire human race, opposing our commands and disturbing the peace and harmony of the provinces subject to us, we ordered that all whom Haman—who is placed over all the provinces, is second to the king, and whom we honor in place of a father—should identify be destroyed by their enemies, together with their wives and children. No one was to pity them, on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month ADAR of the present year, so that these impious men, descending to the underworld on a single day, might restore to our empire the peace that they had disturbed.”

Thus far the copy of the letter.

[Col. 1446D] What follows I found written after the passage where it reads:

“Mordecai went on and did everything that Esther had commanded him.”

Yet it is not found in the Hebrew, nor is it reported as translated by any interpreter at all.

Mordecai pleaded with the Lord, remembering all his works, and said:

“Lord, Lord, almighty king, for all things are placed in your power, and there is no one who can resist your will if you have determined to save Israel. You made heaven and earth and everything contained within the circuit of heaven. You are Lord of all, and there is no one who can resist your majesty. You know everything, and you know that I did this neither out of pride and insult nor from any desire for glory, so that I would not worship the most arrogant Haman. For I would gladly have been ready to kiss even the traces of his feet for Israel’s salvation. But I feared transferring the honor of my God to a human being and worshiping anyone except my God.

“And now, Lord, King God of Abraham, have mercy upon your people, because our enemies intend to destroy us and erase your inheritance. Do not despise your portion, which you redeemed for yourself from Egypt. Hear my prayer and be gracious to your lot and your allotted portion. Turn our mourning into joy, so that, while alive, we may praise your name, Lord, and do not close the mouths of those who sing to you.”

All Israel likewise cried out to the Lord with one mind and one plea, because certain death threatened them.

## [Chapter XIV]

Queen Esther also fled to the Lord, fearing the danger that threatened. After removing her royal garments, she put on clothing suited to tears and mourning. Instead of various perfumes, she filled her head with ashes and dung, humbled her body with fasts, and filled all the places where she had previously been accustomed to rejoice with the tearing of her hair. She pleaded with the Lord God of Israel, saying:

“My Lord, you alone are our king; help me who am solitary, for I have no other helper besides you. My danger is in my own hands. I heard from my father that you, Lord, brought Israel out from all the nations and our ancestors from all their forefathers, in order to possess an everlasting inheritance, and that you did for them as you had spoken. We sinned in your sight, and therefore you delivered us into the hands of our enemies, for we worshiped their gods. You are just, Lord. Now it is enough for them that they oppress us with the harshest [Col. 1447C] servitude. Yet, attributing the strength of their hands to the power of idols, they wish to change your promises, destroy your inheritance, close the mouths of those who praise you, and extinguish the glory of your temple and altar, so that they may open the mouths of the nations, praise the strength of idols, and proclaim a mortal king forever.

“Do not hand over your scepter, Lord, to those who are nothing, lest they laugh at our ruin. Turn their plan back upon them, and destroy the one who began to rage against us. Remember, Lord, and show yourself to us in the time of our tribulation. Give me confidence, [Note: [Col. 1447D] The Regina manuscript reads: ‘Give me confidence, King of the gods and Lord of all power.’] Lord, King of the gods and of all power. Put a well-composed speech in my mouth before the lion, and turn his heart to hatred of our enemy, so that he and all who consent to him may perish.

“But deliver us by your hand and help me, who have no other help but you, Lord, who possess knowledge of all things and know that I hate the glory of the wicked and detest the bed of the uncircumcised and of every foreigner. [Col. 1447D] You know my necessity: that I abhor the sign of my pride and glory that is upon my head in the days of my display; that I detest it like a menstrual cloth; that I do not wear it in the days of my silence; that I have not eaten at Haman’s table; that the king’s banquet has not pleased me; that I have not drunk the wine of libations; and that your servant has never rejoiced from the time I was brought here until the present day, except in you, Lord God of Abraham.

“Strong God above all, hear the voice of those who have no other hope, deliver us from the hand of the wicked, and rescue me from my fear.”

[Col. 1448A] I also found the following added in the Vulgate edition.

## [Chapter XV]

Mordecai—there is no doubt that he is commanding Esther—commanded her to go in to the king and plead for her people and her homeland. He said: “Remember the days of your humiliation, how you were nourished by my hand, because Haman, second to the king, has spoken against us for death. Invoke the Lord, speak to the king on our behalf, and deliver us from death.”

And also the following passage, which is appended:

“On the third day she removed the garments of her adornment and put on her glory. Shining in royal attire, and having invoked God, ruler and savior of all, she took two maidservants. She leaned upon one of them, as though, because of luxury and excessive delicacy, she could not bear to carry her body. The other maidservant followed her mistress, supporting the garments that trailed upon the ground.

“She herself, her face suffused with a rosy color and her eyes gracious and shining, concealed a sorrowful spirit contracted by excessive fear. Entering through all the doors in order, she stood opposite the king, where he sat upon the throne of his kingdom, dressed in royal garments and gleaming with gold and precious stones. His appearance was terrifying.

“When he raised his face and showed the anger of his heart with burning eyes, the queen fell, and, her color changed to pallor, she rested her weary head upon [Note: [Col. 1447D] The same manuscript reads ‘upon the maidservant.’] the little maidservant. God changed the king’s spirit to gentleness. He quickly and fearfully sprang from his throne, took her in his arms, and supported her until she returned to herself, speaking soothingly to her:

“‘What is wrong, Esther? I am your brother; do not be afraid. You will not die, for this law was established not for you but for everyone. Come, then, and touch the scepter.’

“When she remained silent, he took the golden staff, placed it upon her neck, kissed her, and said: ‘Why do you not speak to me?’

“She answered: ‘I see you, lord, like an angel of God, and my heart was troubled by fear of your glory. For you are exceedingly wondrous, lord, [Col. 1448C] and your face is full of grace.’

“As she spoke, she fell again and was nearly lifeless. [Note: [Col. 1448D] The final sentence—‘But the king was troubled, and all his attendants,’ etc.—is missing from the Regina manuscript.] But the king was troubled, and all his attendants comforted her.”

The copy of the letter of King Artaxerxes that he sent on behalf of the Jews to all the provinces of his kingdom follows. This too is not found in the Hebrew volume.

## [Chapter XVI]

“The great King Artaxerxes sends greetings to the commanders and rulers of the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces that obey our command.

“Many people, abusing the kindness of rulers and the honor conferred upon them, have turned to pride. They not only strive to oppress those subject to kings, but, unable to bear the glory given to them [Note: [Col. 1448D] The same manuscript reads: “unable to bear the glory.”], plot against those who granted it. They are not content merely to fail to give thanks for benefits and violate the rights of kindness shown to them; they also imagine that they can escape the judgment of God, who sees all things.

“They have advanced so far in madness that they attempt to overthrow those who diligently discharge the offices entrusted to them and conduct everything in a manner worthy of everyone’s praise, using underground passages of lies, while deceiving with cunning fraud the simple ears of rulers who, by their nature, judge others by themselves. This is proved both by ancient histories and by what happens daily: how the deliberations of kings are corrupted by the evil suggestions of certain men.

“Therefore provision must be made for the peace of all the provinces. You must not think that, if we issue different commands, this arises from fickleness of mind; rather, we pronounce judgment according to the character and necessity of the times, as the welfare of the state demands.

“And so that you may understand more clearly what we are saying, Haman son of Amadathus, Macedonian in spirit and race and foreign to Persian blood, who stained our piety with his cruelty, was received by us as a stranger and experienced such great kindness from us that he was called our father and was worshiped by everyone as second to the king. He was lifted to such a swell of arrogance [Note: [Col. 1449B] The same manuscript reads: ‘lifted to such a degree of arrogance and honor.’] that he attempted to deprive us of both kingdom and life.

“For he sought the death of Mordecai, by whose fidelity and benefactions we live, and of Esther, our partner in the kingdom, together with their entire people, by certain novel and unheard-of devices. His intention was that, after killing them, he might lie in wait for our isolation and transfer the kingdom of Persia to the Macedonians.

“But we found that the Jews, condemned to death by the worst of mortals, were entirely without fault. On the contrary, they use just laws and are children of the highest, greatest, and ever-living God, by whose favor the kingdom was handed down both to our ancestors and to us and is preserved to this day.

“Therefore know that the letters he sent under our name are void. [Col. 1450A] For this crime, both the man who devised it and his entire kindred hang upon gallows before the gates of this city, that is, Susa—not because we repay him, but because God repays him what he deserved.

“Let this edict, which we now send, be posted in all cities, so that the Jews may use their own laws. You must assist them, so that they may kill those who had prepared themselves to destroy them on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called ADAR. For on this day almighty God has turned their mourning and grief into joy.

“Therefore count this day among your other feast days and celebrate it with complete joy, so that in the future it may be known that all who faithfully obey the Persians receive a worthy reward for their loyalty, while those who plot against their kingdom perish for their crime.

“Any province or city that refuses to participate in this solemnity shall perish by sword and fire and be so destroyed that it shall forever be impassable not only to human beings but also to beasts, as an example of contempt and disobedience.”

[Note: [Col. 1449B] After the book of Esther, the Memmian manuscript adds the following as the conclusion of the Hebrew canon of truth:

“THE THIRD ORDER OF THE HAGIOGRAPHA ENDS. THE FOURTH ORDER OF THOSE BOOKS THAT ARE NOT IN THE HEBREW CANON BEGINS.”

These words are written in gold letters in the center of a circular figure expressing the civic crown represented on ancient coins. The manuscript of the biblical codex of the Church of Narbonne has the same text, but in a simpler style:

“THE BOOK OF ESTHER, V. DCC., ENDS. THE THIRD ORDER, OF THE HAGIOGRAPHA, ETC., ENDS.”

Thus it indicates that there are seven hundred verses in the book of Esther, with which the final order of the books of the canon concludes. These words are also partly covered in red pigment and partly in ink. In the Saint-Germain manuscript no. 15 they are written in uncial or capital letters:

“THE END OF ESTHER. THANKS BE TO GOD. AMEN.”

“Thus far the Old Testament has been completed, that is, all the canonical Scriptures”—read: “all the canonical Scripture that makes the twenty-four books”—“which Jerome the presbyter translated from the Hebrew truth into the Latin language. With the greatest diligence and care, wandering through various codices, I sought out the editions, collected them into one body, and transferred them in writing, making a complete volume . . . . The other Scriptures, however, which are not canonical but are called ecclesiastical, are these: the book of Judith, Tobit, the two books of Maccabees, Wisdom, which is called Solomon’s, the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and the book of the Shepherd. It ends in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

The same copyist then appends the book of Judith according to the ancient Latin translation customarily used in the Church before Jerome; concerning this old Vulgate we shall speak in the Appendix to the Old Testament. Let what has been said about the canon suffice for now. MART.] ÷

[Col. 1449] The book of Esther ends.

# Appendix to the First Part of the Divine Library of Saint Jerome

[Col. 1449]

## J. Martianay’s Admonition

What we promised to do here in the annotations on Psalm XLV must now be fulfilled, with interest added. Accordingly, in this appendix to the canon, to satisfy the curiosity of learned readers, we present a considerable portion of Psalm II together with the entire sacred text of Psalm XLIV, or Psalm XLV among the Hebrews, in the vernacular language of the Hebrews but in Latin characters, exactly as the words are set down in a very ancient manuscript of our monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, which contains a threefold Psalter.

Yet lest anything be lost to the instruction of readers through the absence of the Hebrew letters, in the other adjoining column we have placed the Hebrew characters together with their Latin reading according to the vowel points, or the present-day vocalization, of the Masoretes. Thus, at a single glance, the difference between the ancient Hebrew reading and that now current among Hebrew grammarians may immediately be seen.

From this differing reading of the ancient and modern forms, something can also be inferred about the date of our ancient Hebraizing writer. Since in many places he agrees well with the teachers of the Masorah, but in some others occasionally disagrees with them, he seems to have lived near in time to those Jewish masters. Certainly no one who has compared the Hebrew readings of both will deny that he is inferior to Jerome: for one will find in them very different sounds of both vowels and consonants, as the examples below from our scholia demonstrate.

In any case, although the date of this anonymous writer is uncertain to us, one conclusion follows from him beyond all doubt: the Church of Christ was never without men learned in Hebrew who followed Saint Jerome’s footsteps in the study of the divine Scriptures. The ignorance of the heterodox of our own time has taught that the opposite was the case.

Hebrew characters expressed in Latin letters according to the punctuation of the Masoretes.

[Col. 1452A] [Note: [Col. 1453] Scholia on the Hebrew readings of the preceding psalms.

[Col. 1453C] To remove all ambiguity and confusion from our scholia, it will not be out of place to divide into certain classes the differing Hebrew readings of the ancient writers and of the more recent grammarians. First, therefore, we shall speak of variant readings in [Col. 1453D] consonantal letters.

Beth, which they call “softened,” or deprived of the dagesh point, sounds for our Anonymous author almost like a consonantal v; in this he differs in nothing from modern Hebrews. For example, in Psalm II, verse 8, he reads the word *besevet*, which recent grammarians likewise read because of the small point inscribed in the middle of the first beth in the Massoretic copies; when deprived of that point, the second beth is pronounced and read as v. In verses 1 and 12 of the same Psalm II, the same beth, without dagesh, sounds as v: *avedu*, *thovedu*. The diligent reader can observe the same thing in nearly all the verses of the following Psalm XLIV, especially verse 1, in the words *davar* and *tov*, which Jerome read in six hundred places as *dabar* and *tob*; the Anonymous author, however, read them *davar* and *tov*, as is customary today.

[Col. 1454C]

Heth, having a double aspiration, is more often represented by the Anonymous author with a capital H, as in Psalm XLIV, verse 1, *raHas*; verse 3, *Hen*, and so forth. Today we read *rachasch*, *chen*, or *rahhasc* and *hhen*. Thus Jerome and the anonymous writer agree in the pronunciation of this letter, since the holy Doctor recognizes a double aspiration of heth in many places, which the Unknown author sufficiently indicates by the capital form of the character.

Jod, in the future tense of verbs and elsewhere in nouns, he reads according to the sound of g: Psalm XLIV, verse 7, *gippolu*, where the g seems to have been introduced through the pronunciation of scribes in place of consonantal j—*gippolu* for *jippolu*. Psalm II, verses 9 and 13, *jocer* and *jivear*, and so forth; not a few Rabbis support this reading.

Chaph, according to the same author, sometimes sounds like k and sometimes like c. Thus in Psalm II, verse 13, the words *ki* and *col* are expressed in Latin letters. Our Hebraists, however, always pronounce initial kaph as k, reading *kol* just as *ki*. Jerome has *Chi* and *Chol*.

[Col. 1455A]

Samech, the hard s, he renders with a capital S. Thus in Psalm II, verse 8, *AfSe*; verse 13, *HoSe*. In the same way he reads the Ephraimite Sin, which is otherwise called Sin of *Sibolet*. Psalm XLIV, verse 9, *SaSon*. In this sound of the letter samech, both the ancients and the moderns agree.

In the letter *phe* he more often differs from Jerome, because that Anonymous author follows the reading of modern Hebrews in the dagesh, which he reads as p, rather than as *phe* in Jerome’s manner, who recognizes no dagesh. Psalm II, verse 9, *tenapecem*; verse 12, *Pen*; verse 13, *apo*, and so forth. Yet he does not agree in every respect with modern grammarians, who double the sound of p wherever a strong dagesh occurs; hence they read *tenappetsem* and *appo* with a double p, whereas the ancient writer reads them with a single one. Below, however, in Psalm XLIV, verse 7, he doubles the letter p in the word *gippolu*, or *jippolu*.

Tsade deserves more careful observation: the Anonymous author customarily reads and expresses it as c, as above in Psalm II, verse 9, in the word *tenapecem*, and in the same place in *jocer*. In Psalm XLIV, verse 7, however, he reads it almost as a double letter, with *tc*: *Heitcecha*. He therefore comes closer to the reading of modern Hebrews, especially if one bends the letter c as in our vernacular word *façon* and in the name *françois*. It should nevertheless be noted that final tsade has for the same writer the sound of z: *arez*, and so forth.

Thav with dagesh, nowhere heard in Jerome’s books, is everywhere recognized by our Anonymous author together with the disciples of the Massoretes. Hence *teroem* and *tenapecem*, and so forth, which in Jerome would be read with aspirated thav as *theroem* and *thenaphesem*.

[Col. 1456A]

As for the vowels, or vowel signs, this in particular must be observed in the manuscript codex: initial sheva is customarily read according to the sound of the following vowel, as in Psalm II, verses 8 and 13, *saal* for *scheal*, *maat* for *meat*, and so forth. Experts in the Hebrew language know that the ancients once likewise read *Sodom* and *tsabaoth*, although this practice has now fallen out of use, with one exception: the sheva immediately following an unmarked jod, which is not marked with hiriq, as in *liiom*, not *leiom*.

Ayin the Unknown author always expresses as though it were the vowel a, and often also by an enlarged form of the letter with a point inscribed within it. We could not reproduce this care by imitating it, owing to the lack of identical types. Nor are such letter-forms now seen among printers—forms which the very ancient writer devised and drew for the purposes of Hebrew-Latin reading, placing inner points not only in ayin, represented by A, but also in several other letters. They should by no means be imitated in printed books. It is enough to have made these observations. We leave the rest to the investigation of the curious and diligent, lest, by going through everything individually, we should seem—so to speak—to begrudge them the exercise of their diligence.

The reader should nevertheless beware of certain scribal confusions by ancient scribes, and of passages less accurately copied by them in the manuscript. Thus in Psalm II, verse 8, *vaa Huzadcha* occurs instead of *vaa Huzathcha*; in pronunciation these are easily confused, namely, the sound d with the sound th. Likewise in Psalm XLIV, verse 15, *zahad* occurs for *zahab*, d for b; verse 20, *vaheth* for *vahed*. Elsewhere they add the vowel e to the sound of consonantal letters: thus in verse 7 of the same Psalm XLIV, *bleve* for *blev*; verse 14, *Ame* for *Am*, and so forth.

*nachalathecha gojim veettena mimmenni scheal arets aphse vaachuzathecha tenappetsem jotser kichli barzel beschevet terohem schophte hivvaseru haschkilu melachim vehatta arets birhada veghilu bejira adonai eth hivdu derech vothovedu jeenaph pen bar nasschecu kol aschre appo kimhat jivhar ki bo chose*

“Your inheritance: the nations; and I will give you the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall break them with an iron rod; like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them. Now therefore, kings, understand; be instructed, judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the son, lest he become angry and you perish from the way. For his anger will soon burn; blessed are all who trust in him.”
